# Theology Library
## SCHOOL OF THEOLOGY AT CLAREMONT
### California

<margin>
Preparing—an explanation <note>original: elucidation</note> of these mystical implications and events.
</margin>

NOTICE.—The Editor of this work has had a few copies of it hand-corrected throughout. However, because this was done with great carelessness, a further adjustment <note>original: regulation</note> may be necessary in some cases. These copies have been deposited in the British Museum Library, the Bodleian and other libraries at Oxford, the University and other libraries at Cambridge, Trinity College Library in Dublin, the Advocates’ Library in Edinburgh, the Wesleyan Theological Library, and other libraries and literary institutes of Great Britain, as well as the Astor Library in New York, and others. These are intended to serve as references and models <note>original: exemplars</note> for correcting other circulated copies where those changes have not been made, though such correction is advisable. To these additions, the Editor would make a further or *final* addition with the following:

ANNOTATION.—When the reader has properly mastered the studies in this work (which are summarized in the pamphlet titled "A Guide to the Knowledge for a Biography of William Law" bound with this volume), he may find himself in a specific state of mind. If, while meditating upon the revealed mystery and nature of things explained here, and while feeling perfectly satisfied regarding the essential doctrines and practice of religion, he still feels unable to grasp the overall scheme or process of creation and redemption—with its various beginnings and ends, its massive revolutions of events, and its final completion where the circle returns to its starting point in the first opening of heavenly eternity—then he should consider the moral goal of Divine Providence in this process. That goal is to make any further sin <note>original: lapse or falling-away</note> impossible forever by turning the straying wills of all immortal spirits into a *fixed devotion* to and union with the one and only good, perfect, divine will. 

If the student desires to understand how this entire procedure (including the hidden stores of eternal heavenly glory) is truly worthy of INFINITE GOODNESS to have designed and achieved, he is recommended to take certain steps. Presuming he is familiar with the secret knowledge <note>original: arcana</note> of "Animal Magnetism" <note>Animal Magnetism: Also known as Mesmerism; an 18th-century theory regarding an invisible natural force possessed by all living things that could have physical or spiritual effects.</note> and the story of "Gichtel’s <note>Johann Georg Gichtel (1638–1710): A German mystic and follower of Jacob Böhme.</note> deliverance of the soul of his friend," he should read the theological discourses in volumes 4 and 5 of the *Fool of Quality* (1770) <note>A novel by Henry Brooke known for its mystical and pedagogical themes.</note>, along with pages 244–245 of *The Way of Divine Science* <note>original: La Voie de la Science Divine</note> (12mo, Paris, 1805). He should also consider pages 211–217 and other related passages of the present work, and finally, for a stronger and more certain judgment, the contents of treatises 7 and 8 described on pages 687–688 of this same book. 

By these means, a qualified reader may attain perfect freedom and delight in understanding these topics. Furthermore, they may gain insight into the mysteries of the millennial age—as well as the subsequent *final jubilee, or harvest festival, and hallelujah chorus* of all the assembled children of God at the beginning of the reign of eternal heavenly glory. For the powers of the free will of understanding, having reached awareness and experienced themselves, must return to and rest in their original mother, and God will again be ALL IN ALL. [John 17:5, 20-24; Luke 15:2-7, 17-32; Revelation 22:13.]

There appears to be no more necessary information to add to this work as a key or clue to the entire science of true theology. It will now be put into free circulation, *for the honor and glory, true knowledge, and worship of God* <note>original: ad honorem et gloriam, veram scientiam et adorationem Dei</note>. If, however, further explanations are deemed suitable, they will be published for the time being in the journal *Notes and Queries*.

->Dated, *April*, 1861.<-

<meta>This page continues the preface of Christopher Walton’s "Notes and Materials" for a biography of William Law. It focuses on the Editor's intellectual development regarding "Animal Magnetism" and the intended spiritual and philosophical purpose of the book.</meta>

# PREFACE.

> “True metaphysics is the philosophy, and sound mysticism the spirit of religion; and that mystical contemplation—which I have frankly endeavored to reduce to a science—is as superior to any other science as the soul is to the body, and is more or less readable within every attentive heart.”

<margin>From the Library of C. W. Beuve, December 23, 1857</margin>
The Editor’s understanding of the hidden <note>original: recondite</note> and practical knowledge presented in this work has been greatly enlarged and perfected during the several years he has been occupied with it. This was especially true as he approached its conclusion. It was then that he first obtained a true and philosophical insight into the secret <note>original: arcanum</note> of “Animal” or “Vital Magnetism” (as it is called), along with the magical wonders hidden within it as both a science and an art. <note>Animal Magnetism: Also known as Mesmerism; a 19th-century theory regarding a natural energy transference between living objects.</note> He asserts that without this understanding, neither the original revelations of Scripture in their literal truth, nor the purely magical phenomena of Nature in any age, can be properly understood or rationally explained. 

Because of this, the reader should note that only those statements are to be regarded as the Editor’s final conclusions which remain unmodified by later remarks. These later remarks can be found either in the work itself, in the *Introduction to Theosophy* (which immediately followed it), or in the “Corrections and Additions” <note>original: Corrigenda and Addenda</note> placed at the start of this volume, following this present introduction or Preface. A knowledge or understanding of the entire treatise and its references will therefore be necessary before any fair representation of its original contents can be honorably offered to the public.

For the Editor’s aim throughout this work has been truth and the promotion of sound judgment regarding its main subjects. He seeks to establish the kind of judgment that might have characterized divinely illuminated souls—such as William Law, Dionysius Andreas Freher, Johann Georg Gichtel, William Bramwell, Thomas à Kempis, Gregory Lopez, the Apostle Paul, or even our Lord himself—under similar circumstances. This practical and important goal is to establish, once and for all, a universal <note>original: catholic</note> standard of knowledge and judgment regarding the truths of spiritual rebirth <note>original: regeneration</note> and the philosophy of the Gospel in its purest form of faith and practice, from the elementary to the most advanced levels, for all future ages of the—

---

* The ultimate goal of this work, as named hereafter and as its title page suggests, may be described metaphorically as the building of a Temple or Monument of Wisdom. This would be a realization of the ideal <note>original: beau-ideal</note> of a properly developed human mind, according to the highest classic refinements of learning, wit, and literary art; the most complete discoveries of natural science; the most sublime principles of moral philosophy; and the purest lights and holiest achievements of Gospel rebirth <note>original: regeneration</note>, or Christianity. Its immediate design is to find, or to assist in creating, the "artist" or "craftsman" who possesses the architectural genius and technical talent required to build such an edifice—aided, however, by the supervision, advice, and experience of the Editor of the present work.

<meta>This page continues the preface of Christopher Walton’s "Notes and Materials" for a biography of William Law. It describes how Law’s systematic writings provided a logical and "scientific" foundation for the mystical doctrines of self-denial and spiritual rebirth found in earlier devotional authors.</meta>

<page-num>iv</page-num>
<page-type>preface</page-type>

...had been originally derived from those sources of holy learning and sublime religious experience: the devotional schoolmen and their faithful successors, the eminent contemplatives and mystical theologians. In those writings, however—since they were intended for a general audience or for simple moral improvement—the duty of self-denial and surrender to God and to the needs of our neighbor was treated only through exhortation or as religious dogma. 

But in Mr. Law's writings—*The Spirit of Prayer*, *The Way to Divine Knowledge*, *The Spirit of Love*, and his *Collection of Letters*—the core principles and logic of the doctrine were fully revealed. These works explain the philosophy introduced in his book *The Appeal* (which could appropriately be called the *first principles of pure metaphysical science* <note>original: "principia of pure metaphysical science"</note>). Law addresses all the essential points of Christian truth and practice with such a comprehensive grasp and complete *proof*, in the strictest sense of the word, that nothing more needs to be said. He explains the reasons for and the extent of our duty, the necessity of fulfilling it, and the only means by which it can be accomplished.

Through these treatises, along with those mentioned previously, the Editor was introduced to the true, classic doctrines of spiritual or mystical theology, stripped of all irrelevant details. These doctrines concern the "new man" and the "old man" within us—their distinct natures, temperaments, spirits, and their relationship to one another. They also explain the full practical extent of the self-discipline commanded by the Gospel (even though these commands are scattered throughout its pages) for the "crucifixion" and death of the old nature, and the simultaneous resurrection and life of the new nature in its place. 

These two points undoubtedly summarize all the practices and duties of the Gospel. They form the conditions, covenants, and responsibilities of the New Testament established by Christ before his death. By faithfully performing or fulfilling these, every believer is able to enjoy the true benefits of redemption. This is consistent with Christ's universal proclamation: *Unless a man denies himself, takes up his cross daily, and follows me, he cannot be my disciple.* This means one cannot share in His salvation, achieve spiritual rebirth <term>regeneration: the spiritual rebirth or renewal of the soul</term> in this world, or reach His state of blessedness in the world to come. 

Or again: *He that follows me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.* In other words: "He who dies to himself and to the spirit and temperament of this world and of Satan—and whose entire heart and spirit are converted to God *alone*—desires, hungers, lives, and prays only, *Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done*, following my own example. After my resurrection from the dead, ascension, and glorification, such a person shall find a new, holy nature or spirit arising within himself. This spirit enjoys free communion with God and will be a source of every good and blessing to him."

This was the practical Gospel science taught and demonstrated in the works mentioned above. It was presented not just through simple scriptural declarations, but by revealing the very foundations of nature itself. In this way, nature was, so to speak, called upon to testify to the truth of the essential doctrines of the Christian religion.

Through these writings, the Editor was also introduced to the philosophy of Nature—specifically its physical or spiritual foundations and its internal *electro-chemical* operations or combinations. This particular subject is addressed more directly in the last two books, *The Way to Divine Knowledge* and *The Spirit of Love*. While these books form a concluding sequel to *The Appeal*, Mr. Law stated that they were composed as an *Introduction to the writings of Boehme <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), the German mystic referred to in the text as "Behmen."</note>, and to the proper way of reading them*. In these, Law shows that although *Boehme's* writings were a direct revelation from God, they were not intended for people who already understood the true purpose of the Gospel and were sincerely trying to follow its commands—that is, those working out their salvation and seeking regeneration (the perfect renewal of their moral nature in the image of God). For such people,

<meta>This page continues the preface by explaining how William Law’s later works serve as an introduction to the deeper "theosophical" philosophy of Jacob Behmen. It details Law’s argument that spiritual rebirth is a logical, "magical" process of the human will aligning with the divine.</meta>

<page-num>v</page-num>

He observed that they required no further instruction, as they were already duly enlightened and practically focused on the single end and aim of all religion and divine revelation. However, the people to whom these works were immediately applicable were those who, both in theory and practice, were unaware of the true scope and design of the Christian religion. This description applied, one might say, not only to those outside the commonwealth of *Israel* <note>A biblical reference (Ephesians 2:12) to those outside the faith.</note> of whatever name throughout the world, but to the whole of Christendom itself. For the *pure devotees* of religion, though they exist in every sect, were comparatively so few that they were indistinguishable amid the general mass of mere nominal Christians. 

He shows that the unique suitability of such a revelation to the universal wants and necessities of the world consists in this: it offers a fundamental explanation of the nature, power, and origin of the human Will, and of its central relations to the soul and spirit, and all subsequent parts or developments of man’s threefold life as a creature. This involves, therefore, a demonstration of the Divine Nature—in which all created immortal existences “live, move, and have their being”—as well as the Supernatural life of the Deity, in which man has his uncreated origin as an idea or generated image of the Divine Unity. 

He further argues that just as the Deity, by the working of His supernatural Will, generates His own glorious heavenly nature (the perfection of life) as a birth and spirit of love, so man is to do the same. By his will (the "engrafted word" <note>James 1:21</note>), being of the very same eternal origin and possessed in its own degree of the same magical <term>magical: in this context, the word refers to the innate spiritual power of the will to effect internal transformation or "spiritual chemistry."</term> powers, man is to work and generate his own glorious heavenly nature or perfection of life through a similar magical process or new birth, becoming also a spirit of love. 

Mr. Law briefly sets forth this concept in the two treatises last mentioned,* but he refers the reader to the writings of Behmen <note>Jacob Behmen (1575–1624), also known as Jakob Böhme, a German Christian mystic and theosopher.</note> for a full explanation of the subject from every possible perspective. Behmen was raised up and illuminated by God to offer—first to a Christian world that had fallen away from the simplicity and purity of Gospel faith and practice—a logical demonstration of original truth based on self-evident principles. He provided a fundamental resolution to all the great central questions of theology and philosophy that the "spirit of nature" required due to the emergencies of the time. This was intended to perfectly establish those two branches of science on a proper working basis of purification and effective development for the future improvement and regeneration of the world. 

Thus it was that the Editor was introduced, both intellectually and practically, to what Mr. Law terms *God’s last dispensation to the world*—namely, the *opening of the foundation and mystery of all things.* To this mystery, Law says, every <gloss>blindness</gloss>, folly, and vanity <insert>and of himself</insert> of life must, <margin>be forced to</margin> sooner or later, surrender.

On entering into an examination of Behmen’s writings, it was found that in order to obtain a good understanding of their scope and unity—and the relations and harmony of the philosophy† contained in them—they were not to be studied in the order in which they are published in the standard editions...

***

\* To thoroughly master the works of Mr. Law, especially those relating to religious philosophy, the student should begin with the *Answer to the Plain Account of the Sacrament*, include those contained in the *Introduction to Theosophy*, and end with the *Spirit of Love*. These will suffice as an introduction to the philosophy of Behmen, provided the student is well-versed in the metaphysical and mystical knowledge prevailing in the earlier part of Law’s generation, and also in the simple evangelical theology of the Methodists. The student would do well to write out a correct analysis or abstract of their contents; by doing so, he would perceive at a glance the main points, the logical order, the entire drift of the arguments, and how far they seem to support their stated aims and conclusions.

† This philosophy—which necessarily contains the only true refutation and overthrow of all errors, heresies, and infidelities in religious faith and practice, and affords the only logical means of leading the intellectual "heathen" or unbelieving mind into the Gospel faith (both of which objects the Church of Christ is obligated to accomplish)—is revealed and deciphered here for these latter ages. It carries such internal evidence as to prove inconvertibly that it proceeded from the very same Spirit which first opened and announced the Gospel. This counsel of God is admirably suited to the peculiar wants and distresses of the fallen, dark, and ignorant state of Christendom and the world at large—this new revelation of the...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jacob Boehme’s (Behmen’s) progressive spiritual illumination. It explains how his understanding evolved from his first work, the *Aurora*, to his later, more mature treatises, and addresses the resistance his writings faced from the established church.</meta>

of them. For the author’s perceptions at the start of his illumination—or when he first attempted to describe it in writing—were entirely focused on the single object then before his vision: namely, the birth or essence of nature in its sevenfold working unity, or its seven fountain spirits, properties, or qualifications. He describes these simply as his spiritual eye beheld them, without reflecting on or assuming any deeper source for their manifest operation. 

This remark, however, applies only to his first treatise, the *Aurora*, written some seven years before any of his subsequent books. In that work, his descriptions of the seven spirits—due to his lack of understanding at the time regarding the origin of the fourth property (fire)—differ from and are relatively inferior to those in his later treatises, where that point had become clear to him. In his subsequent writings, beginning with *The Threefold Life* (as his spiritual vision* became familiar with the objects constantly presented to it, enabling him to make inferences and reflections), he had evidently come to understand a deeper or higher ground than the sevenfold shifting unit of nature. In the infancy of his illumination and concepts, he had taken this sevenfold unit to be the first or deepest root of things; he later realized it was itself merely a birth and manifestation of a higher, invisible, and otherwise incomprehensible abyss. 

Consequently, his descriptions of the seven properties became settled in the form in which they appear in *The Three Principles* and his later works. His knowledge of God indeed grew deeper and deeper while he was writing his revelations (as he expressly mentions at the start of his *Answers* to the *Forty Questions*). Nor did he, as some have imagined, immediately grasp everything he saw along with all its logical implications. Therefore, the well-disposed reader should accept his descriptions with this in mind. Such a reader will find that his underlying understanding is always consistent and uniform, even though the literal expressions regarding the same point may not always seem to agree or may even appear to contradict each other. And yet, how excusable even greater im-

word and wisdom of God, offering a solution to every question the human mind can ask about its own origin, present state, and future destiny. Despite having existed in print and being published for over two centuries, the writer found upon inquiry that these works were unknown to the church as a whole. Furthermore, where they had been made known to the chief priests and rulers of the church, they had been rejected. This was for reasons similar to those an easy, self-satisfied *farmer*—destitute of any polite learning, science, or art beyond basic arithmetic, reading, and writing, and having no knowledge of or desire for further education—might give to his son to discourage him from seeking a learned upbringing. Namely:

> "To have nothing to do with any such
> supposedly fine-spun, mystical, high-flown, useless, and unscriptural knowledge. This is an attempt to be
> wise *beyond what was written* in the plain, simple word of God, or beyond anything ever heard of by
> your respectable, well-to-do ancestors. They were as good and great as you will ever be;
> and they stuck to the only essential business of life: the good cultivation of their
> farms and the plentiful production of grain, food, and clothing for their wealth and
> comfort."

Similar reasons were presented to the Editor for keeping theological students confined to the simple elements and dogmas of popular Bible Christianity. These critics neither desired nor sought to understand philosophically the nature of that Deity of wisdom, power, and goodness that had created, redeemed, and sustained them. This Deity had chosen to reveal itself understandably to their intellects through the very writings mentioned here. However, as Mr. Law <note>William Law (1686–1761), an English divine and mystic.</note> says, *what God intended by such a revelation must, sooner or later, happen; and attempting to stop its progress will be as futile as trying to delay the coming of the last day.*

* It should be noted here that Boehme was a perfect *clairvoyant* in the highest sense of the term. He was not only "possessed of double consciousness," as Dr. Gregory defines it, but he was not restricted to the inferior astral or illusory nature—unlike modern alleged "seers" and "mediums" who merely reveal the limitations of their own spiritual state in relation to the center and total universe of life and truth. No eye can see beyond the world or principle in which it lives. Instead, Boehme was able to penetrate through all worlds and spheres of being, even to the center of the Divine Majesty itself. Because he was a highly regenerated Gospel Christian, the Divine eye found in him a suitable medium for understanding. To enjoy our original and redeemed privileges of perfect clairvoyance and magical power, it is essential that we, through regeneration, return to our original state and place in creation; then, all such things become natural to us.

perfections in his writings, considering that he <gloss>had</gloss> no sooner written a work—at the earnest urging and entreaties of his friends—than it was immediately taken from him to be copied, and he was set upon some new labor by them. Consequently, there appears to have been no prearranged connection between his various treatises; they were *all independent pieces*, never printed in his lifetime but left scattered abroad as manuscripts throughout the world. It is, therefore, even more wonderful that such a clear serial unity can be found in his writings. Considering his lack of formal education, there is an admirable, easy, and regular descent into the very deepest mysteries of the divine nature; furthermore, such difficult, super-rational matters are described by him with so few externally or superficially objectionable and contradictory terms.

<margin>% /</margin>
This abyssal, hyperspiritual, hyperphysical, supernatural ground alluded to here—or, more properly speaking to us, the *Unground*—contains the potential of all visible light and of all natural senses; indeed, of all powers, colors, and virtues. The Editor might designate this, in modern photographic language, as the "negative" of nature; or, as mathematicians might say, the *infinitely* <note>original: "ab infinitum"</note> negative of the unit; or the root and virgin matrix, or the *central radius* of the first flowing spherical point (for the point is only symbolized by a visible dot, while its real entity is mental or magical). Indeed, it could be described by numerous other negative yet meaningful terms, all of which are truly necessary and important in the formulas and explanations of theosophical science, just as the minus symbols of quantity or number are in algebraic or mathematical demonstrations.

For this abyss—though it seems like nothing to us and to that ground of nature through which it becomes an object for a created understanding—is not "nothing" in and of itself. It contains *everything*, and all things have proceeded out of it—not by necessity, but as the play or sport of its free inclination <note>original: "lubet," meaning a divine longing or desire</note>, good pleasure, or delight. These are either immediate births of its own active knowledge <note>original: "scientz"</note> in eternity, or subsequent combinations of the same that have a beginning in time and, therefore, an end.

In short, Boehme had discovered this abyssal ground to be a mere natureless, emotionless, and creatureless WILL of goodness, light, and truth, containing all the virtues, colors, and powers thereof. It is eternally positioned in a central unity, and from there, it moves into a circumferential or distinguishable sounding development, or "Word of Wisdom." This occurs in what may be termed the infinite abyss or capacity of its own womb, being a magical <note>original: "magia"</note> or desiring nothingness. Meanwhile, he found the sevenfold, twofold unity of nature to be the material or spiritual manifestation of this same universal magic <note>original: "magia"</note>, desiring nothingness, or the capacity of the will. This is fulfilled by its aforementioned inherent inclination <note>original: "lubet"</note>, center, heart, or "allness" of the virtue, power, and glory of light, goodness, and truth. This is a Will which, by its own inherent instinct, flows forth without predetermining this or that, for outside of itself there is nothing. It generates or positions things as it instinctively flows forth, and only magnetically selects within the creaturely manifestations or forms of its *working word* in nature. By this means, Boehme clarifies the great doctrine of *Election* or *Predestination*. This is also the source of his expressions: *All is magical*; *magic is the mother of all things*; and *the eternity is magical*—seeing that all things are the products of Will working in imagination and desire, and they only exist in such a form of life. To return then:

The student or seeker of divine knowledge who has advanced far enough in the process of attaining it to have experienced the simple evangelical doctrine (described in *Romans* 6:17–19 and included in the division of study categorized under the head of "Intercept Continued," inserted hereafter) moves into the next higher practical stage: spiritual or mystical divinity. There, the seeker exercises the discipline of "dying to the self"—or, in other words, is diligently climbing the steep and slippery hill of perfection (in the manner described and recommended in *Philippians* 3:11–14 and *Ephesians* 4:13, etc.). Such a person is therefore being duly prepared for the further or high—

<meta>This page continues the instructions for the spiritual education of a student, specifically recommending a sequence for studying Jacob Boehme’s theosophical works to understand the "abyssal nothing" and the generation of nature through the seven fountain spirits.</meta>

[The high]est branch of *spiritual education* is *theosophy* <term>theosophy: divine wisdom or the study of God through direct experience</term>. This is a clairvoyant contemplation of the entire field of creation from the center of divine wisdom, or the image of God. This image is reopened in the soul by the *appointed divine magnetist* <note>The "divine magnetist" refers to the Holy Spirit or Christ as the attracting power that reorients the soul toward God.</note> for that purpose, serving as the blossom of its regenerated life. This alone is worthy of the name of divine knowledge: to behold the divine separator, the *working word*, the *word that creates* <note>original: "verbum fiat"</note>, or the creating power in all things! It is noted that such a student, when beginning Jacob Boehme’s [Behmen's] theosophical writings, should not confine themselves solely to the earlier treatises. Instead, they should first endeavor to obtain a conception of the entire scope of his philosophy, beginning with that *bottomless nothingness* <note>original: "abyssal nothing"</note> previously mentioned, out of which nature and all things arise. They should then study the *manner of action* of such a birth or generation. In this way, the relationships and distinctions between Deity and Nature, as well as the makeup or electro-chemical properties of the latter, would be properly understood. For this purpose, after reading Boehme's *Epistles*, the student might take up the author’s fifth treatise, the *Book <margin>*</margin> of the Incarnation* previously mentioned—specifically the Second Part. After reading that, they should proceed to the next treatise, the *Six Points*, followed by the *Answers* to the thirteen *Theosophical Questions*, along with the *Three Tables* and the *Clavis* <term>Clavis: Latin for "Key," referring to Boehme's explanatory work providing definitions for his terminology</term>. Having thus grasped, as if on a map or diagram, the author's field of vision in his theosophical contemplations and the original cause of nature’s foundation, the student might then return to the treatise on the *Three Principles or Worlds of Nature*, or *The Threefold Life of Man*. These are recommended by Mr. William Law in *The Way to Divine Knowledge* to obtain a clear, intellectual understanding of the *seven fountain spirits*—the forms of desire or properties that make up the unity of the eternal, original, universal, or divine Nature. This nature consists of two perfectly balanced, opposing principles: dark gloom and shining light. In their center—serving as a point of both union and separation, and as the life of each—is fire, the fourth property. This fire is the eye or opening of the omnipotent, *supernatural, bottomless One*, or Deity. From these seven, every power, quality, motion, essence, and life (both mental and physical), along with every mystery of grace and nature, has its birth, descent, and operation, whether directly or indirectly.

To return now to the current discussion regarding the *origin of the present work*: from what has been related, it can be seen how the Editor pursued his studies of spiritual or mental nature through his acquaintance with Mr. Law. All the steps of his process were based on experimental understanding, not merely speculative opinions. The end of his apprenticeship placed him on the highest ground of contemplative knowledge by introducing him to a true understanding of the principles in Boehme’s writings. At this point, he *felt* he had reached the *original source of all sound information on metaphysical science*. For not a single question can be asked, nor—

Having reached such a height, and being enabled to perceive and comprehensively describe to others the direct and safe—though intricate—path leading to that same desirable viewpoint; and also having made continual descents from that height into the surrounding districts to explore them and confirm by actual verification that it was really the country he was searching for, full of all the treasures of wisdom and philosophy—everything the human mind could possibly desire to possess (and which the enlightened and reflecting people of all ages had ever been secretly longing to discover)—he became even more eager to make the world acquainted with it. He designates these writings as invaluable because—aside from offering an illustration of a classic, well-balanced mind and judgment regarding the accomplishments of universal learning, combined with the spirit of the Christian religion in its most enlightened form of truth and understanding—they contain a clear, rational explanation of the principles of divinity and philosophy found in the deep, mysterious writings of Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), the German mystic</note>. Behmen’s writings, being the spontaneous, simple, and honest outpourings of his pen, written at the request of friends, are not characterized by that high sentiment of *sanctity or holy inspiration* <term>original: "holy breathingness"</term> which distinguishes some of the treatises of the refined practitioners of the spiritual life in the mystic schools, whether of the Roman Catholic or the Lutheran churches of *John Arndt*. So the *popular religion* of the present time, as well as *popular science* (see pages 401–23, 3, 72, 46, etc.), is traceable back to the source, or fundamental revelations, of Behmen!

He considered that the biography of such an individual, if written adequately, would offer edification to all readers—from the simple beginner in knowledge to the learned academic sage, and from the ordinary layman to the most faithful, devoted, and enlightened disciple and minister of Jesus Christ. It could also serve as a general guide and example for the education of youth. This would realize the ideal <note>original: *beau-ideal*</note> of the exalted philosopher of antiquity combined with the pure evangelical Christian and divine theosopher of the present age (as more directly discussed in the "*Advertisement*" at the end of the "Introduction to Theosophy").

Being unskilled in the refined arts of rhetoric himself and conscious of his complete inability to do justice to such a character and work—a work that should serve as a standard model for future ages regarding the true nature and right proportions of secular and Christian knowledge sought through education—the Editor sought help. Though he might act as a consulting architect or surveyor in building this intellectual edifice, he, the Editor, now inquired among his acquaintances in both the church and the world to find someone with the suitable mindset and literary ability for the task. However, his search was in vain. In this situation, it occurred to him to publish an advertisement to the public to find the necessary artistic talent. This advertisement included a description of the primary features and characteristics of Mr. Law’s literary and devotional genius, for he believed that *only such* specific talent could complete the work. This led to the ADVERTISEMENT with which the current treatise begins, and of which it is merely the explanation.

* For surely only a divine sage and an accomplished master of learning and rhetoric—someone also endowed with great wit and extensive experience observing the world—could correctly portray and weave together the sentiments, principles, character, and exemplary life of an exalted Christian philosopher into a masterpiece of biographical literature. This is a person of whom even a somewhat reluctant or prejudiced witness said that "he lived everything he taught and practiced everything he enjoyed." The blatant folly of an individual who has no knowledge or understanding of the mystical workings of spiritual rebirth <term>regeneration</term> attempting to describe the spirit of God's saints for the *public* has rarely been more obvious than in the recent publication titled "*Hours with the Mystics*" (2 vols. 12mo., 1856). In that book, the author reviews the lives and doctrines of the enlightened children of God from past ages with the flippancy and shallow perceptions of a modern penny-newspaper novelist. The author further writes, "*in the swarming fantasies of his own being, the mystic finds the only domain for which he has ever longed*"! In reality, the truly enlightened spiritualist or mystic turns away from and detests all the "swarming fantasies and imaginations of his own natural spirit" or mind. Instead, he seeks and longs only for what the Spirit of *Truth*, dwelling in his newborn soul, chooses to open and reveal within him. This is a sample of the understanding of even the more serious literary critics, whom the world looks to for sound judgment. —This attempt also proved unsuccessful. After some correspondence regarding its primary subject, it was suggested to the Editor that the pure, classical style of argumentative writing required—one that is rigorous in its reasoning and draws its conclusions in a regular sequence, however much it is clothed or concealed by ingenuity and good sense in the simple and graceful style of accomplished rhetoric (as seen, for example, in Mr. Law’s own writings between the years 1717 and 1733)—was not popular in this current age of superficial utilitarian knowledge and mechanical philosophy. It was suggested that such a style would be even less likely to be found among individuals professionally educated for religion. If it existed anywhere, it would probably be among lawyers, whose system of mental training is more favorable to strict logical thought; however, because of their sophistical mindset and their resulting lack of aptitude for the holy contemplation, purity, and simplicity of high Christianity, they were deemed unfit for such an elevated religious and philosophical undertaking.

It then occurred to the Editor—despite the complete incompetence he felt in himself for literary craftsmanship and the necessary preoccupation of his time and attention by secular business—to attempt to draft a kind of specification of the complex talent he deemed necessary to execute the work in question. He planned to accompany this with a sketch of the contents of the writings of the authors who would be the primary subjects of the memorial. He considered that this draft, when printed, might form an octavo <note>A book size where each sheet is folded into eight leaves, resulting in pages of moderate size.</note> pamphlet of about eighty or a hundred pages, through which readers might judge their own ability in various particulars for the desired work. To avoid any delay or further procrastination—whether arising from self-doubt or other causes—he also resolved to send the material to the printer immediately, exactly as he had noted it down from his mental concepts. He intended to make whatever corrections might be necessary in the proof sheets, feeling himself capable of providing the remainder of the material as required, however imperfect it might be in terms of literary art, provided it was clear and distinct. This resolution was put into practice, and *thus, by degrees, the present work arose.* Instead of being comprised of some four or five sheets <note>In printing, a "sheet" refers to a large piece of paper that, when folded, creates multiple pages; five sheets would be a very small book.</note> and completed in as many months as expected, it has been spread over more than that same number of years and expanded to its current dimensions. This was found to be unavoidable in order to provide a full exposition of the subjects deemed proper to be included in the work. Consequently, the work now functions more as a cyclopædia of evangelical truth and divine philosophy—as established by the experience and wisdom of past ages of Christianity—than as a brief general statement of the qualifications of mind, spirit, and literary art required of the individual sought to write a just and adequate biography of Mr. Law.

In conclusion, the Editor may be excused for mentioning the heavy mental strain and labor sustained in compiling this work, which was done almost entirely alone. This is in addition to the great expense incurred, including the collection of all its materials, the purchase of books (and heavy incidental expenses) from various parts of the nation as previously mentioned, the preparation and arrangement of the material for the printer along with editorial and original notices, the revision of the proofs, and the struggle against all the difficulties and frustrations inherent in the proper completion of the book. All of this was undertaken while simultaneously carrying on his commercial affairs, and consequently, much time and attention were taken away from—

Along with all this, one must account for the private and voiced regrets of his friends, both clergy and laypeople, who believed he was suffering from such an obsession or monomania that he would devote his time, labor, and money, and sacrifice his business and personal health (which suffered significantly, along with his other external interests, over the course of the work) to what appeared to them as such an unprofitable project. They saw it as something far outside the usual path of evangelical effort and religious zeal in the present age, despite admitting that *in every other detail of his life, it was his rule and practice to aim for the highest perfection of excellence and utility.*

Nothing would have sustained him in the steady pursuit of his goal amid such a combination of depressing circumstances except for the consciousness and firm conviction that the work in which he was employed was the work of God, of truth, of wisdom, and of the gospel—aimed at the moral, spiritual, and universal improvement of the world, to be proven in its due time. Under these impressions, he pursued his labors and has now reached their conclusion regarding the present work. Notwithstanding its great imperfections, it is adequate for the purpose for which it was compiled: *as a guide to the correct understanding of the mind and character of William Law <note>William Law (1686–1761) was an influential English cleric and mystic whose writings deeply impacted the evangelical movement and influenced figures like John Wesley.</note>, for future scholars and artists to work with in the manner intended by it.* It shall remain as a faithful testimony of the editor’s sincere desire and humble efforts to benefit the world in the most ennobling manner, even for the latest posterity. If he might mention some of the reflections that encouraged him to proceed in his labors, they were as follows:

1. You see your object clearly in view and know the way to attain it: push forward. If you persevere, something valuable will be accomplished, even if the manner of its performance is not satisfying to your own judgment and taste.

2. If you wait until you can do a thing perfectly, or even according to what you might consider the lowest degree of proper execution, you will never do it at all. Do all you can in the circumstances; do not be discouraged even though you cannot compose the work according to the order, style, rules, or classic models of rhetoric in which it should be presented, or as Mr. Law himself would have done it. Only be assured the work is the work of God, and then you may leave the results to Him.

## RECAPITULATION, OR SUMMARY
### OF THIS ENTIRE WORK.

The following advertisement appeared some time ago in a newspaper. However, because the specific skills required might not be clear from the advertisement alone, it was decided to provide a more detailed and thorough explanation of the subject. This led to the creation of the current treatise.

> **WANTED: A gentleman of exceptional literary talent and deep devotional spirit,** at least forty years old. During his academic studies, he should have become well-versed in the case-based moral reasoning <term>casuistry</term> and metaphysics of ancient theology. His writing style should be strictly logical and argumentative, even if that rigor is softened by the elegance and grace of rhetoric. He will assist in writing a sophisticated religious and philosophical biography.

The following series of works and tracts have been selected as general models. By studying these according to the notes attached to each, one can understand the exact nature of the talent required.

I.—*Serious Call to a Holy Life* by *William Law, M.A.*—*The Case of Reason, or Natural Religion, Fairly and Fully Stated, 2nd edition*, by *William Law, M.A.*

These treatises (along with the author’s *Christian Perfection* and his *Three Letters to a Lady Inclined Toward the Church of Rome*) serve as examples of the desired argumentative style. They demonstrate the necessary level of metaphysical knowledge and showcase a masterful use of wit, a vivid imagination, keen observations of life, classic and effective character sketches, and a smooth, comprehensive handling of various topics.

The first of these treatises (which may be said to embody the literary and other perfections of the previously named works) may be taken as a model for the authoritative style and power of philosophical writing that is desired. The biography should be composed in this way from first to last—penned, indeed, with such a holy, reverent glow of spirit as if written by a seraph, so as to inflame the heart of every reader with the love of God and a desire for all holiness and perfection of life.

The preceding notices relate chiefly to the author’s literary qualifications; the following series of works express the foundation of understanding, or the mental outlook, from which the work should be written.

London, 1708. And his *Sermons* in Latin.

Paris, 1755.—*Tour to Alet*, (in Volume Two of *Mary Anne Schimmelpenninck’s Port Royal Memoirs.*)—*Life of Abbot de Rancé* <note>original: "Vie de l’ Abbé de Rancé"</note>, by *Dom Pierre le Nain.*—*De Rancé’s The Sanctity of the Monastic State.* 2 vols. 12mo. Dublin, 1830—focusing on what constitutes the essence of Christianity or practical methods for spiritual rebirth, and absorbing its earnest and serious spirit.

These works are intended to form a proper foundation for the high structure of a perfect Christian, reborn, and divine life. First, they should create in the mind a profound and piercing conviction of the vanity and emptiness of all worldly things and of the degraded, sinful state of human nature; this should lead to an earnest conversion of the soul to God. Secondly, they should arm the mind with a steadfast, immovable purpose to follow Christ fully through the process of spiritual rebirth—following His precepts, counsels, and example. This is the narrow way, the way of the cross, and the way of faith; it is the only true and direct path from defilement to purity, from sin to holiness, from darkness to light, and from death to life. Thirdly, these works should provide the soul with principles to walk confidently and securely on that path. This involves the perfect spirit and power of prayer, self-denial, and detachment from the world. It requires divine love and universal charity, as well as humility, patience, gentleness, endurance, obedience, purity, silence, and resignation. This path offers heavenly tastes of the world to come and demands absolute trust and dependence on God, while placing all earthly and temporary things—all the successes and hardships of this life—beneath one’s feet.

These works are intended to clarify the way—more or less perfect, according to the insights they were granted—in which devoted souls have walked through the process of regeneration or the way of faith. They show how, according to their unique temperaments and dispositions (having first sought and found "the kingdom of God" and his righteousness), they were led to serve their neighbors and the world. But especially, one should study here the practical skills and tools of complete sanctification—even to the total destruction of self-love and self-will in the core of the soul, and the attainment of that purity of heart which alone can see God. Ultimately, these are meant to lead the soul through a natural process of self-conscious, experiential growth in regeneration, up to the very entrance of the temple of Wisdom—the supernatural, intellectual, or divine life.

Rebekah, Balaam, and Job, along with his friends, are cited to prove that it was anciently believed in all nations that there were means by which men and women might come to have some acquaintance and communication with God. The tradition and succession of this through the Colleges of the Prophets among the *Jews*; through the Priestly Colleges of the Eastern *Magi* among the *Egyptians, Chaldeans*, and *Arabians*; and through the Pythagorean and Platonic schools—if it were accurately and judiciously documented—would be a significant work; but this is not to be expected within a few sheets of paper. And as for the *media* <note>methods or instruments</note> which the Gentiles used to attain intimacy and communication with their peculiar Deities, or with the "Soul of the World," or with the supreme Demiurge <note>The artisan-creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note> and Creator, a particular and distinct explanation of them would necessarily lead us into an investigation concerning the ancient theurgic mysteries <note>The practice of rituals performed with the intention of invoking the presence of gods or spirits</note>.—[The next "Magical" Intersection will afford a clue to understanding them.] The spirit of Plotinus and Iamblichus, and also the spirit of Porphyry <note>Three major Neoplatonist philosophers</note>, cannot be thoroughly understood without a more than ordinary insight into these mysteries. The *Porphyrian spirit* is a very great mystery. But as it is in witchcraft, or in demonic possession, so it is also here: the evil demons are able to do nothing by themselves. It is Nature that works all and produces those strange and wonderful operations. They simply know how to apply active forces to passive ones and leave Nature to bring about what they design; the present corrupt state of nature is subservient to this, and they do not fail to add some of their own malice to the process.

Query: Who or what was the stranger who so impressively spoke to **Bohemius** <note>Jacob Böhme (1575–1624), the German mystic</note> when he was a youth (as related in his biography), and what followed from that? Also, regarding the polished platter—by the light of which reflected upon him—he entered a trance of "double consciousness" into the central foundation of all Nature; he was, however, clearly qualified for such a baptism and revelation! Is this not the secret clue to **Bohemius's** character (which we offer here to the wise future editor of his life): namely, that he was a pure, simple child of nature, with a highly delicate spiritual temperament and complexion (evident indeed by the existing portrait of him in this country), and accordingly susceptible to magical or "magnetic" <note>An 18th/19th-century term for hypnotic or psychic influence</note> action? 

This explains his early vision on the *Landskrone* mountain; and also, after being "baptized" by the supposed Rosicrucian, his inner life became even more open, and he became more lucid. And now, seeking God and salvation in the true, orthodox, gospel manner (in the style of William Bramwell <note>A famous Methodist preacher known for intense prayer</note>), specifically through total penitence and earnest, struggling, unyielding faith and prayer, and obtaining what he sought—even the full *liberty* and *witness* of the Spirit—in this state of clear but now greatly increased salvation, being again "magnetized" by the *inward* solar power and essence in the reflection from the polished platter, he became a *perfect clairvoyant*! 

That is, he realized the full privileges of his state at that time as a highly regenerate man regarding both temporal and eternal vision and other senses. From this state, he wrote down his perceptions of Nature as he was able to understand and express them through his natural reason <term>astral reason</term> and imperfect, worldly language <term>Babylonish language</term>. This original view or discovery of **Bohemius's** character, which has occurred to us, is, we believe, the true key to his peculiar genius as shown in his writings; in this respect, it may also serve as a qualifying note to our other descriptions of him in these pages. 

But the true subjects of a proper Theosophical College and its training— — —*Would that some noble-minded philanthropist might dedicate a hundred thousand pounds to the foundation of such a scheme in the name of the holy, holy, holy, eternal* **Sophia** <note>original: "SOPH-IAH," referring to Divine Wisdom</note>, *and to his own high honor!* — — —might, we believe, be made to far surpass **J. B.** <note>Jacob Böhme</note>. They would enjoy equal clarity of spiritual sense but, being thoroughly grounded in scholarship and modern science, would therefore be enabled to explain technically the "mystery" and inherent powers <term>virtues</term> of things, making them of greater practical use to the Church and the world.

The object of this *sixth division* of study in the series has already been sufficiently indicated: namely, to provide the advanced student with a knowledge of all the science and art which has hitherto been revealed and discovered regarding the high refinement of human life, and of the true and lawful mode by which to advance steadily to the very central throne of divine revelation, even to become a **holy artist**, a lord, a prince over nature, to the praise and glory of God. For humanity, as observed before, being now fully redeemed, man is therefore capable of a transcendently exalted spiritual renovation and illumination: (and if of a spiritual renovation, why not of an outward and physical one—even of an Enochian <note>Referring to the biblical Enoch, who was translated to heaven without dying</note> life on earth?) And therefore it ought to be the aim of the enlightened Christian to press on to this high regenerate perfection, or glorified resurrection state of the inner man; to practice the arts of paradisiacal horticulture, first in himself, with his own life and intellect, and then to raise up others to the same faith and inward glory. This attainment, according to its degree, is what restores to man his original prerogatives of dominion *over all temporal creatures*, and opens the latent powers of God and the sciences of Divine Wisdom in everything. Our Lord spoke to his wondering disciples to this effect:—You seem surprised at what I now accomplish, deeming it a miracle: *Truly, far greater works than these shall you* (my faithful, theosophic disciples) *do after my ascension*. St. Paul also, in the same scope of understanding, observes, *Henceforth we know no believer according to the flesh* . . . . (but rather as members of a God of glory in heaven.) And again, *But you are come*, etc. *Hebrews* xii. 22—24. And what St. John declares respecting the paradisiacal glories of the New Jerusalem—that is, of that Christianity in which we are all placed and growing up, if we are of the regeneration—does not need to be detailed in this place. VIII.—The *Old and New Testaments* of the Lord, JESUS CHRIST—the pillar and standard form of evangelical truth. This is the popular and devotional light in which the Holy Scriptures are to be regarded.—The other, or theosophic consideration of them (which provides a proof of their Divine Inspiration, though loose and partial in detail and composed of separate parts), is as brief chronicles of the divine origin or creation, and of the degeneration or bestial-diabolic transmutation of human nature in Adam, its natural head; and then of the entire process of its redemption, re-transformation, and deification, through the “mystery of Christ” in the person of JESUS, as the second and divine head of that nature.—Consequently, the working of these two principles of life—the rational-animal spirit of fallen man and the holy, <term>sophian</term> Spirit of Christ—forms the mystical ground of every narrative in the Scriptures, however historically true they may be; and the line and virtue of the Covenant is the golden thread that runs through and illuminates the whole. Therefore, they conclude by presenting the person of the Second Adam and Conquering Prince, all-perfected, glorified, and divine, and by inviting and admonishing all people to “follow him in the regeneration.”—That is, to cultivate the seed or spirit of grace, of moral holiness or love, of heaven or the heavenly humanity, or the virgin wisdom of God—the “divine nature,” or Christ himself within them—into a powerful and all-predominant life, even to its full maturity or adult development, as visible in him: the “perfect,” “justified,” and “glorified” Son of Man, and heavenly Virgin form of substantial light and Love, in whom the earthly nature or spirit is swallowed up, “hidden in God.” This transformation is therefore possible to be achieved in us—as he is the spi-

[S]piritual, heavenly parent of humanity, and (as the divine nature) the element of our souls, and possessed of omnipotent power over us—if we will only conform to the laws of the divine nature and cooperate with his horticultural, regenerative, unceasing action in us. Those laws and requirements are revealed to us in the gospel, in the precepts and *counsels* of Christ, and in the subsequent explanations and exhortations of his apostles, having been all fulfilled in his own example and process on earth; and which consist in the continual crucifixion of our fallen natural or diabolical spirit, and the renunciation of our animal, earthly will and wisdom: in other words, in a *daily dying* to all *self*, spiritual and natural, and in a turning of the faith, hope, and earnest prayer—or hungering desires of the soul—constantly and absolutely to God; to the love of God, and the humility, meekness, and patience of the divine light, for deliverance from "self" and growth in grace or salvation. This spiritual diligence, labor, watchfulness, and passive submissiveness on our part is to be persevered in until the "*new birth*" *is fully brought forth* in us by our heavenly regenerator and magnetizer; until the *last remains* of "self" in the will are finally immersed in the power of God, and our *life* is thereupon transformed into a *spirit of love*: which, and which alone, is the Christian salvation! The sum and end of the whole is then this: that man (the spirit of his soul being clothed with the regenerate, heavenly humanity, corporeity, or "*flesh and blood of Christ*") may be able in this world to magically re-enter paradise again and "*eat of the tree of life*" in its midst (as witnessed in the experience of Mrs. Pratt, related on pages 588–590 and following), and so walk and act on the earth in *divine power and understanding*;* and that upon his mortal death, he may be found *a qualified subject and participant of those nameless, ravishing manifestations of wisdom, power, might, majesty, and love* which shall eternally spring up and break forth in ever-new wonders, as displays of the riches and glories of the Godhead in the kingdom of heaven, but especially in the souls of its redeemed inhabitants: or, in a word, that he may be a partaker of that same divine glory with which JESUS, the King of Glory and Lord of All—the Alpha and Omega—here exhibits himself crowned! Thus, the *words of the prophecy of this book*, or the "counsel of God" concerning man—in his creation, his fall, and his redemption in Christ—are brought to a close! And such is the theosophic scope, spiritual unity, and divine certainty of the INSPIRED VOLUME, the contents of which may well be termed the blessed gospel—or good tidings of great joy to all people! And how the whole forms a glorious demonstration of the *love of God*: or, that GOD, as *our God*—as in Christ Jesus—is pure LOVE, the POWER OF LOVE! This power is indeed the universal basis of all things and that quickening element wherein, as observed before, our <term>self-constringed</term>, iron-hardened, insensible, ungrateful, unbelieving hearts and souls *have*, or ought to have, their momentary life and being! *Ephesians 3:8-19; 2 Corinthians 2:6, 7, etc.*

<margin>*</margin> * According to the prerogatives of man's first creation, and therefore of his full regeneration; "when that which is outward is (virtually) as that which is inward," and there is no longer the division and degradation of the created Virgin image of God into "male and female," like the animal creation (*Genesis 1:25–27*); but the garment of shame and ignominy—the animal and sexual nature—having been virtually put off by regeneration, the man and the woman are again one in the Lord, who is both the father and spouse, or "bride," of the Virgin generation of humanity. All of which is the correct Christian, *Enochian faith and life on earth*. For Adam in the first creation (when all was completed and perfect) was in this world as a supreme being over it, having no share of its life and nature—that is, no sense or feeling of good and evil as distinct from it—just as an individual in the <term>magnetic sleep</term> or trance has no sensibility of pain or pleasure through the animal body. He was in the world as a heavenly artist, *medium, and <term>magist</term>*, who had power and skill to reveal the wonders of God in every power of outward nature. We read that an angel used at a certain time to come down into a pool at Jerusalem: the water, magnetized by the angel, gave forth its virtues, but the angel felt no impressions of weight or cold from the water. This is an image of Adam's initial freedom from and power over all outward nature. Wherever he went, he could do as this angel did—make every element and elementary thing reveal all the riches, virtues, and powers of God that were hidden in it, without feeling any impressions of any kind from it. This was meant to be the work of both Adam and his offspring: to make all creation *show forth the glory of God* and to spread paradise over all the earth (which at that time existed only in a certain place upon it called the Garden of Eden), until the time came when all the good in this world was to be called back to its original state, and all the evil in every part left to be possessed by the devil and his angels. But since man fell from this state into an animal life and nature, his work has changed, and he must now labor with sweat to till the cursed earth, both for himself and the beasts upon it. He must also toil in great anguish of mind, under the load of the cross, to regain his first heavenly birth of life in the straight and narrow way, strewn with briars and thorns, which has been opened for him by Jesus Christ. The end of this way, when reached, will—as suggested above—re-invest him with his first heavenly prerogatives.

# CONCLUSION. 

Such, then, is the series of works which are considered capable of providing the reader with an accurate general understanding of the deep and universal theological science of the main subject of our proposed biography. It also provides a concept of his far-seeing *faith-based* realizations of the effects that should flow from his own *Elijah-restoring, Baptist-purifying* ministry:—not only in the general spread of a simple, practical Gospel Christianity among the *unsophisticated* of the earth, as we see in progress today; but also regarding the bringing of *intellectual* unbelievers of all nations into the Christian faith. This is yet to be achieved as the final result of the revelation of the "mystery of Christ"—of Deity, Nature, and all things—in BOHEMIUS <note>Jacob Boehme</note>, and of the refinement of all natural knowledge, philosophy and theology, the arts and sciences, mechanical and magical, which has followed and shall follow in the future as a consequence or development of it.

As a close, the following EXTRACT is offered for the reader's consideration:

> *It is because people fail to consider the spirit of holiness as a new nature, a seed of God, and a plant of paradise in the soul—and therefore as something to be nurtured and cherished, cultivated and brought to perfection by care and planning, by skill and method, and by the diligent use of the best tools and most effective means—it is because they do not consider it in this light that so many people benefit so little from it. They live and die as strangers to that inner renewal, that holy, spiritual "oneness" with the glorified nature of the Lord Jesus (John 17:21–24), which they might have achieved if only they had intended to.*
>
> *For though the spirit of devotion is the gift of God and cannot be reached by any mere power of our own, yet it is usually given and never denied to those who seek it correctly and prepare themselves to receive it.*
>
> *And it is amazing to see how eagerly scientists and businessmen use their talents, their wisdom, time, study, application, and effort—how every available help is called to their assistance—when anything is intended and desired in worldly affairs. Yet, it is amazing how dull, foolish, and stagnant they are—how little they use their talents, wisdom, and abilities—to awaken and cultivate the incorruptible seed of grace, or the Light and Spirit of God. This is the source of every divine blessing of holiness, power, and wisdom, and with it every necessary earthly good—implanted and hidden in the depths of the soul.*

This much specifies the talent which is deemed essential for the proper representation of the genius and character of MR. LAW (as intended by this work); or rather, it specifies the means and tools by which the artist who is qualified by nature and education for such a task (having a purely Methodist origin and understanding of religion) may gain the special ability, knowledge, and experience needed to perform it adequately. In short, the goal is to present the portrait of a man which—whether regarding the subject itself or the manner of its execution—may serve as a classic standard or practical model of divine wisdom, sound learning, and the art of rhetoric for all future generations of the British people and of humanity.—*Correspondence on this subject, or for permission to make excerpts from this work, should be addressed to the "Editor of Law's Memorial" and left at 24 Ludgate Street, London. Midsummer, 1856.*

<note>ANNOTATION. In the "Cyclopedia of Biography" recently published by Richard Griffin & Co., Glasgow (1854), the articles relating to mystical theology are all treated according to the false, fantastical, heretical doctrines of Swedenborg—that is, Swedenborg's theological tenets are therein made the standard of divine truth, and of course the ancient "fundamental truths" and "essential principles" of Christianity are labeled "falsities," being opposed to the Baron's "truths." Under the heading of Böhme in that work, the Editor writes: "As an apostle of religion * * * we must look for the real results of his influence in such movements as those of the Moravian Brethren and primitive Methodists; add to which, the most intelligent of the later mystics, followers of Law and Böhme, accepted the *revelations of Swedenborg!*" It is to the bold assertion here placed in italics that attention is now called, and the writer would observe that, in penning it, the author, however writing consistently with the fantastical light of his great master, was stating that which was directly untrue. So far from any intelligent mystic of the school of Böhme and Law, acquainted with the nature and design of their writings, accepting Swedenborg's affirmations, they—whatever they might have thought of these writings before becoming acquainted with those authors—thenceforth abandoned *all serious regard for them* as containing nothing new or advanced in pure religious philosophy, but on the contrary much that was diametrically opposed to the *essential truth and vital interests* of the true gospel religion; and in effect (as observed elsewhere) they are "of no more use to the church of Christ or the Gospel religion than a fifth wheel to a wagon." One first-rate proof of the spirit and institution of the "New Church" of Swedenborg being a new dispensation from that "Lord" who said, *Go into all the world, and preach the Gospel to every creature*, would be the vast number of holy, self-denying missionaries whom the said "new church" has sent forth to preach the gospel to the heathen—especially the poor savages of the South Sea Islands—"to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God," from savagery to refined civilization and happiness!</note>

# APPENDIX to ERRATA.—BÖHME'S WRITINGS.

**A Summary Account of the Works of JACOB BÖHME, in which is revealed the Mystery of the Supernatural DEITY and VIRGIN WISDOM, and of the birth and ground of NATURE; the Creation of Angels, and the Fall of one Hierarchy of them; the Creation of this Gross, Mutable World, or Temporary Principle of Nature; and the Ground and Development, or the entire Mystery of MAN (as ADAM and CHRIST, making up every individual) in his Creation, in the process of his Fall, and in the process of his Restoration, or Cure. Also, with respect to his Individual process of Regeneration, and his ultimate Deification.**

->[*The Emblem at the head of Böhme's Works is an Angel passing through the air, blowing a Trumpet, signifying the Demonstration of the Gospel Religion by a Revelation of universal and self-evident Truth; out of which is sounding forth these words:—To all Christians, Jews, Turks, and Heathens, to All the Nations of the earth, This Trumpet sounds for the Last Time.*]<-

1. *Aurora. The Dawning of the Eternal Day, or the Infancy of Creation.—An unfinished piece,* from the childhood of his illumination. [In which he describes as best he could—as a stammering, timid, unlettered child—the opening panorama of the divine wisdom set before his internal vision. He narrates the circumstances and ground of the angelic creation; the *fall* of the chief of the three hierarchies of it, and the direful effects which ensued from it in eternal nature (by their unbalancing of its *seven balanced powers or forces*); and the subsequent creation of this material, temporal system (from the *condensed, compacted, dark, fiery, fluidic, spoiled materiality and galvanic powers* of the spiritual, angelic world, both good and bad) as the first act of the curative process of the *evil* thus originated in nature. The narrative was broken off by violence before the author came to the creation of Man.—This piece *should not be read* until the reader is quite familiar with J. B.'s other works; as his descriptions here of the *seven spirits* differ from and are relatively inferior to those contained in the subsequent treatises (due to his lack of understanding at the time regarding the origin of the fourth property, the *fire*), where *that point* had become recognized in his understanding. This fourth property is the opening of the life of the *supernatural liberty*, abyssal nothingness, or free, magic **Eye**, in Nature; that is, of the pure Deity in nature.] A. D. 1612.

2. *De Tribus Principiis cum Appendice. Of the Three Principles or Worlds of Nature, with Appendix.*—Describing the Eternal Birth of Nature in its Seven Properties and Two Co-eternal Principles, as well as this Third Principle and the Creation of All Things. Lastly, of **MAN**, as the Crown and Comprehension, or Developed Central Divine Idea of all, and therefore a true Lord and Prince over All. His Fall, with all its circumstances; and his Redemption, by virtue of the 'Mystery' and Process of Christ. With a concurrent evangelical application of the truths developed. A.D. 1618. — [In this work, Man's creation is declared, from which it appears that Man is the noblest being in the universe of God. He is the primal center, the immediate abode, habitation, organism, and personal medium of Deity, who, as the triune, incomprehensible, universal power, or Spirit of life—a mere goodness, light, and truth—has neither form nor visibility except in Man—understand, the **VIRGIN MAN**, as created, and as restored and glorified in Christ. (**OH, MAN! SEEK AND KNOW THYSELF.**)—In this work, Man (who was created as the instrument by which God would heal the disordered, corrupted body of Nature and restore all to its primitive perfection) is described in detail in his original creation, his fall, and his redemption by the "mystery of Christ"; who, as a second Adam, or Man, came to heal and restore the first ruined Adam, and to effect all that which the Deity would have had accomplished by him.—A knowledge of <term>theosophic</term> science, as well as the experimental philosophy of <term>animal magnetism</term>, <term>mediumship</term>, <term>spiritism</term>, <term>alchemy</term>, etc., is, however, essential for a proper understanding of these deep mysteries of nature and magic.]

3. *De Triplici Vita Hominis. Of the Threefold Life of Man, according to the Three Principles.* That is, as the generated Idea, or Supernatural Image of the abyssal triune Will-spirit of the Deity—the **VIRGIN SOPHIA**, incarnated in, and clothed with Eternal and Temporal Nature.—And from the relations of Man's present state of grace and nature, setting forth his practical duties and obligations for the purpose of regeneration and the attainment of the prerogatives of his glorious redemption in Christ. A. D. 1619.

4. *Psychologia Vera cum Supplemento. Forty Questions concerning the Soul of Man, Answered, with Supplement.*—In the *Answer to the First Question* is presented a Symbolical Diagram of the **WONDER-EYE** of the Divine Wisdom, the supernatural Abyss or Habitation of the Triune Deity; with the Central Generation therein (by the Father-Will of the Trinity of Deity) of Eternal Nature, with its Two co-eternal Principles of black Darkness and lustrous Light, and this generated third or mixed temporal Principle included within it. A.D. 1620. [Understand these two eternal principles of *positive* and *negative*, the *no* and the *yes* of the speaking triune Word of Life, the **SUPREME ONE**—that together they constitute Nature, or eternal Nature: not the dark world alone, which is termed the ground or root of nature, but both principles together, in *perfect, indissoluble union*.—By the fall of angels (through the perverse, obstinate, proud, self-willed, ignorant, rebellious misuse of their free, uncontrollable will; being unduly elevated by the sudden perception of their own wonderful beauty, power, and glory)—who had their life and being, or qualities, in this eternal or divine nature—it came to be discovered or experienced how the majestic visibility or "glory of God," or "kingdom of heaven," has this darkness as its basis or ground; and how the life of this dark principle *in itself* is a life of the most horrible wrath, anguish,
