falsehood and misery. From this arose the scriptural and theological term *God's wrath*, or the *wrath of God*—meaning not that the will-spirit of the Deity is wrathful or capable of wrath, for he is the only *good*, pure, and lovely one, the unchangeable love; but that in bringing forth his ineffable, intellectual will-spirit into a perceptible essence or nature—something sensible to creatures through *desire*—this desire, as such, must be the *very opposite* or contrary spirit to his own Being of gentleness, peace, delight, holiness, and happiness. By overcoming or possessing this center, his real goodness, holiness, light, and truth become manifested in a triumphant, glorious life. This twofold *life* is then Nature, eternal Nature, the "divine nature," in which all immortal beings are created to live and enjoy divine happiness. Yet alas, how many will *frustrate* the divine intention and render *ineffective* the divine benevolence toward them in the incarnation, sufferings, and death of Christ, and so fall into the dark, fiery center, the self-contracting generation or root of Nature—the *eternal dying* of the divine liberty, or the life of desire, wrath, and *all misery*.

5. *De Incarnatione Verbi (On the Incarnation of the Word), in Three Parts.*—Part First: Of the Incarnation of Jesus Christ; the kind of Mother she became in the Blessing* and Conception of her Son, Jesus Christ; and how the Eternal Word has become Man.—Part Second: Of the Suffering, Dying, Death, Resurrection, Ascension, and Glorification of Christ, as the first and second Adam. And why we must all *follow* him in the same Process and Way thus opened for us, back to the Throne of God.—Part Third: Of the Tree of the Christian Faith; showing the whole Christian Doctrine of Faith and Practice. Entirely brought forth out of the Supernatural Center, through the Three Principles. A.D. 1620.

6. *Sex Puncta Theosophica (Six Theosophic Points).* Containing a description of the life of the Supernatural Wisdom and Abyss of Deity, and of the Three Principles of Nature, as well as each Principle as it is in itself. Showing how men should seek, find, and know the ground of nature.—7. *Sex Puncta Mystica (Six Mystic Points).* Clearing up certain deep points involved and not resolved in the previous dissertations.—8. *Mysterium Pansophicum (The Pansophic Mystery).* A further diversified, deep consideration concerning the heavenly and earthly mystery of nature, and of the full working and enjoyment of the life of the latter. A.D. 1620.

9. *De Signatura Rerum (The Signature of All Things).* Showing the meaning, virtue, and qualification of the shapes and forms of the creation. And what the beginning, ruin, and cure of everything is, both spiritual and physical. <note>The ground of Physiognomy, Phrenology, Homeopathy, etc. The Language of Nature, or speech of the Divine Wisdom, understandable by her regenerate, clairvoyant children. A book of the sublimest wisdom and angelic melody; and the key to the regeneration of the medical art.</note> A.D. 1621.

*Christosophia (The Way to Christ), and Divine Wisdom. Part One.*—10. *De Regeneratione (On Regeneration).* Of the grounds and reasons of regeneration, being an introduction to the Gospel religion.—11. *De Poenitentia vera (On True Repentance).* A practical entrance upon the way of regeneration, or the new birth.—12. *De Aequanimitate (On True Resignation).* Of true resignation and advancement in the regenerate life. Or, of continually dying to self and submerging the will and desire wholly into the meekness, humility, and love of the supernatural, divine element.—13. *De Tentatione, et 4 Complexionibus (On Temptation and the 4 Complexions).* Of the ground and nature of temptation; where it arises from and how to overcome in the conflict. <note>The first three tracts composed the only book the author published in print; all the rest of his writings were left by him in the hands of his friends in manuscript.</note. A.D. 1622.

14. *Libri Apologetici duo (Two Apologetic Books), against Balthasar Tilken.* Two apologies.—The first, in defense and explanation of the *Aurora*. The second, concerning Predestination; and of the person of Christ and the Virgin Mary, as treated in the previously named Book of the Incarnation. A.D. 1621, 23.— 15. *Anti Stiefelius (Against Stiefel), in two books.* (1) Considerations of E. S.'s book concerning the threefold state of man and the new birth; also of the Last Zion, or New Jerusalem, etc. (2) Concerning the errors of the sects of E. S. and Ezekiel Meth relating to Christian perfection. A.D. 1621, 22.— 16. *Apologia contra G. Richter (Apology against G. Richter), with an apologetic booklet to the Senate of Görlitz.* The author's defense of his printed book *The Way to Christ* and his *Aurora* against the libellous censures of the Primate, G. R. A.D. 1624.

17. *De Electione Gratiae (On the Election of Grace), with an Appendix on Repentance.* Being a fundamental demonstration of the scriptural doctrine of election, or predestination. With an appendix showing the way to attain the clear vision and knowledge of divine mysteries. A.D. 1623. <note>Grounded in the deepest supernatural, abyssal center—the instinct, constitution, or science of the Fountain Word and Creator of all things; and from there traced into and through Nature. And showing the inevitability of that which is evil and that which is good.</note>

18. *Mysterium Magnum (The Great Mystery):* an exposition of the First Book of Moses, called Genesis. In three parts. In which is treated the revelation of the Divine Word through the Three Principles of Nature; and of the origin of the world and the creation. Also, in which the kingdom of nature and the kingdom of grace are explained. A.D. 1623. <note>Demonstrating the literal</note>

## FREHER’S WRITINGS.

**A BRIEF ACCOUNT OF FREHER’S WRITINGS, being Comments upon the above-described Writings of the divine regenerated one and clairvoyant, Böhme. They are entitled, FUNDAMENTA MYSTICA JACOBI BOHEMII TEUTONICI, EXPLICATA. BY ANDREAS DIONYSIUS FREHER. (British Museum, *Add. MSS. 5767-5794.*)**

1. *Serial Elucidations of J. B.'s Principles of Philosophy and Theology*; in EIGHT VOLUMES, with an *Index Volume*. A.D. 1698—1705. Namely:
Vol. A. (1.) On the Deity considered without any Nature or Creature. (2.) On the Deity, as Manifesting Himself through Eternal Nature; with its Seven Properties, Two Principles, and Three Distinctions or Parts.
Vol. B. (§.) An Explanation of J. B.'s Tables of the Deity *outside of Nature*. (3.) Answer to an Objection concerning the *Desire's Attraction of Itself*. (4.) On the further Exterior Manifestation of God, or the Divine Nature, in the Creation of Angels. (§.) Answer to an Objection concerning *Material Causes*. (5.) On the Fall of Lucifer and all his angels.
Vol. C. (6.) On the Creation of this Third or Temporal Principle of Nature, in which we live and have our *Outward Being*.
Vol. D. (7.) On the Fall of Man from his Primeval Glory, down into the Spirit and Grossness of this Astral Principle. (8.) On the Natural Propagation of Man in this now Cursed, Four-element world. (9.) On Man's Regeneration, through the Blood and Death of Christ.

### SECTION I.

The following advertisement appeared some time ago in a public journal; however, as the peculiar talent required might not be exactly understood from the terms of that announcement, it has been thought appropriate to present a more explicit and comprehensive statement regarding the subject; hence the present treatise.

The nature and extent of the employment is also only partially described in the advertisement. In addition to the proposed biography, there would likely be the revision, with notes, of the works of three or more eminent theologians and philosophers—to which the biography is partly intended to serve as an introduction—as well as other devotional literary work.

<margin>a/</margin>It will, of course, be indispensable that the person sought for should already possess a foundation of character, devotional habits, and sound metaphysical, classical, mathematical, and other related learning. This should enable him, by a little practice in adjusting his style and disciplining his thoughts, to exhibit—according to his own genius and the nature of the subject—the specific qualifications of the models presented here for his guidance.

->(ADVERTISEMENT.)<-

> WANTED, a GENTLEMAN of LITERARY TALENT, ASSIDUITY, and PIETY (not under forty years of age), who, during his scholastic training, has been well practiced in the casuistry <note>The study of resolving moral problems or cases of conscience.</note> and metaphysics of ancient divinity. His style of writing should be one of strict argumentation, even if its mathematical severity is dressed in the simplicity and graces of rhetoric. Experience in ascetic devotional authorship would be preferred. He will assist to COLLECT, RESEARCH, and WRITE an ELEVATED PHILOSOPHICAL and RELIGIOUS BIOGRAPHY. Address * * * * *

The following works and tracts have been selected as general models regarding writing style and devotional spirit. From a proper study of these, according to the observations attached to each, as well as the supplementary works (see the following section) and their accompanying remarks—and from various other observations interspersed throughout this treatise—the nature of the required talent may be understood.

I.—**A SERIOUS CALL to a DEVOUT and HOLY LIFE**, (By W. Law, M.A.)
II.—**The CASE of REASON or NATURAL RELIGION**, (By the same.)

These serve as models for a style of strict argumentation and demonstrate the necessary amount of metaphysical knowledge. The former work is to be especially noted for its masterly display of wit and wisdom, and for exhibiting great

The former treatise (which may be said to embody the literary and other perfections of the previously named works) may be taken as a model of the magisterial style and power of philosophic writing required. It presents a condensed, though perfect, declaration of all the essential points of the subjects in question; a full and open exhibition of all the relative truths, from their deepest foundations, in every necessary variety of light; and then a masterly refutation of the elaborate fictions, plausible errors, and ignorant conceptions of the learned antagonist. At the same time, with equal dexterity of talent and irresistible power of conviction, it does not fail to establish in their place lucid demonstrations of the right understanding of the grossly misunderstood truths of revelation and philosophy.

The "Address to the Clergy" may be taken in connection with the "Confutation," and more particularly as a kind of model of the *Elias-Baptist* spirit of divinely animated zeal, irresistible truth, and elevated wisdom in which the biography is to be written. This is because the subject of the biography is to be exhibited as one of the forerunners, or extraordinary messengers coming from God to proclaim the approach of the great day. His original and adopted writings, his whole character, and his form of life—when shown in their true point of view (as will be done here)—afford undeniable evidence to those who have "eyes to see" of his undoubted office and commission once again "to prepare the way of the Lord, and make his paths straight." For though he performed no more outward miracles than the Baptist did, his works and his adopted writings emerged and stand with such a power of divine distinction from all others of these last ages that it may be justly said, from their effects, that they answer in spirit to what was formerly done in the flesh, when "the blind saw, the deaf heard, the lame walked, and to the poor the gospel was preached."

The object of the biography will, therefore, not simply be to set forth the memorial of the individual's private life—and that in a glowing, reverential spirit, for the purpose of holy edification for the Christian, the scholar, the philosopher, and the gentleman—but to represent him in the truth of his mystic character as the *Elias** of God's last dispensation to the world (as observed

Along with modern scientific works containing the latest experiments, theories, and discoveries in Astronomy, Electricity, Magnetism, Geology, and other branches of universal Science.

We now come to **THE WORKS** themselves, the chosen writings of the subject of the proposed biography. The numbers attached to each indicate the order in which they originally stand.

<image-desc>pointing hand (manicule)</image-desc> The foundation of all solid progress in Divine wisdom lying in the renewal of the soul in the image of God, the writer has put together the following treatises, which he has designated **THE GRAMMAR OF WISDOM**, or **ELEMENTS OF THEOSOPHY**, in Three Parts; the instructions and practical exercises of which should be made the daily pursuit of all who would enter philosophy at the right door. A particular description of its contents is inserted here for the guidance of those who desire to understand the works in question, in the way and manner in which they are intended to be received and understood by the world. THE FIRST PART of the Grammar, though not belonging to the works in question, is nevertheless inserted regarding the unity of the treatise.

**GRAMMAR OF WISDOM.**—The FIRST PART [or, "**THE LAW.**"]—This part consists of the first thirteen and last chapters of the "**Serious Call.**" The student should study herewith Law’s "**Christian Perfection**" to the end of chapter 12; then chapters 19 to 23 of the "**Serious Call**," and then the remaining chapters 13 and 14 of the "**Christian Perfection.**"

**THE SECOND PART** [or "**THE GOSPEL**"] is composed of the following tracts of Böhme's "**Way to Christ**," made uniform in literary character with the preceding part.

(b.)—[HERE COMMENCES THE PRACTICE.] The tract *Of True Repentance*:* Or, Of Conviction of Sin, of True Repentance, or the "striving" and "wrestling" Exercises of Living Faith, and of the direct Witness of the Spirit, or Birth of God in the Soul.

(c.)—The Tract "Of The Four Complexions." This treats of Temptation, showing where it arises, whether from our own natural constitution, or Satanic agency, or outward providences, or the perversity of our neighbor; with directions on how to overcome in all trials. It might be briefly described as "The Philosophy of Temptation, or the Warfare in Awakened Souls between the World, the Flesh, and the Devil, and the Seed of the Woman."

(d.)—The Tract "Of True Resignation," which treats of the Spiritual Doctrine of Self-Denial, or of Daily Dying to Self; until all the properties of the old Adam weaken and decay, and the New Man is raised up in his stead. In other words, of "Incipient Sanctification," by the unvarying practice of Love toward God, and in regard to self and the action of external things, of perfect Patience, Meekness, Humility, and Resignation to God: which is accomplished by turning inwardly to the SPIRIT of these virtues now born in the soul (in the process of repentance and regeneration), and dwelling therein as the promised "Comforter," to replace the bodily presence and assistance of Christ, as a Savior from all evils, and an ALL-SUFFICIENT.†

(e.)—The Tract "Of the Supersensual Life," as paraphrased. This treats of the further process of Christian perfection or manifestation of the Divine nature in the soul, and Of Intellectual Illumination.—And here, let all seekers after true knowledge observe, commences the study of divine wisdom. "We preach wisdom among those who are perfect," says St. Paul; not to unconverted men, for they have no senses for it. And that such is the *true* and *natural* order of procedure is apparent at a moment's consideration. "For," as St. Paul again observes, "what man knows the things of a man, except the spirit of a man which is in him;" so likewise of the "Spirit of God." And then he goes on to declare, 'We know the wonderful mysteries of God by the Spirit of God, which is born within us.' As it must be with every other man.

Now, by the quickening action of the spiritual instructions and exercises of the preceding portions of this "Grammar," the incorruptible seed of Grace, or the Divine nature within us, is brought to life (upon the death of our natural serpentine spirit and properties), and is enabled to unfold its latent powers, and to evolve "with a divine elasticity" into light and liberty. Whereupon, the eyes of its spiritual senses or understanding being opened, it learns to recognize the forms and sounds and truths of its native element, the world of Truth, either in its own spirit, or as virtually symbolized in the signatures of outward nature, or contained in the letter of Scripture, or in these writings.—Here then, in the practical progress through the "Grammar of Wisdom," even to the experience of the tract under consideration, lies the key to true philosophy; and here, it is especially observed, the candidate and all should begin who would become proficient in the theosophic school.—From what is stated, it will also be apparent that, should complaints be made of the difficulty of understanding the works about to be described, the fault can only lie with the plaintiffs themselves, who have not entered philosophy by the right door (by which, indeed, the author himself obtained his high knowledge), or have not exercised that patience which the nature of things demands for the apprehension of truth. For just as no one can obtain the products of the terrestrial world except by duly waiting for their development and maturity, so likewise no creaturely intellect can understand the growths of the intellectual universe or world of divine wisdom, except so far as he is born again, or has obtained eyes to see, as he dwells in the light, and as he patiently waits for their birth and revelation (in his own microcosm) according to the unchangeable process of the divine manifestation. To proceed.

(f.)—The Tract "Of the Way from Darkness to True Illumination." This is a Practical Illustration of the preceding tracts, noting the several Experiences of a soul passing through the whole process from sin to holiness or Christian perfection, even to its admission into the light of divine wisdom and child-like apprehension of the philosophy of truth.

THE THIRD PART, [OR "AN ENTRANCE UPON THE SCIENCE OF WISDOM."]—For those who, having practically passed through the preceding course, feel a divine incentive to pursue the study of divine and natural wisdom. The first tract of this third part of the "Grammar of Wisdom" is J. B.'s brief treatise "Of Divine Vision or Contemplation;" and the other consists of his "CLAVIS."—Thus much concerning the "GRAMMAR OF WISDOM."—<insert>~~<unclear>of which see the preface in the first part also the chapters 20, 21, & 22 etc.</unclear>~~</insert>

## (XXI.)—THE CLAVIS, or An EXPLANATION of some PRINCIPAL POINTS and EXPRESSIONS in these WRITINGS.

### THE PREFACE is as follows:—

1.—It is written, *the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit, nor the mystery of the kingdom of God; they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them:* therefore I admonish and exhort the Christian lover of mysteries, if he will study these high writings, and read, search and understand them, that he does not read them outwardly only, with keen speculation and meditation; for in doing so, he shall remain in the outward imaginary ground only, and obtain no more than a counterfeit appearance of them.

2.—For a man's own reason, without the light of God, cannot reach the ground of them; it is impossible, let his wit be ever so high and subtle, for it apprehends only the shadow of it, as if in a mirror.

3.—For Christ says, *without me you can do nothing*; and He is the *light of the world*, and the life of man.

4.—Now if anyone would search the divine ground, that is the divine revelation, he must first consider within himself for what end he desires to know such things; whether he desires to **PRACTICE** that which he might obtain, and bestow it **PURELY** for the glory of God and the welfare of his neighbor; and whether he desires to die to earthliness and his own will, and to live in that which he seeks and desires, and to be one spirit with it.

5.—If he does not have a purpose that—if God should reveal himself and his mysteries to him—he would be one spirit and have one will with him, and wholly resign and yield himself up to him so that God's Spirit might do what he pleases with him and through him, and that God might be his knowledge, will, and deed, he is not yet fit for such knowledge and understanding.

6.—For there are many who seek mysteries and hidden knowledge merely so that they might be respected and highly esteemed by the world, and for their own gain and profit; but they do not attain this ground where the Spirit searches all things, as it is written, *even the deep things of God*.

7.—It must be a totally resigned will in which God himself searches and works, and which continually pierces into God in yielding and resigned humility, seeking nothing but his eternal native country and to serve his neighbor with it, and then it may be attained. And he must begin with effective repentance and amendment, and with prayer, so that his understanding might be opened from within; for then the inward will bring itself into the outward.

8.—But when he reads such writings and yet cannot understand them, he must not immediately throw them away and think it is impossible to understand them. No, he must turn his mind to God, beseeching him for grace and understanding, and read again; and then he shall see more and more in them, **UNTIL AT LENGTH HE IS DRAWN BY THE POWER OF GOD INTO THE VERY DEPTH ITSELF**, and so enters into the supernatural and **SUPERSENSUAL GROUND**, namely, into the Eternal Unity of God (N.B.), where he shall hear unspeakable and effective words of God, which shall bring him back and outward again, by the divine effluence, to the very grossest and simplest matter of the earth, and then back and inward to God again. Then the Spirit of God searches all things with him and through him, and so he is rightly taught and driven by God.

9.—But since the lovers of these writings desire a **CLAVIS**, or Key to my writings, I am ready and willing to please them in it, and will set down a short description of the basis of those unusual words, some of which are taken from nature and sense, and some are the words of uncommon masters, which I have tested according to sense and found them good and fit.

10.—Reason will stumble when it sees heathenish terms and words used in the explanation of natural things, assuming we should use nothing but scripture phrasing (or words borrowed from the Bible). However, such words will not always apply and align themselves with the fundamental explanation of the properties of nature, nor can a man express the ground with them. Also, the wise Heathens and Jews have hidden the deep ground of nature under such words, having well understood that the knowledge of nature is not for everyone, but it belongs only to those whom God by nature has chosen for it, **AND WHO SEEK IT IN THE RIGHT WAY.**

11.—But no one needs to be offended by it: for when God reveals his mysteries to any man, he then also brings him into a state of mind and capacity to express them as God knows is most necessary and profitable in every age, for setting confused tongues and opinions upon the true ground again. Men must not think that it comes by chance or is done by human reason.

12.—The revelations of divine things are opened by the inward ground of the spiritual world and brought into visible forms, just as the Creator will manifest them.

13.—I will now write but a short description of the divine manifestation, yet as much as I can briefly comprise; and explain the unusual words for the better understanding of our books, and set down here the sum of those writings, or a model or epitome of them, **FOR THE CONSIDERATION OR HELP OF BEGINNERS:** the further explanation of it is to be found in the other books.

THE PREFACE is as follows (previous to the reading of which, however, the reader is recommended to read the Preface to the book of "The Three Principles," which may be considered as a General Preface to all the author’s writings):

1.—When we consider the visible world, with its essence and the life of the creatures, we find within it the likeness of the invisible spiritual world, which is hidden in the visible world as the soul is in the body. We see by this that the hidden God is near to all and through all, and yet remains wholly hidden to the visible essence.

2.—We have an example of this in the mind of man, which is an invisible fire that is inclined toward light and darkness—namely, to joy and sorrow—and yet in itself is none of these, but only a cause for them. It is an invisible, incomprehensible fire-source, and yet as to its own essence, it is contained in nothing except the will of life.

3.—The body cannot comprehend the mind, but the mind comprehends the body and brings it to love or dislike. This is likewise to be understood regarding the word and power of God, which is hidden from the visible, sensible elements, yet dwells through and in the elements and works through the sensible life and essence, just as the mind does in the body.

4.—For visible, sensible things are an essence of the invisible: from the invisible and incomprehensible, the visible and comprehensible has proceeded. The visible essence has come to be from the expression or <term>spiration</term> of the invisible power. The invisible spiritual word of divine power works with and through the visible essence, just as the soul does with and through the body.

5.—The inward spiritual soul of man was breathed into the visible image by the speaking-in, or inspiration, of the invisible word of the divine power (as an understanding for the created image), wherein man’s <term>divine science</term> or knowledge of the invisible and visible essence consists.

6.—Thus man has now received ability from the invisible word of God for re-expression, so that he again expresses the hidden word of the <term>divine science</term> into formation and separation, in the manner and form of the temporal creatures, and from this spiritual word according to animals and vegetables; by which the invisible wisdom of God is portrayed and modeled into several distinct forms. As we plainly see, the understanding of man expresses all powers in their property and gives names to all things according to each thing’s property; by which the hidden wisdom is known and understood in its power, and the hidden God is made manifest with the visible things, for the delight and play of the divine power; so that the invisible might play with the visible, and therein introduce itself into the light and sense of itself.

7.—As the mind introduces itself with the body, and by the body into senses and thoughts, whereby it works and acts sensibly to itself; so also the invisible world works through the visible and with the visible world. We are not in any way to imagine that a man cannot search out what the hidden divine world is, and what its operation and essence are, for in the visible essence of the creation we see a figure of the internal spiritual operation of the powerful word.

8.—And we ought not to think otherwise of God than that he is the most internal ground of all essences; and yet in such a way that he cannot be comprehended by anything through the thing's own peculiar power. But as the sun introduces itself with its light and power into the sensible living things, and works with (or in) all things, and also introduces itself into an essence, the same is likewise to be understood concerning the divine word with the life of the creatures.

9.—Seeing then that this visible world is the expressed, formed word, according to God’s love and anger—namely, according to the grand mystery of the eternal spiritual nature, which spiritual world is hidden in the visible—and yet the human soul is a spark out of the eternal speaking word of the <term>divine science</term> and power, and the body an <term>ens</term> of the stars and elements; and also as to the internal ground an <term>ens</term> of heaven, namely, of the hidden world; therefore he has power and ability to speak of the grand mystery, from which all essences originally arise.

10.—Since then the great mysteries—the beginning and origin of all things—happen to us by divine grace, so that we are able (as through the ground of the soul) to understand the same in real knowledge with the inspired word of the <term>divine science</term>, we will write down its ground (so far as it is permitted to us) in this book, as a memorial to ourselves and for the exercise of divine knowledge for the reader.

11.—And I. We will signify and declare what the center and ground of all essences is.
->II. What the divine manifestation is, through the speaking of the word of God.<-
->III. How evil and good have their origin from one only ground—namely, light and darkness, life and death, joy and sorrow—and how it is in its ground; also for what purpose every essence and source is profitable and necessary.<-
->IV. How all things have their ground from the grand mystery—namely, from the <term>spiration</term> of the Eternal One.<-
->V. How the Eternal One introduces itself into sensation, perception, and separation, for the knowledge of itself and the play of the divine power.<-
->VI. How man may attain to the true knowledge of God, and to the knowledge of eternal and temporal nature.<-
->VII. Also how man may come to the real contemplation of the being of all Beings.<-
->VIII. Also of the creation of the world and of all creatures.<-
->IX. And then of the origin, fall, and restoration of man; what he is according to the first <term>Adamical</term> man in the kingdom of nature, and what he is in the new regeneration in the kingdom of grace, and how the new birth occurs.<-
->X. Also what the Old and New Testaments are, each in its understanding.<-

12.—And we will expand this explanation through all the chapters of the first book of Moses; and point out how the Old Testament is a figure of the New, what is to be understood by the deeds of the holy patriarchs; why the Spirit of God had them recorded by Moses; and what the symbols of these written histories look toward and intend, and how the Spirit of God in his children before the time of Christ alluded to the kingdom of Christ through those figures: whereby God has always represented this mercy-seat (or throne of Grace) Christ, through whom he would blot out his anger and manifest his grace.

13.—And we shall show how the entire duration of this world is portrayed and modeled, as in a clockwork mechanism, how it should proceed through time, and what the inward spiritual world, as well as the outward material world, is; also what the inward spiritual man, and then the external man of the essence of this world, is; how time and eternity exist within one another, and how a person may understand all this.

14.—Now if it should happen that when these writings of ours are read, the reader does not immediately grasp and understand them (seeing that this foundation—which nevertheless has its full basis and perfect agreement with both scripture and the light of nature—has for a long time been very obscure, yet by divine grace is given to plain simplicity), let him not despise and reject them, according to the way and custom of the wicked world. Instead, let him look upon the practical foundation which is suggested therein, and give himself up to it, and pray to God for light and understanding; and at last he will rightly understand our basis, and it will find great love and acceptance with him.

15.—But we have written nothing for the proud and haughty pretenders to wisdom, who think they know enough already, yet indeed know nothing at all; whose belly is their god, who only cling to the beast of the Babylonian whore and drink of her poison, and willfully remain in blindness and the devil’s snare. But we have placed (with the spirit of our knowledge) a strong bolt before the understanding of folly, so they cannot grasp our meaning, since they willfully and willingly serve Satan and are not the children of God.

16.—But we desire to be clearly and fundamentally understood by the children of God, and we heartily and readily communicate the knowledge given to us by God, seeing the time for such a revelation has arrived. Therefore, let everyone watch and take heed of what judgment and criticism they pass: everyone shall receive their reward accordingly, and we commend them to the grace of the meek and tender love of Jesus Christ. Amen.

The reader, as he proceeds in the study of these works, should take care to write out the substance or chief points of what he has studied, as well as to read portions aloud and emphatically to others on all possible occasions, and converse with them upon the meaning. *DOCENDO DISCEMUS* <note>By teaching, we learn</note>; and the reason is because all things are in the mind and merely require awakening through the senses. Some philosophers maintain that there are no innate ideas; others, and more correctly, that there are none but innate ideas: "For as the soul was made a partaker of the divine nature by its creation, it possessed (and possesses, when regenerated) the triune life, likeness, and spirit of God, living in its own creaturely life, and therefore had the riches and perfections of the Deity grounded and growing up in that which was living in it. For as it was the life of man that had this image and likeness of God in it, so the unfathomable riches, powers, and perfections of the divine nature came forth in a creaturely state in the birth of the human life. And this is the true ground of our eternal happiness—that is, of that eternal increase of union, perfection, and glory which the redeemed soul will find in God. It is because the image and likeness of God, being like a seed sown into it at its creation, will for all eternity, after its admission into heaven, be made to open more and more of its divine nature, and spring forth in new and further fruits and growths of glory, blessedness, and union with God. And as it is a certain truth that no fruits, flowers, or virtues can be or come forth in any plant except what were first in its seed or root, so no divine glory, perfection, or power can ever come forth in any creature in heaven except what arises from that seed of the Deity sown into it at its creation. Therefore, as surely as the heavenly soul will for all eternity increase in new openings and enlargements of divine union, enjoyment, and perfection in God, so surely is it that in the center, or innermost birth of the soul's life, lie the riches of the divine nature [and therefore all things, and the knowledge of them] as a seed or root of glory given into it by its first created image or likeness to God."

<margin>second</margin>
The following treatise was the first book of this author, written in the infancy of his high knowledge and illumination. It was simply set down as a reminder for himself of what he saw and conceived, but the providence of God made it known and caused it to be much sought after. It will be advisable for the reader, after studying the first thirty-six chapters of the previously mentioned work, to read the answer to the first of the "Forty Questions," then to run over briefly the "Book of the Incarnation," and the first two of the "Six Points." Then, by reading alternately in the book of "The Three Principles" and "The Threefold Life," he will easily arrive at the basis and meaning of the author in the following treatise.

Description of Nature, showing I.—How all was, and came to be in the Beginning. II.—How Nature and the Elements have become creaturely. III.—Also of the Two Qualities, Evil and Good. ## THE AUTHOR'S INTRODUCTION to this book is as follows:—

To this book I have given this name, namely, "The Root or Mother of Philosophy, Astrology, and Theology." And so that you may know what it treats of, observe:—

1.—In Philosophy, it treats of the Divine Power.
> I.—What God is.
> II.—How in the being of God nature, the stars, and the elements are created.
> III.—From where everything has its origin.
> IV.—How heaven and earth were created.
> V.—How angels, men, and devils were created.
> VI.—How heaven and hell, and whatever is creaturely, were created, and what the two qualities are in nature.

All out of a true ground in the knowledge of the spirit, by the impulse and motion of God.

2.—In Astrology, it treats:
> I.—Of the powers of nature, of the stars, and of the elements.
> II.—How all creatures proceeded from there.
> III.—How the same impel and rule all.
> IV.—And work in all, and how good and bad is produced by them in men and beasts.
> V.—From where it comes that good and bad exist and reign in this world.
> VI.—And how the kingdom of heaven and of hell consists therein.

3.—My purpose is not to describe the course, place, and name of all stars, and what their annual conjunction, opposition, quadrat <note>An astrological aspect where two planets are 90 degrees apart.</note>, or the like is; what they yearly and hourly operate, which over a long process of time has been observed by wise, skillful, and expert men, who were rich and expansive in spirit through their diligent contemplation, observation, deep sense, calculation, and computation.

4.—Neither have I studied or learned the same, and I leave that to the learned to discourse upon; but my intention is to write according to the spirit and sense, and not according to speculation.

5.—In Theology, it treats:
> I.—Of the kingdom of Christ, and what its condition is.
> II.—How it is set in opposition to the kingdom of hell.
> III.—How in nature it fights and strives against the kingdom of hell.
> IV.—How men through faith and spirit are able to overcome the kingdom of hell, and triumph in divine power, and obtain eternal salvation, and all this as a victory in the battle.
> V.—How man, through the operation or working in the hellish quality, casts himself into perdition.
> VI.—And what the outcome of both will be at last.

6.—The supreme title is **AURORA**, that is, The Dawning of the Day in the East, or Morning Redness in the Rising of the Sun.

And it is a secret mystery concealed from the wise and prudent of this world, which they themselves shall shortly be aware of; but to those who read this book in singleness of heart, with a desire for the Holy Spirit, who place their hope only in God, it will not be a hidden secret, but a manifest knowledge.

7.—I will not explain this title, but commit it to the judgment of the impartial reader, who wrestles in the good quality of this world.

8.—Now if the critic, who works with his wit in the fierce quality, gets this book into his hands, he will oppose it, as there is always a stirring and opposition between the kingdom of heaven and the kingdom of hell.
> I.—First he will say that I ascend too high into the Deity, which is not an appropriate thing for me to do.
> II.—Then, secondly, he will say that I boast of the Holy Spirit: I had more need to live accordingly, and demonstrate it by wondrous works or miracles.
> III.—Thirdly, he will say that I am not learned enough.
> IV.—Fourthly, he will say that I do it in a vainglorious way.
> V.—Fifthly, he will be much offended at the simplicity of the author, as it is usual in the world to gaze only upon high things, and simplicity is a scandal and offense to it.

9.—To these partial worldly critics, I set in opposition the patriarchs of the first world, who were lowly, despised men, against whom the world and the devil raged, as in the time of Enoch; when the holy fathers preached powerfully of the name of the Lord, they did not ascend with their bodies into heaven and behold all with their eyes: only the Holy Ghost revealed himself in their spirits.

10.—It is seen afterwards in the next world, among the holy patriarchs and prophets, all of whom were lowly, simple men, and some of whom were herdsmen.

11.—And when the **MESSIAH CHRIST**, the champion in the battle in nature, took on humanity, though he was the king and prince of men, yet he kept himself in this world in a low estate and condition, and his apostles were poor, despised fishermen.

12.—Nay, Christ himself returns thanks to his heavenly Father, that he has "concealed these things from the worldly wise men, and revealed them unto babes."

13.—Besides, it is seen how they also were poor sinners, having both the impulses of good and of bad in nature. And yet they reproved and preached against the sins of the world, yes, against their own sins, which they did by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, and not in vainglory.

<meta>This page continues the author's introduction to his work, transitioning from the overarching purpose of the book to the author's personal spiritual experiences, the nature of the soul, and a detailed summary of the chapters to follow.</meta>

14.—They also had no ability from their own strength and power to teach of God’s mysteries in that way, but all was by the impulse of God.

15.—So I also cannot say anything of myself, nor boast or write of anything, except this: that I am a simple man and a poor sinner, and have need to pray daily, "Lord, forgive us our sins," and say with the apostle, “O Lord, you have redeemed us with your blood.”

16.—Neither did I ascend into heaven and behold all the works and creatures of God; but the same heaven is revealed in my spirit, so that I know in the spirit the works and creatures of God.

17.—And besides, the will for that is not my natural will, but it is the impulse of the Spirit; and I have endured many an assault of the devil for it.

18.—But the Spirit of Man is descended not only from the stars and elements, but there is hidden within it a spark of the light and power of God.

19.—It is not an empty word which is set down in Genesis, “God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him.” For it has this sense and meaning: namely, that he is created out of the whole being of the Deity.

20.—The body is from the elements; therefore, it must have elemental food.

21.—The soul has its origin not only from the body—though it is in the body and has its first beginning in the body—yet it also has its source within it from the outside, by and from the air. And so the Holy Spirit rules in it in the same manner as he replenishes and fills all things, and as all things are in God, and so God himself is all.

22.—Seeing then that the Holy Spirit in the soul is creaturely (namely, the property or portion of the soul), it therefore searches even into the Deity and also into nature; for it has its source and descent from the being of the whole Deity.

23.—When it is kindled or enlightened by the Holy Spirit, then it beholds what God its father does, just as a son beholds what his father does at home in his own house.

24.—It is a member or child in the house of the heavenly Father.

25.—And as the eye of man sees even to the stars, from which it has a finite origin and beginning, so the soul also sees even into the divine Being in which it lives.

26.—But as the soul also has its source out of nature, and as in nature there is good and bad, and as man has cast himself through sin into the fierceness or wrath of nature, so that the soul is daily and hourly defiled with sins, it therefore knows only in part.

27.—For the wrath or fierceness in nature reigns now also in the soul. But the Holy Spirit does not go into the wrath or fierceness, but reigns in the source of the soul which is in the light of God, and fights against the wrath or fierceness in the soul.

28.—And therefore the soul cannot attain any perfect knowledge in this life until the end—when light and darkness are separated, and the wrath or fierceness is consumed with the body in the earth; then the soul sees clearly and perfectly in God its father.

29.—But when the soul is kindled or enlightened by the Holy Spirit, then it triumphs in the body like a great fire, which makes the heart and reins <note>The kidneys, historically considered the seat of the emotions.</note> tremble for joy.

30.—But there is not immediately a great and deep knowledge in God its father, but its love toward God its father triumphs in the fire of the Holy Spirit.

31.—Instead, the knowledge of God is sown in the fire of the Holy Spirit, and at first is as small “as a grain of mustard seed,” as Christ makes the comparison; afterwards it grows large like a tree and spreads itself out in God its creator.

32.—Just as a drop of water in the ocean cannot achieve much, but if a great river runs into it, that makes a greater commotion.

33.—But time past, present, and to come, as also depth and height, near and far off, are all one in God—one comprehensibility.

34.—And the holy soul of man sees the same also, but in this world only in part. It happens sometimes that it sees nothing at all, for the devil assaults it furiously in the fierce, wrathful source which is in the soul, and often covers the noble mustard seed; therefore, man must always be in fight and war.

35.—In this manner and knowledge of the Spirit, I will write concerning God our father, in whom are all things and who himself is all; and I will show how all has become distinct and creaturely, and how all drives and moves in the whole tree of life.

36.—Here you shall see: 1. The true ground of the Deity. 2. How all was One Being before the time of the world. 3. How the holy angels were created, and out of what. 4. How the terrible fall of Lucifer, together with his legions, happened. 5. How heaven, earth, stars, and the elements were made. 6. How metals, stones, and other creatures in the earth are generated. 7. How the birth of life is, and the corporeity of all things. 8. What the true heaven is, in which God and his saints dwell. 9. And what the wrath of God is, and the hellish fire. 10. And how all has become kindled and inflamed. In brief, how and what the Being of all Beings is.

37.—The first seven chapters treat very plainly and comprehensively of the being of God and of angels by analogies, so that the reader may, from one step to another, at last come to the deep sense and true ground.

38.—In the eighth chapter begins the depth in the divine Being, and so on—the further, the deeper.

39.—One thing is often repeated and described even more deeply for the reader’s sake, and because of my slow and dull understanding.

40.—That which you do not find sufficiently explained in this book, you will find more clearly in the second and third.

41.—For corruption is the cause why we know only in part and do not have perfect knowledge all at once.

42.—Yet this book is the **WONDER** of the World, which the holy soul will understand well enough. Thus I commit the reader to the meek and holy love of God.

### THE AUTHOR’S PREFACE to this book is as follows; it may serve as a general preface to all his works—

1.—A man can undertake nothing from the beginning of his youth, nor in the whole course of his time in this world, that is more profitable and necessary for him than to learn to know himself: what he is, out of what, from where, and for what he is created, and what his office is. In such serious consideration, he will soon find that he, and all the creatures that exist, all come from God. He will also find, among all the creatures, that he is the most noble creature of them all; from which he will very well perceive God’s intention toward him, in that He has made him lord over all the creatures of this world and has endowed him with mind, reason, and understanding above all the rest of the creatures, especially with speech or language, so that he can distinguish everything that sounds, stirs, moves, or grows, and judge the virtue, effect, and origin of everything; and that all is put under his hand, so that he can direct, use, and manage them according to his will, as pleases him.

2.—Moreover, God has given him higher and greater knowledge than this, in that he can penetrate into the heart of everything and discern what essence, virtue, and property it has—both in the creatures, in earth, stones, trees, herbs, in all movable and immovable things; also in the stars and elements, so that he knows what substance and virtue they have, and that in their virtue all natural sensibility, growth, reproduction, and life consist.

3.—Above all this, God has given him the understanding and perception to know God his Creator; what and from where man is, how he is, and where he is, and out of what he proceeded or was created; and how he is the image, substance, property, and child of the eternal, uncreated, and infinite God, in whom God has His own substance and property, in whom He lives and governs with His Spirit, by which God manages His own work and loves him dearly as His own heart and substance. For man's sake, He created this world with all the creatures that are in it, which for the most part, without the reason and government of man, could not live in such a condition as they do.

4.—Divine wisdom itself stands in such high consideration and has neither number nor end; and therein is the love of God toward man made known, in that man knows what his Creator is, and what He would have him do and leave undone. And it is the most profitable thing for man in this world that he can search for and seek after; for in this, he learns to know himself, what matter and substance he is made of; also from where his understanding <note>thought, perceptibility</note> and sensibility are stirred, and how he is created out of the substance of God. And as a mother brings forth a child out of her own substance, and nourishes it with it, and leaves all her goods to it for its own, making it the possessor of them, so God also does with man, His child; He has created him and preserved him, and made him heir to all His eternal goods. In and by this consideration, divine knowledge buds and grows in man, and love toward God, like that of a child to its parents, so that man loves God his Father because he knows that He is his Father, in whom he lives and has his being, who nourishes him, preserves him, and provides for him; for thus says Christ our brother (who is begotten of the Father to be a Savior and sent into this world): "This is eternal life, that they know Thee to be the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom Thou hast sent."

5.—Now, seeing we ourselves know that we are created out of God’s own substance and made His image, substance, and special inheritance, it is therefore right that we should live in obedience to Him and follow Him, seeing He leads us as a father does his children. And we also have His promise that if we follow Him, we shall obtain the light of eternal life. Without such a consideration as this, we are altogether blind and have no knowledge of God; instead, we run on like dumb beasts, and we look upon ourselves and upon God’s creation as heifers look upon a new door made to their stalls, and set ourselves against God and His will, and so live in opposition and enmity, to the destruction of body and soul, and of God’s noble creatures. We fall into this terrible and abominable darkness because we will not learn to know ourselves—what we are, of what substance, what we shall be, whether we are eternal, or whether we are wholly transitory as the body is; or whether also we must give an account of our matters and doings, seeing we are made lords of all creatures and of the whole creation, and have all this in our power to manage.

6.—Even as we see, know, and find undeniably that God will require an account of all our doings—how we have managed His works—and that when we fall away from Him and His commandments, He will punish us terribly, of which we have fearful examples from the beginning of the world, and among the Jews, Heathens, and Christians, especially the example of the flood, and in Sodom and Gomorrah; also in Pharaoh and the Children of Israel in the Wilderness, and ever since until this very time. Therefore, it is indeed most necessary that we learn to know ourselves, what great vice and wickedness we carry about us, and how horrible the wolves among us are that strive against God and His will.

7.—For there is no one who can excuse himself and plead ignorance, because the will of God is placed and written in our minds, so that we know very well what we should do; and all the

<summary>This page introduces "The Three Principles of the Divine Essence" and features a preface on the necessity of self-knowledge. The author argues that humans are God's most noble creation, endowed with reason to understand the natural world and their own divine origin.</summary>

creatures bear witness against us. Moreover, we have God's law and commandments, so that there is no excuse, but only our drowsy, lazy negligence and carelessness; and so we are found to be slothful, unprofitable servants in the Lord's vineyard.

8.—Lastly, it is of the utmost importance for us to learn to know ourselves, because the devil dwells with us in this world. He is both God's enemy and ours, and he daily misleads us and ensnares us, as he has done from the beginning, so that we might fall away from our God and Father. In this way, he might enlarge his kingdom and rob us of our eternal salvation; as it is written, he goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.

9.—Seeing, therefore, that we are in such horrible danger in this world—surrounded by enemies on every side and having a very unsafe pilgrimage or journey to walk—and above all, we carry our worst enemy within us, which we ourselves hide and do not desire to learn to know, though it is the most horrible guest of all, which casts us headlong into the anger of God. Indeed, it is the very anger of God itself, which throws us into the eternal fire of wrath, into the eternal unquenchable torment. Therefore, it is most necessary for us to learn to know this enemy: what he is, who he is, and where he comes from; how he enters into us, and what in us is properly his own; also what right the devil has over us, and what access or entrance he has into us; how he is allied with our own enemy that dwells within us, how they favor and help one another, and how both of them are God's enemies, continually lying in wait to murder us and bring us to perdition.

10.—Further, we must consider the great reasons why it is very necessary to learn to know ourselves: because we see and know that we must die and perish for the sake of our enemy, who is God's enemy and ours, who dwells in us and is the very half of man. And if he grows so strong in us that he gets the upper hand and becomes predominant, then he throws us into the abyss with all the devils, to dwell there with them eternally in an eternal, unquenchable pain and torment, in an eternal darkness, in a loathsome house, and in an eternal forgetting of all good—indeed, into God's contending will, where our God and all the creatures are our enemies forever.

11.—We have yet greater reasons to learn to know ourselves, because we exist in both good and evil and have the promise of eternal life. If we overcome our own enemy and the devil, we shall be the children of God and live in his kingdom, with and in him, among his holy angels, in eternal joy, brightness, glory, and welfare, in meekness and favor with him, without any touch of evil and without any knowledge of it, in God eternally. Besides, we have the promise that if we overcome and bury our enemy in the earth, we shall rise again at the last day in a new body, which shall be without evil and pain, and live with God in perfect joy, loveliness, and bliss.

12.—Also, we know and understand that we have within us a reasonable soul, which is in God's love and is immortal. If it is not vanquished by its adversary but fights as a spiritual champion against its enemy, God will assist it with his Holy Spirit; he will enlighten it and make it powerful and able to overcome all its enemies. He will fight for it, and upon the overcoming of evil, he will glorify it as a faithful champion and crown it with the brightest crown of heaven.

13.—Now, seeing man knows that he is such a twofold man, with the capacity for both good and evil, and that they are both his own, and that he himself is that one man who is both good and evil; and that he shall have the reward of either of them, and to whichever of them he inclines in this life, to that his soul goes when he dies; and that he shall arise at the last day in power, in his labor and works which he exercised here, and live in them eternally and also be glorified in them—and that shall be his eternal food and subsistence—therefore, it is very necessary for him to learn to know himself: how it is with him, and where the impulse toward good and evil comes from, and what indeed the good and evil actually are in himself, and from where they are stirred; what properly is the origin of all the good and of all the evil; from where and by what means evil came to be in the devils, in men, and in all creatures, seeing the devil was once a holy angel and man was also created good; and why such hostility is found in all creatures, biting, tearing, worrying, and hurting one another, and such enmity, strife, and hatred in all creatures; and that everything is so at odds with itself, as we see it to be not only in the living creatures, but also in the stars, elements, earth, stones, metals, in wood, leaves, and grass—there is a poison and malignity in all things. And it is found that it must be so, or else there would be no life, no mobility, nor would there be any color or virtue, neither density nor rarity, nor any perceptibility or sensibility, but all would be as nothing.

14.—In this high consideration, it is found that all is through and from God himself, and that it is his own substance, which is himself, and he has created it out of himself. The evil belongs to the forming and mobility, and the good to the love. The austere, severe, or contrary will belongs to the joy; as far as the creature is in the light of God, the wrathful and contrary will creates the rising, eternal joy. But if the light of God is extinguished, it creates the rising, painful torment and the hellish fire.

15.—So that it may be understood how all this is, I will describe the "Three Divine Principles," so that in them all may be declared: what God is, what nature is, what the creatures are, what the love and meekness of God are, what God's desiring or will is, what the wrath of God and the devil are, and in conclusion, what joy and sorrow are. I will also describe how all things took a beginning and endure eternally, with the true difference between the eternal and transitory creatures—especially of man and of his soul, what it is, and how it is an eternal creature—and what heaven is, where God and the holy angels and holy men dwell; and what hell is, where the devils dwell; and how all things originally were created and had their being. In sum, WHAT THE ESSENCE OF ALL ESSENCES IS.

16.—Seeing the love of God has favored me with this knowledge, I will set it down in writing as a memorial or remembrance to myself, because we live in this world in such great danger between heaven and hell and must continually wrestle with the devil. If perhaps through weakness I might fall into the anger of God, and thereby the light of my knowledge might be withdrawn from me, this writing may serve to help me recall it to memory and raise it up again. For God wills that all men should be helped and does not will the death of a sinner, but rather that he return, come to him, and live in him eternally; for whose sake he has allowed his own heart, that is, his Son, to become man, so that we might adhere to him and rise again in him, and departing from our sins and enmity, or contrary will, be newborn in him.

17.—Therefore, there is nothing more profitable to man in this world, while he dwells in this miserable, corrupted house of flesh, than to learn to know himself. Now, when he knows him—

<summary>The author emphasizes the urgent need for self-knowledge to combat the internal and external influence of the devil and explains that both good and evil originate from God's own substance. He introduces his work on the "Three Divine Principles" as a guide to understanding the nature of God, the soul, and the origins of all existence.</summary>

himself aright, he also knows his Creator and all the creatures too. He also knows how God intends toward him, and this knowledge is the most acceptable and pleasant to me that I have ever found.

18.—But if it should happen that these writings are read—and perhaps the corrupt world and its fattened swine come upon them and root around in my garden of pleasure, those who can understand nothing but how to scorn, scandalize, reproach, and argue in a proud, haughty way, and thus know neither themselves nor God, much less His children—I do not intend my writing for them. Instead, I shut and lock my book with a strong bolt or bar against such idiots and wild heifers of the devil, who lie over head and ears in the devil’s murdering den and do not know themselves. They do the same thing their teacher, the devil, does, and remain children of the severe anger of God. But I will write plainly and clearly enough here for the children of God. The world and the devil may roar and rage until they reach the abyss, for their hourglass is set; everyone shall reap what they have sown. The hellish fire will sufficiently sting many for their proud, spiteful, and despising arrogance, which they did not believe in while they were here in this life.

19.—Besides, I cannot easily neglect to set this down in writing, because God will require an account of everyone’s gifts and how they have employed them. For He will demand the talent He has bestowed, along with its increase or use, and give it to the one who has gained much. But seeing as I can do no more in this matter, I commit it to His will and proceed to write according to my knowledge.

20.—As for the children of God, they shall perceive and understand my writing for what it is; for it is a very convincing testimony. It may be proved by all the creatures—yes, in all things, especially in man, who is an image and likeness of God. But it remains hidden and obscure to the children of malice or iniquity, and there is a firm seal before it. And though the devil dislikes the scent and flavor and raises a storm from the east to the north, yet a LILY will then grow in the bitter sour tree, with a root as broad as the tree spreads with its branches, bringing its scent and fragrance even into paradise.

21.—A wonderful time is coming. But because it begins in the night, many shall not see it because of their sleep and great drunkenness; yet the sun will shine for the children at midnight. Thus, I commit the reader to the gentle love of God. Amen.

### (IV.)—THE FORTY QUESTIONS CONCERNING THE SOUL ANSWERED.

In the answer to the first question is the figure of the Philosophic Globe, or universal **WONDER-EYE OF ETERNITY**, or Mirror of the Divine Wisdom, along with an explanation of it.

With a summary appendix concerning the soul, the image of the soul, and the **Turba**, which is the destroyer of the image.

The author originally wrote the answers to these questions for the sake of his friend, a certain Dr. B. W. After traveling to various parts of the world in search of ancient occult wisdom, upon his return home, he happened to hear of this author and made his acquaintance. He rejoiced that he had at last found, in a poor cottage in his own neighborhood, what he had traveled so far to seek in vain. He then proceeded to several of the most noted universities in Germany and collected such metaphysical questions concerning the soul as were considered impossible to be resolved fundamentally. He sent this catalogue of questions to the author, from whom he received the answers contained in this book to his complete satisfaction.

<margin>stone /</margin>
Each of the previous books, starting from the first, will be found to be grounded deeper and deeper; and in this fourth treatise, the Great Mystery of the Manifestation of God may be clearly understood. It would seem that successive books are written so that what could not be explained in one might be found in another. It would be well, if possible, if all were compressed into one and the rest laid aside, for the multiplicity of books causes strife and confused understanding because of the grasping conceits of human reason. Reason is completely blind to the mystery, for it stands both outside and within the circle of truth. But whoever applies themselves correctly, according to the indicated process, to understand the center of all beings, and goes so far as to apprehend the **THREE PRINCIPLES** of the Divine Manifestation, will not need either these or any man’s writings; for the whole universe of things will be an open book to their delighted understanding.

**THE QUESTIONS are these:—**

I.—From where the soul proceeded at the beginning?
II.—What is its essence, substance, nature, and property?
III.—How is it created in the image of God?
IV.—What and when was the breathing of it in?
V.—How is it specially fashioned, and what is its form?
VI.—What is its power?
VII.—Whether it is corporeal or not corporeal?
VIII.—In what manner does it come into the body of man?
IX.—In what way does it unite itself with the body?
X.—Whether it is **EX TRADUCE** and propagated in a human bodily manner, or created anew every time and breathed in from God?
XI.—How and where is it seated in man?
XII.—How and what is its illumination?
XIII.—How does it feed upon the Word of God?
XIV.—Whether such a new soul is without sin?
XV.—How does sin enter it, since it is the work and creature of God?
XVI.—How is it kept in such union, both in the Adamic and regenerate body?
XVII.—From where and why is the conflict between the flesh and the spirit?
XVIII.—How does it depart from the body at the death of a man?
XIX.—How is it mortal, and how immortal?
XX.—How does it return to God again?
XXI.—Where does it go when it departs from the body, whether it is saved or not saved?
XXII.—What does every departed soul do? Does it rejoice until the last Judgment Day?
XXIII.—Do the souls of the wicked, without exception (during the time before the Day of Judgment), find even any relief or refreshment?
XXIV.—Do men’s wishes benefit them at all, or do them any sensible good?
XXV.—What is the Hand of God and the Bosom of Abraham?
XXVI.—Does the soul care for people—their friends, children, or goods—and does it know, see, approve, or disapprove of their undertakings?
XXVII.—Does it know this or that art or occupation in which it had sufficient skill while in the body?
XXVIII.—Does it also obtain a more certain knowledge of divine, angelic, earthly, and diabolical matters than it had in the body?
XXIX.—What is its rest, awakening, and glorification?
XXX.—What is the difference between the resurrection of the flesh and of the soul, both of the living and of the dead?
XXXI.—What kind of new glorified bodies shall they have?
XXXII.—What shall their form, condition, joy, and glory be in the next life?
XXXIII.—What kind of matter shall our bodies have in the life to come?
XXXIV.—What is the lamentable and horrible condition of the damned souls?
XXXV.—What is the Enochian life, and how long does it continue?
XXXVI.—What is the soul of the Messiah, or Christ?
XXXVII.—What is the spirit of Christ, which He willingly committed into the hands of His Father?
XXXVIII.—Concerning the things that shall come to pass at the end of the world?
XXXIX.—What and where is Paradise, along with its inhabitants?
XL.—Is it mutable, and what shall it be afterward?

**THE PREFACE** is the letter addressed by the author to his friend, Dr. B., upon returning the answers to him, as follows:—

1.—Beloved Sir, and my good Friend, it is impossible for reason to answer these questions of yours, for they contain the highest and greatest mysteries, which are known to God alone.
2.—Therefore Daniel says to King Nebuchadnezzar: That which the king asks and desires of the learned Chaldeans, Astrologers, and Wise Men, is not in their power. Only the God of Heaven can reveal secret things: It is not in my reason to answer the king; but so that the king may perceive the thoughts of his heart, God has revealed it; not because my reason is greater than that of any living man. <note>Dan. 2:27–28; Gen. 41:16.</note>
3.—So likewise I say to you: you shall be answered, not because my reason is greater than that of any living man, but only so that you may perceive the thoughts, the earnest seeking, and the desire of your heart, it is given to me to answer you.
4.—And you should not seek after these things so anxiously in such a way; they are not found in any outward reason. But to the Spirit of God nothing is impossible: seeing that we are the children of God, and born anew of God in Christ, the son sees very clearly what the father does in his house, and also learns his art and work.
5.—Seeing also that we are the mystery of God, we ought not to suppose that we must not even look upon, nor meddle with, such mysteries as Babylon teaches; for no one takes anything of God's mysteries for himself, unless it is given to him. And St. James says, every good and perfect gift comes from above, from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor alteration.
6.—And since you seek so eagerly after such things, you thereby become the very cause of finding them, for God gives His mysteries both through means and also without means; but so that no man might boast, He often makes use of very humble people for them, so that it might be acknowledged that they come from His hand.
7.—You shall be answered with a very sound and deep answer, yet briefly summarized, not according to outward reason, but according to the spirit of knowledge.
8.—And although I could sufficiently show and demonstrate these things in a longer description; yet since they are all described and explained at length in my other writings, at present I set them down only briefly for the ease and delight of the reader, and so that it may serve as a short memorial of the great mysteries.
9.—But he who desires to know these things fully and fundamentally, let him seek them in my former writings, especially in the third book, and there he has the whole ground of the divine essence; and also of the creation of all things; of that which is eternal, and of that which is perishable; and how everything was made, and has come to be as it is, and acts as it does, and what it shall be in the end.
10.—And therein also lies the key of the <term>Mysterium Magnum</term>, as far as a creature is able to comprehend or bear, and we refer you there for further explanation; and so I commend myself to you, in the brotherly love in Christ.

## (V.)—THE TREATISE OF THE INCARNATION. IN THREE PARTS.

**Part I.**—Of the Mystery of the Becoming Man or Incarnation of Jesus Christ the Son of God; that is, concerning the Virgin Mary, what she was from her origin, and what kind of Mother she became in the Conception of her Son Jesus Christ; and how the Eternal Word has become Man.
**Part II.**—Of Christ's Suffering, Dying, Death, and Resurrection: why He had to die, and how we must enter into Christ's Suffering, Dying, and Death, and arise with and through Him out of His death, and become conformed to His image, and live eternally in Him. Fully brought forth, enlarged, and confirmed out of the Center of all Things, through the Three Principles, very deeply.
**Part III.**—Of the Tree of the Christian Faith: A true instruction on how man may be one spirit with God, and what he must do so that he may work the works of God; wherein the whole Christian doctrine and faith is briefly summarized; also what faith and doctrine are.—An Open Gate to the great secret Arcanum of God, out of the Divine <term>Magia</term>, through the Three Principles of the Divine Essence.

# THE PREFACE to the Great Six Points is as follows:—

1.—We have written this work, not for the irrational beasts, who have the outward form of a man but in their image and spirit are evil and wild beasts, which reveals itself in their character or conditions.

2.—But for the image of man—for those who grow or spring forth out of the bestial image with a human image that belongs to God’s kingdom; who would gladly live and grow in the human image, in the right, true man.

3.—Who are many times and often hindered by the opposing, contrary life, and so remain stuck in the mixed life, panting after the birth of the holy life: for those, these writings are written.

4.—And we advise them not to consider it impossible to understand and know such secret, hidden *arcana*; and we offer this for them to consider and conceive of in a simile.

5.—For instance: there stood a life that had sprouted out of every life and was mixed; but another life grew within that one, out of every life, which—though it grew out of every life—was yet free from every other life, and yet also stood in all the essences of life <note>in all properties or qualities of the life</note>.

6.—And that other new life became enlightened with the light, and that only in itself, so that it could see every other life; yet the other lives could not behold or understand the new life.

7.—It is just so with everyone who, out of the mixed life of evil and good, is born again in and out of God; that very new image born or generated in the life of God beholds every natural life, and nothing is strange or hard to it, for it beholds only its root, out of which it has sprouted or grown.

8.—As we may understand by observing how a beautiful flower or blossom grows out of the wild earth; it is not like the earth, yet with its beautiful beauty it declares the ability or potential of the earth, and how it is mixed with good and evil.

9.—Thus also is every man who is born or generated out of the wild condition and property, back into the right image of God.

10.—For those now who are sprouting and pushing forth toward the **BEAUTIFUL LILY** in the kingdom of God, and who stand in the birth, this book is written, so that they might strengthen their essences in it, and spring or sprout in the life of God, and grow and bear fruit in the tree of Paradise.

11.—And seeing that all the children of God grow in this tree, and every one of them is a branch in that tree, we would therefore have our sap, scent, flavor, and essences imparted to our fellow-branches and sprouts in our tree in which we all stand, and out of which we all sprout and grow, so that our tree of Paradise might be great, and we may rejoice with one another.

12.—And so that one sprout and branch may continually help to cover or shelter the other from the storm, we give this to all the children of this sprout in this tree to ponder kindly; and we commit and commend ourselves to their love and growth.

The Preface to the other Six Points is as follows:—The highly precious knowledge of this book is not attained unless the soul has once overcome in the storm and beaten down the devil, and so has attained the victorious garland or crown of triumph, which the most blessed Virgin chastity sets upon it as a badge of victory and a token that it has overcome in its dear champion Christ; then this wonderful knowledge rises up, yet not with perfection.

# (VII.)—Of the **EARTHLY** and **HEAVENLY MYSTERY**; a **BRIEF SUMMARY**, showing how they stand in one another, and how the Heavenly becomes manifested in the Earthly. **IN NINE SECTIONS.** Wherein is shown what the Turba of all substances is.

Section I.—Of the Eternal Beginning, or Seeking of the Abyss. <note>Of the Origin of all things, which is incomprehensible and without name, described according to the negative terms of Nothing and All, or Abyssal Nothing.</note>

—— III.—Of the Eternal Band. <note>The Seeking in the Will.</note>

—— VIII.—Of the Two Magias or Two Sorts of Religions <note>that distinguish Christians, yes, Jews, Turks, Heathens, and all people: namely Babel, Antichrist, the Mystery of Iniquity, or "Self"; and "the Cross" of Christ, or Humility, Resignation, and Adherence to God, by the grace and power of the engrafted Word or Christ.</note>

### (IX.)—ON DIVINE CONTEMPLATION OR VISION: Briefly showing what the *Mysterium Magnum* is, and how All is from, through, and in God: also how God is so near all things and fills All, yet is comprehended by Nothing. IN TWO PARTS.

☛ This (unfinished) tract is admirably adapted, as it is indeed intended, to serve as an Introduction to the Science of <term>Theosophy</term>, in the Third Part of the GRAMMAR OF WISDOM, previously described.

THE CONTENTS of this treatise <note>on the Perception of Divine and Natural Things in the light of God</note> are as follows:

->FIRST PART.<-

Chapter I.—On Divine Contemplation; what God is, and how humanity shall know His Substance through His Revelation.—The Objections Answered here are these: (1.) Why it seems as if there were no God, and as if all things in the world happened by chance. (2.) Why God, who is Love itself, permits a will contrary to His own, through which creatures suffer such cruel pain and misery, instead of keeping all things in the harmony or balance of goodness. (3.) Why evil should be found alongside good; what its purpose and benefit are.

Chapter II.—On the Mind, Will, and Thoughts of Human Life, how they originate from the Will of God, and how it is an Object or Representation—namely, an Image of God—in which God wills, works, and dwells.—The Objections Answered here are: (1.) Why the mind in the mortal body can become super-cogitative—that is, be introduced into the Supersensual Divine Life and be filled with God.* (2.) How a person may prevent the desiring life from entering into earthly properties.
