* The master of the Grammar of Wisdom will not need, like the author of ****** to go groping about for the reasons and causes of things related therein. That work is a noble specimen of the egregious absurdity of a man devoid of faith—however excellent a condenser of facts and an historian he may be—attempting to write the life of a man of faith and to philosophize upon its incidents. Another proof of the vanity and, moreover, the malice of that author is his insinuation regarding Law. Finding in the course of his research connected with the biography with what force of truth and just sarcasm Law, in his masterly writings, treats the unmanly, contemptible occupations of mere storytelling, sing-song literature, he took the opportunity in his book to cast a stigma upon Law and his writings. He did this not only by joining in the mawkish regrets of a few shallow religionists that a man of Law’s piety and resplendent talents should, “in his later days, have so degenerated into mysticism and the errors (as they call them) of J. B.,” but by slyly insinuating, with an affected air of candor and pity, that he (L.) “who had been the means of turning so many heads, at last sacrificed his own intellect to the mad reveries of J. B.” But what was the end? For all is well that ends well, and all is ill that ends ill. One—the devoted servant and instrument of God, after a life of seventy-five years spent in a continual acquisition of wisdom and piety and in the boundless diffusion of temporal and spiritual benefits to his fellow creatures, and whose intellect seemed to become only more divinely bright and luminous as he approached the heavenly City (his “Tract upon Warburton” being written after he was seventy years old, and his “Address to the Clergy” only a few days before his death)—died as he lived, in the triumph of faith. These were some of his last words: “Away with these polluted garments,” said the dying seraph, “I feel a sacred fire kindled in my soul which has destroyed everything contrary to itself, and shall burn as a flame of divine love to all eternity!” And now, how did it fare on the other side? According to the newspapers, the slanderer himself closed the last years of his life in drivelling idiocy.

<margin>irate</margin>Further, on glancing back over the last fifteen or sixteen pages, and then forward over the same number, may it not be asked here: what but a self-willed, audacious fool or an envious, sophistical knave would dare to reproach the above series of writings as void of sense and light, and publicly revile the author as a madman? They did the same of old to Him who spoke as never man spoke [John 10:20-21], and who, in and through the author of the above works, wrote as man never before wrote. The very sacredness and depth of the subjects considered therein, the systematic manner in which they appear to be treated, the extraordinary common sense and piety sparkling and shining through every line of the prefaces, and the unearthly, seemingly miraculous character of the whole—yet all simply tending to promote the love and knowledge of God and the diffusion of Divine benevolence among mankind—far from provoking the jeers of the conceited and earthly-wise, ought rather to have the same imposing effect upon the mind as the first sight of the author’s books had upon Law, when in the full, fresh bloom of his intellectual powers. This is described by one of his friends thus: “In an intimate interview I had with Mr. Law, a few months before his death (with which I was favored at my particular request), I asked him when and how he first encountered Boehme’s works. He replied that he had often reflected upon it with surprise; that although when a tutor in London he had perhaps rummaged every bookseller’s shop and bookstall in the metropolis [doubtless feeling the need for a much higher philosophical and theological science than even he had yet attained—the true science of God, nature, and all things], yet he had never met with a single book, or even known the title of any book by J. B. The first notice he had of him was from a treatise called ‘Fides et Ratio,’ published at Amsterdam in 1707; soon after which he accidentally obtained one of his best works [the ‘Signatura Rerum’?]. ‘When I first began to read him,’ he said, ‘he put me into a perfect sweat. But as I discerned sound truths and the glimmerings of a deep foundation and sense, even in the passages not then clearly intelligible to me, and found in myself a strong incentive to dig into these writings, I followed the impulse with continual aspirations and prayer to God for his help and divine illumination, if indeed I was called to understand them. By patiently reading in this manner again and again, and from time to time passing over any minor objections and difficulties that stood in my way for the moment, I perceived,’ he said, ‘that my heart felt well, and my understanding kept gradually opening; until at length I discovered the wonderful treasure hidden in this field.’” Such indeed is the way in which all rightly constituted minds receive and examine such writings, <insert>though not according to the frivolous literary method of the juvenile author of ‘Hours with the Mystics’.</insert>

☞ The reader must not be offended, during the perusal of this account of the author’s works, at the seeming tautology, or constant repetition of one and the same unchangeable ground, in his several treatises. For the author (more especially at the commencement of his high illumination), being a poor illiterate man and having no knowledge of regularity in composition, wrote without art, except as a faithful recorder of what he saw and conceived in the *Divine light*. When, therefore, he entered upon the explanation of any particular subject, he always began afresh from the same first ground and full opening of the mystery of nature. But when it is considered that, on such occasions, he never expresses himself in the same terms, but always presents his wonderful subject in a new aspect, and moreover, that he had no idea of his works ever being collected together and published as they are now, but supposed each of them would exist in a separate and independent form in manuscript as a complete treatise of itself—it will appear not only consistent with, but a further instance of the care and condescension of the Divine goodness, that he should have set forth his very sublime knowledge in so simple and childlike a manner, whereby his readers might the more easily come to understand his deep sense and meaning.

16.—But look with me once more at these seeds, and *flowers*, and *fruits*: their ancestors are older than ours by three days. And if the church is one with the Lord, in spirit and in truth; if our life is hidden with Christ in God, what wonder that the expectation of the creation is toward the manifestation of the sons of God? 17.—I believe that Divine powers act, in the present universe, by means of material resistances, which serve as bases, instruments, and coverings of one ineffably and inconceivably glorious Unity, to whose eye all things are ever naked and open.

18.—Philosophers and observers are beginning to be persuaded (I allude chiefly to Dr. Faraday’s researches) that among “the various powers of nature, or physical forces, as they are termed, although producing different classes of results on matter, there exists a close relation:” in fact, they are connected by a common origin, have a reciprocal dependence on one another, and are capable, under certain conditions, of being converted into one another. Electricity is a source of magnetism—magnetism, combined with motion, yields electricity. There exists a relation between these powers and light: and now it is discovered that a ray of light may be magnetized and electrified, and that lines of magnetic force may be rendered luminous. “Motion, chemical affinity, heat, light, electricity, are convertible states of matter,” says Professor Grove.

What wonder is it that these natural mysteries should gradually discover themselves, if all that we call matter has only one origin, and that origin higher than its present state? If matter is only a system of degraded powers, tending to permanent equilibrium, but failing—at one time by excess and another by defect—wherever life is, light cannot be far off.

Light, life, and motion surely tell of Eternity. And we cannot help but begin to entertain the idea that all belonging to time and sense is only a coarse veil, spread between us and eternal beauties, which are ever near, and every now and then sparkle through the coarse covering, impatient for the hour when the hand that wove the temporary veil shall tear it again and show clearly the hidden glory.

<margin>d</margin> 19.—In one closing word: the present creation seems to be only a parenthesis—*a mere parenthesis*. Now, all that is parenthetical finds its full meaning in the context—in that which went before and in that which follows after it. A parenthesis is not without real sense, but it does not have enough sense to stand alone. It is enclosed between the past and the future: we must look to the left and also to the right if we would understand.

Hence it is that angels above, saints below, and “they that shall be,” have only one common hymn and song:—

> “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and is, and is to come! You have created all things, and for Your pleasure they were and are created: heaven and earth are full of Your glory: glory be to You, O Lord, Most High.”

20.—I believe Christ Jesus, the Lord, to be the full, living image, house, form, and glory of God.

I believe the universal church of faithful people to be the body of the Lord.

I believe the creation to be an appendage of the Church.

I believe that the Lord will be seen, glorified, in the Father.

I believe that the church will be seen, glorified, in the Lord.

I believe that all that now ministers to mortality will be swallowed up by life.

In this faith I desire to be active and engaged until the Lord shall come, and bring with Him the kingdom, the power, and the glory, which shall finally establish everywhere the supremacy of God. (1 Corinthians 15.)

## (XIII.)—An APOLOGY CONCERNING PERFECTION: Being a REFUTATION of certain erroneous explanations by E. S. of the following four texts of Scripture; and showing what outward and inward perfection is attainable in this life.

—— IV.—As the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things <note>out</note> of God.—1 Corinthians 11:12.

### THE PREFACE is as follows —

> Courteous Reader, who loves truth! There has lately come into my hands a treatise, sent from good friends who have entreated me to give my exposition of the four texts of Scripture claimed to be explained there. And seeing there are in that treatise some erroneous opinions that run contrary to the Holy Scriptures and which are of great concern to the reader, I am willing to undertake the task and express the meaning according to a right understanding.
> Not that I would judge any man, but for the sake of those who with earnestness seek the pearl of divine knowledge, I would clear up the understanding of those various points, so that the hungering mind may be brought into satisfaction and rest; and so may have occasion to seek with greater earnestness the refreshment of this pearl until we can attain the perfect enjoyment of it in the next life after this tabernacle. <note>2 Corinthians 5:1</note>
> I will therefore set down the true ground of these doctrines and leave it for the consideration of the lovers of divine knowledge.

☛ The chief hindrance that has kept good men from deciding theological differences has been their confining themselves to such a train of thought as has withdrawn their attention from those texts which are most material and necessary to be considered, concerning the WORD which is Christ and God: as it is written—

> *In the Beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; all things were made by it, and without it was nothing made that was made; in it was life, and the life was the light of men; also the light shines in the darkness, though the darkness does not comprehend the light; this is the true light which enlightens every man coming into the world; it was in the world, and the world was made by it.*

These texts are seldom emphasized or considered, but those arguments that can be collected concerning the written word of God (the holy Scriptures) and what they call the word preached in pulpits are urged so much that people are ready to understand the texts concerning the substantial Word of God—the Word of His power, the Word of prophecy, the Word in our hearts, also the creating Word, the Word of wisdom, the Word of life—as meaning the Scriptures only. And men are so violent as to account him heretical who shall venture to question their opinion in his mind: thus, the true understanding partly comes to be veiled from people's eyes.

Some of the learned, also, are very unwilling to take so much trouble as to read and consider what is offered to them in this author, though some sincere lovers of good literature have, by reading him, found that which is more excellent than that upon which they and others had spent their time for a long time together. But they account themselves filled so full with their present wisdom and knowledge that they have no room to desire any other, especially that which cannot be attained without casting away the high esteem of that which they have laid up as a treasure to themselves already; and so every little difficulty of uncouth words or phrases and expressions, which they cannot immediately see to agree with their former opinions, makes them loath to be troubled about that which they think themselves to have more and better knowledge of beforehand. Neither can they in reason be blamed, except that they block up their own way to inestimable treasures which they do not know of, and others not so learned attain; yet which they might have in much greater abundance if they would not suffer their learning to hinder them, which itself would much more further them therein.

Another bar the learned have is this: that they will not allow reasoning and proving by similitudes <note>analogies or metaphors</note>, because such are not demonstrative logical proofs according to the requirements of that art. But he that was more than Solomon, our Savior himself, chose to teach the highest and most precious wisdom through similitudes, hidden under such teaching. And if the writings of the holy prophets and apostles be examined, it will appear that there is not the least thing done in this world but does, by way of similitude, signify and teach to us something of the most transcendent and richest mysteries of eternity. All visions which were the clearest revelations were represented in something or other, in part or in the whole, like that which is in this outward world; though the *thing representing* is but a shadow in respect to the inward substance that is resembled by it—as for instance Christ and faith is a *substance*, and a *rock* is but a *shadow*; and the Holy Spirit, the Word, and God, and the Divine Nature is much more a substance, while the things in this world resembling them are scarcely so much as an exact shadow of them. So also the sun of righteousness, the city of God, the trees in the paradise of God, the fallow ground of our hearts, the grain of mustard seed which the kingdom of heaven is represented by and likened to; a steward, a husbandman, a door, a vine, a sheepfold, a candle set upon a table or put under a bushel, a seething pot with the scum rising up, a rose, a lily, briers, thistles, and thorns, the seven stars, the dragon, the woman, the candlesticks, the temple, the moon, rivers, fountains, fire, brimstone, etc.—every one of these denotes to us some mystery or other in the spiritual world, as will in time to come be manifested; which we could know nothing of, except by way of similitude, but it is the Spirit alone that teaches the mystery by and from them. Neither can we apprehend the demonstration of that which we never saw, except by similitude in those things which the outward man has seen or conceived; for our minds are opened, as the understanding of a child is in learning, and we must be as children to all our great knowledge before, or else we cannot be taught any new thing that is beyond our former reach, apprehension, or capacity. But when the similitude is declared and weighed, the knowledge of the thing itself will be easier, and then the demonstration of it may be briefly and exactly made by those who are teachers in Christ’s school, to scholars exercised in some degree in such spiritual matters: otherwise, that saying of our Savior may well be applied to them, *if you do not believe when I tell you earthly things, how shall you believe if I tell you heavenly matters*.

This may be a just plea for this author’s teaching the mysteries of eternity by examples and similitudes of natural earthly things. And in them he lays open his ground of interpreting the holy Scriptures, by which men try the deepest questions and controversies in religion, so that the seeming differences therein may be cleared and composed; that all may understand them rightly—all Christians, Jews, and Heathens—and so prize them as they ought. And in the following preface to this treatise, he sets down to this effect: that the supposition that God is only far off in a heaven above and beyond the stars and firmament exclusively, and not in everything and everywhere present as to himself substantially and totally, with all that he is in essence in the Unity of the Deity and Trinity of Manifestation in his whole kingdom, power, and glory (though as to the creature not discernible or perceptible, but by his Word revealing himself in and to the creature according to its kind), is the only cause why men cannot satisfy themselves in that great secret <term>arcanum</term> of predestination and other high and necessary mysteries mentioned in the Old and New Testament.

The Heathens would esteem the Scripture if it were but hinted to them how they might consider that that which is mentioned and contained therein (and of which it chiefly is appointed to testify) is the same with that which is in their very hearts; they would rejoice to hear the lively demonstration and effects of that God and his graces, which lie as a deep fountain and well-spring hidden in their own souls; and so they would soon taste the eternal gos—

The Jews, also, cannot be fully persuaded that Jesus Christ, whose name is Immanuel, is and was the true Messiah. Although they shall certainly be converted, as we Christians believe and long to see accomplished, yet they cannot perceive the truth except by understanding how the promised seed was put into, or caused to sprout forth in the soul of Adam and Eve by God after they ate the forbidden fruit. In this way, it became salvation to all men, continually taking effect in those who become the offspring of that seed by forsaking their sins and being obedient to that seed of God—the Word of life, the Word of promise, which is the Word of grace, the Word of God, the Commandment, his Law, his testimonies, his ways, statutes, precepts, and judgments, which are so strongly emphasized in Moses and in the Psalms of David; all of which was Christ in them. Regarding *that* seed in the line of the covenant according to the manifestation in the flesh, Christ Jesus—their Messiah and our Savior—came and took our nature, being born of Mary, and finished our redemption in a human soul like all of ours (which is why he condescends so low as to call us his brothers, though in him dwelt the fullness of the Godhead bodily), and so he worked and perfected our salvation. All should be partakers of the divine nature in him, being born again and growing up in him—that is, in his grace and covenant in their souls—so that he rules in them to subdue the seed of the serpent and the lusts of the flesh in anyone at all. And this is that light that enlightens every man—even every Heathen, Jew, and Christian—at the instant the soul takes life in the womb, thus coming into the fleshly substance of the elementary body of this world.

The Word of the Lord does not contradict itself, neither in its operation in the works of the outward world, nor in the inward teachings of the Holy Spirit in the soul, nor in the written Word of the holy Scriptures,* which were written as holy men spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. This Spirit teaches, and can teach, nothing other than what the holy Word speaks, from which the Spirit proceeds. Therefore, the essential Word is to be considered in every respect before men are able to decide a <unclear>deep</unclear> controversy, question, or doubt in any matter fundamentally. And we see that God's ordinance in the outward world, which we call Providence, does by nature appoint what profession and condition of life everyone shall have; and accordingly, Caiaphas was high priest that year in which Christ was crucified, even though he was inwardly a conspirator against Christ. So also was Judas appointed to be one of the apostles, though inwardly he was a devil; so King Saul was among the prophets, and so also there are many false apostles gone into the world, and many false Christs; but the true ones are what they are in spirit and truth in the inward hidden man of the heart. Therefore, everyone should labor to be that in spirit, mind, soul, and affection in his honest outward calling or office, whether low or high, which is right in the sight of God according to His Word and ordinance, to which he is outwardly called. He should not, under the pretense of an outward calling, think he is such a person without the Spirit, nor should he despise those who are such in spirit, even if they have no outward calling at all. For most of the eminent prophets—and likewise the apostles, disciples, evangelists, elders, bishops, overseers, or pastors, doctors, or teachers—have not been called from the schools of the prophets, nor from among the learned or noble, though some of them have been; and those were called by God as were Moses, Aaron, David, Peter, Paul, Timothy, Barnabas, etc.

And so were all those called who were the first authors and writers of the books of the Old (and New) Testament, although there may be reason to think that the greatest part of it was afterwards delivered to Esdras and his scribes by the angel of God, when it is considered that the most ancient manuscript copy of that Hebrew Bible which is now extant in print was that which the Jews received from Esdras (or Ezra) at the return from the Babylonian captivity. [See Dr. F. Lee's "Dissertation."] For the whole book is consistently written in the Caldee letter, even though there is a difference in the style of several of the books, which the angel knew well how to express to a tittle. And certainly, if Esdras and the rest with him had possessed the originals to transcribe them from, they would not have burnt or buried those hand-writings of the authors. And although the Samaritan Pentateuch is supposed to be the script in which the five books of Moses were written, yet it cannot be the same in content and words, because it differs in several places from the true Hebrew text, and in some places it agrees with the Septuagint Greek translation and not with the Hebrew itself—which was the language Moses was supposed to write in, using the same script as the Samaritan Pentateuch. This is indicated in an introduction to the various languages of the best and most exact edition of the Bible that was ever published in the world, which was produced about two hundred years ago by the labor of the most learned men, knowledgeable in Oriental languages and most versed in the literal text of the Bible. In this edition, it appears that the same person whom the Hebrew calls Ezra, author of one of the books undoubtedly in the canon of the Bible, is translated in the Greek Septuagint as Esdras. The book of Ezra in our English Bibles is accounted the first book of Ezra or Esdras, and the book of Nehemiah the second book of Ezra or Esdras; so the Greek copy of the first and second book of Esdras in our Bibles may rightly be accounted his third and fourth book, as it is in Luther's translation in the German language. And thus, as the law was ordained by angels in the hands of a mediator, who was Moses, so when it was lost, it was restored to Esdras again by the same means [II Esdras, xiv., from 20th verse]. This advances the excellence of the Old Testament beyond any other books before Christ's time for their manner of delivery, in addition to the spirit of prophecy that filled both the first and last authors of the whole book, as is made manifest by a few of the matters spoken and written by them, which have been transmitted to us for our learning by the infinite mercy and goodness of God.

For we may observe how the inward substantial seed of the promise, the seed of God, was hidden and suppressed in the offspring of Adam and Eve, except only in the line of the covenant passing through the loins of many sinful parents, even to Mary, the mother of the Messiah, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was the Son of Adam, who was also the Son

<meta>This page continues the history of divine revelation, tracing how the "Word of life" was maintained from the time of the patriarchs and Moses through the era of Christ and the apostles, eventually leading to the spiritual rediscoveries of the Reformation.</meta>

of God. But the seed continued under the evil life and conduct of the old world before the flood, though they had the preaching of Adam himself, and Abel, Seth, Enoch, Noah, and others. And after the deluge they were more depraved, though under the preaching of Noah, Shem, Eber, etc., until Abraham, to whom God sealed his covenant of promise with circumcision, for a stronger teaching to the outward man, observed by Isaac, Jacob, and his sons the twelve patriarchs, until Moses, who was raised up by God and received a further external clear teaching in the institution of the Passover, as another seal of the covenant; also giving the law of the Ten Commandments, which the outward man had so darkened in the inward heart of almost everyone, with very few exceptions; also the law of sacrifices and other ceremonies, with the judicial law for government of God’s own people; and this dispensation remained all along among a wicked and stubborn generation in the world under the evangelical teachings of the prophets, until Christ himself. Under whose outward teaching, while he was upon the earth, men were so very wicked, that according to his own parable, when the lord sent his son to the vine-dressers, thinking they would have reverenced him, they said, *this is the heir, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours*; and so they did kill him, and cast him out of the vineyard. At this time, (as necessity required) to help the outward man so that the inward Word might grow in him, greater teaching was provided than in the time of Moses or Solomon, he being then incarnate—namely, by the ministry of John the Baptist sealing his covenant by the baptism of water, and a little before Christ’s death by his eating the Passover with his disciples, thus instituting his Last Supper: and yet the apostles could not understand or remember what he told them, nor bear what he would have taught them before his death, not until the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, was sent after his ascension and glorification, who would bring to their remembrance whatever he had told them. And then this great manifestation of the power of God did so spring and spread that many were converted by it who were not prevailed upon by the former teaching; and it reached to Saul, who was also called Paul, and made an apostle of the highest mysteries to the Gentiles, all of which were brought to his knowledge by the Holy Spirit, for he had never heard Christ’s teaching as the other apostles had. And by his preaching, (from a philosophical knowledge of truth), the Gentiles became Christians; but in the following age, the wickedness of Christians was like that of the Jews before, which had caused the Ark of the Testimony, the book of the Law, their temple, city, and country, and every excellent thing they had to be taken away or destroyed; and so these Christians caused the powerful effects of the Holy Spirit to be withdrawn after the death of the first preachers and faithful brothers, until at length thick darkness spread itself over all nations, and there was only left some of the holy men’s writings contained in the Old, and some in the New Testament, which were brought forth to light and put together in a book, or as it is called **THE BIBLE**. The understanding of those writings was small in the following ages, except in those who suffered martyrdom, who declared the power of it by mighty wonders; and though afterward much teaching successively began to spring up, yet the Holy Scriptures were not so closely examined and publicly divulged until Luther, who was helped forward by a little book called *Theologia Germanica*, and the sermons and works of *Taulerus*, compiled in the obscure times before him and printed in the Latin tongue.

About that period Calvin and many others arose, each in his own way searching even more into the letter of the Scripture, whereby various questions were raised in divinity which have not been fully decided and resolved to the satisfaction of the various differing parties by the efforts of all who have labored in scholastic learning to this very day—nor indeed could they be, without the knowledge of the basis of the truth. Yet of all the deep obscure mysteries expounded by this author, <note>concerning the internal dwelling and existence of the one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all, and in all; filling all things in such a way as there is but one air which is the same breath of all living creatures; who is the unknown God whom the heathens ignorantly worshipped, and many Christians, as they call themselves, in these days, who know Him not to be within them, notwithstanding all his preaching by his Word in their hearts, and their reading of the Scripture, and the outward preaching from the written Word; the reason for which is that his indwelling is not so pointedly, strenuously, and frequently pressed in our public preachings as it ought to be:</note>—this of predestination is generally considered the most mysterious, though there are some who, to the great comfort of their souls, have had most mysteries cleared to them in this author, and this among the rest in the treatise under review; which raises a hope in them that the time is at hand wherein all the mysteries of God shall be manifested.

Now, though the Light is in all of our darkest hearts and souls and shines therein, yet if we pay no attention and do not turn toward it, we cannot grasp the light—or rather shall not be grasped by it—nor will the day dawn, neither shall we have any morning in us, as the Hebrew text in Isaiah <note>8:20</note> expresses it; and then we cannot speak according to that Word which is the law and testimony—not that which is written with ink, which does not endure forever, but the real substance of it on the fleshy tables of our hearts, written by the finger of God when he created the soul at the first beginning of life in the womb. <note>Well, therefore, may one, a reader of this author, say of him, that he lays down in everything a kind of celestial divinity; and it is that which endures forever.</note>

He who attends to this Innate Word of life will soon have a clear understanding of the Scriptures, and not only so, but at length attain what those who spoke and wrote them knew; and more than that, for as the time of the world proceeds further toward its limit, that shall be understood of the eternal Word which neither the angels, nor prophets, nor apostles knew—who saw what the angels desired to look into and were not able. For the Word of God is the furthest that can ever possibly be known. ### The Author’s Preface to this Book “Of the Election of Grace,” is as follows:

1.—When reason hears anything said concerning God, indicating what he is according to his being, essence, substance, and will, it imagines that God is some strange thing far away, dwelling outside and beyond the place of this world, high above the stars, and governing only by his spirit with an omnipotent power in the place of this world.
2.—But it supposes that his majesty in the Trinity, where God is especially manifest, dwells in heaven, outside and beyond the place of this world.
3.—And thereupon reason falls into a creaturely opinion, as if God were some strange thing, and as if he did—before the time of the creation of creatures and of this world—hold a consultation within himself in his trinity, by his wisdom, to contrive what he would make, and to what end everything should serve, and so has framed a predestined purpose in himself, what he would ordain everything to be.
4.—From this the contentious opinion has arisen concerning God’s determination regarding man, as if God had in his purpose or predestination chosen one part of men for heaven, to be in his holy habitation, and appointed the other part to eternal damnation, in whom he will manifest his wrath; and that, conversely, in the others who are his chosen and elect, he will manifest his grace.
5.—And so it is thought he has, in his predestination, made a separation so that he might show his power both in love and anger; and therefore everything must of necessity be as it is.
6.—That part ordained to wrath, it is conceived, are so reprobated and hardened by God’s purpose and predestination that there is no possibility left for them to attain the salvation of God; and on the contrary, in the others, there is no possibility of damnation.
7.—And though Holy Scripture speaks almost the very same words, to which creaturely reason agrees—which does not understand at all what God is—yet Scripture, on the other hand, speaks much more to the contrary: that God wills no evil, nor has he purposely by way of predestination made anything that is evil.
8.—Both these contradictions, and how each of them is to be understood in its own ground, we will give to impartial Christian readers—the seekers and lovers of the ground and of the truth—to unite and reconcile them, and establish the true understanding. I say we will give them a short explanation to consider, and present our gift or talents (as it is apprehended and laid hold of in the grace of the highest good) for them to examine with a good intention.
9.—Not meaning thereby to contend against or despise anyone for their conceived opinion, but for a Christian and brotherly joining and uniting of the gifts we have, bestowed upon any of us from divine grace.
10.—The branches and twigs of a tree do not appear identical in form, and yet they stand in one and the same trunk; one gives and introduces entity and virtue into the other, and all flourish and rejoice, blossom and bear fruit in one trunk, without any resentment or dislike of their strength and differences; but each branch labors to bring forth its fruit and harvest.
11.—So it may also well be with our unlike, differing gifts, if we direct our desire into the right, true mother as into our trunk, and each branch of the tree affords the other its virtue in goodwill.
12.—We must not bring ourselves into selfishness and into our own lust of self-love, going forth in pride, wanting to be above our mother in whom we stand and above all her children, and to be a tree of our own.
13.—Neither are we to receive into us the devil’s poison and venom or infection of self, and false or wicked magnetic impressions, from which strife and opposition, as well as rifts, schisms, and divisions arise, so that one twig of the human tree tears and separates itself from the others, does not provide them its ens or being and virtue, and exclaims against them as schismatical, sectarian, apostate, false, and wicked.
14.—It sets itself, and is known as a broken, separated twig before its brother in a false luster or show, from which the multitude of contentions among men have risen.
15.—Of all which we will signify what the origin of contention is, and from where opinions and divisions naturally arise; we will also signify what the true ground of the only religion is.
16.—And we will show from where the opposition from the beginning of the world to this time has proceeded, for the better understanding of the divine will, both according to love and anger, and how it is all fundamentally to be understood.
17.—And we admonish the loving reader to immerse himself in divine humility into God and his fellow branch or brother; and so he may read and understand our received deep sense and apprehension, and be brought from all error into the true rest, where all things rest in the Word and power of God. And we commend him into the working love in the <term>ens</term> or being of Christ, and our well-intended will and desire into his. AMEN.

This treatise also reconciles the differences of opinion about transubstantiation, consubstantiation, and the participation of mere bread and wine; it shows how to understand the right participation of the real flesh and blood of Christ under bread and wine. And since there is a real participation to be had of the flesh and blood of Christ without bread and wine, it shows why the bread and wine were so instituted to be celebrated and communicated. Likewise, seeing that the baptism of the Holy Spirit has often occurred without water, it explains why the baptism of water is necessary to be used, even for those who had previously received the Holy Spirit, as the apostles did.

When all this is understood, it will also appear what the foundation of the preaching of the Word of God is, as it is an ordinance of God; and we shall truly perceive what the essence of all ordinances is (which, in the meaning of the word, is nothing more than a thing ordained or appointed). Thus, it will be easy to perceive how far Christians fall short of rightly valuing the true ordinances, and how eager they are to take for an ordinance that which is not indeed the ordinance of God. * * * But, indeed, we must know God before we can know His ordinances; and to know Him, we must seek Him. ### The Author’s INTRODUCTION is as follows: —

1. All strife and misunderstanding concerning Christ's person, office, and being or substance, as also concerning the testaments he left behind him, in which he works presently, arises from defective creaturely reason. This reason runs only on image-like opinions and does not reach the foundation of this mystery, yet it wants to be a mistress of all things or beings and judge all things; it only loses itself in such image-likeness, breaks itself off from its center, disperses its thoughts, and runs into multiplicity, whereby its foundation is confused, the mind is disquieted, and it does not know itself.

2. No life can stand in certainty unless it remains in its center, from which it has sprung.

3. Since the soul is sprung from God's Word and will, yet has entered into its own lust and desire to will for itself, it cannot reach its first foundation from which it sprung through such searching of self-will. Consequently, it runs outside of its foundation in mere uncertainty until it returns to its origin again.
<note>Otherwise expressed:
(*a.*) In their confusion and running out into multiplicity, the thoughts break themselves off from their chaos, namely from the eternal Word of God and from the eternal Divine speaking. In this spoken Word, all beings—along with understanding, reason, and thoughts—exist and take their foundation and beginning from it.
(*b.*) For if the abyssal, non-natural, uncreaturely God—the eternal ONE—no longer spoke His Word, and that Speaking should cease, there would be no more understanding, reason, or thoughts, nor any Nature or Creature; all beings would be an eternal Nothing. For every life arises from the breathing out of the eternal ONE, namely from the Abyss; and there could be no formability in the eternal ONE, according to which or out of which something might be made.
(*c.*) For if there is a formability to a figure, then there must also have been a cause from which the form arose, and God would not be the ONE Only God, who is without foundation, time, or place; for everything that has a beginning has a foundation. But that which has no beginning is without foundation and form.</note>

4. Every beginning goes out of the eternal ONE—the tri-unity of God—through the breathing out or speaking of the UNITY of God. As a fountain flows from its source, through which flowing forth, the unity brings itself into self-viewing, findingness, and perceptibility, to form and image itself. Every visible and invisible being, both spiritual and corporeal, has taken its origin in the breathing out of the Divine power and is a reflection of the separable will of God, standing with its foundation therein. For the beginning of every being is nothing else but an imagination of the out-flown will of God, which has brought itself into separability, form, and image-likeness; wherein lies the whole creation: and every life consists in its re-breathing and reflection in the same manner.

5. Since human life is an out-flowing and reflection of Divine power, understanding, and skill, it ought to remain in its origin; otherwise, it loses divine knowledge, power, and skill. Through self-speculation, it brings itself into centers of its own and strange imaging, by which its origin becomes darkened and strange.

6. This is known by erroneous reason, which always teaches concerning God yet has no true understanding; it never comes to rest while it runs on in strange imaging.

7. Therefore I say that this is the only cause for why men dispute and strive about God—His word, essence or being, and will: the understanding of man has broken itself off from its origin and now runs on in mere self-will, thoughts, and images in its own lust for selfishness. It imagines for itself another foundation for the Divine willing, in which there is no true knowledge—nor can there be—until the life returns into its origin, namely, into the Divine out-flowing and will.

8. And if this is done, then God's will speaks forth the Divine power and wonders again through the human willing. In this Divine speaking, the life may know and comprehend God's will and frame itself within it. Then there is true divine knowledge and understanding in man's skill when his skill is continually renewed with divine power, and when divine skill presses forth through the life in the same manner as it flowed forth from the divine power and skill in the beginning.

9. As Christ has taught us when He says, "Unless you are converted and become like a child, you shall not enter the kingdom of God." That is, the life must turn itself back into God, from whom it proceeded, and forsake all its own imaging and lust; thus it comes to the divine vision again.

10. All strife about the Divine will and being or essence, by which men despise one another, comes from self-image-likeness: one man comprehends the image of another—namely, his thoughts—and yet cannot rightly understand them. Where one man places himself in the thought and mind of another, bringing what is his own into it and compelling the other's thoughts into his own meaning, he forcibly sets himself above the thoughts and mind of the other. He holds them as his own property and makes a show of them, using them to dominate the thoughts and minds of others; men must worship and reverence his thoughts and mind, holding them to be the Word of God or the speaking of God.

11. Thus man deludes himself and robs God of His honor; he takes God's covenant in his mouth and yet hates the guidance of the Spirit of God, which therefore reproves him in his conscience, showing that he is but an apostate Lucifer who would compel others into his image so they might hold it for the Word of God.

12. But a true man inclines himself to his origin and forsakes all images, desiring no self-imaging of his understanding except what God will frame and speak with and through him. He despises no one but only distinguishes the true from the false, the good from the evil, and teaches the truth with the divine, powerful out-flowing and will.

True understanding is only possible when the soul returns to its source in the eternal Word of God, forsaking its own selfish thoughts and images.</summary>

13.—All dispute concerning God’s being or essence and will is performed in the images of the senses or thoughts without God; for if anyone lives in God and wills with God, why would they need to dispute about God—who or what God is?

14.—But the fact that he disputes about it is a sign that he has never felt it at all in his mind or senses, and it has not been granted to him that God is in him and wills what he wills. It is a certain sign that he wants to exalt his own meaning and image above others, and that he desires dominion.

15.—People should confer together in a friendly way and offer one another their gifts and knowledge in love, testing things with one another and holding to that which is best (1 Thess. 5:21). They should friendly instruct one another and not stand so firmly in their own opinion as if they could not err, seeing as we have a mighty enemy against us who suddenly brings strange images into a person's thoughts and makes people behave arrogantly. This is where sects and schisms originate: namely, from SELFHOOD <note>though God makes the weakness as well as the wickedness of man to show forth His glory</note>.

16.—It lies in no specific person's status that people should suppose that divine understanding must come only from such and such a person; for the Scripture says, *Prove all things, and hold fast that which is good* (1 Thess. 5:21).

17.—The touchstone for this knowledge is, first, the cornerstone, Christ; one should see whether a thing proceeds out of love into love, or whether the love of God alone is purely sought and desired—whether it is done out of humility or pride. Secondly, is it according to the Holy Scripture of the Bible? Thirdly, is it according to the human heart and soul, in which the book of the life of God is incorporated and may very well be read by the children of God? There the true mind has its touchstone within itself and can distinguish all things. If the Holy Spirit dwells in the foundation of the mind, that person has a sufficient touchstone that will lead him into all truth.

18.—Christ’s testaments are a secret mystery and are offered to the minds and thoughts that have departed from and returned again to God. Where life brings itself to God again, the thoughts that return to God are first fed with Divine power and understanding. This afterwards kindles the life so that it hungers after God; to which is afterwards given Christ’s flesh and blood as a pledge and seal, and the Divine essence or substance will be imprinted therein. From this, the life is brought again into its origin: namely, into God’s power and Word.

19.—A false thought or mind in a person is nourished again by its own likeness—namely, from its own conjecture, from pride, or from the subtlety of the serpent. These it desires to exalt and put into an image, and that image is a branch on the tree of Satan.

20.—Now, the person who is fed by the Divine power and spirit in his mind and thoughts is divinely-minded and brings forth good things out of his good heart; but the person who is fed in his thoughts from the power and will of the flesh is only fleshly-minded.

21.—When reason considers Christ’s Testaments and thinks about how Christ can be present in his testaments, it thinks it is done in a literal, image-like manner. And when it knows that it is not done in an image-like manner, then it falls away from that entirely and thinks He is present only in remembrance. For example, when His word is preached, it thinks He works powerfully only in that way; and it thinks the same concerning his testaments—that Christ works only spiritually in faith, and that the testaments are only signs or symbols by which we should instruct ourselves in what He has done for us, only to declare His death and the shedding of His blood and to keep it in lively remembrance for our comfort.

22.—Thus reason understands nothing at all of the kingdom of Christ, much less of His person or His office. In that respect, men dispute and strive about it, wanting to attain it through the searching of reason. All this fails to reach the true understanding, for Christ’s testaments are heavenly, and reason is earthly and worldly. It seeks Christ in time <note>or that which is temporary</note>, and if it does not find Him there according to its power, then it supposes He is present only to the thoughts that cast themselves up to Him in heaven. But this will not renew the life or bring it back into God; it will not cause the new birth.

23.—All strife comes from this: that men do not understand the heaven in which Christ sits at the right hand of God—that He is in this world, and that the world stands in heaven, and heaven in the world, and they are in one another like day and night.

24.—The inward ground of the world, from which the four elements sprang, is heaven—namely, a spiritual world. In that inward power, Christ rules as true God and man through the outward world; for where Christ says (Matthew 28:18, 20), *all power is given to me in heaven and on earth*; also, *I am with you always till the end of the world*; also, *He shall rule over all his enemies till all his enemies are laid under him as a footstool* (1 Cor. 15:25; Psalm 110:1). This is to be understood as His inward kingdom, where He rules in inward power over the outward earthly world and also the hellish world.

25.—For the outward world sprang out of the inward spiritual world—namely, out of light and darkness. This structure, before the office of Christ, stood in the eternal Creator’s office, who from eternity has worked <note>or effected</note> light and darkness—namely, the spiritual world. This structure flowed forth and became visible, brought by God into a creation where light and darkness—namely, good and evil—rule together. In this, hell and pain are understood in the flowing forth of eternal darkness, and the light of nature in the flowing forth of the light. In that place where evil and good rule alike, the kingdom of nature is understood, with hot and cold and all other properties.

26.—God has given this dominion to the office of Christ so that He, being both true God and man, should rule over all the particular nature and self-willing of this kingdom, where evil and good rule within each other. Just as the sun in the visible world rules over evil and good, and with its light and power—and everything that it is—is present everywhere and penetrates into every being, yet in its image-like form does not snatch things away to itself with its outflow, but wholly gives itself into every being while remaining whole, with nothing of its being departing; so also it is to be understood concerning Christ’s person and office. He rules in the inward spiritual world visibly and in the outward world invisibly, and thoroughly penetrates the faithful person's soul, spirit, and heart. And as fire glows through iron, and as the sun works through and through a plant so that the plant becomes solar <note>or filled with the virtue of the sun, and, as it were, so converted by the sun that it becomes wholly of the nature of the sun</note>, so

For all natural knowledge is outward in the world and arises from its <term>astrum</term>, and runs on in conjectures, doubting whether a thing is so or not; but the spirit of God gives assurance in the soul and spirit of his faithful, and witnesses in them that they are God's children, Rom. 8:16.

30.—Now, how this present essential participation is effected, and what the covenant of grace between God and man is (in both the Old and New Testaments), and what BAPTISM and THE SUPPER of Christ are, shall be declared in the following chapters.

31.—THIS FOUNDATION IS ONLY BROUGHT FORTH SO DEEPLY SO THAT ALL WHO STRIVE ABOUT IT MIGHT SEE THE TRUE INWARD FOUNDATION, CEASE FROM STRIFE, AND YIELD THEMSELVES TO THE SIMPLICITY AND LOVE OF JESUS CHRIST. By this, the power of Satan will suddenly be diminished, and all people and nations will see that Christians are the children of God, if they walk in love in this way.

> Though indeed I here dive and search loftily and deep, and set it down very clearly, yet the reader must be told this much: that without the Spirit of God it will be a mystery to him and not understood. Therefore let everyone look well to it regarding what he judges, so that he does not fall into the judgment of God and be captivated by his own <term>turba</term>, and that his own reason does not distract him. This I say, meaning well, and give it to the reader to ponder.

Chap. I.—Of the Foundation of the Old Testament; how this Testament was clearly in the Type among the Jews.
—— II.—Of the Supper of the New Testament: how the Type has become Essence or Substance.
—— III.—How the Disciples of Christ have eaten and drunk Christ's Flesh and Blood: and how that is properly to be understood.
—— IV.—Of the Difference in the Participation of it: what the Wicked receive by this Testament; and how a man should rightly prepare himself for it, so that he may be truly worthy.
—— V.—Of the Contention and Strife among the Learned about Christ's Testaments: how that Strife is a vain and very hurtful thing, and arises (no matter how plausibly it is covered) in the Anger of God, from the Devil's Desire and Will; whereby all brotherly Love and Unity is destroyed, the highly precious Name of God is Blasphemed, and the Holy Spirit in his Divine Wonders is Judged, and becomes despised by Reason.

(b.)—Of **TRUE REPENTANCE**: Showing how Man should stir up Himself in Mind and Will, and what his Consideration and Earnest Purpose should be.

This practical Treatise, with the following and preceding tracts, were the only writings of the author published during his lifetime, the rest of his works being handed about in manuscript only.

The Author's **PREFACE** is as follows:—

> Dear Reader, if you will use this book correctly, and are in good earnest, you shall certainly find the benefit of it. But I desire you may be warned, if you are not in earnest, not to meddle with the precious names of **GOD**, in and by which the most High Holiness is invoked, moved, and powerfully desired, lest they kindle the anger of God in your soul. For we must not abuse the holy names of **GOD**. This little book is only for those who would gladly repent, and have a desire to begin: Such will find what manner of words are in it, and from where they are born. You are herewith commended to the eternal goodness and mercy of God.

**THE CONTENTS** are these:—

Particular I.—How Man must Stir up himself in Mind and Will, and what his Consideration and Earnest Purpose must be, when he will perform powerful and Effectual Repentance; and with what Mind he must appear before God, when he would ask, so as to obtain Remission of Sins.
—— II.—The Process of Repentance, or Way to Conversion; showing what Course a Man shall take who finds in himself, by the former or any other Consideration with which his Mind and Conscience shall have been pierced, a Hunger or Desire to Repent, and yet feels no true sufficient Sorrow for his Sins.
—— III.—A Short Formula of Confession before the Face of God; in which is personified a poor Soul agonizing for Pardon, night and day Wrestling, Groaning, and Struggling into the Divine Liberty, or Principle of Light and Love. Every Seeker according to his Call and Necessity may order or enlarge this Confession as the Holy Ghost shall secretly teach him. What is here set down is only a short Direction.
—— IV.—Concerning what transpires in the Deep of such a Soul; and how many draw back and perish in such a Beginning, as young grafts broken off by the wind, or withered by the heat, for want of perseverance in that tremendous conflict with the powers of darkness. How the soul must never give up the battle, for it cannot be crowned, unless it both fights and overcomes in the storm.
—— V.—A Short Direction how the poor Soul must come before God again, and how it must wrestle on for the noble garland; what kind of weapons it must use, if it will go to combat against the wrath of God, against the devil, the world, and sin, against flesh and blood, against the influence of the stars and elements, and all its other enemies; and what earnestness is required in all this.
—— VI.—A Form of Prayer, showing in what manner the poor seeking soul must pray: though the Holy Spirit forms and frames the prayer for the soul in every heart that *intends to Conquer*.
—— VII.—A Little Direction for the Soul that has been earnest without intermission, how it must meet its Beloved when she knocks in its Center, or most inward shut chamber. ### (c.)—Of TEMPTATION, a TREATISE of the Four COMPLEXIONS : Wherein are provided Consolatory Instructions for a Sad and Assaulted Heart, in the time of Temptation: Showing, also, from where Sadness naturally arises, and how the Assaulting happens. The whole confirmed by several Pertinent and Comforting Texts.

**NOTE.**—This useful and instructive treatise of consolation in time of temptation, very properly follows the preceding tract, the Rudiments of Theosophy. For as the foundation of Christianity taught there is laid in so deep and earnest an exercise of repentance, as shakes the soul of the natural man to the very bottom, and by that concussion stirs up and brings to his view the foul dregs of corruption that have until now lain there undisturbed ever since he came to the years of reason; so the horror of this sight, together with the painful sense of guilt and misery consequent upon it, which the author calls the judgment of the soul or conscience, proves a very severe trial to the young soldier of Christ, at his first entrance upon the warfare. And in some instances it is a long as well as a sharp process; for it may continue for a man many years, as stated in the previous Book of Repentance, if he does not earnestly and speedily put on the armor of Christ. This is a very deplorable condition indeed: but in no subjects does it occur so predominantly as in souls surrounded with the melancholy <term>complexion</term> <note>The dominant temperament or constitutional disposition of a person</note>; especially if they have defiled themselves with much gross sin, or taken up erroneous conceits of their having been rejected by God, or of having out-sinned their day of grace.
This extremity of spiritual distress, of which none can know or conceive the poignant anguish and bitterness who have not in some degree felt the same, has here a friendly relief. Every information is communicated, every advice given, and every consolation administered, which the unhappy case can well require or admit, short of the immediate vital operation of the great Physician of Souls and only sufficient Comforter himself, to whose joyful entrance into the afflicted soul the way is here opened and cleared, by the removal of all these doubts and fears which arise from the soul's ignorance of its own true nature and essence, and of its necessary subjection during its stay in the body, to the influence of the astral powers and its natural complexion. This beneficial knowledge is in the following little tract fundamentally, though briefly, provided: and that from such a divine ground, and with such a satisfactory fullness of conviction, as to leave no doubt of either its truth or worth.

<margin>corrections</margin>
$\times$ * Note, relative to the existing uniform edition (in English) of BEHMEN, Four volumes quarto, Richardson; 1764-81.—It is a common but erroneous supposition that LAW was the editor of this (incomplete) edition of Behmen's Works. Law doubtless intended to produce a new and correct translation of those works, as may be inferred from his book "The Way to Divine Knowledge," and the following Letter to one of his correspondents; but he died in 1761, before the first of the present volumes was finished, if even begun; and all his involvement with it, if any, may be limited to a few verbal <unclear>corrections on the margin</unclear> of one of his own copies of the "Book of the Three Principles," from which they might have been transferred into the above edition. Even the Symbols, or "Figures," which are stated to have been "left by the Rev. W. Law," were only copies he had sketched himself, or had taken from the originals, which were designed by Freher, in illustration of his own Treatises on the Philosophy of Behmen.

<margin>(the other and fellow companion of Mr. Law and Mrs. Hutcheson)</margin>
The fact is, the entire republication of the Works constituting the above edition was undertaken at the sole expense of Mrs. Hutcheson and Mrs. Hester Gibbon, the friends and companions of Law, <unclear>the latter the sister of David Gibbon the historian,</unclear> out of respect to his memory. The chief editor was a Mr. George Ward, assisted by a Mr. Thomas Langcake, two longtime friends and admirers of Law, who used to occasionally correct his pieces for the press while residing in London, and who undoubtedly undertook the duty of editorship at the request of those ladies, to carry out, as far as possible, the designs of their late esteemed friend regarding a New Edition of J. B., as expressed in his later writings. And the reason this edition was not completed was that Mrs. Hutcheson and Mr. Ward died about the time of the publication of the Fourth Volume; Mrs. Gibbon, it appears, was not willing to <unclear>undertake the</unclear> continuation of the work, <unclear>so rather her money to another person</unclear>. All that these parties did as editors was to take the original translations, change the phraseology here and there without reference to the German original (a language it is supposed they did not understand), leave out certain portions of the translators’ prefaces, alter the capitalization of a few words, and manage the Treatises through the press. For some reason or other, they omitted several very important Treatises of the author, which should have been inserted immediately after "The Book of the Incarnation," and in other cases, they disregarded the proper order of the Writings. They also adopted the antiquated Life of Behmen, written by Durand Hotham in 1653, having no other biography at hand, which is influenced by the fantasies and old wives’ tales peculiar to the alchemists of former times. The supposition that this Memoir was edited by Law has been the cause of much dissatisfaction in the minds of his friends and much discredit with the public regarding his good sense and judgment. But, as observed before, Mr. Law had no connection with this edition of Behmen; and, besides, he was as great an enemy to all the pretenses of alchemy or occult science as the most simple-minded Christian believer.

The following is the Letter referred to above, in answer to one recommending Mr. Law to undertake a new edition of Behmen’s Works:—

> "I have several times had the same designs in my mind which you recommend to me, but have never yet been moved enough to begin them * * *. I taught myself the High Dutch Language, on purpose to know the original words of the blessed Jacob * * *. The edition I have is in quarto [1730?] carefully printed from Gichtel’s edition in the year 1715. The translators of J. B., Elliston and Sparrow, are much to be honored for their work; they had great piety and great abilities, and well understood their author, especially Elliston; but the translation is *too heavily loaded with words*, and in many places the *sense is mistaken*."

> "A new translator of J. B. is not to intend to make his author more intelligible by softening or refining his language. His style is what it is, strange and uncommon; not because he lacked learning and skill in words, but because what he saw and conceived was quite new and strange, never seen or spoken of before: and therefore if he was to put it down in writing, words must be used to signify that which they had never done before."

> "If it shall please God that I undertake this work, I shall only endeavor to make J. B. speak as he would have spoken had he written in English. Secondly, to guard the reader at certain places from wrong understandings of his meaning, by adding here and there a note, as occasion requires. Thirdly, and chiefly, by Prefaces or Introductions to prepare and direct the reader in the true use of these writings. This last is most necessary of all, and yet would be entirely needless if the reader would only observe J. B.’s own directions. For there is not an error, defect, or wrong turn which the reader can fall into in the use of these books that is not most plainly set before him by J. B." [WHAT WAS HERE DESIGNED BY MR. LAW, IT IS INTENDED TO SUPPLY IN THE PROPOSED NEW EDITION OF THE WORKS OF BEHMEN.]

> "Many persons of learning in the last century read J. B. with great earnestness, but it was only, as it were, to steal from him certain mysteries of Nature and to run away with the philosopher's stone; and yet nowhere could they see the folly and impossibility of their attempt so fully shown to them as by J. B. himself." In reference to what Law and others have written regarding the true source of the Newtonian philosophy, as well as the supposed original discoveries of other philosophical minds, the following extract from a letter by Law to Dr. Cheyne is appended here: "When Sir Isaac Newton died, large abstracts from Jacob Boehme's works, written in his own hand, were found among his papers. I have this from undoubted authority, as well as the fact that in the earlier part of his life, he was led into a search for the philosopher's tincture from the same author."

> "My witnesses are well-known names of great esteem to you. It is perfectly plain that everything Sir Isaac said about the universality, nature, and effects of attraction—and the first three laws of nature—was not only said but proved in its true and deepest foundation by Jacob Boehme in his first three properties of Eternal Nature; and from there, they are derived into this temporal manifestation. This, added to the information above, is, I think, sufficient justification for having said that 'Sir Isaac could have referred to Boehme for the true foundation,' etc. ->* * *<-"

> "P.S. From the authority mentioned above, I can assure you that Sir Isaac was previously so deep into Jacob Boehme that he, along with a relative named Dr. Newton, set up furnaces and worked for several months in search of the Tincture, purely based on what they understood from him. It is no wonder, then, that attraction, with its two inseparable properties—which in Jacob Boehme constitute the first three properties of Eternal Nature—should become the grand foundation of Newtonian philosophy."

> "I am in too much of a hurry to say anything except in this fragmented way. If you have any requests for me of any kind, a letter must be directed to me at Cliffe, near Oundle, in Northamptonshire."

> "It is my guess that Sir Isaac at first so openly declared his total ignorance of the source or cause of attraction to prevent any suspicion of his being led to it by Boehme's doctrine. It is plain he knew the deep foundation Boehme had given for it. No one can know anything of the Tincture from Boehme, or the means or possibility of attaining it, without knowing and believing, as Boehme does, the foundation of universal attraction. Therefore, Sir Isaac's silence and ignorance of this foundation must have been feigned for certain reasons that can now only be guessed at."

The following is Poiret's note on this author at the end of his "Theologie Germanique," 1700:

> —Jacob Boehme (he says) is the only one—at least whose writings have been available until now—to whom God has revealed the foundation of nature, both in spiritual and physical things. With a central insight into theological or supernatural matters, he also knew from their source the true principles of philosophy, including metaphysics, pneumatics, and true physics. He saw, through inner light and feeling, how God, emerging from the indivisible point of His uniform eternity, manifested Himself to Himself in a perfect Trinity through the ineffable generation of His luminous Word and the procession of His holy and delightful Spirit. He saw how God, having contemplated within Himself the immense virtues, beauties, and delights of His divine forms and their infinite combinations and variations, caused spiritual and physical beings to flow from His Divine Power through His Word and His Spirit, in imitation of the ideas formed by His divine wisdom. He saw how these beings have, in their natural foundation and their luminous and free perfections, properties, beauties, and delights similar and analogous to their originals in God—but with this difference: spiritual beings possess and act upon them in a divine manner and with freedom, while physical beings do so in a lower and more limited way, yet still vividly, with feeling and living instinct. By reducing all forms of spiritual and physical nature to Seven, and their principles to Three (the first two being for spiritual things and the third, which is like a material image of the first two, for the external world), he explained the creation of the Angels and their realm, the fall of the demons, the creation of this world (which is coarser than the angelic world and drawn from the dark chaos caused by the demons corrupting their home), the glorious creation of man, his fall, his restoration through Jesus Christ, and an infinity of other spiritual and natural mysteries.

> When this profound and mysterious author speaks of the foundation of nature and the qualities of things, both divine and natural, he cannot be truly and vividly understood by anyone, no matter how learned or great their intellect (for this consists of feelings), unless God divinely awakens and touches our faculties—which are analogous to His—in a way that would now be beyond the senses or supernatural. This includes our passive senses: the divine ones, which correspond to God, and the natural ones, which correspond to His works. We have lost these, or at least they are drowsy and asleep within us due to the state of corruption and death to which the fall of Adam has reduced us. Without this awakening, no matter how well one might speak of these things after reading...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the divine wisdom that sanctifies the soul, transitioning into an assessment of Jacob Boehme's writings. It highlights the necessity of inner transformation over mere intellectual curiosity and provides a bibliographical history of Boehme’s works and their various editions.</meta>

the breath of God, the holy unction, which sanctifies the soul to be the temple of the Holy Spirit, which instructs it correctly in all things, and searches *τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ*, the depths of God <note>1 Corinthians 2:10</note>. This is the precious pearl, whose beauty is more glorious and whose virtue is more sovereign than the sun: it is a never-failing comfort in all afflictions, a balm for all sores, a panacea for all diseases, a powerful antidote against all poison and death itself. It is that joyful and assured companion and guide which never forsakes a man, but escorts him through this valley of misery and death into the blessed paradise of perfect bliss.

If it be asked, "What is the way to attain to this wisdom?" Behold! Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life, tells you plainly in these words: *If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me*; or, as he says elsewhere, *Unless you be born*

---

again, you cannot see the kingdom of God. Without experiencing this in oneself, even if one reads all the writings of the author, one will nevertheless form only *completely dead* paintings of them, or rather ideas that are as defective as they are unlike their originals—indeed, they would be pure fictions. This is much like a person born blind who, having often heard people talk of light and colors, might later speak of them by hearsay, yet without truly knowing the living meaning of the words he pronounces.

Nevertheless, it is not that one cannot—in proportion to the good disposition of heart and mind that one has—glimpse more or less (though still roughly and in an imperfect manner) several very beautiful truths. From these, one can draw very fine insights and conclusions regarding doctrines, both in theory and practice. But it is not through these that he is most clear to everyone; rather, it is through what he intersperses here and there concerning the corruption of man and the depravity of today's Christianity, conversion, resignation, and the abandonment of the soul to God. He writes of the principles of the Christian life, the duties of man, and the practice of virtue—in short, of what is necessary to know and essential for practice. All of this is touched upon so clearly and strongly in his writings that there is no person of goodwill who cannot understand and appreciate them without difficulty, provided that one approaches them by reading those of his treatises which contain the most of these kinds of truths. Such works include his books on the *Way to Christ* (which make up the second section of the *Theosophic Grammar*), his *Letters*, and even the latter and greater part of his *Mysterium Magnum, or Explanation of Genesis*.

But the natural and proud inclination of a curious spirit does not find as much taste or attraction in these kinds of solid and vital matters as it does in abstract and elevated speculations concerning the principles and forms of nature, their various combinations, the natural effects that may proceed from them, and similar things. Many people, who pride themselves on their esteem for this author's writings, seem more attached to these things than to those he recommends as uniquely essential and as the "Key to Everything"—such as repentance and pure abandonment to God, or pure resignation to His divine will. This resignation is the center and the deepest principle of all, and indeed the only one that is of infinite depth. For to conceive of and penetrate all the greatness, all the light, and all the divine and angelic delights—to possess this knowledge along with that of all nature down to its deepest folds and principles, and to be attached to it—all this is but a natural foundation, limited by the "self" and by personal ownership; it may even degenerate into a diabolical and infernal foundation. But there is neither a created and finite foundation, nor any danger, in the stripping away and resignation of all things under the will of God and in perfect abandonment to Him alone. This involves leaving Him the freedom to give us or refuse us His extraordinary graces and particular insights as He pleases. One should have much more apprehension and distance regarding the possession of these than inclination or desire, for fear that self-love, curiosity, vanity, self-complacency, pride, and spiritual presumption might slip in and establish themselves to our ruin. These are precautions which our author very carefully noted and instilled, and by which he governed himself.

This author was German by nation, born in Lusatia in the year 1575; a Lutheran Protestant by religion, a peasant by birth, and a shoemaker by profession. However, since God enlightened him for the third time and prompted him to record his insights in writing, he worked much less at his trade than with his pen, which has left us thirty treatises, both large and small, without counting his letters. They are all—with the exception of one on the Last Judgment, which is lost—printed in German in various places and at various times, some during the author's lifetime; but the greater part of his writings did not appear until after his death, which occurred in the year 1624. The noble and learned Franckenberg wrote an account of them, as well as of his life, which can be found at the head of the edition of his works reprinted together in Amsterdam in 1682. But the latest and most exact edition of his works is that of I. G. Gichtel, in 4to., 1730, which is very carefully edited. Franckenberg, the same person who under the name *Fr. à Monte* published in Amsterdam in 1647 a Latin abridgment of the *Mystical Theology* of Hugo de Palma, did the same with another small treatise by our author, which appeared in Latin in the year 1650 under the title *Metapsychica de Cœlesti et Terrestri Mysterio*. A jurist named Werdenhagen had already done the same for the *40 Questions of the Soul*, which appeared in 1632 in Amsterdam under the title *Psychologia Vera J. B. T.* These two books are both too obscure and too lacking in necessary explanations, as was the booklet *Theologiæ Christianæ juxta Principia J. Bohemii idea brevior* of 1687, to serve as an introduction to this author's principles for either beginners or the scholars of this century. The one who wrote the treatise *Exercitatio Theoreticorum Copernico-Cœlestium Mathematico-Physico-Theologica*, printed in Hamburg in 1689 (who is the same person who published a German apology for the author in Frankfurt in 1691 under the name Johannes Matthæi, against Mr. Holzhausen, a Lutheran minister in Frankfurt), was much more successful in the third part of his *Exercitatio*. As for the translations of his books into French, this is something that the false delicacy of that language cannot tolerate. To accommodate soft and feminine minds, the French language has allowed itself to be governed by a law to say nothing that appears even slightly obscure to the most negligent readers, on pain of it being dismissed as nonsense—as the translation of the most obscure of his books, *Signatura Rerum*, will no doubt be dismissed. It was published about fifty years ago (1650) in French at Frankfurt under the title *Temporal Mirror of Eternity*—a translation which is, in fact, not a very significant work.
