the reason why nature is only a *desire* is because it exists for the sake of *something else*; and it is also the reason why nature in itself is only a *torment*, because it is only a strong desire and cannot provide for itself that which it wants, but is always working against itself.

Now a desire that cannot be stopped, nor obtain that which it would have, has a threefold opposition, or working, within it, which you may conceive of as follows: the first and *specific* property, or the *one and only* will of the desire as such, is to *have* that which it does not have; and all that it can do toward having it is to act as if it were *seizing it*. This is what makes the desire a *magical compressing, enclosing*, or *astringing*; because that is all that it can do toward seizing that which it would have. But the desire cannot thus magically *astringe, compress*, or strive to enclose without *drawing* or *attracting*; but drawing is *motion*, which is the highest opposition and *resistance* to compressing or holding together. And thus *the desire*, in its magical working, sets out with *two contrary* properties, inseparable from one another and equal in strength; for the motion has no strength except as it is the *drawing* of the desire; and the desire only *draws* in the same degree as it wills to compress and astringe; and therefore the desire, as it astringes, always produces a resistance equal to itself.

Now from this great and equally strong opposition of the *two first* properties of the desire—magically pulling, as I may say, in two contrary ways—there arises, as a necessary birth from both of them, a *third* property, which is emphatically called a *wheel*, or the *whirling anguish* of life. For a thing that can go neither inward nor outward, and yet must exist and move under the equal power of both of them, must whirl or turn around; it has no possibility of doing anything else, or of ceasing to do that. And this whirling opposition of these inseparable properties is the great *anguish* of life, and may properly be called the *hell of nature*; and every lesser torment which any man finds

> “ “Thy kingdom come, thy will be done,” is the one will and one hunger that feeds the soul with the life-giving bread of heaven. This will is always fulfilled; it cannot possibly be sent away empty, for God’s kingdom must manifest itself with all its riches in that soul which wills nothing else. It never was, nor can be lost, except by the will that seeks something else. Hence you may know, with the utmost certainty, that if you have no inward peace, if religious comfort is still lacking, it is because you have more wills than one. For the multiplicity of wills is the very essence of fallen nature; and all its evil, misery, and separation from God lie within it; and as soon as you return to and allow only this one will, you have returned to God and must find the blessedness of his kingdom within you.

> Give yourself up to ever so many good works—read, preach, pray, visit the sick, build hospitals, clothe the naked, etc.—yet if anything else goes along with these, or if in doing them you have anything else that you will and hunger after except that *God’s kingdom may come, and his will be done*, they are not the works of one born again from above, and so cannot be his life-giving food. For the new creature in Christ is *that one will and one hunger that was in Christ*; and therefore where that is lacking, there is lacking that new creature which alone can have its conduct <note>The original term "conversation" refers to one's citizenship or manner of living.</note>, which alone can daily eat and drink at God’s table, receiving in all that it does continual life from “every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.”—”

From what word, and from what mouth of God? Why, only from that hidden, supernatural power of the triune Deity, which speaks and breathes continual nourishment to that heavenly fire, light, and spirit, in and from which all who are around the throne of God have their inward joy beyond all thought, and their outward glory, which can only be represented or hinted to us by pearls, sapphires, and rainbow beauties.

It is from this power of the triune God, working in the fire, light, spirit, and spiritual water (or body) of your new-born creature, that all the good, comfort, and joy of religion which you lack are to be found—and found by nothing but the resurrection of that divine and heavenly nature which came forth in the first man.

Do not take these to be too high-flown words, for they are no higher than the truth; for if that which is in you is not as high as heaven, you will never get there. That heavenly fire, light, and spirit, which make the angelic life entirely divine, must certainly be your inward likeness to God; and what God is and works in angels, he must be and work in you, or you can never be like or equal to them, as Christ has said. To be outwardly glorious as they are, you must wait until this corruptible body has put on incorruption; but to have the same inward glory 
<margin>

</margin>
of the same celestial fire, light, and spirit—burning, shining, and breathing in your inward man as angels have—belongs to you. You were born at first from the triune breath of the living God, and born again of Christ out of Adam’s death, to have and be all that by a wonder of redemption, which was your divine birthright at first by a wonder of creation.

And now, my dear friend, choose your side; would you be honorable in *church* or *state*, put on the full armor of this world, praise what man praises, clothe yourself with all the graces and perfections of the *belles lettres* <note>Fine literature and academic arts.</note>, and be an orator and critic as fast as ever you can, and above all, be strong in the power of flattering words.

But if the other side is your choice; would you be found in Christ and know *the power of his resurrection*: would you taste the powers of the world to come, and find the continual influences of the triune God feeding and keeping up his divine life in your triune soul, you must *give up all* for that *one will and one hunger*, which keeps the angels of God in their full feasts of ever-new and never-ceasing delights in the nameless, boundless riches of eternity.

Think it not hard, or too severe a restraint, to have but *one will and one hunger*; it is no harder a restraint than being kept from all that can bring forth pain and sorrow to your soul; no greater severity than being excluded from every place but the kingdom of God. For to have only this one will and one hunger is to have every evil of life and all enemies put under your feet. It is to have finished with everything that can defile, betray, disappoint, or hurt that eternal nature which must have its life within you. On the other hand, everything that is not the effect and fruit of this one will and one hunger, but added to your life by a selfish will and worldly hunger, must sooner or later be torn from you with the greatest pain, or become food for that gnawing worm which does not die.

Do you ask how you are to come to this one will and one hunger? I refer you to no power of your own, and yet refer you to that which is within yourself.

...in this mixed world, has all its existence and power from the working of these *three properties*: for life can find no troublesome motions or feeling of distress, except in so far as it comes under their power and enters into their whirling wheel.

Now here you may observe that just as this *whirling anguish* of life is a *third state*, necessarily arising from the conflict of the *first two properties* of the desire, so in this material system, every whirling or <term>orbicular motion</term> of any body is solely the effect or product of the conflict of *these first two properties*. For no material thing can whirl or move in a circle until it is under the power of these *first two properties*—that is, until it can go neither inward nor outward and yet is forced to move. This is exactly how the whirling anguish of the desire begins: when it can go neither inward nor outward and yet must remain in motion.

And this may be yet another strict demonstration to you that all the *matter* of this world comes from *spiritual* properties, since all its workings and effects happen according to them. For if matter does nothing except according to these properties, it can be nothing other than what it is because of them and what it receives from them.

Here also—that is, in these *three properties of the desire*—you see the basis and reason for the three great laws of matter and motion, which were recently discovered and are so highly celebrated. You need no longer be told that the illustrious Sir *Isaac* ploughed with *Behmen’s heifer* <note>A biblical idiom from the Book of Judges meaning to solve a riddle using someone else's information; here, it suggests Newton used Jakob Böhme's ideas</note> when he brought forth his discovery of them. In the mathematical system of this great philosopher, these three properties—<term>attraction</term>, <term>equal resistance</term>, and the <term>orbicular motion</term> of the planets as the effect of them, and so on—are only treated as *facts* and *appearances*, the source of which is not claimed to be known. But in our *Behmen*, the illuminated instrument of God, their birth and *power* in eternity is revealed; their eternal beginning is shown, and how and why all worlds, and every life of every creature—whether heavenly, earthly, or hellish—must be within them and from them, and can have no nature, either spi-

---

Angels in heaven are not good and happy because of anything they can do for themselves, but solely by what is done to them. Now, that Holy Spirit which does God’s will in heaven and is the goodness and happiness of all its inhabitants—that same Spirit is every person's portion on earth and the *gift of God within them*. It is only wasted effort to strive by any power of your reason or self-activity to work up this one will and one hunger within you, or to kindle the true intensity of a divine desire by anything your natural self can do. This is as impossible as it would have been for fallen Adam to be his own redeemer, or for a dead man to give life to himself. The one will and one hunger, which alone can consume the true nourishment of the divine life, is nothing other than the divine nature within you, which died in Adam in no other way except by being suppressed and buried for a while under a weight and variety of earthly wills.

Because of this, nothing can put an end to this variety of wills in fallen man (which is his death toward God), and nothing can be the resurrection of the divine nature within him (which is his only salvation), except “the CROSS” of Christ. This does not mean that wooden cross on which he was crucified, but the cross on which he was crucified through the whole course of his life in the flesh. It is our fellowship with him on this cross, throughout the whole course of our lives, that constitutes our union with him; it alone gives power to the divine nature within us to arise out of its death and breathe again in us in one will and one hunger for nothing but God.

To be like-minded with Christ is to live in complete opposition to self, the world, the flesh, and the devil, as he did. This is what it means to belong to him, to be one with him, to have life from him, and to wash our robes in the blood of the Lamb. For we are washed and cleansed by his blood then, and only then, when we drink his blood; and we drink his blood when we willingly drink from the cup that he drank from.

Again, not to be like-minded with Christ is to be separated from him. To have a different mind than he had is to be in the state of those who crucified him. As the Redeemer was, so are those who are redeemed. As Adam was, so are those who are born of him. Life from Adam and life from Christ is the single thing that makes the one our destroyer and the other our redeemer. But to conclude: do not worry in your mind about how you are to have the one will and one hunger which is always eating at God’s table and continually fed with the bread of life; the work is already done for you. “I am the way, the truth, and the life,” says Christ. It is the same as if he had said, *the way is nowhere, the truth is nowhere, the life is nowhere, but in me.* What room is there, therefore, for any learned schemes or further inquiry about the matter? Follow Christ in the denial of *all the wills of self*, and then everything that separates you from God is put away. <insert>Persevere in persistent prayer,</insert> and the heaven-born new creature will come to life in you—the only creature that knows and enjoys the things of God, and finds its daily food of joy in the many blessings that Christ preached on the mount.

Tell me no more, then, of your new skill in *Hebrew* words, of your *Paris* editions of all the ancient fathers, your complete collection of the councils, commentators, and church historians, and so on. Did Christ mean anything like this when he said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life?” Did the apostle mean anything like this when he said, “No man can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit?” You say many of the fathers were great, good, and divine teachers. I say nothing against that, except that he who is *always teaching within you, ever standing and knocking at the door of your heart with the words of eternal life*, is much more great, good, and divine.

You may perhaps ask: why do I continue writing books myself if there is only one true and divine teacher? I answer that although there is only one bridegroom who can provide the blessing of the marriage feast, his servants are sent out to invite the guests. This is the unchangeable difference between Christ’s teaching and the teaching of those who only publish the good news about him. They are not the bridegroom and therefore do not have the bridegroom’s voice. They are not the light, but are only sent to bear witness to it. And as the *Baptist* said, “He must increase, but I must decrease,” so every faithful teacher says of his own doctrine: it must decrease and end as soon as it has led the student to the true teacher.

All that I have written for nearly thirty years has been only to show that we have no master but Christ, nor can we have any living, divine knowledge except from his holy nature *born and revealed in us*. I have not written a word in favor of JACOB BEHMEN except because, *more than any other writer in the world*, he has shown all that is found in the kingdom of grace and the kingdom of nature to be ONE CONTINUAL DEMONSTRATION that dying to self in order to be born again of Christ is the ONLY POSSIBLE SALVATION FOR THE SONS OF FALLEN ADAM.

ritual or material, no kind of happiness or misery, except according to the working power and state of these properties.

<margin>1</margin>
All outward nature, all inward life, is what it is, and works as it works, from this unceasing, powerful attraction, resistance, and whirling.

<margin>2</margin>
Every madness and folly of life is their immediate work, and every good spirit of wisdom and love has all its strength and activity from them. They equally support darkness and light; the one could have no powers of density and coldness, the other no powers of warmth, brightness, and activity, except by and through these three properties acting in a different state. Not a particle of matter stirs, rises, or falls, separates from, or unites with, any other, except under their power. Not a thought of the mind, whether of love or hatred, of joy or trouble, of envy or wrath, of pride and greed, can rise in the spirit of any creature, except as these properties act and stir in it.

<margin>3</margin>
The next and following properties—namely, the fourth, called *fire*; the fifth, called the form of *light and love*; and the sixth, sound, or understanding—only declare the gradual effects of the entrance of the Deity into the first three properties of Nature, changing or bringing their strong wrathful attraction, resistance, and whirling into a life and state of triumphant joy and fullness of satisfaction; this state of peace and joy in one another is called the *seventh property*, or state of nature. And this is what *BEHMEN* <note>Jakob Böhme (1575–1624), a German Christian mystic</note> means by his *Ternarius Sanctus* <note>Latin for "Holy Ternary," referring to the manifestation of the Trinity in nature</note>, which he so often speaks of as *the only place from which he received all that he said and wrote*: he means by it the holy manifestation of the Triune God in the seven properties of Nature, or kingdom of heaven. And from this manifestation of God in the seven properties of nature, or kingdom of heaven, he most wonderfully opens and accounts for all that was done in the first six working days of the creation, showing how each of the six active properties had its peculiar day’s work, until the whole ended, or *rested*, in the sanctified, paradisiacal sabbath of the seventh day, just as nature does in its seventh property.

<margin>4</margin>
And now, sir, you may see, with the greatest clarity, how everything in this world, everything in the soul and body of man, absolutely requires the one redemption of the Gospel. There is but one nature in all created things, whether spiritual or material; they all stand and work upon the same ground: namely, *the first three properties of Nature*. Only that which can illuminate the soul can also give brightness and purity to the body. For there is no grossness, darkness, or opposition in the body except what strictly proceeds from the same cause that makes selfishness, wrath, envy, and torment in the soul; it is but one and the same state and working of the same first three properties of nature. All evil, whether natural or moral, whether of body or spirit, is the sole effect of the wrath and disorder of the spirits of nature, working in and by themselves. And all the good, perfection, and purity of everything, whether spiritual or material, whether it be the body or spirit of man or angel, is solely from the power and presence of the supernatural Deity *dwelling and working in the properties of nature*. For the properties of nature are in themselves nothing else but a mere hunger, want, strife, and opposition, until the fullness and riches of the Deity, entering into them, unites them all in one will and one possession of Light and harmonious Love; which is the one redemption of the Gospel, and the one reason why nothing else but the Heart, or Son, or *Light of God*, can purify nature and creature from all the evil into which they have fallen.

<margin>5</margin>
For nothing can possibly deliver the soul from its *selfish nature* and earthly passions except that one power that can deliver *matter* from its present material properties and turn earth into heaven; and that is for this plain reason: because soul and body, outward nature and inward life, have but one and the same evil in them, and from one and the same cause.

<margin>6</margin>
The unbeliever, therefore, who looks for life and salvation through the use of his reason, acts contrary to the whole nature of everything that he sees and knows of himself and of the nature and state of this world. For, from one end of it to the other, all its material state, all its gross divided elements, declare that they are what they are because the light and love of heaven is not working and manifest in them; and that nothing can take darkness, materiality, rage, storms, and tempests from them except that same heavenly Light and Love which was made flesh to redeem fallen humanity first, and after that the whole material system.

<margin>7</margin>
Can the unbeliever, with his reason, bring the light of this world into the eyes of his body? If not, how can it be less absurd, or more possible, for reason to bring heavenly light into the soul? Can reason hinder the body from being heavy, or remove thickness and darkness from flesh and blood? Yet nothing less than such a power can possibly help the soul out of its fallen and earthly state. For the grossness of flesh and blood is the *natural state* of the fallen soul; and therefore nothing can purify the soul or raise it out of its earthly, corrupt state except that which has all power over all that is *earthly and material* in nature.

<margin>8</margin>
To pretend, therefore, that reason may have sufficient power to remove all hellish depravity and earthly lusts from the soul, while it has not the least power over *sweet or sour* in any one particle of matter in the body, is as highly absurd as if a man should pretend that he has full power to alter the inward, invisible, vegetable life of a plant, but none at all over its outward state, color, leaves, or fruit. The deist, therefore, and not the Christian, stands in need of continual miracles to make good his doctrine. For reason can have no pretense to amend or alter the life of the soul except so far as it can show that it has power to amend and alter the nature and state of the body.

<margin>9</margin>
The unbelieving *Jews* said of our Lord, “How can this man forgive sins?” Christ showed them *how* by appealing to that power which they saw he had over the body: “Is it easier (he says) to say, Thy sins are forgiven thee, or to say, Arise, take up thy bed, and walk?” But the delusion of the unbelieving deist is greater than that of the *Jew*. For the deist sees that his reason has no power over his body; it can remove no disease, blindness, deafness, or lameness from it; and yet he will pretend to have enough power from his reason to help the soul out of all its evil, not knowing that body and soul go hand in hand and are nothing else but the inward and outward state of one and the same life; and that therefore he only who can say to the dead body of Lazarus, “Come forth,” can say to the soul, “Be clean.” *The unbeliever or deist*, therefore, if he pleases, may style himself a natural or a moral philosopher, but with no more truth than he can call himself a *healer* of all the maladies of the body. And for a man to think himself a moral philosopher because he has made a choice collection of syllogisms <note>Formal logical arguments</note> in order to quicken and revive a Divine goodness in the soul, or that no redeemer need come from heaven because human reason, when truly left to itself, has great skill in *chopping logic* <note>Engaging in clever but trivial or over-complicated arguments</note>; this may justly be deemed such an ignorance of the nature of things as is seldom found in the transactions of illiterate and common life. But this by the way.—

To return to our chief subject: the sum of all that has been said is this: all evil, be it what it

will; all misery of every kind, is in its birth, working, and extent, nothing else but Nature left to itself, and under the divided workings of its own hunger, wrath, and contrariety; and therefore there is no possibility for the natural, earthly man to escape eternal hunger, wrath, and contrariety, except solely in the way as the gospel teaches, by denying and dying to self. On the other hand, all the goodness and perfection, all the happiness, glory, and joy, that any intelligent, divine creature can possess, is, and can be, from nothing else but the invisible, uncreated Light and Spirit of God manifesting itself in the properties of the creaturely life, *filling, blessing, and uniting them all in one love, and joy of life.*

<margin>2</margin>
And thus again: there is no possibility of man attaining to any heavenly perfection and happiness, except only in the way of the gospel, by the union of the divine and human nature, by man's being "born again from above," of the *Word* and *Spirit* of God. There is no possibility of any other way, because there is nothing that can possibly change the first properties of life into a heavenly state, but the presence and working power of the Deity united with, and working in them. And therefore the "*Word* was made flesh," and must of all necessity be made flesh, if man is to have a heavenly nature. Now, as all evil, sin, and misery have no beginning, nor power of working, except in the manifestation of nature in its *divided, contrary properties;* so it is certain that man has nothing to turn to, seek, or aspire after, but the lost *Spirit of love.* And therefore it is that God alone can be his Redeemer; because God alone is Love; and *Love* can be nowhere else but in God, and where God dwells and works.——

<margin>3</margin>
Now, the difficulty which you find in attaining to this purity and universality of the Spirit of love is because you seek for it, as I once told you, in the way of reasoning: you would possess it only from a rational conviction of its fitness and loveliness. And as this clear idea does not immediately put you in the real possession of it, your reason begins to waver; and suggests to you that it may be only a *fine notion* that has no ground except in the power of imagination. But this, sir, is all your own error, and as contrary to nature as if you would have your eyes do that which only your hands or feet can do for you. The *Spirit of love* is a *spirit of nature and life;* and all the operations of nature and life are according to the working powers of nature; and every growth and degree of life can only arise in *its own time* and place from its proper cause, and as its genuine effect. Nature and life do nothing by chance or accidentally, but everything in one uniform way. Fire, air, and light do not proceed sometimes from one thing, and sometimes from another; but wherever they are, they are always born in the same manner, and from the same working in the properties of nature. So in like manner, Love is an immutable birth, always proceeding from the same cause, and cannot exist until its own true parents have brought it forth.

<margin>4</margin>
How unreasonable would it be to begin to doubt whether *strength* and *health* of body were real things, or possible to be had, because you could not by the power of your reason take possession of them! Yet this is just like suspecting the PURITY AND PERFECTION OF LOVE to be only a *notion* because your reason cannot bring about its birth in your soul. For reason has no more power of altering the *life and properties of the soul* than of altering the life and properties of the body. That, and *that only*, can cast devils and evil spirits out of the soul, which can say to the storm, "Be still;" and to the leper, "Be clean."——

<margin>5</margin>
The birth of Love is a *form* or *state* of life, and has its fixed place in the *fifth form of nature.* The three first properties or forms of Nature are the *ground* or *bond of life* that is in itself only an extreme hunger, want, strife, and contrariety. And they are in this state so that they may become a proper fuel for the *fourth form* of nature, namely, the *fire* to be kindled in them. You will, perhaps, say, What is this *fire?* What is its nature? And how is it kindled? And how is it that the hunger and anguished state of the properties are a fitness to be a *fuel* for this fire? It may be answered: This hunger and anguish of nature, in its first forms, is its fitness to be changed into a life of light, joy, and happiness: and *that* for this reason, because it is in this hunger and anguish because God is *not* in it. For as nature comes from God, and for this end only, that the Deity may manifest heaven within it, it must stand in a hunger and anguished state until the Deity is manifested in it. And therefore its hunger and anguish is its true *fitness* to be changed into a better state: and this is its *fitness* for the birth of the *fire;* for the fire means nothing, and is nothing else but *that* which changes them into a better state. Not as if fire were a *fourth*, distinct thing that comes into them from *without*, but it is only a fourth state, or condition, into which the same properties are brought.

<margin>6</margin>
The fire, then, is *that* which changes the properties into a *new and heavenly state:* therefore the fire does two things; it alters the state of Nature and brings heaven into it; and therefore it must work from a twofold power; the *Deity* and *nature* must both be in it. It must have some strength from nature, or it could not work in nature; it must have some strength from the Deity, or it could not *overcome* and *change* Nature into a Divine life. Now all this is only to show you *that the fire can only be kindled by the entrance of the Deity, or supernatural God, into a conjunction or union with nature.* And this conjunction of the Deity and nature makes, or brings forth, that state or form of life which is called, and truly is, fire: *first*, because it does *that* in the spiritual properties of nature which fire does in the properties of material nature: and, *secondly*, because it is that alone from which every fire in this world, whether in the life of animal, or vegetable, or inanimate matter, has its source, power, and possibility of burning. The *fire of this world* overcomes its fuel, breaks its nature, alters its state, and changes it into flame and light. But why does it do this? From where does it have this nature and power? It is because it is a *true out-birth* of the eternal fire, which overcomes the darkness, wrath, and contrariety of nature, and changes all its properties into a life of light, joy, and glory. Not a spark of fire could be kindled in this world, nor a ray of light come from any material fire, except because material nature is, in itself, nothing else but the *very properties of eternal nature* existing for a time in a *material state* or condition; and therefore they must work in time as they do in eternity; and consequently there must be fire in this world; it must have the *same birth* and do the *same work* in its *material way* which the eternal fire has and does in spiritual nature.

<margin>7</margin>
And this is the true ground and reason why everything in this world is delivered, as far as it can be, from its earthly impurity and brought into its highest state of existence only by fire; it is because the eternal fire is the *purifier* of eternal Nature and the *opener* of every perfection, light, and glory in it. And if you ask why the eternal fire is the *purifier* of eternal nature, the reason is plain: it is because the eternal fire has its birth, nature, and power from the entrance of the

pure, supernatural Deity into the properties of nature, which properties must change their state and become what they were not before as soon as the Deity *enters* into them. Their darkness, wrath, and conflict are driven out of them, and they work and produce only a life and strength of light, joy, and glory. And this twofold operation—namely, on one hand taking from nature its *wrathful workings*, and on the other hand, opening a glorious manifestation of the Deity in them—is the *whole nature and form* of the fire. This is the reason why, from eternity to eternity, it is and must be the *purifier of eternal nature*; namely, by changing nature into a kingdom of heaven from eternity to eternity. Now, every fire in this world does, and must do, the same thing in its own humble way to the utmost of its power, and can do nothing else. Kindle fire wherever or in whatever you wish, it acts only from and by the power of this *eternal purifying fire*; therefore, it breaks and consumes the *grossness of everything* and makes all that is pure and spiritual come forth out of it. Thus, purification is its one and only work through all material nature, because it is a real outbirth of that eternal fire which purifies eternal nature and changes it into a pure heaven of glory.

The eternal fire is called a *fourth form*, or state of Nature, because it cannot exist except from the first three and has its work in the *fourth place*, in the midst of the seven forms, changing the first three into the last three forms of nature; that is, changing them from their natural into a heavenly state. So, strictly speaking, there are only three forms of nature, corresponding to the threefold working of the Triune Deity. For the last three are not three new or different properties, but are only the first three brought into a new state by the *entrance of the triune Deity* into conjunction with them. This entrance of the supernatural Deity into them is the *consuming of all that is bad in them* and the turning of all their strength into a working life of light, joy, and heavenly glory; therefore, it has the most rightful claim to be called *fire*, as having no other nature and operation in it but the known nature of fire, and also as being *that* from which every fire in this world derives all its nature and power of acting as it does. ——

You once, as I remember, objected to my speaking so much <note>See the last extract</note> of the “*fire of life*,” thinking it was too gross an expression to be taken in its *literal meaning* when mention is made of the eternal fire or the *fire in animal life*. But, sir, fire has only *one nature* through the entire universe of things; and material fire has no more or less of the nature of fire in it than that which is in eternal nature, because it possesses and produces nothing except what it has and works from that source. How easy was it for you to have seen that the fire of the soul and the fire of the body had only *one nature*? How else could they *unite* in their heat? How easy also to have seen that the fire of animal life was the same fire that burns in the kitchen? How else could the kitchen fire be useful to animal life? What good could it do you to come to a wood fire if you wanted the heat of your own life increased? In animal life, the fire is kindled and preserved in such a degree and in such circumstances as to be *life* and the *preservation of life*; and this is its difference from fire kindled in wood that burns it to ashes. It is the same fire, only in a different state, that sustains life and consumes wood; it has no other nature in the wood than in the animal. Just as in water that has only enough fire in it to make it *warm*, and water that is made boiling hot by fire—the same nature and power of fire is in both, only in a different state. Now, will you say that fire is not to be understood literally when it only makes water warm because it is not *red and flaming* as you see it in a burning coal? Yet this would be just as much as to say that fire is not *literally* to be understood in animal life because it is so different from that fire which you see burning in a piece of wood.

And thus, sir, there is no foundation for any objection to all that has been said of fire. It is *one* and the same great power of God in the spiritual and material world: it is the cause of every life and the opener of every power of nature; and its one great work through all nature and every creature, animate and inanimate, is purification and exaltation. It can do nothing else, and that for this plain reason: because its birth is from the entrance of the pure Deity into nature; and therefore it must, in its various states and degrees, be doing only *that* which the entrance of the Deity into nature does. It must bring every natural thing into its highest state. ——

But to go back now to the *Spirit of love* and show you the *time* and *place* of its birth, *BEFORE WHICH IT CAN HAVE NO EXISTENCE IN YOUR SOUL*, no matter what you do to have it.

The fire, you see, is the first overcomer of the hungry, wrathful, self-tormenting state of the properties of Nature; and it only overcomes them because it is the *entrance of the pure Deity* into them; and therefore that which overcomes them is the *light of the Deity*. And this is the true ground and reason why every properly kindled fire must give off light and cannot do otherwise. It is because the eternal fire is only the effect or operation of the *supernatural light* of the Deity entering into nature; and therefore fire must give off light because it is itself only a power of the light; and light can be nowhere in nature except as a *fifth form*, or state of nature, brought forth by the fire. And as light thus brought forth is the *first state* that is *lovely* and *delightful* in nature, so the Spirit of love has its birth only in the light of life and can be nowhere else. For the properties of life have no common good, nothing to rejoice in, until the light is found; therefore, there is no possible beginning of the Spirit of love until then.

The shock that is given to the first three properties of <note>eternal</note> Nature, <note>the ground of the soul</note> by the amazing light of the Deity breaking in upon them, is the operation of the fire that consumes or takes away the wrathful strength and conflict of the properties and forces each of them to shrink away from itself, as it were, and come under the power of this new-risen light.*

* For a modern example and illustration of this operation of God upon the soul—diversified, perhaps, according to the temperament of the individual—the reader might refer to the biographies of Rogers, Bramwell, and others who have sought and found God (so as to be ‘quite clear’ in the ‘blessing of pardon’ and the ‘witness of the Spirit’) by the good old Gospel-style, persistent, Jacob-like wrestling way to Christ described in Behmen’s “*Book of True Repentance*.” And, indeed, may that not be said to be the only sure and direct way to God? <meta>This page continues the discussion of how the properties of nature are transformed into a heavenly state through the operation of divine fire and light, leading to the birth of the Spirit of Love.</meta>

Here all conflict of enmity and wrathful opposition in the properties must cease, because all are united in the *Love of the light*, and all equally helping one another toward a higher enjoyment and delight in it. They are all one triune will, all doing the same thing; namely, all rejoicing in the one love of the light. And IT IS HERE, in this delightful unity of operation, THAT THE SPIRIT OF LOVE IS BORN, in the *fifth property*, or light of life; and it cannot possibly rise up in any creature until the properties of its life are brought into this *fifth state*, thus changed and exalted into a new sensitivity of life. Let me give you this analogy of the matter: imagine a man shut up in a deep cave underground, without ever having seen a ray of light, his body tortured all over with pain, his mind distracted with rage, himself whirling and working with the utmost fury and madness, he knows not over what; and then you have an image of the first properties of life, as they are in themselves, before the fire had done its work in them.

Imagine this man suddenly struck, or entirely surrounded, by such a glare of light that, in the twinkling of an eye, it stopped or struck dead every working of every pain and rage, both in his body and mind; and then you have an image of the operation of the fire, and what it does to the first properties of nature. Now, as soon as the first terror of the light has had its fiery operation and struck dead every working sensibility of distress, imagine this man—as you now well may—in the sweetest peace of mind and bodily sensations, blessed in a new region of light that gives joy to his mind and gratification to every sense. Then the transports, the overflowings of Love and delight in this new state, may give you an image <note>of the New-birth and</note> how the Spirit of Love is and must be born when fire and light have overcome and changed the state of the first properties of nature. It can never exist in any creature until then, nor proceed from any other cause. Thus, sir, you may sufficiently see how vainly you attempt to possess yourself of the Spirit of Love through the power of your reason; and also what a vanity of all vanities there is in the religion of the unbelievers and deists, who will have no other perfection or divine life but what they can obtain from their reason. This is as great a contradiction to nature as if they would have no life or strength of body but that which can be obtained from their faculty of reasoning. For *reason can no more alter or exalt any one property of life in the soul and bring it into its perfect state than it can add one cubit to the stature of the body.* The perfection of every life is impossible to obtain except in the way every flower comes to its perfection; namely, from its own seed and root, and through the various degrees of transformation which must be experienced before the flower is found. IT IS STRICTLY THUS WITH THE PERFECTION OF THE SOUL; all its properties of life must have their true natural birth and growth from one another. The first properties, as its seed and root, must have their natural change into a higher state; like the seed of the flower, they must pass through death into life and be blessed with the fire, light, and spirit of heaven in their passage to it. Just as the seed passes through death into life, blessed by the fire, light, and air of this world until it reaches its final perfection and becomes a beautiful, sweet-smelling flower. And to think that the soul can attain its perfection any other way than by the change and exaltation of its first properties of life—just as the seed has its first properties changed and exalted until it produces its flower—is a total ignorance of the nature of things. For just as whatever dies cannot have a death particular to itself, but the same death in the same way and for the same reasons that any other creature, whether animal or vegetable, ever did or can die; so every life, and degree of life, must come into its state and condition of life in the same way and for the same reasons as life and the perfection of life come into every other living creature, whether in heaven or on earth. Therefore, the deist's religion, or reason, which is intended to raise the soul to its true perfection, is so far from being the religion of nature that it is quite unnatural, and declared to be so by every working in nature. For since reason can neither give life nor death to any one thing in nature, but everything lives or dies according to the working of its own properties, everything—dead and alive—demonstrates that nature asks no counsel of reason nor waits to be directed by it.

Hold it therefore for a certain truth that you can have no good come into your soul except by the one way of a birth from above, from the entrance of the Deity into the properties of your own soul-based life. NATURE MUST BE SET RIGHT, ITS PROPERTIES MUST ENTER INTO THE PROCESS OF A NEW BIRTH, IT MUST WORK TOWARD THE PRODUCTION OF LIGHT, <note>as indicated in Behmen's Way to Christ, in the tract "True Repentance,"</note> BEFORE THE SPIRIT OF LOVE CAN BE BORN IN YOU. For Love is delight, and delight cannot arise in any creature until its nature is in a delightful state, or it possesses that in which it must rejoice. And this is the reason why God must become man; it is because a birth of the Deity must be found in the soul, giving to nature all that it lacks, or the soul can never find itself in a delightful state, working only with the *Spirit of Love.* For while the soul has only its natural life, it can only be in such a state as nature is without God; namely, a state of mere hunger, want, opposition, and conflict for it knows not what. Hence comes all that variety of blind, restless, and opposing passions which govern and torment the life of fallen man. It is because all the properties of nature must work in blindness and do they know not what, until the light of God is found in them. Hence also it is that what is called the wisdom, the honor, the honesty, and the religion of the natural man often does as much harm to himself and others as his pride, ambition, self-love, envy, or revenge; and these are subject to the same whims and caprice. It is because nature is *no better* in one impulse than in another, nor can be, until something supernatural enters into it. We often charge men, both in church and state, with changing their principles; but the charge is too hasty, for no man ever did or can change his principles except by a birth from above. The *natural man*, called in Scripture the *old man*, is steadily the same in heart and spirit in everything he does, whatever variety of names may be given to his actions. For *self* can have no impulse but what *is selfish*, whichever way it goes or whatever it does, either in church or state. And be assured of this: that nature in every man, whether he is learned or unlearned, is *this very self*, and can be nothing else until a birth of the Deity is brought forth in it. There is therefore no possibility of having the Spirit of Love, or any divine goodness, from any power of nature or working of reason. It can only be had in its own time and place; and its time and place is nowhere but where nature is *overcome* by a birth of the life of God in the properties of the soul. And thus you see the infallible truth and absolute necessity of Christian redemption; it is the most demonstrable thing in all nature. The Deity must become man, take a birth in the fallen nature, be united to it, and become the life of it, or the natural man must necessarily be forever and ever in the hell of his own hunger, anguish, opposition, and self-torment; and all for this plain reason, because nature is and can be nothing else but this variety of self-torment until the Deity is manifested and dwelling in it.

And now, sir, you also see the absolute necessity of the gospel doctrine of "*the cross;*" namely, of **DYING TO SELF AS THE ONLY WAY TO LIFE IN GOD.** This "*cross,*" or dying to self, is the *one morality* that does man any good. Imagine as many rules as you like for modeling the moral behavior of man; they all do nothing because they leave nature still alive, and therefore can only help a man with a feigned, hypocritical art of concealing his own inward evil and appearing not to be under its power. And the reason why it must be so is plain: it is because Nature cannot be reformed; it is immutable in its workings and must always be as it is, and never any better or worse than its own untaught workings are. It can no more change from evil to good than darkness can transform itself into light. The one work of morality, therefore, is the one doctrine of **THE CROSS;** namely, to resist and deny nature so that a supernatural power, or Divine goodness, may take possession of it and bring a new Light into it.

In a word, in all the possibilities of things, there are only two states or forms of life: one is Nature, and the other is God manifested in nature; and as God and nature are both within you, you have it in your power to live and work with whichever you choose; but you are under a necessity of doing one or the other. There is no standing still; life goes on and is always bringing forth its realities, whichever way it goes. You have seen that the properties of nature are, and can be, nothing else in their own life but a restless hunger, disquiet, and blind strife—*for they know not what*—until the property of light and love has taken possession of them. Now, when you see this, you see the *true state* of every natural man, whether he is *Caesar* or *Cato*, whether he gloriously murders others or only stabs himself; blind nature does all the work and must be the doer of it until the Christ of God is born in him. For the life of man can be nothing else but a hunger of covetousness, a rising up of pride, envy, and wrath, a medley of contrary passions, doing and undoing it knows not what, because these workings are *essential* to the properties of nature; they must always be hungering and working against one another, striving to be above one another,

* THERE IS NO NEED FOR MANY PRACTICES OR METHODS in this matter. FOR TO DIE TO SELF, or to escape its power, is not and cannot be done by any *active resistance* we can make to it by the powers of nature. For Nature can no more overcome or suppress itself than wrath can heal wrath. As long as Nature acts, nothing but natural works are produced; therefore, the more labor of this kind, the more nature is fed and strengthened with its own food.
But the *one true way* of dying to self is most simple and plain; it requires no arts or methods, no cells, monasteries, or pilgrimages. It is equally practicable for everyone; it is always at hand; it meets you in everything; it is free from all deceit and is never without success.
If you ask what this one true, simple, plain, immediate, and unerring way is, it is the way of patience, meekness, humility, and resignation to God. This is the *truth and perfection* of dying to self; it is nowhere else, nor is it possible to be in anything else but in this state of heart.

---

*Theogenes.* — I readily acknowledge the excellence and perfection of these virtues; but alas, sir, how will this prove the way of overcoming *self* to be *as simple, plain, immediate, and unerring* as you say? For is it not the doctrine of almost all men and all books, and confirmed by our own woeful experience, that a great length of time, exercise, and a variety of practices and methods are necessary and barely sufficient to attain *even one* of these four virtues?

*Theophilus.* — When Christ our Savior was on earth, was there anything more simple, plain, immediate, or unerring than the way to him? Did scribes, Pharisees, publicans, and sinners need any length of time or exercise of rules and methods before they could be admitted to him or have the benefit of faith in him?

*Theogenes.* — I do not understand why you ask this question, nor do I see how it can possibly relate to the matter before us.

*Theophilus.* — It not only relates to it, but is the very heart and *truth* of the matter before us. It is not appealed to as an illustration of our subject; it is our subject itself, only set in a truer and stronger light. For when I refer you to patience, meekness, humility, and resignation to God as the one simple, plain, immediate, and unerring way of dying to self or being saved from it, I call it so for no other reason than because you can *easily* and *immediately*, without art or method, by the mere turning and faith of your mind, have all the *benefit* of these virtues, just as publicans and sinners could be helped and saved by turning to Christ.

*Theogenes.* — But, good sir, would you then have me believe that my turning and giving myself up to these virtues is as certain and immediate a way of being directly possessed and blessed by their good power as when sinners turned to Christ to be helped and saved by him? Surely this is too short a way and has too much of a miracle in it to be expected now.

*Theophilus.* — I WOULD HAVE YOU STRICTLY BELIEVE ALL THIS in the fullest sense of the words. And also believe that the reason why you, or anyone else, vainly endeavors for a long time after—and hardly ever attains—these first-rate virtues is because you seek them in the way they are not to be found: in a multiplicity of human rules, methods, and contrivances, and not in that simplicity of faith in which those who applied to Christ immediately obtained what they asked of him. <note>They are only another name for Christ, 'the Spirit of Love.'</note>

> “Come unto me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you.”

How short, simple, and certain a way to peace and comfort from the misery and burden of sin! What happens now to your length of time and exercise, your rules, methods, and roundabout ways to be delivered from self and the power of sin, and to find the redeeming power and virtue of Christ? Will you say that turning to Christ in faith was *once* indeed the way for *Jews* and heathens to enter into life and be delivered from the power of their sins, but that all this happiness ended as soon as *Pontius Pilate* had nailed this good Redeemer to the cross and thus broke off all *immediate* union and communion between faith and Christ?

WHAT FOLLY WOULD IT BE TO SUPPOSE that Christ, after having finished his great work, overcoming death, and ascending into heaven with all power in heaven and on earth, had become less of a Savior and gave *less certain and immediate* help to those who turn to him by faith now than when he was clothed with the infirmity of our flesh and blood on earth? Does he have less power after he has conquered than while he was only resisting and fighting our enemies? Or does he have less goodwill to assist his church, his own body, now that he is in heaven, than he had to assist publicans, sinners, and heathens before he was glorified as the Redeemer of the world? *Theogenes.*—You seem, sir, to have stepped aside from the point in question, which was not whether my turning, or giving myself up to Christ in faith in him, would do me as much good as it did to those who turned to him when he was upon earth. *Theophilus.*—I have stuck closely, my friend, to the point before us. Let it be supposed that I had given you a form of prayer in these words:

*Theogenes.*—What can I answer you, but that this is a most true and good prayer to Jesus, the Son of the living God? For who else but he was the Lamb of God and the bread that came down?

*Theophilus.*—Well answered, my friend. When, therefore, I exhort you to give yourself up in faith and hope to patience, meekness, humility, and resignation to God, what else do I do but turn you directly to that same faith and hope in the true Lamb of God? For if I ask you what the Lamb of God is and means, must you not tell me that it is, and means, the perfection of patience, meekness, humility, and resignation to God? Can you say it is either more or less than this? Must you not therefore say that a faith of hunger and thirst and a desire for these virtues is, in spirit and truth, the *one very same thing* as a faith of hunger, thirst, and desire for salvation through the Lamb of God? And consequently, that every sincere wish and desire, every inward inclination of your heart that presses after these virtues and longs to be governed by them, is an *immediate, direct application to Christ*. It is worshipping and falling down before him; it is giving yourself up to him and is the very perfection of faith in him.

If you distrust my words, hear the words of Christ himself:

> “Learn of me,” says he, “for I am meek and lowly of heart, and you shall find rest unto your souls.”

Here you have the plain truth of our two points fully asserted: *first*, that to be given up to, or to exist in a *desire* for patience, meekness, humility, and resignation to God, is strictly the same thing as to learn from Christ or to have faith in him. *Secondly*, that this is the one simple, short, and infallible way to overcome, or be delivered from, all the malignancy and burden of Self, expressed in these words: “and you shall find rest unto your souls.”

And all this is because this simple tendency, or inward inclination of your heart to sink down into patience, meekness, humility, and resignation to God, is truly giving up all that you are and all that you have from the fallen *Adam*. It is perfectly leaving all that you have to follow and be with Christ; it is your highest act of faith in him and love for him, the most ardent and earnest declaration of your clinging to him with all your heart and seeking for no salvation but in him and from him. And therefore all the good, blessing, pardon, and deliverance from sin that ever happened to anyone from any kind or degree of faith, hope, and application to Christ, is sure to be had from *this state of heart*, which stands continually turned to him in a hunger and desire to be led and governed by his spirit of patience, meekness, humility, and resignation to God. Oh **Theogenes**, if I could help you to perceive or feel what goodness there is in this state of heart, you would desire it with more eagerness than the thirsty deer desires the water brooks; you would think of nothing and desire nothing but to live in it constantly. It is a security from all evil and all delusion; there is no difficulty or trial, either of body or mind, and no temptation, either within you or without you, that does not have its full remedy in this state of heart. You have no questions to ask of anybody, no new way that you need to inquire after, and no oracle that you need to consult; for while you enclose yourself in patience, meekness, humility, and resignation to God, you are in the very arms of Christ. Your whole heart is his dwelling place, and he lives and works in you as certainly as he lived in and governed that body and soul which he took from the Virgin Mary.

Learn whatever else you will from men and books, or even from Christ himself besides or without these virtues, and you are only a poor wanderer in a barren wilderness where no water of life is to be found. For Christ is nowhere but in these virtues, and where they are, there he is in his

It is only natural to suppose—given the numerous objections made from time to time against those writings by many good (though perhaps unphilosophical) men, as well as by others less deserving of attention—that they would have clearly explained their drift and purpose to enlighten such people. This would leave opponents, if there are any after such an explanation, either to disprove their statement or admit it, and from then on duly respect what they might have ignorantly undervalued until then.

own kingdom. From morning to night, let this be the Christ you follow, and then you will fully escape all the religious delusions in the world and, what is more, all the delusions of your own selfish heart.

For to seek salvation through patience, meekness, humility of heart, and resignation to God is *truly* coming to God through Christ. When these temperaments live and abide in you as the spirit and aim of your life, then Christ is truly in you, and the life you then lead is not yours, but Christ living in you. For this is following Christ with all your power: you cannot possibly pursue him more quickly; you have no other way of walking as he walked, no other way of being like him, of truly believing in him, and of showing your trust in and dependence upon him, except by wholly giving yourself up to what he was: namely, to patience, meekness, humility, and resignation to God. [THE FOUR PROPERTIES OF THE SPIRIT OF LOVE.]

Tell me now, have I sufficiently proved to you the short, simple, and certain way of destroying that "body of Self" which lives and works in the four elements of covetousness, envy, pride, and wrath?

Theogenes — Quite enough. But as for covetousness, thank God, I cannot charge myself with it; it has no power over me—in fact, I naturally loathe it. And I also now clearly see why I have been struggling in vain for so long against other selfish temperaments.

Theophilus — Permit me, my friend, to correct your mistake. If covetousness had no power over you, you would have no other *selfish* temperaments to struggle against. They all die as soon as covetousness stops working in you. You assume covetousness relates only to the wealth of this world. But this is only one single branch of it; its nature is as broad as desire itself, and wherever *selfish desire* exists, the entire evil nature of covetousness is present.

Now, envy, pride, hatred, or wrath cannot possibly exist in you unless there is some *selfish desire* alive in you that is unsatisfied, ungratified, resisted, or disappointed. Therefore, as long as any selfish temperaments—whether envy, uneasiness, complaint, pride, or wrath—are alive in you, you have full proof that all these temperaments are *born and bred in* and from your own covetousness. That is, they come from that same *selfish bad desire* which, when turned toward the wealth of this world, is called covetousness. For all these FOUR ELEMENTS OF SELF, or fallen nature, are tied together in one inseparable bond; they mutually generate and are generated by one another; they share one common life and must all live or all die together. This shows you again the absolute necessity of our *one simple and certain* way of dying to self, and the *absolute insufficiency* of all human means to achieve it.

For consider only this: to be angry at our own anger, to be ashamed of our own pride, and to strongly resolve not to be weak is the peak of all *human endeavors*; yet all of this is the *life* rather than the death of self! There is no help except from a *total despair of all human help.* When a person is brought to such an internal, full conviction as to have no more hope from human means than they hope to see with their hands or hear with their feet, then they are truly prepared to die to self. That is, they give up all thoughts of having or doing anything good in any other way except through a meek, humble, patient, and total resignation of themselves to GOD. All that we do before this *conviction* is done in great IGNORANCE of ourselves, and is full of weakness and impurity. No matter how wonderful our ZEAL may be, if it begins sooner, or proceeds further, or toward any other matter, or in any other way than as led and guided by this conviction, it is full of delusion. No repentance, however long or laborious, is conversion to God until it reaches this STATE. For God must do everything, or everything is nothing; but God cannot do everything until everything is expected from him; and everything is not expected from him until, through a true and *good despair* of every human help, we have no hope, trust, or longing for anything but a patient, meek, humble, and total resignation to God.

And now, my dear friends, I have brought you to the very place for which I desired today’s conversation: to set your feet upon sure ground regarding the Spirit of love. For all the variety of subjects we have passed through has been only a variety of proofs that the *Spirit of Divine Love* can have no place or possibility of birth in any fallen creature until that creature wills and chooses to be dead to *all self* in a patient, meek, humble resignation to the good power and mercy of God.

From this state of heart, the "SPIRIT OF PRAYER" is also born, which is THE DESIRE OF THE SOUL TURNED TO GOD. Stand, therefore, steadfastly in this *will*; let nothing else enter your mind; have no other plan but to nourish and maintain *this* everywhere and in everything.

This latter fact appears so certain that the writer knows an individual who does not hesitate to claim that if he were a profound mathematician and were able to place himself back in the time and circumstances of Sir Isaac’s day, he has no doubt whatever of being able naturally—by force of imagination, thought, research, trials, experiments, etc.—to follow exactly the same path as Sir Isaac did and to arrive at the same results, just as the truth of things revealed itself in his mind. *state of heart, and then your house is built upon a rock; you are safe from all danger; the light of heaven and the love of God will begin their work in you and will bless and sanctify every power of your fallen soul. You will be ready for every kind of virtue and good work and will know what it is to be led by the Spirit of God.*

*Theogenes.* — But, dear Theophilus, though I am so delighted with what you say that I am loath to stop you, permit me to mention a fear that arises within me. Suppose I should find myself so overcome by my own darkness and *selfish temperaments* as to be unable to sink from them into a feeling of this meek, humble, patient, and full resignation to God; what must I then do, or how shall I have the benefit of what you have taught me?

*Theophilus.* — You are then at the very time and place to receive the fullest benefit from it and to practice it with the greatest advantage to yourself. For though this patient, meek resignation is to be exercised regarding all outward things and occurrences of life, it primarily concerns our own inward state: the troubles, perplexities, weaknesses, and disorders of our own fallen souls. And to remain *turned* toward a patient, meek, and humble resignation to God when your own impatience, wrath, pride, and lack of resignation attack you is a higher and more beneficial performance of this duty than when you remain turned toward meekness and patience when attacked by the pride, wrath, or disorderly passions of other people. I say, remain *turned* toward this patient, humble resignation, for this is your true performance of this duty at that time; and though you may have no comfortable feeling of performing it, yet in this state you may always have *one full proof of its truth and reality:* and that is, when you seek for help in no other way, nor in anything else—neither from men nor books—but WHOLLY LEAVE AND GIVE YOURSELF UP TO BE HELPED BY THE MERCY OF GOD. And thus, whatever your state may be, you may always have *the full benefit of this short and sure way of resigning yourself to God.* And the greater the perplexity of your distress is, the nearer you are to the greatest and best relief, provided you only have PATIENCE to expect IT ALL FROM GOD. For nothing brings you so close to divine relief as the *extremity of distress*; for the goodness of God has no other name or nature but as the helper of all that need to be helped; and nothing can possibly hinder you from finding this goodness of God and *every other gift and grace that you need.* Nothing can hinder or delay it but your turning from the only fountain of life and living water to some cracked cistern of your own making—to this or that method, opinion, division, or subdivision among Christians, carnally expecting some great things either from *Samaria* or *Jerusalem*, *Paul* or *Apollos*, which are only and solely to be had by worshipping the Father in *spirit and truth*: which is only done when your whole heart, soul, and spirit trust wholly and solely in the operation of that God *within* you, in whom we live, move, and have our being. AND BE ASSURED of this as a most certain truth: we have neither more nor less of the Divine operation within us because of this or that outward form or manner of life, but strictly in that degree to which our faith, hope, trust, and dependence upon God is more or less within us. [*Dead to Self, and alive to God: who wills this Salvation?*]

What a folly it is, then, to be so often perplexed about the way to God! For nothing is the way to God but our heart; God is nowhere else to be found, and the heart itself cannot find him, or be helped by anything else to find him, except by its own love of him, *faith in him, dependence upon him, resignation to him, and expectation of all from him.* ——

These are short but complete articles of true religion that carry salvation along with them; they make a true and full offering and sacrifice of our whole nature to the *Divine operation*, and also a true and full confession of the holy Trinity in Unity. For as they look wholly to the *Father* as blessing us with the *operation of his own Word and Spirit*, so they truly confess and worship the *Holy Trinity of God*. And as they ascribe everything to, and expect everything from, this Deity *alone*, so they make the truest and best of all confessions: that there is no God but One.

Let, then, *Arians, semi-Arians, and Socinians* <note>Theological groups that historically challenged the traditional doctrine of the Trinity.</note>, who puzzle their laborious brains to make paper images of a Trinity for themselves, have nothing from you but your pity and prayers; your foundation stands sure while you seek for all your salvation through the FATHER, working life in your soul by his OWN WORD and SPIRIT, which dwell in him and are ONE LIFE, BOTH IN HIM AND YOU.

However, to give a popular answer to the question, the writer would say that LAW is the Newton of metaphysics; he would also add, in the words of LAW, that “the ground and mystery of all things was never opened in any man but BEHMEN, and there are good reasons for supposing it will never again be opened in any other man;” that BEHMEN’S mind, therefore (and, in a good sense, our own mind also), as it was reflected as well as possible in the mirror and on the platform of his writings, is a grand mine or garden full of the seeds and births of universal truth; and that LAW (from a living knowledge and experience of it in his own microcosm) is the learned opener, displayer, and demonstrator of its riches and wonders. And if it were further remarked and asked, “since there can be nothing new in religion, and as Christianity is a complete system and a perfect revelation, what then is the use and purpose of these writings, and for whom are they intended?”—in other words, “who are the children of this mystery?” and “are these works profitable for Christians in general, and if so, for what end and to what degree?” The answer is, first, that they are not at all necessary for Christians, any more than the elements of geometry need to be understood by a working farmer or any other person engaged in the essential occupations of agriculture. For what has a working man to do with the philosophy of nature in searching out the *how* and the *why* of her operations? It is enough for him to know the facts of the course of nature without troubling himself about their ground and reasons; and with such knowledge, he pursues his business, sows his seed, and duly reaps enough to survive. Nor are these writings necessary to the great body of people in a Christian country—that is, those who receive as true the series of theorems constituting that branch of revealed truth called Christianity and contained in the Holy Scriptures. For these, accepting the truth of Christian doctrine, do not therefore require or demand a scholarly demonstration of it. Indeed, a fundamental demonstration of the truth of the Christian religion in all its parts, from first principles, would only puzzle and confound such simple souls and distract them from the one essential point, which is the end of all knowledge: the constant practice and personal verification of its truths. This very circumstance has occasionally happened regarding these writings; that is, some simple religious individuals have been greatly injured in their spiritual interests by their improper inquisitiveness into the writings of these authors (as they might have been by meddling with and misusing any other good gift of God), having thereby nearly lost themselves in an incomprehensible labyrinth. And yet, it must be admitted that in doing so, they paid no more regard to the plain nature of things than if they had been trying to master the seventeenth problem of the twelfth book of Euclid without having passed through or even looked at the preliminary books and course of study—and that with the sole object, strange as it may seem, of finding out the “plan of salvation” and saving their souls! Nor are these writings necessary to those happy, well-instructed individuals who are wholly and solely intent upon putting the Gospel revelation to the proof, thereby realizing the present fruits of faith and, it may be added, of the most perfect knowledge. Though they are conscious that there must, in the nature of things, be a deep, mysterious ground and philosophy of truth, they absolutely shut their eyes against any inquiry into it, whether it may have pleased the wisdom of God to reveal it or not. These blessed souls, receiving the truth for the love of it and knowing they may enjoy all the benefits of the most extensive understanding of it without understanding a single reason upon which it is founded, are the right men and heirs of faith; they hear God’s words, believe them, and compel themselves to obey them (even to the least of the commands and exhortations of Jesus Christ and his apostles), and so, in due time, after having served their day and generation according to the

“I come now to an enthusiast whom the doctor has accidentally met with, from whom, it seems, I have borrowed some of my strange notions and would pass them off as my own. For here a stranger, a layman, not even known to the doctor by name—who, for <gloss>all</gloss> he can tell, may be some small retailer of infidelity or a candle-snuffer in the playhouse, who has gained favor with the doctor by no other marks of ability and judgment but his compliments to him and his scurrility toward me—from the authority of this informer, the doctor immediately puts J. B. into his list of enthusiasts. Is this not a proof of what Sir Isaac Newton must have encountered from some great scholars, and to what a speedy refutation he must have exposed himself and the plainest appearances of nature, had he ever referred to the *Teutonic Theosopher?* Now, am I here to suppose that this censure of the doctor’s relating to J. B. is a rashness that has first seized upon him by *chance*; that he never before in his life allowed himself to treat *any man* or *any book* in this manner; that if he took the judgment of another, it was of somebody he knew; if he condemned an author, he always waited until he had read *something* of him, at least an *index*, or a *title page* or *two of his works?* Or am I to suppose that this has been the doctor’s method for over *thirty-seven years*: calling one man an enthusiast, another a fanatic, this a monstrous book, that the most pernicious book of the age, as rashly and hastily, regarding no more of right or wrong in what he affirms of these matters than he has done here regarding J. B.? But I hope the doctor is unique in this spirit; for if it could be supposed that it was common among learned men to get their knowledge of ancient and modern, foreign and domestic enthusiasts as hastily and slightly as the doctor does here, must it not be very dangerous for the unlearned to take any opinions of this kind from them? Must it not be said that *one grain of equity, good sense, and real knowledge is more to be desired than a hundredweight of such learning!*
>
> “When I considered the *fallen soul* as a *fire spirit* deprived of its *proper light*, and therefore becoming of a diabolical nature, I could have pointed to J. B. for the deep and infallible ground of it. But what need was there for that, when I could make the plainest principles of *nature*, the plainest doctrines of *Scripture*, everything that was said of the *fall*, of *heaven*, of *hell*, and the like, to be undeniable proofs of it? What I said in the *second proposition* of the discourse upon *regeneration* concerning the holy trinity of God in *man* does not stand in *that form* of expression anywhere that I know of; but for the true ground and certainty of it, I could have referred to the *Teutonic Theosopher*, to many ancient and modern writers of the greatest name, and to a *venerable record of antiquity* ascribed even to St. Peter himself, where he asserts, even upon the same ground as I have, that because we were created in the image and likeness of God, therefore the triune life arises in us as it does in God, and we have in us the *Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.**
>
> “But what occasion was there for these references when I had so much better proof, when I could show that all which the Scriptures say of the whole nature and manner of our redemption, of the whole *nature* and *form* of baptism, all that they say of the necessity of the *Word* and *Holy Spirit* of God having again a *birth in us*, are absolute decisive proofs of it? I also knew very well that the most essential, fundamental, and joyful doctrines of the Gospel would be *questioned* or received with *difficulty* had I referred to a poor shoemaker for any proof of them; and it may well be believed that the doctor would have been among the *first* and *loudest* of those who would have cried out at my folly and presumption in directing readers to an author whom all the world knew to be an *illiterate enthusiast;* and yet, if all the world knows it as the doctor knows it, all the world may be said to know nothing about it.”—Law’s Animadversions on Trapp’s Reply.

Under this view of things, and with a knowledge of the current methods used to evangelize the intellectual nations of the East, it may be justly remarked how imperfect, futile, wasteful, and unnatural those efforts and means appear for achieving the intended goal! Such a mode of propagating Christianity would seem to have neither reason, nor precedent in the Holy Scriptures, nor analogy in any of the workings of nature or the ordinary actions of life to support it. That some partial good may have resulted from it is beside the point, for every cause must have an effect according to both its nature and its extent. But to proceed as Christians are now doing among sophisticated nations—is it not like starting at the ends of a few branches of a stream and hoping, in due time, to change the nature of the source itself along with its many other branches? This was not the way St. Paul "went to work." St. Paul was the apostle to the *learned* as well as the *unlearned* Gentiles. He received his commission not from man but by revelation from heaven; he was an apostle not so much to those who already possessed the oracles of God (for the original apostles were sent to them) but to the Gentiles of *every name and character*. He was not sent to them until he had been endowed with the knowledge<note>The original text uses an asterisk here to point to the extensive footnote below.</note> of the highest theosophic mysteries, so as to be able to combat and convince, on their own grounds, all that the most profound, deep-thinking, and learned philosophers of Greece—many of them true theists and virtuous men—could or might propose or inquire regarding the doctrines of Christian salvation and the philosophy and "mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ," and of all things in heaven and earth. governed by the highest wisdom and knowledge of adapting cause to effect, what then must be said of our modern attempts at evangelizing the vast, rational, and *highly intellectual* continent of India, Persia, Turkey, or China? It must be said that it is the result of short-sighted advice, of half-thinking, and an inexplicably imperfect study of God’s wisdom and providence, as illustrated in the Holy Scriptures. And what are the effects of such endeavors, beyond the translation of the Scriptures, but a great waste of money, effort, and even life? Let the directors of missionary societies reflect a little upon this strangely overlooked but most essential point (as well as the donors of prize essays at the University of Cambridge and elsewhere, regarding the best means of introducing Christianity among the intellectual Mahommedan and other Asiatic nations), so that their future labors and expenditure may be productive of adequate fruits, being directed to rational ends by rational—indeed, divinely natural—means.

This remedy, it is to be observed, when it has done its work—that is, convinced its subjects of the truth of the gospel revelation, or served as a schoolmaster to lead them to Christ—is, of course, like the law of old, to be *laid aside*, having accomplished the end for which it was given to the world.
