As a discoverer of the false antichristian church, from its first rise in Cain, through every age of the world, to its present state in each and every sect of the currently divided Christendom. (3.) As a guide to the truth of all the mysteries of the kingdom of God. In these three respects, which contain all that anyone could possibly want to know or learn from any teacher, he is the strongest, plainest, most open, intelligible, awakening, and convincing writer that ever was. Regarding all these three matters, he speaks to everyone, as he himself says, *in the sound of a trumpet*. And here, to pretend to be his explainer, or to make him fitter for our understanding in these great matters, is as vain as if a man should pipe through a straw to make the sound of a trumpet better heard by us."

> “Jacob Behmen (he says), in his natural capacity and outward condition of life, was as humble and uneducated as anyone our Lord called to be an apostle; but as a chosen servant of God, he may be placed among those who had received the highest measures of light, wisdom, and knowledge from above. He was no more a human writer, and spoke no more from opinion, conjecture, or reason in what he published to the world, than St. *John* did when he wrote his Revelation. He has no right to be placed among the inspired *writers of the New Testament*; he was no messenger from God of anything new in religion; but the *mystery of all that was old and true* both in religion and nature was opened in him. This is the peculiarity of his character, by which he stands fully distinguished from all the prophets, apostles, and extraordinary messengers of God. They were sent with occasional messages, or to make such alterations in the economy of religion as pleased God. But this man came on no particular errand; he had nothing to alter or add, either in the form or *doctrine* of religion. He had no *new* truths of religion to propose to the world; but all that lay in religion and nature as an unsearchable mystery was, in its *deepest ground*, opened in this instrument of God. And all his works are nothing else but a deep manifestation of the foundations and reasons for what has been done, what is being done, and what is to be done, both in the kingdom of *nature* and the kingdom of *grace*, from the beginning to the end of time. His works, therefore, though immediately from God, do not at all share the *nature* of the Holy Scriptures; they are not offered to the world as necessary to be received, or as a rule of faith and conduct, and therefore no one has any right to complain either of the *depths* of his matter or the peculiarity of his style. They are just as they should be for those who are fit for them; and he who does not like them, or finds himself unqualified for them, has no obligation to read them.
>
> The entire system of Christianity has generally been viewed as a mystery of salvation founded solely on divine pleasure, and as a scheme of redemption to be wholly resolved into the contrivance of the *will* and wisdom of God; and therefore, men can think as differently about it, and fall into as many opinions, as they can regarding the *will* and wisdom of God. Hence has arisen all the speculative opposition to the Gospel: it is because reason, human speculation, and conjecture are always imagining they can form a religion more worthy of the wisdom and designs of the Supreme Being than the Christian religion is, and would be thought to oppose the Gospel only for the honor of God and the divine attributes. This is the great prevailing *idolatry* of the current heathen world, or that part of mankind who are infidels or deists. This body of people, whether they be *clergy* or *laity*, are but *nominal Christians*, because they have little more than the *name* of every mystery of the Gospel: *historical Christians*, because satisfied with the *history* of Gospel salvation: *literal Christians*, because looking only to, and contending only for, the *letter* of the institutions and mysteries of Jesus Christ. For the letter, for the federal rite, and the *figurative* expression of regeneration, they are all zeal and industry; but the *reality* of it, the *true life* of the new birth, they oppose and reject as heartily as the deist does the outward form and letter. Now this *twofold* idolatry of the present heathen and Christian world has its full discovery and confutation in the mystery opened in J. For, in the revelation made to this man, the *first beginning* of all things is opened, the *whole state, the rise, the workings, and the progress* of all nature are revealed, and every doctrine, mystery, and precept of the Gospel are found, not to have sprung from any arbitrary appointment, but to have their *eternal unalterable ground and reason in nature*; and God appears to save us by the methods of the Gospel, because there was NO OTHER POSSIBLE way to save us in all the possibility of Nature. And therefore the idolatrous confidence of the deist in *his own reason*, and of the *nominal Christian* in the *outward letter* of their religion, have equally their full confutation.

To those who confine idolatry to the worship of *such idols*, as the old heathens and *Jews* worshipped, it may seem a paradox to talk of the idolatry of the *present world*, either among Deists or *Christians*. But if we consider things more than words, we shall find that idolatry is nowhere, but where the heart has set up something in the *place of God*, and therefore is everywhere, and in everything, where the heart places that *repose, trust*, and *delight*, which should be placed in God alone. For God is only owned, and confessed to be *our God*, by these acknowledgments and dispositions of our hearts toward him. It is an infallible truth, that all sin has its beginning and continuance in and from idolatry: this alone debauched the former and the latter ages of the world, and is the one source of all the corruption of manners, from the beginning to the end of time. You do not make a golden calf, as the Jews did, to worship; but if mammon is your God, if your life is devoted to pride, ambition, and sensuality, your idolatry is not so obvious, but it is as real as theirs, who danced about a golden calf. You fancy that *Venus* is not your *goddess*, because you are not worshipping a *figured* image of her, in a temple called by her name; but if you look at the odes, the *hymns*, the *songs*, which you love, which lust has inspired, then you may know that *Venus* is the goddess of your heart. It is thus with every object, and in every course of life: that which possesses and governs our heart has usurped the *right and place of God* in it, and has that worship, trust, and devotion of the heart, which is due to God alone: and therefore the idolatry of the present world is only of a different kind from that of the ancient; it is less seen, and less confessed, but not less real, than when carved images and figured idols were adored.

Deism, or the religion of human reason, set up in opposition to the Gospel, is *direct idolatry*, and has every grossness and vanity of image worship. For to put our trust in our own reason, to be content with its light, to resign ourselves up to it, and depend upon it as our guide, is a mistake that has every grossness and vanity of the adoration of an idol. Now this kind of idolatry has overrun all the last ages of the world; it is the last effort of human vanity;* it is the utmost that idolatry can do, both to hide and propagate itself, and is the devil under the appearance of an angel of light. The Gospel has no enemy but this idolatry, and it is as visible in the church, as out of it: hence it is, that the state of the church is so sadly described in the *Revelation of St. John*, for so many ages, as a *spiritual whoredom*.—When the old *Jews* left off the *idols* of the heathens, they fell into an idolatry of another kind, which was this: they idolized the rites and ceremonies of their own true religion; they placed that *confidence in the outward letter*, and expected that good from their outward rites, which they should have placed, sought, and expected from GOD ALONE. This is the idolatry of the rational deist, and the nominal Christian. BUT, WHEN THE MYSTERY OF ALL NATURE AND GRACE, which by the mercy of God has opened itself in the writings of J. B., SHALL FIND ITS CHILDREN, EVERY IDOLATRY, both within and without the church, WILL BE ASHAMED TO SHOW ITSELF.

I prove to the world that his writings are the work of the Holy Spirit? The answer is, I neither intend nor desire to prove this to the world. And if anyone chooses to dispute or deny everything I have said of him, he will meet with no opposition from me. I have given notice of a PEARL; if anyone takes it to be otherwise, or has neither the skill nor the value for pearls, he is at liberty to trample it under his feet. Nothing passes with the world as proof of a divinely inspired writer except miracles; if people can see no other proof but this, it is not in my power to give them better eyes. I suppose the Gospel and all the writings of the New Testament have *internal characters* of their Divine origin for those who can see them; but if they had been left to those internal characters alone, I am inclined to think that the sons of *Cicero*, the disciples of a *Bayle*, or those who stand the highest in such literature would, of all men, be the most indisposed and unwilling to see and acknowledge them.

Had we no miracles for proof of the inspiration of the Scriptures, they would still be what they are: the *true word and wisdom of God*, and there would be the same benefit in believing and receiving them as such. But how can they be proved to come from the Spirit of God? Now, this can only be through an honest simplicity and love of truth, by humility and prayer, and the conversion of the heart to God in the reading of them. These are the only dispositions that could possibly bring any man into a sense and belief of their Divine origin. Therefore, all those critical scholars and rationally wise men, whose inquiries are driven by a love of glory and personal distinction, and who look into those writings for such ends and with such views as they read *other* books, would be of all men the most unable to see and unwilling to acknowledge the very *best truths* of the Holy Scriptures. This is because it is the very nature and purpose of the Scriptures to reveal the vanity and falseness of that light and knowledge which is gained from *human reasoning*, and to subdue that self-sufficiency which is so inseparable from *certain kinds and degrees of human learning*."

On another occasion, he thus briefly describes the mystery revealed in his embraced writings:

> This is clearly the case with that depth and fullness of Divine light and truth, opened by the mercy of God in the poor illiterate BEHMEN, who was so *merely* an instrument of Divine direction as to have no ability to think, speak, or write anything but what *sprung up in him*, or came upon him, as *independently* of himself as a shower of rain falls here or there independently of the place where it falls.

> His works, being an opening of the Spirit of God working in him, are quite outside the common path of man's reasoning wisdom, and proceed no more according to it than the living plant breathes forth its virtues according to such rules of skill as an artist must use to set up a painted, dead figure of it. But as the Spirit of God *worked* in the creation of all things, so the same Spirit worked and opened in the ground and depth of his created soul an inward *sensibility* of it.

> His writings begin where the Spirit of God began at the first rise of Nature and Creature. They are led on by the Spirit of God, *just as it proceeded* in the creation of angels and men, and all this material system of things. The all-creating Spirit of God which did, and still does all things, in every birth and growth of life, opened its process in this chosen instrument: Showing how all things came from a *working will* of the holy TRIUNE incomprehensible GOD, manifesting himself as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, through an outward perceptible working triune power of fire, light, and spirit, both in the eternal heaven and in this temporal transitory state of material nature: Showing from this eternal manifestation of God in the unity and trinity of heavenly fire, light, and spirit, how and what angels and men were in their creation; how they are in and from God, his real offspring, and born partakers of the Divine nature; how their life *began* in and from this Divine Fire, which is the father of Light, generating a birth of Light in their souls, from both of which proceeds the Holy Spirit, or breath of divine Love, in the triune creature, as it does in the triune Creator: Showing how *some* angels and all men are fallen from God and their first state of a Divine triune life in him; what they are in their fallen state, and the difference between the fall of angels and that of man: Showing also how and why there is good and evil in all this temporal world, in all its creatures, animate and inanimate, spiritual and material; and what is meant by the curse that dwells everywhere in it: Showing what are the natures, powers, and qualities of all creatures; the source and reason for their numberless variety; what they have of good in them and how they have it; what is the evil in them, and why there is such *strife* and *enmity* between creatures and creatures, elements and elements; what is meant by it, to what end it works, and when it shall cease;—how and why sin and misery, wrath and death, shall *only reign for a time*, until the Love, the Wisdom, and the Power of God shall, in a *supernatural way* (the mystery of GOD made MAN), triumph over sin, misery, and death; make fallen man rise to the glory of angels, and this material system shake off its curse and enter into an everlasting union with that heaven from which it *fell*."

The following is an extract from a letter of the same individual to the Bishop of London (Dr. Sherlock), in reply to his very complimentary acknowledgment of the published letter addressed to his lordship (containing the 'Confutation of Warburton'):

> "I am conscious that, in my later writings, I have raised a prejudice against me by espousing the writings of JACOB BEHMEN.

> "It was very easy for the world to find fault with me on that account. Matters for censure lie very open to the *critical reader* of his books; though the true ground of every doctrine and article of Christian faith and practice is there opened in such a ravishing, amazing *depth* and clarity of truth and conviction as had never been seen or thought of in any age of the church.

> "To regard him as a divinely-inspired writer will, for many, be proof enough of my being an enthusiast. But I am fully assured that if the most sober and just enemy to enthusiasm had but patience to read him until he in some degree understood his *ground and principles*, be he who he will, Christian or deist, he will find himself forced to think of him as I do, and that without adding either him to the number of apostles or his writings to the sacred canon."

> “I am less affected by any reproach, even from the learned world, on this account, because I think it is apparent enough that, from the beginning of the world, nothing extraordinary in the way of instruction ever came from God without meeting its chief opposition from what was the reigning wisdom and learning of the time.
>
> “The ground and reason why the *wise and prudent* of every age have less disposition and fitness to receive divine light and instruction than *babes and sucklings* lies in the nature of things; it will always be as true as when Christ said it regarding the doctrines which he himself preached to the world.
>
> “I could not refrain from saying this much to your lordship on this topic, but shall now only add my prayers to those of all good men among us, that it would please God to continue that life, which has been so manifestly useful in the most trying times, for the good of this part of the Christian church.”

The remaining extracts are mostly from his familiar letters to his friends:—

> “The charge of Spinozism brought against me by Dr. W. [as also, it may be added, that of Pantheism and other absurd, heterodox accusations*] has all the folly and weakness, etc., etc., that can be well imagined. For as Spinozism is nothing else but a gross confounding of God and Nature, making them out to be only one and the same thing, the full absurdity and absolute impossibility of it can only be fundamentally proved by that doctrine which can go to the bottom of the matter and demonstrate the *essential, eternal, and absolute distinction between God and nature*. This is a thing done over and over, from page to page, in those books from which the doctor has extracted Spinozism, with just as much acuteness as if he spotted rank Warburtonianism in my letter to the right reverend the bishop of London.
>
> “Now, though the difference between God and Nature has always been supposed and believed, the true ground of such distinction—or the *why*, the *how*, and in what way they are essentially different and must be so for all eternity—was to be found in no books until the goodness of God, in a way no less than that of a MIRACLE, enabled a poor illiterate man, in the simplicity of a child, to open and relate the *deep mysterious ground of all things*. In this is shown the *birth and beginning of nature*, or the *first workings* of the inconceivable God—opening and manifesting his hidden triune Deity in an outward state of glory—in the splendor of united fire, light, and spirit, all kindled and distinguished, all united and beautified by the hidden, invisible, inconceivable, supernatural Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—working all the glories in heaven, and every kind of life and blessing on earth, by visible and invisible fire, light, and spirit.
>
> “This is the wonderful *gift of God to these last distracted ages of the world*. As every purpose of God must stand and, sooner or later, produce all that which God intended by it, so the more the wise and the learned in all churches reject this counsel of God, the more they will promote its success over themselves, and only help it to come forth with greater strength and glory to God by being owned and proclaimed by the *mouths of babes and sucklings*.”

---

<note>* The following is one instance from among many others of the stupid, senseless stuff attributed to Behmen and Law by some *highly spiritual professors* of the popular evangelical school, who of course took it for granted that they themselves were competent judges of the depths of orthodox Christian doctrine: “Behmen and Law’s error,” say these luminaries, “is in maintaining that the soul of a believer possesses God’s incommunicable essence, or enters into that union by which the Three are One Jehovah; and John Arndt’s error is that, through the grace of the Lord Jesus, we partake of the Divine nature in the same manner that God exists in himself.” One would have thought such solemn twaddle regarding self-conjured “error” could only be found in the critical reviews of an insane asylum.</note>

In the case referred to in the above letter, Warburton’s pride could never forgive the defeat and mortification he had sustained at the hands of Law, having had his learned ignorance of the philosophy and spirit of Christianity exposed in such a glaring light to the world. Thus, he took every opportunity to excite prejudice against Law by disseminating, among other slanders, a charge against him of maintaining the detestable doctrine of Spinoza and the materialists, which places nature on the throne of God.

> “But Mr. Law’s doctrine only amounts to this (as the reader will already be prepared to hear): that Nature, in her original perfect state and celestial forms, was an outflowing from the ideas of the Divine Wisdom. And he no more supposes that nature in its present degraded state (first by the fall of angels, and afterwards through the fall of man) derived its grossness, darkness, and hard compaction from the Divine nature, than he supposes wicked men to derive their darkness and wrathful essence from it. And yet, that the spirit of man first came forth from God is taught in Scripture. Such as are unacquainted with the principles of the <term>TEUTONIC THEOSOPHER</term>, and have formed their ideas by that dead, erroneous system of philosophy which is commonly received among us, cannot understand the distinction between the materiality of nature in her present state of degradation, bondage, and corruption, and as it is conditioned in the angelic world. There, the luminous material vehicle of a seraph may as far transcend in splendor and thinness the nature of our light in this world as the latter does the darkness and density of a flint stone; indeed, for all we know, the difference may be inconceivably greater. Hence it is that our definition of matter, regarding its essential properties, has nothing to do with heavenly materiality. To take only the property of solidity: how is this compatible with the body of an angel, which can pass through a quarry of the hardest marble as easily as through the yielding air? And if even our present ideas of matter extend to a supposed pure ether, too subtle to be the object of sense, what unassignable gradations may belong to it in the highest heavens? Indeed, what stretch of our understanding or imagination shall fix its bounds and say, 'Thus far shall you go, and no farther'? Who can pronounce it incapable of sensibility? Indeed, who will say that in its further ascent of refinement toward its first cause, it does not rise up to intellectuality? Or that the difference between created spirit and created matter, in its nearest approach to the throne of God, is not specific rather than generic? Indeed, to give the highest flight to hypothesis, who can positively deny that it derives its first and purest essence from the original ideas conceived in the womb of the divine imagination, and by the Almighty FIAT substantiated into created forms?”

—Hartley. See also Paynes’ Letter to Warburton. 8vo. 1761.

Again, referring incidentally to the same subject in another letter to a friend, he may be said to include in his voluntary observations at the end of it another antagonist (Dr. H. <note>Dr. George Horne</note>), who had used exactly the same angry, insulting language as Warburton in a "Letter" he had dared to publish condemning Boehme’s writings. He also expressed similar sentiments in a printed tract titled "Cautions to the Readers of Mr. Law," a copy of which had been sent to Mr. Law by a friend for him to read. The "letter" is such an insignificant production*—being a web of mere misrepresentations and fallacious reasonings based upon disconnected extracts from J. B. <note>Jacob Boehme</note>; in short, an attempt to confuse the matter and thereby deceive a weak mind—that Mr. Law gave no further notice to the writer than what is contained in the ironic remark at the end of the letter mentioned above. The extract from it is as follows:—

> "Let me here, sir, observe to you (he writes) the barefaced slander that Dr. W. has dared

---

*Another production of the same character was the "Letter" to the subject of our proposed biography, published in print in the year 1756. Although it was incomplete, it has very unwisely been included in the standard edition of the writer's works published since his death. Mr. L. alluded to it shortly after it appeared in a letter to a friend who had sent him a copy of it:—"Mr. * * * <note>John Wesley</note> is an ingenious man, and the reason why his letter to me is such a childish composition of emptiness and *rudeness* (!) as is below the character of any man who had been serious in religion for even half a month, is because it was not ability (!) but necessity that put his pen into his hand. He had condemned my books, preached much against them, and, to make all sure, forbade his people from using them. And as a cover for all this, he promised from time to time to write against them. Therefore, an answer had to be made *at any cost*."—And again, in another letter, in answer to one from Lady Huntingdon: "Mr. * * *’s letter did not at all disappoint me. I had no expectation of seeing a better, either regarding the *substance* or the *style* and manner of it. If I knew of any kind of answer that would do him any real good, I would suggest it. But to answer it for the good of anyone else seems to be quite unnecessary. It does not admit of a serious answer because there is *nothing substantial* or properly argumentative in it. And to answer it with ridicule is something I cannot agree to, as I am as unwilling to mock him in a religious garment as I am to do the greatest physical injury to his person. * *

> "As for myself, I seem to have no other part to play, nor any calling to anything else in this hurry and struggle of zeal against zeal in such a variety of forms, but only and fully to assert the true foundation and extensively explain all the reasons for that one inward regeneration. This is equally the one thing necessary to every sect, and the one thing alone that can make every sect, method, or outward form not harmful to those who adhere to it. For every outward form, however attractive or promising, will only help us to be worldly-minded until it is understood to have no other or better nature than that of the *shell* which helps us reach the *kernel*.
>
> "The doctrines I have published are in their best state for the reader as they stand in my books, and will be less useful to him when they are dragged into controversy. For this reason, I can give no help to that.
>
> "This may, perhaps, seem to your ladyship as if I had too high an opinion of what I had done; and I believe such a free way of speaking of my own books in conversation may sometimes have been suspected of smelling too much of self-esteem. But I can truthfully assure you, madam, that when I speak of the *fullness* and *clarity* of my own writings, I feel no more sense of self-sufficiency than when I speak of the health of my own eyes. Nor do I know how to consider the one more than the other to be any merit of my own; and therefore, when any man, great or small, despises, reproaches, or slanders me or my books as devoid of sense, truth, and light, I feel no more inward discomfort, nor think myself any more hurt, than if he had only told the world that my eyes were miserably bad and I could *scarcely see to read, even with the best spectacles!* And so I have no desire to defend the one through controversy more than the other, but contentedly leave them both to be their own proof of what they are.
>
> "I was once a kind of oracle to Mr. * * *. I never suspected anything bad of him, nor ever discovered any kind of falsehood or hypocrisy in him. But during all the time of his intimacy with me, I judged him to be much under the power of his *own spirit*, which seemed to predominate in every good thing or way that his zeal carried him toward.
>
> "It was owing to his unwillingness or inability to give up his own spirit that he was forced into that false and rash criticism which he published against the mystics:—*as enemies to good works, and even tending toward atheism*. A criticism so false and so regardless of right and wrong that hardly anything can exceed it, which is to be found in a preface of his to a book of *hymns!*—But no more of this. Feb. 16, 1756."

The person referred to here, at a more mature period of his life, retreated greatly from his intensity of spirit and strong opposition to everything that did not harmonize with his temperament and peculiar views of the moment. Mr. Henry Brooke of Dublin, a great admirer of Mr. Law and of the most edifying of the spiritual writers, once reproached the individual mentioned above for his rash and groundless criticisms of the mystics, which were permanently inserted in his published writings, journals, etc.; to which he sent the following very worthy and Christian reply:—"April 21, 1783. Dear Harry,—Your letter gave me pleasure, and pain too. It gave me pleasure because it was written in a mild and loving spirit; and it gave me pain because I found it had pained you, whom I so tenderly love and esteem. But I shall do it no more; I sincerely thank you for your kind reproof: it is a precious balm—and will, I trust, in the hands of the Great Physician, be the means of healing my sickness. I am so aware of your real friendship in this that I cannot write without tears. The *words* you mention were too strong; they will no longer fall from my mouth."

Had I only proved, as I have done by a variety of proofs, that *wrath* cannot possibly be in the true God, I would have sufficiently refuted Spinozism; for if there is no wrath, then nothing of nature is in God. But I have gone much further and have, in my last six books, opened

---

The way in which this "indefatigable man of business"—who, if Law might be considered the perfecter of the steam engine and inventor of locomotives, might himself be considered as the managing director of the first English railway company and chief engineer!—proceeded to study and fathom the scope and depth of Behmen’s <note>Jacob Boehme</note> writings (of which he had heard so much said by the learned as containing the revelation of the ground and philosophy of all things, with a fundamental demonstration of all the particular truths of Christianity) is thus naively described by himself in his diary. As, doubtless, his above-mentioned published letter was founded upon such a mode of examination, the reader may form some conjecture of its character and of the probable appropriate description given of it by Law in the above extracts, as also of the value of such an individual’s judgment upon matters out of the sphere of his natural temperament and idiosyncrasy. We may also thereby understand the difference between what is termed *popular evangelical theology* (to the self-activity and energetic character of which all profound exhibitions of Christian truths, requiring time and patience, are unbearable) and *philosophic Gospel truth*, which, possessing all the devotion and solid experience of the former, considers truth, both divine and natural, as a science which must necessarily have a *root, stem, and branches*, and be one undivided whole. Strange as it may seem, such is the very character given of Behmen’s works by an apostolic descendant of the above-mentioned individual, after a very brief acquaintance with them, in these terms: “I have formerly (said he to the writer of these lines in the month of May 1847) read through all systems of metaphysics, and am now convinced that the philosophy of BEHMEN is the only true philosophy. They are, as it were, pieces of the circumference, while this comprises both the *center and the whole of truth*.”

The passage above referred to from the individual’s diary runs thus: “Friday, June 4th, 1742. <note>This was about four years after the period when (see his letter to Mr. Law of May 14th, 1738) he considers he had discovered he was but a “child of hell,” “having the faith of a devil!” etc., though for thirteen years previous he had been a most sincere, devoted Christian. The fact was, he was just emerging out of the legal state into the Gospel state; but the popular character of his religious education, not having made him master of the rationale and scope of Mystic Theology, he had not understood his true state and position in the experience of Christianity. But now that he had passed through the legal state, and also that in the *flesh*, and further had entered into the new birth of the Spirit, or spiritual state of Christianity, he fancied (as almost all new converts do) that he ought to have been in this state from the very first; and thereupon he flies at Mr. Law, his spiritual preceptor, in the letter referred to, for not having taught him this at first. But Mr. Law knew his business too well ever to lead souls imperfectly: he, like his Master, knew the absolute necessity of a deep scriptural foundation for a high superstructure of holiness, and therefore in his first works, he keeps his students under the ministry of the law and of Christ in the *flesh*, until they are grown naturally ready, by a conscious, inwardly felt *WANT* of a radical change—yes, in their very essences—in order to a full deliverance from their present bondage into the glorious liberty of the light of God! And so it occurred in this individual’s case, in God’s own time and way, because he was pressingly desirous, *earnest*, and diligent. But Mr. Law is as free from blame as Kempis or the Holy Spirit himself regarding this individual’s experience; on the contrary, as the instrument of the latter (regarding the *amazing results of this individual’s subsequent career*), “to him, it brings endless honor,” as will be shown in the Biography when demonstrating the former part of the *Elias-Baptist* character of his mission. But to proceed with the extract.</note> “Hence,” says he, “I rode to Beeston. Here I met once more with the works of a celebrated author of whom many great men cannot speak without rapture and the strongest expressions of admiration: I mean Jacob Behmen. The book I now opened was his *Mysterium Magnum, or Exposition of Genesis*. Being conscious of my ignorance, I earnestly besought God to enlighten my understanding. I seriously considered what I read and endeavored to weigh it in the balance of the sanctuary. And what can I say concerning the part I read? I can and must say this much (and that with as much evidence as I can say that two and two make four): it is most sublime nonsense, inimitable bombast, fustian not to be paralleled! etc.” Now, to judge of the soundness of this nonsensical, bombastic, fustian decision, we may substitute for Behmen’s works Euclid, Algebra, Trigonometry, or the whole range of scientific erudition; and instead of the individual, an intelligent, virtuous farmer who has “but one business” at heart—namely, the cultivation of his farm—and who entertains a dignified contempt for all practical knowledge in comparison to the art of raising good crops. Now, suppose this honest farmer, in the course of his journeys, were to meet with some treatises upon the mathematical and other sciences mentioned above, and thereupon kneel down and earnestly beseech God to enlighten his understanding and give him such a knowledge of those sciences that he shall be able at once to perfectly comprehend the treatises. And having “prayed in faith, nothing doubting,” imagine him rising from his knees, seriously opening the works, and as a matter of course, being unable to comprehend them any more than before he “prayed in faith, nothing doubting.” Imagine him now passing his judgment upon them in these words: “I am now assured—yes, with as much certainty as that two and two make four—that these pretended sciences are sublime nonsense, inimitable bombast, fustian not to be <margin>e/</margin> paralleled.” Thus we would have a fair illustration of the above most rational mode of testing the science and orthodoxy of Behmen!

What is most excellent among the *** comes the nearest to what is laid down in their spiritual writings; and had Mr. *** studied them more himself,

Does not God impart and reveal his wisdom to us diversely, as he manifests the tincture of the mystery in the earth through diverse fair plants? Even so it is in us men, who should love one another the more for his revealing his wisdom so variously in us; but he that judges and condemns another in an evil way, only runs on in *self-will* and pride, and is the oppressor in Babel, who stirs up contention and strife."

<margin>d</margin>
The following is another passage, taken from the same individual's published diary; but it ought to be removed from future editions of his works, for if Behmen really was the inspired instrument of God, then to call him an *ingenious madman* is direct blasphemy:—"A few things (he writes) in the second volume of Dr. Byrom's Poems, are taken from Jacob Behmen; to whom I object, not only that he is obscure, (although even this is an inexcusable fault in a writer on practical religion,) not only that his whole hypothesis is unproved, wholly unsupported either by Scripture or reason: but that the ingenious madman over and over contradicts Christian experience, reason, Scripture, and himself." Now all this, starting from the parenthesis, is both utterly false and groundless, and yet he reiterates the same assertions as had already been confuted, and the contrary demonstrated, over and over again. But surely, not another line need be quoted, to show the justice of Mr. Law's remarks, (in the above letter,) upon this individual's subjection to his *own spirit*.—If one more, however, be wanting, here it is, taken from his thirteenth journal:—"St. John (he writes) speaks as high and as deep things as Jacob Behmen. Why, then, does not Jacob speak as plainly as him?"!! The Bible speaks as high and as deep things as Sir Isaac Newton, or a perfect master of the whole range of the sciences; why, then, does not such a philosopher write in the same style as the Bible? Juvenile, disreputable stuff!—and yet, if weighed in the *true balances of the sanctuary*, there never was, nor can be, an objection made to Behmen, possessing more of sound reason, justice, and *strict propriety*, than is contained in this absurd sentence; indeed, where such objections are not traceable to a peculiar idiosyncrasy, they will be invariably found to emanate from a 'fox and grapes' principle of judgment.

And as to the obscurity sometimes complained of in the phrases and writings of Behmen, and of other mystic philosophers and spiritual authors, the objection is without foundation, and can only be made by those who dislike the trouble of applying themselves to understand them. 'All arts and professions have their appropriate terms, suited to their respective provinces, and so has mystical theology, for a much higher reason, namely, as it treats of subjects beyond the reach of nature and natural knowledge, being conversant with the things of a new world and the operations of the Holy Spirit in the soul of believers; which words of familiar use in language cannot properly express the ideas attached to them. And therefore deep spiritual writers are often led to use new words and figures of speech, which may seem very strange and incongruous to those that first enter into this school; but by patience and application they will come to be well understood, yes, approved of by the diligent learner, just as the words of any other language, of which we only become masters by study and practice. But there is also another reason for that venerable obscurity in which we see certain spiritual truths involved, namely, that it may serve as a veil to conceal them the more from those that are not as yet fit for them; and also to guard them against the abuse of such as are of a mocking spirit—(from which some professed Christians are not delivered)—and which would only serve to their greater disadvantage: and therefore our Lord says, *Cast not your pearls before swine*; and for this reason, he couched many Divine truths in parables, only to be known by *those that were in a disposition to receive them*. Now, the veil thus spread over certain sacred truths, to conceal them from the unworthy and profane, answers this good end, namely: such persons, though possessed of the outward expression, yet being unable to come at the meaning but by serious study and pains; such a previous course of discipline and application might serve as a good means to rectify their disorder, to remove their prejudice, and to prepare them as proper vessels to receive the truth. And thus proceeded even the wiser heathens, with respect to what little truth they were possessed of, in the more obscure mysteries of their religion: none were admitted into them until they had passed their novitiate, or preparatory stages of discipline.'

But what is more strange of all, it is now almost a moral certainty that all that peculiarity of doctrine concerning the New-birth (with, however, many invented crudities added to and mixed up with it,) with which the individual here referred to so specially identified himself and all his people, was originally derived, and that in a direct line, from this very Behmen's "Way to Christ," the only treatise he ever published in print, and which was productive of so great a revival of Christianity in his own day, where it was received, and doubtless in subsequent ages, until the time of its translation into this country. The writer has had an opportunity of pursuing his research on this point, since it was touched upon in the note of p. 42: and should any one desire to obtain a glimpse of that fact, until the history of the whole matter be traced out publicly, he has only to make himself acquainted with the life of Behmen, and the above-mentioned effects of his "Way to Christ" in his lifetime; then to peruse the first and second of the individual's journals, and such other passages of the rest as relate to the Moravians, and connect the mystics with them; and then

It was rather singular in this individual (though quite consistent with *prudence*) to omit the insertion in his diary of the correspondence that took place between himself and Mr. Law in the year 1738, as previously alluded to, when he fancied he had made a wonderful discovery about the meaning of "faith" and that Mr. Law had been misleading him, indeed was in darkness and error himself. His executors, however, found the correspondence among his papers after his death and published it in their periodical (1795), both the letters of this individual and those of Mr. Law. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of a humble heart for receiving divine truth, emphasizing that intellectual ability is no substitute for a sense of spiritual poverty and warning against the "Pharisaic" spirit in modern religious institutions.</meta>

son to be content with the success that God gives it. "He who has ears to hear, let him hear," may be enough for you, just as it was for our blessed Lord.

The next thing that belongs to us, which is also godlike, is a true, sincere patience and *meekness*, showing every kind of goodwill and tender affection toward those who turn a deaf ear to us; looking upon it to be just as contrary to God's method, and the good state of our own heart, to dispute with anyone in contentious words, as to fight with him for the truths of salvation.---

"Come to me, all you who *labor and are heavy laden*, and I will give you rest," says our blessed Lord. He called no one else, because no one else had ears to hear, or a heart to receive the truths of redemption.

Every man is a vain debater, until such time as something has disturbed his state, and awakened in him a sensitivity to his own evil and miserable nature. We are all of us afraid of both inward and outward distress; and yet, until distress comes, our life is but a dream, and we have no awakened awareness of our own true state.

We are apt to consider intelligence and abilities as the proper qualifications for the reception of divine truths; and we wonder that a man of a fine understanding should not immediately embrace just and solid doctrines: but the matter is quite otherwise. Had man kept possession of his first rich and glorious state, there would have been no foundation for the gospel redemption; and the doctrine of "the cross" must have appeared quite unreasonable to be pressed upon him: and therefore says our Lord, "To the poor the gospel is preached." It is solely to them, and no one else: that is, to poor fallen man, *who feels* he has lost all the true natural riches and greatness of his first divine life; to him is the gospel [or glad tidings of its restoration] preached. But if a man knows and feels nothing of this poverty of his nature, he is not that person to whom the gospel belongs: it has no more suitability to his state than it had to man before the Fall: and then the greater his intelligence and abilities are, the better he is qualified to show the *folly* of every doctrine of that salvation of which he has no need!

Such a man, though he may be of a humane, noble, generous, and frank nature, of lively intelligence and much candor, is nevertheless entirely ignorant of the depth of the heart of man, and the necessities of human nature. As yet, though he knows it not, he is only at play and pastime, pleasing himself with supposed "deep inquiries after truth," while he is only amusing himself with lively wandering images of this and that, just as they happen to start up in his mind. Could he but see himself in the state of the poor distressed prodigal son, and *find that he himself is the very person recorded there*, he would then, but not until then, see the fitness of that redemption which is offered him by the mercy of God in CHRIST JESUS. But such a person, alas! is rich; he is healthy; light is in his own power, goodness is in his own possession: he feels no distress or darkness; but has a *crucible of reason and judgment* that on every occasion separates gold from dross: and therefore he must be left to himself, to his own elysium, until something more than argument and debate awakens him out of these golden dreams.---

Let us beware also of the religious pharisee, who raves against *spiritual religion*, "because it touches the very heartstring of all systematic divinity," and shakes the very foundation of every BABEL in every country; for not a system of divinity, since systems began, whether Catholic or Protestant, deserves a better name.

All preachers of the true spiritual mystery of the gospel, of a birth, light, and life from above, in and by JESUS CHRIST (who are the mystic writers of every age), ever were, and will be treated by the reigning *fashionable orthodoxy* as enemies to the outward gospel and its services, just as the prophets of God (who were the mystic preachers of the Jewish dispensation) were by the then reigning orthodoxy condemned and despised, for calling people to a spiritual meaning of the dead letter, to a holiness infinitely greater than that of their outward sacrifices, types, and ceremonies.

Whoever he is that has any situation of his own to defend, be it that of a celebrated preacher, a champion for received orthodoxy, a head, a leader, or follower of any sect or party, or particular method; or that seems, both in his own eyes and in the eyes of others, to have made himself significant in any kind of religious distinction; every such person, sooner or later, will find that he has much of *that very same* pride to give up, which hindered the zealous and eminently religious pharisee from converting to Christ in the spirit of a "little child."

Nor does it help the matter, that such a person abounds with *piety* and *excellence* <note>as some of the aforementioned voluntary opponents may do</note>; for Saint Paul was governed by a spirit of great piety, great excellence, and zeal for God. He says of himself, that when he was persecuting the disciples of Christ, he "lived in all good conscience, as touching the law blameless, and according to the strictest sect of the Jewish religion": for the pharisees, though many of them had all that hypocrisy and rottenness which Christ laid to their charge, yet as a sect, they were an order of most confessed and resplendent sanctity; and yet the more earnest and upright they were in this kind of zeal for goodness, the more earnestly they opposed and condemned the heavenly mystery of a *new life from CHRIST*, as appears by Saint Paul.

This sect of the pharisees did not cease with the Jewish church; it only lost its old name; it is still in existence, and springs now in the same manner from the *gospel*, as it did then from the *law*: it has the same place, lives the same life, does the same work, minds the same things, has the same goodness at heart, has the same religious honor and claim to piety in the Christian, as it had in the Jewish church; and as much mistakes the depths of the mystery of the Gospel, as that sect mistook the mystery signified by the letter of the law and the prophets.

It would be easy to show, in several instances, how the leaven of that sect works among us, just as it did among them. "Have any of the rulers believed on him?" was the *orthodox* question of the ancient pharisees. Now, we Christians readily and willingly condemn the weakness and folly of that question; and yet who does not see, that, for the most part, both *priest and people* in every Christian country, live and govern themselves by the folly and weakness of the very same spirit which put that question? For when God, as he has always done from the beginning of the world, raises up private and illiterate persons full of light and wisdom from above, so as to be able to discover all the workings of "*the mystery of iniquity*," and to open the ground, and truth, and absolute necessity of such an inward spirit and life of CHRIST revealed in us, as time, carnal wisdom, and worldly policy, have departed from; when all this is done by the weakest instruments of God, in such a simplicity and fullness of demonstration, as may be justly deemed a MIRACLE, do not clergy and laity get rid of it all, though ever so unanswerable, merely by the strength of the pharisee's

> Let me first premise this much. Every man in his fallen state has all that in him—though in a state of death and hiddenness—which was the *living glory and perfection* of the first created man. Just as the *root* of the lily, in the winter's cold, has all that in it—though as if in a state of death—which was the glory and beauty of the summer's flower. What is hidden in the root of the lily lies no longer in its seeming death than until the spring sun calls forth its life. Now, *one divine dispensation after another is to do that same thing to the fallen soul* which the spring and daily advancing sun do to the lily root; namely, to call it out of its state of death, and make something of its first glory come to life and spring forth out of it. Hence it is that "the kingdom of God (which was that to which Adam died) is like treasure hidden in a field"; and again, "the kingdom of God is within you." But this could not be true unless all that glory which Adam lost was still preserved as a *seed* or shut-up root of life within him: and all this is through the mercy and *free grace* of God, who, foreseeing the fall of Adam, willed that a *seed* of his first glory should be preserved in him, declared and made known to him by a *seed of the woman*, which through the Word made flesh should, in spite of death and hell, grow up to the "fullness of stature in Christ Jesus."
> 
> And as the kingdom of heaven is every man's treasure, as surely within him as his own soul, so that which hides and covers it from us is that awakened, *bestial life* which is called Adam in us; and in which the immortal soul, that was born for heaven, is wedded to the "lusts of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life," and subject to the workings of that satanic nature which our Lord calls the *prince of this world*. And thus it is that every man comes into this world in a twofold state: Adam and Christ are both born in him. And if this was not the state of man, nothing within you would or could ask, as you have done, or have any anxiety after the truth. And your being either led from this true *knowledge* of your state, or having never been *aware* of it, is the *reason* for your having made so many religious inquiries in vain, both from yourself and other people. For nothing can tell you the truth, or establish you in a *just and solid discernment* of right from wrong in doctrines, opinions, and practices of religion, but this home-knowledge of yourself: namely, that Christ and Adam are not only both of them *essentially* within you, but the *whole* of you; that nothing is life or salvation but that which is the *life and growth of Christ* in you; and that all that is done from the *life, the power,* and *natural capacity of the Adamical nature* is heathenish, is mere vanity and death, however gloriously set forth by the natural gifts of intelligence and learning.
>

Satan is known by you in no other way, and can have no other fellowship with you, except as his evil spirit works and manifests itself along with the workings of your own spirit. "Resist the devil, and he will flee from you"; but he is nowhere to be resisted except as a working spirit *within* you; therefore, to resist the devil is to turn from the evil thoughts and motions that arise within you. "Turn to God, and he will turn to you"; but God is a universal spirit, which you cannot locally turn to or from; therefore to turn to God is to cleave to those good thoughts and motions which proceed from his Holy Spirit, dwelling and working in you. This is the God of your life, to whom you are to adhere, listen, and attend, and this is your worshipping him in spirit and in truth. And that is the "devil that goes about like a roaring lion," who has no voice except that which he speaks within you. Therefore, my friend, be at home, and keep close to that which passes within you; for be it what it will, whether it be a good in which you delight or an evil at which you grieve, you could have neither the one nor the other except because a holy God of light and love is essentially dwelling in you. matter is decisively determined: both where truth is found and who can have knowledge of it.

->*Heavenly truth* is nowhere spoken except by the voice of CHRIST, nor heard except by the power of<-
living word and SPIRIT working within you. For if anything else could have been man’s way to God, the WORD would not have been made flesh.

The last words in your question—namely, *to be in the truth*—are well expressed; for to be in the truth is the final state of man returning to God, as declared by Christ himself: “You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free”; free from the blindness and delusion of your own natural reason, and free from forms, doctrines, and opinions which others would impose upon you. To be in the truth is to be where the first holy man was when he was created in the image and likeness of God. When he lost paradise, he lost the truth, and everything he felt, knew, saw, loved, and enjoyed in the earthly, animalistic world into which he had fallen was nothing but separation from God—a veil over his heart and scales over his eyes. Nothing of his *original truth* could be spoken to him, even by God himself, except under the veil of earthly things, symbols, and shadows. “The law was given by Moses,” but Moses had a veil over his face: *the law was a veil, prophecy was a veil, Christ crucified was a veil*, and everything was a veil until “grace and truth came by Jesus Christ” through the power of His HOLY SPIRIT. Therefore, to be in the truth “as it is in Jesus” is to come out from under the veil and to have passed through all those religious eras which would never have begun if they were not meant to end with Christ being spiritually revealed and essentially formed within the soul. So now, in this last era of God’s plan—which is the original truth itself restored—nothing is to be considered, trusted, or sought after except God’s immediate and continual work in the soul through His Holy Spirit. This, sir, is *where* you are to go and *what* you are to do *to be in the truth*. For the truth as it is in Jesus is nothing other than Christ coming in the Spirit, and His coming in the Spirit is nothing other than the first lost *life* of God brought to life and revealed again in the soul. Everything short of this has only the nature of an outward symbol and figure which, at its best, is only temporary. If, therefore, you look to anything but the Spirit, seek any power but that of the Spirit, or expect Christ to be your Savior in any other way than as He is spiritually born within you, you regress from the *grace and truth that came through Jesus* and can at best be only a *legalistic Jew* or a *self-righteous pharisee*. There is no progressing further than these states except by being “born of the Spirit” and living by the Spirit as His child, His instrument, and the holy temple in which He dwells and performs all His good pleasure. Give up this *complete adherence to and dependence upon the Spirit*, act within your own sphere, try to be something of yourself through your own wisdom, and so on—then, even if everything you say or do uses the outward words of the *spiritual gospel* and the outward practices of the spiritual apostles, you are still only in the same position as those who worshipped God with the blood of bulls and goats. For (N.B.) nothing but the Spirit of God can worship God in spirit and in truth.

But you will, *perhaps*, say that you are still no further along because you do not know how to find the *continual guidance* of the Holy Spirit. If you know how to find your own thoughts, you do not need to be at a loss to find the Spirit of God. For you do not have a single thought within you that is not either from the goodness of the *Spirit* or from the evil of the *flesh*. Now, the good and the evil within you, which are always more or less noticeable by turns, both teach you the same *work* and presence of the Spirit of God. For the good could not appear as good, nor could the evil be *felt* as evil, except that the immediate work of the Spirit of God *creates* or *reveals* this difference between them. Therefore, in whatever state you are, the power of God’s Spirit within you reveals itself equally to you; and to find the *immediate, continual*, and essential work of the Spirit of God within you, you only need to recognize what good and evil are felt within you. For all the good that is in any thought or desire is that much of God within you; and while you adhere to and follow a good thought, you follow or are led by the Spirit of God. On the other hand, all that is selfish and wicked in thought or feeling is that much of the spirit of Satan within you, which would not be known or felt as evil except that it is contrary to the immediate, *continual* work of the Spirit of God within you. Turn, therefore, inward; and everything within you will demonstrate the presence and power of God in your soul, and make you find and feel it with the same certainty that you find and feel your own thoughts. Best of all, by doing this you will never be without a living sense of the immediate guidance and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, always equal to your dependence upon it, always leading you from strength to strength in your inner self, until all your knowledge of good and evil becomes nothing more than a pure love for the one and a pure hatred for the other. For the *sole work* of the Spirit of God is to distinguish the good and evil within you, not merely as ideas, but through your feelings. When you are wholly given up to this new-creating work of God, so as to fix your mind upon it, *remain with it*, and *expect everything from it*—this, my friend, will be your return to the rock from which you were carved, your drinking at the fountain of living water, your walking with God, your living by faith, your putting on Christ, your continual hearing of the Word of God, your eating the bread that came down from heaven, your dining with Christ, and following the Lamb wherever He goes!

For all these seemingly different things will be found in every person, according to their capacity, who is wholly devoted to and depending upon the blessed work of God’s Spirit in their soul.

But your mistake, and that of *most Christians*, lies in this: you want to be good through some outward means; you want methods, opinions, forms, and religious rituals to change and elevate your fallen nature and create in you a new heart and a new spirit. That is to say, you want to be good in a way that is *altogether impossible*, for goodness cannot be brought into you from the outside, much less by anything that is created or by the actions of man. This is as impossible as it is for the flesh to sanctify the spirit, or for temporary things to *give life* to things that are eternal.

The image and likeness of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are in every person, prior to any outward work or action that can come from them. It is God within the person that is the only reason why anything they do, observe, or practice can be called godly. If it were not so, man would only have his *existence* from God, but his *goodness* from himself.

All of a person's outward good works are just like their outward good words; they are not good simply because they use them frequently, for they bring no goodness into the person, nor are they of any worth in themselves, except when a good and *godly spirit* expresses itself through them. CHRIST living in the hearer. As he is the only eternal Word of God who speaks forth all the wisdom and wonders of God, so he alone is the Word who speaks forth all the life, wisdom, and goodness that is or can be in any creature; it can have none except what it has in him and from him:

---

of every outward creaturely thing, or work of man, whatever kind it may be—whether *hearing*, *praying*, *singing*, or *preaching*, etc., or practicing any outward rules and observances—they have only the goodness of the outward *Jew*; indeed, they are as vain as *sounding brass* and *tinkling cymbals* unless they are solely the work and fruits of the Spirit of God. For the *divine nature* alone is what can provide the power for any good work, whether in man or angel.

When a man first finds himself stirred up with religious zeal, what does he generally do? He turns all his thoughts *outward*; he runs after *this* or *that* person, he is at the beck and call of every new opinion, and thinks only of finding the "*truth*" by relying on *this* or *that* method or denomination of Christians. If he could find a man who did not want to win him over to his own party and opinion, but instead turned him away from himself and the teachings of men toward a God—not a God read about historically in books or preached about in this or that society, but a God essentially living and working in his soul and every soul—that person he might call a man of God. Such a man would lead him from himself to God, saving him from many vain wanderings and fruitless searches into the Council of Trent, the Synod of Dort, the Augsburg Confession, the Assembly’s Catechism, or the Thirty-nine Articles! For even if he had a hundred articles of faith, if they were anything other than a hundred calls to a Christ come in the spirit—to a God within him as the only possible *light* and teacher of his mind—it would be a hundred times better for him to be without them.

For all of man's blindness and misery lies in this: that he has lost the *knowledge of God as essentially living within him*. By falling under the power of an earthly, beast-like life, he thinks of God only as living in some other world, and so seeks only through intellectual notions to set up an image of an absent God, instead of worshipping the God of life and power in whom he lives, moves, and has his being.

Whoever, therefore, teaches you to expect great things from *this* or *that* sort of opinion, or calls you to anything as *saving* and *redeeming* other than the manifestation of God in your own soul through a birth of the holy nature of Christ within you, is totally ignorant of the whole nature of both the *fall* and the *redemption* of man. For the *first* is nothing less than a *death* to the divine life, or Christ-like nature, which lived in the first man; and the *other* is nothing else but Christ new-born, formed, and *revealed* again in man, as he was at the beginning. These two great truths are most strongly asserted by Christ when he said, “If any man will be my disciple, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.” The phrase “let him *deny himself*” is the fullest declaration and highest proof that he has lost his *first* divine and heavenly nature; he is not *that self* which first came from God, or he could not be called to deny it. If you claim that he has not lost that first heavenly life in God, then you must also say that our Lord calls him to deny, crucify, and renounce that holy and godlike self which was the first gift of God to him.

To read whole libraries on these matters is only to be bewildered in the strife of *fictions* and contradictions about them. But to read this one single line of Christ is to be led into the full, open truth of the whole nature of both the fall and redemption. Indeed, if we were only freed from the *Babel of opinions* which have so long confounded the *first truths* of the gospel, it would be plain from every part of it that nothing could be called the fall of man except his loss of the divine life or nature, nor could anything be called his redemption, or the real means of it, except *solely* that which God *is* and *does* in him. For what can be good, or work good in man, but God or the Divine nature in him? All the divine truths that ever came from God speak only to the *pearl* of the Divine nature that is *hidden* in our earthly *field* of flesh and blood, because nothing else desires them or has any capacity to receive them; that which is divine can only receive divine things from God. And that is why, unless a “*man be born again from above*,” it is not possible for him to see “or enter into the kingdom of God.” That is, the divine life must arise again in the power of a *new birth*, or there is nothing in fallen man that can partake of the kingdom of God. The reason is that “the kingdom of God is righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost,” and therefore it is not possible to be anywhere except where it proceeds from the Holy Spirit.

> “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength.” Now, what is this God whom you are to love in this way? Is it some *abstract idea* that learned men have helped you form of him? Not at all. That would be only a poor fiction of God and a poor fiction of love. God is *all good*, *the only good*, and there is nothing good *besides him*. Therefore, to love God with all your heart, etc., is *to love all goodness*, and to love nothing else but goodness; then, and only then, do you love God with all your heart, and soul, and strength. But now, for what purpose could this command for such a love be given to man unless he essentially partook of the *divine nature*? For to be in heart, soul, and spirit entirely the love of God within yourself would surely be too absurd for anyone to believe [if we did not possess His nature]. Just as surely, therefore, as this command came from truth itself, so it is certain that every person (however reluctant they may be to hear of anything but pleasures and enjoyments in this vain shadow of a life) still has a divine nature concealed within them. When allowed to hear the calls of God, that nature will know the voice of its heavenly Father and long to do his will on earth as it is done in heaven.

The conclusion, then, is this: if to love God with your whole heart and soul is to love all goodness and nothing else but goodness; and if all that is done without this love—whether in religious duties or common life—is but *mere separation from God*, then it must be the grossest blindness to believe you can have any love of God or goodness in any duties you perform, to any extent or degree other than as the eternal Holy Spirit of God lives and loves in you.

Again, to see the divinity of man's origin, you need only read these words: “Be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect.” For what could man have to do with the perfection of God as the rule of his life unless the truth and reality of the divine nature was in him? Could there be any reasonableness in this command, or any suitability in calling us to be good as God is good, unless there *was* that in us which is in God? Or why call us to the perfection of a heavenly Father if we were not the *real children of his heavenly nature*? One might as well order a heavy stone to fly just as its *flying father*, the eagle, does.

We append the following three letters as examples of a rational, enlightened representation of evangelical Christianity, suited either for Christians or—with a little modification—for human nature under any and all creeds, to be considered in connection with the observations on pages 78 to 87:

> “My dear, worthy friend—whom I love and esteem much—your letter, though full of complaints about the state of your heart, was very much to my liking and gives me great hope that God will carry on the good work he has begun in you, and lead you by his Holy Spirit through all those difficulties under which you currently labor.

> The desire you have to be better than you find yourself at present is God's *call* beginning to be heard within you, and it will make itself heard more within you if you only give way to it and revere it as such; humbly believing that he who calls will—and alone can—help you to pay right and full obedience to it.

[suppres]sion is brought upon our first divine life, and also that it is still in a state capable of being revived in us again. For if it were not in a state of death, or suppressed within us, there would be no need to call us to live according to it; for every being naturally acts according to the life that is manifested in it. Nor could we be called to be heavenly, unless the heavenly nature had its seed in our soul, ready to come to life in us.

Lastly, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” is another full proof that God is truly in us, and that the Holy Spirit certainly has an essential birth within us, just as the spirit of this world does. For this precept might as well be given to a *fox* as to a man, if a man did not have something *quite supernatural* in him. For mere nature, and the natural creature, is nothing but mere self, and can work only for and toward itself. And this is not because of any corruption or depravity of nature, but because it is nature's best state, and it can be nothing else, in either man or beast.

“I say to you, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you,” etc. Every word here is proof that nothing but the *new birth from above* can make one a Christian. There is no other nature or spirit that can breathe forth this universal love and benevolence except that same one which, laying aside its own glory, came down from heaven to forgive, to love, to save, and to die for a whole world of enemies and sinners.

This is the Spirit of Christ, which must as essentially live and breathe in you as it did in him; otherwise, all exhortations to do as he did, or to walk as he walked, are in vain. The natural man is entirely separated from this holiness of life; and though he possessed more wisdom of words and more depth of literature than was in Cicero or Aristotle, he would still have as much to die to as the grossest tax collector <note>The original text uses "publican," referring to the biblical tax collectors often paired with Pharisees.</note> or the vainest Pharisee before he could be a new creature in Christ. For the highest improved natural abilities can no more ascend into heaven or clothe flesh and blood with immortality than they can make a man like-minded with Christ in any divine virtue—and that for this one reason: because God and divine goodness are inseparable.

No precept of the gospel assumes that a man has any power to fulfill it, nor does it call upon any natural ability or wisdom of your own to comply with it. Christ and his apostles did not call any man to overcome the corruption and blindness of fallen nature through the learned cultivation of the mind. To them, the wisdom of the learned world was the same pitiable foolishness as the grossest ignorance. They only distinguished them in this way: the one produces a tax collector, who is often converted to Christ, while the other produces a *Pharisee*, who for the most part condemns his remedy. They (Christ and his apostles) taught nothing but death and the denial of all self, and the impossibility of having any one divine temperament except through faith and hope in a new nature, “born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.”

To speak of the operation of the Holy Spirit as only an assistance, or an occasional assistance, falls as short of the truth as saying that Christ shall only assist the resurrection of our bodies. For not a spark of any divine virtue can arise in us except that which must be wholly and solely called forth by that same power which alone can call our dead bodies out of the dust and darkness of the grave on the day of resurrection.

If you turn to your own strength to achieve Christian piety and goodness, or if you are so deceived as to think that learning, logical abilities, critical acuteness, skill in languages, church systems, rules and orders, articles and opinions, are to do for you what the Spirit of Christ did—and alone could do—for the first Christians, then your diligent reading of the history of the gospel will leave you as poor, empty, and dead to the divine life as if you had only been a diligent reader of the history of all the religions in the world. But if all that you trust in, long for, and depend upon is that Holy Spirit which alone enabled the Scripture saints to “call Jesus Lord;” if this is your one faith and one hope, then the divine life which died in Adam will find itself alive again in Christ Jesus. And be assured that nothing but this *new birth* can make a gospel Christian, because nothing else can possibly love, like, do, and be that which Christ preached in his divine Sermon on the Mount. And be assured, also, that when the Spirit of Christ is the spirit that rules in you, there will be *no hard sayings* in the gospel; rather, all that the heavenly Christ taught in the flesh will be like meat and drink to you, and you will have no joy except in walking as he walked—in saying, loving, and doing what he said, loved, and did. And indeed, how could it be otherwise? How can notions, doctrines, and opinions about Christ—what he was and what he did—make you a *new creature* in him? Can anyone be made a Samson or a Solomon by being well-versed in the history of who they were or what they said or did?

Ask no more then, my friend, *Where shall you go, or what shall you do, to be in the truth?* For you can find the truth nowhere but in JESUS, and in him no further than as HIS WHOLE NATURE AND SPIRIT ARE BORN WITHIN YOU.” [And so again I refer you to the practice of Behmen’s <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), a German Christian mystic.</note> “Way to Christ,” as the short and direct way to be born again of the Word and Spirit of God.]
