<meta>This page continues the specific examination of the doctrine of the atonement, moving from the general introduction of Jacob Boehme's insights to a detailed explanation of why Christ's life and sufferings were a natural necessity for human salvation.</meta>

condition of Christ, is only there as his *true* and *natural* qualification to do all that he came to do, in us, and for us. That is to say, Christ was made to be that which he was; he was a seed of life in our first fallen father; he lived as a blessing of promise in the patriarchs, prophets, and *Israel* of God; he was born as a man of a pure virgin; he did all that he did—whether as suffering, dying, conquering, rising, and ascending into heaven—only as so many things, such as naturally, and as truly, according to the nature of things, qualified him to be the producer, or quickener of a Divine life in us, just as the state and condition of *Adam* qualified him to make us the slavish children of earthly, bestial flesh and blood.

This is the comforting doctrine of our redemption; nothing in God but an infinity of love and goodness towards our fallen condition; nothing in Christ, but that which had its necessity in the nature of things, to make him able to give, and us to receive our full salvation from him.

I will now only add, that from the beginning of deism, and from the time of *Socinus*, to this day, not a Socinian or deist has ever seen or opposed this mystery in its true state, as is undeniably plain from all their writings.

And how it could enter into any Christian philosopher's head, to charge this doctrine with destroying the necessity and merits of Christ's death, is exceedingly strange.

For look where you will, no other cause, or reason of the death of Christ, can be found, but in the love of God towards fallen man. Nor could the love of God will or accept of the death of Christ, but because of its absolute necessity, and effective power to do all that for fallen man, which the love of God wanted to be done for him.

God did not, could not love, or like, or desire the sufferings and death of Christ, for what they were in themselves, or as sufferings of the highest kind. No, the higher and greater such sufferings had been, were they only considered in themselves, the less pleasing they would have been to a God that wills nothing but blessing and happiness to everything capable of it.

But all that Christ was, and did, and suffered, was infinitely prized, and highly acceptable to the love of God, because all that Christ was, and did, and suffered in his own person, was *that* which gave him full power to be a common Father of life to all that died in *Adam*.

Had Christ lacked anything that he was or did, or suffered in his own person, he could not have stood in that relation to all mankind as *Adam* had done. Had he not been given to the first fallen man as a *seed of the woman*, as a light of life, “enlightening every man that comes into the world,” he could not have had *his* seed in every man, as *Adam* had, nor been as universal a father of life as *Adam* was of death. Had he not in the fitness or fullness of time, become a man, born of a pure virgin, the first seed of life, in every man, must have remained only as a seed, and could not have come to the fullness of the birth of a new man in Christ Jesus. For the children can have no other state of life, but that which their father first had. And therefore Christ, as the father of a regenerated human race, must first stand in the fullness of that human state which was to be derived from him into all his children.

This is the absolute necessity of Christ’s being all that he was, before he became man; a necessity arising from the nature of the thing. Because he could not possibly have had the relation of a father to all mankind, nor any power to be a quickener of a life of heaven in them, but because he was both God in himself, and a seed of God in all of them.

Now all that Christ was, and did, and suffered, *after* he became man, is from the same necessity founded in the nature of the thing. He suffered on no other account, but because that which he came to do, in, and for the human nature, was, and could be nothing else in itself, but a work of sufferings and death.

A crooked line cannot become straight, but by having all its crookedness given up, or taken from it. And there is but one way possible in nature, for a crooked line to lose its crookedness.

Now the sufferings and death of Christ stand in this kind of necessity. He was made man for our salvation, that is, he took upon him our fallen nature, to bring it out of its evil, crooked state, and set it again in that rectitude in which it was created.

Now there was no more two ways of doing this, than there are two ways of making a crooked line to become straight.

If the life of fallen nature, which Christ had taken upon him, was to be overcome by him, then every kind of suffering and dying, that was a giving up, or departing from the life of fallen nature, was just as necessary, in the nature of the thing, as that the line to be made straight, must give up and part with every kind and degree of its own crookedness.

And therefore the sufferings and death of Christ were, in the nature of the thing, the only possible way of his acting contrary to, and overcoming all the evil that was in the fallen state of man.

The apostle says, “The Captain of our salvation was to be made perfect through sufferings.” This was the ground and reason of his sufferings: had he been without them, he could not have been perfect in himself, as a *son of man*, nor the restorer of perfection in all mankind. But why so? Because his perfection as a son of man, or the captain of human salvation, could only consist in his acting in, and with a spirit suitable to the first created state of perfect man; he must in his spirit be as much above all the good and *evil* of this fallen world, as the first man was.

But now, he could not show that he was of this spirit, that he was above the world, that he was under no power of fallen nature, but lived in the perfection of the first created man. He could not do so, but by showing that all the good of the earthly life was renounced by him, and that all the evil which the world, the malice of men and devils could bring upon him, could not hinder his living wholly and solely to God, and doing his will on earth with the same fullness, as angels do it in heaven.

But had there been any evil in all fallen nature, whether in *life*, *death*, or *hell*, that had not attacked him with all its force, he could not have been said to have *overcome* it. And therefore, as sure as Christ, as the Son of Man, was to overcome the world, death, hell, and Satan, so sure is it, that all the evils which they could possibly bring upon him, were to be felt and suffered by him, as absolutely necessary, in the nature of the thing, to declare his perfection, and prove his superiority over them. Surely, my friend, it is now enough proved to you, how a God all love towards fallen man, must love, like, desire, and delight in all the sufferings of Christ, which alone could enable him, as a Son of Man, to undo, and reverse all that evil, which the first man had done to all his posterity.

Eusebius.—Oh, sir, in what an adorable light is this mystery now placed. And yet in no other

light than that in which the plain letter of all Scripture sets it. No wrath in God, no fictitious atonement, no folly of debtor and creditor,<note>An objection having been made to these words in a letter to the author (which the writer of these lines has in his possession), the author addressed the subject again to remove the concern; this reply may be seen in the collection of his "Letters."</note> no suffering in Christ for suffering’s sake, but a Christ suffering and dying as his same victory over death and hell, just as when he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven.

*Theophilus.*—Surely, now, Eusebius, you plainly enough see wherein the infinite merits, or the prevailing efficacy and glorious power of the sufferings and death of Christ consist; since they were that, in and through which Christ himself came out of the state of fallen nature and gained power to give the same victory to all his brethren of the human race.

Do not wonder, therefore, that the Scriptures so frequently ascribe all our salvation to the sufferings and death of Christ; that we are continually referred to them as the wounds and stripes by which we are healed, as the blood by which we are washed from our sins, as the price (much above gold and precious stones) by which we are bought.

Do not wonder, also, that in the Old Testament, its service, sacrifices, and *ceremonies* were instituted to typify and point at the great sacrifice of Christ, and to keep up a continual hope, strong expectation, and belief in it. And that in the New Testament, the reality, the benefits, and glorious effects of Christ our Passover, being actually sacrificed for us, are so joyfully repeated by every apostle.

It is because Christ, as suffering and dying, was nothing else but Christ conquering and overcoming all the false good and the hellish evil of the fallen state of man.

His resurrection from the grave and ascension into heaven, though great in themselves and necessary parts of our deliverance, were yet but the consequences and genuine effects of his sufferings and death. These were in themselves the reality of his conquest; all his great work was done and effected in them and by them, and his resurrection and ascension were only his entering into the possession of that which his sufferings and death had gained for him.

Do not wonder then, that all the true followers of Christ, the saints of every age, have so gloried in the *cross of Christ*, have imputed such great things to it, and have desired nothing so much as to be partakers of it, to live in constant union with it. It is because his sufferings, his death, and cross were the *fullness* of his victory over all the works of the devil. Not an evil in flesh and blood, not a misery of life, not a chain of death, not a power of hell and darkness, but were all baffled, broken, and overcome by the process of a suffering and dying Christ. Well, therefore, may the cross of Christ be the glory of Christians.

*Eusebius.*—This matter is so solidly and fully cleared up that I am almost ashamed to ask you anything further about it. Yet explain a little more, if you please, how it is that the sufferings and death of Christ gave him power to become a common Father of life to all that died in *Adam*; or how it is that we, by virtue of them, have victory over all the evil of our fallen state.

*Theophilus.*—You are to know, Eusebius, that the Christian religion is no *arbitrary system* of divine worship, but is the one true, real, and only religion of nature; that is, it is wholly founded in the nature of things, has nothing in it supernatural or contrary to the powers and demands of nature; but all that it does is only in, and by, and according to the workings and possibilities of nature.

A religion that is not founded in nature is all fiction and falsity, and as mere a nothing as an *idol*. For as no creature can be or have anything in it but what it is and has from the nature of things, nor have anything done to it, good or harm, but according to the unalterable workings of nature; so no religion can be of any service but that which works with and according to the demands of nature. Nor can any fallen creature be raised out of its fallen state, even by the omnipotence of God, but according to the nature of things, or the unchangeable powers of nature; for nature is the opening and manifestation of the divine omnipotence; it is God’s *power-world*: and therefore all that God does is and must be done in and by the powers of nature. God, though omnipotent, can give no existence to any creature, but it must have that existence in *space* and *time*. Time comes out of the *eternity*, and space comes out of the *infinity* of God. God has an omnipotent power over them, in them, and with them, to make both of them set forth and manifest the wonders of his supernatural Deity. Yet time can only be subservient to the omnipotence of God according to the nature of time, and space can only obey his will according to the nature of space; but neither of them can, by any power, be made to be in a supernatural state, or be anything but what they are in their own nature.

Now right and wrong, good and evil, true and false, happiness and misery are as unchangeable in nature as time and space. And every state and quality that belongs to a creature has its own nature, as unchangeably as time and space have theirs.

Nothing, therefore, can be done to any creature supernaturally, or in a way that is outside or contrary to the powers of nature; but every thing or creature that is to be helped, that is to have any good done to it, or any evil taken out of it, can only have it done so far as the powers of nature are able and rightly directed to effect it.

And this is the true ground of all divine revelation, or that help which the supernatural Deity grants to the fallen state of man. It is not to appoint an arbitrary system of religious homage to God, but solely to point out and provide for man—blinded by his fallen state—that one only religion that, according to the nature of things, can possibly restore to him his lost perfection. This is the truth, the goodness, and the necessity of the Christian religion; it is true, and good, and necessary, because it is as much the one only natural and possible way of overcoming all the evil of fallen man as light is the one only natural, possible thing that can expel darkness.

And therefore it is that all the mysteries of the gospel, however high, are yet true and necessary parts of the one religion of nature; because they are no higher, nor otherwise, than what the *natural state* of fallen man absolutely stands in need of. His nature cannot be helped or raised out of the evils of its present state by anything less than these mysteries; and, therefore, they are in the same truth and justice to be called his *natural religion*, just as that remedy which alone has full power to remove all the evil of a disease may be justly called its *natural remedy*.

<summary>Theophilus explains that Christ's suffering and death were not legalistic penalties but the natural means by which he overcame fallen nature, effectively making Christianity the "religion of nature" because it operates according to the inherent laws of the created world. He argues that divine revelation is not an arbitrary set of rules but a necessary, natural remedy for the fallen human condition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Theophilus explains to Eusebius that Christ’s redemption is not an arbitrary act but a necessary, "natural" process required to restore humanity’s fallen state.</meta>

A religion is not to be deemed natural simply because it has nothing to do with *revelation*; rather, it is the one true religion of *nature* when it contains everything that our natural state stands in need of—everything that can help us out of our present evil and raise and exalt us to all the happiness that our nature is capable of possessing. Supposing, therefore, the Christian scheme of redemption to be all that, and nothing else in itself but what the nature of things absolutely requires it to be, it must, for that very reason, have its *mysteries*.

For the fallen, corrupt, and mortal state of man absolutely requires these two things as its only salvation. *First, the divine life, or the life of God, must be revived again in the soul of man. Secondly, there must be a resurrection of the body in a better state after death.* Now, nothing in the power of man, or in the things of this world, can bring about this salvation. If, therefore, this is to be the salvation of man, then some intervention of the Deity is absolutely necessary, by the very nature of the thing, or man can have no religion that is sufficiently natural; that is to say, no religion that is sufficient or equal to the needs of his nature.

Now this necessary intervention of the Deity, though doing nothing except in a natural way, or according to the nature of things, must be mysterious to man, because it is doing something *more and higher* than his senses or reason ever saw done, or thought possible to be done, either by himself or any of the powers of this world.

And this is the true basis and nature of the mysteries of Christian redemption. They are, in themselves, nothing else but what the nature of things requires them to be, as natural, effective means of our salvation; and all their power operates in a natural way, or through a true fitness of cause for its effect. But they are mysterious to man because they are brought into the scheme of our redemption by the intervention of God, to work in a way and manner above and superior to all that is seen and done in the things of this world.

The mysteries of the gospel, therefore, are so far from showing that the gospel is not the one true religion of nature that they are the greatest proofs of it, since they alone can help man to all that good which his natural state needs to have done for it.

For instance, if the salvation of man absolutely requires the revival or restoration of the divine life in human nature, then nothing can be the one sufficient, true religion of nature except that which has a natural power to do this.

What a massive error it is, therefore, to blame the doctrine that asserts the incarnation of the Son of God, or the necessity of the Word being made flesh; when, in the nature of the thing, nothing but this very mystery can be the natural, effective cause of the renewal of the divine life in human nature, or have any natural power to bring about our salvation.

And now, *Eusebius*, on this basis—namely: (1.) That there is but one true religion, and that it is the religion of nature. (2.) That a religion has no claim to be considered the religion of nature simply because it rejects divine revelation and has only human reason for its guide, but wholly and solely because it contains every good that the natural state of man needs and can receive from religion. (3.) That nothing can be a religious good, or have any real effectiveness as a means of salvation, except that which has its power in and from the natural power of things, or the fitness and sufficiency of a cause to produce its effect. (4.) That the religion of the gospel, in all its mysteries and doctrines, is entirely grounded in the natural powers of things and their fitness to produce their effects. On this basis, I come to answer your question, namely: How is it that the sufferings and death of Christ gave him full power to become a common father of life to all those who died in *Adam*? Or how is it that we, by virtue of them, are delivered out of all the evils of our fallen state?

The sufferings and death of Christ have no *supernatural* effect—that is, one that is above or contrary to nature. This is because the thing itself is impossible; for a thing is only impossible because the nature of things will not allow for it.

The fall of all mankind in *Adam* is not a *supernatural* event or effect, but the natural and necessary consequence of our relationship to him. If *Adam*, at his fall into this earthly life, could have absolutely overcome every power of the world, the flesh, and the devil in the same spirit as Christ did, he would have been his own redeemer, would have risen out of his fall, ascended into paradise, and been the father of a paradisiacal offspring—just as Christ, when he had overcome them all, rose from the dead and ascended into heaven. But *Adam* did not do this, because it was as impossible in the nature of the thing as for a beast to raise itself into an angel. If, therefore, man is to come out of his fallen state, something must be found that, according to the nature of things, has the power to effect it. For it can no more be done *supernaturally* by anything else than it could have been by *Adam*.

Now the matter stood like this: the seed of all mankind was in the loins of fallen *Adam*. This was unalterable in the nature of the thing, and therefore all mankind had to come forth in his fallen state.

Neither can they ever be in any state whatever, whether earthly or heavenly, except by having an earthly man or a heavenly man as their father. For mankind, as such, must by all necessity be born of, and receive the nature which it has from, a man. And this is the true basis and absolute necessity of the one Mediator, the man Christ Jesus. For seeing that mankind must have the birth and nature which they receive from man; seeing they never could have had any relationship to paradise, or any possibility of sharing in it, except because they had a paradisiacal man for their father; seeing they never could have had any relationship to this earthly world, or any possibility of being born earthly, except because they had an earthly man for their father; and seeing all this must be unalterably so forever, it plainly follows that there was an utter impossibility for the seed of *Adam* ever to come out of its fallen state, or ever have another or better life than they had from *Adam*, unless such a son of man could be brought into existence who had the same relationship to all mankind as *Adam* had, was as much in them all as *Adam* was, and had as full power, according to the nature of things, to give a heavenly life to all the seed in *Adam*’s loins as *Adam* had to bring them forth in earthly flesh and blood.

And now, sir, the fact that Christ was this very *Son of Man*, standing in the same fullness of relationship to all mankind as *Adam* did, having his seed as really in them all as *Adam* had, and being as truly and fully qualified according to the nature of things to be a common and universal father of life as *Adam* was of death to all the human race, shall, in a word or two, be made as plain and undeniable as that two and two are four.

<summary>Theophilus argues that Christianity is the "true religion of nature" because it provides the necessary, natural means—specifically the divine life and resurrection—to heal humanity's fallen state. He explains that Christ must be a second "Adam," sharing the same fundamental relationship to all mankind in order to naturally transmit heavenly life as Adam transmitted earthly death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Theophilus and Eusebius, moving from the necessity of divine intervention to the specific "natural" relationship between Christ, Adam, and all of humanity.</meta>

The doctrine of our redemption absolutely asserts that the seed of Christ was sown into the first fallen father of mankind, called the *seed of the woman*, the *bruiser of the serpent*, the *engrafted Word of life*, and called again in the Gospel, "that light which lights every man that comes into the world." Therefore, Christ was in all men, in that same fullness of the relation of a father to all mankind, as *Adam* the first was. Secondly, Christ was born of *Adam's* flesh and blood, took the human nature upon him, and therefore stood as a human creature in the same relation to mankind as *Adam* did. Nothing, therefore, was further lacking in Christ to make him as truly a *natural father of life* to all mankind as *Adam* was at first, except God's appointment of him to that end.

For just as *Adam* could not have been the natural father of mankind except because God created and appointed him for that end, so Christ could not have been the *natural* regenerator, or redeemer of a heavenly life that was lost in all mankind, except because God had appointed and brought him into the world for that end. Now that God did this—that Christ came into the world by divine appointment to be the Savior, the resurrection, and the life of all mankind—is a truth as evident from Scripture as that *Adam* was the first man.

And thus it appears, in the utmost degree of plainness and certainty, that Christ in his *single person* was, according to the nature of things, as fully qualified to be a common *redeemer* as *Adam* was, in his single person, to be a common father of all mankind. He had his *seed* in all mankind, as *Adam* had; he had the human nature, as *Adam* had; and he had the same divine appointment as *Adam* had. But Christ, however qualified to be our redeemer, could not be actually such until he had gone through and done all that by which our redemption was to be effected.

Adam, however qualified, yet could not be the father of a paradisiacal offspring until he had stood his trial and established himself victorious over everything that could test him. In like manner, Christ, however qualified, could not be the Redeemer of all mankind until he had also stood his trial, had overcome *all that* by which *Adam* was overcome, and had established himself triumphantly in that paradise which *Adam* had lost.

Now, as *Adam’s* trial was whether he would keep himself in his paradisiacal state, *above and free from all that was good and evil in this earthly world*, so Christ’s trial was whether as a *Son of Man*, and loaded with the infirmities of fallen *Adam*, sacrificed to all that which the rage and malice of the world, hell, and devils could possibly do to him; whether he, in the midst of all these evils, could live and die with his spirit as contrary to them, as much above them, and as unhurt by them as *Adam* should have lived in paradise.

And then it was that everything which had overcome *Adam* was overcome by Christ, and Christ’s victory did, in the nature of things, as certainly and fully open an entrance for him and all his seed into paradise as *Adam’s* fall cast him and all his seed into the prison and captivity of this earthly, bestial world.

Nothing *supernatural* came to pass in either case, but paradise lost and paradise regained occurred according to the nature of things, or the real power of a cause to produce its effect.

Thus is your question fully answered; namely: How and why the sufferings and death of Christ enabled him to be the author of life to all who died in *Adam*? Just as the fall of *Adam* into this world, under the power of sin, death, hell, and the devil, enabled him to be the common father of death—that is, was the natural, unavoidable cause of our being born under the same captivity—just so, that life, sufferings, and death of Christ, which declared his breaking out from them and superiority over them, must, in the nature of things, as much enable him to be the common author of life. That is, it must as certainly be the *full, natural, effective cause* of our inheriting life from him. Because, by what Christ was in himself, by what *he was in us*, by his whole *state, character*, and the divine appointment, we all had *that natural union* with him and dependence upon him as our head in the way of redemption, just as we had with *Adam* as our head in the way of our natural birth. So that, as it must be said that because *Adam* fell, we must by all necessity be heirs of his fallen state, so, with the same truth and from the same necessity of the thing, it must be said that because Christ our head is risen victorious out of our fallen state, we, as his members and having his seed within us, must be, and are made, heirs of all his glory. Because, in all respects, we are as strictly and intimately connected with and related to him as the *one Redeemer* as we are to *Adam* as the *one father* of all mankind. So that Christ, by his sufferings and death, becoming in all of us our wisdom, our righteousness, our justification, and redemption, is the same sober and solid truth as *Adam*, by his fall, becoming in all of us our foolishness, our impurity, our corruption, and death.

And now, my friends, look back upon all that has been said, and then tell me: is it possible more to exalt or magnify the infinite merits and availing efficacy of the *sufferings and death* of Christ than is done by this doctrine? Or is it not the case that everything said of them in Scripture is here proved, from the very nature of things, to be absolutely true? And again, is it not sufficiently proved to you that the sufferings and death of Christ are not only consistent with the doctrine of a God who is all love, but are the fullest and most absolute proof of it?

Eusebius.—Indeed, *Theophilus*, you have so fully done for us all that we wanted to have done, that we are now ready to take leave of you. AS FOR MY PART, I WANT TO RETURN HOME, TO ENJOY MY BIBLE AND DELIGHT MYSELF WITH READING IT IN THIS COMFORTABLE LIGHT IN WHICH YOU HAVE SET THE WHOLE BASIS AND NATURE OF OUR REDEMPTION. I AM NOW IN FULL POSSESSION OF THIS GLORIOUS TRUTH: THAT GOD IS PURE LOVE—THE MOST GLORIOUS TRUTH THAT CAN POSSESS AND EDIFY THE HEART OF MAN. It drives every evil out of the soul and gives life to every spark of goodness that can possibly be kindled in it. Everything in religion is made amiable by being a service of love to the God of Love.

No sacrifices, sufferings, and death have any place in religion except to satisfy and fulfill that love of God, which could not be satisfied without our salvation. If the Son of God is not spared, if he is delivered up to the rage and malice of men, devils, and hell, it is because, had we not had such a captain of our salvation made perfect through sufferings, it never could have been sung, "*O death, where is thy sting, O grave, where is thy victory!*" It never could have been true that "*as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin, so by one man came the resurrection of the dead:*" it never could have been said that "AS IN ADAM ALL DIE, SO IN CHRIST SHALL ALL BE MADE ALIVE."

<summary>Theophilus argues that Christ is the natural source of life for humanity just as Adam was the natural source of death, grounded in a shared nature and divine appointment. Eusebius concludes that this understanding proves God is pure love and makes the scriptures and the process of redemption clear and comforting.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue involving Theophilus and Eusebius, transitioning into an extract from "The Way to Divine Knowledge" concerning the nature of Gospel Christianity and the necessity of acknowledging the fall of man as the starting point for faith.</meta>

Therefore, dear *Theophilus*, farewell: God is love, and he who has learned to live in the spirit of Love, has learned to live and dwell in God. Love was the beginner of all the works of God, and from eternity to eternity, nothing can come from God but a variety of wonders and works of love over all nature and every creature.

*Theophilus.*—God prosper, *Eusebius*, this spark of heaven in your soul; may it, like the seraphim's coal *taken from the altar*, purify your heart from all its uncleanness.”

Finally, as a close to the present section, we offer the following extract from the “Way to Divine Knowledge” (being the conclusion of the dissertation in the first part of that work, on the *true way of making converts to Christianity*, and recommended to be referred to in that respect on page 78)—containing a description of the ground and nature of GOSPEL CHRISTIANITY in contrast to that *original universal Christianity*, which began with Adam, was the religion of the patriarchs, of Moses, and the prophets, and of every humble penitent man in every part of the world, by whatever name called: Heathen, Mohammedan, Jew, or national Christian:—

“But let me now return to *Humanus*, and ask him, supposing he could not convince a man of the certainty of his fallen state, how he would proceed further with him.

*Humanus.*—Truly, *Theophilus*, I would proceed no further at all; and for this good reason: because I should then have nothing to proceed upon. If I certainly knew of an infallible remedy for every disorder of the eyes, only to be had by going to *China* for it, I should not attempt to persuade a man who believed his eyes to be sound and good to leave all that he had and go to *China* for this infallible remedy for bad eyes.

Now, to press a man to deny himself and leave all that he has in the enjoyments of flesh and blood in order to be reconciled to God, when he believes himself to be in the *same good state* in which God created him, seems to be as wild a project as to desire him who is well pleased with the goodness of his sight to go to the *Indies* to be helped to see.

And, indeed, I know very well from former experience that all discourses about the *reasonableness* of Christianity, the doctrine of the cross, the exceeding love of God in giving so great a *Savior*, with many more things of the like nature, were mere *empty sounds*, heard with the greatest *indifference* and incapable of raising the least seriousness in me, merely because I had not the least *notion* or suspicion of the truth and greatness of my fallen state; and therefore, I was not the man who had any fitness to be affected by these matters. And for this reason, Christ said, <margin>6</margin> *Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you*; as plain as if he said, 'No one else can come to me, nor can anyone else be refreshed by me.'

Here, therefore, in my humble opinion, should all *begin* who would propagate Christianity or make true converts to it, and *here stop*, as Christ did. It is only the weary and heavy laden who are fitted to be converts or refreshed; and therefore, we can in no way help a man to be a Christian, or fit him to be refreshed by *Christ*, but by bringing him into a full awareness of the evil, burden, and vanity of his natural state, until some good Providence awakens him out of it. We should not make proposals to him about the reasonableness of believing in the Holy Trinity, the Incarnation of the Son of God, and the necessity of his sufferings and death, etc.; for this method is as absurd as entering into a solemn debate with a confessed atheist about the reasonableness of worshipping God in spirit and truth. For, just as the existence of a God is the only ground for proving that he ought to be worshipped in spirit and in truth, so the certainty and belief of our fallen state is the only ground for showing the reasonableness of the mysteries of redemption. And he who disowns the fall of man from a divine life has all the same reasons for rejecting the mysteries of our salvation as the atheist has to reject the doctrines of a spiritual worship of God. Therefore, to expose the mysteries of our salvation to the wrangling of a debate with an unbeliever of the fall of man—mysteries which have no other ground to stand upon—is not only helping him to an easy triumph over you, but is the most likely method to prevent him from ever being a Christian. For seeing how easily he can ridicule mysteries which, to him in his present state, can have no reasonableness in them, he is put on the most likely path to living and dying in a hardened contempt of them. Whereas, if you stick close to the *one true ground* of Christianity and only proceed as it proceeds, and make the unbeliever no offers of any other Christianity but that which begins with the acknowledged awareness of the fall of human nature from its first divine life, you stop where you ought to stop and rob him of all power and pretense of meddling with the other mysteries of salvation.

The one business, then, on his hands, if he will hold out against you, must be to deny his reason and senses, and maintain, in spite of both, that man is *not fallen*, but is by nature *holy, just, good, and happy* in both body and soul; and that mankind, and the world they are in, have all that goodness and happiness which they could be supposed to have from an infinitely good and happy God, who can will nothing in the creature but goodness and happiness. Here you bring the deist to his proper work, and all the contradiction to sense and reason will lie on his side: you set Christianity upon its true ground; and whoever thus defends it as it ought to be defended not only does justice to the Christian cause but acts the most kind and friendly part toward those who oppose it merely through a misunderstanding of its true *ground and nature*; which I will venture to say is the case of all sober, well-meaning deists. For *Deism* has no natural foundation or ground of its own to stand upon; it does not grow from any root or strength within itself, but is what it is merely because of the *bad state of Christendom and the miserable use* that heathenish learning and worldly policy have made of the Gospel. If it (*Deism*) seems to itself to be *strong* and *well-grounded*, it is merely because it can so easily object to church doctrines and scholastic opinions: if it seems to itself to be *good*, it is because it can so easily expose the evils which Christians and churches bring upon one another: If it seems to be highly rational, its reason is because it is free from that number of absurdities and contradictions which Christian churches charge against one another. Lastly, if it keeps off all fearful forebodings of the con-

consequences of not receiving the Gospel, it is because it so plainly sees that Christians say, *Hail, Master, kiss the Gospel*, and then break every part of it.

This is the true height, depth, and total strength of Deism or infidelity; it never had any other support within me but this; nor did I ever converse with a Deist who carried the matter higher or farther than this to support their cause. Hence it is that you made so speedy a convert of me, by showing me such a Christianity as I never heard of before, and stripped of everything that gave me power to oppose it. If you had proceeded in the way practiced by most defenders of the Gospel, you would have left me just as you found me, if not more confirmed in my old way. But as you have justly removed all controversy about doctrines from the merits of the cause, and shown that it all lies in this one short, plain, and decisive point—namely, the fall of man—a fall proved and demonstrated to all my senses and reason by every height and depth of nature, by every kind of misery, evil, and sin in the world, and by everything we know of God, ourselves, and the world we live in; the ground and foundation of Christianity is undeniable, and no one can be too speedy a convert to the belief of it. And as you have also shown that the whole nature of the Gospel redemption means nothing but the one true and only possible way of delivering man from his miserable state in this world, Christianity is shown to be the most intelligible and desirable thing that the human heart can think of. And thus, contrary to all expectation, the tables are completely turned; Deism can no longer be founded on argument, and Christianity is as self-evident as our senses. All learning on both sides, either for or against it, is insignificant; Christianity stands upon a foundation quite superior to it, and may be the sure possession of every common man who has sense enough to know whether he is happy or unhappy, good or evil. For this natural knowledge, if adhered to, is every person's sure guide to that *one salvation* preached by the Gospel. This Gospel stands in no more need of learning and critical art now than it did when *Christ* was preaching it upon earth. How absurd would it have been for any critics in *Greek* and *Hebrew* to have followed *Christ* and his apostles as necessary explainers of their hard words, which called for nothing in the hearers but penitent hearts turned to God, and declared that only those who *were of God* could hear the *Word of God*! How strange it would be if *Christ* had chosen only illiterate men to preach the Gospel of the kingdom of God, if only great scholars could rightly understand what they said! Again, supposing learned men alone have the true fitness to understand the word of Scripture, and that the common man is to receive it from them, how must he know which are the scholars who have the right knowledge? From where is he to get this information? For no one needs to be told that ever since learning has held rule in the church, learned doctors have contradicted and condemned one another in every essential point of Christian doctrine. Thousands of learned men tell the uneducated they are lost in this or that church, and thousands of other learned men tell them they are lost if they leave it.

If, therefore, Christianity is in the hands of scholars, how is the common man to find it? Must he, though unable to understand Scripture for lack of learning, decide which learned man is in the right and which is not? If so, the unlearned man has much the greater ability, since he must do for scholars what they cannot do for themselves.

But the truth of the matter is this: Christian redemption <unclear>is foreseen as its ground and necessity, and likewise predestinated before the world began to be effected by that which only could effect it in the whole nature of things, namely the actual process of the incarnate Son of God, as the supernatural philosophy of which, with all its attendant relative mysteries, was first systematically revealed to the world by God, through his chosen servant, JACOB BEHMEN?</unclear> <gloss>is God's mercy to all mankind, but it could not be so if every fallen man, as such, did not have some fitness and capacity to lay hold of it. It must have no dependence upon times and places, or the ages and various conditions of the world, or any outward circumstance of life; as the first man partook of it, so must the last. The learned linguist and the blind, the deaf and the mute, have but one and the same common way of finding life in it. And he who writes large commentaries upon the whole Bible must be saved by *something* just as different from book-knowledge as were those who lived when there was neither book nor any alphabet in the world.</gloss>

For this salvation, which is God's *mercy* to the fallen soul of man, merely as fallen, must be something that meets every person; and which every person, as fallen, has something within that directs them to turn toward it. For as the *fall of man* is the *reason* for this mercy, so the fall must be the *guide* to it; the need must show the thing that is needed. And therefore the manifestation of this one salvation, or mercy to man, must have a nature suitable—not to this or that great reader of history, or able critic in *Hebrew* roots and *Greek* phrases—but suitable to the common state and condition of every son of *Adam*. It must be something as grounded in human nature as the fall itself is, which requires no art to make it known, but to which the common nature of man is the only guide in one person as well as another. Now this *something*, which is thus obvious to every man and which opens the way to Christian redemption in every soul, is *a sense of the vanity and misery of this world, and a prayer of faith and hope to God to be raised to a better state*.

Now in this *awareness*, which every person's own nature leads them into, lies the whole of man's salvation; here the mercy of God and the misery of man meet together; here the *fall* and the *redemption* kiss each other. This is the Christianity that is as old as the *fall*, which alone saved the first man and can alone save the last. This is what all the law and the prophets depend upon, and what fulfills them both; for they have only this end: to turn man from the lusts of this life to a desire, faith, and hope for a better one. Thus the whole of Christian redemption, considered on the part of man, stands in this degree of nearness and plainness to all mankind; it is as simple and plain as feeling our own evil and misery, and as natural as the desire of being saved and delivered from it.

This is the Christianity of which every man must first be made aware—not from hearsay, but as a growth or degree of life within himself—before he can have any fitness or the least pretense to judge or speak a word about the further mysteries of the gospel. But here I stop.

*Theophilus.*—Well, *Humanus*, I have now pushed the matter with you as far as I intended; and you have given me full proof of the truth and solidity of your own conversion, and your ability to do good among your former brethren. You must now enter the ranks with them; not to charge them with ignorance, ill-will, or profaneness of spirit, but only to try, in the spirit of love and meekness, to undeceive them in the same way you have been undeceived; and to show them that Christianity is by no means that thing which you and they have so long disliked.

Nothing could be more correct than your decision not to enter into debates about Gospel doctrines, or to propose their reasonableness to anyone, until he admits he is consciously convinced of the previously mentioned fall of man and truly desires to be saved or delivered from it. And if that time never comes, you must leave him just as incapable of hearing or judging the doctrines of the *Holy Trinity*, the *Incarnation of the Son of God*, or the *operation of the Holy Spirit* as *Epicurus* would be. For every man who clings to this world, who is in love with it and its earthly enjoyments, is a disciple of *Epicurus* and is stuck in the same mire of atheism as he was, whether he is a modern deist, a Catholic or Protestant Christian, an Arian, or an orthodox teacher. All these distinctions are meaningless if this world possesses and governs his heart. For the entire matter depends solely on this: whether heaven or earth holds the heart and rule over man. Nothing separates the worshippers of the true God from idolaters but this: where the earth possesses and rules the heart, everyone is of *one and the same* religion and worships the same God, no matter how they are distinguished by sect or party.

And wherever the heart is weary of the evil and vanity of earthly life and is *looking up to God* for a heavenly nature, everyone there is part of the true religion and is a worshipper of the true God, however distant they may be from one another in time or place. But enough has been said on this matter.

Before we finish, let me just point out to you the true foundation and nature of GOSPEL CHRISTIANITY. I call it this to distinguish it from that *original universal Christianity* which began with *Adam* and was the religion of the patriarchs, of *Moses*, the prophets, and every repentant person in every part of the world who had faith and hope in God to be delivered from the evil of this world.

But once the Son of God was born into and from human nature, had finished all the wonders belonging to our redemption, and sat down at the right hand of God in heaven, then a heavenly kingdom was established on earth. The Holy Spirit came down from heaven or was given to the flock of *Christ* in such a degree of birth and life as never was, nor could be, given to human nature until Christ, the Redeemer of human nature, was glorified. But when the humanity of Christ, our second *Adam*, was glorified and became entirely heavenly, then the heavenly life—the comfort, power, and presence of the Holy Spirit—was the gift he gave to his brothers, friends, and followers whom he had left on earth.

The Holy Spirit descended in the form of divided tongues of fire on the heads of those who were to begin and open the new powers of a *Divine life* established among men. This was the beginning and manifestation of the whole nature and power of GOSPEL CHRISTIANITY, a thing as different from what was called Christianity before as the possession of something hoped for is different from the hope itself, or as deliverance is different from the desire or expectation of it. Because of this, the apostles were new men; they entered into a new kingdom come down from heaven and were enlightened with new light and inflamed with new love. They did not preach about something absent or distant, but about Jesus Christ as the *wisdom and power of God* felt and found within them, and as a power of God ready to be shared as a new birth from above to all who would repent and believe in him. It was to this change of nature, life, and spirit—to this certain, immediate deliverance from the power of sin, to be possessed and governed by the gifts and graces of a heavenly life—that men were then called as true Christianity. The preachers of it bore witness not to something they had heard, but to a power of salvation, a renewal of nature, a birth of heaven, and a sanctification of spirit which they themselves had received. Gospel Christianity then stood on its true foundation; it appeared to be exactly what it was. And what was it? It was an awakened *Divine life* established among men; it was its own proof. It appealed to its proper judge—the heart and conscience of man—which alone was capable of being touched by these offers of a new life.

This is why sinners of all kinds, who felt the burden of their evil natures, were ready to receive these glad tidings. Meanwhile, the *rigid Pharisee, the orthodox priest, and the rational heathen*, though enemies to one another and each proud of his own distinction, all agreed in rejecting and hating a spiritual Savior who was to save them from their carnal selves and the vanity of their own rational, selfish virtues. But after a while, when Christianity had lost its first glory and no longer appeared as a *Divine life awakened* among men—when it was no longer its own proof of the power and Spirit of God manifested within it—then worldly learning and political power were, from age to age, forced to be called the glory and prosperity of the church of Christ. This was so even though in the *Revelation of St. John*, its image is that of a *scarlet whore riding upon the beast*.

Here, therefore, my friend, you must place the true distinction of GOSPEL CHRISTIANITY from all that went before it or that has come after it. It is purely and solely a *Divine life awakened and established among men as the effect and fruit of Christ’s glorification in heaven*. It has no other promise from him except that of his HOLY SPIRIT to be with it as its light, guide, strength, comfort, and protection until the end of the world. Therefore, as Gospel Christians, we belong to the *new covenant of the Holy Spirit*, which is the kingdom of God that came down from heaven on the day of *Pentecost*. This is why it is impossible to see or enter this new kingdom without being *born again of the Spirit*. The apostles and disciples of Christ, though they had been baptized with water, had followed Christ, heard his doctrines, and performed wonders in his name, were at that time only standing near the kingdom of God and preached that it was *at hand*. They had only seen and “known Christ according to the flesh.” They had followed him with great zeal but with very little and low knowledge of either him or his kingdom. For this reason, they were commanded to wait and not act as his ministers in his new glorified state until they were endued with *power from on high*. They received this power when the Holy Spirit, with his divided tongues of fire, came down upon them, making them the enlightened instruments who were to spread the light of a heavenly kingdom over all the world. From that day, GOSPEL CHRISTIANITY began with its true distinction from everything that came before: it was the ministry of the *Spirit*. The ministers of it called the world to nothing but the *gifts and graces of the same Spirit*. They were to look for nothing but *spiritual blessings*, and to trust, hope, and pray for nothing but the *power of that Spirit*, which was to be the *one life and ruling spirit* of this newly-opened kingdom of God. No one could join them or have any part with them except by dying to the wisdom and light of the flesh, so that he might live by the Spirit through faith in Jesus Christ, who had thus called him to his kingdom and glory. Now this Christianity is its own proof; it can

be proved by nothing but itself; it needs neither miracles nor outward witness, but, like the sun, is its own discoverer.

He who adheres only to the history of the facts, doctrines, and institutions of the gospel, without being *born of its spirit*, is only a nominal Christian; he is no nearer to Christ than the Jew who carnally adhered to the letter of the law. They both stand at the same distance from GOSPEL CHRISTIANITY.

Therefore, it is in vain for the modern Christian to appeal to *antiquity*, to *history*, and *ancient churches* to prove that he belongs to Christ; for he can only belong to him by having the power of Christ and the Spirit of God living and dwelling in his renewed *inner person*.

But a learned Christianity, *supported* and *governed* by reason, debate, and criticism—one that is forced to appeal to canons, *councils*, and *ancient customs* to defend itself—has lost its place. It stands on fictitious ground and shows that it cannot appeal to itself or its own works, which alone are the certain and *only* proofs of either a true or a false Christianity.

For the truth of Christianity is the Spirit of God living and working within it; and where this Spirit is *not* its *life*, the outward form is merely like the empty carcass of a departed soul.

For the spiritual life is its own proof, just as natural life is, and needs no outward or external thing to bear witness to it. But if you please, gentlemen, we will finish for now.

Such, then, may be considered a brief <gloss>general</gloss> popular representation of the nature and design of the grand Enochian revelation contained in the series of works previously described, as interpreted by this GREAT ORACLE of Divine wisdom and master of all solid learning and literary accomplishments.

As for a specific and philosophical explanation of the effects that have already followed—and are clearly progressing—in the moral, religious, scientific, and political renewal of this country, other nations, and the world at large, that must, of course, be reserved for the biography. In that work, the *Elias-baptist* character of this notable individual will undoubtedly be demonstrated—incidentally regarding philosophy, but directly in the complete restoration of Christian doctrine to its original evangelical purity of principle and practice, and in laying the groundwork for its dissemination in all its simplicity, power, and effectiveness to the ends of the earth (to be referred to again in this treatise). This fulfills the proclamation of the evangelical prophet regarding the glory of the latter days and the characteristics of its preceding messengers:—(Isaiah 40:3, 4, 5)—

> “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low; the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain. And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all people shall see it together; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken it.”

Indeed, such is the clarity and fullness of light in which every part of Christianity, in both theory and practice, is now presented in the direct and supported works of this learned author, that when seen through such a lens, it may be said to be irresistible.

## SECTION II.

->[BEING PROPERLY A NOTE BELONGING TO THE FOLLOWING SECTION.]<-

The contents of the present section, as described above, originally formed the substance of a note in the next section (which was then the second section) under the divisions numbered VII., VIII., IX., and X. That note contained a recommendation of select and edifying treatises on both active and contemplative divinity by the most spiritually-minded ascetic and mystical writers, with illustrations of their principles and characteristics of piety found in the lives of holy saints from various ages of the church. But because of the great length of the note, it has, upon reflection, been deemed better to make it a section of its own and to place it in the order in which it now appears in this treatise.

The design of the whole is to provide the candidate with a comprehensive and interesting view of mystic theology, or of that science of active and contemplative piety into which Christianity had been resolved by her most devoted, experienced, and learned students down to the early part of the eighteenth century—the era in which the subject of the proposed biography appeared. It omits mention, however, of the English experimental <note>Relating to religion as a matter of personal experience rather than mere theory.</note> and devotional writers, as they are assumed to be familiar to every theological student in this country. It was considered that this goal would be best achieved, consistently with the necessary brevity of the present treatise, by presenting a CATALOG OF ALL THE EMINENT SPIRITUAL OR MYSTIC WRITERS of all ages of the church. This is accompanied by brief general observations upon each, with more extended annotations upon those who appear to deserve more particular notice, either regarding the distinguishing characteristics and qualities of their piety or on any other ground. These annotations also include descriptive notices of other authors and writings of similar or corresponding principles. This has now been done; and, regarding these writings in conjunction with others of a similar character from the English, Greek, and other churches, they may be said to illustrate the great truth that God has "*never left himself without a witness*," but has always delighted to dwell with the children of men whenever he could find detached hearts and purified souls.

It is to be observed, however, that these authors are not to be considered as receiving an indiscriminate endorsement simply because they are mentioned in this catalog or because of any other general favorable observations attached to their names. On the contrary, many of them are to be rejected as either <term>jejune</term> and worthless in themselves, or utterly useless to a Christian of the present day. Only those among them that are truly instructive and edifying will be found specially referred to as such, either in the annotations mentioned above or in the smaller selection of devotional works inserted in the following section of the present treatise. And, assuming the student of experimental religion has passed through the basics of piety to an elevated understanding of the nature, scope, and design—

supposed to represent Mr. Law himself when at college, to whom *Theophilus* is thus made to speak:— “If you, my friend, having read many old *Greek* and *Latin* books, should intend to publish *Homer* or *Caesar’s Commentaries* with critical notes, I should have nothing to object to your ability; you might be as well qualified by such means for such a work as one man is to make baskets, or another traps to catch flies. But if, because of this skill in old *Greek* and *Latin*, you should seem to yourself or others to be well qualified to write notes upon the *spirit* and *meaning* of the words of CHRIST, I should tell you that your undertaking was quite unnatural and as impossible to be free from error as when a blind man undertakes to describe the beauty of different colors.

For the doctrines of redemption belong no more to the natural man than the beauty of colors to him who never saw the light. And from this unnatural procedure it is that the Scriptures are as useful to the *Socinian* or *Arian*, the *Papist* or the *Protestant*; and they can easily, by the light of reason, charge one another with absurdities and refute each other’s opinion, just as two blind men can quarrel and reject each other’s notions of red and green.

Jesus Christ is the light of that heavenly man who died in paradise; and therefore nothing in man but that awakened seed of life that died in paradise can have the least sensitivity or capacity for receiving the redeeming power of Jesus Christ. But *light* and *life* have no dependence upon words or phrases; they both can only proceed from a *birth*, whether it be the light and life of God, or the light and life of this world. How absurd would it be to suppose that a man, naturally blind, must be taught grammar or logic to fit him for the reception of the light of the sun and the knowledge of colors! Yet it is no less absurd than to think that skill in *Hebrew* and *Greek* words <note>or even a knowledge of the most sublime evangelical doctrines</note> can open the light of God and heaven in the soul. If you now, *Academicus*, can set this matter in a *fairer* light, I am ready to hear you.

*Academicus*.—Standing upon the ground that you, *Theophilus*, stand upon, all that you have said of reason, science, historical knowledge, or critical skill in words is unanswerable. For what can all these things avail if redemption is purely a birth of the Divine nature, light, and Spirit of God offered to fallen man; which birth can only be received by the faith, hope, and desire of that inward man which is divine in us? For nothing else can have any hunger or thirst after the divine nature but that which is itself born of it.

Now this true ground of the Christian redemption gives the greatest glory to God and comfort to man. It explains the fact why plain and simple souls, having their inward man kindled into love, hope, and faith in God, are capable of the highest divine illumination; while learned students, full of art and science, can live and die without the least true knowledge of God and Christ, and as slaves to all the lusts of the flesh. For thus, this redemption belongs only to one sort of people, and yet is common to all. It is equally near and equally open to every son of man. There is no difference between learned and unlearned, between *Jew* or *Greek*, *male* or *female*, *Scythian* or *barbarian*, *bond* or *free*; but the same Lord is God over all, and equally near to all who call upon him.—It is told us, as the glory of the divine goodness, that *it gives fodder to the cattle; and feeds the young ravens that cry to it.* What cattle? Surely not only the cattle of *Jacob*; or only the young ravens that cry in the land of *Judah*. Yet this would be much more consistent with the goodness of the one universal God than to hold that only the sons of Jacob, or the children of the circumcision, were in the covenant of God’s redemption.

But now, though this one ground of Christian redemption stands in the highest degree of clarity from Scripture and is absolutely certain from the very nature of the thing; yet, until I met with honest *Rusticus*, I never conversed with any man or read any book that gave me the least hint of it.—When I had taken my degrees, I consulted several great divines to put me in a method of studying divinity. Had I said to them, *Sirs, what must I do to be saved?* they would have prescribed hellebore to me, or directed me to the physician as a disordered enthusiast. And yet I am now fully satisfied that this one question ought to be the sole inquiry of him who desires to be a true *divine*. And were our Savior himself on earth, who surely could do more for me than all the libraries in the world, yet I would need to have asked no more divinity-knowledge of him than is contained in this one question.

It would take up nearly half a day to tell you the work which my learned friends have cut out for me. One told me that *Hebrew* words were everything; that they must be read without points; and then the Old Testament is an opened book: he recommended to me a cartload of lexicons, critics, and commentators upon the *Hebrew Bible*. Another tells me the *Greek Bible* is the best; that it corrects the *Hebrew* in many places, and refers me to a large number of books learnedly written in defense of it. Another tells me that church history is the main matter; that I must begin with the first fathers and follow them through every age of the church, not forgetting to take the lives of the Roman emperors along with me, as shedding great light on the state of the church in their times. Then I must have recourse to all the councils held and the canons made in every age; which would enable me to see, with my own eyes, the great corruptions of the *Council of Trent*. Another, who is not very fond of ancient matters but is wholly focused upon rational Christianity, tells me I need go no higher than the *Reformation*: that *Calvin* and *Cranmer* were very great men; that *Chillingworth* and *Locke* ought always to lie upon my table; that I must get an entire set of those learned volumes written against popery in King *James’s* reign: and also be well versed in all the discourses which Mr. Boyle’s and Lady Moyer’s lectures have produced: And then, says he, you will be a match for our greatest enemies, which are the popish priests and modern deists. My tutor is very *liturgical*; he desires me, of all things, to get all the collections that I can of the *ancient liturgies*,

embracing, as it did, all the theoretical instructions and highest experiences of the most learned doctors and devoted saints of God, when fullest of Divine light, and all the best thoughts and most refined discoveries of evangelical truth from the most erudite contemplatives and practical devotees of all previous ages—

---

and all the authors who treat such matters, who, he says, are very learned and very numerous. He has been many years making observations upon them, and is now clear as to the time when certain little particles entered the liturgies and others were gradually dropped. He has a friend abroad in search of ancient manuscript liturgies; for, by the way, he said at parting, "I have some suspicion that our sacrament of the Lord's Supper is *essentially* defective for lack of having a little water in the wine," etc. Another learned friend tells me the *Clementine Constitutions* is the book of books, and that everything that lies loose and scattered in the New Testament stands there in its true order and form; and though he won't say that Dr. Clarke and Mr. Whiston are right, yet it might be useful for me to read all the *Arian* and *Socinian* writers, provided I stood on my guard and did so with caution. The last person I consulted advised me to get all the histories of the rise and progress of *heresies* and of the lives and characters of heretics. These histories, he said, condense the matter; they bring truth and error clearly into view; and I should find collected in a few pages what would have cost me some years to gather. He also desired me to be well-versed in all the *casuistical writers* and *chief schoolmen*, for they debate matters to the bottom, dissecting every virtue and every vice into its many degrees and parts, and show how near they can come to one another without touching. And this knowledge, he said, might be useful to me when I became a *parish priest*.

Following the advice of all these counselors as well as I could, I lit my candle early in the morning and put it out late at night. I had been sweating in this labor for some years until *Rusticus*, upon our first acquaintance, seeing my way of life, said to me: "Had you lived about seventeen hundred years ago, you would have stood just where I stand now. I cannot read; and therefore," he says, "all these hundreds of thousands of disputing books and doctrine books produced by these seventeen hundred years do not stand in my way; they are the same to me as if they had never existed. And had you lived at the time mentioned, you would have escaped them all just as I do now; because, although you are a very good reader, there were none of them then to be read."

"Could you, therefore, be content to be one of the primitive Christians, who were as good as any who have lived since, you might spare all this labor. Take only the Gospel into your hands; deny yourself; renounce the lusts of the flesh; set your affections on things above; call upon God for His Holy Spirit; walk by faith and not by sight; adore the holy Deity of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost—in whose image and likeness you were at first created, and in whose name and power you have been baptized—to be again the living likeness and holy habitation of His life, light, and Holy Spirit:"

"Look up to Christ as your redeemer, your regenerator, your second *Adam*; look at Him as He truly is: the *wisdom and power of God*, sitting at His right hand in heaven, giving gifts to men; governing, sanctifying, teaching, and enlightening with His Holy Spirit all those who are spiritually-minded, who live in faith, hope, and prayer to be redeemed from the nature and power of this evil world. Follow only this simple, plain spirit of the Gospel, loving God with all your heart and your neighbor as yourself; then you are Christ’s disciple and have His authority to let the dead bury their dead:"

"God is a *spirit* in whom you live and move and have your being; and He does not wait until you are a great scholar, but until you turn from evil and love goodness, to manifest His holy presence, power, and life within you. It is the love of goodness that must do everything for you; this is the art of arts; and when this is the ruling spirit of your heart, then Father, Son, and Holy Ghost will come to you and make their home with you, and lead you into all truth, even if you knew no more of books than I do."

So ended *Rusticus*. It is not easy for me, *Theophilus*, to tell you how much good I received from this simple instruction of honest *Master Rusticus*; for I may well call him "master," since he taught me in so few words a better lesson of wisdom than I had ever heard before.

What a project it was to grasp at the knowledge of all the opinions, doctrines, disputes, heresies, schisms, councils, canons, alterations, additions, inventions, corruptions, reformations, sects, and churches which seventeen hundred years had brought forth throughout the whole Christian world! What a project this was in order to be a *divine*—that is, in order to bear *true witness* to the power of *CHRIST* as a deliverer from the evil of flesh, blood, hell, and death, and as a *raiser of a new birth and life from above*! For as this is the divine work of *CHRIST*, so he alone is a *true and able divine* who can bear a faithful testimony to this divine work of *CHRIST*.

How easy it was for me to have seen with *Rusticus* that all this labyrinth of learned inquiry into such a dark, thorny wilderness of notions, facts, and opinions could mean no more to me now—for my own salvation, my interest in *Christ*, and obtaining the Holy Spirit of God—than if I had lived before it had even begun! But the blind appetite for learning gave me no leisure to understand such a plain truth. I have not finished with books of divinity, indeed; but I will value none as such except those that make known to my heart the *inward power and redemption of JESUS CHRIST*.<note>* such as are recommended in this present treatise for that purpose.</note> Nor will I seek anything even from such books except *that which I ask of God in prayer: namely, how to know better, and to more greatly abhor and resist, the evil that is in my own nature; and how to attain a supernatural birth of the Divine life brought forth in me. Everything else besides this is pushpin*—The shipwrecked man only wants to get to shore. If we saw the truth of our state as he does, we would have *only one want*, and that would be to regain our first created state. There is no misery except in the evil of our own fallen state; this is our shipwreck and great distress. Nor is there any happiness except in having the first life of God and all goodness *opened again in the soul*. He who is not intent upon this "one thing needful" is not a wise Christian, much less a *divine*, or someone qualified to make known to others the mystery of the power of *CHRIST* in the work of redemption. <note>* such as are recommended in this present treatise for that purpose.</note>

of the church. He was to be the instrument for concentrating and simplifying the substance of this science—in all its depth and diversity—as stated in the following section. He aimed to make it understandable to the common people while also laying the foundation for spreading gospel truth, with all its proven power, capacity for growth, and effectiveness, even to the ends of the earth. This was accomplished not by a learned and formal tracing of those practical applications of truth back to their principles and forms in the Holy Scriptures, but (with the help of the mystery revealed in Boehme’s writings) by personally experiencing those discoveries of the Divine life in the soul until they reached full maturity. He then organized his *theological, devotional, and experiential knowledge* into a simple, methodical form for future distribution.

For just as a seed or a grain of wheat in the ear, once fully mature, naturally contains within itself—in a single unit—all the original properties and powers of the first seed (now enriched by their outward expression), and just as it is capable, through careful sowing and cultivation, of producing a great increase and finally a plentiful harvest; so the seed contained in Law’s own writings and those he championed (as mentioned hereafter), being sown in its proper place by God's providence, grew into the *spirit* or *spiritual tree* of Methodism. The blossoming and *full development* of this tree—regardless of what it produces in the meantime, according to God's varied wisdom—will occur in what is mystically called the *time of the* LILY. This is when the kingdom of grace and the kingdom of nature become ONE, as it is promised will happen on earth; that is, when, through a *correct understanding* of the revelation of Boehme, the piety, purity, and perfection of the sons of God shall be crowned with *virgin*-SOPHIA, or Divine wisdom. 

Just as the fertile seed, in the fullness of its display as a lovely aromatic flower (favored by good soil, a healthy atmosphere, and proper scientific cultivation), necessarily shows all the central perfections of its nature that were hidden within it—and just as this perfected development is a *true symbol* and *emblem* of the Divine manifestation as MAN—so may we not justly hope to see the perfect restoration of the original glorious image of God? This image was absolutely redeemed by the second Adam on the very earth created for him. This "great day" <note>p. 5, 6, 52</note> may be closer than is generally believed. For "it is undeniable that the seven thousandth year is but a short time away; and it may be asserted with good reason that the six-day creation will last no longer than until that year arrives." We know that the paradisiacal Sabbath began on the *afternoon* of the sixth day. <note>GENESIS 1:31.</note> And what insightful and reflective mind cannot see, even now, the signs of its immediate arrival in the movements of the great spirit of nature? With its mystical earthquakes and signs, it is overturning mountains and leveling valleys throughout *all nations*, all moving <note>BOEHME, Forty Questions 1:116—129; Mystery of Heaven and Earth 49—60.</note> toward the grand conclusion: the Sabbath unity or rest. May God hasten the time, according to His wisdom and will!

Mr. Law’s opinions regarding truly spiritual mystic and ascetic writers are well known, as they are stated in his published works and will be presented to the reader at the end of this section. However, regarding false mystics—with their transcendentalism and empty reasoning on divine subjects—he held them in the greatest abhorrence. (He referred to those who think they are living members of Christ's mystical body, *the resurrection and the life*, simply because they entertain their imaginations with spiritual, psychological, or metaphysical toys and feel an *inward glow* during such speculations.) It is equally certain that he disapproved of all self-proclaimed visionaries and their supposed revelations. In those who were otherwise devoted to God, he considered such things to indicate a diseased state of Christian understanding and only a hybrid kind of gospel experience. For such vi—

These dangers arise in many ways but consist chiefly of temptations toward SPECULATION and reasoning, thinking they can thus attain knowledge of supersensual matters, or, as the Scriptures say, "by searching to find out God." The reason, indeed, why GICHTEL, the accomplished editor of the standard German edition of Boehme's works—the worthy, the learned, the devout, the Bramwell-spirited, the all-powerful [Hebrews 11:29–34], the highly illuminated, and scientific theosophist, Gichtel—the reason why his light was relatively hidden under a bushel and restricted in its effects (despite what may be said in favor of his case), was because he was not united with a systematic, outward spiritual church. This is all due to a self-deceptive persuasion to which they cling, and by which they deflect the blows of the Spirit in the warnings of their friends—namely, the idea that they are *not called out* and therefore must not run before they are sent. All the while, they overlook or forget what their primary teacher has said on this point: [Theosophic Questions 5:19] that man's mind is like the sense and nerve of the Holy Spirit; and secondly, that God's wisdom and providence work in and through human efforts, either accompanying or overruling them, for nothing *is done by God except through something done by man.*—But how to persuade such individuals out of their fallacies and draw them from their secluded retreats into the light of the Gospel day, while they continue to indulge in their own opinions and imagine they know better than those who have gone through their experience? These individuals admit they could never attain full liberty of soul until they died to their former opinions and entered heartily into outward Christian church action, while also keeping their usual private devotion and theosophic research—how to achieve this is the question.
