<margin>the "Spiritual Combat"</margin>
And what is the reason that the piety of Germany today is in such a poor, sickly, unpurified, and narrow state, relatively speaking, and so uninfluential in the world? The writer concludes this is the case from information received in response to his pertinent inquiries from a devout person who has recently traveled to almost every part of Germany solely to find enlightened theosophists, but who found the truest devotion in private families of the Roman Catholic communion. What, then, can be the reason for this spiritual lethargy in that great nation, except simply that Protestantism there has no bond of union, no simple, systematic, universal religious society to draw it together and direct its motion—such as, for example, original Methodism? If that were provided, its wonderfully talented and, in many cases, holy children—who are now like sheep without a shepherd—would then be able to bring their various talents into the right sphere of action, and Germany would contribute its proper and honorable share of influence to the evangelization of the nations. How, then, is the regeneration of Germany to be achieved? It must be done as the regeneration of England was achieved: by Law's "Christian Perfection" and "Serious Call"; by "Taylor's Holy Living and Dying"; and the three volumes of "Kempis" falling upon and igniting the spirit of a young, ardent, devout Wesley-Ignatius; for similar causes produce similar effects. If these were translated into German with the same purity of language and logic as the first two were in English, and were sent with the Bible to all the German universities, the rest could be left to God.

## CATALOG OF MANY AUTHORS, who have written on MYSTICAL or SPIRITUAL MATTERS; or who have ILLUSTRATED and COMMENDED, or INTERPRETED, or EDITED them.*

->A.<-

**ON INTERNAL ABNEGATION**—anonymous, enlightened, methodical, short.
*ABRIDGMENT of the Slain Lamb, etc.*—see J. Daumont.
*ABRIDGMENT of the Mystical Ways of the Ven. Mother of St. John the Evangelist.* Paris.—cited in her life, published in Paris, 1689.
**ACTA MARTYRUM** [Acts of the Martyrs] sincere and selected.—An excellent book after the divine Scriptures.
*Memorable Actions of the Dominican Fathers of the Low Countries.*
**ADRIANUS ADRIANI.**—*Various works, Belgian.*
**ALBERTUS MAGNUS.**—*Paradise of the Soul. On Cleaving to God.* Cologne. This last one is entirely mystical.
**P. L'ALLEMAND**, Chancellor of the University of Paris.—a pious collector of the final hours of several notable Saints.
**P. L'ALLEMAND**, Louis, *his Life and Doctrine*, Paris.—praised by P. Rigoleuc as enlightened by the Spirit of God.
**DE ALCANTARA**, Peter. His remarkable mortification is praised by St. Teresa.
<margin>e/</margin> **ALETHOPHILI** True Perfection and Happiness in this World.—*German. Solid and vigorous.*
**ALPHONSUS DE MADRIL.**—Methodical, solid, short.
**ALVAREZ**, Balthasar. Devoted to contemplation. His life was written by L. de Ponte and printed in Cologne, 1670.
**ALVAREZ DE PAZ**, Jacobus.—Mystical Theologian, systematic writer, in three folio volumes, Mainz, 1614. In this work, the parts pertaining to Mysticism are in the third volume, making up about a third of it. The rest are ascetic, practical, spiritual, moral, and indeed excellent.
**AMBROSIUS CAMALDULENSIS** Abbot of the Order. Wrote on Dionysius.
**ANDILLIUS**, Robert.—*French translator of Teresa and of the Lives of the Fathers, etc.*
**ANGELA OF FOLIGNO.** Taught by God.

**ANNOTATION.**—The cross of Jesus Christ and the graces resulting from it—that is, the love of the life, virtues, and death of Jesus Christ; the purification of the soul through these; and subsequently the infusion of true celestial and supernatural Theology, and of the flavorful and experimental knowledge of God, His attributes and perfections, redemption, and other divine wonders and very sublime favors—are the element and particular character of St. ANGELA of Foligno. In her reigns a heartiness, simplicity, and sincerity so natural that one feels she is free from all fraud and deception. Her doctrine and life are the substance of the Gospel, entirely pure and practical, and it is a path where self-love can find neither refuge nor support.

<margin>e/</margin> The works and life of this holy Lady, who lived in Foligno in the Duchy of Spoleto four hundred years ago, and who, having been converted while she still had her husband, entered the third order of St. Francis after he died, were published in Latin by her confessor. Besides the editions made in Paris and Cologne, 1601, they are also found in the acts of Bollandus on the fourth of January, which was the day of this saint's death. They have also been published in various languages, namely in French at Paris, and in Flemish at Antwerp, 1628. [Besides those mentioned in that place, the same works of the Blessed Angela are said to have been translated from Latin into the Spanish language and published in the year 1618 by a noble girl of Madrid, Francisca de los Rios, twelve years old.] But as French copies were no longer to be found, a new translation was recently made (in 1696) and published under the title of "The Theology of the Cross of J. C.; or the Works and Life of the Blessed ANGELA of Foligno." Everything has been arranged there in better order.

<margin>e/</margin> Her works contain a very powerfully moving recommendation of the life of J. Christ and of his three inseparable companions: poverty, contempt, and suffering; of prayer; of humility; of spiritual love; of the gifts of God to his lovers; of the sacrament of love; of the presence and dwelling of God in the soul; and of the supernatural communications of God, with necessary precautions against illusions. Her life is divided into three parts: the first contains the description of her conversion, her penance, and her terrible purification; the second, the supernatural ways in which God communicated His consolations, His lights, and knowledge of Himself, His attributes, and things regarding our redemption and salvation; and the third, her final discourses, her Testament, and her most happy death, which occurred in the year 1309. Joined to this edition, one finds the exercises of BLOSIUS on the passion of J. Christ.

The short works of ST. FRANCIS OF ASSISI, printed in Latin in quarto at Antwerp, 1623, with too many remarks by Waddingus, and in small format without remarks at Lyons, 1636, are of the same spirit and character as St. Angela.

<margin>en</margin>Monsieur de BERNIÈRES LOUVIGNI, counselor to the King and Treasurer of France at the office of Caen, died there in 1659—not of any illness, but of the "kiss of love" in the heat of prayer. In terms of his affective style, he closely resembles St. Teresa; however, regarding his subject matter and doctrine, he is entirely in the spirit of St. Angela, whom he greatly admired and imitated. Following her example, he took nothing more to heart than the cross of Jesus Christ, as well as the imitation and teaching of the poverty, abjection, and sufferings of the Son of God—matters which this holy man recommends everywhere as the highest point of perfection in this life. His divine writings are filled with the true spirit of the most solid Christianity. His *Interior Christian*, which has been printed dozens of times in France and translated and published in Flemish and even in Italian, deals generally with the subjects mentioned above, but specifically treats mystical matters, the presence of God, and prayer in books 3 and 7. There was a plan to publish many more of his other works, beginning with the addition of a second volume to the *Interior Christian* and the publication of his divine *Maxims* and excellent *Letters*. However, his *Life* and four other works promised in the preface at the beginning of his *Spiritual Works* have not yet seen the light of day, and perhaps never will, given the daily opposition that worldly, acquired knowledge poses against the advancement of the science infused by the Spirit of God, and the contradiction between the outward piety that dominates everywhere and that which is truly solid, interior, and hidden.

HENRI SUSO, a holy Dominican of the fourteenth century, is also within the spirit and character of St. Angela of Foligno. The old German original of his works can no longer be found, but we have—as with Tauler—a Latin translation by Surius, printed several times in Cologne (the most recent being in 1615). It is from this version that the current German translation was made, also printed in Cologne in 1661. Among his works, the *Dialogue of Eternal Wisdom* with his disciple, *four sermons*, *twelve letters*, *his life* (which is a very beautiful piece written by one of his spiritual daughters, though it is incomplete), his *Meditations on the Passion*, and his *Exercises*, *Hours*, and the *Office of Eternal Wisdom*, have as their primary subject the sufferings and the cross of Jesus, as well as the patience and resignation with which we must participate in them. His *Dialogue of Truth* and *his disciple* treat other sublime and mystical matters, as does his treatise on the *Nine Rocks*, which one must climb to find our beginning again—after first showing, through a description of the corruption then reigning in all ranks of Christendom, how much everyone, both ecclesiastical and secular, had fallen and distanced themselves from God. All his works, except for the *Dialogue of Truth*, were translated into French and printed in Paris in 1614; quite recently (in 1684), a new translation of his *Dialogue of Eternal Wisdom* was published there, dedicated to the Bishop of Meaux.

Suso was a man of incredible mortification, boundless humility, and a sweetness and patience that withstood every trial. He was an incomparable lover of the sacred humanity of the Son of God and His sufferings—a quality he seems to have inherited from his holy Mother, who died on a Good Friday out of pure compassion for the sufferings of the Son of God and the Holy Virgin, who saw Him agonizing on the cross.

<margin>c/</margin>Besides the exercises of Tauler and the meditations of St. Catherine of Siena (which will be mentioned later and are in the character of the cross of Jesus Christ), there is also the greater part of the life of St. Mary Magdalene de Pazzi; *The Sting of Divine Love* by St. BONAVENTURE; *The fourth part of the meditations* of LOUIS DU PONT, whose work is worth more than all imaginable sermons of this time, as there are no necessary Christian truths that are not reduced therein to useful and pious meditation; the *Elevations on the Passion*, by a Father of the Oratory, Paris, 1677; the Flemish book *Sponsus Sanguinum* [The Spouse of Blood], often printed in Antwerp, which includes about twenty formal meditations on the passion of our Lord, the author of which (Michael Zachmorter) is the same as that of the *Thalamus Sponsi* [The Bridal Chamber of the Spouse]. To this I must add (leaving aside several others) another small Flemish book, almost unknown but very solid, titled *The Secret of the State and Life of J.C.*, Amsterdam, 1653. The author was enlightened, though unlearned <note>The text uses "idiot," meaning a simple or uneducated person in this historical context.</note> and a tradesman, named Henri Gerrits, marked by the initials H.G.—Regarding the mental or spiritual sorrows of Christ, which are the most important of all, there exist *Eight excellent Meditations* by an anonymous Virgin, which are usually found attached to the book *Spiritual Combat* by Father Scupoli, and have thus been frequently published.

<margin>direct</margin>
**ANNOTATION.** — The writings and letters of Monsieur Bertot teach the same doctrine as the works of Mons. de Bernières ~~of whom he was the intimate friend and spiritual son~~ and show no less the solidity of his enlightenment and his experiences in the ways of prayer—especially in those of passive prayer in pure and naked faith—than the beautiful talents he had received from God to guide souls capable of His graces, to animate and strengthen those who have already entered upon them, and to preserve both from all illusion.

Those who have seen the *History of the Life of Madame Guyon* written by herself, will no doubt have noticed there that our author was her director during almost the entire time that divine love led her through the hardest and most rigorous paths to make her find the resurrected life in God by the assured means of the cross and total death to self. One will even find among his letters several that were written to this lady, which those who have read her life with some application will easily discern. It is true that she acknowledges that, by a very particular providence—and to take away from her all the supports that might have hindered in her the loss of all "self-life"—he helped her very little regarding her interior state. However, M. Bertot having died at the beginning of the new life into which divine goodness happily made her enter after having delivered her from all her pains, she notes to us that not only did she have some sign of his death, and even that she was the only one to whom he addressed himself, but also that it seemed to him he shared his spirit with her to help her spiritual children.

Indeed, one will find an entire conformity between the principles and advice of this enlightened director and that of this great soul, so deeply instructed by God through long experience in the most interior secrets of His love, which she clarifies with a clarity and ease that even seems to surpass that of her director. He, nonetheless, explains the same subjects with unction and power in a manner that can greatly serve to smooth their difficulties, and to reassure and advance the souls called to these sacred paths, so hidden from the "wise" and those who claim ownership of their own righteousness.

Monsieur Bertot was a native of the diocese of Coutances in Normandy, where he was ordained a priest. He was a great friend of the late Messire Jean de Bernières-Louvigni, Treasurer of France at Caen, so well known for his spiritual works, who died in the odor of great piety on May 13, 1659. After the death of this dear friend, whom he regarded as his spiritual father, he applied himself to directing souls in several communities of nuns. Several persons of consideration of both sexes <insert>[and even some who were engaged in important positions both at court and in the military]</insert> consulted him to learn from him the ways of salvation, and he tried to help them through his instructions and his letters. He continued this exercise until the time that providence attached him to the direction of the Benedictine nuns of the Abbey of Montmartre near Paris, where he remained in this position for about twelve years until his death. He was a man of good counsel and very interior, as will be seen by his works. His experiences had made him realize that to serve

**BOURIGNON**, *Antonia.*

**Annotation.** — This writer affects neither the style nor the sublime subjects of the mystics: she insists only on the substance of evangelical doctrine: self-denial, the mortification of nature, the imitation of Jesus Christ, the practice of virtues, the love of God, and dependence on Him. — Here is the true character of her writings. It is a force that is luminous, free, natural, sweet, solid, simple, easy, for universal use and proportioned to the capacity of everyone and even children; (so writes her admirer, Poiret,) impartial, pure, animating, and which vividly and substantially determines sincere souls toward real and specific acts of conduct, of penance, of abandoning the world and its affections, of self-renunciation, of the love of God, and of dependence on Him through the resignation of our will into His hands, so that by resuming dominion over us as over Adam before the sin, He may restore and subsequently govern all things fully according to His divine will.

<margin>n/</margin> In several other writings, however good they may be, one often perceives things only in general, such that when one wants to come to specific practice, one still does not know quite how to go about it. Here one feels pulled out of this indecision, and one sees oneself shown step by step where to set one's foot. One feels as if led and applied by the hand to the work that must be undertaken, and animated within in a way that is not ordinary. Furthermore, one finds there explanations and uncommon insights into the great principles of the power, goodness, justice, truth, and wisdom of God: on the glorious creation of the world and of man: on his fall and his deplorable and infinite corruption: on Jesus Christ, His birth from Adam,* (!) His functions, His kingdom, that of the Antichrist, the decay of true Christianity in all religions through the fault of their leaders, the destruction of the wicked, and the renewal of the Church and the world. One finds there the essential of religion and virtue, distinguished from their accessories: the annihilation of useless controversies and pernicious heresies: the conduct that must be held in all things: the awakening of the restlessness in which the soul must remain as long as one has not yielded entirely to God; and the discovery of the deceitfulness of the human heart in everyone, and particularly in the false spiritualists and devotees, who, priding themselves on making much of all kinds of spiritual and mystical books, could not hold their ground before these—for which alone they have an aversion that they would like to inspire in everyone, some subtly, and others more overtly: because they see that these truths strip them of their pretended spirituality, and make them appear to their own eyes and to those of others as something quite different than they would like.

Although I find no writers who are fully in the character of Mademoiselle Bourignon such as has just been marked, nevertheless as one of the things that has shone forth the most in—

> * Her works in French are comprised of nineteen volumes, and were published in 12mo in 1686. The editor was the devout and indefatigable Poiret, who was not as discriminating in his approvals as he was talented in defending what he deemed to be the interests of vital Christianity. If an author only wrote in the style he admired, he seemed to adopt all their peculiarities, visions, and revelations, along with what was orthodox in their performances. In the present case, this authoress, along with much that was good and solid, advances several confused and heretical notions (which she had made for herself, doubtless from misconceived scraps of Behmen <note>Jakob Böhme</note>, and other writers) concerning the state of Adam when in paradise—among other things, that ‘Jesus Christ was then born of him,’ (as the “firstborn of the creation,”) who, at Adam's fall, became invisible, only occasionally showing Himself to the patriarchs, prophets, etc., until the time of the Virgin; with a number of similar fantastic conceits, all of which she gives forth as a *pure revelation from God to her!* The Chevalier Ramsay adopts a few of these crudities; as likewise Dr. Garden, in his “Apology for A. Bourignon,” 8vo, London, 1699; also Marsay, and others, of her own country. Seven volumes of her practical works were translated into English and published partly at the expense of the Honorable Robert Boyle. She appears to have been, naturally, of a dark, sour temperament; and, when a young woman, being subjected to severe trials from a cross-grained step-mother and an unfeeling father, she turned to religion with many prayers, fastings, self-denials, and ascetic practices, and in due time, after the ordinary experience of such a complexion, was brought into liberty. Her constitutional temperament seems still to have predominated in her regenerate state, as manifest in her published life and works. The former is about as profitable for perusal as any of her other writings, two or three of which may deserve a reading. There is an affecting anecdote

This is especially true when they consider that just as the clergy took the life of this holy man because of his freedom in telling them the truth (as they also did to Molinos), Mademoiselle Bourignon would have likewise lost her life a hundred times for the same reason, had God not continually prevented her from falling into the hands of her persecutors.

**A CANFELD, Benedictus (Benet of Canfield)**. — *Enlightened, learned.*

<margin>S Leo</margin>
ANNOTATION. — Since this author intended to facilitate the acquisition of perfection by recommending a means that is most evident, incontestable, easy, and complete, he composed a small treatise in Latin, French, and English titled *The Rule of Perfection*. In this work, he reduces everything to the single principle of the *Will of God*, which is the character of his book. This indisputable principle, approved by all Christians and even by all rational creatures, serves greatly to ensure that everything is put into action and practice. It also serves to disillusion those who imagine for themselves, or wish to persuade others, that the spiritual life consists only of some vague, abstract speculations of an idle mind without action. He desires that the Will of God alone be the principle and the goal we look toward in all things. Having divided this will into three parts, based on a passage from the Apostle, namely: the exterior and *good* will; the interior and *pleasing* will; and the intimate or essential, *super-eminent*, and *perfect* will. He spends the first part of his book showing how the Will of God, which concerns our actions, is known through God's law, right reason, the commands of superiors, or the outcome of events that happen to us. This will must be performed or accepted actually, uniquely, voluntarily, confidently, with light, and with promptness. After this, the Will of God makes itself felt within the soul and manifests itself in a luminous and flavorful way, followed by admiration, humiliation, exultation, and the elevation of the spirit to God. This constitutes his second part, followed by a third that treats an intimate and supernatural communication from God Himself. Regarding this communication, the author reports one unique means and two manners of practice, which are applicable to two sorts of people. In both manners, he enumerates several points and various necessary observations and precautions regarding the mystical and interior life. All of these, however, come back to passive annihilation, which is for the fruitful love of contemplation and union; and to active annihilation, which is for practical love, by which one must act spiritually or physically in the world.
<margin>n./</margin>
As this author was learned, he is as methodical and systematic as he is solid, enlightened, and cautious. He does not lack any necessary precaution, not only against false mysticism and false quietude* or the idleness of nature, but also against the confusion one might feel regarding the words and manners of speaking he uses. He shows that these terms were used by the holy doctors who preceded him—a subject that *Sandæus* treated more fully in his Latin work titled *The Key or Dictionary of Mystical Theology*, Cologne, 1640. As also

---

related therein, regarding the pastor of Blatton, George de Lisle, who—having escaped sudden death while in a state of worldly folly and intoxication—was so struck by the goodness of God in preserving him from rushing into perdition that he became a true penitent and a most zealously holy man. He relates his burning devotion to God and love for his neighbor, as well as the great austerities he practiced upon himself. He renounced all studies and all academic learning, keeping only two books: the *Holy Bible* and the *Lives of the Saints*. This man of God read a chapter from the former and a "life" from the latter every day, saying of these two books, "*Here is the doctrine!* (the Bible) *and here is the practice!* (the Lives of the Saints)." He had lived this way for many years when Antonia Bourignon first met him, being then sixty years old; he continued in this state for twelve years more. Her works are now of little value, as whatever is edifying in them—though there is much force in her practical exhortations—may be found in a more attractive form and free from all unprofitable mixtures in other theological and devotional authors. She died in 1680 and was undoubtedly an instrument of Divine wisdom in the renewal of the Gospel spirit. For further details concerning her and the times in which she lived, consult Poiret’s works and the "Apology" for her, published in 1699. I consider Poiret and some others to have been the correspondents in Holland for the Philadelphians of London from 1697 to 1703.

But above all, see Ruusbroec's "On the Adornment of Spiritual Marriage," book II, chapters 76 to 79, which was likely seen by Tauler and explains the matter more fully.*

Dr. Le Brun in his French treatise *Clarification of Mystical Theology*, printed in Rouen, 1659; and very recently the *Archbishop of Cambray* in his *Maxims of the Saints*, which have caused such a stir, and which despite the well-known censures, still have many supporters. These supporters believe that far from the author having taken things too far, some points are actually too weakened and fall far short of the sublime meaning intended by the saints and true mystics.

Canfield's book has been translated into Flemish and several other languages and printed many times. The latest French edition<note>This refers to the French edition of Canfield's *Rule of Perfection*. O immeasurable abyss of the love of God!* A very small Latin summary of his entire book was printed in Lucerne, 1649.

The treatise on *Christian Wisdom*, or the *Science of Uniformity with the Will of God*, which Mr. **D'Argenson**, Counselor to the King, wrote in prison and which was printed in Paris in the year 1651, is based on the same principle as Canfield’s and is no less solid, spiritual, and easy, as well as very well written.

### ANNOTATION.
This illustrious and holy lady of the very noble House of Fieschi, whose father was the Viceroy of Naples, was—though a married woman—one of the most spiritual souls and one of the most perfect lovers of God who has lived on earth for a long time. Her character is defined by a love of God so pure, so elevated, so strong, and so unique that nothing can be found on this subject in the examples or writings of the saints and doctors that approaches the sublimity and strength of this most pure love. Having perfectly possessed and converted her in an instant, it burned in her soul and body throughout her life, allowing her to breathe, practice, say, and write nothing but pure and incomparable Love.

One sees in her and in her writings how this noble and pure love—which seeks only God and His glory alone—comprehends all things in itself: the sovereign end, all the ways, and all the means to reach the highest degree of perfection. She shows how from the source of love flow the knowledge and recognition of our infinite corruption and malice; that of our nothingness and our inability to do good; that of the absurdity of vainglory; the renunciation of oneself and of everything; perfect contrition; the horror of sin; the mortification and sanctification of the body, soul, and spirit; acquiescence to the justice of God; perfect patience; a very lively charity and compassion for one's neighbor; and matters of this nature, which are the duty of all those who wish to be saved. Here and there, she deduces from the same source a thousand beautiful and convincing insights on the most important and difficult matters of theology: on the incomprehensibility of God and His love; on the attributes of His power, wisdom, goodness, mercy, and justice; and on the manner in which they correspond with both good and evil creatures. She writes on grace—its prevention, its universality, its manner of operating, its resistibility, and its efficacy; on free will; the power and impotence of man; his cooperation with God in the work of his salvation; and finally, on all mystical theology and its paths of purification, illumination, the annihilation of the faculties, union, transformation, and deification. All these things are the flowings and glowing radiations of the pure love of the Spirit of God, which filled and governed her.

The works of this great saint, who lived and died in Genoa two centuries ago, were translated from Italian into French and published about one hundred years ago in Paris by the Carthusian Fathers of Bourgfontaine; they were then reprinted several times in Paris and Lyon until 1667. At that time, the style was revised and they were reprinted in Paris, but with more cuts and changes than was appropriate. An attempt was made to remedy this through a new edition published recently in the Netherlands under the title *The Theology of Love, or the Life and Works of St. Catherine of Genoa, 1691*. In this edition, her life (which is a work by her confessor) was divided into three parts: her conversion, her discourses and conversations, and her final hours. Regarding the three Dialogues, the first concerns the fall of the soul, its conversion, and its active purification through the infusion of love; the second, the passive purification of the soul and spirit by new infusions of the same love; and the third, several questions of the soul and answers from God on the nature, causes, operations, and effects of this pure love of God. By this same principle, she also separately explains the nature of the purification of souls after death. All of this is presented in an infinitely solid and touching manner.

The blind saint of Brittany, JEAN DE S. SAMSON, a Discalced Carmelite who died in Rennes in the year 1636. He dictated fully sixty spiritual and mystical treatises on various subjects. However, only two quarto volumes have been printed so far (to my knowledge): the first, containing *his Life, his maxims, and some other treatises*, in Paris, 1651 (this was translated and published in *Latin* at Lyon, 1655); and the second in 1654, which included a reprinting of the first. This latter volume contains his *Contemplations on all the mysteries of salvation*, along with several other small works. Like all the rest, these are nothing but outbursts or torrents of an infinite love that dominates everything. This love leads him to give God the name of his "Love" and his "Dear Love" throughout, and to give his books titles such as *Mirrors and Flames of Love*, *Aspirative Love*, *The Consumption of the Soul in God through Love*, *Soliloquy*, *Epithalamium of the Divine Spouse*, etc. His treatise on aspirative love was recently reprinted in the second volume of the *Theology of the Heart*; an abridgment of his *Maxims* is also found annexed to the latest edition of *Real Theology.*

Among the ancients, it appears from the seven authentic letters of St. IGNATIUS of Antioch that this holy Martyr was entirely of the same spirit and character of divine love. His single letter to the Romans (which Father Ruinard recently published for the first time in Greek with the acts of the martyrdom at the end of his *Acta martyrum sincera*) is a singular and divinely convincing proof of this. The same is true of his six other letters, which have been reprinted several times following the publication by Vossius. Vossius, however, showed too much contempt for the letters called "interpolated" and too much passion against the author of that interpolation. That author intended to provide a kind of paraphrase of the Holy Martyr’s letters rather than to corrupt the text, since he actually preserved all the substance and the character of the spirit of love.

* When I first wrote this, I had not yet been able to see the life of ARMELLE NICOLAS, commonly called "Good Armelle." It was written very solidly in the French language by a certain religious Virgin and printed in Paris in the year 1683, with a second printing following. Otherwise, I would not have hesitated to join her to St. Catherine of Genoa as a true companion, for she was moved by the same dominant principle of burning divine love and was consequently imbued with the same admirable and sacred character. Indeed, it can be asserted that her life and her individual ways of acting are, if not more admirable, certainly more imitable, and therefore of more general utility for everyone. Among all the lives of holy souls I have had the chance to read, I have never seen anything that is simultaneously more admirable, solid, and sublime. The *admirability* lies in the fact that whatever admirable virtues, insights, and graces exist in what is most holy and divine in Christianity, they were all found in a poor, unlearned, and <term>ἀναλφαβήτῳ</term> <note>illiterate</note> peasant woman who acted as a servant throughout her life. The *solidity* consists in the fact that everything in her flowed from the living spirit of the indwelling Christ and was founded on union with Him through living charity. Furthermore, these things were not only imitable but were such that they could be integrated with the actions of life, even external ones. Finally, the *sublimity* was such that even in the highest degree of the Christian spirit, or in the most sublime states mentioned by the Mystics, there was nothing so strong and firm, nothing so arduous and lofty, nothing so spiritual or divine that was not perfectly present in this ignorant, unlearned peasant servant who could not read. For her, a single, most full surrender of her heart to Jesus Christ served as her only school and exercise. I am certain that all those who possess a sincere heart for divine things will gain no less benefit than emotion from this; nor do I doubt that anyone who, at my persuasion, decides to read this admirable life will feel grateful toward me for it. Indeed, so that this good might be shared more widely with everyone, effort was recently made (in the year 1703) to bring this *Life* back to the press in these provinces, in a more correct edition. It was titled *The School of the Pure Love of God, open to the Learned and the Ignorant, in the marvelous life of a poor, unlearned girl, a peasant by birth and a servant by condition, ARMELLE NICOLAS, who recently died in Brittany*, etc. However, it is a pity that someone was found [*History of the Works of the Learned*, 1703] who—by I know not what instinct, certainly not God’s—sought to suppress or invalidate such a great good. At the same time, he confirmed (as many have long noticed) that he is incapable of properly presenting the analysis and contents of any book. By concealing the most solid virtues, truths, and the very core of this life, he collected from it only a few small details that he thought would be either hated or ridiculed by most people, thereby deterring them from this remarkable aid to piety and holiness. By such a shameful trick, even the Holy Bible itself could be traduced by any wicked mind. By the same method, the most upright Protestants could be condemned for having published or praised many pious Roman Catholic writings—such as those of St. Bernard, Kempis, Tauler, the *Life of M. de Renty*, and many others (in which several things could be twisted to incite hatred)—which they ought rather to have exposed to derision and rejected, according to the malignant method of reporting recently used against this incomparable monument of divine Love. But since the author of that report was an intimate friend and companion of the famous mocker of divine men (such as David) and sacred things, Baillet—who even in his last posthumous writing (to which our author is believed to have written a laudatory preface) mockingly cites the divine testimony of Armelle to ridicule human liberty—what wonder is it if our author learned to imitate this method of ridiculing divine things from such a companion? I will not speak now of the things the reporter falsely attributes to the Editor of Armelle’s life to incite envy, since I have already refuted those elsewhere. POIRET. *On Erudition, vol. ii. p. 721.*

## A CRUCE, Joannes. — Most enlightened, Angelic, profound, solid, and learned.

<margin>del</margin>
**ANNOTATION.** — He stands on equal footing with Harphius in sublimity, and even surpasses him in the subjects that are particular to him. His goal is to recommend the purity of the soul* <note>Or rather, to show how, through all-encompassing purity, the soul is both safely prepared for and truly attains union with God.</note> by revealing a sample of God’s caresses and delights with a purified soul. Beyond the way of active purification (which he proposes in a manner very well-suited to purging the minds of the learned who seek God), and the same path as it is achieved through the practice of virtues (where he insists that one should always choose what is least and most painful), the singular character of John of the Cross is that of a nakedness of the soul and its powers so universal that it extends even to stripping away attachment to all sensible and particular graces that God often gives to beginners—whether they come through the senses, the imagination, or the other powers—excepting only the substantial words and substantial touches of God. He guards the soul more than any other author against all spiritual illusions, whatever they may be; so that by following his principles, one will walk with a firm step and far from any danger of illusion in the ways of the Spirit through the purity of naked faith, hope, and charity. — Another part of this sublime author's particular character is the passive purification of both the soul and the spirit, or the immediate preparation for uniting with God; he treats this purification more deeply, in more detail, and more vividly (in his *Dark Night*) than anyone has done before. — And thirdly, he treats (in his *Living Flame of Love*) divine union and its wonders in a much more specific and marvelous way than anyone else; as he also does (in his *Canticle of the Divine Spouse and the Bride*) regarding the various conducts and the fluctuations of loving caresses and bitter trials that pass between God and a soul that has arrived at divine union, but which during this life must be exercised by God in various ways for the ends that God knows.† <note>His works conclude with ten *Letters*, nine *Spiritual Cautions* against the World, the Devil, and the flesh, and one hundred *Spiritual Sentences*; to which he adds at the end this exclamation to God, from which you may recognize the man's spirit and the health and purity of his doctrine: "Lord God, my Lover, if you still remember my iniquities so as not to hear my prayer, do with me according to your will, for this I myself desire; exercise your goodness and mercy, and in them you shall be known. If indeed you wait for my works so that by their intercession you may grant my prayer, give them yourself, Lord, and work them in me; and send also the punishments which it pleases you to accept; and let it be so! But if you do not wish to wait for my works, what, O most Merciful Lord, do you wait for? Why do you delay? Why at last, if grace and mercy are to come, which I ask for in your Son? Take the pittance of my works if it pleases you; and grant me this good since you also will it. Who can escape these lowly ways and limits unless you, O my God, raise him to yourself in the purity of love?"</note>

<margin>u/</margin>
This profound and solid author speaks of things in a way that one clearly feels comes from the source and from experience, which draws much attention and respect to them. He wrote in Spanish, being a Discalced Carmelite of that nation and a coadjutor to St. Teresa in the century when the great schisms occurred that still divide Christendom today. His life, which is available in a short abridgment and in another longer treatise, testifies that he was a soul of Angelic purity—an advantage that gives great weight to all his writings. They were translated and published in Latin at Cologne, 1639; in German at Prague, 1697; and elsewhere in several other languages. There are two French translations: one old version, which was printed in Paris four or five times (the last being in 1665), with the addition of a treatise by another religious man regarding the union of the soul with God, by which he intended to provide a necessary supplement to our author's works. However, this piece is only a rather dry bit of scholasticism, which was rightly omitted in the new translation. This second translation of our author's works, published in Paris in 1694 by Father Maillard, a Jesuit, is of a very pure style; it phrases many things more clearly than the old one and with more felicitous expressions. But beyond the fact that the translator does not seem to have well understood the meaning of some passages, too many omissions were made under the pretext of avoiding repetitions, perhaps as a means to suppress passages that are now inconvenient to many, or of the same nature as those removed from Harphius—of which the explanation of the third stanza of the *Canticle of the Living Flame of Love* could well provide examples. Thus, those who wish to have this author in his full integrity will stick to the first editions, especially since one also finds there three discourses and two books or parts of clarifications§ <note>Those three dissertations, which are found only in the old French translation of the works of John of the Cross, were written by Father Jacobus a Jesu. The two books, or parts of illustrations, which are seen there and also in the Latin translation, are by Father Nicolaus a Jesu Maria, a religious of the same Order as Jacobus a Jesu.</note> regarding both Mystical Theology and its phrases or expressions, as well as those of the author. These treatises clarify those matters and remove many difficulties, both through reasoning and through many authorities produced there to forestall the weakness or malice of those who might interpret them in an unfavorable sense. The latest edition, however, has another advantage: at the end, one finds a very useful collection of all the spiritual maxims of our author, which have been gathered from all his works on all sorts of subjects.|| <note>Indeed, in the preface by the same French interpreter, there is at the beginning an argument of our Author's scope, method, and the subjects treated by him, so succinct and organized that I cannot help but present it here translated into Latin, since it encompasses a very brief yet sufficiently full and solid idea of *Mystical Theology*. It is as follows: "In the beginning, this holy man proposes for himself as an end and scope perfect union with God. Then for..."</note>

<meta>This page continues the bibliographic survey of authors influenced by St. John of the Cross, providing detailed entries for Jean de Jesus-Maria, Thomas à Jesu, and Constantin de Barbançon, along with a theological summary of the unitive path.</meta>

As this Author [St. John of the Cross] gave great weight and a brilliant luster to Mystical Theology in this last century, many who have written on the subject have heavily used and benefited from his insights—some naming him and others not. Here are a few who, in this regard, come more or less close to his character:

Father Jean de Jesus-Maria, in his *Mystical Theology*,* <note>This author owes a great deal to John of the Cross and St. Teresa; indeed, it seems he was led to the experience of divine things by their help. Thus, his book agrees perfectly with the substance of those writers and clearly indicates a man who has experienced divine things. His main point comes down to this: a soul devoted to purity of life and humiliation of spirit, joining its affections to God, is illustrated by the ray of His wisdom. From this, knowing God better and loving Him more excellently, and tasting Him more sweetly after having sighed for Him more ardently, the soul is finally touched by the Holy Spirit. In this most sublime and ineffable touch, it is ultimately gifted with a singular and intimate knowledge and contemplation of God, pure love, and ineffable taste and enjoyment. In this matter, the author establishes the very substance—indeed, the peak—of Mystical Theology, and insists upon it primarily, omitting those things that pertain to the purification of the soul, which are among the preparatory steps and are to be sought from others.</note> written in Latin and translated into French by the early translator of the works of John of the Cross, in Paris, 1666.

Thomas à Jesu, whose Latin treatise on *Divine Prayer*, printed in Antwerp in the year 1623, is in a sense a system of Mystical Theology arranged according to the three ways—purgative, illuminative, and unitive—and supported by many authorities from various spiritual authors. This author also wrote another Latin treatise on *Contemplation*, printed in the same place in the year 1620, where he explains his subject in great detail and supports it with many authorities. The rest of his works are not on this subject. He also wrote a very touching treatise on the sufferings of Jesus Christ.

Father Constantin de Barbançon, a Capuchin, seems to have incorporated many of our author's truths, particularly regarding rigorous purification, in his small and excellent treatise *Secret Paths of Divine Love*, which was published almost simultaneously in French, Latin, and German. It has just been very neatly reprinted in Latin under the title *Veræ Theologiæ Mysticæ Compendium, sive Semitæ occultæ Amoris Divini* (Amsterdam, 1698), and it is indeed a kind of Mystical System. His *Anatomy of the Soul*, in three parts (874 pages), is an addition to the book *Secret Paths*. This author is expert, penetrating, concise, and fruitful.

I would rank among the mystical writers who have particularly benefited from the works of John of the Cross, Father *Victor Galenius*, a Capuchin of Trier, specifically in his Latin treatise, *Summa Practica Theologiæ Mysticæ*, printed in Cologne in the years 1646 and 1652. He sought to benefit indiscriminately from the insights of all sorts of spiritual authors in order to give the public the most universal and extensive of all systems that have yet appeared on mystical matters, both theoretical and practical.

The short treatises *Abridgment of Christian Perfection* and *Internal Abnegation*, or *The Ruin of Self-Love*;† <note>This excellent treatise is found in its entirety among the French works of Cardinal de Berulle, printed in Paris in folio in 1657 under the care of Father François Bourgoin. He attributes the treatise to the Cardinal, but at the same time admits that many doubt this, and that the style and mode of expression differ entirely from the Cardinal's diction. He tries to excuse this with the reason and assertion that the treatise belongs to the Cardinal's early years—specifically his nineteenth year. But this has no appearance of truth: that a book could come from the pen of such a young man which could only proceed from a man of accomplished spirituality and many long years of experience. The very method of treating the subject matter shows and proves a man matured over a long time and practiced in the art of writing methodically and succinctly.</note> written last century in Italian, made public in various languages, and reprinted in the Low Countries in 1690 and 1696, in the first volume of the collections titled *The Theology of the Heart*,§ <note>Both volumes of this book appeared in German in Frankfurt and Leipzig in 1702. But the first treatise of the first volume, *On Christian Perfection*, besides the translations and editions reviewed in the Letter, was formerly printed in German in Nuremberg in 1634, and in Dutch in Antwerp in 1631. A small treatise of almost the same title and argument (*On Perfection*) is found added as a supplement to the anonymous book titled *Faith and Reason Compared*, which was recently (1707) published through my own care. That book presents the principles and main heads of divine and spiritual matters, both theoretical and practical, against more pernicious errors—especially those of the Rationalists as well as lukewarm flatterers—with a vigorous, fruitful, and uncommon solidity, openly and without partisan bias.</note> follow essentially the same principles, via the same paths, and toward the same goal.

---

->“He places at the foundation the mortification of the affections, the internal and external senses, the memory, the intellect, and the will; so that the soul, freed from creatures and from itself, may lift itself to God through the darkness of faith, the firmness of hope, and the fires of divine charity.

Because internal tastes, sensible sweetness, and spiritual fervors are usually added to these first beginnings—by which self-love, mental activity, discursive meditation, and other dispositions that are pleasing and comfortable to corrupt nature are nourished and fostered—he teaches that anyone who tends toward that divine union must remove all these imperfections from themselves. They must renounce material forms or notions of created things, as well as imaginary visions and other operations of that kind, so that they may receive supernatural contemplation through infusion and in a passive way, which leads to the highest good through certain, though very dark, paths.

And from this source, as he shows, proceed dryness, aridities, doubts concerning God and one's own state, restlessness, fears, terrors, despair regarding divine mercy, and other internal anxieties that seem equal even to the torments of Hell to the soul. Meanwhile, God is in this state purifying the soul along with its senses and spiritual powers, making it fit to be united with Him in the purest and most sublime manner.

For as soon as the soul emerges from these hard trials, it enters into high, steady, and constant elevations of love; it tastes rest in the enjoyment of its object; and it is entirely transformed into its Creator. And in this happy transformation, God communicates Himself to the soul, while the soul is united to God Himself, as this great Master of the interior life explains in his *Canticles*.” Thus far the Interpreter.<-

## **D. G. Anonymus Belga (David Georgius)—ill.**

Annotation.—Regarding the anonymous Fleming (who is said to be the same person often marked by the letters D. G. or D. J.)—it has been more than a century since a learned man, who appeared to have a full knowledge of both this author's person and his writings, published a small summary of the substance of his doctrine, which amounts to this:

To bring men back to the true knowledge and true worship of God, from which they had all strayed—some by making their worship consist of purely human, civil, and pharisaic morals and duties; others in the use of certain external ceremonies joined to purely ideal speculations, persuasions, and applications. Instead, true Worship consists in giving one's heart, senses, thoughts, inclinations, and life to God, taking Him as the principle and end of everything one does and wishes to do.

That to return to this state, it is necessary for man to know the terrifying depth of the universal corruption in which he is submerged, both by original sin and by his actual and habitual sins. He must confess, feel, groan for, and deplore this corruption before God, firmly and constantly seeking his real deliverance in Jesus Christ, whose grace and spirit must enter into him, to stop and kill the evil there, and to produce a new life in faith, holiness, justice, and charity. In this way, the heart and spirit are so occupied with heavenly things that henceforth, in every thought, enterprise, work, and word, one always has the high Majesty of God before one's eyes with fear, reverence, and gratitude. And it is in this manner that one will be able to stand before God in the terrifying judgment He is ready to bring upon the earth for the extermination of evil and the restoration of good.

That this is the substance of what he recommends; and as for particular opinions that are not necessary for salvation—such as regarding the nature of Angels, Demons, Hell, the location of Heaven, and similar things—he prescribes his own to no one and leaves everyone free to believe what they discover in the Holy Scriptures according to the measure of light they receive. And indeed, most of the Holy Fathers of the primitive Church held several different and even erroneous opinions on these kinds of subjects, without being any less esteemed or tolerated for it. Regarding sacred assemblies and ceremonies, he believes it is good to use them, both for one's own advancement and for that of the weak and infirm.

The Summarizer adds that he has never seen an Author who has written with so much force and energy, although he has read with considerable care all the writers of any importance in the Christian Church.

The Jurist *Werdenhag* in the preface of his *Latin Introduction to the books of Bodin's Republic*; and *Chrestien Hôbourg*, a Protestant Minister of Germany who wrote, among other books, a *Mystical Theology* and an *Unknown Christ* (in the preface of which he mentions this Author, speaking of him as a person highly enlightened by God). The pious and learned CASTALIO consulted him on the meaning of the Bible, which he translated into Latin, and published the preface only under his advice.

I have heard the same judgment made by several people who had read all his writings and who were, moreover, people of spirit, pious, wise, and even learned or very learned. I have known some who could not read them without feeling moved by compunction to the depths of their hearts and inflamed to the point of admiration. Others have expressed the character of this Author in these very terms:

> "This divine man (they say) took great pains to instill in souls this great principle of true Christianity, which is to know by experience in the divine light the depths of our corruption and misery; to mourn it inwardly with an intimate desire for good and a true aversion to evil; and to believe that one can only be delivered from the one and acquire the other by the grace of Jesus Christ within us."

This same person held this Author to be one of the men who best understood the Scripture. For my part, I can ensure that I have seen nothing but what is good and consistent with the above in those of his books I have read. But if anyone wishes to assure themselves of the character of this Author, they need only consult either his *Letters* or his four small *Manuals*; as well as the extracts recently produced from his writings by Mr. Gottfried Arnoldi, formerly Professor at Giessen, in his *History of Heresies* (in German), which he has just made public.

HERMAN HERBERTS, a Minister of the Reformed Protestants at Gouda more than a century ago, comes very close to the spirit and character of this Author in the excellent Flemish Treatise he published in the year 1584, under the title of *A Short Explanation of the Words of St. Paul, Romans 2:28: He is not a Jew who is one outwardly*, etc. This is a kind of system of positive theology (no offense to Voetius in his *Bibliotheca studiosi Theol.*), the most solid and fruitful that can be found, and for which he wrote a very fine Apology in 1591. He had benefited much from the writings of our Anonymous author, and even contributed (so it is said) to the printing or reprinting of several of his works.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of authors who share the spiritual character of the anonymous Flemish author previously mentioned, specifically focusing on St. Ephrem the Syrian and St. Macarius of Egypt, before providing a bibliographic list of authors under the letter D.</meta>

Deacon of Edessa in the fourth century, a man revered and admired by the whole Christian Church, and of whom St. Chrysostom said: 
> “Where is now this great Ephrem, the goad of the sleepers, the comforter of the afflicted, the master, instructor, and exhorter of the young, the mirror of solitaries, the leader of penitents, the sword and dart against heresies, the receptacle of virtues, the habitation and dwelling of the Holy Spirit?”

This man was (just like our anonymous author) without human letters and without formal study; but the Holy Spirit had poured into his mind and heart the substance and even the very words of all the Holy Scriptures. He had been given a tongue that explained them and imprinted them in the hearts of others in a way that no eloquence of the schools or of nature could approach, as his divine writings bear witness. Indeed, they are nothing but a fabric of the substance and terms of Holy Scripture, aiming to recall the spirit of remorse in hearts, to turn men very sharply away from evil, and to animate them very strongly toward good through every conceivable motive of fear, hope, and love. They were so highly esteemed that they were read publicly in the Eastern Churches. There is a Latin translation that has been printed several times, the latest being from the year 1675 in Cologne. His *Testament*, along with some of his minor works, appeared previously in old French; but there is a new translation by Father Lallemand, Chancellor of the University of Paris, in his book *The Death of the Just*, printed in 1673. One also finds in the *Lives of the Holy Fathers*, translated by Mr. d’Andilly, a piece by the same St. Ephrem, which is the *Life of St. Abraham* and that of his *penitent niece*.

Another Ancient of the same spirit and character is the great and divine ST. MACARIUS of Egypt, a contemporary of Ephrem, a solitary and disciple of St. Anthony. Although a man without formal study, he was nevertheless powerful in miracles, virtues, and words. The fifty *Homilies* we have from him are, in my opinion, the most divine and excellent piece preserved from all Antiquity. It is a work of the Holy Spirit that one can no more tire of reading than his minor works, which are of the same character. One clearly feels that it is the Spirit of God who reveals therein the greatness of man's misery and his captivity under sin and the Devil; the means to escape through Jesus Christ and to live again by His Spirit, which thereafter governs victorious souls and produces in them operations and graces that the world does not know. There is no need to warn those who have eyes to see that they will find there the substance of all Mystical Theology,* even down to the very terms that most strangely surprise those who dislike this divine Theology—all the more so as they are indisposed to it by the darkness of their corrupted reason and the turmoil of their passions.

But we owe to the care of Mr. Pritius the best and most complete edition of all the works of St. Macarius, which he has just recently published in Leipzig (in 1698 and 1699). It is preferable to the others both because of the accuracy with which he corrected the Greek text and revised the Latin version of the Homilies and minor works, and because of the additions of the apophthegms and everything else that could be found by the same Father in Cassian, in Rosweydus, and in the *Monumenta* of Mr. Cotelier.

* <note>It might perhaps not be useless to remark here that this holy Author is one among the ancients (as might also be truly said of Ruysbroeck among the moderns) whom you might deservedly consider as the restorer and a sort of living fountain of true Mystical Theology, even though people generally attribute these roles to DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE. However, the works attributed to Dionysius do not appear to belong to the author whose name they bear; rather, they seem to be by a writer later than our Macarius. Furthermore, they contain little concerning Mystical Theology (which he takes to mean the highest degree of contemplation), as most parts relate to Symbolic or Hierarchical theology—unless you except a few passages here and there in the book on divine names, in the Epistles, and in the very brief booklet on Mystical Theology. This last work, as the only one uniquely pertaining to this subject, was published separately in Greek and Latin with notes and commentaries by CHARLES HERSENTIUS, Priest and Preacher, who also included an Apology for Mystical Theology and an introduction to it, in Paris, 1627, in 8vo. All his works had previously appeared there in Greek and Latin through the care of Lansselius in 1615, and were later published more elegantly in Antwerp in 1634 with the Paraphrases of PACHYMERES and the Scholia of MAXIMUS the Monk, with added notes and commentaries by the editor BALTHASAR CORDERIUS of the Society of Jesus; these were reprinted in Paris in 1644 (2 vols. in folio). They had been translated earlier from Greek into the French language, indeed twice, by Father Jean Golius, son of the celebrated Golius, Royal Professor of Greek; his second translation was published in French with elegant type in 1629, in 4to, at Paris.

Furthermore, Dionysius—or whoever remains hidden under that name—is not unjustly said to have something approaching the character of the Platonists in his way of handling the subject, in his phrasing, and even in certain arguments. This is not to be blamed in a man who could have been previously devoted to that Philosophy; however, he primarily focuses on those things pertaining to the intellectual part of the soul and to those who are more advanced. From this, the less cautious might perhaps more easily find an occasion for useless speculations. But Macarius, affecting no philosophical method or appearance (in which he was ignorant) and no such precision or subtlety, is entirely devoted to simplicity, to methods, to words, and to the element and spirit of the Scriptures, possessing the character of an Apostolic man and a clearly sacred writer. He considers all things that must be both destroyed and built up or restored in the whole man so that he may enjoy God. He is thus entirely practical and life-giving, both externally and internally, suited for beginners and those progressing—in a word, for everyone, without the danger of deception.</note>

* With respect to treatises recommended to be studied by contemplatives, the following extract is from a little 18mo. volume of devotions, entitled *The Holy Practices of a Divine Lover*, printed at Paris in 1657. The author considers the 'active way' as but the stepping stone to the 'perfect, or contemplative divinity.' Among all the practical works which have been presented to the world respecting that way of returning to God, it will, perhaps, be difficult to find one more adapted to the purpose, in connection with the popular writings of Law and Kempis, than Ignatius Loyola's *Spiritual Exercises*, which, it is hoped, will, ere long, be published in a classic English dress, and divested of all unpalatability to Protestant idiosyncrasy. The extract referred to above proceeds thus: "A catalog of such books as may greatly help, comfort, and increase the devotion of contemplative spirits, such as are already well-grounded and instructed in the Catholic faith, and who have passed through the necessary rudiments of active preparations. "A.—All the Venerable Father Augustine Baker's Manuscripts, of the Holy Order of St. Benedict, of the English Congregation, which are kept as precious treasures (as indeed they are) in the English Monastery of Comfort, of the same Order and Congregation, at Cambrai. . . . B.—All St. Bernard's works. St. Bonaventure's little works, or *Opuscula*. Father Bennet of Canfield's *Books of the Three Wills*. C.—The works of Climacus. Cassian's works, corrected. —Many other books (he continues) there are, very proper for you, and which may happen to fall into your hands; but these I only reckon up, so that you may easily find out, O devout reader, what may serve your purpose. But to save you labor, never expect to find any book suited for your purpose written by any of the 'Society of Jesus,' whose genius is in the *active way*, and in that they are excellent and very commendable; but in this contemplative way, few or none have appeared ever since their first institute, over these hundred years."

**Brooke.** Henry Brooke was the nephew of the author of the *Fool of Quality* and other works; whose daughter was the author of the *Relics of Irish Poetry*, etc. Mr. Holdcroft published, at Dublin, St. Helen’s, and Wigan, in one volume 12mo in 1820, all the pieces (except the author’s letters) needed to complete the large quarto edition of Behmen; at the end of which he inserted an extensive catalogue of spiritual books, including almost all that had been translated and published in English up to the middle of the eighteenth century. The Brooke family and their acquaintances were great admirers of Mr. Law and of the truly spiritual mystics. This was also true of the celebrated Hannah More of Bristol, who, with her friend the Rev. Richard Symes, Rector of St. Werburgh (a correspondent of Mr. Law when he was living), and Mr. Thomas Mills the publisher, occasionally met together to converse about their favorite author. It is supposed that Mr. Law’s *Serious Call* provided Hannah More with the original idea for *Cœlebs*; many of the sentiments and characters of that work are feeble imitations of Law’s powerful genius. The Mr. Mills mentioned above was the father of the respected elderly gentleman now residing at Bristol, from whom the writer obtained a great number of manuscripts by Freher, Law, and others, along with other books. These had been preserved in his family for more than half a century, having descended to him directly from immediate friends of Mr. Law and other learned students of Behmen’s philosophy from the last century.

<margin>al/</margin>
<margin>Edward</margin>
Among the most warm-hearted admirers of Law and collectors of the aforementioned manuscripts was a Mr. Edward Fisher of Bath, to whose philanthropy we perhaps owe the preservation of Freher’s invaluable productions. Freher was a profound philosopher (born in Germany), a man of great learning and piety, and of amazing capacity, originality of genius, and strength of mind. The later years of his life he spent in London, where he died in 1728 at the age of seventy-nine. He appears to have been entirely occupied with his manuscript demonstrations and illustrations of Behmen’s writings. He also continually kept a friend with him named Leuchter, a draftsman, to execute the beautiful drawings and symbols with which his demonstrations are so abundantly illustrated, as well as to make copies of them for others. Freher lived on intimate terms with the Rev. Mr. Waple and other admirers of Jacob Behmen’s writings; among whom might, perhaps, be included some of the remaining members of the Philadelphian Society. This society, which began publicly in 1697 and ended its meetings in 1703, maintained correspondence with individuals of similar sentiments in Holland and various parts of the continent. It originally owed its existence to one or two devout persons whose nature of piety was peculiar to the time of Cromwell. These individuals devoted themselves to the study of Behmen’s writings, which had then just been published in English, and then imagined themselves to be the subjects of visions and revelations. They also published these in print until, in about a dozen years or so, the Philadelphian Society was formed. This society, however, the writer considers to have been more immediately brought into existence and kept together by the pious zeal of the learned Francis Lee, who was then the son-in-law of the society's chief heroine, a Mrs. Jane Lead. She was a very devout woman <note>A seeker of visions, as Mr. Law seems to suggest, while he at the same time criticizes the folly of such attempts, knowing that it is God who selects his prophets and it is not for man to take that office upon himself—a truth that does not appear to have occurred to these Philadelphians</note>—her admirers were probably thereby induced to conclude that what she termed her visions were true revelations to her from God, as they found them to be in harmony with Behmen’s principles, with which they might have been acquainted. As for her style, whatever the *modern* reader might say about it, they claimed it was quite consistent with her pretensions and fully equal to that of *Hosea* or other second-rate ancient prophets; indeed, they found a beauty in it that was admirable, if not inimitable! If we were to obtain a general idea of her published visions through a modern illustration, they might be described as what we would expect from devout and sincere, *moaning, squawking, unknown-tongue* professors, had they immersed themselves deeply in the transcendentals of Behmen’s philosophy and then turned into prophetesses. And just as these women obtained supporters for their innocent self-deceptions regarding their "extraordinary vocation" from sincere and pious—though, regarding theological knowledge, partially informed—individuals, so did Mrs. Lead in her day make her converts. These were not only among the simple, but also included some very respectable persons from the University of Oxford; for she captivated the very learned and ingenious Lee, a Fellow of St. John’s, to such a degree that, for a time, he seems to have given up his brilliant talents entirely to the propagation of her views or, as he considered it, the interests of Divine truth. The purpose of the Philadelphian Society may be ascertained by referring to their periodical, *Theosophical Transactions* (1697), of which only five numbers were published, and to Roach’s two publications and others up to 1727. Without Lee, however, the group might never have been heard of, as the other members, including Dr. Hooker, do not appear to have been very eminent in literary ability. But how great Lee’s talents were, and the devotion he brought to the cause, may be inferred from his defense of Mrs. Lead in a long letter he addressed to Dr. Henry Dodwell, who had reproached him for encouraging her groundless enthusiasm and thereby bringing a reproach on the university; it is also evident from his writings in connection with the Philadelphian Society. If an opportunity offers, we hope at the conclusion of this section or elsewhere to provide a few sparkling illustrations of the genius, ability, and Christian science of this celebrated individual—that "most pious, ingenious, and ready writer," as Dr. Hickes is supposed to have called him in that observation. After the dissolution of the Philadelphian Society, Dr. Lee returned again to his accustomed sober occupations of practical philanthropy and incessant activity in the promotion of learning, piety, and the general good of his fellow creatures. He was supposed to be the author of <insert>$\times$ (some of whose manuscript treatises we also hold)</insert> Nelson’s *Feasts and Fasts*, of the second volume of *Kempis’s Christian Pattern* (with the preliminary dissertation therein), and of *Kempis’s Christian Exercise* by Nelson; he was also the translator of Fenelon’s *Pastoral Letter*, besides being the editor of numerous other ingenious and devotional publications, both translations and originals, and perhaps partly the author of Nelson’s *Life of Bull*. <insert>$\times$ In Nelson’s Will in the *Life of Nelson* 1860.</insert> For anyone who has read his prefaces to *Lead’s works* (which he edited), his poems therein, and his writings in connection with the Philadelphian <insert>$\times$</insert>

Society, and the above-mentioned works in the order of their appearance, may perceive the identity of style; and when he compares them with Nelson's own undoubted letters, dedications, etc., he will recognize the difference in the authorship.

Among other “revelations” which this Mrs. Lead published abroad was one which she termed the “Everlasting Gospel,” which was to be preached to the devil and his angels after the restoration of the whole human race; for she claimed that the entire fallen creation, both of men and devils, should return to their original state as brought forth by God—the immutable God of **LOVE** and Goodness, whose designs in creation should not be eternally frustrated. Instead, His glory would be even more infinitely glorified by triumphing over every opposition and self-will of the creature; all of which, after having exhausted itself and been conscious of its own possibilities, should return to the unity and harmony of the Divine life. To overturn such a bold assumption, Freher wrote a deeply grounded philosophical treatise, illustrated with elaborate symbols, demonstrating from Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme</note>, in accordance with Scripture, the absolute impossibility—according to the known powers and possibilities of eternal nature—of the restoration of devils. But when Law, in later life, had obtained a clear philosophical understanding of the whole subject, he declared that both sides stood in the same position: namely, in a necessity of neither affirming nor denying the matter. He believed that neither Behmen nor Scripture sufficiently addressed the question, and that it all depended upon a possibility which at present could not be proved, but if it were possible, it would surely come to pass. 

Another celebrated character who deserves notice in connection with Freher, Law, and others immortally identified with Behmen, is John George Gichtel, the original compiler and publisher of a uniform German edition of Behmen's works with notes. He was a man of the deepest practical piety and, at the same time, the highest scientific and theosophical abilities. His life was published in German at Leyden in 1722, entitled, “The Wonderful and Holy Life of That Elect Instrument and Man of God, John George Gichtel,” as well as his “Theosophia Practica.” These should all be translated into English, preserving their theosophical style. But to return.

Some time after Mr. Law's death, his surviving friends, to whom a few of his manuscripts had been committed for the publication of Behmen, found among them several long extracts in Law's own handwriting, apparently from some eminent writer on theosophical science. These, however, remained with them without further notice for nearly twenty years. About this period, it would seem that Mr. Fisher—who, as stated, had been a strong admirer of Mr. Law's talents and genius—conjectured there must be more memorials of him existing than what had appeared. Feeling that nothing of so great a man should be lost for want of collecting, he commenced an inquiry through Mrs. Gibbon, Mr. Law's nephew Mr. William Law, and Law's remaining intimate friend, Mr. Langcake, who was the joint editor with Mr. Ward of the incomplete four-volume quarto edition of Behmen. One of the results of this inquiry was Mr. Fisher ascertaining the existence of Freher's manuscript works and drawings. 

Thereupon, he began to make further researches and was at last able to discover and purchase (chiefly from the widow of Denis, the bookseller formerly of New Bridge Street, Blackfriars) two almost complete copies of Freher's works, with their numerous and beautiful symbolic illustrations. These he preserved with the utmost care, believing that he possessed a treasure that could not be matched in the world. His admiration, however, grew into a sentiment of enthusiasm; as an amusing illustration of this, the present Mr. Mills related to the writer of these lines the following anecdote, the circumstances being familiar to his memory. 

About the time of Bonaparte's expected invasion of this country, the elder Mr. Mills was suddenly roused from his sleep one night by a loud knocking at the door. Getting up to find the cause, he found there his friend Mr. Fisher in the greatest anxiety. On being asked the reason for this midnight visit, Fisher replied that he had heard of Bonaparte's intended invasion of this country; that the rumor of his descent on the southern coast was all a pretense, for the true secret was that he intended to sail up the Severn directly to Bristol, his object being to get possession of Freher's manuscripts and drawings in Fisher's possession. Since there was no time to be lost, he thought it best to come off at once and consult with his friend Mr. Mills as to the best way of depositing the manuscripts in a place of safety. 

After Mr. Mills succeeded in allaying the fears of his friend, he prevailed upon him to return home again. However, some time later, Mr. Fisher proposed to send one copy of the manuscripts to the Bodleian Library at Oxford and the other to the British Museum, as they would probably be out of the reach of Bonaparte there, in case he should suddenly invade England. Accordingly, one of the copies was forwarded from Bath, where Mr. Fisher resided, to the British Museum, and it is there at present; however, it does not contain all of Freher's works. For some reason, he delayed forwarding the remaining copy to the Bodleian, and at his death, it was purchased by Mr. Mills, who also reverently preserved it, along with other manuscripts and letters of Law and similar valued writers, until his death. It then came into the possession of his son, the present Mr. Mills, and so to the writer of these lines. 

If the reader would judge the beauty and ingenuity of those symbols, he has only to refer to the four-volume imperfect edition of Behmen's works and the illustrations therein. In fact, those are not as beautifully executed as the original designs, all of which were produced by the talent of Freher and Leuchter, as observed before, to illustrate the former's demonstrations of the central philosophy of Behmen. Mr. Fisher and Mr. Mills had some reason for their high esteem of those manuscripts, for they are perhaps the most ingenious manuscript curiosities in existence. It is supposed there is nothing of a similar character, except for the few engraved illustrations in Gichtel's German edition of Behmen.
