> ANNOTATION. — The reader (writes the editor of the abbreviated German life of Gichtel) is here presented with a man of a very peculiar character, a singular saint—and yet a saint. * * *
>
> But in the life of extraordinary persons, such as Gichtel was, [and such as Bramwell's diary had shown him to have been, had it not been destroyed,] if some things appear too wonderful, we ought to remember that we are here in the domain of inward wonders, where he who is experienced may measure and understand according to his experience, but cannot and must not exceed it. For, although his eyes may be opened, yet *all heaven* is not therefore opened to him. — He who has never travelled in the *inward way*, in which wisdom leads her true disciples; he who does not live *entirely* by faith, as did Gichtel, but is still governed by worldly prudence and self-love, may see nothing, and probably will not hesitate to affirm that there is nothing here but refined enthusiasm and "error." Such individuals, however, had better not read Gichtel's life at all: it was not lived for them, neither is it written for them. But to those who are able to take and read this life without offense, and to profit from it, [continues the editor, Kanne, an evangelical Protestant minister,] I have endeavored to make the perusal of it as smooth and easy as I possibly could, and refrained from using the theosophic idiom of the original. This latter, a memoir of 366 8vo pages, rather irregular and heavy in its composition, was published about twelve years after Gichtel's death; together with the third edition of his "Theosophia Practica," which consists of a complete collection of his theosophical letters. The publisher, of both these letters and the memoir, was Gichtel's most intimate friend, Ueberfeldt, who had lived twenty-seven years with him in the closest intimacy; but he was not the author of the memoir, which was written by an anonymous individual who had not known Gichtel personally. The materials for it were supplied by several parties, but principally by the above Ueberfeldt; and the composition was laid before Gichtel's friends for examination, previous to its being sent to the press. That Ueberfeldt was not the author of the work, there is every reason to believe, though, as his own writings show, he could have written it much better than this biographer has done. The reason for his declining the task might have been that, as Gichtel's intimate friend, and constantly involved in his movements, he would have had continual occasion there to speak of himself, and this his great modesty could not endure. His name, which often occurs in the work, he would only permit to be represented by the letter U, desiring, as regarded himself, to remain altogether in the background of the wonderful picture, if it were impossible to be altogether concealed. [A few episodes of Gichtel's life might have been selected for insertion in this place, from the manuscript translation of the abbreviated and popular memoir of Gichtel in the possession of the writer, illustrative of the wonderful, indeed, omnipotent powers of faith, wielded by this Samson-like man of God, and which reside in the soul of all believers, who have, like him, under the light of theosophy, laboriously pursued the counsels of the gospel, and realized the full developments of the Christian life in human nature—the lengths, and breadths,

# GUILLORE, Fr. François. — Solid and learned in Mysticism.

# MADAME GUYON.

**ANNOTATION.** — Everyone knows the famous dispute of the late Monsignor de Fénelon, Archbishop of Cambrai, concerning **PURE LOVE**. But perhaps it is not known that Madame Guyon was the innocent victim of the blind zeal, ambitious jealousy, or political views of the enemies of this illustrious Prelate. One of the means they used to discredit the doctrine of this great man was to represent Madame Guyon—with whom he always had a close connection—as another Priscilla <note>A reference to the follower of Montanus, often used as a pejorative label for female leaders in mystical movements accused of heresy.</note> corrupted by the maxims of false Quietism. During the time her writings were being examined, she composed the work of her *Justifications* to show the conformity of her experiences and expressions with those of authors canonized or approved by the Church.

To read the life and works of Madame Guyon with intelligence and profit, it will perhaps be necessary to give a clear and simple idea of the **DOCTRINE OF THE MYSTICS**. For when it is spoken of, those who blaspheme what they are ignorant of regard it as a mass of obscure terms and bizarre thoughts, which have no foundation except in the heated imagination of weak minds or visionary women. —

2. — *To love God with all our heart; to pray without ceasing; to carry our cross every day:* this is the essence of Christian morality, and at the same time the substance of **MYSTICAL THEOLOGY**. The Gospel proposes Charity as the fulfillment of the law; continual Prayer and Self-abnegation as the two means of achieving it.

3. — God loves Himself supremely and uniquely because He is supremely and uniquely lovable. He loves all His creatures according to the degree they participate more or less in His divine perfections. The perfection of GOD is the rule of His love. Now, the most perfect rule for finite wills is undoubtedly that of the infinite will. Let people dispute, refine, and split hairs as much as they want over the different motives for love; they will never dare to deny that the supreme rule of love is *to love God for Himself and all things for Him*.

This is an immutable truth, founded on the idea we have of the Infinite Being. It is the eternal and universal religion of all intelligences. It is a duty to which the creature is obligated at all times and in all places, even assuming that the soul were to be annihilated after death, or that God never granted it any other knowledge of His infinite perfection than what we have during this life.

The hope of the beatific vision is undoubtedly a divine virtue, a legitimate motive for love, a source of infinite consolation, and a powerful resource against all the temptations and miseries of our exile: but it is not pure Charity. Scripture distinguishes between these two virtues. They must never be confused, nor should one reject chaste hope while recommending pure charity.

<margin>/</margin>What makes people believe that man is incapable of this perfect love is that they judge his capacity by what he does, and not by what he ought to do. Men usually act only by a principle of self-love, more or less refined; and by our own strength, we cannot act otherwise. Just as man is not the true light that enlightens his own mind, likewise he is not the cause of the perfect love that must animate his will. A power superior to man must act unceasingly within him to raise him above himself and make him love according to the immutable law of love.

4. — The first means of attaining this pure charity is Prayer: and the most perfect prayer is to passively receive the impression of God, who carries us unceasingly toward Himself. The Church attributes no other activity to man in a state of grace than that of consenting or dissenting to the *Divine action*, which excites and moves him. It is GOD ALONE who is the moving force of the soul; but the soul can always yield or resist the divine operation, and its most perfect cooperation is that of letting GOD act within it.

First, the will, excited and moved by grace, must make efforts and form multiplied desires and distinct acts to turn away from creatures and toward GOD. But after being accustomed to these frequent returns for a long time, one gradually contracts the habit of living continually in the Divine presence in a simpler, more intimate, and more uniform manner. The soul acts, but it is GOD alone who is the principle of its action. It is He alone who moves it, pushes it, animates it, and draws it; but the soul follows freely what attracts it. This is not inaction or a forced cooperation, but a free concurrence with the Divine action. The more the soul gives itself to it, the stronger and more vigorous this action becomes, like the movement of bodies, which increases in proportion as they fall toward their center.

This is the evangelical Prayer, which Madame Guyon, following the Mystics, calls *passive prayer, the prayer of silence, of rest, etc.* It is neither a multitude of words, nor an effort of thought, nor the enthusiasm of a heated imagination; but a commerce of the heart with God, of which even the simplest are capable. It is not we who pray; it is the Holy Spirit who prays in us, who groans, who desires, and who asks for us what we do not know how to ask for ourselves. According to the style of Holy Scripture, everything appears to be the action of God in man, to which man adds nothing but simple consent or non-resistance.

5. — In proportion as man unites himself thus to God through prayer, he must distance himself from the creature and from self through Renunciation, which is the second means of attaining divine union. The one is a necessary consequence of the other.

This Evangelical Abnegation is not an austerity that surpasses human strength, destroys health, or makes us lead an extraordinary life. Jesus Christ practiced none of these austerities. His life was entirely common on the exterior; but His interior was entirely Divine. The renunciation He proposes leads us not only to flee false pleasures, to combat our gross passions, and to be content with the simple necessities according to our state; but to cut out all frivolous amusements, all activities of the mind, and all the charms of the imagination, which serve only to dissipate us and keep us in a taste for the created. Evangelical Abnegation forbids us the slightest look at the creature outside of God, the slightest pleasure against His order, the

<meta>This page continues the explanation of the doctrine of the Mystics and the life of Madame Guyon, specifically detailing the stages of spiritual abnegation and the "passive" work of God within the soul.</meta>

the least return of vain self-complacency. It makes us love the lowest place—even if we were born into greatness—and find silence and interior solitude amid noise and crowds, as well as poverty of spirit and perfect detachment in the midst of riches. That is not all. This Abnegation leads us to debase the *ego*, that idol so dear to man; to receive with joy that which crucifies it; to bear the imperfections of others with patience and gentleness, our own faults with humility and peace, and the purifying rigors of Divine Justice with surrender and flexibility. This is a universal penance—a martyrdom of love—a mortification, or rather a death that extends over the senses, the spirit, the heart, and the whole man, leaving no refuge for the disordered love of creatures or of self.

6.—It is in this continual Prayer and this evangelical Abnegation that all the mysteries of the interior life consist.

The first operation of God is sensible, pleasant, and full of charms. It leads the soul to act, to fight, and to exercise itself in all the labors of active virtue and outward mortification, in order to detach itself from foreign objects. This is the foundation of the interior life, without which all spirituality must be suspected. At this stage, one tastes a sweet anointing and a savory delight in Prayer. One practices mortification with a noble and masculine vigor. The soul sees its own virtue, sustains itself by its labor, and is charmed by its own courage.

7.—Afterward, God begins another operation in the soul, where it is entirely passive and cooperates only through its surrender. It is then a matter of annihilating the *ego*; and this is what GOD alone can do. It is no longer the soul that fights outwardly; it is GOD who attacks it from within to make it die to itself. He introduces the soul into its own depths. He shows it all the folds and recesses of its self-love. He unveils all its mysteries. The soul sees itself and is horrified by what it sees. Everything within it rises against it; it no longer finds resource in its former fervor, nor in its own righteousness, of which He shows it all the impurities. It falls into a state of weakness; it remains faithful without seeing its own fidelity. All that remains is the firm will to suffer a thousand deaths rather than to displease God. Yet it does not always have the consolation of perceiving this will within itself. As God's action becomes more fundamental, more intimate, and more central, it seems to disappear more and more; but it is no less real. Just as that pure and universal light which illuminates, penetrates, and moves all bodies is itself imperceptible to our coarse eyes—or as self-love, which acts constantly in the natural man, is not always distinguished—so too the action of the WORD, which is the life, light, and love of all intelligences, acts very really in the supernatural man, though in an insensible manner.

8.—God’s design in acting this way is to hide His operation from our self-love. For self-love, no longer taking pleasure in impure delights, sensible objects, or coarse passions, would otherwise establish a new empire upon our very virtues; it would take complacency in its own excellence and corrupt the divine action through a self-idolatry that is all the more dangerous because it is more refined. One would perhaps no longer sin as a man, but one would sin as a Demon through pride and vain complacency. This is why the more advanced states of the spiritual life are filled only with temptations, pains, privations, dryness, uncertainties, miseries, obscurities, desolations, and interior sufferings, until the empire of self-love is destroyed and the kingdom of God, which is within us, is established in the soul.

9.—Then that tumultuous crowd of vague thoughts and disordered passions, which puts the natural man into a perpetual frenzy, ceases. The spirit is delivered from all its useless activities, the will from all its restless agitations, and the whole soul is brought into a peace, a void, and a divine solitude. There, the senses and the imagination, the self-spirit and the self-will, fall silent to listen to ETERNAL WISDOM. Wisdom speaks to the heart, not through visions, nor through revelations, nor through sublime lights, nor through subtle speculations, but in a much more perfect language less subject to illusion: namely, the "all" of God and the "nothingness" of the creature, and the profound homage that "nothing" owes to the "ALL." Then man no longer lives his own life, but JESUS CHRIST lives in him. He is reborn and becomes a child, without cleverness and without self-will. The light of the WORD becomes his only light, and the love of the HOLY SPIRIT his only love. His life is hidden with JESUS CHRIST in GOD, and this new life takes the place of the old life of Adam. This is the regeneration of which the Gospel speaks.

These are the three states of the spiritual life that the Mystics call *Purgative*, *Illuminative*, and *Unitative*, and which MADAME GUYON names *Active*, *Passive*, and *Divine*—that is to say, the renunciation of coarse vices, the destruction of self-love, and the restoration of divine order through pure love.

10.—This is the substance of all the experiences of this Lady. Such was the character of her devotion. Such are the Truths that fill her writings. Eternal Truths founded on sovereign reason. Truths that supreme WISDOM would teach equally to all upright spirits and all humble hearts, even if there were no Revelation. Truths known from the beginning of the world to the holy Patriarchs. Truths that made them walk continually before God without being known by men, like Enoch and Job. TRUTHS drawn from the Gospel, which one would discover there if one knew the gift of GOD and if one resembled those little and simple ones to whom He reveals His mysteries. Truths found more or less developed in the writings of the holiest Fathers of antiquity, such as St. Ignatius, St. Clement of Alexandria, St. Basil, St. Ambrose, St. John Chrysostom, St. Augustine, etc. Truths upon which the great Solitaries nourished themselves in the most fearsome deserts. Truths by which the great founders of Orders—such as St. Francis of Assisi, St. Bernard, St. Teresa, the Blessed John of the Cross, and St. Francis de Sales—have renewed the face of the Church in different centuries. Truths that have engaged an infinite number of Virgins and Religious to bury themselves alive in solitude to give themselves over to those purifying operations of the Divinity, which the noise of the world and the care for earthly things all too often disturb. Truths taught by the most enlightened Doctors of the Church, such as Albert the Great, St. Thomas, St. Bonaventure, Granada, Rodriguez, Sylvius, Cardinal Bona, Gerson, and many others. Finally, Truths whose tradition is universal and immutable in all times and all places.

Of HAMPOOLE, Richard.—Works, Cologne 1536.
From HANSWYCK, Florentinus.—On the Manner of the Divine Presence.
HARMONIA Mundi [Harmony of the World].
HARPHIUS, Henry.—Illuminated, sublime, methodical.

ANNOTATION.—This author approaches the character of Tauler; but he is more methodical, specifies more, and goes much further: one can even say that before him, and perhaps after him, no one has penetrated as he has into the depths of the interior states of a soul abandoned to God; in which one clearly perceives that Rusbrochius <note>Jan van Ruusbroec</note> was of no small help to him. His character is to propose the gradual resurrection of the states of spiritual life in the purified and tested soul. He shows how, after various mortifications, purifications, and trials of the soul, there arise within it, degree by degree, new states of divine life—first active, then passive—in the lower powers of the soul, after that in the superior ones (the memory, the intellect, and the will); then in its fundamental essence, and finally above its being and the operations of its powers, through the investiture made by the three persons of the Holy Trinity, who manifest their adorable operations there. It is the most beautiful, most substantial, and most advanced and profound system of Mystical Theology ever seen.

But to perceive this, one must not follow the order in which the editors have placed his mystical works, which is very poorly conceived. Seeing them under the common title of *Mystical Theology in Three Books*, one would say that the whole is but a single body of Theology divided into as many books as there are constituent parts. However, these three alleged parts are three very different works, each of which is complete by itself. The first, which is the largest and most long-winded, is much more moral than mystical, and has very little to do with our subject. It is properly the second and third that are mystical, and even in the second (titled the *Directory of Contemplatives*) one must have patience until chapter 25 (of the old editions), after which he enters directly into the depths of his subject until the end. His third book, another separate treatise titled the *Eden of Contemplatives*, enters into it much sooner. There he touches again upon the same things as the *Directory*, nevertheless adding new and considerable ones; he explains in more detail what he had touched upon only briefly, and fortifies it with several authorities from the Doctors and Saints. Several other writings are also attributed to him that are hardly found, and which are not to be compared with those I have just mentioned.

Harphius was Guardian of the Franciscans of the strict observance at Mechelen more than two hundred years ago. His Mystical Theology was brought to light in Latin, for the first time at Cologne, in the year 1538, and then in 1556. Father Mabillon is right to prefer these editions for their integrity over all others, although these were subsequently prohibited by the Inquisition—not because of the mystical dogmas, but because of three or four lines against the incapacity of the Directors and Spirituals of that time. The author, after having said in the twelfth chapter of his *Directory* that the perfect—or those who, though not yet perfect, are nonetheless so moved and attracted by the Spirit of God that they are obliged to follow only His attraction—have no need to be under the obedience or direction of men, had added these words: *“especially in this time, in which commonly all the Superiors who lead others are more devoted to external things than to internal ones; so that they understand very little or nothing at all of the inner life; and consequently are an obstacle rather than a help to those who, being drawn by God to this interior life, are subject to their direction. And this is the cause why there is so much laxity and so much lack of mortification among the Religious; I mean to say, it is because they do not regulate their conduct in the manner required by the interior life and the progress one must make there.”* These words caused his disgrace. Thus, they have been removed from the Rome edition of 1585, the Cologne edition of 1611, and others, from which they also removed a word the author used regarding “eternal creatures”; an expression that surpassed their understanding.

The mystical works of this author appeared in French in Paris, in the year 1616, translated by M. de la Mothe-Romaincourt, Counselor to the King: but this language being dated, a new translation—at the very least of his *Directory*, which is his best piece—would not now be out of season. This last treatise is still found in old Flemish, but rarely. This author declares himself strongly against self-interested love in relation to those who wish to strive for perfection.

# I.

ST. IGNATIUS of Antioch.—Apostolic. Sublime in the love of God, profound in humility.
ST. IGNATIUS of Loyola.—Pious exercises, ascetic.

ANNOTATION.—In all his practices of piety until now, (says his biographer,) he had only proposed his own perfection to himself. But God, who destined him for the evangelical ministry, and without his knowledge had already prepared him for it by contempt of the world, by retirement, mortification, and prayer, now gave him other insights and standards. He began to consider that since souls had cost our Savior so much, nothing could be more acceptable to Him than to prevent their eternal ruin; he understood that the glory of God was most revealed in the salvation of souls, purchased with the blood of His Son. These were the sentiments that kindled in him his ardent zeal for souls. *It is not enough (he said) that I serve my Lord; all hearts must love him, all tongues must praise him.*

As soon as he had turned his thoughts toward his neighbor, however dear solitude was to him, he gave it all up; and lest he should frighten away those whom he intended to bring to God, he changed his austere penitential dress for a more decent attire. Moreover, knowing that the ministry to which he was called required health and vigor, he moderated his austerities and partook of ordinary food.

He preached publicly concerning the things of heaven; and to be better heard by the people, who gathered around him to hear him, he stood upon a stone in front of the ancient hospital of St. Lucy. His mortified countenance, his modest air, his words animated with the spirit of truth, and his zealous and affectionate entreaties inspired his listeners with sentiments of the deepest compunction, with the love of virtue, and a horror of vice. But his private ministrations produced wonderful effects; he converted the most obstinate sinners by laying before them the maxims and duties of Christianity, and by causing them to meditate upon them in retirement. Some were so wrought upon that they renounced the world and changed both their manners and their state at the same time.

<margin>(The origin of retreats)</margin>
The many reflections that Ignatius made upon the force and power of the evangelical maxims, and the many trials of their operation both in himself and others, moved him to write a book of SPIRITUAL EXERCISES for the good of souls that live in the world. This book plays such a large part in his history, and is so little known abroad, that it will not be unprofitable to give an account of it.

The SPIRITUAL EXERCISES of Ignatius are something more than a mere collection of meditations and Christian considerations; if they were that and no more, there would be nothing special or new about them.

Ignatius is not the first who has taught us the way of raising our minds to God and of looking into our souls by means of prayer and contemplation. Before him, the various points of meditation were known, such as those concerning the end for which we were created, the enormity of sin, the pains of hell, and the life and death of our Savior; but this much may be said: before him, there was no definite and established method for the reformation of conduct. We owe this method to him, as one enlightened by God, and it was he who, in a systematic way and after a manner altogether new, organized the conversion of a sinner into a holy art, as it were. Knowing, on the one hand, the perverse inclinations of the human heart, and on the other hand, the power and virtue of the particular truths of Christianity to rectify those corruptions when rightly applied, he has set down a process or way by which man, with the aid of grace, may recover himself from his sin and degradation and ascend to the highest degree of Christian perfection. In effect, if we look narrowly into the matter, there is as much difference between the ordinary meditations of religious books and these exercises as there is between the knowledge only of medicinal plants <note>simples</note> and the entire science of medicine—which has its principles and aphorisms (the result of accumulated experience) for the cure of diseases, according to the constitution of bodies, the nature of ailments, and the quality of remedies. But so that the reality of what is stated above may be apparent, we shall here set down the entire order and SCHEME OF IGNATIUS'S SPIRITUAL EXERCISES, which are adapted for a FOUR-WEEK RETREAT for those who desire to ENTER UPON A CHRISTIAN LIFE... (See the account of them in his Life, as also of the original principles, spirit, and rules of the "Society of Jesus.")

INSTRUCTIONS on the way of perfection.

ANNOTATION.—This individual, as already observed, was the reason for the Philadelphian Society, which, after continuing its meetings for some five or six years, was dissolved, its members having thereby “completed their public testimony.” At its first institution, it created some sensation in the capital, because of the respectability and talent of its members, and by its declarations concerning the coming of the Lord and the great natural and moral revolutions which were to precede and follow that event. One of the professed objects of the association was to promote the cultivation of a pure spiritual and practical piety; and indeed, some of the writings that were produced by it for that purpose are most excellent and enlightened works. Meanwhile, the leading members themselves aimed at a highly transcendental knowledge, according to the superior insights which they believed distinguished their age through the writings of Behmen <note>Jakob Böhme</note>, and themselves in particular, as being under the immediate direction of Mrs. Lead. They believed her to be the subject of Divine revelations and a kind of illuminated prophetess of the last times, sent to reveal the Divine counsels regarding the declared approaching restoration of all things. Her pretensions to that office seemed to them to admit of no doubt, both from the nature and character of her published writings and her holy life and conduct. Being of inquisitive and devout minds, and well acquainted with the principles of Behmen’s philosophy—and therefore with what he declares concerning the mystic significance of his revelation—and then considering the mystery of the six days’ creation as well as the Scripture declarations concerning the coming of the Lord; and further observing Mrs. Lead’s great piety (and there are undoubtedly many passages in her writings which show her to have been a deeply experienced person in the interior life), and finding her visions, when divested of her individual way of describing them, to be in harmony with Behmen’s principles and the subjects accordant with their own speculations—I say, considering all these points, they were probably induced by degrees to believe her to be, as she considered herself, extraordinarily inspired by God. *For they deemed it a false principle, and highly subversive of gospel privileges, to maintain that God had ceased to reveal himself to man since the days of the apostles, and that all claims to the same are illusions and merely the fancies of temperament or religious zeal.*

It would not, perhaps, be difficult to analyze Mrs. Lead’s character and demonstrate the philosophy of her prophetic assumptions by considering the constitution of her mind, the character of the piety of the Cromwell-Muggletonian-fanatic days in which she lived, her undirected study of Behmen’s works then first published in English, and the popular spiritual topics of her age; but that does not belong here.

These observations are not to be taken as casting ridicule, or even venturing a final judgment upon her writings, but only to afford a general notion of their character and makeup. But whatever may be thought of her own compositions, there cannot be two opinions as to the merit of the prefaces and poems with which some of her later works have been illustrated by their voluntary publisher, her son-in-law, the learned Francis Lee. Wesley’s hymns may stand on an equality with those poems for the expression of true Christian experience; but there is, perhaps, no poetry extant in English equal to them for the fine classic, sparkling, Pope-like poetic genius applied to the illustration of the spiritualities of the life of faith, according to the true evangelical theory.

The following is a list of her pieces:—1.—*The Heavenly Cloud; or, the Ascension Ladder.* 4to. 1682. pp. 40. 2.—*The Revelation of Revelations; an Essay towards the Unsealing, Opening, and Discovering of the Seven Seals, the Seven Thunders, and the New Jerusalem State.* 4to. 1686. pp. 130. 3.—*The Enochian Walks with God, found out by a Spiritual Traveller.* 4to. 1694. pp. 38. 4.—*The Laws of Paradise; given forth by Wisdom to a Translated Spirit.* 8vo. 1695. pp. 69. 5.—*The Wonders of God’s Creation manifested in the Variety of Eight Worlds, as they were made known experimentally to the Author.* 8vo. 1695. pp. 89. 6.—*The Message to the Philadelphian Society, wherever dispersed over the whole Earth, together with a Call to the several gathered Churches.* 12mo. 1696. pp. 108. 7.—*The Tree of Faith: or, the Tree of Life, springing up in the Paradise of God; from which all the Wonders of the New Creation must proceed.* 12mo. 1696. pp. 122. 8.—*The Ark of Faith, or a Supplement to the Tree of Faith, for the further Confirmation of the same; together with a Discovery of the New World.* 12mo. 1696. pp. 33. 9.—*A Fountain of Gardens, Watered by the Rivers of Divine Pleasure, and springing up in all the variety of Spiritual Plants; blown up by the Pure Breath into a Paradise: Being a continuation of the process of a life according to faith, of the divinely magical knowledge, and of the new creation, in mutual entertainment between the Essential Wisdom and the soul, in her progress through Paradise to Mount Zion and the New Jerusalem: In a Spiritual Diary of the wonderful Experience of a Christian soul, under the conduct of the heavenly Wisdom, from the first vision in April, 1670, to the 2nd of August, 1686.* 4 vols. 12mo. 1697, 1697, 1700, and 1701. 10.—*A Revelation of the Everlasting Gospel Message, which shall never cease to be preached until the hour of Christ’s eternal judgment shall come, whereby will be proclaimed the last love jubilee, in order to the restoration of the whole fallen creation.* 8vo. London, 1697. pp. 39. 11.—*The Ascent to the Mount of Vision.* 4to. 12.—*The Signs of the Times.* 4to. 13.—*The Wars of David, and the Peaceable Reign of Solomon; symbolizing the Times of Warfare and Refreshment of the Saints of the Most High God. To whom a Priestly Kingdom is shortly to be given, after the Order of Melchizedek. Containing, (1.) An Alarm to the Holy Warriors to fight the Battles of the Lamb. (2.) The Glory of Sharon, in the Renovation of Nature, introducing the Kingdom of Christ.* 4to. 14.—*A Second and Third Message to the Philadelphian Society.*

ANNOTATION — on the "Evangelical Pearl." This book is truly anonymous; and Sandaeus is mistaken to attribute it to Eschius, a priest of Antwerp, who did nothing but publish it. It was composed by a holy girl whose doctrine has as its principal foundation the continual presence of God in the soul, like that of the sun in the heaven, to drive out evil and darkness, and to fill its depths with the happy and eternal life: by the action of the Father upon the memory, making it always think vividly of God; by that of the Son upon the understanding, illuminating it with the living and saving light of truth; and by that of the Holy Spirit upon the will, animating it holily with divine love. All of this is by virtue of the merits and mediation of the joyful Spirit, the afflicted soul, and the mortified and dead body of Jesus Christ, so that by imitating him in the way of love, abstinence, and suffering, God may have joy, peace, pleasure, and eternal contentment within us. These are principles that this holy girl inculcates and amplifies everywhere very vividly and with great heart. One finds in this book several beautiful truths and several important principles regarding the depth and faculties of the soul, the presence of God, His operations, etc., which are rarely found elsewhere, and which serve greatly to resolve certain significant difficulties of the interior life and of Mystic Theology.

The *Evangelical Pearl* has been printed several times in French, Latin, German, and Flemish. The French edition is by the Fathers of Bourg-fontaine in Paris, over a century old. They produced it from the Latin edition of Cologne, 1545, which however is not the true original, but a translation by Eschius, where the order is changed to reduce it from three parts into four. But the greatest variation is that, for fear of shocking the learned world by attributing this book to its source—I mean to a girl—they not only removed the first preface, but also changed the feminine terms into masculine terms in the acknowledgment that the first Flemish editor (believed to be the same Eschius) makes at the end of the work: that he was converted to God by the ministry of this girl, whom he calls one of the spouses of God, his servant and his friend. Instead of this, they substituted the masculine terms *servant* and *friend*; as if one should be ashamed to show the truth coming from a woman to disdainful scholars, even though the Holy Spirit often has more of a hold on them than on men, their minds being freer from the clutter of human science, more docile, and more inclined toward piety than those of the learned, whose wisdom, presumption, and pride God is pleased to confound by means so suited to His design, and so mortifying to those proud hearts. Be that as it may, what the same Eschius says of it in the first

The preface of one of the old original *Flemish editions* from *Antwerp* puts the matter beyond all doubt. It is too beautiful not to be included here as a citation—which would otherwise be superfluous—to make up for the suppression of it in the *French* and *Latin* versions.

<margin>delete</margin>
> “This book,” he says, “was written by a virtuous girl, inspired by the Holy Spirit and taught by her own experience. From her youth, she had given herself to the King of Glory, whose footsteps she constantly followed until death, through all sorts of paths, both sweet and bitter. She lived at her Father's house, where submission to a spiritual Father, fasts, prayers, vigils, and other penances subjected her flesh to the spirit. Following this, exercised by great and numerous temptations from the enemy, by a manly resistance, by the bitterness of many spiritual deaths, and by ardent prayers, the grace of God made her surmount her passions and temptations and acquire many virtues. From then on, she was often so absorbed in the conversation of her spirit with God that she forgot business, time for rest, and everything else. The continual watch she kept over her heart to maintain it in purity filled her so strongly with the light and joy of God that all other things were erased from her mind. She was tested like gold by fire in the crucible of suffering, contempt, and persecution from people of the world and devout persons alike; even then, she did nothing but pray and remain firm in the hidden way where God had placed her—always kind, always amiable, always joyful, and praying to God for those who made her suffer. Only God knows the magnitude of the interior pain she felt for the wandering of men and the loss of souls. She took communion every day based on the desire and the merits of her Beloved; and all her practices moved toward this goal: that God might have glory, peace, pleasure, and contentment in her. This she repeated often, even saying at the moment of her death while addressing God, *O Lord, may you have joy, may you have peace and contentment in me!* With these words, she gently gave up her spirit to her God on January 28, 1540, in the 77th year of her age.”

Although her book has been often printed, it is nonetheless quite rare now. The last Flemish printing of it was made in *Antwerp* in the year 1629, and it is one of the most beautiful and faithful. I do not know if it has been updated into better *French*, as the language of the first edition is no longer suitable for use.

Since this book is not only for the passive and contemplative life but also for the active and ascetic life—to which more people are better suited than the former, and which more authors have treated than the other—it will not be out of place to indicate on this occasion some of those authors who have written either for this latter kind of life, or for both together.

Everyone knows that *Thomas à Kempis*, or the book of the *Imitation of Jesus Christ*, is of great help to those who wish to return to themselves, to be imbued with the maxims of the *Gospel*, and to surrender themselves to God through the way of the heart, which follows no artificial method. He insists particularly on detachment from all things and from oneself, and on the duty of giving oneself to God entirely and without reserve. It would be useless to speak of the translations and editions of a book as well-known as this one, which has been published in four books for the use of Protestants.

*The Spiritual Combat*, another very excellent booklet, which the majority of voices attribute to *Father Lorenzo Scupoli*, a *Theatine*, is a manual very well suited to those who, seeking God through the way of the heart, also wish to join to it a more distinct perception and proceed by order and principles. He reduces the entire matter to four principal points: self-distrust, confidence in God, prayer, and the practice or right use of our powers. On each of these points, he gives excellent rules, easy to imprint on the mind so as to remember them when needed, thanks to the clear order he observes. *St. Francis de Sales* recommended this book above all others and called it his "Director." The best and most complete edition should have not 33 but 66 chapters, with a small treatise added on *the peace of the soul or the path to heaven*, and another<note>This is how the author of the excellent booklet *On Peace (or Quiet) of the Soul* (called by others the *Path to Paradise*) is named in the Latin Censure or Approbation by Sylvester de Pardo, Licentiate of Theology, Canon, and Censor of books, given at Antwerp on June 8, 1587; this is attached to the Dutch edition from 's-Hertogenbosch of the year 1613, although the English interpretation and edition of 1700 (which the German edition of Frankfurt in 1706 imitated) names him as de Bovilla.</note> on the mental sorrows of *Jesus Christ*, as found in the translation by *Father Mazotti* printed several times in *Paris*, although that of *Father Brignon* from the year 1688, which is the most *French* and was recently reprinted in *Brussels*, does not have this last treatise. This booklet is also found in *Latin*, in Flemish, and in several other languages.

*The Art or Method of Serving God* by *Alphonse de Madrid* is another exquisite little manual or booklet—solid, entirely practical, essential, methodical, and within everyone's reach. Its goal and the summary of its content is that, through the motive of the glory and will of God, and by recognizing our nothingness by nature and our nothingness through the fall and sin, we should employ ourselves in serving God primarily through the exercise of our spiritual faculties of desire and liberty. This is done by performing penance, by hating ourselves, by praying assiduously, by learning the humility and patience of Jesus Christ, and by taming our passions to arrive at the pure love of God, joined with the legitimate love of our neighbor and ourselves according to God and for Him. I do not know if the author wrote it in *Latin* or *Spanish*; besides these two languages, we also have it in *French* and Flemish. But it is now almost impossible to find.

*Theologia Germanica*<note>Most people think this booklet is named *German Theology* because it was originally written in the German dialect; this was also my opinion. <meta>This page continues the bibliographic review of spiritual and mystical authors, moving from the anonymous author of the "German Theology" to other influential figures like Jean Arndt, Juste Lansberg, and the Desert Fathers.</meta>

foundational and most exquisite, containing almost nothing but the pure principles of true internal and practical Christian Theology. The "all" of God, the "nothingness" of man, the evil of self-appropriation, the abnegation of self and of everything else, the discernment of true light from the false, and of true liberty from the false, etc., are the matters he treats without much method, but in a manner that one feels is very substantial and comes from a soul enlightened by God. The preface of the new French Edition which has just appeared will provide more details. — One of its German Editors, the celebrated *Jean Arndt*, formerly Inspector in the Duchy of Luneburg, had absorbed its spirit, as well as that of *St. Macarius*, which he knew by heart, and of *Tauler*, as appears in all his works of piety and notably in his distinguished book, *True Christianity*. This work, by its manner of presenting all the solid substance of piety and a truly Christian life without ever departing from the authority and the terms of the Holy Scripture, has acquired the universal esteem of everyone.

<margin>aj</margin>
Father ALEXIS DE SALO, a Capuchin, in his *Sure Path to Paradise*, attempts to put into practice—regarding all kinds of things and all our senses, passions, affections, and in all our mental acts—the precept of Jesus Christ so recommended in *German Theology*: that one must renounce *oneself* to follow Him; and he supports everything he teaches with very simple and very natural examples. His book, translated from Italian, was printed in Lyon in 1620, in Douai in 1627, etc.

Father JUSTE LANSBERG, a Carthusian who lived a century ago, wrote solidly and in a touching manner about the interior and spiritual matters of piety and true devotion. His works are comprised of two volumes (in quarto) and five parts, of which the first three are sermons for Sundays, feast days, and the history of the Passion; the other two are treatises on piety, an apology for the monastic life, letters, and devotional verse. He is methodical and follows his text very well in his Sermons without neglecting the internal and allegorical sense. Of his treatises on piety, two were translated into beautiful French a few years ago: one, the *Christian Militia*, or the *Spiritual Combat*, printed in Paris in 1670, which contains salutary instructions for stripping away vices and corruption, and for acquiring virtues and purity in order to reach divine union. The other book translated from the same Author is a *Discourse of Jesus Christ to the Devout Soul in the form of a Letter*, published in Paris in 1674, and this treatise is only the last part of his *Amoris divini Pharetra* (Quiver of Divine Love). This book is an excellent manual of devotion and piety, which contains in summary all the most solid rules for the conduct of a truly Christian life. ERASMUS wrote a small book approaching these two in title and subject matter: it is his *Enchiridion Militis Christiani*, or *Manual of the Christian Soldier*, which is a very good piece; but it is not as "interior" as those of Lansberg and does not go as far. The Spanish Author of the booklet *The Treasure of the Soul*, translated into all sorts of languages under the title of *Desiderius Peregrinus* (at Rotterdam 1674),* is second to none to Lansberg; using an emblem as useful as it is entertaining—a shepherd traveling to find the love of God—he places before our eyes the progress of a soul which, through Christian virtues, sufferings, and divine love, reaches the first fruits of the enjoyment of God. It appears that this Author was a member of a religious order, and therefore Sandius was wrong to claim to attribute it to Servetus in his *Library of the Anti-Trinitarians*.

ALPHONSE RODRIGUEZ, a Jesuit, in his excellent *Practice of Christian Perfection*, treats the same subjects, but with more breadth. He proceeds quite methodically with rules and instructions, which he accompanies with the most beautiful and edifying examples found in the lives of the Holy Fathers of the deserts and other holy souls. This, joined to the great clarity and ease of his book, cannot help but make it very attractive as well as very useful to all kinds of people, even children.

<margin>ne/</margin>
In terms of instructions supported by examples, here are sources that will provide a great quantity. The lives of the Holy Fathers of the deserts, collected by Father Rosweydus, a Jesuit, and published at Antwerp twice in Latin in the year 1615 (which is the most beautiful and correct Edition) and in 1628; and twice in Flemish around the same time. They were also published in German at Frankfurt not long ago. The French, who had only a small part of them in old Gaulish (Middle French), now have them in perfectly beautiful language by the celebrated Translator Monsieur d'Andilly, who nonetheless made too many cuts and omissions; nothing has been restored in either the French reprints or in the new Antwerp edition of the year 1694. It is true that he augmented them with some excellent lives, such as, among others, that of ST. EUTHYMIUS and ST. SABAS.

The Acts of the Martyrs, when they are sincere, such as those collected by Father Ruinart in his book *Acta Martyrum Sincera et Selecta* (Sincere and Selected Acts of the Martyrs), printed in Paris in 1689. The collection of the *Death of the Just* by Father Lallemand, reprinted in the Netherlands in 1673, based on the Paris edition. To which one may join the *Account of the Death of some Monks of La Trappe*, such as that of *Dom Muce* and the Count of *Santena*, reprinted several times in Brussels.

The Conferences of JOHN CASSIAN, a Priest of Marseille with a reputation for holiness in the fifth century, translated from Latin into French and printed in Paris in 1665, but without the 13th Conference, which was imagined to be full of errors on matters of grace, although he knew them better by experience than his censors did, even if he did not explain himself with all the precautions necessary to prevent the opposition of argumentative minds.

The Rules of St. BASIL, the *Institutions of St. DOROTHEUS* (a sixth-century Abbot, translated from Greek into French by the Abbot of la Trappe and printed in Paris in 1686), and *The Holy Ladder* of St. John Climacus (a Father and Abbot of the same century). Of the latter, there are Greek-Latin editions, Latin editions alone, and a double French translation by M. d'Andilly; the first of these was printed separately in Paris in 1653, while the other is found both separately and joined with long notes to the lives of the Desert Fathers, 1675. There are also the works of *Evagrius*, though incomplete, in the Greek-Latin Monuments of Mr. Cotelier (Vol. 3, Paris, 1686), and the *Apophthegms of the Fathers* in the same collection. All these books are filled with very divine instructions and highly animating examples; at the same time, they are very convincing through real effects, showing that the practice of a perfectly Christian, penitent, and spiritual life is neither impossible nor merely an abstract idea.

One could be vividly and beneficially convinced of the same truth by a very great number of other admirable lives of several excellent people from all sorts of states and conditions<note>You will find these collected copiously by many authors among the Roman Catholics; for example, by Laurentius Surius in four volumes, and especially by Bollandus and his associates or successors, Henschenius and Papebroch, etc., who, if they continue, will not stop before the thirtieth volume. The celebrated Arnold collected a volume of most pious lives of those who lived within the last 200 years, and published it under the title *Lives of the Faithful, or Believers*, Halle, 1701, in quarto, in German; it was intended primarily for the use of Protestants, although it also includes some lives of Roman Catholic Saints. Furthermore, regarding my description of such lives as worthy of admiration, there will undoubtedly be those who argue that they should be called worthy of laughter or contempt; but what judgment can "brutish souls" have of divine and spiritual things? They will one day be forced to change their minds—not without shame, though without fruit. See Wisdom of Solomon, chapter 5, verses 1–14.</note>, even those whose memory is still quite recent. However, to avoid offending the scrupulousness of certain people and to avoid wordiness, it will suffice for me to mention only two: one of a man and the other of a girl. The first is the *Life of Monsieur de RENTY*, whose high virtue was recently the admiration of France and all of Paris, where he died in the year 1649. This excellent life, the history of which was given to us by Father St. Jure, a Jesuit (a pious, spiritual, and solid author of several other treatises), is a summary of what is most exquisite in Christian virtues and most solid in true spirituality. One can observe there not only the maxims but also the practice of what true mystics teach regarding the different states of souls, pure love, prayer and contemplation, and other similar matters. These are touched upon, like everything else, in a manner so clear and solid that even readers with the least inclination toward these subjects or toward reading such lives cannot help but have their hearts softened and persuaded. Here is the judgment made of it by a prominent Protestant, who cannot be suspected of partiality or credulity in these matters: *Whatever infatuation one may still have for fables, it must be admitted that the Life of Monsieur de Renty shows none of it. One notices such excellent virtues in it that he who practiced them should justly be placed among the greatest models that France has provided to our century.* These are the words of Mr. Burnet, the (English) Bishop of Salisbury, in his preface to the life of Mr. Bedell; and it is said to be the same person who translated and published the life of M. *de Renty* in English.—The other life I just mentioned I wished to note is *the life of Mother ELIZABETH of the Infant JESUS*, which is in no way inferior to that of M. de Renty. He had served as a guide, along with Father St. Jure and M. de Bernières, to this excellent nun, who died in Paris in the year 1677. Her life was printed in the same place in 1688. The life of the Baroness de CHANTAL is too famous to need a particular recommendation, if only it were not so rare in these countries. [See the *Lives*.]

Furthermore, in reading the lives of the Desert Fathers, one should not be discouraged at first by reading those taken from the Epistles of St. JEROME. These are placed first and, to tell the truth, savor a bit too much of the affected declamations of his rhetoric. Those by RUFINUS, PALLADIUS, THEODORET, and St. SULPICIUS SEVERUS, as well as the collections of JOHN MOSCHUS and several others, are of a simpler, more natural, and more touching character.

Among the authors who have written specifically concerning the matters of Prayer, Meditation, Contemplation, and dependent subjects, here are some of the most familiar and useful.

St. PETER OF ALCANTARA, a friend and contemporary of St. Teresa, wrote a very useful little *Treatise on Prayer and Meditation*, which has been printed several times in Latin, French, and other languages. Similarly, the treatise by HORSTIUS, *Paradisus animae* (Paradise of the Soul), is an exquisite and practical manual on all subjects of Prayer. The first part of the *Thalamus Sponsi* also deals with this matter, as does the first part of the *Introduction to the Devout Life* by St. FRANCIS DE SALES, whose entire book contains very good instructions on piety and conduct for all sorts of people, even those in the high society of the world. This treatise, along with that on the *Love of God* and his *Letters*, is excellent among the works of this author. His character is to try to make the practice of true piety easy for everyone and to inspire peace and solid devotion in all, both through a fair condescension to the dispositions of souls and by a spirit of singular gentleness—a character so recommended by Jesus Christ, and which among the ancients, St. CLEMENT in his divine letter to the Corinthians and St. POLYCARP in his to the Philippians perfectly expressed.

Father NOUET and Father RAPIN, Jesuits, have written very good things on Prayer and its types: the former more extensively in his *Man of Prayer* printed in Paris in 1674, and the other in summary in his *Prayer Without Illusion*. This is the same booklet that was reprinted in the second part of the *Theology of the Heart* under the title *Summary of Mystical Theology*. In the same second part of the *Theology of the Heart*, there is a small treatise by a girl entitled *The Interior Life*, where the matter and types of Prayer are explained with uncommon simplicity and ease. It is explained even more briefly in the fourth conference of that divine booklet, *The Illuminated Shepherd*, which is the first part of that same *Theology of the Heart*. translated from Latin into fine French, and printed at Brussels, 1683; and *Fr. Jean of St. Samson* in his treatise *Aspirative Love*, which is found in the second part of the *Theology of the Heart*, both aim for the same goal through the path of *continual aspirations*. A small French booklet, very solid and very affective, titled *Method for Conversing with God*, printed in Paris in 1685 and reprinted in Brussels some time later, also leads to this.

Father GUILLORÉE, a Jesuit, has six or seven excellent treatises printed more than once in Paris. The *Spiritual Letters of a Cleric*, collected by M. de Lassot and recently published in the same place in five small volumes, can be of great and almost universal use regarding everything concerning the active and exterior life, as well as the interior and contemplative life. The same is true of the excellent *Spiritual Catechism of Father SURIN*, a Jesuit, printed several times (the last in 1693) in Paris, in two volumes; as well as his *Foundations of the Spiritual Life*, reprinted at Liège in 1679. In these, the author—using several sentences of Thomas à Kempis, which he explains in the form of questions and answers—solidly guides his reader to the spiritual life by deducing its most important points, its easiest paths, and the obstacles most necessary to avoid and often the least noticed. The small *Christian Catechism for the Interior Life by M. OLIER*,* superior of the seminary of St. Sulpice, often printed in Paris and even published in Flemish at Louvain in 1686, contains the substance of what its title promises, sticking almost always to the words and clearest instructions of Holy Scripture.

To end with a woman [this section having begun with a woman], let us say a word about the spiritual works of JEANNE DE CAMBRY, a reclusive nun at Lille. Her life, printed separately at Antwerp in 1659, contains many details on God’s guidance of souls. Her works, which appeared together at Tournai in 1665, treat the truths and practice of Christian, interior, and mystical things no less solidly, regularly, or clearly than the writings of the most educated men. In her greatest treatise, which is that of *The Ruin of Self-Love* (which was printed separately in Paris), she treats the entire interior life in order. She explains its states (like Ruysbroeck in his *The Ornament of Spiritual Marriage*) through the emblem of what happens successively in the four seasons of the year. This treatise, divided into four books, speaks in the first of self-love and generally of the graces of God to suppress it; in the second, of the advancement of God’s graces in those making progress, applying several things from the Song of Solomon; in the third, of rigorous privations, temptations, and spiritual trials; and in the fourth, of the restoration of the soul to a perfect state. These last two are very sublime, as well as very appropriate for satisfying the difficulties often blindly raised against interior paths. Her *Mystical Torch*, which is also printed separately, is a short explanation of both the things and the words of the mystical path and theology, as well as a summary of instructions for directors of souls. There are instructions for the direction of families in her treatise *The Reform of Marriage*. That of the *Excellence of Solitude* is more for retired persons; and the *Exercise for Attaining the Love of God*, which is as solid as it is short and methodical, is for everyone’s use, as is the one titled *Lamentation of the Soul Captive in its Mortal Body*. In this, she shows that in whatever kind or state of life one may be—even in the most charming and sublime of the spiritual life—one nevertheless encounters everywhere matters for lamentation and tears. Her manner of expressing things bears the character of a cordial naivety and a solid, strong clarity, fit to convince the mind and heart of those who seek the true Good with sincerity. It seems that there is ordinarily less of this in the writings of men than in those of women.

**ANNOTATION.**—Regarding Protestants (remarks the Editor of the French edition in his Introduction), I admit that the purity of their religion and the simplicity of their ideas do not accommodate the confusing terms of the Mystics. The word "Contemplation" alone frightens them; those of "general view" or "obscure and confused faith" fill them with horror because they smell of Papism. When they hear mention of dryness, divine darkness, dark or resplendent night, inaction, annihilation, the interior path, spiritual martyrdom, active and passive purification, infused contemplation, divine union and transformation, or deification, they cannot imagine how there are people so foolish as to seriously speak of such great poverty.

<meta>This page continues the defense of mystical literature, transitioning from a list of recommended authors to a justification of the specialized terminology used by these writers to describe the interior spiritual life.</meta>

<language>French</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>155</page-num>

But one is asked to consider that the <term>Mystics</term> might well have had good reasons to use these terms, and believed them very appropriate to express the ideas given by the life of JESUS CHRIST resurrected within themselves. We do not intend to justify these ideas at present; we will only say that since no one condemns the terms of Geometry, Architecture, or Painting simply because they do not understand them—due to the conviction that those who possess these arts and sciences have knowledge that the common people do not have, and that they need words unknown to the public to express them—it is also not fair to reject <term>mystical</term> phrases because those who have not studied the theologians who use them do not understand them at the first glance.

Here is the principle of the error: Everyone imagines that religion is something very easy; and they are right. Nothing is easier than to understand the foundations of Christianity and to become a good Christian, since one only needs to attentively consult natural light, read the Gospel, desire to give one's heart to God, and sincerely execute that resolution. But are there many people who do so?

A very false consequence is drawn from this truth. Most of the world is satisfied with a certain moral honesty, or the profession of Christianity, although *self-love* still reigns in the heart, and one is still full of oneself and the world. In this state of mind, people gradually persuade themselves that piety consists only in that, or at most in some attractions of sensible devotion. Consequently, when they hear it said that this is only the state of those who are beginning, and that one must pass as far as renouncing oneself *entirely*, becoming nothing in the presence of God, stifling all one's passions and even one's thoughts and knowledge, and having no spirit or will except the light and good pleasure of God, being united and transformed in him—they imagine that all these big words contain nothing but pure nonsense, and that they are only the visions of a melancholy mind, because they believe themselves to be good people and feel nothing similar. The most suspicious, who are usually the most ignorant, regard these expressions as magical words, invented only to deceive the simple, and containing some secret error.

If the length of a preface allowed me to enter into detail, I could show that many of the <term>Mystics'</term> terms are taken from Holy Scripture, and that they have only used them in the sense of *Jesus Christ* and his *Apostles*; but that requires a separate work. It is enough for me now to assure the reader that they only have to give themselves entirely to God, and make a sincere study of piety and Christian morality, to soon understand the language of the true <term>Mystics</term>. For I exclude from this number certain extravagant individuals who make <term>contemplation</term> consist of raptures and ecstasies; which is undoubtedly the reason why this species of <term>Theology</term> has fallen into contempt among *Protestants* and become the object of admiration for superstitious *Catholics*.

<term>Contemplation</term>, according to *Molinos*, *Malaval*, *John of the Cross*, *Harphius*, and other true <term>Mystics</term>, is nothing other than that state of the soul which always has God before its eyes, which undertakes nothing except to please him, which never murmurs against his orders, which is perfectly resigned to his will, which kisses the hand that strikes it, which regards itself as unworthy of the favors of heaven, which never asks him for miracles or extraordinary graces, which receives good and evil with tranquility and a holy indifference, which believes itself to be nothing, esteems itself as nothing, and wants only what God wants—in a word, it no longer lives for itself; it is *Jesus Christ* who lives in it, and his *Holy Spirit* animates it. It is *this new creature* that *God forms in souls*, which he truly regenerates, and which I cannot describe because I am still too imperfect, and language and expressions fail me. But how could I succeed, since the holy and learned *Usherius* <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh.</note>, having begun a treatise on the nature of <term>sanctification</term> at the request of one of his friends, confessed that he then felt its effects so little that he could only speak of it like a parrot, without knowledge or understanding of what he would have written? The friend to whom he spoke was astonished to hear such an humble confession from a Christian as perfect as *Usherius* was, and whom God had often honored with the gift of *Prophecy*. This devout Prelate continued in these terms:

> "I must tell you that we do not well understand what <term>sanctification</term> and the <term>new creature</term> are; it is nothing less than being brought to a perfect renunciation of one's own will, and an entire submission to the will of God, such that one lives in a continual offering of one's soul to God, in the flames of love, offering oneself to him in sacrifice, like a perfect burnt offering in *Jesus Christ*. There are many people who make profession of *Christianity*; but very few who feel these operations in their soul by experience."

"Let that be so," a *Protestant* will say, "but what does that do to justify the phrases of the <term>Mystics</term>? Why wrap the science of salvation in obscure terms, and make a separate language of what God wants to reveal to all men? Do we not know how much the expressions of the Scholastics have corrupted *Theology*, and that in these kinds of matters, one rarely invents new words without also inventing new things, or obscuring clear ideas, or determining others to a certain sense that God intended to remain suspended and unclear, not having told us more?" I admit that this objection alone would be enough to immediately reject all the new terms of the <term>Mystics</term> if they concerned the mysteries of faith and *speculative Theology*, since new terms are extremely suspect in that context, and they are almost the unique cause of all the disputes and schisms that tear Christianity apart. However, these expressions concern only morality, and mark nothing other than the different dispositions in which a soul finds itself when it has consecrated itself to God, and the various states through which it passes.

Regarding the obscurity of mystical books, it can have various causes. There are *Ideal Mystics*, who study this science out of vanity, as most others do, and who, having no solid piety, can only speak of the effects of grace and the operations of the Holy *Spirit* in souls through imagination or memory, and most often in a false and confused manner. These people, to appear learned, have usually mixed the confused conceptions of *Aristotle's* metaphysics into their mystical explanations, which has finished spoiling this *Theology*.

This obscurity can also proceed from the lack of attention and experience of those who read them. _MYSTICAL SCIENCE is the science of the human heart and the love of God._ One can well

In his introduction to “the Treatise on Daily Communion,” the editor observes the following concerning it:—“The Author proves there that one can and even should receive communion every day, provided that one is not in mortal sin—that is to say, fallen from the state of grace, and in a state of present condemnation. He cites an infinite number of Fathers and scholastic theologians who have supported this sentiment; but if anyone doubts that frequent communion was in use in the primitive Church, he has only to read Letter 289, by Saint Basil addressed to the Lady Cesaria, where this Bishop treats specifically of this matter, and shows from the beginning that it is a good and useful thing to receive communion every day. He testifies that even in his time, they received communion four times a week in his church—on Sunday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday—and even other days, if the memory of some martyr was being celebrated.”

Amsterdam, Cologne, and other places where Protestantism was tolerated, a Roman Inquisition over the press was not established, and a fair degree of religious liberty was enjoyed; namely: *Works of Madame Guyon*, 36 vols.; *Works of Bertot*, 4 vols.; *Works of Bourignon*, 18 vols.; *The Life of Good Armelle*; of *Gregory Lopez*; of the *Marquis de Renty*; *Catherine Adorna*; the *Works and the Life of Angela of Foligno*, with an appendix from *Blosius*; *Theology of the Heart*, containing *The Illuminated Shepherd*, *The Abridgment of Christian Perfection*, *The Ruin of Self-Love*, *The Interior Life*, *Aspirative Love*, *Abridgment of Mystic Theology*, by *Father Rapin*; *Real Theology*, containing an *Apologetic Preface on Mystic Theology*, *German Theology*, *Treatise on the Restoration of Man*, (Marie Henrics) *Letter on Regeneration*, *Spiritual Rules and Maxims taken from those of John of St. Samson*: *Molinos' Spiritual Guide*, etc. concerning *Quietism and the Quietists*; *Theology of the Presence of God, containing the Life, Manners, Conversations, Practice, and Letters of Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection*, etc.; with many other treatises of a similar character.

The labors and services to religion of this very worthy and indefatigable writer cannot, indeed, be properly estimated by us; there may, however, be occasion to refer to him again in connection with the subject of the Philadelphians, or with that of the revival of the life and spirit of Christianity in the early part of the last century, to which, doubtless, the practical writings of Bourignon, through his agency, contributed in some degree. His treatises may be profitably read by the candidate in their proper place—that is, as he shall come to feel a necessity for the knowledge of them; after having become thoroughly a master of the works of that original writer and standard of all scientific as well as practical divinity, who is the subject of this present proposed biography. Should the reader judge for himself the groundless fantasies and grossly heterodox opinions promulgated in Bourignon’s writings (and indiscriminately embraced by Poiret), which she unhesitatingly declares to be truths revealed to her by God—as also the great piety and ability, and the great weakness of her adherents, he has only to refer to pages 44, 52, and 78 of Dr. Garden's “Apology” for her, and the other portions of that work. Poiret thus boldly speaks of the benefits he had derived from her writings in the preface to the fourth volume of his ‘*Divine Economy*,’ but it must be remembered that this was in the *first ardor* of his religious experience: “I honestly profess,” says he, “that had it not been for the writings and conversation of Madame Bourignon, I would have known nothing solid in divine matters, nor indeed in natural ones. All the truths <note>and groundless theories</note> I have proposed in these treatises are only the consequences of her principles, or of my own deductions, which I carried still deeper, encouraged by the light she gave me into all subjects whatsoever. Nay, more, had it not been for the Divine light I received from her, I should, to this day, have been in the darkness of death, in blindness of heart, and in the slavery and idolatry of vain, proud, presumptuous, and chimerically corrupt reason; and such a creature that it would have been better for me never to have been born.

“For whatever knowledge in the Scripture or divinity, in holy or mystical books, I might have acquired before—and I imagined I understood all these very well—yet all was but darkness until, by God's grace, I met with the writings and conversation of this remarkable instrument of God.

“For my own part, I confess I have taken, and do still take, the substance of what she says for truths coming from the mouth of God himself!—being convinced of it in my very soul by such effects as can proceed from God alone <note>an illogical inference</note>. And so I had no hesitation in embracing these truths as sure rules, to consider them thoroughly, and to search out their consequences, knowing that from truth nothing but truth could follow! * * * And I cannot comprehend how anyone whose heart is not willfully set against God can condemn or slight her writings, if he has read them with any attention—or at least the chief of them, such as the *Light of the World*; *Light Risen in Darkness*; *Solid Virtue*; *Antichrist Discovered*; *Renovation of the Gospel Spirit*; the *Touchstone*; and the *Apology* before her life. <note>If the general reader has the strength of understanding to separate the chaff from the wheat in theological writings, and all the mere speculative novelties from true practical Christianity, he may derive profit from a perusal of these works.</note>

Whereas, if the true spirituality of the Christian life was kept within its own bounds, supported only by Scripture doctrines and the plain appearances of nature and experience, human reason would be strangely at a loss to know how to expose it.

and a fondness for singularity, carried even the pious and learned Poiret so far as to defend Bourignon in this and other matters, contrary to the gospel." Marsay's unique *Life* was translated into English in 1772 by a Moravian preacher, at the request of Henry Brooke of Dublin (previously mentioned and author of the poem "Redemption"); it exists only in manuscript, of which the writer has a copy.

Another individual demanding notice on the present occasion is the celebrated Baron Swedenborg, a scientific mineralogist and natural philosopher, who, quitting those relatively obscure studies, appeared in the field of theology about sixteen years before Law’s death. He was a man of a highly cultivated mind, great inductive powers, and research in theoretical science, with a subtle imagination; however, he was totally devoid of that masculine strength, penetration, and severity of judgment which are always found to be the characteristics of powerful common sense and a sound, practical understanding.—<margin>ley/</margin> It is supposed that his mind became ~~first~~ turned to the popular subjects of theology and metaphysics by Law’s *Appeal*, *Animadversions*, and other tracts published at that time; <margin>dage/</margin> ~~and by the uncritical reading of the~~ writings of Jane Lead, Bourignon, Poiret, Englebert, Marsay, Reeve and Muggleton, and other famous visionaries and idealist writers of the German, Dutch, French, English, and other schools—orthodox and spurious, ancient and modern. Then again, his mind was influenced by the recollection of occasional glimmers of deep truth in the works of ancient philosophers, which corresponded with what is so fundamentally, systematically, and freshly revealed in Behmen; and along with all this must be taken into account his observations of the wrangling and jangling concerning "faith and works," and similar literalist topics of knight-errant religionists in his day, who, he clearly perceived, did not understand the core of their subject and were therefore fighting vainly in the dark. To this must also be added the consideration of his experience as a physiologist, his grasp of the truth of the principles of nature, and the philosophy of spirit and body so wonderfully revealed in Behmen, and his endeavor to elaborate that ancient philosophical subject in a scientific manner, divested of Behmen’s technical jargon. For there is not a truth of any importance in all his works that cannot be immediately stripped of the form he gave it and traced back to its source in Behmen’s principles, whether derived directly from him or through his commentators. All these were splendid materials for a man of Swedenborg's peculiar mental constitution, his great power of mental elaboration, calm even temperament, and tireless application to work with; ~~and~~ the results he produced may be seen in his writings after the year 1745. [In a new edition of part of Lead's works, published in 12mo., London: Ogle and Co., 1816, the editor makes the following remark: "Those persons who are favored with a clear understanding of the profound works of Jacob Behmen will also have the skill to separate the pure gold from the harmful and most infectious dross in the writings of the noble, truly excellent, and very learned Emanuel Swedenborg."]

Among the collection of Law's manuscripts that came from Mr. Langcake, copies were found of two informal letters written to a friend and admirer of Swedenborg (supposed to be Hartley), who had sent the writer one of his works, or a summary of it, to read. As there are good grounds for considering Law to have been the author of those letters, we insert them here, leaving them to stand on their own merits. The first proceeds as follows:

> "I here return to you the book of *Dialogues* relating to Swedenborg’s doctrines, which contain the following curiosities:
> "First—That the distinction of personalities, offices, powers, and operations in God is by no means admissible, because God is immutable. See pages 52, etc., 163.
> "That the man Jesus is the Holy Father, consisting of three essences or principles—the Divine, the Proceeding, and the Human; that as the Divine Essence or Principle, he is the Holy Father, even the Jehovah of the Jews, the Creator of all things; that as the Proceeding Essence or Principle (which, it seems, must be distinguished from the Divine), he is the Sanctifier; that as the Human Essence or Principle, he is the Son of God, who suffered and died. See pages 52, 53, 54, 71, 72.
> "Secondly—That the merit, virtue, and effectiveness of Christ’s sufferings consist (not, as is the common faith, in himself, but) in changing the state of man by removing from him the power of hell and darkness, and placing him in a state where he can rise out of evil through a renewal of the parts, powers, and principles of his life in both soul and body, restoring him to both health and uprightness; which, says our author, was all that was necessary for the eternal well-being of the creatures.
> "The Baron, therefore, adds that Christ satisfied himself and made an atonement to himself, etc., and that all this must be so because God is immutable. See pages 55–67.
> "Again, he teaches that Christ is no more a mediator, an advocate, an intercessor, or one who sits at the right hand of God, than he is a door, a vine, a lion, or a lamb; that he is all these alike and figuratively, or in a sense denoting his divine qualities and properties, for which the literal names 'door,' 'mediator,' 'lion,' etc., are expressive signs. See pages 67–75.
> "Now, can any man of learning and in his right senses adopt such meaningless nonsense as the above for Divine revelation, or judge it as anything other than the ramblings of a disturbed brain? Can this be that stable word of sound or rational doctrine [Titus 1:9] by which we shall be able to convince those who oppose us? Furthermore, it is not supported by a single argument or alleged proof, but is merely the *dictum* of a fantastical mineralogist who has shown throughout all his works a notorious ignorance of both the language and the records of theology."
