> “Thirdly—Our author, being embarrassed by the scriptural form of sound words, which would in no way align with his wild fantasies, proceeds to persuade his impressionable disciples—novices in scriptural language and its modes of expression and revelation—with these presumptions: that Divine terms are to be interpreted figuratively, allegorically, symbolically, and mystically whenever an internal sense and interpretation can be devised. And therefore, to spread some appearance of plausibility over these pretenses, he cavalierly undertakes to exemplify his premise regarding the doctrine of the resurrection; assuring us that when we read of the appearance of the Son of Man at the last day, and of his coming in the clouds of heaven, we are to understand even these promises far differently than they are commonly conceived as predictions of real, though future events. He claims we are to understand them figuratively, mystically, and symbolically; that, therefore, the clouds in which Christ (or the Father, or the Holy Spirit) will come are in no way those natural, visible clouds which appear to our sight in the skies (See page 197, 198); for clouds denote veils that cover or obscure; and the clouds mentioned in these parts of Scripture are clouds overshadowing the spiritual or internal sense of the coming of Christ, namely, of his internal appearance to his saints.
> “Then, with a kind of instructional surprise at our simplicity, the baron proceeds to teach us that the book of God’s word is a sealed book (p. 199), wherein the mysteries of truth and Divine wisdom are hidden under an external literal meaning (p. 199, 200). He argues that Christians ought to behold, as in a mirror, the glory of God; and that this vision of him is truly the sign of the coming of the Son of Man in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory! (p. 200, 201.)
> “And since it is a question naturally asked of these new luminaries when and where this coming of Christ is to be expected—since it will not be, as previously believed, an advent literally spread across the clouds of heaven—the answer is that wherever a fresh opening of divine truths is made and a new church established on earth, there this advent of Christ is manifestly displayed, and that is the place of Christ’s coming.
> “Now, to cast a plausible appearance upon this notion, he describes in a similar way the descent of the *New Jerusalem* from God out of heaven; boldly assuring us in the following words: ‘that by it is meant a new dispensation of heavenly righteousness, or a re-publication of the word of God, opened anew, for the purpose of forming a *new church* among men. This (New Jerusalem) must necessarily signify and be the same thing as the Lord’s second coming, as it denotes not the destruction of the earth, but its renovation by purging it from sin and purifying the hearts and lives of mankind through the operation of genuine truth, opened anew from his own holy word.’ (p. 204–6.)
> “Reveries as weak as these would have made Socinus ashamed, even if he were a friend of the baron; he would have rejected such a supporter as a mockery of him—nor do I have the time to examine these follies as they deserve.
> “Although the above are the main doctrines of this book you sent me, interspersed with them we find many false distinctions, Socinian tenets, deistical reasonings, and mystical whims. These are generally so weakly enforced, however, as to be easily recognized, for they reveal not only a total ignorance of Christianity but obviously a disordered intellect.
<margin>[with reference to logical knowledge]</margin>
> “And indeed, a disordered intellect could not have generated the wild absurdities this baron has poured out had he acquired even a moderate amount of theological knowledge. A philosopher who is a novice in the revealed word, when turned enthusiast, is of all men the most liable to heresies; but the enormity of this baron’s delusions proves both the most abject lack of learning, along with the most egregious blindness and infatuation. * * * ”

Julian—the chaste, the temperate, the learned, the pious, the vigilant, the merciful—for so he is characterized by historians.
> “ ‘And by what standard are we to judge the term goodness? From the Scriptures, or from Aristotle’s Ethics? > *and this is that spirit of antichrist of which you have heard that it should come, and even now is already in the world: twisting the word to his own destruction. 2 Peter 3:16.*
>
> “The Christ who is Jesus, and who came in the flesh from God, is the only begotten Son of the Father; to deny him, therefore, is to deny the Son. If someone does not confess that he, this only begotten Son of the Father, has come in the flesh, he is an antichrist. What else can we conclude about your good baron than that he is not light in the Lord, but an antichrist who denies the truth and makes God a liar; or that he has no truth in him?
>
> “And if those who refused him who spoke on earth did not escape, how much less shall they escape who turn away from him who spoke from heaven? What must be the sentence passed upon your good baron? For the word adds: ‘How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?’
>
> “Also, it is not doubted that your good baron denies that any only begotten Son of the holy Father has come into the flesh. He does this more expressly and more dogmatically than either Arius or even Socinus or Crellius; and this, again, without their plea of reasoning or plausibility of argument. He confidently claims the character of a prophet as much as Simon Magus or Mahomet ever did.
>
> “*To deny a begotten Son of the holy Father made flesh is at once to deny all revelation, our Scriptures being the only revelation from God; and by so denying it, he returns mankind to Paganism. To prevent this, the Baptist assures us (John 3:16, 17, 35, 36): 'He who does not believe in the name of the only begotten Son of God shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.' Accordingly, our Lord speaks in his prayer to his Holy Father (John 17:3): 'And this is eternal life, that they might know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.' He also declares the same to the Jews (John 8:24): 'If you do not believe that I am he, you shall die in your sins'—that is, you shall sink down into the aeonian darkness, ignorance, and stupidity, knowing nothing further of yourselves or of my Father than that you yourselves are miserable, and that God is someone or something you do not know.*
>
> “Christianity insists that the belief in an only begotten Son of the holy Father is essential to its profession, and without it, its whole system of doctrines is a chimera. *There are* (says St. John, 1 John 5:7) *three that bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Logos, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are One. And there are three that bear witness on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood* <note>For the authenticity of this passage, see Bengelius.</note> *and these three agree in one* (1 John 2:13), or harmonize in this one testimony: that the Holy Father has begotten a Son, who, having been the creator of all things, is the restorer of all things. For,
>
> “*Firstly: The Spirit, sent from the holy Father and given to the saints on earth, is a testimony of the Father’s acceptance of us, confirming the Gospel report concerning his goodwill toward us in his beloved Son.*
>
> “*Secondly: The water, which corresponds to the second witness, the Logos, signifying our baptism in him, testifies to his acceptance of us as his own property—even as members of his new creation and his new kingdom in the heavens.*
>
> “*This is evident because the element of this new life resides in the Logos as its source; and our baptism testifies to our immersion into this element in Christ, proving our fellowship with him in it. Being buried with Christ into his death, we are raised with him into his new element of life; we are dead with Christ to our old or former nature and stand renewed in Christ in the element of the new creation, alive from the dead.*
>
> “*Thirdly: The blood-witness corresponds to the Holy Spirit and carries his testimony of our acceptance and our life in him no less clearly.*
>
> “*This again is evident because blood is represented as containing life; it is said that the life is in the blood, or the life resides in the blood. The blood, therefore, as the emblem of life, signifies an immortality administered to us by the Spirit of Christ—a principle of genuine life derived for us from the blood of Christ, which is filled with his Spirit, who is life.*
>
> “*The Holy Spirit (who, with the Son of God, is coeval with the Father) and the Logos, although two personalities, are one JEVE; and since the blood of the Logos is ours, his Spirit is also our spirit with it, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 6:17): 'He who is joined to the Lord is one Spirit' (see also John 17:22, 23).*
>
> “*So then, the Spirit given implies our favor with the holy Father; the water in which we are immersed implies our renovation in the element of grace and of the new creation which is in the Logos; and the blood by which we are sanctified implies our immortality, elicited in us by the Spirit of Life. And thus, the whole of Christianity is demonstrated in these three witnesses.*
>
> “*The man Jesus was the one begotten of the holy Spirit of God, an event of mysterious suitability. But it is the Word or Logos who is the begotten of the holy Father—who was from the beginning with God, who was made flesh, who had a glory with the Father before the world existed, and who created all things: thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers. For without him, nothing was made that was made. It is solely through the Logos’s sufferings in the flesh that we are the redeemed of God, reconciled to God, and accepted by the holy Father. He, the Logos, suffered for our sins so that he might bring us to God, who has laid the iniquity of us all upon him, and by whose stripes we are healed.*
>
> “Therefore, the reasonings of Crellius (whom, or whose followers, it seems the baron may have read) are vain—namely, that a God of God cannot be subjected to humiliation or suffering. * * * ”

This much on Swedenborg as a theologian. — The writer recently asked a well-informed gentleman, a professed Swedenborgian, what the *practical merits* or characteristics of the baron's divinity were. Whether its tendency as a scientific Christianity was to make its disciples and students profoundly aware of the radical universal corruption of their nature (through the death which Adam died on the day of his transgression), and at the same time acquainted with their capacity for restoration (through the Divine word of promise); and thereupon to strenuously recommend to them (as the only object deserving of their consideration) the commands and counsels of the Redeemer, in order to obtain that renovation (first in the heart or root of man, secondly in the intellect, and ultimately in body as well as soul). Whether the baron teaches his followers that the possibility of that renovation was procured for them by the triumphant process of Jesus Christ—the eternal Word made flesh, or Divine man, and second head of the human race—through all the states of the fallen human life, conquering all its evils and restoring to it all that it had lost; and that none could partake of redemption except through the Divine nature or Spirit brought to life in them, so as to enable them to follow Jesus Christ victoriously over every evil of life and death, and to overcome even as he overcame. <margin>defect ^</margin> Whether this regeneration and sanctification was the *foundation doctrine of the baron's divinity*: and that consequently, he urges upon his disciples the earnest practice of the gospel—that is, all kinds of self-denial to the old rational animal nature, living by strict religious rules, early rising for devotion, and continuing constant in prayer (many hours of each day *on their knees*), recollection or introversion of the mind, fasting, and other acts of mental and physical mortification, with activity in all goodness toward the souls and bodies of their neighbor; and all in faith, all in order to raise up or cultivate the Divine principle, or living Word of promise grafted into their souls, to perfection: — Whether such was the groundwork and main drift of the baron's divinity, apart from his visions; for he, the inquirer, considered all professed scientific theology, whatever it may declare regarding the mysteries of eternity, to be mere transcendental humbug, unless its manifest primary object was to make man awake to his sin and misery, and to the salvation offered to him in Christ, and thereupon to induce him earnestly to adopt all those self-annihilating practices or exercises of the gospel just referred to, as the means of obtaining that salvation; which, being the restoration of man to the blessings of his original birthright, included in it all possible blessings, even the highest intellectual illumination and divine knowledge. To which the individual candidly replied, that "such was not the main object of the New Jerusalem doctrine; but the baron had, he considered, given a key by which to understand the Revelations and other mysterious parts of Scripture, which he considered a proof of his having been inspired."

How clearly the baron has explained some of the leading mysteries and doctrines of the gospel has been sufficiently mentioned in the two letters above. But regarding his mystical interpretation of the Scriptures, can it, for edification and unction, be at all compared to that of Madame Guyon—woman as she was—or of other deeply spiritual writers who, according to their individual form of understanding, have opened a solid and uniform mystical sense of Scripture? For after the baron's declarations that the last judgment (spoken of in the Revelations) happened in the year 1757; that he had conversed with the inhabitants of the planets; that those of the moon are small, being no larger than children of six or seven years old, yet have the strength of men and roaring voices like thunder which proceed from their abdomen (!); that the angels sleep, and have entrails and the bestial configurations of the fallen, divided humanity, etc. (!) <margin>enormous development ^</margin> with an infinity of other corresponding productions of his analogical and comparative faculty—after this, no one will contend that the baron offers a purely *natural* ground of interpretation. The following is the baron's own word-for-word account of the pentecostal opening of his Divine commission: — "I dined very late at my inn, in London, and was eating very heartily, when, toward the end of my repast, I perceived a kind of mist spread itself before my eyes, and that the floor of the apartment was covered with hideous reptiles. They disappeared: the darkness was dissipated, and I saw, clearly, in the midst of a bright light, a man seated in the corner of the room, who said to me with a terrible voice, *Do not eat so much.* At these words my sight failed me; it afterwards gradually returned, and I found myself alone. On the following night, the same man, surrounded by a radiance of light, again appeared to me, and said, *I am God the Lord, the Creator and Redeemer; I have chosen you to unfold to mankind the interior and spiritual sense of the sacred writings; I will dictate to you what you are to write.*" — Law's identification of Swedenborg's and Mahomet's 'revelations' has more meaning in it than appears at first sight. — Should the reader wish to see what has been said in Swedenborg's favor as an inspired seer and theologian by one of his talented and most enthusiastic admirers, he may consult the apologetic dissertation prefixed to a publication entitled "The Beauties of Emanuel Swedenborg, comprising his opinions and visions, collected from upwards of forty large volumes of his works, closely printed in Latin; with a Preliminary Dissertation upon his Life and Writings, and their relation to the present times. 8vo. G. Hughes, London, 1813. Price, half-a-guinea."

**ANNOTATION.**—The *Spiritual Catechism of Christian Perfection* is the best work of Father SURIN—the most substantial, the most instructive, the most methodical, and the most useful regarding the goal he proposes. He begins by providing a grand and clear idea of Christian perfection; he then enters into the details of the means that lead to it and the obstacles that must be overcome to reach it. Nothing is more precise, clear, and perceptible than what he says of Prayer and Mortification in general, of the practice of virtues, and of the battle against vices and passions in particular.

As he wishes to treat his subject exhaustively, after having spoken of the ordinary conduct of grace, he describes the extraordinary ways into which God leads the souls He wishes to unite particularly to Himself. But he does not express himself in mystical and obscure terms. Everything he says of the passive state, of contemplation, of divine union, and of the great favors that accompany it, is within everyone's reach. He touches upon almost all the points of Mystical Theology most difficult to reconcile with Scholastic Theology; but he does so in such a way that no one can be mistaken, and one can always easily distinguish the condemned sense of the false Mystics from the Catholic sense, which gives everything to the power of grace without taking anything away from the cooperation of free will.

He speaks in several places of divine union and the delights of which it is the source, in order to inspire souls with an ardent desire for the highest perfection. But while he works to expand the hearts of those he instructs and to nourish their spirits on a grand scale by the magnificent ideas he gives them of perfection, he takes particular care to keep their courage within just bounds. He does this by placing their own weakness before their eyes and revealing the illusions into which it is easy to fall when one takes flight prematurely and wanders from the beaten path to indulge in a false elevation. It is to this that he attributes all the disorders of the *Illuminati* and other false Mystics. In accordance with this principle, he shows no mercy to that kind of pride which breeds a love for extraordinary ways, and he seizes every opportunity to recommend fidelity in fulfilling the duties of one's state of life, limiting oneself to accepted practices, preferring obscure virtues to those that are striking, and following the attraction of grace in such a way that it is always submitted to the external law of faith and obedience. So, if one wished to summarize the entire work and reduce the Author’s doctrine to certain main points regarding man's practice and response to God’s designs, one would find little else than an inviolable attachment to common duties and obligations, the care to be recollected, to conquer oneself, to humble oneself, to renounce oneself in everything, to refuse nothing to God, and to distrust one's own insights in order to depend on those of others.

Furthermore, while leading souls toward the most sublime perfection, he takes care to make it understood that he is speaking of Christian perfection, which concerns not only religious persons but also laypeople in the world. And so that the latter may not be mistaken, he goes into the details of their obligations. Reviewing different conditions of life, he helps everyone find in their own state the necessary means to reach the perfection of Christianity and the purest love of God.

Some will perhaps be surprised to see the same subjects return often, and will find it regrettable that the Author did not treat them thoroughly the first time he spoke of them. But they

<meta>This page continues the bibliographic entry and characterization of Jean-Joseph Surin's "Spiritual Catechism," emphasizing his pedagogical method, before moving on to other major mystical figures like Henry Suso, Johannes Tauler, and Jan van Ruysbroeck.</meta>

should reflect that spiritual matters are sometimes so delicate and subtle that they escape the penetration of even a sharp mind, even when it believes it understands them well. The skill of the Master consists in proportioning his instructions to the capacity of those he instructs, and in presenting the same objects under different facets to facilitate understanding for minds of different characters.

This is the method followed by Father Surin when speaking of prayer, contemplation, divine union, and the conduct and extraordinary effects of grace. After giving a general knowledge of these subjects, he moved on to easier ones to provide rest for the minds of his readers, most of whom are unaccustomed to considering spiritual objects. He returned several times to the subjects he had started; and going from clarity to clarity, he gave ideas that were increasingly clear, precise, deep, and extensive—ideas which would have discouraged many of his readers if he had proposed them all at once at the beginning.

It is to be hoped that all who read this work have a taste for the virtues and mysteries of grace treated therein. Father Surin usually confirms what he says with examples drawn from the lives of the greatest saints. These examples might well offend the sensitivity of many worldly people. It is for them to be fair: these kinds of books are not made for profane minds who have no wish to change. But one dares to assure that all those who read this catechism with a sincere desire to profit from it, and to reform their own wisdom according to the spirit of the Gospel and the sentiments of the saints, will gain the advantage the Author intended to provide: which is to instruct themselves thoroughly in their religion, to know themselves, to know God, and to be inflamed with the desire to please Him through the practice of the virtues of the evangelical counsels.

### **TAULERUS, Joannes.**—*illuminatissimus* and *internus.* <note>Most illuminated and inward.</note>

**ANNOTATION.**—This Author, who was a holy and learned Dominican who taught in Cologne and Strasbourg, where he died in the year 1379, is considered one of the most authoritative and significant among the Mystics, all of whom have an extreme deference for his sentiments. In truth, no good people could know him without enjoying his work and giving him their approval. We also see that the wisest Protestants—Doctors Arndt, Müller, and several others, without even excepting Luther or Melanchthon—have given him praises that are in no way inferior to those of Roman Catholics. This can be seen at the beginning of the German edition of his Sermons provided by the pious Arndt, and in the edition of all this author's works by the celebrated D. Spener, which has been reprinted in Frankfurt several times.

The character of this illuminated Author is, in my opinion, this: That the soul—through the mortification of its passions and vices, through the practice of virtues, through detachment, and the abnegation of self, its desires, its will, its self-love, and all its activity, and of every created thing—should return to its interior depth, seeking God there and finally finding Him manifesting Himself through the birth of His Divine Word and the breathing of His Holy Spirit; and that then, through a lasting and continual introversion, the soul preserves itself in this state of interiority, in which God can produce in it His will, His wonders, and His special guidance, though this author speaks of these only generally.

Tauler wrote in an old German language, which is very rarely found. Surius made a Latin translation, printed several times in Paris and Cologne until 1615, which currently serves as the original. We have several German editions provided by both Roman Catholics and Protestants. The Flemish have done the same; but the old Flemish edition of Frankfurt from 1565 is altered, as is the one Mr. Serrarius published in Hoorn about 40 years ago, although otherwise the latter contains more of the author's works than any of the others. The best is that of Antwerp, 1685; it lacks, however, his *Institutions*, his *Letters*, and his *Exercises on the Passion*, but these are found separately. The first two are under the title *Medulla animae* <note>The Marrow of the Soul</note>, of which we have an old French edition, now superseded by a new and very beautiful translation of both his *Institutions*, printed in Paris in 1668, and his *Exercises on the Passion*, printed in the same place the following year, with the *Exercises* of the pious Eschius on the purgative, illuminative, and unitive life joined to them. Father Mabillon, in the Catalogue at the end of his treatise on *Monastic Studies*, places the works of Tauler among the spiritual books translated into French. I have never seen his Sermons there, which are the most significant piece; and I am certain that his treatise on *The Poor Life of Jesus Christ* is found there even less, seeing as it is missing from the Latin of Surius and is only found in German, English, and Flemish.

**RUSBROCHIUS**, a contemporary of Tauler and in some ways his Master, is of almost the same character as him, and even sometimes reaches higher and more methodically. He was a holy Prior of a monastery of canons near Brussels who had almost no formal education and was of great simplicity, but possessed a great holiness and very high contemplation. From this came to him, by way of experience and infusion, a very deep and original knowledge of all Mystical Theology, in which he served as a guide to many. Except for his excellent treatise on the *Adornment of the Spiritual Marriage*, which is still sometimes found in old Flemish and which is one of his principal works, his works are only available in the Latin translation by Surius. They were printed in Cologne three times, the last being in the year 1692. Those

Father JEAN EVANGELISTE, a Capuchin at Louvain, is—or very closely approaches—the character of Tauler in his excellent book *The Kingdom of God in the Soul*. It is written so familiarly, so clearly, and with such a natural and consistent method that it can well serve as an introduction to the understanding of mystical things even for the least perceptive minds. His book is in Flemish and was printed several times in Antwerp from the year 1639 (while he was still living) until 1639. It has also been available in German since 1665;† but the latest Frankfurt editions of the years 1690 and 1692 are augmented by a second treatise, *The Separation of the Soul and the Spirit*, which a Professor from Louvain (*Libertus Fromondus*) had previously printed in Latin and joined to his *Explanation of the Song of Solomon*. This treatise seems more like a recapitulation and a derivation of some main points from his first book—specifically on the *Elevation of the Soul Above Itself*—rather than a sequel to the same book, regardless of what the title says. None of this is yet available in French. This author is remarkable because in his entire book there is not a single word that directly or indirectly touches upon the controversial matters between Christians, so that it is for the edification of all. It is also said that Protestants have contributed to its reprinting, so highly is it regarded, and rightly so. There is also a posthumous *Treatise on the Eucharist* by the same author, which has been translated from Flemish into French and printed in Brussels in 1662.

### ST. TERESA—Taught by God, affecting, and inflaming.

ANNOTATION.—What John of the Cross proposed in a theoretical manner, adapted to the way of the intellect and even, in a way, the scholastic method; that same thing is spread in a practical manner through narratives and productions of personal experience, and in an entirely affective manner suited to the way of the heart, in the writings of St. TERESA. Her character is such that, without affecting any specific method—though she does not lack order—she speaks and writes from pure feelings and pure movements of the heart, of love, and of humility, according to the vivid experiences she had of spiritual and supernatural things. She insists particularly on the way of Prayer, both active and that of quietude or supernatural and unitive passivity; on its degrees, and on the infinite and ineffable graces that God communicates through it to the souls who surrender to it. Her humble, touching, and animated ways, filled with the Spirit of God, soften hearts that still have some inclination toward God, awaken divine love within them, and engrave in souls a deep veneration for the Divine Majesty and the sacred humanity of the Savior, along with a singular admiration for the inexpressible graces and operations of the Most High in hearts that give themselves sincerely to Him.

Everyone knows that this great saint was a Spanish Carmelite. In her works, she describes a good part of her own life (of which the Bishop of Tarazona and Father Ribera have each published a separate, complete history, available in French). Her works, I say, have been translated and published in all sorts of languages, such as in Latin at Cologne in 1626, in

---

<note>* Indeed, in that same year, it was published in Frankfurt, in folio, with a German preface by the celebrated G. Arnold.

These few words about RUYSBROECK in the context of this letter were first written by me after I had looked through some of his books several years ago, of which only a general memory remained. But having read them all more recently, I am forced to confess that Ruysbroeck seems to me, without any difficulty, to be easily the first among all mystics: solid, safe, pious, holy, humble, accommodating himself to the weak, while seeking sublime and secret things with the sublime; profound in sense, a most holy moralist, an incomparable contemplator, an illuminating teacher, inflaming and seizing one with admiration through the revelation of divine secrets and eternal life; experienced in the enjoyment of God and blessed rest—in a word, such a man as I know not whether you will find his like anywhere. If anyone desires to have a summary of Ruysbroeck’s character, or his method and subject matter in his own words, here are the passages from the book *The Seven Guards*, chapter III, which seem relevant:

> "If you wish to cultivate, exercise, and possess LOVE and HOLINESS in the highest degree (and this is indeed his aim; the means and progress follow), it is necessary that you free and strip the INTELLECTUAL power of all forms and images, and through FAITH elevate it above Reason, where the rays of the eternal SUN shine, which will illustrate you with its splendor and teach you all TRUTH; and the truth shall set you free, and will fix and stabilize your naked gaze in formless nakedness... This vision the POWER OF LOVE always follows with naked Love; and in the very act of following, a stream of divine GRACE flows continually, introducing such a soul to the living fountain of the Holy SPIRIT, where the VEINS OF ETERNAL SWEETNESS spring up, inebriating the soul and lifting it above Reason into a kind of wandering or pathless journey, namely into the DESERT OF ETERNAL BLISS itself. And this is the root and substance of true HOLINESS, and from that same root the internal EXERCISES OF VIRTUES continually emerge and proceed; for LOVE cannot be idle."

That these things, and whatever else this Holy Man teaches, are not merely bare words or mere ideas, but the divine experiences of an enlightened mind, is testified by these other words of his, which are also remarkable monuments to his humility:

> "I renounce myself; and to the eternal truth, and the faith of the Holy Catholic Church, and the Doctors who have explained the Sacred Scriptures through the Holy Spirit, I willingly submit myself and my writings. Nevertheless, that which I feel and experience within remains with me, nor can I drive it from my spirit; indeed, even if I could gain the whole world, I could not doubt it, nor despair of the Lord Jesus, thinking He would want to damn me. But if I hear otherwise, I will willingly remain silent."</note>

German editions from 1686, etc., make her sufficiently known. Of the many translations available in French, the most recent and the best is that of Mr. Arnauld d'Andilly, printed several times in Paris, and recently (in 1688) in Antwerp in three small volumes. These include the ancient *Letters* of this Saint which were missing from the Paris editions, though they are somewhat overburdened by the remarks of the Bishop of Osma. I call these letters "ancient" by comparison to two volumes of others that have just been published (in Antwerp, 1698) and which had never appeared before. Of her works, her book the *Interior Castle* is the most sublime; her treatise the *Way of Perfection* is the most familiar and useful; her *Life* written by herself and her *Exclamations* are the most moving; and her *Letters* and *Foundations* are the most pleasant.

Among the authors who share St. Teresa’s character, or come very close to it, St. **Gertrude** is the principal one; not the one from Brabant, but from Germany, a Countess by birth, who was an Abbess of a monastery of nuns of the Order of St. Benedict in the Diocese of Halberstadt about five hundred years ago. She wrote in Latin. I believe that by the title given to her life and revelations, *Insinuations of Divine Piety* (often printed in Cologne, as well as in Paris and Salzburg in 1662), they intended to show that she indeed instilled into hearts a truly divine piety and a very affective love for the Majesty of God. This is particularly evident in the second book of these same *Insinuations*, where she describes her conversion and part of her life in a manner that imitates and even seems to surpass that of St. Augustine in his *Confessions*. Her *Exercises of Divine Love*, which are prayers for her use for every day of the week, are also very affective and touching. They were translated from her Latin and published in French in Paris in 1672; her *Insinuations* were also published a year earlier, as well as in 1687, under the title *The Life and Revelations of St. Gertrude*. <gloss>*</gloss> The translator, though eloquent, did not always fully grasp the meaning of this holy soul, who is considered to have been one of the purest who ever lived on earth.

This saint reminds me of another holy woman of the same name, who wrote the *Confessions of a Loving Soul* in the same style—very touching and capable of softening and inflaming hearts with the love of God. This is **Gertrude More**, a descendant of the famous Chancellor of the same name, formerly a nun at Cambrai, whose book has been printed in English in Paris several times.<gloss>†</gloss>

St. **Catherine**, surnamed **of Siena** because she was born there around the middle of the fourteenth century, is also entirely in the character of St. Teresa. Her *Meditations on the Passion*, printed with her life by her confessor; her six *Dialogues* which she dictated (printed in Latin in Ingolstadt, 1583) and which deal primarily with Christian Doctrine regarding the restoration of man, the love of God, the tears of penance, the Church and the corruption of its ministers, Divine Providence, and obedience; her prayers, which are appended there; and her *Letters* <gloss>‡</gloss> to all sorts of people, published in French in Paris in 1644. Finally, the deference—not to say the submission and obedience—shown to her by all of Christendom without exception, including Popes, Kings, the great and the small, the learned and the unlearned (even though she was merely a simple young woman whose life did not last beyond thirty years), clearly shows that God had given her the gift of touching hearts and affections with the affective and sacred fire with which she herself was completely inflamed.

In the works of Louis de Blois, commonly called **Blosius**, a Benedictine Abbot of Liessies who lived over a century ago, one finds the same spirit and character for softening hearts toward piety; this has led to him being called "pious" almost every time he is mentioned. His works have been collected and published several times in Latin in Antwerp, and various treatises have been translated into different languages.

The *Contemplations on Divine Love* by **Raymond Jordan** (who called himself "the Idiot") are clearly in the same style, as are the treatises usually joined with them: the *Soliloques*, *Meditations*, and the *Manual* that bear the name of St. Augustine. The *Confessions* of St. Augustine, as well as those of **Alonso de Orozco**, preacher to Charles V, are also in this same character of humble and affective love.

* In the introduction to the abridged life of Gichtel, the editor remarks, “If it were ever necessary to attend to what may be said regarding the imitation of highly regenerate and enlightened souls, it is certainly so regarding the example of this singular individual; the rule is this: — *Follow such spirits in the way to heaven, but do not walk precisely in their footsteps as their scrupulous imitator. Go with them to their aim and end, but go at your own pace, holding the Lord’s hand, not theirs. Let their great example excite you to place the rule of the divine life more vividly before your eyes, but do not include in this rule all the exceptions which might take place in them—nay, which are permitted to take place—so that the Divine glory might be the more abundantly displayed in them. In short, walk entirely your own way, imitating their devotion and diligence, courage and fidelity, but not the peculiarities of their path and spiritual process. * * * There is only one who is our way, for He alone is our life. Having his example before our eyes, and resigning ourselves without any presumptuous self-choosing entirely to his wise and gracious guidance, we shall not fail to be led by him in our own path, which is most adapted for us, neither outrunning his will, nor remaining behind it; and thus shall his will be accomplished in us. * * * But just as we should not minutely govern ourselves by such examples, we should as little judge them or measure them by ourselves. * *”*

These very judicious observations may be applicable to the whole of the works recommended in this treatise for reading, by those who desire to understand Christianity in its universality of theory and experience—a science that few have explored, even if they have had any notion of its vast extent and wondrous sublimities.

<margin>X</margin>
For the devout reader must not suppose that any of the numerous ways described here of returning to God are to be the precise rule and model of his own spiritual process. This would, indeed, be a mistake, and yet it is one which an undirected study of mystic books, or of the lives and experiences of spiritual persons, might cause inexperienced readers to fall into, and thereby cause themselves much disquietude. — The object of spiritual books (as implied in the above observations) is to open the reader's understanding to the truth and necessity of God’s action on the soul in order for its renewal, and consequently to induce him to turn wholly to GOD ALONE, in diligent research, in faith and prayer, rather than to lead and constrain him into a *particular* way to that same end. At least, such should be the aim of spiritual authors. And here we see the peculiar characteristic of Law’s and Behmen’s <note>William Law and Jacob Boehme</note> practical writings, which, being the interpretation of Scriptural truth through pure, sound, non-idiosyncratic, undistorted reason, have this advantage over all other instructive and encouraging evangelical books—if only taken by their right handle and duly understood (which, however, is generally very difficult because of the preconceptions and imaginary knowledge of divinity already in the mind)—namely, that they lead their faithful student, according to his particular nature, *directly* to Christ; to Christ, not as a concept, but as ‘the Spirit’ of holiness, life, and redemption. They do not draw him out of his true and proper way to make him walk, as it were, unnaturally in *their* way, as is the case to some degree or other with almost all other devotional writers; instead, they cultivate the divine nature in the soul—the life of grace—according to the individual subject’s natural character, whereby the diversity of the harmony of creation is preserved and accomplished according to Divine wisdom and will.

</margin>
We cannot, perhaps, take a better opportunity than the present to introduce some further warnings concerning the vanity and self-deception to which mere curious readers and students of spiritual books are subject. — Previously observing that, although some of the disadvantages of isolation from outward church communion were referred to in the note on page 127, there was, however, a very common excuse urged in defense of that *temptation* which was then overlooked; namely, ‘that there is so much corruption in every communion that pure-minded, spiritual persons cannot mix with them.’ Now, can this reasoning be anything but fallacious? For does not Christ’s own description of the gospel net—embracing good and bad fish until the end of the world, when the separation is to be made—imply that there will always be corruption and the working of the mystery of iniquity in even the most spiritual Christian societies? And does not Christ’s prayer for his true followers (besides numerous other passages of Scripture, 1 Cor. 5:10, etc.) suppose the same truth, namely: ‘I pray not that you should take them out of the world, but that you should keep them from the evil’? Surely it is only necessary to direct the attention of sincere and devoted retired spiritual worshippers to the truths contained in the above passages, and to assure them of the inconceivably great and surpassing benefits—in respect to growth in grace and high spiritual enjoyments—derivable from the interaction of diverse Christian experience, and of doing good in company with brethren animated by the same spirit of earnest devotion and holy endeavors to promote the glory of God, according to the various operations of the spirit of Christ in them, to induce them at once to unite themselves heartily with an outward section of professing Christians. This is offered as brotherly, well-grounded, experienced counsel. — The points referred to regarding spiritual books are contained in the following quotation, which is another beautiful illustration of the practical wisdom and sublime talent of the subject of our proposed biography:

> “Indeed, *Academicus*, your education has so accustomed you to the pleasure of reading a variety of books that you hardly propose any other end in reading than the entertainment of your mind; thus, the ‘Spirit of Prayer’ has only awakened in you a desire to see another book upon the

<margin>x</margin>
*Philo* has, for these twenty years, been collecting and reading all the spiritual books he can hear of. He reads them as the *critics* read commentators and lexicons: to be precise and exact in telling you the *style, spirit,* and *intent* of this or that spiritual writer; how one is more accurate in this, and the other in that. *Philo* will ride forty miles in winter to have a conversation about spiritual books, or to see a collection larger than his own. *Philo* is amazed at the deadness and insensibility of the Christian world—that they are such strangers to the inward life and spiritual nature of the Christian salvation; he wonders how they can be so zealous for the outward letter and form of ordinances, and so averse to that spiritual life that they all point at as the "one thing needful." But *Philo* never thinks how wonderful it is that a man who knows regeneration to be the whole should yet content himself with the love of books about the new birth, instead of being born again himself. For all that is changed in *Philo* is his taste for books. He is no more dead to the world, no more delivered from himself; he is as fearful of adversity, as fond of prosperity, as easily provoked and pleased with trifles, as much governed by his own *will*, tempers, and passions, and as unwilling to deny his appetites or enter into war with himself as he was twenty years ago. Yet all is well with *Philo*; he has no suspicion of himself; he dates the *newness* of his life and the fullness of his light from the time that he discovered the "pearl of eternity" in spiritual authors.

All this, *Academicus*, is said on your account, so that you may not lose the benefit of this spark of the divine life that is kindled in your soul, but may conform yourself suitably to so great a gift of God.

It demands, at present, an eagerness of another kind than that of much reading, even upon the most spiritual matters.

*Acad.*—I thank you, *Theophilus*, for your goodwill toward me; but I did not imagine my eagerness after such books to be so great and dangerous a mistake. And if I do not yet entirely give in to what you say, it is because a friend of yours has told us (and, as I thought, by way of direction) that he has been a diligent reader of all the spiritual authors <note>See the Concluding Observations of this Section</note> from the apostolic *Dionysius* down to the illuminated *Guyon* and the celebrated *Fenelon of Cambray*; and, therefore, it would never have come into my head to suspect it to be a fault or dangerous to follow his example.

*Theoph.*—I have said nothing, my friend, with a design of hindering your acquaintance with all the truly spiritual writers. I would rather, in a right way, help you to a true intimacy with them; for they are friends of God, entrusted with His secrets, and partakers of the divine nature; and he who converses rightly with them has a happiness that can hardly be overvalued.

My intention is only to lessen, for a time, a spirit of eagerness after much reading, which in your state has more of nature than grace in it—which seeks delight in a variety of new notions and rather gratifies curiosity than reforms the heart.

<margin>Beautiful.</margin>
Suppose you had seen an angel from heaven, who had revealed to you a glimpse of its own internal brightness and of that glorious union in which it lived with God, opening more of itself to the inward sight of your mind than you could either forget or relate. Suppose it had told you, with a piercing word and living impression, that all its own angelic and heavenly brightness was hidden in yourself, concealed from you under a bestial covering of flesh and blood; that this flesh and blood had become the master of it and would not suffer it to breathe, or stir, or come to life in you. Suppose it had told you that all your life had been spent in helping this flesh and blood to more and more power over you, to hinder you from knowing and feeling this divine life within you. Suppose it had told you that, to this day, you had lived in the grossest *self-idolatry*, loving, serving, honoring, and adoring yourself, instead of loving, serving, and adoring God with all your heart, and soul, and spirit: that all your intentions, projects, cares, pleasures, and indulgences had been only so much labor to bring you to the grave in a total ignorance of that great work for which alone you were born into the world.

Suppose it had told you that all this blindness and insensibility of your state was obstinately and willfully brought upon yourself, because you had boldly slighted and resisted all the daily inward and outward calls of God to your soul, and all the teachings, doings, and sufferings of a Son of God to redeem you. Suppose it left you with this *farewell: "O man, awake; your work is great, your time is short, I am your last trumpet; the grave calls for your flesh and blood, your soul must enter into a new lodging. To be born again is to be an angel; not to be born again is to become a devil."*

Tell me now, *Academicus*, what would you expect from a man who had been thus awakened and pierced by the voice of an angel? Could you think he had any sense left if he were not cast into the deepest depth of humility, self-dejection, and self-abhorrence? Casting himself, with a broken heart, at the feet of the divine mercy, desiring nothing but that, from that time, every moment of his life might be given unto God in the most perfect denial of every temper, will, and inclination that nourished the corruption of his nature: wishing and praying from the bottom of his heart that God would lead him into and through *everything*, inwardly and outwardly, that might destroy the evil workings of his nature and awaken all that was holy and heavenly within him; so that the seed of eternity, the spark of life that he had so long quenched and smothered under earthly rubbish, might breathe and come to life in him.

Or would you think he was sufficiently affected by this angelic visit if all that it had awakened in him was only a longing and eager desire to hear the same or another angel talk again?

*Acad.*—O *Theophilus*, you have said enough; for all that is within me consents to the truth and justness of what you have said. I now feel, in the strongest manner, that I have been rather amused than edified by what I have read.

*Theoph.*—A spiritual book, *Academicus*, is a call to as real and total a death to the life of corrupt nature as that which *Adam* died in paradise was to the life of heaven. He, indeed, died at

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Academicus and Theophilus, further exploring the necessity of total self-denial for spiritual regeneration and defining the "self" as the internal source of all spiritual opposition to God.</meta>

— of Father Bardon.

once totally to the divine life in which he was created: but as our body of earth is to last to the end of our lives, so to the end of our earthly life, every step we take, every inch of our road, is to be made up of denial and dying to ourselves. This is because all our redemption consists in our regaining that first life of heaven in the soul, to which *Adam* died in paradise. And therefore the one single work of redemption is the one single work of regeneration, or the raising up of a life, spirit, tempers, and inclinations contrary to that life and spirit which we derive from our earthly fallen parents. To think, therefore, of anything but the continual, total denial of our earthly nature is to overlook the very thing on which everything depends. And to hope for anything, to trust or pray for anything but the *life of God*, or a *birth of heaven* in our souls, is as useless to us as placing our hope and trust in a graven image. Thus says the Christ of God, the one pattern and author of our salvation: “If any man will be my disciple, let him deny himself, hate his own life, take up his daily cross, and follow me.” And again: “Unless a man is born again from above, of water and the Spirit, he cannot see, or enter into, the kingdom of God.”

Now is your time, *Academicus*, to enter deeply into this great truth. You have just come out of the slumber of life and begin to see with new eyes the nature of your salvation. You are charmed with the discovery of a kingdom of heaven hidden within you, and long to be entertained more and more with the nature, progress, and perfection of the new birth, or the opening of the kingdom of God in your soul.

But, my friend, stop a little. It is indeed great joy that the “pearl of great price” is found; but take notice that it is not yours—you can have no possession of it—until, as the merchant did, “you sell all that you have” and buy it. Now, *self is all that you have*; it is your sole possession; you have no goods of your own; nothing is yours but this *self*. The riches of *self* are your *own riches*; but all this *self* is to be parted with before the pearl is yours. Think of a lower price, or be unwilling to give this much for it; plead in your excuse that you keep the commandments, and then you are that very rich young man in the gospel, who went away sorrowful from our Lord when he had said, “if you will be perfect,” that is, if you will obtain the pearl, “sell all that you have and give to the poor.” That is, die to all your *possession of self*, and then you have given all that you have to the poor; all that you have is devoted and used for the love of God and your neighbor. This *selling all, Academicus*, is the measure of your *dying to self*; all of it is to be given up. It is an apostate nature, a *stolen life*, brought forth in rebellion against God; it is a continual departure from him. It corrupts everything it touches; it defiles everything it receives; it turns all the gifts and blessings of God into covetousness, partiality, pride, hatred, and envy. All these tempers are born, bred, and nourished in *self*; they have no other place to live in, no possibility of existence, but in that creature which has fallen from a life in God into a life in *self*.

<margin>Beautiful</margin>
*Acad.*—Please, sir, tell me more plainly what this self is, since so much depends upon it.

*Theoph.*—It is hell, it is the devil, it is darkness, pain, and disquiet. It is the one only enemy of Christ, the great antichrist. It is the scarlet whore, the fiery dragon, the old serpent, the devouring beast that is mentioned in the revelation of St. John.

*Acad.*—You terrify rather than instruct me by this description.

*Theoph.*—It is, indeed, a very frightful matter; it contains everything that man has to dread and hate, to resist and avoid. Yet be assured, my friend, that careless and merry as the world is, every man who is born into it has all these enemies to overcome *within himself*. And every man, until he is in the way of regeneration, is more or less governed by them. No hell in any remote place, no devil that is separate from you, no darkness or pain that is not within you, no antichrist either at Rome or England, no furious beast, no fiery dragon outside or apart from you can do you any hurt. It is your own hell, your own devil, your own beast, your own antichrist, your own dragon, that lives in your own heart’s blood, that alone can hurt you.

Die to this self, to this inward nature, and then all outward enemies are overcome. Live to this self, and then, when this life is over, all that is within you and all that is without you will be nothing else but a mere seeing and feeling of this hell, serpent, beast, and fiery dragon.

See here, *Academicus*, the twofold nature of every man. He has *within him* a redeeming power, the meekness of the heavenly life, called the *Lamb of God*. This seed is surrounded, or encompassed, by the *beast* of fleshly lusts, the *serpent* of guile and subtlety, and the *dragon* of fiery wrath. This is the great trial, or strife of human life: whether a man will live to the lusts of the *beast*, the guile of the *serpent*, and the pride and wrath of the *fiery dragon*, or give himself up to the meekness, the patience, the sweetness, the simplicity, and the humility of the *Lamb of God*.

This is the whole of the matter between God and the creature. On one side, fire and wrath, awakened first by the rebellious angels; and on the other side, the meekness of the Lamb of God, the patience of divine love coming down from heaven to stop and overcome the fire and wrath that has broken out in nature and creature. Your father *Adam* has introduced you into the fire and wrath of the fallen angels, into a world from which paradise has departed. Your flesh and blood is kindled in that sin which first brought forth a murdering *Cain*. But, dear soul, be of good comfort; for the meekness, the *love*, the heart, and the Lamb of God has become man and has set himself in the birth of your own life, so that in him, with him, and by a birth from him, heaven and paradise may be again opened both within you and without you, not for a time, but for all eternity.

Once more, *Academicus*. Every man in this world stands essentially in heaven and in hell, both as to that which is within him and that which is without him: for man and the world are both in the same fallen state. The *curse in the earth* is that same thing in outward nature that the loss of the divine life was to the soul of *Adam*. The whole world in all its nature is nothing else but a *real mixture of heaven and hell*. The sun and the water of this world are what keep under and overcome the darkness, wrath, and fire of hell, and carry on the vegetable and animal life that is in it. The light of the sun blesses all the workings of the elements, and the cool, softening essence of the water keeps under the fire and wrath of nature. In all *animal* creatures,

the birth of *light* in their own life, and the *water* of their own blood, both produced by the light of the sun and the *water of outward nature*, bring forth an *order of earthly creatures* that can enjoy the good that is in this world, in spite of the wrath of hell and the malice of devils.

But man has more than all this; for having been first created as an angel, and intended by the mercy of God to be an angel again, he has the *light* of heaven and the *water* of eternal life. Both were given to *Adam* in that seed of *the woman* which was to bruise the head of the serpent; that is, to overcome the curse, the fire, and wrath, or hell, that was awakened in the fallen soul. So that man has not only, in common with the other animals, the light and water of outward nature to quench the wrath of his own life in this mixed world, but he has the meekness, the light, the love, and the humility of the holy Jesus as a seed of life born in his soul, to bring forth that first image of God in which *Adam* was created.

This, my friend, is the true basis of all true religion: it means nothing, it intends nothing, but to overcome that *earthly life* which overcame *Adam* in the fall, which made him a prisoner of hell and a slave to the corrupt workings of earthly flesh and blood. And therefore you may see, and know with a mathematical certainty, that the one thing necessary for every fallen soul is to die to all the life that we have from this world, so that the life of heaven may be born again in him. The life of this world is the life of the *beast*, the *scarlet whore*, the *old serpent*, and the *fiery dragon*.

Hence it is that sin rides in triumph over church and state, and from the court to the cottage all is overrun with sensuality, guile, falseness, pride, wrath, envy, selfishness, and every form of corruption. Everyone swims away in this torrent, except for the one who hears and attends to the *voice* of the Son of God within him, calling him to die to this life, to take up his cross, and follow him. Much learned effort has often been taken to prove *Rome* or *Constantinople* to be the seat of the beast, the antichrist, the scarlet whore, etc. But, alas! they are not at such a distance from us; they are the properties of fallen human nature and are all alive in our own selves until we are dead or dying to all the spirit and tempers of this world. They are everywhere, in every soul where the heavenly nature and spirit of the holy Jesus are not. But when the human soul turns from itself and turns to God, dies to itself and lives to God in the spirit, tempers, and inclinations of the holy Jesus—loving, pitying, suffering, and praying for all its enemies, and overcoming all evil with good, as this Christ of God did—then, but not until then, are these monsters separated from it. For covetousness and sensuality of all kinds are the very devouring *beast*; religion, governed by a worldly trading spirit and gratifying the partial interests of flesh and blood, is nothing else but the *scarlet whore*; guile, and craft, and cunning are the very essence of the *old serpent*; self-interest and self-exaltation are the whole nature of *antichrist*. Pride, persecution, wrath, hatred, and envy are the very essence of the *fiery dragon*.

This, *Academicus*, is fallen human nature, and this is *the old man* who is alive in everyone, though in various manners, until he is born again from above. To think, therefore, of anything in religion, or to pretend to real holiness without totally dying to this old man, is building castles in the air; it can bring forth nothing but *Satan* in the form of an angel of light. Would you know, *Academicus*, why it is that so many false spirits have appeared in the world, who have deceived themselves and others with false fire and false light, laying claim to *inspirations, illuminations*, and openings of the divine life, pretending to do wonders under *extraordinary calls* from God? It is this: they have turned to God *without turning from themselves*; they would be alive in God before they were dead to their own nature—a thing as impossible in itself as for a grain of wheat to be alive before it dies.

Now, religion in the hands of the self, or corrupt nature, serves only to reveal vices of a worse kind than those in nature left to itself. Hence come all the disorderly passions of religious men, which burn with a worse flame than passions only employed about worldly matters: pride, self-exaltation, hatred, and persecution, under a cloak of religious zeal, will sanctify actions which nature, left to itself, would be ashamed to admit.

You may now see, *Academicus*, with what great reason I have called you, at your first setting out, to this great point: the *total dying to self* as the only foundation of a solid piety. All the fine things you hear or read of an inward and spiritual life in God, all your expectations of the light and Holy Spirit of God, will become a false food to your soul until you seek for them only through death to self.

Observe, sir, the difference that clothes make in those who have it in their power to dress as they please: some are all for show, colors, and glitter; others are quite fantastical and affected in their dress; some have a grave and solemn habit; others are quite simple and plain in their whole manner. Now all this difference of dress is only an outward difference that covers the same poor carcass and leaves it full of all its infirmities. In the same way, all the truths of the gospel, when only embraced and possessed by *the old man*, make only such a superficial difference as is made by clothes. Some put on a solemn, formal, prudent, outside carriage; others appear in all the glitter and show of religious coloring and spiritual attainments; but under all this outside difference, there lies the poor fallen soul, imprisoned and unhelped in its own fallen state. And thus it must be; it is not possible to be otherwise until the spiritual life begins at the true root, grows out of death, and is born in a broken heart—a heart broken off from all its own natural life. Then self-hatred, self-contempt, and self-denial are as suitable to this newborn spirit as self-love, self-esteem, and self-seeking are to the unregenerate man. Let me, therefore, my friend, urge you not to look forward or search for spiritual advancement until you have rightly taken this *first step* in the spiritual life. All your future progress depends upon it: for this depth of religion goes no deeper than the depth of your malady; for sin has its root in the bottom of your soul, it comes to life with your flesh and blood, and breathes in the breath of your natural life; and therefore, until you die to

*Acad.*—Indeed, Theophilus, you have made the difference between true and false religion as plain to me as the difference between light and darkness. But all that you have said, at the same time, is as new to me as if *I had lived in a land where religion had never been named!* But pray, sir, tell me how I am to take *this first step*, which you so much insist upon.
*Theoph.*—You are to turn *wholly from yourself*, and to give yourself up wholly to God, in this or a similar two-fold form of words or thoughts:
<margin>Prayer.</margin>
> "O my God, with all the strength of my soul, assisted by your grace, I desire and resolve to resist and deny all my own will, earthly tempers, selfish views, and inclinations; everything that the spirit of this world and the vanity of fallen nature prompts me to. I give myself up wholly and solely to you, to be all yours—to have, and do, and be, inwardly and outwardly, according to your good pleasure. I desire to live for no other ends, with no other designs, but to accomplish the work which you require of me, as a humble, obedient, faithful, thankful instrument in your hands, to be used as you please."

You are not to content yourself, my friend, with making this offering of yourself to God now and then, or even many times. It must be the daily, the *hourly exercise* of your mind, until it is wrought into your very nature and becomes an *essential state and habit* of your mind; until you feel yourself as habitually *turned from all your own will, selfish ends, and earthly desires* as you are from stealing and murder; until the *whole turn and bent of your spirit points as constantly to God* as the needle touched with the lodestone does to the north. This, sir, is your first and necessary step in the *spiritual life*; this is the key to all the treasures of heaven; this unlocks the sealed book of your soul and makes room for the light and Spirit of God to arise within it. Without *this*, the spiritual life is but *spiritual talk*, and only assists nature in being pleased with a holiness that it does not possess.
The necessity of this first step, and the folly of pretending to succeed without it, is thus represented by our blessed Lord: "What man intending to build a house—"
All our ability and preparation to succeed in this great affair lies in this *first step*. You may perhaps think this a hard saying. But do not go away sorrowful, like the young man in the gospel, because he had great possessions. For, my friend, you little think what a deliverance you will have from all hardships, and what a flow of happiness is found, even in this life, as soon as the soul is *thus dead to self*, freed from its own passions, and wholly given up to God; of which I shall speak to you by and by. I have told you the <term>PRICE OF THE NEW BIRTH</term>. I shall now leave you to consider whether you will be so wise a merchant as to give up all the wealth of the old man for this heavenly <term>PEARL</term>. I do not expect your answer now, but will wait for it until tomorrow. * * *”

A few years at furthest, and we shall see the end of this impious author—whether he dies a broken-hearted penitent, or his body is cast into the ditches, if it is honored with a human burial at all!

**ANNOTATION.**—The following extract from a letter by Dr. F. Lee, found among Law’s papers, concerning some of the objections made against the Contemplative Way, and representing the true nature of that way, may be acceptable to many readers of this treatise:—

> “Without apologizing for myself, I am immediately led to consider the great point of **PASSIVE CONTEMPLATION**, wherein I find that you have been much shocked by some significant objections from a great and active genius. You shall hear, then, my free sentiments upon the matter; and after such a long period of silence, it may be concluded that they are my fixed thoughts, and not the hasty eruptions of any natural or supernatural fire in my spirit.
> 
> It must be confessed that several of the admirers and followers of the Passive State do seem to show too **little** respect for the **sacred** Scriptures, and that some of them even very slightly pass over the mystery of **salvation by the death of Christ**, and seek to find **God** outside of and above the blessed **humanity** of our dear Mediator—which is Jacob’s ladder, by which the angels of God and all **Divine** influences descend from heaven to earth, and re-ascend from earth to heaven. But after I had spoken with Mr. Coester and had heard him fully, I found that it was the unbounded activity of his genius that had carried him too far; and that it was hardly possible for anyone (no matter how sharp) to reach the **punctum** <note>The central point or essential core of an argument.</note> of the question without having first learned to moderate the active faculties or powers of the soul, or without having had (*at least*) some minor experiences regarding this subject matter.
> 
> The **way of Contemplation** ought in the first place to be understood; and this is to be learned either from the philosophers, or else from the Holy Scriptures and the Christian Mystics. Philosophical Contemplation is evidently misunderstood when the exercise of it is condemned in those who were never acquainted with the history of the Gospel or convinced of its truth. For certainly it can be no fault in anyone who never heard of Jesus Christ (or, what is the same thing, could never be satisfied after his best and sincerest endeavors made for that purpose) to go as directly as he can to God in the deepest self-abasement and the most perfect surrender of his will into the hands of the omnipotent Creator and Father. And it is no less evidently misunderstood when the exercise of holy Contemplation is censored in those who are both acquainted with and convinced of the truth of the history of the **Gospel**. For every Christian contemplative who is truly such does not ascend in his spirit above Christ, or put himself in any way outside of Christ; but in the very exercise of Contemplation, he most truly and properly sinks himself down into the heart of Christ—and even more truly and properly than he could possibly have done by all the meditations and reflections imaginable upon the life and sufferings of Christ. Everyone who has had any experience of this must declare it to be so. These meditations and reflections, indeed...

soul are not to be neglected, for they are most useful and beneficial in their proper order. By these, when rightly pursued, we may arrive at <term>Contemplation</term>, and thereby lodge ourselves as if in the bosom of our Beloved. In contemplating His beauty we can never grow weary—the beauty of Him in whom all the treasures and beautiful forms of the Deity are stored, which are never to be revealed except to the single and contemplative eye. The devout and active contemplation of what <term>Christ</term> both did and suffered for us will naturally lead us into that divine and passive contemplation which transcends all meditation and self-action whatever, and which He, by the merits of His precious death and sufferings, has purchased for us. It will bring us successively into that divine peace which passes all understanding and reasoning. It will not cease to carry us on beyond all that the activity of our intellectual abilities is able to reach or apprehend; and then it will allow us gently to fall asleep in His dear arms and to cease from every motion of our own spirit, so that we may be perfectly passive to all the motions and inworkings of that blessed Spirit which, through His merits, is given to us, and which is given to us in the highest degree when we are stripped of all our own acts. Being thus under the guidance of this Spirit, we do not then lie exposed to the subtlety of malicious spirits transforming themselves, but are quite delivered from them. None of the powers of darkness are able to hurt or supplant a soul that continues in this passive and silent state; for it is therein actually surrendered into the hands of the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Under that consideration too, it is truly animated by the Holy Ghost (no less than the body is by the soul) and is made indeed a partaker of the Divine nature in <term>Christ</term>. And <term>Christ</term>, indeed, is the true and proper way of <term>Contemplation</term> (I say to us Christians), and no one comes to the Father but by Him. For it is the Son who comes to the Father, and those who follow the Son must come to God in the same manner as He comes, so that they may even, in a degree, behold His face and, beholding it, be irradiated by the light of His countenance, lifted up and reflected upon them. But He who teaches me to come to the Father has taught me not only to see the Father in Him (as if that alone were permitted), but also to see and contemplate Him in the Father.

The last six chapters of <term>Cardinal Cusanus</term> in his manual <term>Of the Vision of God</term>, by means of simple abstraction (which I have only seen in the English translation of it), lay this down professedly. The book of the *Idiot* does the same; and many others of the best and wisest of the Mystics will be found to agree perfectly on this point when they are thoroughly examined. Indeed, I believe I am able to show even from <term>Dr. Molinos</term> himself that there is no other way to the quiet of the soul in God but through <term>Christ</term>; and that in the very laying aside of all sensible images, He is not laid aside, but may then most truly be beheld in the Father. Nor can I think anything more absurd or self-contradicting than that he should write a book purposely for *Daily Communion* and yet not highly exalt the merits of the death of <term>Christ</term>; or that he should undertake to prescribe this as a proper means for the preservation of this internal quiet, unless he believed that this quiet of the recollected soul in God was both to be acquired and preserved by an union to the humanity of the blessed Jesus, as well as by a communion of the Divine Word arising from it. This must have been the ground of his writing that little treatise, which is not otherwise significant in itself, and will sufficiently vindicate him from the charge of Deism. And I am certain that the French lady, <term>Madame Guyon</term>, is not as great a heretic in this matter as the cabal in France would make her. Her <term>Moyen Court</term> <note>Short Method</note>, which was burned at Paris, has many express passages—some of them very excellent—that set forth <term>Christ</term> as the way. In the article which speaks of the mysteries of redemption, she briefly and fully shows how her method of simple prayer, or of passive <term>Contemplation</term>, does more effectively honor them than any other method which is more complex and active; and how it imprints on us the very *stigma* of our Lord Jesus, so that we are truly said to bear His marks. The method of the <term>Jesuits</term> has always been against this <note>as also the <term>Methodists</term></note>, for which they press the very same argument as our friend does, therefore preferring meditation in their <term>Spiritual Exercises</term> so that they may not put themselves out of the protection of <term>Christ</term> by too much abstraction and silent recollection. On this account, in the last age, they made such a violent opposition against <term>Father Austin Baker</term> and against <term>Dame Gertrude More</term>; whose reasons, which they bring in vindication of their simple and plain way, are perhaps not unworthy of consideration. The <term>Articles of Issy</term>, which are drawn up by the present <term>Bishop of Meaux</term> against the little book of that (allow me to call her so) great woman just mentioned, run in their beaten track and fall into the same mistake as they do. I have written some reflections upon them and have, in some measure, exposed the fallacy of that manner of proceeding by taking them apart and reducing them to mere propositions. These I have some thoughts of printing with the discourse itself to which they belong, and which I have had translated for quite a while, but it is now providentially called for after I had laid it aside. This has given me a surprising satisfaction as to the universality of that method which is so subtly attacked, and no less therefore as to the security and facility of it, the whole interior process being made hereby direct and linear. It has laid open a field which others may pursue with good success.

Many, notwithstanding, must be alarmed at it; but in the end you will see that *truth shall be justified by her children*. And after all the arguments that are in the world, there will be found no other way to arrive at the *truth* but this. It is <term>Contemplation</term> and Abstraction that must lead us through the veil into the <term>Sanctum Sanctorum</term> <note>Holy of Holies</note>, where the originals of truth are preserved, even in that ark of the Divine presence, which is <term>Christ</term>, the Alpha and the Omega of every creature. And it is through Him that we can come with boldness (being first purified by the blood of sprinkling, which cleanses us from every pollution of the flesh through faith) to the throne of Grace, which is the everlasting mercy-seat in the third heaven and inmost sanctuary, where this great High Priest ministers continually and presents such pure contemplative souls as do ascend here upon the wings of the divine eagle to His God and their God. He is the way, and He is the truth of contemplation <note>Note Well</note>, though we may not be always reflecting upon the way while we are in it, nor reasoning about the truth while we possess it, if we are so happy. And <term>Christ</term> being the truth of <term>Contemplation</term>—or that Truth which the contemplator beholds and, beholding, possesses—everyone in such a state or frame is necessarily under the protection of the truth and, consequently, can be in no danger of falling into errors or of being blinded by delusions; because the truth itself dwells in him and he dwells in the truth, being possessed by it in silence and passiveness of spirit, and he walks in the *truth* then when he puts forth what he has learned in this—

internal silence as under this divine possession by the *word of truth*, by passing from rest into action, and so bringing forth all the fruits and powers of the Holy Ghost, in the life of the blessed Jesus, both active and passive; and the truth shall be with him *forever*, as an inward principle of life, and of the resurrection from the dead. He is now in the truth, and the truth is in him; he is vitally united with the truth, and of this union (as it is truly made outside of time,) there can never be a dissolution: so that all the subtle and intriguing spirits of darkness are effectively shut out by this. They have no power to deceive, because when they come they find nothing of their own to mix with; for as much as the creature being silenced, God alone in Christ speaks, moves, and acts. And I think that this is a state both warrantable and Christian, and one that everyone would do well to strive for; there being few incapable of it, and none who may not be made capable of it. <note>See B's Tract of DIVINE VISION, chapter 2, page 26; also, of SUPERSENSUAL LIFE, pages 43, 44., etc.</note> Before we arrive at it, we are *not yet in the Truth*, but are only advancing toward it; neither is the truth (properly speaking) in us, but instead, there is only a shadow or image of the truth. If followed, this will lead us into that of which it is a shadow and an image, as we silently turn our souls inward to the fountain of the Divine Being. And then we may be said to worship God in truth. The more spiritual and the more perfect our worship of God in Christ is, it must of necessity be that much nearer to this state of internal silence and rest: so that Christ our Lord, just as He is in the Heavens, may in us also come to enter into His rest, and to sit down in the soul as * * * *"
