But it is time to finish these observations, contenting ourselves with what we have remarked regarding the characters of several mystical and spiritual authors on the occasion of the ten or twelve principal ones we set out to examine; from which it must now appear to everyone, it seems to me, that this kind of diversity between them—which caused some difficulty—is not an opposition found in the heart or spirit of these authors, nor in the matters and subjects they treat. For example:—

The character of **TAULER**, and of those of his class, which is to return by external things to the internal faculties, and from these into the depths of the soul to God, is the same thing that God commands a hundred times in His word when He calls souls from the outside to the inside; as when He says through Isaiah (46:8), *Transgressors, return to your heart*. In this exhortation, there is evidently the external word which, when heard, requires that one apply the faculty of intelligence to understand its meaning, which desires that one re-enter the depths of one's heart. Thus, like morning mists before a tropical sun, they will dissolve of themselves and hence require no formal refutation.

And surely it is high time to put an end to the Babylonian theology, which under the self-appropriated title of ‘evangelical doctrine,’ seems, for want of an enlightened exposure of its fallacies, to be insidiously making its way even among the more sober orthodox divines of the English church; though, paradoxical as it may appear, with the more universally instructed of the branch evangelical churches, a reaction toward solid practical divinity seems happily to have commenced.

As truth is more attractive and powerful than error, however exciting, when shown in its true aspect and real character, in its fullness of beauty and harmony: so in the scripture doctrine of justification, for instance, the ground of it needs only to be laid bare, and the doctrine displayed in its connection with all other parts of essential truth, to afford a much greater satisfaction to the mind than the ordinary popular erroneous representation of it is calculated to impart. And thus, were the mystification of Christian faith removed, the world would fall back from the practical antinomianism doctrine of ‘salvation by faith alone,’ and similar conceits, to the unity and simplicity of real evangelical Christianity as contained in the plain teachings of Jesus Christ, understood according to their natural meaning and the true theory of the gospel.

For this is the substance of the modern skip-jack divinity as popularly understood: *You are simply to believe in Christ: you are saved by faith alone, not by works (as to the real essence of the salvation-act): only believe and yours is heaven.*

Is it not then high time, we say, to return to the first truths of the gospel—to unreservedly declare and earnestly enforce the strict, self-denying, ascetic injunctions of Him who was opposed to everything that pleased fallen human nature, whose whole life as the leader of men and the way to heaven was entirely contrary to the way and spirit of the world, and who lays it down as an infallible maxim that everything that is popular in the world, yes, and in religion too, is enmity with God! like expecting the ploughboy who is taught reading, writing, and the elements of arithmetic, to be thereby raised into a highly scientific and Christian philosopher.

It must not, however, be supposed by these remarks that any sanction is given to another class of writers who are generally considered the opposites of the modern evangelicals and designated **PUSEYITES**: for these are further removed from the true orthodox standard than the former, though in another direction. The origin of them may be conceived to be in this way: Law’s series of writings have been until now justly represented as demonstrating the whole Biblical revelation—that is, the growth of the tree of Christianity in its patriarchal, legal, prophetic, personal, and perfective developments of the Spirit in the redemption of human nature. Now the ‘Puseyites’ were, so to speak, a premature abortion, or unnatural *self-generation* from Law’s writings; for which, let it be observed, Law is not responsible any more than the Bible is responsible for the misuse of it by self-willed, ignorant interpreters. The ‘Puseyites’ began, as it were, in the middle instead of at the beginning of Christianity; with the prophets, or faith, instead of with Moses or the Law; that is, they were led by imagination rather than divine instinct in their rise and progress as Christian professors. They began to be teachers of Christianity according to particular opinions before they had known it by experience, or had felt in their own souls the *dark centre*, upon the fact and absolutely necessary transformation of which it is altogether grounded; and without such experience, how could they truly teach others? For Christianity is a life, just as *animality* and *diabolism* is a life, and can only be understood by feeling; and no man is a true philosophical teacher of it except he who has been the subject of it in its various births or evolutions, who teaches only what he has experienced and not one iota further. For beyond that, it is all mere notion or fantasy to him, just as is a history of what is happening on the moon. Now this party of unfledged apostles in the seat of learning and divinity, having read the fifth or sixth and perhaps others of the progressive writings of Law—for instance his ‘Animadversions’ and other tracts, his ‘Letters to Hoadley,’ etc.—and having been thereby captivated with the truth and justice of his elevated views and sentiments, and especially of what he says concerning the holiness and dignity of the priesthood and other points favoring their own professional position—they began to urge those views according to their own blind concepts, until at last they finished by such childishness as the ‘Ideal of a Christian Church,’ and some by running over to Rome in search of a *local Christ*, an imaginary salvation, a notional church—in short, a *religion* instead of a *God*. All this, of course, served only to demonstrate afresh that scholastic reason in regard to the ‘things of the Spirit’ was still the same pitiable foolishness to God as it was in the days of St. Paul, and that no man can call *Jesus, Lord, but by the Holy Ghost*.

To speak plainly, these undoubted ‘apostolic successors,’ ‘consecrated priests,’ and young scholars, upon reading the aforementioned treatises of Law, insisted on becoming holy ‘somebodies’; and, having well furnished their minds with the ideas of profound humility, perfect meekness, and the whole array of passive graces, as well as of priestly authority and passive obedience doctrines (all of which are very true as set forth according to the spirit of holiness in the writings of the saints), they began to consider themselves learned in the kingdom of heaven, doctors of the law, and endowed with divine authority. In a word, *self*, under the disguise of an angel of light, would seem to have been at the top and bottom, the beginning and end of the whole scheme; and not being truly converted to God and made actual partakers of scriptural holiness, with a similar conversion of all around them as their sole aim and end.

<margin>Last</margin>
Now here was the difference between them and **WESLEY** and the first Methodists. Wesley began at the *beginning* of Law. He took the “Christian Perfection” and the “Serious Call” as the true classic interpreters of the spirit and practice of the Gospel, and he made the orderly specific doctrines of those books the *exact rule of his life*. He *lived* them to the letter. (Here is the secret of a holy and apostolic life!) And so, having *experimentally* passed into Christianity, into its first state (which those books, as the law, are so admirably calculated to induce), he became prepared for the next development of the Spirit—that is, regeneration or the new birth, being born again out of the weakness and bondage of sin into life, liberty, and *divine* power. And thus, upon the foundation of the Holy Scriptures as seen through the medium of those treatises, and according to the full discoveries of *moral wisdom* so orderly and practically displayed in them, he pursued onwards, and

It would not be very difficult to show that not only the characters, but also the dogmas and the ways of speaking of the Mystic Writers, are in conformity with the truths of the Holy Scriptures, and often use the same terms. Consequently, the errors or imaginary contradictions with which they are reproached only stem from the fact that their adversaries do not understand them; in the same way that the different sects of Christianity draw from the same—

<note>And such an appendage to the church is now both wanted, and might easily be annexed to it, by adopting some of the most soul-affecting hymns, and hymn-tunes, and modes of meetings for spiritual edification, for mutual prayer, and spurring on each member both actively and passively to diligence in the cultivation of holiness, made use of in that society; and by the ministers or leaders throwing off all slavish deference to what the *world* thinks and says, all fears of being *particular*, all love of self-satisfaction as gentlemen and scholars, and the *stiffness* of an unexercised piety and an unpracticed apostolic aggressiveness, which is to be accomplished by entering *heartily* into the great work of converting sinners, and—like Ouranius, Fletcher, or Bramwell—looking upon each member of their flock purely as so many souls committed to their charge by Christ, to watch over, to direct, and to train up for eternal glory; and whose blood he would therefore require at their hands: *hic labor! hoc opus!* Were the English church (with its pure Christian doctrine) blessed with such ministerial agencies, and such discovered improved methods of exercising the powers of the divine nature in the quickening and cultivation of the life of grace, it would speedily swallow up all sectarianism in this country. Under this head, Finney "On Revivals," (the author of which, by the way, is not inferior in originality of genius to Voltaire, ~~the one in the cause of the Gospel, the other in that of unbelief,~~) would be a profitable book for perusal by clergymen.</note>

For the original principles of Methodism are nothing more than the methodical and evangelical principles of Law’s "Call" and "Christian Perfection" carried into practical operation by a number of united Christian brethren, collected together here, and there, and over the land. And though admitting the ignorance, erroneous views, and disorder that have occasionally characterized their doctrines and practices, which however was hardly avoidable; yet the principles, the practice, and discipline of Methodism may be justly considered as embracing the machinery for the entire Christian and political regeneration of a country—yes, and with the addition of the insights indicated in this treatise, of the intellectual as well as the illiterate world. Thus Wesley practiced, and led others to practice, the science which Law in so masterly a manner taught: thus he proceeded; and upon such a foundation, (N.B.) *ever retaining the original practice of Law’s books*, he went on from weakness to strength, from one degree of experience and evangelical ministry to another; always having before his eye the high perfection of Christ, which, through the development of the spirit of Christ in him by regeneration, he knew belonged to him and was the privilege of all believers to attain. Therefore, he so publicly enforced the doctrine of Christian Perfection or "entire Sanctification," knowing, moreover, that the soul must ever be pressing forward in grace, by prayer and self-denial, or it will inevitably retrograde into the rational animal nature of the world.

But this was not the way of the "**Puseyites**." Had they entered religion at the right door, in such simple, earnest, orderly devotion, self-abnegation, heavenly aspiration, and fruitfulness in all kinds of evangelical good works as are taught in the "Christian Perfection" and "Serious Call" as the true spirit and practice of the doctrines of Christ, and so proceeded step by step to the high and sublime experiences of the advanced stages of the Christian life; had they laid such a foundation, and so raised the superstructure, their lives and labors would have exhibited—instead of a vain research after an idol religion and a local, partial, whimsical Deity, with the effusion of such scholastic theological impertinences as the *Tracts for the Times* and similar publications—a nineteenth-century revival of the life and power of Gospel Christianity, and zeal

I will add only one word concerning what might be said: either that I have omitted many authors of this class, making no mention of them, or that I have presented too many, and that this multitude will only cause confusion to those who, wishing to acquire some knowledge of mystical matters through reading, will not know what choice to make and might think that to reach that point one is obliged to read them all. I admit, regarding the first of these points, that critics will be right, as I am not unaware of how many I have left behind. However, it seems to me that more than a hundred, which I have just mentioned, should have been sufficient for my design, which required no more—and perhaps even less. As for the second point, far from intending to suggest that it is necessary for those who wish to be solidly helped in the knowledge of spiritual things to read all these authors, they are told on the contrary that very few of them and very little reading should suffice—provided that they take the opportunity to return within themselves. Instead of amusing themselves with the speculation of dead ideas formed from reading, they should implore the Light and Virtue of God to come and vivify and realize in us the *substance* and *spirit* of the things that the reading has represented to us. But because there are few, or perhaps no places where all these kinds of books are found together—dispersed as they are, some here and others there—and because they are even rare and unknown in many places, it was good to indicate several of them, and even to mark them by the place and time of printing, so as to facilitate for everyone as much as possible the search for and discovery of at least some of them. If persons, driven by a good curiosity for a little more reading than what is strictly necessary, desired to create a kind of small, select library of some spiritual and French books, here are the principal ones I believe could have a place there: *Thomas à Kempis*; *The Spiritual Combat*; *Monsieur de Bernières*; *the four Theologies: of the Heart, of Love, of the Cross, and the Real*; *St. Teresa*; *John of the Cross*; *Madame Guyon*; and *Brother Lawrence*; *Constantine of Barbanson*; *Canfield*; *Gelenius*; *the Lives of the Holy Desert Fathers*; and

for the divine glory in the conversion of sinners, which so eminently distinguished the last century through the instrumentalities of Wesley and others, and again a previous century in the sublime apostolic lives and labors of Ignatius Loyola, Francis Xavier, and that band of devoted, angelic spirits who—before the "mystery-of-iniquity" corruption of their order by their self-seeking "apostolic successors"—diffused the lovely fragrance of the knowledge of God and the blessings of true Christianity wherever they appeared. They proved the truth of their apostleship to all the world by the undeniable miracles that attended it, and which will always attend the accomplished missionary of Jesus Christ. Where are the Xaviers, Loyolas, Wesleys, Fletchers, Bramwells, and Pauls of our days? Does not the present state of the *Christian* and *Gentile* world demand the revisiting of the same Divine Spirit? May this treatise, or that which is sought to be obtained through it, be the providential instrument of rekindling it afresh, even in such a glory as shall meet the radical necessities of all nations.

We have alluded to the benefits of a proper display of the doctrines of salvation—how there is no need for any erroneous, exaggerated representations of them to magnify the grace of God or to promote the salvation of souls. Rather, if shown in their true light and proper point of view, they contain everything to render the Divine character adorable and the state of man certain and comfortable. In illustration of this, and by way of concluding this Note, we propose to take, for instance, the doctrine of Justification (already referred to), and to represent it with that classic clarity and exactness in which it stands in the Holy Scriptures, and in which it therefore ought to be exhibited by all true theologians. We remit the reader for a theosophical demonstration of it to those treatises where it is set forth. This will be found accomplished in the following rough draft found among Mr. Law’s old papers, which was probably sketched out as the substance of a more exact and finished essay to meet the request of one of his correspondents (Francis Okely), who had desired Mr. Law to favor him with a brief scriptural view, according to his understanding, of the doctrine of JUSTIFICATION:

> "The whole world, or all the race of fallen Adam, was, by the *free grace* of God, called and chosen, and enabled to rise from their fallen state.
<margin><unclear>Justified by grace</unclear></margin>
> This free grace of God, on which the salvation of mankind is solely founded, is prior to all good works; it saves us without any regard to works of any kind, and for this plain reason: because this free grace began before any of us were born, or the first man was created. As appears from these plain passages of scripture, \* \* \*. And again, *in hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began*. Titus 1:2.
> This is the first free and general grace of God to the whole fallen race of mankind, and has no dependence upon our works, because it was prior to them all.
<margin>*</margin>
> The second exercise or manifestation of this same free grace of God was at the fall of our first parents. When God, in consequence of that mercy he had for man when his fall was foreseen, now bestowed this free grace upon him by a declaration—and by giving into his soul a Savior, or engrafted Word—in this declaration: *the seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent*.
> Now, this is a second act, or manifestation, of God’s free grace to all mankind. For this grace is as universal as that before the creation, and is only that same free grace actually given and bestowed upon us, which was then only in the decree or promise of God to be given to us.
> This second free grace, manifested by the giving of a Savior, an engrafted Word, a bruiser of the serpent into the essences of Adam’s life—and in him to all who were to descend from him—is a free grace also; that is, it is without our works, because it also is prior to them all.
> Thus our salvation stands on the part of God as not only the offer, but a real and free gift of a Savior, or saving power, into the ground of every man's heart who is born of Adam.
> And this is the only true, free, and general grace of God that concerns the *salvation* of mankind, and is given to us solely from the pure love and mercy of God.

> spark of virtuous desire, or the least striving or tendency toward anything that is good, but what proceeds from this free grace of an inspoken Word, or a bruiser of the serpent that was spoken into our first parents.
>
> Now, if this is an undeniable truth—that God’s free grace has chosen us for salvation in Christ Jesus before the foundation of the world; and, secondly, that this same free grace performed this promise at the fall, and did, prior to all our works, put into our life's essences a bruiser of the serpent, an incorruptible seed of the Word, which seed of life became the beginning of a divine life or salvation that was to be worked out in us. If this *bruiser of the serpent* is that alone from which we have the possibility of a *good desire*, then it will be as plain as the sun at noon how we are to understand those scriptures which ascribe all our righteousness and justification to a free grace of God in Christ, with an *entire exclusion of all our own works*.
>
> Now, as this goodness of God—while it stood only in the divine purpose prior to our creation and works—must necessarily be considered as the sole free gift of God, and as a salvation given to us without any motive, reason, or cause for it except the *pure love* and *free mercy* of God:
>
> So it must be called and looked upon after the creation, and through all the ages of the world, to still be, in the same degree, a sole gift and free grace, as it was before the foundation of the world.
>
> So that it is as absurd to ascribe a man's *salvation* to any works that he has done after he was created as to any works of his before the foundation of the world.
>
> Our justification, considered on the part of God, relates to all mankind.
>
> It implies an offer of a new righteousness in Christ Jesus, which comes as solely *from* God in Christ Jesus, and is as truly a *gift of God*, as our creation was.
>
> It implies a universal ability given to all mankind to be thus righteous and holy in Christ Jesus.
>
> And thus considered on the side of God, it is the same free grace and mere gift of God, and has no more to do with our works than when it was only in the divine purpose before the foundation of the world.
>
> *According as he has chosen us in him before the foundation of the world* (Eph. 1:4), *that we should be holy and without blame before him in love*. This is as if he had said: Before the foundation of the world, so great was the mercy and love of God toward us that we were even then, in the divine decree, created again in Christ Jesus for good works; so that we who were fallen in Adam should again in Christ Jesus be made holy and without blame before him in love.
>
> But now, as all this mercy and redemption began in the divine goodness toward us before the foundation of the world; and as this mercy was freely bestowed in the giving of an inspoken Word, or bruiser of the serpent, to all mankind in our first parents; and as all the possibility of our thinking or deriving any good proceeds solely from this free gift of an inspoken Word, prior to all our works, there is an absolute necessity to say of our salvation, as St. Paul does: *By grace you are saved, not of works, not of yourselves; it is the gift of God*.
>
> When St. Paul says, *by faith you are saved*, he means neither more nor less than that we are saved by Jesus, as Jesus Christ is opposed to works; that is, as it is a salvation that is not our own work, so faith is opposed to our own works or righteousness.
>
> Thus it is that St. Paul, in his Epistles, declares against all the works of man as having no share in the justification of sinners, because he all along considers or looks upon this justification on the part of God; and therefore, in that view in which he considers it, it is as true that our justification is wholly the gift of God, without regard to our works, as it is true that God was moved only by his own *pure mercy* before the foundation of the world to receive *man* in a righteousness of Jesus Christ—or by making Christ as much the revival of a righteousness in us as Adam was the cause of sin being born in us.
>
> And therefore, as it was not our works that brought Adam's sin upon us, so neither was it our works that derived the righteousness into us: this is plain and clear to a demonstration.
>
> Thus much concerning our justification as it is on the part of God: a righteousness offered to us through Jesus Christ.

<margin>Further, what the true principles and what the nature of things are, are all and each fundamentally and philosophically declared in one or another of the works of Behmen and Law.]</margin>

II.—Let us now consider Justification on the part of man.
That there is a justification on the part of man, and that we are to have a share in our justification, or in the acceptance of the justification that is offered to us by God, is certain from these passages of Scripture: *Turn to me, says the Lord, and I will turn to you; Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; Him who comes to me, I will in no wise cast out; Knock and it shall be opened to you; You will not come to me that you might have life; He who believes in me has everlasting Life.*
Here turning, coming, knocking, believing, etc., are things to be done on the part of man for his justification, so that the righteousness of Christ may not be denied to him.
And here, what the Bishop of London has said—that good works are a *necessary condition* of our being justified in the sight of God—is an eternal and immutable truth; and he who denies it denies the gospel; and he who preaches another justification on the part of man is entitled to the anathema threatened for preaching another gospel than that already preached by the apostles.
That there is a justification on the part of man, I have already proved from the foregoing texts. I shall now show that the terms in which that justification is expressed necessarily imply, and expressly call not only for good works as an ingredient in it, but for all such good works as are taught by the gospel.
I shall show that all those works which are called for and demanded as the fruits of faith, are all necessarily demanded to be in faith, to constitute its existence, and that faith is not justifying until it is itself the *fruit of works*—until it has all those good works in a certain degree, which appear afterward in more visible fruits and effects:
And that faith is dead and rotten, and a mere dead fiction of the brain, if it does not itself arise from a converted soul, or from some degrees of goodness in the soul that raises it.
First, *Turn to me, says the Lord, and I will turn to you.—Zech. i. 3.* Now the whole nature of sin consists in our turning, or being turned, from the Lord. There is no sin in the world but what is comprehended under this general notion. Therefore a turning to the Lord necessarily implies a turning from all sin. Can it be thought God here calls upon us to turn to him hypocritically, or without turning sincerely from our sins? If not, then we are to turn from everything that turns us from him; but sin, and all sin, is that alone which turns us from him: therefore we cannot turn to him, but by turning from all sin. That faith is dead and rotten that does not spring from this turning to God. Therefore faith supposes, and is itself the fruit of, some goodness in the soul.
Again, *Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you.* Christ does not say, "come to me with a naked faith that proceeds from no goodness in you," but "come to me all you who labor and are heavy laden," *i.e.*, all you who are laboring against your sins, and are afflicted with the weight and burden of them, and would be glad to be delivered from the sad slavery, "and I will give you that peace and rest that you want." Now, as Christ promises only rest to those who were in this degree of goodness, who stood in this state of struggling with their sins and abhorrence of them, it is undeniable that a faith in him, or a coming to him, that did not proceed from this degree of goodness, would not gain him to be their Savior, or procure rest to their souls. Therefore, a faith that is not the fruit of some good works or workings in the soul, is dead, and not the faith that justifies us through Christ.
*Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.* I take it for granted that, by "the kingdom of heaven is at hand," is meant that the salvation offered to us by God through Jesus Christ is at hand. What is meant by repentance, I suppose I need not explain; therefore I say, that all that is required to make the beginning of a repentance acceptable to God is required to make us fit for the salvation which is offered to us by Jesus Christ; and as Christ can only be received by faith in him, or desire for him, so this faith in or desire for Christ must be founded on repentance, and have so much goodness in it as can make the beginning of a repentance sincere. Therefore, that faith which brings us to Christ, or Christ to us, must be a faith that proceeds from repentance, and is the fruit of it.
*Knock and it shall be opened to you; I am the door, says our blessed Lord:* therefore when we are to knock, it is so that this door may be opened to us. This knocking is a work, and I sup-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on religious sectarianism and the necessity of personal piety, transitioning into a theological examination of how human action and divine grace cooperate in the process of justification.</meta>

Had he been born in England, and had Oxford or Cambridge been his *alma mater*, he might have rivaled our great Bishop Stillingfleet, and would have written as many learned folios against the Church of Rome as Stillingfleet did. And yet I will venture to say that if each church could produce even one man who possessed the piety of an apostle and the impartial *love* of the first Christians in the early church at Jerusalem, a Protestant and a Catholic of this character would not need *half* a sheet of paper to hold their articles of union, nor would it take half an hour before they were of one religion. If, therefore, it should be said that churches are divided, estranged, and made unfriendly to one another by learning, logic, history, and criticism in the hands of *bias*, it would be saying what every particular church proves all too well to be true. If you ask why even the best among the Catholics are very hesitant to acknowledge the validity of the orders of our church, is it because they are afraid of removing any disgrace from the Reformation? If you ask why no Protestants anywhere touch upon the expediency and benefit of celibacy in those who are separated from all worldly concerns to preach the gospel, it is because that would seem to sup—

—pose a good work, because our Lord directs us to it. Therefore, our faith—which is to enter into Christ as the door—must arise from and be accompanied by this "knocking"; and therefore, to a naked faith that is not founded on this knocking, the door of Christ will not be opened.

By this is meant prayer, and therefore such dispositions as prayer requires: namely, *earnestness and persistence*.

> *He who believes in me has everlasting life: If any man comes to me and does not forsake all that he has, if he does not hate his father and mother, yes, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple.* But if he cannot be His disciple, surely he cannot be justified by Him, or receive justification from Him. Therefore, some degree of dying to our own *selfish nature* (which is implied by "hating" our own life), some degree of that renunciation of the world and worldly tempers (which is implied by "forsaking all that we have"), and some degree of detachment from natural love must be implied by our "hating" father and mother, as a preparation for being capable of being justified by Christ.

Our Lord declares that a man is unfit to go to the altar if his brother has anything against him. Now, does the altar call for this degree of holiness, and can it be supposed that Christ does not require it in those who come to Him by faith? Is the gift unfit to be offered unless brotherly love is first present in some degree in the heart? And can we think that a faith which is destitute of this love is the faith that fits us to receive Christ? That such a faith cannot be accepted by Christ so as to obtain justification from Him is plain from our Savior's own words: *if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you.*

> *A faith, therefore, that does not have some degree of this charity in it cannot receive justification through Jesus Christ; and therefore a* **TRUE FAITH IS AS MUCH THE FRUIT OF GOOD WORKS AS IT IS THE PRODUCER OF THE FRUITS OF GOOD WORKS.** <note>See also the note on pages 106–109.</note>

Thus, in summary, on the gospel doctrine of Justification—called by some "justification by faith" and by others "justification by works"—he considered it no differently than our Savior considered it: as implied, according to the analogy of faith, in all His counsels and exhortations. But according to the popular, fallacious representations and distortions of this doctrine—whatever wonderful effects may have followed through the excitement of the imagination of those who receive them—the terms offered by Jesus Christ appear to sober thinkers to be quite a mystification, having no obvious relation to what they have been taught is essential to their individual salvation; indeed, even the words of the Lord of life and glory Himself! 

On the other hand, when the doctrine of justification is shown in its true, natural aspect, as in the above dissertation, free from all "Babylonish" mystifications, then the whole of Scripture appears in perfect harmony. The words of Christ retain their plain, compelling meaning, and the reader sees that he must himself cooperate body and soul with God in his salvation (and not simply "jump" into all the privileges of Christ's kingdom merely by believing). This involves the suppression of the "old man" and his deeds, so that the "new man" (which is a pure birth of Christ, or a seed of Christ) may be raised up in its place. To achieve this, however, besides all kinds of self-denying exercises, the hunger and desire of the soul must be fixed upon God alone, accompanied by all kinds of devotion and good works that may tend to invigorate that new principle of a divine life. 

In short, he sees that obtaining a qualification for Christ's kingdom is exactly that same difficult, laborious work which it is represented to be by our Lord—despite the plausible and attractive representations of the *short cut* to it offered by modern evangelical justification doctrines. This is the sum and substance of the gospel: the way of the Cross, or death to the "old Adam" in all his motivations, and the way of faith, or the exercise of all the graciously implanted principles and powers of the new life, until it is raised up to the full stature of a man in Christ Jesus. Such is the sole purpose of the practical instructions of Holy Scripture; and if we had more of this plain, Christian common sense and less of the "justification by faith" babble sounded from our pulpits, we would have a great deal more genuine faith, devotion, and justifying good works among evangelical professors than we have at present.

And thus uniting in heart and spirit with all that is holy and good in all churches, we enter into the true communion of saints and become real members of the holy catholic church, though we are confined to the outward worship of only one particular part of it. It is in this way that the angels, as ministering spirits, assist, join, unite, and cooperate with everything that is holy and good in every division of mankind.—Thirdly, he must always keep in mind this great truth: that it is the glory of Divine Justice to show no favoritism toward parties or persons, but to remain equally disposed toward what is right and wrong, whether in the Jew or in the Gentile. Therefore, he who would like as God likes and condemn as God condemns must have neither the eyes of the Papist nor the Protestant; he must like a truth no less because *Ignatius Loyola* or *John Bunyan* was very zealous for it, nor have less aversion to any error because a *Doctor Trap* or *George Fox* had brought it forth. Now, if this universal love and impartial justice is the spirit which will judge the world at the last day, how can this spirit be in us too soon or too much? When I was a young scholar at the University, I heard a very religious person say in my father’s house that if he could believe the late King of France was in heaven, he would not know how to wish to go there himself. This was exceedingly shocking to all who heard it; yet something of this kind of temper must be assumed to be more or less present in those who, as a point of orthodoxy, have worked themselves up into a sincere contempt and hatred of those who are divided from them. He who has been used all his life to look with great abhorrence upon those whom he has called superstitious bigots, dreaming visionaries, false saints, hypocritical enthusiasts, etc., must naturally expect they will be treated by God as they have been treated by him; and if he held the keys to the kingdom of heaven, such people would find it hard to get a place in it. But it is very important for us to get rid of this temper before we die; for if nothing but impartial, universal, perfect Love can enter into the kingdom of God, what can be more necessary for us than to be full of this love before we die?

In the Church of Rome, the more we should rejoice to hear that in every age so many eminent spirits, great saints, have appeared in it. We should thankfully behold them as so many *great lights* hung out by God to show the true way to heaven, and as so many joyful proofs that Christ is still present in that church, as well as in other churches, and that the gates of hell have not prevailed or completely overcome it. Who that has the least spark of heaven in their soul can help thinking and rejoicing in this manner at the appearance of a *St. Bernard*, a *Teresa*, a *Francis de Sales*, and others in that church? Who can help praising God that her *invented devotions*, *superstitious use of images*, *invocation of saints*, and so on, have not so suppressed any of the graces and virtues of an evangelical perfection of life, but that among Cardinals, Jesuits, Priests, Friars, Monks, and Nuns, numbers have been found who seemed to live for no other end but to give glory to God and edification to men? Their writings have everything in them that can guide the soul out of the corruption of this life into the highest union with God. And he who, through a *partial orthodoxy*, is diverted from feeding in these *green pastures of life*, or whose just abhorrence of Jesuitical craft and worldly policy keeps him from knowing and reading the works of an *Alvares du Pas*, a *Rodrigues*, a *Du Pont*, a *Guil-*

loree, Father Surin, and similar Jesuits, suffers a greater loss than he can easily imagine. And if any clergyman can read the life of *Bartholomeus a Martyribus*, a Spanish archbishop who sat with great influence at the very Council of Trent, without being edified by it and desiring to read it again and again, I do not know why he should like the lives of the best of the apostolic fathers. O my God! How shall I unlock this mystery of things: in the land of darkness, overrun with superstition, where Divine Worship seems to be all show and ceremony—there, among both priests and people, You have those who are fired with the pure love of You, who renounce everything for You, who are devoted wholly and solely to You, who think of nothing, write of nothing, and desire nothing but the honor, praise, and adoration that is due to You, and who call all the world to the maxims of the gospel and the holiness and perfection of the life of Christ. But in the regions where light has sprung up, from which superstition has fled, where all that is outward in religion seems to be pruned, arranged, and put in its true order—there a cleansed shell, a whitewashed tomb, seems too generally to cover a *dead Christianity*!

The error of all errors, and that which forms the darkest charge against the Roman Church, is persecution—a religious sword drawn against the liberty and freedom of serving God according to our best light; that is, against our worshipping the Father in spirit and in truth. This is the "great whore," the "beast," the "dragon," the "antichrist." Now, although this is the frightening monster of that church, yet even here, who—except perhaps the Church of England—can throw the first stone at her? Where must we look for a church that has renounced this persecuting beast as thoroughly as they have renounced the use of incense, the sprinkling of holy water, or the extreme unction of dying persons? What part of the Reformation abroad has not practiced and defended persecution? What sect of Dissenters at home has not, in their day of power, dreadfully condemned toleration?

When it pleases God to incline the hearts of all princes in the Christian world to destroy this antichristian beast entirely and leave all their subjects in that religious freedom which they have from God, then the light of the Gospel, the benefit of its faith, the power of its ministers, the usefulness of its rites, and the blessing of its sacraments will have a proper time and place to reveal themselves. That religion which has the most *divine power* in it, whose offices and services do the most good to the heart, whose ministers are most of all *devoted to God* and have the most proof of the power and presence of Christ with them <note>See ‘Sigston’s Memoir of Bramwell.’</note>, will become, as it ought to be, the most universal. By this destruction of the beast, nothing but the errors, delusions, corruptions, and fictions of every religion will be left in a helpless state. <note>A prophetic suggestion of the effects that would result from the action and reaction of the *spirit of Methodism*.</note> * * *

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his theological influences, specifically the "Mystical Writers," following his critique of religious persecution and the limitations of "dead Christianity" on the previous page. The text begins under the heading of a postscript.</meta>

[POSTSCRIPT.]

I thank God that I have been a diligent reader throughout all ages of the church, from the apostolic *Dionysius* the *Areopagite* down to the great *Fenelon*, Archbishop of *Cambray*, the illuminated *Guyon*, and *M. Bertot*. Had the Doctor read *St. Cassian*—a chronicler of the lives, spirit, and doctrine of the holy Fathers of the deserts—as often as he had read the story of *Aeneas* and *Dido*, he would have been less astonished by many things in my writings. But I perceive the Doctor to be a complete stranger to writers of this kind, with whom every age of the church has been blessed, and to know no more of the divine *Rusbrochius*, *Thaulerus*, *Suso*, *Harphius*, *Johannes a Cruce*, etc., than he does of *J. B.* For had he known anything about them, he would have known that I am as responsible for the sentiments of all of them as I am for those of *J. B.* For although I never wrote on any subject until I could call it my own—until I was so fully possessed of the truth of it that I could sufficiently prove it in *my own way* without borrowed arguments—yet I have no religious doctrines except those for which the Scriptures and the *first-rate* saints of the church are my witnesses.

<margin>e/</margin>
There have been writers like those I have mentioned in all ages of the church; but since they did not serve the ends of popular learning, did not help people gain *prominence* and advancement in the world, and were useless to academic controversial writers, they dropped out of public use. They were only known—or rather unknown—under the name of Mystical Writers, until at last some people have hardly even heard that name. Yet if a man were to be told what *is* meant by a Mystical Divine, he would have to be told of something as *heavenly*, as great, and as desirable as if he were told what is meant by a living member of the mystical body of Christ. For they were called this for no other reason than as *Moses*, the prophets, and the saints of the Old Testament may be called the spiritual *Israel* or the true mystical *Jews*. These writers began their office of teaching, as *John* the Baptist did, <note>Note well</note> after they *had passed through* every kind of mortification and self-denial, and every kind of trial and purification, both inward and outward. They were deeply learned in all the mysteries of the kingdom of God, not through the use of commentaries or lexicons, or by meditating upon the hearsay of divinity critics, but because *they had passed from death unto life*. They highly reverence and excellently direct the true use of everything that is outward in religion, but like the Psalmist’s *king's daughter, they are all glorious within*. They are truly sons of thunder and sons of consolation; they break open the *whitewashed tombs*; they awaken the heart and show it its *filth* and the rottenness of death, but they do not leave it until the *kingdom of heaven is raised up within it*. If a man has no desire but to be of the spirit of the gospel—to obtain all that renewal of life and spirit which alone can make him *a new creature* in Christ—it is a great misfortune for him to be unacquainted with these writers, or to pass a day without reading something of what they have written. For although the Scriptures are an inexhaustible source of spiritual instruction, leading the heart to the deepest knowledge of all the mysteries of the inward *new life in God* with the greatest plainness and openness of expression, yet a worldly spirit, academic schools, criticism, sectarian interpretation, and controversy have so dried up and distorted everything into a literal outward meaning and a biased sense that much of their spirit is lost. This remains true until these holy writers, who interpret the Scriptures by the same Spirit that wrote them, guide us to the true understanding of them. For in these writers, the Spirit of God speaks a second time, and everything that can awaken, convert, instruct, and inflame the heart with the love of God and all holiness and purity of life is to be found in them with the most irresistible degree of conviction. You will perhaps say, do I then call all the world to these *spiritual books*? No, by no means. But I call all those whom our Savior called to himself in these words:

> “COME TO ME, ALL YOU WHO LABOR AND ARE HEAVY LADEN, AND I WILL REFRESH YOU.”

# POSTSCRIPT.

We have already, in the previous pages, alluded to the Philadelphian Society and to the correspondence which took place between the celebrated "Mr. Henry Dodwell" and Francis Lee (a Fellow of St. John’s College, Oxford) because of the latter’s connection with that society and his reported separation from the communion of the established church. Lee was not only an enlightened, practical Christian, but also deeply versed in the Jewish, Philosophic, and Christian Mystic science of all ages. He brought this knowledge to bear in that controversy in defense of Mrs. Lead’s claims and writings, and of his own conduct in relation to the Philadelphian Society—a society, by the way, which might in a sense be considered a prelude to, or the budding of, that universal evangelical spirit which broke forth in the next generation, as referred to in the Note on page 176. As the subjects of that controversy belong to the considerations of the present treatise—particularly as exhibiting the character of the spiritual theology and transcendental science of this country at the close of the seventeenth century—it may not be inappropriate to insert the most interesting portions of that correspondence as a sequel or Appendix to the present Section, which we now propose to do.

The controversy was begun by Dodwell (who, as the world knows, was not himself orthodox on certain points of Christian doctrine) in a long and learned discourse—addressed to Lee in the most respectful and affectionate protesting terms—in support of ecclesiastical rights, proving the necessity of adhering to the visible communion of the Church and to a strict dependence on its lawfully constituted governors. It began as follows:

> “Shottisbrook, near Maidenhead, in Berkshire. Oct. 12th, 1697.——Worthy Sir,—I was at once both troubled and surprised to hear that so good and so accomplished a person as you are should be engaged in a new separation from that church, for whose principles you had so generously suffered. And I hope you will excuse me if the love of our late common excellent cause, as well as of a common brother and a common defender of it, encourages me to hope that so recent a change has not altogether stopped you from hearing an affectionate protest concerning it. I say this especially because I understand that it is a pretense of loving us, and all those separated from us, better than we can by our principles love one another, that has induced you to have a low opinion of the terms on which we are divided.
> 
> You, who know what it is to reason accurately, I hope will not risk your soul on alluring fancies or warm, inexplicable feelings, which would be more excusable in a person of lesser education. You know that the same Scriptures which require that we should not despise prophecies also warn us of false prophets, and of testing the spirits to see whether they are from God. You may also be pleased to remember that one <term>κριτήριον</term> <note>criterion</note> for testing them is their keeping to the one true communion and observing their duties to their superiors in the station where God has placed them as judges of the spirits. You see the disorders of those who claimed to have the Spirit—and truly so—even in the Apostolic times, when gifted women presumed to exercise their gifts in assemblies of men; you see how the Apostle restrains them from it. When even gifts designed for the public assemblies were used either unedifyingly or in a disorderly way, you may be pleased to remember how the Apostle curbs them even there. * * * [and so forth, at great length, to the conclusion, as follows:] * * * Enthusiasm may be very pleasing and endearing for a time; but though we have many instances of it in history, I never remember it to have lasted more than a generation. Imagination naturally decays when it reaches its highest point, just as it improves until it reaches that height; especially an imagination such as yours, which lacks the signs of the prophets—the external credentials of miracles. It is only the rational obligation for all to depend on the governors of one communion that has preserved a Christian church until now, and may still perpetuate it, if men would be true to the principles of that rational obligation. For God’s sake, do not rob the Church of this security in your trial of new experiments. For your own soul’s sake, do not risk it in such ways as take you away from reasoning. Return to your deserted brothers, and do not contribute to the further divisions and ruin of that small number to which we are reduced, so that I may again be able to justify by principles the signing of myself—Your most affectionate brother, Henry Dodwell.

To the above letter Lee wrote a very explicit reply, as follows:

> Dec. 4th, 1697.——Most dear and worthy Sir,—I consider myself exceedingly obliged to you for both the kindness and the severity of your letter: and I do heartily pray that on the day of reward, this your most generous and Christian intention toward me in particular, and toward the church of Christ in general, may be remembered before God, angels, and men. For I am not able to thank you sufficiently myself, but I am confident this labor of love of yours shall not lose its reward.
> 
> Perhaps also it may not fail in its effect; if not the same effect which you or I expect, yet that which the good Spirit of God has designed for it. I am more inclined to believe this because I have had a most pressing desire, ever since my return to England, to speak with you freely about these very matters which prompted your protesting Letter. I had intended to have revealed to you in all naked simplicity the process by which I have been led, and to lay before you at the same time the ground upon which both I and several others, some in se-

secretly, others more publicly, have been carried out beyond the present ordinary line. Therefore I greatly rejoice that the good Providence of God has at last opened a way for such a mutual communication between us, as may, I hope, be for the glory of God, the edification of his church, the fixing of truth, the detection of the various mazes of empty enthusiasm, and the vindication of the true spirit of prophecy. For whatever you may think, I have not yet made one venture into such paths as to take me away from reasoning, but am as ready to hear what is reasonable, in its proper place, as ever I was in my life. So I beseech you for God’s sake, and for the sake of truth, not to prejudge the case from popular reports, common suspicions, or certain historical applications, which last may in part agree, and in part disagree—sometimes in the circumstances, and often in the very ground itself.

*Sir*, I am not as far from you as you think. For I will readily grant to you what you desire in the following particulars. First, I own that the danger is great to be ensnared by false prophets, and that therefore the spirits are to be tested, whether they be from God. (2.) Next, I own your distinction between the spirit of prophecy and the spirit of enthusiasm, as it is commonly called. (3.) I confess that in the former there is no violence done to the human soul, but that it is left to act freely, and correspondingly to its natural powers. However, I conceive there may be in some (besides the inspiration common to all the prophets in one degree or another) even a sort of Divine impetus or inebriation with the Spirit, wherein the soul, having before freely and voluntarily surrendered itself to God, is sweetly ravished and brought into a full and perfect submission to the <term>πνεῦμα ἡγεμονικὸν</term> <note>the "governing spirit" or "ruling principle"</note>, which I suppose to have been a superior governing principle in this Royal Prophet, that did gently subdue all inferior motions arising from the rational or sensory part. Yet this may not only be resisted, but even quenched in the soul upon which it falls; and consequently the soul, as you assert, is here left free to the disposal of its own will. (4.) I also own that as there is a manifold subordination of spirits, and great diversity of gifts, and likewise of degrees in the same gifts; so in order to a proper regulation of them, there were originally established certain judges of the spirits, who should be themselves more eminently endowed with one of the two superior orders of gifts, to be assigned to the several classes of governors in the church mentioned by St. Paul, Eph. iv. 11, or at least with those of the *third* order specified there. And to these, as to their proper judges, all inferior prophets and spiritual persons were obliged to submit themselves to be tested. To this the establishment of the colleges of the prophets seems to agree, under the leadership of the father or head prophets; and for no other end but this was the gift of <term>Discretio Spirituum</term> <note>the "Discerning of Spirits"</note> afterwards granted in the Christian church, which is so very necessary to all those who should have the power of laying on of hands. (5.) Further, I grant that there was an obligation upon every baptized believer, in order to a communication of influences from Christ, of whatever nature they may be, strictly to adhere to a visible union and communion with the catholic body of the church, and to a subordinate dependence on the head governors and fathers of it, who had received the Holy Spirit and the power to convey the same to others. And in pursuance of this obligation, I never have been, nor am I, against the use of visible means for the regular participation of the gifts and graces of God, and for the keeping up of the fellowship of the saints—which God forbid that I should ever violate. (6.) Lastly, I will grant to you all that you have written, if the case were truly as you have understood it to be; and I will lay my hand upon my mouth and acknowledge that I have opened a way for all heresies, schisms, and enthusiasms by taking away the power of the church, which Christ and his apostles have left for restraining them.

Now in return for these concessions, which I most readily grant, I shall only desire this one from you: namely, that there is a great difference between the visible state of the Church today and the visible state of it in its best and purest ages. If this is allowed, then inferences drawn from the discipline of the church then (though in itself truly excellent) will no more affect us (who live in a state of the church that is in so many ways inferior to it), than inferences drawn 
<margin>a/</margin>
from the constitution of the English government, and from its laws and customs under King Alfred, would affect us (after so many and great revolutions) under the present state of our political affairs. For though indeed the discipline of the primitive Church is generally acknowledged as the standard of ecclesiastical government even today, and the constitution of the Saxon monarchy is not so acknowledged regarding the civil state of this land, yet it must be confessed that there has been such a decline from both that it would (according to common usage) sufficiently argue against several original or primitive customs in that, as well as in this, and against several laws in both that are not of perpetual obligation. And I dare, *Sir*, appeal even to your own self, whether there are not some allowances to be made according to the requirements of time and place. Are there not some exceptions to general and ordinary rules? Was the law of Moses, in more than one particular, not sometimes dispensable to the whole body of the people, and at all times to the prophets? Can the discipline of the Christian church be proved to be more indispensable? That it is ordinarily binding I shall not dispute; indeed, that it may be indispensable as long as it retains its integrity and is practicable, I can readily grant without hurting in the least that cause in which I have been engaged—not suddenly, but after long deliberation. Anyone who takes the pains to consider it must be convinced that it is no ordinary cause. And if its foundation should happen to be true, regarding the claims that are made, as it is both true and extraordinary, it may not improbably justify some extraordinary methods and free those who shall act in pursuance of this extraordinary call from the guilt of Schism. I have now read your Treatise upon that subject, which has caused me to defer my answer to your letter so long, along with some other pressing matters. For I could not be satisfied to read only some parts of it to which you might seem to refer me more immediately; I had to take your own advice given in your preface to read the whole, so that from the strict connection of all the parts with one another, I might better understand the full extent of your hypothesis. I do not at all repent of this, having found it well worthy of the effort, and I therefore thank you for the many significant things I have encountered there. But withal, *Sir*, I leave

...you to judge whether someone with an overheated imagination (as I am supposed to be) could have the patience to read through a book of such size and such close logic.

And after all, I cannot help but maintain my former judgment: that there have been, and are to be, some extraordinary steps of Divine Providence which may supersede ordinary rules and general customs: *which is all that I claim.* For I must freely admit that rules and customs of *general obligation* ought not to be superseded except for great and wise ends, and even then only by an authority sufficient to grant a dispensation in particular cases. In such great and extraordinary emergencies of Providence, no rule or custom can be supposed to bind beforehand. I believe there are very few laws in any country—even those considered fundamental—that are not capable of some restrictions and limitations for the sake of some extraordinary good to that country, especially if they do not tend to subvert the constitution itself, but rather serve to establish it and promote all the ends designed by it, and evidently serve all its interests better than could have been done without such a restriction or limitation.

In all human institutions, this is generally maintained. But, assuming that the government of the Church should be Theocratical, as it was with the Jews and also with the Christians of the earliest and undoubtedly purest ages, it seems to me currently not very unreasonable that there should be, besides certain universal laws and constitutions, some particular mandates as well, or private instructions given to some who may have either a public or secret commission for a special work. Whether this is the case now, and whether my own private situation falls under this, I am willing even to submit to such a strict defender of ecclesiastical rights as yourself, once you are more accurately informed of the circumstances upon which it depends. I am very aware that neither ordinary nor extraordinary illumination can be of any use or authority to others, except insofar as those who enjoy it are able to provide either ordinary or extraordinary proof of it. Yet the extraordinary, even without such proof, may be of use and authority to the individuals themselves, just as the ordinary is to both themselves and others. Furthermore, the extraordinary may possibly be useful and authoritative to others without any extraordinary credentials being externally proclaimed or displayed, if it pleases the Holy Spirit to ratify it in a more internal and secret manner upon their minds—without which, as you know, even the greatest outward miracles will not suffice. Therefore, although I cannot expect to be believed by many at present, or as long as nothing extraordinary appears outwardly, I still do not despair of finding belief in several persons eminent for their wisdom and sobriety through this inward operation of the Spirit. This may happen when it pleases God that many (currently) secret circumstances are brought to light and are carefully examined and impartially looked into. After that, everything you fear concerning me may vanish into wonder, and very formidable arguments may melt away like ice before the sun, as they already have for some people. I will say this much for now: just as the sincerity of my heart in this matter can only be known to God, so I have lacked no effort to satisfy myself as to how I might truly and faithfully follow His guidance, neither allowing myself to be deceived by any, nor seeking to deceive others. And even in that which is most open to objection—if any public or private declarations mean anything—I hope I may be found not to have contributed to any division in the Church of Christ, nor to have transgressed the intent of its primitive discipline which you urged. Indeed, I may possibly be found to have taken the only way that can restore peace, and with it the better part of the discipline of the early church. For let me know, I entreat you, Sir: (1.) Whether there are grounds to expect, by any other method whatever, the restoration of this very discipline or of catholic peace? (2.) What was the foundation of government and order in the Apostolic church, especially in those of Jerusalem and Antioch? (3.) If the principles of our Society in England, of the Restists in Germany, and of the Quietists in Italy and France, should be found fundamentally true (even if not in every detail), is it a different foundation or the same one the Apostles laid? (4.) Whether the Apostles themselves did not write and act as if (what we call) extraordinary powers of the Holy Spirit were intended to remain with the Church until the end? (5.) Whether there are any traces to be found throughout the writings of the whole New Testament from which it can be concluded that Christ intended, or any of his Apostles even knew of, a cessation in the church of either immediate Divine revelation or of miracles? (6.) How long was it before revelation and miracles ceased in the church? (7.) What was the true cause of their cessation? For the common answer to this question is unsatisfactory for many reasons. (8.) Whether this cause may be removed again, and if it can, whether there may not be a return of the same ministry* of the blessed Spirit? (9.) Whether there must not yet be a universal publication of the Gospel before the end of the world? (10.) Whether this publication (if such a thing is to happen) shall not be accompanied by the same signs as the first one? [See Bramwell's "Memoir" for the enduring signs of the Spirit.] And (11.) Whether, before such a great publication, it would not be reasonable to expect certain previous manifestations and intimations for that purpose, chosen by God, which shall not immediately be sealed with open miracles [*of the Spirit*]? If you please to answer these questions at your leisure, you will greatly oblige one who considers it the greatest victory and honor to be overcome by truth—however contrary to his inclination or disadvantageous to his interest—and who hopes even by these principles to justify signing himself: Dear Sir, your most affectionate brother and humble servant, Francis Lee.

The next letter, from Dodwell, is dated Jan. 15th, 1698, and begins this way:—

Dear Sir,—Your kind acceptance of my sincerely intended efforts for the Church's good and yours, and your resolution to be guided by reason, and the pains you have taken (more than I could have presumed to request, however necessary it was for you to give a right judgment concerning the matters debated between us), are great encouragements for me to proceed. I hope that the good God, who has given you such commendable zeal in an age of such general apostasy, will also give you the knowledge by which your zeal must be directed.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence between Henry Dodwell and Francis Lee, following Lee’s previous defense of his mystical views. Dodwell now responds, warning Lee of the dangers of schism and the lack of scriptural evidence for his group's "revelations."</meta>

To return therefore to my former argument (which is all that can be managed in the small space allowed in a letter), I think you have already granted me so much that if you had practiced in the Apostles' times as you do now, your practice would have been censured as injurious to the unity of the Spirit, and therefore schismatic. Your forsaking the assemblies of our lawful Bishops, and your joining in communion with those divided from them based on your Philadelphian principles, must necessarily have been interpreted that way. And no pretensions to the Spirit could then have excused you. For the spirit that led you into separation would, for that very reason, have been judged not to have been the Spirit of Christ, as not holding to the head, because it was different from the spirit of the governors. * * * [and so forth, at extreme length, to the conclusion, thus,] * * *

This case of Tertullian was afterwards so similar to yours, that I think it also deserves your serious consideration. A man so very learned, so zealous, and so pious was, notwithstanding, afterwards seduced out of the communion of the Church and became the head of a schism for much the same reasons as you have, by his too forward zeal for the prophecies of Montanus and his women prophetesses. Vincent of Lérins bemoans his fall with great and very fair acknowledgments of his personal accomplishments. I hope, dear Sir, you will rather give your old deserted brethren an occasion of joy and hearty congratulations for your return, than add to our sufferings the melancholy aggravation of losing you. Add to your former self-denials for the testimony of a good conscience the mortification of submitting to the truth when it appears against you. Be a glorious example of candor and sincerity in this age. Gifts and revelations make a great show, but the way of Charity is preferred before them by the Apostle himself. May God Almighty qualify you for the rewards of your good meaning and good works, by reducing you to that true communion of his peculiar people. So prays your old brother and fellow laborer, Henry Dodwell.

P.S.—I shall be glad to see your *Apology*, though I foresee nothing that can hinder you from being concerned in the consequences of these reasonings, if you give yourself the liberty of promiscuous communions, whatever your pretenses may be for doing so. * * * I wish you would also be pleased to see what Bishop Stillingfleet has written against Mr. Cressy's *Sancta Sophia*. You will there find that the Mystical Divinity, which is the foundation of Quietism, was derived from the Philosophical religion invented by the later Platonists—and among them admired by the great enemy of the Christian religion, Porphyry—rather than from any tradition derived from the Apostles. The pretended Areopagite has given it great authority with those who did not know that he was an impostor; and it seems to be the language of those Platonists that was imitated by that impostor. They seem to understand the mystical unity as a coalescence with God and Christ, which certainly is against the doctrine of Christ. Those expressions in *Theologia Germanica*, a book of that kind, seem to look that way, where the author speaks of renouncing not only *meity* (mine-ness), but also *egoity* (I-ness), and *ipseity* (self-ness). You will understand what I say if you have seen the elegant translation of that author by Castellio.

The reply to the above letter having been deferred, Dodwell addressed to Lee a further communication, which—as it may be supposed to represent the natural sentiments of scholastic theology and sober scripture piety of all times upon the subjects in question—we give at length, with the categorical reply of Dr. Lee, and some subsequent letters. Dodwell's additional communication proceeds thus:

> Dear Sir,—I never received any answer to my second Letter, relating to your new unhappy schism from your old brethren. Since my writing that, I have been at Oxford and seen many books of your mother-in-law [Mrs. Lead], who is the only person of your sect who has had her prophecies published, as far as I know. And her being so, I look on as the best security you have against schisms among yourselves, while you so manifestly favor enthusiastical pretenses for withdrawing your dependence on your lawful ecclesiastical superiors. This security may hold as long as, and no longer than, the rest of you remain more modest and dare not rival your own pretended revelations with hers. But since I have looked into what has been published in her name, I have a worse opinion of your cause than formerly. I find her plainly decrying the trial of her cause by reasoning. This alone would make a wise man suspicious that her cause was not thought defensible by that method of decision, and that those who manage her cause were conscious that it is not defensible that way. Yes, even you yourself interpose such cautions in admitting this, as if your credentials were stronger reasons than any that could be drawn from the nature of the things themselves. But I find no credentials so much as pretended by you yet; no Shekinahs, no signs of the prophets, no miracles, no fulfillings of predictions by answering events. Yet she pretends to equal her own prophecies with the confessedly inspired Scriptures, which had all these testimonials of the Divine authority of those who wrote them. She presumes to warn us not to admit them in the trial of her own pretences to inspiration, contrary to St. Paul, who pronounces an anathema even against an angel from heaven that should presume to teach us any doctrine besides that which we have received. Yet pretending to no external credentials, the enthusiasm itself is far from being an evidence of its own Divine original. Imagination alone is sufficient to represent golden groves and golden cities. Complexion, fevers, and many other diseases affecting the brain make such things appear as plainly as if they were really present. Much more the influence of evil spirits, permitted by Providence in those who break the unity of the good Spirit, which is the bond of the political society of the Church. So far is your discourse (if that discourse be yours) from proving yourself as certain of heaven, in your way of enthusiastical sensation, as you are of London. It is certain that the representing of sensible ideas to the imagination is in the power of the devil, where God is pleased to permit him to exercise that which the Apostle calls <term>ἐνέργειαν τῆς πλάνης</term> in his Energumeni. And I find nothing in your mother-in-law's case that relates immediately to the purely spiritual faculties, which are the proper subject of the true spirit of prophecy.

> Thus every way her case is suspicious: in her distrust of much stronger topics than any she can insist on in favor of her own pretenses, both of reason and authority; and in her being destitute of any external evidences of the Divine original of her pretended familiar conversation with God.
