<meta>This page continues Henry Dodwell’s critique of Francis Lee’s involvement with the Philadelphians, specifically questioning the legitimacy of Jane Lead’s visions and suggesting they were actually authored by Dr. John Pordage.</meta>

...in the suspicious nature of the ability employed here, where there is no security against the intervention of evil spirits, since this ability is the very same through which they are permitted to act by the ordinary rules of Providence. And your case is so far from giving you any security against the intervention of evil spirits that, indeed, evil spirits are the most likely to be expected in the methods you use to attain the Spirit you claim to have. God’s Spirit cannot legitimately be expected except through those means which God has instituted for conveying it. And those are all external means, within the power of those persons whom He has authorized to govern the spiritual society. His way of giving it was by the laying on of the hands of the Apostles, and of their lawful successors who have derived that authority down to the age we live in. Your claim for resolving the current divisions of Christendom is to lead people away from all these outward rituals, even those of Christ’s own institution, under the pretext of a greater perfection than can be consistent with needing them. Christ’s design was even to oblige spiritually gifted persons to proper submission to their governors. This is the principal purpose of St. Paul and St. Clement in their letters to the Corinthians: to prove this obligation. Your design is quite the opposite—to break such persons away from their dependence on their superiors in the spiritual society, on this very pretext of their being "spiritual." The apostolic age distinguished the Gospel state from the Law, even regarding the outward rituals of both: that the legal dispensation was to be succeeded by the evangelical as a more perfect state in this world, but that the Gospel state was everlasting (at least regarding this world) to cut off all claims by enthusiasts for breaking the established institutions of the Gospel. You, on the contrary, claim to abolish all obligations, even to true communion, on the pretext of a more perfect dispensation even in this world. Therefore, the Scripture assumes that all other spirits moving in opposition to that subordination are, for that very reason, different spirits from the one that is the bond of the Church’s unity; and that all divided spirits are also, for that very reason, to be taken as spirits of error and delusion. It deeply concerns you to protect yourselves against the consequences. I hope, dear Sir, you will value your soul more than your family ties, and excuse my frankness regarding a person so nearly related to you; I do this because it is so necessary for considerations much more important than your alliance. I desire to exercise my freedom no further than the cause requires, and with all the sincerity which I value as the best quality in your sect.

I do not know how your mother-in-law is qualified to write in the style in which her books are penned. But I have observed that there are many elements in that style which are quite beyond the education, social circles, or even the reading of women. It consists of many Latin terms, technical terms, the old Platonic mystical divinity, the writings of all the modern enthusiasts, of *Jacob Boehme*, of the judicial astrologers, of the magic oracles, and of the alchemists—too many of which are in English but are not usually encountered. I very much doubt whether she would be able to explain the terms used in the writings that go under her name if she were critically examined about them. But I think I have discovered traces of another, more likely author of them: I mean Dr. Pordage. I find she has been very intimate with him ever since the time she began her prophetic visions. She calls him her fellow-traveler; she generally claims to have her revelations while he was praying by her side. She claims a divine revelation that he was to recover from a very dangerous illness, and shows a great concern for him. And at the end of her first volume of the "Fountain of Gardens," either she or the editor <note>LEE himself</note> has added a testimonial from the Doctor, written in the same enthusiastic style as the revelations themselves, only more accurately and correctly, but just as extravagant. And that extravagance is a detail <note>N.B.</note> that I find none of you besides him are able to imitate with such perfection as he does, as far as I can judge by the prefaces, postscripts, and the tracts in the "Theosophical Transactions." I observed, furthermore, that the reason given for several missing revelations is that they were missing from the Doctor’s copy, and that they were received in the Doctor’s absence. Why should that be the case if she herself had been able and accustomed to write down her own visions? These things make it very suspicious to me that the words and style of all her books are the Doctor’s, and not hers. As to the actual facts, you can have better information than I can, and I earnestly recommend that you look into it for your own satisfaction.

There was really a Dr. John Pordage removed from the parish of Bradfield in Berkshire by the Commissioners in Cromwell’s time, in the year 1654, for doctrines and practices of the same nature as those I suspect in your mother-in-law’s friend. Whether this is the same person, you can know better than I, and you are greatly concerned to inform yourself as accurately as you can; but so many circumstances are similar, and yet so unique, that it would be very difficult for it to be otherwise. That Dr. Pordage was then accused of improper communication with spirits, some of them certainly evil ones. Nor did he deny being troubled by evil spirits for a considerable time. As for such favors as your mother-in-law claims—conversing with God and good spirits—he is so far from denying them that he glories in them. He claims *to have tasted much of that tree of life which grows in the midst of the paradise of God; to have seen through the veil of sensory nature into the spiritual glory of eternity; to have had the rising of Christ’s image within him; to have possessed the secret, hidden treasure of eternity and the outpourings of divine goodness; to have had discoveries of celestial glory, instillations of heavenly dew, and secret touches of the Holy Ghost, brilliant radiations of eternal light, strong motions of divine life, and pleasant streams of eternal love.* I give you his meaning in his own words so that you may see a sample of his style and judge how similar it is to that of your mother-in-law. He did not deny being taken up into heaven, like your mother-in-law, but compared it to that of St. Paul. He was then charged with claiming that *the New Jerusalem had been seen in his house coming down from heaven, and that within it was a globe—which globe was eternity—and in that eternity were all the saints.* He then mentioned a "virgin essence," which is in all likelihood the same one you now call the virgin *Wisdom*, with whom your mother-in-law claims to converse primarily. He was then charged with converting women, and the women so converted were said to practice, as yours are said to do now, the singing of hymns. <note>!</note> He then also claimed a power to bestow the gifts and graces of the Spirit on whomever he pleased. Why, then, should it be wondered at if your mother-in-law derived these visions she claimed from him? Mrs. Pendar, upon a similar or lesser familiarity with him, is said to have had such visions that they made her think herself bewitched by them; they came upon her so unaccountably, and with such obvious tendencies toward wicked and unlawful practices. And it was a frequent practice among the old heretics to make their women—

disciples believe themselves to be prophetesses; just as Simon Magus did with his Helena, Apelles with his Philumena, and Montanus with his Prisca and Maximilla. I wish you would particularly look into Irenæus, book 1, chapter 9, where you will find what arts were used for this purpose by Marcus, the father of the Marcosian heretics, along with the judicious remarks of the Father himself on the philosophy behind it. The same Doctor then claimed that he had seen the *world of devils*, innumerable evil spirits, their order and government; that he had heard, felt, tasted, and smelled *hell in salt and sulfur*, and that by a magical tincturation. "Magical" and "tincturation" are, as I remember, terms also used by your mother-in-law. His use of salt and sulfur shows how he also affected the terminology of chemistry. He also claimed to have seen the *world of angels, and of them without number, bright as the rays, sparkling like diamonds*; that he had tasted and heard the *dews of paradise and harmonious music, etc.*; and he speaks as favorably of magic as your mother-in-law does, and with as much caution, to distinguish it from magic that has a notoriously bad reputation. In short, you will find the notions charged against him then to be in exact agreement with those of your mother-in-law, and the style too, as much as could have been expected after forty years of refining and improving upon them. My authority for what was then charged against the Doctor is Mr. Fowler of Reading’s *Dæmonium Meridianum*, written in the year 1655, where several things are transcribed from the Doctor’s defense of himself in his own words. You may possibly obtain the Doctor’s own book, titled *Innocency Appearing*, etc., which I have not seen; there you may find more instances of his own style and notions, which may make his agreement with your mother even clearer and more certain. If you find upon examination that I have guessed correctly, and that the Doctor is indeed the true author of your mother-in-law's revelations, and that he was indeed guilty of the wickednesses then testified against him, I believe you will not easily believe them to be divine, nor really as pure as they pretend.

Yet even if you could prove your mother-in-law's cause is separate from his, I cannot see how you can avoid very just objections against her writings, even if they were entirely her own. The primitive Christians never spoke as honorably of magic as she does, but condemned all sorts of it—the white as well as the black, to speak in your own language concerning it. The Chaldee or magical Oracles are the oldest monuments, I believe, of that kind, from which any terms have been borrowed into mystical theology. They are certainly older than Porphyry, who grounded his philosophy ἐκ λογίων <note>from the oracles</note> upon them. Yet even the name of magic was of such ill repute among Christians that Simon and his heretical followers, the Gnostics, were then upbraided for ascribing any authority to them. Indeed, how could they do otherwise, when they universally condemned all the heathen demons of every kind—they who condemned all such strange familiarities even with good angels themselves (Colossians 2:18). It was in later, very degenerate ages that a book of magic was forged under our Savior’s name, inscribed to St. Peter and St. Paul; that forged so many magical offices under the names of great saints, which are still extant in manuscripts; that are supposed to have admitted professed magicians into the primary sees of Rome and Constantinople; that leavened so many of the later writings of the later Rabbis, and caused so great a loss of them. In those first and purest times, it was enough to ruin the reputation of any heretic to say they claimed such knowledge. Nor is there any reason to have a better opinion of even this "white magic" because of its great pretensions to purity. The devil has, even in these matters, also transformed himself into an angel of light. Cornelius Agrippa also claimed great purity and prayerfulness; and so do the chemists in their search for the philosopher’s stone, who are another source for the formation of your mother-in-law's style. But God does not promise the rewards of piety to such worldly designs, however plausibly they are presented. And there are no books of the chemists extant that I know of, even in manuscript, dating earlier than the 4th century; so far are they from being consistent with the best and purest ages of our Christian religion. Yet even these pretensions of piety in enthusiasts who cast off their duty seldom meet expectations after the first fires of enthusiasm have evaporated. It would be easy to show this in many instances, but hardly any more remarkably than in the case of Dr. Pordage. However, there is no reason to believe a style is divine and sacred when it is borrowed from the practices of such unjustifiable curiosities.

But this affected innovation in words might have been more tolerable if it had gone no further than words. And indeed, I expected when I first looked into your mother-in-law’s writings that it had gone no further. But I was surprised to find her stumbling into several antiquated heresies, condemned as such in the first and most infallible ages of our Christian religion. She calls her "Virgin Wisdom" a goddess, directly contrary to all that those purest ages declared against the distinction of sex in the Divinity. In this she agrees with no Christians of these times, but only the Gnostic heretics, who made their Aeons ἀῤῥενοθήλεις <note>androgynous</note> and allowed for a Sophia of that sex in the πλήρωμα <note>fullness</note>, no doubt meaning by her the Heavenly Wisdom; besides whom they invented a daughter of hers of an inferior rank, whom they called Achamoth (or if the word were Hebrew, *Chokhmoth*), an inferior terrestrial wisdom also, such as was also admitted in the philosophy of that age. But perhaps the word, having a singular meaning, was rather Egyptian. Your mother makes this same Virgin Wisdom the mother of the Son of God in regards to His eternal generation, directly contrary to St. Paul (Hebrews 7:3), who makes the Son of God ἀπάτορα <note>without father</note> in relation to His humanity, and ἀμήτορα <note>without mother</note> as to His Divinity. Yet your mother makes her Virgin Wisdom born under the sun and Venus; with what possible consistency, when her son is supposed to have created those planets? But this is the likely outcome when an ungoverned imagination manages terms taken from arts not understood by the person using them. And I am inclined to think that the Doctor, though he has made his jargon the study of his life, is not much more skilled in these things than she is. I have elsewhere observed her giving an account of the origin of Good and Evil through two co-eternal principles in the Deity, one good and the other evil, exactly agreeing with the condemned doctrine of Manes and several other heretics of those first ages. But in this age of licentiousness, there is hardly any doctrine of hers of more harmful consequence than her claiming Divine revelation for her doctrine concerning the finiteness of hell’s torments. I hope these heresies will cause you to seriously reconsider where this favor toward enthusiasm is likely to lead you. For my part, I think what I insisted on previously, both in my book on Schism and my first letter, was a just

We now come to Lee’s long Apologetical Letter, in reply to all the unanswered points of the former correspondence of ‘*Mr. Henry Dodwell*’; which was written about the end of the year 1698, but having then been laid aside, was afterwards revived upon fresh prompts, and the conclusion added on April 9, 1699:—

Dear Sir, — You do not need to excuse yourself for any freedom you have taken in a case of such great importance; you have a right to do so for several reasons. And although I did refrain from answering your second Letter, considering that you were not then as well informed about the state of the cause you undertook to oppose as you might be now, I did not do it with the least disrespect to a person who has deserved so much from the Christian world, as well as from the learned. To disagree with you would be very difficult, if I did not have other grounds than what you seem yet to have understood. For I have considered your criticisms of my mother’s books, and have some reason to doubt whether you did not simply settle for a cursory look at them, rather than accurately examining their whole scope and contents. Had you thought it worth your while to do so, some of the more major objections might perhaps have disappeared. And a plain representation of the facts will best determine what weight those general prejudices should have, which are brought to make her case seem suspicious.

II.—The design, then, of her writings <note>see p. 46, pp. 141, 148</note> is to *lead the soul up, as if by various degrees and through several purifications, washings, baptisms, and deaths into the Divine life.* This is most clearly laid out in her first treatise, called the *Heavenly Cloud*, which is the foundation for the rest of her works. Now, in order to attain this, she shows how it is necessary, in the first place, to be dead to the sensory and animal life into which we are all born.

And for this purpose, reason is very useful; she does not distrust it here, but freely uses it herself. But then this is only one end of the ladder, one step toward heaven, or according to her own style, one death. And between the sensory and Divine life, there may still remain a great gap. And it is certain that many get stuck here, who pretend to be great masters of reasoning. And many who have first reasoned themselves out of a spiritual principle and life in religion, have afterwards reasoned themselves out of the very existence of the eternal Word or reason, which is God, and finally out of the very being of a God, by confusing him with the world. It is very true that right reason could never persuade anyone of either of these; but it is enough that the reasoning faculty in man may be so corrupted as to give its assent to that which it should not.

Because of this, it appeared to this inquisitive spirit that there was as absolute a necessity for the mortification and resignation of this faculty also—in its corrupt and unbounded activity—as there was for the sensory and animal part in men. No injury is done here to the light of reason, nor is any just prejudice given against the cause maintained here; rather, a great advantage comes to reason when it is regulated by a superior principle and illuminated by a greater Light, as is claimed in this case, at least. And since there is intentionally a goal to introduce a principle superior to reason—as much as reason is superior to sense—and to use a Light from a higher source, flowing more directly from the Father of Lights into his reflected image when made pure and clear; so far, I do not see why this should be any just cause for prejudice against what is offered, unless it can be clearly proven: (1.) That there is no such superior principle, life, or light. Or (2.) that it is no longer communicable, nor to be expected in the regenerated image of God. Or (3.) that the process taken here for its communication is incorrect. Or lastly, that an error is committed in this process, or in admitting the Divine principle into the soul, and in its application, specification, and determination to particular objects. Besides, I must state this one thing once and for all: you must not expect the same accuracy of expression from a person without formal education as from one who is skilled in the true definitions of terms.

You well know, Sir, that the Spirit of God accommodates Himself to the capacity of the person into whom He flows. Neither the prophets nor the apostles have the same style, or even the same way of thinking. And all the world knows how differently *faith* is understood by the brother of our Lord and the teacher of the Gentiles.

I am confident that the word *reason*, as used by my mother, is taken in quite a different sense from the one you and others may take it in; and that she has as good reasons to diminish it in her sense as you can have to elevate it in yours.

Of this I could give many clear pieces of evidence from her writings. And I do not doubt that you yourself will find these upon a more narrow and strict examination of them, if you think it worth your while. I have never heard of anyone whom inspiration has made into a critic. It is enough if the scope and intent of an author be understood. If more than this were required, the Holy Ghost would never have spoken through fishermen, or would have made them orators and philosophers.

<meta>This text continues the "Apologetical Letter" by Francis Lee, defending the writings of Jane Lead against criticisms. This page specifically addresses the concerns that Lead claims her writings are equal to Scripture and that she lacks the miraculous signs typical of biblical prophets.</meta>

## III.—Another prejudice brought by you against her writings is that she *pretends* to equal her own prophecies with the confessedly inspired Scriptures.

But, dear Sir, what is her claim, I ask? Is it anything more than this: that she believes herself truly inspired by God? What grounds she has for believing so will be considered in their proper place. It is very true that she thinks herself led and taught by the Holy Spirit as truly as the prophets under the Old Testament or the apostles under the New Testament were—that is, according to their degree and nature. Indeed, her own writings may (and should) carry no less authority for her than theirs did for them, since they were likewise confessedly inspired.

For if I have a truly Divine inspiration, it is certain that it is not in my power to give it less credit than I give to the Divine inspiration of another, assuming both are inspirations of the same degree. And there are some grounds, I think, to allow (if possible) greater credit to that which is immediately communicated to myself than to that which is only communicated through others, no matter how well-attested it may be.

Thus far, then, it is certain that it ought not to be a prejudice against the truth of her prophecies that she herself firmly believes their truth and waits for their completion. Nor should it be held against her that she has an assurance equal to that which is universally given by Christians to the ancient prophecies and confessedly inspired writings which testify to the glorious coming of our Lord and blessed Saviour.

But despite this firm and solid assurance in herself, I do not find (either from her writings or from her conversation) that she pretends to compel others to give an equal authority to her writings as they do to the sacred Scriptures. Nor does she demand any authority at all for them that a sober seeker of truth would not be compelled to give of their own accord after the most careful scrutiny.

She has, indeed, published them for the sake of others, following a particular admonition given to her and various coinciding providential events strongly encouraging her—events very contrary to her own expectations, as can be shown from clear signs. But by doing this, she does not impose any new articles of faith or bring any new gospel; she only declares the light which she says was communicated to her, and she leaves everyone free to receive or reject it, since the harm or benefit will be theirs alone.

But she does not doubt, at the same time, that many good souls will be stirred up by the Spirit of God to acknowledge and embrace them, even before Divine wisdom sees it expedient or necessary to confirm them by some external and public mark, which may be given in due time, though not immediately.

## IV.—A further prejudice against her writings is this: that she assumes an authority for them equal to the Scriptures without any of the testimonials of Divine authority that the biblical writers had, such as *Shekhinahs*, signs of the prophets, miracles, and the *fulfillment* of predictions.

As for the first of these, it is true that she does not claim any *visible Shekhinah* such as was suited to the infant state of the Jews; but she claims that which is higher and nobler, substantial and permanent: even the real indwelling of the Holy Ghost as if in His temple.

And if this claim of hers is well-founded, and the truth of it made manifest to her (as it cannot well be supposed otherwise), I cannot see why she may not depend safely upon the Divine principle of light and love. Nor can I see why others who are, or shall be, convinced in the same manner, may not securely trust themselves to this superior way of administration as to a more certain word of prophecy.

## V.—As for the signs of the prophets, they were generally required and given upon particular messages, whether of judgment or mercy. This was seen with Moses in the famous Exodus of Israel, with Samuel regarding the kingdom conferred on Saul, with the man of God regarding the birth of Josiah, with Isaiah in several cases, and with Jeremiah also in several; but these were all specific instances.

But it does not appear that these signs were given by all the prophets, or even by the greatest or most eminent of them, in prophecies of a more universal nature or those that were unspecified as to persons and times.

Of these latter types, instances are frequent in Isaiah alone. Regarding the former, there are two witnesses at once—the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. It does not appear that either of them showed a sign or performed any miracle, though both held the same commission at the same time. And the reason for this may be the difference between the commission of these prophets and that of others who went out with a sign.

For the spirit of prophecy fell upon these men to promote the building of the second temple, which had no need of a new sign. This event occurred punctually with the expiration of the seventy years and was supported by several extraordinary providences occurring at the same time.

Another instance may be that of Daniel, a man highly favored with the revelation of hidden secrets and a most singular gift of interpretation, along with great angelic communications. Yet he brought no external sign other than the verification of what was declared or the outcome of the interpretation. And it may reasonably be wondered whether it might not have been this way also with Amos and some others during the first years of their public prophesying.

Moreover, in the most specific and extraordinary messages, and no matter how public and universal the concern, it does not appear that a sign was always required or given by God through His prophets. Of this there are two signal instances, and there cannot be any more eminent than these.

The first is Noah, who is believed to have prophesied to the old world concerning the approaching deluge no less than one hundred and twenty years before it happened. During all this time, there is not the least probability of a sign being given to that wicked generation, except for that of his own strict righteousness and his building of a strange structure or house—which appeared very extravagant—for the saving of himself and his family.

Here was an express command from God to declare that His Spirit would not strive with man beyond such a limited season. The prophet who was to declare this was to expect no better than—

<meta>This page continues Francis Lee’s defense of Jane Lead, specifically addressing the objection that she lacks the miraculous signs expected of a prophet. Lee argues from historical and biblical precedents that God often withholds such signs.</meta>

<margin>1)</margin> scorn or pity at least from the whole world at that time. There was no faith then upon the earth, and to humor such people with a sign from heaven would have been of little effect, if any. God was not obliged to give it, and it might not have suited the methods of his wisdom to do so. But this righteous man <note>Noah</note>, though laughed at by all, being moved with fear, would not tempt God by demanding a sign for his own vindication; instead, he believed and obeyed, and thereby condemned the unbelieving world, became heir of the righteousness which is by faith, and the father of a new world.

<margin>2)</margin> The second instance of this kind is Jonah, whose commission, according to the modern hypothesis of prophecy, would be very unaccountable. Certainly if Nineveh had been like London, or Assyria like England, they would not have so easily repented, but would have called aloud for signs before they would have listened to the word of the prophet. Therefore shall Nineveh rise up against London, and you, Assyria, against England.

<margin>3)</margin> Regarding this case, when fully and clearly stated, I cannot see anything that can be opposed with any solidity, assuming that matter of fact to be just as it is related. And to suppose the matter to be otherwise—and that there was a sign given when none is mentioned—is altogether unsubstantiated and a begging of the question.

<margin>4)</margin> I am not ignorant that in both these cases, there are good reasons that can be produced why a sign was withheld; but the very same reasons will hold just as well in the present case, as would not be difficult to demonstrate in detail.

<margin>5)</margin> One instance more I cannot omit, of a prophet without a sign, and that is the precursor of our blessed Lord <note>John the Baptist</note>, who though he was a second Elijah, yet neither performed miracles nor showed a sign, yet all men nevertheless acknowledged him as a prophet.

<margin>6)</margin> Therefore he is called only a *voice*, and a voice of one crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Messiah. And though he was afterwards publicly acknowledged by the Messiah himself, yet this was only as a subsequent ministry to ratify a former one, not to give any authoritative sign or seal of its truth; he having, in a manner, already finished his office, being in all places wherever he went, and by some of all ranks of persons, taken for a true prophet.

<margin>7)</margin> And whether his case may not be peculiarly applicable to some in this day, or sometime before the end of the world, as the precursors of the second glorious coming of our Lord and Savior, I leave you, Sir, to consider with as much accuracy as you please.

<margin>8)</margin> VI.—As for miracles, more may be said perhaps for them than for signs. A sign must be a miracle, but neither every miracle, nor even every great miracle, can properly be said to be a sign. And notwithstanding those great miracles which our blessed Savior performed, he refused to give a public and decisive sign, which could not have promoted, but rather would have served to frustrate, the design for which he came into the world.

<margin>9)</margin> Therefore he roundly told his unbelieving countrymen that no other sign should be given them but that of Jonah the prophet; which could not happen without them first putting him to death.

<margin>10)</margin> So there was no proper and public sign during the whole course of his ministry, notwithstanding all his miracles, by which he could be distinguished from Moses and Elijah, or any other great prophet who had performed miracles—even setting aside the signs which they gave as more immediately declaring their Divine mission.

<margin>11)</margin> Indeed, at the beginning of his ministry there was a sign given, but it was not public, being intended (for all that appears) for one single person, who was to bear witness of it by crying, *Behold the Lamb of God*.

<margin>12)</margin> The next sign that he also gave was private, in the presence of only three witnesses: and it was not until he was finishing the last scene of his commission, and was only a precursor to the great promised sign, the sign of Jonah.

<margin>13)</margin> A third sign may be what happened at the very finishing point of his ministry, or the threefold sign of his crucifixion: (1.) The rending of the veil of the Jewish temple. (2.) The earthquake. (3.) The darkness. This also was not so properly a sign as a *wonder*, being too indefinite for the former term strictly taken. And all this together did but make up the beginning of that grand, adequate sign, which had been twice promised in the most solemn and public manner, though not understood by anyone.

<margin>14)</margin> This was presently preached as the true and proper sign of the Messiah, and everywhere throughout the New Testament joined with him, even so far as to have been taken by some for the Godhead of Jesus. That it had all the marks of a true and adequate sign is indubitable, except that it was not exhibited in the open view of those who crucified him (which yet remains to be done); however, this was sufficiently compensated by their sealing of his sepulcher and by many other corroborating evidences.

<margin>15)</margin> Now, if it shall please Him who is exalted above every name to send forth his prophets and messengers in his name to prepare a way for Him against his glorious return, I cannot indeed but conclude that many miracles must be performed through them; and that many concurrent wonders also may be expected is not denied. Notwithstanding this, I doubt very much whether any sign (that is properly so called) ought to be expected or demanded before the sign of the Son of Man shall appear.

<margin>16)</margin> And what that is can be understood from the previously mentioned grand sign. But let this be what it will, or the preceding miracles be ever so many or great, yet to those who inquire after a sign, what they seek may be refused as it was before, and that without any discredit to the Divine glory or truth. And just as only the sign of Jonah the prophet was given by the great Son of man to those of his own generation, so truly shall only the sign of the Son of man be given by his Holy Spirit to those of the last generations of the world. With this, in my opinion, the plain and literal meaning of *Apoc. xi. 2* <note>Revelation 11:2</note> most aptly concurs. For the fulfillment of that passage I do not look either in this or the next age, clearly discerning that it must be the last great event immediately preceding the sound of the last trumpet. In miracles: to which these very writings, though not attested themselves at first by miracles, will most mainly contribute, whenever and by whomever they are rightly digested. This is visibly a principal design of them throughout. And I think no deeper foundation...

can be laid for the restoration of the miraculous powers by the spirit of faith, than what is to be found in them.

If these do not break out immediately, or all at once, but in due season and gradually, I do not see why this should be any disadvantage to these writings of my mother, or any just exception against her claims. It is what she herself has declared again and again, and still declares. Her claims may be firm and valid without external and public miracles to guard them, if Infinite Wisdom shall see fit to begin weakly and insignificantly for a greater manifestation of his glory. But besides, though she may not so much as *claim* to perform miracles, possibly God may sometimes honor his handmaid beyond what she claims; and I do not, therefore, have a worse opinion of her, but a better one.

I do not like to make a mountain out of a molehill; but what I have seen and known within these few years has certainly been too much to confirm either an imposture or a delusion.

VII.—As for the fulfilling of predictions by matching events, which you make another credential of true prophecy, I do not find that this could be claimed by several of the ancient, undoubted prophets during their lifetimes; their prophecies, as you know, were for the most part for a considerable time after their death. By this standard alone, Jonah might have passed for a false prophet; as possibly several of the true prophets did when they were stoned, or otherwise put to death by the public legal authorities for their testimony. It was only after their deaths, when their predictions came to be fulfilled, that those who had previously rejected them came to receive their prophecies and build their tombs. And yet, even on this point, there may perhaps be more reality than what is claimed in the present case. Some things of a private nature may be evidence of this kind to particular persons, which cannot be made so to others. And there may also be some things of a more public nature, predicted or represented in visions, which happened to be confirmed many years later by corresponding events, even when the prediction or vision had been utterly forgotten. An instance of this may be a visionary dream in the beginning of 1678 concerning the public exercise of Roman Catholic worship being tolerated in several parts of this kingdom, in which mention is made of the <term>Pope's vicars</term>; this seems to have been fulfilled seven years later, though it was unnoticed and not found until this very year, following the urgent requests of some persons from abroad requiring what still remains unpublished. [!] And there is one more instance which I cannot help but mention: a vision in December 1688, apparently relating to the peace concluded last year at <term>Ryswick</term> <note>The Treaty of Ryswick (1697) ended the Nine Years' War.</note>. [!]

Nor would it be difficult to find some other parallel instances of predictions that have either been answered by events, or at least have been very applicable to them. But I do not place any very great stress on these; the conviction that I have from other grounds is incomparably greater for me.

VIII.—Another prejudice against her writings is that she *presumes to warn us not to admit even the Scriptures in trial of her own claims to inspiration.*

How far this is true, or how it is understood, may easily be decided. It is true, then, that she claims an immediate revelation of God's mind in some matters not previously revealed in the Scriptures, and in which, consequently, no Scriptural ground may appear. But if this is a just prejudice against her—and if even an angel from heaven may be cursed who teaches any other doctrine than what is clearly expressed in the Scripture—then it will also be, if I mistake not, a prejudice against <term>Catholic tradition</term> <note>In this context, the universal or ancient traditions of the Christian Church.</note> for the same reason. And I am much afraid that the curse will rebound upon the holy fathers themselves of the ancient church, and upon its most renowned councils in many well-known cases. The doctrines of <term>infant baptism</term>, of the change or abandonment of the Jewish Sabbath, of the unity of baptism in opposition to the re-baptism of heretics, of prayers for the dead, along with some others, are certainly ancient doctrines for which it will be very hard to find a satisfactory ground in Scripture; but it would be no less hard to condemn all those who have believed and practiced according to these.

For by the same line of reasoning, I do not see at present why the whole Church may not fall under a curse as well as any single person, if they should receive any other doctrine than what is evidently grounded in Scripture, however consistent it may otherwise be with universal tradition or any other means of knowing the truth. This is, indeed, agreeable enough to the principles of some; but because it is not agreeable to yours, sir, I cannot but promise myself a more generous treatment than if I had fallen among those who would narrow the evidences of truth to public written inspiration, and that, too, interpreted according to their own explanations.

Besides, she does not claim to say that there is no Scriptural ground for the doctrine which she brings, but only honestly confesses that she has not found it. But it may be there, I suppose, despite the fact that she could not find it. If she could not find it there at all, or could not find it there plainly enough to satisfy herself or convince others, this might be cited as an example of her honesty, not of her presumption. For it can be no presumption to declare what God has revealed and has commanded to be declared, but rather a duty.

And if she does really believe that God did by His Spirit reveal this doctrine to her, and command her to declare the same publicly against all kinds of disadvantages—whatever the doctrine may be in itself, and though she may be mistaken as to the revelation—her only crime would be to have acted according to the best of her light, after the most earnest search into this matter by praying and waiting upon God. However, this is not imposed on anyone as an article of faith, and those who cannot digest it may pass it over. Though I think there may be as good grounds even from Scripture itself to make it so as the <term>supralapsarian</term> <note>A Calvinist doctrine regarding God's decrees and the fall of humanity.</note> doctrines which so many confessions of faith have raised to that rank, if not far better grounds.

Again, it is also true that she declares we are not bound to limit ourselves to any previous dispensation or revelation, nor to be so preoccupied with the Scripture itself, or to rely on it, as if nothing more were to be revealed for the benefit and instruction of mankind. And the conclusion which she draws from this is that whatever shall be thus revealed—so far as this shall be made to appear to the person receiving a revelation, or to any other—ought to be no less credited and esteemed than a revelation from the same Spirit of an earlier date. The truth of this is most evident from the very nature of the thing. And this should not be thought of as overriding the authority of the Scripture, nor a detraction from any previous Divine revelation, nor any arbitrary introduction of a new claimed revelation, since what is asserted is based upon this infallible maxim: that God cannot lie, and consequently that whatever was, is, or shall be communicated from Him, either for a more particular or more public benefit, ought to be received with the same reverence.

This is the essence of what she says, so far as I understand her; and it is no more than what everyone believes—that is, if the facts were assumed to be true. I do not find that she anywhere evades the acknowledged Divine authority of former divine revelations to establish her own. Nor does she refute even a single particular that can be determined this way, in order to bring what has been communicated to her to the Holy Scriptures as the standard of true inspiration. On the contrary, I find she is taught by that Spirit which guides her to hold them in the highest esteem, to appeal to them in all they contain, to meditate on them almost continually, and to search into their most hidden depths and concealed truths by and with the assistance of the Holy Inspirer who dictated them. It is the general method of the Spirit by which she is moved, after a revelation or manifestation is given, to apply and confirm it by some text of Scripture, which is then brought to her remembrance and most emphatically unfolded for the proper occasion; this certainly can be no sign of an evil spirit. And I do not think an evil spirit would excite her to call daily for the Scriptures to be read to her, as is her custom. 

But even suppose that she had, in express terms, warned us not to admit even the Scriptures themselves in the trial of her inspirations; however harsh this may sound, it is no worse than what the greatest part of Christians—including the learned, wise, and pious—effectively do regarding many of the doctrines and practices they maintain. It is not that they seek to set themselves apart from the Sacred Writ, but only to avoid all contention over its interpretation, which is so varied according to the different education and habitual prejudices of the readers. This may be a matter of prudent caution for them, based on good and weighty considerations; and if so, it may be the same here as well.

But there is no need for that. I know she is as far from distrusting the authority of the Scripture in her present case as its greatest claimants are. She believes she has a better claim from it to the teachings of the Spirit than any man can bring for his own estate, or than all the world can produce to oppose it.

Now, I will not say (yet) that this is anything more than a vivid imagination. Let it pass for such; it will, however, sufficiently vindicate her from this main charge.

### IX.

It is then a further prejudice against her writings that imagination alone is able to represent and perform all that is reported here.

But I cannot yield to this, based on the following grounds: It is not enough to say that imagination can represent golden ladies and golden cities; doubtless it can do this, along with everything in the book of Revelation.

It can represent all that Daniel or Ezekiel saw, all that Zachary typified, or all that Christ himself spoke in parables. But despite the fact that the sacred representations they exhibited were presented to the imaginative faculty, St. John, Ezekiel, and Daniel are not esteemed any less as true prophets, along with Zachary and others. Nor is it any detraction from the authority of our blessed Master that he chose a method so in agreement with human imagination.

Temperament and fevers may do a great deal, and I do not dispute the power of imagination. But there is no greater sign of a strong imagination than to challenge realities, or to conclude that whatever it *can* do, it *is* doing.

There are some things in my mother’s writings that undoubtedly relate to purely spiritual faculties—some indirectly and others directly. A particular listing of these with respect to those superior faculties of the intellect and will would be too tedious. There are some passages, I think, that visibly tend to enlighten the former, and others that strongly touch the latter. It is impossible that I should think otherwise, or that you yourself should, if only the contents were allowed or supposed to be true. 

For certainly the doctrine of the Spiritual kingdom of Christ; the unity and sanctity of the church; the order and discipline of the apostolical fraternity; the communion of saints; the ministry of angels; the origin of simple spirits; the various mansions allotted to blessed souls; the shared nature with the glorified humanity of the Lord; the nature of a spiritual body; the different steps of transfiguration, transformation, and transubstantiation; the Divine Virgin principle through which the Deity is manifested in nature; the real and spiritual eating <note>manducation</note> of the spiritual internal senses mirrored by the natural and external; the first paradisiacal state of man; the gradual defection and fall; the scale of regeneration; elementary spirits and their receptacles; the various states of purification in other regions; the general restoration of the creation; and others coinciding with these—all are doctrines that, according to their degree, tend as peculiarly to illustrate the understanding as any others that can be named in the Christian religion. And assuming this to be equally true at present, I cannot think that the least question would be made of it. 

Neither would it be an easy task to transcribe all those passages that properly affect the superior will of man and strongly impel it as soon as they are rightly understood. Of this nature are those that lead to a pure and naked dependence upon God; to the incomprehensible peace of God; to that perfect thing described by the Apostle; to a high and masculine faith that can truly be called apostolical; and to the holy and undefiled <term>magia</term> <note>spiritual power or wisdom</note> which proceeds from it, and is the greatest of all wonders in purified and resigned wills, being therefore frequently called the "great mystery."

How many cautions, counsels, exhortations, and encouragements are to be found here for recovering the evangelical spirit among Christians and for waiting for the promise of the Father? I cannot conceive that all of these relate more immediately to any spiritual faculties of the soul, unless the imagination is the seat of the evangelical spirit.

There are also judgments and blessings pronounced: one upon those who obstinately refuse this Spirit, and the other upon all who shall yield themselves to its call as it grows louder and louder. This also bears a relation to the will; it is so consistent with the methods of divine providence and the manner of all ancient, undoubtedly inspired prophets, that I do not know what can be reasonably objected against it, after what has already been considered regarding previous prejudices. By the evidence of this, I am forced to conclude that there are some—indeed many—things in these writings that relate to the faculties which are the proper subject of the true spirit of prophecy.

Not only that, but the very scope and aim of all these writings is to set the mind free from images, to purify all the avenues of the imaginative faculties, and to drive the soul into a super-sensual and super-imaginative state. And however much sensory mediums and images are used in the process toward this attainment—and are used to make the same known to others—they are taken up instead

of words, for their great significance and expressiveness; yet all this is but an artificial way of uncovering the imagination with the greatest familiarity and ease to itself, in order to reach that blessed state of seeing God from, in, and through a simplified and pure heart.

There may be, and really is, a great distinction between imagination and the work of God upon the imagination. The greatest part, if not all, of the angelical ministration consists in this. Therefore, it is not a valid argument to say that the imagination itself is sufficient to represent such objects as realistically as if they were present, unless it is also evident that there could be no operation of God upon it, or co-operation with it through the intervention of angels, to make those objects present to that faculty.

The imagination is properly <term>Speculum Anima</term> (Mirror of the Soul), which in its fallen, corrupted state is filled with innumerable broken images, very inadequate and illogical; but in its restored and pure state, all these images being cast out, it becomes a bright mirror to reflect the immaculate and entire image of God, as it is in the Virgin nature of the Lamb (then seen upon mount Sion). And so through this one image, reflected here, the spirit of the soul, as in a glass, may be said to behold God and the Divine world (all whose figures are adequate and regular), not indeed nakedly and manifestly, but somewhat obscurely and enigmatically.

And thus, in proportion as the imagination is more or less emptied—all the imaginations of the heart of man being evil, and evil altogether—there is (or may be) an admission into it of that vision for which it was originally formed, either in a higher or lower degree. Whether it may be so in this case, or how far it may be, may perhaps be worthy of a wise man's search.

But sixthly, you yourself, dear Sir, seem sensible enough that all could not be the mere effect of imagination, since you are so willing to admit the influence of evil spirits upon it.

Therefore, this prejudice concerning the imagination being insufficient, even according to your own method of reasoning, I shall consider the next prejudice, which instead of strengthening seems to overthrow the former; unless the obsession and influence of an evil spirit should be confused with a constitutional or accidental infirmity, and the same thing might be said at once to be both natural and preternatural.

X.—Another heavier prejudice then remains against her writings, even no less than this: *that it is in the power of the devil to represent sensible ideas to the imagination, where God is pleased to permit him; that there is no security against the intervention of evil spirits in a faculty wherein they are permitted to act by the ordinary rules of providence; and that evil spirits are most likely to be expected in the ways used by us for attaining the Spirit we pretend to have.*

Now if there can be a security against the intervention of evil spirits, even in this faculty, and we actually have this security, then will this prejudice that is leveled against these writings in particular, and against the society in general, fall to the ground.

Now, that there may be a security even in the imagination itself from evil spirits interposing themselves, I think may be proven, not only <term>a posteriori</term> from undeniable instances, but also <term>a priori</term> from the nature of the subject. Now it is firm that every faculty in its original constitution must have its proper certainty; otherwise God would deceive his creature, that is, he would be no God. And as certain as truth cannot be the fountain of either a verbal or essential lie, or as two contradictories are impossible, so certain it is that every faculty, power, or might which proceeds from God, the essential Truth, must attain to its proper object for which it was formed or brought forth; on the condition that everything which would weaken, darken, or impede it is removed out of the way. And when it has attained its object, it must of necessity be certain of this attainment. Intellectual truth is the proper object of human understanding, and though it is possible for the understanding to be mistaken with respect to truth in almost infinite cases, yet it is absolutely impossible for it to be mistaken in some, particularly in those common notions wherein all mankind most unanimously agree. Nay, it is impossible to be mistaken in any, provided the objective truth is fairly and fully presented, and the faculty is sound and free of all prejudices.

Besides, there are some few general rules for finding out and discerning truth, which being strictly observed in their application to particulars, ensures no error can be admitted into the understanding. All of this is likewise applicable to the imaginative faculty, which has its common images wherein there can be no mistake; it has its soundness as well as its infirmity, and its true position as well as its false. And that is to be regulated by such plain, easy rules of discretion as will exclude all illusions.

This is universally true in the various faculties and gifts of God to men, without any exception, whether natural or supernatural, purely spiritual or mixed, internal or external.

Good is the proper object of the Will, to which, according to its true original constitution, it may attain. And Infinite Good, or the supreme Good, is the only true object of the will of man, for which it was formed and capacitated; and to which it may therefore, according to its original formation and native capacity, attain, and having attained, rest satisfied in the possession of its object with an infallible certainty. And though we daily and hourly experience how possible it is for the human will to be misled with respect to good—yea, how very difficult (and almost impossible) it is not to be mistaken or biased in this pursuit—yet where the objective good is clearly and sensibly presented, and the will is unfettered and in the full liberty of the spirit, it is perfectly impossible for it to be misled here, or not to have sufficient security against the deception of apparent good.

Material beings are the proper objects of the external senses, and though it is notorious what innumerable errors have sprung up through these, and what gross and even ridiculous mistakes are made by the unlearned, yet it is altogether impossible for these to occur when the organ is sound and perfect, the object is proportioned to it, and the distance is neither too remote nor too near. There are certain sensations in which all mankind mutually concur; and there are also certain natural rules of addition and subtraction of sensible ideas, of their division and multiplication, and of their negation or abstraction, and comparison, which afford many solid and substantial truths, and cannot in any way lead into error when they are attended to.

Nay, it is impossible for the senses themselves to deceive anyone, since the error is not in them, but in the judgment that is made upon them. And all that has been said with respect to these, and the superior and purely spiritual faculties of the mind, is likewise applicable to the imagination, as could be distinctly shown if I were writing to a person of less penetration.

Thus, then, even the imaginative faculty is capable of its own proper evidence, just as the intellect, the will, or any of the senses are of theirs. Indeed, it is as capable as any faculties or powers whatever, whether angelic or human, since all alike depend equally upon the nature of Divine truth. Nor is it enough to argue that this is only a natural evidence, and therefore to be suspected for fear of a supernatural deception by the subtle insinuation of transformed evil spirits; for if it were in their power to nullify or supersede this evidence, where there is a proper disposition of subject and object, they would be more powerful than God himself, who has willed such evidence to arise from this or that disposition or combination, according to certain immutable and eternal laws of truth. And although as long as this faculty or fountain is impure, and not regenerated from above, there may be no security against the intrusion of such spirits, yet certainly, as this is purified and renovated by the spirit of JESUS, the greatest possible security can be obtained. In comparison to this, the security of external signs and miracles can only be of an inferior degree. Since no evidence from without (no matter how great) is anything, except so far as it is apprehended by, and corresponds with, the internal principle of sensation and perception, by whatever name it is called.

An instance of this, I believe, is the famous ecstasy of the great Pythagoras, when he ran about as an <term>Energumen</term>, or possessed person, crying "*Eureka*," for having found out that noted theorem which is the basis of all trigonometry. He was thus transported out of himself by the energy of truth, so as to forget that he had a body; this transport was caused by the inner action of the truth upon his mind, whereby his animal spirits were so activated through the surprising clarity of what before was very obscure, that his imagination was filled with the ideas relating to such a triangle during the suspension of his outward senses.

This inner action or energy of truth was so powerful only because of the conformity of certain imaginary ideas with one another, and their combination according to such laws as are necessary and self-evident. This conformity, even of imaginary ideas, was in itself a proof vastly superior to any other that could be given. For I believe that no man would think he could have been half so certain of the truth of that proposition if he had spent all his days measuring triangles by rule and compass, or if the whole body of mathematicians at that time had declared it to him, or if any wonderful operation of magic had been performed by any of them for the confirmation of it.

All external proofs, all mechanical figures, and miracles themselves—even to the raising of the dead—would have been given as inferior evidence to that which he had, and which everyone may also have when the first elements and terms of geometry are clearly understood.

Thus it is: every faculty of the soul has its proper evidence and its proper energy, which all other things can never be able to balance or equal.

And here I cannot help but observe that the Divine energy upon the soul is not without good reason so often mentioned by the great Apostle; I should think with some particular regard to these degenerate times, if he may be allowed to have had the spirit of prophecy—as he doubtless had—when he prophesied of the son of Belial (<term>ὁ ανομος</term>, the lawless one), to be manifested "in the energy of Satan," with apparent miracles, signs, and prodigies. But without pretending to decipher this prophecy, I dare be confident, upon as good grounds as we can have for the interpretation of any one text in the whole Scripture, that the application, neither in part nor in whole, ought to be made to the present case.*

Nor can I help but take notice that in seven places where this word <term>Ενεργεια</term> (Energy) is used by St. Paul alone in his Epistles, there are no fewer than six of them where it is certainly taken in a good sense. And in this one place referred to by you, where it is taken in a bad sense, it is only incidental and upon an extraordinary occasion, though for deeper emphasis and impression it is indeed repeated. Why, then, I cannot yet see a ground, either in reason or in Scripture, to conclude that even in this very faculty of the imagination itself, there can be no security against the interference of evil demons, or that there may not be a natural and supernatural evidence in this so-disparaged subject, when it is rightly disposed through the holy energy of God in the soul. This energy may be in any or every part or power of the soul, just as the soul has its energy in any and every part of the body. From this arises that great diversity of <term>ενεργήματα</term> (which I take the liberty to call "Seminal Operations") of the Holy Spirit, mentioned in a very accurate discourse upon this matter by this very Apostle, for the use (as I suppose, at least) not of one age of the Church, any more than of that one particular church alone to which it was immediately addressed, but of all ages of the Church. Some of these are more internal, others more external, and all have a peculiar energy, manifestation, and ministry, different from all the rest.

And for further confirmation of this significant position—that every faculty has its proper evidence as well as its proper object, and that consequently a security can be obtained from all fallacy of any kind—there are not lacking arguments *a posteriori* that I could produce if it were necessary. I could also produce instances in the imaginative faculty of unsuspected truth, <term>κατ ενεργειαν εν μετρω</term> (according to the energy in measure), as the Divine powerful energy is commensurate with it. This faculty was very predominant, or rather exalted, in the prophet Ezekiel, more so than in Daniel himself—that is, more masculine and vivid. And it will not be more difficult to answer how he could be secured against the interference of the spirits of delusion than it will be how some others may also have been secured from them, especially considering those three grand visions: that of the wheels, that of the dead bones, and that of the temple. He and many others have had this security, notwithstanding that the ordinary rules of providence do permit evil spirits to act in the imagination, where Divine visions are also exhibited.

Now, that there may not only be such a security, but that we actually have this security, may—

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the discernment of spirits, transitioning from the internal evidence of the purified imagination to the scriptural grounds for determining when a person is truly abandoned to diabolical delusion.</meta>

can be established on several grounds that are not easily shaken. But, omitting others, I shall focus here on two that are taken from that very passage in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians to which you have been pleased to refer me; these, I believe, necessarily follow from the Apostle's intent. For if I know the cause or causes that expose me to the interference of evil angels transforming themselves, and to their powerful delusion, I also know for certain that my security consists in removing those causes. And if an opposite cause must produce an opposite effect, I must conclude that if the sign of this opposite cause is present, it would be absurd to expect the same effect.

Now, the causes for the Divine permission of evil angels to interfere are expressed as two: (1) an opposition to the Gospel of Christ—and not only that, but even a fixed hatred against it. This opposition is expressed in these words, *not believing the truth* (μη πιστευσαντες τη αληθεια), discrediting the Gospel; and the hatred by these, *they received not the love of the truth* (την αγαπην της αληθειας, ουκ εδεξαντο), meaning they did not admit the love of the Gospel. (2) A stubborn impiety expressed by these words, *taking pleasure in unrighteousness* (ευδοκησαντες εν τη αδικια), as we translate them—entirely approving, acquiescing to, and being possessed by it; resting in it as if it were their nature, rarely (or at least very seldom) moving away from it, but always drawn toward it by a strong personal inclination, with the greatest affection and satisfaction of mind. This was the case of Pharaoh and Ahab in the Old Testament, and of Simon Magus in the New Testament; because of their *infidelity* and *impiety*, they were surrendered by the just judgment of God to believe a delusion after they had willfully resisted the truth.

Conversely, the causes of Divine protection against the interference of evil spirits—preventing them from working in the "deceptiveness of unrighteousness"—are (1) faith and (2) holiness, as both are used here in a broad sense and in the lowest degree they can be properly attributed to any subject. Otherwise, the Apostle’s argument on this point would be weak, the inference he draws to support those in his beloved care would largely fail, and his sacrifice of thanksgiving which he offers to God for them would be extremely flawed (v. 13). From this, I must conclude that even the lowest degree of faith, or belief in the truth, and the very smallest measure of holiness, or sanctification of the spirit, are real, proper, and sufficient safeguards against all fear of diabolical enthusiasm. And wherever the signs of these are found, in any degree or measure whatever, to make such a charge as this, or even to hint at it, is not only most unsafe but also most unreasonable.

Furthermore, if there is even a possibility of doubt in this matter due to the lack of clear signs, there may be greater danger in pronouncing such a severe sentence than you, dear Sir, and many others are currently aware of.

Another deduction that I make from this is that the more intricate points of schism and heresy are not the proper criteria for such an enthusiasm, though they may be the effects of it, and thus might indeed be used as subsequent proofs when the evidence is clear. For this is the most terrible judgment of God that can ever be inflicted against the most stubborn and defiant opponents of the Gospel—specifically in its full scope and after they have knowledge of it. Therefore, it cannot be justly declared against those who are mistaken in their profession of it, regardless of how gross or unfortunate their mistakes may happen to be. Since this "delivery up to Satan" is not for their reformation but for their destruction, it follows a full and decisive judgment against them for their past crimes. It would be very harsh for a most righteous God to do this only for matters of a debatable nature that have been, and are, continually argued on both sides by men of goodwill—matters where it is not impossible for learned and honest men to be deceived.

And just as it would be harsh on God's part, it is even more so for a man to set himself up as a judge in this critical case. For even he himself can never be so universal and orthodox in his own views that a much larger body of Christians will not be against him than for him (not even excepting the Church of Rome). He could not be safe for even one moment from falling under this very same judgment—alongside sorcerers and witches—if he should be so unfortunate as to mistakenly err in a matter about which very few can agree. The majority will certainly agree on this, whichever side he chooses: that he is a schismatic, or a heretic, if not both. Whether he relies on the infallibility of his own reason or the infallibility of someone else—by whatever name it is called—and regardless of whatever sincerity and love of the truth he may truly claim, I do not see how anyone can have even a reasonable security against suffering this sentence in this life (as pronounced against the "firstborn of the devil"), if either schism alone, or schism combined with heresy, is accepted as a true criterion for when enthusiasm is diabolical and when it is not. Unless the irresistibility of Divine truth (in its strictest sense) is maintained, and its specific application is infallibly and irresistibly demonstrated, no other security can be invented. To assert either of these is, I confess, an enthusiasm that I have not yet reached.

Now, God forbid that I should make myself a patron of either schism or heresy by saying this. I know very well their evil and danger; and I continually bow my knees before the God and Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, asking that he may preserve me from both and keep me forever in the unity of his Holy Spirit with all the true Israel. I only beg leave to say that all the lines of reasoning that are or can be drawn from either of these are far too weak to conclude that anyone is under a diabolical influence.

No matter how many or how great the arguments raised from these points may appear, they cannot amount to a proper criterion for the kind of enthusiasm being claimed. Nor can they be accepted as such without running directly counter to the intent of the Apostle, who defines it as consisting of infidelity and impiety when they have reached their crisis. That these alone can be relied on as the inseparable and characteristic signs of all anti-Christian delusions is further evident from historical facts proving the invalidity of any other criteria. It is not only possible for such delusions and obsessions of evil spirits to be found where there is no appearance of schism or heresy, but there have actually been examples of this that can hardly be disputed. Among these, I place Simon Magus and his companions first, as they were still visibly in the communion of the Church and the fellowship of the Apostles. Because of this, the Christian religion fell under the hatred of the times for

In the Apostolic Church of Thyatira, as also in that of Pergamus, it is highly probable that they did not separate themselves from the external communion of the saints, nor did they publicly maintain any heretical doctrine against the catholic faith. And it seems that the faithful Thyatirans were therefore rebuked by Christ because they tolerated in their communion persons guilty of such enormous impieties and idolatrous practices; which they did not fail to cover with some plausible pretexts from the false and evil spirit of prophecy, which moved strongly in them. Apoc. ii. 20. Thus it was even in the first and most pure age of the Church. And how it was in the succeeding and more degenerate ages of the Church, you know, Sir, very well. You know what sort of persons were sometimes raised to the chief patriarchal sees, and how Satan (in a more real sense than is ordinarily understood) might be said to have his throne in the temple of God. I will not now ask what communion there can be between God and Baal? Or how such Asiatic Churches could be utterly exterminated for permitting the evil leaven of Balaam and of Jezebel to creep in among their prophets and teachers, while others who have followed in the same steps should not also be laid in the same bed with them, according to the equal and righteous judgment of God?
These and many more questions would naturally arise; but I am not willing to be burdensome to you, and I leave them only to your consideration, and your free choice to take notice of them or not.

XIII.—Now the summary is this: there is a security to be had against the interference of evil spirits, and that in the imaginative faculty itself. This security is not difficult or complicated, but easy to obtain and to be judged by all Christians. It consists in knowing the reasons for God's permission of such evil spirits to interfere and act in this manner; the preservatives against their interference are faith and holiness, even if only in an inferior degree and measure. Schism and heresy do not by themselves expose one to this danger; they cannot be justly or safely made the presumptive marks of a diabolical energy or enthusiasm. This is no less possible, and no less frequent (if not more so), within the external unity of the true Church than outside of it. Therefore, if the visible unity maintained with the undoubted catholic Church and the external profession of orthodoxy can provide no security against the greatest of all evils, and if some may fall into one or both of those two previously mentioned evils and yet still have a sufficient security (if they wish) from falling into this last one, so long as there is any sincerity remaining in them; I cannot see how it can be denied that we may, or actually do, have a security of this kind that is sufficient for us to rely on, without running into such consequences as you yourself would not be willing to allow. For it will not be difficult to find out—now that there are many living witnesses—whether this person has led a life of infidelity or a life of faith; and especially for these past thirty years, during which she claims more immediate familiarity with the true Spirit, whether it has been a life of impiety or a life of angelic sanctity; whether she has taken pleasure in unrighteousness, or rather in righteousness. If the former is found to be true, then there is no security; but if the latter is true, then there is all the security that can justly be demanded or expected. This security is stronger than miracles themselves. It is all that God is pleased to give, even for the discernment of pretended miracles, in that most perilous case mentioned by the Apostle. And though some may indeed delude themselves through the efforts of a natural enthusiasm, whether innate or accidental, yet it is as impossible for any but the maliciously wicked and the perversely unbelieving to be delivered up to that which is diabolical as it is impossible for God to deceive.
Indeed, should they sometimes even be exposed to this by the course of Divine justice for some willful misconduct against the truth and holiness of God, it would still be impossible for his good Spirit to leave them to the destruction of the Evil One before they have filled up the measure of their iniquities, and not to set bounds to the incursions of the disguised enemy.
There is such a security, then, in this present matter, as great as the justice and truth of God himself.
Since if we have received the love of the truth, or if we have believed it when and so far as it is made manifest, our consciences must accordingly condemn or acquit us. And it cannot but be known to the persons concerned if they have obstinately rejected sanctification or *the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ*, of which they make such frequent mention. And if it may be known to the persons themselves (as it is known to them infallibly), so may it also be known to others, according to the external demonstrations given of either.
As for my own part, I stand before the judgment seat of Christ. But it is well known what my external life has been, and my internal life is known where it ought to be. I dare not justify myself; for if I do, my justification is not true. Only permit me to observe, dear Sir, that you here unknowingly justify me even while you most condemn me. Since if I were truly under the power of Satan, it must have been in vain that you have taken so much trouble to recover me; and all efforts of this kind must necessarily be fruitless, being directly opposite to the expressed will of the Sovereign Judge.

XIV.—There is another general prejudice against these writings: that they were not penned by the person under whose name they are published, but by another—and by one also who was publicly censured for doctrines and practices of an evil nature.
And here I must confess that so much is said, and so well organized, that had it been a matter of fact from some hundreds of years ago, I could never have resisted the force of so many probabilities gathered together, but would have surrendered myself to your opinion. I cannot do that now, however, because the matter is fresh, and because the most plausible conjecture will avail nothing against real experience and tangible demonstration.
For the plain truth is this: I find it was the constant practice of my mother to write down with her own hand day by day all her own experiences and discoveries, along with several memorandums relating to her external as well as internal life. This was observed by her so long as it pleased God
