to permit her the use of her eyes, which lasted for almost a year after I first became acquainted with her. During that time, she secretly described with her own pen the treatise of the *Eight Worlds* (the original of which, so written, I still keep with me), along with some other things not yet published. But since the loss of her sight (caused by the intense exercise of her mind in meditation and recollection, and by much writing), she has been forced to dictate to another—and not always to the same person, but to several different people. Her great facility in all subjects, and upon all subjects presented to her, is quite remarkable.

She did indeed have the assistance of a man of letters for some years, who accidentally (if a Christian may use this word) contributed much to the preservation of the greatest part of her *Diary*.

Because what she wrote was on loose slips of paper, like the Sybilline leaves, he transcribed them for his own private use without any thoughts of publishing them. Consequently, in his haste, he frequently copied the very grammatical errors and false spelling, leaving blank spaces for the words he could not read; some of these were filled in by her own hand, but others were not. Upon comparing the remaining originals with the copies, I do not find any insertion of words to make them look more grand, nor any variation of the style or the sense (except through mistakes in punctuation). The only thing to be admitted regarding the former is that he sometimes moves the verb to the earlier part of the sentence, whereas my mother usually places it at the end.

While this makes the style a little more familiar and natural to the ear, it is actually broken and made weaker. I could provide many examples of this if it were worth dwelling on such small details.

There are also omissions in the copy—of a word, a line, and even, though rarely, of an entire sentence. Indeed, some of the loose papers were forgotten and not transcribed by him (where entire dates are omitted), and others are written twice, word for word.

The very first book she published, titled the *Heavenly Cloud* (printed in 1681, the same year her friend died), was printed from her own manuscript and never transcribed by him, nor was the prose even revised. I dare appeal to you, Sir, whether the style in this book is not the same as that in her recently printed *Diary*, and even in the very parts of it which, being lost in the original, could be found only in the copy.

For some parts of it are printed from the original itself where the copy happened to be lost; as evidence of this, you may see June 20, 1676, page 253, volume 1; and June 30, ’76, page 256, with the note at the end of the former, among others.

But even if there were no such evidence to prove that my mother is indeed the author (next to whatever spirit guides her) of what has been published under her name, I still have daily, undoubted proof of her capacity to write in such a style on all sorts of cases and subjects presented to her from abroad by persons of various nations, ranks, and qualities.

XV.—Nevertheless, a significant doubt will still remain: whether her friend was truly the kind of person some claim him to be. But I have conducted the most careful search into his life that I am able to perform, without the least partiality or favor, and I cannot find him guilty of that black charge so barbarously laid against him. While he was not exempt from human passions and weaknesses, he showed himself to be a diligent combatant in the Christian struggle. From everything I can possibly learn, I must believe him to have been a person of great integrity, of very deep experience in spiritual matters, and of most worthy and holy aims. Such a man was this Dr. John Pordage, who was ejected from the living of Bradfield by Cromwell’s commissioners in a most arbitrary and illegal manner.

But whatever he might have been in 1654 and before that, it is possible that in the space of twenty years—and those spent under the Cross—he might have become a new man. For it was not until about that time, as I understand, that his close friendship with my mother began.

It was in August of 1673 or 1674 (the date is entered differently in two places due to a mistake) that they first agreed to wait together in prayer and pure dedication. From that time until his death, his conduct was such that malice itself can hardly find fault with it; he pressed forward toward the most perfect state attainable, though not without a sense of his imperfections and the many temptations of Satan. In the year 1675, I find noted in his own handwriting how many years he had been earnestly striving after the heavenly pattern contained in the Gospel, complaining how he had fallen short of it and giving the reason for this defect. I find several other private remarks he made regarding his internal state, which demonstrate to me unbeatably that he could not have been a hypocrite; that he was not someone suited for managing secret designs; that he was not deceived by lying spirits; and that he was guilty of neither the doctrines nor the practices with which some have charged him.

He has written a treatise against the errors of the Quakers and has fundamentally overthrown the principles of <term>Rantism</term> in another of his unpublished books. From these and his other remains, it appears that he was an impartial seeker and a sincere lover of truth. Yet, as he said himself, he desired to hold the *just balance with even weights*; so it will be evident to anyone who examines his case that he did indeed receive false weights and measures from others. You cannot help but discover this yourself if you consult even his accusers: there is such confusion among them, such disordered passion, such plain twisting of words, such ridiculous reporting of matters, and throughout it all, such an unchristian behavior that it recoils upon their own heads, hurting them more than him.

Examples of this are clearly found in the author of *Familism Arising out of the Bottomless Pit*, in the *Demonium Meridionum* of Mr. Fowler, and even in Mr. Baxter himself—though with far greater moderation than the others, and only at second hand. If you read his *Apology*, called *Innocency Appearing* (to which the second work claims to be an answer), you will find a clear account of the facts mainly in dispute concerning the appearances of both evil and good spirits, and the manner in which the two contrary kingdoms or worlds were opened, as happened by the will of God in the autumn of 1649. This was also recently reprinted by Mr. Edward Stephens in a treatise concerning witches, etc. <note>Son-in-law of Judge Hale, and author of “Ancient Ascetics.”</note>

And truly, having considered both the printed accounts and other supporting evidence I have found from several people who were closely acquainted with the matter (one of whom was then at All Souls College and went with another Fellow of the same college to...

I must freely say, I see as much reason to confuse Simon Magus and Simon Peter as to confuse Everard the sorcerer and Pordage the divine. St. Peter resisted and overcame his adversary, who had hypocritically suggested himself to be a visible member of the church; so did Dr. Pordage also, by virtue of that promise (not reserved for the Apostles alone, but for every true Christian), *resist the devil and he will fly from you*. This, and no other, was the case at Bradfield.

But it was not an easy combat; it required continual watching and praying, without any interruption, for whole weeks together. While one person slept, others watched and prayed in their turns, and whenever there was even the least flagging, I have heard that the enemy immediately prevailed and recruited his force. But though by the grace of God and the name of Jesus he was forced to flee with his wicked instrument, his malice did not expire here. Instead, he laid a new plot, which took effect five years later, through the excessive zeal of those times and some personal grudges (which it has always been common to cover with the cause of religion) that must not be stirred up again.

But in this I except Mr. Fowler, in whom I believe it might have been pure zeal, for the most part. Of this he (or anyone) could not give a more notable example than in the present case, when all matters are duly weighed. However, even if the Doctor had been ever so guilty, I think it would have been of far better reputation if someone else had undertaken the cause, rather than one who is said to be obliged to him in many ways, and to have been raised through his means from a poor state to what he then was—even to the point of sitting as a judge over his former friend, while he also made himself both a party and a witness for a surer dispatch.

Thus an ungoverned zeal transcends all limits, especially when it flows from rigid principles. For it is no wonder if one who took pleasure in denouncing hell and damnation not only as infinite but also as inevitable—and who, according to those principles, condemned those who knew not their right hand from their left to an irreversible destruction, so as in a flight of enthusiasm to imagine the very place of everlasting terrors to be paved with the souls of little children—it is no wonder, I say, if such a person (if what is generally reported concerning this *Durus Pater* <note>"Hard Father," likely a reference to a strict or Calvinistic theologian</note> is true) should be transported into a fit of zeal upon hearing of matters so extraordinary, so little understood, so misrepresented, and lastly, so loaded with other criminal charges.

But notwithstanding what this severe judge has brought to invalidate the solemn appeal to God made by the Doctor when there was no redress to be expected on earth, and when a re-hearing of his cause (which he sued for) had been denied to him—since he would never afterwards withdraw this appeal by appealing again to man or returning an answer to the accusations of the *Demonium* <note>The demonic entity or the specific accusations involving spirits</note>—I dare not offer to put in my plea against it, but must let it rest where it is. And therefore, I shall also omit many things that might be relevantly urged on this behalf to set right such a distorted case.

This one thing only I cannot help but mention, which in other cases is constantly allowed as certain evidence of a person's credibility, and which the special Providence of God has favored me with here, beyond what I could ever have expected or desired to find. I find among his papers that have fallen into my hands (some of which were never intended to be seen by anyone) several unquestionable marks of an honest nature. And I must observe that he is so far from concealing his own faults and imperfections (as a cunning impostor would have done) that he has in various places brought shame upon himself and thereby given glory to God by his own hand. And he did this when there could be no motivation (at least none presumed) for doing so, except from a generous and open principle that moved within him and the holy guidance of the Spirit of Truth. Hence, he transcribed several admonitions, rebukes, and even some prophetic threats that were expressly leveled against himself. And however secret the cases were to which these referred, he was never less faithful or less diligent in preserving them, doubtless for caution and instruction.

Neither could he indeed hide his infirmities, as far as I can learn, even if he had wanted to. He confesses frankly the dullness of his soul in comprehending or expressing what was revealed to him in the Spirit. He warns against confusing the reasonings of his mind with the illuminations of the Spirit. He complains of his carelessness, of the irregularity of his natural fire, of his pride for some time, and of his too great activity at another. He reports of himself that in Bradfield, a most terrible voice came to him and said, *Take this unprofitable servant, and cast him into outer darkness*. And how, immediately upon this, he was snatched away there in spirit and made to feel the heavy strokes of Divine justice, so as to be able from that experience to describe that world in the manner that he has done.

In this, he owns, even after all the Divine enjoyments and communications he had received, that he was still only an unworthy servant in the eye of God and had strictly deserved to be cast alive into hell, according to that dreadful sentence which sounded in his ear as if from the Sovereign Judge. And if this be the mark of an impostor or of a wizard, I must confess that such a one was this known (or rather unknown) person.

But this is not all; there are many other corroborating circumstances of his truthfulness in this matter particularly, which can be produced if needed. And I must say, if he were not innocent of these charges against him, it may be necessary for us to consider how to clear holy Job and David, of whom it is probable that they were similarly made to undergo the pains of hell in their souls for a season.

This lasted for him, in fits, for some years, during which times the heavens were shut to him and he was continually exposed to the buffeting and scourgings of Satan, so that he was enabled to write, as he solemnly says, what he had heard, seen, felt, and tasted in those dismal regions. And in this very treatise, he takes sufficient notice in a few lines of the injustice of the *Demonium*.

Upon all these considerations, and many others that might be mentioned if I were to write a defense, I am (after the most exact inquiry it is possible to make) fully convinced that this very Dr. John Pordage, who is so much slandered—though he was like other men not quite free from human passions and frailties—yet was a man truly fearing God and hating a lie: yes, that he

XVI.—But there still remains a closer prejudice against these writings; that is, even if we suppose they were not devised by another head or forged upon another’s anvil, there is still enough ground to suspect their origin from the style itself in which they are composed—principally from the honorable mention of *magic* found in them, which goes against the practice of the primitive Christians, who condemned all sorts of it, both white and black.

This is indeed a very significant objection, if you have understood this word in the strict and specific sense in which it is used throughout these writings. But allow me to say that I very much doubt whether you have done so; and it is no wonder if, upon a quick reading, we frequently mistake an author’s sense and find our own meaning there, where perhaps the opposite is true. I have done so myself (even in this very case), and therefore can pardon it in another.

And do not let it seem strange to you, Sir, if my mother condemns "white magic," so-called, no less than the primitive Christians did themselves. I am certain that she does so in the sense it is commonly understood. For the whole scope of her writings is clearly against all manner of intercourse even with good demons and angels through certain religious rites and invocations, and against every degree of communion, confederacy, and familiarity with these (even if it could be obtained *without* such rites), except in and through the Spirit of Jesus. In this, she agrees exactly with the sense of the primitive Christians and is no less distant from Porphyrian magic than they were, when both are rightly understood. But this is the specific design of the *Treatise of the Enochian Walks with God*, where this very subject of the communion of saints and angels is expressly delivered, and the method of attaining this communion is proposed according to her own experience.

Therefore, if there were any of this evil science in her, it would certainly be found here, if anywhere.

Instead, quite the contrary is found; no society is recommended with them except as within the body of Jesus Christ, and no way to arrive at this blessed society is declared except through the life of Christ.

Consequently, she condemns all demon-worship of the paganizing Christians, both ancient and modern, and all that <term>εθηλοθρησκια</term> <note>will-worship</note>, and all that pomp of worshipping angels which was condemned by the Apostle in those of Colossae. She does this by making the body of Christ the sole medium and vehicle (if I may say so) of communication with beatified spirits, and assigning no other mediational natures for calling the soul back to the Deity than this one in Him, in whom the fullness (and that of nature also) resided bodily.

And that false humility, which is the foundation of this sort of magic, is so diametrically opposite to the very character and spirit of these writings that if all the libraries of Europe were searched, it would be hard to find any (since the days of the Apostles) that have less of it, or that more directly press into the very bosom and heart of Jesus!

For this counterfeit humility transforms itself in various ways and is discovered to some extent in most writers, even those of the best reputation, as it is the mother of twin offspring that at one time or another govern all mankind (namely, superstition and infidelity) under several disguises or mazes, by the fair names of piety and prudence. From this it is most evident that it could never be the intent of these writings to honor this "white" magic—whose very foundation they entirely overturn—nor the meaning of the author to introduce into Christianity a cult of demons, which is so contrary to what she everywhere aims for: doing all things in the name and power of the Lord Jesus.

This alone is a sufficient characteristic for me of the truth of her spirit and of her distance from whatever savors of the pretended angelic art, the *Ars Paulina*, or the *Key of Solomon*.

I confess my curiosity has led me in the past to look into these, and by this, I am better able to judge in a matter of this nature. Indeed, among all the prayers I have seen in such curious books, printed or manuscript (of which there are many, some of which are very excellent in their substance), I do not remember even one that was offered up to the Father in the name of the Son, explicitly or implicitly. This is the fundamental error of the magic which the ancient Christians so much condemned, and which to this day (as I am well informed) is really practiced by many nominal Christians, even of high rank. For this very cause, I cannot help but place an exceeding value upon the greatest part of the Collects of the English Liturgy, as they seem most directly leveled against this practical error; the same is true of these or any other writings that tend so much to the exaltation of the mediational dignity of our blessed Savior, as might be demonstrated.

Therefore, the word magic in these writings is not to be understood in any sense contrary to the practice or the belief of the first Christians.

But if you would know in what sense it ought to be taken, you need only accept the author’s own explanation of it. The word *Magia*, she says in a marginal note to a book (the most objectionable of any), *is the created power of the Holy Spirit*; it should be understood this way as often as it is named.—Rev. Rev. p. 51. And again, in another marginal note, she says *Magia* is the faith of the operation [energy] of the Holy Spirit. From this, it is clear she means such a Divine faith as existed in the Apostolic Church, being born in the soul by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit as the gift of Christ, to give a demonstration (both internally and externally) of His kingdom and of the subjection of all nature and every creature to His all-powerful will. And however this may have been degraded or condemned by the later and more corrupt ages of Christianity, I humbly conceive that it was not so by the first and purest. <note>See Freher's Treatises and Law's "Way to Divine Knowledge" for the full justification of Behmen's word Magic.</note>

XVII.—The other objections brought against the style of this author are of far less importance and could be weakened without any difficulty by a simple explanation of the terms that cause offense. And though many of them should appear to be borrowed from the customs of unjustifiable curiosities, there is no reason I know of why this should be a more just prejudice against these than against some others found in the Old Testament and also in the New.

Both Judicial Astrologers and Alchemists find in these writings what is very consistent with their own style. The Chaldean Oracles I do not understand; but when they were used by the enemies of Christianity, who knew how to counterfeit and interpolate them for their own purposes, it was then very reasonable to censure them. In the old Platonic divinity there may be as much truth, I am inclined to think, as in either the old Aristotelian or modern Cartesian divinity. I am sure the style of the first is more agreeable to the primitive antiquity of our Christian religion than either of the last. And if this is any objection at all against my mother's style, it will be just as valid against Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, etc. Whether it is so or not against St. John, I do not say.

As for the style of the modern enthusiasts, and all those you classify under that name, let them speak for themselves. However, a true and a false prophet may have the same manner of speaking; and the same character of style may be exactly imitated by persons with a completely opposite intent. You give the example only of *Jacob Boehme*, who is *little understood by anyone*; for whom there is much to be said to prove him to have been no enthusiast at all, in your sense of the word. I am told that the learned *Zimmermanus* has written a very judicious *Apology* for him against a certain professor at Frankfurt. And I know a person of great accuracy of thought and coolness of mind, as well as *of a most holy and primitive life*, <insert>[FREHER? See Roach's Great Crisis, p. 111.]</insert> *who is undertaking to make him intelligible by a true and genuine representation of his Principles, both of Divinity and Philosophy, after having read all his books in the original more than ten times, though not without the greatest imaginable disgust in the beginning.*

And yet I do not find that J. B. anywhere attributes a sacredness to his style; but on the contrary, he supposes it to be full of his own faults, which he was willing to correct by the advice of learned men, his friends. Therefore, living in a place and age where Paracelsian chemistry was greatly favored by many, it is no wonder if he was persuaded to make use of its terms when they were appropriate.

XVIII.—And indeed there is not a greater, and perhaps more grievous mistake, than to imagine *that every person inspired by God is infallibly directed in the use of the phrases and words that express this inspiration.* For if this were once allowed, many bad consequences would naturally flow, which you can see without me listing them in detail. So, even if those points objected to were real faults in the style—and not only those, but several others unmentioned—it is still possible for the substance of the inspiration itself claimed here to be true.

That this is really so, and that God actually accommodates himself to the infirmities (and even the prejudices) of the instrument he chooses, is not difficult, I think, to prove from the histories of Moses, Joshua, the Prophets, and even from that of the Apostles themselves. Now, this is all that is claimed: that the matter of the Revelation, where it is delivered as a revelation, is true; and that the manner of expressing it has been sufficiently cared for, yet not excessively so. Had the latter been more polished, I would have suspected it more, not less. The *Koran* of *Mahomet* is said to have been written in a far better style than the Gospel of Jesus Christ; and you know there are some who criticize his Apostles for writing like barbarians, yet they do not think they thereby lessen their authority or deny that they were guided by the Holy Spirit. Consequently, they maintain the *matter* they deliver to be no less worthy of regard than if every syllable were externally dictated as if by a local voice; therefore, I proceed to your exceptions against the matter itself.

XIX.—But just as imperfections of style are no justifiable prejudice against the sacred authority of the matter revealed, neither is every mistake in the matter itself derogatory to the principal design of the author, even if truly inspired. Justice requires me to distinguish between matters that are less central and accessory, and those that are fundamental and essential; between what is delivered as an express word of revelation, and what may only be a deduction made from it by the soul to whom the revelation came; and lastly, between what may be conditional and what is positive in a revelation, what is mutable and what is immutable, and what is within nature and what is above nature. And if the foundation is true, even if some errors should be found in the superstructure, I shall not be much concerned by them. For if the foundation is Divine, it must remain when whatever human production built upon it is burned up, despite the fact that it might have come from a very innocent and well-meaning intention. Instances of this are to be found among those whom the Catholic Church has always accounted as saints and lights in their generation.

So, if what is essential and given as a clear, express word of revelation does not fail, and if what is positive, immutable, and above nature declared by this word can stand the test, I do not think we are obliged to invalidate what is written, <gloss>[N.B.]</gloss> even if what is accessory and merely a matter of deduction should indeed fail, and what is conditional, mutable, and within nature should seem to suffer loss. St. Cyprian may have been truly illuminated and may have had many of the more extraordinary Divine favors, visions, and voices, yet it is possible for him to have been mistaken on the point of rebaptism and in his revelation about the elements to be consecrated in the Eucharist. Yet I do not positively say that he was so; much less do I dare be as bold with this holy martyr as some Protestant writers are, being satisfied that he was far from being either a dreamer or a cheat.

St. Chrysostom was a burning light in the Catholic Church and certainly had true inspirations himself, and excited others also to believe and wait for the same. Yet he was certainly mistaken in the prophecy of his return from exile. Of St. Augustine, I do not doubt in the least that he was converted by a revelation, and that he was also afterwards followed by perceptible Divine teachings and intellectual openings; if what he has written of these (especially in his book, *De Magistro*) can be believed, there is no question to be made. But I do not therefore think that he was guided at all times without error, or that there was no need for him to write a book of *Retractations*.

Besides these three instances, there are others no less obvious in antiquity; therefore, I cannot help but greatly wonder at the common misunderstanding that infallibility accompanies all those who at certain times have been inspired by the Holy Ghost for a private or public good—no less than the idea held by some others that impeccability is a consequence of regeneration or an effect of ordinary Divine grace, since there appears to me to be one and the same foundation for both of these. And therefore, I do not see but that there is as much need for a spiritual discernment as for a natural one, according to the diversity of the object, whether from revelation or reason.

Nor would it be more unreasonable to reject the many excellent natural truths that are to be

<meta>This page continues the defense of the author’s mother (Jane Lead) and her spiritual writings, shifting from a discussion of literary style to the nature of spiritual fallibility and the specific theological charge of Gnosticism.</meta>

...found in the most rational writers, which they have learned from the common light of mankind by applying it properly, solely because of some errors with which they may be mixed through either a lack of application or misapplication of that standard; than to cast away (or even undervalue) those Supernatural Truths found in the best spiritual writers, which they have learned from the Divine light—the true Light of the world—by means of a right conversion to and application of it, solely because of some mistake committed in the use of this superior standard.

And if in the former case the error may be discerned by its proper light, which is reason, so likewise in the latter may it be discovered by its proper light, which is the Spirit of God, when it is rightly attended to.

Nor is this any greater disparagement to the true Spirit than it is to true reason.

In some sense it may be said that every man is, or may be, infallible; but in another sense no one is, and perhaps cannot be while we are in these bodies.

And truly I am so far from easily attributing infallibility to anyone, however highly illuminated and favored, that I do indeed doubt whether in its strict sense it can be applicable to any but Christ himself.

That the Apostles themselves might be mistaken—both in their understanding of the Scriptures and of their own revelations at times (without derogating from the foundation of the Christian faith)—there are two notorious instances which I think render it more than probable. One is that of St. James, the brother of our Lord, the most stiff asserter of the perpetual obligation of the Mosaic law, grounded upon some expressions in it and confirmed by its universal interpretation.

The other is that of the great St. Paul, who, having had a particular revelation of the glorious return of our blessed Lord, seems to suppose it was then very near, and as a consequence of this, to confound, as it were, the impending fate of Jerusalem with that of the whole world—a private judgment with a universal one, and a temporal deliverance of the Church with the general resurrection of the saints. From this I conclude that it is possible for those who are at some times extraordinarily assisted by the Holy Ghost, and even *filled* with it, to nevertheless err in matters of both faith and practice where they allow themselves to be guided either by tradition (oral or written) or by their own particular deductions drawn from what is revealed.

And thus it is not so extremely surprising that Nicholas the Deacon, *a person full of the Holy Ghost*, was misled himself, or at least was the cause of misleading others into a pernicious error, by a mistake committed by him (or them) in the latter. This serves to keep all humble, and to ensure that everyone takes heed not to exceed the measure of the Spirit given to them, or to frustrate it with substitute sentiments, either of others or of themselves, which has often been done.

XX.—But how it is in the present case, I shall leave you to determine once I have represented the matter as it is, and not as it may at first seem to be.

There are three points which you take notice of and call *antiquated heresies*, which I shall say nothing to vindicate in this place, but only set them in their true light, whether they be heresy or truth, new or old. The first charge is of Gnosticism, from the appearance of introducing a female personality into the Deity. The truth is this: she is accustomed to speak of *Wisdom* in the same manner as Solomon does in his Proverbs and the author of the Book of *Wisdom*; yes, even as Christ himself does in Matthew 11:19. Upon the reading of the first, she had her first vision: and this was the representation of Wisdom under a female figure, presenting the book of *the Holy Trinity* and promising to unseal it.

She supposes this to be an Effluence or Glance from the whole Deity, but principally from the Father, or αυτοθεος <note>God of Himself</note>, the original source of existence and power. It may be called, in accordance with her meaning, by these several names: *Speculum Trinitatis* <note>Mirror of the Trinity</note>, the Tabernacle of God, the Eternal Shekinah, the Heavenly Bethel, the φως απροσιτον <note>unapproachable light</note>, the Throne of God, the *Mundus Divinus* <note>Divine World</note>, the *Vehicle* or *Chariot* of the Divine nature, the *Chasmal* of Ezekiel, the Hand of God, and even more expressly, the *Right Hand of God* where Christ sits. In the famous prayer of Solomon, it is called *Shamaim* <note>Heavens</note>, and addressed by him in 1 Kings 8:32. And in the prodigal’s confession, it is called ο ουρανος <note>the heaven</note>, Luke 15:18. Many other names are given to it by the sacred writers, by philosophers, and by the *illuminati* in the confessedly purest and most infallible ages of the Church—some expressing one character or property, and some another, of this holy Divine principle through which God is conceived by them to descend into Nature and to clothe himself, as it were, with Nature. This is believed by my mother to be like the matrix of all immortal spirits; and more eminently with a particular regard to man, the *true mother church*, the register and fountain της παλιγγενεσιας <note>of regeneration</note>, which must be entered, or rather re-entered, by all; and the womb of the morning of the resurrection, which was seen in an allegory by one Apostle (Galatians 4:26) and in a vision by another (Revelation 21:2).

She calls this by a harsh expression, the *Spouse* or *Bride* of God; yet not without the warrant of the ancient Prophets and Apostles.

She distinguishes, regarding this, the inexistence in God from eternity and the figurative manifestation in time. Of the former she says that *it lay hidden in the Triune Deity (like a plant in a seed)*; of the latter, *it was taken into God’s bosom*. I do not know that she anywhere expressly calls it a *Goddess*; but among some hundreds of places in her writings where this Eternal Virgin nature is mentioned, in only one I find it said she may be termed so (φυσις θεια <note>divine nature</note>, 2 Peter 1:4), because of her near relation to the Godhead. And it is directly opposed to attributing Divine honors to the blessed Virgin Mary, whom no one will strictly call by this name, or Queen of Heaven, except derivatively. However, even if such a limitation of the word had been omitted, if the reasoning of the Apostle is just (1 Cor. 8:9), as also that of Christ himself (John 10:34, 35, 36), it might not have been as altogether indefensible as it at first appears. This Virgin Divine nature she makes to be the true mother or manifestress of Christ before he was born of the blessed Virgin Mary. But as she distinguishes between the hidden internal existence and the figurative manifestation of this Divine nature, she consequently does the same for the Divine WORD manifested by it. And therefore, as she clearly assumes not only an eternal co-existence and internal existence of the WORD within the majesty of the Father while still unmanifested in the creature (as *Λογος ενδιαθετος* <note>Logos endiathetos</note>, or the MIND), but also a visible shaping of this very Word before time and the creature—in eternity, indeed, but yet not properly from all eternity—in order to a manifestation thereof in the creature and time, as the *Λογος προφορομηνος* <note>Logos prophoromenos</note>, or IMAGE of this mind.

Hence according to this latter view, she asserts Christ to be born, or manifested in a glorious figure, out of the Virgin nature of the unmanifested *Σοφια* <note>Sophia</note>. And this manifestation or birth is called the beginning of the works of God, the firstborn of the creatures, the Divine image, the eternal Adam, the Heavenly Humanity, and the Son of Man which came down from heaven.

By means of which she believes that Christ did really appear to Adam, to Enoch, to Noah, to Abraham, to Moses, and to most of the patriarchs and prophets. So that her meaning is, that just as Christ was born of the Virgin Mary in the frail figure of our sinful flesh, so he was also actually brought forth previously in another, more glorious figure by another Virgin—not of the earth, earthly, but of heaven, heavenly—containing in it the primordial matter and life, out of which all created beings were afterwards to proceed. And that this was the Similitude after which Adam was created in his original purity and beauty, which is called by Moses the similitude (or form) of God, and expressly the God of Israel (Exod. 24:10), and by Ezekiel several times the glory of Jehovah, and perhaps by the apostle *μορφη του Θεου* <note>morphe tou Theou</note> (Phil. 2:6). And it was the Goel <note>or kinsman</note> of Job, that was seen and believed in by him (Chapters 19, 25, 41, 11, 5), and the proper medium of communication between God and man in all ages. The glory that appeared in the Jewish temple sitting between the cherubim, and the tree of life in the superior paradise (on which Adam should have fed had he not sinned), therefore called the bread that came down from heaven (*that is, that of Paradise*), the bread of God, the hidden manna—as being most emphatically the *Ζωη* <note>Zoe</note> and the *Λογος Ζωης* <note>Logos Zoes</note> upon which the whole system of *Λογοι* <note>Logoi</note>, that is angels and men, must live—is very often clearly suggested in these writings.

Her meaning is, that Christ had a celestial form before he had a terrestrial, both generated from a Virgin nature by the omnipotent Father. In the former of which he gave his laws and rules to Moses and the prophets. As also Justin Martyr, Theophilus of Antioch, Tertullian, Cyprian, and Eusebius of Caesarea (besides Origen) do:

And in the fullness of time, he was further clothed by the terrestrial form, for the transformation and glorification of our vile forms. She does not deny anywhere that Christ is the Wisdom of God, as well as the offspring of Wisdom: that is, according to this manifestation. But as the Nicene Fathers themselves thought it no robbery to style Christ "Light of Light," though he is called the *Light*, so also she thinks it no robbery to call him the "Wisdom of Wisdom," or to say that he is generated out of the Wisdom (and Light) of the Father, though he is also rightly called the Wisdom.

She does not mean to assert any diversity of sex in the Deity, as the Gentiles and Gnostics did; she is so far from it that she thinks sex did not even belong to the created Humanity in its first and best state, which was paradisiacal, and that it shall again cease to be in the state of the resurrection.

Whether her sentiment is true or not, I am not concerned; but this much at least it proves: that she can never be guilty of such a gross imagination as she is charged with. Consequently, there ought to be a presumption in her favor, rather than against her, where some metaphorical and symbolic expressions are used that are capable of more senses than one. This would be allowed in another case; therefore, I hope it will not be denied here. Since then it will not be unreasonable to interpret these expressions, or the like, according to the logic of the rest of the sentiments of an Author; since the sacred writers themselves do (under a veil) frequently attribute human passions and members to the Deity, which are interpreted in a high and sober sense; since the titles of male and female, when appropriated to the Divine Being, are equally improper; since the characteristics of both are attributed to it in Holy Scripture according to a sound meaning, and that not only in the prophetic writings but in the very epistles of the Apostles; since the common name of God in the book of Job seems to be of a feminine ending, and no less, also, possibly that most high and lofty name of JAH, so frequent in the book of Psalms; and since the female does constitute part of the Divine character in pure and undefiled nature as well as the male, she being designed as the *glory* and crown of the head; and lastly, since the glory of God may be considered distinct from God himself (though in him and out of him, Heb. 1:3), it does not appear why her words should be interpreted in a low and gross sense when they are capable of a higher one, which is neither dissonant from Scripture or antiquity, nor derogatory to the simplicity and spirituality of the Divine Being.

And in this high sense, she supposes the *glory of God* to have pre-existed in God, as Eve did in Adam, before the *Απαυγασμα* <note>Apaugasma</note> thereof broke forth in the visible person of the *Λογος* <note>Logos</note>, and was produced as if out of the womb of this glory, being no other than the Eternal Wisdom itself (called by her both a Virgin and a Mother) going forth into manifestation in the said glorious Person, by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made that was made. He being properly *Χαρακτηρ της* <unclear>      </unclear> *του Θεου* <note>Charakter tes ... tou Theou</note>, in his laying the foundation of all things and still upholding the same, as her writings elsewhere declare. The meaning of Tertullian, to whom you refer me in another case, may perhaps deserve to be considered a little. In his book against Hermogenes—as if either he had conversed with my mother, or my mother with him—he writes thus:

<margin>1</margin>
> Prophecies and Apostles record that first WISDOM was established as the beginning of his ways for his works. Then also the WORD was brought forth, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. Chapters 18, 23, 49.

<margin>2</margin>
Whether he delivers this as his own private opinion, or as an apostolical tradition; and whether what he has written in other books concerning the Divine body ought to be understood as crudely as it generally is, and not rather soberly—and in the same (or nearly the same) way as the former, according to catholic prescription—I leave to be considered. But if this Father’s meaning in his controversial writings against the heretics of his age is either defensible or excusable in this regard, then my mother’s cause is not as bad as you might imagine, even in the area where it has been thought the weakest.

<margin>3</margin>
Indeed, his and her meanings are so alike that I cannot distinguish them apart; and I have not lacked diligence in finding out what is truly hers, or sincerity in representing it, so that judgment may be passed on it accordingly.

<margin>4</margin>
XXI.—But there is another stumbling block, which is (and unless this block can be removed, all that was said otherwise will be to no purpose): *that she is inconsistent with herself*. Now, whatever foundation there may be for such a charge against her in any other particular, I do not dispute; but in this, I can see none. Well, does she not make the Virgin Wisdom born under the planets Sol and Venus—planets created by her own son? If she does so, I will confess all that you would have me do. And if she does *not*, I trust that the great generosity and integrity of your soul will not let you be ashamed to acknowledge that you have misunderstood her, and also that it will incline you more strongly than ever to forgive another when they are mistaken.

<margin>5</margin>
It is true that she does make use of these terms, which did indeed shock me for a considerable time; but she also forewarns us to take them in a sober sense. She expressly declares only a few lines before that she did not intend the planetary names to mean what the astrologers do, or the inferior and visible planets, which they claim have dominion over man as long as he is in subjection to the curse. Rather, she means the superior and invisible ones, which are so many Divine powers, properties, attributes, modes, energies, etc., that deliver us from the curse. Moreover, it is evident that she speaks not of the birth of wisdom as it is in eternity, but only as it is in time; not of her origin before the world, but of her manifestation in the world; not of her first manifestation in this our orb, but of her descent again into it, after she had been forced (by the fall) to forsake it; not of the progression of the Divine form (or beauty) through the universal system of beings, which was in the beginning, but of that in one particular order of them, which is yet to happen in the end.

<margin>6</margin>
She speaks of its renovation, restitution, reproduction, and regeneration, evidently assuming a previous rise and formation, as is clear both from the main point of that very book from which this objection is raised, and the passage itself to which I suppose it may refer. The words are these: *Therefore it is entirely worthy to be inquired, in what planet the birth of the Virgin may be again RENEWED? Which must be by bright Venus, which must bring forth the mighty birth under Sol; in conjunction with the rest of the SUPERIOR planets, which are all harmonized in one, etc.* Revelation p. 24. And in the manuscript, with some little variation, I read thus: *Which must be by serene Venus, that must bring forth the mighty birth under bright Sol, etc.*

<margin>7</margin>
Again, shortly after, these words also occur: *The Divine mold for her SHAPE is again found according to what it was BEFORE either angels or men were formed, which is not to be portrayed until she comes to be essentially manifested within it.*

<margin>8</margin>
From which it is evident, I think, that she can mean nothing but a certain manifestation to the soul of man—not superficial, but essential—of some pre-existent substance that is spiritu-corporeal. But to express what her mind means by this (which depends upon a thorough understanding of that whole book, and of the nature and progress of the Divine kingdom which she expects) cannot be done in a few words.

<margin>9</margin>
The terms of <term>Sol</term> and <term>Venus</term>, which are not chosen at random, ought for this purpose to be well understood in a sense that is both physical and metaphysical. And however harsh or unjustifiable these may seem, yet they are not without a basis even in Scripture: the one in Psalm 19:4, 5, 6; the other in 2 Peter 1:19 and Revelation 11:28.

<margin>10</margin>
We may call one of them *Light*, and the other *Love*, or *passive Love*. Or we may regard one as the energy of the Son of God, and the other as that of the Divine Spirit. But whatever other names we substitute in their place, there will still remain something in these hieroglyphics that is unexpressed.

<margin>11</margin>
The mystery of the Divine numbers, if there be any such, lies hidden here. And the seven spirits before the Father’s throne, from whom the greatest of mystics wishes grace and peace (Revelation 4), are these superior planets—those high and exalted powers which must all concur, in the most perfect harmony, to the formation and production of this mighty birth, so frequently spoken of in these writings, and to which all the powers and wonders of the kingdom of Christ are assigned.

<margin>12</margin>
She always supposes this to be the way of natural causality, corresponding to outward and fallen nature, and not by such a rushing, temporary influx as descended on most (if not all) in the first proclamation of this kingdom after the ascension of our Lord.

<margin>13</margin>
And this, according to the spirit of these writings, is the establishment of the <term>Melchisedechian</term> priesthood in his members. Upon them He does not merely reflect his image, as the visible sun reflects its image on the waters; but in them he represents himself really and vitally, and produces in them his express likeness, just as the same sun also, in a lower degree, brings forth its likeness in all the subjects of temporal nature. He stands properly as the tree of life in the midst of our <term>vortex</term>, without whom all the visible things contained within it would presently be dead.

<margin>14</margin>
So this royal manifestation, or birth of these holy, priestly <term>Magi</term>, is said to be *under Sol*, that is, under the direct rays and immediate communication of the Divine and invisible Sun, who has become to them the tree of life and immortality, on which they continually feed, without danger from the cherub of Moses or the chariot of Elias.

And such a continued participation in His light and life may, in a sober sense, not unfitly be called an eternal and substantial generation. According to which, everyone who is called of God,

<meta>This page continues the defense of Jane Lead’s mystical theology, specifically addressing the nature of the "Virgin Wisdom" and her role in the spiritual rebirth and the eternal priesthood, building on the previous discussion of Tertullian's views.</meta>

<margin>1</margin>
...as Melchisedec was, he must be both *without father* ($\alpha\pi\alpha\tau\omega\rho$) and *without mother* ($\alpha\mu\eta\tau\omega\rho$) with regard to his eternal generation, according to the express appointment of Christ in Mark 10:29, 30 and Luke 14:26, and also his example in Matthew 12:46—50. From this he will likewise be *without genealogy* ($\alpha\gamma\varepsilon\nu\varepsilon\alpha\lambda\text{o}\gamma\eta\tau\text{o}\varsigma$), that is, without any genealogy, whether paternal or maternal, in this mortal world. He calls no man father on earth and does not depend upon any mother—not even the universal mother of all flesh—as he has one Father in heaven and one mother, which is the New Jerusalem. He is therefore said to be *redeemed*, or separated, *from among men and out of the earth*; he is said to be a virgin—that is, without succession or *end of days*—and is figuratively represented to us as standing outside of this gross atmosphere upon a high and glorious mountain.

<margin>2</margin>
Now, to arrive at this eminent state and honor of the everlasting priesthood belonging to the first fruits, according to the present theory, it is required that there be a preceding state of revelation and a Divine vision opened in the soul. It also requires that all the spiritual faculties, senses, and powers, which will be manifested in the future life, be manifested in this one (p. 43, 44). This state is continually attributed by the author to Wisdom, and in this place is named her *renewed nativity*, as it is distinguished from the succeeding state, which she attributes to the WORD, according to the former distinction of the African father <note>Tertullian</note>. And this state is much more noble than the former. For though the first state is here represented as *exceeding glorious*, and is really so in itself, it falls vastly short of the glory that is revealed in *this other* state. This other state is no less than the very brightness and refulgent character of the glorified person of Christ, as the firstborn from the dead. Therefore, to this state—as derived through Him—is applicable that most eminent decree of God in Psalm 11:7, upon which the order of this priesthood (treated of at length there, p. 92) is founded. She thinks it may as well be called a *birth* as that which is but the beginning of a low and mortal life. The one is a state that is *all glorious within* but vile and contemptible without; the other is glorious outwardly also, and makes the vile become honorable. The one is like the pattern of the other and contains the other in its womb. But for both, there is required the exact harmonization of the powers of the world to come and of the seven principal emanations from the throne of the Divine Majesty, so that nothing is redundant or defective, and nothing is disproportionate or discordant.

<margin>3</margin>
Therefore, it is said they *agree to bring forth* (or manifest) the Mother and then the Son in the Virgin humanity. And just as the fetus receives its figure and form in the womb of its mother and from her earthly matter, so in this author's sense, this state receives both from the *heavenly matter* of undefiled Virgin nature.

<margin>4</margin>
In these writings, they are called by almost as many different names as the most kabbalistic authors have been able to invent, either for the *prima materia* <note>first matter</note> or the *summum bonum* <note>highest good</note> in nature. But the most ordinary names are the *birth of Wisdom* and the *birth of Power*.

<margin>5</margin>
The last consists of that which is the new creation, while the first consists of the idea of it. In this idea, the generative or prolific virtue (expressed here by the term *Magia*) is included; it is therefore called the Divine Venus, in a sense well understood by many of the ancients. And as all generations in the fallen state of Adam's transgression proceed from the earthly and impure Venus (who truly sits as a queen upon the beast of nature and can be said to be the Goddess or idol of all flesh)—that is, as they come out of the same polluted mass and seminal corruption—so do all the heavenly generations. The children of God who are brought forth in regeneration and resurrection, according to the restored state of Christ's righteousness, proceed from this heavenly and pure Venus (that is, as the virgin clothed with the sun) out of the same one undefiled substance and seed of incorruption, which some have significantly named the *One Element*. [Refer here and hereafter to the note on p. 111, which is by this writer.]

Also, just as the planet Venus, when it is a morning star, arises before the sun and yet does not shine by any other light than what proceeds from the sun; so, in like manner, the morning star of Wisdom—allowing for the present hypothesis—may be properly said to arise in the soul before the Sun of the intellectual world comes forth out of his Chuppah <note>bridal canopy or chamber</note>. Yet it may shine in the soul by no other light but what is reflected by this Sun while he remains in the Chuppah; this is a preceding, internal ministration of familiar Divine converse, preparatory to the more public and glorious manifestation which is to succeed in the coming out together of the bridegroom and the bride.

Now, should we suppose the outward sun to be the creator of that outward planetary body, the star of Venus, and that because the light of this star is produced from the light of this sun and is inferior to it; yet, nonetheless, I do not see any inconsistency or even inconvenience in mentioning the said star as being either before the sun or after the sun, according to different perspectives. And so it will be with the superior star of Venus, according to the same hypothesis.

For if there be any such star or power in the intellectual or angelic world corresponding to that which appears to us in the visible heavens—though it be inferior to the light of the intellectual and angelic sun and have no more than a derivative light from its light—yet with respect to manifestation, it may be conveniently and truly said to be before it.

Nor is that which is manifested, in the order of science, known after that by which it is manifested, imaged, generated, or even created; but on the contrary. These different perspectives are sufficiently distinguished by this author.

XXII.—Moreover, that which appears so very confused at first reading, and the mere product of imagination, is perfectly agreeable to the principles of the most *acute and deep Philosophy* that I have ever met with.

And as the most regular system of the universe favors the same, so likewise many passages in the Holy Scripture are not (as far as I can apprehend) otherwise intelligible.

This has been very surprising to me; but I cannot expatiate into particulars here, nor stay to lay down those principles in their proper light, or to produce those passages and apply them as would be necessary. Only, *in transitu* <note>in passing</note>, I observe that as astronomers now make the sun the center of our vortex or world, so do these philosophers make their Sun (as distinguished from both the unoriginated sun and from the first-begotten image of it) the center of every vortex and world, both visible and invisible.

And this sun, in the Septenary System of spirits, they place as the fourth or middlemost; calling

...much if the fourth form, the fourth power, fountain, or spirit of Nature; the Fire, the Holy Fire, <term>Ignis Magorum</term>, the Cross, and Tree of Life, universal and eternal. So that the birth of Wisdom in the soul, by opening within it the secrets of the invisible worlds—the soul becoming like a clear, unspotted mirror to receive their reflections—cannot happen, according to the principles of the *true central philosophy*, except under the fourth form and fountain of nature, i.e., under <term>Sol</term>. And they show, consequently, how this magical birth, originated under the fourth, cannot be brought forth except by the help of the fifth form of nature, called the fountain of Love and Venus, in conjunction with the rest of the superior forms, fountains, powers, and spirits, constituting the <term>wheel of Nature</term>, which some think St. James alludes to in iii. 6. Particularly, they explain the harmonization of the Seven Spirits of God and the conjunction of the seven forms of incorruptible nature in this way: the fifth with the third, the sixth with the second, and the seventh with the first; so that out of each conjunction there arises an eternal harmony in the perfect octave, an eternal circulation of love and joy in the soul. All these Spirits and forms being thus harmonized in *One*, which is the fourth, standing in the midst of the rest, they explain that the fifth contains the sixth in its womb, and the first combination of forms flows into the second; this second is the reproduction in the soul of the image of the *Word*, just as the first was the image of the *Wisdom*. And they explain that the seventh finishes the whole mystery of God in nature, by the third and last combination receiving the other two into itself, which is the Sabbath of nature, beyond which it cannot go.—All this perfectly agrees with what has caused so much scandal in the writings of an illiterate woman. [See p. 43, (e.)]

XXIII.—And this may be enough to show you that she is not inconsistent with herself or with principles in the current account you were pleased to urge. There must be something more than *ungoverned fancy* to speak so consistently with what she has delivered elsewhere, and so in line with the principles of a *certain Philosophy*, which requires more than *ordinary penetration* of spirit to understand even *in part*. Much abler persons are ready to defend the truth of these Principles. However, no matter how much these are disputed, it can hardly be denied that she has written according to them with a wonderful, consistent harmony. It is plain that terms taken from arts she did not understand have nevertheless been managed by her as if she understood them perfectly. Some also understand these two births as occurring both outwardly in nature and inwardly in the soul. In the former interpretation, they say the process of the renovation of all things is hidden, through a new virgin earth and new virgin heaven, according to the famous prophecy of St. Peter applied to this. Also, besides this universal regeneration, which is two-fold, there are grounds in nature to believe in a particular regeneration, likewise two-fold. This regeneration of certain individual subjects, such as plants, etc., which some chemists speak of so much, would—according to the description given—greatly clarify this matter, if it were proper to expand on it here. For this reason, I have heard even some mechanically-minded people, busy with the examination of nature, greatly admire certain passages in her writings; they said they found them to be exactly consistent with the truth of experimental philosophy, of which she herself could not yet be supposed to have any knowledge at all.—Therefore, I conclude that she cannot be justly charged with introducing a difference of sex in the divinity, or with inconsistencies and unintelligible jargon on this point; but that she must have had the assistance of some superior intelligence in her account of wisdom. <note>[! which the reader, in the course of the following pages, may suspect to be Lee himself !]</note>

XXIV.—The next charge against her writings is the Manichean heresy of *two co-eternal principles in the Deity*. But here also, I doubt much whether she has been fully understood. I do not see anything that might seem to favor this except for the private resolution of a question put to her; she does not say she received the answer from any voice or vision, as she frequently does; therefore, it might as well have come from reason as from a more questionable principle. And if she reasons wrongly here on a point that the wisest heads have not been able to unravel, yet what is said elsewhere to be from express revelation may nevertheless be true.

But whether what she declares in the *Postscript to the Enochian Walks* (which is the only passage of this nature) is from her own reasoning or from revelation, her meaning may perhaps not be as heretical as it is at first easy to assume; indeed, it may be as far from the doctrine of <term>Manes</term> as the most common view today. This can be shown from what she delivers elsewhere, speaking again to this very question: she says, "hell, death, destruction, and the lake are of themselves." And if they are of themselves, they are not from God or in God; and there can be no co-eternal principle of evil in or with the Deity from which they could have originated. She opposes the imperfect act of a created being to the perfect act of the Creator: and the confusion and disorder of evil arising from the one, to the unity and harmony of good existing in and flowing from the other. She makes good natural and evil preternatural; good is eternal, without beginning or end, and evil is temporary, having both a beginning and an end. All this seems to me directly opposite to the condemned doctrine of <term>Manes</term> and <term>Valentinian</term>, which makes evil no less natural and eternal than good, and attributes its origin not to the creature but to the Creator himself.

Nor is it simply asserted by her that hell and death, etc., are not of God but of themselves; for it is a conclusion she draws from the premises she had laid down—premises which are exactly consistent with the principles she previously followed in the *Postscript*.

These turn upon the manifestation of God in nature and the breach of the original bond of nature established by Him. Now, as all variety is contained in this bond and branches out from it, as soon as this is broken, disorder and confusion must necessarily arise instead of order and beauty, because the will of the creature is separated from the Divine will to act independently and by itself.

This will appear to be the origin of evil according to her meaning. The only difficulty will be how this variety in the bond could proceed at first out of the eternal Unity. But whatever way is taken to account for the creation, this difficulty will recur just the same.

The easiest way, according to the chain of principles upon which all this turns, is this: The <term>UNITY</term> is the beginning and the center of the variety, which variety was contained in the unity. The variety is generated from the unity and is the goal of the unity, and must return back into the unity; the harmony proceeds from both the unity and variety together. In the unity without the variety, there could be no harmony; and in the variety without the unity, there

could spring up nothing but contrariety. This UNITY, VARIETY, and HARMONY existed before the angelic creation; it was in the angelic creation, and it was after it.

It was before, in, and after all creations whatever in the Deity: and after all creations and revolutions that are to be, it will still be in the Deity, throughout all the circles of eternity, when all shall be in all—Deity in nature and nature in Deity.

<margin>2</margin>
This unity, variety, and harmony were in all the angels at their creation, when they sang together for joy; and it would have forever continued in them all, had not some of them dared to test the *might of their own wills*, by which the harmony was perfectly broken when they did not return back into the unity through a humble resignation of their wills. And so, through the variety, the contrariety broke forth. In this contrariety is evil, and it springs up out of the separation of the perfect band of nature. In this band, while unbroken, every created being was to have existed eternally; and therefore it was called an Eternal Band, and this nature, Eternal Nature—that is, immortal and incorruptible nature. There would have been an eternal circulation of life, light, and love in the unity, through the variety, by the harmony, if this eternal band had not been violated, as to some, in the angelic nature. And there is such an eternal circulation of life, light, and love in all where it has not been violated, or where, having been once violated, it is again renewed.

<margin>3</margin>
On the contrary, while this band remains broken or dislocated, no created being can exist eternally, but is made subject to vanity; there can be no circulation of life in the creature thus made subject. There may, indeed, be a temporal circulation of life in this state, but the vanity which is in the creature, and which flows from the contrariety, cannot live forever. The vanity of the creature is not eternal, but as it stands in the contrariety, it must pass away with the contrariety sooner or later, for it cannot subsist outside of the contrariety. And the contrariety must be at last conquered, unless there be two contrary co-eternal and co-equal principles—that is, two Gods; and being conquered, it must pass away into the harmony. And thus, entering again into the harmony of Divine Love through the most beautiful variety of the heavenly light, it centers in the original unity, which is the very life of God. Therefore, where there is an eternal circulation of life, there must also be an eternal circulation of light and love in the band of perfect nature, without any contrariety or any disharmony.

<margin>4</margin>
And if the creature, through the contrariety and through the disharmony, is made subject to vanity for a long duration of ages—the better to display the wonders of both time and eternity—this contrariety must, in the end, be made subject itself to Him who is the head of the whole creation, the Alpha and beginning of it, in and by whom the variety of all things created were manifested in perfect harmony; and who alone is able to subdue everything to himself. Whereupon, all disharmony in the creature must vanish away, all things being again put under his feet, as it was in the beginning, through the all-powerful harmony of love prevailing over that which has stood in the greatest opposition to it.

<margin>5</margin>
In the contrariety stands all evil, death, darkness, and wrath; in the harmony stands all good, life, light, and love. When the harmony subdues the contrariety of nature, then death is swallowed up in life, darkness in light, and the wrath of God in his love; and all the evil in the creature, whether of sin or of punishment, vanishes away as if it had never been. This is the victory of the Divine Harmony in the spirit of CHRIST.

<margin>6</margin>
But when the contrariety breaks the harmony of nature, whether in angels or in men (which can only happen during the times of their probation), violating the natural subordination of their wills to the Divine will and not centering in the supreme unity from which they primarily originated: all manner of evil must be expected to proceed out of this breach and violation of eternal Nature, according to the degrees of the contrariety and the proportion of the disorder, multiplicity, and confusion arising from it in the creature that has departed from the fountain of its unity.

<margin>7</margin>
Thus death, they say, entered into the world through the transgression (or deviation from the unity) of one head angel, or angelic patriarch, and then of one man, or patriarchal head of the human race. By this, both the angelic and human natures in those hierarchies of Lucifer and Adam were as totally separated and divorced from the original source of their life and from the unity and harmony of the Divine Being, which had before contained the variety in them and kept all in its proper place and station, unviolated. And thus, through this disharmony and separation, life disappeared in death, light vanished in darkness, and love clouded itself in wrath. Yet the life was in death, the light in darkness, and the love in wrath. But the death could not comprehend the life, nor the darkness the light, nor the wrath the love. So the life, the light, and the love were now unmanifested and incomprehended, just as death, darkness, and wrath were before unmanifested and incomprehended, standing only as a faint shadow in the creature; and they could never have been manifested or comprehended by the creature except through the contrariety of feeding on the knowledge of good and evil, life and death, etc. And these should never have been manifested to all eternity except for the better display of the wonders, the glories, and the triumphs of the eternal Life, the eternal Light, and the eternal Love.

<margin>8</margin>
But being manifested, they do not yet have a positive existence in themselves, as everything derived from God has. They do not have their existence in the band of Nature, for that is good, yes, very good; but they have it outside of this band. Therefore, their existence—and consequently the existence of all evil—is more relative than real, more negative than positive.

<margin>9</margin>
For their existence is formally nothing else but the separation and disunion of this sacred band, which was derived from God entire. And their manifestation in nature (as it is now fallen and broken) is but the hiding of the Divine love, light, and life in the creature, or from the creature; so that God becomes to it like a hidden God, an angry God, a God inhabiting thick darkness and a consuming fire. And yet, in this, there is not the least variation in God, the Spirit of eternity. Nor is there any new existence, or new degree of existence, given from this to the spirits in time. Nor is anything new produced (despite this change in the creature) which was not already before in the band of nature, actually or potentially, but only a loss and breach effected in the same.

Notwithstanding which, as God is, so also Nature remains invariable, according to its eternal order that was given to it in the beginning; which is good, and eternally good. So that the good which

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of the author’s mother (likely Jane Lead), moving from the nature of the "eternal band" to the specific origins of evil and its relationship to Divine Justice.</meta>

<margin>1</margin> [Good] in nature has an existence most real and positive, and also eternal; but the evil which is introduced into nature, or manifested by the separation of nature's eternal band and law, does not exist in this manner. Instead, it stands as a dark shadow in opposition to the Divine Light and Truth; and hence death is called a shadow, hell is called outward darkness, and sin is called blindness.

<margin>2</margin> For this blindness and darkness have only a shadowy existence, resulting from the violation of original nature—appearing as angelic in one order of beings, and paradisiacal in another.

<margin>3</margin> And yet, had there not been the potentiality and root of darkness in nature, neither the outward darkness nor the inward blindness could ever have sprung up, or been made to exist in any way within either of these two orders of beings.

<margin>4</margin> And had there not also been something in the Deity to be manifested or glorified through this potentiality and root, it could never have existed in nature in any manner; or even supposing it were in nature, it never could have been brought forth from there. Instead, it must have remained forever hidden as a mere empty and impotent possibility, as it is in the blessed angels and perfect spirits.

<margin>5</margin> Now, what that quality in the Deity is which was to be manifested through this dark root of nature is not difficult to see. It must be good in itself, because it is in the Deity; but it may not be good to the creature, because all that is in the Deity is not communicable or manifestable to any created being, except according to that being's proportion of aptitude.

<margin>6</margin> It cannot be positively evil; but it may be relatively evil where it meets with disproportion and disharmony. Indeed, it must be positively and essentially good, but it may not be good for the creature to taste it.

<margin>7</margin> This is no other than the severe Justice of God, which could not be manifested before the birth of contrariety. This Divine justice is both darkness and light, both death and life, yes, both good and evil, according to different perspectives in the creature. But before the contrariety of the creature arises, it is unmanifested; it exists in the Unity, and not in the divided root of good and evil, wherein the knowledge of it can only be obtained. And this is no less glorious and excellent in itself than the Divine Mercy, which also could not help but remain unmanifested without the existence of contrariety.

<margin>8</margin> But because it is terrible and unbearable to the creature, it bears the relation of evil and encompasses manifold scenes of misery. All of these serve to more fully unfold the mystery of the kingdom of Christ, the beatitudes of the saints in light, and the exceeding riches of the Divine Goodness, as well as to a higher manifestation of the wisdom, power, and holiness of the infinite Creator, which will be eternally surprising. Therefore, if that which is glorious is also terrible, and that which is good in the Creator is evil in the creature when divided from his root, then that which is glorious and good in *Him* may yet, in the creature and with respect to the creature, be termed dreadful and evil. This is said without any design to promote the condemned heresy of Manes, or to deny the unity and simplicity of the Godhead. And this is no more than what the infallibly inspired Divine writers of both the Old and New Testaments have done, of which you cannot help but observe frequent instances. These instances, not having been understood by many for want of a very easy distinction between GOD in Nature and GOD above Nature,<note>Nor was it possible to be understood before God's revelation of "the mystery," or the philosophy of things.</note> has caused them foolishly to make God the author of evil—most of them, indeed, by logical consequence, but some even directly. This would have been impossible to do if they had known how Divine justice or Divine mercy, though they are two in nature, are yet only one in God; or how God in nature, as the supreme universal cause, acts in the divided root of nature while still remaining in His own eternal unity. In this eternal unity all things, according to this writer, are comprehended; and were in the beginning comprehended as they were created and flowed forth out of it, through variety, into the harmony of nature. Thus she constitutes one undivided principle in the Deity, containing all principles, elements, and seeds in an eternal temperature. And she considers the Deity in a transcendental sense, above all that is called material or spiritual, dark or light, mortal or immortal, terrestrial or celestial, and above all names, specific or general. So, matter and spirit, darkness and light, life and death, earth and heaven, may be said to be in God, or not to be in God, according to different relations; and both may be said without injury to the eternal unity and the eternal harmony of God. Now, how far this is from making two co-eternal Gods, or two co-eternal principles in one God—one good, the other evil—how far this is both from the *Chaldean* doctrine regarding their *Oromasdes* and *Arimanius*, or from the *Valentinian* regarding their *Achamoth* and *Ananche*, I leave you, Sir, to determine.

XXV.—The third charge of heresy against her writings is that called the Origenian, for maintaining the finiteness of hell torments.

But if this is a heresy, it is absolutely inconsistent with the origin of good and evil from two co-eternal principles in the Deity. For if they are co-eternal *a parte ante* <term>from the beginning</term>, they must necessarily be co-eternal *a parte post* <term>into the future</term>, and consequently the torments of hell must be as infinite as the joys of heaven. This consequence is so natural and easy that everyone must see it. And therefore, if the torments are to be believed as so infinite in their duration that they do not cease before God ceases to be, it is impossible for me (I must confess) not to agree with the Manichean doctrine, or to refuse to believe in an eternal principle of evil as well as of good—that is, an eternal root and cause of hell in the Deity. But while I believe the torments of hell, and consequently all evil, to be finite, it is impossible for me to believe the principle and root of evil to have been co-eternal with the good *a parte ante*. And therefore, if by such an easy train of thought I am driven to embrace one of these two doctrines, I would much rather incline toward that which makes only the principle of good to be eternal both *a parte ante* and *a parte post*, than toward that which makes the principles of both good and evil to be so in like manner. Since it appears equally absurd to believe in two universal principles (the one good and the other evil) eternal *a parte ante* and yet only one of them eternal *a parte post*; as it is to believe in one universal principle eternal *a parte ante* and two co-eternal principles *a parte post*, standing immutably in opposition to each other.

Therefore, it being impossible for anyone to hold at once the finite duration of evil with Origen, and the infinite duration of it in both respects with *Manes*; and my mother having so professedly expressed herself in favor of the former, and never professedly in favor of the latter, she ought
