not to be accused of believing this, which is so inconsistent and impossible with the other position, and is also absurd, harmful, and blasphemous.

<margin>1</margin>
XXVI.—But that position of the finite duration of evil and the infinite duration of good, however harmful it may seem at first in this age of license, is certainly not against the light of reason or against the honor of the Divine Majesty. There is neither absurdity nor blasphemy in it. And if it is harmful, it must be so to those who do not understand it. In this way, the most undeniable truths of the Christian religion may accidentally be harmful to many. Indeed, it is undeniably true that the common doctrine itself has not been without its harmful consequences.

<margin>2</margin>
And if this doctrine of universal restoration or the final annihilation of evil is reconcilable with the Scriptures (as some men of no small learning and piety assert), then there will not be the slightest shadow of difficulty remaining as to why it should not be embraced. For I consider it no difficulty at all that the books of that great and holy man, whose name is famous for it <note>This refers to Origen of Alexandria</note>, were publicly prohibited about three hundred years after his death by a council that gave the greatest boost to establishing papal supremacy; or that it was privately condemned by some famous persons in the church who were notoriously biased, a hundred and fifty years before and about as many after his death. It does not appear from this that it might not have been a doctrine of the universal Church, or at least held as piously probable in the second and third centuries. Or if it were not then publicly known as a general doctrine, but reserved only among some few who were initiated into the mysteries, it does not appear from that that it should not be published now, or that it is unsound because it was unfit for *every age*.

A clear view of the facts and the truth will be the best evidence that can be desired here.

<margin>3</margin>
XXVII.—The substance of her doctrine on this point is plainly this: angels and men were created by God to be eternally happy by loving and enjoying Him. So that they might eternally love and eternally enjoy God, they were made partakers of the Divine nature at their creation. This participation in the Divine nature consisted in the communication to them of the Divine Life, Divine Light, and Divine Love, by which they were, as it were, branches growing out of the Deity; they were to have lived forever in the Deity as their root and fountain. God communicated himself to angels and to men in the unity of his life, in the variety of lights, and in the harmony of love. He did this so that they might love him, and by loving him, behold him, and by beholding him, be transformed into the exact image of his life, which is eternal life to both the angelic and human creation. By this communication of Himself, he did not intend that any angel or man should hate him forever, should turn away from him forever, or should be transformed forever into a shadow of death. It was in the power of angels and men to interrupt this Divine communication within themselves, but it was not in their power to cut it off totally, any more than it was in their power to create themselves or to annihilate themselves, since it entered into their original constitution.

<margin>4</margin>
The original root of all spirits is the Divine Being, and their beginning or root must not be different from their end. Their author and finisher is God; their beginning and end is Christ; their first and last life is the divine Spirit in harmonious concord and blessed unity.

<margin>5</margin>
One great angel was permitted to go away from the face (that is, the light) of God, and so, leaving his first place and station, he was not only distinct but separated and turned away from his original source. And thus, not keeping his *beginning* and native principality (Jude 1:6) but running from it in the power of his will, he entered into opposition against God and against his beginning, which was the eternal Light of life. And by this, he first broke that heavenly harmony which was in the bond of angelic nature; and instead of it, a sinful disorder broke out. This being broken by one angel, other angels, finding the same liberty in their wills to remain in unity (with God) or to go out in opposition (from God), they immediately consented with him to the latter, which appeared to be the more noble, powerful, and great of the two.

<margin>6</margin>
They found where their might and strength lay, and so they awakened what they could not fathom the nature of. Now their strength was their *fire*: the fire of nature, spiritual and eternal fire.

<margin>7</margin>
This fire was good while it was in union with the spiritual and eternal light, but as soon as it was separated from it, it became evil and the root of all evil. Thus sin was conceived and evil brought forth in the angelic heavens by the fiery strength of the Luciferian spirits, which was not kept within its bounds in a meek humility, and was parted from the Divine Light. Being separated from that light, they could no longer remain in their angelic principle.

<margin>8</margin>
Therefore, man was created by God in their place, and <term>essenced</term> a little lower than they. And by this, it was provided that his fall should not be as great as theirs, if he likewise should not keep his first estate and beginning. He was created upright, but he stood in a free liberty regarding either the good or the evil. Both angels and men were created good, but before the end of their probation, they were to be made immutably good.

<margin>9</margin>
Immutability of good is in God alone, and therefore every creature, intellectual and rational, must be mutable toward good and evil before their fixation in him. But after their fixation in him, as in the fountain of their being, they become immutable toward evil and are unchangeably good, as he is eternally good.

<margin>10</margin>
The image of the Eternal Goodness is also eternal. The *eternal image* of God, in which man was created, could not be destroyed by man, for he stood <term>essenced</term> in it as to his superior part. Yet it might disappear to man by the superposition of another image, which accordingly happened. For the fallen angels, envying this new and heavenly image in man, conspired how they might involve him in the same state as themselves and make him bear their likeness.

<margin>11</margin>
And as he was <term>essenced</term>, as to his inferior part, in that very matter which they knew how to defile and had actually defiled in themselves, they more easily carried out their conspiracy.

<margin>12</margin>
This was the poison and seed of the serpent cast into human nature; and the fountain being poisoned, from this came the infection of all mankind. The universal human nature being infected, a universal antidote was then prepared to expel all the poison. This must have its effect sooner or later and cannot be resisted by any particular, inferior, or subordinate causes. In some, it has its effects in this life, and they are the firstborn and the firstfruits; in others, it does not have effects until after this life, and they are the later born and the latter fruits.

<margin>13</margin>
The principle or seed of sin and defilement in the fall of angels extended to the curse of that heaven where Lucifer was king; and so a hell was prepared there for him and his angels.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the doctrine of universal restoration, specifically outlining the degrees of purification for different souls and the eventual reconciliation of all creation to God.</meta>

<margin>1</margin>
The principle and seed of sin and corruption, and sin in the fall of humanity, extended only to the curse of that earth (along with its atmosphere) of which Adam was king. And so the earth was corrupted and defiled. And death was prepared for him and his descendants. This death is experienced in both soul and body by every person, as everyone is under the same condemnation. And the great degeneration of the soul from the Divine life, and of the body from the paradisiacal life, was a true and literal death when man was cast out onto this accursed earth.

<margin>2</margin>
And corresponding to this twofold death, there is a twofold resurrection to be achieved by every person, but by each one in his own order: the principle and seed of holiness and incorruption extends itself no less universally to all.

<margin>3</margin>
The seed and principle of corruption, passed on to all mankind, has a greater influence in some individuals from the start than in others; yet in no one does it extend so far on its own that anyone shall be condemned for it to the flames of hell. Hell was not prepared for fallen man, but for the devil and his angels. Therefore, none of mankind can be cast into hell, strictly speaking, to suffer the second death, except those who, through unbelief and disobedience, have worked together with the devil and his angels and loved darkness rather than light.

<margin>4</margin>
Consequently, all who die as minors—at or under the age of about twelve years—have a certain world or kingdom allotted to them (which she calls the children's kingdom). There they experience neither the torments of hell nor the joys of heaven for the time being, but are trained there in everything necessary to prepare them for the latter, according to their various previous dispositions and whether they were found within or outside the covenant.

<margin>5</margin>
Likewise, the holy seed naturally holds a greater place in some than in others, as it did in Isaac more than in Ishmael; yet it does not reach so far that anyone shall be admitted into the kingdom simply because of it. Instead, it must be perfected in them, first through the obedience of faith in cooperation with Christ, until they are fully redeemed from the defilement of the earth.

<margin>6</margin>
From this holy seed of Divine Light comes a common illumination, which Heathens, Muslims <note>The original text uses "Mahometans."</note>, and Jews share with Christians as the law written in the hearts of all men. Besides this, there is a special illumination that none but *true Christians* can share; this is the *internal revelation* of Christ’s death, resurrection, ascension, and descent in the powers of the *Holy Spirit* <note>The original text uses "Holy Ghost."</note>, operating and working effectively, by which *regeneration* is perfected.

<margin>7</margin>
Those who have only received the former illumination, however faithful they have been to it, cannot yet be admitted into the kingdom of God for that reason. But since they are not far from it, they are kept in custody, where their souls are protected from evil and the gospel of Christ crucified is preached to them and opened inwardly in mystery, so that they may ascend to where he is.

<margin>8</margin>
Furthermore, among professed Christians who depart from this world, besides those who go to heaven or hell, there is a great number who are imprisoned for a season in certain elementary regions or middle places, until the opposition of evil is finally worked out of them.

<margin>9</margin>
And even among those who have had a significant degree of knowledge and belief in God and Christ, and [N.B.] have seriously labored for the new birth—being truly convinced of their depravity and lost state, and of the necessity of their redemption through Christ—but who have only partially, not clearly, separated themselves from the world, none can immediately enter the kingdom of heaven. Instead, they occupy a higher level in the elementary regions near Paradise. While they do not feel much pain, agony, or sorrow there, they also feel little pleasure or joy, because they cannot achieve the vision of God as long as *any impurity remains*. She believes that no one should oppose the idea that such impurity may be removed after the soul is separated from the body, especially those who deny that perfect purity is attainable while the soul and body are joined; otherwise, few (if any) could be saved.

<margin>10</margin>
All souls, therefore, must pass through the refining and purifying <note>The original uses "calcining," an alchemical term for heating a substance to high temperatures to purify it.</note> regions prepared for their purification, according to the level and degree they achieve here in this life. The more they suffer here [in achieving a state of *perfect love*, humility, meekness, patience, and resignation—for the direct process of which, see pp. 8, 9, and notes on pp. 75, 127, etc.], the less they will have to do and suffer in the life to come, where the difficulty will be much greater.

<margin>11</margin>
Consequently, in the first delivery of this doctrine, these exact words are found: 
> *How many years might you stay in these purging and burning furnaces? One day here, while in the body, would have advanced your work more than years in those centers where you are to be confined. Therefore let this be acceptable, etc.* Enoch Wal. p. 16. <note>Probably referring to the work "Enochian Walks with God" by Jane Leade.</note>

<margin>12</margin>
Thus, all souls, having been created by God to be happy, shall in the end be eternally so after their purification by such ways and methods (in such regions) as Divine Wisdom sees fit. Being first truly humbled, they are then made capable of loving and enjoying God forever, according to the order of their creation, which will be in the unity and harmony of his own life and light within them.

<margin>13</margin>
However, this is generally not to happen until *some considerable time after the thousand-year reign of Christ*, when the high and great saints of all ages of the world shall sit as counselors and judges with him. By virtue of his authority, they will demand all such condemned souls who are held captive in the infernal prisons and set them free from the dominion and tyranny of the prince of darkness.

<margin>14</margin>
This Universal Jubilee of mankind will be the bruising of the devil’s head, which he shall never be able to move again. It will be the removal of the sting of death, the seizing of the prey from the mighty, and the capturing of the treasures of darkness.

<margin>15</margin>
After this jubilee, the angels who fell shall also achieve the end for which they were created and intended by God, and they shall recover their original state, beauty, and brilliance. Seeing themselves now stripped of all their power and become so weak and poor as to have no place or subjects over which to exercise authority, they will be deeply pierced.

<margin>16</margin>
When they are thus humbled, the eternal and pure nature that was implanted in them directly from God at the beginning—and which could never be corrupted or lost—will be stirred up and awakened for their recovery.

<margin>17</margin>
This will be done by the Father of all spirits, the eternal UNITY, who will not fail to gather to himself what is his own and to annihilate whatever is not derived from him. In this way, all conflict in Nature may finally cease, and all things may be reunited to their source, from which they branched out in the beginning through the eternal WORD. So, whether they are things in heaven, or on earth, or things under the earth, they must bow and pay their obedience to the ONE Supreme Being.

<margin>18</margin>
Yet until the wonders of the mystery of iniquity are fulfilled in all fallen worlds, the disobedient angels will refuse to surrender their kingdom or to humble themselves before the throne.

And when this mystery is fulfilled in all its wonders, then will the end be: the end finding the beginning, and Christ becoming (*manifestly*) the *Alpha* and *Omega* of the whole creation, and as the first, so also the last.

But as the order of the transgression of the angels was different from that of men, so also shall the order of their restoration be.

For as the restoration of man was more proper to the Word made flesh, so *their* restoration is more proper to the Father of their spirits, as he is the Spirit of Eternity. And as the Father there moved in the Son, so the Son here will move in the Father, by the same Spirit. And as Christ was the creating Word by which they were created at first, so again the second time will he be: First consuming and devouring all the diabolical nature, by an impregnable fire of Love from the breath of the Almighty, invisibly fanned; and then reintroducing himself by the eternal generation of the Father into their eternal essences; so that being created new, they may be recovered to their primary existence in the Deity and inseparably united with their true original.

Moreover, as God did introduce himself again into the fallen human nature in a corporeal manner, because its depravity was chiefly in the outward birth, called the third principle of nature; so will he into the fallen angelical nature in a *spiritual way*, because its <term>tartarization</term> was chiefly in the inward spiritual root of their essences, called the first principle of nature. And therefore, their fall having been so deep, it cannot be recovered except after a universal and radical dissolution in the second death.

Which death must have its resurrection, as the first death had its own, by a new creation and new generation from the Virgin principle of Wisdom in perfect nature;

Since the foundation of God being in them can never be annihilated, but must abide forever, and so cause in them this angelical resurrection and new angelical creation. For this they are to be prepared and made to believe the same by the ministry of Michael and the rest of the holy angels commissioned by God for this end. For who could not have a sympathy of nature for their fallen brethren and desire that they also should be happy—if it be the will of God—in loving him and ministering before his throne as they do?

This is the sum of her doctrine concerning the general restoration of the creation, as far as I understand it. I have endeavored only to represent it in its true light, as delivered; and having done so, I leave you to judge whether it does indeed give that favor to <term>libertinism</term> which many think.

I would also ask you whether you believe it altogether unreasonable and unfounded? Or whether the contrary is so expressed in Scripture that it is not possible for serious and thoughtful persons to agree with this sentiment?

I do not vindicate it, or think it necessary to do so; but if it were, there is hardly one doctrine about which Christendom is divided for which more can be said.

This uproots <term>Manicheism</term> and also <term>Gnosticism</term>, or the false magical knowledge of the ancient heretics; it having been a fundamental doctrine, you know, of <term>Simon Magus</term> their head, that the God who created Adam was not the supreme God, but an impotent demon only, because he was not sufficient to preserve his work from being marred or to hinder his will from being disobeyed. This puts an end to many otherwise inextricable controversies, throws down the foundation of many ancient and modern opinions very destructive to mankind, reconciles the sentiments and decrees of persons and churches with one another that have been thought most inconsistent, and above all, promotes catholic love and universal peace. ...once the truth of this doctrine is accepted, there are, besides these, several other advantages—too visible to be denied—which will flow from it. XXVIII.—Now, whether the doctrine is true, and whether the revelation supporting it is likewise true, are two different considerations.

I may be convinced of the one, but not of the other; I may be convinced of one by the other; and lastly, I may be convinced of either by various means. But if both should be found to be true (upon a free and just inquiry), then this will be unquestionable evidence, both for that spirit which was the author of such a revelation or revelations, and for the person chosen as the instrument for their conveyance to others.

For though an evil spirit may reveal a truth, it is not to be believed that he will ever reveal a truth to anyone capable of doing so much good in the world, or that he can take satisfaction in foretelling the final destruction of the devil’s kingdom. And though a person may also receive a revelation from a good spirit and not understand it—even, indeed, mistaking some part of it, as some say the very Apostles did (who had a revelation from angels that they should see Christ return in the same manner as they had seen him ascend, yet misapprehended it as if his return was to occur during their lives or very suddenly; and who also misunderstood Christ himself regarding the death of St. John)—I say, though a revelation from a good spirit may not be understood, or may even be misunderstood, the instrument through which it passes is not therefore to be undervalued. Rather, God alone is to be adored and admired, for He knows how to make use of the humblest instruments for His praise.

Let this now suffice for the charge of heresy, as well as for that of enthusiasm.

XXIX.—There remains still the first and last charge to be considered, which is *Schism*. But here, also, the best way will be to represent the state of the case clearly as it is, and then to search for the true *nodus* <note>the core or knot</note> of the question.

The society of which I profess myself a member is not of a single ecclesiastical communion, nor under one civil government. Instead, they belong to different communions and are under several jurisdictions, both temporal and spiritual. They do not intend to dissolve any obligations to the princes and states under which they were born, nor to transfer their allegiance to another where it does not belong because of this alliance. On the contrary, they think themselves bound to the same civil obedience as if such an alliance had never existed.

Likewise, they do not intend to destroy the obligations they have to any rightful or lawful authority in the Church derived from Christ and his Apostles, so as to either assume that authority themselves or transfer it wherever they please. Rather, they aim to maintain the same spiritual obedience that could previously be claimed, based either on the principles of primitive Christianity or the common motives of ecclesiastical peace.

Hence, in Lutheran countries, there are many aspiring with us after the renovation of the angelic spirit and life and the restoration of the Church, yet they do not therefore break off from the communion of which they are subjects, nor withdraw their obedience where they are permitted to pay it without violating an express Divine command.

The same is also true in some kingdoms of the Roman communion, and even in Rome itself. Nor is this entirely unnoticed by our friends who live under the reformation of Calvin.

The true members of this Society, wherever they are dispersed and under whatever kind of government in state or religion they live, never oppose the established constitutions or acknowledged rights of anyone, except where those rights are directly against the law of Nature or the light of the Gospel. They would rather bear with many things and submit themselves for the sake of conscience than run the risk of disturbing the peace and rest of the public by withdrawing from their true superiors and denying them that obedience which Christ has commanded. Yet the object of this obedience may be very easily, and is very commonly, mistaken. Regarding this in the—

<meta>This page continues the defense of the spiritual society's principles, specifically addressing the nature of obedience, the role of the internal Divine call, and a critique of the modern Church's lack of Apostolic spiritual gifts compared to the primitive Church.</meta>

<page-num>218</page-num>

Even within the Roman Church itself, where the practice of this virtue is most prominent, several people have greatly complained; specifically Father Baker and Gertrude More, who wrote expressly against that blind obedience which the Jesuits generally required.

These authors explicitly declare that the true object of obedience is God alone, and that no one can live in true obedience without attending to the internal Divine call, regardless of what their superiors may persuade them to the contrary or what their spiritual directors may dictate. And in this, we cannot help but agree with them; yet we do not think that because of this we separate from the church of which we were previously members, any more than they separated from theirs—unless the church that claims us should either deny this Divine call or prohibit obedience to it.

But I have a far better opinion of the Church of England, in which I have lived until now, than to believe that it would ever be guilty of such an excess as this. Since from its very liturgy, I have learned those very principles which oblige me to act as I do at present. And I have fully declared this in my answer to Philalethes, and could declare it even more abundantly. But be that as it may, the principles of our society are compatible with all due subordination to rightful superiors; and its members are not in favor of leveling all denominations as if there were no difference between them—much less for overthrowing the established institutions of our country—but rather for settling and establishing the true communion.

For though it would be a great absurdity for them, and wholly incompatible with their design, to take it upon themselves to peremptorily and immediately determine the rights of the many contending parties, they do not by this refusal allow any right to an heretical or schismatic communion to take anything away from the true communion (wherever that may be). Instead, they leave all things in the same state, without interfering with anyone except where it is absolutely necessary, and even then, with all imaginable honesty, while still reserving for themselves the liberty to join with those where truth is most prevalent.

They profess, along with the Catholic Church, a true veneration for all the formal institutions of the Gospel; which Gospel they say is *everlasting*, both regarding this world and the next.

They think it is very justifiable to work toward an evangelical perfection; but they do not discard the means that support it under the pretense of already having achieved it. *If they had lived in the age of the Apostles, or at least before the Church was poisoned under nominal Christian emperors, I dare say there would be very little difference between them and you regarding the regular subordination of the gifts of the Spirit, and consequently regarding the testing of spirits. Since God, according to your own most true observation, was pleased to distribute his gifts in such a way that the supreme governors were endowed with the highest gifts and the most undeniable credentials.* For they cannot easily persuade themselves that this is the case in every true communion today, or in every communion that you acknowledge to be a true one.

They say that although there have been, and still are, some excellent persons endowed with the Spirit of God in the highest offices of the Church, there is no general example of this in any single church at this time from which a conclusion may be drawn that the true Spirit of God must necessarily be subject to the decision of the majority of those who are so promoted—as if the gifts of γυβερνησεις <note>governances/administrations</note> and διακρισις πνευματων <note>discernment of spirits</note> belonged to them by inseparable right.

And they suppose that since the worst people are always the most eager to promote themselves under all kinds of systems, both civil and sacred, and since there is no possible security against the intrusion of such people except for a constant miraculous gift of spiritual discernment in the governing part of the Church, therefore no one ought to demand this subjection without more than human credentials for possessing it. Nor should they allow that to be an acceptable form of proof now which would not have been so in the Apostolic age, when no one was admitted as a presbyter—much less the head of the presbytery, or a bishop—without an express Divine call and without a real and perceptible communication of the Apostolic spirit through the laying on of hands. And although Christ never has, nor ever will, withdraw his Spirit from the church or suffer it to be totally eclipsed by the powers of darkness, they cannot help but think that there is a great degeneration today in every part of it; and that God seems to have included all parties under evil—even those who are, above the rest, most catholic—so that all being left without excuse, he might have mercy upon all.

And particularly regarding the legal Church of England: they do not object so much to the evils of the times or the corruption of particular people as they do to the heavy load of sacrilege and Erastianism <note>the doctrine of state supremacy over the church</note> which entered into its very constitution, and which some call the *original sin* of this Church—lamented by both the governors and the subjects, but never yet cured, nor likely to be cured.

And therefore, those who are more immediately concerned in this matter want to be convinced of how a superiority of the Divine Spirit in the governors of the church can be universally and constantly claimed under a constitution such as this, which even those governors themselves lament as imperfect.

Now, no arguments that it *must* be so will be sufficient, unless it actually appears that it <margin>80.</margin> *is* so. And if even the contrary appears *de facto* <note>in fact</note>, in some cases at least, then all reasonings *de jure* <note>by right/law</note> concerning the perpetual succession of the Apostolic Spirit will be insignificant here.

But we think it is evident (if not demonstrable) that this does not actually appear, but rather the contrary, based on the communication of the baptismal Spirit to all the Christian converts in the first churches—whereby not only ordinary graces but even the extraordinary gifts of this Spirit were conveyed—compared with the present administration of this holy introductory mystery, in which the gifts are never, and the graces are but rarely, transmitted. This is confirmed by sad and general experience; for out of ten people who are baptized (whether infants or adults), hardly one is found who can even be claimed to have received the Spirit in baptism as a permanent principle of spiritual life. Many of them never receive it during their whole lives, and most of those who do receive it only do so a long time afterward.

This also appears from the communication of the Pastoral Spirit as it was formerly practiced, compared with what now serves as a substitute for it in even the best reformed churches, as well as in the Roman and Greek ones. And seeing that, *de facto*, the succession of both the pastoral and baptismal Spirit is not perpetual—there being evidently many baptized with water who are not baptized with the Spirit, and many ordained to the pastoral function by the laying on of hands who have not thereby received the Holy Ghost—therefore, as many as are of this spiritual society, can

They do not immediately submit to or acknowledge a superiority of spirit in the pastoral and episcopal order as their exclusive and inseparable right. However, they think themselves obliged to be faithful to that measure of the Spirit of God within them, which they have received either mediately or immediately. This is not at all different from the Spirit which is in the true pastors of a true Church, but is the very same Spirit that has always been in all the true pastors and governors since the time of the Apostles.

They believe that the Epistles of St. Paul and St. Clement to the Corinthians do indeed bind spiritual persons to a due subordination to their spiritual governors; but they also suppose that this subordination was not merely (or chiefly) political, but was according to the various distributions of spiritual gifts—the lower gifts giving way to the greater, according to St. Paul’s list. In this way, all the members of the mystic body were both distinguished from each other and united together into the same bond.

Thus have I represented to you the case of the Unity of the Church and of Schism, as it is understood not by myself alone, but by many persons of good will in other countries, with whom I have true spiritual correspondence and union.

And the sum of all is this: that the Unity of the Church is also the unity of the Spirit (and vice versa), and that there may be a political unity in a true communion without a Spiritual Unity (and vice versa). Those who are of the closest spiritual unity, whether in the same communion or in different communions, are not to break themselves off from their respective political unity as long and as far as they can maintain the spiritual unity. But where political and spiritual unity cannot both be preserved, or cannot be well preserved together, it is safer to withdraw in some things from the political unity of the Church than from the spiritual unity, which is the ground of the political relationship between Church members. <insert>See Gichtel's Letters and Life. — Also Freher's "Microcosm" p. 57</insert>

XXX.—We in England do not observe exactly the same measures as those abroad; but our principles are the same, only our reasons for appearing in a more outward work are different.

And even several of us here, who do not have a sensible, internal call to such a public appearance, choose rather to retire privately and wait in peace for the powers of the Holy Ghost to descend and the kingdom of Christ to come into duly disposed souls. We choose to pray and wrestle together in spirit for the times of restitution, rather than to declare and proclaim openly the external manifestation of what we enjoy secretly without a positive command for doing so. Some, having received such a command, do meet together twice every week as a religious society for the free exercise of spiritual gifts and for the better manifesting of our faith and hope to others, without raising up "altar against altar" or setting up a divided church or communion. In pursuit of this, we do not meet on the Lord's day in the morning, which is a solemn time of public worship and communion everywhere throughout the whole world. Nor do we oppose the doctrine, the discipline, or the worship of the established communion of this nation, nor seek to withdraw any from it so that we may gain them for ourselves.

On the contrary, we have until now acted as friends, while we have been counted as enemies.

Some of us are so far from giving any just occasion of offense that they would willingly not have met on the Lord’s day at all, or at least not until the entire service of the day was performed; they could not be persuaded to yield on this point except for considerations that absolutely necessitated them.

The doctrine of general restitution <note>Universalism or the eventual restoration of all souls to God.</note>, as it is not an article of faith or a term of communion among us, nor even generally understood or maintained by our English Society, is not opposite to the established doctrine of an eternity of future punishment in a scriptural sense, nor to any of the articles agreed to at the beginning of the Reformation.

It is not condemned by any of the four general Councils received by the Church of England, though it was known before them all; nor is it condemned by any of her convocations, as far as I can learn.

Indeed, the doctrine of *preexistence*, which is very closely related to it, has been publicly asserted by some of her learned members without incurring censure or being so much as attacked by a decree of a university.

The doctrine of the guidance of the Holy Ghost is indeed carried much higher than what is commonly taught in her pulpits; but it is not a doctrine contrary to anything she delivers. Instead, it seems most conformable to her principles, or at least easily deducible from them.

The doctrine of the Spirit of WISDOM, and of its being distinct from the WORD as well as one with it, is no less than Apostolical tradition, if we may trust so ancient a writer as Tertullian. And (being rightly stated), it has never been condemned, as far as I know, by either the Catholic Church or this particular church.

Neither do we oppose the discipline of the established Church any more than its doctrine. The private discipline of our Society does not interfere with that, or may very easily be kept from interfering.

And since the discipline of the Church is admittedly defective, we have begun to revive among ourselves privately some of the Apostolical constitutions of the Catholic Church.

That we do not oppose the established worship of this communion may be made evident from many facts, and not only from our solemn declarations, which have been published in the *Reasons, Propositions, and Constitutions* of our society.

Some assist at public worship with much sincerity and devotion; even at the more solemn parts of it, they are no less zealous than the most rigid conformists. We do not, therefore, claim the name of a *Church*, but are contented with an inferior title. We say indeed that this Church is imperfect, and so cannot be accepted by Christ as his true bride. But at the same time, we admit ourselves to be yet imperfect, and therefore we wait to be part of that perfect Church which we surely expect to arise in this nation, to be gathered both out of the episcopal communion and out of *others* that have separated themselves from it, with a design (as we hope) of achieving greater purity. And thus it is mentioned in the *first Message to the Philadelphian Society* by way of a parable: in which the defect of the Reformation, and of all the subsequent reformations in this kingdom, is pointed out, as if by the Spirit of Christ sitting in judgment. [The time draws near: as already and hereafter indicated.]

But since we do at present only wait for the manifestation of a pure Church, which is described there, and do not call ourselves that Church, but only a Society preparatory to it, therefore

though indeed we do encourage others, both publicly and privately, to *join with us in the same expectation*: yet this is not to make them separate or divide from their present communion, despite the imperfections in it, for the sake of greater perfection in discipline or doctrine, but rather to embrace *all that is good and true*, and overlook what is not so in an imperfect church.

This is what we have declared again and again, in every way and on all occasions, and we hold to it, except where there is a clear Divine authority to outweigh the judgment, and some evident and eminent mark of the *Divine will*.

And though we may seem perhaps to allow no special privilege to the true communion, it is because we think there is no great fear that, if truth is set on *equal terms* with error, she must turn her back to her adversary. Indeed, we desire no greater privilege for the truth that we seek than that she may be on equal terms with whatever may contend with her for that name. That is, we require only impartiality and indifference.

We are not in favor of dissolving either spiritual or political unity; but since there may be political unity without spiritual unity even in a true communion, and also spiritual unity sometimes without political unity, therefore we think it our duty never to recede in the least from spiritual unity, however political unity may occasionally be dispensed with. For we have not learned to prefer the case before the jewel. This is the state, and these are the claims of this Society in England.

XXXI.—Now for my own part, I believe in the communion of saints in the holy catholic Church, and whatever my present engagements are, or may seem to be, I hope I shall always study to preserve the same to my utmost ability, wherever it truly exists, and never be found to violate it in any part of the church.

I do also believe that this communion will be better understood than it has been until now (not even excepting the Church of Jerusalem itself, where it did not continue long among the saints, but began to cool), and that <note>N.B.</note> the church will be more *holy* than it is now, or has been at any time.

And in acting according to this belief consists the whole Philadelphian Design. As for any irregularities, whether seeming or real, that may have been committed by myself or others through human frailties in the pursuit of this design, I am not unwilling to take shame upon myself, and I hope I never shall be. But as these do not concern the substance and foundation of the design, I presume that no persons of any sincerity or candor will be very severe in charging them against us. And whatever irregularities and anomalies may remain for a while, they are perhaps no more to be minded than the scaffolding work for some royal building.

I am far from having the least natural inclination toward what I am now engaged in. And whoever thinks it can proceed from passion or interest, I leave him to enjoy his own thoughts until the truth shall vindicate or condemn me. Indeed, if I consulted with flesh and blood, I know I would not find a greater natural aversion in anyone than I do in myself against what the love of God has constrained me to do in these recent proceedings; and regarding this, I hope it may be said of me, as with the apostle, that I *die daily*. For truly it is such a cross, in all outward considerations, *that to speak in confidence to you, I would be of all men most miserable* if I did not have a more than human support to hold me up under it, and the perceptible communion of that Spirit which no one can take from me, to comfort and assure me that I am still a true member of the *Israel of God*.

But because you will doubtless say that this may be nothing but my own warm imagination—even though it brings with it that peace which is not only beyond all imagination but also beyond all understanding—therefore I beg the favor of you to consider:

> *Whether there can be proven, both by right and in fact, such an Apostolic spirit in the governors of any Church today which may not only obligate every member in all cases, ordinary and extraordinary, to hold communion with it, but also to hold communion with no other—even where nothing but what is manifestly Apostolic is required for a term of communion, and wherein no part of the discipline, doctrine, or worship of the said Church is opposed.*
> 
> *Or otherwise, whether a person who does not oppose the discipline, doctrine, or worship of a Church which is imperfect, but is willing to hold communion with it as far as he can with an imperfect Church, may not in some extraordinary cases—such as where he really and truly believes there is a Divine call for it—be permitted to have fellowship with a religious fraternity (not separated) that requires nothing to be believed or practiced which is not clearly Apostolic, without thereby incurring the sin against the Holy Ghost or rebelling against the Apostolic spirit as resident in the governors of the said Church.*

With whomever the credentials of such a Spirit shall be found that can obligate all the members of its communion in this manner, I shall heartily acquiesce and entirely submit myself to their guidance in all cases.

But then these credentials must be very convincing, and the matter of fact solidly established, as well as vindicated by ancient Divine right. Which right, no matter how well vindicated, if it is not yet made evident by facts, is like faith without works.

Now if this is a dead faith, that may possibly be a dead right; or if it is not altogether dead, it may be paralyzed even in a proper sense of the word, instances of which would not be hard to find.

Thus, the stress of this article on Schism, as it is applied here, will lie in this proposition: *There is an uninterrupted succession of the Apostolic Spirit in every true communion, perfect and imperfect, which does without reserve obligate everyone living in such a district to the exclusion of any other spiritual communion, even while not inconsistent with it.*

The consideration of this, and of its consequences, will put an end not only to this dispute, but to many other momentous disputes besides. But until those who claim a right by succession to this Spirit of the Apostles can also show it by *real works*—that is, by the *acts of the Apostles*—I am afraid the matter will not be brought to any resolution. <note>N.B.</note>

XXXII.—In the meantime, whatever may be the censures not only of evil but also of good men, I cannot easily abandon those principles and practices which the sincere research of truth, against the contrary bias of education and constitution—yes, and of interest too, as well as of honor—has led me to embrace. And if you, on your part, require external evidence, I think it no less reasonable that the same should be given to me here, the claims being so very great and the claimants also many. So I heartily pray that the good LORD would illuminate all Bishops,

P.S.—I beg your pardon and Mr. Cherry’s for this tedious delay. It is a mistake that I should ever refer you to any of the *Theosophic Transactions*. I do not know how that arose, except from this: that someone might suppose that letter to be yours which came to me from an unknown hand and is answered in the report on the state of the *Philadelphian Society*. I have several times admitted that I owed you an answer, but I was not willing to show what I had written in this letter before you yourself had seen it. This I thought myself obliged to do by common decency, in addition to that special value which I have for your dear person. I pray God to bless you long for the good of his church, and for something greater in it than has yet appeared.

I do not fear but that I shall be treated by you as a friend, and that you will kindly overlook the minor slips that are of no concern to the main subject. I thought to have struck out some passages that will appear to have been written with a certain warmth that I was not master of; but I have left them in, so that you might have a true and clear view of my inner self. I also beg you to pardon the faults of the transcriber, and to believe that no one is, or can be, more sincerely and cordially yours than your old friend.

Dear and Honored Sir,—The great sense of my own disability, my natural and acquired aversion to a scholarly war, and the particular advice given to me by a learned friend—not to write too soon in defense of my current views which you have attacked, but to wait until I should be able to do so more fundamentally and solidly, as much from higher and clearer experiences in myself as from a greater maturity of the times—along with other contributing causes, both internal and external, made me set aside this Answer. I had written it in response to your second and third Letters in the year 1698, except for the conclusion, which I added on Easter day in the following year, just as I was then going to give the most solemn sign and evidence of my adherence to the Unity of the Church, according even to your own understanding. And I am still ready, on all occasions offered to me, to do the same, and to express—in relation to the national Church where I was educated—my hearty and sincere desire for external and internal union, so far as is consistent with *Catholic* communion and not contrary to the operations of the Holy Spirit, which were undoubtedly given to the Apostolic Churches. By this limitation, I do not intend to excuse myself from any obligation I may be under to maintain the peace of this particular Church to which it pleases God that I should belong, according to his unsearchable wisdom and foreknowledge. I only mean by this that I would not have a lesser obligation take precedence over a greater one, a succeeding one annul that which was prior, or a particular one destroy that which is general; and that I am not to be excluded, by virtue of any private laws or customs in such or such a Church, from obedience to those laws which are either more universal, or more ancient, or that are undeniably derived from a superior authority and a more immediate Divine origin. <note>N.B.</note>

This I do not doubt you will readily agree to; and though we may differ in its application, I think there can be no dispute about the foundation.

If any of the rules or prescriptions of the Church of England as established by law—for the breach of which I am judged by my brethren—can now be proved to have these qualifications, in opposition to what I have been endeavoring to promote in the whole Christian Church these past few years (not without much weakness, and indeed with great reluctance of the flesh), I am content to undergo the severest censure they can pass upon me for the same. And moreover, whatever reparation is in my power to make, I shall be more ready to offer on my own account than anyone is to ask, if the matter appears otherwise upon a strict examination than what I have really thought or asserted it to be.

The matter in which we differ is indeed a matter of great importance; but I cannot concede that I have been engaged in it by the pretences of any mortal. I can have no blind or partial respect for anyone, since I know that Truth is transcendentally more related and more natural to the essence of my soul than any relation, whether of blood or marriage, can be to my body.*

I.—Is it possible for God to deliver over to a spirit of seduction any sincere soul who seeks above all things to please him, who forsakes all things for his sake, and who takes up the cross of Christ in that very thing which is of all others most directly contrary to his nature—and even to deliver him over in the very act of the highest dependence upon the Divine Majesty?

II.—Is it at all consistent with the methods of God to suffer evil and seducing spirits to intrude themselves there, and even actually to bring about their design, where man does not first surrender himself as a prey to their malice and put himself wholly outside the protection of the good spirits?

III.—Are our human frailties, or the ordinary and daily sins which well-disposed souls are subject to in the state of continual combat between the flesh and the spirit, considered before God as an act of such a surrender?

IV.—If they are not, how is it possible for any soul in such a state to be given up by God to a strong and irresistible delusion in the most significant point of his whole life? Or does not the state of warfare necessarily imply that God has not given up such a soul to the deceitfulness of unrighteousness, as the present case suggests?

V.—Is there, in the course of a man’s whole life, a greater, more significant point than marriage,

God is no respecter of persons, so I would gladly be an imitator of Him in this; and should I fail in my research after truth, yet this shall be my comfort: that it is not for want of impartiality and objectivity, but of capacity, which I am sure is not in anyone’s power to change. If it is my misfortune, it shall never be my fault. Yet I cannot help but have better thoughts of the Divine Being, even when considered apart from Christ, and I count nothing more absurd than the imagination that He who is truly called the *Father of Lights* should refuse to be found by those who seek him in sincerity, *for want of sufficient light communicated*; or as if He should permit anyone to be misled by a *false light from the path of truth* who, above all things, earnestly seeks His guidance and wishes to behold nothing but in His light; or lastly, as if He could make one guilty for a default in this case, which it was in His own power to have prevented, and in no one else's. No, surely; the ways of God are equal and impartial, however unequal and partial ours may be. So I need not fear, for I have this abundant consolation springing in my soul: that no one could take greater pains to divest himself of all partiality and bias. It would not be hard for me to provide even clear evidence of this.

I have been so far from venturing my eternal state on appealing fantasies, or from being biased by warm and unaccountable affections, that I have truly examined—with as much accuracy as I am capable of, or as the matter will bear—everything that many people might consider to be so. I have not been afraid of discovering my error, or even of having it discovered to the world; instead, I have labored greatly in that discovery, and perhaps with as much satisfaction as another might take in discovering the errors of others. In this scrutiny which I have made, I have shown no favor or fondness for any person whatever, or for any sentiment whatever, but have considered the weak and indefensible side of both with the very same impartiality as that which is more strong and defensible.

Therefore, I have not failed to declare my dissent wherever I thought the interests of Truth obliged me to do so, without any regard for the status of any who might otherwise appear to have the greatest influence over me. And as I have scrutinized things with such strict severity—finding as many or more objections, I think, than anyone else could find—I am better enabled by this, not only on one hand to judge the truth that may dwell in me (as I firmly and rationally hope), but also better prepared on the other hand to acknowledge freely whatever may not be found conformable to the eternal and unchangeable patterns of Truth.

Now, Sir, I could have almost wished you had either limited yourself to your first argument or had produced others of a general nature, and had not sought for evidence from that particular case which you chose. For I am extremely averse by nature to all personal disputes, especially to those in which my interest or affection may seem in any way to have involved me. Therefore, this also has been one occasion for this long delay in not sending you my answer when it was finished.

Whatever this or that particular case may be, my principles are the same; I have not taken them up suddenly, but have compared them for a long while with the Scripture, and also with universal and Apostolic tradition.

I have brought matters fairly to the test, at least as far as I am able, and have not failed to examine the pretensions of all the various churches and communions, without the bias of either a friend or an adversary. In doing so, I have been greatly astonished at the strangeness of the mutual misrepresentations, at the Babel of words and terms, at the passions over the obscure or less momentous points of Christianity, and at the general decline of all, both from the faith and—

---

on which the happiness or unhappiness of persons does so much depend; and that not only for this present time, but even beyond it? And if we are to believe that Divine care and providence, according to our Saviour’s doctrine, is concerned about every private circumstance of our lives, shall we suppose that it is unconcerned in a matter of such vast importance? Should we suppose He would suffer the great turn of human life to run at random, and submit even the very least and weakest of all God’s children and servants to the play of deluding spirits in this matter?

VI.—Can there be a greater impiety than to commit a villainous act under the mask of religion? Therefore, should not the grounds of evidence for such a charge be proportionate to the crime?

VII.—Might there not have been many successions of jealousies and suspicions against most of the undoubted Prophets of God—yes, even against Christ himself—which might probably be presented with some plausibility, when yet there was nothing of reality at the bottom? And is not human nature the same now as it was then? May not the same pretenses be renewed again many times, by which it may be possible for well-meaning persons to be scandalized and take offense?

VIII.—Were there not passions and contentions sometimes among the Apostles themselves? Were there not suspicions and misreports of one another? Were not some of these reports caused by those who had an immediate mission from the Apostles? Were there not certain of these Apostolic missionaries who, through an excess of zeal, exceeded their commission? Did not some of these lay heavier burdens on others than was either necessary or laudable? Did not others condescend too far, out of weakness or fear? Or were not even their just concessions perversely misinterpreted? Were not the impositions of the one, and the compliance of the other sort, made to have an effect other than what was intended by them? Did not divisions and scandals arise in the churches from these misapprehensions, and from taking sides with those who had a manifest Apostolic commission? Was it ever known that spiritual persons were exempted from the danger of falling into this *partiality*, if they did not keep to the *head* <note>The source or Christ</note>? Were there not very bad consequences drawn both from actions and doctrines that were not only innocent, but holy, by those who had submitted to the Divine authority of the persons? May not the passions and contentions of the (really or supposedly) spiritual persons of today arise from the same ground; and will they not naturally produce the same effects? And is it at all to be wondered at if many evils and scandals arise out of a spiritual jealousy (which is often found lurking in those who are otherwise very good persons), and that this spiritual jealousy arises from a partial consideration of many causes, not always accompanied by an evil will? Therefore, should we not be very careful in accepting reports and jealousies against a brother or a sister, even from such persons as are truly spiritual?

IX.—If the best and most spiritual are capable of being mistaken or misled, either by oversight or an excess of zeal, is it not most advisable to forbear from condemning anyone until—

And I owe the result to certain principles and well-considered axioms that are not flexible, but very rigid. Where the principles I stand on (considered in themselves) are faulty, I shall be glad to be informed. Indeed, I expected that the *Propositions, etc.* of the Philadelphian Society (or something of that kind) might have come under your examination sooner than those books <note>N.B.</note> from which only a guess can be made at what these may be. And truly, I cannot sufficiently wonder that this has generally been the method of most or all of those I have dealt with in this matter: they consider it enough to attack specific writings <note>N.B.</note> that are most obscure and furthest from being understood, or certain sentiments and tenets that we have positively declared are not essential, or our religious meetings as a Society and some practices within them; yet they take no notice of those grounds and elements on which we proceed, and upon which the entire superstructure is built. Whereas, whether anyone receives these writings or not, whether he adheres to such doctrines or leaves them, and whether he is free or not to be present at such exercises, <note>N.B.</note> he may still cling most firmly to the first and common elements. These are universally agreed upon by all who long, as we do, for the renewal (as we believe) of the true evangelical Spirit and of the Apostolic dispensation; and until these are overturned, all other labor spent will have little, if any, effect.

<margin>By Francis Lee.</margin>
But I am convinced that the first principles and common elements of this glorious dispensation (as I take it to be) will not be so easily shaken by anyone as some might imagine, who have thought us more worthy of contempt than notice. Men of the soundest minds have undertaken this task to represent them in their proper light; and what is lacking in me, I do not doubt God will abundantly supply in a short time through the concurrent assistance of others with far deeper learning. I have the honor and happiness of being acquainted with some from several nations <note>N.B.</note> who are expertly skilled in human and Divine knowledge. I am certain they will leave no stone unturned for the sake of Truth, which has been so greatly oppressed through the violence and prejudice of parties. And if our first principles are once established—as some think they may be, almost beyond contradiction—then I do not much fear any attacks that are or shall be made against the superstructure. <note>Who are they? What are their writings, if any?</note>

I proposed some questions to you in my first letter. Had you been pleased to think them worth an answer—for which I could think of no one so well-qualified as yourself—I would have taken it as a particular favor. It might also have contributed much to setting me right if I am in the wrong. But I would not impose any task upon you, however much considering them might help to clarify the truth or reveal the falsehood of certain principles that I cannot abandon, as they appear to me as irresistible as steel.

I find that under the Jewish dispensation, there was the greatest imaginable care for the preservation of the unity of the body through the communications of the Divine Spirit, as if from a visible head. And yet it cannot be denied that, despite this dependence, there have been some who have publicly prophesied in the camp and Church of Israel without any commission from that visible head, and who were not rebuked for doing so after being accused of a schismatic separation.

Even Moses, who certainly was no stranger to the extent of his own authority, and who just before had received an express Divine order to share the same Spirit which—

<column-break/>

there can be a full and thorough hearing of both sides; and if that cannot be, to suspend our judgment, to accept what is clearly good and worthy of approval in anyone, and to cling unmovably to the head? Is this not the safest method that can be taken in both general and particular disputes? Is there any possibility of being preserved otherwise from error and mistake? Or is there a more pernicious error in faith, or a more dangerous mistake in fact, than that which would seat us on the tribunal of Christ by making us transgressors of His law?

X.—If it is against the law of Christ to judge others while we are not sure of being acquitted ourselves, who shall be left to set up a spiritual judicature? Is there anyone but Christ himself who can decide the differences found today among spiritual persons, which could not help but arise from the current twilight light that was prophesied? Therefore, where there is a clear appeal made to His tribunal, should anyone remove it from there? And if there are all the visible signs of joy in the appellant as the decision seems to draw nearer, can there be a more evident sign of the appellant's sincerity?

What follows, however, will perhaps sufficiently instruct us in the nature of this document by Lee, which appears to be a casuistical justification to himself of his marriage against the judgment of his immediate friends, and of Mrs. Lead against the slanders cast upon her as having brought about that event by intrigue; it also informs us of how Lee became acquainted with Mrs. Lead, which led to his marriage with her daughter, probably in the year 1696. His deep devotion to God and pure love of the truth, wherever it might be found and even if its operations were offensive to unregenerate reason, may be inferred from what is related in this treatise. Many of the manuscripts referred to by his daughter in her preface to his posthumous “Dissertations” were recently found by the writer of these lines among Mr. Law’s miscellaneous papers, from which source the extracts given here are obtained. When Law retired from the city in 1740, about three years after the death of his old friend Mr. Gibbon, he apparently borrowed Dr. Lee’s papers to review; and, judging from the carefully written copies he made of many of those papers and from his own later agreement in opinion on certain mysterious theological points in the above ‘Apologetical Letter,’ he must have held a great respect for Lee’s talents as a learned spiritual writer. The paraphrase of the “Supersensual Life,” which was inserted in some of the final issues of the fourth volume of Behmen’s works (published 1781) and there incorrectly stated in a note (perhaps by Langcake?) to have been composed by Mr. Law—since the manuscript was found in his handwriting—was actually written by Lee and merely copied by Law. The writer of these lines possesses both the original by Lee and the copy by Law, along with other curious pieces by Lee, one of which is a *Dialogue between Lazarus and his Sisters after*...</note>

<meta>This page continues Francis Lee’s argument regarding the universality of the Holy Spirit, using the biblical example of Moses and the seventy elders to justify the presence of spiritual gifts outside of formal institutional structures.</meta>

[The Spirit] rested on himself, to a certain select number, he did not dare to prohibit them from prophesying, upon whom the Spirit of God immediately fell, or fell without the ordinary means of conveyance. He did not condemn them for this, as being private spirits, or as breaking the public and external bond of the one Spirit. He did not insist here on his ecclesiastical prerogative, nor did he call on Divine Justice to vindicate his cause on behalf of the true Spirit, as he had done in other cases. But he was so far from condemning them that he justified them; he was so far from confining the gifts of the prophetical Spirit to such a select and separate number, that he even earnestly wished and prayed that the whole *laity* might be made partakers of it.

And do we not also have the example and command of one greater than Moses, not to be rash in condemning all those spirits that do not walk with us in the same external communion? If I am not very much mistaken, there is some such thing that our blessed Lord has taught his disciples. And I do not know how to make any sense of his words if there cannot be a true internal communion of the same Spirit, in some cases, under different external communions. I also think it is an ancient observation that as soon as the Eastern Magi turned aside to seek counsel at Jerusalem—where the true church undoubtedly still was—they lost sight of the star that was given to lead them; it was taken from them while they were consulting with the ordinary leaders. [!]

How applicable this may be, I leave for others to judge. As you know, there is an infinite variety in cases, and it is utterly impossible that any two should be exactly parallel. But this much at least is evident: that the true and genuine Spirit of God is not so limited as some have been apt to imagine in favor of themselves, or of that communion which they espouse to the exclusion of all others. There are many things relating to the economy of Moses and the prophets, as also of Christ and his apostles, that I could heartily wish were thoroughly and impartially considered for this purpose.

And after all that you have written for preserving the unity of the Catholic Church, I am fully persuaded that there are still some things remaining untouched by you which, upon further examination, you will find conducive to universal peace as much as anything you have said so far. Perhaps they may even be more so, given how the spirit of mankind is moving at this time.

It does not seem altogether absurd to me to believe that there may be even in false and contradictory communions sometimes a real participation in that very Spirit which was conferred by our Savior’s baptism. And I cannot find any proof that the true Spirit of prophecy was ever confined by God only to the Jewish church, even while that was his <term>peculium</term> <note>Special possession or property.</note>; nor do I dare to say that He was such a stranger to all the rest of the world as some would have him be. The ways and methods of Divine Wisdom are various—indeed, they are infinite. I can say that if I had not seen it, I would not have believed it. But having seen it, I believe that the Spirit of God blows where it wishes, and no man knows where it comes from or where it goes.

However well the style of one or two persons whom you mention in particular might be explained by such other origins as you name (distinct from that of the Divine Spirit), it is not very significant in my opinion—especially since there is a whole cloud of witnesses who stand up for this very same principle. Nevertheless, I had considered them before, and though much remains that could be said on each of these points, I will refrain. If an atheist or deist should say that the style of the Jewish prophets is very well explained by origins distinct from the Divine Spirit, or if a Jew or Pagan should say that the beginning of St. John's Gospel is very well explained by Platonic philosophy, I do not think you would be moved in the least to diminish the veneration that is certainly due to the Prophets or to St. John. And if I were—

In regard to visions and revelations, Law—like Behmen and all the sensible mystical divines—maintains that they are not at all to be sought after, or even desired, in any part of a religious soul's exercises. <meta>This page continues Francis Lee’s defense of mystical writings and spiritual experiences, transitioning from a general justification of spiritual gifts to an analysis of the specific styles and historical receptions of biblical prophets to provide a precedent for modern visionaries.</meta>

Afraid of saying anything that might seem in any way to contribute toward the reigning Deism and infidelity of the age, I could show in almost every one of the ancient prophets how their style can be explained by different origins. I could also show how both the matter and style in most might have been objected to in those days—not only by Sadducees and those whom the French call *Les Esprits Forts* <note>The "strong spirits," or freethinkers</note>, but even by the stricter sort of religious people among the Jews, and the very precisians and zealots of the law themselves. 

This might be shown not only in Daniel, who was an <term>arch-mage</term> in the Chaldean College, and in Ezekiel, who likewise seems not uninstructed in eastern philosophy and magic; not only in Hosea and Zechariah—where the former's manner of speech is scarcely (if at all) defensible according to the European method of writing, and the latter is truly magical in his style and, in his figures, appears to have written much according to the rules of <term>Oneirocritics</term> <note>The interpretation of dreams</note>—but even in Jeremiah himself. Jeremiah was called to be a prophet from childhood (much like Samuel) and was certainly sanctified for a special ministry from his birth. He was mighty in word and in power, to such a degree that hardly anything higher can be said of a mere man than of him; and yet it can easily be conceived how his prophecies might give offense to the majority of both the clergy and the laity, making them count him as an enemy of the temple, of the law, and of the holy people. It would not be difficult to produce several plausible grounds for this even at this distance of time, from quite a few places in his book; and undoubtedly some others might then have been produced by his enemies, both priests and prophets. And if so great a friend of God as this holy prophet was no better understood or received in his day, we must not think it hard to meet with nearly the same fate in ours. God will vindicate his own glory in his own appointed time; and truth will at last gain the victory over all error and dispel the clouds of misapprehension.

On this account, I have been more extensive in the examination of the particular case itself, on which you place such great weight. I have shown that the various prejudices, both specific and general, are not entirely as legitimate as you concluded upon a cursory look into these books. 

I have shown that the author nowhere denies right reason, but only corrupt reason; nor does he supersede the authority of Scripture, but only the false interpretations of it. I have shown that no doctrine is taught in these revelations which ought to be called *another gospel*, and that the testimonials brought for their authority are not as insufficient as is commonly claimed. I have shown that imagination is not capable of producing all the effects specified in them, and that even for the imagination itself, there are proper criteria of truth which may be very clearly discerned. Furthermore, the claim of physical temperament is likewise precarious and unconvincing; and to retreat to theories of fevers and distempers is a refuge not becoming a wise man. particulars of which, however minutely related, the hearers cannot possibly understand, except for their possible certainty. Yet, as Mr. William Law says, it is in these things that the inquisitiveness of otherwise well-instructed minds is employed, as if it were possible to grasp them; and in another place, that Divine secrets will only be made known in God's own time, and not a *minute sooner*, however men may try to fathom the prophecies. 

Let this be a warning to all visionaries when publishing their favors to the world: let them know that the only possible good such things can do is to lead those (and only those) who have ears to hear, or who are specially suited for such statements, to pursue the same process they themselves pursued before arriving at the state where Wisdom could open her sevenfold gates to them. This consisted simply in a strict conformity to the Gospel's counsels, from the first commencement of repentance to the highest perfection of holiness and purity. 

At the same time, let them warn their readers that these things are simply personal to the subject experiencing them; the reader must not think of seeking or desiring visions, but simply follow on (in the indicated process of the "Grammar of Wisdom") to know the Lord, diligently pursuing that path day by day without drawing back or looking aside, until he attains the true high degree of Christian development and arrives at the portal of Wisdom's temple. And further, that even then, were the gates of Divine revelation to be opened to the newly arrived soul, she is not to demand or expect the self-same revelations she might have read about in others; for the wonders of Divine Wisdom are *infinitely various*, as are the temperaments of the souls she delights to manifest herself to; so that *no two revelations are ever alike*. 

If visionaries—that is, those who were truly holy and have had their <term>ternarius sanctus</term> <note>holy ternary</note> really opened—or their friends who have published their writings (Jakob Böhme is not included here, for he, guided by Wisdom, most wonderfully shields every part of his writings from abuse), if they had only offered these common-sense cautions to their readers, they would have prevented much fanaticism and self-deception. At the same time, they would have honorably provided all necessary protection for the holy doctrine that God has his peculiar blessings for every age, and is ever ready to open the treasury of his Wisdom to such of his devoted, holy children as will prepare themselves by purity of heart for such manifestations—a doctrine inseparably interwoven with enlightened Christianity, however it may be ignorantly slighted or vehemently denounced even by good men. Nor will the Church rise to its proper grade of perfection and glory until this doctrine is duly promoted, though of course only to those who have arrived at a state to receive it. 

These reflections have arisen in the mind of the writer upon reading the prefaces to Jane Lead's works and other pieces by Francis Lee in connection with the Philadelphian Society. Not that he considers her prophetic, mystical, transcendental writings to be of any public utility, or that she was an inspired prophetess, or that her declarations are uniformly true, any more than those of Antoinette Bourignon. But we must, by a natural process, arrive at a certain state in order to grasp the truth, and God in his regulating wisdom brings every persevering seeker into a *state* to know every truth that will benefit him or carry out the secret purposes of Divine Love. Let him who reads judge of this from a *proper state*.

It is well known that I have not wished to encourage anyone to desert the ordinary methods and means of the Christian Religion, upon any pretenses of greater purity or otherwise. But on the contrary, I have both by letter and by word of mouth, frequently admonished and encouraged such as I have found to be of a soaring spirit, to adhere closely to the common rules and ordinances of Christianity; and to remain and wait therein, so that they may arrive at a life of Contemplation, and thereby at the more peculiar favor of God. We both contend for God (permit me to say so); we both call on him as our Father, in the name of his Son, and we both, I hope, seek to please him as such; and both study nothing but the propagation of Truth, and the same blessed interest.
