It is to these last sublime studies, belonging only to those who have actually stripped themselves of the animalistic spirit, and are risen with Christ into his newness of life and light, that we hear so often applied by popular religionists the hackneyed phrase of “being wise above what is written.”—But is it not strange that it should never cross the minds of those who thus so glibly misapply Scripture, to know that what is written in the Word of God can be no slight or easy task, even to such masters of spiritual knowledge as they may deem themselves to be; for as the Word of God, it must be an *exact expression* of the mind of God, of the wisdom of God, of the will of God, which must necessarily lie hidden therein, and which therefore requires no ordinary vision to penetrate and to declare, in its variety, depth, and life-inspiring truth. The Word of God is truly said to contain a revelation of all mysteries and all knowledge; as indeed does the other expressed word of God, the book of Nature; and likewise that still more wonderful expressed word and wisdom, and fullness of the Deity, the book of MAN in his true form of existence, that is, a full-grown Christian; but the reader must have eyes, or he will in vain try to read it, but be like the Jews of old, who said, “are we blind also?” for it is according to the state a man is in that he understands the Scripture, or any revelations of the Deity, in creation, or grace. For instance, if he be as yet in the state of nature, familiar only with scholastic theology, or but imperfectly awakened, he reads and explains the Scripture according to the elementary principles of piety; if he has ascended higher into the school of real regeneration, and practical mystic science, he understands it *further* of the things of the Spirit, of salvation, of the conscious love of God, and growing union with Christ; and if advanced still higher, to the central, most inward, supersensual or theosophic ground, the pinnacle of all Nature, he then finds so much the more sublime testimonies contained in Scripture: but strangely enough, each grade calls the next above it, *enthusiastical or mystical!* Hence it is, that to those who are in the lowest degree of Christian life and understanding, the Scripture only proposes simple things; but in proportion as they return to their true original, and redeemed state, in CHRIST, it becomes to them a clearer and clearer mirror of the grace and love and wisdom and wonders, and deep things of God. Who am I that I should boast in my strength? However, like Job, I must justify myself to the last; and I know that I shall not be utterly cast off by my God, even if all the world should reject me and none of my brothers acknowledge me.

You may please remember that I have never yet, for myself or for others, claimed an exemption from human imperfections or frailties. In the very first public paper relating to our undertaking, it was acknowledged that there was much weakness and imperfection, superfluity, and mixture in the foundation of our Society. Therefore, it may be a bit unfair to tax us with every failure we may really be guilty of—failures of which we are perhaps no less aware than others, though not immediately able to correct. [N.B.] The greatest things have often begun very imperfectly, and I know that you are too wise to despise weak beginnings.

The writings that you criticize appear to the world in great weakness, but this does not hinder the power of God from working through them. They have certainly not been entirely without their credentials or authentic proofs, if intrinsic evidence has any validity here—which is so generally argued for in similar cases.

These credentials may possibly rise higher and higher, and objections may vanish more and more, as it shall please God to favor a poor, despised cause.

Truth needs no more than to be fairly represented; that is the best apology for her that can be made. There is no end to running out into personal controversies, which are for the most part altogether irrelevant and fall away by themselves as soon as there is a right understanding. This I do not doubt but you will find in the particular case before us (human frailties still excepted), and that the veil that is between us being so removed, we shall yet know one another to be brothers in the unity of the same spirit, however variously and seemingly contrary its manifestations may be.

And now, dear Sir, since you seem to request something for the *sake of the public*, I leave you entirely at liberty to do herein what you shall judge proper: and you may command the originals or copies of those letters with which you have favored me whenever you please. I would not have anyone involved in danger on my account; but on the contrary, I could wish myself even a sacrifice for the sake of my brothers, and of my countrymen, and for the peace of Jerusalem, which my soul loves.

The good Lord reward your labor of love for me, your zeal for his name and for catholic unity, and crown you with everlasting blessings in that inheritance of light, which may manifest things hidden as well from your eyes as from mine. May he convince me by his gracious Spirit in whatever I err, or am in the wrong; and confirm me wherever I am in the right, that the gates of hell may never prevail against me, nor the tempests from a raging world overwhelm me. May he also, if I am in the right, give to you in due time such a spirit of wisdom and revelation, that by the most essential illumination of the spiritual eyes and most experimental knowledge, you also may be led to confess that for which I am at this day counted as the offscouring of the earth, and that I may have the joy of signing myself, even according to principles, in the deepest and most real sense, and more than formerly, Your most affectionate brother
Hoxton [Hogsdon], March 25, 1701. ->In the heart of the Lord Jesus, Fra. Lee.<-

to me. The next day being Holy Thursday, and the weather also being bad, I did not go to town. And having considered what Valerianus Magnus has written concerning it in his book, *De Luce Mentium* <note>Of the Light of Minds</note>, I must tell you that I am (whatever you may think of me) one of the greatest admirers of reason in the whole world; that is, of reason in its truest and deepest sense, as the eternal and uniform (though multifaceted) light of all created spirits.

Nor, on the other hand, do I know how to believe the first revelations of our Christian religion without also believing in a succession of the same Spirit (the spirit of revelation) which brought them into the Church; and without believing several other truths which I understand to necessarily depend upon that and to lead into the knowledge of, and communion with, the mystical body of Christ. Perhaps there is a greater connection between what was anciently given by the Divine Spirit and what is still maintained by a few to be so than everyone is aware of. The same Holy Scriptures that forewarn us against a multitude of seducing spirits also warn us sufficiently of those who make the most clear revelations of God of no effect by their human glosses and criticisms; they tell us not only of scoffers and those who resist the Holy Spirit and oppose the second appearance of Christ in the glory and power of his kingdom, but likewise of the virgins themselves, some of whom shall fall asleep and others slumber. I refrain from making the application. But I think it is high time for the world to awake, and for the whole Christian Church to go out from her chamber to meet her bridegroom, who by many signs and voices declares himself to be coming. was the Savior of *Adam*, the *Patriarchs*, and the *Jews*, just as he is our Savior. His body and blood, offered in their sacrifices, was their atonement, just as it is ours, offered upon the cross. His flesh and blood was food and drink, or a *principle of life to them*, as it is to us.

Jesus Christ was theirs just as he is ours; he was the life, substance, and spirit of the law, as he is the life, substance, and spirit of the gospel; only with this difference: that then Christ was covered and received under more outward figures and ceremonies than he is now; we do more openly what was then done more covertly by the *Israel of God*.

His atonement for our sins is not a *transitory thing* that *began and ended* with his passion and death, but it began with the *Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world*; for he was the Lamb of God slain in all their types and sacrifices through every age, until he became the real expiatory sacrifice on the cross for the sins of the world.

When he died upon the cross, his atonement did not then become something that *was over or past* and done, to be remembered only by an act of memory, but it continued increasing in its power and virtue.

As Christ by his death put an end to nothing in religion but types and prefigurations, so by his death he put an end to nothing of his atonement except that which was typical and prefigurative of it. And as he rose from the grave with greater power and strength and became, instead of a *meek and suffering Lamb, a powerful conqueror over death and a royal Priest* over the house of God, so his atonement continued increasing in strength and virtue. <note>N.B.</note>

His atonement was so far from being a thing then finished and *past* when his blood was shed upon the cross, that it was shed for this very end: that he might forever do in *reality* what the high priest did in the *type*, when with the blood of the sacrifice he entered once a year into the holiest of all to make the highest atonement for the people. <note>N.B.</note>

<margin>ca</margin>
Thus Christ, to perform and to continue forever the most powerful way of atoning for us, *by his own blood he entered once into the holy place*—now to appear in the presence of God for us.* Where he continues forever and has an unchangeable priesthood;† and therefore our atonement is *never finished and past*, but is just as *perpetual and unchangeable* as his priesthood. For he can be no longer a priest than while he makes an atonement and intercession for us. And from this, his *unchangeable priesthood*, the apostle argues thus: *wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost who come unto God by him,‡ seeing he ever lives to make intercession for us?* <note>* Heb. 9:24. † 7:24. ‡ 7:25.</note> <note>And yet Law, according to modern theology, is non-evangelical!!</note>

But if he is *able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him*, then his atonement is not *something done and past*, but always in existence, always present, always acting, and always presenting itself everywhere and to every man. And if he is ever living to make intercession for us, then we have a propitiation that never ceases, which is as near to us as it was to the apostles, and will be as present to those who shall be born two thousand years after Christ as it was to those who stood by his cross when he died. Agreeable to this, St. John says, *We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And he is the propitiation for our sins.* He does not say we have had an advocate in this world, but that *we have* one with the Father; nor that Christ *was* our propitiation some time ago, but that he is the propitiation for our sins.

And indeed, Jesus Christ is the atonement for our sins in that same *unlimited, universal, and omnipresent manner* in which he is the *life and light of the world*. And as he is the *light which lights every man that comes into the world*, and is not an actual present light to some and a distant, unpossessed light to others, only to be remembered by an act of *their memory*, so he is the atonement for every man who comes into the world; he is not an *actual, present* atonement to some and a distant atonement to others, only to be remembered by an act of their memory, but is

an atonement *actually* and *really* present to all, just as he is a light actually and really present to all, and to every man who comes into the world.

Therefore, this author's account of *the remembrance in the sacrament* not only contains the absurdities demonstrated above, but is also solely founded upon the grossest of all errors: that the benefits and blessings of Christ, as the Savior of mankind, are something finished and *past*. This is an error that no one could have fallen into if they had even a common knowledge of the first and plainest principles of either the *Jewish* or *Christian* religion. For both these religions are founded upon this *great truth* and assume it in every part: that the benefits and blessings of Christ were always *in existence*, always *active*, and always *present* in and to every age, both before and since the incarnation and death of Christ.

And as this author has been forced to assert that they were things *absent*, *finished*, and *past* in order to make the sacrament consist of an action of the *memory* upon those absent things; so, seeing it is an undeniable truth that they are not things absent, finished, and past, but are as actually present as they ever were or ever could be, it follows according to his own principles that the *remembrance* spoken of in the sacrament cannot possibly signify only an action of the memory, but must necessarily signify such *faith* and *acknowledgment* of Christ as when we are commanded to *remember our Creator* or *believe in God*.

Further, this author proceeds as follows: > *To say that the communion is the actual partaking of all the benefits of Christ's living and dying for us is to place upon one single act of obedience that which our blessed Lord made to depend upon the whole system of all virtues united.* And again, *Such a doctrine as this would, in my opinion, be not only inconsistent with the clearest declarations of the gospel, but directly contradictory and destructive to its main design.*

What this author calls here a *single act* and a single instance of obedience is true only of his own sacrament, which consists only of a *single action of the memory* directed toward Christ at a certain moment in time, and regarding which single action this author expressly says that no prayer is necessary—not even necessary to attend to it, either before or after it. He claims that in its own proper and peculiar nature, it has nothing to do with prayer or devotion of any kind; it can gain no perfection from them, nor be in any degree imperfect in its nature and essence for lack of prayer, because its essence is entirely distinct from prayer.

And therefore, all prayers, thanksgivings, and devotions are to be considered as things distinct from this sacrament, having no relation to its peculiar nature and proper essence.

Hence it is plain that we do not misrepresent this author when we say that he places the whole nature of the sacrament in a *bare, single action of the memory*. For if, as he says, no kind of prayer, devotion, or thanksgiving is of the essence of this sacrament, or can be an essential part of it, then it has all its perfection within itself as a bare act of the memory; it cannot, in its own proper nature or essence, have anything added to it by prayer or taken from it by the lack of prayer. Hence it is also undeniable that this author’s sacrament is not even a *bare act of religion*, nor can it have any more religion in it than if it were the act of a parrot. For no act can be a religious act except insofar and in such a degree as it is an act of *faith*, *love*, and *devotion* to God. But this author’s sacrament will not, as a sacrament, allow faith, love, or devotion to be any part of it; therefore, it cannot be even a bare act of religion.

Indeed, it may and must be said that the correct observation of this author’s sacrament is directly an act of *atheism*. For if it is an act that, in its own nature and according to its peculiar essence, cannot be performed as it is intended unless it be done without *faith*, *love*, and *devotion*

But the essence of this author's sacrament cannot be preserved unless you keep prayer, devotion, and thanksgiving out of it. Therefore, to perform it correctly according to what it is, is to perform an act of atheism.

<margin>a</margin>
And if, at the taking of the bread and wine, you should allow faith, or love, or adoration of God, or thanksgiving to occupy your mind, you might as well have left the sacrament alone; for you have neglected all that in which its whole nature consists and have only been in such a state of devotion as has nothing to do with it, nor can possibly be a part of it. And therefore, if you will perform this sacrament correctly according to this author, you must perform it atheistically; you must stir up such a remembrance as excludes faith, love, devotion, and thanksgiving from being a part of it. And your remembrance is not performed unless it is such a remembrance that these things cannot be a part of.

<margin>b</margin>
The devils are said to believe in God; but why is it that their faith is no religious act, nor of any benefit to them? It is because their faith is only a bare act of believing, just as this author's sacrament has only a bare act of remembering; and that which is the perfection of his sacrament is their wretchedness.

<margin>c</margin>
If you ask this author why faith, and prayer, and adoration, and thanksgiving are not of the essence, or cannot be essential parts of the sacrament, all he has to say is this: that the duty of *prayer is a duty absolutely distinct from the participation of the Lord's Supper*.

<margin>d</margin>
It may and must be granted that prayer, humility, faith, hope, charity, etc., are absolutely distinct from each other; that humility is not prayer, nor is faith, in its proper idea, prayer; and so with the rest. Yet despite this distinction between them, they are all essential to each other. Faith is of the essence of prayer, hope is of the essence of faith, and all of them are essential parts of prayer. Therefore, when this author asserts that prayer is not an essential part of the communion, he is just as much in the right, and has as much truth on his side, as one who says that humility, faith, and hope are not essential to prayer because prayer is distinct from humility, faith, and hope.

<margin>e</margin>
What this author says of the sacrament—that it is one single act, or one single instance of obedience—is only true of his own fiction of a sacrament, which he makes to consist in a single act of the memory; and indeed, it would be highly inconsistent with the gospel to make such a sacrament a means of obtaining the benefits of Christ. But this is not the sacrament of Christ, nor the sacrament which the church of Christ observes.

<margin>g</margin>
For all that relates to our salvation, either on the part of Christ or on our own part, is plainly united in that sacrament which Christ has instituted. All that relates to our salvation on the part of Christ is in the sacrament because he has said that his body and blood are there for the *remission of our sins*, and that his body and blood are there to be eaten and drunk as the food and life of our souls; therefore, Christ as our Savior is wholly there.

<margin>h</margin>
And all that relates to our salvation on our own part is there, because we cannot come to Christ, or find him to be there as he has said he is, unless we come to him with all those qualities and pious dispositions that correspond to him, as he is an atonement for our sins and a principle of life to us; therefore, all that relates to our salvation, either on the part of Christ or on our own part, is plainly united in the sacrament. And to call such a communion *one single act of obedience* is just the same absurdity as to say that the baptism of a heathen converted to Christianity is but one single instance of obedience. For everything that is implied in such a conversion and baptism, whether on the part of Christ or on the part of the person baptized, is implied in this communion.

The *Fountain of Gardens* is by no means an unsuitable title for this work, as with Lee’s embellishments, it may be considered a kind of garden of spiritual recreations for those who are familiar with transcendental exotics and nomenclatures; though it is still but a *pleasure garden*, and that for a few privileged *savants*. The letters of Bromley and Pordage at the end of the first volume are solid and just in sentiment: and the only thing that seems to be missing from them is a resolution of the natural question: *What is the shortest, simplest, most direct road to the blessed state described therein? > *And as the baptism of such a person contains* all *in it that relates to his salvation, either on the part of Christ, or on his own part, and therefore cannot without great ignorance be called a single instance or act of obedience: so it is with the sacrament; it is* all that *to the pious communicant, both on the part of Christ and on his own part, that baptism is to the true converted heathen; and he is made an actual partaker of all the benefits of Christ by it, just as the convert is made so by baptism; and therefore it is the same absurdity to call it a single act or instance of obedience.*
>
> *And as it would be vain and groundless to say that it was inconsistent with the main design of the gospel to make such baptism the* actual *partaking of all the benefits of Christ; so it is equally, if not more so, to say the same thing of communion; because every pious and holy disposition is supposed to be in a higher state in the pious communicant than in the person who piously desires baptism; and therefore, it cannot without much absurdity be supposed that the Sacrament is not as beneficial to the pious communicant as baptism is to the pious convert.*
> 
> *For if Christ has appointed this institution to assure us that he is there, both as the atonement for our sins and a principle of life to us, and we come to it with such pious dispositions as correspond and answer to him in both these respects and make us capable of him; it must be a great absurdity to say that we do not find him there as our atonement, nor receive him as a principle of life to us, nor are made partakers of these benefits of him.*
>
> *If we stand before this atonement without such dispositions as correspond to it, we are as absent from the sacrament of Christ as those who refuse to come to it; if we eat that which is before us in the sacrament without such faith and purity as qualify us to receive the flesh and blood of Christ, we are only eating that which might have been the bread of life to our souls.*
>
> *But if we, according to the condition of our humanity, are that which these two* essential *parts of the sacrament require us to be, then we may and ought as firmly to believe that we are by this sacrament made* actual partakers *of all the benefits of Christ, as that we are saved through Christ and not by ourselves.” [N.B.]*

Whether its contents—coupled with the repeated warnings from Dodwell and his many old, sober, and devout friends—might have had some influence in causing the dissolution of the <term>Philadelphian Society</term> in the following year; or whether Lee might have begun to perceive nothing extraordinary in the times and seasons, despite the high expectations and prophecies of Mrs. Lead and some of her associates, and so his views began to change in some degree, resulting in that outcome—these are points that cannot now be determined. However, as we learn from Lee's history and the date of his works published under the patronage or name of his dear friends Hickes and Nelson, as well as from some papers inserted later, the unquenchable fire of his noble and divine soul did not allow him to sit down in ease or despair, but drove him toward pursuits and employments suited for more universal benefit. He was, truly, “abundant in his labors” for the edification of souls and to promote the cultivation of the highest philosophical science, according to the most perfect discoveries granted by God to mankind. For the reader's pleasure, we propose to give a few more extracts from his papers, by which (along with what has been provided above) a general understanding may be formed of this most estimable character and most ingenious, learned, and devout man.

The letter from Stephens to him continues as follows: “Mr. Lee—I received your letter with the enclosure only last night and have hardly any leisure at present to read them, as the handwriting is small and not very legible, much less to return a long answer, even if I wanted to; but I think it is unnecessary. It is now over a year since I noticed what concerned me in the *Transactions*, and though I immediately made my remarks upon it, I never bothered myself further about it. By this, you may see how little I was concerned for myself in that matter. And I assure you now that you cannot be more ready to ask my pardon than I am free to give it. For I believe that no man can hurt me, but he hurts himself more. The injury I am principally concerned for is what is done to a good cause; and to that extent, you are responsible to yourself to make restitution. There is one thing in these papers for which I must ask for satisfaction: to be informed of the particulars in which I am thought to have used too much severity, to the detriment of a good cause. For to be plain, I strongly suspect the sincerity of those who criticize it, and I believe it is fundamentally nothing but formality and a vain affectation, no better than that of the Ruler of the Synagogue (Luke 13:14). Indeed, I observe so much affectation, ostentation, and self-promotion in what I have seen in print from your Society that this alone would make me suspicious of what other observations confirm for me: that it is far from being any true Christian spiritual society, but is no better than a new sprout of an old sect of enthusiasts, established under a new, impressive name. About three weeks ago, I wrote a discourse one morning to convince some persons how far short they were of a right understanding of the spiritual life. When we afterward came to our morning service, the first lesson for the day was Ezekiel 13, where, after a reproof of the false prophets, he is commanded to prophesy against the false prophetesses—the daughters of his people—who prophesy out of their own hearts. Thereupon, when we had finished, I added what I thought might be appropriate for your consideration, but I do not have time at present to transcribe it. I can only tell you now, in answer to your questions, that it is not only possible but common for God to allow souls (even those as sincere as you imagine) to eat the fruit of their own actions when they presume to follow their own imaginations outside the ordinary path of humility which He has prescribed. This serves to correct those who are correctable and acts as a judgment upon the rest for an example and warning to others. I admonish and advise you as a friend, and in the name of God, to consider better what you do; be careful how you proceed further in this Society, and apply yourself quickly to the proper means of escaping the snare of the subtle enemy. I heartily wish you well and would very willingly take any pains to serve you, but at present I am otherwise engaged. If you resolve to come here, let me know the day two or three days beforehand, lest I should unfortunately be absent. Your affectionate, faithful friend, Edward Stephens."

This is an age that thinks itself superior to all that have ever gone before it in the discovery and improvement of truths; and it cannot be denied that in these recent years, mechanical knowledge has been brought to a very great height, which has had both its good and bad effects in the world. But despite all the imagined or real light in matters either physical or theological that the present age boasts of so much, it may perhaps be aptly enough said of those who cry out the loudest that *the veil is still before their eyes*. And let them imagine what they please and pride themselves in the sharpness of their sight, they must all, sooner or later, be convinced that it will be impossible, without the immediate hand of Christ, to tear away the veil or to penetrate through it into the sanctuary of God or of Nature. This cannot happen unless the great High Priest, bearing the oracle of truth upon his breast, makes a way for them to enter and opens both their eyes and ears so that in seeing they may see, and in hearing they may hear, whatever is written by his finger or spoken by his mouth. But although the *Philadelphian Society* plan was dissolved in 1703, Lee did not abandon his opinion of Lead’s understanding of the Divine mysteries and of her mode of obtaining that understanding, as being assuredly the right way: namely, by constant prayer, deep inward focus of spirit, and silent waiting before God (the soul being in a high degree of regeneration), until the idea, in its birth and development, arose in her mind, and so the truth became understood. For however plainly and clearly deep truth may be described (as it is done in Boehme, in a manner that for simplicity and fullness may be termed miraculous), the theosophical student can only obtain an understanding of the sense by the eternal innate idea of the truth rising like a plant in the mind; only then does he first understand it. By the *theosophical student*, is meant one who has made considerable progress in the divine life; for as truth is the most inward thing of all, nothing less than the immediate powers of the Spirit of God could touch the center of the idea and awaken it into life. If Lead had solely meant by her "*visions and revelations*" this circumstance of the understanding of the deep points of Boehme’s philosophy (which also applies to Pordage), then the writer would fully approve of the term, though by no means of the Muggletonian, fanatical, parabolic clothing in which she dresses them; for the knowledge of a deep point of metaphysical truth is a *real revelation or mental vision*. But if she intentionally included any apparently unscriptural new doctrines, then he would reject her assumptions. And how possible it is for even a most devout woman, by reason of the present disordered and imperfect state, to deceive herself by taking her own conceptions—imperceptibly combined as they are with the truth in her imagination—to be equally of the same origin.

It has occurred to the writer as a strange circumstance that so few, if any, who discuss Boehme have ever considered whether it were not possible to *assist* the student in obtaining an understanding of deep truth. In answer to the question, "How am I to obtain a correct understanding similar to your own?" they reply, "I cannot give it to you, nor could an angel; it must be born in you." This appears to the writer a very unsuitable answer from a philosopher who knows that (whether in spiritual or material nature) like causes produce like effects. According to this, it would follow that the respondent ought to answer the inquirer (supposing the point in question to be a truth) by declaring the method in which he arrived at the understanding. In doing so, he would, as it were, seize the idea at the bottom of the inquirer’s mind and perceptibly trace it through all intricacies and mazes until, so to speak, it reaches the surface and so becomes visible, manifest, and self-evident! Therefore, though he could not give the inquirer the understanding of a deep truth, he might most materially assist him to understand it and much shorten the time otherwise required for obtaining that mental perception. <note>Here reflect upon pp. 199, 200.</note> And what a pity that the whole of Boehme—if his philosophical writings are, as they are, a perfect *chain of truth*, the first link of which reaches to the first conceivable motion of the Unity of God, prior to natural existence, through everything to the end of revelation and thought—what a pity that all is not laid open by those who have obtained an understanding, one of this and another of that mystery, in the manner indicated here. That is, in addition to what FREHER has done.

We will give an example of what is suggested here. And what better topic for the purpose than *Virgin Sophia, the Virgin, the Eternal Virgin, the Wisdom, the Virgin Wisdom, the Looking-glass of Wisdom, God's Wonder-Eye*, etc.: what is more suitable than the *Virgin Wisdom*, which may at first have appeared as fantastic a term and concept to theosophists as it does to ordinary popular and scholastic theology. Thoughts:—The Virgin Wisdom. The Bride of God. The original model of all reflections. Love: its nature is to love; that is its essence, being, and life. It requires an Object: the Unity, or rather Triunity of light and love, has nothing but itself; it wills to know itself. That knowing of itself is its first form; it is its reflection or image, its picture and looking-glass in which it sees itself. It is the science of itself and, so to speak, the embodiment of its riches, beauty, purity, and glory. It is pure Wisdom, the wisdom of the Deity—of the unformed, inconceivable, nameless, supernatural Trinity. It is a *form*, we have said, *and that form is a Virgin*, of no sex but uniting all sexes and perfections, eternally a Virgin, the *image of God*, above all Nature, in eternal fellowship with the Trinity. The whole unformed Spirit of the Deity is eternally manifest in *form*, a virgin form; an eternal Virgin, yet all things are generated (SEEN) in it without touching or affecting its virginity; for it is the universal passive mother of Nature. The archetype of the Virgin Mary, and of St. Paul’s ‘woman’ or wife of ‘the man.’ And when a man beholds his beloved wife with understanding eyes (and hears the music of a sweet hymn tune played and sung by her), he reads in that the philosophy of God’s eternal Virgin Wisdom. But what language can describe the merits, beauty, and perfections of Wisdom? It is the body of the Triune Spirit of the Deity, body being the manifestation of spirit. The Virgin: no man nor woman as such, nor having any affinity with that idea, but a divine ALL-POSSESSING ALL; and only known by creatures as a Virgin. Oh, wonders to contemplate! Now reflect upon the following quotation from Behmen:

> “Thus we say, the Holy Spirit goes forth from the Father and the Son, but where does he go? Into the substantiality, with the glance of the Majesty, wherein the Deity stands revealed. This gateway is called by me in all my writings <term>Ternarius Sanctus</term>: for I mean the Number Three in the Substantiality (that is, in the angelic world), where the Three Persons have revealed themselves.”

Now, therefore, we say very rightly that the Son is the Word of the Father, which the Father speaks. But now the deep mind asks, *where* does he speak it? Behold! The Word is the heart and sounds in the essences of the Father; and the heart speaks it in the mouth of the Father, and in the mouth, the Holy Spirit of the Father comprehends it in his center, and so it goes forth from the Father and the Son into the substantiality, where it stands with the glance of the majesty as a Virgin of the Wisdom of God in <term>Ternario Sancto</term>.

This, which is spoken forth, is an *image* of the Holy Number Three, and a *Virgin*, but without substance, yet a likeness of God. In this Virgin, the Holy Spirit opens the Great Wonders of God the Father, which are in his hidden seals.

Moreover, the Holy Spirit manifests the *opened seals* of the Heart of God in the glance of the Majesty, which stand in the light and are called the *Seven Spirits of God*.

Thus the Image of the Wisdom of God *stands* in substance among the seven *burning spirits* which burn in the light of God (for they are the Divine nature); *and it has the seven stars* (of the hidden seals, which stand in the anger of the Father in his center) *in its hand: for the Heart of God is the power of the Number Three, as the Apocalypse shows in the first chapter*.

This WISDOM of God is an eternal VIRGIN, not a woman, but chastity and purity without blemish, and is like an *image* of God. In her, the Holy Spirit has *discovered* the Image of Angels, as also the Image of Man, which the <term>Verbum Fiat</term> has created.

Therefore consider, O you philosophers, how God created this world in *six days*: for each day's work is a creation of a Spirit in *ternario sancto* <note>the holy ternary or trinity</note>; and the *seventh day* is the rest of the *Sabbath of God*, in the *Seventh Spirit of God*, in which the *Virgin of the Wisdom of God* stands; and in it there is no more any working of anxiety, but the eternal perfection of rest.

For the six spirits must pour out their operations of what is *in* their seals; and they are not known before until they have poured out the power of *their vials* in the principle of this world, which men and creatures bring to *substance and act*, as a building to God's works of wonder.

And when this shall be accomplished, then the hidden Spirits of God (under the seals) enter again into the ether, that is, into their center: and *then* the time of the *seventh seal*, in the substantiality, in the presence of God, *begins*, and the hidden mystery of the kingdom of God is accomplished: as is mentioned in the *revelation of Jesus Christ*, and as we have known in *ternario sancto*.

This Wisdom of God (which is the Virgin of Glory and beauteous ornament, and an Image of the number Three) is (in her figure and image) like angels and men, and she takes her origin in the center on the Cross, like a blossom of a branch, out of the Spirit of God.

For she is the substantiality of the Spirit, which the Spirit of God puts on as a garment, by which he manifests himself, or else his form would not be known: for she is the Spirit's corporeity, and though she is not a corporeal palpable substance like us men, yet she is substantial and visible, but the Spirit is not substantial.

For we men can, in eternity, see no more of the Spirit of God, but only the *glance* of the majesty: and *His glorious power we feel in us*, for it is our life and conducts us.

But we know the Virgin in all her heavenly similitudes or images; though she gives a body to all fruits, she is not the corporeity of the fruit, but the ornament and luster.

The corporeity goes out from the substantiality, which is not the Spirit, but an insufficiency in comparison to the Spirit in which the Number Three dwells; and that substantiality is the Element of God, for there is a life in it (but without understanding) in which the Paradise of God consists, for the Seven Spirits of God work in it, and it is like a growing; and in this consist the *great wonders of God*, according to all essences infinitely.

For every form of the essences brings forth its fruit, which by the wrestling of the *wheel of nature* <note>the cyclic forces of natural birth and transformation</note>, attains its highest ornament and power, and yet passes away as being overcome again, and another rises up which has other essences: and so it is a holy sport, a joy or *fruit* of angels, a fulfilling of the will of every life.

Here again we need an angel's tongue: for the mind always asks *how and where?* For when the deep is spoken of, which is without comprehension and immeasurable, the mind always understands some corporeal thing.

But when I speak of the Virgin of the Wisdom of God, I do not mean a *thing* that is in a place; as also when I speak of the Number Three; but I mean the *whole deep of the Deity, without end and number*.

For we comprehend (before us) the Number Three in the Image, namely, in the Virgin of the Wisdom of God: understand, outside of our person, we see only the majesty of the Deity, for the creature does not comprehend the Number Three in its *appearance to the eye*; but the Spirit of that soul (which stands in the *Divine center*) sees it, but not perfectly.

Might not then the way to the understanding of deep philosophical truth be much *shortened* by *lecturing upon Behmen*, somewhat after the manner attempted to be described above; and would not this be more honoring to God than (as has been the custom until now, *for example*: with Pordage and Lead, and others) for individuals to call public attention to themselves, to their idiosyncratic, confined conceptions and deductions as some pretended new ‘revelation’; instead of all bowing to Behmen, as mathematicians do to Euclid? Both of these authors stand in a corresponding relation to the Holy Scriptures. Behmen must hereafter be the *Euclid’s Elements* of philosophy: we say hereafter, because we embrace Law and Freher as Behmen’s precursor and demonstrator, from the date of the publication of the present Treatise.—And now to return to Lee: whose indefatigable efforts and incessant schemes in the cause of truth, of religion, and heavenly wisdom we have alluded to. > “PROPOSALS for raising a FUND to print BOOKS of MYSTICAL DIVINITY, PHILOSOPHY, and HISTORY. In order to the advancement of the most ancient and universal religion, as professed by Christ and his apostles, and of the most curious and solid learning, throughout all the ages and parts of the world.” And it proceeds thus:—
> “There being at present but very little encouragement in this kingdom for all books of such a nature, they being known but to very few, and coming into the hands of fewer, and there being likely to be in the beginning a great expense, because many hands will be employed (both natives and foreigners), and many books successively published, of which no suitable return can be expected for some time; it is therefore proposed,
> I.—That whoever shall contribute towards a fund for such an end, shall be repaid his money deposited, in books, as they are produced, according to the number they subscribe for. And that the performance of this shall be secured by such trustees as some of the principal subscribers shall agree upon.
> II.—That the books shall be printed carefully, on a fine paper, and with a very good typeface.
> III.—That the profit which is made by the sale of the books, beyond the original fund, shall be made a bank for charitable uses and services most agreeable to the carrying on of this design; and shall be under the regulation of the said trustees.
> IV.—That from the said fund there shall be printed upwards of a hundred sheets the first year; and so on until the contributors and subscribers shall be fully satisfied.
> V.—That every term there shall be published one or more books, papers and stitched tracts excepted.
> VI.—That the ancient Christian Mystics, Macarius, Nilus, etc., shall be set forth in the English tongue very advantageously, with proper annotations.
> VII.—That the best of the Heathen Mystics shall be set forth also after the same manner: with a just parallel between them and the Christian, and a demonstration of the excellency of the latter.
> VIII.—That whatever can be collected of the true ancient Jewish Cabala shall be translated and set forth in like manner, in Latin or English, or in both.

Lee, finding no suitable encouragement for this noble design, in the unquenchable ardor of his zeal, still continued in other ways doing good to the world, as witnessed by his publications that followed the date of these papers, already referred to throughout this Treatise. His great piety and modesty (ever the attendant graces of a truly fine genius) would not allow him to take any glory for himself in the admiration and praise of "man," and hence his numerous works came before the world either anonymously or under the ostensible authorship or patronage of Hickes and Nelson, as already mentioned. But although he would receive no honor while living, God does not forget his faithful servants; and here (singularly enough) at the distance of nearly a century and a half, we are appointed to raise a monument of honor (indeed, one that shall endure while time endures) to this faithful and highly favored servant of Christ, in common with other special kindred sons of wisdom. And what is still more singular, we have been imperceptibly led, without any previous connection with Lee’s writings, to renew by this *second Section*, and this whole *Treatise*, the scheme which he himself proposes in these papers, though more suited to universal benefit. May we hope, then, that the time has come for its practical commencement, and also for that of the following *second paper*, regarding the raising up of an evangelical Theosophical College or Society for the scientific cultivation of the divine life in the soul, to its highest perfection of holiness and supersensual wisdom. <note>That is, so to speak, for the horticultural rearing of heavenly plants and trees that should provide sublimated paradisiacal flowers and fruits; for why should there not be a growth in divine wisdom as in every other principle of life? It is proposed—That a Society, or societies, be formed out of a select number of faithful friends who are persons of a true Christian spirit, experienced in the ways of God, sincere lovers of peace and truth, without partiality to any person or party, and especially in no way inclined to disturb the government, either in Church or State, or to speak evil of dignitaries. And that the formation of such a society or societies—having no other end but the revival of the genuine and primitive spirit of decayed Christianity, and the life of its most renowned professors in the purest ages of the church—be according to the following model:

I.—That the members of this society, as members of it, distinguish themselves by no other name but that of **CHRISTIANS**.

II.—That they unite together purely for the reviving of the life and spirit of primitive Christianity, and for promoting peace and union universally.

III.—That they meet once a week (if not more often), and chiefly on the Lord's day; if possible, without interfering either with the public duties of the day in the churches, or with family duties at home; unless some other time for this is found more convenient.

IV.—That the number of its members does not exceed six or seven, both for the greater liberty of Christian conversation and for several weighty reasons.

V.—That for the preservation of unity and order, every member of this shall have his particular lot and service assigned to him, besides the general ones, according as everyone is fitted by God and Nature for one thing or another.

VI.—That there be a fund of piety established here, according to such regulations and orders as shall be unanimously agreed on by the members, for charitable and pious ends best suiting such a generous and Christian Institution.

VII.—That this society be dedicated to **GOD** through **CHRIST**, so that He may ratify it and say Amen to it by His **HOLY SPIRIT**. And that the feast of its dedication shall be kept annually, with a recollection of the previous year's proceedings and with proper services and offices for the occasion.

Now, since it has been found expedient, after mature deliberation and experience, that no society of this nature contain more than half a dozen members, or seven at most; and that no one be admitted into it without the full consent and hearty goodwill of all; therefore, so that any serious Christians may not be barred from the benefit of this design, it is thought proper to attach here the specimen of an agreement for forming such a society. This is so that they may consider it and accordingly form themselves in a similar manner into a sacred fraternity and fellowship with those to whom they may have the closest relation in spiritual matters, however small their number may be. For only three or four fully united in a society of this kind, having a good agreement in their temperaments and a close sympathy both spiritually and naturally with each other, may be capable of doing far more than three or four hundred loosely combined who seek to carry out the very same end; and they may expect more of the grace and blessing of God, as they are motivated by greater unanimity and concord. The following is a Letter addressed to Dr. Edward Hooker, in Lee’s own handwriting (probably a copy):—

> “Peace be with you: and blessing, and mercy from the mercy-seat of the Lord Jesus Christ in heavenly places. Amen.—Sir,—Though I would not do anything in the least to discompose you in your near preparations for a blessed eternity, yet since it has pleased Divine providence to put into my hands some writings for which you have declared the highest esteem, as well as for the author, your friend, with much regret for the will of the deceased not being fulfilled in this matter; I think myself obliged to propose to you a few questions concerning them, which no one perhaps in the world but yourself can answer for me. And, therefore, despite being a stranger to your person, I must take this boldness with you, for the honor of God, for the interest and propagation of truth, and for justice to the dead, to entreat your resolution of these matters, so far as you are able. If you please to grant me this, and to allow about an hour’s time for declaring your answer, distinctly and separately to what is here proposed, I trust that it shall not be accounted a loss to you; and I shall heartily pray that God may bring you into the great light of his everlasting kingdom, after being first thoroughly purified in the blood of the Lamb. Amen.

The Questions are these:—

We also present the following manuscript, entitled “Short Reflections upon the first original and secondary universal matter:”

I.—The invisible God has brought forth out of himself, in the beginning, a visible matter that was capable of receiving all ideas and forms: to which we may fitly give the name of a subtle spiritual matter, which penetrates all other more gross matters.

II.—In this first original matter, all qualities, elements, and properties were virtually included in the highest degree: for God has created out of the same, in the six days’ creation of this our universe, all planets and visible creatures; and this indeed in such a glorious order, that the infinite wisdom of the Creator is from this clearly revealed to the reasoning creature.

III.—This original matter filled up and occupied, before the creation of this world, the whole space from the heavenly waters above down to the center of the earth. In which place there now exist the created heaven and earth, the Almighty God having in the six days of the Creation divided, distributed, and diffused this first matter into all those planets and various creatures.

IV.—Now, just as this first matter was pure and luminous; so also were the creatures and forms that were created out of it, each in its own kind, luminous and perfect. But because the growth and support of the creatures must follow from the original matter out of which they were created, and because that same matter in the location of this world was already reduced into specific forms; therefore the eternal Creator worked out and produced, by the cooperation of the earthly and heavenly created influences, a second matter, agreeing in all things with the first. This occurs in the same way as in the present earthly defiled world, where a plant that grows out of a grain is altogether like the grain from which it grew, and as in the animal kingdom, where from the seed is again generated such a seed as that from which the living creature came. And in this manner, all creatures materially are resolved into the matter from which they were produced, as into their <term>quintessence</term>, for the bringing forth of their likeness.

V.—To this second matter many names are also given, and because we *rely* most upon the Holy Scripture, among others it is called by the patriarch Jacob the blessing from heaven, with the blessing from the deep, which is otherwise called the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven.

VI.—By this second matter the material creatures were maintained in their property and perfection, until the curse came into the world through sin; by which the will of Man then made all other sublunary creatures and existences partakers of the curse. Therefore also now this second matter is no longer to be obtained in a pure state, but is mixed with filth, as is our sublunary globe.

VII.—But this curse consists properly in this: first of all, that the Creator has moved the earth from its position to a location more remote from the sun, as the true center of the universe, so that the sun cannot enlighten the earth and operate upon and into it as directly and overflowingly with his mild and gentle fire-water-rays as he did before; for which the earth’s remoteness and distance are a great hindrance. In the next place, the earth in and for itself is, by reason of the inherent curse, no longer the same subject as it was, nor as capable and pure as before; so that now the sun, according to the various conditions of the defiled subject and earthly lump, produces from it more terrestrial and intemperate fruits and nourishments, which are not produced by—

The next paper we propose to provide (as indicative of the high science of this individual) is headed, “*A Hundred Queries upon the Mosaic Kabbalah*,” which it would appear he had drawn up as an exercise on the first and second chapters of Genesis, either for himself or some other deep-searching Christian philosophical student; which are these:

I.—Why is this word *Elohim* used in this first chapter of Genesis, and how shall it be properly interpreted? Because it is in the plural number, why is it used with a singular verb? What also is the reason that these two names, *Jehovah* and *Elohim*, are found together in the second chapter, after the completion of the seventh day, and not before?

II.—Why was the earth created before the sun? And why does it now (with all its creatures) desire and thirst for the sun’s power or virtue, even though at that time, when the sun did not exist, it could produce all its growth with its seeds, which it can do no longer?

III.—Since there was yet neither summer nor winter, nor springtime nor harvest, what should be thought of those questions that seek to know in what time of the year the earth was created?

IV.—Why must the sun have been created, since there was such a power in the earth already that it could bring forth all things without the sun? Has the sun then taken its power from the earth? And if so, why does the earth now take it from the sun? Because this power to beget from itself and to be fruitful originally lay in the earth (which must now be done through the mediation of the sun), where has this power gone; and how has it come from the earth to be now in the sun?

V.—Since this power was first in the earth, where was the earth located at that time, which now turns itself around the sun? How could it turn around the sun then, when the sun was not yet created? What was this thing which the earth was longing for at that time? What was there then in place of a sun? How is it to be understood that the sun, which was created later, now has more power in it than the earth, which had not only the same power as the sun has now, but also more? If the sun were a child of the earth, how has this child deprived his mother of her life? But if the fountain of light sprang up alike through the earth and in the place of the sun also, which light was then the greater of the two? What kind of light was it, specifically, which the earth possessed? Was it visible or invisible? From what fountain did it spring, since every light that can be seen by outward eyes now comes from the light of the sun? Why does this light no longer open itself through the earth as it did before?

Now the manifestation of this divine kingdom is various in different persons, and in the same person at different times. Therefore, this variety in the descent of the heavenly and spiritual powers (whether in this principle or in another) and of the joys of the world to come, is here not unfitly symbolized by a *garden, or paradise*; as it was by the King of it himself, in his truly gracious answer to the penitent thief. How varied the manifestation of this *Lebanon-kingdom* will be, no pen can describe and no tongue can express. It is indeed varied, but the manifester all the while is only one; and the essential Word of God, which is the worker of all these things, is most uniform. The guidances, illuminations, and inspirations are very different, but still there is but one way, one light, and one spirit; one Lord, and one God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and of us all, who in these—

XCI.—Could Adam not also have eaten from the tempting tree without any danger if he had first possessed power from the tree of life? And how much more glorious would he have become because of it?

XCII.—Can the tempting tree cause any hurt or annoyance to the man who has a perfect power of Jesus Christ with which to overcome? Or must it not rather be only subservient to him for a greater glory?

XCIII.—Did God shut up Paradise and all its glory for this very purpose: so that Adam might not be tempted even more strongly if he were to be more glorious here?

XCIV.—Was it not God’s great mercy and pity that he set man—who was not found faithful in the smallest things—on a path of humility to learn obedience, so that he might help him up and restore him; there otherwise being no possibility for it if a higher power or station were given to him here?

XCVII.—When man in his <note>blank space in original</note> desire puts the power that is still left to him to a wrong use, and when he steals the things that are God’s and abuses them, and so comes to ruin or undoing, to whose charge is his undoing to be laid?

XCVIII.—In what way must we now be tried and prepared so that we may use our gifts in all purity for our happiness, humbling ourselves and not attempting to fly on high because of them?

XCIX.—Was it not the devil’s fall that he wanted to be like *God*? And does man not still do this same thing? Has he who is the tree of life taught us to do so? Has he not assigned all things to their very foundation, and has he not himself denied all things—yes, even the things to which he himself had right and access? Why should we not listen to him more than to our own lust?

C.—In what way must we now, by continual exercise and striving, set ourselves against our nature and all its lusts, and so continue or go on until we may gain victory from the power of the tree of life—such a grace which, by God’s mercy, is to remain in us substantially and which, either in or after this life, is to keep us in all our trials and to protect and preserve us from the venom and attracting power of ruin, and which is to give us strength or power to reign over it according to the degree to which temptation or trial falls upon us? This trial will surely come upon us because everyone who shall remain in God eternally must pass through trials, either during this life or after it. But in this life it will be better and easier, and after it, it will be infinitely more difficult and painful.

Thus he who is the ABYSSAL UNITY of all beings clothes himself as with various names, rides forth in various powers, wears on his head various crowns, and flashes from his eyes various lights. And yet there is but one crown, one power, and one name, just as there is but one light, which spreads itself into all the variety of colors. This unity and variety of light is well to be noted in the reading of this book, and of all other spiritual treatises whatever, of whatever rank or degree they may be. For God sometimes appears in the darkness, and yet in that darkness there is light; again he appears in the light, and yet darkness may be mixed with this light, until the perfect day springs from on high. Thus he appears to some at a distance, as in a *great and strong wind*; to others in an *earthquake*: in both of which forms he eminently manifested himself through some, about the beginning of the seventeenth century. Then after this, approaching still nearer, he appears to a third sort in the *fire*: as at this very day he powerfully does to some who are known to *Wisdom’s* discipleship. And lastly, he demonstrates his presence to some, as to this his chosen vessel, in a *still small voice*, and in a sweet, gentle, glowing flame. Sometimes God manifests himself to the eye or ear of the receptive heart, according to the various properties, operations, and influences of this or that name which he puts on; of this or that attribute which he communicates; of this or that sphere in which the living wheels of the creatures before the throne of God move. We give the answer to the first of these *Queries*, namely:—" This name, *Elohim*, is the only one of all the Divine names used in the *Cosmopoeia* <note>The creation of the world</note>, or Genesis of the World, by Moses, as expressing in it a sort of plurality or fruitfulness: and by it is to be understood, as the eastern sages declare, the glorious creator or executor, as containing within himself ideally the world to be created; or, as God one and many, or one and all—with regard to that divine all-forming power, which is one and the same in all its manifold productions. And this, therefore, being always expressed in the plural number, is yet paired with a singular verb, to signify the Unity both in God and Nature, under all the multifarious effects and phenomena; and that just as all things orderly spring up from a center into multiplicity by the going forth of *Elohim* into manifestation, so likewise all things are to be reduced by him through that variety back into an Unity. But when the heavens and the earth were perfected in the full harmony of all beings, and *Elohim* had, on the seventh day, finished all his work as the executor of the Incomprehensible substance or abyssal ineffable Deity, by blessing and sanctifying the day of his rest; then the great and venerable Name, which is beyond all expression, as particularly regarding the Divine essence, or essence of essences, was added to that of *Elohim*. And thereupon mention is made of the *generations* of both heaven and earth, as immediately succeeding their creation. This is well to be observed."

The answer to the second *Query* runs thus:—" The creation of the earth is excellently represented to us as being before that of the sun, so that we might not be ignorant that the light which is concentrated in the sun is the very light which was previously concentrated in the earth: and that there must have been a certain fiery and luminous substance in the earth, from the impregnation of the spirit of *Elohim* irradiating those waters in which it lay immersed for some time; which substance was perfectly of a solar nature. . . . . . . . ."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the varying degrees of divine inspiration, transitioning from the manifestation of God’s names to how he calls individuals from all walks of life, followed by specific prayers for a deceased individual and for the ailing Dr. George Hickes.</meta>

proselyte, male or female, young or old. Some he has called from the plow, others from harvesting sycamore trees, and others from their fishing nets; whom he has set over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out and to plant, to throw down and to build up, by the mighty power of his Spirit, according to its various operations and manifestations. It does not matter what the subject is through which the divine influences are received and passed: even if it should be a heathen, as in the case of *Jethro*; or a brute beast, as in the case of *Balaam*. The level, nevertheless, of these influences may be calculated according to the situation, and according to the proximity or distance of the subject—which is to receive them—from the source or center of Divine light, and according to the several channels and ducts through which they must first pass before they are received there. But the all-wise God is never lacking in the preparation of such vessels as may be suitable for the reception of such degrees of his light as he intends to communicate. And this beautiful variety is most remarkable in the writings of the Old Testament, and also in those of the New. For the degree of inspiration that *Moses* had was one thing, and that which *Isaiah* had was another, and that which *Daniel* had was a third. Neither is the inspiration of the writer of the *Chronicles* the same as any of these three: and yet both the one and the other are all from the true, inspiring breath of God. The same may also be observed in the New Testament. But to treat of this would require a long discourse. What has been said here already will suffice for the wise in

<meta>This page continues the editorial commentary on the necessity for a systematic "science" of spiritual experience, critiquing Jane Lead and Pordage for their over-reliance on visions while highlighting Methodism as a practical but incomplete model. It then transitions into a preface defending the continued nature of divine revelation and begins an introductory poem regarding the fall of man and the intervention of Divine Wisdom.</meta>

religious world. But being without such a solid groundwork of instruction and practical demonstration regarding the grand aim and design of the gospel and of Behmen's revelation, her mind—like that of her "companion and fellow-laborer," Pordage—became subject to being turned toward the non-essentials of visions and revelations as if they were *an end* in themselves. The result of this is that, however profound her experience may have been, her works can only be received by enlightened Christians of the present day as a medley of unprofitable, even hurtful, and yet, in some points, most interesting curiosities.

With regard to the above demanded standard treatises of *orderly experiences* and systematic directions, we might again ask why Christianity, as a *positive and progressive science*, should not have its formulas of elementary rules, exercises for acquisition, and tests of advancement, *all exactly laid down*, as in the case of other sciences; why, indeed, should the science and practice of Christ-like perfection not be professedly taught as a part of education, at least to those who desire such an accomplishment? This was the object of a <term>Theosophic College</term>.

Now, though such an institution has been proposed, it is not thereby implied that a set method of cultivating piety, even to a high degree of perfection, is not in existence. *For it may be said, and said truly in a general sense, that Methodism, for instance (to say nothing of its ministerial training, either ancient or modern), is so constituted as to present an exercise to draw forth the spiritual life in very numerous evangelical developments—through its simple original services and preachings; through its wonderful code of experimental and seraphic hymns, with their appropriate tunes; through its prayer meetings (after the evening services on the Lord's day and during the week, but particularly at five and six o'clock every morning—a most efficient means for* holy living, *to get the soul baptized with the* fire, *and* power, *and* full composure *of the Spirit so early each morning, and then to preserve that life in a* full glow *during the day by watchfulness and continual recurrence to the closet); through its class meetings, its band meetings, and, not least, its love feasts; through its demands upon the personal activity of all its members in some evangelical way; and by its systematically taught pecuniary liberality toward the bodies and souls of our neighbor; in short, by its professing to make religion* the business *of all its members, and making all other things subservient to that end.* Through all these particular exercises and principles, Methodism may be said to present a general system for eliciting the Christian life in numerous practical developments (notwithstanding that scarcely one in a hundred of its modern tutors or class leaders either knows or teaches further than the common elements of spiritual arithmetic, and not one in ten thousand understands the higher branches of spiritual mathematics). And if any persons doubt that, we only say: let them go and try it *faithfully* for six months, and then give their judgment. But the object of the institution contemplated here is, as observed, to prove Christianity in all its universality and fullness of divine life, light, and power through a number of variously constituted individuals; and from there to deduce a system of rules, or rather a "Grammar" and "Exercises," for the cultivation of the divine life in the soul, to be improved upon by experience.

This appears to be the *practical* question for us, then, in reference to what has just been stated in the above Preface—that is, the production of a system for the universal training of the spiritual man (whatever may be his individual character and temperament) with the strictness and certainty of academic discipline, according to a standard form of piety and high divine science, corresponding in the latter particular to the discoveries and information provided through the indications of this treatise. [—*To proceed with the continuation of the Preface.*]

As for the removal of that great millstone which is thrown in the way—*namely, that God has ceased to reveal himself to man since the days of the apostles, and that all pretensions to the same are but illusions, and at best but the dreams and fancies of a natural enthusiasm*—I am not very concerned. I well know that the same God, who has already appeared in a most wonderful manner to give his testimony to souls concerning what has been published so far from the same spirit and instrument, will not fail now to give his seal to this, or to what may come to be published hereafter. He will vindicate his honor even in a more ample and fuller manner than he has yet been known to have done since the primitive days of faith. But however the Wisdom of God may show itself at present regarding these particular writings, this millstone must shortly be cast into the sea. Otherwise, the kingdom of God, for which we ought to pray daily, can never come; and it is little better than a mockery of his name to solicit him for the calling of the Jews, the fullness of the Gentiles, and for unity, peace, and concord among all nations* until this beam is removed from before the eye of our spirits. For this purpose, a treatise was written some time ago [by yourself?] to prove not only the *possibility* and the *expediency*, but

### FREHER.

Having, no doubt, excited a legitimate curiosity in the reader to see some of Freher’s writings—from whose discourses Law, as noted, derived full benefit, and which therefore must be read by the student to understand the basic formation of Law’s mind in its theosophical development; and since this section should be seen as representing the highest philosophical, mystical, and theological science available in this country at the start of the last century, we propose to devote the rest of this POSTSCRIPT to a few illustrations of Freher’s genius and talent.
We have already briefly described the character of Freher’s works. It is therefore only necessary to repeat here that they contain a systematic presentation and demonstration of the truths and principles of Boehme’s philosophy. As the author proceeds, he invites or anticipates objections to specific points—whether because they are not easily understood by the honest inquirer, or seem inconsistent with accepted orthodox truth or other parts of Boehme’s writings. He never fails to clear these up before continuing his discourses, caring only for the interests of truth and setting it forth in its full, natural light.
It would be impossible, through any extracts inserted here, to provide an adequate sense of the universality and depth of Freher’s philosophical science. The only goal we can attempt is to present a few glimpses of it, also hoping to generate a demand for the publication of his complete works, as described in the advertisement to be attached to this treatise. Therefore, as an example or illustration of the merits of Freher’s writings suitable for this occasion, we have—despite the difficulty of choosing—selected two or three of the aforementioned Discourses. These address the objections mentioned earlier and provide a summary of his previous explanations of the subjects in question.
The first of these extracts, which briefly treats “Of GOD considered without NATURE or CREATURE,” may be considered an introduction to the rest, and is as follows:

> I.—It is a deeply grounded central axiom of immovable and unquestionable truth—firm and solid throughout all principles and most worthy of being carefully pondered, both at the very beginning of all these writings and especially at the start of this first section—*that no eye can see beyond its own sphere or world, in which it is born, or in which it exists and has its sole essence and its entire faculty of sight*. *Three Princ.* ii. 1—4, etc.; vii. 1, 2, etc. *Baptism*, i. 14. *Sign. Rer.* iii. 6, 7, 8. *Epistles*, v. 2, 3, etc.; xxxii. 3—8.
> II.—According, then, to this fundamental position, it is absolutely impossible for any created intellectual eye to look essentially into that Abyss which is beyond eternal nature, or to distinctly grasp and positively declare, in an affirmative way, *what God is apart from all nature and creation*. Truly, if we were to say that either men or angels were able to do so, our statement would carry the same absurd and contradictory nonsense as if we said that something can act without or beyond its own sphere of activity.
> III.—For every created eye or intellect is a specific thing, having an existence distinct from other things; it is posterior to and situated—regarding all its faculties—within the sphere of eternal
