<meta>This page continues the discussion on the distinction between God as He is in Himself (beyond nature) and God as He is manifested through eternal nature, drawing upon the writings of Jacob Boehme and the commentary of Dionysius Andreas Freher.</meta>

nature. Whereas, without eternal nature, there is and must be an eternal *nothing*, in comparison to all created things in nature: and an eternal *chaos*, or *balanced state*; or an eternal *oneness*, in comparison to that divisibility and innumerable multiplicity that is in nature. In which eternal *nothing, balanced state, and oneness* no creature can exist, nor ever be brought forth; seeing it is self-evident that something and nothing, distinction and balance, multiplicity and oneness, cannot stand together in one and the same sphere, but imply the very highest and most irreconcilable contradiction. <term>THREE PRIN.</term> i. 21, 22. <term>PREDEST.</term>, ii. 56—63.

IV.—But, nevertheless, the created intellect, both in men and angels, considering things *after the fact* as they are in nature, and knowing they came into natural existence from such a deeper original or foundation-essence, which is itself ALL things in the most eminent sense, must necessarily on one side acknowledge all things to have been in that same original fountain before eternal nature; because they came forth from it; and must also on the other side deny anything to have been there in the same way it is now in its created existence, after eternal nature: or else we would say that it has been a creature before it was created.

V.—This we are able to understand; but to declare, further, distinctly and positively, what this original or foundation-essence is in itself, and how all things have been in it before eternal nature, will be much more impossible for us than to understand distinctly, and to declare positively, what and how we have been in the loins of our father Adam. <term>FORTY QUES.</term> i, 341, 347.

VI.—All that we can conceive and say of it is this: that we all, when yet in the loins of Adam, were nothing, lying in one single chaos, without any distinction from each other: which in a sense, and with respect to what we are now, is very true. And yet it is not true without all limitation in an absolute transcendent sense. For we may see that even from this same nothing the apostle can, and does, draw forth a most excellent and emphatic argument to demonstrate the great preeminence of the <term>Melchizedek</term> priesthood above the <term>Levitical</term>, saying that <term>Levi</term>, who received tithes after he was in existence, *paid tithes in Abraham*, when he was yet so much "nothing" as to be only in the loins of his father.

VII.—Though, therefore, our Author has written most deeply and solidly about nature and the creature, so also even of God himself without any nature and creature; yet we are not to think that he had, or could have had, an essential prospect or looking, as it were, *from the beginning* into that most incomprehensible Abyss of all abysses. For no illumination, no matter how high, can afford such a view to any created eye; but only a sight *after the fact*, whereby (in a comparative or negative way) he could and did express that first Original Being, outside of nature, with natural words; being made able to find the most fitting expressions that could be found in outward nature. And of these, I think those three mentioned before are the most accommodating to every capacity.

<margin>Comparison punctuated with the Author's original</margin>
VIII.—But this must yet especially be noticed: that these three expressions (and chiefly that of oneness) relate not only to the creatures, but also to all that God has manifested to be himself through eternal nature. . . . Which is to say that here in this place, where God is considered without any nature and creature, no distinct idea may be had (and shall also not be desired to be had) of the Holy Trinity: no Father, Son, nor Holy Ghost; no Wisdom, no light, glory, majesty, goodness, or holiness are yet here brought forth into distinct manifestation. For though all these things have verily been there also, and must not be said to have had a beginning afterward—much less to be generated by eternal nature—yet they were as yet unknown, incomprehensible, and unmanifest. And this expression, *They were then so, and are now so*, does not imply that ever any change, turning, or alteration was made, for all is eternal and co-eternal, without any beginning or shadow of turning: but we, who live and understand in time and are used to periodical distinctions, cannot express what we conceive of it otherwise but by a *before* and *after*: which yet signifies nothing else but our own distinct idea of one and the same eternal object. This idea is one thing when we consider this eternal object abstractly, as *it is in itself* without all nature: for then it is to us, who are in nature, unknown, hidden, and unintelligible; and it is another thing again when we consider it as manifested through the concurrence of eternal nature: for then we are able to have an understanding or sight of it, more or less, according to that degree in which our eye is illuminated by the eternal light.—Regarding that former consideration, we cannot express it better and more closely than by saying: All these things were (or rather are) an eternal incomprehensible *nothing* when compared to that which we now, after their manifestation through eternal nature, can understand them to be. They are an eternal unintelligible *oneness*, in opposition to our distinct, manifold ideas we can now have of them: they are an eternal inconceivable *balanced state*, in comparison to that distinction we can now conceive in them.—He, therefore, who has but a proper understanding of these three expressions, may easily be freed from being disturbed by such seeming contradictions as might appear in some of those places where <term>JACOB BOEHME</term> writes of *God considered without Nature and Creature*, and may also easily discern what is intermixed here and there relating to his eternal manifestation. Which places are these following: <term>THREEFOLD LIFE</term>, i. 33. <term>FORTY QUEST.</term> i. 24—48., 262—265. <term>INCARN.</term> Part II. i. 29. ii. 1—25.; iii. 1, 2, etc. <term>PREDEST.</term> i. throughout. <term>CONTEMPL. <meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the Divine Being's relationship to eternal nature, specifically addressing how Jacob Boehme (referred to as Teutonicus or Behmen) distinguishes between God as the unmanifested Abyss and God as manifested through nature.</meta>

deepest sense, much different from the way the dark world is called abyssal, both in his own writings and in the Holy Scriptures. It transcends all created capacities and is utterly excluded from any possibility of being an object of either human or angelic understanding. As it was, it still is and will be forever and ever: above, without, beyond, and before eternal nature. This is true even though this nature is, in the sense declared formerly, co-eternal with that Divine Being, so that all priority or successiveness is totally excluded. And sometimes, again (2) he considers this Divine Being, as manifested in and through eternal nature, as **byssal**—or as that which from the former unformed, beginningless, and endless Abyss has introduced itself into a ground, or byss; into perceptibility, or into beginning and end. In this state, it is capable of being understood and enjoyed, in some measure and degree, by understanding creatures created for that purpose; as it was, still is, and will be forever and ever, in and with eternal nature. This is despite the fact that this nature was always, still is, and shall be forever distinct from, and in no way to be confounded with, that Divine Being.

So then, therefore, (3) it is also unquestionable and obvious in all the books of Teutonicus that he uses several various expressions and makes very different descriptions of the Divine Being. These are not applicable interchangeably to both these considerations but must be referred either to the former or to the latter with due distinction.

Though it cannot be denied that he also often uses the same words for both cases, this is mainly because of the insufficiency of our capacities and speech. Both our understanding and our language exist after and under eternal nature, and cannot reach or be furnished with words sufficient to express that which is beyond and before it. Therefore, such expressions as are used in both the former and the latter considerations must be understood distinctly and regulated according to what he has so frequently and plainly warned and laid as a foundation for further study. For this foundation, if observed, cannot help but immediately direct the reader to that distinction which must always be maintained in meaning, even if it cannot always be maintained in outward words. This applies to every expression that is dubious or common (in its outward sound) to both considerations; if neglected, much confusion and seeming contradictions cannot be avoided.

The first result of these three fundamental, unquestionable assertions, which should be justly noted here at the beginning, is this: when Teutonicus considers the Divine Being as before or without all nature and creature, the generation of *eternal nature* and its seven properties is not implied in that consideration—neither tacitly nor explicitly—and must not be conceived as if the mention of it were only left out for the sake of brevity. Instead, this generation of eternal nature in all its properties is utterly and absolutely excluded from that consideration and must be conceived as entirely *posterior* to it. Yet, this posteriority should not be referred to the thing itself, but only to our narrow capacity and confined understanding.

If, in the *first* consideration of the Divine Being, the generation of eternal nature in its properties were looked upon as tacitly implied, the entire distinction between the first and second consideration would be wholly lost. Yet that distinction was laid down as the first foundation, most plainly and clearly, in more than twelve or fifteen places. Besides this, many hundred noble expressions would be rendered senseless; indeed, the whole structure of his entire building would be overthrown. Pray, how can God be considered as without and before all nature if the generation of nature is said to be only left out in the written words, but is to be conceived in the mind as already done? Or how could Teutonicus have said: *so far is God considered without all nature and creature?* Truly, that "so far" can mean nothing else but this: until it comes to the generation of the properties of nature, God is considered without all nature.

But here two objections may be made. The first is this: since there is neither "before" nor "after" in the consideration of God and eternal nature, we cannot but think that these two expressions, *before* and *without* nature, must be equivalent. And since God is considered by Behmen only as in the second principle of light and love, wherein He is distinct from and superior to His dwelling place, he could rightly have said that God is considered without nature, even though in this consideration the whole generation of nature is tacitly implied, even if not always distinctly mentioned.

The answer is, first, as to priority: it was granted already that we ought not to speak of any *before* or *after* with relation to the *thing itself*, but that we must do so with respect to our *apprehension*, which allows us to conceive all these things orderly, since we are not able to apprehend them as they are in themselves, all at once. And secondly, as to the two expressions, *before* and *without*: though they are, on one account, commonly and rightly joined together, they are on another account not at all equivalent, but greatly different from each other in their sense and relation.

For when I say God is considered as *before* eternal nature, this nature is always utterly excluded and must be conceived as absolutely posterior to that consideration, as the *natural* and *common* sense of that word shows sufficiently. But when I say God is considered *without* nature, as Behmen sometimes does, the whole of eternal nature is not always utterly excluded. Instead, only the "left" or inferior restless part of nature is excluded—which is frequently called "nature" by Behmen in an absolute sense, without addition, and in a stricter sense that excludes the other "right," superior, transmuted part. This latter part, in opposition to the former, is not called nature by Behmen, but most significantly "the end of nature," or the "fulfilling" or "satisfying" of nature, or also the "holy" or the "tinctured nature."

So now it is true indeed that when he considers God in that second, superior, transmuted principle of light and love, the generation of the first principle in all its preceding properties is indeed implied and must be conceived as already completed. But what can this signify or prove against our position? This entire consideration of God is not a consideration of God as abyssal, unmanifest, and unintelligible, but as intelligible by creatures—as byssal and manifested in and through eternal nature. It may be called "without nature" also—not because the generation of nature is utterly excluded or looked upon as posterior, but only because it is done through the inferior and restless part into the superior, harmonized part of nature. It is thus truly *without* (but not before) that lower, disharmonized part of nature, which properly and strictly is called nature.

But further, it is absolutely false that Behmen considers God only in that way. For though he uses the same expressions mentioned in this objection—namely, that God is considered *only* in the second principle of light—it is as clear as the day at noon that this *only* is, by himself, limited and—

confined to eternal nature, and especially to its three tinctured and harmonized properties. Thus, it is to say that God, as manifested in eternal nature, is considered only in the second principle. And so, this "only" does not at all imply that there is not a deeper and more central consideration of God, since it is well known that he also considers God as unmanifest, in that abyss where there is neither darkness nor light, etc.; that is, before eternal nature.

The second objection is this: If, in that consideration of the Divine Being which Behmen calls "before and without nature," we do not view the generation as tacitly implied, Behmen will be found full of contradictions; but if we do, all that he says about it is plain. Answer: The exact contrary to this is true. For, as it cannot be denied that there is something deeper, more central, and more unintelligible than eternal nature is—which something is the very same eternal or Abyssal Nothing that the Divine Being is before eternal Nature—if it is either wholly removed or not observed as it ought to be, or if it is mixed and confused with what should be conceived as posterior to it, it is no wonder that contradictory expressions appear in Behmen's work. So, then, this mentioned erroneous position cannot be a proper means to reconcile such contradictions; and though it may provide a clearer view of one superior part of Behmen’s building, it cannot give a plain and full view of the whole structure, nor show the coherence between the foundation and what is built upon it. But let everything, and every expression of it, be placed and viewed in its own proper station—as it is either more distant from or nearer to the center, or as it is even that deepest and most individual center itself—and everything will be free from contradictions.

When two opposite winds meet each other at the same height in our atmosphere, there must necessarily be opposition and strife; for each is resisted by the other, and neither can go its own way until the weaker is driven back or swallowed up by the stronger. But let one blow from east to west at a certain height (for instance, the height of a mountain), and then the other may go freely on its own quite contrary way from west to east in a region above it. This is known to occur many times in our macrocosm and is truly a fine emblem, able to give us good direction in the interpretations we place upon these deep spiritual matters—to imitate these orders and regulated courses of nature. This is all the more true because we have before us a clear pattern from our enlightened author, who constantly did so himself throughout the whole progress he made from the deepest and most central to the highest and most outward circumferential thing. Therefore, if what he has so orderly and gradually declared is to be understood, we must do the same thing by looking at everything in its own place where it stands and where it is expressed by him. By doing so, every lower and more external expression will open a free and clear way to every other that may be either more central or the deepest center itself; and we shall clearly find that as eternal nature is plainly and necessarily implied in the second consideration of the Divine Being, so from the first consideration it is wholly and absolutely excluded—which, in the following discourse, I hope and trust will be sufficiently demonstrated with God's assistance.

IN THE FIRST PLACE, then, I shall say something concerning the Abyssal Nothing and declare the reason why it is so called by BEHMEN.

IN THE NEXT PLACE, I shall say something especially concerning the Trinity, showing (1) from Behmen’s own expressions that a Trinity both before and after eternal nature (but with a great difference in sense) is inseparable from the Unity. (2) What difference exists in the Trinity when considered in this twofold respect. And (3) that, despite this difference, there are not two Trinities, but only one. 

IN THE THIRD PLACE, I shall proceed to the delineation of these four figures, showing (1) that if all four are taken together, they stand in good conformity with that single figure which Behmen himself made in the *Forty Questions*, despite the fact that their outward form might appear as something quite different.

(2) That the first and fourth are to be viewed as only one, despite the fact that in the fourth, several things are added which were wanting in the first. (3) That the addition of those things in the fourth is caused only by the second and third, both of which—even distinct from each other—must have been inserted between the first and the fourth. (4) That nothing in Behmen’s writings (as to this matter concerning the Divine manifestation) may be found which could not be referred to one or the other of these four. (5) That nothing regarding all this matter is omitted, but everything is set in its due place and order (though it was impossible for every particular to have been distinctly expressed by a unique character), and that by everyone that is expressed, some consideration was intended to be represented. This, I say, as far as I can judge, will be the best method.

If anything should be said that contributes to the honor of God, declares the truth, and is beneficial to the reader, all praise and glory shall be given to Him alone, without whose assistance we can do nothing. Amen.

*Ex nihilo nihil fit* <note>Out of nothing, nothing comes.</note>: This was a saying of that famous heathen philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note>, almost idolized by many learned people called Christians. And though it was said by him in opposition to Christian doctrine, it is yet true enough in some sense, limited to that notion which a corrupt natural reason or earthly wisdom could have afforded him regarding that common expression of "nothing." But yet it is not accepted here either on account of his authority or in his heathenish sense, but in the sense of TEUTONICUS, who says the very same in these formal words: *out of nothing, nothing can come forth, but everything must have its root*. And he gives not only a far deeper explanation but also makes a far better use of it than could have been done by any natural philosopher.

If he then says so plainly that out of nothing, nothing can come forth, and if he, notwithstanding this, calls the Divine Being (from whom angels and men came forth as an offspring) an "eternal nothing," it is as clear as anything can be that there must be the greatest difference between the former and the latter "nothing."

Whenever *Teutonicus* says, *Out of nothing nothing can come forth*, it is certain that he takes this "nothing" in that common sense where it is generally said that the whole creation is brought forth by the Creator out of nothing. If he had now said that this Creator himself was "nothing" in this same sense before he created, could anything be more foolish or mad?

If it is such a foolish and abominable thing to form such a negative idea, as mentioned, of that

which was, or rather which is to be conceived, before eternal nature, this eternal nothing before nature must certainly be something. For if we do not conceive it as nothing, we must conceive it as something, there being no third notion either distinct from these, or partaking of them both. But we must of necessity take one, and deny the other. And since it is not nothing, according to Teutonicus's own plain words, it must certainly be something.

But I would not want to be misunderstood here, as I easily might be, if this dilemma should be extended beyond its sphere, and so beyond the sense and intent for which it is taken here. For I know very well that, according to the principles of Teutonicus, in various senses, upon different accounts, and with several respects, that which is considered by him as "before eternal nature" may be called both something and nothing, and may be said again to be neither nothing nor something. And truly he cannot be blamed for such variety and seemingly contradictory expressions.

He could not help it, and no man living upon earth shall be found able to represent these things to the understanding of another with such expressions as would never seem to cross and contradict each other. If the Spirit of God in the revelation could have said of one and the same thing, "it was, and was not, and yet was," nay, could have added, *that here is wisdom*, etc., who can justly complain of Teutonicus? The understanding must supply what is lacking in the expressions, which may be done in part by duly considering that this matter, with its expressions of nothing and something, cannot be referred to one only world or universe, which would make no difference in the sense, but to two extremely different from each other; which is therefore, and must be, the chief cause why one and the same expression is true in relation to the one, and false, or at least much altered in sense, in reference to the other.

This, then, is an evident position of Teutonicus: that the Divine Being, considered as *before* eternal nature, is an eternal *something*, though he so frequently calls it an eternal nothing, which will appear by the following particulars.

We may ask reasonably, what was before the creation of angels and of this world? And we may answer, God. This will be enough for a common or superficial understanding; but more distinctly and theosophically we must answer with Teutonicus, *God and eternal nature*. Now, we cannot ask further, what was before God? But we may ask (in a sense limited as above), what was before eternal nature? meaning not, thereby, that there was any instant in which eternal nature was not, and after which it came to be what it is; but meaning only that there was, and still is, something deeper, or something more internal and central, which is eternal nature’s root, ground, and original, since out of nothing, nothing can come forth. And asking what that was, and is, which just as it does now, so also from eternity, *causes* eternal nature to be what it is, and gave it to have what it has? We must, with Teutonicus, answer, that this is *God, an eternal nothing, a still eternity, an eternal liberty, a resting quiet temperature, a serene light* <note>habitation, says the English interpreter, for want of a fitter expression; but in the true sense of the German word, there is not meant a *habitation* at all, but such a soft and tender *sweetness* or *delightfulness*, (N.B.) as is perceptible, indeed, but very calm; and not so powerfully unfolded or displayed that it might be called a great overwhelming joy; which difference may be more easily understood in our mind by experience than it can be expressed by words</note>:

An unintelligible softness, meekness, stillness, humility; an abyssal Being; a chaos, comprehending itself, or comprehensible by itself; a Wonderful Eye, wherein all the colors, powers, and virtues lay together in such a mixture that they are indeed undiscernible, so that none can tell what it is; and yet they make a most terrible, awful prospect, confounding and consuming every sight that looks upon it. An eternal mirror of wonders; an abyssal powerfulness, all-sufficiency, omniscience, something which is and is not; (N.B.) which is, and dwells in itself, and is *not manifest outside of itself*; something which is nothing and all; a single eternal life or good; and a single will without *desire*, <note>without that desire which tends toward the outside and is the beginning of nature, but not absolutely without any desire. For this eternal will without all nature desires, and only desires, to generate itself in Trinity, or to generate its co-eternal son; which desire, though not conveniently nor properly so called, tends not toward the outside, but keeps within, is free from nature, and has no other object but only this generation, as might be shown from many places of this author.</note> A spiritual, substantial power, working in itself, (N.B.) a sensibility of love; a pleasant, loving taste; a delightful moving of the Holy Ghost in the eternal wisdom; an eternal love, and only love, generating and introducing itself in pure love into trinity; which trinity as yet is not distinguished according to what we can call a distinction in and after nature, and is not, therefore, a proper object of our understanding. JE-HO-VA: Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; a threefold opening and breathing out, working in itself, generating itself, finding and perceiving itself; a divine eternal unity, <note>answering, in a sense and manner, much rather to the 0 than to the number 1.</note> An infinite Triune Being, past all finding out, etc.:

All these expressions may be found in Behmen as an answer to that question: what was before eternal nature? And so we may now see, not only that he expresses it so variously, but also by expressions negative and positive. Nay, sometimes his expressions do so notoriously contradict each other that it might seem as if they were designedly used to frighten away from these mysteries all ill-natured and unworthy readers, and to raise an attention and inquiry after truth in those who had enough consideration and reasonable judgment to think that this author had something of reality in him and was not quite a mad and drunken babbler. For instance, when he says in one place that what is before eternal nature is an eternal life and good; and in another, that the abyss has no life and good; and in another, that there is light and clearness in the abyss, and that there is neither light nor darkness within it. Again, that before eternal nature there is no finding, no perceiving, no knowing of itself; no activity, no mobility, and yet that there is perceiving, knowing, loving, tasting, opening, generating, breathing out, working and moving, etc., before and without eternal nature. And again, when he says plainly, (N.B.) that all the powers, colors, and virtues lay together in one (without distinction), and yet adds in the same place that one power, color, and virtue knows or perceives the other in distinction; and that this is a manifold generating harmony, well tuned and concordant with every sound thereof. Or a speaking word, wherein all the languages, powers, colors, and virtues lay together, and with or by the speaking, they unfold and introduce themselves into a sight or seeing eye.

<meta>This page continues the argument that Jacob Boehme (referred to as "Teutonicus") uses the term "eternal nothing" not to describe a void, but to signify a substantial Being that exists before and beyond the limitations of "eternal nature."</meta>

...prove that *Teutonicus* does not represent that which is before eternal nature as a nothing, but as a something, or true substantial Being.

For since he speaks of it so variously, now in a negative and then again in a positive way, it is undeniable that he would not have us conceive of it as *non ens*, or nothing, but as a real something.

It was necessary, also, for him to use these seemingly contradictory expressions, and to represent it both as nothing and something; neither this nor that alone could have served his ends.

If he had represented it as a something only, he would not have sufficiently declared the infinite distance between that abyssal center and all its outflown, lesser and greater circumferences. He would not have properly exalted it above all that can be named, thought of, spoken of, or comprehended. He would have dangerously misled us and given occasion to conceive of it only as the greatest and most particular something, when it is not such a something that has any other something beside it from which it could be distinguished as a unique something by itself. Instead, it must be quite exempt from the number and order of "somethings" and exalted far above them as a universal ground, source, or center, out of which all things, with all their order, originate.

Just as we see a fine resemblance of this in a center and its circumference: the circumference consists of innumerable little points, fittingly corresponding to so many particular "somethings" placed beside each other.

But the center is only one individual point; as to its quantity, it is no bigger than any of the rest, but as to its qualities, it is the most significant of all, and in a sense as large as all the circumferential points taken together; indeed, upon another account, it is even infinitely larger.

For upon this alone all the circumferential points depend, having from that one point all that they are and have. Indeed, there is none of them, however small, which does not have something answering to it and corresponding with it in the central point as their original source; seeing that even this may be considered not only as a center of its circumference, but also as a circumference of itself. Why, then, we may conceive it as being as large as all the points together in the whole circumference. And when we consider that from this single central point—without any addition to it, subtraction from it, or any change of place or number—innumerable other circles, first smaller and then wider, even *in infinitum*, may be conceived coming forth, this one original central point may well be conceived as infinitely larger than all the circumferential points can be. These are all confined to number, order, and place, and subject to various changes of increase and decrease, while that central point alone is immutable in itself, free from all such imperfections, and nevertheless possesses more eminently within itself everything that exists in all of them; for everything displayed in them is concentrated in that point.

Further, we may conceive of a visible circumference wherein no center visibly appears at all, and yet we are always sure there is and must be a fixed, unalterable point which caused all the points in this circumference to stand in the order they do and to have such a connection with each other. And again, all the points in this circumference exist in divisibility and multiplicity as so many particular parts; so that each of them fills only its own place and is only what it is within its own narrow scope, but nothing more; and none of them can be considered in any way as a whole, and when taken all together, they are but a whole circumference in which no center is implied as a part of it.

But the central point alone is a single, indivisible universe and can be truly called a whole; since it can never be divided into two, nor can it ever admit a second or third beside it; and is, moreover, in a sense and manner, both center and circumference itself. So that it is, and remains unalterably in the whole circumference, an only perfect whole, and an all-fulfilling, all-sufficient all.

Now let a proper application of all this, and more like it, be made to that Abyssal Being, and we shall see that just as a center is no less—but rather more—really something than any point of the circumference, yet it is also really nothing at all to all the points thereof because it does not belong to their number and order, but is that which allows them to have such a number and order. It is incomprehensible to them, but it itself in a sense comprehends them all and had them within itself before they were set forth in number and order out of it. It is excluded from the entire circumference and keeps only its own central residence where none of all the other points can approach. It is of a completely different nature, condition, and properties; and so it may be called, on one side, a real being in itself, but on the other, quite a nothing to them. So also that Abyssal Being before eternal nature, which is the only original source of all things that follow, may be called most significantly a "nothing" with respect to all that originates from it, even though it is a substantial being in itself. Therefore, if he had represented it only as "something" through mere positive expressions, he would have taught us to conceive of it not as an abyssal, incomprehensible (N.B.) Universal Center, but as an "outflown" particular something, which we might have looked upon as if it belonged to the category and order of other particular things. And so he would have led us to form various images of it, as we might have thought most fitting, when they all would be no better than idols of gold and silver.

But now, by telling us not only in one respect (through positive expressions) that it is a Being, but also through negative descriptions that it is nothing to us and to all things that are posterior and exterior, he prevents (if we would understand him) all such mistakes. For he earnestly reminds us that in our inquiry after that which is before eternal nature, we should be very cautious, modest, and sober—not running out too far, and not thinking that we have, or can have, any ability to find such pertinent notions as might correspond to it and provide us with words fit to declare affirmatively what it is. Rather, we should be sure that it utterly vanishes out of all our sight, thoughts, and ideas, so that it can be apprehended, imagined, or expressed by none of them. Indeed, even the nearest and best ideas we can lawfully have of it must be denied again and quite abstracted from every sense they can have or bear in this world. This is to say: it is nothing, and is the reason why he so frequently calls it an eternal nothing.

But then again, on the other side, if he had represented it always and absolutely as nothing, using only negative expressions without affirming anything, he would have erred himself and misled others, quite contradicting his own axiom: that out of nothing, nothing can come forth.

Having thus proved, I think sufficiently, from Boehme's own many expressions (1.) that

<meta>This page continues the argument that Jacob Boehme's "eternal nothing" is not a void but a "being" so exalted and central that it precedes all created "somethings" and properties of nature.</meta>

the generation of eternal nature in all its properties is not implied, but totally excluded from that first consideration of the Divine Being, which he usually calls "without all nature and creature."
(2.) That this Divine Being without nature is not to be conceived according to the usual absolute sense of this latter expression (nothing), but according to the most eminent sense of the former (being). This sense must be abstracted indeed from all conceivable beings in and after nature. Yet it is not abstracted by way of a strict and direct opposition, which would lead us into that common notion of nothing, but by way of a great exaltation above it, in such an eminent manner that we may say it is a being indeed, but a being only in and to itself, having no communion in properties or qualities with any other being; and belonging not to the number and order in which all particular beings stand with a mutual relation to themselves. (3.) That consequently these two expressions, *no-thing* and *being*, must necessarily be joined together in all our discourses and conceptions of it, and that the whole truth cannot be declared in its fullness by either one alone. And (4.) that taking these two expressions in the sense mentioned here is the only true middle way, leading safely through two most dangerous extremes, and making us avoid on one side our forming images of that divine abyssal Being, which we are naturally so much inclined to conceive in forms and figures; and on the other to avoid dishonoring our only true eternal root, or central being, without which no creature could exist. And that, therefore, we must not place it in the circumference, which belongs only to things brought forth, in which circumstance this divine abyssal being is nothing; but that we must place it in its own central residence, where this eternal nothing is a true substantial being—not brought forth, but bringing forth everything that may be called something, in and after eternal and temporal nature: where innumerable "somethings" represent themselves to our eye and understanding, and are yet (only because there are many) nothing else but small particulars, all confined to their own narrow compass; while that central no-thing alone is a whole universe, and an individual, all-filling and all-sufficient.
We must now consider, a little more distinctly, some of our Author's chief affirmative expressions, in order to approach thereby nearer to the most principal matter, which is the consideration of the Trinity, both before and after eternal nature. Some, I say, of his affirmative, not negative, expressions; setting this down as a significant foundation for what is to follow: that his affirmative expressions must prevail in our consideration, and must be more looked into, observed, and insisted upon than his negative ones. Because by doing so, we shall find ourselves enabled to save all his negative expressions also, so that none of them shall be lost or left as useless or insignificant.
On the contrary, if we regard chiefly his negative expressions and insist upon them absolutely and universally, not minding in what particular respect they are used in certain ways, we can in no way save his affirmative expressions, but lose them and make them empty and insignificant, as if they were but frivolous prattling.
We will therefore choose some of his affirmative expressions that shall lead us the nearest way to a decision on these two principal points, which are inseparable from each other and concern (1.) the Divine Abyssal Being's finding, knowing, or perceiving itself; and (2.) its generating itself in Trinity before the generation of eternal nature.
(1.) Then I justly recommend for serious consideration that description of the wonderful eye of eternity, which we meet with in the Second Part of the BOOK OF THE INCARNATION iii. 1, which is to be compared with the following places:—MYSTERY MAGNUM i. 7, 8; PREDESTINATION i. 4—9; FORTY QUESTIONS i. 14—21; DIVINE CONTEMPLATION iii. 6, 7. <note>The references of this discourse are to the German original, from which our English translation differs in the arrangement of the paragraphs.</note>
All these places declare one and the same thing: namely, the Divine Being before and without eternal Nature.
This is evident, also, from his own declarations in the DIVINE CONTEMPLATION iii. 6., according to the German original.
> *We cannot, he says <note>Note Well</note>, say that a nature or creature is to be understood here, but it is the eternal forming of the Divine word and will, where the Spirit of God <note>Note Well</note> has played with himself in the powers of wisdom, and by such formings of similitudes.*
Now this name (of an eye) sufficiently shows that we are to conceive it in a sense as something, which is also still more evident from the attributes he ascribes to it. *He says that this EYE is like (in the sight of a created understanding) a prospect of great wonders, where all colors, powers, and virtues <note>Note Well</note> appear as a most dreadful being, etc.:*
> *That no man indeed can discern distinctly this from that, and that nevertheless it may be looked upon <note>Note Well</note>, yet so that this eye, as a terrible lightning, is confounding and consuming all created sight:*
> *That the wonders in this eye have no number, no ground, and no end; and that only the soulish spirit, which has its origin from there, can be able to understand it. > *That this is a most concordant generating harmony; that the eternal nothing without nature and creature introduces itself into an eye, or an eternal seeing, in order to find and contemplate itself:*
> *That in the unnatural, uncreatural Deity (that is, without all nature and creature), there is but one will, which is called the one only God, willing in himself nothing else but to find and contemplate himself; and that in this <note>Note Well</note> the Trinity and the looking-glass of wisdom, or the eye of eternity is understood. That this eye is not to be compared to a circle, but to a globe, and that all beings were seen there from eternity, without being, or before they had a being. That the spirit of eternity introduces the eye of the soul into it, or opens a prospect of it to the spirit, and only then it can be seen:*
> *That in the abyss there is <note>Note Well</note> no finding, but that the finding is in this abyssal eye, where what eternity is is made manifest. <note>Note Well: this paragraph can by no means be understood if the different senses in which the abyss must be taken are not regarded. conjunction, is an abyss with respect to the posterior world, wherein the generation of eternal nature is understood, concerning which distinction more will be said by and by.]

That this eye makes beginning and end: <note>this expression is very important to observe, and is only made intelligible by the section immediately preceding it. The main emphasis related to that previous part lies in the fact that it does not say that it has, but that it *makes beginning and end*.</note> That there is in this first world an opening; a moving, an out-breathing, a multiplication, a forming of similitudes, etc., all of which the author represents in a simile taken from the mind, will, senses, and thoughts of man. These different things he places expressly and deliberately before the magnetical impression (that is, the first form of eternal nature) out of which afterward joy and sorrow (the first and second principle) come forth.

(2.)—The second affirmative expression to notice here is this: that <term>Teutonicus</term> calls this *eternal Eye the first world*, of which no creature knows anything. It is plain enough that a world is not an empty region, as if it could be conceived as a mere nothing in opposition to something; but that it is a universe, containing everything within itself without exception in one sense, and everything with limitation in another—namely, everything it is capable of, according to its own particular kind. So we find it both in the dark world, and in the holy light world, and in our four-elementary world also.

(3.) He says, in more than a hundred places, that there is a <term>Divine Being</term> within it—a being of all beings, a foundational being—indeed, that this being is that first abyssal world itself, etc. And though he says expressly that this world or being is ineffable and incomprehensible, yet it is deeper than any thought can reach; that it is without properties, without inclination to this or that, and that it has no other being beside, before, or behind itself from which it could be distinguished, or by which it could be touched and affected, etc. Yet all this, and much more like it, cannot make this Divine Being a nothing in itself, but a nothing to all those exterior and posterior beings which are derived from it, in and through the generation of eternal nature.

This he says himself in the plainest words:
> *The Divine Being, before and without nature, is an eternal nothing; though we ought not to call it a nothing, since this nothing is God, an eternal All.*

And again,
> *This eternal being is a pure Nothing to everything that exists after itself.*

What can be clearer than these two expressions? Does he not directly limit this name of "nothing" only to the creatures and to their understanding? And he will not have them call this abyssal being an eternal nothing in relation to itself, but allows them only to call it so with respect to themselves and all their narrow capacities, so that no one presumes to form specific ideas or images of it, etc.

Further, when <term>Behmen</term> says that in this first abyssal world there is the greatest stillness, meekness, quietness, etc., he not only plainly distinguishes this first world from all other subsequent worlds (wherein there is more or less, and in each according to its kind and order, some stirring, moving, working, comprehensibility, thickness, palpability, etc.); but he also expressly grants that even in this first world there are all these things just named—though not according to the sense these names bear in any of the other worlds, but according to its own central station.

And though he says plainly that no creature knows anything of this first world, he limits this by saying elsewhere that the spirit of the soul, which is a creature, may be introduced into it and may be enabled to see *that it is*.

(4.) See especially the <term>Book of PREDESTINATION</term>, i. 4, 7, 20, 21, where we shall find that this first <term>Abyssal Being</term>, before and without eternal nature, is a substantial spiritual power, working lovingly within itself, etc.

(5.) Regarding what <term>Teutonicus</term> says especially about the Trinity in this Abyssal world, see the Second Part of <term>Incarnation</term>, ii. 4, 7; <term>MYST. MAG.</term> viii. 5, 10.

We find that in the <term>Chaos</term> (which is the first abyssal world), there is also the <term>Trinity</term>; indeed, a Trinity must be acknowledged there as soon as a living, understanding Being is granted. Just as there is an eternal seeing in this first world, so there is also an eternal imagination and impregnation of the first will, and furthermore, an eternal generation in the Three (commonly called persons). These are so distinct <note>N.B.</note> from each other that none of them is what the other is, but each is only that which it is itself. The first groundless will generates within itself a grounded, comprehensible will, which is indeed co-eternal with the first will, yet in a sense has an eternal beginning. This second grounded will is the first will’s eternal "something," or its essentiality and perceptibility, through which that first will goes out and introduces itself into an eternal contemplation of itself; this outgoing is the third (person) and is a moving life of the first and second.

That this <term>Tri-une Being</term>, in its outgoing and self-contemplation, has been so from all eternity and has been but one life, one will, *without desire*. In this eternal generation, three things are to be understood: (1) a groundless will; (2) an eternal mind of that will; and (3) an out-breathing, speaking forth, or outgoing from the will and mind (or, as he sometimes says, from the will through the mind, both of which are right and true), which is the spirit of them both. This Trinity before eternal nature cannot yet properly be called Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, and is not yet an object of our understanding; rather, the Trinity is only understood rightly in that exterior manifestation of this abyssal being which is made in and through the generation of the properties of <term>eternal Nature</term>, in which all understanding creatures stand, and beyond which, therefore, none of them can reach.

->*CONCERNING these contradictory (namely, affirmative and negative) expressions of the first divine Abyssal Being, I shall further consider and explain these two things: (I) how they are both true with respect to two different worlds; (II) how they are both true in one and the same abyssal world, with respect only to two different degrees or parts of it.*<-

I.—Concerning the understanding, knowing, and perceiving of itself: both of these are affirmed and denied of the first abyssal being by <term>Teutonicus</term>, and both are consistent with each other in respect to two different worlds.

We heard above that everything that exists before and without the generation of eternal nature is called the *first world* by <term>Behmen</term>. Upon this foundation, I call the *second world* all that which follows immediately after the first, and this is the *whole generation of eternal nature*.

And this naming of the second world, in such a distinction from the first, is to signify nothing more or less than that this or that is so; not with respect to that which is be-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "eternal Eye" and the first world, specifically addressing the distinction between two different senses of the "abyss" and the "byss" in Behmen's work, and justifying his use of negative expressions to describe the Divine Being before the generation of nature.</meta>

before nature, in the chaos or abyss, but to that which is in the generation of eternal nature, and is even that generation itself, conceived in a general idea and extended to all its various properties, without descending to a specific notion of darkness, fire, and light.

But it may be objected against this distinction of a first and second world that Behmen expressly says and confines this "finding and not finding" to the abyss, or first world, without any mention of a second. Answer: This is granted. But then it must also be granted that he very frequently speaks of the Divine Being's knowing and perceiving itself with a manifest relation to that which is not in the first world, but in the generation of eternal nature; declaring that only there is generated what creatures call understanding, knowing, feeling, etc. So, here lies a sufficient reason and ground for viewing his expressions with respect to two very different worlds.

Secondly, Behmen does, indeed, speak only of the abyss, referring only to that in both his affirmative and negative expressions. However, this naming of "abyss" is to be taken in two greatly different senses, which must be carefully distinguished according to what the matter then being considered requires. These two senses both indeed belong to the first world; so we cannot say the abyss in one sense is in the first world and in the other sense in the second, but rather that the abyss is only in that first world and is that first world itself.

But yet these two senses belong to that first world with a great deal of difference.

One sense belongs so entirely to the first world that it can in no way be referred to the second. The other sense also belongs to that first world, yet in a way that implies a certain relation to the second world—a relation that is entirely inseparable from that sense.

For "abyss" is a relative expression for Behmen and cannot be conceived, according to his mind, without its correlate, which is "byss," no more than a father can be conceived without a son. Just as "abyss" is taken in a twofold sense, it also has a twofold relation, or byss, to be taken in a twofold sense, each of which must conform to the world of which it is then spoken.

The whole second world, or the whole generation of eternal nature in its seven chief properties, is byss, though the principal focus aims at the light world only and ends there. And the abyss of this byss is the entire first world, or everything that exists before, without taking any particular notice of what Behmen represents more distinctly therein and calls the Divine Abyssal Being; this is one sense of the word abyss.

This sense, because of the byss corresponding with this abyss, implies not one, but two different worlds, vastly different from each other.

But then again, in that first world alone, before eternal nature, there is—according to Behmen’s own plain words and extensive reasoning—both abyss and byss together; for that Divine Abyssal Being is its own abyss and its own byss.

Since, therefore, this twofold sense of the abyss is plainly founded in Behmen’s writings, the reason for looking at his contradictory expressions—first, with respect to two different worlds, and secondly, with respect to the first abyssal world only—is also plain and solid.

FOR to come now to our main purpose, it will be most proper to briefly represent several circumstantial things relating to those negative expressions, and to recommend them all together for serious consideration: namely, who it was that uttered these negative expressions, and for what purpose he uttered them; of what he speaks; on what account; in what manner, and to what end.

(1.) He who uttered these negative expressions was a creature and, despite his extraordinary gifts, only a small part of the innumerable products of eternal nature, calling himself only a little point or spark. Consequently, he indeed had all his understanding and knowledge from the Divine Being, but only as it is considered not before, but in or after that eternal generation of the properties of eternal nature. Moreover, he was a man who, from his natural birth, was as simple and ignorant as any other, as he frequently confesses. He was a man who not only admitted to knowing nothing of himself but also felt and understood through experience, in a very high degree, that he himself was nothing—in a sense quite different from, and even (N.B.) opposite to, the sense in which he says the Divine Being is an "eternal nothing" before the generation of nature's properties. But he was also a man who, despite all his "nothingness," *was actually permitted to have a glimpse into that eternal nothing and to see that it IS*, though his sight must have been immediately overwhelmed so that he could not see, much less declare affirmatively, what or how it is. And it was such a person who uttered these negative expressions,

(2.)—To creatures, all of the same nature and condition as himself, who are all therefore capable, more or less, of understanding his mind and meaning; yet in such a way that none of them can claim to be sufficient by themselves to understand him. Among these, he directs himself especially to the simple ones, calling himself a "philosopher of the simple" and saying that their simplicity is not to hinder them, but rather to further them and make them more fit for understanding these deep things—which is to say, chiefly and especially, more fit to be admitted (as he was) into the sight of eternal nature and also of that eternal nothing which is before it. There they cannot help but meet with the same experience he met with: namely, to be dazzled and overwhelmed so as to be unable to see distinctly what or how it is, though they may see plainly that it is. Now, to such people he speaks

(3.) Of their deepest abyssal origin; of that which dwells and is what it is only in and to itself, without any relation or tendency toward anything outside itself. Of that which does not desire to *be understood by creatures, but only to be acknowledged* and, in a deep internal silence, awe, and reverence, *to be adored as the deepest and most internal center of all that ever was, is, or shall be hereafter*. This is most different from the considerations of *all the theologians*, in that they all conceive and describe an infinite, good, just, holy, gracious, etc. *Spirit*. That is a consideration of God as manifested in and through eternal nature to creatures; whereas in this first consideration of Him, God is not only without any creature but without all nature also. He is infinitely superior to all conceivable properties and to all words or names, even if they were to signify (N.B.) the greatest imaginable perfections.

If all the perfections we can conceive, or use to express through various names, are much more like lies than truth when attributed to the Divine Being considered as manifested in eternal nature and in relation to creatures (according to what is plainly said by many mystical writers), how much more must they all be lies when attributed to that Divine Abyssal

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the Divine Being as considered by Behmen (Jacob Boehme), specifically addressing why the "abyssal being" is described in negative terms like "Nothing" and "unknowable" when viewed before the generation of nature.</meta>

Being, which Behmen alone considers as dwelling in itself, before and without all nature and creature?

Though in both this consideration and in that one, they may be acknowledged as true in a sense relating to the stammering creatures; for they are not said to be true in one consideration and false in the other. Rather, in both the former and the latter, they may be tolerable and acknowledged as true in a sense entirely relating to creatures. And again, in both this and that, they are false in a sense relating to that Divine Eternal Being itself—though much more false when this is considered as "before" than when it is "in" or "after" eternal nature. This is because all conceptions, words, and names each have their own specific meaning, originating in the generation of the properties of nature and determined by particular understanding creatures. Why, then, no such meaning can be attributed to, or spoken of, that abyssal being before all nature and properties, so as to declare how or what it is in and to itself. Of that abyssal central being he speaks now—

(4.) For that reason, which was mentioned several times and is of the greatest consequence: *viz.*, that a creature, in a certain sense and manner, may be admitted into the sight of it, so as to see *that* it is, even though no creature can fix its eye upon it or endure the sight of it so as to see *what* and *how* it is. This is and must be so out of necessity, not only because of the creature's weak and narrow constitution, but also because of that abyssal being's own nature, which cannot help but melt down, confound, and consume everything belonging to another world.

If the creature itself could be brought (regarding its own particular created existence) into this first abyssal world, it would immediately be dissolved and annihilated as to all its created being; it could not be preserved in its particular created existence.

But the creature itself is not brought into that first world; rather, only the creature's sight—or, as it were, a ray of the creature's seeing or understanding faculty—is admitted into it. Or rather, a small opening of this abyssal depth is made in the spirit of the soul. Through this opening, the spirit must necessarily become sensible of something appearing in that central depth, appearing much like a most terrible lightning. This is because its ray of seeing or understanding is immediately confounded and swallowed up by it, as far as it has looked into that abyssal depth. And he cannot express this "terrible something" more closely or significantly than by calling it an eternal abyssal nothing—both in consideration of its own particular being (which is in a sense, or as it were in part, annihilated by it) and in comparison to so many millions of other particular beings, all of which may be looked upon without danger as proper objects of the understanding. But since the creature itself, as to its own existence, continues to be the same as it was before and cannot be annihilated, its seeing faculty must also continue, since it proceeds from that created natural being.

This, therefore, may now justly be said both to have seen and not to have seen. It has seen because it was really touched and made sensible of such an abyssal being's existence within itself, or its own central world. And it has not seen because it was immediately, as it were, killed, driven back, and confounded, so that it cannot say what it was or how it was, but only that it was not this nor that, nor anything that could be named in all these worlds to which creatures have any access.

For everything that can be looked upon by understanding creatures can also be declared, more or less, as to what or how it is; it may have a name more or less suited to its nature and properties, by which it is not only distinguished from all other "somethings" but is also placed in the number and order of all those other "somethings."

But regarding this abyssal being, everything must be denied that is affirmed of all other things in other worlds. It must be absolutely exempted from every number and order, and cannot be named by any proper name by which it might be distinguished from other "somethings," seeing that there is none besides itself in that first abyssal world.

And this is plainly to say that it is nothing at all with respect to creatures, yet something in and to itself. And this makes it clear why Teutonicus must have spoken of that Divine Abyssal Being—

(5.) In a human way or manner, like a little stammering child, delivering indeed great, true, heavenly, deep, and eternal things, but with an earthly tongue. He has no other words but those of this low, four-elementary world, which are much more insufficient to represent that which cannot be looked upon (and is therefore beyond expression) than the colors of a painter are to represent a visible object vividly. He freely confesses that he speaks of it in such a manner, even when he declares things much inferior to this.

In such a manner, therefore, using such expressions as he could find in this world, he speaks to his fellow creatures:

(6.) For this end and intent: that he may not only exalt (as is his duty) that Divine Abyssal Being above all nature and creature, setting it in its own place, exempt from the number and order of all subsequent "somethings"; but also that he may, according to his command, inform his fellow creatures—as he seriously did—to be cautious in their inquiry, to watch over their own impulses, to restrain the curiosity so natural to them, and, above all, to make no images of that first central or abyssal being by representing it in this or that particular likeness, without which we can conceive of nothing at all. Indeed, they should also know for certain that, despite all his declarations, they cannot achieve any true, proper, affirmative conception of it. While such a conception might be, in a sense, excusable in the second consideration of God as manifested in eternal nature, here in this first consideration it is entirely intolerable, without any limitation—and he never intended to prescribe such a thing to anyone, as shall soon appear.

Let all these six circumstances now be duly considered, and it will appear plainly enough not only why Behmen called this Divine Abyssal Being an eternal Nothing, but also why he said there is no finding, knowing, or understanding within it.

If we understand the generation of eternal nature in its properties, we cannot help but grant that all we apprehend of such expressions, and whatever we are able to say of it with any other words, *are originated in eternal nature*, along with our entire being, knowing, and understanding, etc. So all of this depends entirely upon that eternal generation as a product, result, or consequence, which can by no means be conceived as antecedent to the properties—

He asserts that any attempt by a creature to perceive this depth results in the confusion or symbolic "annihilation" of the creature's understanding, necessitating the use of negative descriptions and earthly metaphors.</summary>

of eternal nature; or if we would presume to conceive it so, we would be presuming to conceive a nature that existed before eternal nature.

If, before eternal nature, there is an eternal chaos or temperature <note>a state of balance or mixture</note>, where all things lie in stillness and equality, without order, number, measure, properties, or qualification; without being distinguished from each other (according to our author's simile, just as fire, light, heat, smoke, air, water, etc., lie in a candle without distinction). And if all distinction related to and perceivable by creatures has its origin in eternal nature—just as the distinction of leaves, branches, and fruits is first performed by an actual moving and concurrent operation of its properties in every particular plant or tree—how can there be, or be conceived, a finding, perceiving, knowing, etc., before eternal nature, where that which is supposed to be found, perceived, known, understood, or seen is not yet distinguished from that which finds, perceives, knows, understands, or sees? And where that ray which is to go forth from the one to the other is not yet generated between them, but lies still in its own nothingness?

It is certainly true and clear that all these mentioned expressions relate to the second world, and further, to the creatures and their understanding after this second world. It must therefore be true and clear also that all these and similar expressions are justly to be denied of that first abyssal being or world. It cannot be expressed strictly and significantly enough, or imprinted into the hearts of men, that there is in that first central world no such thing at all that any creature, in any other circumferential world, can understand, apprehend, or declare with words.

For in this way, that first abyssal being is duly exalted above and totally excluded from the capacity of men and angels. They are all confined to their proper station in due humility: eternal nature is distinguished from and subordinated to that central being from which it had its eternal origin; and this is declared to be always the same in itself and absolutely incommunicable to anything except what is itself in its own abyssal world, which no creature can ever approach, neither in its being nor by its understanding.

All this is clear; for everyone who even acknowledges an invisible spiritual world will readily grant that things in this world (where we now live in such blindness and ignorance), even in the sense they carry in relation to creatures, cannot be attributed to that internal world. How much more, then, must he who acknowledges <term>Behmen's</term> abyssal world be ready to grant that nothing of this external world, in the sense it is understood here, can be attributed to that first eternal world.

But now, if anyone should conclude from this that <term>Behmen</term>, by so positively denying that perceiving, knowing, etc., exist in the first abyssal world—or in the Divine Being before eternal nature—has therefore denied these things in every absolute sense, without any limitation in the widest extent, he would certainly be mistaken. He would be guilty of stretching <term>Behmen's</term> words beyond his intent and contrary to all his affirmative expressions.

LET IT not seem contradictory that affirmative expressions are mentioned above and here again, when it was expressly stated a little before that <term>Behmen</term> never intended to provide his readers with any true, proper, affirmative concept of that first abyssal world.

And again: let it not seem contradictory that it was said above that the creature is not capable of any other sense, perceiving, or knowing, except what comes after and has its origin in the generation of eternal nature—while it is now said here that knowing and perceiving are indeed denied of the abyssal being in the sense relating to creatures, but not denied in every possible sense. For this plainly supposes there is another sense that has no relation to creatures and is nonetheless conceivable by creatures, which cannot be reconciled with that former statement.

**Answer 1.** Regarding the affirmative expressions, I say they are called so only with respect to their verbal construction, where they stand opposite to this or that and are called negative. Thus, it is true, indeed, in a very low, insignificant, and outward sense, that they appear as a fixed and solid position or affirmation. But we should not stick to that if we intend to become more intimately acquainted with <term>Behmen's</term> meaning. For it is also certainly true, in a much deeper and more significant sense, that all those (so-called) affirmative expressions are turned by him into negatives. He never intended to prescribe for, or raise up in his readers, such an affirmative idea of the Divine Abyssal Being as could be called so in an eternal, true reality.

And this appears plainly from the many limitations, cautions, and restrictions evident everywhere in those places where he speaks of that first abyssal world.

By this, he shows sufficiently that all his expressions are negative in their true internal sense, though many of them, in their outward shape and in the language of this world, appear affirmative—something that neither he nor any other person can remedy.

Every affirmative statement attributes something particular to that first abyssal world. In our outward world, this must be tolerated, since the creature cannot do otherwise. However, if the creature has any understanding from a higher principle, it will naturally observe a proper distinction between one world and another. It will not presume to bring any particular thing or sense that is valid in one world into the other, as if it were valid there also. Instead, it will see for itself that nothing which is affirmative in this world (where there is only particularity, division, and conflict) can be affirmative in the first abyssal world, where there is a whole and total, undivided universality.

Affirmative expressions in this world may indeed be attributed to the second world and may be tolerable if their sense is refined and exalted above what they signify here below; this is because there is a connection between them, consisting in the fact that they both exist in and after nature. But as for the first abyssal world, no affirmative statement from this world can be admitted into that one, no matter how much it is refined and exalted. This is because there is no coherence, no analogy, and no mutual correspondence between them, since one exists within nature and the other without nature.

This immense distance makes all affirmative expressions within nature negative or false when applied to what is outside nature. Every affirmative expression creates an image or representation of a thing in a certain form or figure, whether finer and more spiritual, or coarser and more physical.

<summary>The author explains that human concepts like knowing or perceiving cannot be applied to God's "abyssal being" before nature exists, as all distinctions only arise within eternal nature. He argues that while Jacob Boehme uses affirmative language, these terms must be understood as essentially negative when describing a reality that transcends all natural categories.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Boehme, abyssal being, eternal nature, divine essence, negative theology, Ungrund, spiritual world, universality</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Jakob Boehme's use of language to describe the "abyssal world" (the Ungrund), explaining why he often uses affirmative terms for a reality that can only be truly grasped through negative concepts.</meta>

If then, of this first abyssal world, no image in any sense or manner shall be made (though in some sense or manner it must be made of the second world), no affirmative expression has any place here, but must (since we cannot help using them in our speech and writings) be always restrained and confined; whereby then, in our mind, that same is made negative, which in outward words appears affirmative.

All affirmative expressions have a natural inseparable relation to nature and creatures, and are all born in this low four-element world.

If then, all this world, and all nature and creature can show and give us nothing that could be applicable to the first abyssal world; and if no created understanding can be found able to reach that world, and to form from ten thousand affirmative expressions even one true, positive idea of it; all affirmative expressions must be denied again, and are turned thereby into negative, regardless of what their outward appearance in a grammatical construction may be.

If we allow them to form an affirmative idea in our mind, this idea will certainly be false, and contrary to Behmen's sense and intent.

But if we can come to have a right negative idea, this will be the best, the nearest to truth, and the most conformable to our state and duty as creatures. For it is a negative idea which Behmen presses upon his readers, even in the midst of all his affirmative sayings; and beyond a negative idea we cannot climb any higher.

But I would not here be mistaken; for I know and freely grant that of this first abyssal world, there is and must be had one general idea, which may be called (in a partial and broken sense) affirmative, namely: *that it is something in and to itself*.

And by saying that beyond a negative idea we cannot climb any higher, I understand—according to Behmen's own direction—that of this first world we can only say that it is neither this nor that, etc.; but cannot go forward to a sure, determined position, declaring what or how it is. And even if we could, or did, by the very best and most suitable expressions, yet none of them would be without some relation to nature and creature, and to this outward world also. Why then, they all must be denied again, and could leave nothing behind them in our mind but an obscure, and as it were, a broken shadow of an affirmative representation. Which I could demonstrate further from a consideration of all those attributes that are usually given to the Divine Being, considered as in and after eternal nature, if I were not inclined to think it is already proven sufficiently that Behmen is all for negative ideas, and that there is not such a contradiction to be found as was objected above concerning his affirmative expressions. Let us now

Answer secondly, to that other part of the objection, namely: that knowing and perceiving are denied indeed of the abyssal being in that sense which has any relation to creatures, but that it is not denied in each and every sense.

This seems to suppose that there is a certain sense conceivable by creatures which has no relation to creatures.

But herein is no contradiction nor difficulty at all. It is easily understood that a creature cannot be capable of any other sense but what has a relation to creatures, and what comes after eternal nature. But seeing that a creature can know and own that there is still another and deeper world beyond its reach, which is not therefore an object of its understanding; the creature can know also certainly that this or that may be affirmed or denied of that world, in a human way or method, and by such a person as has had a vision of it, as Behmen had.

And if the creature can know and own so much, it can certainly also know more: that all such words and expressions as are thus spoken of it must have a meaning in them. If then, there is a meaning in them, this meaning must be as it were proportionate, not to the second natural, but to the first abyssal world, although it be expressed by natural words, inferior and posterior not only to the first, but also to the second world. And if so, the creature can also easily apprehend by itself that this meaning is not proportionate to its understanding, and that it is not expressed or included in words to be found out and understood for what or how it is in itself (which is deeper than any thought can reach), but that it is only mentioned or shadowed out by natural words, all taken *a posteriori* <note>reasoning from effects to causes</note> from things derived from it, to be known that it exists, and to be owned that it is the deepest, central original of all the subsequent worlds.

Teutonicus speaks of the second world—namely, of eternal nature and its two eternal principles—all with words taken from temporal nature; giving, indeed, to eternal invisible things the same names which are given to temporal and visible things; because these came forth from them and are their visible representatives, and he had no other words to use, cautioning us at the same time that we must observe a distinction in the meaning, lest we should "set cows and calves into heaven" and charge him undeservedly with gross absurdities. <note>N.B.</note>

So he speaks also of the first abyssal world with the same words he uses in the descriptions of the second world, which certainly he does not do so that we should make a confusion of these two worlds (so carefully distinguished by him), but he does it only for the same reason mentioned. This alone might be sufficient to show us that we must observe a distinction in the meaning, which he could not observe in words; and which we can easily observe if we but mind which world it is he speaks of—whether the second, together with its temporal outbirth, wherein all things are displayed in distinction, or the first only, wherein all things are concentrated.

Whatever now is understood from his words by any reader from the lowest to the highest degree, that is a meaning which has a relation to creatures, and a meaning which is natural; and though it be an illuminated understanding, yet this meaning is natural, *i.e.* posterior to, and originated from eternal nature. And though it may be good and true in its kind with respect to the creature and to the illumination, yet this meaning must not be applied to that first abyssal world as if it were able to declare what it is, but must absolutely be denied, since this first world is deeper than any natural sense or thought can reach.

But now, when such a meaning as this is denied, the question is: What is then left, or what benefit can we reap from such descriptions?

Answer: There is left a deeper meaning, excluding the generation of eternal nature, and therefore not conceivable by creatures as to "what" or "how," but only knowable "that" it is. The words of Behmen signify that all our ideas of this first abyssal world must be negative; and that no affirmative one, truly to be called so, can be had of it by any creature.

And our benefit is, that we are by his descriptions advised what, and from whence we are,
