and how far we can reach; and be cautioned also to put a stop to our natural curiosity, etc. This is enough concerning this objection.

**LET US PROCEED** now in our intended method. When Behmen says first negatively that perceiving, knowing, etc., is not in this first abyssal world, by "perceiving" and "knowing" we understand that which is natural to ourselves. This presupposes the generation of eternal nature, upon which we depend with all our senses and perception; we are not able to have any deeper sense of these things than what this generation of eternal nature has endowed us with. So we must acknowledge that all this, and whatever might be named similarly in this particular and natural sense, is not and cannot be in that first abyssal world, which excludes nature.

But when Behmen says again affirmatively that knowing and perceiving, etc., is in the first abyssal world, must this affirmative expression be false because the former negative was true? God forbid! That former negative must have been true because it implies a relation to the second world, which can have no place at all in the first, and must therefore be absolutely denied—indeed, it cannot be denied strictly and vigorously enough.

And this latter affirmative must be true also, because it does not imply any relation to nature or creature, but reflects only upon that first world as it is in itself. And so both this and that are true, in different respects, regarding two most different worlds.

Our greatest stumbling block lies in this: that the same words—knowing, perceiving, etc.—are used in both affirmative and negative expressions. Because we cannot form any difference in our minds between one kind of "knowing" and another, we are apt to think there can be no foundation for the distinction.

But let us only keep this in mind, as Behmen has often told us: that none of our senses, thoughts, or concepts can reach that first abyssal world. This is because we are, in our entire being, only natural; we cannot rise, nor raise up within ourselves, nor send forth any thought beyond eternal nature. We might indeed be inclined to imagine that we send certain thoughts or ideas beyond eternal nature when we try to conceive of that first abyssal world in our minds. But if we stop there, our thoughts remain very lowly and unacquainted with Behmen's meaning in this profound, inexpressible matter.

None of our thoughts can be free from eternal nature or reach beyond its limits, any more than the sound of our words can exceed the range of our voice when we speak in London about the East Indies. Instead, all our thoughts are generated in and by eternal nature; they are inferior to it and are confined by it to mere particulars, just as they are all particulars themselves. Therefore, none of them can break through its borders to enter that first central world, which alone is a complete and universal all.

Now, if all the natural meaning we attach to these expressions of knowing, perceiving, etc., is utterly denied regarding the first abyssal world, then (without our needing to create or worry about another meaning) this position will immediately result from his words: that in his affirmative expressions, there is a sense that is not conceivable in terms of *what* or *how*, but is knowable in terms *that it is*.

Being knowable, this will be found grounded upon the vision of the spirit of the soul; whereas the other, not being conceivable, is grounded upon that sight being dazzled, confounded, and so on.

He who made the eye and prepared the ear, shall he not see and hear?

I know it will be replied here that the *causa efficiens* <note>efficient cause</note> of knowing, etc., in creatures is to be sought in the generation of eternal nature—that is, in the second world and not in the first world, which has no relation to creatures.

This is granted. But then we must ask further: Where does knowing come from in this second world? If it is the "second," then there must be another "first" and deeper world, even that which Behmen expressly calls "God in himself," the first world; then certainly this second world in the generation of eternal nature is descended from the first. We know that God and nature are not to be confused. God in himself is free from nature and is not generated by it, but is prior and superior to it; nonetheless, in another sense, neither of them is prior or posterior, but both are co-eternal. But since it cannot be said of God that He had an eternal beginning in nature, while it can be said of nature that she had an eternal beginning in God; and seeing again that Behmen considers something as being before and outside of eternal nature—which he calls God, Nothing, and All—we must allow that this eternal "Nothing and All" is the only *causa efficiens* <note>efficient cause</note> of that second world and the knowing within it.

It will still be replied that knowing, etc., is not denied absolutely and in every sense regarding the first abyssal world, but that it lies within it only potentially. Thus, as Behmen says, all powers, colors, and virtues lie within it as in a chaos or temperature <note>a state of balanced, undifferentiated qualities</note>, without distinction.

Answer: This chaos, or temperature without distinction, is rightly called so in one sense with reference to the second world and the creatures depending upon it, but it cannot be called so in another sense with respect to the first world itself. For we heard above that Behmen plainly says that in this first abyssal world, the one power, color, virtue, etc., perceives the other in distinction.

Since there is distinction in this first world, in whatever sense it may be, this first world is not a chaos or a temperature in and of itself, though it is still so with respect to the second world.

For if this distinction in the first world is not conceivable by creatures (as the distinction in eternal nature is), but is only knowable "that it is" according to the first world; and if the spirit of the soul, which is admitted into the sight of it, can see that powers, colors, and virtues (three distinct things) lie within it and yet not see them distinctly so as to discern one from the other, then this first world must be a chaos or temperature with respect to that soulful spirit looking upon it and to the second world (where all things are distinct enough to be discernible). But it must also, conversely, not be a chaos or temperature with respect to what it is in and to itself. For since Behmen says that in the first abyssal world, what he calls the Father is not in every sense the same as what he calls the Son; and what he calls the Spirit is not what he calls Wisdom; and similarly the powers are not colors, and so on—therefore, all distinction cannot be absolutely denied.

It is known that Behmen describes the eternal chaos as a most terrible appearance which, like a dreadful flash of lightning, instantly confounds and consumes the sight of the soulful spirit, so that he cannot see *what* it is, but only know *that* it is. What shall we now think of this

description? Can we think that it is given by Teutonicus in order to declare what this wonderful thing is in itself? Does it not have a manifest relation to creatures, and even to creatures only, by saying that it is confounding and consuming? For certainly this cannot be applied to that Eye of eternity with respect to what it is in and to itself, seeing that none will say it is itself, and by itself, confounded in its sight? Therefore, then, it must be quite another thing in and to itself than what it appears to be to a created eye, looking upon it from without.

If this eye sees something, and sees it so that it can bear the sight without being confounded by it, it cannot see (as the spirit of the soul sees) only one thing or one confused chaos; but it must see a numberless number of things, and must in this seeing perceive them as they are—namely, as not yet in being, and so also as not yet distinguished in themselves, but as standing in a possibility to be brought forth into so many distinct beings; and so also as distinguishable in the sight of this eye. For this is plain when we only consider what arises from this sight, or in this eye: namely, a delightful play, and further, a design to bring forth these wonders into being, so that they might appear in a distinct existence, etc.

->Again,<-

if perceiving, knowing, etc., should be absolutely denied of the first abyssal world, I ask what could the name of Wisdom signify?

It is certain that Behmen places Wisdom not only in the second world, or in and after the generation of eternal nature, but also in the first; and he says expressly in a *Clavis* (never, to my knowledge, printed in English): *The Mysterium Magnum without nature, and Wisdom, are utterly one and the same thing.*

We know, indeed, that he speaks of a *Mysterium Magnum* in and after Nature; but this is plainly distinguished from that by this notorious mark of distinction: *without nature*.

Now as to that other denomination of wisdom, he says indeed plainly that Wisdom is properly so called in the second world, implying and presupposing the generation of eternal nature; and that before nature in the first world, it is more properly called a mirror of eternal wonders. But even this twofold denomination shows us that one and the same thing ought to be considered in a different sense, relating to two different worlds. For though he has given us this twofold denomination as proper, yet he uses almost always the same name of wisdom, both in his first consideration before, and his second after the generation of eternal nature. And what is this else but to say that we must not take two quite different things from that which is but one; but must look upon that one thing in two different respects, senses, and degrees, according to the different conditions of the first and second world.

Wisdom, then, is indeed more properly to be called so in and after the generation of eternal nature, wherein it is *Mysterium Magnum* with respect to its being unfolded and displayed afterwards in the creation, chiefly of angels and men; and it presupposes its having been unfolded and displayed in another degree already in the generation of eternal nature.

And Wisdom is indeed more improperly called so before and without nature, where it is *Mysterium Magnum* with respect to its becoming unfolded and displayed the first time, or in the first degree, in the generation of the seven chiefest and innumerable lesser properties of eternal nature; and it presupposes no other antecedent unfolding or displaying.

But yet it is still, both before and after nature, only one and the same thing; and the two different denominations are only to give us notice of two different degrees wherein this one thing is to be considered, if we will not confound the first world with the second.

Wisdom implies in its idea perception, knowledge, and understanding; therefore these are with wisdom both before and after eternal nature.

In the first world, God is considered only *as in himself*, abstractly from all relation, respect, or tendency toward anything outside himself. And in the second, he is considered *as in eternal nature*, or with respect to something which is in a sense outside him and is not himself, but is to be distinguished from him. When, nevertheless, this twofold consideration made by the creature does not make a twofold God, just as it also does not bring in a confusion between the first and second world. So then, according to this distinction, wisdom also must be considered both as in the first world, before, and as in the second, after eternal nature; yet there will not be made thereby two wisdoms, but only one, and no confusion shall be brought in. Rather, a great difference between the first and second consideration of wisdom will be found, consisting chiefly in this: that as wisdom in the second world implies a knowing and understanding what it is to have actually unfolded and displayed the first deepest central world, in and through the generation of eternal nature; to have introduced himself out of the still eternity, or first temperature (which is without all properties), into the second temperature, full of harmonized properties and qualifications; to have brought forth his eternal tender Lubet through the three first restless properties of nature; to have exerted his omnipotent all-sufficiency in the generation of the fourth, by opening therein his own eternal liberty or central groundless world; and to have introduced that eternal lubet through this most dreadful magic fire into that most majestic habitation, which is the second principle of light and love and glory, etc.

So also wisdom in the first world implies a perceiving, knowing, and understanding what it is to live and dwell only in himself, in the calm still eternity or liberty, without fire and light and the properties of nature. But especially and chiefly also—note well—what it is to be in himself alone all-sufficient for all the things performed in the generation of eternal nature. If we own that wisdom in the second world implies perception and knowing in that former more exterior sense, we must own also that wisdom in the first world implies perception and knowledge in this latter more interior sense. For these two can no more be separable from each other than the second world can be separable from the first, or a circumference from its center.

If there is in the first world, before and without nature, no perception, knowledge, etc., then there is also not only no wisdom but also no God, in no sense and manner. But how contrary is this to our *CENTRALIS PHILOSOPHUS*, who says, *God is in himself the first world: God is both the byss and abyss, and yet nothing apprehends him except the true understanding or intellect: and* (note well) *this intellect is God himself.*

->Again,<-

If there were no understanding in this abyss, eternal nature must be looked upon as the only mother of wisdom. But nature is not the mother of wisdom, not even of that wisdom which is considered in the second world; but nature is only that *medium sine qua non*, or that instrument by the use of which the first original mother, or the deepest central womb, which is wisdom before

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jakob Behmen’s descriptions of the first abyssal world and how Wisdom, though initially concentrated in that first world, displays its riches through the generation of eternal nature in the second world.</meta>

nature in the first world, has introduced itself into such a perceptibility, knowledge, and understanding as can be had in the second world only, and as wisdom, therefore, in the first world could not have had at all.

Wisdom cannot conveniently be called a mother, for as she never has borne any other thing—for which reason Behmen calls her a Virgin—so we also cannot say that wisdom in the first world has borne any other or younger wisdom different from herself, as a child differs from its mother. But we say only that wisdom in the first world, wherein she was only in and to herself, has in the second world unfolded and displayed herself and all her secret riches, which were concentrated in the first world:

That so she might be made sensible of what it is to have them thus displayed, and to behold and enjoy them distinctly, in fire, light, glory, joy, etc.: And she might also make herself thereby intelligible, accessible, and communicable, in a sense and manner to creatures; all which she could neither have had nor could have been in the first world, before and without nature.

And though it may be said, if rightly understood, that eternal nature is the mother of wisdom, yet to say so absolutely and universally, without restriction, is nothing less than abominable nonsense. And to conceive that eternal nature has brought forth wisdom, properly so called in the second world, out of itself, or from its own sufficiency, without the concurrence or direction of a deeper antecedent wisdom, and without a previous intent, is utterly inconsistent with Behmen's Theosophy. Which not only places wisdom as well before nature in the first world, as after it in the second, but tells us also, that the first abyssal world will not be such an imperceptible nothing as it is before nature, but will perceive itself in and through the properties of nature; and that it has, therefore, a *fixed intent* and purpose to flow forth out of its still eternity, and to introduce its tender <term>lubet</term> into strength, power, glory, majesty, fire, and light.

All which does show us sufficiently that wisdom in the first world is not an empty name, but that it implies not only a perceiving of its abyssal state, but also a finding of itself able and all-sufficient for performing its intent, namely, for going through the three first properties of dark nature into the fire, and through the fire into the light.

For this is its going into the second world, and its becoming in this world that which it will be, and not yet can be, in the first world.
Further,

> *Behmen says plainly, that in the <term>Mysterium Magnum</term> before and without nature (which is wisdom, as we heard above), there lay eternal nature itself, as a hidden fire, which <note>Note Well</note> is and is not. It is not, for it is in that first world, not only nothing to creatures, but also nothing to itself. And yet it is, for it is in the first world to the eye of eternity that, which wisdom finds herself sufficient, to fit and to prepare as a proper instrument, for her own use and advantage.*

If then, nature lay thus hidden in wisdom, wisdom is not brought forth by nature, but nature by wisdom. And wisdom is but unfolded, displayed, manifested and glorified by nature, which is but as an instrument in her hand. And if so, it cannot but be evident sufficiently, not only that wisdom in the first world before, and wisdom in the second world in and after nature, are not two, but only one; but also that this one wisdom must be considered with a different respect to these two different worlds, and must be taken in such a twofold sense, as mentioned before.

Our simile we had above, taken from a centre and its circumference, may help to illustrate this matter very much.

First we are to take good notice thereof, that the two names center and circumference are both relative, so that neither of them can be, nor be conceived, without or with the exclusion of the other. There may be, and may be conceived indeed, a single point, which can be made a center, but cannot be called a center, nor be conceived so, as long as the notion of a circumference is not implied. And again: there cannot be, nor be conceived any circumference, if a center is not implied and presupposed; though there can be, and be conceived an individual point without relation to a circumference, and even that selfsame point which afterwards is made and called a center, as soon as it has drawn about it its circumference.

So then we have now a notable distinction between a POINT and a CENTER: which distinction, as it does not make either two points nor two centers, so it does also not bring in any change or alteration upon that point, but gives it only a new relation, which it had not before, and obliges us to consider one and the same thing in two different respects. First, as it is only in and to itself, without any relation to this or that outside itself; in which consideration it is called a point, but not a center. And secondly, as it is with this relation to the circumference outside itself, in which consideration it is called a center, not a point, notwithstanding that it still is in itself that very same thing without any alteration, which it was before, when it could not yet have been called a center.

And so this distinction is not generated in our brain, nor laid upon the thing by our contrivance, but is generated in the thing itself; it has its ground in an actual generation, done without us; and is brought from there into our idea, which cannot change or place the order of these names according to its own pleasure, but must needs conceive them as they are in their natural order; according to which, the notion of a point is prior to the notion of a center, and the notion of a center prior again to the notion of a circumference.

For every center is a point, but not every point a center; and no circumference can be, if there be not first a center, from which it may have its being.

Like as also no center can be, which could not first have been a point before it was a center, and which could not still be that same point, though the circumference thereof were utterly removed. Seeing that the circumference depends only upon the center, and cannot be without it what it is, but must lose all its being if the center is abolished. But the center depends not so upon the circumference, for it has something in its own essence, which is deeper and more substantial than this accessory relation. This therefore it keeps and represents under the primary name of a point, and can by abolishing all the circumference, lose nothing but that secondary relative name of a center.

Now in this distinction we shall find a fine and proper emblem of the first world before and without, and of the second world in or after eternal nature; and of those things also that are or may be attributed both to this and that. The *point* shall be an emblem of the first abyssal world, considered only and purely as in and to itself. And the *center* of that first abyssal world again,

<meta>This page continues the logical reconciliation of Jacob Boehme's affirmative and negative descriptions of the Divine Being, specifically addressing the first abyssal world and the distinction between natural and supernatural motion.</meta>

Therefore the creature denies all these things regarding the Divine Abyssal Being, saying positively and absolutely they are not within it, and thus exalting that first Central Being above all that can be conceived, all that is particular, circumferential, and exists in number and order. But in those expressions called affirmative, the creature speaks, as it were, in imitation of that Abyssal Being, which alone knows and understands not only that, but also what and how it is, in and to itself. This Being is rather to be conceived, therefore, as speaking of itself and saying: *I am the Lord your God, but one God, etc.* How this is so is declared by Boehme <note>Jacob Boehme, also referred to as Behmen or Teutonicus</note> and applied to that first central being in the first world, before and without all nature and creature; this may be seen and taken into deep consideration from the first chapter of *Prædestination*. To which, for a conclusion, this one question may be added: What is it that holy angels not only adore, but also adore in such a way that they hide and cover their faces from it?

To which we must necessarily answer: (1.) that their honoring and adoring is chiefly directed toward that deepest, most glorious Being in fire and light, which is so near to them that they are themselves also partakers of that divine nature, like so many particular images or representatives of it, related to it as children to their father. And (2.) the hiding and covering of their faces has a plain relation to that deepest, central, and abyssal being, before and without its manifestation in eternal nature, or in fire and light.

For they are not so near to this, but stand in a sense, as it were, at an infinite distance from it, and can never be able to be admitted into it, though they may be able to look upon it. But just as our natural sight is instantly dazzled and confounded by looking into the bright shining sun, so that our eyes must be shut or covered; so theirs also are dazzled by looking into that first central world. From such a looking upon it, they can know no more of it except that it exists, and must leave the knowledge and understanding of what or how it is to this first abyssal being itself.

Now all these things, calmly and without prejudice considered, are enough to show that both the affirmative and negative expressions of Teutonicus <note>Jacob Boehme</note> are just and true, by observing only such a different respect to two different worlds.

But though thus far all is right, yet all this is not yet far enough, nor does it reach the bottom or represent the full sense and mind of our author.
->*In one will there can be no knowledge of itself.*<-
From his words there will still be the objection: *In one will there can be no knowledge of itself.* Therefore we must now further, in a second consideration, show also that all his expressions, both affirmative and negative, are sound, true, and consistent with each other, in and with respect to the first abyssal world only, without any relation or reflection made upon the second world, or the generation of eternal nature.

II.—In this our Second Consideration then, from which the generation of eternal nature with all its properties is utterly excluded, the naming of this first world, and especially that of the *abyss* and of the *will*, or the first Abyssal Will, are to be considered.

It is true indeed that if this first world, or God in himself, is called by Boehme *abyss* only, and nothing else or more than *abyss*, we cannot attribute any knowing, etc., to it, and only his negative expressions must be true, excluding all those that are affirmative.

And again, if in this *abyss* there is asserted by Boehme only One *Will*, absolutely and in every sense, his plain expression—that in one *will* there can be knowledge of itself—must be true absolutely and without any limitation.

But if we can show from his plain words that in this first world (which is an *abyss* and nothing but an *abyss* with respect to the second world) there is not only an *abyss* but a *byss* <note>A ground or foundation, from the German 'Bündnis' or 'Boden', contrasted with 'Abyss' (without ground)</note> also, in another sense and respect appropriate to the first world. And again, that in this first world (wherein there is one *will* in one sense) there is also in another sense both a first and second *will*, corresponding to that *abyss* and *byss*—which both are in the first world and are inseparable from each other—then all his negative and affirmative expressions must be true together, not only without any loss but also without any contradiction. The negative must be true of the *abyss* or first *will*, and the affirmative of the *byss* or second *will*; thus they shall be true of this first world without any relation to the second.

I shall present an abstract of the first chapter of his *Mysterium Magnum*, making such observations as plainly and undeniably arise from his expressions.

So then he says in chapter 1, verse 2: *God is an eternal nothing; he has neither ground, nor beginning, nor place, and possesses nothing but himself*.

This is certainly spoken of God before and without eternal nature, for he says that he possesses nothing but himself; he is above and beyond all the properties of nature, for all these are not himself, but are after and under him.

Now of this first world, or of God considered as in himself only, he says further: *He is the will of the abyss; He is in himself but one*.

Objection: No generation can exist without motion; now motion is a property of nature, therefore the generation of eternal nature is here implied.

Answer: No natural generation, distinctly conceivable and intelligible by creatures, can be without that motion which is the second property of eternal nature.

But a supernatural generation (called in other places the intellectual life) which is not conceivable distinctly by angels and men as to what or how it is, but only knowable that it is, can exist without that motion which is the second property of nature.

But it will be asked: What distinction can we conceive to be between motion and motion? Or why must we call one natural and the other supernatural? Is not this a distinction of our own invention?

No, this distinction is delivered to us by Boehme and is grounded upon the whole harmonious analogy of all his writings.

For we can conceive such a distinction between motion and motion as we can and ought to conceive between God dwelling in himself in the first world, and as manifested outside himself in the second world; between *lubet* <note>Divine delight or inward longing</note> and desire, neither of which can be conceived without all motion, yet this latter only is natural (or in nature), while the former is supernatural (or above and antecedent to nature). And again, it is the same distinction that exists between generation and generation, or which here is all the very same: between generation and manifestation.

<summary>The author explains how Jacob Boehme’s seemingly contradictory affirmative and negative descriptions of God are resolved by distinguishing between the "abyss" and "byss" within the first divine world. He further differentiates between natural motion and a supernatural "intellectual life" that precedes the generation of eternal nature.</summary>

Read attentively the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth verses of the seventh chapter in the **MYSTERIUM MAGNUM**, where these two positions are distinctly expressed and explained: namely, (1.) *God generates himself in the Trinity: and* (2.) *the Trinity is rightly understood only in his eternal manifestation, or the generation of eternal Nature.*

Is it not undeniably plain here, (1.) that he speaks of a generation within himself, before nature, and (2.) of a manifestation, or generation in eternal nature; and that he distinguishes the one from the other by saying that only the generation in nature is an object of our understanding, but not the generation before and without nature? Again, he says:
> *He has no peculiar room or place where he might dwell; the eternal Wisdom or intellect is his habitation. He is the will of wisdom, and wisdom is his manifestation.*

Now, what is here called wisdom was called above the **MYSTERIUM MAGNUM** without nature and the seeing Eye of eternity; and this wisdom is called again the *habitation* of the first will and its *manifestation*.

Now, who does not see that he speaks here of a manifestation prior to nature, even though in other places, and in another sense and respect, he says rightly and truly that without nature no manifestation could be? Indeed, who does not see that such a manifestation, in such a sense, must of absolute necessity be in God, before and without nature? For truly, a seeing eye implies all this manifestation.

But let us follow our author further.

*v.* 3. *In this eternal generation, three things are to be understood: (1.) an eternal will, (2.) an eternal mind of that will, and (3.) the outgoing from this will and mind, which is a spirit of the will and mind.*

---

Before I proceed any further, it will be useful to make the following observations:

(1.) Whenever Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme</note> declares the generation of eternal nature—considering it not only as to its distinct properties and different operations but also chiefly as to its coming forth out of the abyssal deep, or eternal temperature, or eternal nothing—he considers that nothingness chiefly as a unity. In most places, he makes no mention at all of the Trinity, and in a few, only a short mention.

But on the contrary, when he considers that abyssal deep, or eternal nothingness, only as it is in itself, he makes but little mention of the Unity and insists chiefly, distinctly, and sometimes extensively upon the Trinity.

(2.) The next observation is this: in some places, Behmen gives us a description of God and Nature taken together in conjunction. In this, regarding God, he represents both unity and trinity; and regarding nature, he considers it as already generated or as actually generating, so that he declares the whole process of this generation in all the seven properties. For instance, he does this in the **AURORA**, in the **THREEFOLD LIFE**, in the **CLAVIS**, etc.

And again, in other places he describes God and Nature together, but in such a way that he considers nature as not yet generated, but as still lying in the first abyssal will as a hidden fire, which is and is not. He takes no notice of its distinct properties, but only of its being eternally distinct from God, its only co-eternal source; which nevertheless he considers and represents not only regarding the Unity, but also and chiefly regarding the Trinity. He does this in the **EARTHLY AND HEAVENLY MYSTERY**, from the first text to verse 5 of the fifth text. So also in the **SIX POINTS**, i. 1—33. These places are thought to be the most opposed to all knowledge, etc., and to any Trinity before and without nature, though at the core they are strictly consistent with this first chapter of **MYSTERIUM MAGNUM** and the first chapter of **PREDESTINATION**.

---

Here I will only observe concerning these two places in general:

If Behmen, in the *Nine Texts* and in the **SIX POINTS**, considers God and nature in such a way that, regarding God, he tells us *What the Divine Being is in itself without a principle or what the deepest Divine Being is without nature* (which are his own words, **SIX POINTS**, i. 22 and 30); and in such a way that, regarding nature, he looks upon it as not yet nature or not actually generated, but *as lying still in the first abyssal will, as a fire which does not burn, which is and is not*—and if he nevertheless distinguishes God from nature, or from that which is to be nature afterward, and speaks of a *generation in God, a generation in Trinity, a threefold Spirit*, etc., in the same manner as he does in the first chapter of **MYSTERIUM MAGNUM** and **PREDESTINATION**, it is certain that he gives us in all these places but one and the same description of the Divine Being, containing a generation in Trinity prior to nature and excluding all its properties.

And again, if Behmen in the *Nine Texts* gives us a description of the spiritual and essential or *natural life*, or of God and nature, so that he not only calls the one as well as the other *a life*, expressly speaking of *two lives*,

But also, that in response to these two lives, he speaks of a twofold desire (*Text iv. v. 8*): one of which is for the generation of the word or heart, and the other for the generation of nature. He declares that first generation in the spiritual life in the same manner as he does in the **MYSTERIUM MAGNUM** and **PREDESTINATION**; and says moreover that in the natural life no intellect would exist if the spiritual life were not (N.B. 1.) *desiring, in which desire (not that which follows the generation of nature) the Word is generated from eternity to eternity: from which* (N.B. 2.) *the desiring will goes out eternally into the natural life and opens*, etc.;

It is as plain as anything can be that he asserts in the *Nine Texts* an Intellect and generation in Trinity before and without nature.

But to return to the **Mysterium Magnum**. There he says that *In this eternal generation three things are to be understood.* As for the word *generation*, we must observe that just as it differs from *manifestation* in every common sense and subject, it also differs from it in Behmen's sense and in this deep spiritual matter;

In this, the generation must necessarily precede the manifestation. Now, in that first consideration of the Divine Being, he always uses the word *generation*, and in the second—implying and presupposing nature—he uses that of *manifestation*.

The generation in the Trinity is done and is still occurring before and without nature, from eternity to eternity. But the manifestation of this Trinity is done and is still occurring in the generation of nature.

We cannot say that the Trinity is generated in or through nature, though in a certain limited sense it might be said so, but we cannot say so in an absolute sense without any limitation, if we

<summary>This page explains Jacob Boehme's distinction between the "generation" of the Trinity within the Divine Being and its "manifestation" through nature. It argues that the Trinity exists eternally prior to and independent of nature, though nature serves as the medium for its manifestation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical reconciliation of Jacob Behmen’s theological descriptions, specifically focusing on the distinction between the internal "generation" of the Trinity and its "manifestation" through nature.</meta>

We will not make nature the origin of the Triune Being. But we can say absolutely and in every sense that the Trinity, which was and still is generated within itself, before and without nature, is *manifested in* and through nature, outside of itself. By this manifestation, it is made intelligible—first to God himself (in a certain sense relating to nature, as discussed sufficiently above) and further to creatures also. For although there are not yet any creatures implied in this consideration, it is implied that this manifestation in and through nature made a way for the production of creatures, which could not have been produced without it; it also enabled the Trinity to be an object of a created understanding, which could not have happened if this manifestation had not been made.

We know not only that the generation of nature, in its first three properties, is represented by Behmen as a $\Delta$ and called expressly the "triangle of nature," but also that these three are referred by him distinctly to the Father, Son, and Spirit.

Now, we cannot say that they are referred to them only insofar as the Father, Son, and Spirit are manifest in this generation of nature; but we must also say they are referred to them insofar as the Father, Son, and Spirit are in this eternal generation before and without nature—where they are not yet properly called Father, Son, and Spirit (see *Mysterium Magnum*, vii. 10, 11) though they are still called so very frequently.

For if that Father, Son, and Spirit—which Behmen calls so before nature using names taken from after nature—is the Trinity in this eternal generation, represented by Behmen by such a symbol as $\Delta$ or $\curlywedge$.

Furthermore, if this Trinity is that one eternal life, good, or God, which he commonly calls such in his first consideration of God; and if nature with all its properties has its eternal origin from that one eternal life; then the $\Delta$ in nature cannot but be originated from the Father, Son, and Spirit, or from that Trinity which exists before and without nature. Since this same triangle in nature is the beginning of its manifestation, or the manifestation of itself according to the inferior, restless part of nature. Therefore, this manifestation of the Trinity must be placed in nature, while its generation must be before and without it. Thus, we rightly conceive this generation to be prior and that manifestation to be posterior, yet both are co-eternal and without beginning, though in the different senses mentioned above.

Now, further, this distinction and difference between generation and manifestation can also show us plainly how we are to rightly conceive and place the Unity and Trinity in their due order.

But first we must observe regarding the expression *Unity* that it is used here in the strict and narrow sense in which Behmen uses it in relation to the Trinity alone. It is not used in the larger sense in which he speaks of a "unity," or, if I may say so, of a chaotic oneness of all things in the first *Mysterium Magnum*. This latter unity has a relation—or is rather opposite—not to the Divine Trinity, but to the variety and multiplicity produced in nature, and further in the creation of angels, humans, and all of this third principle. This observation should be carefully noted so that we do not confuse this unity with the other; otherwise, we shall confuse the Trinity with multiplicity and God with nature. [N.B.]

This latter unity, in relation to nature and creatures and to the variety and multiplicity within them, is or was a unity before and without nature only. But in the generation of nature and creature, it is utterly lost, turned into multiplicity, and has ceased to be what it was before nature. Consequently, it cannot be found in nature and creature, considered as nature and creature; for it is their own essentiality to exist entirely in division, distinction, particularity, and variety—if they did not, they would not be nature and creature.

<margin>9</margin> But that former Unity, in relation to the Trinity only, is a unity always and everywhere, and does not cease to be in the generation of the Trinity. It is not lost at all there, nor is it turned into the Trinity, but continues still as an individual unity, diffused, as it were, through the whole Trinity. It is to be found whole without diminution in each of the Three, and whole without alteration in all Three together. For it is the inseparable essentiality of God, both before and after nature, to be only one in a universal, individual Unity.

And though the properties of eternal nature also continue, in a sense, all seven to be but one, yet this oneness is already so different and declined from its former unity—which it had when it still lay as a hidden fire in the first abyssal will—and is now so abolished in the distinct generation of nature and its seven different properties, that it can no longer be found in nature, considered as nature generated, but only by reflecting upon its original source.

Now, this unity is not considered here, but only that former Unity in its strict and narrow sense, in relation to the Divine Trinity.

And regarding this Unity, we say according to Behmen that we cannot place it before and without nature and the Trinity, as if before eternal nature there were nothing but a unity, and as if this unity were only displayed or unfolded into a Trinity in and through nature.

For he says expressly that in this generation (N.B.) three things are to be understood. And again, the *triangle* denotes (N.B.) the *hidden God* (or *God unmanifest*), namely, the *Word or Divine Intellect, which (hidden God) in his eternal, beginningless generation, is threefold, and yet only one in his manifestation.*

Here we see again and again: (1.) that the generation is different from the manifestation of God. (2.) That there is a generation in Trinity (asserted by Behmen) in God himself from eternity to eternity. (3.) God unmanifest (which is nothing else but God before and without nature) is here denoted by a *triangle* and expressly said to be threefold in the beginningless generation. (4.) That this God unmanifest, in one sense relating to nature, is manifest to himself according to his own eternal generation within himself.

For since in this unmanifested state there is mention made of a *Divine Intellect*, a manifestation of God to himself is plainly implied, even though he is unmanifest in nature.

Before and without nature, we are to conceive first the Unity and secondly the Trinity, both as unmanifest to nature but manifest to themselves.

In or after nature, we must again place first the Unity and then the Trinity, but now as manifest and able to be an object of a created understanding—which, for both angels and humans, exists and remains forever and ever in nature, and in nature only.

<summary>This page distinguishes between the internal, eternal generation of the Trinity and its manifestation through nature, which makes God intelligible to creatures. It also clarifies the difference between the essential Unity of the Trinity and the chaotic unity that precedes the multiplicity of nature.</summary>

And so we place no nature between the Unity and Trinity, but only between the unmanifest Tri-unity and the same Tri-unity manifested.

->Again,<-

If we acknowledge, as it cannot be denied, that Behmen distinguishes between an eternal generation of God in himself and an eternal manifestation in nature—saying, in the latter, that there are *three persons*, and in the former, *three things*—we cannot refer the Trinity to this latter state any more than we can to the former only. We must refer it to both, seeing that not only do the three things before nature correspond to the three persons after nature (which are not generated by nature but only manifested), but also that the three things before nature must necessarily be an unfolding of the Unity, just like the three persons in or after nature, though not in the same sense, manner, or degree.

[NOTE.—This and the subsequent discourses should be understood as abstracts from Freher, created by Law for his own use, rather than word-for-word copies of the originals. They differ from the originals in the structure of the paragraphs and in omitting whatever Law considered not worth copying or unnecessary to the discourse. In the <term>MYSTERIUM MAGNUM</term>, iv. 3. in an explanation of the following characters [See 1, 2, 3, and 4 of Note.] he says:
*The superior cross signifies (N.B.) the unformed Word in the Trinity, without any nature; and this character [Note 3.] signifies the formed word, namely, the angelic world.* First, <image-desc>upward-pointing angle or lambda symbol</image-desc>
The "unformed Word" here is the same as "unmanifest," both to be understood with reference to nature, declaring that there is a Trinity unformed and unmanifest in nature, fitly represented by this character <image-desc>upward-pointing angle or lambda symbol</image-desc>, an emblem of the Unity as unfolded in Three.
Secondly, in this character [Note 3.] he represents both the first and the second world together—both the eternal generation and the eternal manifestation of the Trinity. For he says expressly that this superior $+$ is an emblem of the Trinity without any nature, and the [Note 5.] <image-desc>circle with a horizontal line through the center</image-desc> is a character of the angelic world, which is nature in fire and light.
I know, indeed, that in the <term>SIGNATURA RERUM</term>, ch. xiv. 29, he describes this same character [Note 3.] in a manner quite different from this explanation made in the fourth chapter of <term>MYSTERIUM MAGNUM</term>. For there he says, *the superior cross above the circle is the kingdom of glory, which plainly implies the generation of eternal nature.*
But is it any wonder if, from a different perspective, the same word—and likewise the same character—is used to represent different things, or the same thing considered differently?
In the <term>MYSTERIUM MAGNUM</term> he considers the Trinity directly without any nature, but in <term>SIGNATURA RERUM</term> he says not one word of the Trinity either as before or after nature, but considers only the generation of the principles, and especially the production of the fire, which is not mentioned in the <term>Mysterium Magnum</term> at all.
Therefore, in the <term>SIGNATURA RERUM</term>, he rightly places the kingdom of glory, or the angelic world (as the highest in nature, which was the only nature he then considered), in the highest place immediately above the principle of fire.
And in the <term>MYSTERIUM MAGNUM</term> he also rightly places the Trinity without any nature (as the highest of all that can be named) even above the angelic world itself. He represents both the former and the latter by a single character, but by one that is fit for both.
It also appears in this same chapter xiv. 8. of the <term>SIGNATURA RERUM</term> that Behmen had not forgotten what he had said about it in the <term>Mysterium Magnum</term>.
For he says, *This impression is the only mother of the Mysterium’s manifestation (N.B. not of the Mysterium, but of the Mysterium’s manifestation) and is called nature and substance, for it manifests what from eternity has been in the eternal will.*

> We are to understand that in eternity there has been a nature in the eternal will, as an eternal mind, but in the will it was only a spirit. And the substance of its power (sufficiency or ability) was (N.B.) not manifest, except only in the "playing" of the will, which is the eternal wisdom. (N.B. 1.) That here a manifestation is explicitly asserted as well as denied: denied with respect to nature as "generated nature," but asserted with respect to the eternal will. Yet (N.B.) this is not with respect to this will considered strictly as an abyssal will in itself, but considered as *playing* with itself—that is, with its "byss," which byss itself is a manifestation of the first abyssal will. In this view then, nature was manifest in and to that will before it is to be conceived as nature generated and manifested in and to itself.
> (N.B. 2.) That in this playing of the will, the Three, or Trinity, is understood, as our author explicitly declares.
> For this playing is a movement, even that moving life of the Deity, <term>MYSTERIUM MAGNUM</term>, i. 7. And this playing of the abyss in or with its own byss presupposes a generation of this byss—even this eternal generation—wherein we are to understand "three things" before and without their eternal manifestation in and through nature. (N.B. 3.) That this playing is the eternal wisdom. If there is Wisdom (in whatever sense) before and without the manifestation in nature, there is also a Trinity before and without it; for the former implies the latter, and the latter is inseparable from the former. So then our author says here in the <term>SIGNATURA RERUM</term> the very same thing that he says in <term>MYSTERIUM MAGNUM</term>.

But let us go now a little further.
In the <term>Aurora</term>, which was our Author’s first book—written, as he thought, only for himself and, according to his own words, like the speech of a stammering child—we shall not find even one word of the first world, or of the first consideration of God as generating himself in himself in

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Jacob Boehme's evolving understanding of the Trinity as presented in his successive works, moving from his early descriptions in the *Aurora* to his more mature insights in the *Three Principles* and *The Threefold Life*.</meta>

Trinity, outside and above all nature. There is not the least mention of an eternal nothing, temperature, liberty, chaos, *mysterium magnum*, abyssal eye, mirror of wonders, or the eternal generation wherein we are to understand three things, etc. :

But his deepest consideration is only the generation of eternal nature in its seven distinct properties; from which he proceeds immediately to the creation and fall of Lucifer, and further to the creation of this third principle. His account of the seven properties of eternal nature is here and there different from what he declared of them in his following writings; especially concerning the generation of the fire, which is not as distinctly and circumstantially declared as it is afterwards. But the true reason for this is as follows: The understanding of the sevenfold generation—and chiefly of its fourth property—depends a great deal upon an understanding of that eternal liberty, <term>lubet</term>, chaos, and temperature, which exist before and outside of nature. Because he did not yet have an understanding of what exists outside of nature, he could not have declared the generation of the fire from an eternal conjunction of liberty with the dark properties of nature; instead, he could and did declare it only as far as his insight could then reach. Therefore, accordingly, in the *AURORA*, he says very much about the most holy Trinity, but only as it is manifested in and through nature. Although he does not yet use the word "manifestation" as distinct from his eternal generation in himself (for the reason mentioned above), everything he says of the Trinity throughout the whole *Aurora* is to be referred only to the second consideration of God, which implies and presupposes the generation of eternal nature.

So also in the *THREE PRINCIPLES*, his second book, written seven years after the first—when the daylight, as he says, had overtaken the first dawning of the day—we may indeed find a clearer and more distinct explanation and continuation of what he had begun in the *AURORA*, concerning especially the generation of this, our third principle. However, we shall not find anything of this eternal generation of God in himself, outside of all nature, wherein we are to understand three things.

If that former declaration of the Trinity (which implies and presupposes the generation of nature) is the deepest and only declaration of it, why has our author not kept only to this in his following writings? Why has he—or how could he have—given us quite another and, as he says, a deeper consideration of it under such an express title: *so, or so far is God considered as in himself only without all nature.*

May this not show us sufficiently that when he wrote these two books, he did not yet have that great opening of the first abyssal world in his spirit, but only an opening of the second world, or of the generation of eternal nature in its two principles? His description of the Trinity in this beginning is good, true, and solid indeed, but not yet the deepest; he has given us a deeper one in his following books after he had a deeper opening in his spirit. In this deeper description, he speaks as if from another world, and also of another thing; for though he speaks of only one Trinity and not two, yet this one may be called, in a sense and manner, another thing when it is looked upon in the first world and another again when in the second. Why it evidences itself that we ought not to confuse one description with the other, nor to take only one and reject the other—much less to fight with one against the other—but to leave each of them in its own place. The first description, which was given later and is above nature, is of no benefit to us who are in nature, and yet it is necessary to be known <note>if we wish to understand the deepest origin of all that follows</note>. The second description, which was given in the beginning and is in nature, is that which we are only concerned with, and upon which our regeneration and eternal happiness depend. By doing so, we shall lose nothing of his writings, but find all their parts in union and concordance. [N.B.]

Now we find that this latter description of the Divine Being in Trinity, before and outside of nature, was not as full and plain when he first began to have an opening of it as it was later, when it became wider and wider; but as this opening in his spirit proceeded gradually, so also did his understanding and description by degrees.

For in the *THREEFOLD LIFE*, his third book—which might be called his *Aurora* with respect to this particular point—we cannot yet find a distinct consideration of God in Trinity before and outside of nature; yet we may find a plain disposition toward it, and, as it were, a mixture of these two considerations. In Chapter 4, verses 86, 87, and 88, he says, *In the number Three are three centers, which are understood in eternal nature, but (N.B.) outside of nature, they are not understood. For outside of nature (N.B.) the name of God is Majesty, but in nature he is called Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. — That which is outside of nature profits me nothing; I could to all eternity neither see, nor feel, nor fathom it — but since the Majesty (N.B.) has generated nature, and has thus opened or manifested itself therein in three persons, I do rejoice in that opening or manifestation, as a creature living therein eternally.*

Let us observe here: (1) that in this third book of his, our author admits something that he was silent about and doubtless quite ignorant of in the first and second; namely, *that there is something outside of eternal nature.*

(2) That he speaks of a number three and of three centers, both outside of and in eternal nature, with this distinction: that in nature they are understood, and outside of nature they are not understood.

(3) That he uses that relative expression of "three centers" before and outside of eternal nature in correspondence to the "three things" in the *Mysterium Magnum*, and in opposition to the "three persons" manifested in nature. By this, he expressly places before nature not only One, as generating itself into Three, but also Three, as generated out of One in the eternal generation outside of nature, also manifesting themselves to be Three in nature.

(4) That he says positively: Outside of nature, the name of God is *Majesty*; and he gives us this (N.B.) as a reason why the three centers or things outside of nature cannot be understood. This must be further considered shortly.

(5) That he places the three distinct names of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost in nature; and outside of nature, he places only that single name of *Majesty*. This name is one that can by no means be attributed to the Unity if it is considered as abstracted from and antecedent to that eternal generation by which God in himself generates himself in Trinity; rather, it is a name common to all three and must necessarily be attributed to the Tri-unity.

By this, therefore, he combines the Unity with the Trinity before and outside of nature.

(6) The *Majesty* has generated nature; therefore, not the Unity, but the Tri-unity has generated nature.

<summary>This text explores the progression of Jacob Boehme’s theological insight, arguing that his early works focused on God within nature while his later works revealed a deeper understanding of the Trinity existing as "Majesty" before and outside of eternal nature. It emphasizes that these different descriptions are not contradictory but represent a gradual unfolding of spiritual revelation.</summary>

(7.) That he distinctly says, *the Majesty has opened or manifested itself in nature in three persons*. If the Majesty has opened or manifested itself in nature, it has not generated through nature; otherwise, the distinction between generation and manifestation would mean nothing.

But a question will arise here: what sense can there be in the words, *without nature the name of God is Majesty*? Since Boehme says that without nature there is no light, luster, glory, etc.

I know it may be said, to reconcile this: The first abyssal will is before and without nature, and if considered as such, in and for itself, it has no majesty. This first will generated nature, and through nature it generated the second will, which is the first will’s co-eternal son, called by Boehme *nature’s end*, because it is free from nature, it is above nature, and does not belong to nature as one of its properties, even though it is generated in and through nature. Now, in this eternal nature, the Father’s majesty appears, for He is, according to the Scripture, the brightness of His glory. Rightly, therefore, on such an account, could Boehme have said that without nature the name of God is Majesty. For in all four chapters of THE THREEFOLD LIFE, he places the generation of eternal nature between the first will, which is the Father, and the second, which is the Father’s co-eternal Son. He thus sets the Father before, and the Son after nature, but both are free from nature, and above or without it, just like the Father.

This explanation, I grant, is plausible if looked upon from the outside and superficially; for Boehme’s own words plainly say all these things. If there were but that due and true distinction observed between the *eternal generation without nature* and the *eternal manifestation in nature* and through nature, nothing more could be desired. But seeing that in this representation and its application to the majesty without nature a confusion is made between these two, a great mistake is committed.

Yet no one can be blamed for this mistake, because Boehme himself, in this book of THE THREEFOLD LIFE (for the reasons mentioned above), makes a mixture, as it were, of the two considerations of the Divine Being, and many times uses the word *generation* when he speaks of the eternal manifestation. For this, he also cannot be blamed: (1) because at this beginning of his enlightenment, regarding this particular point, he probably could not yet sufficiently discern one from the other; and (2) because, for good reason and with a particular focus, he could well have used the word generation even when discussing the eternal manifestation through nature.

But yet from his following descriptions, when he was more especially focused on this point of the eternal generation in the Trinity before nature, it is clear enough that such a distinction must be observed; and through them, this may also be understood sufficiently—which on its own would not be intelligible enough.

But the mistake in this account or explanation of the word *Majesty* is plain enough from this:
If Boehme, by saying *without nature the name of God is Majesty*, means that majesty which exists after nature and is rightly called "without nature" in the sense and account given above, it must be a wrong and backwards saying when he adds, *the Majesty has generated nature*. For this is absolutely false; rather, he should have said, *nature has generated the Majesty*, for this is true in its own sense and place but cannot be applied here. Since he says the exact opposite—the *Majesty has generated nature*—he shows sufficiently that he does not mean that specific majesty. Therefore, we must look for another sense that may be consistent with his work.

It is certain that the majesty of the Second Principle of light and glory is not understood here. And it is certain also that we cannot compare this passage with any other parallel one in which he might have the same or a similar expression of a Majesty without nature.
Therefore, having observed (1) that this is the only place in which he says, *without nature the name of God is Majesty*, and (2) that this is the first place in which he makes any mention of the Divine Being without nature, as distinct from an eternal manifestation of it in nature, I say now further on this ground: here he had, for the first time, in his spirit that opening of the first abyssal world with such an effect that his sight was instantly confounded and overwhelmed. Thus, in a different sense from what was mentioned above, he had seen and yet not seen or observed; what exists *without nature*, he calls *Majesty*. Not that he had perceived or seen something distinctly that could have given him a proper idea of what we usually call so, but because he could not find a more convenient expression than to call that *Majesty* which his spirit could not bear and was unable to look upon, and which must have been transcendently more terrible and awesome to the eye than the visible majesty of a great Ahasuerus was to Queen Esther, etc.

And that he meant nothing else but this by Majesty may appear from this plain construction of his words: *Without nature the three centers are not understood*. For, says he, *without nature the name of God is Majesty*, giving us this name as a proper reason why the Three before nature cannot be understood. This Majesty, therefore, must denote something that is confounding human understanding—not only by its being so far above it that it cannot be looked upon, but also and even chiefly by its working upon it so strongly that all its natural powers must be overcome by it. All of this he asserts plainly regarding the chaos, or the Eye full of wonders, which exists before nature.

However it may be with this expression, it is undeniable that since this majesty has generated nature—which nature in its first appearance shows us the spiritual figure of a triangle, Δ—the three centers or things without nature must be those three from which this triangle in nature is generated, etc.

We shall pass by his fourth book, the FORTY QUESTIONS, although a significant passage relating to the Majesty without nature might be observed there.

In the fifth book, the INCARNATION, he begins to distinguish expressly the two considerations of God in the Trinity. In Part II, chapter 1, sections 8–12, he shows us the eternity without nature and its eternal stillness, the Eye of eternity, and the mirror of wonders; the first Abyssal Will with its <term>magia</term>, which we are not to search into because it has no origin but comprises or makes itself in itself and is without all nature. (*Therefore*, there is (N.B.) a <term>magia</term> in the eternal generation, which

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Jacob Boehme's work, specifically his distinction between the eternal generation of the Trinity and the generation of nature, clarifying that the Divine Being exists as a self-knowing Trinity prior to and independent of natural manifestation.</meta>

...is distinct and different from that magic which is in and belongs to eternal nature.) *See Six Points, i. 17.*

Furthermore, he speaks of an eternal beginning and an eternal end; of an eternal wisdom or mirror of wonders distinct from the act of seeing and from the eternal Spirit. Most importantly, he also speaks of a *desire* of the first abyssal will, and that this desire draws from itself. He explains this by saying that this desire is the will’s outgoing *lubet* <note>pleasure or delight</note>, or pleasure; *therefore*, it is not that desire for nature, which is its beginning and first property.

<margin>the term "liking" is used</margin>
In Chapter 2, he begins with the eternal *byss* <note>the "ground" or foundation, as opposed to the "abyss" or groundless</note>, which the abyss, he says, *makes in itself*. It makes it by the desire which was called *Lubet* in the previous chapter, and here it is explicitly explained as imagination, thus distinguishing it again from the desire in nature. See this distinction in *SIGNATURA RERUM*, vi. 1, 2, where he plainly says: *The desire is a hungry will and is the natural spirit in its properties, but the lubet comes from liberty; for God is desireless regarding his own being (or in himself), seeing that he lacks nothing; all is his, and he himself is All. But a Lubet* he has, and he is *himself that will to manifest himself,* etc. He wishes to manifest himself in nature, and this manifestation cannot occur without the desire. However, having in himself a *lubet*—in which the eternal generation of the Trinity is implied—he is manifest in and to himself, before and without the manifestation in nature, and cannot help but know himself. <note>In the German, this is "a lust-will."</note>

Our author now further explains this eternal generation as an impregnation of the abyssal will, which creates a *byss* within the abyss. This happens by a motion that is as distinct and different from the second property of nature as the *lubet* is distinct and different from the desire. *And thus,* he says, *we know an eternal abyssal Divine Being, and within it three persons, none of whom is the other: namely, the eternal Will, which is the cause of all beings, is the first—* In this will, the eternal beginning originates through imagination, in which the Will impregnates itself from the Eye of wisdom; this Eye exists with the will in an equal eternity, without ground or beginning. This impregnation is the ground, or *byss*, of the will: the Son, heart, word, sound, or (note) the manifestation of the Abyss. The third person is the Spirit.

To ensure no one imagines that eternal Nature is implied here (because desire, motion, life, etc., are mentioned), he prevents that misunderstanding by explicitly adding: *This is now a short declaration of the Deity in the Abyss, showing how God dwells in himself and is himself the center of generation. But the human mind does not rest satisfied with this; it inquires after Nature—that is, after that from which this world is generated and all things created,* etc.

In his sixth book, titled *SIX POINTS*, i. 1–22, he first speaks of an unessential will which is *dumb, mute, and without knowledge of itself* until the fiery essences are raised within it; these cannot be raised without desire, etc. This causes the misunderstanding that an absolute necessity exists, whereby the generation of nature—from desire to the production of fire—must be implied and presupposed in every consideration of the Trinity.

But let it be noted here that after he spoke of such an unessential will and applied it to the first abyssal will, he immediately proceeds to consider God in Trinity, apart from all nature. He shows us that the first abyssal will (which is indeed unessential, and therefore dumb and mute if considered strictly by itself) is not alone before and without nature. Consequently, it is not unessential, dumb, or mute, but becomes essential in and through its own co-eternal *byss*, generated by the desire—specifically, by what he previously called *lubet*, pleasure, or imagination—and not by *that* desire which is the beginning and first property of nature. For this *byss* is the only essence or essentiality of the abyss. Thus, nature and all its properties are utterly excluded from this consideration and are to be conceived as subsequent.

Thus he says directly, after speaking of the eternal Eye, mirror, etc.: *Here we understand the eternal being of the Divine Trinity, together with the abyssal Wisdom. For the eternal will, comprehending the eye, is the Father; that which is comprehended in the wisdom, wherein the comprehending creates a ground, byss, or center in itself, is the Son or heart; for he is the Word of Life, or (note) his essence, in which the will appears with its glance.*

And so that we may have no fear that nature is implied here, he excludes it this way: *Thus we understand that the Divine Being in Trinity in the abyss dwells in itself and generates a byss within itself.*

Again: *Thus we understand what the Divine Being is in itself without a principle, and what the eternal beginning is in the abyss, and the eternal end in its own byss generated within itself.*

Again: *In that wisdom (in which the eternal generation of the Word in the will was accomplished, and is still being accomplished from eternity to eternity), the eternal principle, like a hidden fire, was known in the figure from eternity, and is still known that way in that wisdom to all eternity.*

Note (1) here: there is something before and without nature which may rightly be called an eternal end, distinct from an eternal beginning. This eternal end is the same as that which, in its eternal manifestation through nature, is called nature’s end. Nevertheless, there is a distinction between them that runs parallel to the distinction between generation and manifestation, *lubet* and desire, three things or centers and three persons, etc.

Note (2): It is expressly asserted here that the principle of fire—which is nature—was not only known but is still known in that wisdom which is implied in the eternal generation of God in himself. It is even known only "in the figure," like a hidden fire; that is, as not yet actually generated or brought forth.

If we are then to understand a Trinity without a principle, and if the principle is known in the wisdom of this Trinity as something still hidden, how can we think that the manifestation of this principle, or the generation of nature, must be implied or presupposed in—or is required as necessary for—the eternal generation of this Trinity? And how can knowing, perceiving, and so on be denied in this Trinity?

It is not only said that it *was* known this way, as if this knowing had ceased by the manifestation of the principle, but it is also expressly said that it *is still* known this way. Therefore, this Trinity and this wisdom must still be a Trinity and a knowing wisdom in itself. It must still be considered as before, without, and above nature, even though nature is actually generated. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

The next in order is the short treatise *THE EARTHLY AND HEAVENLY MYSTERY*, comprised of Nine Texts.
