<meta>This page continues the defense of Jacob Boehme's theology against the charge that he places nature on an equal eternal footing with God, or that the Trinity depends upon nature for its existence. It analyzes Boehme's specific definitions of the "abyss," the "will," and the "seeking."</meta>

> *He begins thus: The abyss is an eternal nothing, but makes an eternal beginning as a seeking. For the nothing is a seeking after something; and yet there is nothing that could give anything; but the seeking itself is the giving of that which is itself also nothing but a desiring seeking. If there is thus a seeking in the nothing, this seeking makes within itself the will to be something, and this will is a spirit, like a thought; this goes out from the seeking and is the seeking’s seeker, for it finds its mother, which is the seeking. And in this we understand that the will is a spirit and is a different thing than the desiring seeking. For the will is an imperceptible and unknowable life; but the seeking is found by the will and is a being within the will. Now it is understood that the seeking is a* magia <note>magic or generative power</note>*, and the will a* magus <note>magician or agent</note>*, and that the will is greater than its* mother*.*

> *Thus we give you, in short, an understanding of* Nature *and the* Spirit of nature*. If, then, the eternal will is free from the seeking, but the seeking is not free from the will—since the will rules over the seeking—we therefore acknowledge the will to be an eternal omnipotence, for it has nothing equal to itself. And the seeking is indeed a movement arising from attraction or desire, but without understanding; it indeed has a life, but without knowledge. Now the will rules the life of the seeking and does with it what it pleases; and though it does something, yet it is not known until that being manifests itself with the will. And thus we recognize the eternal* will-spirit *to be God, and the moving life of the seeking to be* nature*. For nothing comes before them; both are without beginning; each is a cause of the other, and it is an eternal bond. And thus the* will-spirit *is an eternal knowing or understanding of the abyss, and the life of the seeking is an eternal being of the will.*

These are the words of our author, in which he represents God and Nature. From this, it is now inferred and said: We see here that he begins with the first abyssal will and places nature in an equal eternity with the abyss. He not only says the abyss is an eternal nothing, but also that the seeking (or nature) makes this nothing become something within itself—and this is so much the case that he calls this seeking the "mother" of the will, and the will an "imperceptible, unknowable life." Again, he says expressly: "There is nothing earlier than these two; they are both without beginning, and each of them is a cause of the other."

Therefore, the argument goes, we cannot conceive of a Trinity in any sense—nor any knowing, perceiving, or understanding—before and without nature. Instead, we must conceive of such an eternal Nothing, or such a Unity alone, which later becomes Something and is unfolded into Three, not only in nature but also by the help and cooperation of nature. This is the argument drawn from this treatise against the Trinity existing before nature.

Trusting in Divine help, I endeavor to answer it as follows:

(1.) First, I say rightly that in this whole treatise, he has no intention to show us the Trinity directly—neither as considered before nature, nor as within and after nature. His purpose is only, in general, to show the deepest and most internal origin of this, our third principle, and especially of things done and existing within it in states of opposition. This he rightly deduces from the first abyssal will and from that seeking by which he later understands nature, saying that there is nothing earlier than these two. All of this is obvious and evident in itself to every attentive reader of this treatise from beginning to end. Therefore:

(2.) In all these cited words concerning God, he does not speak of God considered as the whole Divine Being. He has no occasion, much less any necessity, to tell us in this place and for this purpose what this Divine Being is in itself or in its own eternal generation.

Rather, he speaks of the abyss only when considered strictly by itself and as abstracted from the byss <note>the "ground" or foundation</note>. This abyss, so considered, is indeed God and may be called so, because it cannot be separated from its byss any further than in our separate analysis; however, it is not fully God, because it does not encompass everything the name of God implies. What we are to understand as God is implied in this separate consideration. <meta>catchword: And</meta>

(3.) In all these words concerning *Nature*, he does not speak of nature as it is when actually generating or generated, but as it is considered before its generation and before it can properly be called nature. This is undeniable from verse 8 in the *Fourth Text* and verse 3 in the *Fifth*, where he calls these two—namely, God and nature—not only *two mysteries*, but also *two principles*.

By calling them "two mysteries," he gives us to understand that neither one is yet unfolded, but that each is viewed as still concentrated within itself; for in his style, this is the meaning of a *mysterium*.

And by calling them "two principles," he shows us plainly enough that he does not use the name "principles" in the sense he uses it when speaking of the three principles throughout all his writings. In that sense, he says himself that God is not a principle. In that sense, Nature is also not a principle in the singular; rather, if considered as generated nature, it consists of the two principles of fire and light, of which the third is a visible offshoot. But he calls them "two principles" in that well-known common sense in which the origins or the most radical beginnings of things are called their "principles." This latter sense is applicable both to God and nature, but the former is not.

If, then, nature is called a principle in the singular—and even joined in conjunction with God, who is called a principle in the same sense—nature must be considered as it was before the generation of fire and light, lying still in the first abyssal will as a hidden fire that "burns and yet does not burn," according to his own expression above.

In this state, or rather in the consideration of this state, it must nevertheless be seen as distinct from the first abyssal will, without any mixture or confusion between them. He shows this distinction between the one principle and the other—or between nature and the first abyssal will—as if at the deepest root. He says nothing at all of its properties; indeed, he does not call it "nature" directly, but "a seeking," and calls the will "a seeker," saying only later that nature is understood by this seeking (that is, in its progress and unfolding). So, therefore, it is plain that in this place he considers nature not yet as generated nature, but nevertheless as distinct from the first abyssal will and (in his own words) a *mysterium* in itself, distinct from that other mysterium which is God—or that aspect of God which Boehme calls the abyss and considers not yet unfolded into a byss. All of this concerning nature agrees precisely not only with this whole treatise but also with the rest of Boehme's writings. <meta>catchword: Now then</meta>

(4.) Our author does not intend in this place to declare what God is in himself—that is, what the whole Divine Being is in its own eternal generation as a Trinity—nor what Nature is in its unfolding and displaying of itself into seven; but only to declare what God and nature are in <meta>catchword: its</meta>

He clarifies that "nature" in this context refers to a pre-generated state of desire, rather than nature as it is commonly understood.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological defense of Jacob Boehme’s descriptions of God and Nature, specifically focusing on the distinction between the internal life of the Trinity and the external manifestation of nature. the deepest root with a mutual respect to each other, before they are to be considered as three and seven, he could well have said: "The Abyss is an eternal nothing, but makes an eternal beginning, which is a seeking," etc. But if he had had an occasion and a mind in this place, as he had in others, to declare what the whole Divine Being is in itself, without nature, without a principle, in its own eternal generation only, he would have turned these words quite another way and would have said, certainly to this effect: "The Abyss is an eternal nothing, but makes an eternal beginning, which is its co-eternal byss, heart, Son, or word," etc. For so we find he has said in many places, especially in the <term>MYSTERIUM MAGNUM</term>. There he not only says of the abyss that it is the will towards something and the father of the beginning to the byss; but also of the byss, that this is the first will's eternal *finding*, and the perceptibility *of it*, the *ens* <note>being or essence</note> (or something) of that abyss, which in comparison to the byss is nothing, notwithstanding that it is also all in itself. And further he calls *that byss the seat or habitation of the abyssal will, the eternal mind, the ground*, and <note>Note Well</note> *the beginning of all beings*.

So then we see clearly that in two different considerations, in a twofold sense, and upon a twofold account, he speaks of a twofold *finding*, and of a twofold *beginning*. Now we cannot take the one only and reject the other, nor can we oppose the one to the other; but we must take each in its own place, and no contradiction can then appear.

The Abyss, which, if strictly and abstractly considered as in and to itself only, is an imperceptible, unknowing, and unmoving being, or nothing, in comparison to all that is posterior, does on the one hand find and perceive himself in himself; and this in and by his byss, which is his only begotten Son, in whom he is well pleased, and which is one with the Father. And on the other hand, the same abyss does find and perceive himself outside himself; and this in and by nature, as yet called here but a seeking. This Nature or seeking is not one with the Father, and is never called by Behmen the Son, heart, word, seat, etc., of God; though he be called the father of nature.

And so also concerning the beginning; the byss is the beginning of something in the eternal generation, when God—namely, the whole Divine Being—is considered as in himself only:

And this seeking is the beginning of something in nature. The two beginnings are well consistent with each other, and neither can destroy nor deny the other.

This I could demonstrate from more than twenty places, but one from this treatise will suffice. See then *Text iv.* 3, 4, 5, and *Text v.* 1. There you shall find that he says not only of an impregnation and generation in the spiritual life, or in God, according to what we heard of it above from many other places, but also <note>Note Well</note> that this generation goes inwards (*introrsum*) into itself, and dwells in itself; while contrariwise the nature-life, or the generation of nature, from this seeking goes outwards (*extrorsum*) towards the outside, or straightway forward.

And though he says also that these two are not without one another, yet he explains himself by adding immediately, *So that there were a separation between them.* Without one another, therefore, they are separate to this extent and upon this account: that without mixture each of them is in itself that which it is, and neither of them does or can comprehend and contain the other in its own essentiality;

Yet there is nevertheless an eternal bond and union between them.

If then this be so, no argument can be brought forth from this saying, "The Abyss makes an eternal beginning, which is a seeking," as if this position must necessarily exclude, or could overthrow, all that he says in twenty other places of an eternal generation of God in himself, and of an eternal beginning in this generation. For, if we shall conceive, according to the words of this treatise just now quoted, that in the Divine Being, from the first abyssal will, one progress is made towards the inside and another towards the outside; we must necessarily conceive also that each of them must have its own beginning.

For the beginning of the one, which must be considered as it were an essential part of it, cannot be a beginning and part of the other; though these two beginnings may be both together at once, and even inseparable from each other.

And if thus in this treatise is inserted an impregnation of the first abyssal will, and such a generation as tends towards the inside and dwells in itself—with a clear distinction from nature, which tends towards the outside and dwells in itself also—it is plain and clear that in this treatise is asserted, though not declared particularly, the selfsame eternal generation before, without, and above all nature, of which we have heard so much until now, and in which we are to understand three things. But,

(5.) It will still be replied, *That Behmen says expressly that there is nothing sooner than these two, namely, the abyss and the seeking.* If then these two are the soonest, we cannot conceive three to be sooner than these two.

*Answer.* In this consideration of God and nature, both looked upon as tending towards the outside, he says rightly that there is nothing sooner than these two.

For in our inquiry, made backwards from the most outward things toward the most internal root of them—where always the remoter cause is conceived as sooner, prior, or deeper than that which is nearer—we cannot proceed any further, and can therefore find nothing sooner than these two. But in that other consideration, in which we say with Behmen that there is an eternal generation whereby God generates himself in himself in Trinity, and this from eternity to eternity, without a principle and without all nature; we may freely say the same words: "There is nothing sooner than these three, namely, the abyss, the byss, and the bond of union between them."

For seeing that the same abyss is the first of these three, and the first also of these two—and this even so that neither here nor there can this abyss be separated from what, in both cases, is joined with it in union;

There is an equal beginning of numeration on both sides, and nothing can here be sooner than the three, just as there also nothing can be sooner than the two; and the three must necessarily be as deep, central, and radical in this latter consideration as the two are in the former. Indeed, we may also say more, with good reason and without contradicting Behmen, that the three are sooner than the two.

For it is plain enough that by saying so we do not mean that there was a time or instant in which the three were and the two were not; which would be most ridiculously said, that the abyss was sooner than the abyss, because the abyss was when the abyss was not.

<summary>The author distinguishes between God's internal eternal generation (the Trinity) and His external generation of nature, arguing that both have a "beginning" in the Abyss without one excluding the other. He explains that the "three" of the Trinity and the "two" of God and nature are equally eternal and central, depending on whether one looks inward or outward.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Boehme, Abyss, byss, nature, Trinity, eternal generation, Mysterium Magnum, seeking, inward movement, outward movement, theological defense</keywords>

--- Page 323 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that while Nature and the Trinity are both co-eternal expressions of the Abyss, the Trinity must be understood as conceptually prior because it is the internal, essential life of God, whereas Nature is the external manifestation.</meta>

But we acknowledge with Boehme that the two are co-eternal to the three; and by saying, "The three were sooner," we mean only that in our regular conception they are to be conceived as if they were sooner, and that it would be a preposterous thing to do to conceive of them otherwise.

Because we cannot say in any sense that the <term>abyss</term> is descended from nature, or from this seeking; rather, we must say that nature, with all that belongs to it, is descended from the <term>abyss</term>. For the <term>abyss</term> makes the seeking, says Boehme, but the seeking does not make the <term>abyss</term>. Therefore, we conceive of this <term>abyss</term> as the very deepest and most internal, central root, driving forth, as it were, in the same instant, two collateral branches: the one toward the inside, and the other toward the outside. In that regard, we say that neither this nor that is sooner, but the <term>abyss</term> itself is sooner than both its branches. But further, on another and deeper account, we see that this same <term>abyss</term> is incomparably more closely related and infinitely more familiar to that branch which is driven forth within than to that which is without. For that which is within is one with itself and equal to itself, generated in its own bosom and dwelling in it forever;

Since that which is without is different from itself, lower in dignity, and used only as an *instrument* in its hand, etc., we can by no means think or say that which is within is descended from, caused, or originated by that which is without. But we must say: that which is without is from that which is within; and that which is within must therefore necessarily be sooner than that which is without.

Now, that which is without shows us presently, in its first unfolding, the spiritual figure of a triangle; and that which is within is nothing else but those three that are to be understood in the generation of God himself in himself. If then these three within are not from the three without, but these latter from the former, the three within are rightly conceived and said to be sooner than the three without.

And to show that this is not a construction of my own, see *SIX POINTS*, chapter 1, verse 9, where, having declared what the <term>abyss</term> is—not as here, with respect and relation to nature, but as considered absolutely in itself—and having told us that it is an eternal seeing Eye, wherein nature lies hidden and is nevertheless seen and known, etc., he says expressly the same words which he says here: 
> *There is nothing sooner than this eye; nothing is before it which was deeper, etc.*

From this, it is now evident that if nature itself in general, and also all that belongs to nature in particular, was seen and known—nay, which is much more significant, is still seen and known in the figure as a hidden fire before or sooner than it is nature generated or unfolded—further, if this seeing and knowing nature implies (as has been proved) the eternal generation in the Trinity; and again, if there is nothing deeper or sooner than this seeing Eye; the Three in the eternal generation within must necessarily be conceived as sooner or deeper than nature, with all its three and seven without.

Nay, from the plain words of this same treatise, it may be sufficiently proved. For he makes an express, plain distinction between *within* and *without*, saying not only in Text v. 1 that one of these two mysteries tends toward the inside and the other toward the outside; but he says also more explicitly in Text iv. 4 that 
> *since the <term>abyss</term> is impregnated, the generation goes toward the inside and dwells in itself, for the essence of the other life (namely, of nature) cannot comprehend this impregnation and cannot be a receiver (or a receptacle) of it. So, therefore, the impregnation must go into itself and must be its own receptacle, which is a son in the eternal Spirit, etc.*

Now it is evident to everyone that that which is within must always be conceived as deeper than that which is without; and seeing that that which is within is always a source, cause, ground, origin, root, etc., of that which is without, then that which is within must in one sense necessarily be conceived as sooner than that which is without, notwithstanding that in another sense, one is as soon as the other.

If then here in this treatise such an impregnation and generation of a Son is asserted as tends toward the inside, with an express exclusion of nature (which is said to go toward the outside and cannot comprehend this generation), then there is in this book, as well as in any other of our author's, an eternal generation asserted—without and above all nature—though it is not particularly declared.
<meta>catchword: But,</meta>

(6.) It is also objected that Boehme places nature next or immediately to the <term>abyss</term>, and that therefore nature must be conceived as standing in the middle, between the <term>abyss</term> and <term>byss</term>, and consequently no Trinity at all can be imagined before and without nature.

Answer. He rightly places nature next or immediately to the <term>abyss</term>, as to that which is the first of all, the deepest and most central. But does it follow from this that nature must be conceived as standing between <term>abyss</term> and <term>byss</term>? By no means; it would follow indeed if it could be shown that Boehme places the <term>byss</term> at a further distance from the <term>abyss</term>, behind or after nature. But no such thing can be found in any of all his writings.

He places the <term>byss</term> not only so near, but also, in a sense, even nearer and more immediately to the <term>abyss</term> than nature; so that <term>abyss</term>, nature, and <term>byss</term> are not to be conceived as three things following one after the other in a direct forward line. Instead, the <term>byss</term> and nature are to be conceived as two collateral branches, the former tending from the <term>abyss</term> toward the inside, and the latter from the same <term>abyss</term> toward the outside. On this, see *MYSTERIUM MAGNUM*, vii. 6. 
> *The Father, he says, is the will of the <term>abyss</term>: he is without all nature or beginning; the will toward something: this (Father) sets himself into a <term>lubet</term> for his own manifestation, and this <term>lubet</term> is the will's or Father's power comprehended; and is his son, heart, and seat; the first eternal beginning in the will, etc.*

Pray, what can be clearer and more supportive of our position? If the <term>byss</term> or Son is the first eternal beginning in the will, how can that beginning which is, in a sense, outside the will (and which the <term>abyss</term> makes with the seeking), be before it and stand between the <term>abyss</term> and the <term>byss</term>? And if this beginning is rightly called the first, as well as that one—so that there is nothing sooner than this, and also nothing sooner than that—must they not both be conceived as two collateral branches?

And must we not say: the seeking is the first in that progress which tends toward the outside, and the <term>byss</term> the first in that generation which is within? If we then will not dismiss or treat as insignificant, trifling chatter what he says of such a distinction between within and without, we cannot but freely see and acknowledge that from his placing nature next and immediately to the <term>abyss</term>, no argument can be taken against an eternal generation in the Trinity without all nature.

(7.) Concerning that part of this argument where it is said that Boehme calls the <term>abyss</term> an eternal nothing, and says the seeking (that is, nature) makes this nothing to be something in it—

<summary>The author argues that while God's internal Trinity and external Nature emerge from the same source, the Trinity is conceptually prior because it is internal and essential, whereas Nature is external and instrumental. He refutes the claim that Nature sits between the Abyss and the Trinity, explaining they are parallel branches from the same divine root.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Boehme, Abyss, Byss, Trinity, Nature, eternal generation, internal vs external, Six Points, Mysterium Magnum, divine will</keywords>

--- Page 324 ---
<meta>This page completes the sentence from the previous page, finishing the word "within itself." It continues the argument that while the abyss and nature are related, the abyss (or its internal "byss") exists as an eternal, self-manifesting eye before and independently of the generation of nature.</meta>

itself, which seeking he therefore explicitly calls the mother and the cause of it; so then we are not to think of any other "something," except what is made in and by nature.

Regarding this, I say, little more needs to be added, for what we have declared so far answers all these things sufficiently. It was demonstrated above that the abyss is not absolutely nothing in and to itself, though it is rightly called nothing in respect and comparison to nature. For the abyss in itself is an eternal seeing Eye, which sees and knows nature, in its form, as a hidden fire, before it is generated nature. Nature, therefore, does not make the abyss become something to itself, and Boehme tells us no such thing, but quite the contrary: he tells us, namely, that nature makes this "nothing" (which before was nothing in and to nature) to be now something in and to itself—that is, in and to nature, not in and to the abyss. How can nature make something in the abyss when nature is not only outside it and tends entirely toward the outside, but also when it is itself made by the abyss to be an eternal beginning, and when this abyss is in itself without beginning—nay, when it is an abyssal seeing Eye, which sees nature before it can even be called nature? Nowhere shall we find in Boehme that nature makes the abyss into an abyss, nor that it is called the mother and the cause of the abyss, but only (take note) of the *will*.

It will be replied: "The abyss and the will are but one; if then nature is the cause of the will, it is the cause of the abyss also." Answer: It is true, they are but one; but it is also true that in this consideration, they are to be finely distinguished, and you may find this distinction plainly enough throughout the first three or four texts of this treatise.

In this consideration, the abyss is prior to the will and is an absolute name, bearing no relation to nature; but the "will" is a relative name and implies an obvious tending toward the outside. The abyss as abyss is nothing to nature, for there is not yet any connection between them; but this abyss as a will toward nature is now concerned with nature, and on this account is something to nature, and no longer something only to itself. The abyss, considered as abyss only and strictly in itself, is not the father of nature, but an eye seeing nature before it is generated nature; but this same abyss, considered as a will toward nature, is the father of nature. Nature, therefore, is not the cause of the abyss being an abyss, but may be called the cause of the abyss having a will toward nature, and further of its being a father of nature. Because since nature was seen in the abyss before it existed as nature, this will is to be conceived as raising itself and tending toward the outside—much in the same way a son may be called the cause of his father being a father, but not the cause of his having been a man, fit and sufficient for his generation. So now this "something," in its progress from the abyss toward the outside, cannot make us fix our eyes upon itself alone and deny that there is any other something except what is made in and by nature. Rather, it directs us to look higher for that "something" which we find in the eternal generation, which turns away, as it were, from nature and tends toward the inside.

For it is plain and obvious everywhere in all the books of Boehme that the <term>byss</term> in this eternal generation is constantly called the Father’s or the abyss’s <term>ens</term>, essence, or "something"—His eternal perception, His Heart, Word, or Son, in whom the Father is well pleased, etc.

Having now, as I hope, sufficiently answered all parts of this great objection, we are to proceed further—

<note>Not finished, because the objector (a Mr. Pierce) admitted he was mistaken and was satisfied by this much, as expressed in the following letter:</note>

> "Sir,—I return many thanks for the opportunity to see these papers. Before this, I did not distinguish between the eternal generation and the eternal manifestation, but conceived the Threefold Spirit in the Abyss to be ungenerated and hidden; but now I understand the Triune Spirit to be generated in the abyss and manifest to itself before nature. And what pleases me much more is to see that none of the former descriptions are denied or laid aside, but are reconciled with the latter ones, which I did not understand beyond the point of eternal nature. I might well have expected more in them than in the former ones, had I considered that the author says, *the descriptions are each deeper than the last, and that he saw more and more.* But not minding this, I took the former to be complete and thought he knew everything at first, even if he was not able to set it all down. For that reason, I set aside what I could not find in them, thinking it was enough to know as far as the eternal nature; so I did not study the later descriptions much, and some I never saw. But now I am glad to find such a harmonious concordance in all of it; I have no objection against anything in these papers, even one of which is more than enough to satisfy me. For I am easily convinced by reasonable arguments, being only a learner, and I never expect to understand all this author has written; I am best when I think I know nothing. I always thought there could be no difference in the understandings of those who love and study this author that could not be easily reconciled."

The third of the selected extracts and abstracts from Freher is titled:

### POSITIONS CONCERNING GOD in UNITY and TRINITY, considered both BEFORE AND AFTER ETERNAL NATURE, according to BOEHME’S CENTRAL THEOSOPHY, as follows:

I.—The first and deepest consideration of God in unity and trinity is not what Jacob Boehme delivered in his *Aurora*, where he always declares and intermixes with it the generation of eternal nature in its seven properties, or fountain spirits.

But the first and deepest is that which he afterwards gave us in most of his following books, where he calls it an eternal generation of God in himself, in trinity, without any nature.

II.—In this first and deepest consideration, God is not to be conceived according to any such definitions as usually ascribe to him all the highest and most glorious attributes—whether they are those generally found and owned by all created spirits to be truly divine perfections, or those expressly mentioned in the Holy Scriptures.

III.—This is the reason for Boehme saying so much about an *eternal nothing, oneness, chaos, temperament, etc.*; for his denying in God *thoughts, deliberations, decrees, consultations, predestinations, etc.* regarding things to be created or governed in this or that manner; and further for his taking wisdom in different senses, placing it sometimes before and then again after the trinity.

IV.—None of the true perfections imaginable are hereby denied in God, not even in this first and deepest consideration without any nature. But the meaning is only this: in this consideration, they cannot yet be a distinct object of our understanding. Because they are still to be

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the Godhead as "nothing" and "all," explaining Jacob Boehme’s distinction between God as He is in Himself (before nature) and God as He relates to the generated world.</meta>

looked upon as not yet unfolded out of their root or center, which he calls a universal "all," no less than an eternal "nothing." And if we do conceive of them by distinct ideas, we only show thereby that our consideration does not go beyond the generation of eternal nature.

V.—It is not asserted here that such definitions of God as may be seen in all the systems of theologians are to be rejected as erroneous and hurtful; rather, they are freely admitted to be good, profitable, and sufficient to instruct men in what they are to know of God for their eternal salvation. But it is asserted only that they are not central and do not declare, as Boehme does, what God is in himself, without nature.

VI.—When God is considered by Boehme without any nature, but yet still with some relation and comparison to creatures, He is said to be an eternal nothing, an ineffable and unintelligible oneness, a most internal ground, root, or source of all created beings, by which none of them can be named, found out, or understood.

VII.—When God is considered without any nature, and as in himself only, without any relation or comparison to creatures, we must say, according to Boehme, that God is a beginningless and endless beginning, delighting in himself and playing with himself in the wonders of his eternal wisdom.

VIII.—In this definition, the Trinity in unity without any nature is contained and expressed. By "God delighting in himself," a single individual being or a unity without distinction is expressed; yet from the second consideration of God, as in and after nature, it does appear that here also—before and without nature—in this same individual being three things are to be understood, so that we can truly say of it, in some but not in every sense, that the first is not the second, and the second is not the third.

IX.—For that which delights is to be conceived as answering to that which, in and after eternal nature, is called Father. That which is delighted in answers to that which afterwards is the Son. And this delight itself answers to that which afterwards is called the Holy Spirit, but here, as before and without nature, it is a moving life of Father and Son.

X.—These three are not to be conceived as if they were three distinct beings, persons, or intellectual spirits existing alongside one another, each having his own understanding, will, etc. This would be making three Gods.

XI.—These three are but one intellectual being, having but one intellect, will, and life. Nevertheless, there is such a distinction between them as is not imaginary, nor yet arbitrary. But it is a distinction *cum fundamento in re* <note>Latin: "with a foundation in the thing itself," meaning a real distinction based on the nature of the object.</note>, representing rightly three and neither more nor less. Boehme distinguishes them thus: he calls them an eternal nothing and an eternal *ens* <note>Being or existence</note>, or something. Again, a beginningless and endless abyss; an eternal beginning and end, or a "byss" coeternal to the abyss; and an *outgoing* or proceeding from that abyss and byss, or also from that abyss through that byss. Again, he calls them the first or abyssal will, the second will—or with the Scripture, the eternal *Word*—and the *moving life of the Deity*. And sometimes Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

XII.—The eternal nothing, answering or assignable to that which after nature is called Father, may be safely conceived so, but with this caution: that we do not think it is "nothing" in and to itself, but only so to all and every created understanding.

And when this nothing itself opens upon the spirit of a soul, it instantly confounds and consumes all its sight, and reduces it, in a sense and manner, into its own nothingness. The generation of the fourth property of eternal nature, wherein this nothing opens, and which is to be met with more or less in the process of regeneration, is not only an unexceptionable witness of all this, but also an instructor able enough to inform us how we are to conceive of this eternal nothing.

XIII.—The eternal *ens*, or something, answerable or assignable to what in and after nature is called Son, may safely be conceived so—as we can conceive an endless, substantial being—but with this caution: that we do not say or think it is so to nature and creature, but only in itself and to that former nothing. For to all created spirits, it is still but nothing, because it is still before, above, and without nature, and can be seen, found out, and entered into by none of them; notwithstanding that it is, in a sense, to be distinguished from that nothing, and that this nothing does see, find, and manifest itself therein, and delight in it as in its own expressed image.

XIV.—Boehme’s frequent expressions of "abyss" and "byss" are all equivalent in sense to those of nothing and something. But because he speaks more distinctly and explicitly of the abyss than of nothing, more is also to be said of it.

When he speaks of this abyss, declaring what it is in and to itself, he never says that it is a nothing, but plainly and expressly in more than twenty-five places, that it is a *beginningless endless Eye*. This eye sees all nature and creature before either this or that can be called so. It sees all the powers, products, numbers, etc., that ever are or can be brought forth into being. But it sees none of these things as external, or as really distinct either from itself or from one another; and therefore sees itself only—that is, in a word, its own central all-sufficiency for all these things.

XV.—Here now is the Divine intellect or Wisdom in its first and deepest sense, which Boehme also calls wisdom expressly and in many places. And here, therefore, that objection saying, "He preposterously places the will before wisdom, and wisdom after the will, contrary to sense and reason," is sufficiently answered and must be regarded as having arisen only from a misunderstanding of him.

For though he places wisdom in another sense, and upon another account, not only after the will but after the Trinity—as he does, for instance, in his *Table of the Principles*—yet here wisdom stands, in this sense, before the will, and the will follows immediately upon it. For

XVI.—Thirdly, when Boehme intends to proceed further and to declare that eternal generation in three—which goes, as it were, on the one side, from this abyss toward the inside, while that of eternal nature in seven tends on the other side, from the same abyss toward the outside—he says: This abyss is, or also has, a will, which he calls the first abyssal will, in distinction from the second will, that of the byss. This expression of a first and second will does not say that there are two wills in the Divine Being; they are one, as the Father and Son are one.

The first will is not to be conceived as a will by itself, for it is not yet that which we use to

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Trinity and the nature of God's will and wisdom as described by Jacob Boehme (Behmen), specifically focusing on the transition from the "abyss" to the "byss."</meta>

call a will, but it is to be conceived as the first imperceptible disposition toward the will. This disposition is in the abyss, but as it is in the abyss, it cannot come to its maturity.

XVII.—The reason why Behmen calls it the first will, when it cannot properly be called a will, is this: That which is in the abyss is the very same thing that is in the byss; in the abyss it is in its deepest root, and in the byss it is a full-grown tree. If, then, that which is in the byss is a will rightly and properly so called, that same thing in the abyss may aptly, though not so properly, be called a will, with the distinction of being the "first." This second will he also calls, according to Scripture, the eternal Word, because this second will is not only an offspring produced out of the first, but chiefly such an offspring as is an express image, manifestation, unfolding, outspeaking, or declaration of all (neither more nor less) that the first will was, or had in its own central depth.

XVIII.—The generation of our own word, within the particular sphere of every person's created being, can be, in a manner or in part, a fine though only shadowy representation of this. For though we usually call only that a "word" which is distinctly formed and pronounced, yet we know that every such formed word has a much deeper root in the inmost recesses of our soul and spirit, even before it comes to be perceptible in our mind.

Further, we know that such a formed word is nothing else but an opening, manifestation, or declaration of what our soul first had unformed in its own depth, or what our will first in itself—and at first even insensibly—was inclined or disposed toward. And then we also know that this is nothing else but that; and that by the formation of an express word, the first disposition toward it in the will only brings forth and exalts itself, and nothing but itself, into such perfection as it could not have had as long as it was unformed in its first original depth.

If, then, that which is expressly formed and spoken forth is rightly called a word, that which this same word was before it was thus formed may well enough be called a word also.

XIX.—In one will, says Behmen, no knowledge of itself can exist. And this is not to say that for a knowledge of itself, two wills in two distinct intellectual beings are required. It means only that in this first abyssal will, if it were alone—without having brought forth and exalted itself into its own formed, expressed image, namely, the second will— no perception or knowledge of itself could exist.

XX.—The abyss is all-power concentrated, and the byss is the same all-power unfolded. Now, this "all" and that "all" must necessarily be one, and no distinction can be found between all and all; neither can there be two different "alls."

XXI.—The communion between these two, which is a living beam proceeding from the first into the second, and through the second (and so from the first and second into the eternal wisdom, delighting and playing in and with its wonders), is the Spirit, called here by Behmen a moving life of the Deity. And this completes this holy, most adorable number Three.

XXII.—To these three, no fourth can be added, and though Behmen says ever so much about an eternal Virgin Wisdom, no quaternity is made.

Immediately after these three, Behmen in his Table places Wisdom, distinguishing the "outgoing" from "that which has gone out," and saying that the outgoing or proceeding forth is the Spirit, and that which has gone out is Wisdom.

Wisdom stands rightly both in the beginning and the end, or both before and after this Trinity, concluding, as it were, the circle of this eternal generation, which was also begun with wisdom.

Wisdom is compared by Behmen not only to a seeing Eye, but also to a Mirror full of wonders. And though he usually sets these two comparisons together, he also distinguishes them plainly enough here and there, so that this twofold comparison may not only show us the twofold sense in which he looks upon wisdom, but also direct us to that twofold place where he positions it, and show why he speaks of it before the will and also again after the Trinity.

When he considers the abyss, not yet as a Father, but as the abyss only, he says affirmatively of it that it is an eternal seeing eye. Here, in this place, there is not yet any mention made of the will, which will makes the first beginning of the abyss being called a Father; and so also, there is not yet a generation of the Son, nor a proceeding of the Spirit to be conceived. Instead, this wisdom or seeing eye is considered only and strictly by itself, in its own eternal center, wherein it sees purely in itself its own radical all-sufficiency for everything that is in any sense posterior—and so not only what may concern nature and creature, but also what belongs to the next following generation itself.

In this first consideration, therefore, the comparison of an eye is more fit than the other of a looking glass, which notoriously implies two things: a certain object, and then also something that it can be an object to.

When Behmen has declared the eternal generation in the Trinity, so that now Father, Son, and Spirit are considered in that distinction wherein they stand—so far that we can say the Father as Father is not the Son, and the Son as Son is not the Spirit, though all three are but one and the same intellectual being—then only, but not before, according to this distinction, a distinction also between wisdom and wisdom appears, and the comparison of a looking glass full of wonders is now more fit and proper than before. Notwithstanding this, wisdom is both then and now the same.

For it is now no longer considered by itself alone as an abyssal eye in its own internal center, but as "gone out" and dilated in the byss, and as in conjunction with this byss; between these two, abyss and byss, there is now a mutual relation, so that it is no longer the wisdom of the abyss, but the wisdom of the Father and the Son. And there is now also something which the wonders of this looking glass can be a passive subject to, namely, a moving active life of the Father and Son, which is the Spirit. For,

XXIII.—In the consideration of the eternal generation only, and not before it, the abyss is considered as outgoing or proceeding forth from itself. If, then, this abyss is a seeing eye in and to itself, this seeing eye goes out and makes itself more external than it was before; namely, in that strict sense, and not any further, in which we can say the Spirit gone out from the abyss is to be considered as more external than the abyss as it is in itself only. Therefore, when this eye, considered as abyssal only, had more strictly (or, as it were, more narrowly) for an object its own central and radical all-sufficiency, it has now—considered as more external, as if in a larger dilation—an infinite multiplicity and variety of wonders. These are to be looked upon not only as distinct from the Spirit, but also as a passive subject of this Spirit, wherein he moves, plays, and delights. This, indeed, is to be such an object as they could not be before, when the Spirit was not yet a moving life gone out from the abyss.

And in relation, therefore, to this spirit, that same eternal wisdom—previously only abyssal, but now in conjunction with the byss—is more aptly compared to a mirror than before, standing as an object before the Spirit and representing all its infinite variety of figures, powers, wonders, etc.

This distinction between Wisdom and wisdom is based as much *on a foundation in reality* as that between the first and second will, or that between Father, Son, and Spirit. And if it is therefore necessary to consider the eternal unity as preceding the trinity, and again the eternal generation in the trinity as following the unity, there is also a need for such a distinct consideration of Wisdom and wisdom, placing wisdom in the one sense before, and in the other sense after, the Trinity.

XXIV.—Wisdom in that first sense and place is called by Behmen the *Mysterium Magnum* without nature, considered in its most internal root or center. And <margin>in</margin> this second sense and place, it is that same *Mysterium Magnum* without nature, but considered as more external, as having emerged or displayed itself from that root.

Wisdom in that first sense and place can be considered as neither active nor passive, because it is abyssal. But in this second sense, *wisdom* is rightly considered as passive only and as incapable of activity; for it is in subordination to the spirit, just as a body is to its life. A body may indeed be living and full of vigor and activity, and yet can never be that life or principle of activity itself; so also wisdom is indeed not without life and yet has no life without the spirit, which is the only life within it. Wisdom in this second sense is as inseparable from the spirit as wisdom in the first sense is from the abyss.

Wisdom in the first sense, compared to a seeing Eye, is the divine intellect—that is, God himself considered only and purely as he is in himself, but not yet as in the Trinity. And in this second sense, compared to a Mirror full of wonders, wisdom (though still divine) is not purely God himself, neither as in Unity nor as in Trinity; rather, it is, as it were, a habitation of God, considered now in the Trinity. This habitation without any nature corresponds to that which exists in and after nature, which is called a most glorious, majestic habitation, or a balanced state in substantiality; this also is not God himself, but is under God, just as every habitation is under its inhabitant.

Yet in all these and similar distinctions, the eternal wonders of wisdom (relating principally to the second sense) are inseparable from that seeing Eye in the first. The wonders of wisdom are tacitly implied in the first sense and more explicitly represented in the second. For the Spirit is now that which sees them and delights in them. And his seeing is no longer only as within himself, but as something emerged and distinct, though not separate, from himself. The next consideration concerns the divine Trinity, both as before* and in and after nature.

It elaborates on how the Abyssal Will generates the Trinity (the Three) and the properties of nature (the Seven) to move from an unmanifest state to a self-aware, glorified manifestation.</meta>

...on the one side, the Father of the Byss, and on the other the Father of Eternal Nature. These are not two fathers, but only one, though the generation is twofold for several reasons. For just as from the first abyssal will towards the *inside*, there proceeds from eternity to eternity a generation in three; so also from the same abyssal will proceeds an eternal generation into seven, which is the generation of eternal nature. In this, the three manifest themselves by approaching the creation of living intellectual beings, to be made after their own triune image, so that they might be known and glorified. For none of them could have been brought forth by or from the three alone, without the seven, which generate themselves mutually and perpetually in that constant process called by Behmen the generation of eternal nature. Why this eternal generation is rightly called an eternal manifestation of the Divine Triune Being is most worthy and necessary to be examined.

The name of a manifestation implies (1.) that there is something which has a being in and to itself; (2.) that this something is unmanifest, hidden, and covered, etc.; (3.) that there is also something to which this manifestation is to be made. Now then, it has been sufficiently proved that the Divine Triune Being without nature is not a "nothing" in and to itself, and is not brought forth by nature from non-being into being.

But since, in this Triune Being, the byss is a manifestation of the abyss to itself, it may be justly asked: What is then further hidden, secret, or unmanifest? And what is that to which a manifestation is required to be made? Answer: Notwithstanding all this manifestation of the abyss by its byss, the whole Triune Being without nature is still unmanifest to itself. And this manifestation is therefore a manifestation of this Triune Being made to itself only, though it is also consequently a manifestation made for the purpose of producing intellectual creatures. None of these could the Triune Being have been made manifest to—indeed, none of which could have been manifested to itself—except through the generation of eternal nature.

XXVI.—The byss is a manifestation of the abyss to itself. For the abyss’s eternal finding, which is the byss, is a manifestation of the abyss to itself. For in the abyss’s eternal finding, wonders, figures, colors, virtues, etc., appear to that moving life of Father and Son, which is the Spirit. All this is true in its sense and degree; yet all this will still not suffice. For all these things are still merely nothing in and to themselves, and have no activity in or with them, but are only like transitory or shadowy images in a looking glass, which are and can do nothing to themselves, though they are something to that Eye which looks upon them. Therefore, no properties are in motion, no sound is heard from them, no harmony arises, no fire burns, and no splendor or light can shine, etc. And though there is a clearness and serenity, yet there is no splendor, luster, and glory.

And on this account, the Spirit cannot, in a full sense, be said to perceive and know himself, or to be manifest to himself, before he effectively knows what it is to have passed through all the inferior properties of nature, and to have exalted himself through the fire into the light of glory. If then this is done in and by the generation of eternal nature, and if it cannot be done any other way, this generation is rightly called a manifestation of the Spirit, and so of the whole Triune Being, made only to itself.

XXVII.—It is plain from this that this manifestation is not, as it were, the removing of a veil or similar impediment from a thing that is covered or concealed by it; no such thing is to be imagined here. For as it is not a manifestation made either to or by any other, but made only by and to that being itself, so it is also an eternal impossibility that this Being could be manifest to itself (in the sense that Behmen takes this word) without or before an actual performance, the intervention of the desire, and its own not being changed into fire, but continuing as the abyssal root of it. So then:

XVII.—The will is fire, and is not fire, just as the abyss is God and is not God.

XVIII.—The abyss, God (in the first sense), or liberty, also becomes light through the process of nature; for he wills both fire and light, which he is not before or without this actual willing and effective executing of the will. And nevertheless,

XIX.—Liberty is not changed into light, in the same sense in which the will is not changed into fire, and the unity is not changed into trinity. And so therefore,

XX.—Liberty also is light, and is not light, just as the will is fire and not fire, and the abyss is God and is not God.

XXI.—This liberty, which is free from those motions of nature that are to produce the fire, and which therefore is without light, is the father of light by its <term>lubet</term>, as the desire is the father of fire; and the Will, comprising them both, is the father of the whole nature.

XXII.—This light shines in one sense and respect downwards into the darkness—the inferior part of nature which does not comprehend it; and in another sense upwards into the liberty, which now as it comprehends the light, is the superior part of nature. It still does not comprehend it; and in another sense upwards into the liberty, which is indeed free from the restless nature, but is no longer (as before) destitute of glorified natural properties. Or also,

XXIII.—This light shines in one sense and respect forwards into nature, though with a great difference as to its inferior and superior parts; and in another sense backwards into its root, which is God (in the first sense, not in the second). And so,

XXIV.—God is that spiritual fire and light which is in eternal nature, according to the Scripture calling God fire and light. And again,

XXV.—God is not that spiritual fire and light which is in eternal nature; according to that fundamental position, agreeable to Scripture, that none of these things is done in the past, or only once, but all is perpetually happening: and that therefore the abyss, abyssal will, or eternal liberty is not changed into fire nor into light, but is perpetually the innermost root and ground of them.

XXVI.—St. John’s expression, *it was, was not, and yet was*, may here also be well noted and applied, no less than his following words, *and here is Wisdom*.

of all what is for this manifestation required. Which is in short a raising up the properties of nature, a passing through them, and an exalting itself thereby into glory and majesty.

This cannot be done by three, and not by less than three; and though the properties of nature are in one respect but three, nay in another also but one; yet in their full expansion, they are also seven; and by three only, this raising, passing through, and exalting cannot be performed.

For that which will thus exalt and manifest itself is in a manner three already; and this manifestation is not a going backwards, or decreasing, but an increasing: and though this Tri-une Being does not itself increase, yet its manifestation is and must be a fruitful progress, laying, as it were, a foundation for an infinite multiplication.

**XXVIII.**—As in this eternal manifestation there must be more than three, so by the same necessity, there can be neither more nor less than seven.

For the three in the eternal generation may be conceived, the first as a <term>terminus a quo</term>, than which nothing is sooner or deeper; the second as a <term>terminus ad quem</term>, beyond which there is no going further; and the third as a medium between them, both distinguishing and combining them. And this threefold degree of progress must in the generation of the properties of nature distinctly be expressed and represented, if the three without nature shall be manifested, and gradually exalted in and by the progress of nature; as it is accordingly expressed in the three principal regions, or parts of nature. And it is this same distinct expression which brings in, or carries along with it of all necessity, the full and perfect number seven, without having less, or wanting more. For when in the eternal generation the <term>terminus a quo</term> is but one, the same cannot be one but must be three; in this eternal manifestation thereof, because there are three in the completed eternal generation, all three together are to be manifested and exalted in this progress of nature.

All three therefore are, as in the end of this progress, so in this beginning thereof also, wherein all three do consequently leave behind them, as it were, these footsteps, which are the three first properties of eternal nature, distinctly by <term>Behmen</term> ascribed to Father, Son, and Spirit.

Now further: as the Three in the eternal generation are not to stand still in this beginning, but must go on unto a full manifestation and exaltation in the light of glory and majesty: so these their first footsteps in nature cannot be left in that state wherein they are in this beginning; but must be fixed and appear in the end of nature also, which is the <term>terminus ad quem</term>, beyond which there is no going further.

And these are the three superior properties of nature, not only answering in one sense to the three first, but also one with them in another. And so there are now six of them.

But now as to the medium between them, which is both to distinguish and to unite them, this can be neither three nor two, but must be one. Two cannot be an exact distinguishing mark between these three and three, for if they are two, they not only can be, but also still need to be distinguished themselves by a third.

Three can also not be such a true distinction, for they are themselves distinguished already by a third standing between one and one. This third therefore would be the distinguishing factor, not between three and three, but between four and four. Again, neither two nor three can be duly uniting these three and three, for this uniting must be done in or by one only indivisible point: The three on the one side stand as it were by themselves in a circle or globe, and so do the three on the other also. Just as then two circles cannot touch one another in more than one point, so it is here to be conceived also. And this one point must be such a one as may be able, not only to keep in itself an exact neutrality between the three and three, but to have also an equal communion with both sides, so as to keep them not only from each other in one respect, but also to bind them both together in another. All which cannot be done by two or three, but by one only. And this is now the fourth property in the generation of eternal nature, standing in the midst between three and—

**A.**—The great controversy between us is this: whether eternal Nature is 'created' by the 'omnipotent will' of God, 'commanding it to come forth out of nothing,' or whether it be out of God, and yet not God, nor a part of God.

**B.**—I affirm according to <term>Behmen</term> that eternal nature is out of God, namely, the first abyssal will. And the reason why we disagree is because we do not both have the same idea of God in this dispute. Your notion of God here is compounded of all the divine attributes as they are delivered in Scripture, and so is a good notion in itself, but not right in this place.

**A.**—If my notion of God is according to the Scripture, must it not be good and true and all-sufficient?

**B.**—It is good and true, nay sufficient also for a true Christian who considers only and declares the wonders and works of God, especially as concerning his dispensations towards creatures. But it is not so for a true Christian Theosopher as <term>Behmen</term> was, who considers and declares what the Scripture is quite silent of, namely: what eternal nature is in its seven properties, what its original and perpetual generation is, by what it is distinguished from God, and how it came to be that manifestation of God here by which further in the creation of angels and men, his works and wonders, and different dispensations about his church were effected. **A.**—Is not God always the same, and what can your notion of God be if you exclude the Divine attributes from it?

As after the creation and fall of men and angels, things or attributes may be conceived and affirmed of God which could not be attributed to him before, without implying any change in God, so no change in God is made by supposing the distinction of divine attributes to arise from his manifestation in eternal nature?

<meta>This page continues the explanation of Jacob Behmen’s (Boehme’s) mystical theology, specifically how the "seven properties of nature" complete the manifestation of the Trinity and how the "abyssal Will" serves as the origin of both the Divine Being and eternal nature.</meta>

three and making up the full and perfect number seven; by which the whole manifestation of the three beyond nature is fully accomplished. So, nothing can be taken from or added to it.

XXIX.—By this eternal generation in seven, the Triune Being beyond nature is manifested to itself, and all the Divine attributes are unfolded from their root.

For all that is required for this manifestation is now performed by the generation of these seven. The fire burns, the light shines; the former in strength and power, the latter in splendor and brightness; the air unites and keeps them in union, being itself neither this nor that. And so the former stillness is now turned into a most glorious region, full of living, moving, working, and all harmonized properties and qualifications; wherein God in Trinity dwells and perceives what it is to have actually exalted himself from an abyss into glory and majesty.

XXX.—The Divine Triune Being was never without this eternal generation in seven, which is therefore inseparable from it, though it may be considered separately by itself. And though Behmen ascribes an eternal beginning to this sevenfold generation, this is not to say that the Divine Being was by itself alone before a beginning was made; but only that this generation in seven is not the first, deepest, or most inward original center.

And this mention, therefore, of a beginning is to be taken only in such a sense as that in which the Byss <note>The "Ground" or "Foundation," from the Greek *byssos*</note> or Son himself, though equally co-eternal with the Father, is rightly said to have an eternal beginning in the will—a beginning which he did not have once at a specific instant, but has still from eternity to eternity.

XXXI.—All that creatures can know, perceive, enjoy, and understand of God is only in and by this eternal generation in seven; which is therefore not to be looked upon as if it were a thing strange to, or separable from God, or not of great importance in the consideration of God. For it is the Divine nature, which all the creatures made after his image must be partakers of if they shall be able to stand before his throne; and without which he can much less be known and understood by them than any particular thing can be known without knowing its nature. Therefore, in a true definition of God, not only the number three ought to be expressed, but also the number seven.

Without the three, the seven could not be; and without the seven, the three could not be manifest. For the seven make, in their generation, those two eternal principles: fire and light. And these two are the same in which the manifestation of the Divine Triune Being beyond nature is accomplished; *the Father's in the fire, the Son's in the light, generated and shining forth out of that fire, and the Spirit's in them both.*

XXXII.—After the three first properties—called by Behmen the triangle in nature and referred distinctly to Father, Son, and Spirit—in the generation of the fourth, which is the fire, the first abyssal Will is opened as an eternal nothing—consuming, melting down, turning, and transmuting, in one sense, into *nothing*, but in another into *something better and more noble*, everything that was made by the three first properties in their fighting and whirling. And this is the Father, whom the Scripture also calls a consuming fire. If, then, this first abyssal will is God—namely, the Father, considered as in himself only without all nature—this same abyssal will, now opened in the generation of this fourth form, *is God in nature.*

From this first manifestation, which is *the Father's in the fire, the second, namely, the Son's in the light, is entirely inseparable.* And so also from these two is the third, which is the Spirit's, called or compared, both in Scripture and by Behmen, to a wind or air—not only proceeding forth from fire and light but also keeping them both in union, according to that outward representation in temporal nature, where we see that *without* air proceeding from [and with] the fire, no fire can burn and consequently no light can shine.

XXXIII.—From this different consideration of the Trinity, it cannot be inferred that Behmen—

B.—I conceive of him, with Behmen, as an eternal nothing. . . .

A.—But have you not yourself in many places said that *without* and *before* eternal nature, which you call an eternal manifestation of God, there is an eternal generation in Trinity, of which Behmen says, "God generates himself in himself from eternity to eternity"?

B.—When in a former discourse I considered in general the eternal generation in Trinity and the co-eternal manifestation—demonstrating (*without considering nature's original*) that this is different from that (which was the matter then in question) and declaring which of these two is deeper and more interior, and which therefore is to be set in the first or chiefest place, and which in the second—I said rightly that the eternal generation goes *before*, and the co-eternal manifestation follows *after*, because of its being lower and exterior, and not because of its having its origin out of that Triune being which is generated in the eternal generation; which might be evident even from this expression of its being co-eternal to it.

But when I now consider especially the origin of eternal nature, and what it is made of (a thing quite different from that former topic), I do not set the Triune being before, or immediately antecedent to, the first property of nature, as if it had such a connection with it as a cause must have with its effect. Instead, I set it, as it were, over against the first property of nature; and the first abyssal will in the midst immediately over them, in this form:

->The first abyssal Will<-

The Triune being in the eternal generation. | The first property of eternal Nature.

For out of this Will, and not out of the Triune being, Behmen says *eternal nature exists*; and this will he calls the Father, both of the eternal generation in the trinity within and of eternal nature without.

From this, it can now be demonstrated also: (1.) that your notion of God, gathered from Scripture, though good and proper in its place and order, and sufficient also for a true Christian, is not sufficient for this matter for a true Christian theosopher searching into the deep things of God, but that Behmen's is. (2.) That from your notion, the seven properties of nature—why the three first must be dark and restless; what the fire is and by what it is produced; where the light comes from and why it arises out of the fire, etc.—cannot be explained, but that all this can be explained from Behmen's. (3.) That his notion, when rightly understood, is free from all offensiveness, and that by his saying, *eternal Nature is out of the first abyssal will*, he does really say much more, and quite another thing, than you do by saying, "It is effected by the will."

It clarifies that the distinction between the Trinity "without nature" and the Trinity "in nature" does not imply two separate Trinities, but rather two states of manifestation of the same Divine Being.</meta>

makes two Trinities: one before and the other after nature. For the first abyssal will, the eternal Word, and the proceeding from both—before and without nature—are the same three that, in and after nature, are called Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. And if his speaking of a first and second will does not create two wills in the Divine Being (which was established above), his speaking of a Trinity without and a Trinity in nature also does not create two Trinities. For as the second will is only an opening, manifestation, and exaltation of the first—having neither more nor less in it than that first—so also the Trinity in nature is only an opening, manifestation, and exaltation of the Trinity without nature, and has in it neither more nor less.

XXXIV.—When we speak with Behmen of an opening, manifestation, or exaltation in the Divine Triune Being, we say the same thing in substance, but more explicitly, what the Scripture says more implicitly when it calls the Son an "express image, character, and brightness of the Father’s glory." For if we are to conceive of the Son in this way, we must also conceive of the Father as having no brightness of glory without the Son. And if so, must we not conceive of the Father without the Son as a sealed-up center, not manifested to himself, and not exalted into a brightness of glory?

The Son’s generation, therefore, which is from eternity to eternity, is nothing else but the Father’s manifestation to himself, made by his own opening, proceeding forth, and exalting himself from a low or deep abyss into the highest seat of glory.

XXXV.—Though there are not two Trinities,* the one before and the other after eternal nature, yet there are several significant differences between the Trinity considered as without and

---

* That there are not Two Trinities.—“Concerning a description of the properties of eternal nature, and how they may be conceived in God, it is true that Behmen’s description is for the most part taken from the process of regeneration experienced in himself, to which process he also directs everyone to follow in their own person. [N.B.]”

There, he will say, if one first finds perceptibly and really what the first three properties are in their being separated from the second three (the superior ones), he shall further find also what they are in their union with them. And *only then, being thus made a partaker again of the Divine Nature*, will he be satisfied regarding this matter himself, though he shall never be able to satisfy another. Therefore, although Behmen has indeed said several things about this, he could not have said them otherwise than in a way that all his expressions are still more or less liable to exceptions and objections; for nothing on earth can be named to declare something in heaven or in God, except as a shadow.

So all the words which he uses in his *Aurora*, where he speaks not only of the first three properties but also specifically of air, water, heat, and cold, and how they are in God; and also these three names—*attraction, mobility, sensibility*—which he uses when he says the first three properties are in God, will still be subject to objection. But how can this be remedied? From where shall an earthly man living on earth have words other than earthly, when the Lord himself from heaven had no other words than earthly so long as he lived on earth in our flesh and spoke to earthly men? This, then, is the only thing that can be said: Let everything that implies an imperfection, either directly or indirectly, be removed and excluded from all the words and notions we can have of the properties of nature. And what we then find remaining in our mind, surpassing outward words, we may say of it: this is (according to the different degrees of our sensibility) either a clearer or a more obscure shadow of what the thing itself is in God.

Concerning the two last mentioned similes, relating in a tolerable sense and manner to the Trinity considered as before, and as in or after eternal nature: the first was taken from a consideration of the soul, and the second of the human will.

The first, which is not as close or fitting as the second, is yet fit enough to illustrate the particular point for which it was presented—which is to show only that we bear within ourselves something that is but one and the same; nay, as I think, it may well be expressed as the very same. Nevertheless, it may not only be considered as in two distinct states or degrees, but shall also be found to be very different in the one from what it is in the other. For the soul, considered as in a child, is the same soul that is in that child when he is a man; but the great differences between that former and this latter state of the same soul are well enough known. And it is especially presupposed (which could also be demonstrated) that nothing is added to the soul from without in this latter state; but everything it now has, which it did not have before, has risen and displayed itself only from its own ground within.

The application can easily be made, and the conclusion is this: just as all this difference does not make two souls, so also our distinct considerations of the same Divine Trinity—with all the differences grounded upon that sure foundation of this eternal generation of nature—does not make two Trinities.

But that other simile, taken from a consideration of the human will—which is more agreeable and applicable in more particulars—can illustrate it better, as may appear by the following positions:

I.—Our will not only may be considered distinctly by everyone, but must be so by a philosopher: first, as it is in its own central root, where it is imperceptible to all later faculties; and secondly, as it is in its activity, where it is plainly perceptible. So also may and must the Divine Being be considered distinctly by a true theosopher, searching with the spirit into the deep things of God.

II.—In this distinct consideration, a philosopher will find several differences between will and will; and so will a theosopher find differences between the Trinity in his first consideration and the same in his second.

III.—A philosopher in a discourse, speaking of this will and that will, may well enough for brevity’s sake call one the first will and the other the second. And so might the theosopher (speaking to understanding people, not ignorant ones, after a previous explanation of his meaning) speak of a first and second Trinity—though indeed Behmen has never done so; he calls only the will "first" and "second."
