<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jacob Behmen’s theology, focusing on the distinction between the Trinity as it exists "without" (prior to) nature and as it is manifested "in and after" nature, emphasizing that these are different perspectives on the same Divine Being.</meta>

as in and after nature; some of which have a relation to creatures, but the most important is that which concerns the Trinity as in and to itself.

<margin>Principles</margin>
The Trinity without nature cannot have any created representative, made after its own image and likeness. However, the Trinity considered as in and after nature can and does have such representatives in an innumerable number—even angels and men—all having (if they have not fallen away from it into disorder by their own fault) within themselves this eternal generation in seven, and so also the two eternal properties of fire and light in their most harmonious union, corresponding to that in which they stand in this eternal manifestation of the most holy Trinity. The deep ground and reason why the Trinity before nature cannot have any created representative of itself is shown to us sufficiently by Behmen. Again,

The Trinity without nature cannot be a proper and direct object of any created understanding, and can never be seen, felt, or enjoyed by either angels or men. Conversely, the Trinity in nature can be and is understood by them—seen in a manner, and even *felt and enjoyed* so that Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, in their distinct communications or influences, can be *discerned* by such souls and spirits as stand with them in a nearer and more intimate union. <note>N.B. you holy Rogers-Fletcher-Bramwell-praying souls on earth!</note> The reason for both of these can easily be given: for if the whole created being of angels and men is and must be inferior and posterior to this eternal generation of nature in its seven properties, all their understanding, feeling, and enjoyment must be strictly confined to it, so that it is impossible for them to reach beyond it.

And if all their created [or regenerated] being is of the same nature in which the Trinity is manifested—even of this eternal nature in its seven properties—they cannot help but understand, see, feel, and enjoy God in Trinity, after whose triune image they are made and of whose Divine nature they partake, even so that he is not ashamed to call them sons, children, gods, etc. <note>N.B. you holy ones! You *experimental theosophers!* You gospel ‘*enthusiasts*,’ as you are called, who have proved and ‘known the truth’ as it is in Jesus. Behold here the sure ground and philosophy of your spiritual discoveries, experiences, and joys!</note>

XXXV.—The greatest difference between the Trinity considered as before, and as in and after eternal nature, is this: that in the second consideration it can properly and directly be called a Trinity, because there is a plain and manifest distinction between the three. This is fittingly figured out and represented, even in outward nature also, by that distinction which is found there between fire, light, and air. And though we say with Behmen that three things are to be understood in this eternal generation without any nature, and again that God generates himself in Trinity—expressions in which a distinction is implied so that we cannot understand them at all without thinking more or less of some distinction between the three—yet we are to say also, according to his instruction, that all intelligible distinction in the Trinity depends upon a raising up of the first three properties of nature by the first abyssal will, which is the Father; further, upon the generating and passing through the fire; and then also upon manifesting the brightness of the Father’s glory in the light or Son. So then we are indeed permitted to conceive the three in the eternal generation with a distinction, because we cannot do otherwise; yet we are also charged to abstract our minds again from all this conceptualization and to deny all our affirmative ideas, according to what he plainly says in *Mysterium Magnum*, chapter vii. 11, 12.

Seeing that we are not able to understand any distinction before and without the distinct generation of eternal nature in its seven properties, etc.

XXXVII.—It is not so much our knowing that there are three without nature, but rather this perceptible distinction in nature which makes us call it a Trinity. For though the three without nature are naturally prior to the Trinity in nature, yet *as to our knowing*, we cannot but say that the Trinity in nature is prior to the three without nature. This is because our understanding arises after nature and goes not forward from what is unmanifest without to its manifestation in nature, but contrariwise from the latter to the former—to the extent that we are directed by what is manifest in nature to know that the same must have been unmanifest without nature. Because we now find in nature a plain, intelligible distinction between the three, we call it rightly and properly a Trinity. And because we further know from this that three also are and must be without nature, we take this denomination of a Trinity from nature and attribute it to that which is without nature also. Although we cannot do so properly, because as soon as we go beyond nature and what is manifest in nature, all distinction is lost and vanishes away out of our sight and perception.

XXXVIII.—A simple and crude analogy may perhaps explain the meaning of this a little more clearly. When we conceive of a small grain of a size just discernible to the eye, we

<column-break/>

what it is, nor have what it has, if the first were not. So also is it with the Tri-unity before nature and the distinct Trinity in and after nature.

V.—The first will cannot be abolished by the second so that it should no longer be what it is in itself, nor can it be transmuted into the second so that it is no longer its inmost ground. Rather, it is always found in our consideration as remaining in its central place without any alteration in itself. So also the Tri-unity is neither abolished nor transmuted by the Trinity in and after nature, but remains always its inmost, deepest ground and will be found so perpetually by angels and men in their searchings into the deep things of God.

VI.—In the second will, the first has nothing added to itself from without; all the difference between the first and second will lies in the fact that in the first everything is concentrated, and in the second everything is displayed out of that center. So also in this Tri-unity and Trinity: if anything came in from the outside, these two could not be one and the same. But since all rises out of the first all-sufficient ground and displays itself by its own all-sufficiency, the Trinity and Tri-unity are one and the same—though there is and must be this difference: the former is, as it were, a deeper center having its own circumference within itself, and the latter is a displaying of that center as in a spiritual circumference, having also its own center within itself.

VII.—Neither our distinct considerations of the will, nor our different denominations of "first" and "second," nor any difference that may be found between them can make two wills so that each of them could be separable from the other and exist only by itself, without or besides the other. So also, all that is said here concerning the Divine Being before and after nature cannot make Two Trinities.”

can visibly distinguish in it a superior, an inferior, and a middle part. But when we now suppose it is lessened and reduced to the quantity of an invisible and impalpable atom, we can perceive nothing more of a distinction; nevertheless, so long as we can conceive it to be an atom, we can also conceive that it still has the same three parts which before were visibly to be discerned. And this notion of its three parts is inseparable from our idea by which we conceive an atom, and must necessarily continue so, even if we should think of it being lessened even to infinity. But if we could suppose this atom were at length entirely spiritualized, and so thereby totally taken away from the number of all corporeal beings (which are all confined to their dimensions, however small), then only would all the distinction in our idea be totally lost together with the name of atom; and nevertheless, there would remain in us the notion of a certain spiritual something, which we could no longer conceive with any distinction.

XXXIX.—In the same way, in a tree, when we see three branches, we see them in a plain and manifest distinction. But when we go back first to the trunk, considering that they lay within it before they came forth out of it, all the manifest distinction has disappeared; and nevertheless, from their being manifestly three, we can justly conclude there were three also in the trunk, because there must necessarily have been a threefold disposition toward them. As long as this disposition is, or can be conceived as, threefold, it cannot be conceived without any kind of distinction, though no distinction is or can be obvious to any of our outward senses. But when we go deeper now, to a consideration of the very seed out of which all this tree with all its branches came forth, we can be said in a sense and manner to go beyond the generation of nature; because in this seed, the actual strife of the first three properties of nature must be conceived as not yet raised up, and so this seed lies in a state of stillness, rest, and nothingness with respect to what afterwards is brought forth out of it. There the distinction may be said to be lost totally; for what distinction can we possibly imagine when we must conceive that the three first properties of nature themselves—which are by their actual strife the beginning of all growth in every tree—have not yet entered into their distinction? But nevertheless, again, from our having observed three branches in the outward manifestation, we cannot but conclude three also must have been in the first original center of this manifestation, which center we may justly think had in its own sphere no sufficiency for more and no disposition for less than three. And thus, so long as we think of or speak of three, not all distinction in every sense can be excluded from our idea, notwithstanding that we are not able to find out or to perceive a distinction in the thing itself.

This now may show us, however obscurely, that it is no contradiction when we say on one hand that the three in the Divine Eternal Being, without nature, are distinguished, and when we say again on the other hand that they are not distinguished. For we say the former with respect to our apprehension, in which we cannot separate every distinction from an idea of "three"; and we say the latter with respect to such a distinction as may properly be called so according to our common sense and manner of expression, in which every distinction is and must be posterior to the generation of eternal nature with its seven properties.

XL.—A hand or foot of a child in the womb, says Behmen, grows forward from within, and before it has any visible figure, it already has its own proper form or signature in the spirit. If then this is so, as it certainly cannot be otherwise, we must of necessity conceive that the spiritual signature of the one cannot be that of the other, but must be in a manner so distinct from it as a full-grown hand is from a foot—and this even long before it can properly be called a hand or foot, and before any distinction between them can appear. And he, therefore, who was able, as Behmen was, to declare this wonderful generation and formation in the womb <note>N.B.</note> from the first beginning in the Spirit to the manifest and visible outbirth of it, would find himself necessitated not only to take the names of the parts or members (for instance, those of hands and feet) from the visible outbirth and to give them to that which is but an invisible disposition toward them in the spirit, but also to tell us sometimes that these members (hands or feet) are distinguished even in this spiritual disposition, and sometimes, again, that they are not distinguished before their distinct figure and formation in fingers and toes can appear.

And by saying so, such a declarer would not contradict himself at all. For they are not distinguished with respect to our sight, and yet they are distinct and must be conceived as distinct; because when they can be called hands and feet upon any account, we are not able to conceive them without any distinction—especially when we know that each of them already has in the spirit, before it comes to the outbirth, its own proper form or peculiar signature. This constrains us to apprehend and own that the signature of a hand cannot be that of a foot, even though as yet neither this nor that can properly be called so.

Therefore, we are to conceive every distinction as being, as it were, in different degrees of increase and decrease; for in the first stirring of the properties of nature, every distinction takes its beginning, and from there it goes forward, increasing gradually, until at length in the outbirth it becomes manifest and plainly discernible. But in our sight and apprehension, going backward from the outbirth to the first root in the spirit, every distinction decreases more and more, until at length it is totally lost. This occurs as soon as we venture to go beyond the generation of nature in its distinct properties.

This, then, was the case with Behmen when he declared the Trinity, considered both as without and as in eternal Nature. And accordingly, he has not contradicted himself when he not only gave us three distinct names of Father, Son, and Spirit in the Trinity without nature, but also told us expressly that we are to understand three things in this eternal generation—and yet tells us again, in outward appearance, quite the contrary, as in *Mysterium Magnum*, chapter vii. 11, 12.

XLI.—The conclusion of this matter will now be this: that we are to conceive the first disposition in the spirit to be, as it were, a hidden, invisible, and imperceptible root of that manifest distinction which can be perceived in an outbirth; and this manifest distinction as being, as it were, the fruit or product of that root. And we say, concerning this twofold consideration of the Trinity: (1) The Trinity considered as in nature differs chiefly from the Trinity without nature in this: that the Trinity in this eternal manifestation is manifestly and, to creatures, intelligibly distinguished, whereas contrariwise all the creatures are not able to find out or understand a distinction in the eternal generation without nature. (2) Just as the first stirring in the properties of nature, which makes a distinction intelligible to creatures, is to be conceived as an invisible root of that visible distinction in its following outbirth (which is a fruit or product), so the three in the eternal generation without

And therefore, (3.) the three in the eternal generation without nature are distinguished by such a distinction as is perceptible and intelligible by and to themselves, but absolutely imperceptible and unintelligible to creatures.

(4.) A distinction, or root of distinction, must exist in these three in the eternal generation, because the first is not the second, the second is not the third, and the third is neither the first nor second. (5.) This distinction must be perceptible to themselves, because the second of these three is an eternal perceiving, finding, and enjoying of the first, caused by the intervention of the third, which is a moving life of both the first and second; and because the Divine Intellect, or Wisdom—which belongs not only to the Father, but also to the Son—exerted and manifested in this eternal generation by the proceeding forth of the Spirit, cannot but imply an eternal understanding of what it is for the first to find, perceive, and enjoy himself in the second, by that moving life which is the third. And if so, this can be nothing other than an intellect touched and affected by, or an eternal understanding of, this distinction. (6.) But this distinction, or rather this root of distinction, must be absolutely imperceptible and unintelligible to all created spirits; because it exists before, without, and above that distinct manifestation of these three made in and by the properties of eternal nature, wherein they live and move; from which they originate and have all that they can be said to have and be; and to which, therefore, all their perception and understanding must be strictly confined, as to a sphere of their activity. So that there cannot be conceived in them any ability, proportion, or capacity for perceiving and understanding that which is beyond this sphere, and which can extend no further than to that eternal manifestation of these three which is made—and could not be made otherwise—by a distinct generation of nature in its seven properties, rightly called the *Seven Fountain Spirits*, with respect to all subsequent created things that have flowed forth, descended, or been breathed out from them.

### XLII.—Whether this eternal manifestation in and by the seven properties of nature is to be regarded as purely voluntary or as absolutely necessary cannot be positively defined from the plain, express words of *Teutonicus* <note>Jacob Boehme</note>. But many things may be observed from his writings by which it can be clear that it is more consistent with his meaning, and much more conformable to the whole construction or coherence of the eternal generation in three with the eternal manifestation thereof in seven, to declare for the latter rather than the former.

### XLIII.—All that can be brought forward to support the idea that this eternal manifestation of the three in seven is purely voluntary will, I think, be summarized as follows:

That the Divine Tri-une Being, in the eternal generation without nature, exists in a fully accomplished perfection, is all-sufficient for, in, and to itself, enjoys itself in a fullness of love and delight, rest and self-satisfaction, and lacks nothing to be added to it which could increase its ever-blessed happiness, etc.

And from this it is now inferred that if this is so, no necessity can be imagined for a more exterior manifestation of the three in seven; but this manifestation must be regarded as purely voluntary, so that it is wholly and only referred to his good will and pleasure. And if he had not been pleased to condescend to it, he would still have lacked nothing, just as nothing is added to him by it.

**Answer.** What is said here against a necessity of the eternal manifestation of the three in seven could almost be argued against a necessity of the eternal generation in the three itself, by saying: The Father is all, and has all in himself, for the Son has no more than what the Father has. And that which is and has all cannot but be satisfied with its own fullness, etc. What necessity, therefore, is there for this Father generating a Son? But just as this reasoning is not valid here, *so it is not valid there*.

### XLIV.—From what was said above concerning an exaltation of the Divine Triune Being, and such a manifestation as is made only by and to itself, as also of its being still only central, not manifest to itself, not unfolded, etc., it is clear that such an idea of the Divine Being without nature as is expressed in this objection by the words "full and accomplished perfection" and "enjoyment of love, delight, and self-satisfaction," etc., is entirely inconsistent with Boehme's principles. For though we do not deny that all Divine perfections are in the Triune Being without nature, yet we say that in this first consideration of God—which is *not total, but only partial*—they are not yet exerted, and cannot become exerted except by the rising up and passing through the properties of nature.

And though, therefore, we rightly say, in one sense, that the Tri-une God without nature lacks nothing, but has all and is all-sufficient in and to himself, so that nothing can be given or added to him which could make him more perfect; yet without contradicting this, we may rightly say also in another sense that the Tri-une God, considered as without nature, lacks something which he does not have in this first consideration. For he lacks a fit and proper medium or subject wherein his all-sufficient perfections may exert, display, and show themselves, so that thereby he may come to *perceive* himself—namely, to perceive what he is in that state wherein they are actually exerted—which medium is the generation of the properties of nature.

And this expression, though gross and rude enough, can give no more offense to any person of sense than this: "The Father, considered as Father only, though he is and has all in himself, does not yet stand in a fully accomplished perfection; for he has no brightness of glory, and therefore lacks a son, or express image of his substance, so that he may thereby come to know and *perceive* himself—namely, what he is in that state wherein the brightness of his glory is actually generated, displayed, and manifested to him." This expression is, in itself, entirely innocent and true enough.

### XLV.—It is clear and evident in itself that by necessity, we do not mean that there is this or that coming upon the eternal will from the outside and binding it down, so that this will were to be conceived first as indifferent, then as moved and drawn, and at length led away from its former indifference. But there is no such thing here.

The eternal will, which is closest to the abyssal eye, and is even that abyssal eye itself, considered in its first disposition toward a progress or proceeding forth, cannot be considered first as standing indifferent between YES and NO, and then as moved and drawn to the YES, by some-

Something coming in from the outside, or from elsewhere, and representing its motives to that eye, or will, thereby causing first a consideration, or deliberation, and then a consent, which the will must now descend to, lying, as it were, powerless under a necessity and not altogether free from weakness, etc. Away with all such and similar thoughts!

In the first central Abyssal Being itself—not outside of it, that is, in that eternal Eye and Will itself, or in its own internal, inseparable essentiality—that thing must be implied which we call a necessity. And if so, it is plain that as this eye or will is most internal and essential to the Divine Being, so also must be that which we call a necessity. Therefore, it cannot but be conceived as being in a most harmonious union and concord with the will; or rather, as the will itself, considered in this necessity, as a peculiar and eminent perfection.

For just as there is an absolute necessity, implying the highest perfection, that God must be a living God—knowing, feeling, and enjoying himself, so that the will does not stand indifferent and requires no prior consultation on whether or not he shall be a living God—so also is there such an absolute necessity, full of perfections and necessarily implied in the Divine essentiality, that the Divine Triune Being must go forth to the generation of eternal Nature. By this, his omnipotent life and power may be unfolded, displayed, and manifested, wherein his infinite perfections may be exerted and exalted through the fire in the light of glory.

### XLVI.
If we but consider the first abyssal will and its first stirring, wherein the eternal generation and manifestation are inseparably connected, and from which both go together—one toward the inside and the other toward the outside—according to what Teutonicus declares of it in many places, and especially in the *Earthly and Heavenly Mysterium*, we shall find clearly enough such an absolute necessity as mentioned, though he himself has never expressed it so.

For the Will intends a manifestation of its own central and radical all-sufficiency, which manifestation is nothing other than an unfolding of his infinite perfections and an exaltation of them, from their being all concentrated as one, as it were, into a glorious circumference, wherein they may appear and work in their distinction. Now, this will can do nothing toward its purpose without a stirring, which is self-evident. And if then this very stirring—inasmuch as it is, in a sense and manner, more exterior than the still and resting will in itself—is nothing other than a beginning of raising up the properties of nature, we cannot conceive it otherwise, nor can we perhaps express it better, than by saying:

There is for the generation of eternal Nature such an absolute internal necessity as does not come upon the will from the outside, or from anything besides itself, but lies in the will and is so near and so essential to the will, so harmoniously united with the will, and therefore also so inseparable from the will, as this will is near and essential to, united with, and inseparable from itself, from which it comes. Seeing that if we conceive that this will intends its manifestation, we must also necessarily conceive that it cannot obtain it without a stirring, but also that this same stirring is the beginning of raising up that fire which previously lay hidden in the will and was not burning; indeed, that this stirring is made for that purpose. And if we must conceive it so, it must necessarily be by that self-same intent, as by that fire, in order to be manifested by it, one single act both to stir and also by this stirring to raise up that fire, to be manifested by it and to be exalted through it into the light of glory. Therefore, none of these three can be considered superfluous, but all three must be acknowledged to stand in an equal degree of necessity, if the will is supposed to intend its own manifestation, the necessity of which cannot be questioned.

### XLVII.
Another argument for such a necessity could be brought forth from a consideration of the Divine Goodness and its communicability. For, as the eternal Will in his infinite wisdom knows himself to be good, so he also knows, and cannot but know, this goodness to be communicable, outflowing, and giving of itself. And as it is not indifferent to the will whether he is good or not, but is his intrinsic essentiality that he must be the supreme good, so it also cannot be thought to be indifferent to him whether or not his goodness shall flow out and communicate itself. But as these two—to be good and to be communicable, or willing to communicate himself—are inseparable from the will and both have an equal ground in the Divine Being, so also a necessity for them must be equal in them both. Yet, just as there is nothing besides him which might make or cause him to be good, so also is there nothing besides which might cause him to communicate his goodness; but this goodness itself, on its own account and from its own internal nature or moving principle, flows out and cannot but flow out without denying or forsaking its own nature and name. And therein lies the necessity of the generation of eternal nature. For 

God; yet it necessarily presupposes the seven distinct properties of eternal nature, without which no creature could have existed, and so also nothing of the divine goodness could have been communicated.

### XLVIII.
Almost the same, but regarding several particulars with a greater emphasis and evidence, could be said concerning the Divine Omnipotence. We cannot properly say, in the first consideration, without all nature, that God is omnipotent; for there is not only nothing in which his omnipotence could appear to himself, but there is also nothing in which or by which he might feel and perceive himself to be omnipotent. Yet this saying does not bring upon him any weakness, impotence, or imperfection; for we do not say that it is eternal nature which makes him omnipotent, but that he himself raises up the properties of eternal nature to afford to himself thereby that necessarily requisite subject wherein and whereby his radical omnipotence may be exerted and made perceptible to himself. And further, we say that it is the generation of the fourth property of nature, or the kindling of the fire—dwelling in it in one respect and passing through it in another—wherein and whereby he can and does perceive himself to be actually and effectively omnipotent, which he cannot do without this generation. Why then, without this generation, we rightly say: He has the ground and root of omnipotence in and purely of himself, but without a manifestation of it, and without feeling and perceiving what this root is in its manifestation.

And so we cannot so properly say he is omnipotent without all nature, but more properly we say he is all-sufficient to show forth his omnipotence in the generation of nature. Which all-suffi-

If we then cannot think it is indifferent to the eternal will whether or not he is actually exerting, feeling, and perceiving himself as an omnipotent God, but if we must conceive a necessity for the affirmative, we must also say: there is implied in the first Abyssal Will such an *absolute necessity*, as declared, for the *generation of eternal nature* in its seven properties.

All the Divine attributes would likewise furnish us with further proofs of this necessity, especially those that have more or less a relation to creatures; and that never could have been manifested or exerted if intellectual creatures had not been created by the Father, redeemed by the Son, and fitted by the Holy Spirit for a communion with the Father and Son.

Moreover, many expressions might be found in the Holy Scriptures which would afford such arguments. As for instance, a threefold, very significant one might be formed from the words of St. John in the *Revelation* concerning the seven spirits, which are, as he says (1) before the throne of God, from which (2) he wishes grace and peace to the churches, and which (3) he places in the middle between the Father and Son, wishing grace and peace, first from him who is, and was, and is to come; in the next place from the seven spirits; and then in the third from Jesus Christ.

But since I think it is demonstrated sufficiently enough that such a necessity lies in the very deepest root, even in the first Abyssal Will itself, it is needless to gather arguments from this and that, which are all but posterior to that abyssal root.

**XLIX.**—Just as in the first consideration of the Divine Being without nature, Wisdom was considered immediately after the Trinity, where it was represented as a mirror full of wonders and in distinction from the Spirit; so it is here also in this second consideration of God, manifested in nature, to be considered after and under the Holy Trinity. Indeed, it is even more proper here than there, because not only was it not yet a proper object of human understanding there, but also because all the names which Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), the German mystic frequently referenced in this text.</note> gives to wisdom in the first consideration (without nature)—when he calls her an *eternal Virgin*, a *mirror full of wonders*, the Spirit's *corporeality, clothing, habitation, instrument*, etc.—are all taken from this second consideration, wherein they are significant and intelligible to creatures. Nevertheless, with respect to them, they are not so in that first consideration, but are used there as well only for want of more convenient terms, and to declare thereby that wisdom in the first consideration is not another thing, but the same thing it is in the second; though it stands now in another, more external and more intelligible condition, state, and degree, wherein it can be a proper object of our understanding, just like the Trinity itself.

And moreover, all that was said before concerning a distinction between the outgoing and that which has gone out, or between the Spirit and wisdom, was to be understood only according to what was declared concerning a distinction between the Three in the eternal generation without nature. But here now, in this second consideration, the distinction is plain enough and can be understood by intellectual creatures.

For there it must have been unintelligible and beyond all their finding out, because it was outside that sphere wherein they live and move and have their being.

But here it must also be intelligible, obvious, and familiar to them, because it is not only within their sphere but also so nearly related to them that they are endowed themselves with it and are expressly called the *children of wisdom*.

**L.**—This distinction between the Spirit and wisdom, or according to Behmen's expression, between the outgoing and that which has gone out, is the chief point in this consideration. And seeing that Behmen himself, in a few words, has pointed as if with his finger to a certain simile, I shall explain it in its particulars. This will sufficiently show that Behmen is absolutely guiltless of the crime many charged him with: that he created a *Quaternity* in the Divine Being.

A wise and powerful king sees in his wisdom, considers with himself, and without any advice from his counselors, ponders in his own mind such things as he knows can promote his own honor and glory and the prosperity of his kingdom. Now, as long as this is only a seeing, contemplating, and pondering in his own mind, it is what it is only in and to himself; but it is nothing at all to his counselors and of no effect in his government; for it is still, in a sense and manner, separated, as it were, from his royal power and authority, which cannot yet exercise or show itself therein, nor do any good thereby to any other, etc.

And this may represent to us the Divine Wisdom, taken in its first and deepest sense, wherein it is Divine intellect compared to a seeing Eye, and not distinct from God, but God himself.

This king, having thus seen and found out in his wisdom how to promote and exalt his glory and the good of his kingdom, further settles himself into a will or resolution to put out a proclamation and to declare his will thereby.

Now this will is indeed the first step toward the declaration of those things that were seen in his wisdom and found expedient and necessary. But as long as it is only a will, prior to a real act and deed, it is still but nothing and of no benefit to all that is outside and subsequent to it—all of which nevertheless depends upon it as upon its original. And this will may be looked upon as a representation of the eternal Father.

When, now further, this will actually goes forth by putting out this intended declaration of itself, we may plainly discern therein three things more, as so many distinct figures of the Son, the Spirit, and that which Behmen calls wisdom in a second, inferior, and more external sense.

The declaration of this royal will, considered as to its sense and substance, which is not visible but intelligible to his subjects, and in itself is nothing else but an express image and manifestation of what the will had first conceived, approved of, and disposed itself to—indeed, strictly such a manifestation as has neither more nor less in it than that very same thing—is a fit representation of the Eternal Son. He has an eternal beginning in the will, as in the Father, of which he is an express image and manifestation, having all that which the Father has, and neither more nor less.

The actual putting out of this declaration, which is an active moving and proceeding forth of this royal will to its manifestation, is distinct both from the will itself and from the declaration of the will also; and yet it is inseparable from the one as well as from the other, because it is

The declaration of this royal will—considered as it is also visible and more external, or as a thing which can be passively said to have gone out from the royal will, being a writing signed by the king's hand and sealed with his seal—is a representation of the eternal wisdom. This is taken in the second, more external sense, wherein it is compared to a mirror, and is not God himself, but proceeds from and under him; just as this writing is also distinct from and under the king, and distinct also from his will and from its declaration, when considered in its invisible sense and substance.

Just as this writing is purely passive, having no life, motion, power, operation, or efficacy, and doing neither good nor evil of itself or by its own ability, so also is wisdom in this latter sense.

But just as the king's will, power, and royal authority—declared in its outgoing, or in the issuing of this declaration—is the only life, activity, and power within it, for which it is honored, esteemed, and justly called royal, and by which it is able and sufficient to do good for the kingdom; seeing that the king's will and royal authority owns it as its own product, is joined with it, operates in it, and in a way quickens it and keeps it alive by maintaining it and executing the ordinances contained in it, etc.—so also the Spirit of God is and acts in and with this wisdom. This wisdom, here most properly in its distinction from the Spirit, is compared to a mirror full of wonders.

Besides this distinction between going out and that which has gone out, or between the Spirit who is God and wisdom which is under God, there is yet another distinction to be noticed: between *this* Wisdom and wisdom itself, or rather (which is more proper according to the expressions of Boehme <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), referred to as "Behmen" in the original text.</note>, who gives the name of wisdom only to what is in the holy Light World) between this mirror and the Mirror.

For as the Spirit itself is now considered in two ways, according to the Two Eternal Principles, and in correspondence to that distinction which is now intelligible between the Father and the Son, so also is this mirror. And as the Spirit is in each of these two eternal worlds according to the property of each, so is this Mirror also in each according to its condition, representing only that which belongs to that part of eternal nature, and having no ability to admit anything that belongs to or pertains to the other part. <note>Note well.</note>

For in the very nature of a Principle, if taken in Boehme’s sense, it is most necessarily and absolutely implied that it has its own dominion in, by, and for itself, according to its own natural constitution, and that it cannot be concerned with anything that is outside its own sphere.

And by this, that great objection raised against Teutonicus—when he had written that *God did not know beforehand the fall of Lucifer*—is sufficiently answered, as may be seen from his own words in the *Aurora* and in his *Apology against Balthasar Tilken*.

The Fourth Extract, selected for insertion on the present occasion, consists of "GENERAL POSITIONS CONCERNING THE DIVINE BEING in UNITY and TRINITY, and ESPECIALLY the GENERATION of ETERNAL NATURE, gathered from our FORMER WRITINGS, according to the MIND of TEUTONICUS; and all taken either IMMEDIATELY FROM his own plain, UNQUESTIONABLE WORDS, or by means of an EVIDENT CONSEQUENCE flowing forth FREELY OUT OF THEM," as follows:

The first and deepest concept the human mind can have of the Divine Being, according to the Scripture, is justly said to be that of Unity: because in our going back from the multiplicity of things to inquire after their origins, we must necessarily stop and rest in the unity, without proceeding any further.

This concept of the unity does not imply that, at any imaginable moment of eternity, the Unity existed so alone by itself, without or before the Trinity; but only that our weak and finite understanding cannot help but apprehend it that way and speak of it so separately. For if the generation of the eternal Word was and is from all eternity, without beginning (which Boehme expressly asserts along with the Scripture), the unity never was without or before the trinity, yet it must be conceived of as being before, for natural reasons.

This Unity—belonging not to the number and order of divided, out-flowed, and multiplied things, but being infinitely deeper than all things and all our possible ideas of them, and having as yet no relation to them—is to be conceived of much rather as we conceive of that negative origin preceding all numbers (expressed in arithmetic by a 0) than as we do of the first positive number 1. And therefore, it is chiefly for this reason that Boehme usually calls this unity an "eternal nothing." <margin>Predestination, i. *Theosophical Questions* i.</margin>

In the concept of this unity, still considered in itself alone, it is necessarily implied that it is without and before all manifestation: still, immovable, quiet, silent, hidden, and dwelling in itself. It is, therefore, well enough expressed by "still eternity," and by Boehme's "temperature" (the first), "abyss," and "eternal liberty"; this latter expression denotes for him a freedom from, and a priority to, all the properties of Nature. For everything that in our concept implies anything of moving, speaking, breathing, etc., implies a receding from the true concept of this unity, and represents more or less implicitly a trinity instead.

All this again does not imply that at any imaginary moment of eternity there has been such a state of rest and silence (which is expressly contradicted by Boehme), but only that our understanding, in its gradual process backwards and inquiry after the deepest original of things, cannot help but apprehend it so. For if by "nature" we understand with Boehme in general a moving, stirring life, and ask thereupon what is outside or before it, we must necessarily answer: a rest and stillness; otherwise, we would be saying there is a moving and stirring without and before motion or mobility.

All that was said until now was in consideration of the Unity as only and strictly in and for itself. But now, regarding this same Unity, Abyss, Nothing, or eternal Liberty, considered with some respect to or in order to eternal nature, Boehme says it *has a Will* and *is a Will*. Both are right, and neither is inconsistent with the other (*God is what he has* <note>Latin: *Deus est quod habet*.</note>), if we only look upon the former as more suited to our manner of understanding and speech, and upon this...

Considering this, we may find Behmen sufficiently reconciled with himself when he says in one place, *God dwells in himself*, and in another, *he dwells in an abyss*, and in a third, *the abyssal nothing is a dwelling-place of the divine Unity*, because here, before and without nature, there is no difference between the abyss and the will, or the dwelling-place and its inhabitant.

This abyssal Will is not yet considered here as in its act, or as a perceptible will, but as in its root. Otherwise, Behmen could not call it abyssal and could not have said *that in this will, nature lies as a hidden fire, which is and is not.* Since in the will, considered in its act, nature no longer lies as a hidden fire, but rather as a fire now manifesting out of the abyss by the generation of gradual properties.

This abyssal Will is now further considered by Behmen as Father, both of the eternal Word in the eternal generation within, and of eternal Nature also in the co-eternal manifestation without.

* The following “Questions” with their answers more directly belong to a subsequent page, but for convenience, we insert the note containing them in this place:—

“ **Question I.**—What goes out of the abyss into the Trinity that is distinct from what goes out of the same into nature? **Answer.** An incommunicable and incomprehensible delight within himself only is in the Trinity. But stirring communicable properties, displaying themselves as a more exterior thing in a perceptible variety, are in Nature. Both the former and the latter are out of the abyss, and one is clearly distinguished from the other. He who sits upon the throne is certainly distinguished from what is before the throne, and both are distinct from the throne itself; this throne (in this consideration) may be the abyss.

— **II.**—Do only incommunicable properties go out into the Trinity, or communicable ones also? **Answer.** I can find no other distinction than what relates to an incommunicability in the first and a communicability in the second; yet it is not as if there were nothing at all, in the strictest sense, communicable in the first, and nothing at all incommunicable in the second. It is only that everything conceived of as communicable in the first is in some sense to be conceived as lessened in degree when it *is communicated* to the second, and progressively more so when communicated to other inferior things.

So that this same thing, which is communicable in the first in a lower sense to the second, is nevertheless incommunicable in a higher sense, because it cannot be communicated to the second in that fullness, extent, or totality of meaning in which it exists in the first alone.

If everything in the first were incommunicable in the strictest sense, and everything in the second were communicable, there would be a total separation between the first and second and no coherence at all. But if it is as has been said, then a connection between them is preserved, and the first nevertheless always retains its due prerogative (which is absolutely incommunicable) above the second. For instance, one may consider in the first that great I AM, which is communicable to the second—namely, to nature—and further still (though with a great alteration of meaning and degree) to angels and to men. And in the second, which in one sense is entirely communicable, there is nevertheless still something of an absolute incommunicability—namely, this: *I am a total or universal basis of all created things.*

This is clearly incommunicable to any creature, though all the properties of nature, both principal and subordinate, are communicable to all in a lower and more exterior sense and degree.

— **III.**—If a creature has the whole natural God in it, does this not make the creature equal to God? **Answer.** No creature, from the lowest to the highest, has the whole natural God in it. For the whole natural God, or God in Nature, is the universal basis of all creatures.

This is His unalterable prerogative; it would imply a clear contradiction if we were to say the creature has or can have this in itself.

The creature indeed has, in a sense, the whole of nature within it—that is, all its properties in their endless variety—but only in these ways: (1) not all those properties are equally manifest in it; and (2) only as in a lower sphere of created being, and not at all in that higher sphere where nature was a whole nature (and remains so in itself) before any creature existed.

Here, therefore, there is no more an equality than there can be between a greater and lesser, or higher and lower circle, conceived in such a way that the lesser and lower is subordinated to and depends upon the greater and higher.

— **IV.**—Can any creature say that it is a part of the natural God? **Answer.** No. Behmen, frequently combining these two expressions, *the natural and creatural God*, directs us to observe that continual distinction of degrees just now briefly mentioned and declared by him in several places.

The *natural God* is God as manifested in and by eternal nature, which He was before any creature existed. And the *creatural God* is indeed the same natural God, yet now no longer considered in that former sense and degree, but in a lower one—namely, as manifested again in a lower and exterior sphere of created beings. In this sphere, all creatures taken collectively are the whole manifestation of the natural God, or the whole creatural God, or all the invisible things of God made visible; just as the whole of outward nature is a complete manifestation of eternal nature, and eternal nature is a manifestation of the unmanifested and unnatural God. <insert>[N.B. *the sense and relations of every word in this paragraph.*]</insert>

Take away all creatures, and there will remain God in nature, or the natural God; but take away all nature and creature, and there will remain God in Himself only. No creature, therefore, can say that it is a part of the natural God, but it may say (in Behmen’s expression) that it is a part of the creatural God; for by this it says no more than that it is a part of the creation, or the manifestation of God through the creation. It also acknowledges thereby that God is always a whole, total, or universal root or basis of all the creatures. <insert>[by the Wisdom and desire of the magia-Will.]</insert>

All this, I think, may well be illustrated by a simile taken from those lesser and greater circles made by a stone cast into still, standing water. In this, the outermost is always most remote from the center and depends upon the one next to it, by which it is also made, but

cannot go out, and so forth. But this will, still considered here as abyssal, can do so because there is not yet a distinct determination implied in its notion, neither toward this side nor that. And if a root, in its gross manner and way, can spread itself forth at once—and by one motion—both to the right hand and to the left, why not much more eminently so for this most universal root of all divided things?

The so-called eternal generation and co-eternal manifestation, according to Behmen, are as it were two collateral branches out of one and the same root. Although, therefore, we cannot say the *same actual will that goes out also goes in* (which Behmen never said), yet we can say with him that the *same abyssal will goes both out and in at once, and displays itself in these two branches*, of which it is the common root, having no distinction within it as long as it is abyssal. Nor can we conceive in it any determination toward this or that, according to Behmen's plain words, saying: *It is without all properties, and has no inclination toward this or that, for it has nothing before, behind, nor besides itself to which it could be inclined.* The two places of Behmen quoted above will justify this answer in almost all their expressions, convincing us that if we conceive of any inclination or determination in this abyssal will, we no longer conceive of a unity, but a duplicity; no longer a temperature, but a distinction and inequality; no longer an unsearchable nothing, but two conceivable somethings—the one inclining and the other being inclined toward; no longer an eternal liberty, but a being tied to this in opposition to that; no longer an abyss where there is no searching or finding, etc., but a byss, having already found something which it tends toward and unites with in its will.

Now further: Behmen says that out of this abyssal Will, by its moving and flowing out, everything comes forth—both in the internal generation in the trinity and in the co-eternal manifestation in nature.

As to the former, no objection is made, for therein God is generated out of God according to the Scripture. But concerning the latter, a question is first raised, and from this, a great objection.

It is asked: Is eternal Nature out of the abyssal will, so that this abyssal will is the (*quasi*) *material cause* of it? Or is it only brought forth out of nothing by an omnipotent power of this will, commanding it to be so? <note>See Note, p. 291, 2.</note>

The answer must be *affirmative* for the former and *negative* for the latter, according to Behmen. However, it must be observed that according to Behmen's foundation and the whole construction of his writings, the concept of a *material cause*—however refined by the addition of *quasi*—is much more impertinent here than an ell would be to measure the height of the wind.

He expressly calls this Abyssal Will a *father of nature*; not a *former*, nor *maker*, nor even *creator*, but a father—a name in which his having generated it or brought it forth out of himself is absolutely implied. But,

The reasons why an *out of nothing* is entirely inconsistent with Behmen's foundation, and an *out of himself* is expressly asserted, may be the following:

(1.) The Abyssal Will, as it is considered here in this beginning of the gradual generation of nature, has no power to command that anything should come forth out of nothing. And though all power is concentrated therein, there is not yet any ability to exert any power; rather, this first out-flowing into desire, and further into the other properties of nature, is made for this very purpose: so that the powers might be exerted, displayed, and brought forth into activity. This is not done before the generation of the fire. And though there is neither a *before* nor *after* in the Divine Being, it might be so in our distinct apprehension. Therefore, Behmen properly places Divine omnipotence in the *fire*, not before it. If we place such an omnipotent commanding power in the first Abyssal Will, we do not understand him and fall into confusion.

(2) The first step of the Abyssal Will out of its abyss into nature is a *desire*. Nothing can be closer to the will than its own raising of itself to take in that which it wills. And this raising—or as Behmen styles it, this sharpening of itself—is called "desire" by him in this beginning part of nature. Who can now say, with any sense, that a desire is brought forth out of nothing by the will's omnipotent command and is thus joined to that will from without? Must we not say that the stirring desire flows out of the still and resting will? That is, it is a desire of that will which intends to manifest itself thereby. And the will itself brings itself forth into desire. For truly the will conceives a desire in itself in one respect and sends it forth out of itself in another, as an external offspring.

(3.) This generation (in its full perfection) is the Divine nature—even that which we shall be made partakers of again in our regeneration, according to Scripture. It is the manifestation of God in his powers and wonders [<term>Ternarius Sanctus</term>]. And what shall hinder us from saying, in one particular sense, that it is God himself (though we rightly say again in another that it is not God, but his manifestation, instrument, etc., of which seeming contradiction we shall speak hereafter), seeing that the Scripture expressly says, *our God is a consuming fire*.

So that none of these circles has the principle or power of making itself a circle, but all depend entirely upon that central point where the first motion was made.

V.—May the creature be worshipped because of its having the whole nature, or natural God, within it? Answer: No creature, as was just said, has within it either the whole nature or the whole creatural God, but is only a part or *particular* of the latter. And its having the whole nature within it in the sense mentioned above contributes nothing toward worship, but is rather directly against it.

Moreover, our worship implies the deepest humiliation of ourselves, with an explicit acknowledgment that the very same thing we worship is that universal ground in which we all live and move and have our being. Since no creature can be this, no creature can be worshipped. In a low and partial sense, we are from our parents; therefore, we are especially commanded to honor them. And this honor runs parallel, in its lower sphere, with that worship in the higher sphere, which therefore can be due to nothing but that which was before the creation, and which would be what it is even if all the creatures were taken away.

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the nature of the Abyssal Will and the origin of eternal nature, specifically addressing how all things—including angels and men—are generated out of God's own being rather than created from an external "nothing."</meta>

Now then, the Divine nature, or that which the Scripture calls *our God*, is not brought forth out of nothing by a commanding, omnipotent power of another God who lives before and without nature.

(4.) This generation of eternal nature is not to be conceived as arbitrary, but as necessary; therefore, it cannot be out of such a "nothing" that is outside of or different from the first Abyssal Will. Instead, it is out of that Nothing which is not only nothing in one respect, but also a universal All in another. This Nothing will not maintain only its former name and being, but must necessarily manifest and display itself in multiplicity and variety to show forth its own abyssal Allness.

(5.) Regarding created and visible things, the Scripture nowhere says that they were brought forth out of nothing, but rather that the *invisible things of God were made visible*. If we, along with the Scripture, are to call them His invisible things, we are not to conceive of them as nothing, though they were nothing to themselves before they became visible. And if this is right and true concerning the lower things of this world, how much more—and in what a higher degree of truth and regularity—must it also be right and true concerning these invisible things themselves, namely, the properties of eternal nature?

Therefore, when we conceive of them (with Behmen) as having lain in the first Abyssal Will like a hidden fire—which was and was not—they are not to be conceived of as nothing, nor as having lain in nothing. Rather, they must be called, as he calls them, His *imperceptible things*, and said to be made perceptible in and by this outflowing eternal generation.

(6.) Angels and men are the children and offspring of God (according to Scripture) and partakers of the Divine nature, bearing His name written upon them. They have that life and light in them which was in the eternal Word, which Word was in and with God, and was God. They have a natural kind of omnipotence in them, for to faith nothing is impossible, etc. Of man especially, the Scripture says that he became a living soul (not by God saying *fiat* <note>Latin: "let it be done"</note> out of nothing, but) by His breathing (out of His own mouth) the breath of life into him; that we must be born again from above and out of God; that His seed remains in us; that He is not only our creator with respect to the body, but also our *father* with respect to the soul and spirit; and that Christ, the only begotten Son in whom the Father is well pleased, called us His brothers, etc.

Let all these things, and many more like them, now be duly pondered, and then the conclusion must be this: that angels and men are generated out of God and not brought forth out of a "nothing" by God’s commanding will. And if so, they must necessarily be so many *living witnesses* that this eternal nature, with all its properties, is also out of God (considered here as the first Abyssal Will); and this is because they have in themselves nothing else but what is and was before them in eternal nature.

At this point, two objections are raised: one taken from the notion of a *material cause*, and the other from an apprehension of darkness being in God, <margin>*</margin> * which is said to be directly

<margin>*</margin> * Concerning darkness in God. Behmen speaks much of an eternal darkness in the first property of nature. It is objected that this darkness must be in God because it is supposed to be in His desire, which is directly contrary to the Scripture, which says expressly, *God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all. 1 John 1:5.*

To this objection, I must answer distinctly with reference to the four particular words of this position: (1) darkness, (2) is or is not, (3) in, (4) God. For each of them will show us that Behmen, by his concept of eternal darkness in the first property of nature, has contradicted neither this passage of Scripture nor any other. I say, therefore:

I. Let the words of the apostle be read, and it will be evident that he understands "darkness" to mean that which is now called so after the fall of angels and men, in notorious opposition to the light.

This is similar to what St. James does in his parallel passage, where he says *that with the Father of light there is no variableness, nor shadow of turning.*

Behmen has never asserted that such a thing as they mean is in God or in the first property of eternal nature; rather, he has asserted the complete contrary. For he expressly says, in conformity with both these apostles, "God is light"; again, "This light shone from all eternity without beginning"; and again, "This shining of the light was never interrupted by any darkness breaking forth and prevailing over it."

Where light is, there is no darkness; and where the light had no beginning, there was no darkness before it. And where the shining light was not interrupted by any darkness, there was no variableness, nor shadow of turning, and no darkness in the light at all. But along with the light, there was (in a sense not intended by these two apostles, but in the sense Behmen uses) that which Behmen calls darkness. He had good reason to call it so, and it is called so in another place even by this same apostle St. John himself; for it was and must have been that which the light from eternity shone into, and that which did not comprehend it, according to his words at the beginning of his gospel.

If, then, the apostle in this passage (1 John 1) understands "darkness" as one thing and Behmen understands it as another, where is the contradiction? There is none, even in the literal sense, but only in a perceived consequence that has no connection to Behmen’s meaning, as shall appear hereafter.

II. By *darkness* in the first property of eternal nature, Behmen understands an astringency or a condensation in a spiritual sense and manner—a state of being "thicker" and more perceptible than the first abyssal will can be. He explains why this must be so, and he calls it darkness because: (1) according to his own account given in plain words, this astringency is the first and deepest ground of what later becomes darkness in and to the creatures when, by departing from their life and light in God, they fall into this astringent darkness, or what he calls *still-standing death*. The Scripture then calls this everywhere by the name of darkness and "everlasting chains of darkness." This expression plainly represents a binding, tightening, and shutting up into death, in opposition to light and life, which are entirely free, open, and liberally giving of themselves.

(2) And he calls it darkness, and has good reason to do so, because in this beginning, partial, and gradual consideration—focusing on the first property of nature only—the fire is not yet pro-

It addresses theological objections regarding the concept of "darkness" in God, clarifying that Behmen's use of the term refers to a spiritual state of astringency necessary for manifestation, not to moral evil.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Jacob Behmen’s theology, specifically addressing objections that his view of "eternal nature" being generated from God's own being—rather than from nothing—confounds God with nature. It also begins to reconcile Behmen’s concept of "darkness" (as a property of nature) with the scriptural claim that there is no darkness in God.</meta>

contrary to the Scripture.
The first objection is this: If eternal nature is not produced out of nothing by the abyssal Will commanding that it should be so, but is brought forth out of itself, then it must be either God or a part of God. This is because this "out of" implies a (*as it were*) material cause and makes God not only an effective but also a constitutive principle of nature; thus, God and nature are confounded, which is entirely intolerable.
To answer this first objection specifically: (1.) Such an objection was not made to Behmen himself, but what he would have said, if the opportunity had been given to him, may be apparent enough even from the simile he used in this matter.
He asks us to consider our mind and thoughts, because we carry within us, and are ourselves the—

<column-break/>

produced, and likewise the light not yet risen out of the fire. If we then must say that wherever there is no fire and light in nature, there is darkness, we cannot help but conceive of this first property as being dark and without light—not because it ever was so in and to God, but because it is now so in and to us when we lose our eternal light and fall into that dark, astringent death. Where then, in Behmen’s sense (meaning by darkness nothing more than a spiritual astringency in the first form of nature), is the contradiction against the apostle's words? Truly there is none at all; on the contrary, we can say that when this apostle says, *The darkness did not comprehend the light* shining into it, he says essentially the same thing that Behmen does: *The astringency in the first property of eternal nature is that which condenses and shuts itself up, so that the shining light can find no receiver, no admittance, or no free and open place—or rather, no such condition—in which it could display itself.*
III.—We must inquire into what the apostle means by God when he says, *Darkness is not in God*. He can best tell us this himself through his own twofold definition of God, saying not only, *God is light*, but also in the same epistle, *God is love*.
Now light and love are that second or superior part of the divine manifestation in eternal nature, which this first beginning, with its harsh astringency, must serve; Behmen commonly calls this the Second Principle. If it is obvious that his entire explanation of this matter leads directly to this point—that in the second principle (the apostle's God of light and love) there not only is not, but also cannot be any darkness at all, neither what the apostle calls darkness nor what Behmen calls so in his consideration of eternal nature before the creation and fall—where then is the contradiction between these two witnesses of the same eternal truth?
Indeed, what is more: if Jacob Behmen’s explanation goes even deeper and tells us more explicitly not only that darkness is *not* in God (that is, not in the Divine Triune Being generating himself in himself), but also that darkness is not in God (that is, not in the first Abyssal Will, which is entirely free, clear, pure, and serene, without any astringency overshadowing or condensing itself, etc.), then it may very well be asked again: where is the contradiction?
IV.—The apostle does not say in an absolute sense, "Darkness does not exist at all," as if he would thereby totally deny its existence and make it a mere nothing. Instead, he says in a limited sense, "It is not in God at all," thereby granting that it is outside of God—that is, according to his own interpretation, without His light and love. Truly he was wise and knew how to reconcile what the angel told him in those seemingly contradictory words: *it was, is not, and yet is*.
And all this is exactly conformable to Jacob Behmen, who says in one sense, *Darkness was from eternity*, and in another, *It was not*. Thus we may easily understand that the one saying, *it was not*, relates to the apostle's words, *not in God at all*; and the other, *it was*, to that other expression, *in itself*.
But now, despite all this distinction (between "in God" and "in itself"), it is undeniable that there is also another sense—not contradicting the former, but supported and implied by it, and confirmed by other scriptural expressions—in which we can safely and soundly say, *Darkness is in God*. We do not mean by this that it touches or infects Him, or brings any alteration, mixture, or variableness to His being as light and love; rather, we mean only that it is *within* (not outside) the boundless sphere or globe of His universal, all-filling being. Therefore, while it is not in Him in one sense, it is comprehended by Him (and therefore not outside Him) in another.
If He is in the darkness and hell as well as in the light and heaven (Psalm 139), the darkness must be within His reach as much as the light, and must have its own existence as much as the light—not outside, but within the infinite latitude (if we may call it that) of His being. Nevertheless, it is in Him *not at all*, but is outside Him—that is, outside His being as light and love.
Therefore, this "in Him" and this *without Him* do not contradict each other at all; for the sense in which we *view Him* in one expression differs from the sense in which He is viewed in the other, making a plain distinction. If we may freely say, "The devil is in God," we may say the same, and in the same sense, of the darkness also, for nothing exists outside of God.
If the devil was once in God and was not annihilated in his fall regarding his created being, he is certainly still in God, though he has left his first dwelling place in light and love. Furthermore, if the apostle Paul could say to the dark, unbelieving, superstitious, and idolatrous Athenians that they lived, moved, and had their being in God, without contradicting his own words to the Ephesians (who had once been just such heathens) that formerly, when they were in that state, they were without Christ and without God:
And lastly, if we can speak this way—tolerably, without offense, and without contradicting the apostles—saying, *The darkness is in God*, understanding even by darkness that same evil thing which is now called so after the fall and in the disordered properties of nature in man; then it is plain that Behmen could speak much more tolerably and with less offense. He could have said, *The darkness is in God*, understanding by darkness that good and necessary thing which was from and is for all eternity in the beginning of the harmonious generation of the properties of eternal nature—namely, the spiritual astringency and condensation which always is and must be in the eternal desire. For though such an expression—*The darkness is in God* (considered as before the creation and fall)—is not to be found in Behmen's writings (he always says, *it is not in God*, not in the Will, but in the Desire), yet I may freely grant that he could have said so without contradicting Scripture. For in this latter harmless sense (according to his foundation), this expression is to be understood.

## V.
That nothing can be in the desire except what is in the will also is ambiguous. In Behmen's sense (of which he is the interpreter), it is utterly false, and the contrary is true: namely, that something is and must be in the desire which is not and cannot be in the will.

Consider the simile used earlier of a moderate appetite and a violent hunger. We know that the former comes first, and, if not satisfied in due time, is always followed by the latter. Consider whether each of them must not necessarily have something in it unique to itself and distinct from the other, by which it is known to be this and not that.

The abyss, as an abyss, has in itself neither light nor darkness. The first Abyssal Will, therefore, also has neither this nor that; but as a will, he wills to have light, to dwell in the light, and to show within it the infinite variety of his own central powers and wonders, so that they may all be manifested and displayed from his own hidden center.

He does not will to have darkness, or to first create a darkness in his abyss and then produce a light out of it; instead, he wills light directly and exclusively.

But now this will (comparable, in an earthly way, to a moderate appetite) cannot be satisfied in this manner. For he cannot have light only by willing it, or, as it were, by playing within himself with it in a pleasant imagination, representing to himself the beauty and glory of the light. What is he then to do?

Should he stop willing the light because he cannot have it merely by willing it? No. For this would be to deny himself, or as it were to despair of his all-sufficiency, and to no longer be a will that wills the light. Not being able to give up this willing of the light, he must continue in it; and what is this continuation but a raising, sharpening, and *setting himself forward*, first into a strong vehement desire, and then further into that whole process which was described earlier. <note>N.B. the process of our regeneration so often referred to in this.</note>

Now this desire, which is the first property of nature—as of a strong, moving, and stirring life—is in its own essential nature attracting, astringent, and condensing. If it were not so, nothing could be produced by it, and no progress would be made from the first abyssal will toward the outside, or toward the production of light; instead, that will would only continue in itself willing the light, without any result of having it. <note>N.B.</note>

This harsh astringency, therefore (which Behmen says is the first and deepest ground of what we now call darkness), is the proper internal and essential character of this desire, by which it is and must be distinguished from the will; for the will, in itself, has nothing of such an astringent attraction and condensation. Now let anyone judge in what sense it can be said that nothing can be in the desire but must be in the will also. Is it not clearly evident that something must be in the desire which cannot be in the will? Just as in a violent hunger, there must certainly be that which cannot be in a moderate appetite.

If, then, this is Behmen’s meaning, it is manifest that the claim of a contradiction between St. John and Behmen is groundless, because it depends only on a conclusion that has no connection with his sense or meaning, nor any ground in his doctrine.

## VI.
By another scriptural expression parallel to this one from St. John, this controversy concerning darkness in God may not only be greatly illustrated but also very well decided. The Scripture says, *Wrath and fury is not in God.* Behmen says this as well.

But may we not also say with the Scripture, *God is a consuming fire*, or what is the same, *a fiery justice is in God?* And when we say so, do we mean anything else but that in God there is something which is wrath and fury in and to the *creatures*, if they awaken it in themselves? Surely wrath and fury are those hands of the living God, of which the Scripture says, *it is a dreadful thing to fall into them.* And yet those hands are also nothing else in God but his consuming fire or his fiery justice.

If, therefore, justice and wrath are *placed* beside each other and conceived in such a way that the former declares what the *hands of the living God* are in and to himself, and the latter what the same are in and to the creature, the Scripture shall be consistent with itself everywhere.

Just such a parallel distinction also exists here between the spiritual astringency in the first property of nature before the creation and the fall, and darkness in the dark world after the fall.

The former is the deepest ground of the latter. This latter (in a certain sense) is not in God, but in the properties of nature disordered by the fall. And the former is also not in God (in a certain sense), but in the exterior moving generation of eternal nature. And just as wrath and fury did not exist before the fall—when there was nonetheless that consuming fire which is now wrath and fury to the disobedient creatures—so also darkness did not exist before the fall, when yet there was that spiritual astringency, etc., which is and creates darkness in and to the creatures when divorced from the light. In the generation of nature, the astringency is good and subservient to the production of both fire and light; but in the dark world after the fall, it is the greatest evil of punishment to creatures, for it is that which binds and shuts up the tincture and its free mobility unto death, and it is the first link of the everlasting chain of darkness.

If, then, Behmen had simply not used the name of darkness in the description of the first property of nature, no contradiction would have been found between St. John and him. But now, since he has used it and given us not only a good reason for doing so but also sufficiently declared what he means by it, he has made it an unjustifiable thing for anyone to focus on the outward word without considering its meaning. This meaning, if understood, cannot help but make this whole objection vanish from sight and convince us of this truth: that he has not contradicted the Scripture.
