<meta>This page continues the exploration of Jacob Behmen’s theology, specifically using the human mind and its thoughts as a simile to explain the relationship between the abyssal Will and the perpetually generating properties of eternal nature.</meta>

He compares thoughts to the perpetually generating properties of nature; for just as the former are a stirring life of the mind, so also are the latter a stirring life of the abyssal, still eternity.

Now, if we consider how the contents of this simile agree or disagree with the notion of a material cause, we shall easily find what Behmen would have said about it.

Only three particulars are sufficient for this present purpose:

(a.) Nothing can be called a material cause, nor be looked upon as running parallel with it in a higher sense, except that which has in, by, and for itself (before it is considered as abstracted from its effect) its own peculiar and particular essences; and these as truly as that material, or *quasi*-material effect which is made up by them, possesses them afterward.

(b.) Those essences, at least in part, if not wholly, must be communicated or transferred from the cause to its effect.

(c.) This transfer or communication necessarily implies that the material, or *quasi*-material cause must always lose, or be deprived of, just as much of its matter or essences as it has communicated to its material or *quasi*-material product.

Now none of these three requirements are applicable to this present simile, and much less to that eternal generation of nature which is represented by it as in a shadow. And therefore Behmen would certainly have rejected this notion of a *quasi*-material cause as altogether irrelevant, and no more fit to conceive anything of this matter in reality than an earthen vessel is to contain a certain quantity of human thoughts. For he expressly declares that just as

(a.) Our mind does not have its own peculiar and particular essences in and by itself, before or considered as abstracted from its thoughts, so also the first abyssal Will has none, and is therefore called by Behmen an *unessential will*. Just as our thoughts themselves are the essences of the mind, which is but a universal root or ground for them, so also the properties of eternal Nature themselves are the essences of their universal root, which is the first abyssal Will.

As our mind cannot be distinguished from its essences, except only by the fact that it is in itself a whole, unchangeable, and immovable being, prior and superior to its essences, but in itself without distinction and perceptibility; seeing that our thoughts are but so many particulars, distinct from the mind and from themselves, because they generate themselves in a perpetual motion and alteration, and thereby make the mind perceptible to itself: so also it is declared by Behmen concerning the first abyssal will and the eternal properties of nature, which perpetually generate themselves.

(b.) If then our mind, in and of itself, without its thoughts, is unessential, no essences of it, neither wholly nor in part, can be communicated from this imagined *quasi*-material cause to its product or effect.

And as our mind is never broken to pieces, nor divided into parts, by sending forth out of itself so many thoughts—and what is more, as our mind itself is never changed or transmuted into thoughts, so as to cease to be what it was, and to no longer be a universal, fruitful root or ground of them—so also all this is rightly applied by Behmen to the first abyssal will. All this again sufficiently declares that, like our mind, this abyssal unessential will can have no manner of communion with what we call a material cause.

(c.) Just as our mind, communicating no essences to its thoughts, can lose nothing at all of its being, nor be deprived of anything by their arising and coming forth out of it—but rather, on the contrary, as it (in a sense and manner) wins and gains thereby, seeing that it thus comes into the manifestation and perception of itself, and shows forth the endless fullness of its own hidden treasury for its own delight—so also this third particular is largely declared in many places and elegantly applied by Behmen to the first abyssal will. This shows again, (first) that the notion of a material cause, though ever so much refined by a *quasi*, and though ever so useful in the lower region of natural things in this our Third Principle, is here, in this consideration of the beginning of eternal nature, altogether irrelevant. And (secondly) that nevertheless, as it is rightly said that our thoughts arise and come forth out of our mind, having no other origin, and are not formed out of nothing by a commanding power of the mind, so also is it rightly said that the properties of eternal nature arise out of the abyssal will, have no other origin but this will, and are not brought forth out of nothing, or merely produced by the will commanding that it should be so.

To this it is now replied: If our understanding of this matter is to be directed by this simile, we shall at length lose all distinction between God and nature; for it is generally agreed that our thoughts are nothing else but the mind itself, variously modified.

If we then say accordingly that eternal nature is in like manner God himself, will this not take away all distinction?

Answer. This objection against Behmen’s simile is of no weight, because its contents actually support his meaning very much and do not count against it at all. But this will become evident by what is now further to be answered to that former great objection, namely,

(2.) It was said above: What shall hinder us from saying, in one respect and sense, that eternal nature is God himself, seeing that this saying is supported by these plain expressions of Scripture: *our God is a consuming fire*, and again, *God is light*? Though we may also rightly say in another sense that eternal nature is not God himself, but only his manifestation or his instrument.

Both things are said by Behmen in plain words. Affirmatively he says in *Aurora*, Chapter 11: *This light is the true Son of God, whom we Christians honor and adore as the second person in the holy Trinity, etc.* And negatively he says again, in plain words, concerning the first three properties of eternal nature, that they have their ground in the Trinity but are not to be understood as if they are God, but only his manifestation. And so of eternal nature in general: that it is to be distinguished from God and is his instrument, or an instrument of the still eternity.

Now from the whole system of all his writings about this matter, it appears sufficiently that he has not thereby contradicted himself in meaning, though the words run directly contrary to each other. For just as we can rightly say, in one respect of his usual simile, that our thoughts are the mind itself—because without our thoughts, we cannot be aware of the mind; all our sensation is confined and all our perception of the mind restricted to our thoughts; and without or abstracted from our thoughts, the mind is, as it were, quite nothing, etc.—and as we can nevertheless rightly say also, according to Behmen’s declaration, that our thoughts are not the mind itself, because the mind is their

ground and root; if it were not there, the thoughts could not arise, nor change, nor multiply. The thoughts are particular things, subsequent and inferior to the mind; and the mind is a whole universe, prior and superior to the thoughts.

The thoughts are a moving, stirring life, while the mind, when abstracted from the thoughts, is a still, immovable rest. The Scripture says that we shall be renewed in the spirit of our mind (not our thoughts); and though we shall certainly be renewed even in our thoughts as well, the Scripture—speaking in this place of the mind and requiring in other parallel places the very bottom or the inmost ground of the heart—shows sufficiently that the thoughts are not the deepest ground in the sight of God, and therefore (in as good a sense as the other can ever be) are not the mind itself.

Though the thoughts are the deepest things in our own sight or perception, they make us say, quite understandably, that they are the mind itself, because we can have no apprehension or sensation of what the mind is without our thoughts.

So also, all of this is rightly applied by Behmen to God and nature; and this simile can safely direct our understanding of this matter, so that nothing of a proper distinction between God and nature is lost, and no contradiction in sense is found. For we can rightly say with Behmen in one sense and respect: Eternal nature is God himself, because it *is that part of the Divine Being which is communicable to the creature* (according to Scripture), both with respect to our understanding and to all our constituent essences. It is that deepest, inmost ground (expressly called God in the Scripture) in which we live and have our being; a ground to which we are confined and deeper than which we cannot reach, but must say in Behmen’s sense that whatever is beyond it is an eternal Nothing. It is *that which we are commanded to worship* as our only God in Trinity, seeing that the Scripture tells us of no other Father but him who calls himself a consuming fire; of no other Son but him who is this Father’s light and brightness; and of no other Holy Spirit but him who proceeds from this fire and light. And lastly, it is that in which our highest good, eternal happiness and glory, or our ultimate end consists, or that in which we are to rest and find peace forever. Rightly, therefore, is it called and acknowledged to be God, *our God*. But despite all this, we can also rightly say with Behmen in another sense and respect: Eternal nature is not God himself, because it is not that most supreme, all-abyssal, all-unsearchable, and altogether incommunicable being who generates himself in himself in Trinity. It is not that (in every imaginable sense) beginningless and endless Unity which, before and without its outflowing, can be conceived of—if not properly as a center, yet as an indivisible point. Instead, it is rather to be likened to a circumference, which in some sense has a beginning and an end.

It is not altogether that groundless ground which has nothing before it from which it could come forth, or which it could depend or rest upon, and which is itself the ground of all that is subsequent; rather, it depends upon this ground, is what it is out of this ground, and if this groundless ground were not, this eternal nature also could not be. What distinction between God and Nature could we desire more? And where is the confusion alleged to be introduced by Behmen’s simile? But with him, and according to Behmen’s sense, we say further:

Of that first, all-abyssal, all-incommunicable, beginningless, endless, groundless, Triune Being (which, because it is in itself only what it is, must necessarily be hidden and unmanifest), this eternal Nature—in the perpetual generation of its seven chief properties, all more or less intelligible and communicable—is a *perpetual manifestation*. And this is also called significantly by Behmen, in another specific respect, a sounding, harmonious instrument which the Spirit of eternity plays upon; and in yet another respect, a tool with which he works, etc.

But here it is replied again: Generation and manifestation are two expressions that are not consistent with each other in one and the same thing. If eternal nature is a generation, how can it be a manifestation? And if it be a manifestation, what sense can there be in calling it a generation?

Answer: Eternal nature is a *manifestation* with respect to what is before and outside of it, for that is made manifest by it; and it is a *generation* chiefly with respect to itself, for it is not only generated once, as we might conceive of it, but is also generating perpetually—that is, standing perpetually in the same incessant, unalterable generation of its properties. When it is considered as being in the first abyssal Will (where Behmen says it lay as a hidden fire, which is and is not), it is unmanifest. But when it is considered as coming forth, in the first three properties, out of that hidden ground, this very coming forth is its *generation*. It is significantly called so because it does not come forth from beside that will, but out of it; which in common speech cannot be expressed otherwise than by saying that it is generated, or born, out of that womb in which it lay. And this same generation is a *manifestation* also, no less significantly called so: (1.) with respect to itself, because that which was a hidden fire, which was and was not, is now a manifest and freely burning fire, of which it cannot be said, "It is and is not," but only, "It is." And (2.) with respect also to the first abyssal Will, which was not manifest and could not be manifest without this generation, but is now manifested by the same. This is because it has not only shown forth its own hidden, central all-sufficiency for such a generation but is also now itself this manifested, free-burning fire, which it was not and could not have been without this generation of the first three properties of nature. But I have reason to hope this will be further cleared by what I still have to answer regarding that former great objection. For

(1.) The author does not say that the <term>central fire</term> moved by its own selfish desire. Rather, he says that when the <term>central fire</term> of the own will (that fire which is—if separated from the light—the matrix or mother of its own will) moved, and when it introduced itself into a *greater desire* for its own contemplation and formation, then the creation was done. It is as plain as day that this "greater desire" was not that evil, accursed <term>self-desire</term>, or selfishness, which he says in verse 4 was cast out from the working of God and shut up in darkness. Instead, it was a good, necessary, regulated, and blessed desire, not cast out from God's working but utilized in His work; it was not shut up in darkness but brought forth to the light. For when the <term>central fire</term> moved and introduced itself into this greater desire, the <term>eternal ideas</term> came to be figured or formed as creatures, to the praise of the wonders of God.

(2.) He does not say that by this motion of the <term>central fire</term>, the eternal will of God was *stirred* (passively) in both fires. Instead, he says the exact opposite: namely, that the eternal will of God *stirred* (actively) the <term>central fire</term> (that one only substance or being mentioned in verse 2) and that He stirred it in or as to both fires, into which this One Being is distinguished in the <term>Two eternal Principles</term>.

If he had said the former, he would have, on one hand, dethroned the eternal will of God by placing a motion of eternal nature—especially its inferior fiery part—above Him. On the other hand, he would have shown himself to be a kind advocate for the <term>apostatized angels</term>, instructing them how to plead their cause against the Creator. But since he says the latter, he is clear and free from both these errors.

(3.) He speaks distinctly of two—nay, I may say (knowing what and how, though I cannot presume to make it intelligible enough) of three very different things, which you seem, Sir, to take as only one and the same, or at least to make but a little distinction between them. You indeed mention both the <term>central fire</term> and <term>anger-fire</term>, but you do not consider how they are two, despite the fact that they are also only one; and you think that in this single expression of <term>anger-fire</term>, you have the whole matter perfectly implied. However, our author does not use such a single and general expression in this place, but speaks very carefully and in great detail, saying in verse 4, *In this motion (of the central fire) the hellish foundation of God's anger broke forth also along with it.*

Whether it is expressed so distinctly in the English translation, I cannot tell; but I can say this: none of these details is to be neglected if his meaning is not to be wronged. None is superfluous; they are all significant and sufficient to demonstrate that he asserted no such thing as is expressed in your question.

We must have formed an idea of this two- or threefold distinction in our minds, if not from a deep internal ground, then at least from being very familiar with his style or manner of expression. If we have attained the former, he cannot be misunderstood at all, and if the latter, not easily. The <term>central fire</term> and <term>anger-fire</term> are, in one more distant sense, truly only one; but in another nearer sense, they are also really two.

Just as on one side the <term>central fire</term> is only one substance with the <term>light-fire</term> (verse 2), though there is still a great distinction between these two; so on the other, the <term>central fire</term> is also one with the <term>anger-fire</term>, and yet there is a far greater distance between these latter two than between the former two. For the former two can and do actually exist together, both in God and in creatures, but the latter two can by no means exist together, neither in God nor in creatures.

In God, there is a <term>central fire</term>, but not an <term>anger-fire</term>, neither before nor after the fall of angels. In creatures, if there is an <term>anger-fire</term>, there is no <term>central fire</term>; for by falling into that, they are immediately banished out of this; and that which before was a <term>central fire</term> in them has now become an <term>anger-fire</term>—not in God, but in themselves.

The <term>central fire</term> is properly the <term>First Principle</term>, the great strong city of God the Father, the residence of His living power and almightiness. This was never and can never be an <term>anger-fire</term>, unless we wish to think that the eternal Father is angry with His only begotten Son.

Indeed, we cannot say that it is an <term>anger-fire</term> in Him even now, after the fall of angels and men. For God is not angry with the devil; He is still the same from eternity to eternity and does not change. But the devil is angry with God, and so the <term>anger-fire</term> is only the devil's residence, for he has changed the <term>central fire</term> into an <term>anger-fire</term>, not in God, but in himself.

If they were both angry with each other, they would both live within the same residence, which cannot be asserted without blasphemy.

So far, I think this is intelligible enough, but there is still another and more subtle distinction to be made, reaching much deeper and not easily grasped without actual experience.

And this lies in the fact that our author does not use your single expression, "*The anger-fire broke forth*," but rather "*the hellish foundation of God's anger*," which he also calls especially <term>Satan</term> or the <term>dragon</term>. Regarding this, one may see what he says in <term>Theosophical Question</term> xiii. 10, 11, compared to xi. 3–6. If this is understood, it will show with the clearest evidence that he does not assert what your question, Sir, expresses. But fearing rightly that I might not be able to explain myself intelligibly enough regarding this particular point, and seeing that it can be sufficiently proven by other means, I shall set this aside. Moreover, I am sensible of the fact that nothing can suffice as evidence for you unless this particular expression of "*breaking forth*" is cleared up, so that you may accept what he means by saying, *The hellish foundation of God's anger broke also forth along with the motion of the central fire*, and this in the creation of angels, certainly before their fall.

For here, I think, lies the only knot which gave occasion to this question, and for which the English translation of these third and fourth verses (which I have now seen) gave you a just reason, seeing that it is very wrong and must mislead the reader.

Therefore, I am all the more concerned in my mind about how to lay open most plainly our author's sense in this serious matter, which is truly of great importance and has many significant consequences.

And I think I cannot do it better than by first considering the whole order and connection of all that is said here in this fourth <term>Theosophical Question</term>. Thus, it will appear manifest not only that his meaning is good—conforming to all his writings, simple and childlike—but also that it is well and significantly expressed. It is expressed in such a way that it does not justify or excuse the fallen angels, but only exalts the glory of their Creator.

What was the first origin or principal cause of the creation of angels, or what made the first beginning toward it? To say it was a motion of eternal Nature, or of one part of it (such as the fire), and this by its own <term>self-desire</term>—a motion by which the will of God was stirred, caused, or perhaps necessitated to create—would be the greatest nonsense in the world.

<margin>2
been
^</margin>
But it was the eternal Will himself, desiring that those eternal ideas should be substantial living creatures, formed for his praise and glory. And this view, and not the former one, can be shown to be consistent with all our author's writings. But further,

<margin>3</margin>
Could the eternal ideas become substantial created beings without an actual moving of that from which they were to consist, or which was to make up their being? To say they could would be great nonsense again. Truly, that from which they should come forth, which was <term>eternal Nature</term>, must have both been moved and must have moved itself also, in different respects. But being moved must have been prior, and this moving itself posterior, as an effect of the former. For we know that <term>eternal Nature</term> was itself, in its own essentiality, a perpetual moving without rest, or an eternal, never-ceasing generation. But if this eternal moving (without being moved particularly by the only supreme power) could have been sufficient to bring about the creation of angels, then the angels must have been equally co-eternal with <term>eternal Nature</term> and could not acknowledge any other superior creator. It was, then, the eternal Will of God himself who first moved and stirred this <term>eternal Nature</term>, which was to make up their created being; and only then—not before, but after it was thus moved and stirred—was it able to move itself further and effectively toward the creation.

<margin>4</margin>
No creation, then, existed or could have existed until first the eternal Will had actually stirred <term>eternal Nature</term>.

<margin>5</margin>
In <term>eternal Nature</term> now, there were, before the creation of angels, the two central fires: the anger fire and love fire; now so called (Note Well) *a posteriori*, after they both are manifested by the fall in a separation from each other. But at that time they could not have been called so; their only name was Fire and Light in a most harmonious union, one single substance, *v. 2.* If, then, <term>eternal Nature</term> was that which had to be moved or stirred by the eternal Will, it must have been moved in, or as, both fires—not as an anger and love fire (because it was not so before the fall), but as fire and light.

<margin>6</margin>
For these two—and not just one or the other alone, but both together jointly and in union with each other—were to break forth. This is properly and emphatically expressed in this way, for it was truly a breaking forth out of or through their own sphere (where they previously existed without living, substantial creatures) into an *external manifestation*, or into innumerable self-subsisting beings. All these beings bear that one eternal fire and light within themselves, and all are nothing else but glorious fire-flames illuminated by the light, like so many little individual representatives of their Father and Creator, that great universal All-in-All, both in fire and light.

<margin>7</margin>
No living creature can be generated in this <term>Third Principle</term> unless it has the fire of temporal nature united to its light in the generation of its life; and these two cannot be separated from each other unless the creature dies.

<margin>8
¥</margin>
So also, out of <term>eternal Nature</term>, no living creature could have been brought forth unless it had its eternal fire and light united to each other in its generation or creation. It must also keep them in that union if it wishes to live and not fall into eternal death. And just as these two, after they have broken forth in union into the creature, cannot be separated from each other without its destruction, they also could not have been separated from each other before or during their breaking forth. For life is in the fire, and without the fire, the light is dead. And again, out of the fire only, without the light, no glorious holy angels could have been brought forth (we might say devils could have been, if there had been such a creator who could have delighted in creating devils, which God forbid we should even think). For holiness and glory are in the light, and without the light, the fire is only dark, obscure, and unholy—profane and foreign to the most Holy and Almighty, whose dwelling place is fire and light in union, but neither one nor the other alone. But further,

<margin>9</margin>
When <term>eternal Nature</term> was thus moved and stirred in both fires by the eternal Will, what was the consequence or effect? We see there were several different effects, all linked together and succeeding each other (at least according to our way of understanding) so that the following always depended upon the one immediately preceding it.

<margin>10</margin>
The first was that <term>eternal Nature</term> moved itself also; and why should it not move toward creation when it was moved to do so by the only superior eternal Will?

<margin>11</margin>
It is certainly nothing more than an instrument in his hand, and yet it must not be conceived as a dead, senseless, immovable instrument, like an axe or hammer in the hand of a carpenter. For it was itself, in its own essentiality, an eternal moving generation. Therefore, it must be conceived as a living, faithful, and obedient servant who indeed has the principle of life and motion in his own limbs, but is nevertheless only an instrument of his master. He does not move toward this or that design unless he is first moved and stirred to it by his master's command, as he also lacks the ability to perform it without being commissioned and empowered by his authority.

<margin>12</margin>
This motion in <term>eternal Nature</term> was in, or as, both fires; for it was moved as to both, because both were in union and both were one, just as Father and Son are one.

<margin>13</margin>
But as the fire is naturally prior because it is the root of the light, and the light is posterior because it comes from the fire, the first or chief motion (the beginning-motion) is also ascribed to the fire and not to the light. Previously, the author had spoken of two central fires and said they were but one, but now he must also speak distinctly of that <term>central fire</term> in particular, in which lies the principal efficacy or the foundational power of formation or generation. Since this is in the fire and not in the light, he says rightly that the *central fire of the own will moved*. He shows by this that the beginning of the motion toward creation in <term>eternal Nature</term> was, and had to be, made in the fire and not in the light.

<margin>14</margin>
And regarding this fire, he does not say it moved with its own <term>self-desire</term>, nor does he say it moved in its own will (for it was sufficiently declared that it did not move until it was moved and commanded to move by the eternal Will). Instead, he says plainly that it moved and introduced itself into a *greater desire*, which shows a completely different meaning than the English translation expresses. But as to why he calls it the <term>central fire</term> of the "own will," several good reasons could be given, but this is the

The most important point, namely, is that he must have now distinguished the two central fires, if he were to declare clearly what he intended. If he then had to distinguish the first central fire from the second, he could not have done it better than by a designation taken from its own proper, essential, and inseparable character—one not common to both fires, but specifically proper to that first one alone.

But seeing that such a character was not yet revealed, neither before nor during the creation—both fires standing then as a single Being in the most harmonious union—he must have taken <margin>1</margin> a convenient distinguishing designation *after the fact*, following the fall of angels. And there he found the proper character of this first central fire was *own will*, immediately after or during the fall of angels. This character is absolutely proper to the fire, but cannot be shared with the light.

For in the fire, and not in the light, the own will arises and lives whenever and as soon as a divorce is made between them. In the fire, and not in the light, is that eternal substantial life which cannot die or cease, being an indissoluble circling band of the first four properties of nature, generating themselves always mutually and therefore also perpetually, if once joined together by the kindling of the fire. On the contrary, that life which is in the light can die, or <margin>2</margin> cease and pass away, as it actually died in the fall of angels when own will arose in the fire, where it still lives as if in its proper residence. And so that first central fire is justly called the fire of own will; though I freely admit that all is not yet said by this, but it is called so with another and deeper respect as well. If I were to bring that forth, I could neither do it in few words, nor perhaps in a way that would be understood well enough. Seeing then (1) that what is now said is not contrary to that, (2) that it is a great deal plainer, and (3) exactly conforms to all our author's writings, I shall pass it by and proceed.

The next consequence depending upon the first, and almost coinciding with it, is this: That when the central fire moved, it introduced itself into a greater desire. As the moving before was ascribed specifically to the fire and not to the light, because of its priority and its having the <margin>3</margin> principal power of formation or generation in itself above the light, so this greater desire is also ascribed specifically to the fire and not to the light, though the light is excluded in neither case. Just as eternal Nature in its own intrinsic essence was from eternity a moving generation regarding both fires, so it was also a desire from eternity regarding both fires.

How will and desire in a true and real sense may and must be attributed to all its seven source properties—and indeed, to all its lesser, innumerable subordinate powers as well—shall be discussed in the consideration of the second question. Here we are only to say that eternal nature in general was <margin>4</margin> and had (for being and having cannot be distinguished here) a desire from eternity; and that this desire is not that which is specifically attributed to its first attracting form, whose proper sphere of activity was only the perpetual generation and infinite multiplication of the forms and powers of eternal nature within its own circumference.

But this desire currently being discussed, which became a greater desire by being stirred by the eternal will, was reaching out, as it were, beyond that sphere; for its object was to break out into an external manifestation and to bring forth living, intellectual, substantial, and self-subsisting creatures, in which it might display and show forth the infinite variety of its powers and <margin>5</margin> wonders. And though this desire was kept under control, both on the part of the eternal will by his absolute sovereignty until he chose to move, and on the side of eternal nature as well by its submission and faithful obedience to its Lord and Master; yet nevertheless, there was in its own internal ground a desire. It continued as such a desire until it became a greater, more living and vigorous—indeed, a more exerted and effective desire—by being moved and stirred in both fires. For by that, it was now raised up like a spark of fire that was previously covered with ashes; it was commissioned by it and mightily empowered to break out regarding both fires, according to its desire, into an external, substantial manifestation.

Therefore, it must be clear that this greater desire is not that selfish desire which bears the number and mark of selfishness, but is as distant from it as the south is from the north, or the day from the night. For while that is an untimely, monstrous birth and even <margin>6</margin> from the womb a professed enemy to the eternal will of God, this one is surrounded for its defense, both before and after, by the eternal will itself. Seeing that, from before, it has the preceding movement of the eternal will, of which movement it is the proper intended effect and offspring; and after it, it has its own immediately following effect and offspring as well, which tended again to the praise and honor of the eternal will. For,

The third consequence, depending upon the former two and especially upon the second, is now this: That the eternal ideas became substantial creatures, to the glory of their Creator. Here <margin>7</margin> then, the actual breaking forth of the two central fires out of eternal nature into an external manifestation is to be considered; and that which is further said in verse 4 to have also *broken forth* along with them—namely, the hellish foundation of God's anger—is to be considered here regarding its breaking forth as well.

For they are inseparably joined together, as in reality itself (when the great wheel of eternal nature in its whole universality is considered, comprising everything that lay within it and came out <margin>8</margin> of it), so also in these expressions of our author; therefore, they must also be joined in our consideration.

Previously, only two things were spoken of, which were called two central fires, but now <margin>9</margin> there also comes forth a third, which indeed always lay implicitly beneath the first two as their root and ground, but did not then come explicitly into consideration.

For it is one and the same thing, whether they are named two central fires, or darkness, fire, and light. The only difference is that the former double expression and then this latter threefold expression are more suited to a particular state of things that may be considered differently. As these three now make up the whole of eternal nature and are three such essential parts <margin>10</margin> of it—as body, soul, and spirit are of man—so they must all three have broken forth into the creation of angels, if they were to be truly children of the Living God, generated out of eternal nature after the likeness of their Father. But they did not all three break forth in the same sense, degree, and manner, but each in such a sense as it is able to bear, and each according to its own order and degree, in which it stood from eternity with respect to the other two; either deeper into the bottomless center or higher exalted in the visible surface.

As to the two central fires, it can now be plain enough from what was said of them before, that their breaking forth was a most glorious, real, and visible manifestation of fire and

light, in a most intimate union, displayed in a countless variety and multiplicity of illustrious, shining flames of fire, which were so many living, intellectual, blessed, and holy-substantial creatures, all bearing the holy name of Trinity and Unity, both in and upon themselves; and all being the natural children of God, generated in eternal nature after his own image and likeness, which is (in eternal nature) nothing else but fire and light.

But what shall we say further regarding the breaking forth of darkness, represented in such dreadful expressions as the "hellish foundation of God's anger"? In what sense can this have broken forth also, and even along with fire and light? What communion between them can be so much as dreamed of?

Answer: Let it first be well noted and attentively remembered that, and how, darkness was from eternity; that it was not, and yet was; in what place or station it was with respect to fire and light; in what condition it was, considered in and to itself; and chiefly that it was good, no less than fire and light in its own kind, rank, and order. Let all this be well considered and understood, and it must of itself appear what this breaking forth of the darkness was, and that there must indeed be given another definition of it than that of the former breaking forth. Nevertheless, all that our author says regarding it is properly, well, and significantly expressed; and especially that this expression of "breaking forth" is justly used as well with respect to darkness as with respect to fire and light.

If we should see a ladder of three steps and consider it as a semi-diameter of a circle, and as breaking forth into a circular motion, we could not but say that this same and single breaking forth is common to all three steps. Thus, it is as properly applicable to the lowest as to the highest, but not to every one indiscriminately in the same way, seeing that each of them must keep to its own place and order. The highest touches the outermost circumference, and there it breaks forth into motion, making the greatest and most significant circle of all. The middle is lower and smaller; its breaking forth into motion is in its own inferior degree, and its circle cannot be of the same extent. But the lowest must still keep to the center and can make no perceptible circle at all, even though it does break forth into motion at the same instant in that center, no less than the superior two. None of these can break forth alone; likewise, the two superior ones cannot break forth by themselves alone without the assistance and concurrence of this third and lowest, if the whole ladder is not to be spoiled and broken into pieces.

Now, let these three ladder steps be darkness, fire, and light, and let this circle be that universal wheel of eternity, considered as it ought to be—namely, that only its circumference, and that which reaches the circumference, is visible and manifest, but its center, and that which lies within it or is annexed to it, is altogether invisible, secret, and unknown. Then this simple simile may easily show its own true application, so far as it has any shadow of resemblance, for much more is not to be expected. For it is not an improper resemblance and may at least explain to us this much: that just as surely as many legions of living, substantial creatures were brought forth in eternal nature by its breaking forth into an exterior manifestation, so also, and in the same degree of reality, all these holy angels must have had in themselves all three essential parts of eternal nature. These stood in every particular <term>microcosm</term> of eternity in the very same order in which they stood in the <term>macrocosm</term> of it, and in which order they were also all three harmoniously broken forth into motion to make up so many representatives of that greatest universal "All in All."

Therefore, from this united and harmonized breaking forth, they must have had an eternal light in the supreme, most excellent, and most manifested circumferential place of their created being. There they had it also, and have it still (as many of them as kept their habitation in the light), giving and being to them all their glory, beauty, delight, and happiness.

Further, they must have also had an eternal fire in the middle place of their being, united to the light and generating it, but standing lower and in an inferior degree of dignity; as they had and have it also, giving and being to them all their life, strength, power, and activity. Thirdly, they must have also had an eternal darkness in the lowest, most hidden, and central place of their being, united to the fire and providing it with its essences, but not standing with it in the same degree of nobility. And so they have it also, giving and being to them the central foundation and root of their fire and light, keeping these two in their order and preserving them in their union and glory, as long as it is itself kept down by them and fixed to the center. <note>Note Well</note>

Just as the lowest ladder-step is the only cause of a regulated circular motion only by means of its being fixed to the center—which motion must become irregular and all disordered as soon as this is turned aside from the center and breaks forth to move in or nearer to the surface.

If, then, they had these three things in such an order, they had the darkness under their feet, according to what is said of their eternal Father himself, whose children they are, and whose likeness they must therefore bear if they are to be his representatives. And if so, this darkness was not evil, not hell, and not anger or anger-fire, as long as it was under their feet; and nothing to this sense or purpose was ever said by Behmen.

He says indeed here, "The hellish foundation of God's anger broke forth," but how can these three things be spoken of distinctly in an earthly language now after the fall, and by such creatures as participate themselves in that lamentable fall, except by such distinct denominations as of necessity must be taken from what these things are now to creatures in their disorder and divorce? He does not say, "The hell broke forth," nor "the anger-fire broke forth," for that would be saying God was angry with his creatures, prepared hell for them before he created them, and cast them into it at their creation. And from where could hell and anger have broken forth into the creation when there was neither one nor the other in all the vast extent of eternity? If we believe there was nothing else before the creation but God in fire and light, how or where, from what source, or to what end could there have been hell and anger? Could that central fire of God the Almighty have been hell? And what could have been angry with each other, seeing there was nothing else but himself alone in fire and light?

But this is the thing: there was in eternal Nature that which, after the fall, could have been nothing else but hell and anger-fire to rebellious creatures. Not that it had been changed in itself, but because they manifested it in themselves in disorder.

And this broke forth in the creation; but in this breaking forth, it was only fire and light, or life and glory—and not hell and anger, no more than it is now to those holy angels who kept

And though it was darkness in and to itself, as to its own particular essentiality, yet it was not, and could also not have been manifested as darkness, seeing that it was kept under by fire and light, so that there could not appear what it was—and necessarily must be—when separated from fire and light. And therefore Behmen calls it not positively hell, nor the anger-fire itself, but only the hellish foundation of God's anger, or that which must of necessity have been hell itself, built, as it were, upon this dark foundation as soon as it was raised up out of its bottomless pit.

<margin>1</margin>
And this, he says, also broke forth along with fire and light: significantly suggesting that it did not break forth alone in its own strength and power, and so not in its own dark shape; that it did not break forth in disunion from fire and light, and so not with its own self-desire, which it was not permitted, as shall now follow. And that it did not break forth in the first place, but in its lowest order and degree, or as it were after them as an appendix.

<margin>2</margin>
And this hellish foundation, he says further, God has cast out from his working and has shut it up into darkness. How could he have expressed more plainly that this hellish foundation did not break forth into such a manifestation as fire and light?

<margin>3</margin>
Truly, if God has cast it out, it could not have crept or broken in, and if God has shut it up into darkness, then certainly it did not come to be manifested in the light. And so this breaking forth regarding the darkness must have quite another sense, which we shall find out soon.

<margin>4</margin>
But it will be asked and said, What is meant here by this casting out and shutting up in darkness? If there was not an evil thing in eternal Nature, intending to break forth toward destruction, why must it have been resisted like this by God and cast forth from his working? If it was good and useful, why was it not permitted to stand in its lot? And if evil and hurtful, from where did it have its origin? Or how could it have been said that all was good in eternal nature before the fall?

<margin>5</margin>
Answer. It was said before that eternal Nature had and was a *desire* to bring forth its wonders in a more exterior manifestation. If this was so, it was not so in this or that particular part of it, but in the *whole* in general, and in *each part* of it in particular. So that it *must* have been in the fire as well as in the light, and in the darkness as well as in them both. And if so, even reason itself may tell us that if each of these three desired to be made manifest, none of them could desire to be made so according to the nature and condition of the other, but each only according to that which was its own. Each could only desire to bring forth its own wonders. Just as the light could not desire to be darkness, so could it also not desire to bring forth the wonders of darkness, and *vice versa*.

<margin>6</margin>
But as each is confined to its own particular essentiality, by which it must be what it is, so this *desire* of each must also be naturally confined to its own proper essentiality, as being a proper consequence of it, inseparably annexed to it, and wholly depending upon it. So that it is inclined only to bring forth that which it has in itself, as sufficient only for that, and further for nothing more.

<margin>7</margin>
As also each of these three still desires, and is not only naturally inclined, willing, and ready to manifest its own secret wonders, but does it also effectively—each in its own region, being now enabled to do so by the fall of angels and men: and this both in the Two Principles of eternal nature, and in this Third also, as in their bipartite temporal outbirth.

<margin>8</margin>
All this desiring now (considered as in eternal nature before the fall and creation, and as purely abstracted from all relation and reference to creatures) is good, and must be so if eternal nature shall be what it is meant to be.

<margin>9</margin>
No "own will" or self-desire may be found there; which could only then be said if we could imagine that the light desired to be fire, and the darkness to be light, or the fire either this or that. Nothing is here inordinate, and so nothing is also hurtful or noxious, but all is profitable and useful because all is in its order, and so also serviceable to the whole manifestation of the eternal Will. Nothing is here to be restrained, cast out, shut up, or pressed down, but each must stand in its lot, and each must have its share in that eternal, first seven-fold and further infinite generation which existed before the creation of angels. And as each *must* be what it is, so each *must* also be for that which it has in its own peculiar ground and bottom.

<margin>10</margin>
But now, as soon as this desiring is spoken of with any respect to creatures, or to their creation, there is immediately a digression from that pure, abstracted sense; and this goodness fails more or less, growing weaker and weaker, and always declining gradually from its primeval purity as much as the creature is considered in conjunction with it.

<margin>11</margin>
If all these things that are in eternal nature—always and in every respect good, both to God, and to each other, and to themselves—could be good in and to creatures also, always and in every respect, in what way would the creature be less or inferior than God? What prerogative could the Creator have above the creature? What distinction could there be between order and disorder? And what could it signify that God is called a God of order? To say "This God of order could, according to his omnipotence, have manifested all these three things according to their threefold desire in that order in which they stood from eternity, and so this goodness must have continued," is true indeed in that sense which was spoken of before and, as I think, sufficiently declared; but it is false in the sense we are speaking of now. For their eternal order consisted in this: that only the light was manifested, shining into the darkness, and that the darkness was unmanifest, not comprehending the light, and being nevertheless subservient to the generation of fire, out of which the light could shine and could manifest—in its own manifestation—all the powers of both darkness and fire, but not in their own dark, fiery qualifications, but transmuted according to its own soft, meek, and tender essentiality.

<margin>12</margin>
It is the first fundamental truth that there was nothing evil in eternal nature. Just as there was also nothing (properly) good, because of this same reason: that it had no evil in opposition to it, from which it could be distinguished by such a name as "good." But since this opposition is effectively made in the fall, we have no expression nearer to the truth than this: we say that all that was in eternal nature was good—not in opposition to any evil that then existed, but to that which was afterwards manifested in the fall.

<margin>13</margin>
But nevertheless, there is also further a second fundamental truth, well-consistent with and immediately annexed to it, *namely*: There was that in eternal nature which must have been evil in and to creatures as soon as they manifested it in themselves, though it was good and profitable be-

<margin>/</margin>Therefore, in and for itself, and to them also, so long as it was unmanifest in them. And here we shall find that which must have been restrained, cast out from the working of God, and shut up in darkness. For therein lay all the danger, and the root of declining from good into evil, when it cannot nevertheless be attributed to the thing itself, considered in that former abstracted sense, but only to this conjunction with the creature, in this latter relative sense.

<margin>2</margin>But how, and what was this? It was that natural desire, inclination, and readiness to bring forth its own dark powers. And how could this have been evil and dangerous in the very creation, and yet have been good in eternity when abstracted from the creation? If this is not understood, all the rest will for the most part remain obscure; and therefore, being certainly much concerned with it, I must make it as plain as I can.

<margin>3</margin>We must then, according to the direction of *Teutonicus* <note>Jacob Boehme</note>, (though he does not propose it in such a way or method), conceive it thus:

<margin>4</margin>(1.) In that pure abstracted sense from all creatures and creation, these three things in eternal nature were all three manifest and all three hidden, in different respects. All three were manifest, but each only in and to itself; and therefore all three must also have been hidden, each with respect to the other two. When we then find this expression in *Teutonicus*, which he uses frequently, "The darkness was manifested in itself from eternity," it is not to be passed by thoughtlessly, for it has its deep, true, significant, and wide-reaching sense. I know not how to express it more closely in other words than by saying: As the darkness was in and to itself, when it was nothing to the light, so it was also, and must have been, manifest in and to itself, when it was not manifest in and to the light. For it was, and if it was, it was only that same thing which it was, and nothing else. And this being what it was, cannot but imply a manifestation of what it was, corresponding to that sense in which it existed and relating only to itself.

<margin>5</margin>In that sense, then, in which it existed and in which it was manifest, it had also an inseparable desire to be manifest, or to continue to be what it was. And this desire was then good, necessary, and profitable, not bringing in any evil or disorder. For it was not a desire reaching beyond its own sphere, or intending to destroy the light by breaking forth out of its own limits into the light's region, but only to generate and bring forth its own dark powers, and so to preserve its own being in its own region. All this must have been so and continued so without alteration, for it was subservient to the light. If it had not been so, no fire could have been generated, having no essences except from its root, and so the light could not have shone out of the fire and could have had nothing to shine into. For its nature is to shine into the darkness, and that of the darkness is to not comprehend the light. But,

<margin>6</margin>(2.) As soon as creatures and their creation are spoken of, there is a departure made from this pure abstracted sense, and this desire can no longer be considered in isolation or by itself alone. Instead, all three must now be considered as in conjunction, breaking forth and entering each from its own deeper particular sphere into one only compounded, lesser, lower, and weaker sphere, in order to make up—all three together—every particular angelical being. In which, or with respect to which, this desire of darkness can no longer be considered so single, pure, and closed to itself, for it now has an external object which it can lay hold on and make a claim to, no less than fire and light, seeing it is no less than they a third essential part of it.

<margin>7</margin>And as by the moving of the eternal Will in both fires, the central fire especially introduced itself into a greater desire, so did also the *light*, and no less the *darkness*, each in its order and place, and according to its condition. Nevertheless, even in this greater desire also, there was no evil, nor any danger, as far as it can be conceived by itself alone, abstracted from the creature; for it had not, nay, could also not have changed itself, and no alteration was brought upon it from without. But only in its conjunction with this external object was there an evil danger of disorder and confusion conceived, as it were, in the womb—not as an absolute necessity, but as a possibility of being brought forth into real existence. And so the former goodness, consistent with that pure abstracted sense, is now inconsistent—at least as to the same degree of it—with this latter relative sense. This is not because of its being changed, but because of its now having the ability and possibility, in this external object, to be changed by this dark desire being stirred, raised up, and manifested beyond that sense in which it was manifest before. This could not have been done before by itself without the creature, but could now be done by the creature, as it was indeed done soon thereafter by some of them in their fall.

<margin>8</margin>But could not this dark desire have been kept under or in order, in and by the creature, so that its goodness and profitableness had been continued without alteration? Certainly it could, for so it was also, and still is, with all those holy angels who kept their habitation in the light. For it could not have broken forth into a manifestation of itself, nor could it have necessitated any creature to raise it up. Certainly it could do so no more than fire lying hidden in a flint stone can break forth to consume houses if not brought forth by a living agent, and no more than it can necessitate or constrain any living person to strike it out of steel and flint. But if this is now done by a living creature, and evil consequences come forth from this action, who can be blamed as the author of evil?

<margin>9</margin>So, therefore, all and every evil has its only origin in the creature, and not in this dark desire considered in itself without the creature. For in its conjunction with the creature the danger was conceived, and by the creature's own activity, the evil was effectively born. This desire of darkness implies, in and of itself, nothing else but a bringing forth of its own powers, that is, a preservation of its own being; and this is good, for it is consistent with order and is according to its own natural and eternal right. But this same desire of darkness, when in conjunction with the creature, also further implies disorder, destruction, rebellion, and insurrection against the light; and this is evil. If, then, the former can be separated from the latter—as it really can be and was before there was any creature—there can be no evil, and none could have been in eternity before the creation. But if this latter cannot be separated in the creature from the former—as it certainly cannot by any means—that former goodness fails when this desire is considered in conjunction with the creature. It fails in such a way that the fault is on the side of the creature, and not on the side of this desire. <note>Let God be glorified by the demonstration and publication of the Truth.</note>

<margin>10</margin>Which even in the creature itself does not properly and directly intend the destruction of the creature, but only its own manifestation and increase.

<margin>11</margin>Nay, what is much more: even now after the disordered manifestation of this dark desire, when it is really hell, darkness, torment, anguish, and anger-fire, we may still find some evident and

Therefore, the origin of evil lies in the creature's own activity and choice, not in the fundamental properties of eternal nature itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the explanation of the "hellish foundation" and the "working of God," specifically addressing the three senses in which this foundation can be said to have "broken forth" or been restrained during the creation and fall of angels.</meta>

most significant traces of this distinction, declaring plainly that everything that is or can be conceived of as evil lies only on the side of the creature, and not on the side of that which came out of eternal nature to be manifested by the creature. For hellish darkness and the fire of anger would immediately be good and only good, without any mixture of evil, and could no longer bear such dreadful names, if only the *self-will* of creatures—in relation to which they are and must be evil—could be taken away, abolished, and annihilated. This is certainly a sure and solid truth, and it is most worthy of deep consideration.

But I think it can now be plain enough from this what our author means by the *breaking forth of the hellish foundation of God’s anger*. It must be spoken of in different senses, and I do not see how to represent these differences better than by saying: It broke forth, and it did not break forth, and yet it broke forth. For we may find in this fourth theosophical question, compared with the fourteenth question, a threefold sense that matches this threefold expression, even though we do not find such a specific construction of words.

(1.) *It broke forth*, since all the holy angels, in their creation, must have been composed of darkness, fire, and light, according to the likeness of their Father in eternal nature. But it broke forth in its proper order, for it was not made manifest and did not enter into the surface or the highest visible circumference of the angelic beings, but remained below at the center, as the lowest step of this eternal ladder.

And yet it entered into them, and into every one of them, to be the root and ground of their fire and light.

This entry into them was its breaking forth from its own uncreated eternity into a lower and external degree of many particular created beings.

(2.) *It broke not forth*, in the sense that implies hell, or the fire of anger, properly so called now after its manifestation. For here it was cast out and shut up. This is not to be understood so crudely as if the darkness had a rebellious will or desire to be hell, and to break forth in flames of anger-fire to destroy the light and disturb the whole creation of God; such a rebellious will, like a raging, furious devil, would have had to be resisted by force and violence and bound with eternal chains of darkness.

For what ridiculous nonsense would this be, and what strange monsters would be generated from it?

Certainly, not even the slightest shadow of this can be found in all the writings of *Teutonicus* <note>Jacob Boehme</note>, unless they are ignorantly or maliciously perverted.

The darkness indeed had a will or desire, or a natural internal propensity and inclination to enter into manifestation and to bring forth its own powers and wonders in and through the creature; this was as natural to it as it is to fire and light. And this was good and not evil, as far as it can be considered without connection to the creature; for it implies no rebellion against the light, no disorder, or destruction of anything in eternal nature, but only its own generation, manifestation, and preservation of its own being. This being must be preserved in its own state and condition and is preserved in eternal nature by the cooperation of fire and light themselves.

But it was not good in this connection with the creature, for there it necessarily implies and carries with it the undoing of the light in the creature, and thus the creature’s destruction and rebellion against the eternal will of their Creator, who would not have had them be creatures of darkness, but of light.

Therefore, in the creation of these beings, this will and desire of darkness was not used by the Creator in the same way he used the desire for light; instead, he cast it out. From where? From his "working," says our author—not absolutely from the creature, for darkness had to be the third essential part of it, hidden in its innermost, deepest center—but he cast it out from his working. What is this but to say: He did not open the dark bottomless pit, but shut it up in its own abyssal center; he brought forth no hellish wonders and created no devils, but only holy angels of light, who were all bright and glorious shining flames of fire, having the darkness—along with all its dark will, desire, and inclination—under their feet.

Therefore, this hellish foundation of God’s anger did not break forth, and could not have broken forth, in the creation of angels; but it did so later in their fall, when this desire of darkness was stirred, raised up, mightily assisted, and effectively brought forth by their own activity, working in the dark and false <term>magia</term> of their own will. But nevertheless again,

(3.) *It broke yet forth* even in this creation itself.

And what is this "breaking forth" other than a closer advancement—not from non-being into being, but from a state of pure, absolute impossibility of ever coming into being, to a state of possibility, or, one might say, a good hope for being? For before the creation, it was eternally impossible that darkness should ever have been manifested beyond the sense and degree in which it was and had to be manifested in and to itself;

Since not only could it not have manifested itself any further, but it also could not have desired or been inclined to do so, because there was nothing in which or to which it could have been manifested. But now there were millions of external living objects, all capable of receiving its manifestation into their own ground (where it lay unmanifest), and all also able themselves to bring it into manifestation, both within and without themselves.

There was then a possibility, and a door, as it were, was opened in the creation through which it could creep in and come into manifestation; not indeed by its own power, but by the creature’s assistance and cooperation—if they should be so curious and desirous as to unlock its secret pit and thus enter into a manifest union with it. Experience has shown us in the fall of angels—and can still show us daily in our own actual transgressions—that they could do this by their own will and desire: these two desires, that of darkness and that of living creatures, can enter into, unite, and mingle with each other more easily than black can unite and mingle with black.

And here that *greater desire*, into which eternal nature introduced itself after being stirred up in both fires, may be found with respect to darkness. For while it previously had a desire to be manifest and to remain so (in the sense that it was manifest in and to itself according to its eternal right), it now acquired a greater desire: to be manifest in the creation as well. This greater desire was cast out by the Creator, not because it was evil in itself when separated from the creature, but because it was inconsistent with the state in which he intended the creatures to exist for his own praise and glory, and for their own happiness.

And this, says <term>Teutonicus</term> now further (v. 5), was the ground and cause of <term>Lucifer</term>'s fall. But if we were to imagine a cause by which he were made excusable in the least, we would be quite mistaken. It drew and tempted him indeed, but only within him, and not from outside of him. So it was only his own lust that tempted him; and he had to be tempted just as <term>Adam</term> and all the rest of the holy angels were. It drew and tempted them all, but it compelled none; otherwise, they all must have fallen no less than <term>Lucifer</term> with his legions. But since the greater part stood immovable in the truth and light, he also could have stood and kept his own lust under foot.

And then this darkness, with all its attractions, would have darkened him as little as his fire could have burned him, or could have consumed his shining light.

Of man, the Scripture says, *Thy perdition is from yourself*; despite the fact that man had this same living, strong, and mighty prince of darkness against him in his temptation. For it was only himself; and this, therefore, was properly that which was afterwards in him. But had he prevailed against this, everything that was outside of him would not have hurt him.

And if it was so with man, how much more is <term>Lucifer</term>'s perdition from himself, who did not have such a living, strong, and cunning adversary against him from the outside as he later became to man. He did not remain in the truth, and he did not keep his home in the light, says the Scripture; and so it makes only himself, and nothing outside of him, the cause or causer of his destruction.

I shall now only try to illustrate this entire matter a little more in its chief particulars by a suitable comparison, obvious to reason and the senses.

From the creation of this world, everything that has since been manifested in it, both good and evil, lay hidden and secret in the manifold powers and energies of temporal nature. And so, all things successively and gradually, each in its appointed time, should be brought forth into manifestation. Among so many others, let us consider only that evil, harmful, and destructive invention of gunpowder, which certainly did not flow from the properties of light and love, but out of darkness, from this hellish foundation of God's anger; seeing it is notoriously made up of the first three properties of darkness, and only by the cooperation of the fourth is it enabled to show forth its stupendous effects.

Just as this really lay in the powers of temporal nature from its very beginning, so too did this nature have a desire to bring it forth into manifestation. As it still has such a desire, and as the energies of the stars and elements, and all that is set to work or has a share in the government of this principle—from the highest official down to the lowest—is capable of this desire, each in its order, degree, and according to its ability. But especially the spirit of this world [desires to bring] forth into manifestation all that lies hidden in the secret recesses of his kingdom. For his government and the execution of his office consist of this; he being ordained to manifest both good and evil in this, his mixed third principle, wherein everything is still good if considered in and of itself.

This desire then in the spirit of this world, especially regarding the manifestation of gunpowder, was absolutely good in him (in such a goodness as this principle can be capable of), as far as it can be considered only in itself and purely separate from men. For though we may say it of the devil, we cannot say of the spirit of this world that he desired or intended for so many thousands of living men and beasts to be killed and destroyed by it; rather, his desire implies nothing else but that a faithful execution of his office might be made by the manifestation of those powers and wonders which he was ordained to reveal. But as soon as it is considered in conjunction with man, this goodness fails immediately—not because it had changed in itself, but because its manifestation is inconsistent with the condition of sinful man.

This manifestation and its effects could not have broken forth on its own, or by the sufficiency of this desire alone, however strong it might have been, and despite the fact that all the materials required for it existed; rather, it lacked a living agent, or such an intellectual instrument that could be able and fit to make a proportional mixture and composition of it, and to prepare whatever else was required for its harmful use. And this could have been no one else but man. Animals were not able, and the devils were not either, because of their being cast out from this principle, so as to have no power in it at all.

It therefore could not have broken forth before the creation of man; there it was in a state of absolute impossibility. But in his creation, we may say it advanced nearer, or made, as it were, the first step of advancing from a state of impossibility to possibility, for that external living agent, with whom this desire could join, was now in existence. But in his fall, the connection between them was actually made; and in this connection, all the evil that ever arose from it was actually conceived in the womb.

The objection that might be raised here—that it seems a necessity is laid upon man, by which he was forced to fall, because otherwise the spirit of this world could not have manifested its wonders and secret powers, and that his being created with a natural inclination toward them must have been in vain—is of no significance at all. Man was free and not compelled to join his imagination with the spirit of this world; and if he had kept it under control, he himself would nevertheless have manifested its wonders, though in quite another and much more glorious way—not as a foolish captive and servant, but as a wise ruler and master of it. But now, in his fall or his joining with it, a wide gate was opened through which this hellish invention could gain ready entrance into this world, in such a harmful way as it still exists today.

Nevertheless, it was still unknown to mankind for several thousand years, during all of which time it could not have been called evil if considered purely in and of itself, as it is a wonder of the powers of nature. And, which is the most important thing and the conclusion of all, when it finally broke forth into actual manifestation after such a long period of ages, it carried no killing and destroying evil along with it out of absolute, compelling necessity; rather, all that evil already lay within man himself. For it could not have forced anyone to kill his fellow creature with it, though it may have occasioned and tempted many, who yet were all free so that they could have left it alone—if they all had kept their own evil lusts of hatred, envy, etc., under foot.

But this is enough. What further might be said and applied conveniently to our purpose can easily present itself, if duly considered and compared.

I shall now speak briefly, Sir, concerning your second Question, which was this:

What is the true notion of own self-desire as it relates to fire and forms, and such like things that are in themselves inanimate; since will and desire, in the proper sense of speech, belong only to intellectual and rational beings?

Answer. Several things are expressed here, which must first be noticed somewhat distinctly before a direct answer can be given to this question. But, though many things properly belonging and subservient to this come to my mind, yet for the sake of brevity I shall set down only some of them in the following positions:

I.—It is not the right way toward truth and wisdom to create or settle outward notions, and to fix our minds upon spoken or written words; but the only way is, according to the direction of the Scripture (repeated and insisted upon most earnestly by <term>Teutonicus</term>), to *ask of God, who gives to all men liberally and without reproach.*

II.—If this is given by God and is *obtained* internally in the soul, it is authorized by its giver to regulate the proper use of outward speech, which cannot, in turn, regulate the internal truth. For,

III.—It is unquestionably true that our proper use of outward speech must be subject to a proper internal sense; seeing that it must depend upon this alone, and that it ought not to aspire to any higher dignity than to be a faithful interpreter of it.

IV.—It is no less true that all that we can call a good—nay, the very best—proper use of speech is but earthly, imperfect, powerless, and shadowy (in comparison to inward light and substance). It is full of confusion (because our Jerusalem speech is lost, and this is but born in Babel), and always subject to being understood differently, according to the different constitutions of hearers or readers, none of whom can grasp any outward expression more accurately than he himself *stands within the truth*.

V.—Many things are said with a good propriety of speech (according to our sense and understanding), even in the Scripture itself, condescending to our capacity, which yet are all technically improper, and if regulated by that outward standard of speech, utterly false; yet they are really true in their own internal sense, which, if it should or could be exactly represented, would be entirely inconsistent with the standard of earthly speech. Providing instances would be tedious. This alone, concerning the deliberation or consultation of God and his decrees following from it, could provide sufficient evidence.

VI.—It must rightly be asked: By what ground, or in what sense, can the <term>seven spirits of God</term> before his throne be placed in the category of inanimate things? Or what is the true notion of being inanimate? Seeing that the prophet <term>Ezekiel</term> testifies of those four which he saw as a fourfold <term>seven wheels</term> full of eyes, that they had a living Spirit within them; and seeing further that they are the origin of so many thousand animate beings. For the fact that they are called seven wheels and seven burning lamps, and that neither wheel nor lamp upon earth is animate, can signify nothing at all.

Truly our author had found a true internal and real sense, which cannot be outdone by any standard of earthly speech.

VII.—"He that made the eye, shall he not see? and shall he not hear that prepared the ear?" says the Scripture of God, who nevertheless has neither eyes nor ears; yet he has them both far above all standards of earthly speech, in such a true internal sense as is consistent with eternity and with his transcendent being.

And as this is said of God, so it may also be said in its lower, subordinate sense of <term>eternal Nature</term>.

VIII.—All the forms thereof *see, hear, feel, smell,* and *taste* each other, truly, really, and properly, in such truth, reality, and propriety as is consistent with their eternity, though not with the capacity of sinful man; who lost his intellectual eye and all internal senses, and is only able to look into time—and even then in such a way that it might justly be doubted whether he should more properly be called blind or seeing.

IX.—How these five senses are applicable to the forms of <term>eternal nature</term>, or how they see and feel each other, is asked in vain and would be explained in vain, even if it were by an angel from heaven, if we are not ourselves acquainted inwardly with the movements and operations of <term>eternal nature</term> in its restored, harmonious union. All that our author says of it <note>N.B.</note> is not to explain it to any other so that it should be understood from his outward words by turning them into regular notions, but only to stir up everyone who complains of unintelligibility *to seek and ask for understanding from God,* where he may certainly find it, according to his appointed measure, just as he found it, who before was as ignorant of it as anyone else on earth. For,

X.—Just as it is impossible to be understood if we are not acquainted with the operations of <term>eternal nature</term> within ourselves, it is just as possible and easy if we are; for then it declares itself most sensibly and needs no declaration from outside. It is seen and felt in the mind of man, as a *living word* of God is spoken, heard, and understood without any outward sound and without the means of any language.

XI.—If these things are so, *will* and *desire* cannot be so foreign to the seven forms of <term>eternal Nature</term> as they might seem, if we were to think that the standard of earthly speech which we are used to is a good and proper rule for these eternal, immeasurable things to be regulated by.

XII.—It might rightly be asked here whether a little newborn child has will and desire, and especially its own will and self-desire. I am sure enough that it can neither be directly and positively affirmed nor denied, but a harmonious mixture and union must be made of Yes and No. If we should consider this a little deeper, much would be found in it relevant to this present matter concerning the seven forms of <term>eternal nature</term>.

XIII.—Each of them, considered as if by itself alone (though none can be alone), has its own will and desire.

And this (1) is its own immutable essentiality. (2) It lies in its own immutable essentiality. These two cannot be distinguished from each other in <term>eternal nature</term>; they are one and the same thing, but from the effects and consequences, we find the distinction after the fall in
