creatures. It is rightly said (1.) that it is its own immutable essentiality; for it is that by which it is, and continues to be what it is, and cannot be any other thing or property. It can also have no inclination, no possibility, nor any kind of ability to be, or to become, any other thing than what it is. And so it is not an acting, stirring, or working activity, as we conceive in the notions of will and desire, for there is no occasion for it. It is quietly what it is, and does not need to be occupied with a moving will or a desire to be, or to maintain its being; for there is no opposition which it could or must resist by exerting any act of will or desire.

It stands (notwithstanding that it truly has its own particular essentiality for itself) in the closest union with all the others, making up with them one single harmonized substance. But seeing further, that this same thing afterwards in fallen creatures becomes an individual will and self-centered desire with respect to these seven disharmonious properties—when they are scattered and brought into opposition against each other in creatures—it is also rightly said (2.) that will and desire lay in the immutable essentiality of each of these seven forms: for it arises only from there and shows itself forth immediately. Each is departing from union and withdrawing into that which is its own; each is contrary to all the others and now has a natural, strong desire (inclination or propensity is not enough here), or a fixed, obstinate will, to stand by itself upon its own foundation; to exclude all the others, to prevail against each and every one, and only to preserve and maintain its own particular being. This could not be so if, in the first harmonized original (when all seven were united into only one substance and ruled by only one will of light and love), each of them did not have its own particular, immutable essentiality.

So then there was no individual will, nor any personal self-desire in eternity before the fall of angels; nothing of the kind was ever said by <term>Teutonicus</term>, who declares expressly in more than fifty places, not only that it had its origin in the fall, but also that it could not have been in eternity before the fall. However, that potential must have been within it, which, when introduced into an external manifestation and so communicated to creatures, could, in and by them, have been stirred and raised up in discord and opposition. And this was that seven-fold, particular, immutable essentiality of the Seven Eternal Properties, by which each of them must have been only that which it was. For the first could not have been the sixth, nor the second the fifth, etc. But they altogether could have surrendered their will and total being into the whole; all loving, desiring, and embracing each other in union and harmony, and so making up only one will and substance.

But when they were now stirred up in the deepest central root by Lucifer and his angels, this union and submission to the will of light and love was broken and disturbed; each recalled, as it were, that which was its own to itself, acted according to what it was able to do in its own essentiality, and showed forth what it was when departed from union.

And so there must arise seven particular, not only different but also contrary wills and desires, which the *Revelation of St. John* represents by the emblem of the *seven heads of the dragon, the seven mountains, and the seven heads of the scarlet-colored beast, upon which the harlot sits, etc.*

### The following paper contains a representation of “The GROWTH of VEGETABLES, regarding their ANNUAL RENEWAL in the Springtime, as described by BEHMEN:” —

I.—Heaven and earth make up but one principle and are the two chief constituent parts of it, to be compared in a sense to male and female; so that the concurrence of them both is necessarily required for the generation of all sorts and kinds of earthly things.

II.—The properties of Nature therefore in the earth, which on the third day of the creation (when they were in conjunction with the eternal Word moving them especially) could produce all sorts and kinds of vegetables without the concurrence of the sun, can now do the same no more. But, because they are half dead and impotent after the fall and curse, they now want the sun's heat and light to be thereby raised up, stirred, and enlivened.

III.—All the Seven chief Properties of nature, together with their lesser subordinate qualities, are in every seed, but in various degrees and orders; so that some of them lie more or less deeply hidden within it, and others are more outward and nearer to activity, according to their different kinds. But all are without a manifest distinction, as if they were all but one and the same thing; therefore, they must also be without manifesting or exerting their various distinct faculties until the seed is thrown into the ground.

IV.—All the same properties are in the earth also, but in several degrees and orders, variously different according to the different conditions of places; and in the earth no less than in the seed, they are impotent, shut up in death, and overpowered by its cold astringency. Because the earth then has its own center cast down from the sun—indeed, set as it were in opposition against it, so that it must be more passive than active—its properties could never be able to raise up any quality in the seed unless they were first raised up themselves by the influence of heat and light from the sun.

V.—When this begins to happen and then proceeds further gradually, the Properties begin to be stirred and are enabled gradually to operate, each of them according to its own nature; for the heat, which is the next degree to the light, is unfolded and raised successively more and more out of the cold astringency. And so, therefore, an agreeable conjunction or union is made between the properties of the earth and those of the seed, which latter are taken in, supported, and strengthened by the former. Provided,

VI.—That the properties of that peculiar ground or place where the seed is sown are not too contrary in their constitution, but agree more or less with the properties of the seed in their condition, order, or kind. For otherwise, the grain or seed is indeed taken in by the earth, but the properties of that seed are not taken in by the properties of the earth, seeing that there can be no conjunction, or at least no agreeable living union, between them. And from this, therefore, arises a slow and weak vegetation, or else sterility and a total corruption of the seed. Behmen illustrates this by an analogy taken from a mother's entire kindness and affection toward her own natural son, compared to the same mother's lesser tenderness or total carelessness toward a step-son.

VII.—These two then in conjunction, namely: (1.) the natural contrariety and strife of the first three properties in the earth and seed; and (2.) the sun's influencing power, not only raising up that strife

...by its heat, but also by gradually reconciling it in its light, are the cause of each and every instance of growth.

And this is in a harmonious correspondence to the two eternal principles. For just as Eternal Nature always tends forward in and through the war and strife of the first three dark properties toward their transformation into peace, light, and glory—which it obtains in the second principle of light and love—so too does Temporal Nature always tend or press forward toward its perfection in its kind. This is a transformation of its inferior, striving properties, to be made in and by the light or tincture of outward nature, which is hidden in everything and is fully achieved in the full maturity of every fruit.

**VIII.**—This connection between these two is always broken in the winter by the then-predominant astringent cold. But as soon as the properties of the earth can have their heat stirred and raised in them again, this connection is renewed, and their strife begins anew. From this it follows that every tree produces new twigs and branches yearly; and from every root or seed, a new growth springs up, which is described more particularly by Behmen as follows.

**IX.**—The sun's heat warms and stirs the *quality* of water, or the water spirit, and thus also the material water or sap, both in the earth and in the seed. Then the light of nature springs up *in* and with that sweet water spirit, which makes all the other properties move and stir as well. For there is now a mutual affecting, touching, penetrating, and working of the properties upon one another, though each of them constantly keeps to its own natural inclination and therefore cannot help but act accordingly.

**X.**—All the other qualities, besides the sweet water and light, being in themselves only dark, harsh, cold, rough, astringent, bitter, dry, etc., are thereby naturally made aware that this light and water are their end and aim, or their only desirable treasure, refreshing, softening, healing, and reconciling them. Therefore, in their sensitivity or natural tendency, pressing toward perfection, the growth is now carried on by their own natural strife and opposition. For the seed is now impregnated with a new life according to its kind.—<note>By *sensibility* here is meant a natural tendency or inclination toward that which brings them to their perfection. This may rationally be conceived to stand in such proportion or analogy to sensibility as the proportion between the knowledge and reason of man and that which more or less corresponds to it in beasts.</note>

**XI.**—This new life, being still surrounded by death and encompassed by a gross, hard, unprofitable husk, shell, and so on, cannot spring up beyond it—and so cannot manifest or exert itself—except by breaking through that dead enclosure, shedding it, and leaving it behind in the earth. Here lies that death so often spoken of by Behmen and applied to regeneration, according to the words of Christ: "The grain of wheat cannot bring forth fruit, except it fall into the ground and die."

**XII.**—In this mutual affecting and touching of all the qualities, the sweet water-spirit *tasting*, as it were, the bitter and harsh qualities, naturally stretches itself out, fleeing or retiring from them as much as it can. Behmen illustrates this with a *comparison* of a man tasting an astringent, bitter gall, who naturally *gags* at it and widens his palate, showing thereby a natural antipathy against astringency and bitterness.—<note>This word *tasting* is an expression similar to the former one, *sensibility*. Together with what now follows, it may be illustrated by what we see several such liquids of contrary or disagreeing qualities do when mixed together.</note>

**XIII.**—But this sweet quality with its water and sap, thus fleeing and retiring in its antipathy from the bitter and astringent, only makes them more eager to follow after it. It causes the astringent spirit especially to press more earnestly upon it. This "causing" is nothing else but a more lively stirring and raising up of its internal property, desiring to be refreshed by that sweet water, to satisfy its own natural dryness, and to have such a fit subject before it as may be capable of its operation.

**XIV.**—This operation is, according to the natural inseparable constitution of this astringent quality, a continual attracting, coagulating and (in conjunction with the heat) a drying and thickening of the water or sap. By this, the sap comes to have a certain visible color and a tangible, shaped body according to the kind of the original seed.

**XV.**—This fleeing and pursuing continues until the water is all consumed and the sweet quality is made entirely weak, so that it can eventually retreat no further. This is the true growing or vegetation in this four-element world, where it can only be done successively, gradually, and little by little. For,

**XVI.**—This sweet quality with its water, kindled more and more from above by the sun's heat and pressed upon from below by the bitter and harsh qualities, cannot but flee and retreat in its natural antipathy more and more. It not only first springs up above the ground and stretches itself out on every side in a circle, but also presses directly forward, or rather upward toward the sun, as if to escape their violence. But being always further and further pursued by the other opposites, and especially by the astringent quality, it cannot but be successively more and more coagulated and compacted; and so, therefore, a long and round stock or stalk grows up.

**XVII.**—The stalk is always thicker at the bottom and thinner or smaller above at the top, decreasing in its quantity little by little. This is because the sweet water-spirit first has its full strength but loses it successively more and more, until at length it grows so weak and powerless that it cannot retreat any higher but must submit and be, as it were, captivated by the other properties.

**XVIII.**—The different colors and their changes, occurring separately in one and the same plant—where we may see that the herb or plant first appears whitish below and then changes into green, brown, yellowish, etc.—are from the various predominances of the different qualities in the outermost surface of the stalk, affected by the sun's heat and light.

**XIX.**—The branches, leaves, knots, and so on, all have their origin from that continual strife between the contrary qualities, which is sometimes carried on more regularly and gently, and sometimes with storm or violence. The latter especially is the cause of knots; it must be assumed wherever we see a knot that there has been such a vehement assault made upon the sweet water that it was almost at its end, but it had the strength to escape and get through again. [In the *Signatura Rerum*, Behmen declares this formation of the knots, etc., much more deeply, reflecting more upon the generation of eternal nature, saying for instance, "Each of the properties pursue..."]

the sweet water: Mars raves and rages, Mercury is terrified by it; and Saturn, by his strong impression, makes this terror or crack (which is <term>salnitral</term>, according to the third property of nature) corporeal; and thus the knots come to be. In this terror, Mercury moves to the side and takes Venus along with him, which causes a spreading forth of twigs and branches, etc.

XX.—When the water is so far spent and dried up, or coagulated and compacted by the sun’s heat from without and the first astringent property within—and consequently the sweet quality has lost so much of its strength that it can no longer press forward to preserve itself—it is necessitated to yield to the contrary qualities. It does this by spreading out the small residue of its sweet watery essence, as if in a round court or ball, and admitting all the other qualities into it. And this now is the generation of a round bud or head, which the astringent spirit compacts, and wherein all the rest further act their parts, each of them according to its own natural aim, until another grain or seed is produced within it in perfect likeness to that first seed from which this growth came forth.

XXI.—In this bud, the sweet quality with its water may now be compared in a sense to a pregnant woman, who, having conceived a seed (the other crude qualities) into her womb, must now herself bring it further to maturity and labor for its opening and bringing forth. For this sweet water must bring forth from here the proper natural children of all the other properties.

XXII.—These children are the various leaves of the flowers and blossoms, of such various and sometimes also mixed colors. All of these are no longer (like the green leaves were on the stem below) of the water quality’s nature and condition, but according to that of all the other qualities and their manifold combinations, etc.

For the sweet water, now impregnated with all these qualities, cannot bring forth children according to its own nature, but must bring them forth according to the constitution of that seed with which it is impregnated.

XXIII.—When these red, white, yellow, blue, and other children are brought forth, their sweet mother grows faint and weary and is not able to nourish them very long. For they are not only very tender in themselves but also, with respect to this mother, are in a certain sense only like her stepchildren. This is because they were not generated freely, nor from, nor according to her own natural quality, but according to the others, and as if by constraint, when the sweet quality had decayed and all the others had overpowered and captivated her.

XXIV.—When, therefore, the sun’s heat from without presses upon these tender flowers and blossoms, all the qualities in them are stirred up and enlivened. For the spirit of life—even that true vegetable life which is in every plant according to its kind—is now exalted in them to the highest degree. Since these tender flowers are too weak for this strong spirit and cannot bear it, they must surrender their various noble virtues, which they send out from them in a lively, pleasant smell or perfume; but they themselves must soon after fall away and wither. And so now the plant’s growth decreases and turns back or downward, in a good and true sense, though in another sense it still goes forward toward the maturity of the seed or fruit.

XXV.—For in this flourishing and blossoming of plants (even of thorns and thistles also), a conjunction is made manifest, more or less, between time and eternity, or earth and paradise.

And eternity, as it were, beholds or represents itself in time by a visible image, partaking more or less of both. For in this smell especially, something of a paradisical property is opened. This does not mean that the smell itself—as far as it can be perceived by the earthly sense or nose—is purely paradisical, for it is according to the condition of this third principle; rather, it means only that something of a paradisical property lies and opens itself within it more or less, according to the different kinds of plants.

XXVI.—This paradisical property also shows forth its own signature through the many beautiful colors, while the temporal earthly property expresses its character through the subtle green leaves surrounding the blossoms and flowers.

For the various colors are according to the various dispositions of all the other qualities besides that of the sweet water, and they are also rightly called their colors. Yet they are not absolutely their own, such that they could produce them without a concurrence of the hidden inward world. But there is in this blossoming a transmutation (of the <term>sulphur</term> and its <term>sal</term>, says Behmen, wherein all the qualities are understood) into paradise, or into a paradisical property and joy. <note>Note: This is another such expression like several we had above, and it is used by Behmen frequently on various occasions and regarding different matters. In the sense that the harsh, dark, and bitter qualities can be conceived as naturally desiring their perfection, reconciliation, rest, and satisfaction, they may also be said to be rejoiced—that is, content, satisfied, and acquiescent—when they have obtained it. Moreover, a real and proper joy, delight, and pleasure is caused and raised in man when he beholds the wonderful workmanship of God in Nature, especially when he understands how a paradisical property is manifest in it.</note>

XXVII.—In this conjunction now between time and eternity, or earth and paradise, consists that highest degree into which the spirit of life in all plants (each according to its kind and capacity) is or can be exalted; and this degree can now rise no higher. For though that other stage might also be called the principal thing, but only with respect to the inward hidden world—and manifested in such a manner in the pleasant smell and taste of the fruits—yet what is done here in the blossoming is the principal thing with respect to this outward, four-elementary world, and the chief benefit brought forth by it to creatures. From here, therefore, the growth turns, as it were, back or downward toward earthliness.

XXVIII.—Seeing that the kingdom of this outward world is only temporal, having its own dominion or government as a principle by itself, and lying moreover under the curse and vanity, this paradisical property with its image, character, and signature cannot stay very long in it, but soon withdraws into its own center. And this <term>third principle</term>, according to its own natural right or privilege given to it on the third day of creation and confirmed immediately after the deluge, is only for such a grain or seed to be brought forth from the blossom as may be perfectly according to the sort and kind of the first, and may have in it the same quality and capacity of bringing forth and multiplying again in the same manner.

And thus the Circle of Vegetation is ended or concluded, by the end’s returning into its own beginning. <note>As Time or Temporal Nature herself shall terminate, pages 5, 6.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the physical growth of plants to a spiritual and alchemical explanation of human redemption and the "Philosophical Work," drawing parallels between the fall of Adam and the processes described in Jacob Behmen’s (Boehme's) *Signatura Rerum*.</meta>

[If space allowed, we might now continue to present further illustrations of the workings of the seven properties of nature in this temporal birth, but the present may suffice for our purpose of displaying the divine science of Behmen and Freher, and its substantial concentration in LAW.]

The following curious and interesting paper, consistent with the tone and spirit of this entire treatise, has also been selected for insertion with the preceding extracts. It is entitled "THE PROCESS IN THE PHILOSOPHICAL WORK, considered as thoroughly ANALOGICAL with that in MAN’S REDEMPTION through JESUS CHRIST; and REPRESENTED by POSITIONS given of it, as to its PRINCIPAL POINTS in BEHMEN’S SIGNATURA RERUM, chapters vii, x, xi, xii:"—

I.—Adam's original state in paradise, and the manner in which he corrupted himself and his entire created being by his lustful imagination for the knowledge of good and evil, is correctly spoken of by this author, not only at the beginning of his description, but also frequently repeated and variously expressed throughout his entire discourse. For if man does not understand his own corrupted nature, and the curse under which he himself lies, how can he be expected to understand the nature and curse of the earth? Or upon what ground can he presume to deliver such a specific thing from that curse, or to be instrumental in this deliverance? This is the true artist's only business.

II.—As long as Adam remained in a pure, paradisiacal innocence, the eternal Word and power of life (called by Behmen the *heavenly mercury*) was his leader and had predominance in him. His life, which was a clear, flaming fire, burned in and was nourished by that pure spiritual oil of the Divine substance; which, together with the holy water of eternal life, is generated in the angelic world. Therefore, this could not help but give forth a glorious, bright, shining light.

III.—Through the power of his imagination, or lust for the knowledge of good and evil, that which was then still kept under in him, and so was hidden from him—namely, the outward watery property—became manifest in his holy oil and gained predominance in it. This oil, therefore, now overpowered by it, could no longer be such a suitable food and benefit to his fire as it was before. And so his fire not only lost its shining light, but also became corrupted itself; for it was obscured and made entirely impotent. And his mercury, which before in his holy oil had caused and raised up paradisiacal joy and triumph according to its moving and stirring property, was now made into a stinging, agonizing poison, according to its own natural constitution, which it does and must remain in when it is before or without the light.

IV.—Nothing of the Divine substance was thereby corrupted, poisoned, or turned into evil, though sometimes certain expressions used in respect to man may seem, in outward appearance, to say something of the kind. For that which was in man of the Divine substance faded, disappeared, or died indeed, but only with respect to man; seeing that this disappearing was but a re-entry into its own secret origin, and so but a returning to God, the giver of it.

When, on the contrary, the created mercury—that is, man’s own life—went forth with its will, desire, and lust out of eternity into time, the former union was broken. Upon this breach, its own natural property and character could not help but be made manifest immediately. Because of this manifestation, which should never have been made according to the will of God, it is now rightly called corrupted, poisoned, and turned into evil; yet all this does not reach the Divine substance, nor the holy life of God, but only that of man.

V.—This is the substance of what Behmen largely declares concerning man's paradisiacal state and his falling away from it under the curse. Here he also brings in, for a clearer illustration, not only the fall of Lucifer—saying of him that his desire was to test the fiery mercury, just as man desired to test the watery—but also the serpent with its poison, saying that in the strongest and most poisonous mercury the highest tincture lies, yet not in its own natural property, etc. All of this he represents as a most proper and pertinent introduction to this discourse on the philosophical work.

VI.—Immediately after the fall of man, God said to the serpent, "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; her seed shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." And herein the philosopher's stone or tincture lies implicitly. For though this primarily concerns man, yet secondarily it concerns the whole creation also; and this bruising of the serpent's head is done both spiritually and physically, and both in time and in eternity, and though in different degrees, yet in a parallel process or method, both here and there.

VII.—The serpent's sting points to the fire of wrath, and the woman's seed to the fire of light and love. These two are in everything; and in the curse, the former became predominant in outward nature. This latter must now be raised up again, and by its shining through the wrath, it must subdue and keep it under, taking away its predominant power so that it may keep and exercise only its true natural office as a servant in and to the light. These two may no longer stand in contrariety and opposition to each other, but be one single thing, harmonized by light and love, and reintroduced into paradise. And when the dark, poisoned mercury is thus tinctured, his agonizing death is turned into triumphant life and joy, and his former dark desire into a new desire of light and love; which of itself is now able to create in itself a pure substance of love and light—namely, a heavenly body out of an earthly one.

VIII.—The whole work is summarized in this: that two things must be reduced back into one, even into such a one as they were from the beginning before they became two; a heavenly thing and an earthly one are to be joined. The former must be admitted or received into itself by the latter and must change it into its own heavenly quality. Earth must be turned inward, and heaven outward, etc. This the mercury that is within does all by himself; the artist is not to do it, nor can he do it. He is only to join together those ingredients that are required and leave the work to be done by that workman who is already within.

Yet nevertheless, Understanding and Faith are required in him; and by this latter especially he is to cooperate if his design is to take effect. For his design is nothing less than to extract a body from the curse and to raise it up from the dead, which can never be done by him who is still dead himself,<note>The following letter from the chief subject of the present treatise, and of the proposed biography,</note> both in his understanding and as to his internal life.

IX.—With all this, the process in the regeneration of man runs exactly parallel. Only consider for yourself the heavenly humanity of the Regenerator, and the earthly humanity of poor fallen man, who is to be regenerated: consider that the former must be received or taken in by the latter, and that this must allow itself to be subdued, changed, kept under, and turned inward by that. Consider that faith in man is absolutely required, by which he must in a sense cooperate indeed; but for all this, he cannot make himself a child of God, but must allow himself to be made so by the eternal speaking Word, which in the philosophical process is called by Behmen the *heavenly mercury*. This also at the end of time, as in the most complete period of the regeneration, will raise up his body again, which then shall no longer be earthly, but heavenly, and conforming to his own glorified body.

Consider all this in its true coherence and dependence upon the unique love and free grace of God: and you will certainly find that the entire description of this process is nothing else but a sound, true, and solid explanation of these words of St. John: *As many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe in his name*.

X.—In these words also lies plainly the possibility of obtaining perfection in the philosophical work, which is rightly and firmly grounded upon this by Behmen.

For if God gave us, out of his infinite love, that which is the greatest and highest, how could he have withheld from us that which is much lesser and lower? If man, in this divine power,

---

—who is, indeed, only so presented to the contemplation of the world as a personification and *standard model* of the most perfect natural development of a sound understanding, through all solid human knowledge and accomplishments, and all the experimental states of Christianity, even up to the highest intellectual science embraced in the grand mystery of all things revealed by God in Behmen—the following letter, we say, may be not unsuitably appended to the present extract. From this, the candidate will further perceive the perfect, non-idiosyncratic understanding faculty of this great genius, and the practical gospel character of all his profound science; which, like that of the Saviour himself, of Paul, of Behmen, and of all rightly illuminated prophets of all ages, could only tend to the furtherance of the one Gospel design: the conversion of sinners and unbelievers of all nations, people, and tongues.

And here we take a fresh occasion to observe, for the consideration of the candidate, that all that evangelical applicability which the personal ministry and writings of the inspired Paul possessed in reference to the generation of his day, and to the church at large since, *that same suitableness and adaptation to the present state of the unconverted intellectual world* is contained in the writings of Behmen, Freher, and Law. Indeed, the chief of these latter, or rather the whole of them jointly, are but a *further birth* of that same Spirit which brought forth the former; proceeding as immediately from the same will and wisdom, and God and Father of all. These are strong statements, but they are the results of a clear apprehension of such a truth. And we do not doubt that a similar conviction will be forced upon others who are familiar with the works in question, after a perusal of the several sections of this treatise.

The letter in question was written by Law to an intimate friend, who possibly—like many mystical and natural philosophers of the last century (even Newton himself, as referred to in the note on p. 46), and as a few even in our day—might have been dabbling in alchemical studies and experiments in search of the philosopher's stone. However, they were not sufficiently versed in the mystery of truth to perceive the futility of all such attempts without not only an apprehension of the union and mutual cooperation of the powers of eternal and temporal nature (which can only be the result of a high degree of sanctity, devotion, and purity, such as might be expected in a *Theo-sophic College*), but also of an especial appointment by God to that end, for the same purposes indeed as St. Paul was endowed with his divine wisdom and miraculous virtue.

But how few even of our modern rational Christians, with all their learning and ingenuity, have the sagacity or a *will* to perceive this essential truth: that the attainment and manipulative exercise of high illumination must be founded in the simple experimental religion of the Gospel, in death to the old man, and the real resurrection of the new life of Christ—the light of eternity—in the soul. In a word, by actually passing through all the mystical deaths and births in the soul which stand between human corruption and the light of God. The letter is as follows:—

> “My dear L——,—I cannot tell you how much I love you. But that which of all things I have most at heart with regard to you is the real progress of your soul in the divine life. Heaven seems to be awakened in you. It is a tender plant; it requires stillness, meekness, and the unity of the heart, totally given up to the unknown workings of the Spirit of God, which will do all its work in the calm soul that has no hunger or desire but to escape out of the mire of its earthly life into its lost union and life in God.
>
> I mention this out of a fear of your giving into an eagerness for many things which, though seemingly innocent, yet divide and weaken the workings of the divine life within you. For a *multiplicity of wills* is the *only evil*, disease, and misery, both of our souls and bodies. That which can make the soul have *one will* and *one love* is the *universal tincture* both for soul and body: and it is nothing else. That alone can take the fall or curse out of the body which can take it out of the soul. For the curse through all nature and creature is but one and the same thing, namely, the absence of the heavenly power. Heaven is dead in gold, just as it is dead in man; and its heavenly tincture can only be made alive in the same manner, and from the same power, as the inward man is born again of the water and spirit from above.
>
> Our outward man must be tormented, crucified, and mortified in the fire of our own flesh and blood: and then it is as the impure gold in the crucible heated by earthly fire. But as no fiery torments of our own flesh and blood can glorify our inward man and set him in his first angelic state, so no outward fire can torment gold into its first heavenly state. Our Lord said to the crucified thief, *Today you shall be with me in Paradise*.
>
> Now no one is a *divine Magus* until he is thus qualified to say to his subject, *Today you shall be with me in Paradise*. If he himself is not in paradise, he can do no paradisiacal work.—But, my friend, let not what I say here set you to disputing this point with anyone, for I say it for a quite contrary end: to show you the vanity of all such discourse. My dear soul, adieu. Oct. 16th, 1752.”

<meta>This page continues the argument that if man, through free grace, can triumph over spiritual death and the devil, he should also be enabled to triumph over the physical curse of the earth, provided he possesses the necessary spiritual qualities.</meta>

bestowed upon him by free grace, can truly rule and triumph again over sin, death, the devil, and hell, to whom he made himself subject by his lust, Why should he not also be enabled thereby, to rule and triumph again over the curse in the earth, which he brought into it by the same lust? This latter is but a natural consequence of the former; indeed, an inconsiderable one in comparison to it. Truly it is inseparable from it, *if that former be really attained, and provided that all the qualities that are required for it are truly found in the artist or Philosopher.*

XI.—All these qualities are, as in their principal sum and substance, concentrated in this: *that the artist first must have the curse transmuted in himself into the heavenly blessing, through the holy tincturing blood of Jesus Christ.* Which Behmen sometimes expresses this way: He must first be, and really have that same thing in himself, which he will make or introduce into metals outside of himself. And this he frequently presses home to everyone, warning earnestly and calling heaven and earth to be witnesses, *that none shall presume to meddle with the curse in the earth, before he is really delivered, as to his inward man, from that curse in himself; otherwise* he may expect to earn nothing but a curse instead of a blessing. Before this, his own internal deliverance, he may indeed have many fine notions of this work in his brain; *but the real process cannot be manifest in him, and so cannot be understood by him in that experimental fullness and exactness which is required.*

XII.—This same point he also offers for the serious consideration of such a person, under these and similar philosophical terms: He is to know that his Mercury is kindled in the fiery Mars, and burns in the eternal Saturn, in the terrible impression of darkness; his Venus is captivated, his water dried up, his Jupiter has become a fool, his Sun is darkened, and his Moon turned into a black night. And now there is no other remedy but to take Venus (the eternal love of God) and to introduce that into his poisoned Mercury and Mars, so that they may be tinctured by it, and then his sun will shine again and Jupiter rejoice, etc. This he represents afterward in plain words from his own way, practice, and experience.

XIII.—Yet all this, though really attained, will not yet be fully sufficient. For there is not only a sufficient *ability* for this work and a sufficient *understanding* of its process required (which I do not doubt Behmen had), but there is also required a *special calling* to it, which he did not have. Without this calling, the artist goes only in his own will, even if his meaning and intent, as far as he thinks, were ever so good and pure. And this call he must be able to discern by its own internal character—which it carries along with and within itself—from his own natural impulse. That impulse may easily delude him under the specious appearance of a divine call, whereby the spirit of this world (which from its own internal constitution is mightily in favor of such an undertaking) will certainly mislead him into various dangers.

XIV.—When these two more general requisites—namely, (1) an experimental understanding from the artist's process in his own regeneration, and (2) a Divine call for this undertaking—are truly found in him, two other more particular qualities will still be required in him when he is to make a beginning of his work. And these are represented by Behmen from that parable of our Lord concerning a man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and was robbed and wounded by highwaymen; saying, that the artist must truly and wholly stand in the figure of the merciful Samaritan and must have both his *will* and *eyes*. His will, so that he may desire nothing else but to heal and restore that which is wounded and broken; his eyes, so that he may be able to discern that wounded body which he is to heal, and which is not easily discerned—and not by everyone—because of its great corruption.

XV.—These eyes he shall have the greatest need of in his very first beginning, to choose the proper matter for this work. This is called by Behmen and described parabolically as *That evil child, which has run from its mother's house (from Jerusalem to Jericho) and desired to be in itself, or to stand by itself upon its own bottom.* And this must be sought for in Saturn; which Saturn, therefore, the artist must have sharp and piercing eyes to look into, both as to eternal and temporal nature. For the wrath of God, by its strong astringent impression (he says), has shut it up into the chamber of death. Not that it has turned the same into Saturn <note>Which I think is to say that it has not turned into lead.</note>, but it keeps it imprisoned in the Saturnine death, in the first cold, hard, dark, astringent property; which is called the great still-standing death, because as yet there is no mobility of life in it.

XVI.—When this proper matter is found in Saturn, the artist may go to work, but only so *that he considers and follows that same PROCESS which God observed in the redemption of mankind through Jesus Christ (in which twofold holy Name, the general process was clearly understood by Behmen from the language of Nature), even from his conception and nativity, to his resurrection and ascension.* So doing, he may come to find the joyful feast of Pentecost, namely, that desirable tincture in outward nature, which corresponds to that holy spiritual tincture whereby St. Peter, in his first public sermon on the day of Pentecost, tinctured three thousand souls at once. Now observe:

XVII.—When the human mercury, the outspoken word of the human life, was infected and poisoned by the serpent, or made manifest in its own natural quality (which it has in itself before and without the light), God did not reject humanity so as to annihilate it wholly and make another new and strange Adam, but he regenerated that which was spoiled. And this he effected not by any such new or strange thing which humanity had not had in it before, but by that self-same holy divine mercury which at first was breathed into Adam to make him an image and likeness of God. This he reintroduced again into the poisoned humanity and thereby made a good, sure, and solid disposition for its new regeneration. And this was done in the immaculate conception of Jesus Christ. For in that, a conjunction was made between the eternal speaking Word and the human outspoken word, mercury, or human life, now poisoned in man and full of self or own will.

XVIII.—This must be the first consideration of the artist, to be well observed, so that he may be sure to act accordingly and not bring his subject matter to the fire without such a previous conjunction; if he does not wish to work in vain and make himself ridiculous. And for an illustration of this, this may serve: in the Second Principle of light, the love-desire (that is, the first property of eternal nature, but considered as in the fifth) makes a pure crystalline substantiality. And in there, the divine mercury is the eternal holy Word and understanding: but in the first principle, where-

In the harsh, astringent desire, a dark, obscure substantiality is made; this same mercury is a principal part, or chief property, of the wrath of God, and an original source of all mobility and moving power. This mercury, therefore (considered as in the outspoken Word, or life of man), after it was turned away from the second principle of light and love, and was made manifest according to its own wrathful property in the first, could not have been restored or brought back again except by that very same mercury which was first breathed into man. This mercury was not altered in the light and love of God, though it was altered in man, in whom it disappeared and lost its former pre-eminence. Now, regaining this lost pre-eminence again—either in man or in any other creature, according to its own kind—is nothing else but that same tincturing and transmuting which is spoken of in all this discourse. Therefore, the pre-eminence of that heavenly mercury must necessarily reproduce such a pure light's substantiality as that which disappeared in man by his fall, and in the earth by the curse. [Let him who reads, understand.]

XIX.—In the account from St. Luke concerning what the child Jesus did with his parents in the twelfth year of his age, a representation is seen of the inward and outward world, and of their different wills. For the inward will in Jesus first broke the natural will of his parents when he remained in the temple without their knowledge or consent; indeed, he also said, as if rebuking them, *How is it that you sought me? Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business?*

And then again, the will of this outward world in his parents broke the inward will in Jesus, for he went down with them to Nazareth and was subject to them. This shows to the artist that in his work he shall soon find such a twofold will also. The will of the inward world will not initially condescend and be subject to his will.

But if he does not cease to seek after it, as Mary did, and *wrestles with it all night like Jacob, with a full resignation of his own will (which is the will of this outward world), this Divine will will at length condescend to him and go down with him; for it is, as it were, broken or conquered by his will.*

XX.—Here the artist, or *magus*, is to know that he is not to bring that will or tendency toward perfection into this matter from the outside, but that it already lies within it.

He must only *first in himself* be capable of the Divine will, and then with his own renewed or tinctured will—which here is his *magical faith*—he must handle his subject matter. In this way, the will toward perfection, which indeed lies in the matter but remains still and immovable, may be stirred up and brought into conjunction with his human tinctured will, and so also with the Divine will. Furthermore, this Divine will may press forward or outward to meet with and bless that outward will, which presses backward or inward from corruption into God's love and mercy.

XXI.—*This point is highly recommended to the artist, not only to consider and understand but also to make his continual practice. Because the Philosophical baptism, for the most part, consists of this, and this practice is its very first beginning.* This alone can make him able to baptize truly and rightly, for he is to baptize his matter not only with the water of the outward world but also with that of the inward world. More on this hereafter.

XXII.—The poor fallen humanity, considered barely as it was in and of itself—namely, as broken, spoiled, and poisoned—was not cast immediately into the fiery furnace and melted down by the wrath of God; but, as said before, a conjunction was first made between the earthly and heavenly humanity.

Neither did the great fiery trial come upon it immediately after this conjunction; rather, a long and wonderful process was held before it came to that great earnestness. First, the humanity was to be baptized with water in the Jordan and with water from above the firmament. Furthermore, it was led into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil; this devil <note>N.B.</note> was not put into the humanity but permitted to stand against it and to offer to it all that the first Adam was tempted with. And during all this time of forty days, no outward food was given to this newly baptized humanity, but it was to live upon its own life's mercury <note>mercurius</note>—namely, the eternal Word proceeding from the mouth of God, according to the answer the Lord Jesus gave to the devil. After this, he came forth in public, preached, and did great wonders in all the seven properties of nature. And though at length even his human body was really glorified upon the holy mount and seen so by three of his disciples, yet by all this, the full perfection was not yet wrought out; the very greatest and sharpest trial was still to come. Corresponding to all this process, the Philosophical work must also be carried on, and the artist will see a continual parallelism. But at length, he will also find that all of this, though it was shown to him in a most glorious appearance, is still short of perfection and is all, as it were, preliminary.

XXIII.—By the Philosophical baptism, if it be truly performed, the hunger after the heavenly substantiality *is stirred and raised up again* in the dead mercury, which lies in impotence and hungers only after its own property, being of itself not capable of either desiring or admitting any other <note>N.B.</note>.

And by this hunger, that heavenly substantiality is *drawn in*, with its own peculiar will, desire, or inclination, which is nothing else but a readiness or tendency to become manifest with its life in death. And herein is the first beginning of a new body, or rather of a seed from which a new body is to come forth in its due time.

XXIV.—What this Philosophical Baptism is, and the absolute necessity of it, may be represented thus: Every hunger is a desire after such a thing as is conformable to that hunger, for no hunger can exist for that which is disagreeing or contrary to it. The dead, corrupted mercury then has a hunger indeed, but only (according to its own condition in the curse) after death, wrath, poison, etc. If now such a dead and wrathful thing as it hungers after is given to this hunger, the death within it must necessarily increase, and its wrathfulness must be strengthened by it. But if life is presented to this hunger, or a living, heavenly property is offered, death is not at all able to receive it. To this death, therefore, the death and wrath of God must be given, but within this death and wrath, the heavenly substantiality. And this is the Philosophical baptism, for this is that earthly and heavenly water, in the first of which is death and in the second, life. Both must be together, for the reason is now plain why this baptism cannot be performed by either one alone. But when it is thus rightly done, this baptism—namely, that which is heavenly—swallows up into death that which is earthly and wrathful, and exalts its own new life therein. However, this does not happen immediately, just as it was not done in Christ immediately after his baptism. [Along with this, consider portions of the Note of p. 3: for every dis-

XXV.—This philosophical baptism is nothing but a conjunction to be made between the fiery and the watery mercury. The fiery must be baptized with the watery. And this is what Behmen means by saying obscurely: take care only for this, that you baptize the mercury with its own baptism. For this watery mercury is its own—that is, it is that which <margin>before</margin> <insert>^</insert> the fall and the curse it enjoyed and rejoiced in as its most precious treasure, by which its fiery, poisonous wrath was kept down and prevented from becoming manifest. But when these two were separated from each other, a breach was made which cannot be healed again except by a renewed conjunction between them. It is the same in animals and in fallen man, only different in degree.

The conjunction of male and female, which is absolutely required for the multiplication of every kind of living creature (which also has something corresponding to it in vegetables), may be a good illustration of this. And therefore it is—

XXVI.—That Behmen calls this very same thing, which is here now called the philosophical baptism, a matrimony or espousal, when he plainly says not only that a fair, loving virgin of its own kind must be given in marriage to the earthly, wrathful mercury, but also that this same giving is the philosophical baptism.

And again he says, "The woman’s (not the man’s) seed shall bruise the serpent’s head." The man has the fire-spirit in his tincture, and the woman has the water-spirit in hers.

This latter must baptize, soften, and overcome the former, and so transmute its strong fiery hunger for wrath into a tender desire for love; and herein lies the baptism of nature. In this steadfast desire for love, these two are at last turned into one, so that they are no longer male and female, fire and water in opposition, but a masculine virgin with both tinctures in union. But before this is wholly achieved, and as long as they are in the process toward it, Behmen calls them throughout this discourse the *young man and the virgin*, or also the bride and the bridegroom.

XXVII.—Immediately after the baptism of Christ, he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. A serious consideration of the whole process in this threefold temptation is highly recommended to the artist. For in this philosophical work the same must also be done, in total correspondence to the three particulars therein relating to the first three properties. All this is largely declared by Behmen, the sum and substance of which is this:

XXVIII.—The human soul, or the whole of humanity as an image of the eternal speaking Word, was now tested—after God had reintroduced into it a spark of his eternal love—to see whether it would return to its original state and place and be an instrument for God to be played upon by his Holy Spirit in his love, or whether it would rather continue in its own will and allow the devil to play upon its instrument in the wrath and anger of God. And so in the philosophical work also, the earthly poisonous mercury, after it is now joined again to the heavenly, is tested to see whether it will leave its own natural wrathful property and allow itself to be turned into its first, pure, and crystalline condition, in which it stood before the curse, or whether it will instead continue in its own awakened and now dominant quality.

XXIX.—In our Lord Jesus Christ, the human will rejected all the devil’s presentations and offerings, resigned itself, and entered wholly into the first mother’s womb, according to his words to Nicodemus, etc. And so in the philosophical work, if it goes well and right, the artist will see that when the tempter comes, the young man (or mercury) gives himself up wholly to the first mother, and she will swallow him up as if into nothing. At this the artist will be amazed and terrified, thinking that all is lost and undone, for he sees nothing and has lost all appearance of heaven. He must have patience; that which is impossible in his sight is not so in the powers of nature.

XXX.—The wilderness where this temptation takes place is, in this philosophical work, the outward, earthly, dry, desolate, and barren body.

In this, the young man (or the mercury) is not able to stand against the devil unless he lays hold of his virgin and is supported by her. He is, therefore, to unite with her, to cast his will and desire into her love, and to eat of her bread, not of his own natural quality, just as Christ our Lord, during all the forty days of his temptation, ate only of the eternal speaking Word and would not eat of that bread which he could have made out of the stones. All of this is nothing but the mercury admitting and receiving the heavenly tincture into its own poisonous quality, and allowing the serpent’s head—the fiery, wrathful property—to be bruised thereby within itself. If he does not do this, the devil will prevail and keep him captive in that state in which he exists when separated from his virgin. But if he does, the devil must withdraw, and the virgin takes his seed from him into her womb. [As Note on p. 71.]

XXXI.—What the devil is in this work, the artist (says Behmen) will easily know, but he does not call him by any plain or distinct name. Doubtless, it is some other wrathful, dark, and poisonous matter that may be fitly compared to the devil, and may be able to perform the devil’s office in this process because of the similar qualities in both. Thus he says: the artist shall take care not to allow this tempting devil to be too furious or too wrathful, but proportionate, etc.

And again, on the other hand, that he should not be too weak, for otherwise the mercury would not be sufficiently assaulted by him and might, like a hungry wolf, swallow up his baptism, return to his own wrathful property, and still continue as that same poisonous thing he was before.

XXXII.—At the end of forty days, when the devil had ended all the temptation, he had to depart from the Lord Christ, and the angels came and ministered to him. This also the artist is to observe especially well, for he himself stood here in the fiery trial also, and may now perceive infallibly whether or not he is fit for and accounted worthy of his work. If at the end of forty days, in correspondence to the process of Christ, the angels do not appear, he may surely think of himself that he is not yet fit and worthy; and of his fiery masculine mercury, that it does not yet stand in a proper internal union with the watery feminine, but that it is still the same in its own wrathful property as it was before, and that the devil has prevailed. But if he sees the sign of the angels, he may rejoice and be sure that the bridegroom is in his bride, and she in him, and that his work can prosper. What this sign of the angels is, the author does not say expressly; it must be some new, delightful appearance, by its own character as intelligible to the artist as that was intelligible to him when he previously saw nothing and had lost the appearance of heaven.

XXXIII.—Immediately after this temptation and the overcoming of the devil, the Lord Christ

began his public office, not only by preaching, rebuking, and instructing the people, but also by working many great miracles through all the properties of nature. For instance: in Saturn, he raised the dead; in Luna, he changed water into wine and fed five thousand men with five loaves of bread; in Jupiter, he made the most wise and understanding apostles out of ignorant and simple fishermen; in Mercury, he made the deaf hear and the mute speak, and he healed the lepers; in Mars, he drove out demons from the possessed; in Venus, he loved his brothers and sisters in his humanity and freely gave his life unto death. Only six of the properties are listed here; the seventh, which is Sol, standing in the middle and uniting three and three, is not mentioned here because it belongs to full perfection. That perfection was only attained when he had risen from the dead, ascended to heaven, and poured out the holy tincturing spirit on the day of Pentecost. But the fact that Behmen has good reason for distinctly referring all miraculous deeds to the seven properties of nature could be sufficiently demonstrated from his writings, were it necessary.

XXXIV.—All this the artist shall now clearly see—that there is an exact correspondence in the Philosophical work once the forty-day temptation has ended successfully. In Saturn, he shall see that the mercury now raises from death that same substance in which it was previously imprisoned. In Luna, he shall see that it feeds and nourishes that substance when nothing is outwardly produced by which it could be fed and nourished; and again, that the deadly water is exalted and turned into wine, having now achieved (just as wine has) a union of fiery and watery virtue. In Jupiter, he shall see the four elements, each by itself, and their colors, and the rainbow upon which Christ sits for judgment in the outspoken mercury; he shall be greatly amazed by it and perceive that the wisdom of God plays and delights in it. For friendly Jupiter shows his properties here in such a way as God will, in due time, change this world and transmute it into paradise.

In Mercury, he shall see that heaven separates itself from the earth, and that it sinks back into the earth and changes it into its own color, and that mercury purifies the matter, etc. In Mars, he shall see that Jupiter, within the Mercury, casts a black fire-smoke upward from the matter, which will coagulate like soot in a chimney. This is the poisonous hunger in the mercury, which is rightly compared to the devil because, according to its own kind, it has the devil's qualities. What Christ did in Venus, the artist shall see most gloriously in the Philosophical work. For as soon as this black devil is expelled from the matter, Venus appears in her virginity, in great beauty and glory, which is a fine type or emblem of the great love of Christ.

XXXV.—Now, when this appears, the artist rejoices and reasonably thinks his work is finished and that he has obtained the treasure of the world; but he shall soon find himself extremely disappointed. For when he tests it, he shall find it is only Venus—still a female and not yet a pure and perfect virgin with both tinctures united into one. Just as in Christ, the eternal speaking Word had indeed worked out all these wondrous deeds through his humanity, and yet full perfection could not be made manifest in it—his human body could not be glorified, and much less could he have poured out the Holy Spirit—before he had passed through the great anger of God, or death and hell. So also in this philosophical work: although all these glorious things have appeared in the properties of nature, the universal tincture is not yet fixed and manifest. Everything seen so far was only transient, and the greatest work to be done for this fixation and manifestation still remains. For all seven properties must be made totally pure and crystalline before they can be paradisiacal, and each of them has its own peculiar process when it is to move from the wrathful into the paradisiacal life. In that life, all seven must have only one will—namely, that of love—and all their former individual wills, in which each acted for itself in opposition to the others, must be utterly swallowed up. Only then are they fixed and able to endure the fire, for then no Turba can exist within them anymore.

This is then further effected by a process corresponding to what was observed in the suffering and death of Christ.

XXXVI.—As soon as the regenerator of mankind came into this world from above and was given the name of a king, the civil government could not endure him; he was immediately persecuted by Herod and at length crucified by Pilate, though he had plainly declared that his kingdom was not of this world. And because this newborn king did not come with royal state and splendor, nor with such outward power as the Jews expected and hoped for at the coming of their Messiah, the ecclesiastical government, represented by the high priest and Pharisees, would not receive him.

And since he acknowledged himself to be the Son of God and a king of truth, and said he had come to save his people from their sins and darkness and from the wrath to come, the devil also could not endure him. There was immediately a strong opposition against all three of these together. So also in this philosophical work: as soon as Venus appears in her beauty, with her own natural character and in preparation for perfection, there is a great alarm, opposition, and insurrection against her, manifest in Saturn, Mercury, and Mars. The first of these is a true figure of the civil government, the second of the ecclesiastical state, and the third of the devil. And as these three together were the chief agents that brought the Lord of Life and Glory to his death, so in this philosophical work, the three inferior, wrathful properties—Saturn, Mercury, and Mars—are rightly called by Behmen the murderers of Venus.

XXXVII.—This great opposition and uproar against the Lord Christ had no other basis in internal truth and reality than this: that he was from above, while all three of these were from beneath.

Deep, great, and many things are comprised in these few words, and the essential nature of a Principle (taken in Behmen's sense) is understood through them. If the Lord had come out of their own dark, harsh, bitter, and wrathful root, and if he had appeared to preserve and establish it in its own selfish and willful qualities, they would have received him very kindly, and no opposition would have been made.

But he was from another principle and came only to destroy the works of the devil in this world and to recall its inhabitants to light, love, and truth. Now, all this was bad news to these three parties, for none of them was willing to be stripped of its selfish greatness, dignity, strength, and power; therefore, they all three at length agreed to his crucifixion. So also

In this philosophical work, there is no other basis for this great opposition but this very same: that Venus is from above, while these three are from beneath, united in one wrathful sphere and unwilling to be deprived of their natural power and dominance.

Heaven now stands in hell, on earth, and will transmute them both into paradise; and hell perceives its ruin is inevitable if it receives this child from heaven into itself, and therefore it swells up against it and opposes all it can. But by this very opposition, it must and does only promote its own destruction, as was also done in the process of Christ.

XXXVIII.—Here it might be objected: How can all this be consistent with what was done and declared above—namely, that the matter was purified, the devil expelled, and the sign of the angels appeared, and so on?

For if so, from where can such a wrathful, hellish opposition now arise? The answer given to this by Behmen himself (though only implicitly, and not so directly) is of the greatest importance, not only in this philosophical process but also especially in the process of man’s regeneration. When Mercury, he says, is awakened from the death of Saturn’s strong impression and receives manna (heavenly food, the substantiality of light and love, his own true virgin, the water of life, the philosophical baptism) into the mouth of his poisonous property, a joyful crack [shriek] indeed arises; for it is as if a light were kindled in the darkness, and a paradisiacal joy and triumph arises in the midst of the wrath. When Mercury now gets a twinkling glimpse of this in Mars, the wrathfulness is terrified by the love and sinks back, just as in the generation of the second principle out of the first; and the angelic properties appear as in a glimpse.

And so this is (*Note:* not yet a transmutation, but) like a transmutation, though it is only transient and not yet fixed.

If, therefore, a fixed and radical transmutation is to be achieved, the same process that was like a transmutation must be repeated again, but in a far higher or rather deeper degree. It can also be repeated because the harsh, bitter, wrathful, and hellish properties were until now suppressed only in part, but not fully rooted out and radically turned into one single will. They are therefore now raised afresh by this appearance of Venus—indeed, even much more than they were before—and they stand up in opposition against her to maintain their own natural rights. So here also, in a sense, the words of Christ are true: "I have come to kindle a fire, and to bring a sword and enmity upon the earth," etc.

XXXIX.—This opposition in this philosophical work is between three and three, just as it is in the generation of eternal nature.

Yet this is to be understood in a way that the previous position can support, in which it was asserted that nothing here is yet permanent and fixed. So it was also in the process with the Lord Christ: when he was going into the intense severity of the wrath and anger of God in order to complete his great work, he said expressly of himself, "I am not alone, but the Father is with me." At that time, he had with him on the one side (or from above) the Father, who was unalterable in one sense, though changeable in another regarding the sensitivity of his outward human person. This may be seen by his woeful cry on the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me!" As for the objection some now make concerning a wrong translation of these words, it is not to be regarded, because the meaning of them is not what they imagine. And on the other side (or from beneath), he had with him, though in a very low degree and in a significant sense, the common ignorant people, who received and accompanied him with great joy and cheers when he came riding on a donkey into Jerusalem. So also in this philosophical work, Venus is not alone, but, as it were, Jupiter is with her from above, and Luna is with her from beneath—Luna being a true figure of that common, simple, ignorant crowd. This Luna holds with Venus as long as things go well for her—that is, so long as Saturn, Mercury, and Mars do not actually exert their malice against her. But when these three murderers arise and forcibly try to put her to death or swallow her up into their wrathful pit, then Luna also changes her color and inclination, just as the common people changed their will and, instead of their former "hosanna," now cried out, "Crucify, crucify him!"

XL.—In the process of Christ, when it comes to the great earnestness, one must consider not only what was done to him outwardly by the Pharisees and High Priests, but also what was done within his own person—in body, soul, and spirit.

The two eternal principles—namely, the fire-world with its properties of wrath and anger, and the holy light-world with pure love and the light’s substantiality (or heavenly flesh and blood)—were both manifest in him and stood open against one another. The great work of redemption could not have been performed unless they entered into one another *essentially*; otherwise, no solid, fixed, and permanent transmutation of the first into the second could have been achieved.

This now caused an inexpressible terror in the humanity of Christ—namely, in his whole person, considered in all the three worlds or principles. For love was struck with terror and trembled at the rough, harsh, bitter death into which it was to give itself up, so as to be swallowed up by the wrathful properties of anger, which were all now distinctly raised up and acting according to their own nature. And anger was also struck with terror and trembled at the appearance of love, in which it was to lose its own wrathful and now predominant life. And so, from this, the outward human body in this third principle was also so violently struck with terror and trembling that its sweat was like great drops of blood falling down to the ground. Yet he then said, "Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not my will, but yours be done." These words are to be understood as spoken by the whole person of Christ—namely, in each world and property, according to the different condition of each.

For the first principle, or anger, said, "Let this cup of love be removed from me, so that I may keep my dominion over men because of their transgression." We may see an excellent type of this in Moses, when the wrath of God said to him, "Leave me alone, so that I may devour this disobedient people." But Moses, as a figure of Christ, and Christ in the highest operation of love, would not let him, but replied—first, indeed, to the same purpose—"If it be possible, let this cup pass from me," but then immediately added, "Yet not my will, but yours be done." By this, the human will of Christ, regarding this third principle, resigned itself wholly and submitted to the will of the angry Father, being obedient even to death on the cross.

So also in this philosophical work, when it comes to this great earnestness, the artist shall plainly perceive a great terror and trembling within it. He shall see that Mercury especially, which is the

<meta>This page continues the alchemical allegory comparing the "Philosophical Work" to the Passion of Christ, focusing on the trial and suffering of Venus as she is oppressed by the wrathful planetary properties of Saturn, Mercury, and Mars.</meta>

XLI.—In the process of Christ, the devil said, or thought within himself, "I am alone the great monarch in the fire; Saturn is my might, and Mercury is my life, and I am in and through them a god and prince of this world, and will therefore not allow such a one as calls himself a Prince of Love to rule here, but I will devour him in my wrath, together with his love." This he intended indeed, with the concurrence of the two principal properties of this outward world, Saturn and Mercury—the civil and ecclesiastical government. Thus also in the Philosophical work the artist shall plainly see that Venus, which is entirely passive and wholly resigned to enter into the dragon’s jaws, is surrounded on every side by Saturn, Mercury, and Mars; nay, also that they lay hold on her and bind her by injecting their poisonous rays upon her, etc.

XLII.—In the first place, Mars brings Venus to Mercury, just as the devil’s agents in the anger of God brought the Lord first to the high priest. But as this priest was already beforehand biased with hatred against him, and did not duly or truly test him, nor could look into his internal will and work of love, but looked upon him only from without, examined him superficially, and concluded that since he did not stand with them in the same will, way, and form, he was not to be tolerated among the living. But seeing that he could not execute his design to kill him, he sent him to Pilate with the character of an evildoer who had deserved death. So also in this philosophical work, this very same is the true internal signature of Mercury against Venus.

He was already before possessed with his own hateful quality and stood in opposition against her, and is therefore not able to test, much less to approve of, the loving property of Venus, but has only a will and ability to murder her. But seeing that there is in Venus another living Mercury from above, he cannot destroy her by his own power, but must confederate himself with Saturn; and unto him he delivers this Venus to be killed, just as Christ was delivered to Pontius Pilate to be crucified.

XLIII.—Pilate, a governor or lord in the dark Saturnine impression, did little inquire after or concern himself about the spiritual doctrine, light, love, and truth of Christ, but only about the government; and upon this account alone—of Christ’s being against Caesar, and his own desire to be accounted Caesar’s friend—he sentenced him to death. So here also in the philosophical work, Saturn, the dark astringent property, does not at all concern itself with this or that internal loving quality of Venus, being unable to receive anything of it into its own essence; but this great contest is only for dominance. Saturn will not lose the friendship of Mars and Mercury, which are both with him in the same sphere and jointly make up their own government therein, which must necessarily be overthrown if Venus should be permitted to arise and shine there with her light and love. And therefore he carries out that which is well-pleasing to them, and which they think may serve their wrathful government.

XLIV.—Pilate sent the Lord Christ to Herod, and he mocked him and put on him a long white garment. In this philosophical work, Herod the king corresponds to Sol, who is also a king in his own principle. And this Sol puts upon Venus a simple, lunar-like white color; for it perceives that there lies in Venus a solar, kingly power, and therefore it gives to her the white color from the property of eternal liberty, and would gladly see her open her powers there from the fire’s center and show herself in a golden luster. If Venus did this, she would indeed be a master over Mars and Mercury, but only in this outward world—a ruler in the wrath, just as this Sol is. But as the Lord said to Pilate, "My kingdom is not of this world," and would answer nothing to Herod, nor meet his expectation by working a miracle before him—because in this white garment he stood only before the justice of God and represented the poor, fallen Adam in his false self-love, of which this white robe was a very significant figure, deeply declared by Boehme. So also in the philosophical work, a breaking forth of the solar power in a golden luster from the fire’s center, tinting this white lunar appearance of Venus, is expected all in vain; because the pure union and universal tincture cannot be made manifest except first all the dark wrath and poison of Saturn, Mercury, and Mars be wholly drowned and swallowed up in blood and death.

XLV.—Herod sent the Lord Christ back again to Pilate, and he, by his soldiers, stripped him, put on him a scarlet robe, scourged him, put on his head a crown of thorns, and showed him to the multitude, who cried out, "Crucify him," etc. So also in the philosophical work, Venus is delivered again to Saturn, and he, with his strong, dark impression, lays hold of her, strips her of her fair robe, and puts on her a scarlet color, in which the wrath of Mars is lodged. This color is from Saturn’s and Mercury’s property mixed with the fiery Mars, as the artist shall distinctly see. When, now, the Lord Christ in this royal robe—which was put upon him only in scorn—was presented to the Pharisees, priests, and people, they all cried out, "Away with him, we own no other king but Caesar." So also, when Venus in this royal color appears to Mercury, Saturn, and Mars, and Luna also, they all together with one consent reject her; that is, they dart forth their malignant, poisonous, fiery rays upon her and imprint the same in her by the sharp impression of Saturn, so that the artist shall see distinctly that Venus is as if scourged and full of spots. And moreover, which is indeed the greatest wonder, he shall exactly see that the crown of thorns, with its sharp, stinging prickles, is put upon her.

For as the whole process in the suffering and death of Christ is a detailed representation of everything the first Adam had acted in his transgression, but in a quite contrary way—which is distinctly shown and declared by Boehme—and as the condition of man in the fall is the same as the earth’s condition in the curse, differing from it only in degree, as he sufficiently demonstrates; so also the manner and process of their restoration cannot but be alike in both.

And as the Lord Christ in all his sufferings was most profoundly humble and only passive, in a full submission to his Father’s pleasure, so also, in this philosophical work, Venus is wholly quiet and passive, etc.
