(*f.*) Concerning the words of Christ, *I thirst*, and the vinegar mingled with gall, which he would not drink after tasting, these are profoundly declared (1.) as an outward, most significant figure of what was transacted inwardly between the holy name Jesus and the anger of God awakened in the human soul. The name Jesus thirsted after the salvation of men and would gladly have tasted the pure living water in the human property; but the anger of God in the soul gave itself into this thirsting love-desire, which the love would not drink, but yielded itself up in full resignation and obedience. Vinegar and gall are the proper figure of the human soul—namely, of those properties in which the human soul essentially stands when it is without the light. The soul, now given here again into the holy light’s substantiality (which was in Adam), disappeared, etc. This caused such a two-fold crack, or shriek, as was explained in the generation of eternal nature.

The first terrible crack made the earth quake and rent the rocks asunder, etc. The second joyful crack raised the dead bodies of those who had hoped and waited for the coming of the Messias, and also rent the veil in the temple from top to bottom, now uniting human time with eternity, etc. And (2.) as to the <term>philosophical work</term>, in which Venus also thirsts after the manifestation and predominance of the fire of love; but Mercury, in the <term>sulphur</term> of Mars and Saturn, presses himself into her with his killing <term>menstruum</term>, which is the greatest poison of the dark, wrathful source. But Venus, instead of drinking it down, yields herself up wholly to it, as if she actually died. From this, the great darkness in the <term>philosophical work</term> arises, so that the whole matter becomes as black as a raven.

(*g.*) When the inward sun of the eternal light’s principle in humanity had given itself up into the dark wrath and anger of God, the outward sun in this third principle—which takes all its radiance and luster from that inward sun as a representation or mirror of it—could not shine. For if its root or deepest ground (considered as being in the region of this world) went down into darkness to renew this principle into the light, the offshoot of this root, the outward sun, must necessarily have been darkened, contrary to the common course of nature. This occurred from the sixth hour of the day until the ninth, which was the time of the first Adam’s sleep, etc. In the <term>philosophical work</term>, as the artist shall see all that God has done in and with humanity when he was to redeem and bring it again into paradise, so he shall also see, in correspondence to this great supernatural darkness, that when Venus thus yields up her life (upon which all her radiance and luster depend), all her beauty must disappear, and darkness comes up instead. He shall see also that not only Venus in the three wrathful properties, but also these three themselves within Venus, lose their life altogether, and all is now as black and dark as a coal. For here now life and death lie together, still and quiet in the will of God and at his sole disposal. The whole is now reduced to the *beginning* and stands in that order in which it stood before the creation. Nature’s *end* is now attained, and all has fallen back into the power of the first <term>Fiat</term>.

(*h.*) After this, the Lord cried out, *My God, why hast thou forsaken me?* The eternal, speaking Word now stood still in humanity; that is, it did not operate within it so as to be sensibly felt. For the heavenly humanity, which disappeared in Adam and was quickened again in Christ, was to bruise the head of the wrath in the fiery soul and change the soul’s fire into a clear, shining sun. So that this might be done, humanity had to be introduced into this wrath by the eternal, speaking Word, and by the same Word, through this wrath and death, into the solar or paradise-like life. When this was done, humanity could not help but feel that wrath in the soul, and in the same instant of this feeling, it could not feel the presence and power of the eternal speaking Word as it could and did before, etc. And this was the forsaking.

So also in the <term>philosophical work</term>, when the wrathful properties swallow up the life of Venus, which is to change them into <term>Sol</term> and to make all seven become one, Venus is forsaken.

And this makes her lose her color and become dark. (*i.*) Just as the Lord Christ—after all his powerful works, overcoming the devil in the temptation, and the transfiguration of his human body—was to go through all these sufferings and at length die wholly on the cross, thereby frustrating, in a sense and manner, the expectations of all his disciples; and just as he had no other gate or way than death through which he could have entered into his glory and drawn his members after him; so also in this <term>philosophical work</term>, the artist has until now indeed seen many wonderful things and very glorious appearances, which gave him great hope and expectation; yet despite all this, his expectation is now, in a sense, quite overthrown. All yields up its former life and activity; there is no more any stirring, moving, or operating. All the properties are in the crown-number, scattered in thousands, and so entered into the *<term>first mysterium</term>*, in that state in which they were before the creation. The meaning is not that the outward materiality is made invisible or quite annihilated, but only that all the powers within it—which the outflowing properties had from the *<term>eternal speaking Word</term>*, and which were raised up against each other in opposition, each of them according to its own nature—are now at the end of their activity in *self-will* and earthly inclination, and have fallen back into the power of the eternal speaking Word. They have no other way nor gate but this death, through which they could enter from the curse into their original blessing. But when they are thus dead to themselves and in the hand of the eternal Word, this cannot but raise them up again to glory, as by a new creation, corresponding to the resurrection of Christ.

(k.) The Lord Christ indeed died as to his humanity from this world, but he took the same human body again in his resurrection and left nothing of it behind except the government of the four elements, in which the wrath, curse, and mortality lie, etc. So in this *<term>philosophical work</term>* also, the first matter is not abolished, but only the curse within it is destroyed in the four elements, and the first life in the one eternal element is raised up again; and therefore it is now six, and can endure the fire. A glorious new body is now raised up out of the black darkness in a beautiful white color, but one that has a hidden brilliance in it, so that the color cannot be exactly discerned until it resolves itself and the new desire for love emerges. And then in Saturn's center, but in Jupiter's and Venus's property, the sun arises. This is in the *<term>Fiat</term>*, like a new creation; and when this is done, all the properties unanimously cast forth their desire into *<term>Sol</term>*. And then the color is turned into a mixture of white and red, from fire and light in union—that is, into yellow, which is the color of majesty.

(l.) The appearance of love to the wrathful properties of darkness causes, as mentioned above, a great crack, shriek, or terror. The wrathfulness is mightily aggravated by this appearance of love and presses vehemently into her to swallow her up into death, which it actually does. But since no death can be within it, love only sinks down, yields itself up into these murdering properties, and displays among them its own loving essence, which they must keep within them and cannot get rid of. But even this is a poison to death and a plague to hell. For the wrathful properties are also mightily terrified at this entry of love into them, which is so strange and contrary to their own qualities, and which makes them all weak and powerless, so that they must lose their own will, strength, and dominance, etc.

So it was done in the death of Christ, and in such a manner (largely and excellently declared by *Behmen*). Death and the curse in humanity were killed and destroyed in and by the death of Christ, who, after his resurrection, no longer had the form of a male in his human body, but that of a paradisiacal virgin, as Adam had before his fall. And so it is also in this *<term>philosophical work</term>*. In this terror, crack, and mutual killing (though there is properly no death, but only a transformation or union of two into one), when Venus yields up her life to the wrathful properties, and when these, having lost their dominance, are raised up again to a new life, the *virgin gives her pearl to the young man as a possession*. And so the life of anger and the life of love are no longer two, but only one; no longer a male and female property, but a whole *virgin*, with both tinctures united into one. When the artist then sees the red blood of the young man rise from death and come forth out of the black darkness, together in union with the white color of the virgin, he may then know that he has the *<term>great arcanum of the world</term>* and such a treasure as is inestimable.

Several more things might be added from *Behmen*, which would afford many excellent considerations. But these may be sufficient to show that harmonious analogy which exists between the restoration of fallen man through *Jesus Christ* and the restoration of cursed nature in the *<term>Philosophical Work</term>*.

For Behmen, as observed in the note on p. 320, and as we trust will be fully manifest through the instrument of the present treatise and the proposed biography, stands before the world in the character of the last great prophet of the gospel dispensation. These further extracts, then, consist of “MISCELLANEOUS OBSERVATIONS occasioned by the REVEREND EDWARD WAPLE’S own WRITINGS about JACOB BEHMEN, which he desired ME TO CORRECT.”<margin>and CO</margin> How these critical remarks display Freher’s universal and exact knowledge of Behmen’s mind and writings, and justify Lee’s poetic address, *In sum, second to you* (p. 253), will be for the reader to consider. They proceed as follows:—

Page 33. *Question: Do they mean that the Father and Son, etc.? Answer:* They take the words of the *Scripture* that call God fire and light, not metaphorically but in their plain natural sense; and they mean that the Father and Son (*as in nature*) are formally that spiritual fire and light. But as *outside of nature*, they are in fire and light as in something distinct from themselves. For the Will, as abyssal or outside of nature, is not yet fire; and the eternal liberty or that state of tranquility, which exists before or deeper than and outside of nature, is not yet light. But in the process of nature, the will—or rather the desire, or the will in and by its desire—becomes fire, and the liberty becomes light, according to the extensive explanation of the seven properties of eternal nature.

Page 44. *Last Question: What reason do they give for their translation of John 1:1, besides the order of the words? Answer:* They say that a translation of the apostle’s words, as is done in the English version by saying *the Word was God* instead of *God was the Word*, is inconsistent with the deep mysterious description of the Godhead and with the sense intended therein. It is also inconsistent (in this place) with the order of eternal generation; and it takes away the greatest emphasis and force of an argument that can be obtained from this, which lies in his own construction of these words. For the apostle’s intent is to show by these words both union and distinction in the Godhead, and even to show it by going directly forward, as it were, from the center, *God* (or the first abyssal will), to the circumference, *Word* (or the express character of His substance). This order is perverted by transposing the words, and the weight of it is lost. For the apostle’s words in their original order imply that the only true eternal God, considered as the Father or first abyssal will—not indeed as being an abyssal will, but as having set Himself forth in an express image of His substance—was Himself that Word which was with Him in the beginning, He being Himself both the first and the last, the beginning and the end. This is not implied when these words are rearranged. And so, the apostle, having said immediately before, *the Word was with God*, and having declared thereby a distinction between *God* (the first abyssal will) and the *Word* (the <term>byss</term>); and saying now further, *and God was that Word*, declares again the highest union between them. He does this from the center or abyssal will forward, in the natural order of generation, toward that which is the center’s circumference, so to speak, and not backward from the circumference to the center. For this center is that circumference in an eminent way, as containing it and being able to bring it forth; but this circumference is not that center reciprocally, in the same sense, emphasis, and consequence. In short, Behmen’s explanation of this Scripture passage cannot have half as much life and deep, weighty sense as it has when these words are transposed, which in the German Bible are rightly rendered according to the Greek original.

Page 45. *Question: But do they mean that they have one and the same numerical or individual essence or substance—that three essentialities are but one essence? Answer:* The last two similes mentioned in this question are undoubtedly the best and most fitting. The first, of heat, light, and air, is one that Behmen uses frequently; and the second, of the three faculties of the soul (though I would rather say fire, light, and <term>tincture</term>), is taken from the image of God, to the consideration of which Behmen usually directs his reader. But whether now, or how these latter three, or those former three, shall be called (in scholastic terms) numerically, individually, identically, or specifically the same, I am not able to say, as I am not sufficiently acquainted with the emphasis and importance of these words.

Page 48. *Question 1: Do they consider the eternal glorious Light to be God or a creature? Answer:* The person asking this question, before he can be answered, must first be asked what he understands by *God*? Or, in which of the two senses (the last one represented and admitted to be quite plain) he uses the word *God* in this question. For the answer to it must be given accordingly. I cannot answer so simply and generally that *it is an eternal emanation from God*. For this answer is not distinct, but lies in confusion, breeds a world of other confusions, and leaves everything in the dark. In the question, God is used in the second sense, which appears sufficiently from all the following discourse until page 62 and beyond; whereas in the answer, I cannot but take it in the *first sense*. If I say *an eternal emanation from God*, I must understand *God* as an abyss, as not yet light, as not yet a most perfect being, but still as a central, incomprehensible unity, which is not *God* in the *second sense*. All that is discussed in the next following question, therefore, is irrelevant, since it opposes something which in the preceding answer (according to Behmen’s principles) is not asserted; it is all based on this mistake: that it is not considered what Behmen understands here by *God*.

Page 50. *Question and Answer 1:* This very same point just mentioned is even more evident in the discourse concerning a "necessary emanation," which is generally claimed to be an undoubted error. For a necessary emanation from God—if God is taken in the second sense, as by those who oppose and contradict such a necessity—might indeed be granted to be an error. But if Behmen takes God here in the first sense—and they cannot or will not consider what he means by God, namely, only and solely the *abyss*, and how he declares (N.B. <note>Latin: *nota bene*, note well</note>) what this abyss is—and yet will charge him with an undoubted error, they show themselves to be full of nonsense and irrationality. For I suppose they will not deny that it is *necessary* (not arbitrary or accidental) that God is light in one sense, and that He dwells in the light in another. And if so, it is necessary that the abyss should not continue in an abyssal state, but be unfolded and bring forth such emanations as it does. *Objection:* This unfolding is done in the eternal generation of the Three, which we can grant to be necessary, but what necessity is there for an unfolding in Seven also? *Answer:* (1.) This unfolding is not done in the eternal generation of the three; for if there is a Tri-unity rather than a Trinity, it is (I don't know what to call it) a . . . . rather than an unfolding. This unfolding, therefore, must be done in seven, by which the three are made known distinctly. (2.) If the central life and light is a state of rest and clarity (see page 62 at the end and page 64 at the beginning) without exulting joy and a bright diffused glory, there is a palpable necessity for such an unfolding in seven, if we will not think it indifferent whether the Divine Being exists in an exulting joy and glory, or whe—

If the abyss is not a most perfect being in 그 sense in which God is generally and rightly called so; what error is it then to say, "Out of the abyss the divine perfections must be unfolded"? It is rather an undoubted error to leave it indifferent whether God be a most perfect being or not. To conceive therefore, in the first place, of this most perfect being, and then to speak in the second place of necessary emanations from it, is directly contrary to Behmen, and is the true ground of all this confusion and endless as well as needless controversy.

Page 54. It is commonly asserted that nothing can emanate from God, except by . . . . . . . . . . which is not God in the highest sense of that word. Here again all that has now been spoken of shows itself as clear as day. For they commonly take "God" in the highest or most complete sense of that word—namely, in that which I called the second: if then Behmen does not take it so in this matter, but in the first and deepest sense, do they not fight against a shadow of their own making; and how can they pretend to an understanding of what he says? Let it be as true as can be agreed upon among themselves that nothing can emanate from God which is not God in the highest sense (namely, when they take God, as they do, in the highest, fullest, or second sense); when Behmen takes it in the first or deepest sense, as he does in this matter, such a position applied to that first sense is utterly false, and the direct contrary is true. Consider only what he says of the abyss, and you may find that something emanates from it (*not by way of creating efficiency out of nothing*) which is not the abyss, nor can be the abyss for this same reason, because it is emanated or unfolded out of the abyss. This, therefore, is not God, and cannot be God in that sense in which the abyss is God, but on the one side in a higher sense, and on the other in a lower. *Summa summarum:* this unhappy dispute arises only from not minding what Behmen means by God in this matter, and yet presuming to try and judge him by what others have said from another principle; which indeed is not fair, but is a way of dealing with him as we would not want to be dealt with ourselves.

Page 66, et seq. Concerning what is discussed here regarding *two Trinities*, I see and say only this: that even this controversy also arises, at least for the most part, from the same ground of *confounding the one sense of "God" with the other*. According to such a manner of arguing, it might as well be claimed that Behmen makes two Gods—the one imperfect and the other perfect—and the one within the other. In the order of our conceptions (*yet with a foundation in the thing itself*), going backward from the creatures, or into the deep, there is a *Tri-unity* beyond or deeper than the *Trinity*; and further, an *abyssal Unity* beyond or deeper than the *Tri-unity*. But just as the Unity and Tri-unity make neither two Gods, nor two unities, nor two tri-unities one within the other—notwithstanding that the unity is truly in the tri-unity, and that both this and that is God—so the tri-unity and trinity make neither two tri-unities nor two trinities one within the other. This is true notwithstanding that this latter is represented as actually fire, light, and air, and the former not actually so, but only potentially; and notwithstanding also that the unity and the tri-unity are in the trinity. Just as the Son is in the Father as in his original, and the Father is in the Son as in his express image, which nevertheless does not make two Gods.

As to the Priscillians and Gnostics, and what they held regarding this, I can say nothing. It may be they had a deeper understanding than the account we have of them suggests; and their being condemned in a synod* signifies nothing at all to me, who am fully persuaded that at first the Lord of Life and Glory himself was condemned by the generality of the whole Jewish church, with as much,

But first we take the occasion to observe (though such an announcement belongs more appropriately to a Preface, if one shall be found necessary) that this treatise, to be duly understood, should be read regularly from the beginning. It has been drawn up in the intervals of daily commercial occupations, from only a general scheme or conception of its form and contents, just as the sheets were demanded by the printer. The editor, moreover, does not possess literary talent and has had no other preparation for the work than the singularly providential possession of the manuscripts, treatises, and almost all the books of reference necessary for the compilation of a biography, such as is sought to be obtained here. Therefore, as in such cases, a logical uniformity will not be found in the arrangement and composition of the work. On account of these circumstances—the editor's not being a practical master of logical composition (clearness of conception and clarity of expression having been his sole aim) and his having to gather and decisively arrange the matter as it has been required by the printer—it is recommended to the reader not to satisfy himself with dipping here and there into the work, but to give it a *regular reading from the beginning*. The printing of it began in the month of November of last year and has continued up to the present time, the month of September, 1848; it is intended to proceed until the circle line of the scheme is drawn around all the points necessary to be embraced in a treatise of such a character. This is designed as an index to the quintessence of all orthodox metaphysical, spiritual, or mystical science (the science of the saints, enlarged to its true philosophical extent) and to the direct attainment of all that is experimental therein, from the lowest to the highest supersensual degree, according to the personification of such human and divine wisdom in the ~~scholastically~~ accomplished, naturally developed, ~~square, straight, undeviating, Christlike, standard~~ mind of WILLIAM LAW. These general directions or rude outlines can be hereafter filled up to their full proportions for universal benefit, and practically applied by those who shall be qualified and called to the work.

With respect to the reference on pages 252 and 253, the writer, a few days ago, met with a work which, on examining its matter and style more closely, he has no doubt is the ‘Treatise’ in question, written by Lee. The title-page runs as follows: “The General Delusion of Christians, regarding the ways of God’s revealing himself to and by the Prophets, proved from Scripture and Primitive Antiquity. And many principles of Scoffers, Atheists, Sadducees, and wild Enthusiasts, refuted. The whole adapted, as much as possible, to the simplest capacity. In four parts. ‘Prophecy came not [οὐἠνέχθη, was not, or was brought] at any time by the will of man; but holy men of God spoke [φερομένοι, being moved] by [υπο, by] the Holy Spirit.’ 8vo. London, 1713.”

Page 98. *A. 1. They may be said to be partakers*—not necessarily. It may be granted the creation of angels and men was done by God freely and contingently, not necessarily, but this participation upon a presupposition that God would have such creatures after his own image and likeness is not free nor contingent, but necessary. For he could not have created them after his image and likeness without making them partakers of his Divine nature, though it is true that this participation is only after a creaturely manner, derivatively.

Page 100. *A. 1.—They assert the fire of this emanation to be immortal as well as the light.* This is true absolutely in eternal nature, but not so in the creature. And therefore I cannot say what further follows, and consequently the soul as well as the Spirit. For though the light and spirit do not die in or to God, yet they died in and to the creature; that is, the creature lost them and was separated from them, and retained only its own natural principle of immortality, or continued only to be a living soul in its own fiery nature, but not a blessed image of God in the light.

Page 102. *A. 1. Because here it is asked, What do they deliver concerning the manner of this emanation’s coming out of God?* I think it might be more distinct if it were answered thus: They say, that upon the desire’s actual moving and attracting, various other properties or spiritual motions arise, as are necessary for the production of a spiritual fire, and further of the light, and that so this emanation is eternally produced or brought out of the unproduced, unmade, or self-existent abyss of all things, in which, considered as an abyssal will and Father of nature, it is to be conceived of as a hidden fire and light—not meaning that it was actually fire and light, and hidden as if behind a veil, but that it still was lying potentially in those not yet moving spiritual properties or motions, by the united concurrence of which it must have been manifested or brought into action.

Page 116. To the particulars of this answer could be added, I think, in the first or second place (for it will be directly relating to the question, and is plainly Behmen’s ground), <margin><image-desc>A horizontal line with a caret symbol (^) pointing upwards placed above it.</image-desc></margin> That the desire is not in God, that is, not in the abyss, nor in the Abyssal Will, and much less therefore in the Tri-unity or Trinity. For though we may say the fire is in the abyss, as a hidden and not yet burning fire; and so also the desire is therein, as a hidden and not yet desiring or actual desire; yet we must say also from the plain and contrary nature of the abyss and desire, that the desire, as soon as it is conceived to be actual desire and actually attracting, is no more in the abyss, but has gone forth the first step out of it. And if then the desire, as hidden in the abyss, is not yet attracting, filling, and darkening, this filling and darkening which is in the desire, as already gone out and attracting actually, can also not be in the abyss, but only in the first step from the abyss—which first step having never been without or separated from the *fifth, sixth, and seventh*, it never was also in that first step otherwise than according to our necessary conception.

Page 126. *A. 2. Out of their possible, uncreated, ideal state.* Seeing that in the next following answer, a reason is given why they cannot properly be called creatures, I think they should also not be said there to have been in an *uncreated state*; *abyssal state* would be my expression.

It is strange, we say, that the pious and devout Lee could be induced to write at all in judgment upon so super-rational and delicate a subject as is implied in the history of the Montanists, or indeed upon any devoted individuals whose lives were characterized by a strict practice of gospel piety outwardly, and by great self-denial, total separation from the spirit of the world, and earnest continual prayer in their private walk and conversation.

How differently does the divinely wise and apostolic Freher speak and write in the passages to which these remarks are a note, as on every other occasion. And who that knows anything of experimental religion is not aware that a man must become a fool to the world to be truly wise in the sight of Christ and God? And though human prudence (under the character of sober orthodoxy) may talk mightily wisely about the necessity of *avoiding particularity* (and, whether in synod or individuals, will judge and condemn accordingly), yet he that dares not be so weak as to be particular in his religious course will not only fail in the attainments of evangelical perfection, but be often obliged to avoid the most substantial duties of Christian piety.

In the answer, no ground for it is shown, but it is only said that they think it may be illustrated from what occurs in this world, etc. Whereas Behmen certainly had a deep and solid ground for it, and had not taken it up by reasoning from what is in this world; which ground, in short, was his breaking in the Spirit through the gates of hell into the light-world, and therefore having this generation, as to both principles, opened in his own soul. A ground certainly not to be shaken by devils, and much less by men, of which all his writings testify sufficiently.

Page 138. Q. 1. What ground is there for their asserting that these seven Spirits are the *instruments under God of the Divine nature in man?* This seems to me very obscure and ambiguous, for these seven spirits (as is also said in the next following answer) are God's eternal nature, and this nature and these seven Spirits are called by Behmen "God's instruments by which he works," which is plain. But to call the seven Spirits "instruments under God of the Divine nature in man" seems to be as much as to say they are instruments of themselves, or nature is its own agent and its own instrument, or these seven spirits are so distinct from nature that nature can be an agent and these seven Spirits the instruments of this agent; which is not asserted by Behmen, nor could any ground be found for such an assertion.

<margin>[Vol. II.]</margin> Page 1. Q. 1. Considering that knowledge is not the *manifestation itself*, but rather an effect and consequence of it, I would be inclined to think that either this first question might be formed differently, or if it should remain as it is, that something more might be expressed in the answer, namely, this or something similar:—it is such an effective and solid understanding (chiefly and summarily) of God and man as cannot be had except by a manifestation of the Spirit from Christ, in whom are hidden, etc.

Q. 2. For significant reasons, I would, for my part, change the order of these two particulars, saying: 1st, in the renewed spirit of the mind, from the Word and light of God as in its only true place; and 2ndly, in the Scriptures as a direction toward it and a testimony of it. John 5:39, 40.

Q. 3. The words *not in the same measure*, I would either leave out entirely or change them to these—*not in the same manner*. Because the Word and light of God, considered in humanity and with respect to the several ages of the church, was from the beginning and will be until the end of time increasing, unfolding, and displaying itself more and more, like a tree in its boughs, greater and lesser branches, blossoms, and fruits. This simile is frequently used and excellently declared by Behmen; so that it does not detract from the honor and due unquestionable prerogative of the Apostles to say that after their time such and such a person had the Word and light of God in the same, or even in a greater measure; but their prerogative is sufficiently asserted by owning that none had it for the same purpose. Just as it does not detract from the honor of large, significant boughs to say that they are not as adorned with a variety of buds and blossoms, nor as richly laden with fruits, as the lesser branches are which yet come forth out of them, are supported by them, and stand upon them as their foundation.

Q. 4. Great and various are the ends for which the Word and light of God was given, especially to Behmen; and he certainly received it not for his own sake only, but also for a *general benefit which is yet to be expected*. Therefore, I think that at least something of that in the answer to this question might be mentioned. For instance—it was given him, as he says in the AURORA, to declare to the world the morning redness of the coming day, and to Babel its downfall, and to warn the children of God who are dispersed in all its streets. Again, for an unfolding and explaining of those many deep mysteries that lay hidden in the letter of the Scriptures and were not understood, but must now in this latter age of the world be brought to light, according to the prophecy of Zech. 14:7—"In the evening it shall be light"; and this (Note Well) in order to prepare for the coming in of the Jews, Turks, and Heathens, etc.

Q. 2. This expression, *they may have erred in what they have delivered*, I think might be a little restrained or limited by adding:—*they may have erred as to this or that particular circumstance of what they have delivered*.

Page 5. Q. *last*. When it is declared here in whom or to whom the Word and light of God can become a shining lamp and a living oracle, all the qualifications, so excellently expressed here, are indeed sufficient for everyone to attain the former; but as to the latter, I think something is wanting: for such children of God in whom his Word shall become a living oracle are not only to have all those qualifications on their side, but something from the side of God is also further required for it, namely, they must be expressly chosen or preordained for it by God, who intends to make use of them as his extraordinary messengers. <insert>[The Lord will always choose his own prophets. Page 7. Q. *last*. Q. *last*. *Knowing and loving* are here in the question, and in the answer *knowing and delighting* are combined, and both ascribed to the unity before the act of willing, which I think cannot remain so, because it gives occasion for a confused understanding and raises a great objection; for, if we consider in God a *loving himself*, we must necessarily imply (1) a *lover*, (2) a *beloved*, and (3) a *ray of love*; and so our consideration represents a Trinity to us before the act of willing, which is inconsistent with the Unity. But a *knowing himself* may be acknowledged before this act of willing in the Unity; for in it is the Divine intellect, called by Behmen an *abyssal Eye*. This cannot but know himself as one, and is therefore consistent with the Unity, and does not at all imply a Trinity, because it is not considered any further than as a knowing only his central all-sufficiency for all that is in any sense posterior, or as it is expressed sufficiently here in the answer, *as a knowing himself as one*, which is the same as all in one. It is true, indeed, that knowing and loving himself are inseparable from each other in God, but they cannot be so in our separate, gradual, imperfect consideration, in which we cannot help but look upon each in its own prior or posterior place. Just as knowing precedes loving in our rational conception, so our consideration justly places such a knowing in the eternal Unity; and as next to the Unity the Trinity comes

Page 25. A. 2. When *spiritual fire and light* are mentioned, and that our first parents were created in this image of God, I think it might be clarified by adding: "regarding the invisible, spiritual man," or "regarding soul and spirit." This is not because it was not true or clearly enough expressed for those with understanding, but only so that it does not become a stumbling block to those who lack it, who might immediately cry out that it is contrary to Scripture, etc.

Page 37. What is discussed here regarding the will needs, in my opinion, to be further clarified. I see that there is mention of another will, distinct from the will of the Unity and subordinate to it. However, the generation of eternal nature begins with desire and presupposes no other will but that same first Abyssal Will, which is the will of the Unity. It cannot be distinct from itself, even though it wills two things that are exceedingly distinct from one another. In the eternal generation of the Trinity, the first will is the Father, and the second will is the Son. Now, this second will (in the first consideration of God as He is in Himself, rightly viewed as existing before nature, or as if nature were not yet generated) is here, in the second consideration of God as manifest in nature, also rightly set aside as if it were not yet generated. In our consideration, there must be a "going back" to the first abyssal will, which is the only generator of both the second will (by introducing itself into an eternal <term>lubet</term><note>A term used by Jacob Behmen meaning a 'divine longing' or 'delight'.</note>) and of eternal nature as well (by introducing itself into an attracting desire). The first and second wills are therefore distinct, as Father and Son are. But Behmen nowhere represents this first will as generating another will distinct from itself and prior to desire, but only as introducing itself immediately into desire, just as it introduces itself immediately into a <term>lubet</term>.

Page 41. Q. 1. Darkness becomes an evil of punishment when it exists separately from the light—not universally in every creature, but only in those who were created for the light and abandoned their proper home. For there are creatures in the darkness for whom darkness is good, and the light would be evil, pain, torment, and destruction.

Page 43. Q. 1. This description of the seven spirits is, in my opinion, not yet sufficient or distinct enough. They are not all equally pure, simple, living, and active. For instance, the second is, in a spiritual sense and manner, thicker and grosser than the first; the third is a composition or mixture of the first and second. Only the first six are living and active, while deadness, impotence, and passivity belong to the seventh. Therefore, this question might be answered in this way or something similar: they conceive of the first six spirits as living and acting beings, and of the seventh as their passive, spiritual body, of which the six are the life and in which they both work and rest in different respects.

And here, after this first question, would be the proper place to add several more things, some of which are very necessary for understanding Behmen’s mind: namely, that each of them is distinct from all the rest by its own peculiar essential character, which makes it precisely that specific property and not another. Despite this, they are not seven distinct things, but seven properties of one thing; for this reason, they are commonly called the seven properties of eternal nature. They are not to be conceived as standing outside or beside each other, like the representation of seven distinct lamps in the vision of St. John, but as within each other, like the fourfold wheel in Ezekiel's vision. They are in one respect but one, in another seven, and in another three, according to the Holy Trinity. The first and seventh, second and sixth, and third and fifth should be seen as one and the same, with only this distinction: when they are called the first, second, and third, they are "before" the fire; when they are called the fifth, sixth, and seventh, they are "after" it. This makes the most significant distinction between the two groups of three. None of them is properly the "first" or "second," etc., but they are only called so according to our human conception. There is a reciprocal and perpetual generation between them; each requires all the other six for its own generation and is required in turn for the generation of each of the others. Each of them receives the impression of all the other six, so that here also, in a sense, it is true that <term>quidlibet est in quolibet</term><note>Latin for "anything is in anything," expressing the interconnectedness of all things.</note>; from which an infinite variety and multiplicity of wonders in the kingdom of glory arises, etc.

Q. 2. Regarding the last three words, *light or glory, and joy*, I would arrange them as: light, joy, and glory. This is because of their correspondence to the last three properties: joy is usually referred to the sixth, and glory to the seventh, as Behmen commonly does.

Q. 4. There must be a seventh, not only to unite the six but also to make the distinction between the three distinct opposites manifest, which is achieved by the fire. This distinguishing role is just as necessary (if not more so) to observe and understand as the unifying one. For we would not be able to perceive darkness and light in their distinction—or rather, their opposition—if there were no fire, which has darkness before it and light after it.

Q. last. In the answer, it says, "*the joy arising from it a sixth, and the kingdom of joy a seventh*." Here I would rather say: "the kingdom of glory." I do not mean that the previous expression was false, but I suggest this for the sake of a clearer relationship to the properties, and because the difference between "joy" and "the kingdom of joy" is not clearly explained.

Page 45. Q. 1. Since Behmen did not argue that four spirits are required for spiritual fire based on a similar necessity for the production of material fire—but instead had eternal nature opened to him before temporal nature, and concluded from the former to the latter (indeed, he knew nothing of these new philosophical experiments, as is said later)—I am inclined to think it would be better if this question were phrased this way: "Do you have anything for confirmation or illustration that four spirits are required?" Otherwise, the question seems to imply that Behmen previously understood the generation of fire in external nature and reasoned from that to the eternal. What is said in the answer, being entirely proper, true, clear, and sufficient, might nevertheless be retained, *mutatis tantum mutandis, grammaticæ constructionis gratia*<note>Latin: "making only the necessary changes for the sake of grammatical construction."</note>.

Page 47. Q. 1. Here I cannot see why it is called *the fifth spirit*, from which the light arises. This light is itself the fifth spirit, or the fifth spiritual property, arising not from the fifth but from the fourth—namely, from the fire—as the answer also declares.

<margin>1.</margin> Page 53. Q. 1. Grace and peace from the one divine essence, or threefold Spirit only, considered as in himself alone without the creature, cannot be profitable to man. Man has broken or disharmonized within himself the seven properties of the divine nature, has fallen thereby into misery, strife, and restlessness, and now lacks grace and peace. All the grace outside of him cannot profit him if there is not peace made within him; this peace therefore depends upon that grace, and from that grace this peace must be brought into man. But it cannot be brought into him except by an actual reconciling and re-harmonizing of the disordered properties of his human nature. And seeing this human nature is an offspring of the Divine nature, or of God as manifested in his eternal nature, to this disharmonized nature therefore is rightly wished, not only grace, but also peace, and not only (1.) from God, as the only original source of all grace and peace, but also (2.) from the seven Spirits before his throne, as the seven Divine open Fountains, out of which the human nature flowed forth, and to which it must be brought back again, if man shall be a partaker again of the Divine nature, as he was in the beginning. And (3.) also from Jesus Christ as the King and Head of men, in whom all this reconciliation was first effected, and by whom it is to be effected further in all his members. And in this consideration (as might be sufficiently demonstrated), lies certainly the true ground of this Apostolic wish. But that it is not used so by any of the other Apostles, nay even not by St. John himself, except only in this mystical and prophetical book of his, shows us sufficiently that it was not then the time for the opening and understanding of this mystery, but that this book was written only for the future ages and generations then to come.

<margin>2.</margin> Page 53. Q. ult. Instead of the words *flowing out from them*, I would rather say—flowing out through them, or being unfolded, displayed, or manifested by them. For the former, in my opinion, seems to make the seven properties a source of the Divine attributes, when their source (if we may so speak, for properly they have none) is in the abyssal Unity or central All-sufficiency before and without the properties of nature, and by them they are only unfolded out of their centre.

<margin>3.</margin> Page 55. Q. 1. Here I think it would be necessary to say something, though ever so little, concerning this expression, *before*. Not that an understanding reader should have need of it, but only to remove a stumbling block from the sight of the ignorant.

<margin>4.</margin> Q. 2. A little more connection between this *Q.* and *A.* would exist if in the answer the word *distinctly* were added to the words *to know and perceive*. And here might be considered also what Behmen frequently objects to himself, and also answers sufficiently: namely, whether all the foregoing consideration of God in general, and this question of his distinct knowledge in particular, does not import a beginning of the Divine Triune Being, or at least of the manifestation thereof. And whether Behmen’s expression of an *eternal beginning* might not be so represented that no man of sense could find a contradiction in it.

<margin>d</margin> And here we take the opportunity to say, in reference to the compilation and authorship of the Biography, that what is WANTED in short, as the sum and the object of the present treatise, and as necessary in the nature of the thing, is AN EDITOR, who, while proving himself an exact historian, a solid universal scholar, a just thinker, a profound philosopher, and a deeply-experienced, enlightened Christian, shall produce a masterly picture or biography of the individual in all the features and developments of his mind and character;—interweaving the few incidents of his life that have been preserved with such tender and manly reflections, and filling up the vacancies in his history with such elevated and charming natural conceptions and observations, and interspersing the whole with such touches and relief of sublime instruction, though popularly expressed, as shall irresistibly inspire the reader with a fervent admiration of true wisdom and piety, and also *fire* him with an ardent and indomitable resolution to immediately begin the pursuit of evangelical perfection and the imitation of so perfect a model of a learned and accomplished English gentleman, philosopher, and Christian. The whole is to be rendered as captivating, by the dignity and importance of the diversified subjects upon which it treats in so uniformly felicitous and masterly a manner, as by the condescending tenderness, nobility, and wisdom of its sentiments, and the classic purity, elegance, and sweeping rhetorical and <unclear>stately logical</unclear> <note>The words 'stately logical' are heavily crossed out in the original text.</note> power of its composition:—all of which qualifications a solid, duly-constituted ordinary genius may engraft upon itself by diligence and a close study of the models referred to, and through the directions and specifications interspersed throughout the present treatise. In a word, as none but a Law could design and execute a perfect biography of a man, a scholar, a philosopher, and a Christian; so this treatise aims solely at creating another Law, possessed of all the talents of the former, with all the highest practical experiences, discoveries, and divine manifestations in human nature that have distinguished these last ages added to them: for without a beau-ideal or model of a perfect man in all his characteristic features and particulars, how shall mankind be elevated to their proper redeemed perfection, and how shall the Gospel produce its full results. To proceed.

The town of King’s Cliffe is situated in the northern part of the county of Northampton, at about equal distances from the counties of Huntingdon, Lincoln, and Rutland, and is a place of great antiquity. Though now of small extent and secluded from the great highways intersecting the country north and south, it was anciently famous as a royal residence of the monarchs of England; but in later ages, it has obtained a much greater honor and celebrity by being the birthplace of the individual who is to form the chief subject of the proposed biography, the justly celebrated oracle of wisdom, truth, and goodness, WILLIAM LAW.

not confined to abrupt precipices, but is used also to designate the side of a hill. <note>See *Dugdale’s Warwickshire*, word Cliffe. Cliffe is the chief town of the East Bailiwick of the Forest of Rockingham. It is called the Bailiwick of Cliffe. This forest division contains three walks: Morehay, containing [unclear]; Sulchay, containing 1028 acres, 2 roods, 33 perches; and Westhay, 1147 acres, 3 roods, 16 perches.</note>

It is situated on the northern acclivity of a valley in that district of the county of Northampton which was formerly the Forest of Rockingham. A brook runs through it that rises near Corby, in the western part of the forest, and joins its waters to the Nene in the Lordship of Fotheringhay.

The lands, not only in this valley but in smaller ramifications of it, bear testimony to the use the inhabitants made of the iron ore in the time of the Romans, with which the stone in many parts is united. Indeed the church, which probably occupies the place of one much older (for there was a church here in the time of the Saxons), is on the site of a smelting-house, as testified by the numerous pieces of slag mixed with the earth in the north side of the churchyard and in other parts of it. In digging a grave in the north-western part of the churchyard in 1829, the bottom of a furnace was discovered. From coins found in other lordships—namely, Laxton and Bulwick, near spots where the smelting of iron was practiced—it appears that the Romans were the workers of it. There were extensive quarries of freestone in this lordship, which supplied materials for building many of the ecclesiastical and domestic structures in this part of England. The lordship also abounds in mineral springs, one of which issues from a stone basin in a wood called Spa Sale, on the south-west of the parish. The spot where it rises was paved and surrounded by stone benches about a century ago, and contained a bath for the limbs of cripples. Of the quality of the water, the following account has been given: “It both smells and tastes of iron. It will deposit a white sediment with oil of tartar; and with galls it precipitates a purple sediment; but it turns to an opaque red with logwood, and a deep green with syrup of violets. A gallon yields one hundred and forty grains of sediment, seventy-five of which are limestone and ochre, and sixty-five a calcareous nitre. From various experiments, it appears that this water is of a chalybeate laxative nature, impregnated with iron and calcareous nitre, with a small quantity of sea salt and an earthy substance. It has been used with great success in disorders from obstructions and in eruptions of the skin; it has also cured several lame persons.” <note>The Rev. John Boughton, formerly Fellow of St. John’s College, Cambridge, was the first person who observed this spring to be a mineral water. In 1670, or about that time, it was approved of and publicly recommended by the learned Dr. Thomas Browne, a physician then residing at Cliffe. Morton, from whom this information is obtained, proceeds to state that ever since then it has been much applied to and deservedly celebrated for the real services it has done for those who drink it for various distempers, especially those arising from obstructions. It has likewise been successfully used externally, by way of bathing or lotion. And there is a suitable cistern of stone at a convenient distance from the spring to take in water for the use of those who have cutaneous diseases or ulcers. — *Morton’s Natural History of Northamptonshire*, p. 274, published in 1712.</note>

*...containing all things, and being contained by none, and containing them just as their infinite foundation or center, from which they proceed and in which they rest. In this description, these two specific words, center and rest, require an addition by which the former may be distinctly determined and the latter more explained, so as to be made applicable to all things. For seeing that eternal nature is also rightly called the center of all things from which they proceed, this center must necessarily be distinguished from that one. And though we cannot conceive of two centers in one circumference, one beside the other, yet we can conceive of one being deeper than the other, so that from this deeper one the whole circumference, together with its exterior center, can proceed. Therefore, this deeper center (God in himself) must be distinguished from that center which is nature, by calling it the first, or the deepest and inmost. And further, seeing that the classification of all things also includes the devil, this expression—"in which they rest" (if understood in a sense relating to the <term>Sabbath</term>)—belongs only to nature and is not applicable to the devil. Therefore, it must be explained so that nothing more than this may be understood by it: God is the primary foundational being upon which all things stand and rest, so that there is no further progress beyond it to any deeper cause from which they could have proceeded. For it is true that God is in the devil as well, as the deepest center of that whole circumference, in which he is also one of its innumerable particular things. Our early historians mention a battle fought here in 778, between Aldulf, son of Bosa, general of the army of Ethelred, king of the Northumbrians, and Adelbald and Heardbert, who were rebelling against that monarch. Without pretending to claim absolute credit for this report, it may be appropriate to mention that there was a part of the brook, in the meadow eastward of the town, which until the time of the enclosure in 1809 retained the name of the Battle Green Pit.

The last Saxon possessor of this lordship was Earl Algar, whose brother had a seat at Chesterton in Huntingdonshire, and whose family, it is supposed, continues to the present day and is seated at Chell House near Newcastle in Staffordshire.

The first of the family to be characterized by a surname was Goisfred (or Geoffrey) de Clive, chaplain to Henry I, who, because of his marriage with a princess of the Saxon race, was more lenient to the former inhabitants than his predecessors, and raised his chaplain to the See of Hereford on December 26, 1115. Goisfred is represented by Godwin as a man of great temperance and frugality. He died on February 3, 1119, and was buried in the north wall of Hereford Cathedral.

At Aston Hall in Warwickshire, on glass, were paintings of the Saxon owners of Clive, supposed to have been copied from monastic illustrations of great antiquity; they were represented in their coat of arms, on which some bore the eagle displayed with one head, and others with two.

In the time of Edward the Confessor, when Earl Algar possessed it, the manor of Clive was his freehold and valued at £7 per year. At the general survey after the Conquest, it was in the hands of the crown and rated at £10 per year. It then contained the following quantity of land: one <term>hide</term> and two <term>virgates</term>. Two <term>carucates</term>, with one servant, were in <term>demesne</term>; and seven <term>villeins</term>, with a priest and six cottagers, had five <term>carucates</term>. There was a mill with a twelve-pence yearly rent; four acres of meadow, with a wood a mile long and half a mile broad. Writers differ materially as to the quantity of land contained in a <term>hide</term>; and without attempting to dive into the meaning of the term as used here, but taking a <term>carucate</term> to represent one hundred acres and a <term>virgate</term> twenty-four acres, the contents of the lordship at the time of the Conquest were two thousand one hundred and four acres, besides a wood a mile long and half a mile broad, excluding those parts of the parish which were within the forest boundary and not attached to the lordship.

In the reign of Henry II, it was estimated to contain one <term>hide</term> and a half, and half a <term>virgate</term>.

The Manor House, or King’s Palace, is reported to have stood on the south side of the churchyard and extended to an open space toward the east, still called the HALL YARD (hereafter mentioned as the residence of the Rev. W. Law, Mrs. Hutcheson, and Miss Gibbon). **Page 67. Q. 1.** This very same comes again, for there it is said, *such a kingdom is eternally generated by the seven spirits of God's eternal nature, when it is generated only by the six, and is itself the seventh.*

**Page 68. Q. ult.** The answer to this question combines two considerations, vastly different from each other, which makes the sense obscure and must therefore be altered. Fire and light are indeed always and everywhere to be conceived as distinct, for the one can never be, nor become the other; each must keep eternally to its own peculiar essentiality. But in this kingdom, the distinction between their properties is not perceivable, for the fire is made mild and softened by water and light, and is not known in its own natural fiery properties, but is overpowered by the light, which rules in this kingdom, using indeed the fire's powers as its instrument, but qualifying everything according to its own tender and well-doing qualities. And this is what makes fire and light unseparated in this kingdom, though they are separable in and by the creature. But what more is said in this answer, namely, *that they are to be conceived as two distinct, self-subsistent, and self-sufficient lives or spheres of activity, which they call principles,* can here have no place at all, for this is quite another consideration. And though the two principles may be conceived so (with a good explanation both as to their being self-subsistent and self-sufficient) now, after the fall and separation, yet they cannot be conceived so as before his fall. And further, that they cannot be conceived so in this substance is evident of itself, because this substance, or this kingdom of light and glory, is itself the one of these two eternal principles, the other of which should never have been known or perceived if Lucifer had not manifested it.

Charters still exist, and particularly the Harleian Manuscripts (No. 5511) give some insight into these proceedings. From them it appears that King John was at Cliffe on the twenty-fifth of July, 1208; in 1216, he was at Bedford on the fifteenth of September of that year; at Cambridge on the sixteenth, and at Clyve on the twentieth of September. At all of these places he signed mandates, which are dated there. In the year 1229, December the ninth, Henry the Third occupied his house at Clyve, as appears by a brief, *pro feodo Comitis Flandriæ*, signed there on that day. In the year 1230, the inhabitants accounted to the Exchequer in £30, for the farm of their township. The same year, Stephen de Segrave, sheriff of the county, in the articles of his accounts, charged for the carriage of four hogsheads of wine from Baston to Clyve: a proof that the palace was in use. In 1236, Henry the Third settled the manor upon his queen, Eleanor, second daughter of Raymond Berenger, Count of Provence, as part of her dowry. In 1247, the 30th year of Henry the Third, four pounds, six shillings, and four pence were expended in repairing the buildings belonging to the Crown; and in 1249, he (Henry the Third) granted the inhabitants a fair for three days, beginning on St. Luke's Eve. This he renewed in 1258, on consideration of their paying to the crown fifty shillings per annum, in advance, for the farm of their township. The grant of a market seems to have been at an earlier date. And the grant for the fair was again renewed in the 1st year of James the First, 1604, in consideration of the great suffering of the inhabitants by fire, and the discontinuance of the fair and market on that account. By the Rolls for the year 1274, it appears that King Edward the First visited his house at this place in that year; being at Westminster on the twenty-first of October, at Northampton from the third to the eleventh of November, and at Clyve on the twenty-second, when he signed the patent, *de homagio Lewellini Principis Walliæ*. A.D. 1274.—*Pat. 3 ed. 1. m. 36. in Turr. Lond.*

In 1293, upon the decease of Eleanor, the queen dowager, who died a nun in the nunnery of Ambresbury in Wiltshire, the manor was given, during the king's pleasure, to Elias de Hanvill. During the time it was possessed by the queen, there was a priest officiating in the royal free chapel of the palace of Cliffe; as appears from the accounts of the year 1247, when the sheriff charged to the exchequer one shilling, paid to the chaplain celebrating divine service in the chapel at Cliffe.

So that this denomination cannot be determined or tied up to a fixed constant sense, which would be universally applicable everywhere, but must be taken variously, according to the subject matter. Yet so much may be said in general: that it always implies a particularity of things stirring and moving, descended from this or that, which—considered before this particularity—is to be looked upon not only as a universal, but also more or less as hidden and unknown, and manifested distinctly in and through its essences. Powers and virtues are, in one respect, one and the same thing, but in another distinct, by a distinction that corresponds to the one between fire and light. Thus, powers have a nearer relation to the strong and mighty, lively, energetic, penetrating source of fire, and virtues to the soft, mild, lovely, refreshing, amiable, tincturing light. Colors are no different from what we call colors in this external world, except that they are that heavenly and (to our eyes) invisible original, of which our colors are but an obscure, transitory, and shadowy resemblance; namely, a resemblance suitable to the condition of this world of the four elements. The colors in the holy light-world must necessarily be as much more noble than ours as that eternal light is more noble than our perishable light of the sun. From this, the difference between ideas, essences, powers, virtues, and colors may appear sufficiently; and moreover, it can also be plain that one and the same particular thing can be capable of three or four, if not all, of these denominations, if it is only considered in different respects.

In 1330, August 8th, Edward III was at his manor house of Clive, where he signed a document, *De Rege ap Griffyn et Wallensibus de adhæsione Edmundi de Wadestok, nuper Comitis Kantiæ arestandis. From this time to 1440, there does not appear to be any document relating to this place. It probably continued to be held by the Crown during that period. At that time, it appears that the tenants of the manor were much impoverished, and that the manor itself (by which may be meant the mansion house, as well as other things belonging to the manor) had fallen into decay; this induced the Crown to make a reduction of their fee-farm rents for forty years.

A remission of their rents was also made in the second year of Edward IV, 1462, on account of a fire which burnt down a great part of the town. The tradition of this fire continued until the time of Bridges, the historian of Northamptonshire; and upwards of one hundred houses, which were not rebuilt, are said to have been destroyed by it.

From the reign of Edward IV to that of George III, the manor<note>Valued, by order of the Commonwealth (1650), at £22 13s. 4d.; in the 10th year of James I, it was demised to Sir Thomas Howard for sixty years; on the 22nd of April, 1698, to Richard Marriot, Gentleman; to the Earl of Exeter in 1715 for thirty-one years, having been previously (September 23rd, 1706) assigned by Marriot to that earl.—*Reports of Surveyor-General of Crown Lands, Office of Woods and Forests.*</note> was held by the Crown and leased to different persons. At the time of the enclosure of the parish, which took place in 1809 under the authority of an Act of Parliament, the Marquis of Exeter was the lessee, who collected the fee-farm rents, amounting to £40, and paid £22 annually out of the demesnes. Since that time, the Marquis of Exeter has possessed the fee simple of the manor, by purchase from the Commissioners for the Management of the Crown Lands.

The inhabitants, being tenants in ancient demesne, are exempt from the payment of tolls throughout England. By this is meant all tolls except those taken on turnpike roads, which, being regulated by statute, are laid indiscriminately on all who use them.

About a quarter of a mile west of the church, an embankment crosses the valley; through the north end of which an opening has been made as a passage for the waters of the stream. This embankment, or bay, improperly called "the Bees," was the head of a piece of water belonging to the Crown, which occupied a large portion of the meadows now called the fish pools. The sluices were still standing not many years before Bridges wrote his history. To the royal mansion belonged also an extensive park, lying on the eastern side of the lordship, containing eleven hundred and thirty-six acres, forest measure; that is, eighteen hundred and fifty-four acres, statute measure; two acres of forest measure being equal to three statute acres. It was enclosed with a fence, partly of stone and partly of wood, by the tenants of Apethorpe and Wood-Newton Manors, in the twenty-second year of Edward the Third, 1349; the crown finding the materials, and care being taken that this service of theirs should not be drawn into a precedent. The park continued in the crown until the eighth year of Henry the Eighth, 1517, when the keepership of it was granted to David Cecil, and to his son Richard Cecil. William, Lord Burghley, in the reign of Elizabeth, disparked it, and settled on his hospital at Stamford Baron £100 per annum, to be paid out of its rents, and thirteen loads of fine wood from the wood growing in the park. Thomas, Earl of Exeter, also settled a rent charge on the park for the hospital at Liddington, in the county of Rutland. His descendant is still in possession of it.

Within the bounds of the Bailiwick are the whole walk of Westhay, and a large portion of the walk of Morehay, anciently part of the forest of Clyve; as the East Bailiwick of the forest of Rockingham was called in several ancient documents, such as in the thirty-eighth year of Henry the Third, 1253. <note>Containing one thousand one hundred and forty-seven acres, three roods, and sixteen poles.—*MS. The forest or bailiwick of Clyve originally comprehended the following parishes: Fotheringhay, Nassington, Yarwell, Woodnewton, Apethorpe, Southwick, Blatherwick, Bulwick, Finshed, Duddington, Collyweston, Easton, Benefield, Deenethorpe, and Cliffe. It may be observed that the forest lands, comprehended within certain bounds and included in the ancient perambulations, were not parochial.

We find that in the seventeenth year of Edward the Third, Cotterstock Chantry obtained the tithes of certain assarts <note>Land cleared of forest and converted to arable use.</note>, particularly in Horshaw and Calvhay, in Cliffe Forest, which the parson of Cliffe had been unjustly accustomed to receive. These tithes were also confirmed to them by the Bishop of Lincoln, Clare, in the seventeenth year of Edward the Third, m. 5, and the Register of Thomas Beke, Bishop of Lincoln.

The walk of Westhay, the coppices, with the privilege of cutting down all the woods, underwoods, and trees growing on the premises for ledgebote, palebote, gatebote, and railbote <note>Legal rights to take wood for the repair of hedges, pales, gates, and rails.</note>, with all the tops, lops, and branches, were sold at the end of the seventeenth century to the ancestor of the Marquis of Exeter. Previous to that time they were possessed by the Earl of Westmoreland, who possesses the walk of Morehay in fee.

The lordship was enclosed under the sanction of an Act of Parliament passed in the year 1809, when several allotments of land were conveyed to the rector in lieu of all tithes.

    Page 73. *Final Question. Their souls consist of fire and light.* Here I must observe that when Behmen considers soul and spirit, distinguishing each from the other as to its own specific being, he attributes fire to the soul and light to the spirit. He says expressly that the soul, considered strictly by itself, has in its being nothing but fire with its dark root—that is, the first four properties before the light, which is the fifth. And if we say the souls of angels consist of fire and light, we must admit that Lucifer, by losing his light, lost something of his soul, which cannot be proven.
    Page 75, line 1. *Their spirits are of a heavenly power, etc.* This may remain, and it does not contradict what was just said of the soul but can be reconciled with Behmen’s views, as could be sufficiently shown if there were a necessity for it. Therefore, in our full restoration, we shall indeed be equal to the angels, but we shall also have something more than they do, in the consideration of which they shall not be equal to us. For we shall eternally keep that body from this third principle as well, and this is the body to which the resurrection belongs, not the angelic one. For if the angelic body is born again in regeneration, it does not die in the dissolution of the four-element body but passes through death into life—or rather, has already passed into life in Jesus Christ. If we say only—"their bodies are like that which Adam had"—without any further addition, limitation, or explanation (especially now at the beginning when nothing has been said of Adam’s body), we shall open the door for a great objection to be raised from Scripture, which says that Adam’s body was taken from the earth. I think this should be prevented, as it can easily be done by giving a hint of that distinction between one body and another, which undoubtedly will be discussed hereafter.
    Page 75. *Final Question.* Regarding their food, Behmen says it is all kinds of true, real, substantial fruit, corresponding to that variety which we have in our world, and that they take it with their hands like us, etc. Besides the testimony of those who have seen it, this is logically based on the fact that this world was one of the three angelic kingdoms, as it shall be again after the end of time. Therefore, at the creation, no new thing was brought into it that had not existed before; rather, only that which existed before was altered and brought into such a denser materiality that its former prince [Lucifer] could no longer make use of it. Behmen says this is suggested by the words of Moses, stating that everything came forth *after its kind*. Regarding what is further said on page 77 about the fire-light and watery parts of that fruit and their twofold effects, I do not recall finding it declared this way by Behmen; nevertheless, it may be consistent enough with his views if a few words were added to clarify that this is not the only or principal thing that softens their central fire and causes their humility.

Page 79. Final Question. This expression, *ignorant of the time*, might give occasion to think that they claim the angels were created during or after the days of the creation, since the beginning of the first day is the beginning of time, and before this there was no time. To prevent this, I think this question, "When were the angels created?" might be answered this way:—They believe them to have been created before the six days of the creation, but do not tell us how long before, rather professing themselves to be ignorant of it.

Further, in this answer it would be most proper to declare a little more plainly, and more significantly, the difference between their fire and light, to lay a foundation for what follows, since so much depends upon this: namely—fire was absolutely their own property, which they could not lose; it was their own nature, which could not be taken from them without them ceasing to be creatures; but they could not cease to be creatures once they were created. But light was not their own property in the same way; it was only their inheritance, given to them as a portion by their Father, who wanted them to be creatures after his own image, and who would not have taken it from them if they had remained obedient sons. They could, therefore, lose this inheritance without losing their created nature.

Page 81. Question 1. I think this question ought to be formed a little differently. For (1.) they did not have a law that could properly be said to be *given to them*; since this implies they were creatures before this law was given, whereas this law was rather natural to them, inseparable from their being creatures, innate in them, or born with them as they became creatures. As soon as they can be conceived as intellectual creatures, their intellect must also be conceived as sufficient to tell them that since they had not made themselves, they were not to alter their Maker’s making. And this was their entire law, and their whole duty was comprised within it.

(2.) This was not a *peculiar* or particular law, commanding them this or that particular thing, but it was that universal law, which may rightly be called so, because: (1.) it is extended to all and every kind of understanding creatures, none of which can be created without having this law imprinted, from its very first beginning, into its intellect. And, (2.) because it is the true, eternal root and ground of all the particular laws whatsoever *in this inferior world*.

Or thus:—and then they would have fallen into darkness before they had extinguished their light themselves.

of Nassington, for that of Lincoln, with a canonry annexed. Patron, John, tenth Earl of Westmoreland.

The church is dedicated to All Saints, and consists of a nave, aisles, transepts, and chancel, at the junction of which rises a plain pyramidal steeple, of about ninety feet in height. The length of the fabric from east to west is one hundred and five feet, ten inches; the transepts, from north to south, fifty-eight feet, six inches; and the width of the nave and aisles is forty-four feet, seven inches. At the north-east angle of the steeple is a pier of three semi-shafts and capitals, with several mouldings, evidently designed to support an arch; and we may reasonably believe that there was formerly a chapel on the north side of the chancel, opening into it through the arch for which this pier was a support.

The present structure is composed of various styles of architecture, and has evidently undergone considerable change since its first erection. At the west end, the point of the old roof may easily be traced. This, with the steeple, appears to be of the twelfth century, and probably as far back as 1150. A clerestory was added, apparently about the middle of the fourteenth century (1350). To this date the west window of the nave may also be referred. The chancel seems to be of the fifteenth century, and the east window of the north transept, somewhat later. It was inserted, probably, when the chapel alluded to was demolished. The steeple exhibits four semi-circular headed windows, seen from within; each divided by a rude shaft, with a capital supporting the ends of two smaller arches of similar curvature. One of these is open, the others are partially walled up. It is remarkable that the arches in the basement of the steeple are of the pointed style, which is not easily accountable unless we may suppose that, when the character of the architecture was changed in the fourteenth century, the workman was bold enough to insert them in the place of others of the Norman style. The windows in the bell chamber are pointed, with nailhead and billet mouldings, divided by a slender shaft. The aisles are separated from the nave by four drop arches, of bold and well-executed mouldings, supported by octagonal piers, with ogee mouldings and embattled capitals.

The font is circular, ornamented by quatrefoils enclosed in a plain circular border. In 1818, this was surmounted by a rich cover of dark oak in the form of an octagonal spire, crocketed, having each of its sides carved and pierced with quatrefoils. On four of these are the angel, the lion, the bull, and the eagle, being emblems of the four evangelists. On the intermediate sides are a rose tree, with the legend, *Sum Rosa Sharonis*; a lily, with *et Lilum Convallium*; a vine, with *Sum Vitis et Vos Palmetes*; and a rock, with water springing from it, having the sun rising over it, and *Venite ad istas aqua*.

The open or free seats are terminated by panels, with good oak tracery, brought from the church at Fotheringhay in 1818. The materials of which the desk and pulpit are composed are similar, and were also brought from the church of Fotheringhay at the same time. On the seventeenth of May, 1841, Lord Exeter conveyed a piece of land for the enlargement of the churchyard.

**Q. 3.** In the words, *over God’s meek love and light*, which they despised, the *words and light* must necessarily be left out. **Page 87. Q. ult. A.** Yes: they assume according to Scripture: 1st, That God is love and light. 2ndly, That God is also fire and might, together with his hidden root of darkness. And 3rdly, That darkness, fire, and light are all three required to make a creature after the image and likeness of God. And now, based on these premises, they say—that which came out of God, namely, out of love and light, cannot be capable of such a state of damnation; but as it is his free gift, so it returns to the giver when the creature severs itself from it by turning its will and obedience away from it. But that which came out of God’s fire and might remains alone in such a case and cannot be lost, because it is the creature’s natural property, or that which causes it to be a creature. And this now, since it consists entirely of moving, stirring, and active properties, cannot but work according to its own internal nature and essences. This working is nothing else than a perceivable manifestation of its own natural property, made in, to, and by the creature itself.
