To the inhabitants of these houses, Mrs. Hester Gibbon (aunt to the historian), who died in June 1790, left three hundred pounds by her will. It was bequeathed to a Mr. William Law, senior, <margin>his cousin /</margin> of King’s Cliffe, and his <unclear>son</unclear>, Mr. William Law, junior, then of Stamford (afterwards of King’s Cliffe), attorney-at-law, in trust to invest the same at interest, or in government securities, and to pay the said interest weekly to the poor women in Thorpe’s almshouses. But the successors of Mr. William Law, junior, in Mrs. Gibbon’s property at King’s Cliffe, regularly pay the interest weekly.

To this bequest must be added the interest of one hundred pounds stock, 3 percent consolidated annuities, left to these almswomen by the will of Mrs. Ann de Rippe of London, dated 1804; this is regularly paid by her executor, Mr. Lawrence Redhead.

In the year 1688, Mr. Richard Wildbore gave five pounds per year for the teaching of eight of the poorest boys, born and resident in this parish, to read and write; and he charged a tenement in Park-street and a field called “Willowbed” for the payment of it forever.

In the year 1727, the Rev. WILLIAM LAW, formerly a Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and a native of this town (the subject of our special notice), founded a school for the education and full clothing of fourteen poor girls of King’s Cliffe, with a salary for a mistress to instruct them in reading, knitting, and useful needlework. He afterwards built a schoolhouse and school, and two tenements for two poor old unmarried women or widows of King’s Cliffe, with a weekly allowance. He appointed the same trustees as will be mentioned later in the account of Mrs. Hutcheson’s charity, and vested in them the schoolhouse, almshouses, and premises, along with a freehold estate at Northorpe in Lincolnshire. He also gave the trustees a small collection of books, part of which is for the use of the inhabitants of King’s Cliffe and its neighborhood, and the other part for the clergy; the audit room in the house of the master of Mrs. Hutcheson’s school is fitted up for the books.

In 1745, Mrs. Elizabeth Hutcheson, widow of Archibald Hutcheson of London, esquire, founded a school in this town for the education and full clothing of eighteen poor boys of the town of King’s Cliffe (since increased to twenty), with a salary for a master to teach them reading, writing, and the useful parts of arithmetic.

And this manifestation now is what we call a state of damnation, which this creature must naturally and of necessity be capable of, because it does not come upon it from the outside, but is raised by itself out of its own ground. Among the inhabitants of this place, as already observed, the most memorable was the Rev. WILLIAM LAW, the founder of the school and almshouses already mentioned. The name Law occurs in the early registers of the parish, and it is probable that the family resided here some time prior to 1590, the date when the parish register begins. At that time, it appears there were four families of the same name living in King’s Cliffe: William, Thomas, Robert, and Giles. It cannot be stated precisely from which of these he was descended, but most probably from Thomas, the son of George Law, who is styled "gentleman," baptized May 30, 1626, as it appears that his grandfather, as well as his father, bore that Christian name. Their arms, on a token dated 1659, are an ermine field charged with a chevron.

His father, who was baptized September 25, 1657, was a grocer and chandler, and carried on an extensive business in a house which he himself had built on the north side of the principal street, in the center of the town. Having acquired a competent knowledge of the learned languages, LAW was admitted into Emmanuel College, Cambridge, on June 7, 1705, where he took the degrees of Bachelor and Master of Arts. He was elected to a Fellowship in 1711, as a result of which he entered into Holy Orders. He retained his Fellowship until 1716, when, by refusing to take the oath of allegiance to King George the First, he forfeited his Fellowship and all prospect of advancement in the church.

A. Whether these things, or whether the properties themselves of temporal nature are meant. And to this question now I would answer thus:

A. It is that same eternal Word which breathed them forth in the beginning, yet not considered as being in that manifest and perceptible act which was done in the days of the creation and entered into rest at the end of it; but as in its secret continuing in and with all things, upholding and still enabling them (by the powers of either eternal or temporal nature, or by both of them together) to increase and multiply according to their kind.

[That word, *Be fruitful and multiply*, was not an outward sounding speech, but an internal living power, going forth and communicating something like itself, though only as a shadowy resemblance and according to the creature’s capacity. This communicated power is only transient and perishable, just as the creature is itself: while that which has communicated it is constant, fixed, and permanent, and is even that without the continuation of which in and with all things, nothing could subsist. Concerning this the Scripture says, *He upholds all things by the Word of his power*; and again, *Your* (according to the German translation) *imperishable Spirit is in all things*.]

Page 103. *A.* 1. I think it might be very proper here, if not necessary, to say—that as the seven planets and fixed stars are such representations above, so the seven metals and minerals are also the same below. For our earth, being made up of the coarsest residues, or most corrupted matter gathered from all the corners of this wasted kingdom and compacted into one globe, must necessarily have in it something answering to what is, besides it, finer and more subtle or ethereal in the whole region. And this is certainly the ground (though some other reasons, no less considerable, might be given) of that saying of Hermes, <term>Id quod est inferius est sicut id quod est superius</term> <note>That which is below is like that which is above.</note>

Concerning now the following description of the three first properties, I have nothing of importance to say; but shall only gather from <term>Behmen</term> <note>Jacob Boehme</note> what I may find here or there is attributed to each of them. If it might serve to insert this or that particular thing, significant expression, or circumstance, it would be well and profitable; and if not, no hurt can be done by it. As to the *first*, then,

(Page 103. *A. final.*) Behmen uses the words *of a spiritual sharpness, harshness, grossness, darkness, etc.* and says that of these three (<term>sal</term>, <term>sulphur</term>, and <term>mercury</term>, commonly called the three principles of things by natural philosophers), the first—namely, *sal*—is this same first property. Of this he also says that it is the greatest and most potent, the beginning of strength and might, the <term>Fiat</term> (though never by itself alone), and the keeper of all things; a drying and shutting up into death; a taking in unto oneself, and a true mother of selfishness; a cause of sound, noise, etc.; the beginning of every formation; a magnetism, or magnetical impression and coagulation of itself, filling and darkening itself, etc.

(Page 105. *Q.* 1.) This second quality is the motion of the magnetical drawing in; a cause of all creaturely life, a trembling, stinging bitterness, or a stinger, stirrer, rager, and breaker; the cause of the essences; the beginning of enmity, and of all contrariety, and also of all qualification; the cause of distinction, speech, intellect, five senses, etc. This spirit (N.B.) is restless (or rather restlessness itself), and is yet the seeker after rest, making its own unquietness by its very seeking. It is a ground of bitter woe, and yet the true root of life; and the <term>vulcanus</term>, striking the fire (namely, of or to the life). It is a cause of all sensibility and feeling; a ground of the air in the outward world: it is the outflown moveable word; and in the creation this was the separator or divider in the powers.

(Page 105. *Q.* 2.) This *third* quality makes the triangle in nature, and is a whirling wheel, taken in, and as it were swallowing up into death the bitter essences, but giving forth out of it another life. It is a cause of death and life, and of the twofold fire—namely, of the first and second principle. Its proper name is anguish; its qualification, wrath and anger; and its materiality, <term>sulphur</term>. It has a twofold fire in it, namely, a cold and a hot one, and is the devil’s chief seat. Without the light it is the true foundation of hell; and in the light the cause of eternal joy, etc.

Considering, Sir, that this matter concerning the three first properties is of such great importance, so fundamental, and has so much depending upon it, I cannot but recommend to your consideration whether it would not be necessary that several things about it be declared more distinctly and circumstantially, such that the things belonging more properly and immediately to eternal nature were always placed first, and that then a descent were made to temporal—

Page 107. *Final Question. Where and how does this water spirit arise?* A. It arises in the light, and is that same thing which before the light was called harshness. The manner of its arising is this—when the fire in the three first dark properties is enkindled, it makes in them a (twofold) great crack, or terror, called so with respect to creatures with senses, who, if it were done in them, could not but feel the greatest terror. This harshness then, being thus terrified, (in the second crack) loses immediately, or, as it were, dies to its former nature, and is made soft and thin, and qualified according to the meek and tender properties of the light; wherein it is now the water spirit, or that whose immediate production in the spiritual materiality is water.

Page 108. *Q. What do they mean by the sweetness of the water?* A. They mean that tinctured and transmuted quality, with relation especially to the spiritual taste, which the water now has in the light, in opposition to that which it had before in the first harshness: and they distinguish thereby the water of light and life from that of death and darkness.

*A. 2. Therefore, I am of the opinion that either this word *mercurial* might be left out, or something might be added by which this obscurity could be taken away, and needless objections prevented. And then, it will not be well enough to say only—those things sound most which have this spirit in them, seeing that it was owned just before that all things have it in them. Therefore, it must needs be more proper to say—most in them, or—which have it sufficiently stirring in them, etc.

Page 111. *A. 3. Page 115. *A. in conjunction with his will (which they call the fiat).* This, I think, is not plainly enough expressed; for it might be understood as if the will (alone) were called by them the fiat, which it is not, as it was observed before. And then, instead of *will*, I would rather say, *eternal Word*. Because here one is not speaking of a purpose, but of the execution of it, or of a present act and deed, which the will may be conceived indeed as preceding; but the *Word* is rightly conceived as nearer, and as actually engaged therein. And therefore the *Word* (in that conjunction) more properly than the *will*, was the *fiat in act*; by which the will is not excluded, but manifestly presupposed.

Ibid. *(which they take to be the meaning of the word created.)* This might justly be put in after the words, *compacting its earth*, for as it stands before them, it does but misrepresent their meaning. Seeing that by the word *created*, they do not understand—he prepared the chaotic angelical world, which is a more general expression—but they understand precisely this compacting.

In the same place. *And its heaven—into a state of purity.* I cannot see that it is fit or proper to say that heaven was compacted into a state of purity.

For (1.) the word *compacted* is more suitable for the earth than for heaven, which might rather be said to have been *condensed* (or if there is any other more appropriate expression) to show the difference between heaven and earth. These two could not have been equally capable of the same degree of condensation or compaction. And (2.) heaven cannot be said to be condensed into a state of purity. Because this purity does not depend directly upon its creation or condensation (which very word already implies something of impurity, since it is a change from its former state into another, made on such a sad account), but only upon its being, as it were, swept and cleansed of those gross impurities that were scattered everywhere. When these were gathered and compacted into one place, the rest of this region was free from them and became more fit to receive another shape and condition, much inferior to its former one. And this only is meant by Behmen, when he speaks of that state which the English interpreter has expressed as purity.

Page 116. *A. 1. To the last words, "which there was not before,"* I think something could be most appropriately added from what was blotted out opposite page 117, namely: "and that they might be a habitation, fitted and prepared for those innumerable kinds of creatures that were to be in them."

Page 117. *A. 2.* All that is declared here is right and true; only this may be observed: that not only the compaction into tangible materiality in particular, but also more generally, the whole condensation or out-breathing—coagulated into another inferior kind of coarser substance (though ever so fine in comparison to the earth)—was the proper means by which the devil's power was broken, his kingdom taken from him, and he disabled from exercising his wickedness any further there through his dark and false magic.

Page 118. *That it might be a principle, existing in itself.* Since this designation of a "principle," in its full sense—in which Behmen usually takes it—is not applicable to the earthly globe but to the whole macrocosm, I think it would be more acceptable if it were a little limited, by saying: "that it might be as a principle in some sense existing in itself"; for it cannot be said that it exists in itself in every sense.

Page 119. *Q. 1.* This answer also is right and true enough, but only the last two lines of it may be called obscure and could easily be made clearer and more free from objections. For they do not say nor mean that the earth was restored to an acceptable state directly or only by its revolutions, but by the different works, effects, and products of the six active spirits, which performed their various operations in and on the earth and cooperated successively in this restoration during the time of these revolutions.

*Q. 2. Why the earth's revolution is made in a natural day* cannot well be asked or answered. Because, if we think to ask this, we must necessarily presuppose an idea of the length of a natural day before the idea of the earth's revolution, which we cannot rationally do. We see that the earth's revolution is the only thing that made from the beginning, and still makes, all the natural days, determining their constant length; and without or before it, no natural day can be conceived, nor can any measure of its length be imagined. And so, this question cannot be answered any more than this: "Why does a natural day have precisely the length it has?" This would be the same as if we asked, "Why does the earth not move either more quickly or more slowly than it does?"—which no one will presume to answer adequately based on natural reasons. And yet this question must be formed in even this way with respect to the first three revolutions, which did not yet make a natural day, and were nevertheless performed in the same space of time which is now the proper, constant length of one.

Page 123. *A. 1. If to the last words, "by the motion of his Spirit," were added "upon the waters,"* it would be more evident that this relates to the description by Moses.

They say, therefore, in short: (1.) That on this fourth day, the production of the planetary orb, with all the fixed stars, being a visible outbirth and representation of the seven chief spirits, both of eternal and temporal nature, with all their inferior or subordinate qualities, was made in a manner answering to that in which they were themselves from eternity, and are still generated.

(2.) That the fourth spirit of eternal nature, the magic fire, broke forth and fixed its representative in the center of our vortex, which is the sun.

(3.) That several particular circumstances relating to the first astringent property—considered both before and after that saying, "Let there be light" (all which they do not fail to declare sufficiently)—are most necessary to be well understood and considered together, in order to be informed and convinced by them that this first spirit of nature, the cause of cold, produced its representative (at this kindling of the fire) in the remotest *orbit* from the center, called *Saturn*, which is, according to their doctrine (agreeing with that of the ancients), a cold planet.

(4.) That at the same kindling of the fire in the sun, the fierce, terrible crack (always naturally preceding the fire’s clear flame and light) was projected, or rather fled up from the center with a dreadful force, according to its own natural birthright; and took along with it, for its substantial being, the fire's wrathfulness. And so this ascended until the sun's light, now rising and displaying itself, overpowered it and stopped its raging fury. This <note>sphere</note> they now say is *Mars*, the representative of the third anguishing and whirling spirit, whose office is to stir and move all that is movable in this whole macrocosm, and especially the planetary wheel. <note>That illustration concerning the projection of stars in fireworks is here deliberately left out, not because it was altogether unfit, but only so as not to give occasion for the concept that a visible fiery globe was ejected from the sun, whereas Behmen says no such thing. It was an invisible spiritual property, whose bodily being became visible when the light had conquered and stopped its course, and then appeared visibly in that planet, *whereupon the planet's motion commenced*. It would appear that Newton did not clearly apprehend the *exact sense of Behmen on this point*.</note>

(5.) That this light (considered not as to its shine or glance, but as to its power and virtue) having thus stopped the course of Mars, left behind its fierce wrathfulness and ascended still higher as a soft, rising life, according to its own natural right, until it came to Saturn's harsh, astringent sphere of activity, by whose compressive power it was resisted and made unable to rise higher. There it therefore remained and, by taking possession of that place, became the fifth spirit's representative, which is *Jupiter*, the meekness in outward nature, and rightly therefore situated between the astringent cold of Saturn and the fierce fire of Mars, as a temperament between them.

The first harshness was broken; the same, but transformed, and being now the mild water-spirit, *sunk* humbly and softly down and became a visible representative of the fifth spirit in *Venus*. They say it has an inherent light of its own <note>As well as a borrowed light from the sun; I do not remember that Behmen says this, nor can I find it through all my searching.</note> (which is asserted by some recent astronomers) and tempers the fierceness of the heat of Mars.

(7.) That this sinking continued from the property of Venus, so that the power of the first harshness—now softened in and by the light—sunk deeper down and became a visible representative of the sixth spirit, which is *Mercury*.

(8.) That this sinking continued further from Mercury also and reached its conclusion in the *Moon*, which they say represents the seventh spirit of eternal nature, partaking of the qualities of all the others, and therefore more fit to receive them and transmit them to our sublunary world.

(9.) That the seven planets have a wonderful efficacy upon ——, etc. Page 135.—§ 8.

Regarding the difficulty that the planets have such gross and obscure bodies that they cannot be imagined to have been projected from the sun, it can be plain enough from this short description that Behmen says nothing at all of such a gross material projection. Instead, he describes a spiritual generation, or *displaying of the spiritual properties*, which must have occurred in this macrocosm at the kindling of the fire in its center, according to the manner of their eternal generation. In this, the nature and office of fire is to display all properties and make them manifest in their distinction. Seeing then that this was now done in a manner and degree inferior to that eternal generation—namely, in a temporal principle, in specific locations and measurable distances, etc.—these planets, as to their several chief qualities predominant in them and giving them their distinct names, may well enough be said to have been projected from the sun. This is because the kindling of the sun was their origin, or the cause of their being made visible in this temporal world. It is not said that the sun generated them; Behmen expressly denies this. And much less is it said that so many vast, gross, and obscure bodies were ejected from the sun. But only that at this kindling of the fire in the sun, such and such spiritual properties were raised and stirred up, so that they moved each according to its own nature—some mounting up from the center on high, and others sinking down in opposition—and this according to their predominant powers and virtues. 

But regarding their corporeal being now, it must be supposed that each of them acquired it in its own place or sphere, where it still stands at a proportionate distance from the center, according to Behmen’s plain words. He says sometimes of one or the other (which must be applied to all) that they were created in *that place*. For if we consider what he means by *created* (which was declared above), it will be self-evident that this saying cannot be reconciled with the other—that they were projected—unless we understand the latter as a descent of their spiritual properties from the center, and the former as a thickening of their vast material bodies. If it should be objected that it was said above (§ 4) that Mars took the wrathfulness along with it from the center as its body, etc., it is easily and solidly answered: in such a sense it may be said of all of them that they took this or that from the center as a body. But this was only such a body as our thoughts are bodies of the spirit within them (mentioned above, p. 113). Each of them must indeed have had that kind of body even in the first beginning of their departure from the center. But that this body was not yet that vast, gross, obscure globe in which they appear today is evident enough. This spiritual body, therefore, was afterward immediately created or thickened in their several places, according to the difference of their spirituality. So that none of them can be reasonably imagined to be altogether like our earth. Nay, also, none of them can be such as the moon is, which is the nearest to earthliness and has a mixture of them all, notwithstanding that they all may be equally obscure in themselves, etc.

And thus, I think, the chief difficulty is sufficiently removed, so that it can be tolerable to say, in the sense mentioned, that the planets were projected from the sun at the kindling of the fire in the center, though Behmen never uses the word projection or ejection. Instead, he speaks rather of their own free displaying and departing from the center (though this was caused by the fire), either by flying up or sinking down, according to the manner of their generation in eternal nature.

Page 139. § 1. *manifested out of the fire of nature, etc.* This manner of expression, as to my——

### III.—A PRAYER, on entering into holy Orders.

Therefore, for my part, I would rather say this—breathed forth out of the dark and light worlds, and manifested by the kindling of the fire in the sun, as in the center of our vortex, etc.

§ 2. Since the fixed stars are not only a representation of energies, but also energies themselves—though in an inferior degree and order than those of which they are a representation—I am inclined to think it would be appropriate and necessary, after the words, *energies of eternal nature*, to add this or something similar: exercising in temporal nature, and after a temporal manner, the same powers and energies that are originally in eternal nature, out of which they were breathed, etc.

For though it follows afterward (§ 3) clearly enough that they are of wonderful effectiveness, yet it is not expressed that this effectiveness depends only upon this: their being representatives of as many energies of eternal nature.

Page 139. § 3. *on all things here below.* Since this effectiveness cannot absolutely be restricted to things here below, though this may make up the greatest part of it—especially with respect to man—I think it would be most proper to say: of wonderful effectiveness in the whole extent of this temporal universe, and especially on all things here below.

Regarding all the rest of the expressions in this paragraph, I must say it is so obscure that I cannot grasp the proper meaning. The distinct, specific expressions, looked upon each by themselves, are indeed plain and true enough, but the connection between them creates great obscurity—which yet may be so only to my sight, for want of a sufficient understanding of a good English style.

Between § 3 and § 4, I think something could be most properly inserted which might make clearer what is said in § 4, and might also show, at least implicitly, a ground and reason for it: namely, that good and evil, wrath, anger, and love are manifest in the stars, and this because of their threefold origin, which is the dark, fire, and light worlds, of whose powers and energies (brought by Lucifer into contrariety) they are effective representatives.

And then, in any other convenient place, several more things could be added, according to Behmen, though they are only arbitrary and may be left out as well—for instance: That they have among them their orders and degrees, both of size or visible magnitude, and also of different superior and inferior dignities and offices, in analogy to the angelic kingdoms and also to the governments on earth. That, in one sense and respect, they all stand in discord, disharmony, contrariety, and opposition, and yet in another, they together make up but one great harmonious instrument: just as many larger and smaller, thicker and thinner strings of one or more musical instruments can make a melodious, concordant tune as well as a discordant, unpleasant noise, according to the skill or intent of the hand that moves them. That the whole of nature, with all its powers and energies, is totally in every one of them, but only one power is primarily predominant or manifest in each of them; therefore, there are not as many natures as there are stars, but all the stars together are the whole of nature, or the manifestation of all the powers of nature. That they are in a continual anxious turning or rolling from the wrath-fire kindled by Lucifer and his legions. That they are fixed, each in its own place, because this third principle is to stand in a constant, abiding generation until the end of time; and all manner of life on the earth shall be generated always by one and the same operation, and after the same manner. That they may draw, incline, or dispose man toward good and evil, and many times toward great wickedness, but cannot constrain or force a necessity upon him, etc.

Behmen says only in general that the hour of birth can bring a great change to that power which the constellation that was present at the time of conception would have in man. Or that the constellation at the hour of a man’s birth does alter very much of that natural temper and inclination; and doubtless also much of those accidents or chances concerning temporal prosperity and misfortunes which he would have, or which would befall him, from the power of the constellation that was present at the time of his conception. constellation, called by him a magic astrum, which must indeed necessarily conform to the figure of that firmamental constellation that was present both at his conception and at his birth; however, it cannot be restricted or exclusively referred to either the former or the latter alone. Therefore, it must be referred to both of them in union together: namely, to the latter as grounded upon the former, and to the former as partly altered and partly confirmed by the latter. And in the second place, in chapter 58—where nothing at all is said regarding either man's conception or birth, and even the word constellation is not so much as mentioned—Boehme declares only what a great difference there is between natural and supernatural figures, dreams, and visions. He says that the dreams of Pharaoh were out of eternal nature, above the operation and figure of the stars and elements, and that even this was the true reason why the Egyptian magi, who were merely naturalists, could not give him an interpretation of them. Now, it indeed cannot be denied that here also Pharaoh must have had, in his outward natural constellation of the stars, such a figure as corresponded to that which came out of eternal nature, and by which he was to be that person under whose reign such a great and notable alteration of the Egyptian kingdom should come to pass. But whether this natural constellation was more to be referred to the hour of his conception, or to that of his birth, or also to both of them together, I think nobody can presume to determine.

*Ibid. Q. 2.* As to the influences of the planets and stars upon civil governments, Boehme also says nothing in particular and nothing directly. But in general and in many places, he admits that civil governments, and the various occurrences, revolutions, and alterations within them, do depend upon these influences; for they are (in such a form and manner) but a natural order and constitution of the spirit of this world. Though indeed, as to their substance, he also freely grants that they have a basis in eternal nature. And, moreover, all this dependence upon the starry influences stands only under the *inspection* and *direction* of the Most High, whose operating instrument all this temporal nature with *all its influences* is. This may justly and significantly be called an operating instrument, using a similarity taken from a watch and frequently used by Boehme. For a watch, with all its parts and wheels, is but a dead, impotent, and immovable instrument by itself; yet it is nevertheless operating by its own communicated capacity, if it is but once wound up and directed by its master.

Concerning their influences upon the weather, Boehme says indeed expressly and distinctly that the stars and planets cause fair weather, rain, hail, snow, excessive heat, frost, etc. <note>as indeed is undoubted, as with nativities, etc., but who can calculate them all in a *given point?*</note> But he goes no further into any particular account, declaring which of the stars especially, or what manner of the planetary aspects, cause such or such a kind of weather. Instead, he refers us to the skillful astrologers, saying that they found it out, at least for the most part, by long and diligent observations, etc.

Q. 3.* The meaning of the planetary wheel in Boehme's threefold life, regarding its turning, winding, or bending more and more toward the inside, is not to be understood in relation to the outward appearance of the planetary bodies. For it is well known that all seven stand in an equal degree of outwardness, in one and the same outward or third principle, and all seven have an equal share in being visible objects of one and the same firmamental eye. But it is to be understood in relation to that which is invisible in the planets, though not incomprehensible, and which belongs inseparably to the entire generation of this third principle, considered in its union with and dependence upon the twofold inward world. For this, when considered thus, does not stand with its seven different parts in the same degree of outwardness, and is not intelligible all at once, or to an intellect that remains fixed in one and the same station. For these seven different parts do not, and indeed cannot, have an equal share in being intelligible objects of one and the same human intellect, unless it is, as it were, repositioned seven times. This is because they turn deeper and deeper, according to Boehme's figure, as if into a deep pit, wherein the center must be conceived as being at the bottom and the windings all moving more and more upward, until the outermost, which alone may be visible to that eye that stands at the mouth of that pit. <note>Not as a circular line winding inward by seven turns to a point, but to a central ground; for all the windings and the ground are of equal magnitude or circumference, though represented on a plain surface as ending in a point.</note> That eye, therefore, must be conceived as having to go down deeper and deeper itself if it is to behold each of these windings one after the other. planets together, if they were all elevated above its horizon. But one and the same human intellect cannot see all the windings of this planetary wheel without its own being really translocated—that is, without its own being really generated deeper and deeper, or introduced into one winding after another. For that which is seen or understood is always a veiling or covering of that which follows next. Which covering <note>Note well</note> is not only in that planetary wheel, considered as being outside of man in the macrocosm; but it is in the same manner in man himself also, who otherwise could not be called a microcosm. In man himself, therefore, <note>Note well</note> all these coverings must be removed, and so his intellect will be thereby, as it were, transplaced and enabled to see what otherwise is in vain for him to undertake. I cannot represent the meaning of this planetary wheel any more plainly. Boehme says expressly and intelligibly, not only that it cannot be delineated by figures and not expressed by words, but also that it cannot be understood, except by the spirit, who may understand it in himself; namely, if he be made able to see and behold himself, what and how he is, for *as this planetary wheel is, so is the Spirit also*. And then also, he directs us to consider for an illustration of this, the three different principles wherein we may find the same, or at least something very similar. For all three principles are in every man (just as all the seven windings of this planetary wheel are in every man also), and yet only that is seen and felt by him in which he stands, or which is manifest in him; and by that same manifestation of itself, it always excludes, covers, or hides the other two. If these shall be manifested or opened in his sensibility, he must be brought away from his former station, which is, as it were, a translocation, or a real transport from one into another. A human soul, if in this natural earthly body only, can be sensible only of this third principle and of things belonging to it, and cannot all this while see or feel the first and second. If it has departed from the body and entered into the dark world, it can no longer be sensible of the third and can have no perception of the second. But if it is in the second, the first is shut up from it, and of the third it can have no sensation. And though in this outward world one and the same soul may have, at different times, more or less a real sensibility of all three, yet there will always be required and presupposed something of a real translocation, in a spiritual sense. For no principle can be seen or felt, except by those creatures that are actually within it.

German. In August 1718, his mother died, and by her will left his brother George and him in trust to dispose of her real and personal estate at King's Cliffe, and to divide it equally among her children, then consisting of George, Thomas, WILLIAM, Benjamin, Farmery, and Margaret. The deed of release, which is dated 1726, states that the amount paid to each of the then survivors was one hundred and fifteen pounds only. To Margaret, who was now married to Edward Hayne of Ashbourne, in Derbyshire, had also been devised the household goods, linen, and plate. Giles, the third brother, is said to have had children, though no memorial is preserved of them; nor likewise of Christopher, who probably died in infancy.

Thomas, the second brother, married and settled at Warmington, and afterwards at King's Cliffe. He is described as a yeoman and had two sons and five daughters: namely, William, a linendraper in Sun-court, Cornhill, London, born in 1713, died unmarried in 1790; Sarah, born in 1709, died 1784; Margaret, born in 1716; Ellen, born in 1718; Mary, who, "for sixteen years of the best part of her life," attended on Mrs. Hutcheson, was born in 1724 and died in 1803; Elizabeth, born 1727; and Nathaniel, who left one son and two daughters: namely, Henry, who succeeded to his uncle's business in London and had children by his second wife, a Miss Rogers—three children, all sons: John, in holy orders, rector of ——, in Hants; William, in a mercantile warehouse, who married and had two sons; and Thomas, with an insurance broker. Susanna, the elder daughter of Nathaniel, was married to a Mr. Skey; and Sarah, the younger, was unmarried.

...covers, as shall be said shortly.

What further is added here concerning—an outward quintessence of things, in which the spirit of this world opens itself and resides, out of which he has the power of flowing out, and which is his inward and more immediate body, etc.—cannot, in my opinion, be reconciled in all particulars to what Boehme says in that passage to which the last lines direct me, namely, *CLAVIS, verses 96–105, German edition.* This is the only place sufficient to declare what he means by the spirit of this world, which, says Boehme, is hidden in the four elements, just as the soul is in the body, and is nothing else but an outflow and actual power from the sun and stars. Its habitation, in which it works, is spiritual, surrounded by the four elements. This spiritual habitation is (1.) A sharp magnetic power, from the first property of eternal nature. (2.) An outflow from the inward motion, or second property—this I call the fiery mercury in the spirit of this world, for this is the mobility of all things, a separator of powers, and a shaper of forms or figures. (3.) A sensibility in this motion and sharpness, etc., from the third property of eternal nature. These three properties the ancient philosophers called sulfur, mercury, and salt, according to the matters which are generated out of them within the four elements when this (threefold) spirit coagulates or becomes substantial. In this ground the four elements also lie, and are not separated from it, nor are they something distinct; rather, they are only the manifestation of this spiritual ground, like a house or habitation of the spirit in which it works, etc.

The words "which outward quintessence, the inward and more immediate body of this spirit (*for the four elements are its outward body*), they call *salniter*," etc., are, in my view, entirely obscure, and I do not think they can give anyone a clear and distinct understanding of the matter. For (1.) I cannot find that Boehme calls the *salniter* a body of the spirit of this world. (2.) I cannot understand what is meant here by *salniter*. That visible materiality, which is an ingredient of gunpowder, cannot be meant, seeing that this *salniter* is called an inward and more immediate body; whereas that substance is equally outward or distant, in the same degree from the spirit, as the outward salt, brimstone, and quicksilver. And that which is more inward in this outward *salniter* is its being (in correspondence to eternal nature) that crack <note>Boehme uses "crack" or "Schrack" to describe a sudden spiritual transition or lightning-like flash</note> in which all the properties are separated and displayed. But this also cannot be meant here, because the crack, as a separator and displayer of all the properties, cannot be conceived as a body of the spirit of this world. (3.) This body or *salniter* is called a quintessence of everything, which can no more be applicable to this *salnitrous* crack than to the tangible *salnitral* substance. (4.) It is called an outward quintessence, and this makes everything even more obscure. For every quintessence is the most inward part of that thing whose quintessence it is said to be. And though it might be understood in respect to this outward world, and so thereby distinguished from a heavenly quintessence of paradisiacal things, yet this will not be sufficient to explain it, as long as it is not declared, both as to this outward and to that inward world, how the salnitrous crack can be called the quintessence of all things, which I see no possibility of doing.

<margin>Curate Dr. Hey</margin>
Having left Cambridge upon his resolution not to take the oath of allegiance to King George the First, his next appearance in public was in London, in the year 1717, engaged in the Bangorian controversy; but whether at that time, or from the period of his relinquishing his Fellowship up to the year 1726, he held any paid appointment does not now appear. Report states him to have officiated as a curate in London and to have had very considerable livings offered to him by or through his friend, Dr. Sherlock, afterwards Bishop of London; but as he always remained true to his non-juring principles, it is almost certain that he did not again officiate in the church. In the above memorable and most important controversy, however, he laid the foundation of his future fame; the ability he displayed therein gained him the notice and respect of many who were opposed to the high church principles which he had adopted at the university and, at that early period of his life, so strongly and persuasively advocated. [According to the ‘Preacher’s Assistant,’ vol. ii. 1737, he published a single sermon in 1718, on 1 Corinthians 12:3; but after making researches in the chief libraries throughout the country and in private collections of tracts, the author has not been able to find or hear of such a discourse. His Thanksgiving Sermon of 1713 may be seen in Queen’s College Library, Cambridge.]

The ‘Answer to the Fable of the Bees,’ published in 1721, was the next issue from his pen and may be considered as a good specimen of the gentlemanly tone of ironical banter in which supporters of vice and disbelief—men of education—ought to be met and dealt with by the public guardian of religion and moral virtue.

Some few years later, in the year 1726, he published a tract against stage entertainment, which was then characterized by the most open obscenity of sentiment and language. In this tract, entitled ‘The Absolute Unlawfulness of the Stage Entertainment, Fully Demonstrated,’ he exhibits that power of close yet agreeable argumentation for which his writings have been so highly commended. And notwithstanding the ridicule which Gibbon, Dennis, and others have attempted to cast upon this performance, it is to the honor of Mr. Law that no admirer of sound reasoning who was a Christian ever found fault with it, nor is it possible indeed for such a person to do so without doing violence to his

In the last lines, where three salnitrous substances are mentioned—(1) a visible one, (2) a heavenly one, and (3) a divine one—a clear mistake has been made. For the heavenly and the divine, if both are called and conceived as substances, cannot be distinguished except by referring the former to God as he is considered *within* nature, and the latter to God as he is *outside* of nature. But in the Divine Being outside of nature, there is no such thing; everything must be referred only to the generation of nature. The salnitrous crack, in or at the entrance of the fourth form, is what may be called divine, but it is not yet a divine substance. However, in heaven—namely, in the seventh form—there is undoubtedly such a substance, of which the salnitral substance on earth is a visible image. Yet this heavenly substance is not a shadowy image of another divine salnitrous substance; rather, it is a body or crystalline material being, expressed and made substantial by that salnitrous crack (not substance) which occurs in the generation of eternal nature. This is caused by the conjunction between eternal liberty and the dark forms of nature; even our visible salniter in this world proves to partake of both of these, according to its lower manner and degree.

Page 142. No. 7. Regarding this, I have only to observe that instead of these words—*this outflown word is not the pure Deity, but his outflown word, by which, etc.*—the sense could be expressed with more grace and greater significance thus: "this outflown word is not the pure Deity, but such an outflown power as that by which, etc."

Page 142. No. 8. Here, concerning common salniter and its preparation, philosophical mercury, oil of sulfur, oil of vitriol, spirit of nitre, and the character L signifying gold, etc., I have nothing to say, neither for nor against; the author may perhaps be able to prove it, but experience must confirm it. I am only a little puzzled by the first expression, where it is said, *the matter of the philosophical work is the five vowels, which signify common salniter.* I cannot see what relation these two can have to one another. In the entire description of this work (in *SIGNATURA RERUM*), Behmen never uses the expression "five vowels." And although the very thing he understands by that—namely, the divine life, power, virtue, the Spirit of God, and the true spirit of understanding from the second principle of light, etc.—is absolutely required for this work, I am unable to grasp how the five vowels can be called the "matter." Nevertheless, there may be something there that is beyond the reach of my capacity.

Page 143. No. 9. The signal star, mentioned not only in the *MYSTERIUM MAGNUM* but also in several other books and places, has a twofold meaning, relating most evidently to the discovery of both the inward eternal and the outward temporal nature. According to his own words, he says, *Two suns have risen and shine for us.* And again, *the signal star is as great as the whole world, etc.* With respect to the first, he chiefly understands this great manifestation concerning the generation of eternal nature in its seven-fold wheel; it was in respect to this that he called his first book *AURORA, Day-break, Morning Redness, etc.* And so this signal star, in this first sense, is nothing other than that which some others now call the morning star of Wisdom, relating especially to the mysteries of the kingdom of Christ, which cannot be fundamentally understood

The *Christian Perfection* was published in the year 1726 (where it was composed does not now appear), and the *Serious Call* followed only a year later. We now come to one of the most eventful periods of his life from a philosophical point of view; for these two books may be said to be responsible, under God, for the present religious, moral, social, commercial, and political glory of this highly favored country—the grand providential instrument for the evangelization and moral liberation of all nations. But this subject must be left to be fully considered in its proper place, in the proposed larger memorial of Mr. Law.

The following is the impartial opinion of the great and good Bishop Wilson concerning the *Christian Perfection*, contained in a letter addressed by him to Lady Elizabeth Hastings, of blessed memory, dated Warrington, September 13th, 1729:

> " — His *Christian Perfection* (he writes) fell into my hands by a similar providence: and after reading it over and over, I recommended it so heartily to a friend of mine near London that he procured eighteen copies for each of our parochial libraries. I have recommended it to my clergy in the most moving manner as the likeliest way to bring them to a most serious temper. I have considered the most exceptionable passages in that book. I dare not say he is altogether in the wrong. That point of — selling all and giving to the poor, he truly explains to be the disposing, in our sincere intention, of whatever we enjoy above what is necessary for our own and the honest support of our families, for pious and charitable uses and the relief of our needy fellow members. We are to part with our superfluities with the same cheerfulness and ease of mind as if we had sold our estates and were only disposing of someone else's income. I need not tell you, Madam, the happiness of such a disposition and how acceptable it must be to God; and that our blessed Savior laid that injunction upon his followers not to torment them, but to set them above the world to make them truly easy in it. As to the passage about — not going to law on any occasion whatever regarding private injuries, I dare not condemn it until I see much worse effects follow from practicing it by those who have tried the experiment; as you know, Madam, some sects of people have done without any great visible inconvenience. And whether one who resolves to do so might not expect a peculiar providence to watch over him for good, or a more extraordinary reward for his faith and sufferings in obedience to the commands of his Savior, is something that ought to be well considered before we peremptorily condemn such a doctrine.
> "I will, God willing, for I do not have time to say more now, give your ladyship the summary of the whole book in a few words, just as I met with them some time ago in a book by Erasmus—a person whom God raised up just at the time of the Reformation to set people on the right path after the Christian world had been led into error and superstition for several ages:

<margin>Pages 143 and 145. No. 12.</margin> Several things are expressed here concerning <term>salniter</term>, which will doubtless be able to declare his meaning more intelligibly. That <term>salniter</term> was not created, but only made *substantial* at the creation, is very strange in my apprehension; but seeing that I do not know what peculiar notion he may have of the word "created," and what distinction he may make between "created" and "made *substantial*," I can say nothing more against it. That <term>salniter</term> brings the fire of God to man is no less strange than the former point, though indeed I see obscurely, and as it were at a distance, something in it, if it is not understood of the "out-birth"—namely, of <term>salniter</term> as created, or as made *substantial* at the creation—but of that which Behmen calls the <term>salnitrous shrack</term>, wherein the two eternal kingdoms are severed, and in this world the four elements are displayed, etc. But if Mr. Pierce reflects, as I suppose by this expression, upon the philosophical work especially, meaning that <term>salniter</term>—even common <term>salniter</term> as before—is that matter which brings the philosophical fire into the artist's work, there may be something more in it, which I shall not presume to judge nor censure. That <term>salniter</term> is the *instrument of God* by which he works is true indeed, if it is referred again to the whole of nature, in all its properties, as God's distinction and operation. That the <term>separator</term> is in this *substantial* word, and that it is *the spirit of this world*; as people who should be strangers to the lusts of the flesh, by studying in the body the life of angels; who should have no need of divorce, as they are able to mend or to bear with patience all the evils of the married state; who should be strangers to oaths, as those who will neither distrust nor deceive anybody; who set not their hearts upon increasing their substance, as they have laid up their treasure in heaven; who should not be transported with vain glory, because they refer all the glory to Christ alone; who should be void of all ambition, being disposed that the greater they are, the more they submit to all men for Christ's sake; who should avoid wrath, and much more revenge, as they study to deserve well of those who deserve ill of them; whose lives should be so without blame as to force even infidels to speak well of them; who should be born again to the purity, simplicity, and teachable temper of infants; who should live like the fowls of the air, without anxiety; among whom there should be the same concern and good understanding as among members of the same body; where the abundance of some should supply the wants of others, and the evils of one member be mitigated by the good offices and compassions of others; who should be conspicuous as a city on a hill, so that everyone around them might be instructed by their example, and act as salt to secure the rest from corruption; to whom this life should seem vile, and only to be endured in submission to the will of God; and who, relying upon the invisible power of Christ, are always diligently preparing for that day when they shall enter upon a lasting happiness.—I am, Madam, &c. &c. Thomas, Sodor and Man."

In the year 1727, as related, Mr. Law founded a school in his native town for the instruction and clothing of fourteen girls (now increased to twenty), to which, sometime afterwards, alms-houses were added for two poor old women, inhabitants of King's Cliffe.

With what resources he accomplished this is not now known; but report states that, shortly after the publication of *Christian Perfection*, while standing one day in the shop of his publisher in London, a person dressed as a gentleman’s servant accosted him, inquiring if he was the Rev. Mr. Law; and being answered in the affirmative, placed a letter in his hands and departed. Upon opening the letter, it was found to contain a bank note for one thousand pounds from some anonymous individual. If this anecdote is true, the money so presented, along with what he possessed from the division of his mother’s property at this time and other resources, might have contributed to the foundation of this charity. But such was not the only gift of money Mr. Law received in his lifetime from admirers of his writings and also from strangers to his person. With regard to his works, his arrangement with his publishers (according to documents in the possession of the writer) was that the latter should have the entire profit of the first editions of each. As therefore the principal of them ran through six or eight editions, it is very possible that he derived some pecuniary benefit from that source.

The *Serious Call* was the next production of his pen; but it is a work so well known by devout and well-informed persons that little needs to be said respecting it in this place; especially as its theological character has been so repeatedly explained in the present treatise as containing a demonstration, in logical order, free from all sectarian idiosyncrasy, of the pure spirit and practice of the gospel, according to the personal teachings of Christ and the basis of the apostolic writings—in brief, a systematic method of pure and perfect devotion to God, and of evangelical outreach toward our unconverted neighbor.

Every medicine should and would do this if rightly prepared—that is, if it were first delivered from the conflict of the four elements and exalted according to his description; yet, for all that, it would not resist all sorts of evils from the *astrum*, but only those for which it is specifically prepared. For it would not yet be the blessed universal tincture.

Page 145. Q. 1. *What do they say concerning the oil of life?* A. In order to understand what they say concerning the oil of life, it is absolutely necessary first to understand what they deliver concerning the generation of eternal nature in general, and in particular, the generation of the water of life in the second principle of light. From this water, this oil is entirely inseparable, and it is the more spiritual part of it—the fatness, as it were, or unctuosity. The conjunction between the soft eternal liberty and the harsh, strong desire causes the generation or kindling of the fire in eternal nature. From the latter of these two, a life comes to be which stands in, and is itself, a fire; and from the former comes a water and oil, which is the fuel of that fire and life. By the water, it is refreshed and preserved; in the oil, it burns and flames, and from this oil especially, it gains a shine or glow. If this is now transferred to the life of man, it may easily be understood what Behmen says: that every sickness is more or less a spoiling, poisoning, or a darting of impurity or contrary properties into the oil of life, etc.

Q. 2. *What do they teach concerning the philosophical work?* A. They teach in substance that the process of the universal tincture for transmuting metals and healing the body (attainable if all the requisites are truly found in the artist) is the very same as the process of the holy spiritual tincture for the soul of man, attainable in regeneration. They teach that in both cases, this process is very short in itself; that the life of man, and so of metals—as also of the whole of nature and all things within it—stands in seven properties. They teach that these seven properties are now under the curse and exist in mere strife and contrariety, each of them being manifest in its own natural quality in opposition to all the rest; that is, each of them, according to Behmen—

---

It is, however, deserving of record as an interesting circumstance that almost all the individuals who have been examples of great piety and eminently instrumental in the moral regeneration of this country during the last hundred years have been mainly indebted for their spirit and principles to this and the last-mentioned treatise. In this consideration, the thousands of other individuals who have, indirectly or directly, derived their piety and usefulness from such a source will also be taken into account. And this is true not only in our own country, but on the great continent of America, where it has been related to the writer that, at the present day, there is scarcely a devout family in any of the numerous towns of the United States in which the *Serious Call* is not among the number of its standard books of piety.

It was about this time that Mr. Law entered into the family of Edward Gibbon, Esq., of Putney, as tutor to his only son, Edward (afterwards the father of the historian), with whom, at the commencement of the year 1727, he proceeded to Emanuel College, Cambridge, and remained during his stay at that university. As the *Serious Call* was published in 1728, it was probably written by Mr. Law during the intervals of his teaching duties, and possibly for the immediate benefit of his pupil, just as Fenelon wrote his *Telemachus* for the Duke of Burgundy; though the idea of such a work had doubtless suggested itself to him as he proceeded with the *Christian Perfection*, particularly while writing the ninth, tenth, and twelfth chapters of that treatise. It is reported that he also gave occasional instructions to the two daughters of Mr. Gibbon while residing with the family at Putney, where he remained as a friend for some eight or nine years after his pupil had finished his education, much respected and esteemed by all who enjoyed the pleasure of his acquaintance.

During this period, he pursued his theological studies with avidity, while his writings had rendered him so celebrated that he was consulted by serious persons, both in person and by letter, as a kind of oracle or spiritual director. To these people, he did not fail to afford every necessary instruction for their several cases, to remove their doubts and scruples, and to satisfy their minds. Among the more memorable of his spiritual children and patients were the celebrated brothers John and Charles Wesley; the former of whom, in the mature part of his life, resumed all the veneration and respect for Law's exalted piety and wisdom with which he had been so irresistibly impressed in his earlier years, but which he had suddenly cast aside upon adopting some peculiar views and opinions on certain points of religious doctrine. Reference has been made to this circumstance, however, in a preceding note, and therein to the periodical of 1797 for a further and full understanding of the subject in question.

Another of Mr. Law's correspondents was a Miss Dodwell, daughter of the learned Mr. Henry Dodwell. Overlooking the simple guidance of the Word of God and the all-sufficiency of the Holy Spirit for sincere seekers of truth, she had so bewildered herself in the labyrinth of argumentative controversy concerning schism and other ecclesiastical questions that her mind became filled with doubts about the sufficiency of God’s grace in the ordinances of the established church of this country, of which she was a member. She was also perplexed about absolute decrees, the dispensations of providence, and other mysterious subjects. In this state of mind, she forwarded some papers to Mr. Law, wherein, among other details of her case, she expressed a desire to join the Church of Rome so that she might be delivered from the anxiety of thinking for herself in matters of religion and might have a sufficient authority to which she could resign herself absolutely. This gave him the occasion to—

men’s usual expression, has its own selfish will. This strife cannot be reconciled unless such a death enters into these seven properties as may break and destroy their own will—namely, such a life as by its own essentiality may be first a death to them, and then also able to raise them up again into one harmonious life and will. All this is done according to the constant, unalterable generation of eternal nature, wherein there are indeed the same seven properties, but not seven contrary wills, all being harmonized and overpowered in and by the fifth property of love and light. When this re-harmonizing of the properties in the philosophical work is done, the universal tincture is prepared, the curse is removed, earth is turned in, and heaven is turned out. This, therefore, is also able to re-harmonize all the seven disordered properties, both in the metals of the earth and in the diseased bodies of men.

Q. *ult.* Why must gold be purified seven times? A. Because it must be brought through all the seven properties of nature, and in each of them a specific work must be done. For as they are all seven under the curse, so they are all seven impure and need to pass through the purifying fire seven times if that gold or silver shall reach its perfection. In the first melting, the harsh quality—the gross, hard, stony dross—is melted away. In the second, the harsh death in the water is separated; for in this second property the sweet water was killed or spoiled and turned into the quality of a poisonous <term>aqua fortis</term>, which is the worst of all and must now, in this second melting, be cast out. In the third, the bitter death must be melted down—namely, the stirring, raging, breaking, and stinging property which makes the gold and silver brittle, so that it is not malleable before this is conquered also. In the fourth, the fire-spirit must be destroyed; and then the matter begins to be like gold or silver, according to that property which is predominant within it; but it is not yet tough and pure enough. In the fifth melting, the life arises in the property of light and love; and according to this, the matter which is left from the previous trials gets again that virtue which from the first origin has been the property of that fountain-spirit which is predominant therein. In the sixth, this life, having risen in the fifth, stirs, and from this stirring the metal gets its clear, ringing sound according to its kind. Here, says Behmen, the greatest care is to be taken that the fire may not be too strong, or else this new life is easily kindled again in the properties of wrath, and the whole matter is burned to a hard, useless dross. In the seventh melting it comes (provided that the same care is taken about the fire, which must be more subtle or temperate than in the sixth) to that perfection which it is capable of in this third principle; and it has only this defect: that the spirit therein must leave its metallic body in a hard palpability and cannot exalt it as he did before the wrath-fire was kindled in the fall of Lucifer.

The next public emergency which called forth the services of his powerful and undaunted pen was the refutation of Deism or infidelity, another rampant vice of that age among men of education. The occasion for this was the appearance of Tindal’s book, ‘Christianity as old as the Creation,’ to which he wrote an answer entitled the ‘Case of Reason or Natural Religion, fairly and fully stated.’ Concerning this work—which is a perfect model of classical argumentation, written in the most easy, natural manner, and as such ought to form a regular class book in schools, it being revised and corrected by the author in a second edition in the year 1752—a correspondent of the ‘Gentleman’s Magazine’ gives a very judicious opinion in a letter to that periodical in the month of October 1800, which, notwithstanding the irrelevancy of certain portions of it, we insert at length for its general interest. It may just be remarked that although Gibbon claims to give a slight critical review of Law’s early writings, he entirely omits any notice of this absolute refutation and ironical exposure of infidelity. The letter proceeds as follows:

> “Sir,—In addition to what your ingenious correspondent has related concerning that good and truly great man, the Rev. W. Law, commonly called the mystic divine, give me leave to observe that many years ago I was acquainted with some of his admirers, from whom I understood that Mr. Law was a bachelor all his life; that in person he was a stocky man and rather of a dark complexion, though remarkably cheerful in his temper; that such was his love of privacy and a state of contemplation, that it was very seldom indeed that he passed more than two hours in the company of any person. With a very small inheritance, also, Mr. Law was remarkably charitable; but it was principally confined to his poor neighbors and the manufacturers of wooden ware in and about King’s Cliffe; in which view, it is related that he would only eat off a wooden platter. In these exercises of Christian charity, he also engaged the two ladies with whom he resided. Their object was not to encourage the idle and dissolute, but to promote and facilitate the good intentions and efforts of the industrious.

> “Whether the ‘Serious Call’ be Mr. Law’s masterpiece, I have some doubt; I should give the prize to his ‘Case of Reason,’ stated in answer to ‘Christianity as old as the Creation.’ The style and conclusions are almost as plain and convincing as any of the deductions in common arithmetic; and at this present time, as the public is not quite cured of the preference it has lately entertained for the French goddess of reason, I presume a cheap edition of that work by Mr. Law,

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Jacob Boehme's mystical philosophy, specifically regarding the nature of souls and spirits in animals and the elements, followed by a series of testimonials and critical praise for William Law’s work, *A Serious Call to a Holy Life*.</meta>

The distinction between souls and spirits is not, in fact, much emphasized or insisted upon by Boehme. Nevertheless, it is clear enough from his declarations that they also contain both souls and spirits—or something corresponding, in its lower temporal kind and degree, to that significant difference found in man. Therefore, if a precise and careful distinction is not intended, it may be said well enough, *souls or spirits*. But if a more distinct listing were to be made, it would be much better to say *souls and spirits*, with a short addition explaining that the former refers particularly to the stars and the latter to the sun. Much could be said about this from Boehme’s foundations.

Page 147, No. 3. *Their bodies were made, etc.* Here I would, for my part, rather say *brought forth*; not that the former phrase was altogether unfit or irrelevant, but only because it seems (at least to me) to represent the matter too crudely, as if there had been a specific maker from the outside using his hands or tools. In reality, they all emerged freely out of the elements when the eternal Word moved, thereby enabling them to bring forth, in distinction and variety, those visible images or outbirths of their invisible powers.

No. 4. *from which the visible, etc.* Since the elements and compounded bodies differ in degree, and since there is a descent from the former to the latter—so that the elements are to be considered as joined to the invisible principles—when it is said *from what compounded bodies arise*, I think it would be proper to structure the sentence like this: from which (invisible principles) the *visible elements*, and *further* (or lower) *also, in conjunction with them, the compounded bodies arise*.

No. 5. *those are unclean, etc.* Since this uncleanness cannot be limited to terrestrial animals—because Moses declares some water creatures to be unclean as well—it would be better to say more generally: those are unclean that had, in their origin, a property of the dark world more or less predominant in their particular kind.

Between numbers 5 and 6, the following details could be inserted, though there is no necessity for it:

That living creatures exist in all four elements, and in each according to its constitution. This is because of the unbreakable connection of all the elements in one universal ground, due to which none of them is excluded from those gifts and abilities required for bringing forth their own unique offspring. That from the food and habitat of every animal, its origin can be more or less discerned. That tame and friendly beasts are, with respect to their origin, more closely related to the one element, while the wild and less manageable ones are closer to the four elements. That the state and condition of living creatures before the Fall of man was very different from what it is now, after the Fall and the curse. That in all living creatures, a character of the Holy Trinity may be found, though in none of them so clearly and em-

The following interesting letter from a clergyman may also be worth including here; it was originally addressed to the editor of *Lloyd’s Evening Post*:

->— *Sunt certa piacula, quae te* <-
->*Ter pure lecto poterunt recreare libello.* — Hor. <-

"Scarborough, Dec. 21st, 1771. Sir—As I have a universal love and esteem for all mankind, so particularly for my brothers in the established church, of which I would consider myself an unworthy member if I did not take every opportunity to do good, according to the abilities with which God has empowered me. But as I have always thought a concern for men’s souls to be preferable to that of their bodies, I have in a more special manner extended my charity to that better part. We live in an age where numerous objects present themselves to our view who are destitute of every virtue that can make them worthy of divine favor; and, consequently, there will never be a lack of occasions for exercising ourselves in a laudable effort for their amendment. I, for my part, though I live (when at home) in a small country village, have had sufficient work on my hands to bring my parishioners to any tolerable degree of piety and goodness. I preached and labored among them incessantly, and yet, after all, was convinced my work had been as fruitless as casting pearls before swine; the drunkard continued his nightly practices, and the voice of the swearer was still heard in our streets. However, I was determined to leave no means untried for bringing this profane and stubborn people to a sense of their duty. Accordingly, I purchased many religious books and distributed them among them; but, alas! I could perceive no visible effects. In short, I had the grief to find that all my labor had proved in vain, and was ready to cry out with St. Paul, *Who is sufficient for these things?* Around this time, I happened to read a treatise by Mr. Law entitled *A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life*, with which (if I may be allowed the expression) I was so charmed and greatly edified that I resolved my flock should partake of the same spiritual food. I therefore gave each person in my parish one of those useful books and charged them, upon my blessing (for I consider them as my children), to carefully read the same. My perseverance was now rewarded with success, and I had the satisfaction of seeing my people reclaimed from a life of folly and impiety to a life of holiness and devotion.

Before I conclude, I must beg leave to recommend the aforementioned book to the reading of all your readers; and I heartily wish they may receive as much benefit from it as those have who are committed to my charge."

Page 149. *at the end.* Two different things are requested here in a single question, which must nonetheless be divided into two parts. The first concerns the two <term>tinctures</term> and their division, and the second concerns the <term>magia</term> and the appearance of animals within it. (1.) Regarding the first, I believe this may be a sufficient explanation of it, made as briefly as possible. Fire and water are and must be present in the generation of eternal nature, and therefore in temporal nature as well. Whenever and wherever eternal nature exists in its proper harmonious order, these two cannot help but be united, or exist in a most internal union. Consequently, this union is holy, pure, and heavenly, and the creatures in which this union exists must also be so. Now then, seeing that this third principle was corrupted and all its properties thrown out of harmony by the fall of Lucifer; seeing further that it was not to be immediately restored to its primeval glory and dignity, but was to be established for an appointed time in a lower and external condition—where it cannot be called holy, pure, and heavenly, but rather mixed, transitory, and elementary; and again, seeing that nevertheless, in this mixed state, it should have the whole of nature, or all the properties of nature, working and generating within it; therefore, these two—which cannot be separated from nature—must necessarily have been divided in this third principle. Yet this was done so that (since it is but one world) a communion or mutual communication between them might remain, both in the overall government or generation of this temporal nature and in the particular creatures belonging to and governed by it. Now this division was made accordingly on the second day of creation—not in any particular place or thing, but generally throughout the entire extent of this region—so that a perpetual communication might exist between that which is superior and that which is inferior. Therefore, when living creatures were produced to be temporal, mixed, four-elementary beings—rather than eternal, holy, one-elementary creatures—they must also have been formed in and according to this division. For since their origin was only in, and their end only for, this mixed world, they could not have been gifted with that holy union of which only heavenly creatures are capable. But man, having a higher origin, did not come out of this divided, twofold source; rather, according to the end for which he was designed, he possessed the whole of eternal nature in its proper harmonious order and union within his own single person. Therefore, just as it was impossible for him to be a twofold male and female image in his first creation, it was also impossible for animals *not* to be males and females, or—which is the same thing—not to have the two <term>tinctures</term> in their division. For the <term>tincture</term> here, in respect to living creatures, may be sufficiently described by saying that it is that tender, loving inclination toward that which, from its first origin in eternal nature, is its nearest and most internal part. Although I freely grant that a deeper description could be given by saying it is rather that ground which, in animals, is the root of that inclination—that which stirs it up, that which flows out into it, and which
