->This excellent treatise is written in a *strong and vigorous style*, and abounds with many new and sublime thoughts. In short, one may say of this book, as Sir Richard Steele said of a discourse by Dr. South, that it contains whatever wit and wisdom can put together; and I will venture to add that whoever sits down without prejudice and attentively reads it through will rise a wiser man and a better Christian.<- <note>Correction: The 'Serious Call' was first published in 1729, not 1728.</note>

It would, perhaps, be difficult to imagine a finer illustration of Mr. Law's solid and universal theological knowledge than this circumstance: that individuals who had begun their religious course under the discipline and guidance of his practical books and conversation, but were later induced to abandon his rules based on the plausible representation of a shorter "way to Christ" and salvation than the experimental path of the Old Testament in which they were traveling—that they, upon glancing again over the elementary treatises of their early studies some twenty or thirty years later, expecting to find low and superficial knowledge, should find, to their great surprise, the author's level of understanding to be clearly as much superior to their own (despite all their supposed evangelical light) as when they first placed themselves under his direction. Like the continental tourist who, having set out to climb a neighboring mountain, looks up after traveling for twenty or thirty hours and, to his astonishment, finds it towering above him at almost the same distance—though in more imposing majesty—as when he began his excursion.

But the full merits of his genius as an evangelical divine cannot be properly appreciated until the spirit of his mind, as portrayed in his writings, has been traced through all the degrees of the Christian life up to its last or highest point. To this point, as an able minister of the *Spirit and not of the letter*, he conducts his faithful follower and disciple, introducing him perceptively into immediate communion with the triune Deity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, thus making him a worshiper of God "in spirit and in truth." For as such is the sole end of all divine dispensations and institutions, so it is the design and fulfillment of all his teachings as an enlightened interpreter of religious truth.

These latter ministries are contained in that series of his works beginning with the *Spirit of Prayer* and ending with the *Address to the Clergy*. The last words of the latter, written only a few days before his death, were, by a singular coincidence, those of his master, the "Great Teacher" himself, at the close of his earthly ministry:
> "All that Christ was, did, suffered, dying in the flesh, and ascending into heaven, was for this sole end: to purchase for all his followers a new birth, new life, and new light, in and by the Spirit of God restored to them, and living in them, as the support, comforter, and guide into the truth. And this was his, *Lo I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.*"

—The first series of his theological works may be considered to end with the *Three Letters to a Lady Inclined to the Church of Rome*; the second series to begin with his discourse *On the Sacrament*; and the last, as just stated, with the *Spirit of Prayer*.

It should be well noted, however, that the true understanding and benefit of his writings can only be obtained by passing through them experimentally, in regular order, from the beginning. Indeed, the reason why complaints have been made against his later works is solely because *half-instructed Christians*, or totally unqualified readers—instead of entering upon and pursuing the study of them in that way (which followed the order of spiritual nature and the process of the Holy Scriptures)—have, as it were, jumped into the midst of his last dissertations. Consequently, they found themselves out of their depth, with nothing to cling

It has been observed that they escaped from God not through irreligion, but through a religion—and a divinely appointed religion at that. Though they had no direct intercourse with God, they dealt with ordinances of His own appointment, and by these they pacified their consciences. Here was their great delusion: they came to have a religion for their God, instead of having God for their religion. And is it not so even in our own day, under the full light of the Gospel? Are not "evangelical doctrines" treated in the same way, as "blessed," "soul-saving," and "comforting"? Is not the "atonement" and "death of Christ"—the "finished work of Christ," as it is called—clutched in the conscience as a rest and a confidence, while the religious practitioner is neither living *crucified to the world* (with its goods and ills underfoot), nor worshiping God spiritually, nor trusting in Him immediately and entirely? Thus, what was done by the ancient children of God with their ordinances—is it not acted out over and over again in all ages? At one period by the bronze serpent, at another by rosaries and crucifixes and the intercession of saints, at another by the church and apostolic successions, and at another by evangelical doctrines—while only a *mystical* "seven thousand" are ever found who worship God "in spirit and in truth."

An equally rational and substantial answer might also be given to the objections made by the same type of people at another time against his early publications, *Christian Perfection* and the *Serious Call*. They say these works do not dwell enough upon "faith in the atonement" in connection with prayer, self-denial, humility, universal love, resignation, and other constant exercises of devotion to God, which are so fundamentally taught in those works. They claim that through these, the devout soul might (in their terminology) "at once obtain pardon" and rise out of self-abasement, penitence, and humble confidence in the mercy of God into "joy," "peace," and "salvation."

<margin>Wesley was highly pleased ) ^</margin> But such complaints might be made against the Old Testament dispensation itself regarding its practical character. It serves as the mystical childhood of man's spiritual renewal (the whole Bible itself being the entire symbol) and as only a preparatory school for Christ—a ritual of physical ordinances, washings, and purifications that serve as confessions and memorials of an inward spiritual pollution, and as sure types and figures of a cleansing and deliverance from it. This induces its subjects, in the full assurance of faith and hope, to call upon God for deliverance without understanding how or when that should be accomplished. Why, it may be asked, why were these devout worshippers not led to Christ at once—that is, suddenly turned from children into men? "Why put a foundation below the foundation?" The Mosaic and prophetic dispensations might just as rightly be objected to as these two fundamental treatises by Mr. Law; for they are both of the same mystical character regarding the soul that is to be restored to perfection.

However, as the coming of Christ—both in the flesh and in the spirit—was suitably timed to the preceding dispensations, and His entire process was figurative of our own renewal, so did the analogy truly hold in Mr. Law’s experience and writings. Therefore, in his succeeding works—the *Sacrament Book*, the *Tract on Regeneration*, and the *Serious Answer to Trap* <note>Joseph Trapp</note>—everything will be found stated not only to strengthen the hope and assure the faith of a devout, penitent soul, but they, as it were, *lift him up into the heavenly sanctuary itself. There stands the true high priest with the blood of the sacrifice, forever making the full, perfect, and effectual atonement and intercession.* There, moreover, he sees, as it were, the title-deeds to every degree of salvation, purity, holiness, and wisdom he may desire to possess—indeed, making him the "heir of God and joint-heir with Christ" and (according to 1 Corinthians 3:20–22) of "all things." Thus, indeed, it challenges him not to "believe."

revelation and intercourse with fallen man. But what is the end of such truth, and of the knowledge of it? Not to induce those who for the first time apprehend it to believe themselves "justified," "pardoned," or "saved," and so to settle down and rejoice as having made a grand advance in religion, or as having received some extraordinary manifestations of the divine favor (which is too commonly done); but rather to set them upon "working out their salvation" with "fear and trembling," yet with all the courage, cheerfulness, and gratitude which the conviction of the love and gracious assistance of God, and the certainty of final triumph and endless glorification with Christ, are calculated to inspire. It is to strengthen their souls with holy resolutions, to magnanimously "fight the good fight of faith, and lay hold of eternal life." Thus leading them necessarily into the true order of spiritual advancement; namely, to feel their own nothingness, and the absolute necessity of the new birth, and a total, momentary dependence upon God alone in every step of their progress; which only deserves the name of "conversion" or "salvation." Such, then, being the basis of understanding for Mr. Law’s practical treatises, where do the objections against them stand? And who can henceforth utter them, but those who are imperfectly acquainted with the theory of true Christian theology?

The summary of the matter (with respect to Mr. Law’s evangelical knowledge and systematic exhibition of practical Christian truth) is this, or may be thus represented: He, as a wise master-builder, profoundly versed in the ancient science of spiritual architecture—which, by the way, seems now to be almost lost—not only designs a noble building, complete and perfect in all its parts, but lays the basis broad and solid upon the eternal "foundation that is laid," the rock Christ Jesus, and from there proceeds to raise the superstructure in due order and degree, according to the principles of the science and his own practical experience. Such being the case, he has no occasion during the construction to be perpetually reminding himself that he must "believe" in the rock upon which he is building (for he knows it to be firm and steadfast, and laid by God purposely for him to build upon); nor does he regard the diversified opinions of professors of imaginary evangelical architecture. One party among them, on examining the ground floor of the building, laments his lack of "comforting views of the principles of building," because he keeps the rock or "foundation in the background," or at all events is not always talking about it at every step of his progress. Another avers that he ought to rest his whole hope on the "finished work" of the foundation, for that is the true evangelical way of building; while a third pities him as a most "unscriptural" workman, claiming that he is seeking to raise his building by his "own works," and so detracting from the merits of the foundation; whereas they believe he ought to do nothing more than "merely believe" in the rock, and then the superstructure would rise of itself, for St. Paul teaches "justification," as well as "sanctification," to be "by faith alone." But disregarding all this Babylonian confusion of scripture science, he soberly proceeds with his labors until the top stone is put on. When the whole is completed according to the Gospel model, he gives glory to God for his free grace in providing a ground or rock so sure and steadfast whereon to erect his building, and for providing all the materials for its construction, and for enduing him with wisdom, strength, and perseverance to complete it, though at the cost of all worldly satisfactions. Such is a figurative representation of the basis of Mr. Law’s understanding in his devotional writings; and such is the character of the critical observations which have been made upon them by some modern professors of divinity.

To proceed with the narrative. Another of Mr. Law’s correspondents was the celebrated Dr. Byrom of Manchester, formerly a Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, a poet of renown in his day, and an inventor of stenography <note>Stenography is the practice or manner of writing in shorthand.</note>. He was a great admirer of Law’s genius—so much so, indeed, as in later years to put into verse copious selections from his writings and to voluntarily carry on a controversy in his defense with the celebrated Dr. Warburton, against the perverse attacks of that indiscreet writer. To these attacks Mr. Law himself paid no attention until the appearance of the "Divine Legation," when he took up his pen and wrote his famous "Letter" to Bishop Sherlock on that work, and thereby so effectually silenced his antagonist that the latter did not venture either to reply to that letter or to mention Law's name again in public until after Law's death, which was some years later. (*See Payne’s Letter to the Bishop of Gloucester, 1761.—Dr. Byrom’s Poems.*)

A large inheritance of fortune rendering Dr. Byrom independent of his profession as a physician, he became a great reader and collector of the books and writings recommended or approved of by Mr. Law, and also published a new edition of Behmen’s "Way to Christ" in 1752. His estate and library have descended into the inheritance of a lady by the name of Atherton, residing in the

neighborhood of Manchester, who is as distinguished for her high Christian principles and princely liberality in the cause of religion and charity, as was her worthy predecessor for his estimable old English character and benevolent attempts to diffuse the love and practice of religion and virtue among all mankind. In the year 1736, he wrote to Mr. Law, stating that one of his relations, a devout woman, was on the point of leaving the Church of England to join the Quakers, which he was anxious to prevent, and therefore requested Mr. Law, as a writer in whose piety and judgment the party in question had expressed great confidence, to address her, in dissuasion from her purpose, giving him the grounds of her secession. He accordingly wrote five letters (dated November and December, 1736), wherein he considers the several points of her case, and forwarded them to Dr. Byrom, with a request that they might be returned to him again; possibly with a view to revision and publication, but which did not take place, and they are now in the possession of the writer of these lines.

At the close of this same year, his ancient friend, Mr. Gibbon, died. This necessarily led to a change in his domestic circumstances, though he did not finally retire from the town until about four years after that event. Whether any pecuniary mark of respect was bequeathed to him in the will of the deceased does not appear, though an allusion in the letter of one of his correspondents might suggest a conjecture to that effect.

As already stated, it was between the years 1733 and 1736 that he first became acquainted with those writings with which his name has become so identified, that he is now scarcely known by any other distinction. That may be considered another important epoch and eventful circumstance in his life; not so much on account of what has ensued from it so far, as what may justly be expected, but as yet lies in the inscrutable womb of Providence: though the nature of those writings, the intrinsic necessities of mankind, the prophecies of revelation, the progressing developments of the great spirit of nature, and the relative state of the world, may enable an enlightened mind to form some general guesses as to what those events shall be, and when they shall be brought to birth. In a letter to a friend (November, 1754), Mr. Law expresses himself thus: "But all pretences and endeavors to hinder the opening of the mystery revealed by God in Jacob Behmen, and its bearing down all before it, will be as vain as so many attempts to prevent or retard the coming of the last day." In order to understand the exact sense of this wonderful author, he took the extraordinary pains and trouble to make himself thoroughly acquainted with the German language, in which the writings in question were originally composed and published.

fancied improvements upon common Christianity. The great Origen was one of the first instances of this kind; he was celebrated as the oracle of learning and as a possessor of all the sciences. Along with this, he led a very pious and disciplined life, full of contempt for the world. But for my own part, I would have left his conversation, his deep discoveries, and his allegorical explanations of Scripture, to spend my time and learn religion with a poor mechanic I have read about somewhere, whose heart and life were governed by this spirit: "I am nothing, I have nothing, I am worth nothing: I desire nothing but to love, adore, praise, and obey God, in everything and for everything."

If the world were to see this remark upon learning, they would in all probability attribute it to my own lack of learning; and though they would be very right in judging my pretensions to learning not to be great, yet it would be unjust to think me an entire stranger to its nature.

But I profess to you that whatever talents or learning I possess, I think it as necessary to live under a continual apprehension of them being a snare and temptation to me as I would any worldly distinctions, whether of riches or dignity, that I might possess. I desire no other improvement of science or knowledge, nor to see into any depths, except those that penitence, humility, faith, hope, charity, the pure love of God, and an absolute resignation to his providence shall discover to me. These virtues fill the mind with more light and knowledge of God than all the libraries of learning in the world; they are a much shorter and surer way to the possession and enjoyment of Divine Truth than turning over the endless volumes of the learned. They are the keys of divine knowledge and afford an easy entrance to those who keep them; they make us "friends of God" and, as such, always in a state of finding his certain care and guidance over us. They are, as it were, so many inward eyes of the soul, always receiving a sufficiency of light from God. We are never at a loss or in perplexity except when some of these divine virtues are either too imperfectly practiced or wholly neglected by us.

I take the matter to be exactly like this in relation to the discourses about the *restoration of all things, etc.*; they are about something that we have not the least knowledge of, nor any faculties or foundation for such knowledge. We have nothing certain or plain within ourselves about it, and so we have nothing to oppose to anything we are told; we are, therefore, easily taken in by every writer who has the talents and abilities to form an agreeable scheme of it.

Again, there is another thing which prepares our minds to receive such discourses. The irrecoverable state of men or angels is a dreadful thought to us; our sense of misery, tenderness, and compassion for our fellow creatures makes us wish that no creatures might fall into it. We are unable to show how such a state could result from the infinite wisdom, goodness, and perfection of God, and so we are greatly prepared to think every scheme is rational and well-grounded if it puts an end to such a state.

But then we must consider that we are governed here by our passions and weakness, and only form a God according to our own conceptions. We must consider that the infinite wisdom, goodness, and perfection of God is the fathomless object of our faith and adoration, and not of our comprehension; and to pretend to know what God must do, by virtue of such attributes, in the vast compass of the future regarding his fallen creatures, is as absurd as to pretend to be infinitely wise ourselves. For just as God is so for this reason only—because he knows what infinite wisdom, goodness, and perfection require of him—if we knew that, we would be in the same state of perfection.

The inability to account for the present disordered state of the creation has made many philosophers turn into atheists and deny an all-wise and good providence. But these poor men are self-condemned and fall into the greatest of all absurdities only to avoid a difficulty that has no absurdity in it. They deny the providence of an infinitely perfect being because they cannot account for such a providence in the present state of things; and yet, if there were such a providence, it could not be what it is supposed to be unless it were infinitely above their comprehension. This is their great self-condemnation and absurdity.

Again, they reject a first and governing cause of infinite wisdom and goodness because they see much evil and disorder in the world.

But why do they conclude this? It is from their own sense of wisdom and goodness; they feel such a goodness and benevolence in themselves that they would not permit what they see per-

mitted in the present state of things; and, therefore, they conclude that such a state cannot come from, or be under the direction of, a cause of infinite wisdom and goodness.

But here they are again in a state of self-condemnation and caught in the greatest of absurdities. For if they feel wisdom and goodness in themselves, where did they get them? Just as their existence is infallible proof that something has always existed—as everything finite is proof of something infinite of the same kind—so their own wisdom and goodness is plain and infallible proof that the cause from which they proceed, and under which they exist, is infinitely wise and good.

Therefore, for a being to use his own wisdom and goodness to argue that the First Cause lacks both is as absurd as if he were to conclude from his own power and life that the First Cause, from which he proceeds and under which he exists, lacks power and life.

These absurdities must be accepted by those who are too "reasonable" to adore an infinitely wise and incomprehensible providence.

Deep and long thinking about the providence of God has the appearance of a very pious exercise; and a zeal to present it in some new light, or to refute adversaries in some better way than using common texts of Scripture, has often betrayed well-meaning men into actions prejudicial to religion. That which they intended as a support to religion has helped the adversary oppose it with a greater show of argument.

I am not against using all the arguments that reason and learning can provide us in defense of religion; but I think we are much mistaken when we place our chief strength there and conclude that Christianity must prosper, or infidelity decline, according to how well all objections and difficulties are cleared up and solved.

For just as religion never entered the fallen world in that way—by condescending to explain all the difficulties or answer the objections that ignorance, malice, self-love, pride, curiosity, wit, or worldly learning could bring against it—and as no revelation from God ever dealt with this kind of adversary in such a manner, it is contrary to reason to think that it must be supported in that way now or at any other time.

For these temperaments have no right or claim to be answered or satisfied in their own way. Since they are merely disorders or corruptions of the soul, they are to have no relief from religion except that of *dying before it*. To give pride, self-love, or curiosity the answers they demand would be to maintain the disorder of fallen spirits, who, as such, can only be saved by a religion that calls them to *self-renunciation, to penitence, humility, faith, and absolute resignation to God*.

If speculative instructions and the resolution of doubts had been the right way to deliver man from the corruption and disorders of his nature; if precise and definite decisions regarding the difficulties and depths of providence had been a necessary requirement for entering into the spirit of Christianity; can it be thought that our blessed Lord would have said, "Unless you are converted and become like little children, you cannot enter into the kingdom of God"?

But if an infant-like simplicity, if self-renunciation, if humility of heart, and a total resignation of ourselves to the wisdom and goodness of God are the proper and necessary dispositions of the soul that is to be saved through Christ, it cannot well be thought that Christianity is best defended, or the hearts of people best assisted to receive or adhere to it, when speculative decisions on matters of faith are most studied and appealed to.

If all who wish Christianity well and desire to stop the growth of infidelity would oppose it with their lives and demonstrate the practice of true Christian virtues in defense of religion, infidelity would sink into the greatest shame and confusion, and Christianity would be proven to common sense with more than mathematical certainty. But the misfortune is that, in every attack, we think something is lacking in terms of argument, and so we strain our thoughts for something new in the way of reasoning; whereas the enemy is in his state of strength and we are in our state of weakness because we are doing nothing but arguing and contending for a dead Christianity. If we only began its defense by entering upon *new lives*, the old arguments would be sufficient.

You ask, "When discoveries of this kind are thrown in our way, is it a matter of strict duty to reject them instead of entertaining them, and should we not rather be grateful for them? And if we may

not give them the credit of Divine revelation, yet may we not entertain such things as probabilities, as a harmless entertainment of one's busy thoughts, as things that may innocently be believed or rejected?' I do not deny that there are such things.

But if I knew of anybody who wanted them, or sought relief in them, I should caution him against them; for such entertainment of our busy thoughts is often as dangerous as the entertainment of our restless passions; because the activity and curiosity of our minds is quite prejudicial to true devotion and piety of heart.

If it could be supposed that these probabilities would always be considered as we at first received them, there would be very little to be said for them; for why should our mind, which should be always in a state of reverence and adoration of divine truths, feeding itself with solid enjoyment and satisfaction in them, seek for religious amusement in groundless imaginations? For, supposing (what is here supposed) that they may be as innocently denied as believed, they can only be groundless imaginations. But when we consider the weakness of our minds, how easily they are affected with what they admit, and how soon that which was thought of only as an amusement or bare probability is changed into a solid truth or fundamental point, we shall find that such entertainment is a dangerous indulgence of our thoughts.

The matter you here propose seems to be taking this very turn upon your own mind: you propose it as an innocent probability, or speculative amusement of one's busy thoughts; yet, a few lines after, you say, 'This does not, therefore, seem to be a matter of mere speculation, but of great use and benefit:' and perhaps a little longer dwelling upon it would make you take it for a fundamental point, and that Christianity could not be received without it; and so the entertainment of busy thoughts would drive you upon a rock. Humility, faith, and a total resignation of ourselves to the fathomless depths of the divine providence are our only guard against this danger.

As the fall of our first parents, though in innocence, seems to be owing to the desire of a knowledge not suitable to their state; so we sin in the same temper when our curiosity searches for a higher knowledge than that which is revealed to us. It is an excellent saying of the son of Sirach:

> 'Seek not out the things that are too hard for you; neither search the things that are above your strength; but what is commanded you, think upon those things with reverence. For it is not necessary for you to see with your eyes the things that are in secret. Many are deceived by their own vain opinion, and an evil suspicion has overthrown their judgment.' Chap. iii.

I hope I shall not offend you by observing of your great and good father, whose memory I esteem and reverence, that his chief foible seems to have lain in a temper too speculative; and, perhaps, you may have some reason to resist and guard against it, as a temper to which you have a natural inclination. <insert>[Surely *Lee* is here referred to, not *Dodwell*.]</insert>

But be that as it will, I think I may assure you of this: that however such curiosity might be innocently indulged, yet, if upon a principle of humility, faith, and resignation to God, you deny it, you will be a much greater gainer by the exercise of these virtues in such an instance of self-denial than you could possibly be by any knowledge such curiosity would lead you into.

You may perhaps think that I have too often recourse to these virtues and seek for too much support from them; but, Madam, they are the highest virtues of the most enlightened souls; and as they lead the mind farthest into the truest, deepest knowledge of the mysteries of God, so the best knowledge of the mysteries of God gives the greatest height and strength to these virtues. And when a Christian is at the height of all the perfection which the spirit and grace of the Gospel leads to, though he has been with St. Paul in the third heavens, he will then be, more than ever, all humility, all faith, and all resignation to God; and will find all language too weak to express that fullness and extent in which he desires to practice these virtues.

As to the matter proposed, it cannot well be looked upon as a harmless probability, because the tenor of Scripture, both as obvious to common sense and as interpreted by the constant general belief of the church, is contrary to it; and therefore, until it shall please God to give some *new revelation* of this matter, and show its consistency with the *divine revelation already made*, there seems to be no room for an innocent reception of it.

(1.) The description given here of the heavenly property is applicable to the paradisical as well. (2.) Between the paradisical and heavenly property, and thus also the body, I cannot find that Behmen makes any other considerable difference except for a higher and lower degree or dignity relating to the two different states of the first Adam. For the paradisical, as the lower, was manifested when he was in paradise upon earth and should have continued so until this third principle had been recalled into eternity; and the heavenly, as the higher, should then have been manifested when he was to be translated and exalted from this paradise into heaven. Since this first order is now broken by his fall, and his blessed eternal state must now be regained in quite another way—namely, by a regeneration out of water and Spirit—Behmen, when declaring this way and speaking of that body which he is to put on in the regeneration, no longer takes much notice of a distinction between a heavenly and paradisical body, but uses these two terms interchangeably. He sometimes calls man's newborn body paradisical, but frequently also heavenly; notwithstanding that we still rightly acknowledge, with him, a difference of degree between paradise and heaven. With this one assurance of the *infinitely infinite goodness of God*, I resign myself, my friends, relations, men, and angels, to the adorable and yet incomprehensible disposal of his wisdom; content and happy with this thought, that myself and all creatures will not only be treated with a goodness and benevolence like mine, but with a goodness so *exceedingly superior* to it, as *no thought can comprehend, or language describe*.

It is always in your power to express to God your want of these virtues, and your earnest desire to practice them in the most perfect manner, and to find your strength and protection in them; and so long as you do so, you will put yourself into a condition to say, with the apostle, *When I am weak, then am I strong.*"

Such were his principles, and such his counsels, <note>doubtless, in the above extract delicately referring to Jane Lead's professed "Revelations"</note> at this time, which was about two years previous to meeting with the writings of Behmen in question.

Now when all these circumstances are taken into consideration—his education, his judgment, his principles in favor of pure theology, and his prejudices against any improvement or expansion upon common Christianity—and then his taking up a book at an old bookstall and reading the title page, thus: "Concerning the Three Principles of the Divine Essence, of the eternal dark, light, and the temporary world: showing what the soul, the image, and the spirit of the soul are; as also what angels, heaven, and paradise are: how Adam was before the fall, in the fall, and after the fall: and what the wrath of God, sin, death, the devils, and hell are: how all things have been, now are, and how they shall be at the last." Then, his turning over to the contents, perusing a page or two, and finding—though the language was strange—a deep and solid sense couched within it; every sentence, indeed, seeming to awaken a secret and previously unfelt knowledge in the depths of his mind; the author being, moreover, clearly a man of the purest, truest, and most lively evangelical experience—

When all these things are considered—what, it is remarked, must have been the power of truth to produce such effects as did then follow in a mind so constituted as his was! So furnished with defenses against the insidious entrance of every species of error, and, as just shown, so averse to receiving even the most seemingly innocent knowledge beyond what was openly contained in the sacred scriptures. Nor can it be any wonder that the first insight into those writings, as he stated to a friend, *put him into a perfect sweat.*
->For,<-

<margin>tial /</margin>
Here, the secret mystery of all things, of all time, of all eternity, appeared to be fundamentally opened. Here, all that lay in religion and nature as an unsearchable mystery, and which had so often been the subject of his reverent thoughts and contemplations, was revealed in its deepest ground. Here, in short, was presented the key to the universe of intellectual and physical nature, to all its laws, powers, and operations everywhere and in every individual thing. Here, in an instant, was unveiled the true ground and source of the Newtonian philosophy, and here the head-spring of all future solid progress in all branches of divine and natural, metaphysical and experimental philosophy. And finally, here was the *natural means* by which to bring all nations, and people, and tongues into the understanding, belief, and acknowledgment of the one only true faith of the Christian revelation. And the instrument—through which this incontestably all-but-a-miracle was accomplished—was a poor, illiterate man, whose only qualifications for the free divine action upon him seemed to have been his earnest devotion to God, his Christian simplicity, and perfect abandonment of self-will! So much with respect to his first acquaintance with Behmen's writings.

new Jerusalem, which, insofar as its coming down is certainly paradisical, and is yet not said to come down out of paradise, but from God out of heaven. (3.) The simile of the gold in the ore, or the tincture in metals, is not applicable to the heavenly body in the paradisical state: nor is it ever so used by Behmen; because there is no such difference between these two pure internal things, as there is between the other two external things; one of them alone being pure, and the other entirely impure.

<margin>1</margin> But with respect to man's fallen state and new regeneration, he uses this simile frequently, comparing the ore (or, as he commonly expresses it, the hard, gross, rough stone) to man’s corrupt four-elementary body, or flesh and blood, which cannot inherit the kingdom of God; and the gold or tincture to the regenerated body, born from above, of water and spirit; which he calls sometimes heavenly, because it is from heaven; and sometimes also paradisical, because it cannot be had in man as heavenly, unless it be first had as paradisical. Why then this question, *What do they mean by this heavenly property?* I would answer in such a manner—They mean the same paradisical property as to substance, both being of the water and spirit of eternal life; but they consider it as higher and more inward, and with a particular relation to that exalted state which Adam, if he had not transgressed, was to have been taken up into, after the end of time, in the perfect restoration of this third principle. And then, for the sake of more distinction, I would add further this following question and answer:

<margin>2</margin> **Q. Is this paradisical and heavenly property still in all men? A.** The paradisical and heavenly property lies still in all, though in different degrees, as a possibility for their regeneration and

wards came to be with respect to metaphysical science. And what Boyle said in his ‘Usefulness of Natural Philosophy,’ that ‘man is born the interpreter and priest of nature, ordained to celebrate divine service, not only *in* it, but *for* it,’ is applicable to him in the highest sense. And further, what Kepler was to Newton, that Freher may be considered to have been to Law. Indeed, the analogy that runs between the development of the two branches of science, physics and metaphysics, since both had been placed upon a correct basis through Behmen (to be contemplated in the third chapter, from § 4, of ‘Maclaurin’s Account of Newton’s Discoveries’) is most remarkable. Unhappily, however, the pursuit of the latter branch, since Law’s day, on the only sound basis, has been as much disregarded as the former has been cultivated; which, if the reason of things were duly considered, must surely appear a strange circumstance, for there is the same positive truth in one as in the other, inasmuch as they relate to nothing more or less than the inside and outside of the same thing. As the powers and instinct of nature have in them a governing power and wisdom, so it cannot but be highly profitable to know the philosophy of the superior principles, their union and co-operation with the inferior natural powers, but above all, their relation to the supreme unity of all powers, with all the relative philosophy thereof, both of grace and nature: which is the science in question, based upon the soundest principles, and capable of endless research and *experiment*.

The appearance, in 1737, of a book entitled ‘A Plain Account of the Nature and End of the Sacrament’ afforded him an opportunity of appearing again before the public, equipped, indeed, with fresh powers, as the champion and interpreter of revealed truth, which he had derived from his newly-discovered original source in the writings of Behmen, though as yet he ventured to use them but sparingly and inoffensively. His answer to the work in question is entitled ‘A Demonstration of the Gross and Fundamental Errors, in A Plain Account, etc.’; and to those who desire to see through the imperfect common notions of that divine institution, and to obtain a clear understanding of its real nature and character, it may be heartily recommended for reading, as much on the ground of edification as of instruction. The latter portion of it, ‘explaining the nature and extent of the redemption of all mankind by Jesus Christ,’ may, as already mentioned, be considered an introduction to that grand system of fundamental and practical truth, or of true philosophical divinity, which is opened to the world in so noble and captivating a manner in all his subsequent writings.

His works, from this period, have been descriptively divided into two series: the first embracing the active and contemplative divinity of all ages and sections of devoted Christians, purified and raised to its highest perfection; and the second, consisting of an ascent from there into that cloudless atmosphere from which St. John wrote his epistles, and where he also, pierced through and through with the divine light, was constrained to break forth in the same strain, proclaiming, with all the powers of his ravished soul, that *God is love*, mere love, *the spirit of love*, and love only; and to endeavor henceforth, by all the ingenuity of divine and human wisdom, to draw all the world to the full belief of that truth. His experience in such respect answered to that of the twenty-four elders around the throne, whose highest adoration of the divine glory is the expression of the simplest truth, namely, ‘you are worthy to receive honor and glory, for you have created all things, and for your glory they are and were created’—an unvarying devotion of all those whose inward state is a sense of the nothingness of the creature and the *all of God*.

His chief study and employment, around this particular period, would appear to have been making himself master of the substance of Freher’s writings and copying out those portions of them which he deemed desirable to possess. Part of the extracts thus made, though somewhat altered in their form of paragraphs and with occasional shortenings, have been inserted in the preceding pages of this treatise. Nor was he negligent in making researches after other enlightened writers upon theosophical science, as also upon spiritual quickening truth. For the time was at hand when his high evangelical knowledge was to be called into service, as he himself afterwards, in the midst of its exercise, thus writes to a lady of quality, who was much involved with the great movements referred to there: ‘As for myself (he observes), I seem to myself to have no other part to act, nor any call to anything else, in this hurry and struggle of zeal against zeal in such a variety of forms, but only and fully to assert the true ground, and largely open all the reasons of that one inward regeneration, which is equally the one thing needful to every sect, and the one thing alone that can make every sect, or method, or outward form, not hurtful to those who adhere to it.’

With respect to his opinions concerning the merits of the peculiar and extraordinary religious professors and writers, foreign and domestic, of the previous and then present generation, whose works were much read by certain descriptions of so-called spiritual individuals around this time, the statement of them must be left to another occasion, as his recorded observations upon them varied according to his experience at the time of writing and the supposed requirements regarding the edification of his correspondents who had requested them. —course, he remarked in conversation about Marsay <note>Charles Hector de St. George Marquis de Marsay (1688–1763), a Franco-German quietist and mystic.</note>, a sort of French-German mystic writer of his day, that "the best of what he had written was translated in the Scottish volume; that his sending souls to the moon and stars for purification was a mere fiction," (a particular which, though modified, the celebrated Swedish mystic, Swedenborg, appears to have adopted after him;) "and though he says that he writes entirely from a revelation from God, yet it may be proved that he has borrowed largely from Madame Guion;" that "Marsay, Madame Bourignon, [Jane Lead,] and other mystics who were continually pretending to revelations and deep openings in the divine life, should show their ground," and then he (Mr. Law) added, that "*the ground of all things was never opened in any man but Behmen, and perhaps never would be opened in any other man.*" In reply to a letter from Dr. Cheyne concerning Marsay and the above-mentioned spiritual writers among the Protestants, he said, "it would have been just as well if there had been none in the mystic way among them;" but his opinions on this point have been already expressed in the note on page 157. In reference to certain descriptions of professed converts to religion, he wrote in another letter to a friend: "Such persons, when they become religious, will talk of religion just as they used to talk and decide about everything before. I have met with very few people who are free from the foible of turning all their awakened zeal into curiosity." And in the course of a conversation, he observed that "a man’s taking up merely a new opinion in religious matters was of no more use or consequence to him (while it remained only an opinion) than getting himself a new hat." Also, that "every Christian had four states to pass through in the process of his return to God: namely, the state of nature—the state under the law—the state under Christ come in the flesh—and the state under Christ come in the spirit;" but that the experience of each state necessarily varied according to the temperament and character of the individual subject. Speaking of Gregory Lopez, the Spanish hermit in Peru [with whom might be classed Brother Nicolaus, the Swiss hermit], Mr. Law said that "he was the man that his writings require—not merely a good man, but a *highly divine soul*; but that he had nothing to say about the peculiarity of *his outward life*." [If Mr. Law had lived to the present day, he would have pointed to Bramwell <note>William Bramwell (1759–1818), a prominent Methodist evangelist known for his intense prayer life.</note> as being of the same first-class divine character, if not—as an apostolic evangelist treading, like his master, the common paths of life and showing how the common people may live according to the scriptural rule and standard—even more to his mind than any preceding person.] And, alluding to Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection, described in "*The Theology of the Presence of God, Cologne, 1710*," which was translated by Dr. Heylin in a book entitled "*Devotional Tracts, 1720*," Mr. Law observed that "he was a living example of the divine life, and did not, like most of the rudimentary, formalist divines and scholastic mystics, divide and subdivide it into various invented rules and gradations; which he condemned." As he also expressed himself in a letter to one of his correspondents: "Again, (through the same talkative spirit) you tell me it is objected by some that I never make any distinction between repentance, justification, and sanctification: and you have more than once called upon me to speak to this matter. You add, 'Here' (that is, in this distinction of these three words, thus understood) 'is the beginning, the middle, and the end of the work of the triune God upon the soul. Happy are they who experience these great and important things.' Now, Sir, if you and the objectors are in possession of this happiness, feeling the benefit of these three words *thus distinguished*, I have said nothing to rob you of that happiness. And you might call to mind that a much greater teacher than I am, who justly calls himself *the light of the world, the way, the truth, and the life*, never makes any more mention of this distinction than is to be found in my books. If, therefore, they are defective or blameworthy for lack of this distinction, how will you excuse the four Gospels?" The above series of observations, it will be kept in mind, were expressed towards the close of Mr. Law’s ministry: his opinions from time to time to his various correspondents will, as noted above, belong to a more complete history of his life.

Marsay was the strange and fanciful writer he was looking into when accosted by P. Böhler, the newly arrived Moravian, in Somerset Gardens in 1738. It would appear that Böhler had some personal knowledge of that writer, which Law, being then informed of, was induced to make a few inquiries about. Whereupon, Böhler—whose knowledge and experience of Christian truth had doubtless impressed him with a just opinion of the unprofitable, un-gospel character of Marsay’s views and writings—might have hastily concluded that Law, who had been previously represented to him as attached to the mystics, was of a similar turn of mind. And so, as is common with zealous sticklers for exciting interpretations of gospel doctrines, he would peremptorily judge him accordingly and not hesitate to express his opinion to those friends who asked for it. This may account for those groundless and injudicious letters that were addressed to Law by his former pupil shortly after this interview, as already referred to; these letters, however sincere and well-meaning, betray the uncertainty and imperfection of the writer’s theological science at

It might have made this outline of Mr. Law's history more interesting to have inserted examples of his talent, selected from his several treatises, as they have successively come under review; as also to have introduced some of his letters, written during the periods of his life already considered, to illustrate his style and progress of thought. But as the present notices are rather of the nature of a general sketch of his life, with the lights and shades broadly but correctly thrown over the chief points of the landscape, as a guide to a minute and perfect delineation of the whole in a finished drawing by a master artist; and as such an attempt would have extended this outline beyond the limits which its present position would afford, it has been deemed proper, as a general rule, to defer such insertions, either to the proposed larger biography, or to a second and more correct and polished edition of the present work, if called for. In which case, the whole would be revised and corrected by competent parties, so as to render it a standard reference book, or directory of pure evangelical and metaphysical science, according to the latest experimental discoveries and developments. It would also be printed in larger type, being then adapted for popular reading; whereas, now it is in the character of a pioneer, to prepare the way for a new era in science, embracing the unity, connection, and dependence of supersensuals and physics.

There have been few, if any, writers who have made, or been qualified to make, Law's character and talents their special study, and approached anything like an apprehension of his basis of understanding. Mr. Richard Tighe, in 1813, published a brief but inexact memorial of Law, from some slight information which he had collected on a visit to King's Cliffe, and from a perusal of his works. But he had, manifestly, no philosophical perception of the constitution of Law's mind, as appears by his book; in which, also, his religious idiosyncrasy is but too evident. And though reference has sometimes been made to Coleridge in such respect, yet he must be considered to have been as far removed from Law's sphere of mind as the former individual, and equally as incapable of offering a just representation of him. For his piety, according to report and appearances, was like his genius, mere ideality, not resulting in exalted, practical virtue. It was not of the genuine gospel stamp, beginning in a broken and contrite heart, and proceeding by the degrees of faith, of earnest prayer, self-denial, watching, fasting, and such like exercises, and cultivation of the divine life, to perfection; and therefore, whatever might have been his philosophical imagination through the reading of the higher departments of Law, <term>Behmen</term>, and others, he was incapacitated for such a task.

<margin>with the classics of foreign literature translated into English</margin>
To describe the character of Law, who, as before observed, is considered by the writer—after looking over eminent individuals of antiquity and later times—to be the finest classic specimen of a perfect common-sense mind, uniformly developed through all the solid attainments and accomplishments of human erudition, sterling wisdom, and enlightened, impartial piety, that has ever appeared; as much beyond Socrates or Epictetus as full Christianity is an improvement upon the most perfect light that preceded it ————— to describe his character justly and universally, the author must be radically of a similar mental organization and complexion; and have been subjected to a similar course of universal Spartan mental training and studies; (he would have to carry himself back to view the state of learning, religion, and leading circumstances of Law's epoch, accompanying him *Mentor-like* in his understanding, and from there to proceed up to the present time;) and he must, especially, have passed through a similar course of evangelical ascetic piety and religious experience. — *Secondly*, he must be free of all idiosyncrasy, having been led through all the partialities and imperfections of the several sections of Christianity, so as to have reached the center of truth; and further, be able to express and demonstrate the justness of his perceptions, so that all his readers who are capable of sound reasoning shall be irresistibly convinced of it, though, when they recede back to their own several positions in the circumference of truth, and measure his declarations by the standard of their own oblique light and imaginary conceptions, or personal interest, they shall agree in rejecting them as "mystical" and "erroneous." — *Thirdly*, he ought to be an individual of a searching, exact, and philosophical turn, of at least forty years of age, and to have been brought up, as to religious communion, among the <term>Methodists</term>. Such should be some of the chief characteristics or qualifications of the individual who is to do justice to the portraiture of Law.

Those who are familiar with Gibbon's autobiographical memoirs will have noticed his remarks and critical observations on Mr. Law and his writings. Upon a close scrutiny of them, from a right point of vision, it may afford matter for speculation whether Gibbon's perusal of those writings (whatever had been the results of his researches into history, devoid of the light of faith), did not, in reality, remove from under him the entire ground of his skepticism. Hence may be accounted for the peculiar modest tone of those observations, considering their author. Though for him to have turned confessor, and thereby invalidated his pretensions to the character of a philo-

Q. *What was breathed into this threefold body?* A. A threefold breath of life, in relation to the threefold manifestation of God, made in the two eternal principles and in this third temporal principle—all three of which must have concurred and contributed to the creation and perfection of man, the true image and likeness of God.

sopher—to expect him thus to have died to self, pride, honor, and interest in the beginning of his religious convictions, is not warranted by the observations of experience. The power of faith must be increased in the believer to such a degree as to force nature into subservience before she will consent to the performance of pure and magnanimous virtue.

Among the observations in question, the following remarkable sentence may be noticed on the present occasion:—“His theological writings (he states), which our domestic concerns induced me to read, preserve an amiable, though imperfect, sort of life, in my opinion; but here, perhaps, I pronounce with more confidence than knowledge on the merits of the man no pen can justify.” What, is there no pen that can do justice to the merits of Mr. Law? Remarkable words, indeed—and the more remarkable coming from so thoughtful, *and*, in some instances, judicious a writer, so penetrating and critical a judge of mental ability as the historian Gibbon. But they were the words of sobriety, carefully considered, and uttered by one who, whatever he may affect by a “perhaps,” was, doubtless, as intimately conversant with the character of Law’s private life (through the conversations of his own father upon the subject) as with the nature of his sublime genius from his writings. This is why he could place upon record that immortal panegyric upon the author of *Christian Perfection*, *Serious Call*, and *Answer to Trapp*, that *he lived all he taught, and practiced all he commanded*.

And had Gibbon been able to enter into further particulars without seemingly compromising himself in the way mentioned above, or giving ground for suspicion of his real sentiments, he might, possibly, have added (from the same source) that—his life, from his youth to seventy-five years of age, was *one continual growth in knowledge, piety, wisdom, and truth*. He did not, like the rest of men of learning and genius, after their leaving the university and on the completion of an enlarged course of theological studies (such as set forth in Dupin’s translated work), settle down to the ease and quietness of domestic life; but with his usual academic severity, and according to his unvaried principle of living by strict rule, he proceeded *onward to fresh attainments*—now fathoming the recorded spiritual or mystical science of all ages, making all that was evangelical, just, and solid in it his own. And further, that he did not stop there, but, moved by an insatiable desire and impulse after wisdom and perfection, he was finally led into the highest sphere of science, namely, into the contemplation of the supra-sensual ground of the divine wisdom and its relation to all future being, of nature and creature. The philosophy of this, he discovered, had been revealed by God through Behmen, though the popular class of mankind (as is, indeed, unavoidable) considered the contents of that author’s works to be “stupendous reveries.” And further still, he might have stated (from the same source of information, for letters are still in existence referring to the fact) concerning the “regular and good life” at King’s Cliffe his father had witnessed when on a visit there, and to the “discipline” of which, even during so short a period, he had attributed an improvement in his bodily health. He might have told how, according to his (the historian’s) aunt Hester’s own manuscripts still in existence, Mr. Law died as he lived, “in the perfect vigor of his faculties, as if he had not attained to half the age of man.” His whole conversation, in the intervals of the agonies of his nephritic <note>A kidney-related disease</note> and mortal affliction, consisted either of cries of adoration to the triune Deity of love or declarations concerning the new birth and full “opening of the divine life in the soul, to be all;” and that “after taking leave of everybody in the most affecting manner, he expired in divine raptures.” Such might have been the character of some further particulars respecting Mr. Law, had Gibbon permitted himself to insert them.

The following quotation from a friendly letter of Law to the Dr. Byrom mentioned before—who had turned part of his writings into poetry and was then further engaged in the same occupation—is inserted here to show the effects of Law’s writings on some of the learned deistical writers of his day, from which to infer the effect that could not fail to be derived from a solid and continuous perusal of them by so clear-headed a man as Gibbon:—“I have (he writes) lately received two or three sheets of paper, the remarks of a very learned and ingenious deist upon the *Appeal*, written to a gentleman in London who sent them to me. They are written with great spirit and vivacity, but leave the *Appeal* as unhurt as the northern archdeacon did. He promises to give it a reconsideration, and says this of it: *I sincerely admit the preference of Mr. Law’s system to any I ever met with; and since some religion is necessary for the mass of mankind, I could wish to see his system established—a spiritual elizium.* He ends his strictures by saying of the author of the *Appeal*, whom I look upon as one of the greatest and best divines that ever did honor to mankind—He has this postscript, namely: *I have read Dr. Byrom’s poem. I think it an admirable one; and were I to believe the Fall at all, it certainly should be his [Law’s] system of it, far preferably to that of the bishops. [1751.]*”

*Q.* But since we cannot consider them, nor speak of them all three at once, is there not a specific reason they should be viewed in order and distinction, as a first, second, and third?
*A.* Yes, there is a good reason why the fiery breath may be considered as the first, the light as the second, and the airy as the third. This reason is grounded not only in the order of eternal and temporal nature, but also in the order in which man's life was intended to continue in harmony with the eternal being and will of his Creator, who ordered His light to stand in the middle and to rule both on the right hand and on the left; as it is so with Himself in His threefold manifestation through eternal and temporal nature.
*Q.* What, then, was that first breath? *A.* A spiritual fire from the first principle of eternal nature; which, therefore, had its first four properties in their own mutual generation, so joined together that they can never again be dissolved.
*Q.* What is this properly called in man? *A.* When considered separately and on its own, it is specifically and primarily called the soul, and described as a dry, hungry, anxious fire, or fire-eye, having the center of its birth within itself, and being the proper root and only origin of life, though it is also life itself.

And whether by one or more enlightened men of God, full of the purest human and divine learning, justice shall be done not only to Law, but to truth itself—revealing her undivided unity and multiplicity, and yet her <margin>a</margin> harmony in nature and grace. For if she is only shown in the beginning and end of all her patterns and developments, from the center to the farthest reach of natural being (symbolized in the connection of the parts of every living natural form), then shall 'all nations' and people proclaim regarding the author of Christianity, as the unbelievers of old did when they cried out: "The Lord, he is God; the Lord, he is God."
As to this point, some further remarks—which the specific character of this brief memorial will require to be inserted later in the subject's order, explaining the fundamental relationship of Law to the advanced physical science of today—may suggest that the time is closer than is commonly supposed. For, indeed, the science of the present time has seemed to the writer to stand in a position somewhat similar to that of astronomical <margin>b</margin> or cosmic science at the close of Kepler's life, when he declared that it belonged to the next generation to discover the true system of the material universe, and that God would not fail to reveal it—in this way, an observant, insightful, and enlightened mind may justly judge the approach of great natural events. For all the necessary practical discoveries and experiments for that purpose were then available, and nothing was missing but the metaphysical key to the subject, by which the latter and the former could be made to match; which, accordingly, had been prepared by divine wisdom and revealed in Behmen. His demonstrations of the ground and constituent qualities of Nature, of the Three Principles of the eternal dark, light, and temporal universe, and of the magnetic tendencies and instincts of all things toward their respective centers and to one another—along with other corresponding laws and relations, all existing in number, weight, and measure—were translated by Newton (as far as they related to this temporal or material principle) into the mathematical and philosophical concepts of human reason, and so produced his system. Just as the state of science at that time gave birth to the Newtonian system, it has occurred to the writer that the current state of physical science seems to stand in a similar position—nothing being wanted but a true theosopher, also acquainted with all the advancements and theories of experimental philosophy, to reveal openly to the world the entire clockwork of nature from the center to the outermost edge of dead and solid matter—in a word, her science, and working powers, properties, and effects in everything; such a person is implied in the following allusion by Mr. Law:
> "But would you divinely know the mysteries of nature, the ground and reason of good and evil in this world, the relationship and connection between the visible and the invisible world, and how the things of time proceed from, are influenced by, and depend upon the things and powers of eternity, there is only one key of entrance; nothing can open the vision but seeing with the eyes of that same love which began and carries on all that exists, and works in visible and invisible nature."
<margin>c</margin> As he likewise describes the qualifications of a true scientific theologian: "Would you divinely know (he continues) the mysteries of grace and salvation, would you go forth as a faithful witness of gospel truths, wait until this fire of divine love has finished its perfect work within you. For until your heart is an altar on which this heavenly fire never goes out, you are dead in yourself, and can only be a speaker of dead words about things that never had any life within you. For without a real birth of *this divine love in the essence of your soul*, no matter how learned and polite you may be, your heart is only the dark heart of fallen Adam, and your knowledge of the kingdom of God will be only like that which Cain had." Let but such a philosopher arise (a master of the science of Behmen, Freher, and Law), having his inward eye opened as implied in the above quotation, and at the same time being familiar with the whole sphere of physical science, and then truth—or in other words, wisdom—shall be justified by her children; then it shall be understood how Law may be termed the Newton of metaphysics. But, as observed, the initial tracing of this fact belongs to a later place in this memorial.
And without such a twofold light and qualification, the disconnected theories and experiments of modern philosophy (the former, in many cases, being pure imagination) will unavoidably continue to be only a kind of schoolboy's scientific recreation and theorizing, instead of the clear understanding of divine philosophers. Such philosophers dwell spiritually in Him who sits upon the threefold rainbow throne in the center of nature, as the true life and light of angels and men, and see all things in His light: who is Christ and God.

Q. *If it is thus an immortal life itself, why then is it also said to be the proper root and only origin of life?* A. When life is taken to mean that eternal, glorious, and blessed life that man was created for and is redeemed into, this soulish being is nothing else but the root and origin of it; having, in itself alone, no glory or blessedness, but only restlessness and mere anxiety. But when "life" suggests a never-ceasing continuation in its will, desire, and sensibility, it is also an immortal living being in its own right, which can never stop being what it is or doing what it does, according to its own peculiar fiery nature.

Q. *What was the second breath?* A. A spiritual light from the second principle of eternal nature, called strictly and specifically the spirit, or the spirit of the soul; and described as a glorious flaming breath of light and love, illuminating, imbuing <note>tincturing</note>, and harmonizing all the fiery properties of the soul, and making it a holy angel of God, endowed with Divine wisdom, and fit to stand and worship before His throne.

As he was not versed in it, he wished to form a conception of how far it had come to discovering the foundation and constitution of nature. And though he was a mere beginner in the elements of theosophy, he found himself, while reading that treatise, in somewhat familiar territory, being able to translate its technical language into its true mother tongue, and to trace the phenomena described therein—of powers, motions, primary forms, and so on—back to their essential foundation and relationships as set forth in Behmen. But to return to the narrative.

In the year 1739, Mr. Law published his '*Grounds and Reasons of Christian Regeneration, offered to the consideration of Christians and Deists*.' In this work, he writes as a philosopher to philosophers, desiring nothing to be granted except what will be easily conceded by honest and rational minds. He introduces the discourse this way: "Though (says he) the subject is specific, and seems only to relate to one point, yet the things which come under consideration extend to matters of the most general importance, and contain the most moving reasons to awaken and convert the heart, both of the Deist and of the Christian. — For (he continues) it is my intent to search and lay open the true grounds and reasons of the Christian new birth, so that the things said may equally reach both these sorts of readers. — For the Deists and unbelievers have a great share of my compassionate feelings, and I can never think or write of the infinite blessings of the Christian redemption without feeling in my heart an eager longing to see them become happy partakers of them. — And as one naturally believes what one strongly wishes, so I cannot help hoping that both Christians and Deists will find truths here of such a nature as must, in some degree, touch their hearts, if they are not read with prejudice and aversion."

One of the goals of this treatise was, undoubtedly, to counteract the evil effects of the wild and exaggerated descriptions of the gospel doctrine of the 'new birth,' which were so common at its general proclamation throughout this country around the time he wrote this work. This could only be accomplished by a fundamental and philosophical handling of the subject, showing, by a chain of strict logic, the nature and necessity of regeneration, with the means and circumstances attending it, according to the sense of scripture and the testimony of enlightened children of God who had experienced it.

It has been considered out of place in the present general narrative to accompany the notices of Mr. Law's works with selections from each to illustrate his genius and views at the respective periods when he wrote them. However, having made some observations in a previous paragraph with reference to a prevailing fallacy—that the feeling of surprise and joy which the mind experiences on first grasping the truth of the ever-perpetuated 'atonement' and 'intercession' of Christ is not regeneration itself, as is too commonly taught (even by those who have been the subjects of regeneration, for want of a clearer understanding of the *doctrine thereof*)—it may be advisable, in this instance, to depart from the original rule and give an extract from the work under notice, which describes what *that faith is* which saves the soul. It shows that the blessing of the new birth is not any mere intellectual perception, but only and solely the opening or germination of the holy Spirit of God in the soul of man, or of the soul in God. Its nature and effects are, or may be, as distinct and perceptible as those of a birth into this world, or of a man who had been imprisoned in bitter cold and darkness suddenly emerging into all the delightful sensations of light and earthly comforts. The only way to such a birth is the ancient *Jacob-way* of wrestling prayer.

For as nature, whether spiritual or temporal, always proceeds in one uniform way, so the causes and effects of the new birth are the same in all ages. That persevering, faithful prayer and wrestling with God—which made Jacob a prince in Israel, Behmen a pure original fountain of divine wisdom, and Hester Ann Rogers a conscious subject of the distinct operations of the triune Spirit of love and a model of practical gospel holiness (spreading the fragrance of the vital knowledge of Christ and winning souls for heaven wherever she appeared)—must be the same process for every soul that will realize equal results, according to its <term>signature</term>. There is nothing artificial or to be obtained *by a trick*, or through the knowledge of an easier or 'shorter way' in this matter; but all who will reap the full blessings of the gospel dispensation can only do so in the standard gospel-way: by absolutely breaking with earthly reason, and dying to all that *the world, the flesh, and the devil* have in them and place upon them; and then, summoning all the powers of an omnipotent faith, *breaking through the barriers of death and hell which surround the soul, into the light of God*.

Further, from the confusion of ideas upon this particular point have arisen the crude conceptions and misrepresentations of the doctrine of the 'witness of the spirit,' which would clarify itself at once if we only considered what the new birth really is. Q. How does the spirit chiefly differ from the soul? A. Just as the second principle in eternal nature differs from the first; and as in temporal nature light does from fire. For as the light is a product of the fire, upon which—notwithstanding its own quite contrary constitution—it so depends as to have no being of itself without it, so also is and does the spirit in relation to the soul.

Though the spirit and scope of the practical remarks will not be fully apprehended by a mere abstract perusal of them, they rather require a duly prepared reader who is in communion with some zealous and spiritual outward church, and such a season as, for instance, on returning from some of its solemn devotional services, when the mind is deeply impressed with the stupendous and affecting concerns of eternity and the soul’s everlasting state. The extract, then, proposed for insertion on the present occasion, is as follows:—

> “The reason why we know so little of Jesus Christ as our *Saviour, atonement, and justification*, why we are so destitute of *that faith* in him which alone can change, rectify, and redeem our souls, and why we live starving in the coldness and deadness of an historical, *hearsay-religion* is this: we are strangers to our own inward misery and *wants*; we do not know that we live in the jaws of *death and hell*; we keep all things quiet within us, partly by *outward forms* and modes of religion and morality, and partly by the comforts, cares, and delights of *this world*. Hence it is that we consent to receive a Saviour as we consent to admit of the four gospels—because only four are received by the church. We believe in a Saviour not because we feel an *absolute want* of one, but because we have been told there is one, and that it would be a rebellion against God to reject him. We believe in Christ as our atonement just as we believe that he cast seven devils out of Mary Magdalene; and so we are no more helped, delivered, and justified by believing that he is our atonement than by believing that he cured Mary Magdalene.

> True faith is a coming to Jesus Christ to be saved and delivered from a sinful nature, as the Canaanitish woman came to him and would not be denied. It is a faith of *love*, a faith of *hunger*, a faith of *thirst*, a faith of *certainty*, and firm assurance, that in love and longing, and hunger, and thirst, and full assurance, will lay hold on Christ as its loving, assured, certain, and infallible Saviour and atonement.

> It is this faith that breaks off all the bars and chains of death and hell in the soul; it is to this faith that he always says what he said in the gospel: *Your faith has saved you, your sins are forgiven you; go in peace.* Nothing can be denied to this faith; all things are possible to it; and he who thus seeks Christ must find him to be his salvation.

> On the other hand, all things will be dull and heavy, difficult and impossible to us; we shall toil all the night and take nothing; we shall be tired with resisting temptations and grow old and stiff in our sins and infirmities if we do not, with a strong, full, loving, and joyful assurance, seek and come to Christ for every kind and degree of strength, salvation, and redemption. We must come to Christ as the blind, the sick, and the leprous came to him, expecting *everything* from him and nothing from themselves. When we *have this faith*, then it is that Christ *can do all his mighty work in us*.

> Tempers and inclinations are the *fruits* of the new-born nature, and not the nature itself; and as fruits and flowers are entirely distinct and different from the root and the tree, and necessarily suppose the root and the tree before they can be brought forth, so holy tempers and inclinations are distinct from, and posterior to, that nature which is to produce them as its fruits.

> And if holy tempers, rightly purified, could really arise or be brought forth in us without a change first made in the root or nature that is to bring them forth, it would be no absurdity to say that *men may gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles*.

> But if our blessed Lord has declared this to be contrary to the nature of things, and has further said that the tree *must first be made good before it can bring forth good fruit*, then we can, with sufficient ground of assurance, say that our nature must first be made good—its root and stock must be new-made or regenerated again—before it can bring forth the fruits of a holy, Christ-like walk and conversation.

> The whole nature of the Christian religion stands upon these *two great pillars*, namely, the greatness of our *fall* and the greatness of our *redemption*. In the full and true knowledge of these truths lie all the reasons of deep humility, penitence, and self-denial, and also all the motives and incitements to a most hearty, sincere, and total concession to God.
