A. An <term>astral and elemental life</term> from this outward world; which life especially made him a living creature in this created temporal principle, and allowed him to have communion in his essences with all things within it. Just as the former two, and especially the second, made him rule over them as a mighty, glorious prince, and not to have their own twofold qualities manifest and active in his pure paradisiacal life and body.
Q. *Which of these three was that breath of life which Moses says was breathed into man’s nostrils?*
A. Since all three were but one life, and were all three breathed together by one single act, standing in such a connection as the three principles are connected in only one, though a gradual manifestation of God; they were all three that breath of life (or according to the Hebrew text, *lives*) which made man a living soul. Nevertheless, this particular expression of breathing into his nostrils is properly applicable to this third one only. For the former two, being much deeper and interior, could not have been breathed from without into his nostrils, but were rather raised and breathed from within, each out of its own internal world.
Q. *Can any ground be shown for a confirmation of this?*
A. Yes, it could be confirmed in several ways, but this one alone can do it sufficiently: in the death of man, this third <term>astral and elemental breath</term> is the only mortal life that goes out of his nostrils again, into that same outward receptacle from which it had its origin; and there it can be perceived, like smoke arising from a candle as soon as it is extinguished. While the soul and spirit are much deeper and interior, and do not go through his nostrils from within into this outward world, but go rather out of this

these truths.
And until these two great truths have both awakened and enlightened our minds, all reformation and pretense to amendment is but a dead and superficial thing, a mere garment of deceit to hide us from ourselves and others.
Nothing can truly awaken a sinner but a true sense of the deep, inward possession and power that sin has in him. When he sees that sin begins with his being, that it rises up in the essences of his nature, and lives in the <term>first forms</term> of his life, and that he lies thus chained and barred up in the very jaws of death and hell, as unable to alter his own state as to create another creature; when along with this knowledge, he sees that the free grace of God has provided him a remedy equal to his distress, that He has given him the *holy blood and life* of Jesus Christ, the true Son of God [by the "incorruptible seed" of the "engrafted word" of promise], entering as deep into his soul as sin has entered, to change the <term>first forms</term> and essences of his life, and bring forth in them a new birth of a Divine nature—that is, to be an immortal image of the holy Trinity, everlastingly safe, blessed, and enriched in the bosom of the *Father, Son, and Holy Ghost*; when a man once truly knows and feels these two truths, there seems to be no more that you need do for him. You can tell him of no humility, penitence, or self-abasement but what is less than his own heart suggests to him. Humility can only be feigned or false before this conviction. He can now no more take any degree of good to himself than assume any share in the creation of angels; and all pride or self-esteem of any kind seems to him to contain as great a lie as if he were to say that he helped to create himself.
You need not tell him that he must turn to God with all his strength, with all his heart, all his soul, and all his spirit; for all that he can offer to God already seems to him less than the least of His mercies toward him. He has so seen the exceeding love of God in the manner and degree of his redemption that it would be the greatest pain to him to do anything except from a motive of divine love. As his soul has found God to be all love, so it has but one desire, and that is to be itself all love of God. This is the conviction and conversion that necessarily arises from a right understanding of these truths; the soul is thereby wholly consecrated to God, and can like, or love, or do nothing but what it can in some way or another turn into a service of love toward Him. But where these truths are not understood or not acknowledged, it is not to be wondered at if religion has no root that is able to bring forth its proper fruits.
And if the generality of Christians are a number of dead, superficial believers in Christian doctrines—as unwilling to have the *spirit* as to part with the form of their religion, loath to hear of any kind of *self-denial*, fond of worldly *ease*, indulgence, and *riches*, unwilling to be called to the *perfection* of the gospel; professing, preaching, and practicing religion merely as the custom of the sect or church they belong to requires—these are delusions that must happen to those who, however they may talk about the "corruption of human nature" and the "way of simple faith," do not yet know the true nature of their own fallen soul and what kind of regeneration alone can save them.
Thus the difference may be seen between true regeneration and a lively apprehension of the certainty and efficiency of the "atonement" and mediation of Christ as the ground of human salvation. But for a full, unequivocal elucidation of the subject, the reader is referred to Behmen’s Tract of "*True Repentance*"; by the practical study of its directions, it will be found that regeneration is the actual enkindling of the life and light of God in the soul, which is more or less powerful and sensible as the soul is more or less qualified for it. Therefore, nothing can effect it but the immediate action of God Himself, nor by any other than the natural means exemplified there: namely, of continuous ardor or vehemence of desire on the part of the soul directed toward God, and yet not even then until its resignation, self-abandonment, humility, and faith are complete and so capable of it: "all things are possible [to be done] to him who has faith." It may be well to remark that this process in its essential character and beginning will also be found to be as diametrically opposed to the insidious, self-delusive "quiet-turning of the spirit inwards"—with its consequent unproductiveness of that burning and shining devotion, holiness, and outflowing practical godliness which are represented in scripture as the inseparable fruits of true healthy regeneration—as it is to the boisterous outward action of the self-willed, uninformed young professor or the ignorant enthusiast.
To close these observations, the following extract of a letter from Mr. Law to one of his correspondents (dated Oct. 12th, 1757) may be appropriately inserted here:—"My unknown friend in Christ Jesus, I am glad that you are so heartily affected and so deeply instructed in the things of God. It is a happiness that no one knows, or can know, but he who is possessed of it."

**Q.** *How does this third life differ from the other two?*
**A.** Just as time differs from eternity, out of which it came, and into which it is to be returned again. Or, as this third mixed world differs from the two eternal principles. Or, as air differs from fire and light; all three are clearly different enough, and yet all three are so firmly combined that none of them can exist without the other two.
**Q.** *What do your authors call this third life in man?*
**A.** They call it the *astral spirit*, the *exterior spirit*, the *outward part of the soul*, the *transitory, mortal soul*, etc. Not that it was mortal from its beginning; but because it is now mortal since man’s transgression, and cannot help but be mortal because of the earthliness manifested in his body.
Page 171. *In what do they place the image of God, after which Adam was created?*
God created man in his image, not as he is in himself unmanifested, but as manifested—not only in eternal nature, but also now in temporal nature; man was created after (and not before) the creation of this temporal nature. If, then, this manifestation of God was now threefold—namely, according to the two inward worlds and to this third outward world—man also, who was to be a complete image of the manifested God and a prince of this outward world, must have had all these three as essential parts of his created human being. Therefore, the entire image of God did not consist only in the soul’s fire illuminated by its light (which might indeed be said of the holy angels, created before the creation of this world), but in all these three considered in their proper order and relation to each other, as they currently stand.

This is the necessary effect of regeneration; it brings forth nothing but the nature of Christ in the soul. All that Christ was toward sinners is, in its degree, found in the truly regenerate man. <note>Note well.</note>

> He cannot murmur or complain, though he sees foxes have their holes and birds their nests, but he has nowhere to lay his head. He must turn the other cheek to the smiter; he cannot revile the reviler; he is as free from censuring and judging his brother as a newborn infant. Since all he has to rejoice in is the unmerited, free love and compassion of God toward his own once-wretched state, he has no eyes but those of love and compassion toward those who are only as blind and dead as he was, until the Giver of life and light did for him what he did for Lazarus, lying in the grave.

To proceed.
In the early part of the year 1740, Mr. Law appeared again in print. The occasion for this was the publication of a sermon by one Dr. Trap, a High Church zealot. In this sermon, after picking apart isolated portions of *Christian Perfection* and the *Serious Call*, he attributed the great religious movements then beginning throughout this country to those two practical treatises. He said that "upon their appearance, he had prophesied they would do harm, and so it had happened (he added), for shortly afterward up sprang the Methodists." This was a conjecture regarding their results that was true enough, if Jeremy Taylor’s *Holy Living and Dying* had also been associated with them. This was also reaffirmed some twelve years later—though mistakenly as a reproach—by the previously mentioned Doctor Warburton. Upon reading the journals and other publications of the chief leader of that group, Warburton remarked, with his usual coarseness of expression, that *“Mr. Law fathered Methodism, and Count Zinzendorf was its wet-nurse,”* or words of a similar meaning. However, Dr. Trap in his sermon had shown no moderation toward the subject of his criticism, asserting that those treatises “contained false and scandalous doctrine, reproachful to the Christian religion, and deserving of public censure.”

To this discourse, Mr. Law then published a reply titled *An Earnest and Serious Answer to Dr. Trap’s Discourse of the Sin, Folly, and Danger of being Righteous Overmuch*. In this, he sufficiently justifies his own writings while probing to the quick the principles and sentiments of the doctor’s sermon. He tests them not by the conventions and customs of a church established by law, but by the perfect standard of the spirit and counsels of Christ and his apostles, and the practice of the church in its first and purest state. In it, he also complains of a serious defect in the doctor’s discourse. Although the doctor deprecated the evils of being “righteous overmuch” throughout the sermon—calling it the *“baneful plague of enthusiasm”*—he failed to define for his hearers the right and proper measure of sober gospel piety, or to show how far it ought to regulate a man’s spirit and conduct in the world. By this omission, the doctor had left himself open to the charge of that *“half-thinkingness”* which he had heartily attributed to “enthusiastic pretenders to a more than ordinary degree of sanctity.” This essential deficiency, however, Mr. Law takes it upon himself to supply in his *Answer*, rather than taking for granted—as the doctor did—that his readers were sufficiently versed in the holy requirements of evangelical Christianity. He does this with a master hand, showing himself to be a learned scribe in the kingdom of God, bringing forth out of his treasury of theoretical and experimental knowledge things both new and old.

In the life of the Redeemer, who declared that he “came to do not his own will, but the will of him that sent him,” it will undoubtedly have been the subject of the reader’s reflections that he did not wait for extraordinary or singular occasions to perform his mighty works. Instead, he timed his actions and discourses to the common events and circumstances that each day brought forth, turning them into a means of showing the glory of God. This is undoubtedly the true order of cooperating with Divine wisdom and providence. Furthermore, although occasions seem to have arisen entirely by what is termed “chance”—sometimes as the product of natural causes, and at others as the result of malice or ignorance on the part of men, whether from the reigning orthodoxy of the time or the common people—they seem to have been the very circumstances needed for his personal ministry to convey his divine instructions down to all future ages of mankind.

Why, then, this question might be thus answered— **A.** They place it in his having all the three principles in his created being which God has likewise himself, as manifested in eternal and temporal nature; but especially do they place it in that due order according to which the first and third were to be subject and ministering to the second, which alone was to be predominant. **Q.** *Do they not exclude by this all those perfections of holiness, wisdom, dominion, etc., in which the image of God in man is commonly said to have consisted?* **A.** No; but they consider all such glorious attributes as posterior consequential things, which of necessity must have resulted from the union of these three, and none of which could have failed or been prevented from proceeding forth from it freely, as long as he stood without alteration in the order of this threefold life: which, therefore, they look upon as the very basis of all his perfections, and think, therefore, they have sufficient reason to say, that in this order, chiefly and fundamentally, the image of God is to be placed.

Now as it pleased the wisdom of God thus to act in the life of our blessed Savior, so does it please him to act in a similar manner in those in whom the same Spirit rules and governs, who are called out of the common path of life to be extraordinary guides to the rest of the world; they being constituted for such office by their great devotion and experience in the spiritual life of Christ, their clear, uniform perception and impartial love of religious truth, and the possession of sound learning: qualifications which may naturally be conceived to be indispensable in those to whom the *‘word of wisdom’* is especially given, in these last and more accomplished ages of Christianity. Accordingly, these features will be found to signally mark the whole of Mr. Law’s career as a moral and religious instructor. All his works bear this peculiar stamp of being well-timed, both as to occasion and matter, and full of the most natural, profound, and lasting instruction. And as he combined within himself the quintessence or substantiality of all solid human erudition, as well as theological science, which he brought to bear in due proportion on whatever subject engaged his pen, so his writings must remain standards, regarding the subjects upon which they severally treat, to all posterity.
But, if one more than another of his works illustrates the principle that has just been stated (though, where all are of equal judgment, it would be, perhaps, improper to make any distinction) of turning everyday events in an elevated spirit of wisdom to their right ends—the glory of God and the edification of men—it may be said to be the treatise under consideration, namely, the *‘Earnest and Serious Answer to Dr. Trap’s Sermon;’* to which may be appropriately added the *‘Animadversions upon Dr. Trap’s Reply,’* mentioned hereafter, as forming together a lively epitome or mirror of evangelical Christianity. And the reader of those treatises will have only to refer to the biographies of some acknowledged examples of holiness and perfection, whose lives were, according to their particular form and complexion, a natural exhibition of the regenerated and highly developed spirit of Christ in human nature, after the gospel model and character—take, for instance, as a modern life, *‘Sigston’s Memoir of Bramwell,’* or, among those of past times, numbers which are just sketched in *‘Butler’s Lives of the Saints’*—to be convinced of the justice of such an observation. Indeed, it is far from speaking too highly of this brief discourse to say that it is not unworthy of the most devout and judicious bishop that ever addressed an assemblage of clergy; being just what might be expected from the Spirit of Christ speaking through an erudite apostle to these last times (as he spoke by his forerunner to the characters of his own day). This, however, is but a common characteristic of all Mr. Law’s ministry, as the reader who is acquainted with his works is doubtless prepared to affirm. Happy would it be for this nation if those portions of the treatises in question, relating to the nature and design of the Christian religion, the duties and obligations of the pastoral office, and the true character and requirements of divine love, were, in conjunction with the author’s practical treatises, *‘Jeremy Taylor’s Holy Living and Dying,’* and other works that will be mentioned in the following section, made a regular study in every theological institution and the daily meditation of every administrator of apostolic functions throughout these kingdoms.
Further, with this treatise may be deemed to be completed the series of elementary instructions and directions for the full development and sober guidance of the new evangelical spirit, which arose into fresh manifestation at this period—as the result of his own instrumentality, and, as to its peculiarity of experimental character and missionary zeal (through the Moravians), that of Behmen. Whose little book of the *‘Way to Christ,’* even in his own day, according to the account in his life, had begun its operation; and which, especially the tracts *‘of Repentance’* and *‘of the Four Complexions’* within it, will be found, on examination, to be both original and containing the rudiments of all that was solid, practical, and evangelically effective in the principles and economy of the *‘Church of the United Brethren,’* which, derived from there, was placed upon the foundation of *‘Methodism.’* The term *‘Methodists,’* as already stated, devoid of all mystery concerning its origin, was given, and that very naturally and appropriately, to the individuals who associated themselves together to practice the methodical devotion to God of the *‘Serious Call’* and *‘Christian Perfection.’*
All these interesting facts, taken from authentic sources, with the chain of connection between them, and the manifest instrumentality of the whole in the advancing regeneration of the world, in an evangelical sense; as also concerning the germ and growth of the present and progressing universal improvement and greatness of this country (as of its ancient dependencies), where the principles of civil and religious liberty have had a free course of operation, will require to be set forth in the proposed larger biography. <meta>This page continues a series of questions and answers regarding the distinction between paradise and the Garden of Eden, as well as the nature of the "spirit of life." Q. *What was the paradise, or Garden of Eden, in which this glorious person was placed?* A. The Garden of Eden is not to be confused with paradise, seeing that *no beast can enter paradise*, whereas all the beasts were brought before Adam in the Garden of Eden. Though these two are also not to be separated, but acknowledged in their union; indeed, if a proper distinction between them is understood, the Garden of Eden may well enough be called paradise in some sense and respect.

Q. *What distinctions do your authors make between these two, which are commonly understood to be one and the same?* A. They say, with good reason, that paradise was a holy spiritual state in Adam's mind, or in all the essences of his spirit, soul, and body. But the Garden of Eden was a specific, limited place on earth, or a part of the earthly globe, which remained a part of it even though paradise was lost and gone in Adam's fall.

Q. *In what respect and sense, then, can this garden be called paradise?* A. It can be called so (and for the sake of distinction it may be called the *local paradise*), because it had a paradisiacal property manifest and predominant in it, which was not so in any other place on the earth.

Q. *What was this paradisiacal property, and what were its effects in this garden?* A. It was a quintessential or "one-element" principle of vegetation, producing the most excellent, incorruptible plants of all sorts, in which the four elements were not manifest in their opposition; these fruits, therefore, were fit for man, while no beast was capable of eating them.

The "*Appeal to all who Doubt or disbelieve the truths of the Gospel, whether they be Deists, Arians, Socinians, or nominal Christians, wherein the true grounds and reasons of the whole Christian faith and life are plainly and fully demonstrated*," was the next independent treatise that issued from his pen. This appeared in the same year as the preceding tract and was accompanied by an "Appendix," being the previously mentioned "*Animadversions upon Dr. Trap’s reply*." It would seem that this individual did not have the discretion to keep silence under the rebuke he had received in the "*Earnest and Serious Answer*"; but (not considering the puny ability and vulnerability of a mere scholastic theologian and state churchman, in comparison to the giant-like qualifications of a true mystical divine, who, besides being equipped with all the standard acquisitions of learning, has "the world, the flesh, and the devil" under his feet), he had to venture once again to take up the cudgels and try his hand against such a perfect master of the science of evangelical theology in both its theory and practice, and so accomplished a controversialist as his antagonist.

This reply accordingly drew forth a rejoinder from Law, being the "*Animadversions*" in question. In this work, as may be surmised, the doctor’s professional reputation was entirely laid prostrate, though it had already become the subject of popular discussion and ridicule; one of the publications that appeared on the occasion was ironically entitled, "*Dr. Trap vindicated from the charge of being a Christian*." This latter discourse, as observed, is a most felicitous conclusion to its predecessor and is of an equally providential character, as it afforded its Elias-spirited author the opportunity to complete what he might have previously left unsaid for the purification and good of the church. The following extract, taken from the former treatise—as it exhibits his heavenly enkindled spirit in both these discourses, serves to justify what has just been stated concerning his mystic vocation, and is of great practical importance regarding the best interests of Christianity—may be deemed suitable for insertion here:

> “The whole Christian world, from the time of our Savior to this day, has been praying, *Thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven*. Sacraments, divine worship, and the order of the clergy are appointed as ministerial helps for this end: to raise, set up, and establish this kingdom of God on earth. The fall of man brought forth the *kingdom of this world*; sin, in all shapes, is nothing else but the *will of man* driving forward in a state of self-motion and self-government, following the workings of a nature *broken off* from its dependency upon and union with the divine will. All the evil and misery in the creation arises *only and solely* from this one cause. There is not the smallest degree of distraction, pain, or punishment, either within us or without us, but what is owing to this—namely, that man stands *out of* his place, is *not in, under, and united to God* as he should be, as the nature of things requires. God created everything to partake of *His own nature*, to have some degree and share of His own life and happiness. Nothing can be good or evil, happy or unhappy, but as it does or does not stand in the same degree of *divine life* in which it was created, receiving in God and from God all the good it is capable of, and cooperating with and under Him according to the nature of its powers and perfections. As soon as it turns to *itself*, and would, as it were, have a *sound of its own*, it breaks off from the *divine harmony* and falls into the misery of its own discord; all its workings then are only so many types of torment or ways of feeling its own poverty. The redemption of mankind can only be effected, and the harmony of creation can only be restored, when the will of God is the will of every creature. For this reason, our blessed Lord, having taken upon Himself a created nature, so continually declares against doing anything of Himself and always appeals to the will of God as the only motive

A paradisiacal property still lies, indeed, in all things, yet it is no longer manifest or predominant in them, but is entirely surrounded and infected by a four-elemental corruption; and for this reason, therefore, it cannot be said absolutely to be the very same. For if it were, all things would still be paradisiacal and incorruptible, as they were then. Man, too, would still be in paradise and enjoy a paradisiacal state, both internally and externally, as he did then, when he was in this garden in paradise.

Q. What do your authors say about this paradisiacal state? A. Many great, glorious, and most significant things. For instance, regarding this internal paradisiacal state, they say that it consisted in an entire subjection of all his external faculties to his immortal <term>fire-light-soul</term>, and of both to the holy Will, Word, and Spirit of God; in a childlike, innocent mind; in a continual holy communion with God and Angels; in being filled with angelic joys, delights, and praises; in being endowed with divine wisdom and understanding all the creatures of this world; in an ability to look into all their essences and to have dominion over all, etc. And as for his external paradisiacal state, they specifically describe (1) the glorious condition of his body, which could freely pass through earth and stones without being held back, resisted, or hurt by anything. (2) His living, indeed, in a temporal principle, but standing not so much in time as in eternity; having no night, no weariness, nor sleep within him, and not needing to breathe the outward air as he must do now. (3) The manner of his eating and drinking, which was done in his mouth only, without filling a stomach and emptying it again; but almost as the sun swallows up water, and

and end of everything he did, saying that it was his *food and drink to do the will of Him who sent Him*.

What, now, can be so desirable to a sober, sensible man as to have the vain, disorderly passions of his own corrupted heart removed from him, to be filled with such unity, love, and concord as flows from God, to stand united to and cooperating with the divine goodness, willing nothing but what God wills, loving nothing but what God loves, and doing all the good that he can to every creature from a principle of love and conformity to God? Then the kingdom of God has come, and His will is done in that soul, just as it is done in heaven. Then heaven itself is in the soul, and the life and conversation of the soul is in heaven. The curse of this world is removed from such a man; he walks upon consecrated ground, and everything he meets, everything that happens to him, helps advance his union and communion with God. —— For it is the state of our *will* that determines the state of our life; when we receive everything from God and do everything for God, everything does us the same good and helps us to the same degree of happiness. *Sickness and health, prosperity and adversity* bless and purify such a soul in the same degree; as it turns everything toward God, so everything becomes divine to it. For he who seeks God in everything is sure to find God in everything. When we thus live entirely for God, God is entirely ours, and we are then happy in all the happiness of God; for by uniting with Him in heart, and will, and spirit, we are united to all that He is and has in Himself. This is the purity and perfection of life that we pray for in the *Lord’s Prayer*, that *God’s kingdom may come, and his will be done in us, as it is in heaven*. And we can be sure that this is not only necessary but attainable by us, otherwise our Savior would not have made it a part of our daily prayer. —— It may now, then, justly be asked: have we yet obtained that for which we have been so long and so universally praying? Can we look upon the church of this nation as drawing near, or even tending toward this state of perfection? Can we be taken to any parish, whether in town or country, where it can truthfully be said of any one pastor and his flock that the kingdom of God is coming there, and His will begins to be done on earth as it is in heaven? Can we, therefore, find any one parish where the pastor does not have great reason to reject the doctor’s <note>Likely referring to Dr. Trapp, whom William Law critiqued.</note> discourse and to pray both for himself and his flock that they may enter much further into the spirit and practice of Christianity than they have yet entered, that the gospel may have much greater power over them than it has yet had, and that they all may, with a most awakening conviction, see and understand what it is that has made so divine and powerful a religion so lacking in its proper effect upon them? —— For if this is the case—if we stand at this amazing distance from that state of perfection to which Christ has called us, even though we have His infallible promise to be with us to the end of the world, to assist us with such power and strength from above as to obtain and do everything that we pray for through a right faith in Him and conformity to His laws and example; if this is the case, does it not seem as if heaven and earth call upon every minister of the gospel to take some share of this miserable state of things upon himself and to endeavor to convince both himself and his flock that they have not yet been Christians in true earnest? That they have professed Christ with the tempers of Jews and Heathens; that they have not yet entered into the narrow way that leads to life; that they have not yet enough renounced the world, not enough denied themselves, not enough emptied their hearts of passions harmful to piety, not enough offered and devoted themselves to God, not enough made the spirit of religion the spirit of their lives, not enough sought for strength and deliverance from sin by a firm and living faith in Jesus Christ, who is made righteousness and sanctification to every sinner who turns to God through faith in him; not enough prayed and desired that they might be born again of God by the awakening and quickening of the incorruptible seed of divine life in their souls, so that Christ may be truly said to be formed in them; not enough prayed and desired to be everywhere and on all occasions under the perpetual influence and guidance of the Holy Spirit, that they may think, and say, and do everything by His holy inspiration; not enough looked to that first and great commandment of loving God with our whole heart and whole strength; not enough endeavored to keep the next, which is like it, that of loving our neighbor as we love ourselves; not enough renounced such fashions, customs, and conformities to the world as greatly corrupt the heart and grieve and separate the Holy Spirit from it. —— Now, in whichever way we consider the lamentable state of religion among us—whether they be evils within or outside the church—no evil can be removed, nor any remedy be procured by us of the clergy, except in this one way: that every individual of the order, from the highest to the lowest, begin in right earnest with himself, open the book of his own heart and life, and consider seriously in the presence of God whether, according to his degree in the ecclesiastical function, the world has had its due share of *salt and light* from him; whether all that is in the world—*the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life*—have been so openly, so constantly discouraged and renounced by him that the whole form of his life has been one loud

*Q. But what evidence can be given for the belief in all these things, which seem impossible for man to know?* A. Paradise is not annihilated or destroyed, but is still the same now in itself as it was then, though it is veiled by the curse, and fallen man is not in it. If, then, there is a possibility that man can be raised up from the fall and curse, and can be admitted again into paradise in his renewed, inward part—and this even during his outward life—there must also be a possibility for such a person to know what paradise is; what the first Adam was, and what his paradisiacal state was. If I have changed one flock or station for another, or added one position to another, have I done it in *singleness of heart, as unto the Lord, and not for myself?* Has all that I have sought or done of this kind been *only from this motive* and with this view: that I might be more truly faithful to him who has called me, and be more and more spent and sacrificed for the salvation of souls? Have I neglected no means of fitting and preparing myself for the illumination of God’s Holy Spirit, which alone can enable me in any measure to speak to and work upon the hearts and consciences of men? Have I earnestly longed and labored after every kind and degree of inward and outward holiness, and *purity of body, soul, and spirit, so that my standing at the altar* may be acceptable to God, and my prayers and intercessions for my flock *may be very effective before him?* Has my own *self-denial, renunciation of the world, and love of the cross of Christ* enabled me to preach those duties in their *full extent?* Has my own strictly pious use of the things of this world, my own readiness to relieve and assist every creature to the utmost extent of my ability, fitted me to call others to these things with power and authority? Have all ages and conditions of people under my care had their proper instruction and warning from me, so that I have spared no folly, vanity, indulgence, or conformity to the world that hurts men’s souls and hinders their progress in piety? Have I done all that by my prayers and preaching, life and example, which Christ expects from those whom he has commanded to feed his sheep? Can my flock, by looking at me, see what virtues they lack? Can they, by following me, be led to every kind and degree of Christian perfection? Lastly, has the will of God and the spirit of the gospel been the beginning and end, the reason and motive, the rule and measure, of my liking or disliking, doing or not doing, everything among those people with whom I have lived as their minister? These are a few of the questions that the present state of religion in this *island* calls upon every minister of the gospel to examine and try himself by.——For as the *order of the clergy* is instituted for no other end than the *preservation of religion and true piety in the world*; so when any age is more than ordinarily sunk in vice and impiety, the *whole order of the clergy*, and every member of it, have great reason not only to be deeply afflicted, but greatly frightened by it, and to suspect and fear their own conduct, since that which is their *particular work* has had *so little success.* They have great reason to apprehend that it is some degenerate—

ground, this question is more deeply and distinctly to be answered. Adam, in paradise, must be considered as being in a twofold, different state. (1.) As he was before the first beginning of his wandering imagination, only and purely a workmanship of God, having his threefold life from the mouth of his Creator, and being an entire image of him, made in purity, without any defilement or disposition toward it. In this state, he had in him all the characters expressed of the perfections of him whose image he was—namely, so far as they could have been expressed in, or be communicable to the creature. And (2.) as he was in the first beginning, and further carrying on more and more his own work of a lustful imagination, taking delight gradually more and more in things inferior to himself. In this state, that holy image of God was not yet indeed wholly destroyed, but, nevertheless, already more or less polluted; and it began with the beginning of his own work to decrease, decreasing still further always as much as that work did increase. Now, in this latter state—namely, in the first beginning of it, not in that former—the command was given to him. The command is to be considered as posterior, and presupposing a previous beginning, or a ready disposition to the transgression; while the transgression is to be looked upon as prior, and as that which had given occasion for the command. For the command, *Thou shalt not eat*, presupposes the tree of knowledge. Now, this tree was not there before, but was brought forth by the concurrence of Adam's lusting imagination, and presupposes, therefore, a beginning of the transgression, or a moving, active disposition toward it; and so the command is posterior both to this and that. All this is conformable to that order which the apostle observed, saying, *Because of the transgression the law came in*; but

This does not suppose that it is in the power of our order to regulate the manners of people as we please; it only supposes that of all human means it has the greatest effect; and that when any nation or people are either *very good* or *very bad*, the behavior of the clergy may reasonably be reckoned to have greatly contributed to it. — Let us all, therefore, of the clergy, who have any right sense of the nature of our order, any true love for our brethren in it, awaken and stir up one another to a faithful diligence in our callings—not such as may secure us from public scandal and the laws of the land, but such a faithful diligence as the nature of our office, the spirit of the gospel, and the present decay of religion calls for. Let us beseech and entreat one another deeply to consider the great need that this poor nation has of a zealous, pious, exemplary, disinterested, and laborious clergy; to consider the *dreadful judgments of God* that may justly be expected to fall first upon *our own heads*, if this true, only relief and remedy is not procured by *all of us*, according to the utmost of our ability. — It is now no time for *ease, indulgence, or worldly repose*; all is to be renounced, all is to be sacrificed; and we must, in the spirit of martyrdom, awaken the world into a *faith and love* of the gospel. Now is the time that *we must give up all our worldly regards, forsake all that we have, that we must hate father and mother, wife and children, and brothers and sisters, yes, and our own lives also*, or we cannot be *faithful* ministers of Jesus Christ. The same spirit which first planted the gospel is now required to recover and restore it among us. We must break off our chains of worldly prudence and come forth in the *spirit and power of the gospel*; so live, and speak, and act, whether in the pulpit or out of it, that all who see and hear us may be forced to confess that God is in us of a truth, and that his Holy Spirit has sent us. A ministry that does not have *this power*, that does not have *full proof*, both to themselves and others, that the Holy Spirit is thus *with them*, opening the kingdom of God in their own souls, and enabling them to preach it to others with spirit and power, must answer to God for their lack of it. <note>[Here and throughout, consider the remarks on page 378: "Further, etc."]</note>

To ask whether the assistance of the Holy Spirit is to be ordinary or extraordinary is as needless and groundless a distinction as to ask whether a minister of the gospel ought to be an *ordinary* or *extraordinary* good man. The operation of the Holy Spirit in us since the fall is a *supernatural power*, and therefore, in a just sense, *always extraordinary*, because enabling us to be and do that which the ordinary power of fallen nature is insufficient for; but it is more or less restored to us as we are more or less fitted to receive it. And all that assistance or renovation of the Holy Spirit which an apostle might expect, for the raising of his own personal holiness to its greatest height, or for enabling him with *spirit and power to move, affect, and convert the hearts of men to the faith of the gospel, may be justly expected now* by such ministers of the gospel as do all that an apostle did to obtain and receive it. Our religion is founded on this doctrine: that we are to be *born again of the Holy Spirit*,—that it is to be the *breath and life of our new-born inward man*,—that there is *no sanctification of the heart, no illumination of the mind, no knowledge of divine mysteries, no love of holy things possible to be had, but in and by the motion and life of this Holy Spirit renewed or born again in us*;—that *its life, motion and power in us increases according to our faith, prayers, and desires for it.*

Is it not now a *flat denial* of all this to say, as is said by some, *that the establishment of the gospel in the world, together with the assistance of human learning and languages, has been the reason why the assistance of the Holy Ghost is abated, and become only such as may be called ordinary?* For if we consult either scripture or experience, must it not be said that *worldly peace and prosperity need as much to be sanctified by the Holy Spirit as persecution and distress?* That *human learning and knowledge need as high degrees of divine grace and help as human ignorance?* Is not the blindness, the infatuation and corruption of *men of letters* as notorious as that of *unlearned men?* Does an editor of *Terence, Horace, or Virgil* receive such illumination from plays and poetry? Do cardinals and pluralists receive so much unction and assistance from human establishments as to need *less* to be led and governed by the Holy Spirit of God? Or will we say that a critical study of divided languages, and a religion established in worldly ease and peace, are not only in themselves free from danger and corruption, but have so much of the nature of the Holy Spirit of God in them that they can be to us in his stead, and make his sanctifying operations upon us needed in a *less degree?*

On the part of God, our redemption in Jesus Christ and our sanctification by the Holy Ghost stand always in the same degree of nearness and fullness to all of us; there is hardly a chapter in the New Testament that can be understood, or its doctrines observed, except upon the supposition of this great truth. we do not come to the perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, it is not because Christ has now become our Redeemer only in an ordinary way or degree, but it is because we have not so turned to him, not so turned from ourselves, and not so counted all things but dung so that we might win Christ and be found in him, as the first saints did. If the Holy Spirit does not now renew, quicken, move, and sanctify our hearts in such a degree, and fill us with such degrees of divine light and love as was done in the first age of the church, it is not because this sanctifying Spirit has committed some part of his work to human learning, and so has become our sanctifier only in a lesser and ordinary degree, but it is because we ourselves have forsaken *this fountain of living waters*, and *hewn out broken cisterns for ourselves*; it is because we have grieved this Holy Spirit, resisted his motions, quenched his holy fire, and under an outward profession of Christ, have kept up that old man, with his deeds, which cannot be the temple and habitation of the Holy Spirit.

If, therefore, we have any true sense of the nature and weight of our ecclesiastical calling, any desire to do the *full work of the ministry*, to satisfy the wants and necessities of our flocks; if we have any fear of being condemned as useless, insignificant laborers in Christ’s vineyard, it is high time to awaken from this dream of an *ordinary and extraordinary* sanctification of the Holy Spirit; it serves only to keep us unsanctified, shut up in death, in the dead workings of our own corrupted nature, to keep us learnedly content with our state, as if we were rich, and increased in goods, and had need of nothing, and hinders us from knowing that we are *wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked*.

Several of the clergy, whose lot has fallen in this corrupt age, may be supposed to have taken the sacred office upon them and to have lived in it, not enough according to its nature and spirit, merely through the degeneracy of the times, and from a consideration that they are well enough, according to the measure of religion that now passes in the world. And perhaps there are few, if any, of the order, however eminent for good works, whose virtues have not received some abatement from the same cause. This, therefore, may be added as another reason why all the clergy of this land should search into their lives and conduct with the utmost severity, and bring everything to the test of the letter and spirit of the gospel.

The Christian religion has not had its proper effect, nor obtained its intended end, until it has so established the kingdom of God among us that his will is done on earth as it is done in heaven. This is the perfection that every Christian, when advancing forward in the several degrees of holiness and purification, is to *tend toward and aspire after*. And if those who are to be taught are to be thus separated from an earthly nature, thus emptied of all worldly passions, and thus dead to the workings of self-will and self-love, so that the Spirit of God may be all in all in them, what manner of men ought they to be who are to *teach, promote, advance, and lead* the way to this purity and perfection? What a distance ought he to be from every appearance of pride, who is to draw others to love and practice the profound humility of the blessed Jesus? How ought he to deny his appetites, to humble his body, and be steady in all kinds of self-denial, who should convince his flock that *they who sow to the flesh, shall of the flesh reap destruction*? How heavenly-minded, how devoted to God, how attentive to the one thing needful, how unspotted from the world ought he to be, who is to persuade others that they cannot possibly serve *God and mammon*? How empty ought he to be of all selfish cunning, all worldly policy, all arts and methods of ambition, who is to fix it deep in the hearts of his hearers that unless they become as little children, they cannot see nor enter into the kingdom of God? What open hands and open heart ought he to have, what an extent of charity ought to be visible in him, who is to bring his flock to this faith: that *it is more blessed to give than to receive*? How remarkably, undeniably plain, open, sincere, undesigning, and faithful should he be, who is to recommend, plant, and establish sincerity, plainness, simplicity, truth, and innocence among his flock? There is such a necessary fitness in these things that the force and power of religion must be much prevented when its precepts are recommended to the world by those who excuse themselves from the plain and open practice of them. <note>Consider Bramwell!</note>

The office of the ministry is of the highest nature; it is a trust which no language can sufficiently express; and the unfaithful discharge of it is, of all conditions in life, the most dreadful. To be charged with the *death and blood of souls* by that God who laid down his life to redeem them is a condemnation that will carry more of guilt and punishment in it than any other. Would you know the office of a Christian pastor, you must look at the *office of Christ*; would you know what manner of spirit he ought to be of, you must look at the spirit of Christ. For the work of the ministry is only the work of Christ committed to other hands, who are to supply his absence, to be here in his stead, to be doing the same things and with the same spirit that he did, until the end of the world.

Q. Do they give any reason why the first Adam was tempted? A. Yes, they give several reasons, all centered on this point—that there was an absolute necessity for it. For they say that just as there was a necessity by which Adam must have had a threefold life in him if he were to be a complete image and likeness of God and a prince in this created world, there was also the same necessity that he must have been tempted if he were to possess the throne of fallen Lucifer. They demonstrate this necessity chiefly from the very nature, combination, and internal constitution of that threefold life.

Q. But his threefold life stood, as you said before, in a good and excellent combination, order, agreement, and harmony, as only one, because only one was manifest and predominant in him, which was the paradisiacal; how then could this have caused or necessitated a temptation? A. His threefold life did indeed stand that way within him, and even this made him a complete image of God. But it did not stand so outside of him in the three great worlds of which he was an epitome, and each of which had a natural communion, correspondence, or sympathy with that part in man which was extracted from it; for in those worlds, it was disordered and out of harmony due to the false <term>magia</term> of Lucifer. From this, the cause of the temptation can be clearly seen.

in the work of the ministry; but then it should be well *considered* that it is only honorable in the same sense as saying that nothing is more honorable than to suffer as a martyr. It is an honor as different from all worldly status and distinction as the glory of Christ upon the cross is different from the triumph of an earthly prince. Therefore, when we think of the honor and dignity of the pastoral function, we should be careful to remember that it is only the honor of *dying a martyr*—an honor of humbling, abasing, and sacrificing ourselves with Christ, and continuing the exercise of his suffering priesthood for the salvation of the world. The holy office is often considered only as an authoritative commission to minister in holy things, but it is much more than this; it is a call and command to act with the spirit of Christ, to represent his purity, to continue his holiness, to bear a part of his sacrifice, and to devote oneself to the good of others as he did. A priest who has only his ordination to distinguish him lacks as much to make him a true priest as Judas lacked to make him a true apostle. For though holiness gives no man a commission to exercise the pastoral office, yet all who are called to it are as much ordained and appointed to a unique holiness of life as they are to the administration of the sacraments; and when they cease to be *light and salt* to the rest of the world, they sin against the pastoral office as greatly as those who enter it without any authority.

For the sacred office is God's appointment to continue through all ages of the world the spirit and power of Christ, for reconciling men to God in the same manner and by the same means of holiness, sacrifice, and devotion that Christ exercised when he was upon earth. We need no other proof of this than this one saying of our blessed Lord: *As my Father has sent me, so I send you*. That is, for all the purposes for which I have come into the world, for all those same purposes I send you into it—to be there in my place, to fill my absence, to carry on the work that I have begun, to exercise my power, to act with my spirit, and to continue the exercise of my love, labor, and suffering for the salvation of mankind. To be sent by our blessed Lord for the same purposes as he was sent into the world is such an appointment to all kinds and degrees of holiness that it can never be rightly fulfilled except by giving and devoting ourselves wholly and absolutely to God.

Imagine that you had lived with our blessed Lord when he was upon earth, that you had learned the dignity and divinity of his person, that you had seen the love which he bore toward mankind, and that you had entered into the glorious designs of his kingdom, which was to convert the inhabitants of the earth—poor creatures of flesh and blood—into sons of God and heirs of eternal glory.

Imagine that you had seen him after his resurrection, when he had redeemed the world and conquered sin, death, and hell, and was about to take possession of his throne. Imagine that then, in that state, you had seen him commission some of his followers to be priests and intercessors with God on earth as he had been—to feed, nourish, and watch over his flock as he had done, to lead them with such exemplary holiness, such love of God, such compassion for sinners, such contempt for the world, such poverty of spirit, and such obedience and resignation as they saw in him as an example. Had you been present at all this, how would you then have heard and felt these words: *As my Father has sent me, so I send you?*

What sentiments of piety, what magnificence of spirit, and what exalted holiness would you have expected from those who were called to succeed so great a master in so great a work? Could you think they could be fit for this office, or were like enough to him who had called them to it, unless they had renounced and sacrificed everything for its sake? Could you think that any concern but that of the church of God was proper for them? Would you not admit that the conversion of sinners to God ought to have been their *one and only* labor and effort? That they were to seek no other happiness in this world than their Lord and Master had done, but consider themselves called away from the common affairs, ease, and pleasures of life to be in Christ's place toward the rest of mankind, to conduct them safely to eternal happiness?

Now, when we consider the apostles in this light—as being the first who were entrusted with the care of souls directly by Christ himself—we can see no degree of zeal, no height of piety, no compassion for sinners, no concern for the honor of God, no contempt for sufferings, no disregard for worldly interest, no vigils or mortifications, and no fervors of devotion to which we of the clergy are not equally obliged. For the salvation of mankind is still the same glorious, great, and necessary work that it was in their days; it is still to be carried on by the same means, and it is now in the hands of the clergy as it was then in theirs. If it was their happiness and glory to be faithful to him who called them, to forget the petty interests of flesh and blood, and to have nothing at heart but the advancement of God's kingdom, we shall fail both in happiness and glory if we seek them in any other way. If an apostle, considering the weight of reconciling souls to God, is forced to cry out, *Who is sufficient for these things?* shall we think any care but that which is greatest is sufficient to make us stand uncondemned before God? For though the temporal sword is not always drawn against them, nor are they forced to flee from one city to another, yet the world, the flesh, and the devil have, perhaps, never so much difficulty to be resisted as in temporal prosperity; nor do the ministers of Christ ever have more occasion to put on all their armor than when the world is given up to ease, and peace, and plenty. Swarms of vice steal upon us in these seasons, the spirit and life of religion is in danger of being lost, and the salvation of souls is made more difficult than in the most perilous times. And how is such a state of temptation to be resisted, such a torrent of vice to be opposed, except by the clergy showing themselves *visible* and *conspicuous* examples of all the contrary virtues? When mankind is wallowing in debauchery, wantoning in pleasures, and given up to vanity and luxury in all shapes, it is then the duty of the faithful minister, by being crucified to the world, to proclaim himself the messenger of a crucified Savior, and to make his own self-denying, mortified, and heavenly life a *plain, open, and constant reproof* of all vain indulgences. For to yield to, or fall in with the softness, vanity, indulgence, or avarice of the world, is the same infidelity and breach of trust in the sacred office as to depart from the true faith and fall in with some abominable heresy.

And here I cannot help addressing myself with great affection to all my younger brethren of the clergy. According to the course of nature, you are likely to have the care of the church wholly upon your hands in a short time; and therefore, it is chiefly from you that the restoration of true piety is to be expected in this nation. I beseech you, therefore, for your own sakes, for the gospel’s sake, for the sake of mankind, to devote yourselves *wholly* to the love and service of God. As you are yet but beginners in this great office, you have it in your power to make your lives the greatest happiness both to yourselves and the whole nation. You are entered into *holy orders* in degenerate times, where *trade* and *traffic* have seized upon all holy things; and it will be easy for you, without fear, to swim along with the corrupt stream, and to look upon anyone as an enemy or *enthusiast* who would save you from being lost in it. But think, my dear brethren, think in time, what remorse you are treasuring up for yourselves if you live to look back upon a loose, negligent, corrupt, disorderly, worldly, and unedifying life, spent among those whose blood will be required at your hands. Think, on the other hand, how blessedly your employment will end if, by your *voices, your lives, and labors*, you put a stop to the overflowings of iniquity, restore the spirit of the early clergy, and make all your flock bless and praise God for having sent you among them.

—Lay this down as an infallible principle: that an *entire, absolute renunciation of all worldly interest* is the only possible foundation of that exalted virtue which your station requires. Without this, all attempts at an exemplary piety are in vain. If you want anything from the world by way of *status* and *exaltation*, you shut the power of your Redeemer out of your own souls; and, instead of converting, you corrupt the hearts of those who are around you. Detest, therefore, with the utmost abhorrence, all desires of making your fortunes, either by *promotions* or *rich marriages*, and let it be your only ambition to stand at the top of every virtue as *visible guides and patterns* to all who aspire after the perfection of holiness. Consider yourselves merely as the *messengers of God* who are solely sent into the world on his errand, and think it happiness enough that you are called to the *same business* for which the Son of God was born into the world.—I do not call you away from a sober use of human learning, but I would like to persuade you to think nothing worthy of your notice in *books and study* except that which directly applies to the *amendment of the heart*, which makes you more holy, more divine, and more heavenly than you would be without it. You want nothing but to have the *corruption of your natural birth removed*, to have the nature, life, and spirit of Jesus Christ derived into you; as this is all that you want, so let this be all that you seek from books, study, or men. This is the *only certain way* to become eminent divines, instructed for the kingdom of heaven.—And above all, let me tell you that the *book of all books is your own heart*, in which are written and engraved the deepest lessons of divine instruction; learn, therefore, to be deeply attentive to the presence of God in your hearts, who is *always speaking, always instructing, always illuminating* that heart that is attentive to him. Here you will meet the divine light in its *proper place*, in that depth of your souls where the *birth of the Son of God* and the *proceeding of the Holy Spirit* are always ready to spring up in you. And be assured of this: that as much as you have of *inward attention* to God in your hearts, of *inward love and adherence* to his holy light and spirit within you, as much as you have of real, unaffected *humility and meekness*, as much as you are dead to your *own will and self-love*, as much as you have of *purity of heart*, so much—*and no more, nor any further*—do you see and know the truths of God. These virtues are the *only eyes, and ears, and senses, and heart* by which you will know and understand everything in Scripture, in that *manner* and in that degree in which God would have it understood, both for your own good and the good of other people.—It was owing to this *purity of heart and attendance upon God* that an an-

<margin>(1)</margin>...a reason why the sensitive soul tempted Adam. For although these reasons are now all true, in a sense, they were not true in the same sense before the fall; or, at least, the full sense as it applies to Adam in paradise is not expressed by them. For Adam, giving names to all the beasts and being able to look deeply into all their essences, origins, constitutions, and properties, etc., *knew certainly the internal forms of all things*. In a word, the whole of nature, with all its powers and wonders, stood open before him, and he had knowledge of it. If this had not been the case, he could not have been tempted as he was; but then he also could not have been a prince and ruler of this principle. His temptation and fall, therefore, was not because he desired *a knowledge of the wonders and forms of things*, but because he had such a knowledge of all the wonders and powers outside of him, and he desired to know them within himself also, in a sensible manifestation of *their contrarieties*. And this was the knowledge of good and evil, which he did not have yet, and could not have had without falling down himself from his eminent station in and under the same twofold government of good and evil. That former knowledge was well consistent with his paradisiacal state—indeed, it was a precious jewel of his crown—while this latter was his utter destruction. Not knowing whether I have expressed my meaning and intent clearly enough, I cannot help but declare it again by saying that Adam knew well enough that there were contrary qualities and qualifications outside of him in all the things of outward nature. This knowledge was an eminent perfection of his, without which he could not have been what he was ordained to be in this world; and this, therefore, was not what he lusted after. But because of this, he came to lust after an experimental knowledge, or his own sensation of these contrary qualities within himself. His sensitive soul would prove itself actually by feeling and tasting how it would be with itself when these contrary qualities were manifest, each in its own operation. And this was the thing that was agreeable to the nature of the sensitive soul.

(Page 175), something similar is said, indeed, regarding the words, but not regarding this sense, namely: *which experimental practical knowledge, I suppose, was the thing chiefly desired by the sensitive soul*. This, I say, has almost the same expressions, *but is, for all that, greatly different in sense*. For I cannot understand it otherwise than that it means only a setting of forms to work in things outside of him, because I see it is said afterward *to be now so useful and praiseworthy*. And this is indeed so now, and was also so before; for it was an eminent part of Adam’s dominion over all things. But for this same reason, it was not that which the sensitive soul so blindly desired. For it was never useful nor praiseworthy, but always hurtful and accursed, that Adam set to work the forms of nature within himself; because of this, he must now bear in soul and body all the disharmonized properties in their contrary operations, and has fallen into sin, anxiety, vexation of spirit, trouble, misery, all manner of sickness, and death.

<margin>3</margin>Page 175. *Last Q.* In the first part of the answer to this question, if I were to form it, I would leave out those things that are brought in only as probable, and would rather put this No. 1 into such a construction:

<margin>4</margin>Q. *Did not Adam resist the temptation?* A. Not faithfully, and therefore also not successfully, for he was wearied and overcome by it. As appears:

<margin>5</margin>1. By his desiring a helpmate, or a female associate, as he saw all the rest of the living creatures had. When God said, *It is not good that the man should be alone*, it declares sufficiently that an alteration or change, more or less, from good into not good, was already made in man—and by man himself, because it was not by God. If, then, it was by man, it must necessarily have been from his not resisting faithfully the appetite of his sensitive soul. And that this appetite was not only in general for a sensual knowledge of good and evil, but also in particular *for such a helpmate*, can be manifest from the event, in which that very thing he desired was given to him.

<margin>6</margin>2. His falling asleep argues, etc.

<margin>7</margin>3. The divulsion <note>the pulling apart or separation of Eve from Adam</note>, etc. Here, instead of saying, as if in uncertainty, *he seems to have been overcome*, I, for my part, would rather say positively—he was overcome; or, at least, as is frequently said—they say he was overcome by the temptation.

<margin>8</margin>Page 177. *Last Q.* and 178. What is here objected concerning the honorableness of the matrimonial state could have been objected also (*merely changing the circumstances*) against the doctrine of our Savior concerning polygamy. This doctrine seemed no less offensive to the Jews, and reflecting poorly upon Moses and the law, than this may seem to reflect upon the words of the apostle. If I were asked, "Was there something not good in Adam, and what was it when he desired a female helpmate?" I would answer, it was that same thing which the Lord called the *hardness of the heart*, because of which Moses had permitted polygamy. Not that it was so gross in Adam and in such an outward manifestation as it was in the Jews; but yet it was the same internal root out of which this hardness came forth afterward. If, then, this hardness was not good in the Jews when manifested in this world, its root also could not have been good in Adam when first conceived by his sensitive part in the paradisiacal state. "From the beginning it was not so," says the Lord, that man should be married to more than one wife; and yet he would not say absolutely that the law and Moses’s permission were not good. So also we may justly say: From that first beginning which is to answer to that ultimate end, where, according to the Lord’s own words, *there shall be neither marrying nor being given in marriage*, it was not so. And yet we do not say thereby that the permission and institution of God was not good; but we say only that it was made by God because man had already departed, in his imagination and desire, from the first, most pure, and best paradisiacal state; which departure of man was certainly not good. In the creation of this world, God saw all his works, that they were all good; and yet all this goodness is hardly comparable to that goodness which Lucifer had destroyed, and to which this world shall be brought back again. So then there is goodness and goodness, not indeed fighting against each other as good and evil, but nevertheless distinct and different in degree and order; so that when both are compared, the one is better, but when considered separately, each is good by itself. What then can this objection signify against the apostle’s word? He says, indeed, the matrimonial state is honorable, and shall

Line 1. *A perfect virgin, with fire and light in union.* This must here needs be expressed with an addition of these or similar words—*with fire and light, and with the two tinctures thereof in union:* or shorter, thus—*with the two tinctures of fire and light in union.* For the union of the tinctures in one person presupposes and implies also an union of fire and light, and is therefore enough to describe Adam as a perfect paradisiacal virgin; but the union of fire and light only, without an union of the two tinctures, is here, in this place, not enough, where Adam is considered not only as a single person, but also immediately as divided into two: so that an account is to be given of what was divided, and what was given to each divided part. Not fire and light, but only the two tinctures thereof were divided. For Eve had a fiery soul, or soulish fire, as well as Adam, and had also a shining light, as well as he; and had therefore fire and light in union, neither more nor less than he. But for all that, neither he nor she was any more such a perfect paradisiacal virgin as Adam had been before his sleep.

Page 187. *Q.* What do they mean by the two tinctures? *A.* I know not how to express it better than by what I have expressed already, saying that they mean the two generating powers in man, out of the two eternal principles; neither of which can be complete by itself, nor be satisfied with itself alone; but each must embrace the other, find its accomplishment therein, and be enabled thereby to produce a living image after its likeness.

*Q. Which of these two was left to Adam? And is there a reason to be found why that which was given to Eve could not as well have been reserved to him, so that Eve might have had that which now Adam has?* *A.* The temptation before Adam's sleep was chiefly about propagation, and especially was it in his fiery soul; for therein the lust was conceived, and the desire arose after a female associate. That part, therefore, of the propagating power which was inseparable from his soulish fire, must necessarily have been reserved to him; and that was the strong, fiery, masculine tincture. And so then that other part which he was not willing to have had further within himself in a paradisiacal integrity, but without or besides himself, after the manner of all the beasts, must necessarily have been taken out of him and given to Eve. And this was the weaker watery female tincture, not able (for want of fire) to raise up a life by itself.

*A.* No; because (1.) in the womb of Eve no union of the two tinctures, according to the right of eternal nature, was, nor could have been made; but only an outward familiar conjunction, which soon after must have been turned into disagreement and strife. And moreover (2.) both tinctures were defiled, *etc.* Concerning the next following words, I observe this, that Eve did not expect such *a birth, or such a paradisiacal virgin;* because after her being turned out of paradise, she knew paradise no more, and much less what a paradisiacal virgin was. But she expected (according to her understanding the promise of the serpent treader) a valiant champion against the devil, who should conquer him after an outward earthly manner, *etc.* And this she called *a man from the Lord.* But as she was disappointed in her blind opinion, so she must have been disappointed much more if she had or could have expected a paradisiacal virgin.

<margin>(3)</margin> Q. *I do not well know what you mean by the tincture of the serpent, nor what the subtlety in this tincture is; pray, Sir, therefore satisfy me in these doubts?* <note>Here I am to show the reason why I left out the word "twofold," together with this whole question: "Why do you assert this creature alone to have this tincture?" and then also why I say the "subtlety in the tincture," instead of the "property of subtlety."</note>

(1.) It is plain enough that one and the same thing, and under the same name, may be considered and spoken of differently with respect to different qualities, powers, operations, and effects. Now then, the tincture is here not considered any more as that propagating power which, upon its division, became twofold (as it was spoken of above), but as a power operating upon another thing outside of itself, influencing it, and communicating or conveying this or that to it. The tincture is a powerful thing, whose true name, says Behmen, is wonderful; none can name it but he to whom it is given, and he can name it only in himself, but not outside himself to another. It is not the spirit itself, but the spirit's and soul's habitation and instrument. Through the tincture, the soul can overthrow mountains and do all those wonderful things that the Lord and his apostles did. It is indeed in all things whatsoever, yet not in one as in another, but in every thing according to <margin>(4)</margin> its nature and condition. All communication between intellectual creatures is done by the tincture; all thoughts and senses arise in it, and without it there could be no seeing, hearing, feeling, etc. This, therefore, in the serpent, the devil used to transfuse his poison into Eve, which he could not have done so by his own tincture alone. Now then, it is apparent that it is one thing when Behmen speaks of *two tinctures*, and another when he speaks of a *twofold tincture*. For the former has a particular relation to the two divided propagating powers in male and female; but the latter refers to the twofold means of communication between intellectual creatures: which here, in the case of the serpent, was the outward and inward tincture. The outward, from the astral light of this outward principle, was that which Eve could immediately be sensible of and receptive to, and which the devil could not have entered into immediately. But the inward, from the inward dark-world's properties, was that which the devil had free entrance into, and by which he could direct that outward one also; and so through this outward one, convey and transfuse his hidden poison into Eve's tincture, if she would listen to the serpent's speech. So then, it is evident that this question, *why the serpent alone had this twofold tincture* (if the twofold tincture be understood as now declared), has no sense in it: for it is nowhere said that the serpent had it alone, but only that the serpent had it in a manner and degree more fit for the devil's use than any other beast of the field. But if it be understood of the two divided tinctures in male and female, it does not belong to this place at all and is therefore justly left out. And though I might well have said *twofold tincture* in the sense mentioned, instead of *tincture* only, I also left out the word *twofold* to avoid such lengthiness, and because the matter can be, and is (as I think), represented intelligibly enough even if this word is not used.

(2.) Instead of the *property of subtlety*, I say only the *subtlety in the tincture*; because that former expression is a pure Germanism, and the translator might rather have said the *subtle property in the tincture*: for, to my thinking, the former represents, as it were, three different things, namely: (1.) a tincture, (2.) a subtlety in this tincture, and (3.) a property causing this subtlety; when there are but two. What subtlety is, I think, is seen and known in this world sufficiently, wherein yet it is but an "outbirth" from the dark-world and must be described from the properties of <margin>(5)</margin> both of them together in conjunction. That which is wisdom in the holy light-world is subtlety in this astral light-world; and in the dark world, we have no proper peculiar name for it, but call it subtlety also, though certainly a distinction ought always to be observed. When, therefore, Moses says that *the serpent was more subtle than any beast of the field*, he says in substance nothing else but that the serpent (1.) with respect to the dark-world, was more than any other beast infected, possessed, and filled with its properties; and (2.) that with respect to the outward light-world, it was more than any other of a friendly, fallacious, false-loving, penetrating, and insinuating temper; those inward dark and wrathful properties being thus, in a sense, corrected and tinctured, or raised to a specious appearance. And so in these two together in conjunction, this subtlety consisted; therefore, the serpent was the fittest for the devil's use, who wanted such an instrument. Now, this subtlety is not the tincture itself, but *in* the tincture; and by the tincture, as by a proper vehicle, it was conveyed to and transfused into the tincture of Eve. For it is not essential to, nor inseparable from, the tincture, but shall be separated from it again; it came to be there only by the devil's false magia. Therefore, the sense is rightly expressed by saying the *subtlety in the tincture*.
