(2.) That this tree was exactly such a tree, and neither better nor worse, than our fruit trees are today, which we eat from after the curse.

(3.) That the difference between this forbidden tree and all the other trees in the Garden of Eden was exactly the same as the difference between our current earthly bodies and that paradisical body which man had then; the quintessential property was then predominant in all the other trees, while in this tree alone the four elements in their strife and opposition were manifest.

(4.) That it was called the tree of knowledge of good and evil because man, not having previously had an experiential knowledge of these two in their oppositions, could only come to have a knowledge and feeling of them in his soul and body by eating of this tree.

(5.) That no creature can live without food, but every creature, according to its kind, must eat the fruits of that world in which it is to live. Therefore, in this tree an infinite mercy of God appears; for God, foreseeing the fall of man and not wishing him to fall into the dark world, ordered all things so that by eating a four-elemental fruit, he might fall into this outward mixed world. Its four elements, being only so many outpourings of the pure quintessential element, may be brought back again to their root, and therefore man may also be brought back to his original state.

(6.) That this tree did not come forth with the rest of the vegetation on the third day of creation, but was afterward brought forth out of the earth by the strong magical imagination and desire of Adam, when he had already deviated from his initial paradisical perfection.

->Page 199. A. 1.<-

Seeing that this objection has a fine outward appearance, I think it would be necessary to answer it more specifically; and for this reason, there might be added to the last words of the question, *What reason can they give for this assertion?*

**A.** They believe they have a solid basis to firmly believe that they do not contradict Moses any more than he seems to contradict himself when he says in Genesis 1, *Male and female created He them* [supposing this expression is not contrasting the sexes but relates to the creation of animals in distinction to man]; and in the second chapter, *He took a rib and made a woman*. But some of their plainest and most obvious reasons for this assertion may be these:

(1.) This tree was not entirely good, much less "very good," and therefore we cannot say that it was made by God on the third day with all the rest of the vegetation. For on the fifth day God saw everything which He had made, and behold, it was very good.
(2.) It brings great harm to the honor of God to say that He made such a tree grow out of the ground while man still stood in his complete integrity; for this would be the same as saying directly that God Himself gave the first occasion for the Fall, or that God tempted him and laid a snare at his feet by setting desirable fruit before him and yet commanding him not to desire or touch it. Yet God is not a tempter to evil, and we can show the right and true basis of this temptation.
(3.) This assertion is entirely consistent with Adam's princely state and mighty power; and if this is joined to a consideration of his threefold life, it is a strong, convincing proof to those who can understand its constitution that this tree did not come forth before, but after the beginning of his deviation; and that he brought it forth himself, though God is not absolutely excluded in every sense. And although Moses mentions this tree before he says that God brought man into the garden, it is evident enough that Moses, in all this narrative, is not so precise and accurate as to put everything in an exact order.
(4.) As it is greatly harmful to the honor of God to attribute any appearance of evil to Him—which must happen by saying He made this tree grow without any participation from man and before man could contribute to it—so it is, conversely, highly exalting to His honor, goodness, and tenderness toward man to ascribe all evil, in its greatest extent, to the devil and man. This is done by saying that when man, through the instigation of the devil, lusted and longed for such food, only then—but not before—did God give it to him or allow him to have it; and yet God sufficiently declared His displeasure by commanding him, "You shall not eat of it," and telling him of his great danger.
(5.) Just as someone who says, *God gave or raised up a king to the house of Israel*, is not contradicted by one who orderly describes the manner of this raising up, saying: *The tribes of Israel first departed in their hearts from the Lord their God and rejected Him, that He should not be their king; then they urgently desired, not from God but from the prophet, that he should set a king over them after the manner of all the nations; and so by this desire they were themselves the immediate cause of this kingdom and of all their subsequent calamities*. In the same way, Moses—in what he says regarding God’s actions concerning this tree—is not contradicted by someone who explains that the strong desire of Adam (after his imagination had departed from the Lord, his Father and Teacher) was the proper and immediate cause of this tree coming forth from the ground.

**Q.** *How could such an evil, infecting tree grow in paradise?* — **A.** Thinking still, Sir, on your last question, I might well ask in return: How could such a tree as you describe have been brought forth by God, the only good, without an immediate operation by man himself, and even before he was infected by the devil? But to resolve this new doubt as well, I must say there is no difficulty in the matter at all. For this tree did not grow in paradise, but in the garden of Eden, and even in the midst of it where Adam and Eve were tempted. We discussed before the difference between paradise and the garden of Eden; and from that, you may easily understand that this tree was as little in paradise as the devil or the serpent was. But it could be in the garden, in which all the other trees were paradisical; for only the predominance of either the quintessential or the four-elementary property creates the difference.

**Q.** *Why is this tree of knowledge said to have stood in the midst of the garden?* — **A.** As all outward things are figures or signatures of inward things, so was this as well. Adam and Eve were tested as if in the midst between the three principles, having all three within them but being not yet fixed in any of them; and corresponding to this, the tempting tree also stood outwardly in the midst of the garden. ...being in the midst is chiefly and in the first place attributed to the *tree of life*, representing the second principle of pure eternal life, which stands in the midst, between the first and third; but to the *tree of knowledge* it is attributed only secondarily and consequently. For there were not two trees in number, standing one beside the other, but only one manifest in two principles. As to its outward figure in this world, it could not help but stand in the midst of the garden because it stood, in its inward representation, in that midst; and this was in conformity to the second principle standing in the midst, between the first eternal and the third temporal world.

*Q. How can this assertion of one tree be consistent with the description by Moses, who tells us expressly of two?* A. Because the *tree of knowledge* contained corruptibility and death, it was not indeed the *tree of life*, just as this four-element world is not paradise. But just as paradise exists only without the qualities of this world, though not without the location of it, so also was this *tree of life* related to the *tree of knowledge*. As then, on the former account, Moses rightly speaks of two trees, so on the latter, it is also rightly spoken of as only one, yet one that is twofold, or manifest in two different principles; and Moses is not contradicted at all.

*Q. This distinction and difference between these two trees, which you say were but one, still needs to be better illustrated.* A. There was such a distinction and difference between them as there was between man's outward astral and inward soulish spirit. When his imagination wandered out, he found in the midst of the garden an object represented to his astral spirit by the spirit of this world, which invited him to eat so that he might gain an experimental knowledge of good and evil. And when he withdrew his imagination from this and turned inward, he found in the midst of the garden (though it might now more properly be said, in the midst of paradise) an object represented to his superior soulish spirit by the spirit of God, which invited him to eat so that he might be strengthened and enabled to go forward toward being confirmed in that higher eternal life into which he was to have been translated at the end of this temporal world. And so there was the greatest difference, even to the point of contrariety, between these two objects. And yet they were not two such trees as stood beside or outside one another, each upon a distinct spot of ground, such that they could have been seen at once from one position by the very same faculty of sight. And though they both were always before him, yet each of them affected only that part of him which it was conformable to, and he was aware only of that to which his imagination applied itself. And as he was but one man, or one soul with an interior and exterior spirit, so was this but one tree, with an interior and exterior appearance, answering to his twofold spirit.

*Q. How did this tree of life differ from the other paradisical trees? And to what end was it set before him in the midst, as you say, of paradise?* A. The very name of it shows us that it was more highly graduated or more dignified than the rest of the paradisical trees. For though they also contained nothing of death, they bore fruits only for man's then-present paradisical life, whereas this tree offered him fruits from that higher heavenly life, which he was to have been confirmed in eternally had he endured his trial faithfully. Therefore, it was also set before him in the midst of paradise to show him that this paradise, then upon earth, was still only a circumferential state, as it were, from which he was to enter into a higher or deeper central rest. But it was set before him especially because of this temptation, so that he might have the strongest antidote against the devil's poison, hidden under the veil of the spirit of this world. This was so that he might be altogether inexcusable and later find no fault with his loving Father and Creator; but that God, as he is just, might also be justified in all his works by man, who must necessarily admit that God did not want him to fall, but did everything for him that he could do, consistently with the free will he had given him. When, therefore, Eve neglected this and applied herself to the tree of knowledge, and gave Adam some of its fruit also, they both could not help but fall, by their own fault, into death, and lose not only the tree of life but all the rest of the paradisical fruits as well.

Though I do not exactly know what they understand by <term>universal grace</term>, yet I think this supposition, which is passed by in silence here in the answer as if it were all granted, should be answered in a sense inclining more or less to the negative by showing a difference between them. This difference consists in this: that universal grace is that ability in all men, which is freely given to them after the fall, to turn their will, desire, and imagination toward God again—who offers them a gift—and to receive the same from him; whereas this ingrafted word is that divine gift itself, though still considered only as a little seed. Both this and that are one and the same thing. Behmen considers chiefly the first—the primary and more imperceptible origin of the seed—in that place from which, as the Scripture witnesses, are the issues of life. He does not focus so directly on that which is secondary, which he nevertheless plainly expresses and asserts in several other places. Physicians, on the other hand, consider chiefly that which is closer to observation and physical sensation; they do not focus so directly on what is first and primary, though they also do not deny it, but assert and express it plainly by saying it is conveyed from the heart. Behmen does not say that the semen is refined in the heart, but that the beginning of its generation occurs in the heart, not in the spermatic arteries. For the heart, as the chief residence of life, is nearer and more immediately related to the brain—the residence of the astral spirit—than those arteries are. Therefore, the first operation is performed upon the heart by the agent in the brain, and then it is conveyed down from the heart; I am sure the physicians will neither deny nor contradict this. Furthermore, I see they disagree here, more or less, among themselves; for some add the nervous juice, the *succus nutritius* <note>nutritive juice</note>, or *succus genitalis* <note>genital juice</note> to the animal spirits. But Behmen will disagree with none of them, having asserted that, in the broadest sense, all the powers and virtues of the whole body are comprised in the seed. Regarding their last point in this position—namely, that the gross parts of the semen serve as a vehicle to the spirituous parts, etc.—he will be found not only to stand in entire agreement, but also to be better able than any or all of them to declare, from his internal vision, what and from where those grosser and more spirituous parts originate, what caused such a difference between them, and how the former came to be as gross and beast-like as they are.

(2.) Physicians say that females have no *semen*; their *testiculi* <note>testicles, used historically for gonads</note> are *ovaria* <note>ovaries</note>. From this, it is concluded that Behmen, by saying much about female semen, must contradict their physical observations. However, I think this contradiction is only apparent and lies in a different understanding of the word *semen*. They grant that females have something in them necessary for generation—even something that contains the lineaments of the fetus before the knowledge of a man, and which is meant to drop into the *fundus uteri* <note>the bottom or base of the uterus</note> like a seed into the ground. Now, I cannot see why this may not appropriately be called a seed or semen, especially when Scripture itself speaks of the "woman's seed." Therefore, when physicians say females have no semen, I cannot believe they intend to set up their physical observations as a witness against Scripture, but only that their meaning is this: what the woman has is not like the semen of the man and lacks those requirements they believe are necessary in the man's semen. If this or something similar is their meaning, it is not contrary to Behmen. For he nowhere says that the female semen is entirely of that kind, or that it is generated in exactly the same form as the male's, though he also says nothing of that form of an *ovum* <note>egg</note>—whether he knew of it or not, I cannot determine. It is at least apparent, from his statement that hands and feet have their signatures in the center before they appear outwardly, that he knew more than he expressed. But let this also be noted: since physicians say little of what must precede every generation—namely, will, imagination, lust, and desire, which are of significant importance—and since these things exist and operate in females as well as in males, why should they be entirely without effect in them when they are so effective in men? May we not reasonably think that their astral spirit in the brain, acting upon the same object as in males, must also have the same effect in them, according to their unique kind or female constitution? And could not, therefore, a *massa* (or whatever else it might be called), consisting chiefly of more spirituous parts, be raised up thereby from the blood of the heart and then conveyed into their *ova* to stir and influence them with a concupiscence <note>strong desire or lust</note> for the male semen? Truly, if they have—as physicians admit—their spermatic arteries and vessels just like men do, they must have them in vain and for no purpose (or at least the physicians must name them so in vain) if they do not contribute at all to the generation of the seed. But I will not be dogmatic about this, as I do not pretend to be a natural philosopher. I say only that what I have now offered for consideration is not inconsistent with Behmen, and that I can as yet see nothing in all that the physicians say in this second position that is directly contrary to him.

(3.) The points made in this third position belong partly to the preceding second position and have already been considered. Partly they will be repeated in the following positions and shall be considered then. Partly, also, they depend only upon females having *ovaria*. Therefore, it is plain that if this can be consistent with Behmen, then whatever depends upon it can have nothing in it directly contrary to him.

(4.) Here also, at least on one side, a harmony can be perceived. Although some discord may be observed on the other side, since this discord is only about a matter delivered by physicians from their reasoning and not from physical observation, nothing in it can be set in opposition to Behmen as being able in any way to detract from his authority. *The seed of the male*, they say, *is no part of the conception, but only the active principle or efficient cause of the fetus.* Above (in the 1st position), they acknowledged that masculine seed has both gross and spirituous parts. Now then, if they make these spirituous parts the active principle of the fetus, Behmen shall agree with them well enough. But as for the gross parts, which they themselves call merely a vehicle for the spirituous parts, I think no one will deny that they are mixed in sexual intercourse with the clear liquid in the female *ovum*; otherwise, how could it be impregnated by them? And if so, it might well be asked what sort of microscopes allowed them to discover that only this clear liquid, and not also that which is mixed with it, is the matter or passive principle of the fetus? Male and female are "one flesh," says the Scripture; now this one flesh in two persons jointly generates a third flesh. What ground then can be shown why the female alone should generate the flesh, and the male should contribute nothing to the substance of the flesh but only be its active principle, when it is so plain that the masculine seed is more fleshly, or closer to flesh, than that clear water of the female.

As some physicians declare, this can be consistent with Behmen, as appears sufficiently from the previous observations. I shall add only this, regarding the two different words, *fecundated* and *impregnated*: they seem themselves to tacitly or implicitly grant that the male semen is not only an active principle—namely, in its spirituous parts—but also, in its gross parts, a part of the matter or passive principle of the fetus. For *impregnation* is proper to the latter, and *fecundation* to the former, and these two cannot be attributed to both promiscuously. If the male seed fecundates the female ovum, it works upon it and enables its faculties to bring forth that which they cannot bring forth by themselves alone; but if it impregnates the ovum, it only makes it thick and swelling—not by working upon it, but by adding or infusing something into it which is compatible with it. The gross parts themselves cannot fecundate it, or else they would be the active principle themselves, rather than a gross vehicle for it. Likewise, the spirituous parts cannot impregnate it—namely, directly and immediately by themselves—or else they would be merely a gross vehicle without activity. And if these two roles were attributed to each of them promiscuously, the distinction (which is real enough) between grossness and spirituosity in one and the same seed would signify nothing at all.

(6.) In this sixth position, there is nothing that requires any reconciliation with Behmen. Those who *profess they do not know, etc.*, might learn something about it from him; and others, who *think their opinion to be very probable*, might be further confirmed by him and gain a clearer sight, seeing it is undeniable that he has explained this matter more deeply than they were able to do.

(7.) This position held by some, though it is rejected by others, certainly has something in it which is not absolutely to be rejected. Of the *animalcules* <note>microscopic organisms or spermatozoa</note> in the male semen I will say nothing, though I think something might be said for it, though perhaps not in their sense. I will say only that it is most consistent with Behmen that the lineaments of the fetus are within it, no less than in the female ovum; though, I am sure, they are so deeply and secretly hidden that they shall not be discerned by any microscope, but found only by such an eye as Behmen had, whose words we heard above. And though perhaps these lineaments may be nearer to appearing in the female ovum, yet this cannot be a sufficient ground to assert that they are not in the male seed at all. The second part of this position—saying that the conception is in that animated male semen, and not in the *ova* of the females, which they take to be only the receptacles of the male semen—though it is likewise rejected by others, nevertheless has some part of truth in it. It is also consistent with Behmen to that extent, which will become more and more evident hereafter. Therefore, this mutual rejection among the learned physicians themselves cannot detract from Behmen’s authority, but rather from their own; it must instead exalt him the more, because by his principles many of their assertions can be reconciled, and their sparks of truth, scattered here and there among them, can be distinguished from what is false.

(8.) *The heart is not the seat of our affections, etc.* What is asserted here is so exceedingly consistent with Behmen that this whole position (if only one small and inconsiderable particular be excepted) is more deserving than any of the former to be excluded from the sentence in the first words of this question, which says, *our philosophers and physicians teach us otherwise.* If by the seat of our affections is understood 그 particular place where they reside, act, and play their parts, it is true that it is not the heart, but the fantastic or astral mind. But if the ground from which they first came into the astral mind is understood—and out of which they may still be raised up by the imagination, some more and others less—it is true again that it is the heart. For our Lord says himself, *Out of the heart come evil thoughts*; and Solomon warns, *Watch over your heart with all diligence, for out of it are the issues of life.* Both this and that Behmen well understood and asserted distinctly. He has not asserted that this *love*, which indeed is one of our affections, arises, resides, and plays in the heart; but rather that by this love’s playing in the fantastic mind, the *first conceptions* (as it is well expressed in this position) or rough drafts of the sperm are begun. But as this is only an active spiritual play in the brain, it must have a certain passive and material object or instrument, which is the blood of the heart, from which it is further conveyed to the testicles. Brain and heart must both concur; for that which is active in the brain raises up that which otherwise would be quiet in the heart. What the author of this position further adds regarding a particular point that seems very probable to him does not need to be examined, because his probability can be no argument against Behmen. But what he says at last—of the *imagination’s assisting in the business of generation, always in order to coition, etc.*; and of its *marking the fetus, etc.*—is as good and true as anything that could be expected from him. Why, then, I cannot see how this position can be brought in as an instruction of the physicians contrary to Behmen.

This now being so far proven—that the pretended differences and contrarieties are not as many, as great, as significant, or as deep as they were first believed to be, and that nothing has yet been shown from the physical experiences of the physicians which could demonstrate Behmen to be in the wrong—it can now appear sufficiently what is to be replied to those two questions proposed in the conclusion, page 217, the last section, namely:

(1.) *That the conception is in both male and female.* For as every child is generated from the sinful will and lust of both father and mother, so everyone also bears both his father’s and mother’s flesh and blood. If the male semen is not a part of the conception in its fleshy grossness, as well as being an active principle of the fetus in its spirituosity, what can the words of the Scripture signify when it says, *Adam begat a son after his own likeness?* A chief part of his own likeness was certainly his gross, earthly, mortal body, out of which his fleshy seed proceeded. And again, what can it signify when the Scripture says that *the children of this world are born of the flesh, and of the will of man?* If the whole being of man and woman consisted only of soul and body, a greater outward appearance of probability for that other opinion might be found. But since there are in the whole human being not only these two, but three distinct things—body, soul, and spirit—and all three are in both the man and woman; yet so that the soul, as to

This flesh, in the man especially and chiefly, is to do the outward work in generation. It is apparent, from a due consideration of all these things, that all these three parts do and must concur in this business, each in its kind and order, and according to its ability. And the male semen is not only an active principle of the fetus in its spirituosity, but also a passive part in the conception, as to its grosser and exterior being of fleshliness.

(2.) The spirituous part of the male semen, or that semen considered *κατὰ δύναμιν* <note>according to its power or potentiality</note>, and the limpid, prolific liquor in the ova of the female, are not to be accounted the two tinctures themselves, but only two things coming very near to them. The tinctures themselves are prior and higher, more spiritual and of far larger extent than to be concerned only with this particular generating business; whereas these two things are notoriously posterior and lower, more material, and appointed only for this peculiar work, in the consideration of which they may be accounted the two chief and most immediate instruments of the tinctures. As to the males, indeed, much of this account will depend upon the different considerations of their semen: for this *κατὰ δύναμιν* might be so far extended that but little of a discernible difference between its spirituosity and the tincture would be left; though it can never be so far extended that the tincture in itself should not always have a pre-eminence of priority and universality. But as to the females and their ovum, wherein the limpid liquor cannot be considered in such a great, active spirituosity, the distinction or difference between this and the tincture is much plainer. For the limpid liquor, with the lineaments of the fetus, is in them not only before the knowledge of man, but also before the maturity of their tincture; during all this time, this ovum is not fit for generation, nor can it be fecundated by the male semen, though it might, perhaps (for I am not positive in it), be impregnated by it. But the female's own tincture, after it has come to its maturity, must first fit, prepare, and make it capable of being impregnated and fecundated by the male seed, which no one of any reasonable sense can deny. And so it is now in the males also, *mutatis mutandis* <note>with the necessary changes having been made</note>. For the tinctures in them both, playing first in their astral minds, stir up the seed and raise the lust and desire for carnal conjunction, which is the consequence and effect of it, just as that is the first active principle.

And now I am to go back to the first six positions on page 211, which are to represent this same matter according to the sense of Behmen; for in them also, I meet with several things which I think must necessarily be altered. Yet I shall not enlarge by making particular observations upon them, but think it may be enough to set down only the positions so that the sense of Behmen, according to my best apprehension, might be expressed; which accordingly will be in the following manner:—

(1.) That the only true ground of this natural generation or propagation is to be found in the two divided tinctures, which, when they come to their maturity in male and female, cannot but press forward naturally for their reunion.

(2.) That this pressing forward is first done in the astral spirit, whose residence is the brain, and whose open gates are the eyes, wherein the tinctures of male and female mutually meet, lay hold on, and unite with one another.

(3.) That this kind of union in the astral spirit is that natural love, which is one of the chief agents in this business.

(4.) That this love-union, as long as it is in the spirit only, is indeed much purer than afterwards, when the flesh comes to concur with it; but that it cannot fully satisfy that natural inclination of the tinctures, nor stop their further pressing forward, because they are generating powers, which cannot generate (because of their being divided) without the concurrence of that flesh or body in which they live and act.

(5.) That because of this constant pressing forward, which is turned into a fervent desire for fleshly copulation, this flesh is mightily stirred and—according to the different conditions of the several instruments and vessels proper and requisite for that business—severally affected and acted upon.

(6.) That this affecting and acting touches in the first place, and as our chief consideration, the heart.

(7.) That from the sweet water or oil which is in the blood of the heart, a mass is drawn together or coagulated, and that this is filled, not only with the animal spirits, but also with all the powers and virtues of the whole human body.

(8.) That this coagulation is the generation of that semen which is now fit for propagation, when it was not so before. And that this has a fiery tincture in the man, but a watery one in the woman.

(9.) That these two masses and tinctures, or generating powers, united in the womb, are the causes of the conception and fetus; the male semen being both a part in the conception and an active principle of the fetus.

(10.) That each of these two masses is a triune substance, being not only fleshly and producing the mortal body, but also having in it—though in different degrees—the two eternal principles. And that none of these three is manifest or comprehensible to the others, but each in its own sphere only; and yet all three are in such a combination as the two inward worlds are with this outward third world.

This, now, according to my best apprehension, is Behmen's sense, and from here it may appear that several of the other positions of the physicians—and also that sentiment which is given of it in general—cannot be left as it is expressed in this conference, because the contrariety is not as great as first imagined. (3.) Just as this latter person also does not, by his enumeration, contradict the former, who may have left out such a detail, either because he did not have a sufficient understanding of it, or because he could declare all that he intended without it. From all this, now, (5.) This conclusion, doing justice to each party, may be drawn: First, in general, physicians and anatomists are better able to show the superficial appearance of these lower visible things, which belong to their profession and upon which they only bestow their time and labor to little further purpose than to satisfy their natural curiosity (which yet always remains in the dark, as they must own themselves); and Behmen is better able to show the spiritual inward ground from the two internal worlds, which no microscope can reach into; and this is for a far greater use and benefit, tending to man's regeneration, which is always attended, more or less, with light. And then, in particular, as the physicians in this present matter may be in the right, so Behmen is not in the wrong, any more than the Scripture is. And so therefore, between these two parties there is no more contradiction than between A and B, when A says the meeting was in such a house, and B says the congregation was in such a particular chamber of that house.

Page 219.—221. Here the further process in the natural generation is represented in five positions, according to the sense of Behmen. And here I must observe—as to the first, That when it is said, *the two tinctures in union are much delighted with each other, and there is something paradisiacal in that delight*; this is expressed too generally, and not so as to represent the sense of Behmen faithfully. For that which is called by him paradisiacal is not in the mutual delight of the tinctures so long as they are, or can be said in a sense to be, in union, nor even so long as they are *delighted with each other*, but only in their very first meeting and receiving one another, when the seed is sown by the male into the female; where it is, he says, but for a moment, and vanishes away immediately, being but a small obscure glimpse, and not to be referred at all to what the beast-like flesh is sensible of.

At No. 3. That when there is mentioned a following strife to produce the *paradisiacal image* which *Adam* lost, this strife is not sufficiently represented by referring it to the two tinctures only. It must be referred and declared also (though not so properly here, where this strife is as yet all but in love and friendliness, yet soon after, when there is spoken, No. 5, of their being oppressed and polluted) as to the spirit of this world, and the four elements, and that which Behmen calls the *fiat*; all which distinct things are mightily (each in its order and degree) for the bringing forth of a paradisiacal image. And if it were not so with them, nothing else but a beast (though in an outward human form of body) and beast-like senses could be produced. So also

No. 4. This incapacity to produce that paradisiacal image belongs not only to the two divided tinctures, but also to all these things now mentioned, which all have the same natural inclination.

At No 5. Concerning the *blood's being taken into the matrix*, I am inclined to think that this also might be more circumstantially expressed. Chiefly when it is said the tinctures retire, it will be necessary to be more distinct, and to say in what sense this is a retiring. For it is not an absolute and total departure, but only as to that clearness and purity which in that state they are capable of. Whereby it would show itself, that it might better and more properly be said (in the singular)—the tincture retires. Again, here is nothing said of that great alteration which is made in the blood, which yet is the chief thing in this consideration, that makes, nay constrains the tincture to withdraw, as to its former clearness and purity. I know what to do, and think it is enough to have observed only these things for now. It may be best to let them rest at present until a revision can be made, because in the meantime, this or that might be more cleared up in the following discourse, so that unnecessary repetitions may be avoided. I have only to say a little more about what is replied regarding these five positions.

<margin>(1)</margin> Physicians, it is said, deny that any of the mother's blood is taken into the womb <note>matrix</note>. But since the ground they think they have for this is not expressed, I cannot say more to it, except that their denial seems to come from not knowing what the blood and "tincture" are. I have not found that they mention anything concerning the tincture, which is of the greatest importance in this matter. If this is the case for them, their denial signifies nothing at all.

<margin>(2)</margin> But concerning especially the menstrual blood's <note>menstrua's</note> being poisonous, which they also deny, at least in part (if I do not misunderstand what is said here); it should be observed that Behmen, in asserting them to be poisonous, does not use the word "poison" as they seem to do in relation to this outward world—where adders, toads, arsenic, mercury, aqua-fortis, etc., are called poisonous. Instead, he uses it in a more mysterious sense, relating to the lost paradisiacal world. He explains this by adding that in the menstrual blood lies the greatest antipathy and contrariety to holiness and purity. [Consider here what the Scripture says when it compares all our righteousness to "filthy rags" <note>pannus menstruatus; see Isaiah 64:6</note>.] In this sense, if the physicians denied the menstrual blood to be poisonous, I could only have a very low opinion of them and little value for their understanding of the fall of man from the one paradisiacal world into this world of four elements. Moreover, it is remarkable that Behmen had familiar conversations with many physicians and graduated doctors; indeed, he had written the same thing about the menstrual blood to an eminent one among them, and yet it was never heard that any of them contradicted him or valued him less afterward than they did before.

<margin>(3)</margin> Page 223. *Q. What do they mean by the essences' death to paradise?* This question not being answered, and I not being able to answer it in two or three lines, I shall declare the meaning, and leave, Sir, to you the finding out of better expressions and a shorter construction of it. It is easily intelligible that this "death" in every individual generation is not the same as the death of all the first Adam's essences in his transgression, but only an effect and an indispensable consequence of it. For because he lived in paradise before, he could have died to it or lost that life. But here in his natural propagation, the essences had no previous life in paradise, and therefore cannot properly or directly be said to die to it, or to lose what they do not have. This is the meaning: in every generation of human life, there is a process tending toward the production of the paradisiacal life and image. The two tinctures <note>the male and female spiritual qualities</note>, in their meeting and receiving each other, follow that way and process in a sense conformable to their now divided state; and therefore, as declared above, they endeavor to produce it and expect it. This process would always have been successful if Adam had not fallen, so that in every one of his offspring, that life and image would have been generated. But now, in this natural propagation after the fall, a stop is put to that process, making it always ineffective. This happens at the very point where the paradisiacal life and image are meant to arise. This stop is partly due to what happens in the blood, and partly also to what the spirit of this world does in the essences. He <note>the spirit of this world</note> insinuates himself into them, captivates them, exalts himself in them, obstructs the rising of a paradisiacal life, and forces them to bring forth an astral life and light and a beast-like image in his service instead. This is their death to paradise—different from the first Adam's death in that his death was an extinguishing of his paradisiacal life and light, while this is a violent prevention, because of which the same life cannot be kindled again.

Page 223. *Q. 1 & 2., together with their answers.* The things following (immediately and primarily) from or upon the former disorder and death are not mentioned here at all. For nothing is said here of the "crack" <note>or schrack</note>, the terror and trembling, the great alteration in the tincture, and the consternation in the *fiat*, the spirit of this world, and all the essences. All of these are spiritual things, upon which everything done in the seminal mass depends; Behmen deduces and declares them according to the laws of generation, which are constantly the same in both eternal and temporal nature. By answering, therefore, *A motion of the whole coagulated seminal mass, etc.*, the question is only half-answered, and only as to the lower and later part. Without the higher and prior part, it cannot be understood according to Behmen's mind, much less can it represent his meaning to someone unacquainted with him. When it is then asked again, *What follows from this motion*, and answered, *A distinction of the mass*, it cannot help but cause several misapprehensions. For the single word *motion* will not express what needs to be said. A motion, in some sense and respect, existed before also, even from the beginning of conception; therefore, how this is different from that one should be explained. Furthermore, I cannot see how this *motion* and the distinction of the mass could be represented as two so evidently different things, with one following the other. It is not as if a motion is first made in the mass, and then—as a following event at a perceptible distance—the parts are distinguished. Rather, the distinction is made within this motion; this very motion differs from what came before because it is the distinction of the parts itself. And though one might still imagine some difference between them, it will never be so distinct that they should be represented as two separate things following one after the other; this is even less appropriate because the most important thing—a great tumultuous motion in the spiritual properties—is not mentioned at all. From this, a transition should immediately be made to the distinction and formation of the parts, which would then clearly imply a motion in the seminal mass, seeing as it cannot be distinguished or formed into parts without motion. But when a motion of the mass is placed so distinctly by itself alone, before the distinction and formation of the parts (saying one is preceding and the other following), the formation of the parts is attributed only to something done in the seminal mass, when it should be attributed primarily to something done in the spiritual properties. Therefore, I think the shortest way would be to combine these two questions and answers into one.

Page 223. *Q. last No. 1.* Here I cannot help but observe, in passing, that by these people—here styled *the most experienced philosophers and physicians*—everything is completely overturned that was previously so positively asserted by others, based on visual experience, concerning the features in the egg <note>ovum</note>. I do not know what to make of this contradiction; for I thought they had found it to be so with the help of microscopes, and had reason to believe that everyone using the same means could not help but see the same thing, so that no one could contradict it further. But when they now assure us that the features are in the egg in an *imperceptible manner*, and that nothing appears but a clear crystalline liquid, they are directly contrary to each other. However, none of them can be contrary to Behmen, because the assertion of an "imperceptible manner" is plainly his own, and the other he has not dealt with at all, and so has not contradicted it. But it would be consistent with him, if it were really true, as it was expressed and represented above.

Page 225. No. 5. This confession of *much obscurity* is not only to exalt Behmen more, but also to confirm what he has said: *namely*, that without an understanding of the generation of eternal nature, and of the spiritual properties and essences (which physicians commonly know little about), these things cannot be understood; and that no anatomist can be able to find out and show the true ground, even if he should dissect many thousands of men and beasts.

Page 227. *A. 1. And it is easy to understand that he who had such a deep understanding of eternal and temporal nature, regarding the manner of its generation, and could show (as far as permitted) the internal ground of every external thing in this natural propagation of man, could not have been ignorant of the order in which everything is done. This is because this order depends chiefly upon an order in eternal nature, and then also upon an order in those spiritual properties and essences that come after eternal nature, but before this formation of the parts and limbs.

*Ibid. A. 1. By gripping and binding down the hard property (which itself is also flying up with all the rest), the *fiat* puts a stop to its ascent; and so the *fiat*, through this hard property (which, now being gripped and bound, cannot rise any further), forms the skull.

*So also accordingly, ibid., by the same compacting astringent spirit.* If to these words were added, *which in conjunction with the eternal Word, is the fiat*, the sense of Behmen would be completely expressed; it is not so if this is left out.

*Ibid.*, again. *The nerves only are called the conduit-pipes of the tincture, and of the powers of the stars;* but the *veins* seem to be excluded from this, because they are placed afterward alone, without this title; yet this description belongs no less to the veins than to the nerves—indeed, in my view, to the veins more especially.

Page 235. *A. 2. Concerning this water of the heart*, Behmen says—that it corresponds to the water of the soul, just as the soul's water corresponds to the water in the generation of eternal nature. He states that this blood and water correspond to the water above and the water under the firmament; the water above the firmament (*namely*, in the creature, and in a sense relating to the creature) is blood, and the water under it is this water of the heart. He explains that in these two, two kingdoms are understood, and that the soul resides in the blood, and the outward spirit resides in this water.

...properly place the four elements in however different parts of the body; none can do altogether wrong, for the whole body is composed of the four elements; but let everyone declare his reason, according to his own particular understanding and the degree of it. Let one say, the air's residence is the nostrils, because the Scripture says that the breath of man is in the nostrils; another, it is the lungs, because they draw in the air and breathe it out again; a third, it is the entire cavity of the body, because no vacuum can be allowed to exist within it: they all say something, each according to his measure of understanding, and all three may well enough agree if they only compare their different reasons and take each of them in its proper sense and place. And I also disagree with none of them, though according to my gift of understanding, and the sense and respect in which I look upon the four elements, I cannot say otherwise than that the air’s residence is the bladder, and the spirit of the earth’s residence is the lungs. Many things could be said for Boehme to show, not only that his saying is not unaccountable, but also that he himself has given a good account of it, though not directly, because such a thing was not objected to him. Page 239. *A. ult.* The essences stretched forth for nourishment are compacted and formed into hands. This is expressed clearly enough to those who truly understand anything of Boehme in this matter; but since it is very subject to a crude and gross apprehension because of its excessive brevity, it must be more fully represented. For I see it is understood and gathered from this as if the hands were grasping for such or such nourishment to be taken by the fetus and put into its mouth, when there is no such thing. That such a gross apprehension is easily made appears from the reply here (page 241), where it is said that it cannot be accounted for because the fetus lies with its hands lifted up to the head, etc., and seeks nourishment with its mouth, etc.; all of which cannot even shake, much less overthrow, what Boehme says, who has a deeper basis for his words than what can be reached from the outside. He does not say the hands are stretched forth for any nourishment; but as he declares all this matter from an invisible spiritual root, so it is also to be understood accordingly. Let the hands of the fetus lie which way they will, their chief office, after they are hands in this world, is to stretch out and grasp earthly food for nourishment. And before they were formed and visible hands, such a disposition was in the spirit of the soul, because of its being infected and possessed by the four-elementary qualities. And however the fetus in the womb is nourished, Boehme does not say that it is nourished by taking this or that food with its hands, but that the four-elementary spirit, according to its own internal essentiality, is even then already—as it is always—inclined toward elementary fruit or food, even such as Adam had eaten in the Garden of Eden; and that this spirit, having gained predominance over the spirit of the soul, now shows his power over him in this natural generation, so that the latter must, in obedience to him, stretch forth his essences toward that which he, as ruler, lusted after; and that from this stretching forth, which at that time is still only a thing done in the spirit, such fleshly hands come to be as are no longer able to stretch forth after the fruits of the tree of life, etc.

Page 241. *A. 2.* What they mean by the *spirit of the soul's fetching the essences of the earth to feed upon* can be understood, I think, sufficiently from what was just now declared: namely, that it is not an outward actual work or doing, but a mere prelude in the spirit of the soul, who is captivated, ruled, and drawn away by the spirit of this world. The essences of the earth, considered in their outbirth <note>external manifestation or product</note>, are indeed all that the natural body feeds upon or is nourished by, both while it is still in the mother's womb and afterwards, when in this outward world; for even in the womb, all the nourishment of the fetus, whatever it may be, is earthly, not paradisiacal, but of the essences of the earth, making such an earthly flesh as must necessarily return into earth. But Boehme does not go down so low, nor make it his business to tell us, in the manner of physicians, what specifically the fetus in the womb is nourished by; but has enough to declare this prelude in the spirit, and to show the ground of man's earthliness regarding his body, and earthly-mindedness regarding his spirit. And so his entire, most excellent dialogue between the four elements and the spirit of the soul, in the *Three Principles*, is to be understood accordingly.

Page 241. *A. 3.* Concerning the *stomach and the guts* they say (all in a sense relating to and depending upon the former) that the stomach has its origin from the same ground of the four-elementary food desired and necessarily required by the spirit of this world in the fetus, according to his own nature, which the spirit of the soul must submit to; though as yet it is still, as said above, only a prelude in the spirit of things that must unavoidably come to pass. For if there is in the spirit such a previous disposition and natural tendency toward earthly food, a receptacle fit for it must be prepared in this natural generation, which receptacle is the stomach. And because the grossness of the earth is not fit for nourishment, and is also not desired but seriously objected to in the spiritual dialogue of the four elements, and resolved that it shall be cast out—just as it was also cast out, or in a sense precipitated down, in the creation of the macrocosm—an opening of the body, therefore, must be made, and a passage must be provided from the stomach downwards, through which this grossness may be carried out; and this is the guts.

Page 241. *A. 4. No. 1. And 243. No. 2.* What is said here concerning the *tongue and eyes* cannot stand as expressed here; but I do not see what I could do more, beyond what I did formerly. To declare this matter even tolerably well without great wordiness is impossible; and to make a large digression here to a thing which is to be supposed long before would not be proper. Therefore, I should think it best if this question were answered in this or a similar manner:—
A. They say that the formation of the tongue and eyes belong together, as done by one and the same process, but in two distinct parts of it. This process they deeply declare from what they suppose is done in the generation of eternal nature, and in man's regeneration also.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Jacob Behmen's works, transitioning from the discussion of the physical and spiritual elements of the body to an analysis of the "language of nature" and "signatures" as described in his book *Signatura Rerum*.</meta>

Page 247. *A. ult.* No. 1. *The language of nature in general*, must here be described more generally. For it is not only (as is said here) each thing manifesting its *inward predominant power and property*; but also its whole inward constitution, showing the entire mixture and combination of *all its powers and properties*, whether more or less predominant, or more or less subject and subservient. So that, indeed, the predominant power and property is the main thing that can be discerned from the outward signature, but it is not everything; seeing that all the properties, and their different degrees (which is the most important thing), may be discerned. And this is done, not by some outward sign (*in singulari*), but by the whole outward form, figure, shape, color, smell, taste, etc., and everything that is within it or can be an object of our outward senses; though the name *signature* has a more special relation to the visible appearance of things.

No. 2. *the one language, etc.* This one language, before the division of tongues, as to the outward formation and sound of words (for something beyond this is implied in that name), was not different from any of the now divided languages or their dialects, except only by having been the mother or root of them, which in the division was lost or swallowed up. It was not, therefore, any of those languages that were used afterward, though a great affinity with it may have remained in Hebrew, Chaldean, or any other such as was afterward spoken in the oriental countries. And Behmen does not tell us what language it was, and how this or that thing was called in it, but only that the nearest to it is Hebrew.

No. 3. *The division was not chiefly and primarily in the language*, as to the outward sound and formation of words, but in the mind and understanding (wherein what Behmen calls the sensual tongue and the mental tongue is to be placed); and this now being divided and confounded in different families, their outward language consequently must necessarily have been confounded also. So that, as they were barbarians to each other in their intellect, they must also necessarily become so in their words, each of them calling one and the same thing by different names, not proper to the true internal signature of that thing, and this was the division.

Page 249. Line 3. *a whole treatise.* By this I suppose Behmen’s SIGNATURA RERUM is meant; but if this be the meaning, I cannot see how it could be said, *they have written a whole treatise concerning the signatures of men*; seeing that this book is only generally concerning the signatures of all things; and that which is mentioned in it concerning men especially is very little, and all only in general also; so that hardly anything particular regarding the different signatures of men can be learned from it.

As to all the following *ten positions*, I must observe in general that whereas both the inward and outward signatures are mentioned in them, and yet no distinction between them went before, nor any declaration of what is meant by each of them; this cannot but bring an obscurity upon the whole matter, and a disorder also in the placement of its particulars; which obscurity could largely be removed by altering something in the order of these positions; but chiefly by declaring, in the first place, not only that there is a distinction to be observed between the inward and outward signature, but also what is to be understood by both: namely, that the outward signatures are but the visible signs, marks, and express characters—perceptible by other senses as well—of the *inward invisible* signatures, which are all imperceptible by themselves without the outward. And that these latter are not the spirits of men themselves, but, as it were, their vessels or receptacles, by which the spirits of men are set in innumerable distinctions and differences, which differences further are manifested to others by the outward signatures, derived down from the inward and representing them exactly; so that the imperceptible form and figure of the outward must be the very same as the imperceptible form of the inward. Behmen compares this inward imperceptible signature to a lute standing still, that is, not played upon. For as a lute, furnished with strings, must have a certain signature, form, or something either of harmony or discordance in its strings, by which it is distinguished from all other lutes; further, as this signature cannot be perceived by any means unless the strings are touched and moved; again, as the perceptible sound of these strings, caused by this touching and moving them, is but a discovery and outward manifestation of that interior signature, from which, as to the form, it cannot differ at all; and lastly, as this inward signature would not be the spirit of the lute itself, but only its instrument, if the lute were, like man, an understanding creature; so also is it, in a sense and manner, regarding all these four particulars with man: which I think is intelligibly enough declared by Behmen in the first chapter of his SIGNATURA RERUM.

*Ibid.* No. 4. I do not see why these words, *under the Spirit of God*, should be inserted here; seeing that by this freedom is not to be understood a free liberty, indifferent to good and evil, as if man were not to give an account and be punished with justice if he moves from the former to the latter; but only an ability to take in, or to raise up, or to move towards the one as well as the other. And if it is said here that he has such an ability *under the Spirit of God*, it would almost be the same as saying—or at least it might easily be so understood—that the Spirit of God assisted him in moving toward evil as well as toward good, which would be quite intolerable. This same idea is clearly and rightly expressed thus: under the Spirit of God, or the spirit of Satan and of this world.

Page 259. Q. 2. is asked especially, *What do they mean by the sowing and seed of the soul?* But in the following positions, though I find something is said about this, I do not find a direct answer given concerning these two expressions. Therefore, I shall only observe briefly that by "sowing," Behmen means the natural work of begetting; he calls it a sowing (just as the apostle, speaking of our natural body being buried after death in another respect, says it is "sown"), because it is only the placement, as it were, of the first rudiments of the soul into that natural place where they are to be orderly disposed, and then to be brought forth again no longer as rudiments, but as a perfect living soul. And concerning the "seed of the soul," it is plain that if there is a reason why this work may be compared to a sowing, there will also be a reason why a "seed" may be spoken of. And this reason can be even clearer if we only consider that the soul—namely, that which truly and really is and may be called a living soul—is not sown; instead, only those spiritual properties that become the soul through their own proper process lie in the seed of the man, and these are sown in and with this seed. If, then, they are the substance of which the soul is afterward composed and consists, they may significantly be called the seed of the soul while they are not yet so far advanced in their process as actually to be made a *living and immortal soul*.

Page 261. No. 6. *These propagated essences were not actually living (but only in potentia), until the conception of the fetus.* And again, No. 7. *At the conception, an actual life, or living soul, was generated out of them.* These assertions are not at all consistent with Behmen; indeed, I do not see how they can be conceived as consistent with themselves. (1.) Not with Behmen, for he expressly says that the soul is not generated at the conception of the fetus, but at the formation of its parts and members, or after the formation of some of them; and that before this time there is no immortal life in the fetus. All life in general before this time is not denied: the propagating essences could not help but be actually living, each in and for itself; but they could not be an actually living soul until their process was completed. The end of this process is their being indissolubly joined together in this fetus, and only then are they and can they be called an immortal soul. (2.) These two assertions are also not well-consistent with themselves; for the conception of the fetus occurs in and with the propagation of the essences; or if there is any distinction between them, it must be very small and subtle, seeing that conception implies propagated essences, and essences cannot be called propagated before the conception is done. If, then, the living soul is generated at the conception, according to No. 7, what time could there have been before this generation and conception in which the essences might be called propagated and asserted, according to No. 6, not to have been actually living until the conception of the fetus? This is because this conception cannot be separated from the propagation of the essences.

Page 264. Q. *What is the limit of a star?* To this question, Behmen has plainly and directly answered that the very place or point where a planet stood at the time of creation is its limit and its <term>seculum</term> <note>Latin for an age, cycle, or lifetime</note>; and whenever it comes to that place again, everything over which it has been a sovereign master is broken. But, he says further, this must be rightly understood—this limit of the planet must agree with the crown of the stars—and here lies the reason why we cannot find out the time of our death, because we do not exactly know the limit of our leader: for we must not only know the number of that, but also the number of the sign, if we wish to know the limit of our life. *THREEFOLD LIFE*, XVIII. 11, 12, 13. I cannot give a sufficient account of what this agreement with the crown of the stars is, or what this number is; but I can observe, as anyone easily can, that the thing which inevitably breaks off our life is not only Saturn's arrival at the place or point where it was created, but that something more is required for that to happen. If that were the only factor, we might reasonably conclude that nobody could live longer than the years Saturn requires to complete its whole circuit and return to the place of its creation; yet this is utterly false, as our own experience proves.

Page 266. Q. 1. *How could the outward kingdom be taken from Enoch and Elijah without dying and without this painful death?* This question has two parts or members to be answered distinctly: 1. How could it happen without dying? and 2. How without this painful death? Regarding the first, it may be answered: (1.) Behmen says it is not yet absolutely or totally taken from them; they still have the body of the <term>turba</term> <note>In Boehme's philosophy, the state of confusion or wrath in nature</note>, the outward kingdom, and Adam's flesh. But because they also have the inward kingdom, they exist in both the inward and outward <term>mysterium</term> <note>The hidden or spiritual source from which the physical world is manifested</note> with a twofold body; and this outward <term>mysterium</term> must eventually release that outward body, which is to appear before the great tribunal of Christ just like the bodies of all other men. (2.) The apostle says, *We shall not all die, but be changed.* If, then, in this transformation, the outward kingdom can be taken from many thousands without dying and without violating the original universal sentence of death, it could also have been taken from these two persons, in whom it was done for such peculiar and eminent purposes (regarding this, see the 35th of the *FORTY QUESTIONS of the Soul*). (3.) As for how it was or could have been done, Behmen says the inward kingdom swallowed up the outward within them (especially in Enoch) and kept it suppressed, or excluded it from its own manifestation.

Regarding the second part, it may be said: (1.) Behmen says the spirit of the soul feels no pain, but only the soulish fire-life, from which its matter is broken off. Now, we cannot tell whether or not these two persons felt any pain in their soulish fire-life, or how much or how little of it they felt. Truly, the feeling of pain must be greater or less depending on whether there is more or less of such matter surrounding the soul, and whether that matter is held onto, loved, and clung to more or less by the fire-life. That this matter was very minimal in Enoch especially, and was eventually not cared for at all, is witnessed by his walking with God for three hundred years. (2.) Painfulness, in every sense, is not always an inseparable companion of death, nor is it so for every person or every kind of death. Several sorts of death may be found, both natural and violent, which do not deserve to be called, in any significant sense, a painful death.

But it may be remarked once more that, without the publication in question, there probably would have been no disclosure of the real source of Newtonian philosophy—undoubtedly the greatest intellectual wonder of these recent ages. Lastly, it will not escape observation how suitably the Tract in question serves as an appendix, or in effect a kind of introductory discourse, to the author's great original work accompanying it, entitled *The Appeal*. In short, regarding this second or *Animadversion Tract*, it may be said that without it, an essential link would be missing in the chain of Mr. Law’s <term>Elias-ministration</term> <note>A ministry like that of the prophet Elijah, intended to reform or restore true religion</note> as the classic regenerator of the doctrines of religion and metaphysics, setting them forth in their original purity and simplicity and displaying their true foundation and mutual relations. By this means, it may be incidentally remarked, the learned and ingenious were provided with a key to the few isolated, wonder-exciting phenomena that constituted the knowledge of electricity, chemistry, etc., in those days, and to the systematic cultivation of those sciences that took place afterward. It is, however, as observed before, much to be lamented that so little progress has been made until now in correct philosophical knowledge. Philosophers of today ought to have been able to demonstrate, with intellectual clarity and through experiment, every grade or birth from the spiritual foundation or center to the circumference of nature, and vice versa. Instead, they experiment in darkness and blindness, without a knowledge of the principles, and are thus unable to reach back beyond a certain degree. The sum of all their discoveries (as appears from the lectures delivered in November of last year, 1848) is merely a specific explanation <insert>of what</insert> was largely and definitely stated two hundred years ago. All this must be attributed to a too narrow regard for the dictates of what may be called the subordinate agencies in the construction of the present edifice of practical science, and a lack of understanding—if not knowledge—of those writings upon which it was originally founded. Though it must be admitted that, to attain such an understanding, a different course of study would be required than what is generally considered necessary or desirable for the mere outward practitioner to pursue. Page 266. *Q. 2. How is the soul united to the body, and kept in its proper union?* *A.* The soul, if regenerated, is united to the inward paradisiacal body, and they both together to the outward Adamic flesh; just as the first principle is united to the second, and both of them to this outward third principle, which without this union could not exist, and yet has no union with them regarding their true internal essence. If, then, the soul stands between these two, as if in the middle, it can be kept in union with both if it always remembers its own position and duty within them; for during this time, all three must, in their order, be subservient to the manifestation of the wonders of God. In this respect, regarding only the current fallen and restoring state, this may be called a *proper union*, though it might not be called so in comparison to what the first Adam departed from.

*Ibid. Q. 3. How was it breathed into man?* This has been declared already several times, and I could say nothing more now than what was said previously. The *breathing into man* is not properly applicable to the soul discussed here, but to the third life, which was breathed from without into his nostrils; while the true immortal soul was raised from the depths within, brought forth, and introduced into his heart.

Page 266. *Q. 4. What is the food of the soul?* *A.* If the soul is considered only in a natural, unregenerate state, its food consists of the outward complexion (namely, the same quality that is predominant in her), the astral spirit, carnal pleasures and sensual delights, the works of her own hands, the manifold objects of this third principle, etc. These she draws in through her lust, longing, and desire, and feeds upon through her imagination. But as for regenerated souls, what answer could be expected here except the one the Lord from heaven gave himself, when saying, *My flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed?*

*Ibid. Q. 5. What is meant by the fire-spirit of understanding, and the council-house of the seven spirits?* *A.* To say "the fire-spirit of understanding" is simply to say "the spirit of understanding"; the word "fire" is added to the spirit only to give the reader of Behmen <note>Jacob Böhme</note> a deeper sense and to give this name a greater weight of emphasis. Specifically, it is to show and recall to his mind what he so many times insisted upon: that the true spirit must have passed through the fire, and that before the fire, there is no true understanding. As to that other expression, *the council house of the seven spirits*, I see no difficulty in it. The seven spirits are in man, and in him they may be considered in various ways. If they are considered with specific respect to man's contriving or designing this or that, in which they all must be employed, they may be compared to many counselors; and if so, that place, sphere, or region, in which

Deity: and this, in the first place, from considerations independent of written revelation; and, in the second place, from the revelation of the Lord Jesus; and from the whole to point out the inferences most necessary for and useful to mankind." The following are the chief topics touched upon in the 'Appeal:' CHAPTER I.—"Of creation in general. Of the origin of the soul. From where will and thought come in the creature. Why the will is free. The origin of evil solely from the creature. This world not a first immediate creation of God. How the world comes to be in its present state. The first perfection of man. All things prove a trinity in God. Man has the triune nature of God in him. Arianism and deism refuted by nature. That life is uniform through all creatures. That there is but one kind of death to be found in all nature. The fallen soul has the nature of hell in it. Regeneration is a real birth of a divine life in the soul. That there is but one salvation possible in nature. This salvation is only to be had from Jesus Christ. All the deists' faith and hope proved to be false." CHAPTER II.—"Of eternal and temporal nature. How nature is from God, and the scene of his action. How the creatures are out of it. Temporal nature created out of that which is eternal. The fallen angels brought the first disorders into nature. This world created to repair those disorders. From where good and evil come in everything of this world. How heaven and hell make up the whole of this world. How the fire of this world differs from eternal fire; and the matter of this world from the materiality of heaven. Eternal nature is the kingdom of heaven, the blessed manifestation of the triune God. God is mere love and goodness. How wrath and anger came to be ascribed to him. Of fire in general. Of the unbeginning fire. Of the spirituality of fire. How fire comes to be in material things. From where the possibility of kindling fire in the things of this world arises. Every man is and must be the kindler of his own eternal fire." CHAPTER III.—"The true ground of all the doctrines of the gospel discovered. Why Adam could make no atonement for his sins. Why and how Jesus Christ alone can make this atonement. From where the shedding of blood for the remission of sins comes. What wrath or anger it is that is quenched and atoned for by the blood of Christ. Of the last sufferings of Christ. Why and how we must eat the flesh and drink the blood of Jesus Christ."

Such is a summary of the contents of this treatise, which, for its natural and edifying philosophy, the clear, forcible, and original manner in which the author handles his profound subjects, and the classic simplicity of its diction, may not inaptly be termed the *principia* of true metaphysics; as may be somewhat inferred from a perusal of the contents of pages 52—63 of the present work, which constitute the second chapter of the 'Appeal,' as recited above. This name, it may be further suggested, will lose none of its propriety when considering the numerous fresh directions and impulses to philosophical thought the treatise has originated, and is ever calculated to ori-

Page 267. No. 2. *The soul taken generally, or for the whole inward man.* Seeing that by "the whole inward man," the new-born body is always—and sometimes even chiefly—understood; which is not yet contained or implied in the denomination of the soul in this present consideration; I think it would be more proper to say—the soul taken generally, or for the whole spiritual being, as far as it is distinct from what is bodily.

*Ibid. Q. 1. What are ideas and images of things in the mind? A.* Such representations of <term>intelligible objects</term> are like the images in a mirror are of visible ones; arising also in the mind by the same necessity by which these do in a mirror, if an object is set before it. Because the mind of man, being in itself most quiet, empty, and undetermined to any sort of act or motion, stands in the same relation—and carries the same neutral disposition—to things conceivable in all the worlds out of which it is brought forth, which a mirror carries to things visible in this particular world, wherein and whereout it is made. Yet with this difference, that whereas a material mirror is capable only of receiving passively and keeping an image immovably within it as long as the object stands before it, this spiritual mirror is capable also of admitting from its own side something of activity. By this, its images and ideas may be altered, compounded, divided, displaced, and transfigured into innumerable shapes; though, indeed, at that point, it is no longer strictly called the mind, but comes under another consideration and another name as well.

*Ibid. Q. 2. Do we see all things in God? A.* In some sense, generally corresponding to that in which we are said in the Scripture to live, move, and have our being in God, we may be said also to see all things in God. But as true as this is in one sense, it is also true in another—that the greatest part of mankind does not live in God, but in themselves, or in their selfishness; and that their very light, the only proper means of seeing, is darkness. How, then, can such a person be said to see all things or anything in God? To answer, therefore, this general question with a simple and general "yes" or "no" is absolutely impossible. But let the eyes, the things, the worlds, and above all, those senses wherein the name of God may be differently understood, be duly distinguished; and then of some it may be affirmed more or less, and of others it must be either totally or more or less denied.

Page 269. No. 6. All that is said here concerning *subtlety* is true indeed, but might be clearer if it were expressed in this way, or in a manner like this:

Subtlety is considered (1) as it is in the <term>first principle</term> only, where it arises chiefly from its own <term>tincture</term>, and is devilish—or if it might be so expressed, the devil’s intellect—having in its generation the first three forms of nature only. And (2) as it is in this, our <term>third principle</term>, wherein it is indeed tinctured, softened, made glistening, and in some measure transformed by the outward <term>astral light</term>; but nevertheless, it remains earthly, sensual, devilish, and always evil from its own proper root, which is rooted in the dark world, and which no amount of tincturing with astral light is able to truly turn into good.
