originate in the minds of its readers, according to their peculiar genius or idiosyncrasy. In some, it awakens a train of reflections that, owing to their sober practical turn, has ended in the exposition of the general features of a new system of physical science, also providing a clue to its regular pursuit and development. In others of a more sublimated or abstract nature, it either opens a new sphere of intellectual research or furnishes them with a clearer and more steady light in the prosecution of their favorite studies: in neither case severing (as is the custom of modern blind philosophy) what are inseparably joined together—namely, God and nature—but considering them in their respective mutual relations; either according to the present material system and from there ascending to the spiritual ground of things, or <term>a priori</term> <note>From the cause to the effect.</note> from the understood birth and constitution of original nature—the great and only working life and power—through its elaborations and phenomena in degraded matter. Or it may be in some *few cases* of regenerated and divinely harmonized understandings, who are also conversant with the facts and theories of experimental science (not ingenious visionaries but true alchemical artists), tracing by an unbroken chain the manifestation of the powers and wisdom of the supernatural unity, in and through visible and invisible nature.

With this work (taking the book on ‘the Sacrament’ as its introduction and the “Way to Divine Knowledge,” “Spirit of Love,” and ‘Tract on Warburton’ as its sequels), it may be said, as previously observed, that the latter series of Mr. Law’s ministerial writings began. These, in contrast to all others that had preceded them in support of the truths of Christianity, were immediately addressed to men of intellect and education everywhere, whose strong, logically-constituted, and well-disposed minds were unable to receive the leading partial, irrational theories, dogmas, and doctrines of popular Christianity.

But, to return to the subject of the preceding observations: without enumerating the many instances in which the work in question is stated to have inspired the genius of individuals whose contributions to mental or physical science have been received with admiration and gratitude by the world (which would be out of place in a memorial like the present, which is merely indicative of the general characteristics of Mr. Law’s life and ministry, presenting them in the true aspect in which they will need to be viewed by a capable and concise biographer), it may be proper here to specify one of the most notable of those results, the origin of which has been so little suspected until now. One reason for the latter may have been the lack of a suitable mental constitution on the part of inquirers, and their not having the proper means and books for the pursuit of such an investigation. For the tracing of the authorship of a science cannot be done <term>a posteriori</term> <note>From the effect to the cause.</note>; rather, there must be brought to it a familiar knowledge of the antecedent or concurrent relative circumstances of the time, and of the private life and favorite studies of the individual to whom the chief merit of the discovery is attributed—advantages and qualifications that are seldom found united in experimental historians.

Now, it is the settled conviction of the writer that the modern science of electricity, galvanism, chemistry, etc., is primarily indebted for its origin and purification to the work under review, and essentially therein to Behmen <note>Jacob Böhme</note>, who was the first to declare the true principles of all things in a philosophical manner. Page 269. No. 7. *Reason has for its object only*, etc. Here it may be argued that reason is able, in a sense and manner, to make all things, without exception, the objects of her speculation, whether they be transitory or eternal, and in whatever principle they exist. And this objection would be prevented if some words were inserted, e.g.: *reason has for its proper and adequate object only the transitory things of this world, and even them also, since the fall, only in part and with great obscurity.*

Page 271. Line 6. *but not the primitive faculty.* Here I do not see how this particular assertion could be defended. As the spirit of this world, the elements, and all the things of this principle are still the same now as they were before the curse was pronounced upon them—though they are not altogether in the same condition—so reason also, which did not come into man from without through the fall but was in him before the fall, must necessarily be the same faculty. This remains true even though it no longer has, in its usurped dominion, the same qualities which it had then, in its ministry and subordination to the superior faculties.

*Ibid.* Line 6, 7. *nor does it distinguish men from brutes.* Although this is certainly true, I think it might be expressed with a little more moderation, so that it might not be as offensive as may be justly feared. For that eminent degree which reason has in man, and which no brutes can reach, brings at least enough in his favor that it makes him more noble than any of them—indeed, than all of them taken together. Though, indeed, that which completely exempts him from their order is not to be found in reason, but in understanding.

Page 273. No. 22. *The soul, by its will, turns itself from darkness into light.* This is true, indeed, if rightly understood; but it might be expressed more carefully, so that no one might take the opportunity to say that Behmen makes the will the savior of its soul, which might be inferred from this under a plausible appearance. It is true that Behmen sometimes speaks this way in brief, presupposing that his reader has read and understood his plain and sufficient exposition of it, and is able to take these concise words in a sense conformable to it. *The soul,* he says expressly, *cannot enter or turn itself into the light, which was extinguished in the fall; but it can turn into that deep or ground wherein it was extinguished; and therein is he also, who is the light of the world, able and ready to kindle the light in that soul again.* This turning of the soul is now done by the will and cannot be done without it. Therefore, the soul (which thus can never meet with disappointment) turning into that ground and being taken into the light by him who has surely promised he will in no way cast out such a one, may well enough be said, in a concise way of speaking, *to turn by its will from darkness into light.* This should be understood such that only the lesser medium is named, the <term>sine qua non</term> which is on the soul's side; and yet the greater medium, which is only effective on the side of the light's principle, is not thereby excluded.

No. 23 *The will may be broken, but it is better, etc.* This is a little obscure, for it may be taken in two different senses, and I cannot sufficiently discern which of them is intended here. For (1) the will, as to itself, before an evil act is performed, is said to be made substantial if it has only come forth into a perceptible determination, design, or purpose. And (2) the will is also said to be made substantial in and by its act and deed, really performed and executed. This

published (as also of the theory of magnetism, etc.), may be easily found by a reference to the works that had then appeared regarding it. It may be said to have consisted in the practice of a few isolated, trifling experiments or juggling tricks, with such simple instruments as the infancy of the science had invented to collect electricity and exhibit its phenomena; for not even the <term>Leyden phial</term> was then in existence. This treatise, however, and more immediately that portion of it relating to fire (see pages 61—64, mentioned before, as also 74—75), founded upon what Behmen and Freher have so fully declared, was destined to recall the minds of the ingenious and learned from the mere practice of experiment to the consideration of the philosophy of the great power which was thereby presented to their notice. Indeed, Sir Isaac Newton, with that penetration so peculiar to himself, had—from his intimate acquaintance with Behmen—mentioned throughout his writings the existence of a pure, elastic medium of <term>ethereal fire</term>, which was the root or ground of the four elements, and doubtless had earnestly longed for the means of demonstrating it to the senses; but the instruments with which to exhibit its nature and powers had not yet been invented, so Sir Isaac died without seeing his conjectures—or rather, his knowledge—verified. But he died in assured faith and hope that it was reserved for a later period to open the science in a systematic manner; until, in short, after the appearance of Mr. Law's treatise, the work under notice, in the year 1740. Accordingly, in observing the progress of its development, we find that in 1744, Berkeley's "Siris" was published, which contained a further outward practical elucidation of the science opened in the "Appeal," confirmed by what the ancient sages had written upon it. Then in the year 1746, Freke published his treatise upon electricity, which may be said to be the first direct approximation toward a systematic consideration of the subject. He thus introduced that work to the public:—

> "When I first entered on this subject of electricity (he writes), I intended only to put some thoughts in writing concerning it, so that I might more easily convey them to the understandings of those whom I hoped would be more likely than I to go further with it. And as nobody, either here or abroad, had published anything touching the cause from which it was produced, I chose to show the beginning I had made to some friends, in whose opinion concerning natural knowledge I had great reliance. I told them I thought my difficulty would be to convey what I had to propose on this new subject to them with the necessary clearness, as my intention was to observe the utmost brevity in it.
> After I had read it to them, they assured me that what I had written was perfectly intelligible, and that it gave them many new ideas respecting this phenomenon, and they were very earnest with me to print it for the sake of the public.
> I was not, however, inclined to comply with their requests until I had shown it to a person who is most justly distinguished for his great candor and superlative understanding in all natural knowledge; and he likewise having expressed his wishes to see it in print, I could not but look on his desire as a command. * * *"

Page 274. *Q. What do they say of dreams? A.* They say that natural dreams are magic images, represented by the firmamental constellation, and seen by man’s astral spirit in his own peculiar magic star (*astrum*); which star, they say, is nothing more than an epitomized figure, expressing, as it were, in a small compass, the vast extent of his great firmamental constellation. That is, the whole scheme of the astral heaven in the macrocosm, with all its energies and possible contingencies, lies in every man, according to that peculiar form or posture in which it stood at the time of his conception and birth. And this in the superior astral heavens, being like a watch and unfolding itself successively, also represents its operations successively by similar images in those inferior heavens which in man correspond to them. And so of supernatural dreams, also, they speak in almost the same manner, mentioning only, instead of an exterior firmamental constellation, an interior eternal one, which all men have in the greatest variety in the deeper ground of their soul and spirit, out of eternal nature.

Page 275. No. 25. *the astral and sensitive soul.* Here I would say rather *astral or sensitive*, because they are not two, but one; though these two expressions are both appropriate and may represent a distinction to us, consisting in this: that the former shows more of its origin, and the latter more of its quality. But this being of no great importance, I would not have mentioned it if the occasion had not been given by what is said on the same page—

No. 3. *the sensitive soul is a glass of the third principle.* For here it would be much more proper to say, instead of *sensitive*, the *astral soul* or *astral spirit*; seeing that the third life, soul, or spirit in man—not as it is a sensitive light, but as it is an astral spirit—is a mirror (glass) of this third principle. The reason for this is so plainly laid down by Boehme in the fifth of the <term>FORTY QUESTIONS</term> that I cannot see what difficulty can be found in it. Everything that is in the whole third principle, and all its properties, lie here and represent themselves as in a mirror; and this is exactly why man is rightly called a microcosm. It was that same mirror in which the powers and wonders of this principle were represented to Adam; in which he delighted to see them, and into which he turned his imagination and will, until it was fixed and captivated within it.

Page 275. Last line. *that it cannot be regenerated.* This is too absolute and general. Boehme says only that it is not regenerated during the time of this outward third principle, just as the earthly mortal body, during all this time, is also not regenerated. And the reasons, of which many and great ones may be given, are sufficient for the astral spirit as well as for the earthly body; because they are both equally under the spirit of this third principle.

This tract now forms the second part of his (Freke’s) “Treatise on the Nature and Property of Fire,” published in 1752, and consisting of three essays on the following subjects: “(1) Showing the cause of vitality and muscular motion, with many other phenomena: (2) On electricity: (3) Showing the mechanical cause of magnetism, and why the compass varies in the manner it does.” How this work is deducible from the ‘Appeal’ is left to those who are familiar with the latter to consider; as is also its natural tendency to awaken the attention of the ingenious to the subject upon which it treats, inciting them to pursue an inquiry which, however faintly traced out in these its first beginnings, promised to lead to the most important scientific results. And what did follow from that will be manifest on a perusal of Lovett’s publications and philosophical essays, and others of the same era.

...in Christ, I observe (1.) that because these are not the formal words of Scripture (which never and nowhere says so), instead of *from all eternity*, one might say, *from before the foundation of the world*. This is not as if there were indeed a great or important weight in this alteration; but only because several reflections could be made upon it based on Behmen's principles; and then, also, because there is no reason why the proper words of the Apostle should be altered in this way.

(2.) The interpretation of these words is represented in such a way that it gives occasion to call it *uncommon*; and to think that it delivers more, if not quite another and different thing, from what theologians generally take these words to mean; nay, also to suspect it of having some conformity with what the Gnostics and Valentinians asserted. But seeing it can be sufficiently proven that Behmen's interpretation of that Scriptural expression contains nothing else nor more than what theologians generally will be ready to grant, and what their plain sense expressed in Question 3 means; I rightly conceive that it would be much better, nay, even necessary, to represent this answer in some other terms; and then to make no mention of those early heretics and their eternal Æons. For certainly, *nodus est hic in scirpo quæsitus* <note>a knot is sought here in a bulrush; a Latin proverb meaning to look for a difficulty where there is none</note>; and without any necessity, Behmen is slandered, at least with a suspicion of having communion with those ancient fables. The plain words both of the Scripture and of theologians in general—*fallen man was chosen*, etc.—must necessarily presuppose that the fall of man was seen by God before man was a creature; and this must necessarily imply that it was not seen as a thing actually done outside of God, but as an image or idea in God's eternal wisdom, an expression which I think no one can be offended by. If this is so, the restorer also of this fallen image must have been seen, and must have been appointed in that wisdom; for all this the word *chosen* does imply. If, then, they both were seen in this way, they were not seen as at a distance from one another, but as in conjunction and union with one another. The second Adam must have been seen as entering into the first Adam's nature and restoring it; and the first as restored in the second. But now, all this having had no being outside of God before the foundation of the world, but having been only in the wisdom of God—a foresight of what was to have a future being in time—has and can have no other sense but that very same which our theologians generally express by saying—*man was chosen in Christ, considered as to be incarnate, or as already incarnate in the divine decrees*. And that this is Behmen's sense, containing neither more nor less, could be shown from twenty places in his writings. But now, contrary to this sense, or at least very much different from it, these words in Answer 2—*the second person entered into the image or idea of man, represented, etc.*—seem to be understood as if there was made, before the foundation of the world, a strange kind of incarnation and conjunction; or as if the eternal Word had already taken upon him the nature of that fallen image or idea then. However, Behmen plainly declares that by *entering into that image*, he means nothing else but that there was seen in the eternal wisdom not only the *fall of man*, but also the fallen man restored in and by the eternal Word; or that foresight of the eternal Word's future entering into the fallen human nature. If, therefore, only these words were expressed otherwise, or at least a little explained, it could not be replied that, *This interpretation is uncommon, and the Gnostics and Valentinians have asserted some such thing, etc.*

exhibit those various operations of it which amazed so much at first, especially in the property of its velocity, which is strictly that of our ideas, congenial with and perhaps generated by the same element. But, my God! what an opening has this discovery given, if duly improved, if once regularly pursued from its first principles and reduced into a regular system. Probably in such a case, experimentalists would no longer have reason to complain of the *oddity* or whims of electricity.

The statics of the elementary fire might doubtless, by a progression of deductions from certain axioms, be ascertained so as to account for all its seeming irregularities, as well as produce far nobler and more essential discoveries than have hitherto employed those gentlemen who are scanning the effects before having sufficiently looked deeply into and simplified that cause which, without a compliment, you appear to me to have first pointed out. They must go back to the element of this fire before they can hope to go usefully forward with their discoveries in it. This I can safely aver, that neither Boerhaave nor Stahl nor indeed any author I ever read could afford me the least satisfaction, especially about the principles of vitality (a point I mention only as the most interesting example of the necessity of fire to all nature), before your notion of it let in at once upon my understanding a flood of light. I was indeed never the dupe of that philosophical gibberish of nervous fluid, ether, etc., which, proving nothing to the senses, established nothing; whereas, the existence of this elementary fire realized to our senses accounts almost palpably to me for almost all the operations of nature. This appears probable from a research into its properties; as, for example, its extreme subtlety, velocity, and expansiveness, all of which may be experimentally ascertained and subordinated by certain laws. So that, should this system not be a dream, the component parts of the world will be simplified and reduced into two primary elements of matter: the body, and fire—the soul of the world, or that vivifying spirit, the necessity of which to nature was perceived only in glimpses by the great Sir Isaac Newton, who sought for it in a nitrous salt; surely with less probability than in fire, the nature of which he appears grievously to have mistaken. ***”

Such is our notice of Freke's publication, as one of the results of the ‘Appeal.’ And what further ensued upon it, and from the former work, is left to be traced out by the reader who is interested in the subject. He will doubtless find, by a little research, how in England and throughout the polished states of Europe, as also in America (by Franklin, who imported and republished some of Law's writings, with other esteemed English works), the attention of philosophers was now becoming turned to electricity, with the view of establishing a regular science upon it.

Passing over, for the present, any notice of Lovett's publications in 1756, 1766, and 1774, of Hoadly's and Wilson's in 1756, and of Jones's in 1762—being the chief with which we shall have to do, and upon which a few reconciliatory observations may be needful—the next period to which attention will be called (in order to present the point in question in a lucid light) is the year 1762, when in the month of April a Letter appeared in the “Gentleman's Magazine,” openly referring to Mr. Law and Behmen as the first philosophical demonstrators of the ground of nature, or of those powers which were now classed under the name of electricity.

In the year 1771, the Rev. Richard Symes, Rector of St. Werburgh, Bristol, published a short treatise under the title of “Fire Analysed; or the several parts of which it is composed demonstrated by Experiments.” This gentleman was the author of the anonymous letter just referred to, which he re-inserted in the latter publication, of which, indeed, it may be said to form the basis. As this treatise is very rare to find, and its contents are extremely relevant to the subject under discussion, we propose here to present a long extract from it, as follows: —

> ### CHAPTER I. INTRODUCTION. — *Treating of the Contrary Powers that are in Nature, both within and without man; and of the rich treasures to be found in the writings of Jacob Behmen and Mr. Law.*
> 
> The majority of mankind pass through life without reflection. No one, comparatively speaking, seeks to know himself, or inquires how he is related to nature, or nature to him. Having seen how others come into the world, this satisfies him as to his own existence; and as most are only concerned with how to preserve and indulge themselves, his concern carries him no further than to follow in their footsteps. But now and then someone arises who ventures out of this general path, not satisfied with the mere acts of eating, drinking, and sleeping; he begins to consider the end of existence, and this leads him to inquire into nature, its qualities, and what it consists of. Such a person, reader, allow me to say (it is spoken without vanity), is the author of this treatise.—— Perceiving throughout nature qualities that are completely opposite, this awakened his attention to consider why and for what reason there was nothing either within or without him that did not have its opposite. Externally, his eye clearly saw it. *Internally*, his own feeling was his evidence. Within, he felt the contrary qualities of anger and love, rage and meekness, joy and sorrow, etc. Without, he perceived fire and water, light and darkness, heat and cold, calms and tempests, etc. Now, in himself, he observed these contrary qualities often stirred up and exerting an uncontrollable power. If anger arose, it hurried him to acts that reason condemned but could not prevent. If sorrow was stirred up, joy disappeared, the memory of it was gone, and it was as though it had never existed. ——Now these two contrary qualities, he felt, had a power to suppress and overcome each other; and also, at the same time, they were acted upon and called forth independently of his will. Good news called forth joy. Bad news stirred up sorrow. Now this shows that man has powers within him that sounds and objects can do more with than has ever yet been achieved by the much-touted ability of reason.——And as it is thus with the powers of joy and sorrow, so it is with rage and meekness. They are equally and independently of reason stirred up in us, but with this difference: the former seems more prevalent in mankind than the latter; the latter has its stirrings and often meets with incidents that call it into action, even in the most hot-tempered; but the former prevails for the most part in man. The first two children born to Eve are striking instances of the power of these two contrary qualities ruling and governing in the heart of man. In Cain, rage ruled and governed; in Abel, meekness; but Cain’s rage got the mastery over Abel’s meekness.
> 
> But now as to *external nature*, where the will of man cannot reach, there the contrary qualities are regulated by an all-wise but invisible agent. The heat and cold are wisely tempered; neither is allowed to destroy the other. The earth annually brings forth countless productions for the service of man; but yet, were these contrary qualities allowed to work blindly by themselves, vegetation would cease and every earthly life would end. For if the heat prevailed, all would be burnt up. If the cold, all would be one frozen and solid mass. And yet I think it cannot but be visible to everyone how necessary heat and cold are in the creation, and that they are always at work, but at the same time governed and directed by an all-wise and all-powerful agent; because if they were left to themselves, the one would soon be the death of the other.
> 
> While my inquisitive mind was searching into these things, and yet unable to find out the

...why and for what reason such opposite qualities should exist in nature, I providentially met with two authors in whose writings these mysteries are explained and nature is, as it were, dissected. These authors are *Jacob Behmen* and *Mr. Law*; whose works may be justly compared to a mine full of the richest ores. The seeker and inquirer after truth will find in them material of so precious and sublime a nature as must satisfy the most enlarged capacity. Some indeed, who have casually stumbled upon them—either prejudiced in favor of their own supposed knowledge or having no taste for the truths contained in them—have despised and treated them with contempt; but so it has been and always will be with eminent men. They will have their despisers as well as admirers; but scorn and contempt can never invalidate truth. Truth will ever and invariably remain truth, regardless of how numerous its opponents may be. But that these men have revealed the deepest truths in their writings, if experiments are any criterion by which to judge, I will make clear and evident through those that are incontrovertible. However, how I became able to prove the secrets of nature through experiments, as laid open by *Jacob Behmen* and *Mr. Law* in their writings, shall be the subject of the next chapter.

## CHAPTER II.—*Explaining by Experiments the arcana and wonders of Nature, as opened in the works of Jacob Behmen and Mr. Law.*

My attention was piqued by a book published by *Mr. Lovett* of Worcester, setting forth a variety of cures performed by electricity. I had seen an electrical machine many years before this and had tried all the common experiments that were then known; for very little had been written on the subject, and that was by no means satisfactory, as no one was able to trace the cause of the striking appearances raised by an electrical apparatus. Therefore, like other strange sights which affect us less the more often they are seen, so it happened with electrical experiments. They tired me and then naturally sank into neglect; for having lost their power to hold my attention, and despairing of ever reaching the cause, I left it where I then thought it was: impenetrably hidden among *occult qualities*. But reading in *Mr. Lovett* of its medicinal virtue, this roused my attention to a more accurate investigation and to search more minutely for what I had previously given up as undiscoverable. I tried every experiment my imagination suggested and at last discovered the secret I sought for. But here I admit that I owe my success to a letter from the *Abbé Nollet*, published in the ‘Gentleman’s Magazine’ of August 1759. The Abbé was then conducting experiments and maintained in his letter that there were two currents in the electrical fire that were diametrically opposite. This hint was enough for me, as I was already sufficiently convinced that there were qualities in nature directly contrary and opposite to each other, both from my own experience and from *Jacob Behmen’s* and *Mr. Law’s* writings. But now I was able to demonstrate this truth by experiment and to bring into open view these hidden, secret working powers, known to us only by their effects. But what was more, I found now that I could prove by experiments to the senses that there were seven properties in nature, as set forth and maintained in the books of the two eminent writers mentioned above, the basis of which are the two opposite qualities previously mentioned. Such a discovery, as may naturally be imagined, made me desirous of publishing it to the world in hopes that some more capable hand might throw more light upon the subject; accordingly, I sent the following letter to the ‘Gentleman’s Magazine,’ which was published in the month of April 1762:

### A Letter to the editor of the ‘Gentleman’s Magazine:’ wherein the principles of electricity are proved by experiments to be the same with those of *Jacob Behmen’s* and *Mr. Law’s* philosophy.

My design is not to make myself known; I write only for information and to encourage some more capable person to finish what I consider to be only the outlines of a most important discovery. For if *Jacob Behmen’s* and *Mr. Law’s* philosophy can be proved by electricity, and, vice versa, electricity can be ex-

'But not to detain you longer from what I intend to present in as small a space as possible, the following are my experiments to prove that Mr. Law's philosophy is the same as that which the electrical machine reveals to our senses.

'Mr. Law says there are seven properties in Nature. Indeed, he does not say this as the first discoverer of this great mystery, for he is honest enough to tell us from whom he received it; but since he was a perfect master of it and has given it to us in a style easier to understand at first than that of Jacob Behmen, from whom he took it, I do not hesitate to call it Mr. Law's philosophy.

'In proving these seven properties, Mr. Law says Nature originates from the will of the Deity, <insert>[willing to be manifest in an expressed life of nature and creature; for the Deity, being light and love, must as such communicate.]</insert> This he explains in the following manner:

'Will <insert>[in action]</insert> is desire; now desire <insert>[as such]</insert> has these properties essentially belonging to it: *compressing, enclosing, or shutting up; and reaching out, drawing, or attracting.* Now the first of these—*compressing, enclosing, or shutting up*—is contrary to the last—*drawing or attracting*—for the first has no motion in it, but only wills to compress, hold together, or endeavors to remain in stillness; but the last has motion in it, and therefore is contrary to it and never continues in a quiet state.

'Now these two properties, brought forth by the same will, have *equal strength* and *equal power*, and always act in opposition to each other. This opposition unavoidably produces a third property <insert>[in the same act]</insert>, namely, a *whirling*; for as the holding fast and the going out are equal in strength and power to each other, and because of each other's opposition, neither can go backward or forward, up or down—each acting equally against the other—a *whirling round* must be caused.

'Now these three—the *holding fast*, the *going out*, and the *whirling round*—all necessarily arising from the will of the Deity, or constituting a discovery of it, Mr. Law calls the first three properties of nature. The fourth property, he says, is *fire*, produced from the <insert>[intense]</insert> violent agitation, motion, and anguish of the first three. The fifth property, he says, is *light*. The sixth is *life*; and by the seventh, as Jacob Behmen also does, he means *spirit*, <insert>[spiritual manifestation or body, pure nature, the fulfillment of desire.]</insert> <insert>[As the Deity no sooner wills than carries it out, so this generation of nature is an instantaneous, beginningless act, though it is conceivably divided this way as to its order.]</insert>

'Now I prove by the help of the electrical machine that these seven properties are in <insert>[this temporal out-birth of]</insert> nature, exactly as Mr. Law has described them, in the following manner:

'On the conductor, I tie several threads about four inches long; I then take a hoop, the diameter of which does not exceed the atmosphere I am able to raise by the friction of the globe, and tie some threads upon it of equal length with those I tie on the conductor. This done, I place the conductor exactly in the center of the hoop, and upon setting the machine in motion, all the threads are immediately extended—those on the conductor with their points toward those on the hoop, and those on the hoop toward those on the conductor.

'This phenomenon, so contrary to everything I have ever seen yet, greatly astonished me. For if we blow with our lips, everything within the reach of the blast flies away from us, not toward us; but here, although there is a manifest blast issuing from the conductor (for it may be felt against the hand), yet the threads on the hoop, instead of flying away in the same direction as those on the conductor, act directly opposite and point toward them. This is evident proof that there are two streams or currents, one issuing to the conductor and the other from it; or, in other words, that there are two properties in nature always acting contrary to each other, the one *attracting*, the other *repelling*.

'(Note. — The Abbé Nollet, through a variety of experiments, has now put this beyond all doubt. Dr. Watson tells us these experiments are sixty in number and are exceedingly well chosen to prove the simultaneous inflow and outflow of electrical matter.)

'I will only add one more experiment, which I am not certain is included in the Abbé Nollet's: suspend a bottle on the end of a conductor supported either on glass or silk; let there be nothing near the bottle, and it will be found impossible to charge it; but apply a finger to the side, and it will be filled and give a shock. To the finger, it appears as if the matter that ran in at the top discharged itself at the side; but the charging of the bottle shows this to be a deception, and proves at the same time that for every spark that came out of the bottle, a spark went into it from the finger as well; for these two opposite powers can only be divided by words; where one acts, the other is always present. But to put this beyond dispute, remove the finger and hold the point of a pin at a distance of four or five inches, and a flame will be seen rushing from it, and the bottle will fill and be charged just as well as if the finger had been kept close to it. — N.B. This *flame* reveals another secret to us, namely, that it is not air but real fire that issues toward the bottle. ‘But here, perhaps, it may be objected that I carry matters too far in thinking I have discovered two contrary properties in nature, when it is evidently no more than a strange appearance produced by an electrical machine, just as the vibration of a pendulum is produced by the weight and wheels of a clock. This objection, as it is natural to make it, I thought proper to mention and then remove, so that we may have the way clear before us.

‘The vibration of the pendulum is nothing more than an effect, of which the structure of the clock is the cause. But the electrical machine is not the cause of these strange appearances; it is only the means of making visible to us what is hidden in nature, just as the striking together of a flint and a steel is the means of bringing forth to our sight the fire that lay hidden within them. The collision of the flint and steel is not the cause or creator of fire, but only a means of making visible what before was shut up and concealed from our sight.

‘In the same manner acts the friction of the globe against the cushion; the friction does not create these strange appearances, but is only a means of making them visible. Therefore, I conclude that what we see does not begin to exist only when the machine is put in motion; rather, the machine is a wonderful discoverer of the hidden properties of nature, which are always acting in the same manner, though so secretly that our bare sight cannot discover them.

‘Now, I prove from the Leyden experiment that these two properties acting thus contrary to each other are the cause of a continual whirling, wheel, or circle <note>In modern terms, an electrical circuit.</note>.

‘It is well known to all electricians that unless a circle be made between the bottom and top of a charged bottle, no shock can possibly be given; but let a bottle be charged and then a communication made between the bottom and top, and something of unparalleled force will be found to act within it. But without making a circle, we cannot gain any knowledge of its power. However, its strength is now so far established that nothing is found able to stand against it, and by the help of large jars, its power may be increased to a most astonishing degree.

‘Now these three properties made visible by the help of the electrical machine are clearly Jacob Behmen’s and Mr. Law’s first three properties of nature.

‘The fourth property, *fire*, will not require me to say much about it, for it is well known that it is real fire that bursts forth from the charged jar or bottle in the explosion; and that it will set fire to spirits and properly prepared combustibles.

‘The fifth property, *light*, follows from the fire. This also requires no more to be said than that whoever has seen the fire burst from the bottle must have seen light; indeed, so much light may be produced by the machine with the help of an air-pump as even to read large print by it.

‘The sixth property is [*sound, understanding,*] life. Now that fire is the radix <note>The root or source.</note> of life evidently appears from the following experiment: let a cat and a candle be put together into an oven; let the door have a pane of glass fixed in the middle, so that no air can penetrate it, and then let the door be closely luted <note>Sealed with a substance like clay or cement to make it airtight.</note> to the mouth of the oven, and you will perceive that the same fire that is necessary to keep up the flame of the candle is necessary also for the life of the cat; for the instant the candle goes out, that instant the cat dies. See Freke on Fire, p. 33.

‘The seventh property is *spirit [developed]*. The machine makes this as evident as all the rest, for when it is put in motion, there issues from the end of the conductor a spirit, or air (for they are both the same) that may be felt; and, in sensation, it is not unlike what we produce when we softly blow upon our hand with contracted lips. Now here the machine ceases; here its discoveries end. It has no more properties to display, unless we call its lately discovered medical virtue another property; but this must not be looked upon as another property, as all the rest clearly and distinctly are, but rather a blessed effect of the whole.

‘Now, is it not astonishing that these two men, Jacob Behmen and Mr. Law, should write so clearly and so justly of nature without the help of any instrument to assist them? Jacob Behmen expressly writes in the style in which an electrician would express himself; for he speaks of the fire bursting forth with a violent crack, and so exactly describes the noise and flash that one would think, at first glance, he had seen the fire collected in a bottle and discharged. [See Behmen’s ‘Threefold Life,’ small 4to. pages 16, 17, 18.]

No one I have heard of ever made the slightest objection to the letter above, but my hope was that someone or other would have shed greater light on the subject; for many people were at that time conducting experiments, and several since then have written on the subject. They have incontestably proved that what used to be called electric matter is real fire, and that it exists and is to be found everywhere. However, no one has yet attempted to show what this fire is, where it comes from, or whether it is a single unit or composed of parts. This I shall endeavor to elucidate in the following chapters.

“God is a pure spirit, who from eternity to eternity ever was, and ever must be blessed, by his will or inclination toward an ever-blessed goodness. This strong desire for blessing is, in order (though not in time), the first fervent principle, and is what is called in God 'the Father' or 'eternal fire.' And this fiery desire for blessing eternally generates the Son, or second principle, of divine light and love toward every possible subject or capacity for blessedness; and from the fire and light proceeds the third principle, the active Spirit, wise and powerful to accomplish every intention of happiness. And these three are one GOD and have but one will. Yet in nature and in the creature, they have three distinct operations, and by such distinction they produce all the infinite variety of sensibilities, powers, virtues, forms, colors, flavors, sounds, etc., that from eternity to eternity ever did or can arise throughout all space, or the universe of nature and the creature.

<margin>3</margin>
This triune Deity of LOVE eternally perceived and found himself in the outflow or body of his own kindling spirit, even in the substantiality of internal, ineffable, and unapproachable light. This substantiality of light is the heaven of God himself, and by its influence, it makes the heaven of nature and the creature. It is universal but incomprehensible; communicable but not divisible in the creator, though divisible in the fallen creature. Out of it no creature ever was or can be made, because it is everywhere; and wherever it is, there is the inseparable Unity of the Trinity of God. <note>N.B. To be understood throughout according to the distinctions of the Note on page 292, etc., and other passages of Freher’s papers to the same effect.</note>

<margin>4</margin>
This eternal Spirit of desire, love, and operation toward all goodness, dwelling in his own body or external substantiality of internal light, through his desire for manifestation in the blessedness of creatures, produced an internal capacity or ground of creation. This capacity was not God, though it was in God; yet it was, as it were, outside or external to God. It was a *want*, not a *filling*; a *capacity*, not an *inhabitant*; the *craver*, not the *gratifier*; the *workshop*, not the *operator*; the *dark subject of the illuminator*; *nature*, not God. <note>Nature is like the body and mirror to God, in which he perceives himself and works all his wonders. In like manner, darkness is a body and mirror to light, by which all its glories become reflected and apparent. And thus evil is like a body and mirror of goodness, wherein goodness is seen in all its beauty and delightfulness.</note>

<margin>5</margin>
And into this dark capacity, or *infinite want*, called nature, the fervent desire of the Father eternally entered and brought itself into divisibility, thereby producing an infinite, though unintelligent, desire throughout nature, analogous to the intellectual desire of the Deity. It was a desire from God, but not the desire that *is* in God; it was nature’s desire, but not God’s desire, though imparted to nature by the desire of God. And this desire in nature produces attraction, or a threefold working of properties throughout the infinity of nature. The *first property* of this attraction is called astringency, or a strong pulling in or shutting up. The *second property* of this attraction is a strong expansion or going out in order to pull in (for the desire for compression or holding must move out to get something to compress or hold, and so produces a resistance equal to itself; and the moving out of the desire, merely in order to pull in, produces an act of compression that equally resists the act of expansion). Because these two properties eternally beget each other and are equally strong, though contrary to each other, they produce a *third property* called anguish, or the whirling motion of the first two properties, that can never rest from an equal compression and expansion, a pulling in and a rushing out in order to attract, until desire—which is the ground of their operation—fails.

Now, though these three properties of nature were received into the heaven of God and were illuminated and blessed thereby, they neither changed their nature nor their manner of working: for the first property of astringency became the compression or realizing of every kind of happiness; the second property of expansion went out with the Holy Spirit into the light and the love in order to realize and bring the same into itself; and the third property of the whirling anguish became a rapture and restless enjoyment of the blessedness into which the first two properties were assumed.

## CHAPTER III.—Proving that there is only One Fire in all nature, and demonstrating by experiments that fire is the Life of All Things.

<margin>7</margin> Custom, which too often tyrannizes over our understanding, has until now arbitrarily fixed the epithet *electric* to a machine, which seems most likely to be the most wonderful instrument ever yet discovered, either for its usefulness already found out in the medical way, or for experiments in natural philosophy. But I will not contend with custom here; it is of too stubborn a nature to yield to reason or argument. I would only endeavor to free the reader’s ideas from confusion, lest when I speak of *electric fire*, he should imagine it is something dependent on or produced by the apparatus. I would therefore remark here that there are not in nature *two fires*, or fires of a different quality from each other, but that the fire by which we warm ourselves is the very same as that made visible by an electrical apparatus. <margin>X</margin>
Fire is the most wonderful of anything we deal with: and yet scarcely is anyone’s curiosity or astonishment raised by it. The reason is that continual use overcomes our attention. Knowing how to procure fire whenever we want it, we are no more concerned than to get those materials that can furnish us with enough of it for all our purposes; thus, day after day, we let pass unnoticed the most *astonishing* of all the elements. Even chemists, who make so much use of fire, have never yet, as I have read, entered further into it than to try its effects and how far it would operate. But now it is found to be compounded of several parts; by the help of an electrical machine, we can analyze it and show all its properties distinctly to the senses.

But as I have here spoken of the chemists, I will mention an incident that happened when I was once trying experiments. A very ingenious chemist being present, I asked him if he would taste the fire; the question startled him, but seeing me do it, he was encouraged to try, but rose from the chair with astonishment. “I taste,” he said, “*an acid*, and now I know what I never could account for before: that it is the *acid* in fire that gives the *spicula* <note>Spicula: Sharp, needle-like points or particles.</note> to *precipitate*.” This observation I thought too curious to omit. But as well as being tasted, the fire may also be smelled, for after a machine has been worked for some time in a closed room, a strong smell of sulfur may be perceived. But no more of this now. I would speak here expressly of fire, and not of its properties.

It was the opinion of the ancients that fire was in everything; indeed, that everything living, whether animal or vegetable, owed its life to it; for this reason, they called it the *anima mundi* <note>Anima mundi: Soul of the world.</note>. From where they got this truth, or from what experiments they drew their conclusions, it is not material to inquire; an electrical machine will verify it to our senses.

Jacob Behmen <note>Jacob Behmen: Also known as Jakob Böhme (1575–1624), a German Christian mystic and theologian.</note> tells us his knowledge of nature was opened in him by God. This is an assertion that many may call his *ipse dixit* <note>Ipse dixit: An unproven assertion; literally, "he himself said it."</note>; be that as it may, it reduces us to this dilemma: either to allow or deny what he says. If we deny it, to what or whom shall we attribute those deep and wonderful discoveries that are to be found in his writings, and which experiment proves to be true? Many have been the abuses poured upon him from every quarter; but which should be most regarded: the ravings of folly, or the evidence of the senses?

Mr. Boyle, in his book on the *Usefulness of Experimental Natural Philosophy*, says, like a man of candor (p. 283), “Perhaps neither nature nor mankind is much indebted to those who too rigidly or narrowly circumscribe or confine the operations of nature, and do not so much as allow themselves or others to try whether it is possible for nature, excited and managed by art, to perform diverse things which they never yet saw done, or work by diverse ways differing from any which, by the common principles taught in the schools, they are able to give a satisfactory account of.”

Jacob Behmen and Mr. Law have written, I own, of nature quite differently from all other writers. But is this a reason for rejecting what they have said? Galileo, the famous inventor of the telescope, for maintaining the Copernican system—a system now generally received—was twice thrown into the prison of the Inquisition as a heretic. But because his persecutors, the Jesuits, did not then believe that the sun was a fixed body and that the earth moved around it, were his assertions any less true? Time and experience have removed this prejudice and fixed the error on the right persons. “One shall rarely meet,” says the author of Galileo’s life, “with a more glaring instance of blindness and bigotry.” To condemn an author because he has written contrary to our preconceived opinion is as good an argument of sound sense and understanding as to pronounce that fruit bad and good for nothing which we have never tasted.

When Jacob Behmen was strictly examined at the Saxon court by men of the greatest learning, professors in every science brought together for this purpose by the Elector, they discovered so much honesty, candor, and good sense that not one of them condemned him, even though he said many things to them far beyond their comprehension. What he declared was from an insight given by God into nature. [His mind stood in the center, and God’s eye opened itself in him, so that he saw with the divine eye.] Now that there is a power in nature always at work is evident from the effects. But what is this power? It is *fire*. The tenderest leaf on the highest tree shows at its furthest part that there is life, but what causes this life? It is *fire*.

But so that no one may say this is my *ipse dixit*, the two following experiments are here introduced so that the senses may have full proof of the assertion:

<margin>X</margin>
(1.) Pluck a branch from any plant, the leaves of which would not be too heavy for the power you are able to raise with your machine, and observe when its leaves begin to droop; at this crisis, place it on your glasses and electrify it, and you will see that the *fire* will have the same effect upon it as when it was growing upon the plant; the *fire* will pervade and circulate through every part of it and make it appear as if it were living.

(2.) Take two plants of equal size and similar appearance in pots; electrify one of them for ten minutes or a quarter of an hour every morning. In a few days, you will see a manifest difference. The electrified plant will outstrip and look much more flourishing than the other. Now, what stronger proof than this can we have that *fire*, as Jacob Behmen and Mr. Law assert, is the *root of life*. In the plant growing in the garden, we can only see the effect of the vivifying power swiftly pervading and rapidly circulating through every part. In the electrified plant, we see the cause as well as perceive the effect of the subtle fluid.

I shall conclude this chapter with a passage from Mr. Law’s ‘Appeal’ relevant to my present subject:—
> “The reader,” (he says,) “ought not to wonder or be offended at the frequent mention of the word *fire*, which is used to denote the true nature and state of the soul. For both *nature and Scripture* continually speak the same language. For wherever there is mention of life, light, or love in the Scripture, there fire is necessarily supposed, as being that in which all life and light and love must necessarily arise; and therefore the Scriptures speak as often of fire as they do of life and light and love, because the one necessarily includes the other. For all life, whether it be *vegetable, sensitive, animal, or intellectual*, is only a kindled fire of life in such a variety of states, and every dead insensitive thing is only so because its fire is quenched or shut up in a hard compression. If, therefore, we will speak of the *true ground* of the fallen state of men and angels, we are not at liberty to think of it under any other idea, or speak of it in any other manner than as the *darkened fire* of their life, unable to kindle itself into light and love. Do not the Scriptures strictly confine us to this idea of hell? So it is not any particular philosophy or affected singularity of expression that makes me speak in this manner of the soul, but because all nature and Scripture force us to confess that the root of all and every life stands, and must necessarily stand, in the *properties of fire*.
>
> “The holy Scriptures also speak much of fire in the ideas which they give us both of the divine nature and of created spirits, whether they be saved or lost: the former as becoming flames of heavenly light and love, the latter as dark firebrands of hell.
> 
> “It should be no reason for us to think *grossly* of fire just because it is seen in so many *gross things* of this world. For how is it seen in them? Why, only as a *destroyer*, a *consumer*, and *refiner* of all grossness, as a kindler of life and light out of death and darkness. So in all the appearances of fire, even in earthly things, we have reason to look upon it as something of a heavenly, exalting, and glorious nature, as that which disperses death, darkness, and grossness, and raises the power and glory of every life.
>
> “There is but *one fire* throughout all nature and creation, existing only in different states and conditions. The fire that is in the *light of the sun* is the same fire that is in the *darkness of the flint*. That fire which is in the life of our bodies is the life of our souls; that which *burns wood* to pieces is the same which *upholds the beautiful forms* of angels. It is the same fire that burns straw that will at last melt the sun; the same fire that brightens a diamond is darkened in a *flint*. It is the same fire that kindles life in an animal that kindled it in angels. In an angel, it is an eternal fire of an eternal life; in an animal, it is the same fire brought into a temporary condition, and therefore can only kindle a life that is temporary; the same fire that is mere wrath in a devil is the sweetness of flaming love in an angel; and the same fire which is the majestic glory of heaven makes the horror of hell.”

*You see that every fire gives light, and you see also that air goes forth from the source of the fire; and you know very well that if the fire had no air to blow it up, it would be smothered, as all fires are smothered when they have no air. Verse 136: You see that all fire must have matter, or else it will not burn; understand it thus: the fire produces air and, in the air, water, and it powerfully attracts the air with the water into itself again, whereby the source of the fire is so calmed that it shines; for without water no fire shines. If no water can be produced in a thing, the fire will not shine in that thing. In the "Book of Regeneration," verse 19: Who would believe that fire generates water and that the origin of fire could be in water, if we did not see it with our eyes in storms of thunder, lightning, and rain; and did not also find that in living creatures the fire in the body dwells in the blood, and that the blood is the mother of the fire, and the fire the father of the blood.*

But Behmen has gone much deeper than this, even to the properties preceding fire, which were shown before in Chapter II and proved by the first experiment. But I would ask here: what is that heat, and from where does it come, that warms the body and by which—for as long as it warms, but no longer—the limbs are enabled to perform their functions? Shall I be answered that it is the blood that causes this internal warmth by its speed, friction, and rubbing through the veins and arteries? But then, what causes this rapid circulation? There must be some power to put the blood in motion. Experiments have now established beyond all doubt that it is fire—the fire of which every rational, animal, and vegetable life consists. But look back to Chapter II, experiments the first and second, and there you will see how the first three properties of nature work, which precede fire. The electrical machine shows our senses that there is a continual inflow and outflow, and that these two opposites, always acting against each other, cause a whirling or circulation, and that this violent motion produces fire. So, wherever there is fire, there is always a *going in and going out* and a whirling around or circulation.

Now, what difficulty is there, after seeing these experiments which show how nature works, to account for the systole and diastole of the heart? For if the soul is a fire—and from where can heat come but from fire?—and if its seat is in the blood of the heart, as Behmen declares, then as long as the soul [or life] continues there, there must be attraction, repulsion, and circulation.

Many had imagined that fire was the cause because they did not know how to account for motion without it; but then, not knowing the nature of fire or that there were any properties in nature preceding it, the more they attempted an explanation, the more they found themselves confused. Eventually, others took up the subject and attempted to explain the systole and diastole of the heart from the pressure of the atmosphere, but with just as little success, for all proceeded on doubtful hypotheses. But what need is there for supposition now? An electrical machine shows us the way nature works. It makes the hidden and invisible fire clear to our senses. And by trying experiments on either the vegetable or human system, we shall find the fire of which the life of each consists to be the same; for if it were a foreign and mismatched fire, it would greatly injure the human frame rather than assist it. It would not mix as naturally as it does with the blood but would instead cause it to boil and do the greatest harm to the constitution, whereas nothing of this is seen. The only change that can be perceived is that it acts as a stimulus and quickens the motion of the blood. The pulse beats a few times more per minute. But the variety of cures that electricity has performed speaks more strongly and loudly for this claim than anything I can possibly say in support of it. I wish I could as easily prove—to prevent the critic's complaints—what I am going further to suggest on the subject: namely, that the redness of the blood, which has puzzled so many, is caused by fire. But what is more likely? If all colors are found by experiments to be contained in light, and if we know of no light without fire, to what else can we with so much reason attribute the redness of the blood? I have never yet found a better cause, but if anyone can show a better one, I will readily and cheerfully give up my conjecture. But alas! How little do we know! What reason the wisest men have to regret their ignorance! What a mystery is *fire!* Who thinks that his life consists of *fire!* How unknown is man to himself! But we see such is the force of some men’s fire that it drives them into depths deeper than they can understand. How many hundreds of books have been written that no one now thinks are worth reading? How many volumes has a plausible hypothesis produced, all of which the next age has soon turned into waste paper? A hypothesis, however pleasing, cannot stand for long. Busy imagination is always at work to pull it down and build something of its own, no more durable, on its ruins. But I will end this digression here, if it is a digression, and proceed to the next chapter to show the usefulness of experiments.

Mr. Boyle, in his tenth essay "Of men’s great ignorance of the uses of natural things," begins his first section with these words:

> "I consider, in the first place, that there are very few of the works of nature that have been sufficiently considered and are thoroughly known, even regarding those qualities and other attributes of this or that body (or other physical thing) which belong properly to it, and are not thought to be so relative to other bodies. It is not only in the earthly globe, but in almost every body to be met with in it, that there may be a kind of *terra incognita* <note>unknown land</note>, or undetected part, whose discovery is reserved for our future diligence."

Now this *terra incognita*, this undetected part, no man more diligently strove to find out than Mr. Boyle; he spent his life trying experiments, fully convinced that they were of the utmost importance for investigating nature. The great Boerhaave was of this same way of thinking. In an oration in 1725, "On the method of obtaining certainty in physics," he asserts that "we are entirely ignorant of the first principles of things, and that all our knowledge of their qualities is derived either from such experiments as subject them to our senses, or from consequences deduced from those experiments by an exact method of reasoning."

But no one was more convinced of the utility of this method than Sir Isaac Newton. But if such improvements in the electrical apparatus had been made in his days as have been made in these, what would they not have enabled him to do? It would have helped him to demonstrate to the sight his attractive and repulsive powers, and saved him the labor of writing so much about them, which only very few capacities have been able to comprehend. Sir Isaac undoubtedly had an uncommon genius; but shall we say he was self-taught regarding his doctrine of attraction and repulsion? Mr. Law knew otherwise and was not afraid to tell the world so. <note>See note, p. 83.</note> Sir Isaac Newton was undoubtedly a *great man*; but he certainly borrowed his attractive and repulsive powers from Behmen; for had he been possessed of instruments, as we now have, by which he could have clearly shown them, he would not have been silent; but it is all too plain he was unwilling to declare from where he had his knowledge. As for Behmen, he honestly and without disguise declares he derived his knowledge from God. And who but God, the author of nature, can unfold the laws of nature?

Now after having mentioned Mr. Boyle, Dr. Boerhaave, and Sir Isaac Newton, it would be doing an injustice to my subject not to mention the ingenious Dr. Watson, who has written on electricity in both experimental and medical ways; the result of his inquiries I find drawn up ready to my hand in a dictionary lately published under the article on electricity.

> "Mr. Watson’s system naturally leads him to ask: by what name shall we call this extraordinary power, based on its effects in these operations? Shall we call it electricity because it is a principle neither generated nor destroyed, because it is everywhere and always present, and ready to show itself in its effects—though latent and unobserved—until it is brought into action and made visible by some process? Because it penetrates and unites itself to the densest and hardest bodies, and because of its immense velocity, shall we—along with Theophrastus, Boerhaave, Nieuenhit, Gravesand, and other philosophers—call it elementary fire? Or shall we—because it contains the substance of light and fire, and because of the extreme smallness of its parts as it passes through most bodies we are acquainted with—name it, with Homberg and the chemists, the chemical sulfurous principle, which according to the doctrine of these gentlemen is universally spread? Whatever we call it, it seems certain that this power has many surprising properties and cannot help but be of great importance in the system of the universe."

—This is by far the best and most rational observation I have ever met with regarding electricity. The *terra incognita*, or undetected part, sought for so long and unsuccessfully by Mr. Boyle, has fortunately been hit upon by Dr. Watson. The power called electrical (a trivial term we are obliged to submit to through custom) is indeed of the greatest importance in the structure of the universe. This I have already demonstrated through several clear and convincing experiments. I would only further observe here that this power or principle is truly everywhere, though unobserved, and that it is not "generated" when made visible by experiments any more than fire can be said to be generated from the collision of a flint and steel; for if there were no fire within them, we might strike forever, but never produce it.

Do we need to spend any more time guessing from where the fire shall come that will cause the final conflagration? Some have supposed that it will happen by fire from heaven. Some believe there is a central fire that will burst forth. And others think it is more likely to happen from a fiery comet. But all these are weak conjectures and cannot be supported. However, experiments have now released us from these uncertainties; they discover and manifest to our senses such a plenty of fire that we know of no place, nor anything, in which it is not to be found. Now, this horrid state—miserable beyond description—must be yours if you die <note>without being regenerated in the essence of your soul, thereby</note> refusing the light of God.

I will now attempt to explain what causes the shock we feel when electrified:
By the first and second experiments in chapter two, the eye has clear proof that there are in nature two powers diametrically opposite to each other; these powers never cease working in this manner, but the opposition brings forth another motion, namely, a whirling round. Now, whoever comes within the circle made by a chain or wire between the bottom and top of a charged jar will feel a shock or stroke as if a bystander had struck him. This stroke clearly occurs from the two contending powers; for passing contrary ways with such sudden swiftness and power through the body, they distend the vessels. This sudden and quick distention causes the sensation so much like an unexpected blow. Small animals killed by electricity show this beyond contradiction. Their vessels, being too delicate to bear the power of the shock, immediately burst.
I conclude by sharing the invention of a planetarium, which curiously shows the motions of the planets:
I have a round table, the diameter of which is nearly three feet, and the height twenty inches. In the middle of this table, I place a round, well-polished plate of pewter, eighteen inches in diameter. On this plate, I place six brass orbits, fastened to one another in such a manner that six glass balls, about three-quarters of an inch in diameter, can easily run between the orbits. Under the edge of the outside orbit, I put four supporters of sealing-wax to raise the orbits above the pewter plate, so that the glass balls may just touch the inside edges of the orbits and have nothing to hinder their revolving. Over the orbits, at a distance of about two feet, I suspend a gilded copper globe, about nine inches in diameter, to represent the sun. From this, I fasten to one of the orbits a wire as small as a hair; then by means of another small wire, reaching from the conductor to the gilded globe, I communicate the fire to it. From the globe, it passes by the wire to the orbits, and from the orbits to the balls, which, being caught between the contending powers, are put in motion and driven round swiftly between the orbits. But at the same time that they run between the orbits, they also revolve on their axes, so that two motions are communicated to them; and besides this, one half of the balls is illuminated.

Page 301. Q. 2. *How do they conceive of the union of the Godhead with humanity?* A. As a union between the soul and spirit. *Not* that they would compare the Godhead in Christ to the spirit of man, and his humanity to the soul; but only to say by this, that just as the union of these two makes up one single perfect intellectual being, which cannot be made up by either of them alone, so the union of the Godhead with humanity makes up the only personal second Adam and mediator between God and man, which cannot be formed by either of them alone. Man had wandered away from the love of God, and a real separation was made between them: a real reconciliation and reunion, therefore, was necessary, if man were not to be lost forever. But seeing that in man there was no power to reconcile and unite himself to God again, God therefore—not as Father (because men *belonged* to the Father already, and had fallen, moreover, into the Father's fiery center), but as Son (because he is the Father's light and love, which man greatly needed after his fall)—had to unite himself to humanity. This was not only to reconcile his children to the light world by his sufferings and death, but also to be their head and king, etc.: all of which required such a personal union of the Godhead with humanity as we may conceive between the spirit, soul, and body.

Page 301. Q. 3. *Since the Divine essence is everywhere the same, wherein lies the difference of its union with Christ from its union with any other man or creature?* A. It is true that the Divine essence is everywhere the same, but only in itself, without regard to man or other creatures; for with respect to them, it is notorious that it is not everywhere the same—that is, it is not equally manifest in all of them, nor does it communicate itself to all of them in the same manner and degree. Otherwise, all men would be equal in knowledge, sanctification, glory, etc., and no different degrees could be found between them. Therefore, that there is and must be a difference cannot be anything but plain; and that this difference lies chiefly in this, that this union is a personal union, is also evident: for the God-man, Jesus Christ, is one individual person, and a person in the Holy Trinity—indeed, the only person, seeing that without him we cannot conceive of another person in the Trinity, according to the common definition we have of this name. But such a thing cannot be said of any other man, no matter how highly united to God. Another difference the Scripture shows us by saying that *in him the fullness of the Godhead dwells, and that in him all the treasures of wisdom lie:* which cannot be said of any other angel or man, but all have only their particular gifts according to the measure of their capacities, and as their different offices and stations require.

But if the machine in this experiment could be kept out of sight, the beholders would be greatly astonished; but while they see the apparatus, they are apt to conclude that it is the cause, whereas the machine is only instrumental. After these extracts, and the references made in them and previously to the authors who wrote upon the science in its infancy, as also to the treatises of Behmen, in which it lies hidden and apparent to the understanding eye, it will be unnecessary on the present occasion to attempt a full or further resolution of the point in question; but it may suffice to direct the ingenious reader who feels interested in it how to pursue the inquiry. Therefore, such a person, having as a groundwork a familiar acquaintance with the principles of Law and Behmen (to which such a clear introduction is provided in the present treatise, and without which he will be unqualified to pursue such research), is now recommended to read Lovett's very interesting work, the 'Electrical Philosopher,' 8vo. 1774, and also his 'Philosophical Essays,' 8vo. 1766, and the writings of the authors referred to in those treatises. And the result will undoubtedly be a conviction similar to that experienced by the writer of these lines: that the philosophical discoveries of the last century, in connection with the above-mentioned branch of science, are to be traced for their source to the work of Mr. Law now under consideration, namely, the 'Appeal,' along with his other described accompanying writings.

How is the second person in the Trinity more united to the human nature than the Father and the Holy Ghost?* Answer: Just as the light is more united to the <term>light-world</term> than the fire; for though we are not to think of any division or separation, yet from the light immediately, and not from the fire, the <term>light-world</term> has its name and properties. But, to sum up these observations, should the reader desire to obtain a just apprehension of the truth of things, and consequently a full view of the nature, imperfections, and deficiencies of all the popular systems of philosophy, he must, in the first place, learn to understand the “three principles of the Divine manifestation.” Without this, however learned he may be, either in philosophy or divinity, he will conceive of nature and divine truth only as the blind do of colors. Secondly, he will then apprehend how body is, in all worlds, the manifestation of spirit; and that nothing lives or moves in all the universe but spirit alone. Thirdly, he will understand what the dead and living materiality of this world is, and how it originated. Fourthly, he will then understand what the elastic medium of unexcited <term>electricity</term> is, namely, the womb or ground of the four elements, and of all temporal creaturely life and materiality, as of paradise itself. No. 2. *God has no consultation within himself, etc.* Although this may be sufficient for those who understand <term>Behmen</term>’s ground, it is not so for others; for it is only an assertion without a reason or demonstration. Therefore, I think the reason which <term>Behmen</term> gives might well be added, namely: *If God (here considered [N.B.] as in himself only, without any will toward nature and creature) had a consultation within himself, there must be something before, behind, or beside him about which he consulted; there must be a cause moving him to this consultation, and a beginning of it; there must also be thoughts and a variety of different conceptions in him, making such or such images and representations of things, and comparisons of this method with that, until one was found in which this or that could best be performed, etc.* But now, since he is in himself alone an universal all, will, power, sufficiency, ground, beginning, and end of all things, without any alteration, no such thing has any place in him. This reason, I think, is the more necessary to be added, and expressed as significantly as possible, because it is certain that if this is not well understood and kept in mind, there can never be a true understanding of <term>Behmen</term>’s sense.

No. 4. *God, as manifested, eternally willed or purposed, and eternally generated a root of evil.* This position is not consistent with <term>Behmen</term>; and although there is added immediately, *which being good in itself, etc.* yet this cannot rectify what is wrong in it. (Though we do not say that this latter was generated from such a purpose, or directly to that end; but we can give another substantial reason why it must have been generated as it was.) > “ Philadelphia, Dec. 18th. 1767.—My dear sir,—I thank you sincerely for your kind and affectionate letter. Your letter, therefore, was in every respect favorable to my wishes; and I flatter myself that I shall be indulged with a continuance of your favors. My heart has for some years been deeply sensible of a fallen state, and I long groaned for deliverance from the bondage of my earthly life. I saw clearly that physical and moral evil were predominant in the present state of things, and that the whole human race were involved in a situation which I could not reconcile with the wisdom, goodness, and justice of God in creating them. The Christian religion seemed to me covered with darkness and difficulty; I read most of the deistical writers, and most of the answers to them. I was sometimes a deist and sometimes a Christian. I never could understand the doctrine of the trinity; and had an irreconcilable aversion to the systematical notion of atonement and satisfaction. A wrathful God, whose anger could only be appeased by the blood of his own Son, poured out in behalf of sinners, always appeared to me next to blasphemous.
