*Page 302.* This other question is proposed, pertaining to this: *But how will you avoid the consequences charged upon the <term>reprobatists</term>, if you assert that God, etc.* Answer: If <term>Behmen</term> asserts that *God as manifested*, or *God's eternal nature*, or *his formed word in eternal nature, willed and generated evil*, it will be true that the consequences charged upon the <term>reprobatists</term> <note>believers in the doctrine of unconditional reprobation or predestined damnation</note> cannot be avoided. But if it can be shown that no such thing is asserted by <term>Behmen</term>, then no such question can be proposed. And seeing this question as proposed depends only upon the previous erroneous position, No. 4, namely, *God as manifested, eternally willed or purposed, and eternally generated a root of evil*, which position is justly denied and corrected; this question, therefore, would not require any further answer, if <term>Behmen</term>'s ELECTION, Chapter 6, verse 82, etc., were not quoted, and the expression of a *formed word* did not need to be cleared up: so that it may be demonstrated that <term>Behmen</term> asserts no such thing as this question mentions. Let us see then what he says in Chapter 6, verse 82, etc. I cannot find (and I am sure it cannot be found in any other place throughout all his writings) that he says, *God as manifested, or God's eternal nature, or his formed word in eternal nature, willed and generated evil*. He does say this last part, it is true, in almost those exact words, but in no such sense as could result in those consequences that are charged upon the <term>reprobatists</term>, which shall be evidenced shortly. His own words relating to this matter are these—*In whatever has severed itself into the good, in that he wills the good; and in whatever has separated itself into the evil, in that he wills the evil; as the Scripture says, Such as the people are, such a god they have.* These words he explains according to his gift in the following positions and expressions—*All beginnings, decrees, and predetermined purposes arise in the formed word through nature. All evil proceeds from and out of nature and creature. The hardening in nature and creature originates in the knowledge or root of the creaturely self, so that if it turns itself into the wrath of nature, then it is laid hold of and hardened in it. All that where it is written, He hardens their hearts, etc., is performed and effected in the formed word of the eternal and temporary nature.* Now let us in the first place inquire: what is it that he calls the *formed word*? He answers himself in Chapter 6, verse 104, *Adam is the outspoken, formed, creaturely word, and in this* (not outside, but in this) *formed word, evil is willed and generated.* But how, by whose instinct or direction, and by what means? Has God, as manifested, willed evil, and so that he might execute his will, put such a will to evil into this formed word? Or has he generated evil through it, as through or by his instrument? No; God forbid. Has God's eternal nature willed it, and has this generated evil in this formed word? No; far be this also. Has then this formed word itself willed and generated evil? Yes; but not in the sense that this expression might be and is taken in this question, and which could produce such consequences as are charged upon the <term>reprobatists</term>. Well, what is then the meaning of this expression? Answer: This is the meaning: this formed word, namely, *Adam*, not as he was formed by God—*in*, as it is said here, or *out of*, as it might be better phrased—but as he departed from that formation, or in his departing from the order of eternal nature, willed and generated evil. From what root, and by what means? Answer: Out of the root of his own free will, and by means of his own misuse of it. And that this is the only origin of evil, and its efficient cause, is <term>Behmen</term>'s constant doctrine, and was rightly asserted as such in the last words of the fourth position. If, then, it is not God, nor eternal nature, but only man misusing his free will (which in the knowledge or root of the creaturely self <note>N.B. (Note Well)</note> is prior or antecedent to the acts and deeds of his own formed human nature) who has willed and generated evil contrary to the will of God and contrary to the order of nature, what consequence can be drawn from this and charged either upon God or his eternal nature? Truly, the sun cannot be clearer or more blameless than this assertion is. If anyone should object and say, "If God had not given man a free will, he could not have misused it; and therefore, the giver is the cause of the mischief done by this misuse," I think he would not be worthy of being answered further (though <term>Behmen</term> has answered sufficiently) than by telling him the words of Scripture: *Woe to him who says to his Maker, Why have you made me thus?* But here it will now be asked: Why then does <term>Behmen</term> say so expressly, *All evil proceeds from and out of nature and creature?* Is this not to charge nature as well as the creature? Providence at length made me acquainted with Mr. <term>Law</term>'s writings; and here the grand <term>desideratum</term> <note>essential thing or desire</note> was found. His ‘Address to the Clergy’ was the first of his books that fell into my hands. I took it up with much prejudice in my mind against the author, whom I had always heard spoken of as an enthusiast. But I had not read half the pamphlet before my heart was visited with such sensations as I never felt before. My mind, which had until then been unsettled, dark, doubting, and yet anxious to find the truth, became serene, calm, and sweetly composed. I felt as if I had entered another world, with a new set of ideas, notions, and sensibilities. I was happy beyond expression. I had found my God; I had found my Redeemer; I had found the origin and source of my disorder, and the only means of consolation and a perfect cure. Since this blessed period, all my doubts and difficulties have left me. I see plainly that there is no other road to heaven but that which was trod by Jesus Christ himself; *the same process must every individual of our fallen race pass through, before we can ascend with him to the heaven of heavens—a painful process, it is true;—self-denial, mortification, total contempt of the world, and death of the outward life, accompanied by earnest and continual prayer, are the only method by which we are to be divested of our fallen, and clothed with our redeemed life.* The purifying fire, light, and spirit of heaven must consume the animal nature and change it into a cloud of glory, a white robe, and a house not built with hands. <meta>This page continues the theological argument that God is not the author of evil, asserting that evil originates solely from the creature's misuse of free will, while also providing a personal account of a student’s journey from traditional scholasticism to mystical philosophy.</meta>

does not contradict by this saying what was said above—namely, that all evil proceeds out of man’s misusing his free will. A hundred places of his can plainly show that his meaning is not that evil lay in eternal nature, much less that God has laid it there and willed or intended that man should bring it forth from it, as he may bring forth the poison out of an adder, where it lay before. Rather, it means that man brought the evil into his own nature out of his own will. God’s eternal nature is all order, regularity, and harmony; and so was man’s formed nature also: no evil lay in either one. But in man’s free will lay the possibility of misusing it; which also was not evil, and would never have been evil (for it was essential to the will’s freedom) if it had not gone out into an action of misuse. This free will, in its deepest root, is naturally prior (as mentioned above) to the acts or workings of man’s nature. When, therefore, this received the first subtle inclination to turn away from the regularity and harmony of God’s eternal nature and his own formed nature, the evil was conceived in the womb of that free will. This turning consequently broke the order of nature and made it all irregular; and then, in this now broken nature, the evil was generated and went forth in act and deed. And so it was introduced into nature, and nevertheless proceeds also now out of nature. Therefore, man’s formed nature (and much less God’s eternal nature) cannot be charged with being the origin of evil; but only man, or the creature Lucifer before man, must be charged with having misused his free will and disturbed the order of nature. This disturbance is itself the chief evil and did not lie beforehand in nature, which never would have broken nor disturbed itself. And therefore, to show that no evil proceeds from God, Behmen joins nature and creature together and says it proceeds from them. Not from nature as it is regular and harmonious in God and holy angels, and as it was in man—as if this had any evil in it or were or could be an origin of evil (for the free will is deeper and prior to all the acts of nature)—but from nature as it is now turned upside down by man’s misusing his free will. If, then, man’s own nature, before being disordered, cannot be charged with an evil intent or purpose, how much less can God’s eternal nature be charged with such an evil thing?

This, I think, is clear enough to answer the question concerning the consequences charged upon the <term>Reprobatists</term>. But there is still something remaining, namely these words of Behmen: *In whatever has separated itself into the evil, therein he wills the evil*. This will still be a stumbling block to those who do not understand, according to Behmen's gift and declaration, what God is, but always imagine and frame, as he says, some strange thing far off when they speak of God. To represent his sense intelligibly to such people will be the most difficult, if not an impossible, thing. Yet I will, in the name of God, endeavor to do something for the sake of brevity in these following positions: — I conceive with Behmen, and know it is his mind,

1. That **God is love**: and that this definition, given to us by the Spirit of love in St. John, is the most beneficial and the only sufficient one for a true Christian; who, in all his way homeward to his Father, where he shall meet with many trials, is to own, to adore, and to worship in spirit and in truth no other God but **love**.

2. That, notwithstanding this definition, there are many things not attributable to love, and yet attributed to God in plain expressions of the Scripture.

3. That therefore, only for the sake of our own better understanding, we may use the name "God" when we speak of our only adorable good, which is **love**. And when we meet with anything different from, inconsistent with, or contrary to the properties of love and light, we may use either that of **universal being**, or also that of wrath and fire, according to the requirements and different conditions of the subject matter.

4. That this distinction between God and universal Being, or between light and fire, love and wrath—as it did not exist before, nor in the creation of angels, but came in only by their fall—does not make a division in God the universal Being, but is only to be referred to the division made in the creatures. It is nevertheless attributable to God so far as the creature's existence necessarily depends upon God's being, as shall further appear. Attributable, I say, because it is actually attributed to him in the Scripture, calling him in plain words not only **light and love**, but also a **consuming fire**.

5. That in God, as he is love, all his obedient creatures live, and move, and have their being; but that a creature may rebel against God (that is, against love) and may cease to live and move and have its being in God (that is, in love).

6. That no creature, though rebellious, may cease to live and move and have its being in God (that is, in the universal Being).

7. That if the creature ceases to live and move and have its being in love, which is its heaven, it must necessarily at that same instant begin to live and move and have its being in wrath, which is its hell.

I have taken the liberty to lay my thoughts in this short, disorganized manner before you, so that you might see whether they correspond with your own, and how far the mystical writers have contributed to satisfy my mind by directing me to a right pursuit of truth. I had all the advantages of a liberal education that this country and England together could afford, having begun my studies at the college in this city and finished them in the usual way at Clare Hall, in the university of Cambridge. I was always dissatisfied with the philosophy of our schools, and metaphysics, though a favorite study, appeared to me quite superficial in the way they are commonly taught. I now see in what points they failed, and how far short they stopped in their inquiries after the truth. They had no ground and bottom to stand upon, and in metaphysics as well as divinity, they greatly erred in the very first setting off. For what true philosophy or sound divinity could be expected from two such senseless and absurd opinions as are universally maintained in all modern systems, namely: a world created out of nothing, and a wrathful God. But I will say no more. * * *

8. That God is in hell as well as in heaven, which the Scripture tells us expressly; and from this expression, it is evident that the name "God" is taken with different meanings in the Scripture. For God, according to St. John’s definition, is not in hell, because love cannot be in hell, just as wrath cannot be in heaven. If, then, the words of the scripture in PSALM 139:8 are true, telling us God is in hell, he must be there as he is a <term>universal Being</term>; or as <term>Behmen</term> <note>Jacob Boehme</note> declares it, He is manifest in hell as well as in heaven, yet not in the same manner of manifestation, but in each according to its state; so that in heaven is his love, and in hell his wrath.

9. That all the evil spirits have forsaken God, have departed and broken off from God, and have left their first home in God—that is, in the love and light.

10. That the evil spirits have not departed, nor can they be broken off from God—that is, from the <term>universal Being</term>; and they can never leave their home, or their living, moving, and having their being within it. But they are still in God, though not in his love and light, and he is still in them, but not in the way he was in them at their first creation.

11. That, therefore, there is still a bond between God and the evil spirits; yet not that bond of perfection which is love, but an unbreakable bond, tying and keeping them together. This bond consists of the fact that their created being so depends upon God’s universal Being that it could not exist, even for one moment, if God’s being should or could withdraw from them.

12. That this bond is what keeps them still in subjection, so that they must be obedient even against their will and without their knowledge; they must, by constraint, do his will according to that world into which they have fallen—even that will of his which is manifest in the wrath. They have made themselves subjects and slaves to this wrathful will by departing from the freedom of the sons of God.

13. That this bond implies a manifestation of God, the <term>universal Being</term>, in them, and an influence upon them according to what they have made themselves capable of. So it is a fundamental truth: in whatever intellectual creature God is not manifest and influencing it according to his love, in that same creature he must be manifest and influencing it according to his wrath. Because they cannot be broken off from his universal being, they must live, move, and have their Being either in his love or in his wrath.

14. That love and wrath were not both manifest before, nor during the creation of angels, but only love. Therefore, the wrath had no will or power then, except *in potentia* <note>potentially</note>, and upon the assumption of being stirred up by the creature; for it never would nor could have raised itself up. But now, after being raised up in and by the creature, it has a will as well as love, and a power of influencing whatever it can reach.

15. That this raising up of the wrath, and giving it a will and power, did not tear the will of love in two, nor create two contrary wills in God, who is only good. Instead, it only opened a twofold door and way in the <term>formed word</term> of God, or in the creature. In this way, that single will of God which he had in the creation—namely, that he will be glorified in his creatures—is now performed in two ways and in two contrary worlds: he is now glorified not only in the salvation of his children but also in the destruction of his enemies, according to the plain expressions of Scripture.

16. That the fact that this twofold door was not opened by God, nor decreed and predetermined by him to be opened by the creature, gives sufficient evidence that God was not manifest and had no will in the wrath before and during the creation of angels; nor did he ever will or purpose to be manifest or to have a will in it. For if he had, he would have willed or purposed that his own will be broken, which would truly be to make two contrary wills in God.

17. That <term>Behmen</term> <note>Jacob Boehme</note>, therefore, instructs us correctly by saying that all the decrees and purposes, reprobations, hardenings of heart, etc., do not originate in God before and apart from the creature, but in the <term>formed word</term>, or in the creature, after it has misused its free will and separated itself into evil.

18. That, now that this door of wrath is open, God is manifest and has a will within it. For although the act of manifestation and its effects belong to the creature and are in the creature, yet the wrath is his. It is not outside but within the scope of his universal Being, from which the creature cannot be broken off and without which it can have no existence. The wrath, indeed, is not in him as he is our God, according to St. John’s definition: for then hell would be heaven and heaven would be hell; but it is in his universal Being, which contains all things and without which nothing can exist. For the properties of nature, ignited in the creature, are his, and so the wrath is his, according to the plain words of the Scripture. He is in it, though his love is not in it, and he is its ruler, disposer, and the one who pours it forth. *A fire is kindled, he says* (namely, by the creature;

18. (For he does not say, "I have kindled it"), and shall *burn to the lowest hell*. And again, *See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no God with me: I kill, and I make alive*, etc. Pray, who is this *I*? Truly it is not God in love, as he was only so before and during the creation of angels; for love does not kill. Nor is it God in wrath, for wrath does not make alive; and yet it is God, even he with whom there is no other God. It is God, therefore, in his <term>universal Being</term>: for he contains and speaks of both love and wrath, and both life and death, or heaven and hell; in both of which He is now manifest, and has a will and power, because the creature, by misusing its free will, has separated itself into evil.

19. Regarding this wrath and wrathful will, it can be rightly said: In whatever creature God is manifest in wrath, in that creature he cannot will nor do what he can and will do in another creature where he is manifest in love. This is because wrath cannot will and do what love wills and does; otherwise it would not be wrath, but love—and *the reverse is also true*.

20. This willing and doing in the wrath exists indeed in the creature only, and not outside of it, and is originally the creature’s. This is because not only was the wrath powerless before and during the creation of angels, but it is also still powerless in itself; it has no will or power except in the creature, and even in the creature no further than it is given life and empowered by the creature's own will and self-action.

->But,<-

21. Nevertheless, this willing and doing in the wrath is also attributable to God, as he is a <term>universal Being</term>: (1) because of that bond and dependence of the creature's being upon his being, as spoken of above. (2) Because the wrath is his, and was his from eternity, before it was wrath, and when it was sealed up among his secret treasures. (3) Because many things are said in Scripture about the wrath and are expressly attributed to God.

22. Just as in the kingdom of love and light, its inhabitants cannot work without the cooperation of the Holy Spirit of God (which is raised in them by their own act of humbling themselves, so that all their works—as also all our good works in this mixed world—are the works of God, though they are also truly the works of those who are his active instruments); so also in the kingdom of wrath and darkness, its prisoners cannot work without the cooperation of the spirit of wrath. This spirit is raised and empowered in them by their own act of exalting themselves, so that all their works are indeed truly and properly their own—in fact, much more their own than in the kingdom of light. And yet, in some sense and respect, they are also the works of the wrathful Spirit of God and of those dark properties of nature to which they have made themselves subject. This is because there is no living or moving, neither in this kingdom nor in that, without the *spirit* of this kingdom, or of *that*.

23. These words of the Apostle, *To whom you yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants you are*, etc., though spoken by him in reference to another matter, are also rightly applicable here. Just as they are now true in a particular sense regarding the mixed multitude of Adam’s children, so they were also true in substance from the beginning in a more general sense. Indeed, the truth of these words is passed down to all the children of man even from the beginning of Lucifer's fall.

24. Therefore, just as a servant either does his master's will freely or must do it by constraint, so in both these kingdoms the will of the spirit that is master there is done. However, there is this great difference: in the kingdom of light, the will of the Holy Spirit of God is done freely, willingly, and joyfully, through that innate principle of love which the holy angels adhered to from their creation in full obedience and resignation. But in the kingdom of wrath, the will of the wrathful spirit of God is done in trembling and, in a sense, by constraint. For though it is truly and most properly their own will which the devils do—because it is not the will of God, in and for which they were created, but a will they raised up in and of themselves from their own foundation and endeavored to execute, as they still do—yet this expression "their own will" does not make them absolute or sovereign lords and masters of the kingdom of wrath. Rather, they are only servants of it and prisoners within it. For by their own will, they have manifested and empowered the wrathful spirit of God; they have yielded themselves up in obedience to him, and they must do his will continually, even in and by the doing of their own will.

25. Accordingly, God, as love, wills and works nothing in the devil, and the devil works nothing in God, because he has separated himself from God and is dead to love; thus, that bond or communion of willing and working in the light that existed between them at their creation is broken. But the devil, who is a living and active creature, wills and works in the wrath of God, and the wrath or wrathful Spirit wills and works in the devil, because it lives and is manifest in him, ruling over him like a master over his servants or a jailer over his prisoners. There is now a bond or communion of willing and working between them because when that first bond in the light was broken, this other bond in the darkness must necessarily have been—

26. That this willing and working in the wrath, considered from the creature's side, consists chiefly in this: that the creature, having departed from the will and work of love, having rejected the influence and cooperation of the holy Spirit of God, and having turned itself into the dark wrathful properties of nature, still moves and acts in them. It forms innumerable strange, false, monstrous, and lying forms or images—in thoughts, words, and deeds—which are all absolutely evil, without any limitation, and are mere abominations to the holy will and Spirit of God in the kingdom of love and light.

27. That this willing and working in the wrath, as far as it is attributable to God (as he is manifest within it, and whose wrath it is), consists not only in this: that the active and restless properties of wrath—which are, and must be, subservient to his manifestation in light and love—exert their own natural powers in the creatures fallen into them, and give them continually food and, as it were, materials for their forming and imaging; but also in this: that the Spirit of this wrathful kingdom (who is the Spirit of God, the very same who in the kingdom of love is the Holy Spirit, but in this kingdom is manifest as a Spirit of the fiery anger of God) delights, strengthens, and exalts himself within it, and wills that it shall be so, that he may manifest and show forth through them the wonders of this kingdom. Just as we might imagine in an earthly analogy, that an ignited fire delights in dry wood, strengthens and elevates itself within it, and wills—or naturally inclines—to have such fuel continually, so that it may have something to consume and to show forth its power; all in direct opposition to the kingdom of light and love.

28. That all this, on the side of God, as manifested in the wrath, is good, and no evil may be found in it, though it is the highest evil of punishment to the creature. For in this his justice is manifest, giving to each creature, in due measure and right proportion, not only what it deserves, but also what it wills and what it still makes for itself; for the works of their hands are their food. And this justice is as good in and to him as his mercy, though not so to the creature; indeed, it is as essential to him and as inseparable from him on this side of the evil creature's own will, as his love and mercy are on the other side of the creature's good, resigned will. In this also, the wonders of the deep beneath are brought forth into manifestation, and thereby the great and holy name of God is magnified and exalted, even by this, contrary to their will and without their understanding it—though the creatures, as much as they are able, intend to revile and blaspheme it. Therefore Boehme <note>Behmen</note> rightly says that just as the holy angels praise God freely in his love and light, so the devils must praise him in his wrath, though not intending to do so.

desire that his widow should choose a retired and religious life; and, in recommending it to her, stated that he knew no person who would be so likely to prove beneficial and agreeable to her in such respect as his friend Mr. Law, if she could be situated within reach of his society.

To fulfill the last counsels of her affectionate husband was the early endeavor of Mrs. Hutcheson; and after some little delay and correspondence with Mr. Law, a plan was proposed by the latter to Miss Hester Gibbon. Miss Gibbon was as yet without any fixed plan of life and, it would appear, looked up to Mr. Law as her confidential friend, whereby her own private wishes and the objective of Mrs. Hutcheson might equally be attained. The two ladies consenting to live together, he took a house for them at Thrapstone, a small market town in Northamptonshire about ten miles from King's Cliffe, where he was now settled. Here, in the summer of 1743, they took up their residence, but remained only a short time, not finding the situation altogether suited to their tastes. Mr. Law then suggested that King's Cliffe might prove a more agreeable retreat and also better adapted to their views and intentions, being a much larger place and having more poor people within it. For it was their design, among other good works in which they proposed to employ their fortunes (following the counsels of the *Serious Call*), to establish schools for the clothing and education of the children of the poor, as well as the continual relief of poverty and want. They acquiescing in this proposal, Mr. Law refitted a roomy house in a part of the town called the "Hall Yard," already mentioned as the ancient site of the palace of King John. And here, in the following year, 1744, the two ladies joined their good friend and spiritual adviser, being now settled down for the remainder of their lives. This house belonged to Mr. Law, having, it is said, been the property of his father; ~~and at his death, he bequeathed it, with all his other effects,~~ to Miss Gibbon. It had a good garden attached and a field of pasture ground; at the extreme point of the latter, at about a quarter of a mile distance, stand the small almshouses which he built. Some adjoining land was purchased and added to it at different times by Miss Gibbon, and the whole was bequeathed by her to Mr. William Law, the son of Mr. Law's nephew, a solicitor, who, dying unmarried, bequeathed it to his brother Mr. Thomas Law, the father of the present worthy possessor of the estate.

Shortly after their arrival in the same year, Mrs. Hutcheson planted an acorn in one corner of the garden attached to the house, which grew up and is now a towering oak, measuring about four yards around the trunk and the largest tree in the neighborhood. This fine tree is said to have been visited from time to time by noblemen and gentlemen to ascertain the size to which an oak would grow in half or three-quarters of a century, with the view of planting a park or forest of such trees; though one must take into account the special care which had been bestowed upon this particular tree, of which, by the nature of things, forest trees must be deprived.

Page 302. Q. 2. *How shall we know when the word "God" in Scripture signifies God only, and when it signifies (his) nature*? A. If Behmen is understood concerning these two different considerations of *God*, it can be known without great difficulty, at least for the most part (yet only according to the measure of that understanding), which of the words of the *Scripture* are to be referred to the former, and which of them to the latter. For though *God*, as he is in himself only, without all nature and creature, is not an object of our understanding; and though, therefore, the *Scripture* does not instruct us directly on this point by telling and declaring what he is, yet it tells us that he is. There are places in the *Scripture* in which one thing or expression may belong to the former, another to the latter, and a third to both, in a different sense. But I do not think that any place may be found which only and altogether may be referred to the former; though there are many that only and altogether belong to the latter. For this is certain, and may be a sure and constant rule: that all the places and expressions wherein *God* is spoken of with relation to creatures, especially to men—so that either he is represented to them as their loving *God* and *Father*, as their *King* and *Lawgiver*, as their dreadful judge, etc., or they are instructed concerning his Divine attributes of righteousness, justice, mercy, omniscience, long-suffering, fatherly care and providence, etc.—and case would necessarily require.

As near as can be determined, the annual income of *Mrs. Gibbon* was from five to seven hundred pounds, and that of *Mrs. Hutcheson* about two thousand pounds; none of which, it is believed, was retained or allowed to accumulate. As the expenditure within the house was remarkably frugal, the spending outside must have been great; so great, indeed, as to make those at *Cliffe*, who remembered *Mr. Law* and his companions, say in relating it to parties still living there, that their acts of charity were boundless. The report of such generosity spread to places far from *Cliffe* and produced applications from many whose wants were of a different character than those of food and clothing; who were often gratified by charitable donations.

The domestic arrangements of the establishment being completed, *Mrs. Hutcheson*, under the advice and superintendence of *Mr. Law*, immediately set about the building and foundation of the *Charities* already described, the first of which was completed before the close of the ensuing year, 1745. The following particular account of it, taken from the printed original, may be deemed of interest here:—

### CHAPTER I.—It is thought proper to set forth this short account of these *Charitable Foundations* for several reasons:

(1.) That our present worthy and much-esteemed Trustees, who have had the goodness to accept the care and protection of them, may, by this little abstract of the state, nature, and appointment of these *Charities*, have as little trouble as possible in acquainting themselves with all that is material in them, and have a full and certain insight into all the particulars of the destination.

(2.) That succeeding Trustees, as vacancies shall happen, may at their first entrance upon the trust—without the trouble of reading and searching through the long deeds of settlement—know all that is material in them, and have a full and certain insight into all the particulars of the nature and constitution of the several *Charities* which, by their election, they take upon themselves to keep up in their true uses and operation.

(3.) That hereby, as much as possible, all deviation from the first, true, and legally established order of these *Foundations*—which length of time is apt to produce in most things—may be prevented; there being a considerable number of these little printed books to be carefully preserved for the future, one of which is constantly to be given to every new Trustee at the time of his election.

(4.) That the *Town of King’s Cliffe*, for whose sole benefit these several *Charities* are established, may be fully acquainted with all that is granted and given to them in the original Deeds of these *Foundations*; both as to the nature, place, and value of the Estates, and the several uses to which they are appointed.

That by this means they may become true and proper witnesses of the right use and application of these *Charities*; and also be enabled how to complain, and where to seek for redress, if in later times any misapplication of them should happen.

Page 302. *Q. last. How can you avoid the texts in Scripture, which attribute reprobation to God himself?* A. No text in Scripture attributes reprobation to God as he is in himself only, without nature and creature; and though the Scripture does not determine this so expressly by saying—"God as in nature and creature," yet (1.) the whole series and linked harmony of the truth in its particulars, and (2.) also the various senses in which we cannot deny that the word "God" is used in Scripture, sufficiently prove this assertion. Let us not stick to words and notions, but consider only and even simply, without subtleties, *what reprobation is.* We shall find it is an essential shutting up of the kingdom of light and love, and an excluding of the creature from it; implying that the creature has been there, and presupposing that it is no longer capable of it, or no longer fit to dwell there any longer. Now where is that text in Scripture that asserts either that God willed or purposed in himself from eternity, before the creature existed, that it should be excluded from having communion with him in his kingdom of light, love, and glory? Or that he himself, by his own doing, has cast the creature out and shut the door upon it? Does not the Scripture plainly tell us that angels and man were created to have communion with God, and to praise him in his light and glory? That the devil did not stand or remain in the truth, but left his habitation in the light; and that man lost his paradisiacal state by the devil’s cunning craft and his own sinful lust? Truly, we must take this to be the first action on the creature’s side; and then we may take that other to be the consequence of it, which the Scripture tells us was done by God: namely, the devil was cast out, and his place was no more found in heaven, and Adam was driven out of the garden. As no man of any sound sense can make this latter act the foundation and the former the superstructure, so also no man can separate these two from one another; but both together in conjunction are or make up what we call *reprobation.* This, in substance and reality, is nothing else but that God, who before was manifest in the creature in his love, becomes now manifest there in wrath; because (1.) the creature in its own will is no longer capable of his manifestation in love, and (2.) because without him, as manifested either in love or wrath, there is for the creature no living, moving, nor having any being. From all this it is evident that reprobation is to be attributed much more to the creature than to God, and to God as he is without the creature, not at all. If we would consider man especially, whom both election and reprobation concern, the matter would be even more evident. But not to run out into this wide, open field, I shall say only this in short, according to Behmen’s declaration: Adam, with all his posterity, was to be as a harmonious instrument, which the Spirit of love manifest in him would play upon; and as to his own person, he was actually made and prepared so. But the spirit of this world creeping in, disordered its strings (the pro-

### Page 303. No. 5.

The reason for what is asserted in this position, declared in these last words, *because the evil would have been from him*, cannot give us a right idea of the matter; for it supposes, as it were, that God could have willed or foreordained all things which have come to pass, but left it to free choice, upon consideration that if he had done so, the evil would have been from him. This has only a very superficial sense, and does not rightly represent what God is, according to Behmen's gift and declaration. It is true indeed, that if it were lawful for us to say God willed or foreordained all that came to pass, it would be lawful also to say the evil is from him, and he has willed it. But as this latter is the devil's lying assertion, so that former is not much better; seeing that this depends upon that, and that is the ground of this. As we therefore rightly say, God cannot will evil, any more than he can lie or die, so we must also say positively, and hold it firmly, that God not only did not will and foreordain, but also *could not have* willed and foreordained all things which have come to pass—namely, those that relate to the manifestation of his wrath; because God is love, and was manifest in light and love only, before and during the creation of angels, but in his wrath he was never manifest before the fall. Now God, as love, could not have willed or foreordained that the wrath should be made manifest, and get a predominance in his creatures, whom he purposed to create in and for his light, love, and glory (if we think he could, we do not yet understand with Behmen what a principle is): and in his wrath he could never have been manifested, nor could his wrath have manifested itself, if the creature had not manifested it; no more—

No, his love cannot be concerned with *anything*, nor take any notice of what is in and belongs to the wrath; except only so far, that it has an *eternal will, most essential to itself, to overcome the same, and to exalt itself over it, where it pleases, and where it is not resisted by the creature's own willful continuing in its free will.* And therefore, when God foresaw that the creature would misuse its free will, fall into his wrath, and manifest the same in itself, he—according to this eternal essential will in his love—willed, purposed, or foreordained that the wrath manifested in *man* should be broken and overcome by love, in and through the humanity of Jesus Christ; and that so the first manifestation of love in man should return to him again, to the end that love might exalt itself, and triumph over the wrath, and show forth forever what it is. And therefore also this is the only purpose or foreordaining of which the Scripture tells us, that *it was made before the foundation of the world.* But no such will or purpose concerning the wrath—namely, that this should be made manifest—can be found in any place in all the Scripture. So then, the manifestation of the wrath is only and wholly to be attributed to the creature's misusing its free will. And so it is not enough to say, "*God did not*," but we must say, "*He could not will*" or foreordain all things that come to pass.

Page 305. No. 6. God foresaw in his anger. This expression is right and good, frequently used by Behmen, and well enough understood by those who are acquainted with his style. But all this notwithstanding, the more to accommodate the understanding of those who easily find doubts in words and might here think or ask, "Had God an anger before the creatures were made and fallen? He must then have been angry with himself, etc."? I think it might be expressed this way: God foresaw in the natural qualification of the three first properties of nature. For in God there was no anger before the fall, nor is there in him even now; but in the first properties of nature, if divorced from the rest (which may be done in a creature, but not in God), there is such a qualification that is and must be wrath and anger in that creature that has made this divorce in itself. And this is called his anger because these properties, and their natural, necessary qualifications—all good and harmonious in his eternal nature—are his. So therefore, when Behmen calls it *his anger before the fall*, he does it only because it is that which, after the fall, is called so in Scripture; explaining himself sufficiently: that it had not, nor could have had this name before the fall, which it has now after it, because it was then in God not such a thing as it is now in the creature; no, <note>N.B.</note> *that it is not anger in God properly, but only in the creature, and attributable to God no further than as he is manifest in the creature, and as the creature's being depends upon his being.*

(2.) No man under twenty or above forty years of age is capable of being received as a candidate for the mastership: this is an absolute disqualification.
(3.) No one but a single woman, either a maiden or a widow, between twenty and forty years of age, is capable of being elected to be a mistress of the school. And if she marries after her election, she is to be immediately discharged, and a new one chosen in her place.

(5.) The election of a master or mistress is to be as speedy as is found to be convenient, not exceeding (if possible) three weeks from the time of the vacancy.
(6.) When two or three or any number of persons properly qualified are proposed by the Trustees, the election is always to be made by ballot.

The salary is punctually to be paid by four quarterly payments, at the four great quarters of the year, five pounds at each quarter-day. And every Lady Day quarter he is to be paid thirty shillings over and above his quarterly payments to buy firewood for the school.
(10.) The Salary settled upon the Mistress for teaching fourteen girls is ten pounds a year, to be paid by quarterly payments like the master's above-mentioned, and at the Lady Day quarter she is to receive thirty shillings over and above that quarterly payment to buy firewood for the school.
(11.) If the master or the mistress shall be found taking in, or teaching in their respective schools, any other scholar or scholars than such as are of the Foundation and put in by the Trustees, then twenty shillings for every such scholar shall be deducted from the salary of the master or mistress so offending; and if the same offence is afterwards committed again, such master or mistress is forthwith to be removed and another chosen in his or her stead.
(12.) If a master or mistress shall be found to neglect the daily business of the school, or suffer the scholars to absent themselves from it; if anything scandalous is sufficiently proved against either of them; or if they be not of a perfectly sober, decent, and Christian behavior, and of good example to the children, the Trustees are earnestly requested not to suffer the continuance of such a master or mistress—*a more pious and virtuous education of the children than that of a common school being the one great end chiefly intended by these Foundations:* which end must be frustrated unless it be an unchangeable rule constantly to discharge the master or mistress as soon as they fall into any scandalous irregularity of life and cease to give a good example to the children.
(13.) The master or mistress is not to be removed or discharged from their office except by such a number of Trustees, and such notice given to all of them, as is required in the choice of a new master.

But, for the edification of some types of readers, it may not be inappropriate to insert here the following observations immediately relating to the point in question, extracted from a published letter by Mr. Law:

> "...thus do these three states of man fully show that our first perfection, our miserable fall, and blessed redemption, have all that they have in them, whether of glory or misery, merely and solely because God alone is all that is good, and can be nothing else but good toward the creature; and that neither angel nor man can be happy or miserable, except because he either has, or has not, this one *God* of goodness essentially living and operating in him.
>
> How many things called religion are cut off at once here! Since nothing is life, happiness, and glory except the one essential operation of the triune God of love and goodness within us; nothing is death, evil, or misery except the departure or turning from this essential God of our lives to something that we would have from ourselves, or from the creatures that are around us. And how greatly is he deluded who, living among the throng of religious schemes, thinks this, or that, or *anything in nature, can be his atonement, his reconciliation, and union with God, except the spirit, the body, and the blood of Christ, forming themselves into a ‘new creature’ within him.* Then, and then only, is he that first man whom God created, in whom alone He can be well pleased; but until then, he is that man whom the cherub’s two-edged flaming sword will not allow to enter into paradise. How are we now to regain that first birth of Christ? Simply in the same way that Adam had it at first. What did he then do toward it? How did he help forward God’s creating power? Now, creating again, or restoring a first life in God, is exactly the same thing, and the same sole work of God, as creating us at first; and therefore we can have no more share of power in the one than in the other. Nothing is required of us as creatures fallen from God, nor is anything required of us regarding our growth in God, except not to *resist* what God is doing toward our *new creation*.
>
> What God is doing toward our new creation had its beginning before the foundation of the world. *In Christ Jesus (says St. Paul), we were chosen before the foundation of the world:* which is the same as saying that God, out of His great mercy, had chosen to preserve a ‘seed of the word’ and spirit of God in fallen man, which, through the mediation of an incarnate God, should revive into 그 fullness of stature in Christ Jesus in which Adam was first created. And all this work of God toward a new creation is by that same essential operation of God in us, which at first created us in His image and likeness. And therefore nothing belongs to man in it, except only to yield himself up to it, and not resist it.
>
> Now, who is it that may be said to resist it? Answer: It is everyone who does not *deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow Christ.* For everything except this is that flesh that wars against the Spirit. The whole life of the natural man resists all that essential operation of God which would create us again in Christ Jesus. Furthermore, every religious man resists it in, and by, and through the whole course of his religion, if he takes anything to be the truth of piety, the truth of devotion, or the truth of religious worship except faith, hope, trust, and dependence upon that alone which the all-creating word and all-sanctifying spirit of God, inwardly, essentially,

## CHAP. IV.—Of several other Particulars essential to these Foundations.

(1.) The Rector of King’s Cliffe for the time being is always to be a Trustee. As soon as he is inducted into the living of King’s Cliffe and begins his first residence, he has a right to claim admission into the trust. (N.B.) No other person from King’s Cliffe is ever to be a Trustee; whoever he may be, or of whatever rank, he is utterly incapable of being admitted or chosen for any share of this trust.

(2.) Future Trustees are to be constantly and forever chosen from the neighboring gentry and clergy, living no more than four miles distance from King’s Cliffe. [By order of the Court of Chancery, December 22, 1826, the limits prescribed by the existing rules and regulations regarding the residence of the Trustees are extended to a distance of eight miles from the parish of King’s Cliffe.]

(3.) Every Trustee has an equal right to place scholars in the school; but no Trustee is to place more than two until every Trustee has placed the same number.

(4.) The Agent for the Trustees is to keep a bound register book of the names of the children, their ages, the time of their entrance, and which Trustee placed them in the school. His business is to receive the rents, make the weekly and other payments, provide everything wanted in the schools, and observe the same method of clothing the children as has been practiced until now. At the general audit, the week after Easter, he is to lay his accounts before the Trustees to be examined and passed by them.

(5.) The surplus money at every audit is either to be reserved in part for occasional demands, or the whole is to be used for such purposes as the Trustees, at their annual audit, shall please to appoint; only under this restriction, that such money cannot be used in any other way except for the sole use and benefit of some of the members of these two Foundations. [By an Order of the Court of Chancery, December 22, 1826, the Trustees shall have the power from time to time, and at all times hereafter as they shall think fit, to apply the accumulated and accruing surplus rents and profits (if any) of the said trust estates when received—but not to charge the same with the repayment of any sum of money by way of anticipation, mortgage, or otherwise—toward the building of any additional almshouse or almshouses, or any new schoolhouse or schoolhouses, on such part of the trust estates as shall be most convenient for the purpose. Nevertheless, this must be done so that the currently prescribed numbers of women and scholars—or as many of them as the parish of King’s Cliffe will furnish—and the currently prescribed salaries of the schoolmaster and schoolmistress for the time being, are not reduced or diminished because of the expense of any such additional building as mentioned above.]

(6.) All orders made by the Trustees at their audit are to be entered into a book by the agent in their presence, so that at their next meeting the observance of such orders may be inquired into, and such alterations or additions may be further made as the Trustees shall judge proper.

(7.) It is the joint request of Mrs. Hutcheson and Mr. Law that, now and hereafter, the Agent for the Trustees be that relative of Mr. Law who shall keep such a shop in this town as currently exists. But (N.B.) no such tradesman, nor any other relative of Mr. Law who lives in King’s Cliffe, has any claim to this office by right; nor is he further recommended...

and work vitally in his soul."

From these, and the former passages to the same effect, the *clouded, downcast, and penitent reader* will perceive how Christ is a perpetual atonement for the sins of the whole world; that he abides in the depth of the soul as an *ever-present, infallible* remedy for all human misery, like a "well of water, springing up unto everlasting life," ready to wash away our iniquities and to impart the Divine nature to us. He will see that by his process and conquest, Christ now possesses such omnipotent power over "all things in heaven and earth," and bears such infinite, inexpressible love to our souls, that nothing in the whole universe of being shall be able to separate us from him again (Rom. viii. 38, 39), with the single exception, however, of our own *unwillingness* to be saved by him.

Whoever you are, then, (dear reader,) though you may be as vile as a whole life of willful, accumulated sins and backslidings could have made you, only believe these glad tidings and heartily embrace the gospel; *only cast off all obstructions to your spiritual renewal* by taking up the cross, through self-denial, mortification, earnest and continued prayer, total separation from the world, and the love and practice of all goodness. If you only cooperate in this way with your covenanted, omnipotent Redeemer, who is now waiting for you in the source and depth of your soul (one chief method for which is living by a spiritual rule), salvation will soon open itself in your heart.

And should you also desire a clear *intellectual* understanding of the truth and progress of your renewal, then know what Christ, as your indwelling sanctifier, is: namely, holiness, purity, peace, love, and God. (Oh, meditate much upon these words: holiness—purity—peace—love—God!) Know also that, as your actual Saviour in all your inward and outward trials of self and the world, he is the spirit of meekness, of humility, of patience, and of resignation to God. Turn your faith, then, wholly and solely to Christ under these various phases and manifestations of the one and only Spirit of truth and goodness *within you*; indeed, do so with the same fullness of assurance and earnestness of desire as the lame, the sick, and the blind applied to him to be healed when he was in the flesh. In this way, you may enjoy a rational conviction as well as perceptible evidence of being *born of God*.

Ibid. Line 3. *if it had been infused into them.* This expression does not describe the matter consistently with Behmen, though he may have used the same words in another context and with other circumstances. For in one sense, the *love was infused into the demons*; that is, it was given, offered, and presented so that it shone upon them, drawing, calling, and inviting them no less than all the rest of the holy angels. This was an infusion in the sense that Behmen describes in the parable of a thistle, into which the *sun* continually infuses its light, warmth, and essence, having no other will or inclination in itself but to do the same good to the thistle that it does to the rose; yet the thistle, despite all this loving-kindness of the sun, still remains a stinging thistle. But in another sense, we must also say that the love could not have been *infused into the demons*; for how can wine be infused into a vessel already full of foul water? The wine may indeed be poured out over the vessel, and so was the love poured over the demons; but the vessel cannot take it in. Neither could they, because their own will, which they were full of, could not receive it. In short, God did all the good he could do for them, as he is unchangeable and has no other will but to do them good; but they did nothing, nor would they do anything, of what was their duty to do.

### CHAP. V.—Of the Election of the Widows and Elderly Unmarried Women, etc.

(1.) Upon the death of a widow or the occurrence of a vacancy, no single woman is to be chosen to fill her place immediately. Instead, four, or at least three, of the most elderly widows are always to be nominated by the Trustees, and the election of every individual widow is always to be made by ballot from such a number, in the presence of the Trustees. <insert>[By Order of the Court of Chancery, Dec. 22nd, 1826: In cases where a vacancy happens in an almshouse and there is only one poor woman qualified to fill it, it shall be lawful for the Trustees at that time to elect her to it immediately, without waiting until there is a sufficient number of poor women to proceed to a ballot; and two poor women duly qualified shall be deemed a sufficient number for proceeding to a ballot.]</insert>

(2.) No widows are eligible to be elected except those from the town of King's-Cliffe, nor are any eligible to participate in the ballot who have already received the parish allowance for their support. <insert>[By order of the Court of Chancery, Dec. 22nd, 1826: All elderly and deserving women, whether unmarried or widows, of the parish of King's-Cliffe, who have not received parochial relief, shall be qualified for admission into the said almshouses.]</insert>

(3.) The two houses at Mr. Law's school are as open to elderly unmarried women as to widows, provided they have the proper qualifications.

(4.) No election of a widow or elderly unmarried woman is to proceed until all the Trustees have been notified of the vacancy and the day appointed for filling it. Nor is any election to be made unless three of the Trustees are present to oversee the ballot.

(5.) None are looked upon as qualified to be chosen merely because they are old and poor, but only those elderly and poor women who have a good reputation for their *sobriety, industry*, and *Christian behavior* in their various stations. The lack of these virtuous qualifications is not to be excused; it being our whole desire and intention by these provisions to reward the virtue and merit of such elderly women, and to prevent them from falling into the hardship of a parish allowance in the time of their age and infirmities.

(6.) Therefore, if in any future times any elderly women of bad manners or unchristian behavior, who have had the reputation of being idle, gossiping, or slothful persons, should be nominated or permitted to take part in a ballot for any of these houses, such a disregard for virtuous qualifications would be as great a violation of the nature and design of these charities as if young women, or persons from another parish, were chosen for them.

(7.) No elderly widow or unmarried woman who has more than forty shillings a year of her own is eligible to be elected. <insert>[By Order of the Court of Chancery, Dec. 22nd, 1826: No such poor woman as described above, who has an income of her own of five pounds a year, shall be disqualified for such admission, but all poor women having more than five pounds a year shall be excluded.]</insert>

(8.) The names of the women who are admitted by the Trustees as qualified are each to be written separately on a piece of paper, folded in the same form, and sealed up. They are to be

Page 305. No. 6. *permitted both for good ends.* I say nothing directly against this expression, knowing not only that it is most common, but also that we cannot well avoid it. But I must say, nevertheless, that it is not sufficient to explain the depth of the matter; because God's permitting the fall for good ends seems to presuppose that he could and would have hindered it, if he had not seen good ends in it. This cannot be said by anyone who understands, as Behmen does, what God is. For such a person will grant indeed that the fall must serve good ends; but he will also say that God could not have hindered it. He will be able to understand that by saying so, he does not make God impotent, nor take anything away from his omnipotence, any more than by saying God cannot save him who will not be saved—or, what is the same thing, someone who will not give up his own will. This is a good and true assertion. Therefore, no ill consequences follow from saying "God could not," but rather they might follow in abundance from saying "God could have hindered the fall and did not," while he nevertheless still says of himself, *As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner.*

Page 305. No. 7. To the last words might well and pertinently be added—or a predestined purpose of the free gift of grace. Because Behmen calls it that as well, and it is of good consequence to express that all of this is acknowledged to be free grace. This is so that when something is later said about the human will and its required turning, it may not be so easily mistaken as if salvation were ascribed by Behmen to man's will.

*Ibid.* No. 8. I see no reason why here, after these first words, *God purposed or willed by an eternal will in himself*, these words are added: *which they call election*, ROMANS 6:16. For (1.) It is certain that Behmen does not call this will "election." (2.) That which is expressed in the first four lines of this position might rather be called God's universal call; which is so different from election that the Scripture attributes the former to many, and the latter to few. And (3.) In the quotation of the Scripture there must be a mistake, so that one passage is set for another; seeing that in ROMANS 6:16, nothing can be found which could be referred to here. But I think what Saint Paul says is meant here instead, namely, that man was *chosen in Christ from before the foundation of the world*. And if this is meant, it is true indeed that it is the first ground of election—indeed, in a sense, election itself—so far as it could be in God before man was a creature. But it is not yet what Behmen calls election when he declares what it is in its full sense, from which it is greatly different. For that which was done in God from before the foundation of the world reaches all men; as is said in this position, that God willed to put his grace into all men's hearts, without any condition required of them. But that which is properly called election reaches not all, but only a few; because not all, but (alas!) only a few fulfill the condition that is required here: namely, to turn their wills into that grace.

Page 305. No. 9. Here I would not say, *those who call it God's clock-work*, but rather—and they compare it to a clock-work. Because, though Behmen sometimes calls it that when he discusses it, yet it is not an appropriate name by which this outward mystery could be distinguished from the inward. But as the word *mysterium* is common to both and is distinguished by "outward" and "inward," so also can this name of *clock-work* be, etc.

(17.) No holidays are to be allowed in either school, except those of Christmas, Easter, and Whitsuntide. In harvest time they are allowed to glean in the fields for their parents, after each of them has said one lesson early in the morning.

Different things, expressed there so briefly, make the meaning very obscure to my eyes; but perhaps it is not so in the eyes of others. In particular, I have to observe: (1.) The words, *which God for wise and good ends permitted to remain in him*, are tolerable indeed; but it would reach much closer to the root of the matter if it were said—that this principle of evil cannot but remain in him until the day of judgment, which is appointed for a separation of good and evil. (2.) The words on page 307, *which is reprobation*, are true, but do not give the whole or full sense of what reprobation is, according to Behmen's depth and the sense in which he frequently uses this word. For, when a man, not having turned out of the principle of evil, is rejected by God for all eternity, this is indeed his reprobation in its accomplishment and irrevocability. But Behmen also calls that reprobation (and likewise election) which occurs within a man during his lifetime, in which it may be revoked and altered. For instance: as long as a man remains voluntarily under the power of the principle of evil, he is actually reprobated and rejected, because he is actually excluded from communion with God in His love and light. But such a man may, during this life, turn his will and elect the principle of grace in him; and then he is, by that, actually re-elected, because he comes to have actual communion with God in love and light. Though this also is not yet unalterable; for he may turn away from grace again, and if he does, he is reprobated again, etc. And still deeper, Behmen also declares how all these alterations a man makes in time may be conceived and said—such a man was elected or reprobated from eternity, notwithstanding that he changes his will several times. (3.) The words on page 306, *with his will, or at least a desire*, may indeed be taken in a right sense, but may also easily provide an occasion to object to something, which might be prevented by saying—if he does not turn out of it effectively, or at least with an earnest desire to do so.

Page 307. No. 11. is called—*God’s manifestation in anger, awakened by man’s sins, and his formed word in man, which is the fire, etc.* Here the meaning is very ambiguous; for, for my part, I can hardly discern whether the meaning is this: that the principle of the evil of punishment in man is called God's formed word in man; or whether it is this: that anger is awakened by man's sins and by his formed word. And though I have reason to believe it should be the former, yet I do not see how the following definition can be applicable to this formed word, when it is said, *it is the fire in man separated from the light, upon a misuse of its free will*; though it is applicable to the principle of the evil of punishment in man. From which it then appears that this principle is not called by Behmen "God's formed word in man." But the thing is to be conceived this way: Behmen calls the whole man a formed word of God, from his very creation, before the fire in him was separated from the light upon a misuse of his free will. And now, after it is separated, just as man retains the name of a creature despite this separation, so he may also retain that of a "formed word," and may be called so: not as if this title were now so proper to him, and exactly declared what he is (which might rather be declared by calling him deformed); but only because he is still the same creature in substance who was formed by God, despite the fact that he has deformed himself. But to give the name of a "formed word" directly to the fire in man separated from the light is not excusable. And though it may be that Behmen has such words, they will certainly stand with him in quite another construction. Therefore, then, I think this particular of—

Page 307. No. 12. If it is said here how they call the *principle of grace*, the most accurate and usual name with Behmen will be this—that they call it the *second purpose of God in the blessed name Jesus*; just as they call the first purpose, according to which Adam was created, the first predestined will or purpose of righteousness, out of the Father's property. I could not find where Behmen calls that former one *God's temporary will of grace in the creature*, though I inquired much after it. If he does, it will be very seldom, and the circumstances, or the whole structure of his discourse, must declare why he calls it *temporary*. But the name mentioned is very much in use with him.

Ibid. Last line. *The actual as well as original sins of parents are propagated*. Although this is right and true in its proper sense, I fear it will meet with opposition and be thought contrary to the Scripture, where it says, *The son shall not die for the sins of the father, but each shall die for his own sins*. Therefore, I think it might be explained a little for this purpose—that by the propagation of actual sins, no more is meant than that the actual sins of the parents infect and pollute their natural seed, and thereby make the turning of the will in their children more difficult for them than it would be if their essences were not so infected.

Ibid. (Page 309.) The words, *from Adam as out of one lump*, might either be left out or put into another construction; because as they stand now, they make the sense obscure, at least to me. That this propagation is derived from Adam down to this day is understood of itself; and that it was true in Cain, the first-born of a woman, as well as in all other children born after him, is no less evident. We may see a plain instance of this (according to Behmen's declaration) in that foolish persuasion of Eve, who thought in a carnal way that she had gained the man of the Lord who would be the treader on the serpent. For this principle was so predominant in her first child that, instead of bruising the serpent's head in himself, he bruised the head of his brother—even of him who was a type of the serpent-treader.

Ibid. To the last words, *heavenly bodies concur*, I think could be pertinently added—either aggravating this infection, if their aspects are bad, or lessening it by putting a stop to the effects thereof, if they are favorable.

Ibid. No. 13. *although a <term>turba</term> enters into the seed*. Instead of this, I would rather say—although a <term>turba</term> may enter into the seed even of good parents. This is because a <term>turba</term> already exists originally, more or less, in every seed of both good and evil parents. This <term>turba</term> is not spoken of here, but rather a <term>turba</term> which may enter; not one that enters necessarily and always into every seed of good parents, but only one which may enter from exterior accidents or actions, or also from evil influences of the stars, etc.

Ibid. *they reach not God*, is right and true, and if I remember correctly, it is Behmen's own verbal expression; but it would be plainer and less exposed to objections if it were said with a more specific conclusion, as Behmen sometimes uses to define this expression—*they reach not God in his light, love, and glory*.

Jesus Christ undertook from eternity to redeem fallen mankind, who were elected or chosen in him from before the foundation of the world. And I would make this alteration only because Behmen says, in a place where he explains this text, *When Lucifer fell, the foundation of the world was not yet laid;* and he suggests by this, as it seems, that we should understand the choosing of man in Christ Jesus as following in order after the fall of Lucifer. For he also says in another place, *If Lucifer had not fallen, man would not have been created.* Because Lucifer indeed fell before time (seeing that time began only with the creation of heaven and earth), but not from all eternity, we may say better—man was chosen from eternity, rather than from *all* eternity. And then also the following expression, *from before the foundation of the world*, is the Scripture's own, which therefore may be kept more safely than that phrase, *from all eternity.*

Page 310. Q. But can they will this? A. Yes: for (1.) this willing is not a *work* or action, but rather a resting or ceasing from the works of their own will. If they can work in their own will, why not also rest from this work of theirs? Especially when there is no constraining force from the outside compelling them irresistibly to work, but only that force which is the nature of their own-will itself, and which cannot be called irresistible, as shall appear further. (2.) This resting is not to be done by a power of their own, but by use of the power of that first grace freely given to them for that end; which would be no grace, and can signify nothing to man, if it does not enable him so far that he can will this. (3.) This willing is required by God as the first ground or beginning of their restoration on their part; and God can require nothing of man except what he has enabled him to do. (4.) Man's own will excludes God and shuts the door against him: and to say—God shall open this door, not man, is to say—God shall open the eyes of a man who shuts them willfully so that he may see the sun; and man is not required to do it, even though he can open them by that motor faculty which God has placed in his eyelids. (5.) A wheel running the opposite way to how it should run according to its master's will must first be stopped before it can be set by him to run the way he pleases. And it is evident from the difference between a wheel, which is only dead and passive, and a human will, which is a living, active thing, that this first stopping of the human own-will cannot be done by God, but must be done by man. But it is especially and chiefly evident from the nature of a will. And that this does not make God impotent is also evident from this: that while it is rightly said in one respect—God cannot, but man must do it; it is also rightly said in another—God does it, and has done it, because it is he alone from whom man has this stopping grace. (6.) If we say, man cannot will, we must say, God does

But now this latter idea, that God should hinder him, is false; therefore, the former idea, that man is able to will, must be true. (7.) If by this assertion, "man can will," it were meant that this willing is so effective that he could thereby take for himself strength, salvation, life, and light, it would indeed be false; because it would rob God of what is due to him alone and attribute to man what no creature is capable of. But because it means nothing more than that he can stop his headstrong course of self-will and thus be emptied of himself—and consequently be able to receive the salvation, life, and light that God will then give him—it must be true. On one hand, it is consistent with the honor of God, to whom every good gift is ascribed; on the other, it agrees with the nature of a rational, living, and moving creature, who can justly be required to first stop taking in his own evil things before he receives the good gifts of God. (8.) The testimonies of those who have had not only a real experience in the work of regeneration, but also especially enlightened eyes to see deeply into what man is, what is in man, and what man's will is—all of which lead to the destruction of his self-will—are far more firm and valuable than anything reason can suggest in defense of self-will. (9.) The testimonies of the Scripture plainly confirm that man can will; and even these alone should convince us of this truth and suppress everything that would rebel against it. Moses, the mediator of the old covenant, says expressly, *I call heaven and earth as witnesses today against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life, etc.* Tell me, what does this saying and this command mean if man cannot choose life by standing still and listening to the voice of God? And Jesus, the great Mediator of the New Testament, says: *O Jerusalem—how often would I have gathered your children together—and you would not.* Tell me, how could he have blamed them for not willing, and for thereby resisting his will, if they could not have willed and cooperated with his will?

Page 315. Line 5. *in which fire in man they remain, even after they are forgiven;* which forgiveness is the first justification or forgiveness. One might object that the Scripture says nothing of a first and second justification, etc. Therefore, I think it could be made clearer so the meaning appears distinctly as this: sins remain in the central fire, not only so they appear no more if the soul moves forward directly and constantly, but also so they appear and seize the soul again immediately if it turns back. Therefore, regarding those who go directly forward, this justification does not need to be called the "first," because it is not followed by another that could be called the "second." But regarding those who fall back and yet later rise and return again, it may be called the first, because the same process is then repeated a second time in them. However, if we understand the word "first" simply as a beginning or first degree of justification, which increases more and more from then on, there is no difficulty in the matter, nor do I see how any such objection could be made against it.

Page 315. No. 21. *Christ’s dying in them.* This, I think, should either be left out entirely or explained by adding something like—or Christ’s dying made their own in them. An ignorant person might easily misunderstand the meaning and think the words of Scripture are a strong objection against it, where it is said, "Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more."

Ibid. *We are to fulfill all the law of righteousness by the Divine substance in us.* This also might easily be misunderstood and therefore needs to be expressed more clearly. One might think it means that the Lord Christ’s fulfillment is defective and insufficient unless we complete it by our own fulfillment through works or suffering. Whereas the meaning is simply this—that it is defective in us, or unprofitable to us, if we do not have within us that Divine substance which has sufficiently fulfilled the entire law. By having that substance in us and being conformed to it, our own great lack of Divine righteousness is truly filled. Therefore, we are rightly said to fulfill it, though it is not we who do it, but he in us; just as the apostle says, *I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me*.
