<meta>This page continues the theological critique and refinement of terminology related to the process of salvation and regeneration, specifically discussing the roles of Christ, the Father, and the Holy Spirit, followed by a set of prayers and a concluding note on William Law's charitable works at King's-Cliffe.</meta>

<margin>1</margin> of them is superfluous, and none can be separated from the rest. That principal thing is this, according to the Gospel, of which it is the whole sum and substance in short, (namely) The sinner is saved in and by Jesus Christ, whom the Father has sent, to bring him back, upon his narrow way, from under the powers of darkness, into his kingdom of light. Now herein, they will say, all these names are contained, and do declare this only truth, but so that each of them has its own peculiar relation, either to this or to that particular part of it. And so, *redemption* expresses in general this whole work, but with a chief respect to the Saviour himself, through whom man is redeemed, and to that great price he paid for him. *Pardon of sins* represents the same redemption, but as in its beginning, or as to its first effect on the side of man. *Justification* represents the same again, but with a relation to the Father, by and before whom, he whose sins are pardoned, is justified as one that has fulfilled all the law; and thus also owned to have now a free access to himself, through him who is himself his justification in him. *Purification* declares of this redeeming and justifying work, that though it be worked out and completed by Jesus Christ at once, yet it is not so in man, who needs continually and gradually more and more to be redeemed from his daily sins, failings, and infirmities, as long as he is upon the way; and even this is nothing else but a gradual purification, which also indicates something of the condition of this way, namely, that it is narrow, full of crosses, trials, temptations, etc., as so many proper means by which this purification is effected. <margin>/</margin> *Sanctification* represents that same again, but so as to express more especially, in opposition to man's former sinful state, what by this redemption, justification, and purification is effected in him, both as to himself, and as in the sight of God, namely, holiness, without which he cannot see the kingdom of light. And *regeneration* expresses in general again this whole saving work, but so that it declares on the side of man, what it is in and to him; how that which the Saviour has done for him comes to be done also in him, and so also by what means it is made profitable to him: indicating also, moreover, not only his having been degenerated, but also his being redeemed effectually, in such a process as is directly opposite to his first natural generation.

<margin>2</margin> Page 317. No. 23. *He leads a new life from a new principle, as Christ did after his resurrection.* These last words, *as Christ did after his resurrection*, I find might better be left out, because they cannot be applicable, without a great limitation, to this new life of man. And in the places quoted out of the *MYSTERIUM MAGNUM*, xxxix. 8, 9.; and *ELECTION*, x. 99, 100, I can see nothing to support such a construction. For though this is true, that in such a regenerated man Christ is really risen; and this also, that such a man leads a new life from a new principle, yet this new life cannot be compared to the life of Christ after his resurrection, but might rather be compared to his life in this world, before his death. Seeing that the soul of such a man is not yet, as his soul was, separated from the mortal body, and so not yet entered into that paradisical state which he entered into at his death and resurrection; and that this expression, *of leading a new life from a new principle*, implies only a ruling over and keeping under sin in the flesh, in opposition to the old Adam's life, which he lived before his regeneration, when sin was predominant therein: in which sense we cannot say at all that Christ led such a life after his resurrection. And though this new life of a regenerated man, considered as to itself only, and as abstracted from what it is still joined to, may be truly said to be in and with Christ, according to St. Paul's word, *Our conversation is in heaven*, so that, in some sense, it may be said to be comparable to the life of Christ; yet this sense belongs not at all to this outward principle, and is not in this world, but in its own heaven: nay, this life is not yet manifest, but, according to the Scripture, *hidden with Christ in God*, and therefore not yet such a life as Christ lived after his resurrection, who wholly lived in paradise, and was able to show forth the glory thereof to others. And moreover, I cannot see that it would be a fit expression to say, Christ after his resurrection led a new life from a new principle: for one might presently reply, that this was as much as to say, He led, before his death, an old life, from another or old principle; whereas, all his life was from the same principle, and he was the new or second Adam, not only after his resurrection, but also before his death.

<margin>1</margin>
Christ in man, but man in Christ; which is, regarding the grammatical construction, quite the contrary. But just as the words of Scripture rightly express what the apostle intended to convey in that passage concerning what was done before the foundation of the world in the general election mentioned above; so also Behmen’s words rightly and significantly express what he intended to convey regarding that particular election of which our Savior says, *many are called, but few are chosen*. For in the former, man was chosen in Christ; and in the latter, the same sense is not actually nullified or contradicted. But more significantly, and much more helpfully to Behmen’s discourse and specific intent—instead of saying "man is chosen in Christ"—the apostle could have said, "Christ is chosen in man." This is because he was declaring that in this election, nothing is regarded or looked upon by God except Christ, and that all that is not Christ, or of Christ in man, is reprobated. If, then, out of the countless number of men, none are chosen except for this reason: that they have Christ within them, and that they are living members of that head which alone has a right to the kingdom of heaven, may we not just as well say, in one sense, that only Christ is chosen in man, as we may say in another that man is chosen only in Christ? Indeed, if everything in such a man, besides his being a living member of Christ, is to be reprobated, what then do we think is left in man that could be said to be chosen, except Christ alone? We may find another sense exactly parallel to this in the words of our Savior, saying, *None ascends up into heaven, but he who came down from heaven, even the Son of man who is in heaven*. In those words, he attributes to himself alone that which he makes all his living members partakers of; for they also ascend with him for no other reason but this same one: that they are his living members, and have within them—indeed, also are within him—that which came down from heaven. This he knew and affirmed, and yet, despite this, he speaks so plainly in these words of himself only, excluding everything that he is not himself. If we, then, can say soundly, truly, and accurately enough, based on our Savior’s own words, that none ascends into heaven but Christ, why may we not also say in the same sense that none is chosen by God (to ascend into heaven) but Christ—even Christ in his living members?

So that upon this particular account, we are not only spirit of his spirit, but also flesh of his flesh; and we therefore justly bear his name, as children ought to bear the name of their Father.

For although Behmen, in the passages quoted from the THREE PRINCIPLES, does not make such a distinction himself, it appears sufficiently from a comparison of his other writings that this is his meaning.

Page 321. *Q. 2. But if it be omnipresent it will then be God. A. No; because it has only a circumferential, etc.* I had previously used that expression of a central omnipresence in relation to God, but not that other expression of a circumferential one. And though the former might seem to carry the latter along with it—which would also be well enough and not harmful at all, if taken in a deeper sense than I see it being taken when the reply is: *If it is only circumferentially everywhere, it is not omnipresent, because it is not centrally present*. For then it would be evident that this objection means nothing, and that the one element is truly also centrally present in one sense—namely, in that which is required for its own kind of omnipresence—but not in another, namely, not in that which is attributable to God alone. Though, as I say, the former expression of "centrally" might seem to carry along with it this latter one of "circumferentially," yet here it does not do so in this matter; because I had declared what I mean by "centrally," and that I do not use this word as in opposition to a circumference (where a center is distinct as a small point in the middle and present nowhere but in its own narrow central place). Instead, I use it as in opposition to an "out-birth" or surface, of which this so-called center is the internal ground or foundation—as great as, or even greater than, the whole out-birth or the entire circumference (if we choose to call it that). From this, I further showed a great and even a twofold difference between omnipresence as attributed to God alone, and omnipresence (though I wish we had another word for it here) as attributable to the <term>one element</term>. And all this was declared, to my thinking (as I also said in its conclusion), so as to be not only intelligible enough, but even palpable, as it were, and obvious to common sense. Seeing, then, that if I should explain this distinction as requested in the next following question, I could not do it without another wordy explanation, nor hope to be clearer than I was in that previous declaration, I think, therefore, these expressions of "central" and "circumferential" might be completely set aside, and the question here proposed: *If the*

This is also a practice no less earnestly recommended by the eminently pious bishop, Jeremy Taylor, in his "Holy Living and Dying," as by the most experienced masters of the spiritual life in all ages. And indeed, without a regular recurrence to God, physically as well as mentally, at stated times during each day by all persons—whatever their spiritual knowledge and attainments—the life of God cannot be maintained in the soul according to that true classic order of increase and development. This development was the design of the all-wise Redeemer and vine-dresser of souls to promote through his discourses on the efficacy of frequent and persistent prayer, by his divine sermon on the mount concerning the duties and exercises that are to support the spiritual life (as it is generated by prayer as well as being the fruit of it), and by the example of his own continual practice, both in "the flesh" and in "the spirit," in "strong crying and tears," and "groanings that cannot be uttered." In short, the spirit of prayer is the only standard of a Gospel Christian: not particular opinions upon so-called evangelical doctrines like free grace, justification by faith, election, and the like; not studied discourses upon the fulfillment of prophecy, the downfall of popery, or the second coming of Christ; not even fervent exhortations to repentance and holiness, nor yet an ability to kindle a flame of seraphic love in the hearts of an audience; but regular, earnest psychical and physical devotion, and that outward conduct which flows from such a state of heart.

<meta>This page continues the theological discussion regarding spiritual principles, specifically addressing the distinction between the omnipresence of God and that of the "one element," followed by specific textual corrections and reflections on the necessity of constant prayer.</meta>

If one element is omnipresent, it would then be God; this might be answered as follows: No; because there is a very great difference between what we mean by the omnipresence of God and the omnipresence of the one eternal element. For when we say God is omnipresent, we understand that he is everywhere without any kind of extension or expansion of his being; he fills all things, dwells in all, and both gives life to and supports every external being by his presence, yet remains himself free from them all and is contained by none of them. All of this is attributable to his omnipresence alone. But when we say (for lack of a better expression) that the one element is omnipresent, we mean only this: that in this outward world (of which it is the foundation on one part), there is no place imaginable where we could not say, "The one element is there," but in its own interior principle. For if the spiritual foundation, root, or bottom were not there, its external manifestation—the out-birth—could not be there either. 

This answer, I think, should be sufficient. But if it were thought necessary, it could be explained further by stating that although we can say in a good and deep sense that God was omnipresent from all eternity, it would be great nonsense to say He was everywhere before the creation. Because before the creation, just as there was no time, there was also no "where" or "there," nor any place but himself alone, who requires no place for his being, but is much deeper than any place, etc. Only with the out-birth did place and locality begin to exist; and therefore this out-birth, being neither greater nor less, but exactly as large as place and locality are, cannot but be said to be omnipresent—that is, in every place. This is because there is no place outside or beyond its own extent, even though God exists outside or beyond it, as he is not confined to it nor contained by it, and requires no place at all, etc. 

This outward world is not God, nor is it suspected of being made god-like by saying of it, in such a sense, that it is omnipresent to itself. This can rightly be said because there is no place within it where it is not manifest, more or less, according to its own four-elementary nature, etc. Likewise, the spirit of this world is not God, and yet is omnipresent to the whole extent of its entire region; for there is not the smallest point within it where we could say he is not there, etc. Heaven and all the "heavens of heavens" are not God, because the Scripture says of them that they do not contain him; and yet they must be omnipresent to him, because wherever he is, either within or without this world, he is in heaven. We cannot say that he is in heaven only with a part of his being and that the other part is extended beyond all heavens; rather, we must say he is entirely in heaven and entirely also beyond all heavens. So the scriptural expression, *they do not contain him*, does not mean that he is extended outside or beyond them, but that he is deeper or more inward than all the heavens, etc. 

The same is to be said also of the one eternal element; and this omnipresence of it, now declared and limited sufficiently (I hope), cannot make it to be God, nor equal to God. This is because it is not thereby raised from or beyond its state as a spiritual corporality into that much deeper and purely spiritual Being which is God, from whom, by whom, and to whom it exists and has that interior holy being which it possesses, etc.

Page 327. *A. 4. life and strength from the death of the outward old man.* Seeing that the inward man, being of a completely different nature, can receive nothing from the outward man; and the outward can only, by his own death, make way or open a free place for the inward to display his life and strength from his own internal principle, I think it might be said more properly *through* or *by* the death than *from* the death; if this "from" implies what I think it does, in which I may be mistaken.

Page 329. *A. 2. as a descent into its own hell.* Here I believe that the word *as* might well be left out; because this feeling of the soul’s own agonizing properties is really a descent into its own hell.

Page 331. *No. 3. Upon this death, etc.* This particular (based on several considerations, for which an account can be given if desired) I would rather express this way, or in any other manner like this: "Into this death the soul must give itself up as quite lost; and through this death it must sink down into that foundation where Christ dwells, and from which he is to raise a new life in it."

Page 331. Last line. *doubt—arises from the weakness of the fire of the spirit.* Though this may have a good and true sense, I think it might be said more directly and particularly: "from the division in the fire of the soul, which partly reaches toward God and partly clings to the spirit of this world." For in this way, the true cause of this weakness would be expressed.

Page 333. *In the answer to the final question.* That which seems to me to be the most important detail is omitted, namely: that God’s pardoning of sins is inseparable from a real departure from sin, leaving it behind, or, as it were, beneath us, and entering into a different region where sin cannot follow us, but must be drowned in the blood of Christ.

Page 335. *No. 3. his former sins and guilt remain.* That they remain was said in the previous point, No. 2; it would be more expressive if it were said here: "his former sins and guilt seize him again," for then he returns back into their own territory.

"How often," remarked an eminent modern saint to one of his friends while on his deathbed, "do we say we want to live nearer to God. The great evil is that we do not resolutely pray more. We must have time for secret prayer, taken from business or sleep if we have no leisure. Has anyone ever resolved to do this in the strength of God without actually living nearer to God? It has been my rule and constant practice for some years," he continued, "to pray at least six times a day in secret; and with less than this, I have found I could not maintain uninterrupted union with God." 

Or, as the holy Bramwell (who was perhaps the most perfect resemblance of our Lord in mind, spirit, temperament, manner, conduct, constancy and earnestness of devotion, indifference to self and the world, zeal for the glory of God, and success in winning souls that has ever appeared since the apostolic age) wrote in a letter to a friend, which the latter published after his death (and which, with some other extracts, we propose here to quote as an enlightened practical interpretation of the views of Mr. Law regarding the spirit and practice of prayer): "I am," he said, "striving to live as near to God as anyone I have ever known—yes, as near as Saint Paul himself. I read his character more frequently and study more closely his indifference to the world, his zeal, his love for souls, his labors, his being always ready for his death, and his desiring rather to be with Christ. But I am more than ever convinced that, to accomplish this, I must make the absolute most of my time. I must sleep no more, and eat and drink no more, than nature requires; and this calls for daily self-denial, such as I believe our Lord meant in his divine..."

<margin>/</margin>Page 337. Last Question. *How then does it attain rest?* This question might very well be answered in more detail in this or a similar manner. Answer: By sinking down into that ground where light can be ignited by Christ; for every moment remaining still is a continuation of this miserable state, and every rising up is an increase of the same; but sinking down is the only way for escaping from it.

<margin>2</margin>Page 343. Question 1. *What is that principle, and why do they call it liberty?* Answer: It is (with respect to souls, which are but creatures) that internal supernatural state of rest and peace which Christ promised to those who would come to him, take his yoke upon them, and follow after him. And they call it *liberty* because it is free from, and superior to, all those violent commotions that exist and act in the inferior, restless part of nature.

<margin>3</margin>Page 343. *Answer 3. United in one will, namely the will of the soul and the will of God.* This explanation of the words *in one will*, referring them to a union of God’s will with the will of the soul, cannot be maintained. For in this description of the <term>tincture</term>, they mean no other wills but the will of fire and the will of light, which are to be united into one, so that the fire may no longer have its own fiery will—that is, its own destroying and consuming nature or natural inclination according to its fiery properties—but may have them subdued to the light, to act in harmony with it, etc. The union of the soul’s will with the will of God, and their becoming one, is not denied here; it is only stated what is meant by *one will* in this definition of the <term>tincture</term>.

<margin>4</margin>Page 343. Question. *What do they mean by the virtue of fire, and the virtue of light?* Answer: They mean that wonderful efficacy which arises from the union of fire and light, which cannot be expected from either one alone; and which is chiefly a unifying and harmonizing virtue, able and sufficient to restore to their proper order and agreement all the disharmonized properties of eternal nature in the soul, and so of temporal nature also, in all things.

<margin>5</margin>Page 345. Question 2. *Are there not several other lights besides the true one, and how shall we distinguish them from it?* Answer: If you ask in relation to others, how to distinguish the true light from the false ones in other persons outside of you who make a noise and show of it, so that you may not follow them and be misled or deluded by any of them, they will tell you (1) that just as no man in this outward world follows a light which only another sees, or claims to see, unless he thereby plainly admits himself to be blind; so also, and even much more (according to our Savior’s plain doctrine), must it be in the inward world and upon our way to salvation. (2) Then they will ask you again what rules or directions you can give to such a blind man in this world on how to distinguish the light of the sun from that of the moon, and these two from that of a burning candle; whether all your efforts would not be in vain, because the light is an object for a seeing eye only, and where this is not, a discerning eye cannot be? But, nevertheless, (3) they will tell you also that no man is so blind as not to have something of the *true light*, however little, shining in his own conscience; for Christ is the light *enlightening every man that comes into this world*. Therefore, if he will take heed to follow it always and never run before it—even if he hears many pretenders to great and high things—and if he takes nothing from them except what he sees agreeing and conforming to what this light plainly shows and directs him to, his walk will always be secure. In doing so, he shall never follow another light outside of himself, but only that which shines in himself and is given to him to be his leader.

But if you ask how one may distinguish in himself the true light from the false ones, you must take this true light either in its fullness or in a lesser degree. If you take it in its fullness, they will answer that it cannot be discerned except by him who has really seen it so; and if anyone has seen it in its fullness, he wants no direction from outside on how to discern it from a false light, or from a true lesser one, because it carries along with it, in its own essence, such a mark or character as cannot be doubted. Christ, manifesting himself to a soul according to his promise, wants no testimony from either angels or men to prove him to be the Sun of Righteousness; and such a soul does not need to see any other evidence but his own light to distinguish him from a devil transformed into an angel of light; but with its own seeing eyes it shall see, according to his plain words, *that he is in the Father, and the Father is in him.* But if you take this true light in a certain inferior, beginning, or increasing degree, shining while the soul is still only on the way to full regeneration or the manifestation of Christ, they will give you several marks of discernment, of which this one alone may be sufficient for everyone: namely, the true light always has three inseparable companions: the *cross, love, and humility.* Every light that shows a way how to avoid, escape, or refuse the cross; how to favor selfishness and to maintain the soul’s life according to its fiery properties so that its own essential cross may not be made known, etc.; every light that is not truly accompanied by love (according to the plain doctrine of Saint John)—light and love being not only of one and the same Second Principle, but also of one and the same first property of it—and every light that leads not downwards into our own nothingness—

A. ult. *from the collision of the first four, etc.* Instead of this, I would much rather say—from the kindling of the fire, which, by its flying up, displays, or as it were, disperses the soulish properties and essences, and makes them stand in such a spiritual figure as is like a cross, etc.

Q. ult. *How do they conceive the light to arise in the soul?* The answer to this question says *that the light is water rarefied, made thin and clear; and so places the water before the light, as a material cause before its product:* I cannot conceive it so, but must with Behmen say that the light is prior. For, though in eternal nature, light and water are inseparable and co-eternal, yet I cannot help but understand with him that materiality comes forth from spirituality, *not vice versa*; and that the light, as a pure spirituality, arises in the fifth form; but the water, as a spiritual materiality, in the seventh, etc. The conjunction of the eternal liberty with the restless part of nature kindles the fire; the separation of these two again, or the distinct exerting of each one’s peculiar quality, is the breaking forth of the light. So that, according to Behmen, the light is not water rarefied, but the free liberty sharpened by the harshness of nature. For this, I refer to what was said about it in the discourse on the seven forms of eternal nature.
<margin>2</margin>
For as the light arises in eternal nature, so it does, *with the necessary changes having been made*, in the soul also. Water may be the air or ether condensed, and so it will be true that air or ether must be water rarefied; but air or ether is not yet light, but only that <term>expansum</term> <note>the vast expanse or firmament</note> which is made so thin and clear that the light can shine through it. Therefore, I would answer this question in this way. A. They conceive that when the sharp properties of the soulish nature reach the liberty, they break out in a clear and open flame; and thereby this liberty, which before was nothing to the soul, becomes its "something," stands in union with it, gives to it its own meekness, and receives from the sharp fiery properties again that glance or luster which disappeared in Adam’s fall, and which it cannot have without the fire; just as the soulish fire cannot have a clear flame without this liberty. And as therefore now fire and light are in love and union, so all the properties of the fiery nature must also burn in love.

Page 355. Q. 1. *What is inward Divine hearing?* The place quoted out of the PRAYER-BOOK, page 10, I hardly know how to make plainer. The meaning is in substance this—It is a power opened again, and restored to the fallen humanity by free grace in Jesus Christ; by which the human soul is enabled to approach confidently to the mercy-seat erected in its own ground, and there to hear God speaking in it, according to David’s words, saying, *I will hear what the Lord will speak in me.* This speaking is a real word, not only sounding according to the light world’s condition, but also operating, effecting, and giving forth something of what it speaks; which in substance is nothing else but his mercy bestowed on us in and through Jesus Christ. But I can add further—it bears a true analogy to the outward sense of hearing, and is a perception of something answering to a plain and express or articulate human speech, though not comparable to any kind of earthly languages; and the soul, though it may never have perceived the like before, needs no instruction, but understands what is said immediately, the very first time, without any doubt, plainer and clearer than it can ever understand anything spoken in this world.

As to the other two senses, namely smelling and feeling, which the next following question on page 335 asks, *whether they say anything?* I cannot but answer that Behmen says indeed nothing of them (especially not of the former) in particular; but it is nevertheless evident enough that they also bear such an analogy to what is called so in our outward life, and that they are different powers of the new regenerated life, restored to humanity in and by Jesus Christ.

For, just as on one side, everything that any other soul in reality and truth enjoys of such heavenly motions and visitations cannot help me in the salvation of my own soul if it remains outside me; so also on the other, everything that he falsely pretends to enjoy, or what he (in a delusion, or as it were, in a drunkenness from the astral spirit) believes himself to enjoy and to be directly from heaven, cannot hurt me if I leave it outside me, neither approving nor condemning it until a clear, sufficient evidence is given to me.

<meta>This page continues the theological critique and instructions for spiritual development, focusing on distinguishing true inspiration from false, the nature of resurrection from sin, and the union of the soul with Christ.</meta>

Rules for distinguishing *false inspirations and enthusiasms from true ones* have been prescribed by many others, I suppose, much better than I could ever do; and so, therefore, I beg to be excused. Nevertheless, not to be completely unhelpful, I will set down only this threefold rule from my own practice, which I, for my part, am well satisfied with. One thing I know is absolutely necessary, as the only great fundamental point or work to be done in my own soul no less than in any other; namely, in short, the slaying of the fiery soulish dragon, and the raising again of that new life that is held captive *under him*. Now, all inward motions that point to this, or lead and direct toward it plainly, sensibly, and more or less effectively, cannot but be good and true. All that plainly, sensibly, and more or less effectively tends to the contrary must of necessity be false. And all that does not have such plainness and sensibility in and with it, under whatever shape it may appear, is not to be curiously searched into, and is of itself neither profitable nor hurtful; though it can be made to be both one and the other, according to my own different behavior regarding it.

<margin>2</margin>
Page 360. *Q. What is death to sin, and resurrection from it?* A. Death to sin is the soul's continual putting it off, going out from it, and leaving it behind; and its resurrection from sin is its continual entering into and laying hold of that opposite degree of a new life of righteousness, seeking the things that are above; which degree of life every particular degree of dying is immediately followed by and joined with.

<margin>3</margin>
Page 361. No. 8. *The pearl may be lost and regained, but with difficulty, when it has disappeared.* This is true indeed, yet not so universally as it is expressed here, but only in its place, or kind and degree of disappearing. For there is also a total loss or disappearing, after which Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme</note> expressly says it cannot be regained; namely, when it was once obtained, and is so lost as the Epistle to the Hebrews declares it. For then another sacrifice for sin would be required; whereas there neither is nor can be any other but that which once was made in the Lord's death on the cross.

<margin>4</margin>
Page 363. After these twelve particulars, still another I think might pertinently be added, containing in substance—that all this order and method now propounded is not exactly and punctually to be applied universally to every individual person; but that every one is led to the same end indeed, and through the same principal ways, yet not exactly in this order through all the little by-paths, as the Spirit of God is pleased, and sees it most expedient for every one, according to his peculiar constitution.

<margin>5</margin>
Page 363. *Q. ult. What do they mean by union to Christ? and is the soul united to his personality or natural body, soul and spirit; or only to his Divinity and universal body?* First I observe, that I see not why Christ's personality, as to the most outward part thereof, here in this place, where it is especially distinguished from his universal body, is called *natural*: for though it be natural indeed, yet it cannot by this denomination be distinguished from his universal body, which is natural also. And therefore, I think it would be better to say—to his personality in body, soul, etc. And then I answer to this question thus. A. By union to Christ they mean nothing else but what he meant himself, in his last sermon to his disciples, and in his simile of the vine and branches, which are and must be in union with the vine, if they shall be able to bear fruit. And as now his personality in body, soul, and spirit, cannot be separated from his divinity and universal body, so also none of these distinct things can be separated or excluded from his union to the soul, but all must be implied therein, though not all in a full equality of sense, because not all can be equally capable of this union; which will therefore differ so, as a union between a branch and tree differs from a union between a father and his children, and as both these kinds of union differ again from the union in a red-hot iron, between iron and fire.

<margin>6</margin>
Page 365. *Q. 1. In what sense are they said to put on Christ's righteousness, who put on Christ, or Christ's universal body?* A. In the same sense in which we can rightly say, we put on the first Adam's unrighteousness, by putting on in our natural generation his universal body into which he fell. For, in his first paradisiacal body he was righteous before God: now that body never sinned, nor put on any unrighteousness, but it disappeared only in his transgression. If then Christ has brought and formed it again into paradisiacal flesh and blood, and if he is in this body the righteousness before God, in opposition to the first Adam's unrighteousness; we, by putting on him, or his universal body, by concurrence and efficacy of his personal body, must needs put on not only righteousness, but also his righteousness; and cannot in this body be looked upon otherwise than as if we had never sinned, that, and all that which has sinned, being put to death.

<margin>7</margin>
Page 365. This kindled fire now desires food from that principle with which it is joined in love; and this food (be it taken and con-

all around you.—I know it is neither procured nor retained by the number of times of prayer; yet if you are fully in earnest, you will be often before the Lord on your knees, pouring out your heart and pleading with him, till your cup is full and running over."      Thus much in illustration of the true evangelical practice of devotion, and of the right objects and mode of its exercise. For without a specific object in view in devotion, and that object the only one contemplated by the gospel, namely regeneration, or the crucifixion of the old carnal man and the raising up of the new Christlike nature in his stead, to which all the other parts and acts of religion are likewise to be directed—without this mystical knowledge we say, we may offer up very regular and dutiful prayers and supplications, but shall probably never attain to the true end of prayer above mentioned, namely a real death to self and a real birth of the Spirit, a rising out of ourselves and an entrance into the light and life and liberty, and real enjoyment of God, into a state of Christlike perfection and stability in Divine virtue. Now as without doubt this character of devotion (though including its numerous degrees, from the simple regular devotion of the school before alluded to even to the highest accomplishment of it as exhibited in the life of a Bramwell or a Lopez) was implied in Mr. Law's <note>William Law</note> discourses on devotion and recommendations of regular hours of prayer, in his 'Christian Perfection,' chap. xii., and 'Serious Call,' from chap. xiv., may we not venture to conclude it to have been his own practice? No. 4. *They advise fasting, etc.* In the THREEFOLD LIFE, Chapter xvi. 31., where Behmen says something about fasting, I can find nothing but what is very plain and consistent with what was just now said. He means by fasting nothing else but (besides a continually temperate, sober life) sometimes an abstinence from all eating and drinking, yet without appointing certain days, times, and seasons for it, but leaving that to everyone’s discretion according to their circumstances; and he says that as earthly food fills the belly, and the excess of it makes it heavy and unable to work, so the earthly spirit fills and saturates the soul, and makes it unfit for spiritual things; and that then the Spirit of God departs from such a soul, at least for that time, finding no open place to dwell and work within it.

<margin>2</margin>
Page 367. No. 7. *That prayers are to be made with respect to the eternal internal powers of the days, etc.* I find nowhere that Behmen says such a thing; but this is how the matter stands—In all the printed prayer books of his nation, various and specific morning and evening prayers are prescribed for every day, some of which are made with respect to the seven days of the creation. Accordingly, then, Behmen, knowing the mystery of it more deeply than those common books (which mention only the creatures brought forth on such or such a day), wrote his prayers with a deeper respect to the eternal powers thereof; yet he never said that the prayers were to be made, or must be made so, by everyone. As he himself had no necessity placed upon him to do so, so he has not laid it upon any other; but he that can and will, and understands what he does, may do so freely.

<margin>3</margin>
Page 367. No. 7. *That prayers are to be made with respect to the eternal internal powers of the week, or seven spirits.* The more I look it over and consider it, the less I can find of such a thing. No such expression may be found in the German original: and in those few prayers the author has set down, he makes only sometimes an allusion or accommodation to those planets after which the day is called, and raises the mind above them into that which is their deeper ground; and this very sparingly too, not as if he had designed an equal exactness everywhere, but only as this or that was obvious to his mind. So, for instance, in the first prayer of this kind, on Monday noon, he says nothing at all in a specific or proper reference to this day and hour, but only a general contemplation of his state, both as to the creation, fall, and restoration thereof; which, as he also says himself in the title, may be used whenever one finds himself thus touched in his devotion. In the second, for the same day and hour, he considers (as the title says) the day’s quality, and raises the mind into the inward moon, which is the heavenly substantiality. But in the words of the prayer itself, everyone may see that there is nothing specifically expressed which did or could belong to this day more than to any other. In the third, on Monday evening, which the title says concerns a descent of the mind, just as the former was an ascent of it, nothing more can be discerned but an allusion to the outward moon’s changeableness, increase, and decrease, and this only obscurely as well. The substance of it is a contemplation of our misery, both spiritual and bodily, and an earnest groaning for deliverance; all of which is not in a specific manner more fit and proper on a Monday noon than on any other day and hour. On Tuesday, no further trace of such an allusion or accommodation appears at all; for he immediately begins to consider the ten commandments, without giving a reason for it. And though it might be said that he chose this matter for this day because of that communion or relation between the fiery Mars and this fiery law, yet it is as fit and proper, and as necessary also, for any other day as it is for this. And so, if he had not been prevented by death, he might easily have found matters fit more or less for every day, or capable of such an accommodation, but not altogether applicable to only one, with the exclusion of the rest.

But the whole substance in general he has set down himself in these or similar words—Every true prayer is not only a desiring, longing, and asking, but also an obtaining, taking in, and possessing. Page 369, Concerning Behmen's sense of the ten commandments. His interpretation, as to the
<margin>1</margin> first, goes not so directly nor principally upon what is common—namely, a plurality of gods, making and having idols, or loving and applying one's heart to this or that creature, etc.—though all these things are included as particular lesser branches; but the chief thing is that he says a full relying or depending upon and cleaving to God only, an acting and working of the soul's will with and under God only, a ruling with him over all creatures without appropriating anything to itself, a casting the soul's desire into his love only, and in a word, a leaving and going out from selfhood in the very deepest sense, ground, and bottom, is required in this commandment. And even selfhood is that principal other god which man set up in his first transgression, and which is still the maker of all the other gods or idols, numberless in variety, which everyone sets up according to the peculiar constitution of his corrupted nature.

<margin>2</margin> Of the second Behmen has nothing, because it is not in the Lutheran church. Dr. Luther has left it out, saying that it is but an explanation of the first words. <note>The original numbering of the commandments of Behmen was altered in the arrangement, on p. 44.</note>

<margin>3</margin> Of the third (which in the Lutheran church is the second), he says that it reaches much further and deeper than is generally understood; and that the name of God is taken in vain not only in cursing and swearing, and where the name *God* is directly and expressly named vainly, but also in a more general sense in all our speech and every word of it, even if there is no express mention made of God, if the word is not according to simplicity and truth, but formed more or less by the serpent's <term>ens</term> <note>Being or essence</note> in us. And his reasoning for this is briefly this: Adam had his speaking faculty out of eternal nature, wherein all the names or powers of God are manifest, moving and working; and his giving names to everything was an imitation of their being spoken or brought forth into being and substance by God. Although this is now lost in the fall, regarding man's paradisiacal speech, yet something answering to it, according to this third principle, still lies in human speech and in all languages. And whereas now before the fall, all the words were formed in conformity to and by the concurrence—nay, the predominance—of the holy names and powers of God in the light world, they are now formed more or less in conformity and by the concurrence—nay, many times in a full predominance—of the serpent's ens. By which then all manner of false, abominable images are figured, and so the powers of eternal nature and the names of God are abused in the same manner as the devils do, though it be in another principle, wherein there is a mixture of good and evil. Concerning all of which, Behmen has a large, plain, and very intelligible discourse in the *Mysterium Magnum, Chapter 22.*

<margin>4</margin> In the fourth (which Dr. Luther has only in these words—*You shall hallow the Sabbath*, leaving out all the rest), Behmen leaves indeed the seventh day of the week as an outward symbol in its place, and owns that the hallowing of it is commanded here; but he also insists chiefly upon that internal Sabbath which Adam was set into in paradise, and which we are to come into again in Jesus Christ—namely, a ceasing from our own will and work, and resting in the love of God, so that he may work in us. For if this is the true inward ground of that outward practice, the law, being spiritual, certainly understands the inward in the first place, and the outward in the second, as being subordinate to that. And so also,

<margin>5</margin> In the fifth he owns indeed that we are commanded to honor our outward natural parents; but he also makes a deeper application of it, saying that God is our Father, and his spoken word in eternal nature is our mother, in whose womb we are conceived and nourished, and into which we are to return again from the strange mother of this world. *If I am your Father (as the Lord says by the prophet), where is my honor given me by you? etc.*

Here now Behmen's prayers upon the ten commandments are at an end; but what he would have said in substance upon some of the rest may easily be gathered from several other places, namely:

<margin>6</margin> In the sixth he would not only have reflected upon killing our neighbor with the hand or with the tongue, which is commonly understood there, but also chiefly upon that spiritual killing, stifling, and keeping under (called "crucifying" in the Scripture) Christ and his spirit in ourselves.

<margin>7</margin> In the seventh he would certainly have spoken of that marriage bond the first Adam was tied with to the heavenly virgin, the wife of his youth, against which we all still deal treacherously, more or less.

<margin>8</margin> In the eighth he would not only have said that all manner of deceit used in the world to cheat our neighbor of his goods is forbidden, but also chiefly the appropriating to oneself anything, whether of spiritual gifts or of worldly possessions. For though even these latter may be held by a right and lawful title, yet the soul directly commits a robbery with respect to God, if it does

As to the *ninth* and *tenth*, I find nothing but what would be consistent with what is ordinarily understood there.

Page 369. Q. 3. The particular sentiments concerning those three or four requisites may be these following, namely: They say,

(1.) That the narrow way, as to its inside, is the *inward process of regeneration*; and as to its outside, a *course* or *manner of life contrary to that of the wicked world*.

(2.) That as to the former, or inside, it is called the narrow way chiefly because everyone shall meet upon it with manifold temptations, and as it were, many narrow holes, through which the will-spirit of the soul must creep, and everywhere be stripped of something which his natural will is not willing to be deprived of.

(3.) That these are those manifold particular deaths mentioned above, every one of which is followed immediately by such a degree of life as is always answering proportionately to the preceding degree of death.

(4.) That it is called also the narrow way especially on this account: because those who walk upon it shall find a great opposition from the anger of God, kindled in the whole of fallen humanity, which if they fight against it with his love, will many times press the soul down so much, as if whole mountains lay upon it, and bring it into such a narrowness that, as to all its sensibility in that state, the whole world is too narrow for it.

(5.) That as to the latter, or outside, it is also justly called the narrow way because of the great oppositions and difficulties from the world and our own corrupt flesh, which both invite and draw the soul one way, while laying innumerable impediments in the other; this cannot but make the same to be as it were a small foot-path, in comparison to that broader way that leads into perdition.

(6.) That both in this and that—namely, both inwardly and outwardly—the cross and the yoke of Christ is to be taken up and carried after him.

(7.) That by so doing, the wickedness of the mixed world must necessarily be avoided; for he who bears the cross of Christ certainly cannot walk in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of the scornful.

(8.) That this wickedness is in general expressed by the apostle's *lust of the eye, lust of the flesh, and pride of life*: and what each of them is more particularly, everyone will be told in his own conscience, if he is but willing to hear its voice.

(9.) That all this, thus practiced, is nothing else in its very ground and bottom but a continual SELF-RESIGNATION; for it is always a leaving behind of its own will, and giving up itself into the will of God.
<meta>catchword: And</meta>

(10.) That all this in its order and progress is also nothing else but the WAY FROM DARKNESS TO TRUE ILLUMINATION; for the soul, they say, is not capable of true illumination as long as it is filled and darkened by all manner of impurities in its own will; just as water is not capable of receiving the sun's light and representing its image as long as it is thick and muddy: but when the soul, putting off all that is of that nature and kind, resigns itself to God, his light is ready to illuminate the soul, and the soul, like purified water, is able to receive that illumination.

Page 368. Q. *What are God's calls to repentance?* A. Here it is not asked, I suppose, with respect to anything that is outside of man—as, for instance, the word preached, public and private calamities, pestilence, earthquake, and the like, which may all well be called so—but only with respect to what is done by God in man himself. Thereupon they will answer that these calls are the secret motions and dictates of everyone's conscience; for this does tell him that he *is to depart from evil and do good*. In the conscience, God meets the sinner, and no one living can say that he never heard such a call in his life.

Page 370. Q. *What do they mean by this shape?* A. They mean that spiritual figure or image which is opposite to the soul's former divine image, and which the beastly properties and qualities it is infected with must necessarily represent to the intellectual eye, considering them and finding a conformity between the soul and such or such a brutish creature. For as everything has its outward form or figure according to the various compositions of its parts and dimensions, so it must also have, answering to that, its inward shape or figure, arising from the various combinations of its spiritual properties. And if the soul had once the image of God when all its properties were harmonized, it must now necessarily have that of a beast when they all stand in disharmony and exert such operations as are consistent with those of a beast, whether tame and harmless, or wild and hurtful. <note>N.B. The ground of the asserted heathen doctrine of the transmigration of souls.</note>

of whom in their declaration of this state, nothing is more common than for them to speak of a transcending, surpassing, or leaving behind or beneath; of being raised above and transported beyond all creatures, *holy angels, and even themselves as well*; and of an entering, sinking down, and *melting away into an uncreated abyss*, etc. And they do not mean by this that a soul ever sheds its nature or its status as a creature, or that other creatures no longer exist alongside it in the same level of being; but only that it enters into such a state of holy silence that no creature is perceived, and the soul has no other object before it but that which is uncreated. And that they mean nothing else but this, you may clearly perceive from these words of the famous mystic, M. Eckhard, saying, "A sacred interlude arose within me—that is, a holy silence of all exterior things—and even all my interior faculties were at rest, with the sweetest joy of a heart seeking heavenly things, with a forgetfulness of all things and a full denial of myself, so that only the knowledge of you, O God, remained. . . . Then I was carried into forgetfulness of myself, into You, . . . . I was led by the Holy Spirit into the abyss," etc.

Page 375. *A.* 3. No. 1. As this first position is expressed here, it cannot remain consistent with Behmen’s mind; but I think it might well be expressed this way:—that God’s essence of love and meekness (or the divine virtue—*virtue* belonging more properly to the second principle, and power more properly to the first principle—the fire of love, the holy light’s virtue, the heavenly <term>ens</term> or substance) was, before the fall, a spiritual oil and water in and to the soul, by which its fire was refreshed, fed, and strengthened, and its shining light kept and preserved.

Page 377. Q. 1. *Why is a medium necessary; cannot God forgive sins without it?* A. If by forgiveness of sins, one understands only the kind of pardoning by which an earthly prince may clear or pardon a criminal, God not only can do so, but has actually done so with our first parents. But now the soul lacked not only such a forgiveness, but also a new birth; and this new birth could not be brought forth in him without a previous undoing, drowning, or washing away of the sin in the "old man," which cannot be done without a medium. And just as there is a necessity for a mediator, so there is also for a medium, acting as an instrument of that mediator. This medium is blood and water: *without the shedding of blood, there is no remission of sins*; and the Mediator came *not with blood only, but with water and blood*. In baptism, though the Mediator’s blood is not excluded, the water is primarily considered (as the beginning, ground, or if it might be said so, the first rudiments of blood); because this also makes the beginning, or in a sense lays the ground, for that new birth. And the reason why it must be water, and not any other thing, depends upon the inward ground of man’s paradisical body, which he had lost and lacked. If, then, there was and is the same analogy between the *inward* and *outward* water that exists between the paradisical and elementary body of man, the reason is plain why elementary water must be used in outward baptism. Moreover, man is to lay hold of God through the Mediator by his will, faith, and imagination—and, consequently, also on that medium which the Mediator uses; for it is plain that he cannot lay hold of God, nor come to God, immediately. By his fall, his will, faith, and imagination have departed to such a distance from God and are so corrupted that they cannot—especially in this beginning of regeneration—lay hold directly and immediately on God’s pure spiritual being. Similarly, God in his holiness cannot lay hold on, nor be united immediately to, the soul in this state. Therefore, a medium fit for both is necessarily required, in which they both may meet. And on God’s side, this medium can be no other than the inward water of eternal life, because this is the same materiality of light in which God had created man; and on the side of the outward man or body, it is the earthly or elementary water, because man’s body has also become earthly or elementary, etc.

Page 377. Q. 4. *Why was elementary water made use of as an outward medium?* The chief reason for this was just given; and that which is requested here to be made plainer (from the *Two Testaments*, iv. 9.) can have no obscurity if one only considers man’s falling away from that principle of meekness where God dwells, which was shut off from man as to his spirit, soul, and body. For if there is in baptism such an infusing of the water of eternal life into the soul, the soul thereby has, as it were, a little gate reopened to her, which in its progress may be made wider and wider, and through which she may go out from her own natural fiery properties into the light, love, and meekness of God; for which end this gate is also opened in baptism. In the other place (*Three Principles*, xxiii, 28.), this same thing is also said, though with different and deeper words, and more circumstantially, to show that as the beginning of life is, so also must be the order in regeneration, etc.

Page 379. *trembling.* I remember that I was recently asked why trembling was necessary for repentance. Now, in the places quoted (namely, pages 20 and 21), I find in the <note>German</note> no such word as could be correctly expressed by "trembling"; rather, that word signifies properly and directly a *violent breaking*. Why this is necessary, he gives a plain reason, which may be illustrated by the comparison of a hard stone that is unable to receive any impression until its hardness is first broken, or of a lump of ice which must first be melted into water, etc.

<meta>This page continues the theological and philosophical examination of Jacob Behmen’s (Boehme’s) teachings, specifically contrasting the nature of baptism and the sacraments between the Old and New Testaments, before transitioning into a discussion on the universal principles of truth across different traditions.</meta>

*Page 383. Q. 2. How did John’s baptism differ from our Saviour’s?* **A.** (1.) John baptized only with a spirit of anointing for repentance, in order for the forgiveness of sins; but Christ *with fire and the Holy Spirit*. (2.) John’s baptism was to prepare the way for the baptism of the spirit of Christ. And, therefore, also (3.) John’s baptism did not yet have those glorious effects which our Saviour’s baptism had after his resurrection, because, in John’s baptism, the Holy Spirit—in a certain true sense—was not yet present; the blood of atonement was not yet shed, and the anointing tincture was not yet prepared. But, nevertheless, John’s baptism did not belong to the types of the Old Testament, but stood, as it were, in the middle, between those types of the old and the real substance of the New Testament, partaking somewhat of both, and being, therefore, different from both.

*Page 383. Q. 3. Why was John of the lineage of the priests?* **A.** Because, as the types were now to be brought out of their shadow into the substance, or out of the law-covenant into the covenant of grace; so also that agent, which in this beginning was used, must first have been endowed with the spirit of the law-covenant—as the priests especially were, who handled the circumcision and bloody sacrifices—so that with this spirit a beginning, and from this a progress, might be made into the covenant of grace. In this progress, the former might be overtaken and fulfilled by the latter: which could not have been so if John had not been of the lineage of the priests; rather, the order, coherence, and harmony of the whole would have been broken in this part.

*Page 383. Q. 4. What was Christ’s baptism by John? or why was Christ himself baptized?* **A.** Christ, as a public person and representative of the whole human race, and as one who was to go through the whole process of regeneration, necessarily had to make this beginning by being baptized by John: for thus (he says himself), *it becomes us to fulfill all righteousness*.

*Ibid. Q. last. What is the true order of administering baptism?* Here, I think, the practice of the primitive Christians, as researched in church history, might give the best answer. In the place quoted from the <term>THREE PRINCIPLES</term>, <term>xxiii. 30</term>, <term>Behmen</term> represents it very simply, and without any ceremonies, considering only the sprinkling of the water in the name of the holy Trinity as the only necessary and principal transaction.

*Page 385. Q. 1. Why does baptism precede the Eucharist, or Lord’s Supper?* **A.** Because the beginning or generation of the new life (which is made in baptism) must necessarily precede the feeding or nourishing of the same, which is done in the <term>Lord’s Supper</term>.

*Ibid. Q. 4. How, or in what sense, were these types of it?* **A.** As in the <term>Lord’s Supper</term>, a union is made between man and what man feeds upon; so, also, was such a union made in the paschal lamb, in the sacrifices, and also in the showbread (though only in its kind and degree, according to the nature of that dispensation of the covenant). But as these things did not have the real heavenly substance manifested within them, but were only like shadows of it—pointing at it, directing toward it, and showing what was to be expected, believed, and hoped for—so, also, they could not fill nor satisfy the partakers with that heavenly substance itself, whose types they were. Nevertheless, they were such a medium by the right use of which men approached in faith unto God, and God drew near in mercy unto men. Therefore, not only (1.) the bare likeness which existed between these shadows of the Old and the real substance of the New Testament, but also (2.) that benefit which the church of God received by them, and, more especially, (3.) that ordinance by which they were so instituted with a reference to the substance to be manifested in Christ, caused them to be called holy things and types of it.

*Ibid. Q. 5. How were they brought into substance by Christ?* **A.** Successively and gradually in his incarnation and whole process of suffering and death, resurrection, and ascension. For the real substance of the New Testament, in opposition to the shadows of the Old, is nothing else [but the perfect image of God, the heavenly humanity, the holy tincture of light and love, the bread and water of life, etc.: all which in and to the first Adam had disappeared and withdrawn into its own principle or heaven]. When, therefore, in the second Adam all this came down from heaven again, and when he had fulfilled all righteousness, and had gone through death and hell, and had led captivity captive, and communicated these things or heavenly gifts to believers, both dead and living, then the types of it necessarily had to end; for there was no more need of feeding on things that only represented as in a picture what was to come, but a taking in (as to the inward man), and being really fed and clothed with and by the heavenly things themselves, that were typified before.

*Page 387. Q. 1. Is Christ’s particular soul given to believers?* **A.** Yes, in such a sense as the spiritual being of a soul can sustain; not implying that the individual soul of his human person is transported out of him into the persons of believers, making them to be Christ, but only that between his soul and the souls of believers such a union is made, as there was before between the first Adam’s soul and the souls of all his children, which makes him the root and them the branches. For if his light, inseparable from his soul, enkindles and tinctures their fiery souls, they

Page 387. Q. 2. *Is his particular glorified body given to believers, or only his universal spiritual body?* A. Both together in conjunction; for neither of them can be given without the other. And though the former may be considered chiefly as the giver, and the latter as the gift, yet it is not so in this case as our reason tells us it is with other gifts and givers. This is plain from the nature of the thing and may be illustrated by the simile of the sun’s particular glorious light-body standing in a circumscribed place, and the sun’s universal unformed body extended throughout all this principle.

*Ibid.* Q. 3. *If this were true, would not his particular body be omnipresent as well as his universal body?* A. No, no more than the sun’s particular body is required to be omnipresent as well as its universal body; even though, without the cooperation of its particular body, nothing could be formed in or of its universal body in all the world. For, if there is given a power and virtue of Christ’s spiritual formed body, this power and virtue is certainly in and of his particular body, and proceeds from the same and stirs his universal body; and, without this proceeding from his particular body, or flesh and blood (which he says is meat and drink indeed), no paradisiacal bodies and mystical members of him could be generated in and of his universal body.

Page 387. Q. 5. *What is the true meaning of these words of Christ, Take, eat, this is my flesh?* A. The words of Christ must, according to Saint Paul’s doctrine, be spiritually discerned by a spiritual man, for they are, as the Lord himself said, *spirit and life*; and, therefore, they must be distinguished, but not separated, from that outward act which he then performed when he spoke these words. He took the bread in his hands and broke it, and gave it to them: this was an outward visible act in this elementary world, in which they saw with their firmamental eyes nothing more than what any of us would have seen if we had been present then, namely, that he had natural bread in his hands, not flesh; and so, also, not blood in the cup, but wine. But now, if he had given them no more than what they thus saw and took, he would have fed only their earthly stomach and natural life in this world, which would have profited them nothing toward the kingdom of heaven. His words, therefore, cannot be principally referred to that elementary bread which they saw and took; for truly that bread was not his body, which was to be broken for them for the remission of sins, though it was—according to Saint Paul’s explanation—a communion of, or had communion with, his body. He gave them, at the same time, together with this bread and wine, as belonging to the inward heavenly world, his real flesh and blood, to be taken by their inward man; and to this his words, being spirit and life, must be principally referred. And, though they are not to be separated from the outward elements, yet to each must be attributed only that which it is capable of: and in this act, the two principles—namely, the outward and inward—must always be joined and kept in mind together, so that the outward visible act is referred to this world and to the outward man, but the words of Christ, which he says are *spirit and life*, are referred to the inward man. The connection between them must be understood in that communion which the bread has with his body, and the wine with his blood, consisting not only in that assimilation which is in the breaking and pouring out (attributed both to this and that), but also, and even chiefly, in the interior quickening and strengthening <term>tincture</term>, which is the highest element, regarding this outward principle, in bread and wine. So far, therefore, the Calvinists say well enough that bread and wine are a *symbol* or *sign*, for indeed they are so; but when they add *only* a sign, and a sign of an absent or far-distant thing, this is false. The place quoted from BEHMEN’S THREEFOLD LIFE, which is said to be incorrectly translated, is in substance this—The outward mouth of Christ’s disciples took and gave to the stomach that bread which Christ gave to them; but that word, when Christ said, *Eat, this is my body*, was, or came forth from Christ’s eternal or inward body, and was surrounded with heavenly flesh and blood: this the soul took, and put it on as a new body. Thus there were together at once in the hand of Christ two kingdoms, or two principles, namely, a heavenly one and an earthly one; but you must know that the heavenly cannot be contained and carried about from place to place by the earthly, etc. Now, from this it can be plain enough that all that was said of this above is conformable to this, and that the true meaning of these words of Christ, *Take, eat, this is my body*, cannot be apprehended, found out, or understood in one principle only, nor by a man who lives and is immersed only in this outward principle. Furthermore, it is from this that all the disputes arise, and necessarily must arise, between the divided parties of Christendom. And lastly, the true meaning of these words of Christ (when in each principle that which is within it and belongs to it is understood, and when they both are taken jointly and each is attributed what it is capable of) will be this—(1.) With reference to the inward world, Take and eat with your inward man, will, faith, desire, etc.—this (not this visible bread, for this is not in the

<margin>*Ibid* Page 387. A. last. No, but it is under them, etc.</margin>
Although this answer is sufficient, if it is rightly understood, so that I have nothing to say against it, yet it may easily also be misunderstood, seeing that the words *in* and *under* are a little ambiguous, and bring therefore along with them something of an obscurity. For as there is indeed a true sense wherein we can say, This invisible body is *not in but under the outward elements*, so there is another also, no less true, wherein we can say again, it is *in the outward elements*, namely, just as paradise is in this world, and it is not *under*, but *above them*. It is then indeed in the outward elements, yet not as if in their sphere of being, or as belonging to their kind; but it is under them, or hidden as it were behind their veil.

Page 390. Q. 1. *Is Christ’s body only participated of in the use of bread and wine?* A. No: for Christ has not confined himself to this use of bread and wine, but to the faith of man: which faith, if it is always living and operating, may always eat and drink of Christ’s flesh and blood, whenever it turns itself toward them, and makes them its object; which it can do as well without, as with the use of bread and wine.

Ibid. Q. 2. *Why then is that outward medium made use of?* A. (1.) Because of reasons like those that in baptism required an outward elementary medium: for man also had become outward and elementary, and having disordered himself in all the principles, he wanted a restoration in all of them; and in order to do that, each principle in him was to be fed by its own likeness. (2.) Because of the communion of saints in this outward principle: for there is in the use of this bread and wine a holy band of union tied, even outwardly also between the members of Christ, participating in this common food; which union cannot be made in this outward principle without an outward medium.

Page 390. Q. 3. *To what end is the tincture of the elements conveyed to the soul?* A. Although the tincture of the elements is not properly or directly conveyed to the soul, but to its own likeness in man, yet it may be said also to be conveyed to the soul, as the chief agent in man; and though this tincture is made use of but as a medium, so that no ultimate end may be fixed upon it, yet it may be said also, that it is done to this end, that the soul might have again, in due order and purity, what she had, as to every principle, before the fall.

Ibid. Q. 4. To these two particulars, this third one might reasonably be added——to complete the image of God in man, which does not consist in soul and spirit only, but in spirit, soul, and body.

Ibid. Q. 5. *Why has the soul need of food?* A. Because it is not a self-existent nor independent being. This makes even the holy angels also have need of something for their food: and from the intrinsic essentiality of the two eternal principles, the reason is yet more plain and evident. The first cannot exist without being continually fed, softened, and sustained by the second, and so thereby kept in union with it. But if that first be torn asunder in the creature from the second, it can be nothing else but a perpetual hunger and dryness, never filled nor satisfied, etc. And for such a state the soul was not, nay, could not have been created.

Ibid. Q. 6. *Why has the soul need of a body?* A. The soul, considered as after and with respect to the fall, must of necessity, and according to plain reason, have need of what she lost in the fall, which was her glorious body: and considered absolutely in its creation, and as to its own soulish being, it had need of a body also, because it was to be a full image of God, as manifested in and through eternal nature, wherein there are not only the fiery, but also the light’s properties, and the heavenly corporality as well as pure spirituality.

After the two particulars here mentioned, I think could well be added——(3.) because it has continual need of keeping faithfully to that fraternal band or association, and therefore also of renewing frequently that covenant or confederation, which in this sacrament is made between the members of Christ, in opposition to Satan, the world, and their sinful flesh.

it is capable of. The lusts of the gross body are condemned by God, and his judgment and curse lie upon them, both when a man eats this bread and wine and when he abstains from them: everyone will grant this. Now then, when a man receives this mysterious bread and wine, the testament or covenant of grace—and all that on God's side belongs to it, depends upon it, or is a necessary consequence of it—is stirred within or upon that man, and therefore that judgment upon the lustful outward flesh is also stirred. If, then, the receiver of this bread and wine is in a state of renewal and able to receive Christ’s body, he receives it as to his inward man; but he also receives, as to his outward man, that judgment of his sinful flesh. Indeed, by this, his inward man is strengthened to judge, break, and kill his own lusts in the flesh. But if he is not in a state of renewal, he indeed receives that judgment under the elements, yet he cannot be aware of it; instead, a greater enlivening and strengthening of his own lusts occurs, and Satan gains a wider gateway of entrance into him. Therefore, only the man who is in a state of renewal can receive it profitably in this way, for the destruction of his outward sinful man and the increase of his inward holy man.

Page 392. *Q. penultimate. Why may infants not receive this sacrament?* **A.** Because they cannot examine themselves, nor discern the Lord’s body; nor do they have a will, faith, desire, or hunger for it, nor any awareness of their need for it, but only that foundation in which these things may be raised in their own time. But especially also because they as yet know nothing of that brotherly bond of union and communion of saints, which everyone is to enter into freely, willingly, with a due understanding and an earnest purpose suitable to it; this is the chief end of this outward sacrament, and it cannot be required of infants.

*Ibid. Q. ultimate. What was the true apostolical way of celebrating the Lord’s supper?* **A.** The records of antiquity may give the best account of this. What Behmen says of it is very brief, making no reflection upon any ceremonies, but mentioning only that which is declared by St. Paul.

Page 394. *Q. 4. May it not be called a commemorative or representative sacrifice?* **A.** That there is in this supper not only a commemoration but also a representation of the Lord’s sacrifice is true and plain, both from the words of our Savior and from his breaking the bread. But on what account it should be called such a sacrifice, I cannot see. Christ is not offered up to God in this supper; rather, only a remembrance is made of his having been offered up once on the cross. Instead, he offers and presents himself with all his benefits to man; if man yields himself up to obedience, he is himself a living sacrifice, and ought to be so not only in this celebration of the Lord’s supper, but also in all his life. <note>See LAW ‘On the Sacrament,’ on this point.</note>

Page 394. *How do we eat of the sacrifice of Christ by eating of the Lord’s supper?* **A.** Not only by a thankful commemoration of his sacrifice, made once for us and apart from us on the cross, but also and even chiefly by taking into ourselves and strengthening our inward life with its effectual power. This power is to crucify and kill the lusts and love of this world and of ourselves in our mortal bodies and astral mind; and so we are made, in different respects, a living sacrifice ourselves, both as every communicant in particular and as the whole fraternity in general.

*Ibid. Q. ultimate. What do they mean by the inward word?* **A.** The self-living, and therefore also quickening, enlivening, comforting, raising, and upholding Spirit, power, and virtue, which is contained in and thus hidden under the outward word. Not everyone, and no man always according to his own will, can be aware of it when he looks upon the outward letter—which kills, and kills only, if it is separated from that Spirit. This inward hidden word is different from the outward letter in the same way as, for instance, an almond kernel is from the almond shell, or as pure sweet honey is from the wax frame in which it is contained.

Page 396. *A. 3. These differences between the calls of the inward word are obscure and have something of confusion in them; and I, not knowing from what places they are taken and expressed in this way, can say only this about them in general: namely, that all men are called, and the differences of these calls are on the side of those who are called, rather than on the side of the Word or Spirit calling them. For everyone hears these calls only according to his state, or the progress made in his way, or also his disposition for entering into the way. In some, the Word is indeed unformed, and in them there is very little or no disposition at all to obey their call so that it might be formed; in others, it is in a beginning of formation, more or less, but not yet fixed; and in others again, it is really born and has made its home in them, etc.*

Page 396. *Q. 4.
