Page 398. *A*. 2. *No; none but such are true members*. Since this speaks only of the invisible church, or of those (as was explained on page 396, *A. last*) who are in Christ, I cannot understand why it is said here that *none but such are true members*, by which it is plainly granted that those who are not in Christ are false or dead members; whereas they are no members at all of the Church (which can have no dead members), but only of the outward mixed congregation.

Page 399. *Q*. 1. *What do they mean by Antichrist?* A. That mystery of iniquity (common to all the divided parties of Christendom, and manifesting itself more in some and less in others, according to their different circumstances) which indeed professes the name of Christ, but lives and acts contrary to the spirit, will, and example of Christ; not allowing itself to be taught, led, and guided by him, but setting itself up and suppressing all the rest according to its own will, for its own selfish ends, and upon the principles of its own corrupt reason—all tending to greatness, splendor, and the love of this world.

Ibid. *Q*. 3. *Which do they account the chief error with the Antichristian papacy?* A. The departure from the leading of the Spirit of Christ, according to the pattern of his love and humility, and the exalting of itself into a worldly state—and then also persecuting those who resist or witness against it—cannot but be the chief error, because it is the ground and deep foundation of all the rest. But if this question means the chief error in opinions or articles of confession, I could not say, in particular, which is the chief; but I think that for several of them something might be produced which could make it the chief in this or that particular respect.

Ibid. *Q*. 4. *In what consists the Antichristianism of the Reformation?* A. Although this has already been answered, at least in part, in the question above—*What do they mean by Antichrist*—yet this may be said here in particular: that it consists in not granting the Spirit of Christ his right and due, namely, his inward dominion over the souls of men. Instead, they presume to be their own leaders and teachers, directing people not to Christ *in everyone's own ground*, but to their particular parties and the outward rites, ordinances, words, doctrines, and ceremonies thereof, all crying, "Look, here is Christ!" And then again, it consists in hating, persecuting, and killing one another—at least with the tongue, if not with an outward sword.

Page 400. *A*. 1. *soon after the time of the apostles*. Since the preceding point regarding a false church within the true one is universal and extends to the whole course of time from the beginning of the human race, this point also might be represented more universally, and its beginning be placed in the time of Cain rather than after that of the apostles. This is even more appropriate because, at the beginning of this answer, it was said, *They give an account of the state of the church, from the beginning to the end of the world*.

Page 400. *No*. 5. *The golden candlesticks were withdrawn, etc.* Behmen's meaning in these expressions is, in plain words, this: The glorious light of the gospel and the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit of God—which the Lamb of God had bestowed on the church after he had satisfied the Father's fiery anger and justice and broken the seven seals of the book of life in humanity—were taken away and sealed up again when the church would walk no more in that light. They were hidden from the church under the same seven seals of the Father's wrath; why then, instead, the seven vials of his anger and indignation were poured out from his throne, etc.

Ibid. *No*. 8. *not wholly free from wickedness, strife, and contention, etc.* In that state of the church which Behmen calls Zion, no such thing will exist; nor has he anywhere declared his mind in such a way, but said only that Zion will not be so universal that no wicked man will be left on earth. If strife and contention should still exist in that state, what advantage could it have over the beginning or infant state of the apostolic churches? Moreover, many places in the Scripture speak expressly and directly to the contrary.

Page 401. *Q. Do they admit a supreme pastor or pope?* A. They admit none currently in existence; and as for the future, I can say nothing for certain. The words of Behmen cited from the <term>Forty Questions</term>, Answer 39, do not argue plainly enough for this purpose; rather, if they are compared to some of his other passages and expressions, it is plain that he understands them to refer to Christ, the only head of the church and only true shepherd and bishop of souls.

Q. 3. *Will not their errors and superstitions be counted as sinful by God?* **A.** They will be burned up in the final fire, like straw and stubble; and so they shall suffer the loss of these things, which were—if not directly sins—at least so many effects and products of sin, and unable to endure the fire.

Ibid Q. 4. *What should an honest, simple Christian do amidst a variety of sects and contentions?* **A.** He should not involve himself in contentions, but keep his heart peaceful within himself and in love with all men, of whatever persuasion they may be. He should focus on nothing but the inward work of the Spirit of God upon his soul in all his outward performances, knowing that nothing can benefit him or make him acceptable to God except his own being made a new creature in Jesus Christ.

Page 404. Q. 2. *Please, what do they mean by these last two assertions?* **A.** They do not mean that the civil magistrate is the head of the church—that is, of those who are in Christ—but only of the outward congregation as it exists in this world. In this role, the magistrate is ordained, authorized, and commissioned by God to oversee and care for the welfare of his subjects. They also mean that the priests have no such outward power, commission, and authority given to them by God or Jesus Christ, but that their power and authority is only spiritual. Therefore, with respect to the outward congregation, they are not rulers or governors, but rather servants of the same regarding outward functions; nevertheless, with respect to the spiritual kingdom of Christ, they are not servants, but are or ought to be fathers or elders, excelling their flock in age (of the inward new man) and in experience of things belonging to the kingdom of heaven. This makes them worthy of double honor, which is never applicable to any servant.

Page 403. Q. *Do they say that a layman may administer the sacraments and perform the other parts of the ministerial function?* **A.** In Christ there is no distinction between a priest and a layman, but all who are anointed with his Spirit are priests. All, therefore, by virtue of this anointing, may undoubtedly administer the sacraments and perform all other parts of the ministerial function; that is, they are in themselves sufficiently qualified for it by the Spirit of Christ. But on the other hand, seeing that there is such a distinction in the outward congregation and that God is a God of order, no layman may attempt to do such a thing, except in cases of necessity where no priest can be found.

Page 405. Q. *Is not confession to a priest and absolution by him of great use, even if he has only ordinary gifts?* **A.** To those who have only an ordinary understanding of things belonging to the kingdom of Christ, it may be of great edification; but it cannot be established as a universal rule for all.

Q. 2. *What do they say of tithes?* **A.** No more than that Abraham’s giving of tithes to Melchizedek denotes an inward mystery, or is a figure of the full restoration of man, or of the recreating of God's image in him again. <term>Man</term> is to give the tenth property of the human properties of his <term>soulish fire</term> to Christ; and Christ gives his blessing into it—his love-fire, light's tincture, and heavenly substantiality (just as Melchizedek, the type of Christ, gave bread and wine with his blessing). By the conjunction of these two, the image of God in man is completed. If it should be asked, what is meant by the tenth property of the human properties of the soulish fire? I must confess that I cannot sufficiently penetrate <term>Behmen's</term> sense; but I think, nevertheless, that it may be enough to understand simply the whole fiery soul, without dividing it between Christ and the spirit of this world. For as there is a fullness of counting in the number ten (which is also true of, and even originates from, the ten forms or <term>eternal properties of fire</term>) and a falling back into the first, so the whole soul must first fall back into its ground and be first given up wholly (which it cannot be if it is not at the end of its own counting in selfishness) before it can receive this blessing and be reunited to the heavenly substantiality in Christ. Q. 2. *What do they say concerning death?* This question is particularly answered later on page 422, and this only may be added:—that death is a shutting up or suffocating of the tincture, and that the most terrible thing in it is the dissolution of the four elements, which is a breaking off of the *third principle* from the first. Because this *third principle* was now so nearly consubstantiated with man—having captivated him and taken possession of his will—this breaking off cannot help but be dreadful to him, and accompanied with pains, more or less, according to the inward and outward condition of his soul and body.

*Ibid.* Q. 4. *What do they say concerning the resurrection, and the day of judgment?* A. Concerning the resurrection, it is spoken of later on page 430, but this might be added more specifically:—that the dead shall hear the voice or call of God from within, namely, in the depth of their own souls, whether they are in happiness in the *second principle*, or in misery in the *first principle*. And that every particular receptacle—namely, that of earth, water, air, etc.—when the universal *mysterium* is moved, must give forth again all that it has taken of man. Concerning the day of judgment something is also said on page 430, and this might be added:—that in a manner contrary to, or going as it were backward from that order in which the world was created, its dissolution shall be. That the *fire of nature* (not an elementary fire, which would not consume earth and stones) shall kindle itself. That in this kindling the separation of good and evil in all things is to be done, everything entering into its own principle; and that this strictly is the last day, time being then no more.

*Ibid.* Q. 5. *Do they tell us what will be the state of things after the day of judgment?* A. As to this, I think they say nothing except what in general may be expressed, as is commonly done, by an eternal happiness in the vision and enjoyment of God, and an endless misery in the separation from his light and love.

*Ibid.* No. 8. *saints war not as Christians, but as heathens.* These words are universally true, without limitation or exception. But if this limitation mentioned here be added—namely, *when they war unlawfully and seek self-interest*—this position is inconsistent with No. 4. And the matter is plain. If any war unlawfully and seek self-interest, they do not war as saints; this is self-evident. But if the saints (as in this instance Abraham was) war lawfully and seek no self-interest, they do not indeed war as those heathens, but also not as saints; for all this lawfulness is only in and belongs merely to this outward principle, in which there is a mixture of good and evil, of right and unright, and of which even the saints also are children—that is, natural men or heathens, as to their outward man. This therefore (not their inward sanctified ground) is the property which wars in them; and the only difference between the wars of these heathens and heathens, so vastly different from each other (the former being merely heathens and nothing else, and the latter heathens only as to their outward man, but saints within), consists in this: that the merely heathens seek self-interest, war for ambition and greed, rouse up their own heathenish property, and manage their war in

I do not see how this *spiritual subtlety* from the MYSTERIUM MAGNUM, lviii. 24, etc., can be referred to this place; for it has a completely spiritual sense, not relating at all to outward possessions in this world, but to the wonders of outward nature, showing how they may be taken along with us through death, and brought into the kingdom of Christ, in the holy light-world.

*Ibid.* No. 10. If governors are truly in the inward process of regeneration, as Joseph was, they cannot help but notice how God carries on his work in them after a spiritual manner, in the spirit of love and tenderness, and for their good: and, in conformity with that, they also cannot help but manage all things concerning their subjects in a creaturely manner, in the same spirit, and to the same end. But if they are not, it is no wonder that they do not govern as Joseph did, but as we see they generally do.

Page 422. No. 7. *near and far off are all one.* The meaning of this expression is plain and simple. If there were a distinction between *near* and *far off* in the light and love of God, God would not be everywhere in the light or angelic world equally. Those who are in it are not nearer to him when they are in the kingdom of Christ, nor further from him when they are in that of Michael. *Near and far off* are things belonging to this outward principle, as is time; if one is dissolved, the other must be dissolved also: yet even in this principle, something similar may be observed in our mind, spirit, thoughts, etc. In respect to these, it is no further to the West Indies than to Westminster; our thoughts are able to be as swiftly in one place as in the other. John Engelbrecht, in his *Vision of Heaven and Hell*, says, I remember, that what might be accounted as a thousand miles from him, he could see and discern as plainly and distinctly as that which was next to him. So that, indeed, all manner of distance is utterly excluded from the creatures in the light-world; but that, nevertheless, all "near" and "far off" from God have lost all their distinction in that world, etc.

No. 13. *bad wishes or curses hurt them.* Here, I think, this caution might be added—that it is not appropriate for the children of God, nor lawful, to curse or wish bad wishes upon damned souls: because they thus sow their seed into hell, and will certainly reap the fruits of it if a revocation is not made by repentance.

Page 426. No. 14. To the first part of this position might be added—chiefly if this is done at their departure from this body; which is also expressly added by Behmen. For afterwards indeed, though it is not denied as utterly impossible, yet it is not a thing so easily done. And in the latter part of this position, Behmen's meaning is not expressed, which is this—The soulish spirit of a living saint may go along with his departing brother to assist him in his way through darkness and fire; but when he is in the light, he can no longer help him to have a greater glorification, but that spirit returns to its own soul: and the glorification of his brother is not from the assistance, prayers, or help of any other, but only from and according to his own essence, will, and works.

*Ibid.* No. 17. This raising and disturbing cannot be extended universally to all the departed blessed souls. And accordingly, there appear some glimpses of the most deep mystical Oriental learning here and there, which is not discovered in any books, and therefore some of the learned men of Europe think it may be past their reach; but they will find that foundation in this author which will make such things easy to be understood, for the time of disclosing those foundations so plainly was not until now, that the mysteries which have been hidden since the world began should be revealed. No. 21. *Abraham's bosom is the Christian church, etc.* Since "Abraham's bosom" might be understood as if it meant the Christian church militant—which, though true enough in a certain sense, is not used that way in Scripture or by Behmen—there might only be added a word or two declaring that it is the Christian church as it exists in the second principle of light.

The perfectly regenerate have their new body and soul, but in different principles, etc. Behmen says no such thing: what the English translation says, I cannot tell, nor can I see what sense there could be in those words. He says expressly, between those souls that have not yet put on their new body and those that have, there is indeed still a gulf, but not a principle; for they are both in one principle. If, then, different souls in such different states are in one and the same principle, how could one individual person have his soul in one principle and his body in another, different from that? And again, Behmen does not say, "They have their body in paradise, and they have their souls upon the cross"; but rather they *shall have it so*, or they *shall be brought into paradise again, etc.* But this is Behmen's meaning, and the plain construction of his discourse is this: Those souls that in this life have put on the body of Christ must, nevertheless, still wait for the resurrection of their paradisiacal body. For though they are indeed in paradise in the paradisiacal world, they are not yet in paradise in the same way they were at first created in Adam and introduced into paradise. This third principle has not yet been turned into paradise in its completed fullness; therefore, their inward and outward body cannot be enjoyed by them before the resurrection of their paradisiacal body into paradise, to remain there forever. It shall, therefore, be brought into it again, and the soul shall be upon the cross of the ternary in the mouth of God, from where it came, etc. No separation of soul and body is to be thought of here; but, as in the first creation the whole man was formed and spoken or breathed forth by God into paradise, so in the full restoration it shall be done again. Soul and body are now indeed in God and in paradise; and the soul especially is upon (not in, nor under the cross, as it was during this lifetime, but upon) the cross, in the majesty, surrounded with light. But with respect to the future state, it is still, as it were, in His mouth, or the power of breathing it forth into its lost primeval state; and by that mouth of God, it is not yet breathed forth or introduced into paradise as restored and manifested in this third principle—which also cannot be done before the resurrection of the body and the separation of good and evil in this mixed world.

Those who led their lives in such a way came to understand those mysteries about which these things were written. And in several nations, their wisdom has had several names, which has caused our age to take all the names of the various parts of wisdom and sort them into arts, among which the *Magia* and *Cabala* are accounted the most mystical. The *Magia* consists in knowing how things have come to be, and the *Cabala* in knowing how the words and forms (or signatures) of things express the reality of the inward mystery. But he who knows "the mystery" knows both these and all the branches of the tree of wisdom in all real arts and sciences, and the true meaning of every idea in every thought, thing, sound, and letter in every language. And therefore this author, having this true knowledge, could well explain the letters of the names of GOD—the meaning of which, he says, is well-understood in the language of every thought, thing, sound, and letter in every language. And therefore, just as "not one jot or tittle of the word of God shall pass away till all be fulfilled," so there is no tittle of any letter that has proceeded from that eternal, essential WORD (as all things have) that is not understood in that word from which it came—even in the voice of all men and the sounds of all other creatures. Also, the letters and syllables of a word in one language express something of the mystery more exquisitely than those of another; and therefore (I believe) the author sometimes explains words borrowed from Hebrew and Greek, some Latin words, and other technical terms, as well as German words—and not always words of his own native language only—according to their meaning in the language of nature. For that language shows, in everyone's mother-tongue, the greatest mysteries that have ever existed in the nature of anything, within the letters of the word by which it is expressed. Therefore, let everyone value those expositions of his according to their high worth; for the knowledge of that language is only taught by the spirit of the letter.

The first reflection which naturally suggests itself, after a careful reading of the above '*Observations*,' is this: What a noble popular compendium of theology and classic textbook of Christian doctrine Mr. Waple's work would have formed if the above corrections and alterations had been introduced into it! In the preface to '*Waple's Sermons*,' 3 volumes, octavo, which were published after his death, a brief memorial of the author is inserted, containing the following passages which may perhaps lead to further light being thrown on the subject:

> "As for the author [of these Sermons], of whom some account might be expected here, since he was careful that his life should indeed be hidden from the world; and as certain private memoirs of his own life written by himself (which he told an intimate friend about in confidence *some years before his death*) were *probably* destroyed by him together with *some other valuable papers* when he began to fear the approach of his death, *lest it might happen that someone or other might make a bad use of them*, since they are not now to be found after the strictest search made for them; the reader must be content (without having the veil drawn from that which was hidden with Christ in God) with that most authentic testimony which he has left of himself in his last will and testament, in which the true picture of his mind can be seen." In another place it is mentioned that "he gave a very large and curious collection of books, which he had been amassing at great expense for several years, to the library of Sion College in this city." In another, it is observed concerning him that "his great reserve may indeed be considered a fault by some; and *I do not deny* (continues the editor) that because of it we have lost some *excellent productions* of his, *of various kinds*. But he was a person who had so studied human nature and was so well acquainted with its motives that he found all too much reason for his general distrust, both of himself and of the rest of mankind."

From these passages it would appear that his papers were destroyed, and among them the manuscripts in question; nevertheless, may we not venture to hope that the results of so much study and labor—which they undoubtedly were, and which had been corrected with so much pains and exactness as we have seen, and which were in themselves of such intrinsic value and excellence, contributing to the best interests of mankind in the diffusion of Divine light and truth and the promotion of practical piety—have, by the providence of God, been preserved and will yet be brought to light in due time.

*...passing away before etc. in the Apocalypse.*

*Of transmutation and annihilation with respect to this third principle.* Our common concept of this is exceedingly low, and why. Illustrated only by day and night. Shadows, chimeras, etc., cannot be annihilated, and why. Nor changed into each other. What place is; and what it is to dwell in itself.

*Of annihilation with respect to eternal nature.* What is annihilation? None can exist, and why? In Adam's fall there was no annihilation, but only, etc.: so also in his restoration. No, in this, the first three cannot be so deeply annihilated or swallowed up, as etc. Even all our evil works shall follow us. Even much more the three eternal roots thereof. If man could fall again, where would he fall? etc.

*Of transmutation with respect to eternal nature.* None can exist, and why. Distinction and oneness must be together, the former looking forward, the latter backward. Each is to keep to its own peculiar office. They are not only three in the temperament, but also seven in the temperament, and in nature, and in the midst between temperament and nature. This is further explained by showing how *nature* is understood differently. Upon this difference, the different enumeration of the forms depends. Why there is no passage from darkness into light, except through the fire. Hence it is evident the three forms on the left hand cannot be *transmuted* into the three on the right hand, so as etc. And what further follows is for this demonstration also.

*Here we find the two eternal principles.* By an eternal opposition is meant quite another thing than etc. (1.) Not as day and night by turns. (2.) Not as black and white in one surface. God knew not the fall of Lucifer. (3.) Not as good and evil. In eternity there is but one good thing. Friendship and harmony between darkness, fire, and light, declared by root, stock, and branches. Darkness, fire, and light—all three are good, not good and evil with respect to themselves; nay, to creatures also etc. Where the opposition of good and evil is. Behmen could not so much as have dreamed of an eternal opposition of good and evil. The question: "How could he write of this so positively, and with such an assurance?" is answered.

*What this eternal opposition is,* is declared by looking on the first step, made out of the eternal unity or oneness. There is really opposition, but all is good, not good and evil. *Will* and *desire*, how they are one; and how they are two. And the differences between them. All is good. Eternal will is neither darkness nor light. Desire is necessarily dark, but (Note) not without *itself*. The will is not *desire*. The difference is exceedingly subtle; but remember this is the first step. *God* and *nature* are not confounded by Behmen. Will and desire are as light and darkness. Who can find here such an opposition as that of good and evil? To whom could darkness have been evil? What reason is there to call it evil? But here lies the knot etc. Adam's nakedness. The light was not properly "good" from eternity <note>In the sense of a moral quality distinguished from an opposite evil</note>. Darkness would never have done any hurt, if etc. After all this, what shall we say of God? etc. A state may be attained wherein all this opposition has vanished away. Behmen is justly called *PHILOSOPHUS CENTRALIS*.

*The consequences of this consideration.* An objection that the three forms are thus transmuted only by halves is answered. John 1:5, *the light shines into darkness, but the darkness comprehended it not*. Why can it not, or will it not? is answered. Why not, when it is a desire after light? is answered.

*How darkness was; was not and yet was.* So the glorious transmutation was done, not done, and yet done. Lucifer could not have been the cause of darkness being what it is now, if it had not been something in and to itself before. This is demonstrated (1.) because God has not created it so; and Lucifer is but a destroyer. Beginning and end appear in a broken ring. (2.) Because, if darkness were quite annihilated by the light, Lucifer must have annulled this annihilation. And is thus set upon the great white throne. (3.) Because, if the three interior forms were transmuted into the three superior forms, so as etc., Lucifer was stronger than this omnipotent transmuting tincture, and went directly forward etc.

*Darkness had no beginning, and darkness had a beginning; both are true.* The higher and more intellectual truth of the former is demonstrated. (1.) Upon the supposition that darkness was created by God in Lucifer's fall: by showing what *nothing* is; and that darkness must have been something to the abyssal eye before it was something to itself. Eternal without beginning. (2.) Upon the supposition that darkness was not created, but only manifested: by showing that then it must have been something hidden before this manifestation. Eternally something without beginning.

A strong objection—that darkness is merely a *privation of light*—is answered. This is done chiefly by considering this privation within ourselves, or in our fallen and reborn condition. A foundational axiom is: God has dwelt in the light from eternity.

A summary of all that has been declared so far. There is no path, neither on the right hand nor on the left, but that which leads us to this truth: that darkness had no beginning. For whether we say (1) darkness had a beginning, or (2) light had no beginning, or (3) light had a beginning, it all leads to the same conclusion. The meaning of this expression is defined by saying it is an eternal beginning, or a beginning without a beginning. These two positions—that darkness had no beginning, and that darkness had a beginning—are compared: both are accepted as being without contradiction, but the former is much preferred as being deeper, more solid, truly central, and therefore not obvious to everyone.

The conclusion. A symbolic figure or illustration showing balance—nature—and balance.

### (III.)—A DISCOURSE IN ANSWER TO AN OBJECTION CONCERNING THE DESIRE’S ATTRACTING ITSELF.

Compelling reasons for this discourse. Light cannot be seized by force through deep speculation. The premise, and the consequences said to follow from it. The next immediate consequence, flowing forth freely. The *will* is not a *desire*, and the *desire* is not a *will*. Differences between them. Desire has nothing outside of itself to attract. What is meant by the phrase *attracts itself*. At this stage, there is no distinction yet between the attractor and the attracted.

A fitting simile, drawn from our mind and senses, runs from here through the entire discourse. The next immediate consequence. The difference between the mind and the senses, and thus between God and nature. There is a *self* in the latter.

Desire *attracting itself* is a meaningful expression. It is explained using our simile and applied to eternal nature. *This self* is the only thing by which reason is deluded. By a sharp investigation into what is attracted, nothing can be found, neither within nor without. Objection: Such a state is attracted as the desire will raise itself into. Answer: This is true on the left hand, but false on the right, etc. And everything that follows further is in answer to this objection:

That (1) a state of rest is not attracted by the desire is demonstrated from the nature of attraction, which is an approach toward union; whereas, on the contrary, etc. That (2) this state of rest in our senses and the light in eternal nature are not what the desire is filled and permeated with. (3) What it properly is that the desire fills itself with, and which is attracted by it. "Full of light" is to be understood according to the left hand. The light of the moon and of astral reason are closely related to, etc. Self or selfishness. Covetousness, as the second element of hell, is almost the same—devouring heaven and paradise, and yet remaining nothing but itself. Conclusion.

### (IV.)—AN EXPLANATION OF THAT SCHEME OR FIGURE BY TEUTONICUS, (being the First of the THREE TABLES, see page 27) WHEREIN GOD IS CONSIDERED IN THE UNITY AND TRINITY, APART FROM ALL NATURE AND CREATED BEINGS. This discourse, shortly after its commencement, was interrupted for AN EXPLANATION, which is given here, of the TABLE OF THE DIVINE REVELATION (see p. 32) appended to the book *The Election of Grace*.

God (the Trinity) is incomprehensible and indescribable; and why? Poiret's *Superficial and Solid Learning*. "Thou canst not see my face." From his (even positive) expressions, we are to learn what God is not, rather than what He is. *Nothing* is a positive expression; and Boehme's positive expressions lead us only to a negative understanding: for example, *meekness* and *softness*. A paraphrase upon THEOS. Questions 1, 1-2. Introductory observations. The Scheme. Every letter, word, and syllable of which is set down significantly and exactly in its proper place and relation, and must be so regarded, or the greatest confusion will be caused. . . [Here the discourse is interrupted, and the other Table is requested to be explained.]

Boehme's scheme of God (the Trinity). *Manifestation* is a progress from the internal or central to the outer circumference. *Abyssal nothing and all* is most obscure, and yet it is a key. *Abyss* and *byss* are explained by a resemblance we carry of them within ourselves. And references for abyss and byss. *Nothing*, meaning none of all particular "somethings." *The all rectifies nothing*. *Nothing* is used here primarily with respect to its own *something*. *Has a will and is a will* (God here is not distinct from His habitation), both are consistent. Thus far, the Unity.

The *Father*. Boehme is justified in saying the *Father* is a *dark valley without the Son*.

### (V.) — OF THE FURTHER EXTERNAL MANIFESTATION OF GOD, THROUGH THE CREATION OF ANGELS.
->Wherein material causes are treated.<-

The first movement of God toward the *creation of angels* shall not be investigated. A proof that the Angels are *out of God*. They are children of God, who is fire and light, having darkness under his feet; this was first manifested in their fall, when they acted like *Ham*; which is proved by Paul: *If we are the offspring of God, the Godhead is not like, etc.* If Angels were made out of nothing, then their fall must have been a relapse into nothing, not a downfall into darkness. Reason thinks to honor God more, etc., but he is not more honored by an image of gold than by one of clay. Speculation is the mother of all our inventions. Consider what this *nothing* is, and the impossibility will show itself. God cannot send forth his word beyond the infinite sphere of his all-encompassing existence.

If angels are not from God, what is the meaning of their *bearing his name written upon them?* What is that *spark of divine being* found in all the mystics? What is that *breath of life* breathed into man? If the life, which was the light of man, was in God and was God *before man was made*, how did it come into man, *if not out of God?* And what is the *seed of God, remaining, etc.*? From where do the wonderful magic powers of angels and the stupendous effects of faith in men come? Our *regeneration* gives an all-sufficient testimony. *We must be born again, from above.* If not so, what can the mysterious communion signify, typified by the first *Adam* and his *wife*? What are the names: Christ’s, God’s, Savior’s? What is it to be like him; *sitting upon his throne*; to become one spirit with him; to *ascend with him into heaven?* What is the distinction between a son and a servant? *Go to my brothers. I ascend to my Father and your Father.* The devil's cunning craft. The foundation of Christianity is dangerously undermined and deprived of its essence if this truth be denied; it is acknowledged by many who will *come from the east and from the west, etc.*

The consequences examined, by similes:—I. *If out of God, they are God* is shown to be false. The true consequences are: (1.) They are distinct and different persons. (2.) They bear his name. Females relating to regeneration. (3.) They are like him—men and whole persons. (4.) They are under his direction and government. All this follows exactly regarding God and his children, and the reason why. But (5.) as an addition, it is freely granted: *If out of God, they are Gods.* Reasons are given, both from before and after eternal nature, why this consequence—*they are God*—is false; and why this—*they are Gods; and if Gods out of God, they are not God*—is true.

II. *If out of God, they must be part of God.* This is shown in our simile (1.) to be false, regarding the soul and spirit, but (2.) it is granted to come a little nearer regarding the body. Therefore, we should look into the magical generation. But to give greater satisfaction, we will keep to our simile. Wherein it is shown again that the consequence is false in the common, grossest sense; and the scriptural concept of *partaking of the divine nature* is the only true immediate consequence, in this world as in that superior world also.

If this partaking of the divine nature is such a stumbling block, who laid it in our way? Our saying they are "out of nothing" is a far greater and more real obstacle. The strange consequences of this *out of nothing* are touched upon. The *in him* (which might more easily) does not confound God and creature, and no offense is taken. Why then take offense at the *out of him*? They are equally gross in their utmost sense looking toward materiality. Both the *in him* and the *out of him* are infinitely surpassed by *our being one, as he is one with the Father.* Here is the proper argument for reason's saying, "We are confounded with God." But that we are not is plainly proved. What hurt (if; if; if) would be done to say, *we are part of God*? So Boehme has said of Lucifer; regarding not the enticing words which human wisdom teaches. So our Lord Jesus also: *I am the true vine, etc.*; not concerned what his

words, and other conventional forms and combinations might seem, any more than we attempt to explain the mysteries hidden in the corresponding symbols, hieroglyphics, and other characters of Persian, Hindu, Chinese, and Egyptian philosophy; such specialized learning being discoverable by a study of the respective books that treat those subjects. But what is aimed at here is to indicate that system of fundamental truth which was the basis and subject of those national and distinguished modes of representation, through which they may be severally reconciled with each other and with Christianity—assuming indeed, which is incontestable, that the original inventors, the primitive philosophers, and their successors, were men of at least equal ingenuity, strength of intellect, and integrity of mind as ourselves, and that truth and nature were the objects of their contemplations, and not merely lying inventions of the spirit of error. And this we consider to be achieved by displaying, in an orderly and demonstrative manner, the scope and sense of Boehme; in the center of whose mind, as we have already sufficiently expressed our conviction, the birth—or rather the inward and outward manifestation—of truth, of divine wisdom, and of nature, was originally opened anew. This was done in regard to the evangelical purposes of God, and also in accordance with the epoch of time. For, as the holy trinity of Father, Son, and Spirit (who is truth itself, and whose word is truth) have each had their manifestation in the great acting mystery of redemption for man and creation, so there remained only the manifestation of *wisdom*—the personal or virginal embodiment of the triune spirit of truth and love—to complete the revelation of the Divine nature to man. We declare this manifestation to have been opened in Boehme, not to end with himself, but with regard to all Christendom and to the world, to be henceforth carried forward in its proper developments and discoveries, until the end finds the beginning, and they are clearly one. For, as in the order of consideration, Divine wisdom flows from, or is the perfection and crown of, the triune life in God, so must it do and

Transition to the third alleged consequence, namely, *material cause*; and why the analyzing of it is undertaken.

What is meant by materiality. *Material and visible are not the same as spiritual and invisible; this is shown from "if our earthly house," etc. Materiality and material cause in this temporal world, what they are. There is a great difference between matter and spirit in general, and a far greater difference between our gross matter and the pure matter of the eternal world.* Yet, we say "out of" regarding (1) material things, (2) spiritual things, and (3) both material *and* spiritual things; who then does not see the great difference in meaning? What is implied in the phrase "out of" when said in the grossest sense. Material cause considered again. A carved image out of wood. A plant out of the earth; its smell and colors. A spark of fire out of steel and flint. Storehouses of wrath. Treasures sealed up. Similarly, the storehouse of mercy.* Up to this point, it is in opposition to what is brought forth *out of material causes by nature*. Now, in opposition to what is *out of material causes by art*, it was intended to have considered man. The effects of divine and dark magia. That nothing is impossible to him who believes. Joshua. These two, *out of themselves and without a material cause*, must be joined together. Reasons why. The former implies they are not "out of nothing" because they act forward. The latter implies (1) they do not have and do not need a material cause; this is proved from their acting forward. Material causes do *not go on to infinity*. There is a gulf. Orderly coherence without interruption in the Divine manifestation. Secondly and chiefly, they do not correspond to a material cause; this is proved from their necessary unalterableness. By saying *this or that, we break, etc.*, but by joining the former two, we maintain union and distinction. If you say *out of nothing*, what prerogative do you leave to God? He is *Alpha and Omega*. Thus, he is not confused with creatures, but rather, etc. The *out of nothing* is not utterly rejected. If eternal nature is out of him (as is plain from the desire), all that is out of eternal nature is out of him also. *The will of God is the only cause of all things*; this is true, but often misunderstood. *The band of union; the eternal character.* <term>☉</term>. This is the reason why we cannot say "out of nothing." And why there is no possibility of reducing anything into nothing. *Objection:*—Such a band empties the fullness of God and places a constraint upon him. *Answered* by rectifying *this* and utterly denying *that*. *This discussion of material causes is now closed.*

the seventh form of eternal nature, out of all the powers and virtues of God, etc. All these different expressions may easily be found to agree with each other, without any contradiction, if the *sevenfold generation of eternal nature is more or less understood*.

He says that God, by moving himself (*the ground of which moving on the side of God—as has been mentioned already several times—is the only thing we do not know, and which shall not be inquired after by any creature*), has shaped an image of himself, like a little God. Or that the word of God, *verbum Domini*, laid hold of the fountain spirits, apprehending them by the *fiat* in his will, and compacting them, or as it were driving them together, as if from an expansion into narrowness. By this compacting and driving together (as was done again afterwards, more outwardly and crudely, regarding the materiality of this third principle), their creation was effected, of which may be especially considered what he says in *AURORA*, xvi. 13–21, and *I. INCARNATION*, ii. 1–25.

But if it should be objected and said, "What Behmen says in these two places is unintelligible—why could he not have declared it more plainly to remove offenses and obstacles, and to end controversies? It must be an absolute impossibility to understand this creation distinctly, and so he may be suspected of not having understood himself, etc."? It may be answered with confidence and truth that these two places, and also all his others, are much more intelligible than all the chemical writers are in their enigmatic descriptions of the process of their philosophical work. Indeed, they are altogether unintelligible to everyone who is not himself a true philosopher and possessor of the art, and does not have the spirit of understanding in himself; for to such people they are intelligible enough. But why should others complain of their darkness and unintelligibility? Or how can they say that there is an absolute impossibility to understand and to declare this philosophical process plainly, seeing that the only reason they are so abstruse and reserved in their words is that exceeding great danger which clearly lies in a plain publication of this secret work—not only with respect to the world, but also to themselves? Of this they are accustomed to say that they would lose even their eternal salvation if they should go beyond their limits in making known to the world that which God will have kept secret from its eyes. If this can sufficiently excuse their enigmatic way of writing about it, why shall it not also much more excuse the abstruse expressions of Behmen, used in this matter especially? This is not only because no other utterance was given to him, but also because he did so willingly and purposely regarding several circumstances of it, seeing that this is indeed of a far greater importance and of much more dangerous consequences to the children of men than that could ever be. *If Lucifer had not known (these are his plain words) the manner and method of the creation, and the whole working process of the magical powers, he might have been a holy angel to this very day.* And so he also says further that God placed another exterior king into the room of Lucifer in this third principle, whom he could name indeed but would forbear from doing so because of the dark *magia*; and though he named him afterwards in another place intelligibly enough, because this is not of such great importance, yet he was so cautious in his expressions that he said no more than what he was permitted to say. Several further instances of this kind could also be produced from his writings if necessity required it. But to return to our present matter: the whole tenth and eleventh chapters of his MYSTERIUM MAGNUM are worthy of serious consideration and may be found to be a great deal plainer regarding this or that particular than the two former mentioned places.

*There he says expressly that this great danger was always, and is yet still, the only reason why this magical generation was kept so very secret from the beginning of the world until this present day; though we nevertheless cannot say that it was altogether unknown and unintelligible in its entirety to all the children of Adam, which would not be true. Just as he also does not say it, but grants plainly that, for instance, Moses indeed had a true knowledge and understanding of it. Though it was not always according to his own pleasure, nor in his own reason and capacity, yet he had it—and must have had it—at that moment when those magical powers were opened in him, and when the spirit of his will and imagination was concurring with them in an actual performance of those works he was called and commanded to effect by them.*

To say, therefore, "It is absolutely unintelligible," is to deny that man's internal depth is a dwelling place of those magical powers, and that his will and imagination are a living agent capable of being instructed by the Spirit of eternity—the only supreme director of the divine *magia*—how to act and work. This yet cannot be denied. If man really acts with them and performs this or that stupendous work by them, he certainly knows the way, manner, and method by which his work is done, and can also declare it to others if he is permitted. Otherwise, would it not be the same absurdity as if we should grant on the one hand that a skillful watchmaker can make, and has actually made, a curious artificial watch, but would pretend on the other that it is beyond his understanding and quite unintelligible to him, and that he therefore cannot tell or declare to anybody how he made it? As for BEHMEN, it is to me—and I am sure to many others also—beyond all doubt and question that he truly had a true and deep understanding (not in his reason, but in his eternal spirit) of the manner and process of the whole creation; nay, that he really and fundamentally understood even the way and method of necromancy itself—not in practice as the devil's agents do, but in its ground and depth, where they are blind and ignorant. But none can pretend that he should have declared these magical powers in such a way that the children of men could play with them according to their good pleasure. <note>Which they would assuredly do, as their present vain researches in alchemy—without first of all becoming truly converted to God, evangelically regenerate, and pure in heart—do testify.</note> He has done faithfully what he was commanded to do; that is, he has declared them plainly and intelligibly enough regarding that which can serve us in the process of regeneration. There can be no difficulty to him who desires earnestly to follow that direction given through him by the Spirit of God. Let us therefore first pass through this process <note>to be set forth in the GRAMMAR and EXERCISES of WISDOM with all simplicity, order, and amplitude</note> and arrive at that gate which he—

And this I may say confidently, knowing that I say the truth, and knowing it not only because Behmen says the same through other expressions (whose authority is justly much esteemed and valued by me), but because I also *know another testimony of it*, which is of far greater authority than one thousand outward witnesses can be. ### (VII.)—OF THE CREATION OF THIS OUTWARD THIRD PRINCIPLE, IN WHICH WE LIVE, MOVE, AND HAVE OUR OUTWARD BEING.

What the creation is and why it was made. The beginning of time implies an end. The common opinion (though in a sense not harmful) is debunked. A twofold objection—that Behmen makes Lucifer either a creator of earth and stones or a binder of the sovereign will of God—is answered. Regarding the first, the whole matter is largely represented. Regarding the second, it is shown that it stands upon a false hypothesis, and the whole matter is further and more fully declared, according to the description given by Moses in Genesis 1:1, *In the beginning*, etc. [Because of its importance, we provide the entirety of the above section, up to the dissertation on Genesis 1:1, as follows:]

> "From what was said before, it might already be plain, but it is here to be made plainer, that the fall of Lucifer was the only (*causa sine qua non* <note>An indispensable condition or cause.</note>) cause, or rather the only occasion, of the creation of this, our third principle. This is nothing more than a temporary, coagulated out-breathing or exhalation, and thus a visible representation and manifestation of the two interior, eternal, and invisible principles. These were brought into war and opposition to each other by Lucifer, but settled again in this world by the infinite wisdom and power of God in such a combination, order, proportion, and harmony that (notwithstanding all their contradictions, in which they both act their parts upon this one visible stage) they must both be subservient to keeping out and keeping down their former prince, and to the greater manifestation of the glory of the omnipotent Creator. And so, this creation is not the bringing forth of any new or strange thing that had not existed before in any way; it is only an alteration of that state which existed before the fall in the particular kingdom or region of Lucifer. This alteration was made by God for the better, after Lucifer had brought about an alteration for the worse. For he had utterly spoiled, darkened, and wasted it, turning a pleasant angelic garden into a dark den of lions, dragons, and tigers, a habitation of devils, and a stronghold of every foul, unclean, and hateful spirit. It would still be so if God (the Father especially, to whom this first movement in the creation is properly and fundamentally attributed) had not moved himself and had not made another opposite alteration of the whole state of this kingdom. This was done chiefly by the light and water in this third principle, which he produced again, but of an inferior and exterior kind and degree compared to what it had been before it was spoiled by Lucifer. For by this, on one hand, the prince of darkness was utterly cast out from all his former possessions; and by this, on the other hand, the pure, transparent materiality, or the seventh form of eternal nature (which in this particular region had been darkened, obscured, and grossly compacted by him), was taken away from his tyrannical dominion and placed in a kind of middle state or tolerable condition. From this state (though it must now, during the time of this mixture of good and evil, be subject to vanity), it can and shall be purified and refined by fire again, and so be restored to its primeval, glorious transparency. Therefore, this first creation, brought about by a previous spoiling, necessarily carries with it a second or new creation, or a restoration to the primeval state; and this beginning of time absolutely implies an end of time as well. This is so natural and inseparable that *Teutonicus* <note>Jacob Boehme.</note> had no hesitation in saying *that if we knew exactly the hour and minute of that sixth day in which the creation was accomplished, we could also know the year and day of that fiery trial by which it shall be delivered again from the bondage of corruption*; for the beginning and the end are entirely alike, and the latter is most naturally—or according to the immutable laws of eternal nature—contained in the former. Here then, to have a proper conception of what the creation is in general, before we come to consider it particularly, that *common opinion* which is generally held regarding it is in the first place to be removed. For though it may be pleaded that it is not only consistent with the outward letter of the Scripture, but it may be granted also that it can be consistent with piety and integrity of heart—so as to do no hurt to those who hold it in simplicity of mind because they are not able to look into the deeper ground—yet, nevertheless, it is inconsistent with the hidden wisdom of God, which is behind the *veil of Moses*. It may do such harm to an enquiring mind as to keep it from the understanding of those secret mysteries that were implied indeed from the very beginning in the outward letter of the Scripture, but not unfolded to the generality of mankind, except only now in this latter age of the world. In this age, they will *manifest themselves*, though not to all sorts of people indiscriminately, but only to those who *seek wisdom where it can be found*, and who cannot be contented with a broken superficial knowledge, but desire instantly to look deeper into the *eternal ground*, to understand the whole connection between eternity and time, and to apprehend how and why the latter, out of an absolute necessity (namely, after the *fall of Lucifer*), must have been brought forth out of that, and why it must also of the same necessity be swallowed up into that again.

This common opinion, then, considers the creation of this world as a work of the free, predetermined, or foreappointed will and pleasure of God only and solely, without making any reflection upon the preceding fall of Lucifer, as if it had no communion nor connection with it at all. It thinks that by saying God was pleased in his infinite wisdom to make this third principle, and all the creatures in it, as they are now, or (if it is able to look a little further) as they were before the fall of man and the curse was pronounced upon them, it has expressed the whole mystery so solidly and deeply that nothing more can be added, but that we must fully rest with this free will and pleasure of God and ought not to inquire any further. Now, let this superficial opinion stand in its place for the *common people*, to whom it may be sufficient and well enough, if they only make a good use and application of it to a Christian-like behavior; but as to *Christian philosophers*, it is certainly very short of being sufficient to reach the ground and bottom. For these (to mention only two or three general instances, and to pass over an innumerable multitude of details) will never say *that it was the free, foreappointed will and good pleasure of God, the Father of Light, with whom is no darkness at all, nor any variableness nor shadow of turning, that there should have been darkness upon the face of the deep; nor that the earth, for even one single moment, should have been without form and void.* Nor can they grant that it was his prefixed holy will and intention (arisen and established absolutely in his own counsel, before and without any reflection upon what was actually done by his rebellious creatures) that there should be such dry, barren, howling wildernesses upon earth, full of predatory beasts and venomous worms, insects, and serpents, and such rough, hard, and horrid rocks and stones, which never were nor can be of any use to man, whom yet all the creatures of this world were designed to be put in subjection to. But the cause of all such and similar things, and most especially of that never-ceasing strife and war, by which both living and lifeless creatures upon earth do continually persecute, murder, and destroy one another, must certainly be found somewhere else, and not be attributed to the absolute holy will and good pleasure of God the Almighty, who is only goodness itself, and in no way good and evil. This is the sentiment of *Christian philosophers*, who yet will not proclaim it publicly to the indiscriminate multitude (clergymen as well as laypeople) because they know that it cannot be understood nor accepted by any, unless they are such as are able to look into the ground of eternal nature, and to give a satisfactory answer to that objection which here presently arises.

For our dark natural reason, having no true idea of what the creation was, cannot but say, <insert>[Objection]</insert> If God had not himself alone created all visible and invisible things, without any exception, then there must have been some other creator besides him. And if he had not created them according to his own unlimited will and foreappointed pleasure, as they now are, then there must have been some creature that hindered his absolute sovereign will and constrained him to make them so and so, when otherwise he could have made them better, and settled them in a state of perfect harmony, without any contrariety, hurtfulness, war, and opposition. This creature now could not be supposed to have been any other but even Lucifer himself with his angels; which yet to say or think would be an abominable thing, etc. This same was not only objected to *Teutonicus* <note>Jacob Boehme</note> by some that misunderstood his writings and could not apprehend the *generation of eternal nature*, but it was also most perversely laid to his charge by others, who claimed he held such a doctrine as that Lucifer had made the earth, rocks, and stones, and the venomous and hurtful creatures, and was thus a creator of them, besides Him of whom the Scripture says *that he created heaven and earth and all that is therein:*—whereby we are the more confirmed (said those ignorant opponents) that this shoemaker intended to teach us afresh that old damnable doctrine of *Manes* <note>The founder of Manichaeism</note>, babbling of two contrary Gods, a white or good, and a black or evil one. But truly this is all so far from his mind and sense that it has no communion with it at all, as may plainly appear to everyone who has even a small understanding of the process in the mutual generation of the forms of eternal nature, and will but search a little into this matter. But I think it most proper and necessary that this objection should be examined and answered, before we descend to a particular consideration of this creation; and this for a defense of the truth and innocence of our author. It has two parts, both of which are to be considered distinctly: for it says (1) that Teutonicus made Lucifer a maker or creator of earth and stones; and (2) that he makes him a binder or controller of the free sovereign will of God, whom he constrained to bring forth the creatures of this world in such or such a condition.

Before the revolt of Lucifer, as long as he was a holy angel of light, all the seven forms of eternal nature stood in the most perfect union and harmony, both within himself and outside of him in his entire kingdom. Therefore, the six properties generated the *seventh* most gently, softly, and sweetly, in a clear, pure, crystalline transparency, according to the *nature of the light*; which then had the predominance over all the rest, as they still do throughout all the other kingdoms and regions of all the holy angels who kept their habitation in the light, and as they shall do again in the place of this now defiled and cursed third principle also, when they shall be re-harmonized, and the whole principle be purified by fire, and so be restored to its former glorious condition. When Lucifer, in unanimous concurrence with all his angels, by his perverse will, desire, faith, or *magia*, stirred up the fourth form of fire—first and chiefly within himself, intending to raise it up above all the rest and to exalt himself therein as an almighty, most sovereign monarch—the whole harmonious order of eternal nature in his created being was immediately broken. But this could not have been done only in and to his own particular creature; instead, by this very act and deed, his fiery spirit also actually went forth from him in his false *magia* into all that was outside and besides him, intending to conquer and to trample everything under his feet, and so to be alone the supreme all in all. Thus, he then poisoned, infected, and polluted all that he could enter into; all that gave him any admittance, or in any way yielded to his will. He stung like a *fiery serpent*, not only into the other angelic thrones and provoked them to do the same as he did—from which came the *war in heaven between Michael and the Dragon*—but he also went out against God himself, his father and creator, intending to bring him into subjection. The whole harmonious order of eternal nature, therefore, wherein darkness and fire had stood from all eternity in subordination to the light, was thus immediately broken outside of his particular creature as well, wherever he could get any admittance. It was not broken indeed as to God his creator, for God was truly too strong for him; nor was it broken as to the rest of the holy, obedient angels, for they resisted him and kept him out; but it was broken in his own entire region or kingdom, for only there could he prevail, seeing that it stood in subjection under him and was, by birthright, his natural due possession, of which he then was the only king and ruler. There, therefore, he found a free admittance and compliance with his will, with the four first forms of nature, which he could raise up and so subdue the rest. Throughout his entire dominion, therefore, but nowhere else beyond it (though he intended it everywhere), the harmonious order of eternal nature was actually broken. For that which before stood in the middle between *three* and *three* was now, by his false *magia*, dislocated and removed from its appointed place, and could no longer keep down the darkness beneath, nor any longer give forth a shining glorious light above. So, therefore, the three inferior forms on the left hand—swallowed up before from all eternity by the three superior on the right—came to be raised up out of their hidden deep, and were set in opposition and enabled to act according to their own will and inclination. Why they also immediately exerted their own peculiar qualifications, most intrinsic and natural to them when not kept under by the lightness of light and love. What their peculiar qualifications were was formerly mentioned sufficiently, and is now plainly to be seen here by those fruits or products they brought forth immediately. To generate the seventh form of materiality is common to all the six, and none of them can be excluded from it; whether they stand in union or in disharmony, they can never cease to generate the seventh. Materiality, therefore, must still have been generated in all this disorder and confusion, no less than before in their concordance. But what kind of materiality could now have been generated here, when these three inferior forms of darkness had gained the predominance? All the former purity, sweetness, clearness, softness, and meekness was abolished: the whole region had before been full of light and glory; but now that was extinguished, and there was *darkness upon the face of the deep*. Before, it was a dwelling place of meekness, tranquility, and love; but now, it was turned into fierceness, tumult, wrath, envy, hatred, and anger. The harshness now having the greatest hand in the generation of the seventh form, attracted, constricted, and compacted, without any resistance or restraint, with the extreme force and vehemence; and this still so much the more and stronger as it was more stirred up and exasperated, on one side by its own stinging prickle, and on the other side by its own turbulent whirling wheel. The seventh form, therefore, which should have been generated sweetly and gently—pure, transparent, thin, subtle, fine, and crystalline by the predominant concurrence of the three superior forms of light—could no longer be generated that way within the sphere of this disharmonized region; but must now have been generated only according to the predominant property of the three inferior forms of darkness—that is, it must have been made dark, thick, gross, obscure, hard, rough, heavy, earthy, stony, and rocky. And this happened not only in such or such a particular place of this region, as this earthly globe is now, but everywhere throughout this whole kingdom, though not everywhere equally alike; but here more and there less, according to the various conditions of several places different from each other; and according also to the different activities of those diabolical agents that stirred and exasperated the forms of nature either more or less, or after this or that peculiar manner. Just as we may observe an outward resemblance of this in ice, frozen out of soft water or another liquid, which happens everywhere in all the world wherever this constricting power can prevail; and yet it is not done everywhere equally alike, but more in one place and less in another, according to the different conditions of those liquids that are capable of being frozen, and according also to the various degrees of this freezing force.

But who can say here with any sense that he gives him the character of a maker or creator? Is he not manifestly represented in all his pages and lines as a breaker and destroyer? For he is not said to have himself generated the dark, gross, impure materiality; but the three first forms of dark-

darkness, in their predominance over the three properties of light, have generated it so, as soon as they had extinguished and swallowed up the light. But Lucifer is only said to have been the chief agent who stirred them up to it, by his strong stirring and intensifying the violence of the harshness and fiery strength; and the Scripture says this itself implicitly when it calls him *<term>Apollyon</term>*, and more explicitly, *a liar and murderer from the beginning*. And though he were even expressly said to have generated the dark and coarse impure materiality—in such a sense as now in this world a dark, false magician may be said to produce or generate this or that material thing (which he does not by himself, or by his own ability, but by the forms of nature, which he in a disordered and malicious way abuses, and which alone can properly be said to have produced it)—yet even then also, this production made by Lucifer from the beginning could not at all be called, nor be considered as, a making or creating work. It was only a perverting, breaking, defiling, and destroying of that which before was holy, clear, and pure. 

Teutonicus <note>Jakob Böhme</note>, therefore, did not make him a maker of earth and stones, but he made him a spoiler and destroyer of that blessed crystalline earth, which he used to call *<term>ternarius sanctus</term>* <note>the holy ternary</note>, and which had been full of the light and glory of God, as well in his kingdom *when he was an angel of light*, as in the other angelic regions. And he says that he was the *only cause* of that first spoiled condition of the earth, described thus in the beginning of the first chapter of Genesis: *The earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep*. 

But if these opponents think this to be contrary to the truth, let them declare more solidly what the Scripture means by calling him a destroyer and murderer from the beginning, and let them show us what he destroyed and murdered before the creation of this world. Did he not murder the light in his own creaturely being, and in his whole region, and raise up in its place the darkness, of which he is prince to this day? And did he not waste his own kingdom, his glorious inheritance, his holy, clear, paradisiacal earth—the seventh form of eternal nature, his pleasant angelic garden, full of glory and delight—making it really dark and empty, void and without form, and destitute of all that beauty with which it had been adorned by his Father and Creator? So that Teutonicus might well say of him, *If all trees were writers, all their branches pens, all the mountains books, and all waters ink, they would not be sufficient to describe that lamentable condition which Lucifer with his angels brought upon his region*. 

As little, therefore, as he had created that former pure transparent earth where he lived in the light before his fall, just as little did he create this outward earth. He caused, indeed, the forms and powers of darkness to generate—in their predominance over the light—such a dark, dead, dry, rough, and coarse materiality everywhere throughout his whole region. But it was God, and He only, who created—that is, formed and settled together in one globe—this dispersed impure matter, and rectified it again by restoring to it light and water, in the same manner as it had before (though not in the same internal degree of glory, beauty, and excellence, which was not to be done in this beginning of time, but to be reserved to the end of it, as will appear hereafter). He replenished it with innumerable creatures of all sorts and kinds, all representing those that were also before upon that former paradisiacal earth. Certainly Lucifer would destroy these and make them void and without form again if his power were equal to his will, for he is a destroyer of all the creatures of God, and a setter up of his own dark lying figures, formed by his own will in his false <term>magia</term>. So it is a great ignorance and misapprehension, if not a great perversity, to say that Teutonicus made Lucifer a maker or creator of earth and stones.

But now further, as to that *second* part of this objection, by which it is said that [*Objection*] if it was not the free, preordained will and full pleasure of God that the creatures of this world should be as they are, then Lucifer must have hindered and constrained Him to make them so, when otherwise He could have made them better and settled them in a state of perfect harmony without any contrariety, hurtfulness, venom, war, and opposition, etc. [*Answer*] This is quite erroneous and stands upon that false hypothesis that the creation of this third principle has no connection with the fall of Lucifer, but is a free, pre-designed work of God to be considered without any reflection upon what was done by this revolting angel. This is justly called a false hypothesis, because this creation is a work of God *<term>a posteriori</term>*, made only to rectify and restore that which was spoiled and destroyed. For if Lucifer had not fallen, no creation of this third principle would have been brought forth, nor could any alteration have been made in this region; for it stood already in the highest degree of glory, light, and dignity, and must have continued the glorious inheritance and possession of their great prince and hierarch forever and ever. Whether God would have been pleased to create some other things, and so to have manifested His goodness and glory to some other creatures besides the holy angels, or whether He would not, we are not to determine; but only this we may freely say: that if Lucifer had not revolted, and by his revolt laid—

Therefore, this third principle could not have been made—especially not in this region—as a distinct representation and manifestation of their various divided properties, as it is and must be now. If, then, there was no pre-appointed will and decree in the counsel of God (prior to and without consideration of this sad apostasy of Lucifer) to create this third principle and to manifest within it a visible figure of the two eternal principles in their opposition to each other, how could this will of God have been hindered or limited? And how can he, who is only restoring a thing spoiled by another, be said to be forced by that spoiler to restore it in such a way, and to use that very spoiling for the greater illustration of his own honor and glory? It may indeed be said that he is prompted to accommodate his wisdom to the condition and circumstances of that spoiled thing; and this, in a sense, may also be said of God. But how can this be more derogatory to his honor and glory than it is when we say (and say rightly, according to the truth) that he created such angels as could revolt against him, and that he gave them such thrones and possessions as could be spoiled and wasted by them? Considering that by their revolt they did no harm at all to him, but harmed only themselves; and that he has restored, and will restore, what was spoiled, so that even this spoiling itself shall serve for the greater exaltation of his power, honor, and glory.

The fall of Lucifer was indeed foreseen from all eternity in the mirror of eternal wonders, and so was the creation of this world. Although there is or was no real "before" or "after" in that eternal all-seeing eye, yet with respect to our understanding, the fall of Lucifer comes first (as it also did actually), and the creation of this third principle follows—and follows in such a way that it depends upon that fall and was not decreed beforehand, or without respect to it, but only in consequence and relation to it. For when these things stood in this depraved state, what was to be done both with Lucifer and with his corrupted region? Should God have left him alone, so as to give over this whole kingdom into his absolute power, to exercise his sad tyrannical dominion according to his own will, in defiance of God and all his holy angels? No, this could not have been done at all. For this region was not Lucifer’s property; his Creator was the only proprietor of it. It was only given to him by birthright as an inheritance, which it was very just for God to thrust him out of and to take from him. 

Moreover, this region—especially considering the <term>seventh form of nature</term> within it—neither had nor could have revolted or committed any iniquity against its Creator. It stood only in mere passivity and had to allow itself to be defiled and polluted, having no ability to resist because it was only a generated body without any activity of its own. It could not, therefore, hinder its alteration and pollution brought upon it by the now predominant forms of darkness. How then, or by what equity, could it have been punished by being given over to the arbitrary government of this apostatized prince of darkness? He must indeed have had it subject to him (until the power of omnipotence appeared for its deliverance in the subsequent creation), but this was by constraint, not willingly. For it is natural and intrinsic to every thing—even the most senseless thing—to incline toward continuing in its own state rather than being brought down into a lower and worse condition.

It was then not only justice and equity on God’s part, but also a matter of the highest necessity for the maintenance of his honor and glory to take this region away from the subjection of this rebellious angel. But this alone could not have been sufficient for its restoration; it also had to be further refined and purified by fire, and so restored to its former beauty and excellence. For it was defiled and corrupted so that the glory of God could not appear, nor dwell, nor represent and manifest itself within it. But furthermore, this purification by fire, and thus this full restoration into the original glory, could not have been done immediately. For it was a vacant throne, destitute of its natural prince; and in the counsel of the most Holy Trinity, it was decreed that another king should be raised up instead of Lucifer, in quite another way and manner, to whom this region should be given for an eternal possession. For so says the Scripture to this purpose, that *we were chosen in Jesus Christ before the foundation of the world*. And although this king should have been Adam the First, it was also seen and known beforehand that he would not stand firm in the hour of his temptation but would fall back, and thereby bring another defilement upon this region again.
