But another expedient was in the meantime found in the wisdom of God, by which his whole will and counsel most wisely could be performed; and this was the creation of this, our outward third principle, in which the two interior principles are indeed left in their opposition to each other (not by any necessity or constraint laid upon the Creator by his rebellious creature, but by his own wisdom, for the greater manifestation of his glory and the greater confusion of his spoiler). Both actually send forth their influences into it according to their various divided properties, but are nevertheless so far harmonized and knit together in order, measure, weight, and proportion that neither of them can entirely prevail against the other. The dark and fiery principle, which is destroying in its own nature when alone predominant, cannot exert its power and dominion alone, but must only serve the principle of light to move and stir it up, so that they both concurrently may be subservient to produce and manifest the secret wonders of God, whose shadows shall appear hereafter in eternity. Together, they may both keep out and under their former prince, who is now only a prince of darkness. For though he may have access in that dark and fiery part—with respect to which he is also still called a prince of this world—yet seeing that this is nowhere alone, but has always and everywhere more or less an opposite part of light and water with it, he is everywhere resisted and excluded, except where men, by their own malice, give him an open door. And moreover, this whole principle, seeing that it is of quite another and exterior condition, nature, and order than that in which he was created, avails him nothing at all; nor can he make any use of it, though he still is and lives within its sphere. He can see no more in the light of this principle than he can in his own darkness; and the water of this principle can refresh him no more than his own fire can. So, therefore, he is only disappointed and deluded in all his designs, while the glory of his Creator is exalted in all his works. And there is rejoicing even in heaven among the holy angels because of the creation of this outward world, by which this whole region is delivered from his tyranny and is set in such a state from which (after the time shall be accomplished in which it must be subject to vanity because of the transgression of man) it may be restored into its primeval dignity, and so reunited to the other two angelical hierarchies.

So then, the creation of this third principle is not at all such a work as is commonly apprehended by *the common people*, but quite another thing. To declare and demonstrate this, much more might indeed be added, but it will evidence itself more and more hereafter. Here, therefore, it may suffice only to have said in general: that it is nothing else but a transformation of this whole polluted kingdom of Lucifer into another exterior state and inferior degree of goodness, light, and dignity, made in order to bring it up again in due time through the purifying fire into that primeval glory in which it stood before the fire was stirred up and the darkness set in opposition against the light.

Having thus seen the connection between the fall of Lucifer and the creation of this third principle, and what this creation is in general, and having given, I think, a sufficient answer to that twofold objection, we are now further to consider this whole outward creation more particularly, according to the description given of it by Moses. *In the beginning then God created the heaven and the earth*, says Moses. *By the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth*, says David. And *In the beginning was the word, and the word was with God, and God was the word; the same was in the beginning with God: all things were made by him, and without him was not anything made that was made, etc.,* says the apostle John. All three say harmoniously one and the same thing regarding the creation, though the words of the Apostle reach further and imply much more than those of Moses and of David. For this *beginning* which Moses speaks of is only the beginning of time which, according to his following description, must of necessity have been brought forth after the fall of Lucifer. But the *beginning* mentioned by St. John is not this beginning of time only; for by saying that without the Word, which was in the beginning with God, nothing was made that was made, he manifestly includes the creation of angels also, which truly had its beginning before the beginning of the creation of this third principle. Whereas Moses says nothing at all explicitly of the creation of angels nor of their fall, but was only—and (for reasons declared elsewhere) very shortly and obscurely too—to describe the outward creation of this, our visible world.

We must say indeed, that the creation of angels had a beginning, for though their natures were eternal, yet they were not formed or shaped creatures from eternity; but we cannot say this beginning implies a time, any more than we can say it implies such or such a specific extension of space and place; though really something answering to both is implied, which because it surpasses our external condition, wherein all things are densely compacted, our earthly language has no name to express or represent it suitably: for though it does not imply a time, yet it implies a lower state than eternity is, when considered absolutely in itself, without any respect to creatures. *The mighty angel in the Revelation swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven and earth, and the things that are therein, that there should be time no longer, but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, the mystery of God should be finished. Now this mystery of God entirely relates to man, created after the creation of heaven and earth, and all of the things that are therein. If then there shall be time no longer after the finishing of this mystery of God, there was also no time before this mystery of God had its actual beginning in the creation of heaven and earth and the things therein, though there had been another beginning already before in the angelic creation.*

It may seem superfluous to insist so much upon this difference, the notion of which may be plain and well-known enough, but I think it is not so, because these two beginnings are not yet all that the words of St. John apply to; but we shall find two other beginnings more, both of which are much deeper and far more intrinsic, because they are without any relation to creatures, and they differ also from each other by such a difference as might be said in this or that respect to bear some analogy to the way the beginning of time differs from the beginning of the creation of angels. Seeing then that these two later beginnings are nearer to us (because both were created after the image and likeness of God), and are therefore more understandable, we must look upon them with attention and develop in our mind a true idea of that difference by which they are to be distinguished from each other, if we expect to have any good understanding of those other two beginnings that are much more obscure and remote from our eyes. For all four are to be taken notice of, if the expression of the Apostle, and that excellent explanation which <term>Teutonicus</term> <note>Jacob Boehme</note> provides, shall be fully understood.

If we then look deeper, beyond both this and that creation into the generation of eternal nature, we shall find that something like a beginning is to be understood there also, which is implied in the naming of a principle, and which has been spoken of sufficiently before, where it was called an *eternal beginning* or a *beginning without beginning*. And this is the lower beginning of these latter two, answering in different respects both to the beginning made in the angelic creation and to the following beginning of time in the outward creation also. For as to both these, eternal nature has, as it were, successively and gradually descended—down lower and lower—and has manifested in the former more secretly and as a unified whole, and in the latter more openly and separately, all its hidden powers and energies. For in the beginning of the angelic creation, its darkness and fire, though both were indeed cooperating subserviently, were still hidden and kept in subjection, and the light only was made manifest in all the holy angels. On the contrary, in the beginning of time, or in the outward creation, it has openly displayed both darkness, fire, and light in a plain distinction and division, obvious everywhere, and has even made a visible and temporary representation of each of them particularly.

But further, if we now look deeper again beyond eternal nature and its eternal beginning itself, into that transcendent, bottomless, and incomprehensible generation of God, who there generates all things, or spreads himself forth into Father, Son, and Spirit—spoken of lately in the explanation of that SCHEME or TABLE which considers God without any nature and creature—even there also there is still, in a higher and more obscure sense, a beginning; or rather, something seen as if from afar off, and only answering to it in relation to our understanding, to be conceived. This, more than any of the former, indeed lacks a specific and more suitable *name*; for this word "beginning" is much too crude and low; but seeing we have no better, we must call it a beginning too, and be contented with that difference by which we can distinguish it from all the others in the understanding of our mind. For it is rightly said also, that a real ground of this our understanding is in the thing itself; which would be plainer on both sides if we could have another and more significant name than that of a beginning. And this is the inmost or deepest beginning of all, beyond which there is no other to be looked for anymore, and is answering in different—

Therefore, this correspondence—by which this deepest abyssal (or rather <term>byssal</term>) beginning corresponds to the beginning in the generation of eternal nature—is as far above its correspondence to the angelic beginning as God the Creator is above the creatures. To declare that, and how, the Father and Son are *one* and not *two*, and yet also *two* and not *one*, it is first shown what <term>Teutonicus</term> <note>Jacob Boehme</note> understands by *Unity*, by *Abyss*, by *God*, by *Father*, and by *Son*, *Word*, or *Byss*. The real ground of the Father and Son being one is this: that not only is the Son in the Father, but also the Father is in the Son. *How the Father can be in the Son when the Son is in the Father is explained. That the Father and Son are one, not two, is demonstrated: (1.) In the Father is all, and in the Son is all that is in the Godhead. (2.) The glory is the Father's, and the glory is the Son's. (3.) The Father's is all power, and the Son's is all power. (4.) I am the first and the last. (5.) No man has seen God; yet we have seen with our eyes. Again, that the Father and Son are also *two*, not *one*, is declared and demonstrated by the Abyss not being a Byss, and the Byss not being an Abyss (and later, further explained by the words "with God"). "God" is not always understood in the same sense and respect. *The many strongholds of antitrinitarians. Reason cannot be pulled down by another reason, but only by etc.*

God is his own beginning and his own end. Two, and one. God was the Word in which was life. In the following words, the Apostle descends down to things, and so to eternal nature, which is the first of things.*

As to the *second beginning*, these words of Saint John are explained in several points. *<term>Lubet</term> <note>Divine delight or longing</note> with desire; why and how. How it goes along with it, explained by a simile. The first original will was itself that lubet, and itself that strong desire; declared and proved. All things (all the forms of eternal nature) were made (or caused to be what they are) by him; declared particularly regarding all seven forms.*

As to the *third* and *fourth beginning, "without him was not any etc.,"* because everything in eternal nature was made by him. *"In him was life"* must be understood with respect to the fall. In the Father without the Son, there is no life for men and angels. *"Father, men were yours... I give to them."*

Furthermore, one should understand that, without deliberately offending reason and common sense, one cannot envision any *unveiling of divine things* in the theological REVELATIONS contained in the books of Moses, the Prophets, or the Evangelists; since the great truths that their sacred texts teach us remain obscurely hidden from the common man. It is true that they only speak and think this way because the foundation of their theological knowledge is SCHOLASTICISM.

If, therefore, while not penetrating the secret of *re-veiled things* themselves, their pleasure is to talk to us about these *mystic Revelations* as if they had unveiled divine and eternal truths, it is obvious that their assertion in this regard remains inherently vain—both because the facts negate it and because the word REVELATIO expresses the opposite. Consequently, it should appear to us only as a *Scholastic Thesis* or an *exercise*, suited to sharpen the spiritual senses of the youth. In fact, one cannot engage in a scholastic dispute over propositions so revolting to human judgment without the young *Scholar* being vividly struck by it, which leaves a stronger impression in his imagination of the *natural truth* that is only fictitiously contested.

I admire more than anyone the exquisite work of this celebrated author; because, having found the secret of his Kabbalah, his same Key of the Number 5 served to introduce me into his magnificent **PENTATEUCH**. I followed him there step-by-step, and after decomposing his artificial bouquets of Greek, Arabic, Syriac, and Chaldean flowers, I recognized in him a profound science, a genius fertile in sublime ideas, and infinite art in their arrangement; but I also recognized that the **HOLY THINGS** he re-veiled there, to make them serve the glory of the only God we adore, had been previously veiled.

Yes, Egypt was mystically imbued with them since the great Hermes, its legislator—that is, more than fifteen centuries before Moses was born. They served there for the worship of seven principal gods, honored under a **SUPREME GOD** called the Only Uncreated. Chaldea, Syria, and Greece adopted the same religion and called it "Ethnic," that is, national, because by following it, one was considered to form a single nation. Let us observe that <term>Moyse</term> <note>Moses</note>, being raised at the court of a King of Egypt, must have received an excellent education there, to which he joined a superior sagacity of mind. From this, one must judge that it was easier for him than for any other to be perfectly initiated into the **Arcana of Worship** which was then rendered to the Gods, Demi-Gods, and Heroes. Must it be that our modern scholars have not even studied their names, and that they represent to themselves only vain and frivolous stories when reading the learned collection we call **FABULÆ GENTILIUM ET PAGANORUM** <note>Fables of the Gentiles and Pagans</note>?

This title declares to us that among the subjects, both Arab and Greek, of the Monarch of Egypt, those who were qualified as **GENTILES** and **PAGANI**—that is to say, the common people and the villagers—must have believed the literal words of these sacred stories without understanding them. But it follows that the Great Lords, without perhaps knowing how to explain them, knew at least that their text contained essentially true enigmas. It further follows that the veil must have been entirely lifted, whether for the Eagles of Philosophy or for the **NATURAL ADEPTS**, such as were both the Kings and those whom it pleased them to raise to the dignity of *Prince of the Priests*.

It is astonishing that the lives of the Gods, Demi-Gods, and Heroes of pagan antiquity—in which no pretext of religion could have deterred us from examining deeply—should likewise be for us a purely scholastic science. What! Everyone takes pride in not being ignorant of the various texts, and yet no one applies themselves to penetrating the wonders of Nature which are enclosed within them. What a fine merit for a man of wit to have burdened his memory with what he does not understand.

If <term>Moyse</term> had limited himself to such a ridiculous and fruitless pastime, he would never have discovered, grasped, and admired the allegorical beauties of these fables. When he understood them well, they...

He therefore undertook to work on an *entirely new veil*, which, woven with a *historical thread*, just like that of Hermes, represented only human characters in place of the fictional Egyptian deities: the task was for these *figurative* men, by re-veiling the same physical truths of which *gods and demigods had until then been the symbol*, to express them through a *narrative structure* that was worthy of succeeding the ancient one.

This does not mean the eruption of the fire in the center on the fourth day, but, etc. References for the *spirit of this world*; for *salt, sulfur, and mercury*; for the *eternal one element*; and for the so-called *four elements*. *The fifth day.* (1.) From the fourth day, the emergence of this third property is properly to be counted. (2.) The opening of this fifth "jovial" <note>pertaining to the planet Jupiter</note> motion out of the fourth. (3.) Boehme considers all the *living creatures* here on this day, and why. (4.) They are not made from so many pieces of clay. Concerning their origin, Boehme’s expressions differ and yet agree. Why. This is extensively explained, and Boehme is vindicated as not contradicting but giving the true sense of Moses. Variety, the *astrum* <note>the celestial or stellar influence</note>. Aftersound.

(5.) *Four kinds of living creatures*, and in each of these varieties a subordinate, countless variety; why. A difficulty concerning the fire’s *astrum* is resolved. (6.) Distinction into two sexes. The cause of their propagation is seeking for love. Only the serpent is excepted from the division of sexes. (7.) Several creatures have a mixed origin, coming from two "mothers." (8.) Some have blood, others do not; the latter exist through the devil’s will. (9.) Some are clean, others unclean, and the reason for this.

(10.) *The final cause of their creation*, declared in connection with what is to be considered both before and after. (11.) The necessity of this appearing in the eternal magia. (12.) The condition of the living creatures before the fall, regarding their food, clothing, and cruel, wrathful properties. (13.) None is able to speak; yet the birds understand the language of nature in their own way. The Tower of Babel. (14.) In all things there is a character of the Trinity, but in none so much as in man. Animals exist only for food and propagation. References for the *living creatures*.

*The sixth day.* Everything that Boehme says about the *creation of man* depends upon the *seven properties*, the two principles, and the *fall of Lucifer*. (1.) The origin and formation of his body. *Haadamah*, *Haarez*—Boehme’s different names for it. A two-fold, and also three-fold body, etc.; this must be left to him *who has the true pearl* in the state of regeneration. References for man’s body.

(2.) The breathing in was *one life*, but also *three, or three-fold*: fire, light, and air. *Spiraculum vitarum* <note>The breath of lives</note>. This triplicity is demonstrated. First, the airy breath, the outward part of the soul; the exterior spirit; the mortal soul, explained. Secondly, the *fiery breath*; properly the soul; the worm that does not die; why. Dry, magic-fire. The Cross. The fire-eye: the root and origin of life, yet also life itself. Thirdly, the flaming breath of light and love; properly the spirit of the soul; properly that noble creature because of which the eternal Word was made flesh. Hence it is plain, first, that just as in eternity, so also here the fiery soul stands in the midst. Secondly, their different degrees of nobility. Thirdly, that the soul is only an inseparable property of man. References to Boehme for this threefold breathing.

(3.) The *image of God* is commonly described in a way that is not erroneous, but imperfect. No man is blamed for this, and why. It consisted chiefly and fundamentally in this threefold life, and in the union and order of these three. Both regarding this and that declaration: *man had no law, but an engrafted principle, truth*, as an excellent character of uniformity with his Creator; until this, because of his wavering, was turned into a law. References to Boehme for what has been said of the image of God.

*The seventh day.* From the *work* and *rest of God*, it is clear that these seven days signify quite another thing than, etc. (1.) In outward nature, there was an order and succession of these seven days. But (2.) with respect to eternity, work and rest are equally co-eternal and perpetually together. (3.) In what sense the seventh is prior to the sixth. This is declared as a key to several obscure places. (4.) For example, the first day took its beginning out of the seventh day. (5.) The seventh day in eternal nature is always combined with the first. (6.) *God rested on the seventh day*, in the substantial balance, or the end of nature, etc. (7.) Boehme’s various names for this seventh day in eternal nature. (8.) This seventh day considered with a particular respect to man: first, as in his creation; (9.) further, as in his fallen state; (10.) and lastly, as in his restoration. The seventh

## (VIII.)—OF THE FALL OF MAN, FROM HIS PRIMEVAL GLORY AND PERFECTION, DOWN INTO AND UNDER THE DOMINION OF THE SPIRIT OF THIS WORLD.

Man's primitive state of glory and perfection, in the strictest sense, is always taken to mean the state he was in when he was but one single person. This state is considered: (1.) As to the foundation-pillar. The interior body penetrated the exterior, like red-hot iron. (2.) As to the manner of *his eating and drinking*. The greening <gloss>paradisiacalizing</gloss> of the one element through the earth, the outward local paradise. (3.) As to his magical generation. Eternal nature was not torn asunder when he was *formed upon the cross* and brought away from it into another world, etc. (4.) As to his clothing. He was naked, yet clothed in iron and fire. (5.) As to his labor. Why the tincture is so much searched after, and why it is found by so very few. References for these subjects.

The *first forty days*. Boehme <note>Jacob Boehme, often spelled Behmen in early English translations.</note> does not contradict Moses. Every number *forty* in Scripture is related to this. The five instances... relating to the five degrees of nature. The processes of the first and second Adam are parallel. References for these forty days. The great mystery of iniquity was conceived. Adam began little by little, etc. The tree of knowledge arose; the law came in, etc. But we will consider in these first forty days only the following three things in general:—

*First*, That, and why, Adam must have been tempted. This lies both in understanding (1.) what he was, and (2.) for what end he was created. But it lies much deeper in our own internal ground. The word *temptation* is not yet proper here. Temptation here is a representation of each principle in man's three-fold looking-glass. This is explained. Let none blame God. The necessity of such a *temptation* <gloss>or trial</gloss>, and more arguments for the same. References to Boehme.

*Secondly*, How, and by whom, man was tempted. This might now seem superfluous, but it is not. The *spiritus mundi* <term>spirit of the world</term> comes here chiefly into consideration, and why. There was no such evil design as to kill, etc., in anyone but the devil. His twofold design: (1.) To manifest his wonders; (2.) to obtain the Eternal Virgin, who is manifest only in man. He is the original of all delusions. References.

*Thirdly*, The end and consequence of this temptation. Sleep and death. The simile of oil in a burning lamp. As was Adam's eating, so was his death in sleep. References for Adam's sleep. The *production of the woman*, explained in eighteen positions: (1.) The generation of eternal nature and man's original state in the first creation must be understood. (2.) Man's return <note>To the background of eternity, and a birth deeper than his Virgin nature</note> to the holy name of Jesus, who was now the second Creator. (3.) Adam's body was really broken. (12.) The rib shows her to be the weaker part. (13.) Christ came from the woman only, yet he was a man, and why. (16.) It is not meant that Adam had only a soul and Eve only a spirit. Why can these two not bring forth the whole image again? > The Scholastic School was, and will always be, an ingenious bit of trifling, whether it treats of holy things or profane things; and, consequently, our Schools of Theology do not dictate, and should not dictate, any document that can be essentially instructive regarding the foundation of CHRISTIANITY.

I shall strengthen the mind of my reader in this *truth*, which is indubitable in itself, if I show him that *Philosophy* and the *Science of Letters* are likewise merely trifled with by all those *scholastic* professors who today have the false reputation of teaching them to us.

No one will disagree that the two excellent books which have transmitted to us—one, that famous *Law of the Gods and Demigods*, which was devised for the Egyptians by the great Hermes; the other, the *Law of the Patriarchs*, which was written by Moses for the Hebrews—make, and will forever make, these two legislators revered as *philosophers* who were perfectly instructed in the *secrets of nature*, and no less versed in the *science of letters*.

If, then, the lessons given to us on *Letters* and *Philosophy* were not pure *scholasticism*, is it not evident that after having applied ourselves to our studies under renowned professors—each of us having then become *literate* and a *philosopher*—we could penetrate the philosophical texts of these two authors? But we see that those who claim to be *philosophers* and *literate people*, as well as the *scholastic* doctors who were their masters, understand only that the first book contains *allegorical fables* and the second our *figures of Genesis*.

### IX.—OF THE NATURAL PROPAGATION OF MAN, IN THIS NOW CURSED FOUR-ELEMENTARY WORLD.

The title is ambiguous. *Bivium* <gloss>a parting of the ways</gloss>, in THE THREE PRINCIPLES and MYSTERIUM MAGNUM, thus:—"Our author, having hitherto at large treated of the fall and curse, and of man's being driven out of the garden of Eden, stands now as it were at the parting of a way, the two different paths of which do bear the same name indeed, but are nevertheless so much distinguished from each other that they cannot be walked in or looked over at once, though they may be at different times, which he also himself has done, going through the one in his MYSTERIUM MAGNUM, and through the other in THE THREE PRINCIPLES.

In the MYSTERIUM MAGNUM he now further declares how this Adamical Tree (for so he styles the first progenitor of all the earthly generations) has set forth and displayed himself in branches great and little, both into a numberless multitude as to individual particulars, and multiplicity

<column-break/>

has so greatly misled the minds of most men that today the *title of* PHILOSOPHER is prostituted without the slightest discernment.

It is given first to the authors of systems, whose works fail for lack of a firm foundation or a fundamental ground; so that, although they are well-expressed, even luminous and profound in their genre, they can exactly serve only to *theorize* on the various *rotations* of several globes far from ours, and on the *attractions* or *repulsions* differently perceived in the atoms that surround them: such are the famous Newton, Descartes, Gassendi, Leibniz, and several others, who were certainly much less PHILOSOPHERS than *Molière* or *La Fontaine* have been.

This uncompromised name is likewise granted to our modern contemplators of the *leaves*, *flowers*, and *fruits* of the *Tree* of the *Universe*; who have in no way exposed the *Animating Principle* to our eyes. They are nevertheless worthy of being read and admired, because they have joined to their exact and curious descriptions all the charms of an elegantly and clearly concise style: such are *Buffon* and *Daubenton*, *Pluche*, the *Encyclopedist* authors, and some *Academicians* of reputation.

Yes, if the dissection of *visible bodies* were capable of making us perfectly know THE SPIRIT OF LIFE WHICH ANIMATED THEM, the research of these scholars in natural curiosities could then form part of *Philosophy*: But none of their works can lead us to discern the *magnetic essence of the philosophers*; that *magic and sacred fire* that the Vestal Virgins had to maintain with such care, according to the beautiful figure of Numa; that CUPID of the Latins, who was born from the *Venus of the Greeks*; in a word, that true Principle of the *natural love of living things*, which the syllabic Kabbalah of the Greeks has made me recognize in their name Φιλ-ία [Philia], because it thus contains Φιλίας-ία [Philias-ia], THE FORCE AND VOICE OF LOVE. It is the profound science of this alone which has at all times been able to constitute PHILOSOPHERS.

Our moderns are ridiculously imbued with a completely different meaning lent to this name by the *Schools*; they have persuaded them, as it were, that Philosophy must mean the *Love of Wisdom*. From this frivolous interpretation arises a hypothesis even further removed from reason: namely, that men who take the tone of moralists, or who flatter themselves with correcting moral vices through their writings, can, as *lovers of wisdom*, be qualified as *philosophers*.

That is not all. Our *scholastic doctors* even dare to suggest that a solitary, austere, misanthropic man has a right to this qualification; and I do not know if they will not soon confer it upon those *new purists of the French language* [A.D. 1771] who apparently make us notice their extreme *wisdom* when they multiply their efforts so that we might write as people pronounce today, and not as they pronounced in the past: if they have conceived the grand design of thereby making every vestige of the Greek and Latin etymology of our words disappear, they may well succeed. Ha! I truly see that such a beautiful enterprise must have them named both SAGES and SCHOLARS, according to the style of our Schools.

Be that as it may, let us pray all modern scholars to remember the *rules of Greek syntax*: they teach us that in names composed of two substantives, it was always the genitive that had to start the word: *Geography*, *Geometry*, *Astrology*, *Astronomy*, *Theology*, *Etymology*, and so many other Greek compounds which our language has retained the use of, are proof of this. That is why if one had wanted to form from the two substantives Φιλία [Philia] and Σοφία [Sophia] a single name that

If it expressed the *Love of Wisdom*, the construction of this word would necessarily have been <term>SOPHOPHILY</term>, and not at all <term>PHILOSOPHY</term>.

I will add that those who translate the Greek name Σοφία as *Wisdom* have not perfectly understood the Latin expression <term>SAPIENTIA</term>, by which it is faithfully rendered. <term>SAPIENTIA</term> comes from the verb <term>SAPIO</term>: it expresses *the art of <term>SAVORING</term> the substance of things*, and this is not at all what we understand by our *Wisdom*, which is not the subject of the Greek name Φιloσοφία.

Does one want a second proof? It is dictated to everyone by common sense alone. Each of us knows that the ancient Philosophers were *Scholars*, and that Philosophy was actually a *Science*. One would not say that *the act of loving wisdom* constitutes a real *Science*, since this *Love* is in itself incapable of making us scholars. But the *knowledge of the Love* innate in all beings—of that *Magnet*, or *magnetic attraction*, which the Creator inserted into the essence of Nature in order to perpetuate the revolving duration of its various productions—announces itself as a very vast, very profound Science, and one very difficult to master eminently. Now, that is the science of the *Philosophers*.

Someone will object that <term>VOLTAIRE</term>, who wrote *on Philosophy*, must know it; and that this famous author interprets the name as *the Love of Wisdom*. I know this; but it results in no other proof than that <term>VOLTAIRE</term> himself—that happy Genius, so fertile in ideas both vigorous and brilliant, so admirable in his always new and rich way of expressing them, so revolted against the prejudices that seemed to him to *offend Reason*—never reflected seriously on either the Greek name Φιλοσοφία or the true consistency of the <term>SCHOOLS</term>, from which alone he could have taken this flawed interpretation. From this, he will allow me to conclude that his <term>TREATISE ON PHILOSOPHY</term> must have no relation to the Science that the ancients characterized by this name, to which it is certain he will never apply himself.

<term>LETTERS</term>.—I will astonish my reader much more if, after having proved to him that *Philosophy* is not at all known by the scholars of our century, I add that they are no more versed in <term>LETTERS</term>, and that it is only through scholastic language that they claim to be *Literate People*. The proof follows. <note>[The Candidate will especially note what follows.]</note>

<term>LETTERS</term> naturally express by their name *literal figures*, which serve us in putting the words of a speech onto paper. I see that we are taught in childhood to distinguish characters, to assemble them, and to pronounce the words they compose, *exactly as one trains parrots*.

As a result of this method of the <term>SCHOOLS</term>, it happens that no one thinks to reflect anymore on the *form of each LETTER*, to research its *signification*, and to fundamentally conceive of its *beauties*. Yet it is the *beauties included in their form* that caused them to be named, by the most just of all titles, <term>THE BELLES LETTRES</term>; and it seems that everyone today is ignorant of this.

It is clear that the *form*, which was essentially distinctive of <term>LETTERS</term> in their origin, could not have been a matter of indifference: for the goal was to represent through them what one wanted to communicate without speaking, in order to instruct those who were absent, or posterity, about what could not be told to them in person.

The first thing after the union of the tinctures is *strife* and *fighting*; between what these occur, and for what they wrestle—namely, the heavenly Virgin, as revealed by the tincture. Why no Virgin can be produced. A forewarning: (1.) concerning the outward character of male and female. (2.) Concerning the order of all these things.

The female tincture takes the blood *to hold it fast*, etc.; as explained by the generation of water in eternal nature, which, as the water of life, has all powers.

Just as there is a delusion in the two tinctures, so it is in the *spiritus mundi* [spirit of the world] (even more than in the tincture). And so it is in the *fiat* [creative command] as well; but in both, it is *necessary* and *beneficial*. This is explained by the sweetness of the blood. The expressions of *thinking, delighting*, etc., are explained and defended through analogies.

All delight is turned into anxiety: (1.) by the *spiritus mundi* introducing the four elements. Longing. The tincture's withdrawal, yet it still remains. The *spiritus mundi* is more confined in its delusion. (2.) By the blood being stifled, which causes tumult and uproar. In these two things lies the first essential death to paradise. From this, we will judge that the *first* LETTER *of radical words* must have been more specifically characteristic of the object expressed by each of these words, especially since it declares to us the *first* representative idea of the *object* that affected the ingenious Author of LETTERS when he tried to depict what he would have said. But since the same idea, represented in a *Figure*, can be applied differently to several objects, it was clearly necessary to join one or more other *literal Figures* to this first LETTER to better define the particular object being shown. This is undoubtedly how the different words of writing were formed.

Those who have truly *studied* BELLES LETTRES must have first focused on positively knowing the *ideas signified by the form of each one*, and then on combining their various connections to discover what was originally symbolized by the words we call ROOTS.

When one has well-studied, thoroughly deepened, and clearly recognized the express *Meaning* of all the *radical words* of any language, it is believed that one must have become very learned—especially if one has rectified or ensured the accuracy of their discoveries by tracing them back etymologically to the *Mother Tongue* from which the roots of our languages are drawn. For then, as soon as one casts their eyes upon the *Letters* that compose the *Name* of either a *Plant*, a *Mineral*, or whatever else it may be, one perceives the *Use* and the *Property* of the *Plant*, and the *Nature* and the particular *Quality* of the *Mineral*. In a word, one penetrates into the *Essence* of each thing, because it was natural to specify the Essence of each thing by representing it with Characters that would make it sensible to our understanding. This is the only science that can constitute a *LETTERED MAN*.

All the Philosophers of Antiquity possessed this exact and radical knowledge of their *Letters*. Therefore, when they wished to write in a way that could only be understood by the Learned, they would invent a Story, a Dream, or any other fictitious Narrative using PROPER NAMES that concealed, through their literal Characters, the Secret of the Author's thoughts. <note>Take notice.</note>

Consequently, one could only learn the Secrets of the PHILOSOPHERS by decomposing *the mystical words of their works*, which, if they were not proper names, were always written in distinctive Characters. The eye of the *lettered man* would have distinguished them even without that, but one undoubtedly understands that it was always necessary to be initiated into the meaning of the *literal Figures* so that, after having understood the Names whose *Decomposition* was necessary, one could ensure the meaning that each *decomposed part* was meant to express.

The knowledge of what was to be decomposed in a philosophical writing was called the *Science of the Cabala*, because the Greek term <term>τὸ ΚΑΒΒΑΛΕΙΝ</term> means exactly: "WHAT THE WISE MAN SEES IS TO BE DECOMPOSED." It was truly an art that required much Knowledge, because certain mystical words were not to be dissected by *Letters*, but by *Syllabes*. From this comes our distinction between the *Great* CABALA and the *Syllabic* CABALA. The latter was much more practiced by authors, both Chaldean and Greek, and we shall see that it is sufficient to penetrate the writings of Moses, the Prophets, and the Evangelists.

There were LETTERS of a particular form that were consecrated solely for the *Mysteries of the Egyptian Law*. They were called by the Chaldeans and the Arabs... *Divani*, that is to say...

### *The DIVINE FOUNDATIONS of Genesis.*

--- I have said that the learned Moses, a worthy rival of the Great Hermes, had enclosed within the Names, the Years, and the miraculous Deeds of his PATRIARCHS the same documents that he had recognized and admired in the Theogony of the EGYPTIANS: to enable my reader to judge for themselves, let us lift the *mystical veils* with which THE GODS *of Paganism* and THE *Israelite* PATRIARCHS were equally covered.

I suppose that one has read all the historians who have written on the deities, the laws, and the religious rites of Egypt. The Phoenician Sanchoniatho reports them as a philosopher: I do not know if Manetho was well-informed about the fine fragments he collected: *Herodotus*, by pretending to have made a journey, he says, among the Egyptians to learn about them, lets me see that he had no need to leave his study, and that he did not write blindly. Regarding *Diodorus*, *Eusebius*, and *Plutarch*, those were only historians, without possessing in any way the philosophical secrets of Egypt: Among the authors who have written after them, the most faithful is *Du Pin*: but the *Researches of Dorigny* have more merit regarding the subject of the GODS.

One sees in all of them that the *religion of the Egyptians* prescribed for them the same use of *circumcision*, *ablutions*, *divine festivals*, and *annual sacrifices*: the same respect for the *priesthood*, for the *temples*, for the *oracles of KINGS*, of JUDGES, and of PROPHETS; the same *commandments*, *legal sanctions*, and *moral advice*, which later formed the *basis of the Mosaic religion*.

I suppose also that attention will have been paid to the first dynasties of the Egyptian kings; to those KINGS, GODS OF THE WORLD, from whom they believed their sovereigns were descended: It is evident that, as a consequence of this opinion, they must have considered themselves *the most noble nation on Earth*, and *the most favored by the graces of the Eternal*, just as the Jews called themselves *the people of God*.

One must also have observed that, according to the *divine and royal chronicles of the Egyptians*, the origin of that kingdom went back to the creation of the world; and that the Israelites similarly believed they had, in their annals, an uninterrupted lineage since the first man created.

I conclude from this preliminarily, seeing that the two systems of legislation of Hermes and Moses are uniform in their *legal object* and in their *radical principles*, "That these two philosophers could not have necessarily taught anything about GOD and NATURE except the same truths, and therefore the same origin of the universe, the same, single, and perpetual religion, despite the extreme dissimilarity—

### X.—OF MAN’S REGENERATION, THROUGH THE BLOOD AND DEATH OF CHRIST.

This is Behmen’s *only aim*. The humblest need not complain of obscurity; the strongest will find strong meat enough, etc. The excuse of this writer, who only writes according to the measure of his experience. Behmen’s *passages* in great abundance.

I admit that my conclusion is contested by a *very general prejudice*. I admit further that this prejudice must appear well-founded as long as one does not clearly see the IDENTITY OF DOCTRINE that I claim exists in the midst of the diversity of the two histories and the two forms of worship; but if I prove it, doubt will cease; and for this purpose, it is only a matter of releasing the *dogmatic substance from the double figures that have veiled it from us so differently*.

<margin>Arabia is omitted</margin> Let us begin by examining in depth what this *dogmatic substance* was in the *Egyptian religion*; a religion so beautiful that not only the entire country of the Mizraim <note>Missorains</note>, which included the Thebaid and Ethiopia along with our modern Egypt, but also Arabia, Nubia, and the rest of Africa; Syria, Chaldea, Babylonia, Persia, and India in Asia; Greece, Italy, and the other southern countries of Europe, received it unanimously as DIVINE LAW, upon seeing the marvelous text that the great Hermes entitled with four Arabic letters: : : : <term>Thooth</term>. Their meaning was DEUS IGNIS—IGNIS DEUS, that is to say, [Hebrews 12:29] *God is a pure fire—the pure fire is God*.

### First DOGMA.—

Every Egyptian had to believe that there was ONE SUPREME GOD, *without a name*, because no name could define him, and without a beginning. The qualifications of this supreme God were: *the only Uncreated, the truly Living, the unknown God, the Spirit Father of all the Gods*. To invoke him, they used the term : : <term>Allah</term>, or : : <term>Allah</term>, under which he is still worshiped today throughout the East; but its literal expression is SPIRIT-STONE: it designated *the divine Spirit as being the foundation stone of all things*.

They used the Arabic letter which is pronounced o, ou, and u to characterize him: this letter is a symbol of pure fire. They also added the letter : : KH, corresponding to the X of the Greeks, which formed : : : <term>Khou</term>: there still exists among the Muslims an infinite respect for this divine name, which is repeated while invoking the supreme Being with enthusiasm up to one hundred and one times by a type of their priests called the *Shouting Dervishes* <note>Derviches-Crieurs</note>. The hieroglyphic meaning of this second letter is STRONG SPIRIT, so that the two letters together say *pure fire of the strong spirit*, and consequently, of God.

Others joined to the symbolic letter of pure fire the letter : : a, which, as the first letter of the alphabet, announced the Principle: thus : : <term>aou</term> expressed FIRE PRINCIPLE, or the pure fire which is our Principle.

But the *figure of the supreme God*, which appears to have been the most famous first among the Mizraim Arabs, and then among all the other peoples of paganism, was to double the letter : : u, making the first a consonant, and to join to it the Arabic word : : : : : <term>Elkhan</term>, which means *the Sovereign, or the Monarch*; regarding the first two letters, they signified *Fire of pure Fire*: and as this fire of pure fire is that which animates us, it was natural to recognize it as the <term>KHAN</term>, or the universal Monarch: this was expressed by the emblematic name : : : : : <term>Vuelkhan</term>, which was pronounced, by the ordinary elision, <term>Vulkhan</term>, and from which the Phoenicians made their God of Fire, VULCANUS.

One will not be surprised, now that one radically knows this ancient *Egyptian figure* of THE UNCREATED BEING, by the testimony given to us by the historians of Egypt, that *the first temple of this kingdom was dedicated to the God VULCAN*: it is as if they were saying that its dedication was TO THE FIRE OF PURE FIRE, TO THE MASTER OF THE WORLD. This obliges me to develop the Phoenician fable, according to which we see this same **VULCAN** of the Egyptians qualified as the Son of the god **JUPITER** and the goddess **JUNO**, husband of the goddess **VENUS**, and the maker of the divine thunderbolts, which he places at the disposal of **JUPITER**.

My reader undoubtedly knows that **JUPITER**, announced in his history as the King of the Heavens, has been a very expressive symbol of the Spirit of the Air; he is not unaware that the air contains a vivifying fire, which is truly incorporated into its substance: from there, as the Spirit that reigns in the air universally distributes this **DIVINE FIRE** by which we are all vivified, he well deserved to be named the Father of Life, or the Father of the God of Fire, who alone is the life of every living being. This is only a repetition of what his name expresses, since ***Iou Pater*** signifies the Father of the Unique, that is to say, of God.

The name of **JUNO**, which is given to him as a wife, means exactly the Thought of God, in Greek ***Iou Noos***, MENS UNICI <note>Mind of the Unique</note>: in fact, if the Spirit of the Air (which the philosophers more commonly name the Spirit of the Universe) acts only according to the will of the unique Being, or of God—as we cannot doubt—the **THOUGHT OF GOD** must be as if married to this aerial spirit; and one conceives, regarding the vital fire of which this same spirit is called the father, that only the **THOUGHT OF GOD** could naturally have given birth to it.

Because **Venus** was the goddess of generation, the necessity of her marriage with **THE GOD OF FIRE** becomes evident; for the pure fire of the Eternal is alone capable of animating the generative spirit of creatures. Finally, as lightning and thunder always have the God of Fire for their principle, one senses that Vulcan must necessarily form and administer to Jupiter all his thunderbolts.

Everyone must perceive, in the midst of this theogonic fabric of the Phoenicians, a philosophical instruction for the living: they are taught by allegory that although the pure fire of the divine essence is the only source of life and animation for all beings, we nevertheless receive our spirit of life, emanating from His animating fire, only after it has taken an elementary substance in the spiritual body of our human nature; and this because only human elements can instill in us, make us capable of feeling, and cause us to preserve its divine impression.

Let us observe that, in the Law of Moses, the supreme Being preserved the Egyptian descriptions of the only uncreated, the unnamed living one, and the Stone-spirit; Moses added only that He was **THE ONLY GOD**. He only wished to change in the law of Hermes the plurality of his gods, which led the ignorant people to direct an adoration due to the Creator alone toward beings who were constantly created: this is why he included, in his historical figure of **ISAAC** son of **ABRAHAM**, the same instruction he had discovered under the emblem of **VULCAN** son of **JUPITER**. My reader is about to understand this.

Would it be chimerical? Should M. A. not understand that the *ternary* must be found everywhere, since nature, all the beings that compose it, and all the facts it presents to us, are but the varied results of the existence of an uncreated trinity, or the manifestation of the powers of a triune being?
If it should happen that the three persons of the Christian Trinity were three co-eternal faculties of the same essence—as this essence is undoubtedly, as we have established more than once, the unique and real cause of all existences, and of all physical, moral, or spiritual facts—should not the *divine ternary* manifest itself universally in the sciences, which are but descriptions; in grammar, which is the expression of our faculties; in the arts, which are but those faculties put into action in accordance with pre-existing mathematical laws; in governments, which are political bodies; and finally, and principally, in man, the most perfect of creatures, the very image of the divine model? * * *
I must observe, before leaving the subject of numbers, that M. de Maistre subordinates mathematics itself to metaphysics: he knew this science too well not to know that sensible numbers proceed from intellectual numbers. In mathematics, in fact, as in all others, the essence comes before the form, the force before the movement, unity before the number, and the point before extension. *Would numbers exist without the pre-existence of uncreated unity?* Did this unity not contain them *potentially*, since all emanate from it, adding to it zero, which is nothing but *nothingness*? In the science of extension, it is certain that geometers always presuppose the existence of the point, without length, width, or depth—a supposition in agreement with the essence of things, for it is this point, outside of space, which generates the straight line that itself forms the surface, which is alone necessary thereafter to construct solids and measure extension, which is thus derived itself from the non-extended point, since it is entirely composed of surfaces, etc. The entire edifice of mathematics is therefore based on metaphysical notions existing in our understanding and modeled after intellectual mathematics. It is the same with axioms: why do we not demand a demonstration of them? Because we find within ourselves the *a priori* certainty that they are true; but why are they true? Because uncreated unity, in generating all numbers and all beings, has characterized their relationships in an invariable manner, and because our souls—also emanated from *this first unity* which has so magnificently endowed them—possess within themselves *the innate knowledge of these relationships*. But enough on this article, which will seem too abstract.</margin>

B.'s philosophy and divinity, according to the A. B. C. D. E. Dissertations mentioned above, "which," Freher there adds, "he desired me to correct and complete."

But further, it is evident to the writer that these "Dissertations" were the writings which Law chiefly consulted after making the acquaintance of Behmen (about <term>A.D. 1733</term>), that is, after he had for a sufficient time studied his works alone, so as to have obtained a practical and general knowledge of them; as he, in his "Way to Divine Knowledge," page 240, directs the searcher after truth and wisdom to do; and likewise recommended to the Reverend Mr. Neve in a letter to him, a copy of which has already appeared in this work. Indeed, it would appear that his first philosophical writings (including the "Appeal") were founded upon the special explanations of the particular subjects upon which they severally treat, contained in the above-described "Dissertations"; as likewise, the leading work of the "last series" of his writings was founded upon certain portions of other of Freher's treatises—to be, however, more particularly referred to in the brief memorial introduced below. In Freher's writings, then, he enjoyed the advantage of a resolution of all doubts and difficulties with respect to the exact sense of Behmen, or to particular points of hidden truth that might have been the subject of his meditations.——And now we arrive at the cause or reason of the entire change in his character of thought, which ensued between the year 1732, when the "Three Letters to a Lady inclined to Rome" were written, and the period of 1737–40 mentioned above, which until now has not been clearly understood. And indeed, it is difficult to conceive the possibility of obtaining such a thorough, fundamental understanding of Behmen—as is implied in the authorship of the treatises which issued from Law's pen during the latter mentioned period—from a brief, unassisted study of his books, even taking into account Law's amazing capacity, penetration, and strength of understanding; but now the matter is plain. In addition to his own study and understanding of Behmen, he had the advantage of Freher's—serial and methodical, general and particular, direct and annotatory explanations, with their symbolic and other illustrations of the scope and sense of that author. Freher, himself a native of Germany, was a man of profound erudition, "of great accuracy of thought, and coolness of mind, as well as of a most holy and primitive life," so writes the learned Dr. Francis Lee from his own personal knowledge, "who had read all Behmen's books in the original more than ten times, though not without the greatest possible disgust in the beginning." Thus it was that Law obtained his acute and penetrating understanding of Behmen; which, nevertheless, was peculiar to himself and could only be the result of such theosophical instructions falling upon such a ready and prepared genius, accomplished casuist and logician, and orthodox theologian and mystical divine as he was in the year 1732; and hence the variation, or rather the philosophic enlargement of his views, so strikingly manifest in his subsequent public writings.——The Candidate will, therefore, in his considerations of the latter division of Law's <term>mystic-Elias</term> character, not fail to assign to Freher his proper place in the providential formation of it.

<meta>This page transitions from a discussion of Dionysius Andreas Freher and William Law to a biographical entry for Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin, a French mystic influenced by similar spiritual traditions. Saint-Martin (Louis-Claude de), a learned and profound spiritualist known as *the Unknown Philosopher*, was born in Amboise to a noble family on January 18, 1743. He owed to an attentive stepmother the first elements of that gentle and pious education which, he said, made him love God and men throughout his entire life. At the college of Pont-Levoy, where he had been placed early on, the book he enjoyed the most was that of Abadie, titled *The Art of Knowing Oneself*: it was to the reading of this work that he attributed his detachment from the things of this world. But intended by his parents for the judiciary, he focused during his law course more on the natural foundations of justice than on the rules of jurisprudence, the study of which he found repulsive. * * *

Despite his taste for internal philosophy, a career no less active than that of military exercises opened to him. Initiated through formulas, rites, and practices into operations called *theurgic*, which were directed by Martinez Pasqualis (see the *Universal Biography*), leader of the sect called the <term>Martinists</term>, he often asked him: *Master, what! is all this then necessary to know God?* This path, which consisted of perceptible manifestations, had not at all seduced our philosopher. It was, however, by this route that he entered the path of spiritualism. The doctrine of this school—whose members took the Hebrew title of <term>Cohen</term> (Priests), and which Martinez presented as a secret public teaching of which he had received the tradition—is found set forth in a mysterious manner in the first works of Saint-Martin, and especially in his *Natural Table of the Relations between God, Man, etc.*

After the death of Martinez, the school was transferred to Lyon. It was there that, armed with a doctrine opposed to that of the <term>Encyclopedists</term> (which threatened only too much to spread), Saint-Martin—destined in a sense to combat philosophical atheism, just as he would one day directly attack revolutionary materialism—published his book *Of Errors*, etc. In destroying the erroneous doctrines of a so-called philosophy of nature and history, he recalls man to the *Truth founded on the very Principle of science, and on the nature of the intellectual being*; but he employs the traditions of Scripture only to support his proofs, or enigmatically, so as not to too greatly offend readers imbued with the theories coming out of the workshop of the Baron d'Holbach. This same school of Pasqualis, whose operations ceased in 1778, came to be merged in Paris into the society of the <term>G. P.</term>, or into that of the <term>Philalethes</term>, professing in appearance the doctrine of Martinez and that of <term>Swedenborg</term>, but seeking the truth less than *the great work*. Saint-Martin was invited in 1784 to this last meeting; but he refused to participate in the operations of its members, whom he judged to speak and act only as pure <term>Freemasons</term>, and not as true initiates (that is to say, united to their Principle).

Saint-Martin willingly attended meetings where people occupied themselves in good faith with exercises that announced active virtues. The manifestations of an intellectual order, obtained by perceptible means, revealed to him in the sessions of Martinez a science of spirits; the visions of Swedenborg, of a sentimental order, revealed a science of souls. As for the phenomena of <term>somnambulic magnetism</term>, which he followed in Lyon, he regarded them as being of an inferior perceptible order; * * *

A lover of everything that could make him recognize a truth, especially in the sciences subject to exact principles, the study of mathematics (which Saint-Martin engaged in to discover the spirit that might be hidden in the knowledge of numbers) caused his connection with Lalande; but they were too incompatible, and it lasted only a short time. Although he did not believe in Lalande’s atheism, he nevertheless saw him positioned in such a way as to sink deeper and deeper into that system. * *

<meta>This page continues the biography of Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin, detailing his discovery of Jacob Boehme’s works and his subsequent travels and personal character. It was in Strasbourg that, through a friend (Mrs. Boechlin), he became acquainted with the works of the Teutonic philosopher, **JACOB BOEHME**, who was regarded in France as a visionary. At an advanced age, Saint-Martin studied the German language in order to understand and translate for his own use the works of this famous "illuminated" thinker into French. These works revealed to him what he had only glimpsed in the documents of his first master. From then on, he always regarded Boehme as THE GREATEST HUMAN LIGHT THAT HAD EVER APPEARED. Saint-Martin visited England, where in 1787 he connected with Ambassador Barthélemy and became acquainted with the works of William Law, which contain a summary of J. Boehme’s books. In 1788, he traveled to Rome with Prince Alexis Gallitzin, who spoke these remarkable words to Mr. Fortia d'Urban: "I have only truly been a man since I have known Mr. de Saint-Martin." * *

The internal and reflective view by which man seeks to achieve within himself the knowledge of the very Principle of reality—a view far superior to Kant's purely rational intuition—is the idea that ultimately dominates the author's writings. This is true even in his less serious works, where he hid his philosophy when the subject allowed for satire. A tone of gaiety, which occasionally escaped him and for which he reproached himself, was more a matter of his mood than his meditative mindset or his character, which tended toward simple kindness. * *

At that time, the elevated views and sentiments that made him admire his "good German philosopher" extended even into the natural questions he treated. Based on his increasingly productive insights, he was inclined to discover an internal and invisible world beneath temporal and visible nature—a world which, in his view, nature was meant to reveal to the intellectual and moral man through cultivation. Thus, he could not remain a stranger to any science. He followed the progress of discoveries in every branch of knowledge and compared their data with what he had acquired from Jacob Boehme and his own reflections. It was by searching through this unknown world that he composed and produced *The Spirit of Things*, in which he strives to lift a corner of the veil and shed some light on a nature that seemed to him to have been unveiled by a kind of inspiration only for Boehme's eyes. In this hypothesis, one can understand that since the sciences he had explored were then much less advanced than they are today—except for what the knowledge of the internal man could reveal to him through meditation—he necessarily lagged behind in several of his explanations. These do not always agree with new discoveries, besides the fact that they necessarily depart from received opinions.

Despite the extent of his knowledge and the originality of his ideas, which led him to relate everything to his spiritualism, people admired Saint-Martin’s sound judgment and his simple, lovable modesty. His sociable character and communicative spirit would undoubtedly have gained him many followers, but he did not seek to make proselytes: he only wanted friends who were disciples, not merely of his books, but of themselves. He kept a journal of his relationships; and just as the translations of his beloved philosopher were provisions for his old age, he regarded his new friends as acquisitions, judging himself very rich in "rents of souls." Seeing his humble air and simple exterior, one would not suspect the profound knowledge, the extraordinary insights, or the high virtues he possessed. But the candor, the peace of his conversations, and, one might say, the atmosphere of benevolence that seemed to spread around him, manifested the wise man and the "new man" that philosophy and religion had formed. * *

One can judge that the hopes of a man who had such a sharp hunger for realities could not—

Motion is the ever self-manifesting, and consequently, progressive God. The primary sphere is rotating, for it originated through motion; however, the motion of the sphere cannot be progressive, for it fills everything. God is a rotating globe. God did not find matter co-eternal with himself and, like an architect, arrange it to his fancy; rather, out of his own eternal omnipotence and by his simple will, he evoked the world from nothing into existence. Without light, the universe is not only dark, but it does not even exist. Light is the universe, and every finite thing is only a different position of light. The universe is a thoroughly illuminating globe, a rotating globe of light. Light and heat were the first phenomena of the world. Heat with light, however, is fire. Fire is the totality of ether; it is God manifested in his totality. Before his determination to create a world, God was darkness; in the first act of creation, however, he appeared as fire. There is no higher or more perfect symbol of divinity than fire. God's whole consciousness, apart from individual thoughts, is fire. The Holy Scriptures therefore usually describe God appearing in the form of fire—as a burning bush, a flame. The universe is nothing other than a rotating globe of fire."

Although Saint-Martin was still quite well-known then, this philosopher was generally so little understood by the world that the public newspapers, announcing his death, confused him with Martinez-Pasqualis, his master, who died in 1779 in Saint-Domingue. Although the disciple was considered the head of a religious doctrine, his sentiments, as has been said, were far from being dictated by private or exclusive views. *** It is not that Saint-Martin (as the author of the *St. Petersburg Evenings* suggested) did not believe in the legitimacy of the Christian priesthood; but he thought that the institution of Christ could be realized everywhere through sincere faith in the powers and merits of the Redeemer.

How could a writer professing such an indulgent Christianity have incurred, on the other hand, the hostility of the so-called apostles of tolerance and philanthropy? It was because his religion was neither political nor feigned; the clarity that came from his conviction, despite the clouds in which he seemed to wrap himself, offended the "enlightenment" of the pseudo-philosophy of the time. Saint-Martin wrote much, and his books always develop by degrees, with more strength and clarity, the religious character they bear. They have, moreover, been commented upon and partially translated, but mainly into the languages of Northern Europe.

One will see, by a general glance at the author's doctrine—of which each of his writings offers a particular viewpoint—that it is not surprising that minds led astray by passion or abandoned to the errors of the senses could neither understand nor appreciate him. But it is permissible to believe that as moral ideas and reviving religious sentiments become simpler while being purified through more extensive intellectual culture, we will feel the need to oppose an enlightened and reasonable spiritualism to that tendency of the natural sciences toward a materialism which attributes faculties and functions to physical organs, and which makes passive and blind agents the principle of activity and intelligence.

The works of Saint-Martin aim not only to explain nature through man, but to trace all our knowledge back to the Principle of which the human spirit can become the center.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Saint-Martin's philosophy, contrasting it with Plato, Descartes, Leibniz, and Kant, and highlighting the influence of Martines de Pasqually and Jacob Boehme. It then transitions into a mystical commentary on the figure of Enoch and the unification of divine knowledge, before returning to the biographical account of William Law and his charitable activities.</meta>

Present nature, fallen and divided from itself and from man, nevertheless preserves in its laws—as man does in several of his faculties—a disposition to return to its original unity. Through this double relationship, nature puts itself in harmony with man, just as man aligns himself with his Principle. It follows from this that the *Nosce te ipsum* <note>Know thyself</note> must embrace within the idea of the "self" both the notion of the rational self and that of the spiritual self. This knowledge is therefore not the simple theory of a type or subject of our ideas, which Plato concludes from the notion of an archetype, derived itself from the ideas of unity and object. Descartes and Leibniz also descend, through a common idea, from the abstract to the sensible; but after rising from the subject to the object, the first does so by way of conception, and the second by way of *apperception*. Kant, not exceeding the limit of the sensible, separates the abstract object from the subject, and leaves it in the rank of general notions for which his intuitive reason cannot account. According to Saint-Martin, man, taken as the subject, does not simply conceive or perceive the abstract object of his thought: he receives it, but from a source other than that of sensible impressions (<note>see below, no. II.</note>). Furthermore, the man who gathers himself, and who renounces all external things through his will, operates and obtains the intimate knowledge of the very Principle of thought or speech—that is, of his Prototype, or the Word, of which he is originally the image and type. The divine Being thus reveals itself to the spirit of man; and, at the same time, the knowledge related to ourselves and the nature of things is manifested. It is toward this original nature, where man was in harmony with his Principle, that he must strive through his work and desire, by uniting his will to that of the Restorer. Then, the divine image is reformed; the human soul is regenerated; the beauties of order are discovered, and communication between God and man is restored.

We see, from this overview of Saint-Martin’s doctrine, that the spiritualism—whose path was first opened to him by Pasqualis and then smoothed by JACOB BOEHME—was no longer simply the science of Spirits, but that of *God*. The mystics of the Middle Ages and those of Fenelon’s school, by uniting themselves through contemplation to their Principle, following the doctrine of their master Ruysbroeck, were absorbed into God through affection. HERE IS A HIGHER DOOR; it is not only the affective faculty, but the intellectual faculty, which knows its divine Principle within itself, and through it, the model of that nature which Malebranche saw not actively in himself, but speculatively in God. Saint-Martin discovers the type of this nature in his inner being through an active and spiritual operation, which is the seed of knowledge. It is toward this goal that the author's works, in the order of their composition, appear to lead, marking progressively the route he followed, which others may follow in the same career.

Considered first as an author, and then as a translator, the one is still only the extension or the complement of the other, because it is always the same spirit:

<margin>
[See Vol I Stilling's Works pp. 223]
</margin>

I. *Of Errors and of Truth, or Men Recalled to the Universal Principle of Science.* By an Unknown Philosopher. Edinburgh (Lyon) 1775, in 8º. The author, who rarely followed his own will in writing, but rather the advice of his friends, was indignant to read in Boulanger that religions were born of the fear caused by the catastrophes of nature. He wrote this book to show, as has been said, in the very nature of man, the sensible knowledge of an active and intelligent cause—the true source of allegories, mysteries, institutions, and laws. While the Holbachian school, through the voice of Voltaire, sometimes treated this enigmatic book as insane and absurd—and yet nevertheless prided itself on providing a sequel to it—the philosopher of Bern, struck by the truths it seemed to contain under a veil, initiated a correspondence with its author, whose work he regarded as that of the most profound writer of this century. The so-called *Sequel to Errors and Truth, etc.* (Salmonopolis (Paris), 1784, in 8º), was identified by Saint-Martin as fraudulent and tainted by the vice of the false systems he was fighting. <note>It is a most admirable burlesque on the original.</note> Indeed, the *Unknown Philosopher* had said that the will constituted the essential and fundamental faculty of man; and it is by contradicting him that one dares to interpret him when it is said (page 7) that the will is only a modification of the brain by which man is disposed to put his organs into play. Does one not already seem to hear the materialist doctrine of Cabanis and the school of Gall? <note>Pooh!</note>

II. *Natural Table of the Relationships that Exist Between God, Man, and the Universe*, with the epigraph (taken from the previous work, according to the author’s custom): *Explain things by man, and not man by things*, 2 parts Edinburgh (Lyon), 1782, in 8º. In this work, composed in Paris according to the advice of some friends, the author infers, from the superiority of man’s faculties and his acts over the sense organs and their productions, that the existence of nature—whether general or particular—is equally the product of creative powers superior to this result. However, man is in a state of dependence on physical things, of which he only acquires an idea through the impression they make on his organs. But he has, at the same time, notions of another class: ideas of law and power, of order and unity, of wisdom and justice. He is thus dependent on his intellectual and moral ideas, just as he is on ideas drawn from the senses. Now, those intellectual ideas do not come from the senses; they therefore originate from another source: from external faculties that produce thoughts in him. But from where was this dependence born? From the disorder produced by an inferior cause, which opposed the superior cause and ceased to remain within its law. Man...

<column-break/>

original institution were the results of Mr. Law's own foresight, judgment, and experience, we may infer that this subject occupied much of his attention during the first three years of his residence with the ladies at King's-Cliffe, and more or less, indeed, until the foundations were finally completed.

Unfortunately, no regular documents exist containing an account of the precise economy of the family at the Hall Yard. In the absence of such, however, we insert the following traditions which have been handed down as the testimony of contemporary witnesses, collected nearly half a century ago. These memorials will necessarily encompass the period now under review, up to the year 1749, when the "First Part" of the "Spirit of Prayer" was published, as well as the subsequent portion of Mr. Law's life.

Mr. Law rose early each morning, probably about five o'clock, spending some time in devotion; after which he breakfasted, generally on a cup of chocolate, in his bedroom, and then commenced his studies. He deemed early rising for prayer (with strict temperance, and occasional fasting) to be important aids in the cultivation of the regenerate or divine life in the soul, which in every step of its progress must be founded upon mortification and self-denial. In common with the faithful children of God of all ages, he steadily kept his eye on the process and example of the crucified Jesus, who St. Mark informs us, "rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed": an intimation, by the way, which is received without murmuring or disputing by all those who, desiring to follow Christ in the regeneration and a sure path to eternal glory, carefully examine the rule and practice of his daily life. But for Mr. Law's own sentiments on the evangelical duty and advantages of early rising, we refer the reader to the "Serious Call," chapter 14; as also to the following chapter, for the ground and reasons of another most important help to devotion: namely, that of chanting a psalm, singing a hymn, reading aloud the apostolic exhortations, and vocal earnest supplication, to be persevered in for a sufficient time until the mind becomes flexible, resigned, and enabled to stay itself upon God; along with, moreover, other little arts and discoveries calculated to kindle and maintain the spirit of devotion.

<margin>
had a small farm and ^
</margin>

An act of charity very appropriately commenced the outward employments of each day, which had been thus early consecrated to God. As we learn from the notices referred to, Mr. Law kept four cows; the produce of which, beyond what was required for his household, he gave to the poor, distributing the milk every morning with his own hands, and doubtless accompanying the gift with a few words of friendly discourse or spiritual counsel, according to the circumstances of the recipients of his bounty. The order and devotion of a religious house would appear to have regulated all the movements of this family. At nine o'clock a bell was rung for family devotion, of which the Collects and Psalms for the day formed a portion. From the very impressive and edifying performance of this duty, Mr. Law retired in silence to his chamber, where he passed the morning in study; not infrequently, indeed, interrupted by the message of some poor beggar asking for aid, which never failed to secure his immediate attention. Advancing to a window of his sleeping apartment (which at that time overlooked the courtyard of the house, though it is now blocked up), he inquired into the particular needs of his suppliants, and caused relief to be administered in the shape of either money, apparel, or food. Ever sensitively alive to the tender impulses of a spiritually enlightened charity, he manifested proportionate displeasure if room was not found on the kitchen fire for a vessel for the poor: and sometimes he has been known to leave his studies in order to taste the broth which had been made for them, to be satisfied that it was sufficiently nutritious. In the winter season, he occasionally added ale and wine to these charitable provisions.

In the matter of charity, as in every other characteristic of an elevated Christian philanthropy, the daily life of Mr. Law was strictly conformable to the principles he has so admirably inculcated.
