indicated, and graphically illustrated in his early fundamental treatises. Indeed, it would have been a matter of surprise if the case had been otherwise; it being an irreconcilable paradox to suppose a Christian moralist with a well-balanced intellect, an enlightened understanding, and an honest heart, could write justly and nobly in praise of benevolence without practicing its dictates; and doing so with a freedom and universality of spirit, rather than under the constraint of an unwelcome reflection or warning of conscience.

The principles of wisdom and piety set forth in Mr. Law’s elementary writings, and the characters under which they are delineated, may therefore be regarded as so many diversified phases or features of the foundation of his own mind, uniformly discovered as occasions afforded. But in none, perhaps, of those characters do we find his sublime spirit as a *Gospel sage* more admirably displayed than in that of *Ouranius*, in his “*Serious Call*,” chapter 21. In this simple yet finely conceived portraiture, and the accompanying reflections, is set forth the true spirit of a Christian pastor—such a one as we may well presume Mr. Law would have been, if Divine providence had not called him out from among his brethren and prepared him, by a course of suitable discipline, to perform those more exalted evangelical functions which it is our particular calling in this treatise to indicate. As few readers of these pages may have been so happy as to have seen a fine specimen of the genuine Anglican Christian pastor—at once a gentleman by birth and training, and by education, having carried off the highest honors which the pure mathematical and classical training of the University of Cambridge awards to her faithful and favored sons; and as being appropriate to the scope and design of this treatise, which is that of pointing out the way to the highest perfection in all solid and edifying erudition, we would here especially direct the attention of the reader to the character in question. We only incidentally observe that it was the *intended*, zealous, and laborious conformity to this exemplary model, joined with the general study of the practical writings of Mr. Law and other spiritual interpreters of the Gospel, that the celebrated Flechère of Madeley attained such an eminent degree of personal sanctity, and whose character has been so justly held up to admiration as an illustrious instance of a faithful teacher and pastor of souls. And yet, truth requires us to say also that the ideal portrait in question is only what is commonly to be met with in real life, in the conversation of hundreds of the devoted laborers of the Society of Jesus, as well as in the more ancient devotees and bishops of the original branches of Christianity. But in no modern work, or rather republication, is the true pastoral spirit—burning with seraphic devotion, with the cultivation of high personal holiness, and zeal for the salvation of souls—more forcibly exhibited than in De Rancé’s treatise “*On the Monastic State*”; which, therefore (with other works to be mentioned hereafter) is strongly recommended to the study of the young English ecclesiastic who desires to adequately and worthily fulfill the high and holy function of the pastoral office—that is, after the mastery and acquisition of the principles of Mr. Law’s two practical treatises, his “*Three Letters to a Lady*,” and his “*Answers to Trapp*.” And it was, doubtless, owing to the study of such accomplished examples of the true devotional and pastoral spirit, as is contained in the writings referred to here, that the pious Bishop Jeremy Taylor—the ideal personification and standard of Anglican Church practical divinity—attained such a sublime spirit of devotion, whose popular writings have had such a happy influence on this nation.

With respect to the exercise of charity, we may incidentally observe that every man has his own proper calling, and of necessity, the sphere of action appertaining to it; and provided he is faithful to it, he is not to be judged for not pursuing a path which the irrational understanding of a zealot might assign to him, after his own particular way. Some ordinarily have no other means presented to them of practicing the duty of charity than by almsgiving; others, only by contributions toward the maintenance of hospitals, dispensaries, and public institutions for the cleanliness and comfort, or the visitation and relief, of the sick and distressed of the lower orders of society; and others, according to their circumstances in life and religious associations, only by collecting money for the promotion of the evangelization of the heathen. And this, so far as it is applied to the regeneration of *savage nations*, or in preparing the way for the approaching induction of the intellectual heathen into the Christian faith by translations of the original *Scriptures* into their respective tongues, is undoubtedly a most admirable charity. Among other means of exercising a noble-minded charity may be mentioned the erection of Christian oratories for the preaching of the Gospel, as well as for devotion, in populous neighborhoods where there exists a deficiency of the ordinary means of moral and spiritual edification. If the resources dedicated to such purposes were even to be extended to the adorning of the interior of the Christian sanctuary with such scientific embellishments as are calculated to impress the mind of the worshippers with noble and exalted ideas of the Divine nature, and to induce a solemnity of spirit in the place where the honor and presence of the Most High more immediately resides, such expenditure would be anything but a mistaken charity. But of all institutions of the present day commanding the sympathy and generosity of philanthropists, there are none which possess a more evangelical character, or are more deserving of universal support, than *City Missions and Ragged School Institutes*. These may be considered the great moral discovery of the present age, just as the form and aggressive spirit of simple Bible Christianity (and the call and qualification of all the lay members of the mystical body of Christ to activity in the evangelical work—as local preachers, as missionaries, or as auxiliaries to that office, as exhorters, as leaders of bands and classes, etc., all without exception being employed in doing good and promoting the success of the Gospel) was that of a century ago. This was originated by Mr. Law’s practical treatises providentially falling upon rightly prepared minds to put their purified principles into working effect. Now, these are a few of the various modes in which, in our own day, persons professing Christianity may be considered to be called to the exercise of charity. But in Mr. Law’s case (which is now under review), his peculiar calling, as regards the subordinate personal exercise of this duty, arose from his relative position as an inhabitant of a remote inland town. This resulted in the establishment of the foundations already noticed, and in the regular distribution of all he possessed—after satisfying his own moderate necessities—to those who were in want. Indeed, his whole life was a course of most diffusive charity, exerting itself in every kind of good, without distinction or respect of persons, both to the souls and bodies of all who could re-

Among the articles of clothing which he provided for the needy were shirts made of strong, coarse linen. So that he might not give away what he himself could not thankfully receive, he always wore them himself first to confirm that fact through experience, after which they were washed and distributed. It can hardly be a matter of wonder that a hand so open, and a heart so liberal and humane, should be subject to occasional deception; accordingly, instances of hypocrisy are narrated regarding beggars who were known to change their better clothing for rags while sheltered by the projecting buttresses of the neighboring church, and thus disguised, return for relief to the well-known window. Though suspicions at times crossed his mind, Mr. Law would give his applicants the benefit of the doubt. The result of all this (says the narrator) was that King’s Cliffe became the resort of the idle and worthless, and obtained a reputation for poverty which the place did not deserve. This caused so much annoyance to the inhabitants that the rector, Mr. Piemont, endeavored to put an end to the supposedly misguided benevolence of Mr. Law and his companions by openly preaching against them from the pulpit.

The following curious document, found among Miss Gibbon’s papers in the handwriting of Mr. Law, throws some light on this affair. The writer possesses a duplicate copy, clearly written out by Miss Gibbon, to which are attached the respective original signatures of the parties from whom it was intended to come: —

> “King’s Cliffe, Feb. 21st, 1753. — A Letter to the writer and signers of a certain paper presented to George Lynn, Esq., and the neighboring justices of the peace, praying for justice and judgment against us on behalf of this parish, as being, among other things, the cause of the miserable poverty of the said parish.
> “We observe that a great part of this paper contains an idle narration of such matters as the justices can provide no relief for. Therefore, we must believe that they are related only as an opportunity to prefer a complaint against us and to prevent that gratitude which is due to us from the parish.
> “Ever since we came to this place, full of goodwill to do all the good in it that we could, we have been denounced from the pulpit in the most outrageous manner; and scarcely a Sunday has passed without instructing the people with some disgraceful comments cast upon us. No one can be a stranger to this, except he who is a stranger to the church.
> “But we were determined to bear this treatment from the pulpit for the sake of that good which we so much wished for the parish, looking upon it as unreasonable that the town should suffer for the unchristian behavior of its rector. But since so many significant inhabitants of the town have thought it proper, in conjunction with their minister, to sign their names to the truth and justice of this complaint against us—as helping to increase the poverty of the town—we have also thought it proper to make known to all the parish that we will no longer do them this injury, but will grant them all that relief ourselves for which they have applied to the justices. We will immediately put a stop to everything that we have done here; as for this place, all is at an end, unless such reasons for our staying here should arise as do not yet appear to us. And we have no doubt that every gentleman in the neighborhood, whether he is a justice of the peace or not, and every person of sense and goodness, will approve of our resolution. — Your hearty friends and well-wishers—ELIZABETH HUTCHESON, HESTER GIBBON, WILLIAM LAW.
> “The parish officers are desired to call a meeting of all the parish and let this letter be read to them. If they refuse this, we shall ourselves send it from house to house.
> “P.S.—When this is done, we shall draw up a detailed memorial of our case: of the great expense we have been at since we came here; the nature and manner of Mr. Law’s school for girls for nearly thirty years past; the manner of Mrs. Hutcheson’s school and hospital for widows; also the nature and manner of our daily charity to all the poor in general and to particular families in distress that must otherwise have fallen to the parish—along with the reasons for our departing from all these methods and leaving the town. This memorial is to be presented to the bishop and all the gentry in the neighborhood.”

After this representation of the case, probably to a few of the principal complainers, the matter seems to have died away, as the rector, we have seen, was named one of the trustees of the above-mentioned foundations in the following year. Thus, the worthy trio were left to pursue their charitable activities under a more favorable judgment, if not with the entire agreement, of those who had complained against them.

At twelve o’clock noon in winter, and at one in summer, dinner was laid on the table, of which Mr. Law ate very moderately, allowing himself one glass of wine. Report states that he ate his food from a trencher, or wooden platter, in the ancient college fashion—not because of any dislike for the luxury of earthenware, but either because he considered that plates dulled the knives, or (which is more probable) because of his desire to encourage the manufacture of woodenware, as woodturning was a trade peculiar to the town of King’s Cliffe.

We have seen that the family were called together for devotional exercises at nine in the morning; immediately after dinner, they reassembled for the same purpose. That duty performed, Mr. Law once more retired to his study and remained there a few hours, rejoining the ladies at the tea table. He did not ordinarily partake of this refreshment, but substituted a raisin or two from his pocket, generally standing and indulging in cheerful conversation. After tea, exercises of piety were resumed and varied by the servants taking turns reading a chapter from the Bible. How edifying and devotional these exercises were made—clarifying the purpose and mind of the Holy Spirit through this exalted sage—may be well conceived by the regenerate child of God from the following brief extracts from Mr. Law’s practical writings, being short paraphrases of St. Paul’s exhortation to a life of holiness and consecration to God. As in the following examples: —

> “Forasmuch as you know (says the apostle) that you were not redeemed with corruptible things, as

> “As if the apostle had said: Because you know you were made capable of this state of holiness, entered into a society with Christ, and made heirs of his glory—not by any human means, but by such a mysterious example of love as infinitely exceeds everything that can be thought of in this world; since God has redeemed you to himself, and to your own happiness, at so great a price, how base and shameful must it be if you do not from now on devote yourselves wholly to the glory of God, and become holy, as he who has called you is holy?
>
> “Again, (the apostle says) *You know how we exhorted, comforted, and charged every one of you; that you would walk worthy of God, who has called you to his kingdom and glory.*
>
> “You, perhaps, have often heard these words without ever thinking how much they required of you. And yet you cannot consider them without perceiving to what an eminent state of holiness they call you.
>
> “For how can the holiness of the Christian life be set before you in higher terms than when it is represented to you as *walking worthy of God*? Can you think of any reductions of virtue, any neglects of devotion, that are consistent with a life that is to be made *worthy of God*? Can you suppose that any man walks in this way except he who watches over all his steps and considers how everything he does may be done in the spirit of holiness? And yet, as high as these expressions carry this holiness, it is here plainly made the necessary holiness of all Christians. For the apostle does not here exhort his fellow *apostles* and *saints* to this holiness, but he commands *all Christians* to strive for it. *We charged,* says he, *every one of you, that you would walk worthy of God, who has called you to his kingdom and glory.*
>
> “Again, (St. Peter says) *If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God; if any man minister, let him do it as of the ability that God gives; that God in all things may be glorified in Jesus Christ.*
>
> “Do you not here plainly perceive your high calling? Are Christians to live in such purity of heart, such union with Christ, and holiness of life, that when they speak, they shall speak as the very oracles and mouthpiece of God? Are they so to act and serve that all who know them may see and feel that they act not of their own will, but by the sole power and inspiration of the Holy Spirit? And all for this very just and eternal reason, *That God alone may be glorified in Jesus Christ*—”

In this way, without the help of second-hand and dull commentaries, Mr. Law opened the minds of his little audience to understand the scriptures, introducing them into the very heart and spirit of the gospel at this time. In this way did this wise and devout man stir himself up, along with his friends, servants, and all the members of his little household, to be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord; continually looking for and hastening toward the coming of the day of God. The effects of his heavenly instructions and example were the cultivation in them of a serene and devout mind, full of gratitude and love to God, and of heavenly peace and benevolence toward all mankind.

This latter devotional exercise being ended, Mr. Law mostly took a brisk walk in the fields for physical exercise and for meditation, returning early to an evening meal. At half-past eight, the family reassembled for the last religious service of the day, after which the subject of our memoir withdrew to his room. There, before lying down to sleep, it is reported that he smoked a pipe and drank a glass of water. The hearthstone of this room, which is now just as it was when he left it, is worn away in two places, caused by the rubbing of his feet, which were subject to cold as a consequence of his studious habits. At nine o’clock, the whole family retired to rest.

In defense and support of the wisdom of this strict and regular daily devotion, and of its universal practicality in a modified degree, we insert the following extract, which is also consistent with the theme of this treatise:

> “It will perhaps be thought by some people that these times of devotion *come too frequently*; that they can only be observed by people of great leisure and ought not to be pressed upon the majority of men, who have the *cares of families, trades, and employments*; nor upon the *gentry*, whose status and position in the world cannot allow for this frequency of devotion. And that it is only fit for monasteries and nunneries, or such people as have no more to do in the world than they have.
>
> “To this it is answered,
>
> “*First*, That this method of devotion is not pressed upon any sort of people as *absolutely* <note>The original text spells this "absolutety"</note> necessary, but recommended to *all people* as the *best*, the *happiest*, and the *most perfect* way of life.
>
> “And if a great and exemplary devotion is as much the greatest happiness and perfection of a *merchant*, a *soldier*, or a *man of high status*, as it is the greatest happiness and perfection of the most *retired contemplative life*, then it is as appropriate to recommend it without any reductions to one order of men as to another. Because happiness and perfection are of the same worth and value to all people.
>
> “The gentleman and tradesman may, and must, spend much of their time differently from the pious monk in the cloister or the contemplative hermit in the desert; but then, as the monk and hermit lose the purpose of retirement unless they make it all useful to devotion, so the gentleman and merchant fail in the greatest purposes of a *social life*, and live to their loss in the world, unless devotion is their *chief and governing disposition*.
>
> “It is certainly very *honest* and *respectable* for people to engage in trades and employments; it is reasonable for gentlemen to manage their *estates and families* well and take such recreations as are appropriate to their status. But then every gentleman and tradesman loses the greatest happiness of creation, and is robbed of something that is greater than all employments, distinctions, and pleasures of the world, if he does not live more for *piety and devotion* than for anything else in the world.
>
> “Here are therefore no excuses made for men of *business and status* in the world. First, because it would be to excuse them from that which is the greatest purpose of living, and would only be finding so many reasons for making them *less beneficial* to themselves and *less useful* to God and the world.
>
> “*Secondly*, because most men of business and status engage *too far* in worldly matters—much further than the reasons of human life or the necessities of the world require.
>
> “*Merchants and tradesmen*, for instance, are generally ten times further engaged in business than

they need; this is so far from being a reasonable excuse for their lack of time for devotion that it is their crime, and must be condemned as a blameworthy instance of greed and ambition.
“The gentry and people of *importance* either give themselves up to state employments or to the gratification of their passions in a life of gaiety and debauchery; and if these things might be admitted as allowable *distractions* from devotion, devotion must be considered a minor part of life.
“Unless gentlemen can show that they have a God other than the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; a nature other than that which is derived from Adam; a religion other than the Christian, it is useless to plead their status, dignity, and pleasures as reasons for not preparing their souls for God through a strict and regular devotion.
“For since piety and devotion are the common, unchangeable means of saving all the souls in the world that shall be saved, there is nothing left for the *gentleman*, the *soldier*, and the *tradesman* but to ensure that their various *statuses* be made states of exact and solid piety through care, watchfulness, meditation, and prayer.
“If a merchant, having refrained from excessive business so that he might quietly attend the service of God, should therefore die worth twenty thousand pounds instead of fifty thousand, could anyone say that he had mistaken his *calling* or left the world as a *loser*?
“If a gentleman had killed fewer foxes or been less frequent at balls, games, and merry meetings because set parts of his time had been given to retirement, meditation, and devotion, could it be thought that when he left the world, he would regret the loss of those hours he had given to the care and improvement of his soul?
“If a tradesman, by aspiring after *Christian perfection* and frequently retiring from his business, should leave his children to live by their own honest labor instead of leaving them fortunes to spend in *luxury* and *idleness*, could it be said that he had made a wrong use of the world because he showed his children that he had more regard for that which is eternal than for that which is so soon to end?
“Since, therefore, devotion is not only the best and most desirable practice in a monastery, but the best and most desirable practice for all people as human beings in every state of life, those who desire to be excused from it because they are men of *importance*, *estates*, and *business* are no wiser than those who would desire to be excused from *health* and *happiness* because they were men of *importance* and *wealth*.
“I cannot see why every gentleman, merchant, or soldier should not put these questions seriously to himself:—*What is the best thing for me to intend and aim for in all my actions? How shall I make the most of human life? What paths shall I wish I had taken when I am leaving the world?*
“Now, to be this wise and to make this much use of our reason seems to be only a *small and necessary piece of wisdom*. For how can we claim to have sense and judgment if we do not dare to seriously consider and govern our lives by what such questions require of us?” To return.

Mr. Law and his companions, Mrs. Hutcheson and Miss Gibbon, were constant in their attendance at church whenever divine service was performed. After the morning service on Wednesdays and Fridays, it was their custom to go out for a ride; Mr. Law and Miss Gibbon were on horseback, and Mrs. Hutcheson—along with the Honorable Misses Hatton, their neighbors (who usually dined with them every other Friday), or any other visitor staying with them—traveled in the carriage. <note>Query: who was the niece of Mrs. Hutcheson who was with her at King’s Cliffe in 1746?</note> Their path on these occasions was around the fields of King’s Cliffe, or rather through certain roads that crossed the fields, as the estate <note>lordship</note> was not then enclosed by hedges as it is now.

Regarding the regular occupations of the ladies, aside from the time dedicated to outward acts of charity among their neighbors or spent in private devotion, it appears they consisted of filling their minds with the *instructions of wisdom and the impressions of eternity* by transcribing daily portions from the writings of ancient ascetic and spiritual divines, as if they were *school exercises or themes*. Many of these manuscripts still exist in Miss Gibbon’s handwriting, comprising selections from Thaulerus <note>Johannes Tauler</note> and other deeply experimental writers of the same class, including copies of some of Lee’s manuscripts, which had probably been given to them for that purpose by Mr. Law. The writer also has a manuscript of Mrs. Hutcheson’s, which is a translation of a tract in the second volume of Madame Guyon’s “Opuscules”—a volume little known to English Christians, but full of suggestive and profitable instruction, especially the pieces in it by Father <note>Père</note> La Combe for the eradication of self-love and the establishment of perfect charity in the soul. This is also from Lee.

Music was, of course, a favorite recreation for a philosopher so familiar with the *ground and powers of nature* as Mr. Law was. On the day of the annual audit of the charities founded by Mrs. Hutcheson and himself, it was their custom to host the trustees for dinner, after which Miss Gibbon played the organ. It was at the Easter audit of 1761 that Mr. Law caught a cold which ended in his death about ten days later, affecting the seat of that *kidney condition* <note>nephritic affection</note> to which he was subject.——The reader who is familiar with his practical writings may remember how, in recommending singing and chanting during private devotion, “*he tries to show that everyone can sing well enough for the purposes of devotion; and though the art or science of running through a range of notes with mathematical precision may not be possessed by all to such a degree as to qualify them for giving delight to others, yet the psalms should certainly be chanted in both private and public worship. This may have given rise to a custom at the church of King’s Cliffe, where several parts of the service are performed in that manner; the rector of the time perhaps conceded the point to his suggestions.*”

The collector of some of the details related here also remarks that some idea may be formed of Mr. Law’s knowledge of languages and style of reading from the collection of books bequeathed by him for the use of his townsmen, which is now in the schoolhouse at King’s Cliffe. Part of his private library, however, we have good reason to know has been dispersed; “indeed,” said a member of the family to the writer of these lines, “around the year 1800 or 1801, boxes upon boxes full of volumes were sold by the extravagant heirs of Miss Gibbon’s property, Mr. William Law

Since no authentic portrait of Mr. Law exists (for it should be mentioned that the one inserted in the unauthorized edition of the *Serious Call*, referred to in the note on page 105, is merely imaginary and, in all probability, as foolish and inconsistent in its claims as the literary preface to that book), we take the opportunity in this account of his domestic life to provide a sketch of his personal appearance, as accurately as can be gathered from the records left behind, aided by our knowledge of his character. <note>If our efforts to obtain possession of his skull should be successful, we might then, perhaps, be able to offer a more accurate and complete description of his appearance; his hardy, frugal, physical training, and classically educated mind, make it probable that nature in him was orderly and true, and that his intellectual and sensory organs, with their qualities, were a manifestation of his natural spirit.</note> In height, Mr. Law was slightly above average; his frame was not fat, but strongly built, and kept in healthy condition by the strict discipline and regularity of his habits. The general shape of his face was round, and he had a direct and pleasing fluency of speech. He had well-proportioned features, which were enhanced by a cheerful, open expression, and probably became more distinct as he grew older—the natural result of his strong judgment and the scholarly seriousness of his youth. His complexion was ruddy; his eyes were gray, clear, and lively, sparkling with noble kindness and with the sharp wit which, as his writings show, was always controlled like a well-trained but spirited horse by his superior wisdom. His general manner was lively and natural, and although his behavior and conversation among his friends were those of a sage, we have the testimony of Mr. Hartley (who was then the rector of Winwick, in a note to his *Defense of the Mystic Writers* at the end of his *Paradise Restored*) that he was used to seeing company and was a man of open conversation. A sister of the famous Wesleys, who saw him once, but whose opinion may have been somewhat influenced by her study of the strict and holy principles of his practical books—as well as by what her brothers might have reported regarding his authoritative speech and seeming gloominess and lack of feeling when they consulted him personally—describes him as the very image of the Law itself for severity and seriousness. But as proof that the idea of this extreme strictness being characteristic of Mr. Law’s usual appearance and manner could not be entirely correct, the writer has a letter by Mr. Thomas Langcake. In it, he remembers often seeing Mr. Law playing with his nephew's children after dinner, tossing them up and down on his foot with great sweetness and simplicity. His noble, affectionate nature can also be seen in his correspondence with his private friends. There is a common report that his mind was so kind and benevolent that he could never look with pleasure on a bird in a cage, but instead longed to set the captive free; and, when he could do so without causing offense, he would open the latch of the cage door to give the little inhabitant a chance to escape. Perhaps the gravity of his looks and behavior was slightly increased by the plainness of his dress, which usually consisted of a clerical hat with the loops turned down, a black coat, and a gray wig. Regarding his behavior, while he was open and free to the humble and sincere, he may have intentionally adopted a rigid manner toward the flattering Moravian and sectarian leaders who, as we find in his letters, occasionally approached him with a great show of respect and humility; he might have thought they had come "to spy out the nakedness of the land."

The presence of Mr. Law undoubtedly helped make the establishment at Hall Yard a blessed place of retreat for the two ladies, whose income was dedicated to acts of charity, and all their time to pious, rational, and useful pursuits. This religious retirement, under the guidance of a wise and spiritual advisor, and this use of their wealth and time—so contrary to the empty customs of the fashionable world—was simply in accordance with the common principles of Christianity, as explained in the earlier chapters of the *Serious Call*. This is not to mention the special providence of God in calling Mr. Law, like another John the Baptist, into the silence of a wilderness, where he might, without distraction, carry out the rest of his unique mission to the world, through the help of the two wealthy and honorable women who were his companions, whose respect he fully repaid through the acts of kindness and religious guidance he provided to them.

For Mr. Law’s relationship with these ladies was not merely that of a spiritual guide; he was also their overseeing guardian and advisor in matters requiring business skills, prudence, and judgment. Among the examples we have of his services in this regard is the following, in which the historian Gibbon is mentioned again.

The elder Gibbon, the historian’s grandfather, was a staunch, orthodox old gentleman in both religion and politics (as may be assumed from his choosing the author of the *Unlawfulness of the Stage Entertainment Demonstrated*, *Christian Perfection*, and *Three Letters to Hoadley* to be the tutor for his only son). He likely had sufficient reason for his dissatisfaction with the social circles his son entered through marriage after a tour of Europe. The historian, in his self-centered autobiography, claims this was the reason his grandfather enriched his two daughters, Catherine and Hester, at the expense of his only son. There is no direct evidence that the historian’s mother came from an irreligious family, but it appears (from original letters now in the writer's possession) that his father was closely acquainted with certain well-known freethinkers or atheists at or soon after her death in 1747, when the historian was about ten years old. It is by no means an unlikely conclusion that these connections were brought about by his marriage, and perhaps both by his tour of the Continent without an advisor or companion, except for his "cousin, Ned Acton." For Gibbon remarks significantly regarding his father and Mr. Law: "The mind of a saint is either above or below the present world; and while the pupil went on his travels, the tutor remained at Putney, the much-honored friend and spiritual director to the whole family." Regardless, we find that the historian’s father married again in 1755 to a relative of the Mallets, who were certainly freethinkers or infidels. He had introduced his niece, Miss Elliston, to them; she was the only child of his sister Catherine, who had married around the years 1733–1734. <note>Mr. Mallet edited the posthumous works of Bolingbroke in 1756 and was undoubtedly well known before then for his interest in that philosophy.</note>

This young lady was the heiress of a very considerable estate and an orphan, her father and only surviving parent having died in 1747—the same year as the historian’s mother. It seems she resided first with a relative at Dew’s Hall and afterwards with her uncle, Mr. Gibbon, at Putney. Through him, she became acquainted with Mr. and Mrs. Mallet, who were people of fashion and apparently well-connected with the aristocracy. Sometime before Mr. Gibbon’s second marriage, around 1754, Miss Elliston left his home without consulting her uncle. Influenced by the people mentioned, she went to live with them, which greatly concerned her pious aunt, Miss Hester Gibbon, when she heard the news at King’s Cliffe. Shortly afterward, while visiting town, Miss Hester took the opportunity to protest to her niece about the impropriety of the connection she had formed. Perhaps she feared that this influence would become permanent—which is exactly what happened the following year when Miss Elliston married Edward Eliot, Esq., who was later created Lord Eliot of Port Eliot. The letters we are about to quote (and others) suggest that the argument on this subject was conducted with considerable harshness and a dictatorial manner by Miss Gibbon, who had also experienced an open break with her brother over the same issue. As a result, Miss Gibbon was allowed to leave town without her niece or any other family member visiting to offer the usual courtesy of a farewell. However, the following letter (the original being before us) immediately followed Miss Gibbon to King’s Cliffe:

> “Putney, June 12, 1755.—Madam—As I allowed you to leave town without wishing you a good journey, I think myself bound to give you some reason for such behavior. I would not have lacked respect for you if you had not first given cause for it by what you chose to say of my *friends*; for such I have always found them, at all times and on all occasions. My ingratitude would therefore be of the blackest kind should I hesitate for a moment, in any place or before any people, to confess the obligations I owe them and to defend their character wherever it was slandered.
>
> “I could not answer the harmful expressions you used toward them, especially toward Mrs. Mallet, to your face as I should have; but now the contradiction will be much stronger, as you will have it in writing. If it were the last sentence I should ever speak, these would be my words: *That the slander was as false as heaven is true*.
>
> “As this may be the last request I ever make of you, I beg you to keep this letter so that if the time ever *should* come—as you predict it will—you may confront me with my own handwriting; but until then, it will be my justification.
>
> “I have been so busy preparing for a long journey that I am going to take, that I have not had time to write to you before.
>
> “As the nature of what was said was too shocking to be repeated to anyone involved, it is almost unnecessary to assure you that the contents of this letter were dictated solely by the real sentiments of—Madam, your obedient humble servant, CATHERINE ELLISTON.”

Upon reading this very spirited letter from the young lady, her aunt was undoubtedly quite annoyed and immediately drafted the following reply, which is certainly not a masterpiece of classical composition. Our motive for preserving it is simply to illustrate Mr. Law’s services by contrasting it with the reply that was actually sent.

> “If Miss Elliston had not lost all sense of duty both to God and man, she would not treat the woman who is her nearest female relative and her only surviving godmother in such a saucy and contemptible manner. This is for no other reason than my acting as appropriately as I could in those roles I hold toward her—and she may remember, if she pleases, that I told her this when we last spoke together. If ever her heart comes to be softened with prayer and turned to God in true humility, she will then be shocked by this letter, which she has earnestly desired me to treasure up, though it must be considered a monument of shame to all sincere, sober-minded Christians who read it. That you may begin the preparation for a happy eternity and be quickly freed from the *bonds* of blasphemy, hypocrisy, and infidelity is the heartfelt prayer of—Your truly affectionate Aunt.”

Before sending this "elegant" outburst, Miss Gibbon submitted it to Mr. Law, who naturally saw that its style and contents would neither bring credit to the writer nor achieve the purpose for which it was sent. He therefore took up his pen and rewrote it for her (immediately, as the manuscript now before us shows) in the following terms. The reader will observe that a remarkable grace of expression and weight of reason is infused into this transformed document, which must have struck the fair—and, as events proved, innocent—Catherine like an electric shock. This happy and powerful style of writing was a major feature of Mr. Law's genius: habits of thinking and speaking justly, and in musical rhythm, with a store of pungent and refreshing wit and irony always ready, were thoroughly formed in his mind. However, it may be questioned whether he would have sharpened the retort so much if it were not for his wish to please his friend Miss Gibbon. The improved version of the letter continues as follows:

> “My dear Niece—For so I must call you and think of you, despite all the steps you have taken, or may take in the future, to alienate my mind from you.
>
> “For neither religion nor nature will allow me to forget or disregard the twofold relationship I bear to you, being your closest blood relative and the only surviving relative who stood as sponsor for you when you were consecrated to God at your baptism. Nor will I ever, by God's grace, say or do anything to you except in accordance with these relationships, and as fits all that goodness which I wish for both myself and you.
>
> “You had no reason to write to me except as your aunt, and therefore to write in a style

Thus far, in illustration of the point in question, with respect to the affairs of Miss Gibbon. But we cannot allow the opportunity to pass without throwing a little further light on the sentiments of her nephew, the historian, as we are enabled to do by some other documents from which the above are taken.

We previously indicated (p. 371-2) our conviction of the change which took place in his opinions after reading the just and noble representations of the nature and design of Christianity contained in the writings of Mr. Law. This occurred when the leisure afforded by the interval between the completion of his great work and the commencement of his autobiography permitted him to review his own position calmly and reflectively. He was then able to judge more dispassionately both of philosophy and religion than he had been able to do while hotly engaged in historical researches, and gazing vacantly at the strange contradiction which everywhere met his eye between the faith and practice of the professed Christian world. That conjecture is completely confirmed by the following two letters to Miss Gibbon, the first of which is from the historian’s friend, Lord Sheffield:—

> "Sheffield-house, 27 Oct. 1786.—Madam—I have delayed the pleasure of writing to you (and it has been with much concern) because I could say nothing satisfactory to you relative to the wreck of last winter. I mentioned in a former letter that the Customs officers had put a padlock on the store where the wrecked wine was placed, and insist that it must remain one year and a day before you can consider it as your property. I was inclined to break the padlock, but I was apprehensive of involving you in a lawsuit with the commissioners of the Customs. I have tried other means to no purpose, but as the year and day will now soon finish, we cannot be delayed much longer. * * *
> 
> "I had the pleasure of hearing of Mr. Gibbon this morning, by a letter from Sir Henry Clinton, which mentions that he had seen him in good health, about a fortnight ago, at Lausanne. You say you wish he would let alone publishing more. He finds his works a very necessary financial resource; but you may be assured that he will publish nothing in future in the least disrespectful to the Christian religion. The continuation of his history may lead him to mention the establishment of the Mohammedan religion, which he may do without offense. Lady Sheffield begs leave to join her best compliments with mine.—I am, Madam, Your most faithful, humble servant—SHEFFIELD."

If any doubt should still linger in the mind of the reader as to the real meaning and reason of the assurance given at the end of the above letter, it will doubtless be removed by the following, written by the historian himself about three years later to the same lady, his aunt. Penned for her private satisfaction, it is perfectly explicit and far removed from suspicion as speaking the real sentiments of his heart. Its contents are as follows:—

> "Sheffield-place, June 30, 1788.—Dear Madam—I was truly disappointed that you could not admit my visit this spring, and still more concerned at the motive of your refusal; yet I was glad to hear of your illness from your own pen: the steadiness of your hand and style gave the most pleasing assurance of your strength; and I most sincerely hope that your recovery will be completed and established by the return of summer. I am now preparing, by a last visit to Lord and Lady Sheffield, for my departure to the continent, and I purpose being at Lausanne before the end of next month. I feel as I ought your kind anxiety at my leaving England, but you will not disapprove of my choosing the place most agreeable to my circumstances and temper, and I need not remind you that all countries are under the care of the same Providence. Your good wishes and advice will not, I trust, be thrown away on a barren soil, and whatever you may have been told of my opinions, I can assure you with truth that I consider religion as the best guide of youth and the best support of old age; that I firmly believe there is less real happiness in the business and pleasures of the world than in the life which you have chosen of devotion and retirement. Lord and Lady Eliot have passed the winter in Cornwall, but I have seen their sons in town. Poor Sir

Stanier Porter is still alive, that is all I can say, but his strength is decaying, and his understanding is quite gone. To return from this digression. A further illustration of Mr. Law's talent as a *man of business*, and his services, might be given from the concerns of Mrs. Hutcheson, but this may be reserved for the proposed larger biography. Other examples from Mr. Law's extensive correspondence, not only during the period under review, but after the publication of the "Spirit of Prayer" and subsequent works, may be noticed in due time in the following pages. What has been related above will suffice to acquaint the reader with the intellectual and religious light which Mr. Law threw around him in domestic life, and the genius, so to speak, with which its ordinary commonplace business was managed under his direction, as well as the amiability, the dignity, and the piety which governed all his intercourse with his friends. We now propose to take a view of him in his more retired and contemplative life; and for that purpose shall go back to the years 1747 and 1748, when, being freed from all outward anxieties, he became permanently settled at King's Cliffe.

<margin>ll/</margin> His study was a recess or little cell, about four feet square, partitioned off from his bedchamber by wainscoting. Looking through the ancient mullion window which lighted this apartment, the eye of its occupant would rest on the cheerful garden belonging to the house, and from there out to a distance on a peaceful rural landscape. The only furniture this recess contained was a chair, a writing table, the *sacred Scriptures*, the complete works of *Behmen* in the original, with the translations of several in English, the manuscript writings of Freher, the papers of Francis Lee, and various other select authors, in print and manuscript, who had minutely examined, one this and another that particular aspect of the foundation of divine and natural truth, which both in its general and relative character was familiar to his comprehensive and exact understanding. In the quiet of this retired closet (which he has just entered), behold now the Christian philosopher: selecting from his little collection, and perusing for a sufficient period of time some soul-stirring devotional fragment, and then solemnly committing himself to God in faithful prayer. Now lifted up in the ardor of vocal adoration and persistent entreaty, and, having received the infusion or baptism of *complete composure*, then prostrating himself, body and soul, in deep silence before the interior central throne of divine revelation; and, according to his high supersensual science—(as philosophically set forth in the third part of the Grammar of Wisdom, and diversely illustrated in the experimental writings of Tauler, Evangelista, Canfield, and other eminent orthodox mystical divines, not omitting to mention Francis Lee;) behold him, we say—presenting the now passive, desireless, resigned mirror-eye of his purified will and intellect to the free, active, joyful, beyond-thought researches of the Spirit of Wisdom and openings of the Divine Life. From these theosophic contemplations he in due time arose to note down his insights, which so far as was necessary he afterwards translated into that "Babel" form of thought and language common to the present state of mankind. As Mr. Law knew God to be both *all truth* and the *knowledge of it*, so he sought for wisdom where and how only it could be found; hence the exercises mentioned above, and hence he so emphatically insists upon Christian regeneration, and its several advanced stages and growths, as the sole gate to true divine science, regarding both intellectual and physical nature. <note>See B's. 3f. Life, iii. 29-33 ; iv. 23,24.</note>

We have stated, on pages 225-227, that Mr. Law obtained the loan of Lee's manuscripts, which remained with him until his death, and not being returned, came into the possession of Miss Gibbon and her successors in the property at King's Cliffe. Since the note referred to was written, these manuscripts have passed into the possession of the writer of these lines, but he regrets to say that the "Life" of Dr. Francis Lee, as mentioned by his daughter (Mrs. Deborah Jemima De La Fontaine) in the preface to the "Dissertations," is not among them; nor does it appear upon inquiry to have been there for the last half-century; which gives reason to fear that it has been either stolen by someone who formerly had access to the documents, or that it had been borrowed and not returned. It is to be hoped that this most interesting and most valuable document, drawn up by Dr. Thomas Haywood, will yet be discovered, for the interests of enlightened evangelical piety, and the benefit and delight of the lovers and seekers of accomplished Christian science. It is no little praise of Lee that he was esteemed by such a perfected, original, and unique theologian as Mr. Law; considering how very few could be admired by him for pure, simple, experimental gospel theology and original researches in divine philosophy; the mass of religious authors (especially of the Protestant school), with few exceptions, being but as it were feeble, stumbling schoolboys in comparison to his sublime, masterful understanding of the scheme, the nature, and the design of "the mystery" of Christianity: which indeed encompasses "all things"—God, nature, creature, and all the possibilities and actualities of the workings of truth and error.

The reader has already had an opportunity to peruse some of the outpourings of this highly gifted soul and brilliant, devout genius, Lee. Beginning with the faithful practice of pure Anglican church piety, as exhibited in her Order of Common Prayer, which he carried to its highest proficiency; and from there ascending, through the gate of a felt regeneration, the mystic ladder of the progressive births and growths of the divine life—(by the use of true and assured means, discovered by him in the mystical spiritual writers, and consisting equally in a daily dying to self, and an actual rising on the wings of persistent faith and prayer, watchfulness and contemplation)—Lee presents a fine example of an ingenious, high cultivation of the spiritual life, having a constant reference to, and virtual experience of, the *process of Christ*: though the unmortified proponents of a merely elementary Christianity vainly imagine that in the more advanced or mystical stages of Christian experience (where the crucifixion of all self is to be carried on by the concentration of the spirit of humility), the patient (yet active) subjects of this state lose sight of Christ as their mediator and high priest before God. This point was particularly referred to by Lee in his letter on "Passive Contemplation," inserted on page 91; the conclusion of which, on account of its relation to the subject of our present observations, we purpose now to present to the reader, and should an opportunity occur, to insert also some further additional illustrations of the author's pious erudition, mental power, and poetic talent. > “——on his throne. By this, he becomes our everlasting priest and king as well as a prophet, to reveal to us the whole will of God, and the length and depth and breadth of his love toward us. He offers up in us pure incense, which contains nothing of human composition; and he commands in us both as the King of Righteousness and also as the Prince of Peace, with an absolute scepter, and without dividing his dominion with anyone. All this is nothing but the natural result of that Passive Contemplation for which I am contending, as you will easily find with a little application; because Christ himself, as he is the union of God and man, is both *the way and the truth* of it.
>
> Moreover, as he is the way and the truth, so also is he the life of pure Contemplation; and the soul that arrives at it may then truly cry out, *It is no longer I that live, but Christ that lives in me.* For the soul in this state does not properly live its own life: it does not reason; but he who is the eternal reason reasons in the soul, or gives himself, and in himself all things to be seen. It does not will; but he who came into the world to do the will of the Father has come into the soul to do his will, and he alone wills there, in such a manner that the will of the Father, of Christ, and of the soul are all three but one will. It does not remember, for all old things have passed away, and it is (for that season) as if redeemed out of the earth and temporal nature; only the spirit of Christ brings to remembrance whatever pleases him. It does not imagine, being lifted out of and above all images by being brought into the possession of the truth itself; but the truth images itself upon the soul, in which all the ideas of the archetypal and angelic worlds are contained and will spring forth. Thus this divine imagination of the truth makes all things new in the soul, as likewise in all nature internal and external, and is the proper medium or instrument of the new creation, and of the new Jerusalem descending out of heaven. It does not perceive, being out of the bodily senses and carried away into a state that is altogether supersensual, which no eye has seen, nor tongue can express; but the body of Christ being the body of his whole church, and no less of every particular member, the soul, after its purification, is taken into the body of Christ, <note>N.B.</note> and in that state it sees and hears the heavenly objects and sounds by a free and passive reception of them into the mind, which becomes the *mind of Christ*. 
> 
> But until souls are purified from the mortal body by the <insert>advanced</insert> prayer of simple abstraction, there can be no such free and pure reception of the divine objects, lights, voices, and tastes; instead, there must still be some impurity and mixture adhering to them, which will remain as long as any activity of their own remains, or so long as they are not perfectly separated from the body of sin in the exercise of Contemplation and così united to the body of righteousness, which is Christ. So that in this is the greatest security; and the life of Contemplation is a most strong fortress, against which none of the gates of hell shall be able to prevail, because it is the very life of Christ in the soul. He who has arrived at the blessed state <note>as Mr. Law, in the profound devotional absorption in which he was lately regarded, for he had these very papers before his eyes, with the demonstrative instructions of Behmen, a synopsis by Freher of the P. Evangelista's “Kingdom of God in the soul,” etc., etc.</note> performs no acts of *his own life*, but is led and acted upon wholly (yet freely) by the divine life in him. He has no reasoning, will, memory, imagination, or sensation which he can call his own; but all is surrendered up, and all proceeds again from a *new spring of life*, which is not his but Christ’s. 
> 
> And in this new life, which can never be perfectly attained without Contemplation, the will of our God is to be done by us on earth as it is done by the angels in heaven, who, though they are continually contemplating his face, are also always ready to be sent forth as ministering spirits from him to execute all his commands. By this means, we also feed upon the hidden manna; we sup with Christ and Christ with us, the door being opened to Him by naked faith, in a total abstraction from the flesh and its senses. So there is an end of iniquity and transgression, and we are cleansed from all sin by the blood of the Lamb to walk with him in white. And then, following him in white, we are made priests with him and intercessors for others, so that they likewise may obtain mercy and be purified from every evil that so easily besets them, being brought into the same state of holy contemplation and called up again into their original inheritance of divine light. Thus we come to live as if translated out of the wilderness of this wicked world and are secured against all temptations, having our citizenship in heaven, where the malice of the evil one (τοῦ πονηροῦ) cannot reach us. The kingdom of God is made manifest in our souls, and his power is revealed, and his glory is spread forth to the complete confusion of the creature; and then that new name is given upon the white stone, by which the name of our Heavenly Father is no less hallowed on the earth than in the heavens. For it is the very name of this our Heavenly Father (whom we can now most truly call so) written and sealed upon us invisibly and visibly. 
> 
> And having once obtained this name <note>N.B. the true scope of the mind of Jesus; he looked no lower than at the high perfection and glory of an original and redeemed birthright</note>, there is nothing which we shall ask in it, either for ourselves or for others, but it shall be perfectly and fully answered. We shall not pray afterwards in vain any single petition of that prayer which Christ has taught us, but shall see the complete fulfillment of it both in ourselves and in all those for whom and with whom we pray. Thus it appears that the life of Contemplation is the life of Christ in the soul, the life of God in man, and the wonderful gate of the Holy Spirit and its powers. It is not only justifiable but praiseworthy to wrestle against the senses, and even against all the imaginations and thoughts of our own hearts, by means of the highest and most perfect abstraction, and to strive for the goal of this life, to believe and pray...

<meta>This page continues the discourse on "Passive Contemplation" by Dr. Francis Lee, defending the practice of silent spiritual waiting against potential criticisms and linking it to both biblical tradition and established mystical writings.</meta>

December 1790, praised this work highly as one of the books he had most enjoyed, although he ingenuously admits that he understood little of the underlying doctrine.

...for it, to withdraw and wait often in the presence of God, and so, by ceasing from all our own operations and all self-will—however apparently good they may seem—to stand still and see what Christ, our life, will do for us and in us as soon as we have thereby given ourselves up to his sole and immediate guidance. And if this is unchristian, I do not know what is Christian; it is the way in which I desire to be found, the truth that I seek, and the life that will not make me ashamed before the face of my righteous Judge. <note>And if this is the highest truth, what is Swedenborgian theology but pure anti-Christian fantasy and delusion, or "madness," as expressed below?</note>

If I have now clarified this point for you, or rather if I have been made an instrument to direct you to Him who alone is able to clarify it, and to clarify it fully, I shall heartily rejoice in *Him*; and you will have cause to say that "Great is the truth." However, I have used only one topic, whereas I could have used many others. Nevertheless, it is the one I consider most significant, as it was also the first that came to my mind; there being nothing more strongly imprinted upon it than this axiom of my blessed Lord, *I am the way, the truth, and the life*; or this dear salutation from his adorable mouth: "I will be your way, your truth, and your life." This is so far from being exhausted by what I have said about it that I do not doubt you will be able to say much more and to draw from it many corollaries that are both delightful and profitable in the Christian race. As for other arguments, it would be quite unnecessary to heap them together if this one is able to withstand the shock; and if this will not, a multitude will not help, or will help but little. I find many arguments in both the Gospels and the Epistles that establish the doctrine for which I have been pleading and serve to remove that major objection of our friend (and with it all other objections too), doing so unanswerably, if I understand them. You will also easily find these for yourself using the key that has been given here. But not only the New Testament, but also the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets will be found, after a proper inquiry, to patronize and recommend to us the state of Silent Abstraction, and to lead us in the noble path of Contemplation, following Enoch, Moses, Elijah, David, and other great worthies. Everything contained under the institution of sacrifices and the entire Levitical Law has a reference to this matter, whether near or more remote. The tabernacle and the temple can never be understood without it; the office of the high priest will still be little better than a riddle, even after all the history we have of his antitype; and the establishment of the Schools of the Prophets would be most absurd and unaccountable. The truth of all is within the veil, and there is no passing there except by the contemplative soul; and none can assist the soul in breaking through the veil—by the deepest denial of her own power and the most profound exercise of Contemplation and silent watchfulness—but Christ alone. Therefore, as Christ is the fulfillment of the Law and of the Prophets, so also is Contemplation the key that leads us into their inner chambers and the mirror in which we may behold all their wonders.

But despite all this, it must be confessed <note>N.B.</note> that the too early pursuit of and striving after this state may be highly dangerous to many souls; for many would be glad to be at the end of the journey before they have perhaps taken two or three fair steps in it. And <note>N.B.</note> souls that come to it unprepared very often overwhelm themselves and make shipwreck of the death of Christ and of the resurrection from the dead, putting themselves outside of his protection because they are not led by his Spirit, but by their own. Therefore, if we have a longing to enter into this most excellent path, we must not fail to pray to the Father assiduously and confidently that he would give us his Holy Spirit to purify us in spirit, soul, and body, so that we may be fit to walk therein. And especially, we ought never to let the word of our Lord slip from our minds: that it is the *pure in heart* who shall contemplate God, and therefore no others can contemplate him. For the blessing concerns both this life and the next, as do the rest of the blessings. We are taught from the mount that purity of heart is necessary to attain the vision of God in this blessed state of the kingdom of heaven upon earth—this silent path of peace and joy inexpressible—and without this *purity*, all Contemplation <note>or visionism</note> that can be claimed, however glittering it may appear to some, is nothing but mere rantism and madness. Therefore, Dear Sir, I do not doubt that you will *seek after holiness*, wait at wisdom's gates, and be obedient to her discipline so that, after a due term of days <note>that is, by unceasing diligence in prayer, watchfulness, mortification, and dying to all self</note>, you may be admitted into her palace and advanced to this state. This state is so very lovely and desirable that every hour (if your heart is struck, as I believe it is) will seem like a year until you can attain it. So it was for the ancient hermits and the holy fathers (whose names those who are most against us regard with such due reverence), who never thought they could do or suffer enough to be made partakers of this heavenly gift. This was very far from being a remnant of Paganism in them, as is claimed, unless the belief in a Deity may be called so too. And supposing that it were so, it would necessarily have reintroduced total Paganism again, since they still represented this state as a state of communion between the Divine Word and the soul, which (under that supposition) must have been nothing other than a state of communion with impure demons and the malicious spirit of darkness, presenting themselves to them in the name of Christ, the heavenly Word. I leave you to consider the consequences, which are too many for me to mention. Thus, these holy men did not retain this as a part of the pagan religion, but only as a true (and precious) remnant of the patriarchal religion which the pagans had transferred and corrupted; they, therefore, restored and brought it back according to the primitive design, and also according to the clearer Light which was now revealed to them in the face of Jesus Christ, manifested in the truth.

There is a book by Benedictus Anglus which, to settle you fully regarding this matter, deserves to be recommended for your reading if you can procure it in either Latin or English. It is titled *De Triplici Voluntate Dei* <note>Of the Triple Will of God</note>; the first two parts of which are called in English *The Rule of Perfection*, and the third *The Bright Star*. <note>Canfield's "Rule of Perfection," already recommended by the writer here, the third part only after the acquisition of the two previous parts.</note> I have found much benefit from it, but the last part in the English version lacks that unity found in the two former ones. The sum of all is contained in the exercise of the *Divine Will*.

Now the activity of a soul that has arrived at this state will not be less, but greater than it was before; it will be more central and deeper, but not so noticeable and outward. For by being made

Since the notes on pages 221–223 and 226–227 were inserted in this work, the writer has discovered among the rest of Lee’s papers (which recently came into his possession) the adjacent portions of their interesting contents. It now appears they originally consisted of three documents drawn up by Lee to accompany a letter (which we also possess) written by him in September 1702 to his "very worthy friend, the Reverend Mr. Stevens of Cane Wood" (Edward Stevens, the author of *Ancient Ascetics* and *Theologia Mystica*). Stevens's opinions on the Philadelphians and Lee's connection with them may be gathered from his letter inserted in the note on page 221. Lee was eager to justify his principles and actions in that relationship to him. The paper headed "Some Questions" (page 221) was marked C when it accompanied the letter, and the one containing the "Case" of his connection with Mrs. Lead and the Philadelphians was marked B. We have not yet discovered the "A" paper, so we cannot present it. Considering the great interest attached to the case of Lee, Mrs. Lead, and the Philadelphian Society, we feel it appropriate to make a further digression from the direct course of our narrative to present the beginning of the document given in the note on page 226 (which starts there with the words "of seventy years old" and ends on the following page), as follows:

> **(B.) The Case [of Scandal]**—"A" [Mrs. Jane Lead], an elderly, devoted matron, having left the world and retired to end her days in a private cell, suddenly finds herself much noticed outside her own country. This occurred because of a book or two written and printed more than ten years earlier, but now sent for the first time into a neighboring land, seemingly by chance, from a merchant to his correspondent and friend there. Consequently, first one book and then another is translated without delay into the languages of two major nations, and they are greedily devoured by many pious souls. Furthermore, testimonials are continually given regarding the good effects produced by reading them. A great inquiry is made after the author. "B" [Mr. Tischer of Rotterdam], the person who translated these into the most widely spoken language, takes the opportunity to write to her. He presses "A" very hard to share a copy of the manuscripts she had with her, having heard that she had written much. "A" is persuaded to grant his request, and thus a correspondence was established between "A" and "B." Many others profess an eager desire for it, including some men of learning. At the same time, "C" [Lee himself], a young man of good education then traveling homeward, meets some of these people at different stages—certainly the first of them not without a very extraordinary hand of Providence, being made to return to the place where he was. Two were Doctors of Medicine [Dr. Scot at Zol and Dr. B. at the Hague], and the third was a merchant [Mr. Finley at Rotterdam], who was notable for both learning and prudence. This was at the very last stage, when "C" was just about to cross the sea to his own country. The merchant, being more specifically acquainted with "C" than the others (who were both total strangers), recommends that upon his return, he should visit "A." He gives him directions on how to find her and is anxious for a transcript of her writings. "C" returns and remembers his commission. He also meets two other people traveling to his country, who were young students of divinity and unfamiliar with the language; part of their goal was to see and speak with "A." These three, meeting together at a friend's house soon after "C's" return, make an appointment to visit "A" at her place of retirement. She received everyone to their satisfaction, with "C" serving as an interpreter for the two strangers. This was followed by other visits, through which "C" managed to see all her writings. These consisted mostly of loose papers, like the Sibylline leaves, written down occasionally for her own private memory and recollection, except for those that had been transcribed by an old friend of hers. From these, "C" collects and publishes a little book (possibly the *Laws of Paradise*); which was immediately translated here for the benefit of foreigners by another of "A's" visitors [Mr. Freher] from a distant country, and was published by "B." While many claimed to be greatly edified by this, some who had previously been satisfied with "A" began to show their dissatisfaction. They judged that this tended mainly toward promoting a monastic or hermit-like faith, which might have very bad consequences and be destructive to society and commerce. Consequently, other suspicions were raised by some anti-Papists, and several arguments were offered as proof that "A's" books were contrary to the spirit of the Reformation and proceeded from mere Popish "enthusiasm." This jealousy might have been somewhat increased by her conversation with "C," who was himself under suspicion for refusing to qualify himself <note>Likely referring to Lee's refusal as a Non-juror to take the required oaths for public or academic office.</note> according to the example of others in the same condition and character as him. Thus, as "A" gained many friends and enemies, "C" also became involved with "A" through the publication of this book. "C" did not know how to desert "A," thinking himself bound in generosity to stand by her to the utmost, as well as in

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Dr. Francis Lee (referred to as "C") and his spiritual relationship with Jane Lead (referred to as "A"), detailing Lee's personal hardships, his role as her secretary during her blindness, and his total surrender to Divine providence.</meta>

Christianity, without some compelling and evident reasons appearing to the contrary. Since these did not appear to him, and this publication had been undertaken not only by him but also at his own suggestion, there was no turning back. At the same time, letters from across the seas, through the mediation of B, came frequently to A; and A still shared them with C. Some of these concerned very significant arising affairs and were from people of prominence in the world: to all of these, A responded and provided satisfaction in resolving several most difficult and weighty cases. But whatever arrived or was sent back always passed through the hands of C; nothing of any kind was hidden from him. Thus, by degrees, a spiritual relationship was unknowingly formed between A and C: A looked upon C as a spiritual son given to her in her old age, and C looked upon A as a spiritual mother. Furthermore, A’s eyesight failed very quickly due to a cataract forming in her eyes, which made her unable to carry on the foreign correspondence that had now begun and was increasing daily. It was no longer possible, by the help of her own eyes and hands alone, to handle the burden that had been laid upon her without her seeking or even thinking of it. While this darkness in A grew, C transcribed the letters of A as long as A had enough light to write a line legibly; when this was no longer possible, A dictated to the pen of C all that she intended to write, either for herself or for others, in which C was very precise.

At the same time, C was wholly disengaged from the world and lost to it. <insert>[“In January 1682, Lee was admitted as a Fellow of St. John’s, Oxford (having entered in 1679); he continued there for about seven years afterward. But upon the Revolution which happened both in Church and State, he was obliged to leave a university life and took the opportunity to travel to foreign parts, returning to England about the end of the year 1694. However, not returning to the college to reside there and qualify himself after being summoned, his fellowship was declared void at the next election. On June 25, 1708, he was admitted into the Royal College of Physicians as a Licentiate by Dr. Edward Brown, the president, who was the son of the famous Sir Thomas Brown.” This is from another of Lee's own manuscripts.]</insert> He had recently experienced some surprising alarms calling him to a spiritual retreat, and certain strong impulses and inclinations drove him to it in a nearly irresistible manner. It had pleased God to remove from him by death, not long before, certain great friends who had a very intimate affection for him, by which he was released so that he might depend solely upon the Divine Majesty. He had met with some very harsh treatment from the spirit of this world and was condemned to lose quite a handsome estate for being unable to prove the sealing of a deed within less than twenty-four hours, when he was over a thousand miles away; and this was decided by the highest court in the nation. He was also at this very time expelled from the college of which he was a member and had been for many years. He could have lived there with much contentment and pleasure, had there not been certain propositions to which he could in no way submit without violating his conscience. By this means, he was not only deprived of a comfortable livelihood that was for life, but also of all those advantages he might gain from an academic retirement, which were dear to him for several reasons. Now, only a small annuity was left to him, which likewise had never yet been paid, though several years of it were due, and payment had been denied despite repeated applications. So, C, being in effect stripped of all he had, was exposed naked to the more immediate care and guardianship of that providence which had always provided for him in many notable extremities and had strangely watched over him even from his infancy. Being in this state, he desired to fulfill the will of God entirely, in whatever might relate to him, and he cast himself completely and blindly upon God's most wise direction in all things, especially in whatever might be of the greatest concern in his future life, frequently repeating these verses to himself:—

> Behold, great God, me in the desert cast! — Behold me on the ocean rudely tossed!
> Do you constrain: — I'll kiss your chain.
> Wherever you will, my Lord, your steps I'll trace: — And unrepining follow you apace.

In the meantime, C carefully observed all that passed, compared one event with another, and examined the claims of A as well as he could, so that he might know what was the true and acceptable will of God. And while C labored to gain an actual and particular knowledge of the determination of Divine providence, so far as it was lawful or possible for him, he found in the life of A, after a strict examination, many things that overruled the guidance of human prudence and determined him to enter upon a life of faith. In this naked faith and total surrender of himself to God, he found a great deal of ease, and God sometimes wonderfully answered him. Yet C was made to encounter manifold temptations and trials; the God of this world took on various shapes both to frighten and allure him. Doubts were frequently and subtly injected into him concerning this state of life; and at the very same time, a most singular offer was laid before him, beyond all that he dared presume to think of <insert>[from a certain lord's daughter]</insert>, to pull him away entirely from the thoughts of such a life of dependence. This continued for quite a while, and it would have been impossible for C not to accept it, had not the grace of God strongly pleaded with him in this manner: *Will you do that which, though lawful in itself, may be the cause of any evil report against religion?* So, C could find no inward ease except in quitting all worldly expectations and in cleaving to God alone in the nakedness of faith, both in temporal and spiritual matters. Now, whereas there was trouble in the world, the peace which A had outside of the world was so pleasing to C that everything distressed him which tended in the least to keep him still in the world. The light of God’s countenance seemed to C to shine peculiarly upon A: her enemies were made to be at peace with her, her friends were multiplied on all sides, her low estate was transformed as if in a dream, and an invisible hand brought in supplies continually—even in abundance—to the great astonishment of C, who could only remember something like it in ancient history. There was nothing but the decay of her sight to afflict her, and this made it inconvenient for her to be alone. A being now upwards <insert>[resumed at p. 226,]</insert> . . . . .
