**Q. I.**—*What conception or idea is to be had of Divine Wisdom to reconcile with it that personal apparition of her in the figure of a human Virgin, who performs several personal transactions, such as instructing, leading, giving laws, etc.?*

**ANSWER.**—However strange this may appear, it is no more than what may be well defended from the best and most authentic authors, if a proper examination is made of them. And, in short, it cannot be unknown how this figurative idea of Divine Wisdom is warrantable from the sacred writers, just as that of human wisdom is in like manner warrantable from secular writers. Not only Solomon in his Proverbs and Mystic Song, along with the Sapiential book called Apocryphal by us—but certainly held in the highest veneration by the Hellenistic school and primitive Christians—and the Visions of Esdras (who seems to be cited even in the gospel itself as a true prophet).

But Christ himself represents Wisdom to us under the very same conception, attributing to her a personal act and giving us an idea of her equivalent to that of a mother, by mentioning her *children*. The disciple who lay in his bosom and best understood his mind is perfectly in agreement with this, being confirmed by what was shown to him in heaven of this nature; he has left the church an account of two such personal apparitions: the one of the heavenly woman impregnated by the Divine seed (Rev. xii) and the other of the Divine bride and mother of Jerusalem, descending from God to pitch her tabernacle on the earth (Rev. xxi). And what need is there after this to mention the apparition of such a female to St. Hermas, an immediate successor of the apostles, at the beginning of his prophetic visitations; and the Laws of Admonitions, with the parables and visions which were afterwards given to him? Or what need is there to show how in succeeding ages some holy and separated souls have been visited by God much in the same manner, though they themselves may not perhaps have understood, or may even have mistaken, such Divine communications and appearances, which are portrayed according to certain eternal schemes in the

Such an investigation as this might be very curious, but there is no necessity for it; there being a higher and greater, and more undisputed authority to justify this way of writing concerning *Wisdom*, if we only have an ear to hear her voice as she speaks in the Scriptures. Since its authority is allowed, what need is there for any other secondary reasons? Or what necessity is there to declare the (deepest) ground for why the whole Church (both Jewish and Gentile) is always represented under the figure of a single female person, and therefore called *Our holy Mother the Church*? Or why great abuses and superstitions have sprung up regarding the mother of our Lord, the blessed Virgin Mary? The titles, both in the Greek and Latin churches, were (at first) truly given to her, but were misunderstood afterward and misapplied; yet there is a respect due to her from all generations, as distinguished from that false devotion which the ignorant zeal of many has prompted them to give. For without entering into such particular inquiries, it is, I suppose, sufficiently evident both from what has been delivered here and elsewhere regarding this point, that the personal appearance of Wisdom in such a figure, and her performing several personal actions, is in no way inconsistent with the sacred writers, but very conformable to their sentiments and modes of expression.

And as for the same representation of Wisdom by secular authors, much also might be said. But there is one instance of this so full, so particular, and so significant, that to add any others after it would be quite redundant: it is that Platonic work of Boethius, which may deservedly be called his philosophical masterpiece. In it, as a perfect Deist, he handles the matter of *Consolation* in five books, without any regard to the principles of Christianity. Human wisdom, or philosophy, is represented here as a grave and majestic matron; she is made to perform the part of a mother or tutor, and is introduced not only in a personal figure, but many personal actions are attributed to her, such as giving counsel and warnings, instructing, confuting, reproving, and the like. The whole work is nothing else but a continual intercourse and communion between her and her disciple. And whether he be considered as expressing the sentiments of either Pagan or Christian theology, the matter will be much the same. For if the former, then we have the sense of the Gentiles according to the light of nature, with universal tradition delivering down this figurative idea of the inward teacher as a female principle, or as a passive form of supersensory light shining into the mind, and a soft, gentle flow from the Divine Being, transforming and even *deifying* the soul, so that the wise man becomes a god *by participation* (see proposition X of the third book). But if the latter, then there is no doubt to be made whether this is a new, recent conception of the heavenly Wisdom, or whether it is an old one, entertained by the Christian church from time immemorial. To say that this is a symbolic representation will achieve very little; for if even that is supposed, we must grant at least that what is represented under it must correspond to that which represents it. And herein lies the key which reveals the true origin of Gentile theology and shows us from where the great and horrible abuse of their secret mysteries sprang. For what more ridiculous absurdity can there be than to make Wisdom a Goddess, generated from Jupiter alone and leaping out of his skull as soon as it was split apart for that purpose, if we understand this *literally*, as the words first sound? But if we look upon the Pallas or the Minerva of the Pagans merely as a symbol of the Divine generation of Wisdom in human souls, and of its original pre-existence in the Divine intellect before its descent and manifestation in nature, then all will be very instructive. But this cannot be easily explained as it should be in a few words; and therefore, passing over it here, I shall only hint in general that the idea of a Divine Virgin existing in God, and proceeding from God by outward manifestation to teach and enlighten souls—by the assistance of the separator of nature (or of a spiritual and vital flame which may break apart the thick, Saturnine density that is in every fallen birth, thereby to make a passage for the Light, as a pure virgin and Divine essence to burst forth and be clothed in a personal figure of glory)—from wherever this was derived, it was really known to the wise Heathens and must necessarily have something more in it than is commonly understood. Human wisdom indeed may be mistaken for the Divine, but this does not alter the case at all, though the consequence of such a mistake is in itself most fatal. So this is sufficient to show that such a figurative idea of wisdom is no strange thing, but is justifiable from sacred and secular writers. This being established, let us then consider what is the true conception of Divine wisdom that corresponds to this figurative idea of a Virgin and to her personal appearance, not only to this enlightened author but to several others also <insert>[faithful practitioners of the GRAMMAR OF WISDOM, see p. 42]</insert>. The conceptions of this are exceedingly various, which causes the greatest confusion for want of attention; I shall endeavor to list the more principal ones, so that a just and adequate conception may be formed from them all.

1.—By Divine Wisdom we may understand the unmanifested Divine intellect, the uncreated and unbegotten light, the bottomless mind of the divine Unity. Thus Wisdom is not distinct from the Father but is both in him and one with him.

2.—By it we may understand the manifested Divine intellect, the originated and begotten light, or light of light, and the bottomless mind of the divine fruitfulness, by which all things are made. Thus the name of Wisdom is attributed to the eternal Word, or Son, and is both in the Son and one with the Son.

3.—By it we may understand the manifestation itself of the intellect, light, and mind of the Deity; or the revelation of both Father and Son to the Spirit (or most central ground) of the soul. And thus it most properly belongs to the Holy Spirit, who is therefore correctly called a Spirit of wisdom and revelation.

4.—By it we may understand the abstract Idea of the whole Divine Being, as manifesting itself through a tri-unity of principle in Father, Son, and Spirit; or as the intellectual conception of the Deity in itself, according to all its essential relations, whether this conception or idea is original and uncommunicated, as in the fountain, or originated and communicated, as in the streams.

5.—By it we may understand this very idea, as passing through and invested by pure and incorruptible Nature: or the total Divine idea embodied, which is by a more outward substantializing of it in the creation. Thus it is the same with what some call the *one element*, and

others, the universal body of the <term>λόγος</term> (Logos). It is also called the heavenly humanity of Christ, the tabernacle of God, and by many other names.

6.—By it, we may understand the image of this embodied idea; or its individuation into a personal form or figure, being clothed with the angelic nature.

7.—By it, we may understand this individual image as descending in its own personal form and representing itself even in a true human Virgin. This virgin is thereby properly made the representative of Wisdom. And this representation may be in one person or more.

Besides these, there are two general conceptions of the Divine Wisdom, either as it existed *before* Nature or as it exists *in* Nature; these correspond to the twofold conception of the Deity—that is, to the Divine *tri-unity* before nature and the Divine *trinity* in nature. According to the first, this holy Principle is fitly represented by an *eye*; and according to the second by a *mirror*. Abundant instances of both, which are by no means insignificant, could be brought from the *Revelation of Revelations* and from most of the other books published by the same author.

Now, if we do not distinguish between these many different conceptions, it is not at all surprising if we fall into great confusion, and either take offense or run into gross abuses. This happens by the mistake of what is, in itself, most true and most honorable to the Divine Being, through the misapplication of this or that idea which we may have adopted. Such an idea, though perfectly true in itself, may not yet contain the whole truth or be perfectly true according to the specific relations to which it is applied. The first conception of Wisdom, for instance, is most clearly and undoubtedly true in itself. But nothing would be more absurd or have more dangerous consequences than if I should therefore deny the second to be true, and oppose the Nicene Fathers who call Christ—just as he is *God of God*—also *Light of Light* or *Wisdom of Wisdom*. And if I should grant the second but not allow the third also, what do I do but contradict the Holy Spirit himself as he speaks in the scriptures? If Wisdom is a spirit and is called the Spirit of Wisdom in both the Old and New Testaments, then he is one with wisdom, just as the Son and Father are one with it. 

Or if I should allow all three but oppose the fourth, what else do I do in effect but deny the Creation, or the first manifestation of the Deity in nature? This cannot be unless the Divine Idea of it is supposed to pre-exist. This one, universal, all-comprehensive Idea is called the <term>Ἔσοπτρον ἀκηλίδωτον</term> (unspotted mirror), or the immaculate virgin mirror of the Divine energy, by the Book of Wisdom, and the <term>Εἰκὼν</term> (Eikon) or the portrait of the omnipotent goodness, chapter 7, verse 26. It is this idea which the Lord possessed within himself in the beginning of his way—which is his progression into Nature—before his works of old; and which was manifested by the eternal Word going forth triumphantly in that same way. This was established both from everlasting—that is, before any manifestation of nature, or in the silent eternity—and from the *beginning of all time*, as a preparation for the said manifestation. It existed before the earth was made, and when there were no *depths*, etc., for the earth was made according to it, as were the depths, etc. It was the <term>matrix</term> of all lives, seeds, and forms in the three kingdoms of nature, and that great <term>Exemplar</term> of the world, infinitely co-extended with the Divine Being. According to it, therefore, both the heavens were prepared and the *abyss* was encompassed at once. Hence, it is described as God's most familiar friend or intimate companion, and as the Divine *delight* and *sport*. For all of this, see Proverbs 8:22–32. 

This conception of Wisdom is no less real than any of the previous three and could be deduced at length from the words of Wisdom's greatest favorite, and from the wise <term>Siracides</term> also, if it were thought necessary. But if we confuse this conception of Divine Wisdom with any of the others, we must expect to be quickly lost in a maze of our own imaginations. And should we stop here and cast away the three remaining ones, the danger will be found no less serious upon an important consideration of the whole. For if there is no embodiment of the Divine idea, then the creation must necessarily have stopped at the very beginning; and nothing creaturely could have been brought forth out of the supreme Fountain of Being except simple and naked spirits. The existence of anything else <term>in rerum natura</term> (in the nature of things) would be an utter impossibility if that supposition were allowed. 

Also, if there is no individuation of the prolific Divine idea when it is embodied, many absurdities must follow, along with consequences highly derogatory to the unity and simplicity of God, as well as to the order of beings; it would even be destructive of the principles of individuation in every creature. Lastly, if this individual Idea of the Divine glory—being thus invested with a Divine corporeity, or an <term>ἀπόρροια</term> (outflowing) of the one heavenly and all-formed substance—may not personally represent itself wherever it chooses, in such vessels of Divine light and grace as are made fit to receive and able to bear it; then the hope of Christ's kingdom must be at an end, and we shall never be made virgins to follow the Lamb. Were this not so, the marriage of him and his bride could never be celebrated, as will appear more clearly when we come to consider the next question. As long as we keep these conceptions of the Divine Wisdom distinct from each other, according to its gradual manifestations and descent into nature, there is little or no significant difficulty. But if we blend these together, there is nothing in the world so preposterous and absurd that would not follow. A thousand instances could easily be given in the first three or four, and perhaps ten times as many in the last.

To form now a general conception of Wisdom out of all these, I consider it as an eternal Divine principle (or most holy energy) of fruitfulness in the Godhead, which exists before, in, and after Nature. By this principle, the Godhead—having first beheld and comprehended everything within itself—afterward images itself forth in everything it so beheld and comprehended. Through it, the Godhead brings forth from eternity its first-begotten image, and from that, innumerable subordinate images from the beginning of time onward, for an eternal spirit of Divine joy and harmony in the creature. This principle, or energy, originally exists in the Father and is one spirit with the Father, being like the *Eye* or intellect to the Spirit of Eternity. By this, the Word is eternally generated as the only begotten Son of the Father, in whom the fullness of his wisdom substantially dwells; and by whom the triumphing light of his intellect is eternally manifested through the virtual powers of the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father by the Son into every created image, addressed according to the capacity of each. Thus, Wisdom is truly to be considered as the *Idea* and

<header>V. *The New Man, Paris, ibid. year IV (1792), 1 vol. in 8º. This is an exhortation rather than a teaching. He wrote it in Strasbourg, in 1790, on the advice of the Chevalier Silverhielm,*</header>

Mirror of the blessed Trinity, as well as of all creatures that originate from it; and as such, it may descend and clothe itself with both a universal and a particular body, and personify its glory in a proper subject. Therefore, it is well worth noting that the origin of Wisdom, or her pre-existent state in God, is expressly distinguished from her nativity, or manifestation in a glorious female figure, by those very writings that have been so heavily censored for introducing a female personality into the nature of the Divine Being. For in the *Manifestation concerning the Eight Worlds*, Wisdom’s eternal origin is clearly declared to be *from the triune Deity, being a Virgin hidden in God from all eternity*; but her nativity, or manifest glory in the form of a female virgin, is not so described; for as to *this*, she was *brought forth in time* (§ 16, p. 31). And this is later explained by an example taken from Adam, who was certainly created in God's image; therefore, just as Eve must have originally pre-existed within him before she could be taken out of him (if the image corresponds to the archetype, or life), so also must it have been in the case concerning the origin and manifestation of this virgin of Divine Wisdom—the one being necessarily before nature, and the other necessarily in nature. Now, concerning her personal appearance in the figure of a human Virgin, there can be no question as to which of these it was; for *outside of nature* there certainly can be no figurative manifestation, nor appearance of any distinct personality. And if it were in nature (as it most certainly was), there can be no real difficulty remaining as to why God might not, if he pleased, present himself in this way; and through such a living embodied idea, transact all that is recorded and *reveal in human nature the mystery of the three-sealed book*, as it was shown in the vision.

Q. II.—*Whether this Divine Wisdom is something other than the Spirit of God which dwells in sanctified souls, and communicates the gifts of the Spirit to them (Isa. 11:2), and produces the fruits of the Spirit in them? (Gal. 5:22).*

ANSWER.—*Divine Wisdom* and the *Spirit of God* are inseparably united: *Wisdom* cannot exist without the Spirit, nor can the Spirit exist without Wisdom. Yet they are not entirely the same, regardless of which previously mentioned sense is used; there is a real distinction between them, despite the union of their essences. Therefore, we ought not to confuse their substance for the sake of this unity, which also exists between God and his angels. For this union of essences is perfectly consistent with the truest distinction: just as the angels of God are united with God in their essence, and are thereby commissioned to go forth in his name, yet are nevertheless truly distinct from him. And so also there is a union of essences and natures between God and man, as in the person of the Lord Jesus Christ; and consequently also in the persons of all his saints, as members of him. But as this union is without confusion of substance both in Christ and in the saints, so it is also in the present case of Wisdom and the Holy Spirit, who are indeed undivided but not the same in the ground of their *being*. For the Holy Spirit, as essentially united with the Wisdom of God, enters into holy souls, making them friends of God by communicating his *gifts* to them and producing his *fruits* in them. Divine Wisdom does not properly and of itself communicate these gifts or produce these fruits, but only infuses her nature into man, as if by irradiation. To this infused nature of wisdom, the gifts of the Spirit are solely communicable, and in it alone are its fruits producible. And as every generation requires (1) the seed and (2) the nature, so too must there be a concurrence of these two in the regeneration of the human soul: the Holy Spirit producing the birth of Love (that is, Christ within) through the nature of Wisdom, as the principle of Divine fertility in everything, without which the seed of God would be as if dead and completely closed up. In this Divine generation of souls, or their new birth, the seed is properly conferred by the Spirit; and the nature into which the seed is received, and by which it is made to bear fruit, proceeds from Wisdom. Thus we are to understand that Christ, according to the flesh, was conceived by the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary (blessed for all generations)—not only because she was an earthly virgin, but because the heavenly Virgin of God’s wisdom had chosen to represent herself outwardly through her (according to the seventh and lowest meaning of this name mentioned in the answer to the first Question), for the purpose of bringing forth again, according to the eternal pattern in the heavens, the highest birth of God in its lowest manifestation, under the covering of a lowly and corruptible nature. Therefore, that Holy One who was born of her was most truly (according to the words of the angel) called *the Son of God*, since in this temporal generation he was conceived both from a Divine seed and a Divine nature—just as he was in that which was called *eternal*. This is true whether by "eternal" we understand his generation in the bosom of *the Father* from all eternity, as manifested to the Father alone, or his generation from the said bosom of his father in eternity, yet at the beginning of time, by which he was brought forth into a figurative image and personality as the firstborn of all creatures, *for the creation of both the angelic and this world*. Now, this bosom of God is no other than the virgin spirit of Wisdom, the holy and eternal principle of Divine fruitfulness, and that *Womb* of eternity alluded to in Psalm 110:3. In that passage, the Hebrew word <term>RECHEM</term>, translated as "womb" (which Jewish writers also call <term>Beth-ha-Rechem</term>, i.e., the house of mercy), is very emphatic and proper; it most vividly sets forth Divine compassion as manifesting itself in Christ. In this regard, it is notable what the most learned Jews write concerning the words of the Law: *Sanctify to me all the firstborn, whatever opens the womb* (Exod. 13:2). They say that all the firstborn belong to <term>Cochmah</term>, that is, the *Wisdom of God*, as being the first emanation from the Divine Being, through which the Supreme Unity (which they call the *Crown*) descends into nature and creature to manifest the heavenly kingdom of the Messiah throughout, by and in all the archetypal numbers and modes of being. Moreover, they say that the name of the *firstborn* is given to the kingdom itself (which is the archetypal number). The reason for this is that the birthright of the kingdom, according to the mystic scale of Divine forms, proceeds *out of the opening of the virgin fountain, or womb, of the Divine Wisdom*; by this, the *Paternal Unity* is manifested in glorious variety and exhibited in all the descending forms as the *only immortal King*. and so proceeds to prove that by the male is meant the Divine Word, which he calls *Tiphereth*, or the fullness of all the Divine emanations and the beautiful image; and that by the female is meant the bride of this divine Word, which is the Church—that is, the body of this fullness and the bright mirror of all the perfections of this image, for which reason she is called the *kingdom*; also the *queen*, and the *king's daughter*; the sister-spouse of the great Solomon, the princess, the heavenly *Sarah*, *Jerusalem*, the *Virgin of Sion*; and by various other names corresponding with these! This *opening*, they say, is made by the Law, in obedience to all its *affirmative* precepts; the number of which they calculate to be exactly the same as the number of the Hebrew word used for the *womb*, which is 248: thereby expressing how it is by the opening of the heavenly matrix in the fallen nature that an influx is received from the Father of Lights. Hence then it appears that, according to their parabolical manner of writing, the right of the firstborn to a priestly kingdom, or a royal priesthood, does consist in the opening of a virgin womb; and that there is also a womb of eternal or incorruptible Virginity in the heavens, from which proceeds a twofold birth, male and female, in the perfect image of God. These are reunited together as one eternally by the highest nuptial tie, the Spirit of God. And thus the bridegroom and bride, or Christ and his Church, are both made to be truly the offspring of God, and to reflect his glory in a similar way by means of heavenly generation; with this only difference: that as Christ is the living portraiture of the *Divine Essence*, which is the more inward and radical notion of the Deity; so is the Church the similitude and representative of the *Divine Nature*, which is somewhat more outward, and acts as the byss <note>abyss or foundation</note>, or ground, of the Spirit of eternity, or Supreme Unity. We should not be carried away here into a more precise or detailed investigation into the understanding of the Jews and the Sages of the Eastern nations regarding the Divine matrimony of heaven and earth, God and Man, than is currently necessary. This understanding is: “That the marriage of Christ and his Church, in the descent of the New Jerusalem on earth, can never be consummated unless there is such an essential relationship pre-existing in Heaven and flowing from the Divine Nature itself; and that the souls who are made his bride cannot otherwise be called *virgins*, except as the heavenly Virgin and embodied idea of the Divine Being in the superior Jerusalem impersonates itself in them, and so becomes to them the true *tabernacle* of God, Revelation 21:3.” For Christ and the Church are but one complete image of GOD: he is indeed the head; but as the head is not completed without the members, neither is Christ complete without the incorporation of the Church, which is truly his body; being flesh of his flesh and bone of his bone, in a sense no less real than that in which it was first spoken concerning the terrestrial Eve, the bride of the terrestrial Adam. Therefore they are not to be considered two, but one. This is the highest ground of the *unity* of the Church, and why it is even called *Christ* (Acts 9:4, 5). 

And great is the mystery of this marriage, which in truth is no more than a reunion of what was previously *one*, just as Adam was one before the formation of Eve, being $\dot{\alpha}\rho\rho\epsilon\nu\acute{o}\theta\eta\lambda\upsilon\varsigma$ <note>androgynous or male-female</note> (as some of the Ancients called him), or a complete Angelic Virgin, both male and female within himself; possessing both the principles of self-multiplication individually concentrated within him in a spiritual and heavenly manner. Now this most essential relationship of two such principles in Adam (which were also distinct from, though united with, the inspiration of the Almighty—that *breath of lives* mentioned in Genesis 2:7), while he stood in the original (and most perfect) constitution of nature as created after the likeness of GOD, does not only suppose: (1) a pre-existent harmony of these principles in the creation according to the highest degree of Unity, which may be called *individual*; (2) a separation or division of them after the creation, or a procession from Unity into a Duality that is proportionate to and concordant with it; and (3) a reunion of the duality, in and through the harmony of the separated principles, by the mystical knot which reconstitutes them as one, as they were at first, though not perfectly in the same manner and degree. But it also supposes something analogous to each of these three to have had a previous existence in the Divine Archetypes; and likewise that the eternal marriage celebrated forever in heaven between GOD and his immaculate consort, WISDOM, cannot make Wisdom fully one with the Holy Spirit, however inseparably she is united with Him. 

Therefore, this essential and most intimate relationship—both of the first Adam to his Eve, and of the second Adam to the second Eve, his heavenly bride—must necessarily flow from the Divine nature itself. Without an embodied Idea of His being having been brought forth from God in the virgin mirror and matrix of the celestial Jerusalem, there would have been no production of either a first or a second Eve; and consequently, the marriage of the Lamb and his bride would never be celebrated. Indeed, what is even more, there could have been no such thing as human generation on the earth. 

But even if both possibilities were granted, the actual celebration of this blessed marriage would not follow unless all who are to make up the bride are first made virgins, and then made *one virgin*. For he who is himself a Virgin will not admit any but virgins into his closest intimacy; hence, all those who follow him in his kingdom of Mount Zion are virgins. From this, the virgins love him because of his name poured forth upon them, by which they are made like him through the oil of consecration with which they are similarly anointed; and so they are impelled to run after him by the fragrance of his good ointments, typified by that sacred and most mysterious composition under the Law which was not to touch man’s flesh (Exodus 30:32). This is why the High Priest was obliged to marry a virgin, and one without the slightest blemish. 

And then secondly, as the bride of Christ can be only one, he says, *My undefiled* (that is, *my virgin*) *is one* (Song of Solomon 6:9); so unless all these virgins, who are the daughters of the heavenly Jerusalem, become *one*, as their mother is one, they cannot be made the bride prepared for her husband, or be one with him who is one with himself and one with the Father. [See <note>Jacob Boehme’s</note> *Incar.* I. xi. xii.] Now it is impossible that they should ever be made virgins in the highest and truest sense of the word without that virginity which was originally in Adam before the formation of Eve being restored again. But (according to what has been previously stated) this can never be restored unless there were a heavenly pre-existent Virginity, according to which Adam was imaged. And it would be even more impossible to have all these numberless virgins re-incorporated, $\dot{\alpha}\nu\alpha\kappa\epsilon\phi\alpha\lambda\alpha\iota\omicron\acute{\upsilon}\sigma\theta\alpha\iota$ <note>recapitulated or gathered together in one</note> (Ephesians 1:10), unless they had all proceeded out of one. If they are not born of the one undefiled womb of the everlasting morning—the pure, embodied Idea and bright mirror of the Divine Triune Being—if they are not generated from above, or regenerated by the *living* virgin water of God’s Wisdom as well as the *fire* of the Spirit (which is the masculine and active power contained by the other in all angelic generations), this holy virginity of the saints and their subsequent reunion and re-incorporation with one another and with Christ, in the express and full sense given by Scripture, would be expected in vain. Our hopes for the kingdom of Christ, along with all the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, would be nothing more than a pleasant fantasy. 

Therefore, it follows that a *virgin spirit* must necessarily descend from God out of heaven as the blessed womb of all heavenly and angelic births, and that this spirit may so make itself present and embody itself in man that man may truly become the *tabernacle* of God for the celebration of the wedding of Christ and his bride. It also clearly appears from this that this spirit, however indissolubly united with the Holy Spirit, is yet really distinct from him. The one is more active, the other more passive: the one provides the angelic fire in the new heavenly generation, while the other provides the angelic water. Nothing more needs to be added to this observation intended for the descent of the New Jerusalem in the kingdom of Christ, among many others that might be made from the preceding Table, which may possibly provide some significant light to some readers. With the twofold birth—male and female—from Divine Wisdom, or the generation of the Messiah and his Church (or kingdom), thus being explained to some extent according to principles acknowledged by the most learned among the Jews, this might be sufficient

Nevertheless, for the fuller explanation of what David spoke in spirit concerning the everlasting womb of the heavenly daybreak, or the Aurora of the angelic kingdom, when he beheld the generation of the Messiah from it and called him *Lord*, even though he was to be his *son*; and also because I do not know that this matter has been fundamentally handled by anyone yet, I shall offer some further thoughts for the consideration of those who are wise in heart regarding this great and holy secret of a Virgin nature, both as it exists in God and flows from God: so that everyone who will only listen may easily understand it, and see how it is distinguished from the essential Word and from the Holy Spirit, as properly understood.<note>See Jacob Boehme’s *Three Tables*, the First Table.</note> Nevertheless, it should still be remembered that, due to their inseparable union, the operations, affections, and roles of one may be attributed to the other; so that what properly belongs to Wisdom may very well be ascribed to the Spirit of God, just as what belongs more properly to the Spirit may be ascribed in the same way to Wisdom, which is like the Divine vehicle and chariot in which he rides triumphantly into Nature. The same thing may also be said of Christ regarding both of these: this is a caution to be carefully noted for the sake of greater clarity when reading most spiritual writers. The considerations follow:— 

Consideration I. The Hebrew word *Rechem*, wherever it is found in Scripture—whether interpreted as the *womb* or as *mercy*—when applied to God, may be said to express not only a principle of paternity but also of maternity existing in the Deity regarding the higher orders of created beings. And wherever the same is used plurally, as it most frequently is in relation to the Divine Being, it may fitly signify the super-excellence of this most holy principle, which cannot be expressed by any singular word; this is also why the most common name for God in this language has a plural ending, as is well known: this primarily denotes the super-excellent Majesty of the omnipotent Creator of all things, without detracting at all from the Unity of the Godhead; just as this signifies the super-excelling glory of Divine kindness toward his creatures, wanting to include them in the unity of life. And by both, we are to understand the communicativeness and fecundity of the Divine nature, without which no creation or generation could exist in any of the worlds, visible or invisible. Now there cannot be a more refreshing and delightful consideration than this, <insert>which is the primary guide to the final series of Mr. Law's writings,</insert> That the very principle of Divine fecundity, by which and out of which all things whatever are produced, is nothing other than the fountain and womb of LOVE; yes, the womb of all tender loves in the creature, and of all mercy both in God and in it; the beginning of the creation of God, from which heaven and earth first sprang forth, the male and female offspring from which countless births were to proceed; the universal and original womb, the *womb of wombs*! It was from this holy womb, eternal fountain, and most essential principle of Divine Mercifulness, that judgment was swallowed up by mercy, as if by one bright sudden glance, even when the terrors of the Law were thundered forth in such astonishing majesty. For it was from this promise, first made to the woman's seed, that it should *destroy the curse in nature*; and from this, not just some, but all generations were to be blessed: thus the curse of the Law for idolatry was to end in only four generations, but the covenant of mercy was to be extended even to a thousand generations. In a thousand, all are included. Therefore, Scripture emphasizes the *eternity* of Divine mercy so much: and God is pleased not only to attribute to himself the heart and affections of a mother, but even to declare the most eminent perfection of this principle in him—both in its intensity and extent—far above anything that can be found in a natural mother; and the impossibility for him to forget or utterly and eternally cast away his offspring: Why the Prophet Habakkuk, in his most lofty psalm, calls on God to remember RECHEM, or the womb of mercy, in the midst of wrath (*ch. iii. 2*). Many passages in both the Law and the Prophets harmonize sweetly with this; but especially in the Psalms, such as xc., cvi., and cvii.; and Lamentations iii. This is why he is said to repent of evil according to the multitude of his mercies. And just as Christ, according to his earthly birth, is said to have been born of the *mercy* of God, as the most tender and maternal principle of Divine life, so are we, according to our heavenly paternity, said to be regenerated from there in the same way; that is, out of the same abyssal womb of Divine Compasions, and through the visitation of that heavenly daybreak, or blessed Aurora, which opens the *light of the world* to those who live in these shades of mortality, brings forth the *everlasting day*, and introduces the firstborn image of the Father of lights among us who sat in darkness—most properly called the *Sun of righteousness*. And here we may also observe that just as the MERCY OF GOD, both in the generation of his Son (whether eternal or temporal) and in the regeneration of all who bear his image and name, chiefly expresses to us the illustrious prototype of all *maternity*; so does the WILL OF GOD in both of these express to us the most illustrious prototype of all *paternity*. Therefore, we cannot receive the power to become sons of God in the *new birth* except by the united manifestation of both as one; by being born of the *will* of God, through which he becomes our father in heaven; and according to his *abundant mercy*, through which he shows us the tender heart of a mother: and his love for the church is compared to that of a mother for her firstborn. All this may be implied in the word RECHEM, according to its true interpretation as it refers to God; this could easily be further explained by a diligent comparison of Scripture. But I must refrain: and I shall only, to conclude this First Consideration, mention one passage, which is very significant, as it declares how the fountain and womb of Divine mercy is opened in the covenant of blessing by separation from the *cursed thing*, and how there must be in God a great prototype and exemplar of all maternity and fecundity. *Nothing of the cursed thing shall cling to your hand* <gloss>whatever tends in any way to separate you from the LORD as your God, and the author and fountain of your being; and to make you idolize the creature by your mind's attachment to it, must be utterly renounced and forsaken by you as the accursed thing which, by clinging to you, will certainly deprive you of the blessing of the covenant made to the woman's seed, and sacramentally ra-</gloss>

*Consideration II.* The most common name of God—which in the history of the creation alone is used no less than thirty-two times—is even asserted by the Jewish writers who have written most learnedly upon it to be of a *feminine* nature; and that the repetition of it so many times in the first chapter of Genesis answers exactly to the thirty-two *Paths of Wisdom*. Hence the ancient book of *Jetrivah*, attributed to the Patriarch Abraham, begins this way: *By the thirty-two wonderful paths of wisdom has the Lord of Hosts framed and shaped his world.* Also in another cabalistic treatise, called the *Gate of Light*, the name of God by which the world was created is interpreted this way, and its feminine signification is expressly declared. And as the womb of eternity out of which all things are produced by God is most hidden, these paths are therefore called by a name which signifies *hidden*; and Wisdom herself is called the most high path of all, which comprehends the rest within it, and to which that passage in Job ought to be referred: *There is a path which no bird knows, and which the vulture's eye has not seen*, ch. 28:7; from which the other thirty-one draw all their influence, in the various modes of the corporification of the Divine idea, by the omnipotence of the eternal Word. Therefore all the works of God's creation are made accordingly to proceed from this secret womb and pure ideal fountain, called the *door of the world*; and are outwardly manifested and wrought out from their invisible forms (agreeably to the doctrine which some deduce from Heb. 11:3), by the opening of this wonderful matrix in nature, according to all those secret channels and ducts of Divine wisdom, which they call PELIOTH, that is, "concealed." &nbsp; * &nbsp; * &nbsp; *

*Consideration III.* The *morning* which is mentioned in the generation of Christ by David is properly that *redness* which is between the darkness and the light, or the night and the day: which should be well noted if we would understand the basis from which not only the creation, but *judgment* also is attributed by the mystical doctors of the Jews to that Divine Name, which is both the first and most frequent in the whole Bible. For though it may seem harsh to them to ascribe judgment and severity to the female nature rather than to the male, they nevertheless have respect here to the gradual manifestation in nature of the firstborn of the creatures; to his triumphant exit against the fallen princes and angels at the creation; and to the restoration of lapsed souls from darkness into light, through the red fire of Divine judgment, from which the glorious light breaks forth, as out of a hidden womb, and with exulting joy springs out visibly to run the course of the wonders of God in love. This morning redness is called the bride-chamber, or the secret CHUPPAH in which the bridegroom was to prepare himself, as mentioned in Psalm 19:5: it is that out of which the Divine Word, like a glorious sun, arises; coming as a bridegroom out of his chamber, and rejoicing like a giant to run his race through the whole circuit of nature. For this answers exactly to the meaning of the word SHAIHAR, which is not the light itself, but the triumphant breaking forth of the light from and out of the darkness: from which, among all the Divine goings forth (which are many), that of victory is peculiarly ascribed to it, as the opposition of the powers of darkness is thereby conquered and subdued. And because this conquest of the day, in outward nature, always begins in the East, the east is therefore held sacred to the eternal daybreak of Wisdom; and the Magi, who are the children of wisdom, are said to come out of the East. And in agreement with this, all the kingdoms of the earth are commanded to sing praises to Him who rides upon the heaven of heavens toward the east, Ps. 68:33; not only according to the Septuagint and St. Jerome, but other ancient versions: by which is described the victorious outgoing of the Divine Word from the paradisiacal East; as might clearly be made to appear from the whole drift of the psalm, as also from that particular name of God used here, which is universally accounted by the Jewish nation as the manifestatrix of the ineffable Name; even as the light of the Son manifests the light of the Father, which is otherwise inaccessible, appearing to the creature as thick

This most high East is called in another psalm the *beginning of heaven*, and in the Mosaical Genesis of the world it seems to be assumed as the BEGINNING not only of heaven, but of earth also—that is, of the universal system of things. And therefore, the name of the EAST may be applied quite appropriately by the prophet Zacharias to the Messiah, as this very WORD incarnating itself by a power from the Divine East; from which also his star was seen to appear in the East. And perhaps this may have been understood by the Syriac interpreter, in whom it is found, *From the east has he sent forth his voice*: which is certainly applicable to the eternal *Word*, that is significantly expressed by the most ancient Chaldean paraphrast on the Pentateuch as both the *Word of God*, and the *Word which is God*. But this *Beginning*, or East from on high (ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψος, in the prophetic song of Zacharias), must be distinct both from the *Word*, which went forth saying, "Let there be," and it was so; and from the *Spirit of Elohim* which moved upon the chaotic matter. Nor is it perfectly the same either with the *Light*, which arose in the east, being clouded under the veil of mortal flesh; or with the *Holy Ghost*, who overshadowed the Virgin for the bringing forth of this *Light of Life* in such a form, in order to the manifestation of the wonders of God’s wisdom and grace. As the *Word and Spirit* are not the same as one another, but distinct: so neither is the *Beginning*, or *Divine day-spring*, the same as either; despite the fact that the former is in it, and the latter is with it eternally and inseparably.

In visible nature there is no difficulty at all in distinguishing the redness of the morning from the full day: and if we cannot make this distinction in invisible nature also, may we not rather suspect a defect in ourselves, than stubbornly proceed to conclude that what we cannot immediately understand does not exist at all? The Hebrew word which has been mentioned, and which is chosen by God’s Spirit to express the generation of Christ from the womb of eternity, as an eternal Priest and King, is no less distinguished in sense from another word, which is translated as the *morning* as well, without the least distinction; but it signifies the perfect light of the day. Therefore, just as the victory of the Divine name is attributed to the former, so the *glory of it*, or the triumphant pomp of Christ’s kingdom, is allotted to the latter, according to the *scale of Divine numbers*. This word is found in the account of the creation throughout; and there may perhaps be more of a *mystery* in it than is ordinarily noticed. Now, just as in *redness* there is a mixture of darkness and light, or of the light hidden and the light manifest, so it is to be supposed also in some sense in the womb of the Divine *Aurora*, the *eternal seminary of light*. And from this mixture it is called the *measure of judgment*: and, according to it, this world is observed to have been created, in the going forth of that Divine Name which is communicable to all the administrators of justice, both angels and men, both supreme and subordinate.

Consideration IV. This *Morning-redness*, which the wise men have watched for in all ages, and sought to understand and behold, so that they might know thereby the *mystery* not only of the creation and generation of all things from a Divine Beginning, and out of a holy *Virgin Materiality* and celestial womb, but also their regeneration from and out of the same; and which is to be considered both as the fountain of mercy, and as the measure of justice in the Deity introducing itself into nature, and is the true heavenly *Day-spring and East* from which all the Divine measures descend; is further represented to us under the name of *Place*. And hence it is that some of the Ancients may have been grossly misunderstood, as if they did really assert the co-eternity of place and matter with God, according to the common conception of those terms. It is true that some philosophers of significant standing, and in no way atheistical, have maintained the pre-existence of both place and matter from all eternity: but their meaning in this was altogether different from what many of their dull followers have thought it to be. *It is manifest that the philosophy of the Ancients was extremely corrupted from that purity in which it was originally delivered by the founders of schools (several of whom were persons of a Divine genius, and highly enlightened with the Spirit of Wisdom from above) through their successors and disciples; sometimes for want of attention or penetration, and perhaps at other times even through maliciousness itself:* as the history of the Atomical Philosophy alone may serve abundantly to demonstrate, together with the origin of the sect of the Sadducees among the Jews, and most of the ancient heresies among the Christians. Nor is it less certain that in this most ancient philosophy, after the fullest and freest inquiry made into it, there must be understood by their "eternal place"—which includes the eternal matter filling it—the very same thing which the Hebrew school means by that Divine Name, by which they used to express the omnipresence of the Deity, even the name HA-MAKOM, *i. e. the Place*. By which holy Name of God they would teach that the world is not properly the *place* of God, but that God rather is the *place* of the world; and that all place is in God, and from God alone, all creatures being circumscribed by the Divine essence and nature; so that He may super-eminently be called the *place*, or universal receptacle of all beings, in which they exist, live, and act. Now this Divine title, or name, is attributed by them to the wisdom of God, which is also called for the same reason BETH HA-OLAM, *or the House of the world*. And it is favored likewise by the very origin of the word, which is from a root that signifies to rise, ascend, stand up, or awake; and from that particular mode of it in which the Hebrew language is so elegant in expressing that which makes or causes a thing to be, with but one word. By this it is insinuated that the Divine Beginning, Day-spring, and East of the heavenly Wisdom, as it is in God before Nature, is the true awakening principle of all generated and created beings; out of which, as their eternal matrix, they have proceeded, in which they actually subsist, and by which they are continually comprehended: and that all intellectual and material creatures do first rise and ascend from this beginning, which is in God and with God from all eternity; and do stand up out of their ideas, being brought forth into real existence. And this may not be very distant from what some, greatly enlightened in the mysteries of God and Nature within the last generation, have called (as I remember) the *field of the great potter*, into which the Holy Ghost, for the creation of all things, is said to descend, going forth from the Father (who is the potter) by and through the eternal Word or Son; according to the Father’s will, manifesting itself in the voice of the Word, which is the out-flown FIAT of the Son. It is not perhaps quite the same, but it is at least included in and depending on it: it is a different consideration of it from the former; and

Therefore, this eternal Place, or field, is originally to be distinguished from the Spirit itself which flows upon it, and consequently also in its operations. It is also called, to the same effect, *Beth Ha-Jotrer*, the house of the potter; in which the furnace is generally attributed to Wisdom alone, but the wheel both to eternal Wisdom and eternal Nature. In this house of the great potter, by means of its holy magical furnace, which is eternally burning, the Spirit of God manifests its omnipotence; but the Spirit is not one with the furnace, but feeds it incessantly. Let him who has wisdom study here to become still more wise, and by descending into this abyssal House, or place, where the immortal fire is kept, consider the origin of all the vessels of nature, according to their various markings; and behold the restoration of the broken vessels by the light of the everlasting morning, arising still brighter and brighter! Furthermore, some have thought this aforementioned notion absolutely necessary to defend and explain the Unity of the blessed Trinity in the Divine Nature, as in one mutual common *Schecina* or dwelling; so that the Divine Wisdom, as the heaven of the glorious Trinity, is the everlasting *Hammakom*—place, or *location*—of both the Father, Son, and Spirit, the house and temple of God in the supernatural East: it is *Domus Sacro-Sancto Trinititatis*, the residence of the most holy Number Three. This may be set forth under several emblems; but the most ordinary seems to be the manner of writing the great name of God, everywhere found in the Jewish writings. Which is this\*; and \* <insert>י ו ו ו</insert> it deserves well to be heeded. For whoever was the first inventor of this manner of expressing the ineffable nature of the Divine Being, it appears more than probable that he must have been acquainted with something above the ordinary understanding, not only of Jews but even of Christians [probably through Moses, from the *Egyptian Colleges*]. But the explanation of this may lead too far.

From these and similar papers, extracts, and notices interspersed throughout this treatise (with equally clear representations that might be offered of the pure cabalistic and other forms of divine science), the reader will now be able to obtain a conception of the gems of theosophical literature which Mr. Law possessed and contemplated in his retirement. Having by his side the sublimest discoveries and—according to the elucidation of the spiritual scope of the patriarchal histories in Boehme's "**MYSTERIUM MAGNUM**"—the most standard and scriptural forms of divine knowledge: all clustering instinctively around the one grand central object of the gospel, the earnest pursuit of regeneration and the perfection of the divine life in the soul.

And here may be recognized the special providence of God with respect to Mr. Law as the future regenerator of Christianity and philosophy. Since this is the practical end of all knowledge and all ministrations, it was the one simple end and design of all his pursuits and instructions to others. Whatever diversity of view regarding Christian truth or deep experimental research into heavenly mysteries he encountered in the course of his studies, they only entered his mind to be restored to their primitive ground and unity of conception, as originally contained in the Holy Scriptures, and to be reproduced accordingly, as occasion required, in the most correct and classic diction. Hence, his writings must ever remain standard guides to gospel erudition and divine wisdom.

In our notices of Lee and elsewhere, we have occasionally alluded to the necessity of discriminating between those writers who belong to the category of true mystical divines and mere visionary pretenders to a knowledge of spiritual and heavenly things. We may now incidentally make a few reflections upon the proofs of which all true mystical religion and philosophy are capable, or the pure standard principles by which all pretensions of this kind must be tested; these may be said to be (along with others that the enlightened future editor of the proposed larger Biography may see fit to provide):

*First*. If the sole aim of the individual laying claim to spirituality, from the commencement to the *end of their course*, is purity, holiness, and perfect Christ-likeness of spirit, temper, and practice.

*Second*. If this aim is *continually* derived from and directed by the dictates of the gospel.

*Third*. If it is founded on a clear conviction of the necessity of an absolute rejection of all natural inclinations, habits, reasonings, pride, ease, and gratifications of the *old Adam*, and an entire death to all the most inward spiritual workings of self, self-love, and self-seeking. And

*Fourth*, In an equally clear understanding of the relations of Christ in and to the engrafted word, abiding in the ground of the soul as an all-sufficient, all-present, all-ready, and all-powerful Savior, regenerator, and sanctifier (1 Cor. 1:30).

*Fifth*. If the practice is simply and really in accordance with such understandings—namely, that of constant and earnest supplication (mostly *a genibus* <note>Latin: on one's knees</note>), with the exercise of unfailing patience, as the one direct royal way to true relief and advancement in spirituality; all according to the plain, undeniable teachings of Christ in the parable of the importunate widow and similar examples. In this may be implied being in communion with some lively, zealous, devout section or society of experimental Christians, so as to partake of their various gifts, and all hearty, well-directed endeavors to promote the universal happiness and salvation of our neighbor and the world.

*Sixth*. If, in this process, the individual has attained to the life and *walk of pure faith*, where every thought and operation of inferior nature is brought into captivity to the obedience of Christ; and the body as well as the spirit is continually surrendered to God, to His sole direction, guidance, and support—where the soul is firmly grounded in the element of perfect peace and love, and the whole man walks by the secret principles of the "strange," "mystical," "unearthly" life of the holy Jesus. To enter this state, closely studying all that the most

<margin>•</margin>Lastly, if the soul—having pursued its path faithfully and without interruption through these simple means of mortification and self-denial, of prayer and patience, and through the probationary exercises and inevitable experiences of the life of *pure faith*, of doing and suffering—has attained to full salvation and restoration to the perfect image of God; in a word, to perfect purity of heart and Divine illumination (Vision or Contemplation). In the course of this, the mind, having explored and possessed itself of all the various treasures of mystical wisdom and knowledge gathered and bequeathed by highly gifted and enlightened souls of all ages and parts of the world, finally limits itself to only two books: namely, the Holy Scriptures and Behmen. These latter writings are a standard interpretation and key to the will and wisdom of the Holy Spirit as contained in the Bible. We say *finally limits itself to two books*, for herein lies its peculiar danger, the rock upon which we may say so many have split. For by reason of the present exigency and state of human nature, however refined by Christianity, orthodox experience has shown that tables of stone or outward signatures or indices of the life of truth are necessary to preserve the imagination, will, and desire—or the life of the soul—in a divine classic order of motion and operation.

Such, then, are the general principles by which the validity of all claims to divine illumination may be tested, especially to an *extraordinary mission* from God. That is, whether the individual's piety be of the ancient cast and character, of burning devotion and holiness; whether he be a man entirely of God's workmanship, without crooked, partial, or selfish idiosyncrasies, but of an original, universal divine spirit and understanding; in whom the highest erudition and gifts of wisdom are manifestly concentrated, yet all crowned with the most solid judgment and pure gospel simplicity, suited indeed to the real vital wants and necessities of mankind and the current age of the world.

Now, how these characteristics are summed up in the person and genius of Mr. Law, the reader will be enabled to form his own conclusion from what has been related concerning his early principles and the subsequent progress of his understanding. Writing to a friend (as already quoted), Mr. Law says, 

> "I have had all that I can have from books; the rest I leave to God." 

And, on another occasion:

> "Next to the Scriptures, my only book is the illuminated Behmen. And him I only follow so far as he helps to open in me that which God has opened in him, concerning the death and the life of the fallen and redeemed man. The whole kingdom of grace and nature was opened in him. And the whole kingdom of grace and nature lies hidden in myself. And therefore in reading him, I am always at home, and kept close to the kingdom of God that is within me."

The subject of regeneration is indeed the essence and goal of all Behmen's writings, however fundamentally he opens up the mysteries of nature and truth. And the student of divine wisdom may here be directed to begin his course by mastering the first eight chapters of "The Book of the Threefold Life," which appear to have been in great favor with Mr. Law. But it is in the "MYSTERIUM MAGNUM," in the history of the patriarchs, that Behmen more particularly portrays, as it were, the holy harmonizing of the Spirit of God on its organism or instrument, the regenerate soul; in the very natural and just, yet wonderful descriptions of the kingdom of Christ, as couched in the exact narratives of the Book of Genesis. <insert>[Query: Is there any particular history of the Antediluvians in the Egyptian Colleges which had been preserved in the ark?]</insert>

And this consideration, by the way, may serve to show us how wonderful a man Moses must have been to write such a book; how full of God, how enlightened his mind, and how pure his heart! Upon which point we find a MS. fragment by Lee, wherein he alludes to Moses in the following terms:

> "The Holy Scripture is a wellspring of life and light. And what St. Paul has said of the essential Word of God may be said also of his written word: namely, that all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God are therein included. The first of the books of Scripture is Genesis; and the author who wrote it is Moses.

If we consider the person of this holy man of God, we shall find nothing in him but what is great and extraordinary. He was educated as the adopted son of a princess, who had a design of rendering him worthy to be king; and he was instructed in all the [deep divine and natural wisdom, and] sciences of the sages of Egypt, whose reputation was then famous among the learned.

If we have regard to antiquity, he was beyond comparison more ancient than all those authors so illustrious in the world who have earned Greece the name of the mother of science and arts. For he lived nearly five hundred years before Homer, eight hundred years before the philosopher Thales, who was the first to treat of Nature; nine hundred years before Pythagoras, and more than eleven hundred years before Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, who were the chiefs and masters of all the wisdom of the Greeks.

If we consider what greatness appears in his writings, and in the whole course of his life, we shall find that without being able to borrow any light from all secular antiquity, or reap any assistance from it—as he flourished before it in the world with great luster—he was at the same time an orator, a poet, a historian, a philosopher, a lawgiver, a divine, a prophet; more than a prophet; more than a sovereign pontiff, for as much as he consecrated the high priest; the minister of God, with whom he dealt as one friend deals with another; the leader of his people; lastly, to say all in a word, the master and arbiter of nature, the interpreter of heaven, the vanquisher of kings, the God of Pharaoh.

All these qualifications, both human and divine, were collected and united in Moses, so that he might possess an authority to which everyone should be obliged to pay the same deference as to that of God himself.

<note>ANNOTATION.—Speaking of the path of *pure faith*, the life of Jesus, and regeneration—the main road to purity of heart and Divine vision or *Contemplation*—we may here take the opportunity (for the encouragement and assurance of those who are prepared to enter upon that path, as well as for the benefit of the ordinary reader) to define the nature of the two guides and lights of human nature, faith and reason, and to set forth their relative distinctions and merits. Through which one may immediately perceive the transcendent superiority in understanding and judgment that the disciple of faith possesses over the mere rationalist, however well-furnished his brain may be with the dead notions and images of worldly scholarship. This may be represented as follows: — X

> “Faith signifies (1.) the principle of receiving and grasping whatever is communicated to the soul by any other being whatsoever; (2.) the act of receiving and grasping what is communicated to the soul by God, which is properly called *faith in God*; (3.) the act of receiving and grasping all that is more immediately communicated to the soul through Christ, purely based on the testimony of his word, which is properly called *faith in Christ*; (4.) the act of receiving and grasping what is communicated to the passive intellect from God, through Christ, *by the Holy Spirit*, based upon the inward sense and experience of his operation.
> 
> In it may be distinguished (1.) the principle of faith which receives the Divine impression of ideas, both simple and compound; (2.) the threefold act of this principle, according to the different manners and degrees of this divine impression on the soul; (3.) the threefold *product* of this threefold act—as from the Father, Word, and Spirit—bearing witness in the soul.
> 
> Reason signifies (1.) the principle of thought in general, both direct and reflective; (2.) the gift of understanding, or speculative wisdom, which is otherwise called *common sense*; (3.) prudence, or *practical wisdom*, which properly concerns human life; (4.) justice and equity; (5.) the cause or ground of a thing; (6.) the Divine Word or Wisdom (<term>λόγος</term>), the second person in the holy Trinity and the universal light of minds; (7.) the active intellect, or the principle of reflective thought in man.
> 
> In it may be distinguished (1.) the reasoning principle or rationality; (2.) the act of this principle or reasoning; (3.) the product of this act, or the *argument*; (4.) the matter of the argument or *ideas*.

Hence we deduce the following Propositions: — (I.) Human reason is not the *image* of God. (II.) *It is not an essential part of the soul.* (III.) *The soul may exist without it.* (IV.) The soul *may be happy without it.* (V.) The soul may be happy *eternally* without it. (VI.) It *may* be doubted whether in the *intermediate state* the soul does *not actually* exist without it. (VII.) It may even be doubted whether reason has any portion at all in the kingdom of heaven. (VIII.) Reason is a *superficial faculty.* (IX.) All the knowledge acquired by reason is merely superficial. (X.) Reason is in itself a dry and sterile power. (XI.) All the knowledge acquired by it is likewise dry and sterile. (XII.) The origin of reason is no higher than *nature*. (XIII.) It is derived from the secondary intellect, or soul of the world, through the operation of the *seven lords and spirits of nature*. (XIV.) The *judgment* of reason cannot extend beyond its origin. (XV.) The *certainty* of reason is not the highest certainty. (XVI.) There is a certainty even in natural things higher than that of reason, and of which reason can in no way judge. (XVII.) The *evidence of faith* is not inferior to that of reason. (XVIII.) The evidence of faith is not only equal, but even superior to that of reason. (XIX.) The *method of faith* is subject to *no* delusion. (XX.) The *method of reason* is subject to an infinity of delusions and errors. (XXI.) The *physical* certainty from reason is subject to error. (XXII.) The *metaphysical* certainty from reason is subject to error. (XXIII.) The *mathematical* certainty itself is not exempt from the possibility of mistake in several cases. (XXIV.) *Moral* certainty from reason is *only very imperfect*; and is mistaken daily in almost an infinity of cases, even by the *sharpest* reasoners. (XXV.) *Divine* certainty greatly transcends all reason. (XXVI.) This divine certainty is *only* attainable by divine faith. (XXVII.) Human reason can be *no adequate cause* of divine faith. (XXVIII.) Human reason cannot be even a *partial cause* of divine faith. (XXIX.) The *more* anyone has of divine faith, the *more* sound is his reason. (XXX.) Reason is capable of being *illuminated* by faith. (XXXI.) Without faith reason is *dark*. (XXXII.) It is *less* of an absurdity to contradict reason than faith.” All of which, indeed, will be even more apparent if we otherwise reflect that faith is to the truly regenerated man of Christ's kingdom what reason is to the natural man of this world. Hence, when the order of things is inverted—when, by a faithful following of the Gospel counsels, the old man is essentially subdued and fading away, and the new man is rising up in his stead—then to that man, in whom this redemption is in actual process, the rule and path of *pure faith* is of the utmost certainty; and just as he is dead to himself and the astral influences of time, and is alive to God and the powers of the divine world, to that extent does the evidence of faith transcend that of reason. The question—as with all others of mystical divinity, however transcendentally treated according to the respective idiosyncrasies of the writers upon it and their theology—simply resolves itself into the original Gospel distinctions of the old and new man, the *fallen rational Adam* and the new divine principle or *quickening Spirit of Christ*, as to which of these is the true light and guide of the life and will of the soul. (See also note, p. 69.)</note>

Mr. Law, in his “Letter on Warburton,” has, in his usual complete perfection of thought and language, so clearly and comprehensively explained this subject, that we may be excused for inserting the essence of his argument on the present occasion, which is as follows: —

> “For faith is nothing other than so much of the nature and spirit of Christ, born and living in us. *I came*, says Christ, *not to do my own will, but the will of him that sent me. My food and drink is to do the will of him that sent me.* This is the whole nature and perfection of faith. And as no one but Christ had the power to say this about himself, so no one can have or live in this faith, except because the divine nature of Christ is truly born and formed in him, and has become the life of his life, and the spirit of his spirit. * * *”

In short, these two—faith and reasoning—have always divided, and will always divide, all mankind, from the beginning to the end of the world, into two sorts of people fully distinct from each other.

The *faithful*, throughout every age, are of the seed of the woman, the children of God, and the heirs of his redemption through Jesus Christ.

The *reasoners* are of the seed of the serpent; they are the heathens of every age, and the true heirs of that confusion which happened to the first builders of the tower of *Babel*.

To live by *faith* is to be truly and fully in a covenant with God; to live by *reasoning* is to be merely and solely in a pact with ourselves, with our own vanity and blindness.

To live by *faith* is to live with God in the spirit and power of prayer, in self-denial, in disregard for the world, in divine love, in heavenly foretastes of the world to come, in humility, in patience, long-suffering, obedience, resignation, and *absolute trust and dependence upon God, with everything temporal and earthly under one's feet.*

To live by *reasoning* is to be a prey of the old serpent, eating dust with him, groveling in the mud of all earthly passions, consumed by pride, embittered by envy, tools and dupes of ourselves, lifted up by false hopes, cast down by vain fears, and slaves to all the good and evil things of this world; one day elated by learned praise, the next dejected by the unlucky loss of it; yet plodding on year after year, defining words and ideas, dissecting doctrines and opinions, making all arguments and all objections appear their best, sifting and refining all notions, conjectures, and criticisms, until death brings the same total end to *all the wonders* of the intellectual structure that a cleaning broom does to the wonders of a spider's web, so skillfully spun at the expense of its own life-force.

This is the unalterable difference between a life of faith and a life of reasoning in the things of God; the former is from God and works with God, and therefore it saves; it makes one whole, and all things are possible to it. The latter is from the serpent and works with the serpent, and therefore vain opinions, false judgments, errors, and delusions are inseparable from it and can only belong to it.

Every scholar, every debater of this world—indeed, every man—has been where *Eve* was and has done what she did when she sought for *wisdom* that *did not* come from God. All the libraries of the world are full proof of the remaining power of that first sinful thirst for it; they are full of a knowledge that does not come from God, and therefore proceeds from that first fountain of cunning that opened her eyes. For as there cannot possibly be any goodness in man except so far as the divine goodness is living and working good in him, so there cannot be any *divine truth or knowledge* in man except so far as God's truth and knowledge *are opened, living, and working in him*, because God alone is all truth and the knowledge of it."

We now conclude this Annotation on the life of pure *faith*, the outward characteristics of which are as varied as the spiritual temperaments and life circumstances of those who practice it, though "peculiarity," "strangeness," and "singularity" must, in some good measure, be attributed to the conduct and behavior of all who travel that narrow way.

---

The profound knowledge the Egyptian *scholars* possessed regarding the powers of nature, and their ability to control and direct them, are clearly evidenced to us by the accounts of Scripture. As this subject is essentially related to the theme of our present work, we shall here present to the reader what Boehme has written upon this point, regarding the dreams of Pharaoh, which could not be interpreted by the magicians he summoned for that purpose.

> "These dreams of Pharaoh (he writes) were presented to him by God; therefore no *magus* or naturalist could interpret them. For the natural *magus* has power only in nature, only in that which nature forms in its working; he cannot comprehend or advise on that which the Word of God models and frames. But a prophet has power to interpret that, for he is a *divine magus*, as Joseph was here.

> With the Egyptians, the magic art and skill were common; but when they were misused for witchcraft, they were eradicated, although they remained among the heathens until the kingdom of Christ, when *Divine Magia* arose. Then *natural magia* was suppressed among the Christians, which in the beginning was good to suppress, for the heathen faith was thereby diminished and extinguished, and the magic images of nature, which they honored as gods, were rooted out of men's hearts.

> But when the *Christian faith* became common, then other *magi* arose—namely, the sects in Christendom—which they set up as gods instead of the images of heathen idols, and they promoted greater *delusions* than the heathens did with their magic idols.

> For the heathens looked upon the foundation of the possibility and working of nature; but these set themselves above the foundation of nature, merely in an historical faith, saying that men ought to *believe* that which they contrive.

> As at this very day nominal Christendom is full of such *magi*, who no longer have any natural understanding of either God or nature among them, but only an *empty babbling* about a supernatural magic foundation. In this, they have set themselves up as idol gods, understanding neither the *divine* nor *natural magia*, so that the world is made completely blind by them. From this, contention and strife in faith and religion have arisen, so that men *talk* much about faith, one pulling this way and another that way, and creating a multitude of *opinions* which are altogether worse than the heathen images, which indeed had their ground and foundation in nature. But these *images* have no foundation either in nature or in the supernatural divine faith; they are dumb idols, and their ministers are *Baal's* ministers.

> And as it was highly necessary and good that *natural magia* should be discontinued among Christians where the faith of Christ was manifest, so (N.B.) now at present it is much more necessary that *natural magia* were again made manifest. This is so that nominal Christendom's idols, which it makes for itself, might be made manifest and *known* through nature; so that man might know the outspoken or expressed formed Word of God in nature, as well as the new regeneration and the fall and perdition. Thereby, the contrived supernatural *idols* might be suppressed, and men might at length learn to understand the *Scriptures* in nature. Since men will not con-

Returning to the previously mentioned proofs or standard principles of stages in evangelical spirituality and divine illumination, we may remark as a result that this actual "entrance into life" and "enjoyment of the *true light*" is founded in the simple laws of nature. It has been more or less realized by truly devout mystics in every age of the world and among every description of Theists—Oriental, Jewish, and Christian (especially the Roman Catholic section)—though it was never *philosophically* understood (since the loss of the original ancient Adamic tradition and antediluvian philosophy of the Egyptian Colleges) until the basis of nature and the gospel covenant was freshly opened, distinctively and universally (as a final reflection of the mirror of divine wisdom), in Behmen. Nor *could* it be experienced in its high and hallowed perfection until the opening and diffusion of the heavenly powers over all flesh on the day of Pentecost. Nor yet can it be experienced by any individual until this process and Pentecostal baptism has had an actual verification in his own spirit.

We might mention Lead as a true member of this kingdom, though through the distorted, parabolic style of religious conception peculiar to the unlearned and devout of those days—and by taking Behmen the wrong way—she, as is evident from her diary, was mainly on the lookout for extraordinary dispensations (in which she was to act a leading part), visions, and revelations. (To these she might also have been encouraged by her similarly inclined "fellow-laborer," Pordage.)
