<margin>History or</margin>
The knowledge and experience of the mystery, in a certain measure and degree, not only existed formerly among the ancient peoples of the East (doubtless passed down to them from Egypt), but may be justly concluded to still be in existence, constituting the essence of their present philosophy and theology. For truth, not error, must be the focus of study for devout minds and enlightened understandings, though its foundations may not be understood by the majority of scholars, but only by the devout and highly-gifted contemplatives among them. Its chief seat, as we have said, in the earliest ages was in ancient Egypt, where it was abused* and gradually merged into a false or profane "magic," resulting from human reason trying to penetrate divine things with an earthly will. Indeed, a spark of it may be perceived glimmering in what we must call the empty rationality and trickery of the phenomena of modern "mesmerism and clairvoyance"; though we also add that valuable results may be anticipated when the power is exercised and the manipulation performed by regenerate intellects and <term>physiciens</term>, in whom the light-world's tincture has regained its native rule. From this ancient wellspring may also have been derived, at first as a pure stream, the modern pretended "science" of freemasonry and other secret doctrines (and ideal moralities that dull reason would put in the place of the Gospel), which have finally discharged themselves into the various sinks of tradition and speculative philosophy. [* Just as several high Christian mysteries have since been in the West—for example, the Virgin Mary substituted for the Virgin Sophia, transubstantiation for the universal heavenly humanity (or one element "spirit and life") of Christ, purgatory for etc. 
<margin>A</margin>
Also as the worship of fire with the Persians and other Orientals, the Mexicans, and ancient Britons, etc. (<term>Brahminical Druids</term>), substituted for that Divine fire or "Father of lights" of the Holy Trinity before the incarnation and completed redemption of Jesus Christ. Also, as the doctrine of the *Metempsychosis*, from rational speculation upon certain secret natural truths—not to be stated openly, though known to the early Brahmins—that the body is in *all worlds* the manifestation of spirit with its qualities, as stated in the note on page 70; along with many others, understandable to the *theosophical critic*. Such a critic will easily detect the basis of the initiation rites and ceremonies, penances, sacrifices, and religious practices of the Hindus (*Maurice, vol. 5*) and of the ancient Eleusinian or theurgic mysteries, as well as the occult scope and process of the enlightened alchemist.

And here we would again advise our modern evangelical propagandists to consider what they are doing in attempting to, so to speak, convert India, Persia, and China to Christianity. The secret of their success must lie in the *manifestation of the truth*, not from popular conventional principles, but from its deep eternal ground, as comprised in the expression of St. Paul: "the mystery of God and the Father, and Christ," and nature, and all things. And in demonstrating their principles, they must also, if necessary, be able to perform the works which those principles will enable them to do if carried out to their proper theosophical development: even to indicate, from an intellectual perception, the good and the evil in all natural things, and their various relations and proportions, with the qualifications needed to harmonize the hostile, disordered properties in bodies; yes, even to heal the sick by a touch, to take up any deadly thing, and to have none of the powers of darkness be able in any way to manifest their nature upon them, but to be instantly transformed into heavenly splendor and health.——

After the above digression and observations relating to Mr. Law's private or mental biography, we now resume our narrative, having thereby prepared the way for the next subject: the further elucidation of his character as the *evangelist and prophet of the last dispensation*. Before proceeding, however, we must be excused for expressing our hope that we shall not have, as a result of our suggestions, a new sect of Muggletonians, Philadelphians, French prophets, and other fanatics, or Swedenborgian visionaries, rising up and, like so many "thieves and robbers," climbing into the sheepfold "some other way," instead of entering by the one door of earnest enlightened devotion (based upon a self-evident knowledge of the principles and working powers of spiritual nature) continued for years. This will probably be the case if mere reasoning and imaginative transcendentalists obtain this book before they are acquainted with Gospel regeneration, according to the practical scale of progress and the cautionary annotations of the "Grammar of Wisdom." However, we ourselves will be no party to such abuse, as we shall endeavor to prevent this work from being distributed indiscriminately, and shall also keep our eye upon any new religious, magical, magnetical, or alchemical pretenders that may hereafter arise, so as to discern if they really spring from it.

We have shown by the foregoing remarks how Mr. Law's understanding became matured for his later works. Outwardly, this happened by his masterly understanding of Behmen, aided by the demonstrations of Freher and the supporting explanations of Lee, and based upon his previous acquaintance with the highest French, Spanish, and Italian masters of experimental mystical science. And inwardly, it happened by his own cultivation of the divine life and the immersion of his spirit in the internal abyss of the divine power and life. The clear views which his understanding (thus enlightened and perfected) had now obtained regarding the grand practical and scientific scope of Christianity still remain to be noticed, so that the reader may duly appreciate the eminence on which he stood—and indeed still stands—distinguished not merely from the common order, but even from the most eminent of Christian divines and philosophers. From this position (having now maintained a *silence of eight years* after laying the groundwork of the "Appeal"), he composed all his *future works*, beginning with the "Spirit of Prayer."

With regard, then, to his comprehensive evangelical views at this period, as well as the general plan into which all his later works may be said to fall, we shall endeavor to make it quite clear by a SERIES OF QUOTATIONS. As to the effects of what we shall thus reveal upon the theology and practice not only of Christendom but of the whole world, we must leave the reader to make his own reflections after he has read the entire statement. His astonishment will perhaps be indescribable (after due meditation on the subject) that Christendom should have remained for this last century so ignorant, in effect, of the important knowledge of such distinctions as are represented here, and which indeed evidently appear to be the truth. I.—(a.) In a conversation which Mr. Law once had with a friend, he remarked that every man has four states of experience to pass through in the course of his Christian process, namely: (1.) that of nature in which he is born; (2.) that under the law; (3.) that under Christ come in the flesh; and (4.) that of the Spirit.

(b.) From Mr. Law's "*Treatise on Christian Regeneration*."——"It may freely be granted that conversion to God is often very *sudden and instantaneous*, unexpectedly raised from a variety of occasions. Thus, one by seeing only a *withered tree*, another by reading the lives and deaths of the *antediluvian fathers*, one by hearing of *heaven*, another of *hell*, one by reading of the *love* or *wrath of God*, another of the *sufferings of Christ*, may find himself, as it were, *melted* into penitence all of a sudden. It may be granted also, that the greatest sinner may in a moment be converted to God, and feel himself wounded to such a degree, as perhaps those never were who have been turning to God all their lives.

But then it is to be observed, that this suddenness of change, or flash of conviction, is by no means of the *essence* of true conversion, and is no more to be demanded in ourselves or others than such a light from heaven as shone around *St. Paul* and cast him to the ground. *Secondly*, that no one is to expect or require that another should receive his conversion or awakening from the *same cause*, or in the same manner as he has done—that is, *that heaven, or hell, or the justice, or love of God, or faith in Christ, either as our light or our atonement*, must necessarily be the *first awakening* of the soul, because it has been so with him. *Thirdly*, that this stroke of conversion is not to be considered as signifying our high state of a new birth in Christ, or a proof that we are suddenly made new creatures, but that we are thus suddenly called and *stirred up* to look after a newness of nature. *Fourthly*, that this sensibility, or manifest feeling of the operations of God upon our souls, which we have experienced in these first awakenings, is not to be expected or desired to go along with us through the course of our purification. *Fifthly*, that REGENERATION, or the renewal of our first birth and state, is something *entirely distinct* from this first sudden conversion or *call* to repentance; that it is not a thing done in an instant, but is a certain *process, a gradual release* from our captivity and disorder, consisting of *several stages and degrees*, both of death and life, which the soul must go through before it can have thoroughly put off the old man.——I will not say that this must necessarily be in the same degree in all, or that there cannot be any exception to this. But this much is true and certain: that Jesus Christ is our *pattern*; that *what he did for us, we are also to do for ourselves*; or, in other words, *we must follow him in the regeneration*.——For what he did, he did both as our *atonement and example*; his process, or course of life, temptations, sufferings, denying his own will, death, and resurrection, were all done and gone through on our account, because the human soul required *such a process of regeneration and redemption*; because only in such a gradual process could all that was lost in Adam be restored to us again. And therefore it is beyond all doubt that *this process is to be looked upon as the established method of our purification*."

(c.) From his "*Collection of Letters*."——"Jesus Christ is the only peace, and rest, and satisfaction of human life. This is absolute and admits of no exception. Miracles and demonstrations, you see, are in vain, until Moses and the prophets are believed.

Now Moses is sin, *made known by the law*, and the prophets are faith and hope in God. And these two things must *have their state and work* in the soul before it can have any benefit from Christ and his miracles. If you would therefore give some check to the growth of suicide and madness, it cannot be by attacking them in themselves, or speaking to the unreasonableness of their particular nature; this is as useless as a miracle to him who hears neither Moses nor the prophets.

II.—From Mr. Law’s “*Spirit of Love*,” being a specific dissertation on legal and evangelical Christianity; in which is seen the difference between a *servant* of God and a *child* of God; between what is called a *good Christian* and a *regenerate believer*; between that goodness which arises from a rational conviction of the mind and a sincere effort to keep the Divine commands in a regular and virtuous life, and that which is the effect of the power and presence of Christ, or the life of God born again and fully revealed in the soul—the defining or proper name of which is the *Spirit of Love*. In short, it is the difference between the *way* and the *end* of religion.

“*Eusebius*. Please, Theophilus, proceed as you wish to expose my faults in the *Spirit of Love*, for I am earnestly desirous of being set right in so important a matter.

Theogenes. Let me first observe to *Eusebius* that I am afraid the matter is much worse with me than it is with him. For though this doctrine seems to have captured all my heart, as it is a doctrine, yet I am continually thrown off by it in practice; I find myself as much under the power of my old temper and passions as I was before I was so full of this doctrine.

Theophilus. You are to know, my friends, that every kind of *virtue* and *goodness* may be brought into us in *two different ways*. They may be taught to us outwardly by men, by *rules* and *precepts*; and they may be inwardly *born in us*, as the genuine birth of our own renewed spirit. In the first way, as we learn them only from men through rules and instructional records, they, at best, only change our outward behavior and leave our heart in its natural state. They only put our passions under a forced restraint, which will occasionally break forth despite the dead letter of precept and doctrine. Now this way of learning and attaining goodness, though thus imperfect, is yet absolutely necessary in the nature of things and must first have its time, place, and work in us; yet it is only for a time, as *the law was a schoolmaster leading to the gospel*. We must first be infants in doctrine, as well as in strength, before we can be men. But of all this outward instruction, whether from good men or the *letter of scripture*, it must be said, as the apostle says of the law, that ‘it makes nothing perfect’; and yet it is highly necessary in order to reach perfection.

The true perfection and profitability of the holy written word of God is fully set forth by St. Paul to Timothy. ‘From a child (he says) you have known the scriptures, which are able to make you wise unto salvation, which is by faith in Christ Jesus.’ Now these scriptures were the law and the prophets, for Timothy had known no other from his youth. And like them, all other scriptures since have no other good or benefit in them except as they lead and direct us to a salvation that is not to be had in themselves, but through faith in Christ Jesus. Their teaching is only to teach us where to seek and to find the *fountain* and source of all *light* and knowledge.

Of the law, says the apostle, ‘it was a schoolmaster to Christ;’ of the prophets, he says the same. ‘You have (says he) a more sure word of prophecy, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a light that shines in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star arises in your hearts.’ The same thing is to be affirmed of the letter of the *New Testament*; it is but our schoolmaster to Christ, a light like that of prophecy, to which we are to pay great attention until Christ, as the dawning of the day or the morning star, arises in our hearts. Nor can the thing possibly be otherwise; no instruction that comes in the form of words can do more for us than sounds and words can do; they can only direct us to something that is better than themselves, which can be the true light, life, spirit, and power of holiness in us.

*Eusebius*. I cannot deny what you say, and yet it seems to me to detract from scripture.

Theophilus. Would you then have me say that the *written word of God* is that Word of God which lives and abides forever; that Word which is the wisdom and power of God; that Word which was with God, which was God, by whom all things were made; that Word of God which was made flesh for the redemption of the world; that Word of God of which we must be born again; that Word which ‘enlightens everyone who comes into the world;’ that Word which in Christ Jesus ‘has become wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification’ in us; would you have me say that all this is to be understood of the *written word of God*? But if this cannot possibly be, then all that I have said is granted—namely, that Jesus alone is that Word of God who can be the light, life, and salvation of fallen man. Or how is it possible to more greatly exalt the letter of scripture than by acknowledging it to be a true, outward verbal guidance to the one only true light and salvation of man?

Suppose you had been a true disciple of *John the Baptist*, whose only office was to prepare the way for Christ; how could you have more honored his office, or declared your fidelity to him, than by going from his teaching to be taught by that Christ to whom he directed you? The Baptist was, indeed, a ‘burning and a shining light,’ and so are the holy scriptures; but ‘he was not that light, but was sent to bear witness of that light. "every man who comes into the world."

What a folly it would be to say that you had undervalued the role and character of *John* the *Baptist*, because he was not allowed to be the light itself, but only a true witness of it and a guide to it? Now, if you can show that the written word in the Bible can have any other, or higher role or power, than such a *ministerial* one as the *baptist* had, I am ready to hear you.

*Eusebius.* There is no possibility of doing that.

*Theophilus.* But if that is not possible to be done, then you have come to the full proof of this point: namely, that there are two ways of attaining knowledge, goodness, virtue, etc.—the one by the ministry of outward, verbal instruction, either by men or books, and the other by an inward birth of divine light, goodness, and virtue in our own renewed spirit; and that the former is only for the sake of the latter, and of *no benefit* to us, except as it carries us farther than itself, to be united in heart and spirit with the light, and word, and Spirit of God. Just as the *baptist* would have been of no benefit to his disciples unless he had been their guide from himself to Christ.

But to come now closer to our subject at hand.

From this twofold light or teaching, there necessarily arises a twofold state of virtue and goodness. For as the teacher or teaching is, so is the state and manner of the goodness that can be gained from it. Every effect must be according to the cause that produces it. If you learn virtue and goodness only from outward means, from men or books, you may be virtuous and good according to *time*, and *place*, and outward forms; you may do works of humility, works of love and benevolence, and use times and forms of prayer; all this virtue and goodness is suitable to this kind of teaching and may very well be gained from it. But the *spirit* of prayer, the *spirit* of love, and the spirit of humility, or of any other virtue, are *only* to be attained by the *operation of the light and spirit of God*, not outwardly teaching, but *inwardly bringing forth a new-born spirit within us*.

And now, let me tell you both, that it is much to be feared that you *still* stand only under this outward teaching; your good works are only done in obedience to such rules, precepts, and doctrines as your *reason* assents to, but are not the fruits of a new-born spirit within you. But until you are thus renewed in the spirit of your minds, your *virtues* are only *taught* practices, and grafted upon a corrupt foundation. Everything you do will be a mixture of good and bad; your humility will lead you to pride, your charity to others will nourish your own self-love, and as your prayers increase, so will the opinion of your own sanctity. Because until the heart is purified to the bottom, and has felt the axe at the root of its evil (which cannot be done by outward instruction), everything that proceeds from it partakes of its impurity and corruption. <note>Here consider the distinction between lecture-teaching and preaching, Unitarianism, Swedenborgianism, and all the other imperfect and heterodox religious schemes, and ancient orthodox gospel Christianity.</note>

Now that *Theogenes* is only under the law, or outward instruction, is too plain from the complaint that he made of himself. For notwithstanding his progress in the <note>mystical</note> doctrine of love, he finds all the passions of his corrupt nature still alive in him, and himself only altered in doctrine and opinion.

The same may well be suspected of you, *Eusebius*, who are so mistaken in the *spirit* of love that you fancy yourself to be wholly possessed of it for no other reason than because you embrace it, as it were, with open arms, and think of nothing but living under its power. Whereas, if the spirit of love was *really born in you* from its own seed, you would account for its birth and power in you in quite another manner than you have done here; you would have known the price that you had paid for it, and how many *deaths* you had *suffered* before the spirit of love came to life in you.

*Eusebius.* But surely, sir, imperfect as our virtues are, I hope we may yet be truly said to be in a state of grace; and if so, we are under something more than mere outward instruction. Besides, you know very well that it is a principle with both of us <note>as with our spiritual friends, the Quakers,</note> to expect all our goodness from the *spirit of God dwelling and working in us*. We live in faith and hope of the divine operation; and therefore I must say that your judgment of us seems to be more severe than just.

*Theophilus.* Dear sir, I judge neither of you, nor have I said one word by way of accusation. So far from it, I love and approve the state you are both in. It is good and happy for *Theogenes* that he feels and confesses that his natural dispositions are not yet subdued by doctrine and precept. It is good and happy for you also that you are so highly delighted with the *doctrine* of love, for by this means each of you has your true preparation for further advancement. And though your states have this difference, yet the same error was common to both of you. You both fancied you had as much of the Spirit of love as you could or ought to have; and therefore *Theogenes* wondered he had no more benefit from it, and you wondered that I should desire to lead you farther into it. And therefore, to deliver you from this error, I have desired this discussion upon the *practical foundation* of the Spirit of love, so that neither of you <note>nor, if you please, your spiritual friends, the Quakers</note> lose the benefit of that good state in which you stand.

*Eusebius.* Please, therefore, proceed as you wish. For we have nothing so much at heart as to have the *truth* and *purity* of this divine love brought forth in us. For as it is the highest perfection that I adore in God, so I can neither wish nor desire anything for myself but to be *totally* governed by it. I could as willingly consent to lose my whole being as to find the power of love lost in my soul. Neither doctrine, nor mystery, nor precept has any delight for me, except as it calls forth the birth, growth, and exercise of that spirit which does all that it does toward God and man under the one law of LOVE. Whatever, therefore, you can say to me, either to increase the power, manifest the defects, or remove the impediments of divine love in my soul, will be heartily welcome to me.

*Theophilus.* I apprehend that you do not yet know what Divine love is in itself, nor what is its nature and power in the soul of man. For Divine love is *perfect peace and joy*; it is a *freedom from all disquiet*; it is all contentment and pure happiness; and it makes everything rejoice in itself. Love

# VIII. Discours en réponse au citoyen Garat, professeur d’entendement humain aux écoles normales, sur l’existence d’un sens moral, et sur la distinction entre les sensations et la connaissance.

...is the *Christ* of God; wherever it comes, it comes as the blessing and happiness of every natural life, as the restorer of every lost perfection, a redeemer from all evil, a fulfiller of all righteousness, and a peace of God, which passes all understanding. Throughout the universe of things, nothing is uneasy, unsatisfied, or restless, except because it is not governed by love, or because its nature has not reached or attained the *full birth of the spirit of love*. For when that is done, every hunger is satisfied, and all complaining, murmuring, accusing, resenting, revenging, and striving are as totally suppressed and overcome as the coldness, thickness, and horror of darkness are suppressed and overcome by the breaking forth of the light. If you ask why the spirit of love cannot be *displeased*, cannot be *disappointed*, cannot complain, accuse, resent, or murmur, it is because Divine love desires nothing but itself; it is its own good; it has all when it has itself, because nothing is good but itself and its own working; for love is God; "and he who dwells in love, dwells in God." Tell me now, *Eusebius*, are you thus blessed in the spirit of love? <note>Have you attained to this degree of regeneration and renewal in the divine light? Is this the *Christianity* you enjoy?</note>

*Eusebius.* Would you have me tell you that I am an angel, and without the infirmities of human flesh and blood?

*Theophilus.* No; but I would have you judge your state of love by these angelic tempers, and not by any fervor or heat that you find in yourself. For exactly as much and as far as you are freed from the *folly of all earthly affections*, from all disquiet, trouble, and complaint about this or that, just so much and so far has the spirit of love come to life in you. For Divine love is a *new life* and *new nature*, and introduces you into a new world; it puts an end to all your former opinions, notions, and tempers; it opens new senses in you and makes you see high to be low, and low to be high; wisdom to be foolishness, and foolishness wisdom; it makes prosperity and adversity, praise and dispraise, equally nothing. "When I was a child (says the apostle), I thought as a child, I spoke as a child, but when I became a man, I put away childish things." While man is under the *power of nature*, governed only by worldly wisdom, his life (however old he may be) is quite *childish*; everything about him only awakens childish thoughts and pursuits in him; all that he sees and hears, all that he desires or fears, likes or dislikes; that which he gets and that which he loses; that which he has and that which he does not have, serve only to carry him from this fiction of evil to that fiction of good, from one vanity of peace to another vanity of trouble! But when Divine love is born in the soul, all childish images of good and evil are done away, and all the *sensibility* of them is lost, as the stars lose their *visibility* when the sun has risen.

*Theogenes.* That this is the true power of the *Spirit of Divine love*, I am fully convinced by my own uneasiness at finding that my natural tempers are not overcome by it. For where else could I have this trouble, except because that little dawning I have of the Spirit of love in me makes just demands to be the one light, breath, and power of my life, and to have all that is within me overcome and governed by it. And therefore I find I must either silence this small voice of newly risen love within me, or have no rest from complaints and self-condemnation until my whole nature is brought into subjection to it.

*Theophilus.* Most rightly judged, *Theogenes*; and now we are fairly brought to the one great practical point on which all our proficiency in the spirit of love entirely depends. Namely, *that all that we are and all that we have from Adam, as fallen, must be given up, absolutely denied and resisted* <note>that is, by a faithful conformity to the Gospel counsels</note>, *if the birth of divine love* <note>the full birth of the Holy Spirit</note> *is to be brought forth in us.* For all that we are by nature is in full contrariety to this Divine love, nor can it be otherwise; a death to itself is its only cure, or rather only that can make it subservient to good. \* \* \* "Neither notions, nor speculations, nor heat, nor fervor, nor rules, nor methods can bring it forth. It is the *child of light*, and cannot possibly have any birth in you, except only and solely from the light of God rising in your own soul, as it rises in heavenly beings. But *the light of God cannot arise or be found in you by any art or contrivance of your own, but only and solely in the way of that faith, prayer, meekness, humility, and patience which waits, trusts, resigns to, and expects all from the inward, living, life-giving operation of the triune God within you; creating, quickening, and reviving in your fallen soul that birth, image, and likeness of the holy Trinity in which the first father of mankind was created.*"

*Theogenes.* You need say no more, *Theophilus*; you have not only removed that difficulty which brought us here, but have, by a variety of things, fixed and confirmed us in a full belief of that great truth elsewhere asserted—namely, "That there is but one salvation for all mankind, and that is the *life of God in the soul.*" And also, "that there is but one *possible* way for man to attain this life of God—not one for a *Jew*, another for a *Christian*, and a third for an oriental *Heathen*. No: God is one, human nature is one, salvation is one, and the way to it is one, and that is the *faith or desire of the soul turned wholly to God.*"

Therefore, dear *Theophilus*, adieu. If we see you no more in this life, you have sufficiently taught us how to seek and find every kind of goodness, blessing, and happiness in *God alone.*

# --- Essai relatif a la question proposée par l'institut : Déterminer l'influence des signes sur la formation des idées, avec l'epigraphe : Nascuntur ideæ fiunt signa, an VII (1799), in-8º.—Le Croco-

...kingdom of heaven. Thus says the apostle, "You are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells within you. Now if a person does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him." Consequently, if one does not belong to him, he can perform no divine service to him. Nor can any worship cease to be carnal, or become divine, except by its being *all* that it is, and doing *all* that it does, through the power and presence of Christ *dwelling in our souls*, helping us by his *Holy Spirit* to cry in truth and reality, "Abba, Father."

The New Testament never calls us to do or offer, nor allows anything to be done or offered to God as a divine service or worship, except what is done in the truth and reality of faith, hope, love, and obedience to God.

But throughout the New Testament, no faith, no hope, and no love is considered true and godly except that faith, hope, etc., which *solely* proceeds from, and is the *fruit* of, the Holy Spirit living, dwelling, and working in our whole heart, soul, and spirit.

This spirituality of the Christian religion is the reason why it was first preached to the world under the name of the *kingdom of God*. This is because under this new dispensation—freed from the veils, shadows, and figures of good things absent or yet to come—*God himself* is manifested, ruling in and over us as an *essential light* of our lives, an *indwelling word* of power, and a *life-giving spirit* within us. He forms us by a *new creation* to become a "chosen generation, a royal priesthood," to "offer spiritual sacrifices to God through a new and living way, which Christ has consecrated for us." The truth and perfection of this state is plainly set forth by the following prayer of Christ: "That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; I in them, and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one, and that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them." 

Now, regarding the truth and certainty of this spiritual kingdom—in which there are only spiritual worshippers *baptized from above* into a union and communion with the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit through the mysterious union of God and man in the one mediator Jesus Christ—regarding the truth, I say, of this spiritual state of Christianity, we have the clearest words of Christ. He expressly declared that the *Jerusalem service*, and consequently every service that *shares its nature*, was to end with the establishment of *his church*.

> "Believe me," he says, "the hour is coming when you shall worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. But the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth; for the Father seeks such people to worship him."

Therefore, it must be certain to the highest degree that Christ cannot, nor could he, establish any other kind of worship or worshippers except those the Father seeks, because he and his Father were one, both in will and work. The reason and necessity for this kind of worship is added by Christ in the following words: "God is a spirit, and those who worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

Therefore, if Christ had not only and solely established this truth of spiritual worship, he would have been merely another Moses. Though he would be a better teacher, he would still only be like a *schoolmaster* pointing to some higher state of religion that was *still lacking* and *had to be revealed* if man *was to be restored* to his true state of life, union, and happiness in and with the Divine nature. For as God is a spirit and our life is spiritual, no religious worship can reach its true perfection or bring us into the possession of our highest good until it raises everything that is spirit and life within us into *union and communion with the spirit and life in God*."

<note>These quotations will have afforded the reader a further glimpse into what we mean by the above-mentioned "distinctions," and how the universal teaching of the churches and the duties enjoined in them—in which the preachers and hearers rest as the *end*—are but *the way to the end*. This end is one degree further and consists in the *new birth* of Gospel Christianity, as explained above. However excellent and sublime such general discourses may be, the people are but *imperfectly taught* Christianity if they are not directed to its ultimate stage—namely, that of *Christ come in the Spirit*—which consists in an entire death to the spirit of the world and to self, and an entire living and breathing in the elements of Christ’s *new kingdom* upon earth. But we continue.</note>

IV.—From the *Gospel of St. John*, the great, chief mystical disciple of a mystical-speaking Master. Throughout all of our Lord’s discourses as related here, it is manifest that to "believe" in him implies, simply and universally, the *total following of him*: walking in the steps of his process and perfect obedience to his counsels and precepts. The result of this should be the enjoyment of "the light of life," "no condemnation," "freedom or liberty indeed"—in short, the *new birth and new creation*. In accordance with this view, understand the implications of *Romans* 10:4–17. But what we especially refer to here is *John* 7:37, 39: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his heart shall flow rivers of living water. <note>Note.</note> But he said this concerning the *Spirit*, which those <note>throughout all ages</note> who believe in him <note>that is, should actually take him for their Lord, King, Priest, Prophet, and everything</note> should receive; for the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified."

V.—(a.) From the "*Address to the Clergy*." "That the Jewish and Christian Church stand today in the same kind of apostasy or fallen state must be manifest to everyone who will not shut his eyes to it. Why are the Jews in a fallen state? It is because they have refused Him who, in his whole process, was the truth, the substance, the life, and the fulfillment of all that was outwardly taught and prescribed in their law and prophets.

But it is not as easy to see that the *whole Christian church* is in a fallen state, and for the same reason: because they have fallen or turned away from that Holy Spirit who was promised and given to be the *one and only* power, life, and fulfillment of all that was *outwardly taught and prescribed by the gospel*. For the coming of the Holy Spirit was the same completeness and fulfillment of the whole gospel as the coming of Christ was the completeness and *fulfillment of the law*. The Jew, therefore, with his Old Testament—not acknowledging Christ in all his process to be the truth, life, and fulfillment of their law—is in the same state of apostasy as the Christian with his New Testament who does not acknowledge the Holy Spirit in all his operations to be *his only light, guide, and governor*. Therefore, where the Holy Spirit is not recognized and received as the *whole power* and life of the gospel state, it is no wonder that Christians have no more gospel virtues than the Jews have patriarchal holiness, or that the same lusts and vices which prosper among the Jews should break forth with as much strength in fallen Christendom. For if the New Testament does not result in the *coming of the Holy Spirit*, with *fullness of power over sin, hell, and the devil*, it is no better a help to heaven than the Old Testament would be without the coming of a Messiah.——Need I now say any more to demonstrate the truth of what I first said was the one thing absolutely essential, and only available for man’s salvation, namely: the Spirit of God brought again to his *first power of life in us*. This was the glory of man’s creation, and this alone can be the glory of his redemption. All besides this that passes for a *time* between God and man, whatever it may be, shows only our fall and distance from God; in its best state, it has only the nature of a good road, which is only good because that which we *need is at the end of it*. While God calls us by various outward dispensations, by earthly things, figurative institutions, etc., it is full proof that we are not yet *in* our true state, or that union with God which *is intended by our redemption*.

God said to Moses, *Put off your shoes, for the place whereon you stand is holy ground*. Now, what God said to Moses is the very same thing that circumcision, the law, sacrifices, and sacraments say to man. They are in themselves nothing else but outward signs of *inward impurity and lost holiness*; they can do no more in themselves than indicate, point toward, and direct us to an *inward life and new birth from above, which is to be sought after*.

But here lies the great mistake, or rather the idolatrous abuse of all God’s outward dispensations. They are taken for the thing itself—for the truth and essence of religion. What the learned Jews did with the outward letter of their law, the same is done by learned *Christians* with the outward letter of the gospel.——Why did the Jewish church so furiously and obstinately cry out against Christ, "Let him be crucified"? It was because their ears, trained only in the literal word, their worldly spirit, and their temple-orthodoxy would not tolerate hearing of an inward Savior. They could not bear to hear of being born again of his Spirit, of eating his flesh and drinking his blood, or of his dwelling in them and they in him. To have their law of ordinances and their temple-pomp *submerged* into such *mystical madness* as this was such enthusiastic jargon to their ears that it forced their sober, rational theology to call Christ "Beelzebub," and his doctrine "blasphemy"—and all for the sake of Moses and *rabbinic orthodoxy*.

Need it now be asked whether the *true Christ of the gospel* is any less blasphemed or less crucified by that Christian theology which rejects an inward Christ—a Savior living and working in the soul as its inward light and life, generating his own nature and spirit in it as its *only redemption*? Is not the theology that rejects all this as "mystical madness" that very same old Jewish wisdom appearing in Christian theology? It is the same wisdom that said of Christ, when he was teaching these very things, *He is mad; why do you listen to him?*
-> * * * <-

If it now be asked where this spiritual blindness comes from—this blindness which from age to age mistakes and defeats all the gracious designs of God toward fallen mankind—look at the origin of the first sin and you will see it all. Had *Eve* desired no knowledge except what came *from God*, Paradise would have remained the home for her and all her offspring. If, after Paradise was lost, *Jews* and Christians had desired no knowledge except what came *from God*, the law and prophets would have kept the Jew close to the first tree of life, and the Christian church would have been a kingdom of God and a communion of saints to this day.

Look where you will through the whole nature of things; no divine wisdom, knowledge, goodness, or deliverance from sin are anywhere to be found for fallen man except in these *two points*: (1.) *A total, entire entrance into the whole process of Christ*; (2.) *A total surrender to, and sole dependence upon, the continual operation of the Holy Spirit, or Christ come again in the spirit*, to be our never-ceasing light, teacher, and guide in all those ways of virtue in *which he himself walked while in the flesh*. Everything besides this, call it by what name you will, is but dead work—a vain labor of the "old man" trying to create himself anew.——And here let it be well observed that the whole of that mystical divinity, to which a *Jewish orthodoxy* is such an enemy today, consists of these two points. For nothing else is meant or taught by it but a total dying to *self* (called the process or cross of Christ) so that a new creature (called Christ in us, or Christ come in the Spirit) may be born in the purity and perfection of the first man’s union with God. Now, if the Christian world forgets or departs from *this one mystical way of salvation*—if anything else is thought of or trusted in except the cross of Christ and the *Spirit of Christ*—then, even though churches, preachers, prayers, and sacraments are everywhere in plenty, nothing better can come of it than a Christian kingdom of *pagan vices, alongside a mere lip-service belief in a holy catholic church and the communion of saints!*”

### VI.—From the “Way to Divine Knowledge.”
The passage indicated here has already been inserted in this book on pages 120-1; the reader is therefore referred there to read it. It will be found to sum up all the preceding QUOTATIONS into a clear view of the distinction between universal piety or Christianity, and that which is declared by the gospel: namely, *a divine life that had been lost by humanity, restored to it again as the effect and fruit of the glorification of the second Adam, Jesus Christ. Also, how the powers of this Divine life are opened upon all human nature, regarding its engrafted divine principle, and are ever ready and instant to act and produce a new creation*. So much so that (to quote the words of Mr. Law) “a root set in the finest soil, in the best climate, and blessed with all that sun, air, and rain can do for it, is not in so sure a way of growing to perfection as every man may be whose *well-instructed* mind and spirit aspires after all that which God is ready and infinitely desirous to give him.” With that passage, therefore, we conclude these QUOTATIONS, having brought forward more than enough to clarify the tone of our remarks at the beginning, and to open the eyes of Christians generally to a subject of such infinite importance to their welfare. **[End of the SERIES OF QUOTATIONS.]**

instructors who had preceded him, such as Cudworth, Barrow, Taylor, Hall, Horneck, South, Bull, Dean Sherlock, P. Browne, and many more, both of our own and other churches. It can hardly be said that any of them dug deeper to plant the tree of a solid and universal Christian piety, or used more moving considerations and encouraging earnestness to induce the willing and diligent cultivation of it, than Mr. Law does in his "**Christian Perfection**" and "**Serious Call**." Yet these works are still on *this side of mystical theology, or the true spiritual life of Christianity.* — For although *writings of this class are admirable in their way—as dissertations on the beauty, obligations, and blessings of holiness, and its conformity to the divine nature; or as instructions in the arts and benefits of devotion; or as containing, in orderly discourses, that wisdom and purity of morals taught by Christ in the flesh—yet, as this must be said to be their goal, and since they do not directly point, as if with a finger, to the new birth of Christ, or his coming again in the Spirit, as the one thing needful, they necessarily stop short of the true scope of the gospel. For this alone is its sum and substance, and without it, the gospel is not truly preached.*

Such, however, was the character of the doctrine proposed in Christian churches and religious publications up to Mr. Law's day (and we may add, it is even still so), often with the recommendation of a long, impractical course of self-discipline as the means of attaining a settled state of holiness and the fulfillment of the evangelical law. — For instance, at the close of a sermon by the pious Archbishop Tillotson, we find him making the following observation: — "**All that now remains is to reflect upon what has been said, and to urge you and myself to act accordingly. For everything is nothing if we do not practice what we so plainly see to be our duty.... I foresee (he continues) what will be said (because I have heard it so often said in similar cases), namely: That there is not one word of Jesus Christ in all of this. [To which I reply] no more is there in the text. And yet [N.B.] I hope that Jesus Christ is truly preached whenever his will and laws, and the duties enjoined by the Christian religion, are urged upon us!!**"

So little did this pious and learned Archbishop (and his contemporaries, as we have said) comprehend the true nature and aim of the "preaching of Christ," or Gospel Christianity; of which, nevertheless, they were the authorized public ministers. And as for the high prerogatives and experimental privileges of the restored divine life and powers, they were only regarded as the dreams of "enthusiasts" or "mystic idiots," and of course were never alluded to as either desirable or possible to attain. — Or let it be allowed that some few pastors and teachers have intellectually as well as experimentally understood the nature of the gospel state, in distinction to that of eternal and immutable morality and piety with the express sanction of heaven; yet they have not *exactly defined the nature and relations of each in a precise and rational system of theology, nor turned them into a simple practical science adapted to all mankind.* They have failed to do this by not referring, in short, their hearers or readers to the mystical process of Christ as the example of that course of spiritual operation which every soul that is to be saved must essentially undergo. And much less have they opened the way and exhibited its respective orderly steps, leading to the heights and depths and lengths and breadths of the love, the wisdom, and the power of God. — We do not say, indeed, that theologians have been absolutely to blame for this lack of precise discrimination regarding the system of Christianity, because without the revelations of Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme</note> (whose writings, we have said, are the opening of the mystery of wisdom, and as such the gospel of these last days), it would not be possible to fathom the subject philosophically.

Yet as this is the most valuable science in the world, we do maintain the transcendent dignity of Mr. Law as a doctor of the ministration of the *Spirit*. He alone, among all the learned theologians and philosophers of these recent ages, was sensible of the Babel-like state of Christendom and demonstrated the means of restoring it to its lost purity and perfection: (namely, by the preaching of the new birth, and the process of Christ as the way to it—not only on gospel authority for the masses, but by explaining its grounds and reasons for the learned and intellectual); this constitutes the sum of his later works now under consideration. Although we may add, in these Mr. Law does not—nor indeed, as a logical writer, could he—lay as much stress upon the circumstantial modes of the birth itself, as that was expressly done, once and for all, in its proper place and order in his works. Instead, he teaches the soul how to grow up in God without hindrance, using all spiritual aids, like a sprouting acorn growing into a powerful oak tree. Nor will his regularly-educated pupils be subject to the same sudden surprises as those souls are who, being ignorant of the science of Christianity, are suddenly called to be the experimental subjects of it. For these students are taught the truth of their relations, what to expect, and how to overcome and remain steadfast in all cases of trial and temptation, amid all the adverse action of the winds and torrents attending their growth and progress—namely, by a manly, enlightened faith, a sure immovable hope, an unlimited patience, and an absolute resignation, in accordance with the assurances and promises of the gospel.

We once more, before proceeding further, request the reader to *bear in mind these "distinctions" between the law of Christianity and its true spiritual character.* Many indeed will pretend to understand these distinctions even in their vast practical comprehensiveness, and will perhaps designate the contents of this statement as simple elementary knowledge. Be it so; but who, we ask, has described them philosophically, from their foundation? Even the truly spiritual among the Methodists—for want of this exact apprehension—could never describe in a rational, demonstrative manner the ground of their own experience and the true original difference between the evangelical and the (so to speak) scholastic doctrine, regarding the practice and enjoyment, or theory of Christianity. And as to the Quakers—though, by the way, true Methodism, when judiciously and efficiently worked out to its proper limit of social and personal development, will elevate the soul in spirituality and divine communion much beyond any means which the doctrine and discipline of the "Friends" can afford (and the pure practical and mystical theology of the "Roman Church" even higher still)—as to this body of religionists, we say, because they lay so much stress upon the Holy Spirit's influences, they will be found to be practically and almost universally subject to two grand errors. First, in considering the ordinary conscience as the true evangelical light; and secondly, in fixing the minds of their people almost exclusively upon this abstract truism: that all spiritual life must come from the inspiration of the Holy Ghost. By this, a deadly indolence of soul is induced; the individuals naturally conclude that it is of no use attempting to do anything toward

To proceed. We have observed that Mr. Law maintained a wise silence for eight years—which, as he was to be the personification of a standard educated mind *passing through Christianity*, was doubtless so regulated by Divine wisdom. We have also remarked that his works were, individually and collectively, the transcripts of his own experience; this is said to have been the substance of Miss Gibbon's reply when she was requested to write Mr. Law's life. <insert>)</insert> Until the year 1732, he had preached the gospel of the law, or the *duties and obligations* of wisdom and devotion; but now, after the intervening growth of his mind (as shown by his *Sacrament Book, Regeneration Tract*, and his *Replies to Trap*), it had become his high privilege and duty to preach the *gospel of the Spirit* in all its nakedness and fullness. He does indeed speak of the new birth and the influences of the Holy Spirit in exalted terms in the aforementioned works; and in his specific treatise on *Regeneration*, as quoted in the note on page 375, he clearly exhibits the *orthodox* mode of our proper entrance into the spiritual life. Yet, in those works, he must be said to have reflected more particularly upon the truth of the doctrine of the old and new man, and of that sublime holiness which the Gospel sets before us, than upon the *means and power* by which alone the practice of the latter could be freely and universally fulfilled. This contemplation necessarily precedes the high Johannine experience of the *Spirit of love*—the special subject of these, his last writings.

As regards the particular occasion that called him forth from this silence to write the "*Spirit of Prayer*," we consider it to have been his reading of certain passages in the manuscripts of Freher. While copying the productions of that elevated genius, the discovery of the philosophy that God is pure LOVE, and that his wisdom and power are only operative in overcoming all evil with good, suddenly broke forth like the full blaze of midday sunshine upon his enraptured understanding. Turn back as far as the text on page 418 and read through to page 430; the reader will then begin to perceive the gradual ascent of Law’s mind until, at page 432, he finds himself positioned at that ethereal height from which Saint John (as we have previously stated in reference to Mr. Law, page 369) wrote his Epistles, where truly faith is lost in sight. So we owe the existence of Mr. Law's *Spirit of Prayer* and subsequent works (as we have said of his grand work, the "*Appeal*"), under Divine Providence, to his readings in Freher. Anyone copying the passages referred to will, if in a proper state of advancement, feel compelled to write in a similar strain. Such is the irresistible effect of Law's reasoning and of the heavenly melody that runs through the doctrine of LOVE in this and all his later works.

treatises—we mean upon impartial and unbiased minds, endowed with sufficient *logical capacity* for understanding; that it is not a far-fetched idea to imagine his readers rising up in their study, in the middle of a discourse, and exclaiming, “These are the first books in the world!” This is in accordance with what has been observed—that pure, original truth, when rightly represented, is much more captivating and agreeable to the mind than error; and that there is an intellectual sense latent in the soul which, having been present at the very creation of all things, even at the very birth and Aurora of eternity, or nature, immediately recognizes the objects of its native landscape, and its kindred relations of pure, original truth.

The “First Part” of the “Spirit of Prayer,” which may be called the practical deduction of the “Appeal,” (which every logical mind ought, after adequate reflection, to make for itself, in which case the former work alone would have been sufficient for the meditation and practice of a whole lifetime,) was, as we have stated, published in 1749. It is described on its title page as: “**The Spirit of Prayer; or the Soul rising out of the Vanity of Time, into the Riches of Eternity.**” It consists of two chapters, which treat of the following subjects:—

CHAPTER I.—The indifference and insensibility of men in general to their eternal interests. The original state of man as the son of God, and therefore a living image of the Triune Deity. His trial and fall. The commencement of his redemption. His real nature and state because of sin. How it differs from that of the fallen angels. The means of his salvation, or recovery of the life, or light and Holy Spirit of God. The new birth is not a figurative expression, but a real, living process. The whole chapter is a familiar discourse on matters preparatory to the *Spirit of Prayer*. CHAPTER II.—In what salvation or the regenerate life consists. The manifestation of the nature, life, and spirit of Jesus Christ in the new inward man. The means of attaining such a state lie in faith, or the right direction and earnest action of the desire. How the ground or *principium*, which is the engrafted word or incorruptible seed of Christ, lies latent in every soul. Its opening or manifestation is the only way of salvation. The tokens by which the regenerate spirit discovers itself. All depends on obedience or adherence to it. The infallible truths by which we may be assured that our dependence is well-founded. The abandonment of *self*, and the true nature and worth of self-denial and mortification. No activity of our own is of any avail to salvation. The only way is the desire of the soul turned toward God.

All sectarianism is, of course, extinguished in this work, which makes the whole universe of nature and grace understandable, under one governing idea and plan, as an edifice of pure love. This in itself is an argument for the truth of the philosophy that it opens up, because truth itself is unsectarian, unlimited, and universal in its embrace—not confined to Christendom, but comprehending all the human race “in the outstretched arms of its catholic love.” As the actual application of such a philosophy to the highest interests of man, the “First Part” of the “Spirit of Prayer” may be considered a universal practical grammar, or introduction to gospel Christianity. This was necessary to be presented as a text, or preliminary to what was to follow:—Mr. Law’s calling being now to preach the gospel to the educated, who, not having fathomed the philosophy of the *Nosce te ipsum*, and being indeed entirely ignorant of their own nature and condition, are unbelievers in the truth of that redemption into which they are born, and which only requires the assent of their own wills to become their salvation. Accordingly, it does not argue based on the presumed corruption of human nature, as is common with all books of a popular religious tendency, but shows the actual ground of its existence in the fall of a whole hierarchy of angels and the creation of this world.—For which reason, by the way, it may be considered as especially addressed to such as deny the existence of pure malignity, and consequently the necessity of any such redemption and salvation as that of the Christian religion. <margin>certain</margin> To this class, not to mention ~~Q. Fournier, along with other~~ imaginative, deep-searching reasoners and speculative propounders of social theories, belongs a small number of self-confident and deluded, though otherwise intelligent and educated individuals. (The writer has been informed that these individuals consider themselves a body of some importance, as the representatives of what they call modern philosophy; that is, they hold deistical opinions on the assumption that supposed revelations have been exactly parallel and equal in all ages to the growth of the mind.) To all such, it is only necessary to say that the light of pure truth now shines with midday radiance—through the fundamental philosophy of Behmen and the demonstrations of it by Freher and Law, displaying the entire constitution and relations of the moral universe. Through this, they may discover the world of fantasy (and therefore of error) in which they dwell, and obtain every information for the resolution of those points which they have been vainly endeavoring to determine by their own helpless, groping reason. After this intimation, therefore, they will have no title to be listened to by any enlightened philosopher until they have examined these authors (commencing with the latter portion of Mr. Law’s “Demonstration, etc. relating to the Sacrament,” 8vo., 1737), but their writings must only be regarded as another form of the riff-raff, ephemeral literature of the age.

By this, in fact, the human spirit is stirred and affected to its profoundest root and depth—like the deep subsoil in farming when turned up and exposed to the vivifying influence of the sun and elements. Before moving on from the "**First Part**" of the "**Spirit of Prayer**," we should mention that it was taken to America and published there by Benjamin Franklin. This is proven by a copy which was in the hands of the writer in 1846, being one of the standard old English tracts that Franklin's common-sense mind immediately recognized as immortal. We mentioned this previously when showing the direct connection of the "*Appeal*" with the modern science of electricity.

The pure simplicity and heavenly clarity of Mr. Law's mind and understanding in Divine matters at this particular time may be inferred from the following spiritual letters, addressed to one who had sought his advice and direction. The first was written around the time the *First Part* of the "**Spirit of Prayer**" was published, and the second shortly afterward.

The first of these letters, with some modifications, has already been included in this treatise on pages 104-105, ending with the words, "thy Holy Spirit"; the reader is referred to that section. The writer now regrets that the originals were not always exactly copied.

The second letter began as follows:—"My dear, worthy friend—whom I heartily love in the unity of the spirit of Christ. I received your long letter sometime last month and read it with much pleasure. For as long as it was, I did not wish it to be shorter. I bless God for that good and right spirit which breathed through every part of it. Since it required no immediate answer and you left the timing to me, I did not intend to write until last week, but I have been hindered by unexpected affairs from fulfilling my intention until now.

> Your judgment failed you in nothing except in thinking your letter could be disagreeable to me, or that my reply was delayed for that reason. I love every creature, but people of your spirit inspire in me every holy affection of honor and esteem. Love, with its fruits of meekness, patience, and humility, is all that I wish for myself and every human being. For this is what it means to live in God, united to Him both for time and eternity.
> 
> Would you be done with error, doubt, and delusion? Consider the Deity (as I have said) to be the greatest love, the greatest meekness, the greatest sweetness—the eternal, unchangeable Will to be a good and a blessing to every creature. All the misery, darkness, and death of fallen angels and fallen men consists in their having lost this Divine nature. Consider yourself, and all the fallen world, as having nothing to seek or wish for, except to draw into the life of your soul—through the *spirit of prayer*—rays and sparks of this divine, meek, loving, and tender nature of God. Consider the holy Jesus as the gift of God to your soul, to begin and finish the birth of God and heaven within you, despite every inward or outward enemy. These three infallible truths, if heartily embraced and made the nourishment of your soul, shorten and secure the way to heaven and leave no room for error, doubt, or delusion. The poverty of our fallen nature, the depraved workings of flesh and blood, and the corrupt temperaments of our polluted birth in this world do us no harm as long as the *spirit of prayer* works against them and longs for the primary birth of the light and spirit of heaven.
> 
> *All our natural evil ceases to be our own evil as soon as our will-spirit turns away from it. It then changes its nature, loses all its poison and death, and only becomes our holy cross, upon which we happily die from self and this world into the kingdom of heaven.*
> 
> I congratulate you greatly on your manner of prayer. Practiced this way, it becomes the life of the soul and the true food of eternity. Keep in this state of devotion to God, and then you will certainly find it to be the way of *rising out of the vanity of time into the riches of eternity.*
> 
> Do not expect or look for the same degrees of emotional fervor. The matter does not lie there. Nature will have its share, but its ups and downs are to be overlooked. While your *will-spirit* is good and set right, the changes of physical fervor do not lessen your union with God. It is the *abyss of the heart*—an unfathomable depth of eternity within us, as much above emotional fervor as heaven is above earth—that works our way to God and unites us with heaven. This *abyss of the heart* is the divine nature and power within us, which never calls upon God in vain; whether helped or deserted by bodily fervor, it penetrates through all outward nature as easily and effectively as our thoughts can leave our bodies and reach into the regions of eternity. I am, with sincere prayers to God for you, your truly affectionate friend and servant—W. LAW."

Among the many correspondents at this time who sought his spiritual counsel was also a Mr. George Ward, who afterward (along with the Mr. Langcake to whom the above letters were addressed) became Law's confidential and friendly agent in London for the correction and supervision of the printing of some of his publications. Ward was also the editor of the incomplete edition of Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme</note>, published in four large volumes after Mr. Law's death at the sole expense of Mrs. Hutcheson, with Mr. Law's name included on the title page. The edition of Behmen that Mr. Law intended to publish would have been an original translation, while this one was only the old (and, on the whole, very excellent) one reprinted, with changes according to the preference of Mr. Ward, who also added a few plates to each volume copied from the designs of Freher found among Mr. Law's papers. A standard edition of Behmen (as well as Freher and Law) is still required; it should be edited not by a speculative bookseller’s employee but, as previously suggested, by a properly trained and enlightened theosopher—the kind this treatise seeks to create. Indeed, we hope to be the instrument for giving this to the world, or it may be an appropriate output of a *Theosophic College or Society*. *But to return.*

We find that Mr. Law had resolved to publish the "**Spirit of Prayer**" in two parts, with a certain interval between them. In this time, he might observe the reception of the *First Part* and be guided by it regarding the structure and contents of the remainder, or those portions of it which may be considered as merely secondary to its main design.

In glancing over the vast field of the subject before him, as he considered how to begin work again, he perceived with his usual wisdom that one of the evils and vanities that would accompany the opening of the philosophy of religion for some of the individuals he was addressing would be the excitement of a *spirit of curiosity* rather than of regret and self-improvement. As he observed to a friend, he had met very few people whose awaken-

This "Second Part" of the "Spirit of Prayer" was published in the year 1750 and was composed by Mr. Law in the form of *Three Dialogues*, as he considered that mode of presentation best suited to showcase his subject. The *dramatis personæ* introduced therein, including the author himself, are four in number. The first, *Academicus*, is represented as a man of learning and talents, thoroughly versed in scholastic metaphysics and theology, but like our modern divines (with few exceptions), wholly unaware of the real nature, depth, and necessity of the *new birth*, which he regards as a figurative expression; he prides himself upon his choice collection of the works of the Church Fathers and other spiritual authors. *Rusticus*, another speaker, is a simple, uneducated English farmer of the old school, possessed of a vigorous understanding and strong natural sense. Having been deeply affected by the solemn and awakening truths set forth with such unprecedented clarity in the "First Part," he had put everything into immediate practice and reaped the benefits of such a common-sense approach. Before meeting with Mr. Law’s book, he had not had even the remotest conception of the possibility of this experimental knowledge of the gospel, even though he was a regular attendant at his parish church. This was because Christianity had never been presented to him in its true natural light, but only as seen through the perspective of the ordinary university or self-styled evangelical theology. *Humanus*, a third participant, who is introduced as a *silent listener* to the conversations and agrees to remain so until the end, may be regarded as a personification of that large class of sober-thinking, honest unbelievers best known in this country as deists, but which includes every class of well-educated free-thinkers. In short, he is a fair representation of *humanity* in the best state possible without the gospel; he is not altogether unfavorable to the claims of Revelation, but because he has no knowledge of its real grounds and implications, he lacks that rational conviction of its divine origin and understanding of its true nature. Such understanding is almost the indispensable condition for a man of judgment and sincerity who is an unbeliever to begin the evangelical life. The candidate should keep in mind the scope of his character. Lastly, *Theophilus* may be regarded as the representative of Mr. Law in the character of a true theosopher, or heaven-illumined sage. His task is to reveal the universal scheme of God's revelations in all its scope and implications, and to place the gospel in its true light. He does this by demonstrating that God's procedure in nature and grace is the same, and that the highest conformity to Christian truths is strictly in accord with the unchangeable laws of the physical and intellectual universe.

The contents of the SECOND PART, or, more strictly, the subjects demonstrated by *Theophilus* in the course of these conversations, are as follows:

FIRST DIALOGUE.—Introduction on the vanity of knowledge without religion. Spiritual books are only useful as calls to the absolute renunciation of self and the beginning of the new life. The nature of *self* is described, and the necessity of its complete offering or death is demonstrated. The actual grounds of this necessity lie in the nature of things, and not in the arbitrary provisions of God’s providence. How the will of the creature stands between God and nature as the only opener of all good and evil. Its turning to God in absolute faith and earnestness of desire is the means of bringing heaven into the soul. The accordance of these doctrines with Scripture. There is only one death and only one life in all nature. A defense of the "Appeal."

SECOND DIALOGUE.—The philosophy of the Gospel doctrine of redemption and salvation continued. How Adam existed in his state of perfection. The gradual fall and the division of Adam into male and female. The means of human recovery through the covenant of "the seed of the woman." The argument for the renunciation of self and the world is resumed on the rational ground of this philosophy. In what consists the great apostasy, the sin of all sins, and the heresy of all heresies. Hours and forms of prayer considered.

THIRD DIALOGUE.—The difficulty attending the total conversion of the heart to God. The whole nature must be parted with, yet man has no possibility of doing it himself. The omnipotence of the love of God, and how it overcomes all evil and opposition when the heart turns wholly to Him. How it has followed man from the beginning as the "Immanuel," or seed of Christ, treasured in every soul. The beginning of salvation through the germination of this seed. The new creature formed, or the Spirit of God dwelling and working in man. How this Spirit is obtained and recognized so as to avoid delusion. The prayer of this Spirit is the only genuine devotion. No other spirit in man works toward salvation. The consistency of this doctrine with free will. Prayer is the continual and habitual state of the will, according to whether it works with the Spirit of God or the spirit of fallen nature. All its goodness depends on the continuity and earnestness of the will's state or desire. The outward expression of prayer is justly distinguished. To what extent manuals of devotion are profitable. The degrees of prayer, or steps of the spiritual life. Why the movement of the Holy Spirit is the source of every aspiration to unite with the goodness and holiness of God. How this Spirit is known by the pure, free, universal goodness, meekness, and love which it breathes. These temperaments in man are the certain effect of its presence and influence.

These subjects are not only treated in the strictly argumentative manner and captivating style peculiar to the author, but they are also elucidated from Scripture throughout. This demonstrates the exact conformity of their philosophical development with the gospel and with the simple, experimental facts regarding personal regeneration and the conversion of the soul to God. Their range is, of course, much more extensive than that of evangelical truth as commonly lived. Each of these foregoing states has its time, its variety of workings, its trials, temptations, and purifications, which can only be known by experience and the passage through them.
