<note>As a suggestion to the *candidate*, we would incidentally remark regarding the inefficient mental training of theologians in the present age, and since the severe logic and metaphysics of the schools have ceased to form a part of a theological education. The lawyers are the only well-trained rationalists in this country at the present day. At the close of the seventeenth and commencement of the eighteenth century, theologians were the men of genius—the first spirits of the age as to mental science and power; but now, it has been remarked, they are the most inadequately educated of any profession, being unpracticed in close and just philosophic argumentation. A better representation of the relative character of their abilities cannot perhaps be afforded than in the critical remarks which appeared in *The Times* journal upon the mental flaccidity of the poet Southey, in the early part of March of the present year (1851), in the last two columns of the review in question. Southey, as to intellectual power, may there represent theologians of the present day, while Law, in his "*Case of Reason*," may stand for the divines of the age we have referred to. The lawyers, we repeat, now occupy the place in the field of well-disciplined reasoning power and judgment which was possessed by the divines of a former age, and are therefore much more fitted to be Christian philosophers, and to defend, support, and propagate the Christian mystery, than those whose education professes to constitute them for such office. Surely such a state of things is not to the honor of Christianity, and ought to be at once remedied. *See the proposed Appendix to SECTION III., on* ‘*Christian Education*,’ *regarding how to effect this*.</note>

It should be kept in mind that the contents of the “Spirit of Prayer” and succeeding works were not offered by the author as an essential study for the simple, evangelical Christian; but are adapted for those whose minds are so constituted as to make them capable of apprehending and indeed of demanding the philosophy or fundamental ground of the religion they are called to practice; that class, in short, whether of nominal Christians or of those who have not as yet professed Christianity, which as we have said, is represented by the characters of *Academicus* and *Humanus*.

Our reason for calling attention to this fact so repeatedly is the frequent misapprehension of Law’s mind by those who look into the “Spirit of Prayer” and expect to find exactly what the title would suggest according to their own rote understanding of theology. It is common among such persons to condemn the author for a style of writing which they regard as far-fetched and unprofitable; for introducing, as they say, a philosophy into the gospel which it has no need of, and which serves only to mystify it. And it is true enough that such people will not find in it what it was never intended they should find, especially on a first or second cursory perusal, and without any previous acquaintance with the circumstances of the case and the universal evangelical scheme of which it forms a part. For examples of this class of objectors, we might point to Horne, Venn, Jones, the devout Adams, Wesley, and other names famous in the annals of modern popular English Christianity.

To show the groundlessness of these objections, it might be sufficient to refer the reader to the contents of the “Spirit of Prayer” as we have given them above, the logical unity of which, and the single purpose which connects the various subjects together, being sufficiently apparent. However, by way of further illustrating that purpose, we will here insert an extract from the last Dialogue of the Second Part, and after that three interesting letters. In giving the latter, we shall only be carrying on the thread of our narrative. The extract in question proceeds as follows:

> “Theoph. Your earnest desire, *Academicus*, to live in the spirit of prayer and be truly governed by it, is a most excellent desire; for to be a man of prayer is what the apostle means by ‘living in the spirit, and having our conduct in heaven.’ It is to have done, not only with the confessed vices, but with the allowed follies and vanities of this world. To tell such a soul of the innocence of levity, that it need not run away from idle discourse, vain gaiety, and trifling mirth as being the harmless relief of our heavy natures, is like telling the *flame* that it need not always be ascending upwards. But here you are to observe that this spirit of prayer is not to be taught to you by a book, or brought into you by an art from without; but must be an inward birth that must arise from your own fire and light within you, as the air arises from the fire and light of this world. For the spirit of every being, be it what or where it will, is only the breath or spirit that proceeds from its own fire and light. In vegetative, sensitive, and intellectual creatures, it is all in the same manner; spirit is the third form of its life, and is the birth that proceeds from the other two, and is the manifestation of their nature and qualities. For such as the fire and light are, such and no other, neither higher nor lower, neither better nor worse, is the spirit that proceeds from them. Now the reason why all and every life does and must stand in this form is wholly and solely from this: because the Deity, the one source and fountain of all life, is a triune God, whose third form is, and is called, the Spirit of God, proceeding from the Father and the Son.

> The painful sense and feeling of what you are, kindled into a working state of sensibility by the light of God within you, is the fire and light from which your spirit of prayer proceeds. In its first kindling, nothing is found or felt but pain, wrath, and darkness, as is seen in the first kindling of every heat or fire. And therefore its first prayer is nothing else but a sense of penitence, self-condemnation, confession, and humility. It feels nothing but its own misery, and so is all humility. This prayer of humility is met by Divine love; the mercifulness of God embraces it; and then its prayer is changed into hymns, and songs, and thanksgivings. When this state of fervor has done its work, has melted away all earthly passions and affections, and left no inclination in the soul but to delight in God alone, then its prayer changes again. It has now come so near to God, and has found such union with Him, that it does not so much pray as live in God. Its prayer is not any particular action, is not the work of any particular faculty, and is not confined to times, or words, or place, but is the work of its whole being; which continually stands in fullness of faith, in purity of love, in absolute resignation to do and be what and how its Beloved pleases. This is the last state of the *spirit of prayer*, and is its highest union with God in this

The only and infallible way to go safely through all the difficulties, trials, temptations, dryness, or opposition of our own evil tempers, is this: it is *to expect nothing from ourselves, to trust to nothing in ourselves, but in everything expect and depend upon GOD for relief.* KEEP A FIRM HOLD ON THIS *thread*, and then let your way be what it will—darkness, temptation, or the rebellion of nature—you will be led through it all to a union with God. For nothing hurts us in any state except an expectation of something in it, and from it, which we should only expect from God. We are looking for our own virtue, our own piety, our own goodness, and so we live on in our own poverty and weakness; today pleased and comforted with the seeming strength and firmness of *our own pious tempers*, and fancying ourselves to be something; tomorrow, fallen into our own mire, we are dejected, but not humbled; we grieve, but it is only the grief of pride at seeing our perfection is not such as we vainly imagined. And thus it will be until the whole turn of our minds is so changed that we as fully see and know *our inability to have any goodness of our own, just as we know we cannot have a life of our own.*

For since nothing is, or can be, good in us except the *life of God manifested in us*, how can this be had but from God alone? When we are happily brought to *this conviction*, then we are done with all thoughts of being our own builders; the whole spirit of our mind becomes a mere *faith*, and *hope*, and *trust in the sole operation of God’s holy Spirit*. We look no more to any other power to be formed into new creatures in Christ than we look to any other power for the resurrection of our bodies at the last day. From this it may be seen that the trials of every state are its greatest blessings; they do for us what we most of all need to have done: they *force us to know our nothingness, and the all of God.* * * *

The best instruction that I can give you, as helpful or preparatory to the *spirit of prayer*, is already fully given where we have set forth the *original perfection, the miserable fall, and the glorious redemption of man*. It is the true knowledge of these great things that *can do all for you which human instruction can do*. These things must fill you with a dislike of your present state, drive all earthly desires out of your soul, and create an earnest longing after your first perfection.

For prayer cannot be taught to you by giving you a book of prayers, but by awakening in you a true sense and knowledge of what you are and what you should be; so that you may see, know, and feel what things you lack and are to pray for. For a man does not, and cannot, pray for anything just because a fine petition is placed in his hands, but because his own condition *is a reason and motive for his asking for it.* <note>N.B.</note> And therefore it is that the “SPIRIT OF PRAYER” in the “First Part” began with a full discovery and proof of these high and important matters! At the sight of these, the world and all that is in it shrinks into nothing; and everything—past, present, and to come—awakens in our hearts a continual prayer and longing desire after God, Christ, and eternity.”——

The first of the three letters we proposed to provide after this extract was written by Mr. Law to the same friend as the two epistles inserted a few pages back (a Mr. Thomas Langcake, at that time one of the writing clerks employed in the business of the Bank of England, Threadneedle Street). It is so relevant to our remarks in vindication of Mr. Law from the charges brought against him regarding the philosophy which it was his business to develop in this second ministration—as the ground of all nature and grace (which some called “speculative, vain, and precarious,” rather than practical, devout, and edifying)—that it may well be allowed to speak for itself. It is hardly necessary to remark that the practice described in this letter is the sum and end of all true, orthodox philosophy, and what Solomon meant by his “conclusion of the whole matter” after having experienced all the delights of wisdom, genius, sense, and all that this world can afford.

> “My dear Langcake,—I am greatly rejoiced that you express such a deep sense of the benefit of prayer; and I hope you will every day be more and more raised to, and united with God by it.
>
> I love no mysterious depths or heights of speculation, covet no knowledge, and want to see no ground of nature, grace, and creature, except so far as it brings me nearer to God, forces me to forget and renounce everything for Him, to do everything in Him and for Him, and to give every breath, movement, stirring, intention, and desire of my heart, soul, spirit, and life to Him.
>
> It is for the sake of this spirit of prayer that I have endeavored to present so many points of religion in such a light as must dispose the reader willingly to give up all he inherits from his fallen father, to be all hunger and thirst *after God*, and to have no thought or care but how to be wholly His devoted instrument—everywhere and in everything His adoring, joyful, and thankful servant.
>
> When it is the one ruling, never-ceasing desire of our hearts that God may be the beginning and end, the reason and motive, of our doing or not doing, from morning to night; then everywhere, whether speaking or silent, whether inwardly or outwardly employed, we are equally offered up to the Eternal Spirit, have our life in Him and from Him, and are united to Him by that *spirit of prayer* which is the comfort, the support, the strength, and security of the soul traveling, by the help of God, through the vanity of time into the riches of eternity.
>
> My dear friend, keep your eyes shut and ears stopped to everything that is not a step in that ladder which reaches from earth to heaven.
>
> Reading is good, hearing is good, conversation and meditation are good; but they are only good at certain times and occasions, to a certain degree, and must be used and governed with such caution as we use when we eat, drink, and refresh ourselves, or they will bring forth in us the fruits of intemperance. But the *spirit of prayer* is for all times and all occasions; it is a lamp that is to be ever burning, a light ever shining. Everything calls for it, everything is to be done in it and governed by it. Because it is, and means, and wills nothing else but the totality of the soul—not doing this or that, but being wholly, incessantly given up to God, to be where, and what, and how He pleases.
>
> This state of absolute resignation, naked faith, and pure love of God is the highest perfection and most purified life of those who are ‘born again from above’ and through the Divine power become ‘sons of God.’ And it is neither more nor less than what our blessed Redeemer has called and qualified us to long and aspire after in these words: ‘*Thy kingdom come; thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.*’

Near the conclusion of yours, you say, "you have of late, etc.," as already given on page 110, to the words, "Dear soul Adieu."

If the reader recalls the state of what is termed the religious world during the period under review, it will not surprise them that Mr. Law's publications brought many letters to Kings-cliffe about points of doctrine and practice in spiritual matters. These were often from people who were personally unknown to the author, and his consistent kindness in replying to them must have made serious demands on his time; for it is hardly necessary to say that a spirit of benevolence such as he evidently possessed could no more fail him in this respect than in the other acts of charity he habitually practiced. Sometimes, indeed, when he realized that such inquiries proceeded from idle curiosity rather than any sincere desire for instruction, he would purposely refrain from replying to them. This can be gathered from the following letter, which is nonetheless a good example of the pains he took in advising those who were disposed to seek his counsel, or who were prevented from reaping the full benefit of his works because they lacked proper training in the principles of Christian wisdom and found it difficult to cast away the imaginary notions of a theology not based on Scripture. <note>The Christian student might find it a profitable exercise to write out a clean copy of Mr. Law's letters as a means of understanding the depth of his thoughts and judgment.</note>

The gentleman thus addressed was a "Mr. William Briggs," a subordinate officer of the customs in London. But what Mr. Law says will apply equally well to the whole tribe of self-elected critics of his theology.

> Kings-cliffe. March 18th, 1751.—My dear Friend—I thank God it is neither because of age nor infirmities, nor any unwillingness to serve you, that I have not answered your letters, but from a just sense of the unreasonableness of employing both you and myself in such a manner. Be patient, and receive in the spirit of meekness what follows; and remember that *love is my God and wrath my Devil*, and then you may reap the fruits of Love from the following letter, though written in a way and manner so contrary to your expectation.
> 
> There is hardly anything more hurtful to true spirituality (the life of God in the soul), than a *talkative, inquisitive, active, busy, reasoning spirit* that is always at work with its own ideas, and never so content as when talking, hearing, or writing upon points, distinctions, and definitions of religious doctrines. This may as truly be called an earthly, worldly spirit, and as great an enemy to conversion from darkness to light, from flesh to spirit, as that of the old Athenians, who spent all their time, as St. Paul tells us, in telling or hearing some new thing.
> 
> To be trained up in the school of *reason*, and to have learned from *Locke* or *Le Clerc*, and similar masters, how to be *reasonable Christians*, is to be taught how to be content with eating dust and serpent's food instead of the tree of life. Our reason is an earth-born offspring; it is the Judas of our own nature; the serpent that began, effected, continues, and keeps up our fall and separation from God. And the deceitful cultivation of it, under the specious sounds of *clear and distinct ideas*, etc., has done more hurt to the gospel in these latter ages than any of its declared enemies.
> 
> Hence the Church is divided into numerous parts; hence there are Deists, Arians, and Socinians. Hence the zeal of modern reformers is divided into a number of little subdivisions, each under the light of *clear ideas* and verbal distinctions, contending for small terms of regulation and inventions of their own, while the life of Christ, the one church of God, is not lived, but learnedly given up for a life of reason.
> 
> *Ho! everyone who thirsts, says our Lord, let him come and drink.* It is only hunger and thirst that receives even the smallest degree of the heavenly life. If we are not as weary and as afraid of the spirit of reason as of any other earthly lust, we cannot become such children as can alone enter into the kingdom of God.
> 
> To apply this to the matter at hand. In the year '46, I had your first letter, telling me you had read my *Appeal*, and that by a pure light from heaven, you understood what you read—that it contained the depth of sound mysteries, etc. This was sufficient reason for contentment; but behold, at page 205, your reasoning enemy came to life in you, and helped you to a long list of questions about the holy sacrament.
> 
> I answered that letter immediately, because it was your first, and because I believed a good spark of the Divine life was kindled in you. I showed you that every question was unnecessary, groundless, and conjured up by the sole activity of blind reason, in direct opposition to the plainest doctrine of *The Appeal*. You owned the truth of all this and confessed yourself a dull scholar in the school of Christ.
> 
> The benefit that you ought to have received from this should have been to know that inward enemy to divine light that is so active within you, and that your reasoning activity was your own serpent within you; and that all your safety consisted in turning a deaf ear to all its suggestions, knowing that they could help you only to such illumination as the serpent procured for our sinful parents.
> 
> In the year '49, when *The Spirit of Prayer* was published, you sent me a letter of objections to that. You admitted the book to be most excellent; but behold, the serpent again came to your assistance and showed you how strange a doctrine there was in it, namely, that the holy Trinity was free from, and incapable of wrath, though the Scriptures abounded with declarations of the wrath, fury, etc., of God.
> 
> This letter I laid aside among those that were to have no answer from me, because it was fully answered in *The Appeal* and in that book; and you were here again committing the same fault of which I had before made you aware. Your persistence forced an answer from me. You seemed to support yourself by saying, "that a sincere minister of Christ had preached several sermons against that doctrine." You should have said that *prejudice*, supported by human reason and the sound of words, had been so many times declaiming against a most heavenly truth.
> 
> To say that there was no wrath, fury, vengeance, and damnation belonging to sin and sinners would be to fly in the face of plain Scripture: but to say that none of these things are inherent

<meta>This page continues William Law’s firm rebuke to Mr. William Briggs, transitioning from a discussion of divine nature to a critique of Briggs’s over-reliance on human reason and his "talkative spirit" in religious matters.</meta>

*the man through this [evangelical] way where Jacob Boehme entered so deeply according to Saint-Martin, being much preferable to the ways opened by the contemplative visions of the Mystics; or the manifes-*

qualities in the holy Trinity of God, but as separate from him, as impossible to be in him and of him as sin, hell, and the devil; is a truth, infinitely sound, infinitely lovely, and the most solid, comfortable foundation of all religious faith, love, and resignation to God.

To observe now some other instances of the delusion of your reasoning activity. "Common ideas" you say, (I suppose you meant common minds) "can hardly receive anything that is not almost apparent to their senses. All metaphysical reasonings are to them unprofitable." I quote these words only for what follows, where you say, "for this reason, I believe, the divine writings were written with the utmost freedom from anything above the comprehension of the unlearned reader."

Now, Sir, let this show you the vanity of indulging a talkative spirit; for were you not too much under its power, you could not have brought forth such words as these, or think them fit matter for our correspondence. For is not all Scripture from the first chapter of Genesis to the last chapter of the Revelation to St. John, a direct and full contradiction to this assertion, namely: "written with the utmost freedom from anything above the comprehension of the unlearned reader?" Might you not as justly have said, "written with the utmost freedom from letters, syllables, and words?"

Are not all the libraries in the Christian world a demonstration that the Scriptures are not open and plain to our reason and senses? Does the Scripture anywhere give this character of itself, which you have given; or is the plainness of the letter to common minds ever appealed to as the key to Scripture truths? Hear our blessed Lord, *He that is of God hears God's word*. And every prophet and apostle directs only to this key. *The natural man*, says the apostle (*that is the man of reason and sense*), *does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, nor can he know them*. But why not? It is because they can only be discerned by the spirit of God. *We have also*, says another apostle, *a sure word of prophecy, to which you do well to take heed, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns, and the day-star arises in your hearts*. See here, again, the key that opens the Scriptures; not the plainness of the letter, but the day-star, the spirit of God arising in the heart. All Scripture, whether plain or obscure, is not understood until the anointing from above teaches all things to the reader.

See another instance of the vain activity of this talkative spirit. You go on and say, "The more spiritual men make the Scripture their rule in speaking, writing, etc., the more good they will do to all those around them." For how unreasonable is it for you, or anyone else, to tell a spiritual man how he should speak or write? For no one is a spiritual man except so far as he is led by the Spirit; and to tell him how he should speak is directing the Spirit of God. And when any speaker or writer adopts any kind or manner of language, it is a certain proof that he is under his own direction, and not following or governed by the true Spirit of God opening itself in him.

Again, through the same talkative spirit you tell me, "It is objected by some that I never make any distinction between repentance, justification, and sanctification." And you have more than once called upon me to speak to this matter. You add, "Here (that is, in this distinction of these three words, thus understood) is the beginning, the middle, and the end of the work of the triune God upon the soul. Happy are they who experience these good and important things."

Now, Sir, if you and the objectors are in possession of this happiness, feeling the benefit of these three words, thus distinguished, I have said nothing to rob you of that happiness. And you might call to mind that a much greater teacher than I am—who justly calls himself the light of the world, the way, the truth, and the life—never makes any more mention of this distinction than is to be found in my books. If therefore they are defective, or blameworthy for lack of this distinction, how will you excuse the four gospels?

Bear with patience, my dear friend, this great and useful truth, namely, that all your letters to me are, from the beginning to the end, of the same kind with the passages I have here remarked: mere hasty, needless, fruitless words, brought forth by a talkative spirit, which is the spirit you need to have cast out of you. You must have seen in common life that when a man has this tendency, he is neither wise nor useful in his discourse; he becomes tiresome to everybody, and never talks to the purpose because he is always talking.

I consider you to have good intellectual abilities and an awakened sense of piety; but neither sense nor piety can bring forth their proper fruits when under the power of a talkative spirit. You tell me that "the greatest part of my Second Part of *The Spirit of Prayer* gave you great consolation; that it contains that pure and Christian philosophy which leads the fallen man to find eternity in himself, and Jesus Christ the source of all true happiness." Oh, Sir! is it possible for you to see and know this, and yet make no better use of it? What has the heart to wish or seek from men and books after such a philosophy as this is found? But now, instead of saying to yourself, as you should have done, "It is enough! the mystery of salvation is here opened; in this light will I thankfully give up myself to God for the remainder of my life"; (instead of thus thinking,) my book had not been published a week before you sent me word of a great fright you were in, lest a certain notion there advanced should "give occasion to the enemy not only to cavil, but to blaspheme."

But, my dear friend, this is again mere talk; you have no such fear. For if you had this fear in the smallest degree, how could you possibly ask my leave to publish this very notion in a newspaper? In my book, grounded, guarded, and supported as it is, there is no room to be afraid of anyone seeing it; but for a serious person to remove it out of its place, where it stands supported by a pure Christian philosophy, to place it among the trash and babble of a newspaper, is as wise a plan to preserve it from the ill use of the enemy as if it were to be placed at the end of a playbook <note>A book containing dramatic plays, often regarded as worldly or trivial entertainment in this context.</note>.

You say "On the sixth day Adam was formed; the same day put into Eden; the same day God said, It is not good; the same day caused a deep sleep; the same day took a rib from his side, and made the woman." And then you add these wonderfully strange words, namely, "All this being without force gathered from the holy Scriptures, I cannot find the least room to suppose that Adam had lost much of his perfection before his Eve was taken out of him."

Suppose anyone should say, “Three days after the creation of Adam, God put him into Paradise; three days after that he said, It is not good that man should be alone; three days after that he caused a deep sleep, etc.; three days after that he took a rib from him, and made it into a woman;” and should then add, “All this being gathered from Scripture without distortion,” you could not help seeing the grossness of such an assertion; and yet, gross as it would be, it is exactly your own. For the Scripture is just as far from telling you that all these things were done in one and the same day as it is from telling you of these three days. And, therefore, to claim Scripture for this one day is the same gross abuse of it as to claim it for the three days.

Try your own assertion this way. Say, Moses informs us that an hour or two after man was created, God said, It is not good, etc.; an hour or two after that, God caused a deep sleep to fall upon him; an hour or two after that, He took a rib from him, etc. Here you may see not only distortion, but forgery and fiction forced into the Scriptures. Now your assertion does, in reality, all this violence to Scripture; it supposes all this which is here charged upon Moses. For to say that you gather all this without distortion from Moses is the same as saying that Moses has freely and of his own accord told you all this. Again, your believing all these great things to be done in a few hours of one and the same day is, you say, the reason why you cannot admit my doctrine: that Adam was in a declining state before Eve was taken out of him.

But to show you that this also is mere talk, you need only remember your own words, where you say, “Who can tell that each day was not a thousand of our years?”

Now the supposition is the highest absurdity; but since you suppose it to be possible, according to your own logic it may be said, “Who can tell but that Adam might have been nine hundred and ninety years old before his Eve was taken out of him?” Now, my friend, what has robbed you of the peace and comfort you should have found in this pure and Christian philosophy? Not any whim of mine, nor Moses, but a fiction of your own—that all these great things were done in a few hours.

Now, had Moses expressly said that all these things were done in one short day between morning and night, how difficult would it have been to believe it! For the very nature of all these things calls for some distance of time between them. And every one of them must be supposed to have some preceding great cause and occasion that brought it about.

Thus, Adam was created with the eyes of eternity, and had only just awakened into an angelic life and light; will you suppose him immediately in a deep sleep, without some great matter having been the occasion of it? Again, created like the angels, neither male nor female but both natures united in him, will you suppose that this angelic dignity was taken from him before he had done anything to give cause for being thus altered and brought into a likeness to earthly animals? <note>Query: is this truth not specifically represented in the antithesis of Gen. 1:24–27? See the French translation.</note>

You may easily observe that the great things which I say of Adam are not deduced from the literal text of Moses, but are only shown to be consistent with it. Just as the doctrine of an *eternity* and *Christ within us* is not declared from what Moses speaks of Christ, but is only shown to be conformable to it, and to have had its first dark beginning in his “seed of the woman.” But all, regarding both these matters, is stated and proved from the divine philosophy of our redemption revealed in the gospel. It is the knowledge of Christ and his redemption that gives the true knowledge of the first Adam. This I have shown in all my books, from the *Answer to the Plain Account*, etc., to this day. Thus, in the Second Part of *The Spirit of Prayer*, p. 86: “It may be affirmed, as surely as it is from Scripture, that Christ became our second Adam to help us to *such a birth*; so surely is it from Scripture that we should have had the *same birth from our first parent*.” All my proof is of this kind, taken from the nature of our Redeemer and his redemption; and that is variously expressed and asserted throughout all my books.

But it is time to be done; let me only add this parting word. Consider how much true light God has granted to you; and what is best of all, has awakened in you a sincere love of it. Let not the activity of your reason meddle with it or turn it into a speculative entertainment; but give up your heart to it, in true simplicity, to live in it.

For truth is to be lived; nothing finds it, nothing enjoys it, but life. And nothing lives in us but our heart; and the heart has but one life, and that is love with all its *fruitful workings*. Expect no light, therefore, except from the love of God; for the light and the love of God are inseparable, and they have no communion except with one another. And just as great and true as your love is, just so great and true is your light. Reason may for a while have its fancied treasures, but they are only the treasures of earthly light. Christ and God and heaven are only found, felt, and known by an ardent love of them. <note>Note well.</note>

Go on in Love, and then you go on in light. When all that is within you is only so much *humility, meekness, and flames of love to God*, then you are truly risen from the *death* that Adam died. Your way of life is justly said to be in heaven; Christ is revealed in you; and you are one of those of whom he says, *The glory which you gave me, I have given them; I in them, and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one.*

These three virtues, which are only three in human sounds, are one and the same undivided and indivisible thing: namely, the tendency of the soul from SELF TO GOD. No virtue has the least degree of salvation in it, except so far as this tendency is found in it. This is the *one thing* on our part.

On the other hand, God is one, and grace is one. Ask not for distinctions and definitions in the work of grace; for grace has but one work, just as the *sun* has but one work, from its first enlivening the dead seed to the full, ripe harvest.

The true church of God is the *Spirit of God* and Christ, and those who are united in obedience to this Spirit are all of the one true church of God. Love nothing in books or doctrines but that which directs you wholly and solely to the spirit of God. Everything else is but a loss of time, and only putting *empty cups* to our mouths. If you once come to know what a blessing it is to stand always humbly devoted to, and waiting solely for, the light and spirit of God—expecting no kind or degree of good from anything else—you will then not only know, but feel, what a folly and hurt it

With the next letter, our present observations on the "Spirit of Prayer" and the correspondence more immediately connected with it will naturally close. But we cannot dismiss the subject without remarking how impossible it is to describe the contents of such a book in a manner at all adequate to its merits, or comparable with the picture which it "daguerreotypes" <note>An early photographic process; here used metaphorically to mean a vivid, permanent impression.</note> on the mind. It will be received differently, indeed, as we have already suggested, by two classes of persons, but it cannot be thoughtfully read without making a decided impression on all. Those reflecting and sincere-minded readers who have been inexperienced in methodical practices and arts of devotion, but whose imagination and judgment have been well cultivated, form the class who are most likely to be affected by the heavenly light which streams through its pages and the melodious tone of its sentences; perhaps more so because of the freshness of a subject which is not usually found in philosophical works, and which presents itself to them in the light of a discovery. While on the other hand, those who have been somewhat devoted to exercises of prayer according to the simple prescription of the gospel may have less admiration for this particular work than for the early productions of the same hand—deeming its fundamental explanations of practical Christian truth as already known to them; though in effect, it may be no more *known* than a simple proposition in Euclid may be said to be known by them before they have mastered its demonstration for themselves. Each class, however, will be captivated by what is comparatively original and extraordinary in the writer, and by the sudden awakening of unsuspected truths and trains of thought in the mind.

The third letter is as follows, addressed to Mr. Langcake. The objections to which it alludes were afterward sent to Mr. Law and elicited some further remarks from him in a letter which we shall quote later, as belonging to the early part of 1752:—

> "Kings-cliffe. September 7th, 1751.—My dear worthy friend—Yours of the 27th of this month gave me great pleasure, as it informed me of the recovery of your health. But most of all am I pleased with finding the heavenly effects of the Divine operation on your soul; and I have only to implore you to give yourself up entirely to the good Spirit of God, which has opened in your soul so deep a sensitivity and conviction of divine truths.
> Expect no life, light, strength, or comfort, except from the Spirit of God dwelling and manifesting His own goodness in your soul.—The best of men and the best of books can only do you good so far as they turn you away from themselves and every human thing, to seek, have, and receive every kind of good from God alone; not a distant or an absent God, but a God living, moving, and always working in the spirit and heart of your soul.
> They never find God who seek for Him by reasoning and speculation. For, since God is the highest Spirit and the highest life, nothing but a similar spirit and a similar life can unite with Him, or find, feel, or know anything of Him.
> Hence it is that faith, hope, and love turned toward God are the only possible, and also infallible, means of obtaining a true and living knowledge of Him. And the reason is plain; it is because by these holy dispositions, which are the workings of spirit and life within us, we seek the God of life where He is, we call upon Him with His own voice, and we draw near to Him by His own spirit. For nothing can breathe forth faith, love, and hope to God except *that* spirit and life which is of God, and therefore presses through flesh and blood toward Him and readily unites with Him.
> Keep firmly to this assertion in your own letter: that 'neither reasoning nor learning can ever introduce a spark of heaven into our souls.' There is not a more infallible truth in the world than this. But if this is so, then you have nothing to seek, nor anything to fear, from reason.
> Life and death are the things in question. Neither of them is the product of reasoning or learning, but each is a state of the soul, and they differ in this way: death is the *lack*, and life is the *enjoyment*, of its highest good. Reason, therefore, and learning have no power here, except by their vain activity to keep the soul insensible to that life and death, one of which is always growing within it according to how the will and desire of the heart work.—Add reason to a vegetable, and you add nothing to its life or death. Its life and fruitfulness lie in the soundness of its root, the goodness of the soil, and the nourishment it derives from air and light. Heaven and hell grow this way in the soul of every man; his heart is his root, and if that is turned away from all evil, it is then like the plant in a good soil. When it hungers and thirsts after the divine life, it then infallibly draws the light and spirit of God into it; these are infinitely more ready and willing to live and produce fruit in the soul than light and air are to enter into the plant that hungers after them. For the soul has its breath, and being, and life for no other purpose than that the Triune God may manifest the riches and powers of His own life in it.
> Thus hunger is everything, and in all worlds everything lives in it and by it. Nothing else eats or partakes of life, and everything eats according to its own hunger; and everything hungers after its own mother—that is, everything has a natural magnetic tendency to partake of that from which it had its being, and can only find its rest in that from which it came. Dead as well as living things bear witness to this truth. Stones fall to the earth and sparks fly upward for this reason only: because everything must tend toward that from which it came.
> Were not angels, and the souls of men, breathed forth from God as so many real offsprings

The following, it would appear from the manuscript copy, formed part of the present letter:—

"I am very willing to receive the *Objections* to *The Appeal*, though I am incapable of disputing with anyone in the defense of it. I wrote it only for those who want such light as is discovered there.

'Come unto me all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you,' says our blessed Lord. He called no one else, because no one else has ears to hear or a heart to receive the truths of redemption. Every man is a vain disputer until such time as something has disturbed his state and awakened a sensitivity to his own evil and miserable nature. We are all afraid of both inward and outward distress; and yet until distress comes, our life is but a dream, and we have no awakened awareness of our true state.

We are apt to consider talents and *abilities* as the proper qualifications for receiving divine truths, and we wonder that a man of fine understanding should not immediately embrace just and solid doctrines. But the matter is quite otherwise. Had man kept possession of his first rich and glorious state, there would have been no foundation for the Gospel redemption, and the doctrine of the cross must have appeared quite unreasonable to be pressed upon him. Therefore, says our Lord, '*the Gospel is preached to the poor.*' It is solely to them and no one else; that is, to poor fallen man, who has lost all the true natural riches and greatness of his first divine life—to him is the Gospel preached.

But if a man *knows* and *feels* nothing of this poverty of his nature, he is not the person to whom the Gospel belongs. <note>It is to such a person that the latter part of Mr. Law's 'The Sacrament Book' is especially addressed.</note> It has no more suitability to his state than it had to man before the fall; and thus, the greater his talents and abilities are, the better qualified he is to show the folly of every doctrine of that salvation for which he feels no need. I mention this only to show you that you are not to be surprised at the use your friend has made of *The Appeal*, despite his good talents and natural abilities. *The Appeal* may be hated and laughed at, but that is all the harm that learned reason can do to it.

I am much pleased with your saying that you could be perfectly satisfied even if you never had another letter from me. If you seal up the *Objections* addressed to me and send them in an envelope (if they are not over the postal weight limit), addressed to the Right Honorable Lord Viscount Hatton at Kirby in Northamptonshire, you will have no need for a frank, and I shall receive them without expense."

For other letters illustrating Mr. Law's settled spirit of understanding, pure evangelical simplicity, and union with the divine light at the time he wrote the *Spirit of Prayer* and supplementary pieces, we must refer the reader to the published "Collection of Letters," according to their respective dates, and to any that may be provided hereafter.

The suggestion conveyed at the end of the following passage, which we cite from the second part of the *Spirit of Prayer*, will show what Mr. Law was then occupied with in his study:—

"For without the *reality* of a new birth, founded on the certainty of a *real* death in the fall of Adam, the Christian scheme is but a skeleton of empty words, a list of strange mysteries between God and man that do nothing and have nothing to do.

On the other hand, look now at the things set forth in *The Appeal* concerning the fall of angels, the nature and effects of their revolt, and the creation of this world as deduced from that. They neither abandon nor oppose any literal word or doctrine of Scripture. They add nothing to religion except the full proof of all its articles; they intend nothing but to reveal the original basis and true reason for the Christian redemption and the absolute necessity of it being exactly as the Gospel declares. Now, the *letter* of Scripture does not do this in explicit words; it does not set forth the *why* and how things are, either in nature or grace; it does not teach the *basis* or *philosophy* of the Christian faith; it contents itself with bare *facts* and *doctrines* and calls for simple faith and obedience. It is no wonder, therefore, that when the *natural* and *necessary* basis of the Christian redemption is revealed, the literal text of Scripture is not appealed to *step by step* for everything that is said. The *Sadducees* denied that there was any resurrection at all, and they did this because they could not find it in the *explicit letter* of the five books of *Moses*. Yet it seems that the resurrection was plainly and strongly taught there; for our Lord said, 'That the dead shall rise again, Moses showed at the bush, when he called the Lord the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. For he is not the God of the dead, but of the living' (*Luke* 20:37–38). This shows us that a thing may be fully and sufficiently proved from Scripture even if it is not plainly expressed in the literal text.

And this is how the matter stands regarding those great and edifying truths set forth in *The Appeal*. They are truly scriptural; they have their *basis* and *authority* from Scripture, though they are not as open and express in the literal text as matters of faith and essential doctrine are. For is not the fall of angels a scriptural truth? Is not the desolation that their fall brought into nature, and into the very location of this world, a scriptural truth? What else can be meant by 'darkness upon the face of the deep'? What darkness or what deep could it be, if not in the place of this world? What does the letter of Scripture show but that out of this darkness, these waters, and this state of the deep—once the Spirit and light of God entered them—He brought forth the earth, the stars, the sun, and all the elements into the form of a new world?

To ask for a particular text of Scripture saying in so many explicit words that the location of this world is the very place and extent of the kingdom of the fallen angels is quite ridiculous and without the least basis in reason, as is sufficiently shown in *The Appeal*. For does not our Lord expressly call the *devil* 'a prince of this world'? But how could this name belong to him unless he were here in his own *original region* and *territories*, and still possessed some power until all the evil..."

that he has raised in it shall be entirely separated from it? For, if this world were not raised out of the *materials* of the fallen angels’ kingdom, and if the wrath, fire, and darkness of *their fall* did not still remain to some degree in every part of this world, they could have no more power in it than they have in heaven. They would be as entirely incapable of seeing or entering into it as they are of seeing or entering into the kingdom of heaven; for they have nothing but evil in their nature. They can touch nothing, move nothing, see nothing, feel nothing, taste nothing, and act in nothing but that *very evil*, darkness, fire, wrath, and disorder which they first awakened and kindled both in themselves and their kingdom. And therefore it is a truth of the utmost certainty that they can be nowhere but where there is something of that evil still remaining which they brought forth. And this may pass as a demonstration (if there is any such thing) that the Scriptures themselves demonstrate the location of this world to be the very place and region in which the angels fell. And they are still here, because their kingdom is not wholly delivered from all the evil they have raised in it, but is to stand for a time only in a state of recovery. Here they themselves must see, despite all the rage and malice of their fiery darts, that the *mystery of a Lamb of God born upon earth* will raise creatures of flesh and blood, amidst the ruins of their spoiled kingdom, to be a host of angels in heaven restored; while they themselves are plunged into a hell that is cut off from everything but their own wrath, fire, and darkness. And all this, *Academicus*, is to make it known through all the regions of eternity that *pride* can degrade the highest angels into devils, and *humility* raise fallen flesh and blood to the thrones of angels. This, *this* is the great end of God’s raising a new creation out of the fallen kingdom of angels; for this end it stands in its state of war—a war between the fire and pride of fallen angels, and the meekness and humility of the Lamb of God. It stands for its thousands of years in this strife, so that the last trumpet may sound this great truth through all the heights and depths of eternity: “That evil can have no beginning but from pride, nor any end but from humility.”

O *Academicus*, what blindness there is in the world! What a stir there is among mankind about religion, and yet almost all seem to be afraid of *that* in which alone is salvation!

Poor mortals! What is the one wish and desire of your hearts? What is it that you call *happiness* and a matter of rejoicing? Is it not when everything around you helps you to stand upon higher ground, gives full nourishment to self-esteem, and gratifies every pride of life? And yet life itself is the loss of everything, unless *pride* is overcome. O stop for a while in contemplation of this great truth! It is a truth as unchangeable as God; it is written and spoken through all nature; heaven and earth, fallen angels, and redeemed men all bear witness to it. The truth is this: *Pride must die in you, or nothing of heaven can live in you.* Under the banner of this truth, give yourselves up to the meek and humble spirit of the holy Jesus, the overcomer of all fire, pride, and wrath. This is the one way, the one truth, and the one life: there is no other open door into the sheepfold of God. Everything else is the *working* of the devil in the fallen nature of man. Humility must sow the seed, or there can be no reaping in heaven. Do not look at pride only as an unbecoming temper, nor at humility only as a decent virtue; for the one is death, and the other is life; the one is all hell, and the other is *all heaven*.

As much as you have of pride, that much you have of the fallen angel alive in you; as much as you have of true humility, that much you have of the Lamb of God within you. If you could see with your eyes what every stirring of pride does to your soul, you would beg everything you meet to tear the viper from you, even at the loss of a hand or an eye. If you could see what a sweet, divine, transforming power there is in humility—what a heavenly water of life it gives to the *fiery breath* of your soul, how it expels the poison of your fallen nature, and makes room for the Spirit of God to live in you—you would rather wish to be the footstool of all the world than to lack the smallest degree of it. Excuse this little digression, *Academicus*, if it is one; for the subject we were on forced me into it.

*Acad.* Indeed, Sir, the lesson you have given here is the same that the whole nature of the fall of angels, and the whole nature of the redemption of man, daily reads to every creature; and he, who alone can redeem the world, has plainly shown us what the life and spirit of our redemption must consist of when he says, “Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly of heart.” Now if this lesson is unlearned, we must be said to have left our Master, as those disciples did “who went back, and walked no more with him.” But if you please, *Theophilus*, we will now break off until the afternoon. —

*Theoph.* Allow me first, *Academicus*, just to mention one point more, to show you still further how unreasonably your friends object that *The Appeal* lacks the plain letter of Scripture. Now let it be supposed that the account of the fall of angels, the creation, etc., given in *The Appeal*, does not have enough Scripture. Take then the contrary opinion, which is that of your friends, namely: That all worlds, and all things, are created *out of nothing*.

Show me now, *Academicus*—I do not say a text, but even the smallest *hint* of Scripture—that by all the art of commentary can even be drawn to look that way. It is a *fiction*, full of the grossest absurdities, and contrary to everything that we know, either from nature or Scripture, concerning the rise, and birth, and nature of things that have begun to be. *Adam* was not created out of nothing; for the letter of Moses tells us in the plainest words *from what* he was created or formed, both as to his inward and his outward nature. He tells us also as expressly *from what Eve*, the next creature, was created. But from the time of *Adam* and *Eve*, the creation of every human creature is a birth out of its parents’ body and soul, or whole nature. And to show us how all things, or worlds, as well as all living creatures, are not created out of nothing, St. *Paul* appeals to this very account that *Moses* gives of the woman being formed “out of the man”; but “all things (says he) are out of God,” (1 Cor. 11:12). Here this fiction of a creation out of nothing is absolutely removed from the whole system of created things, or things which begin to be, by the plain and open letter of Scripture; for St. Paul’s doctrine is that *all things come into being out of God, in the same reality as the woman was formed or created out of man.* So again, “There is to us but one God, out of whom are all things,” (1 Cor. 8:6); for as you know, the Greek should be translated not *of*, but *out of* God; not of, but *out of* the man. The fiction, therefore, which I

> speak of is not only without but expressly *contrary to* the plain letter of Scripture. For everything that we see, every creature that has life, is, by the Scriptural account, a *birth from something else*. And here, Sir, you are to take notice of a *maxim* that cannot be denied: the reason why *anything proceeds from a birth* is the reason why *everything must do so*. For a birth would not exist in nature except that birth is the *only* procedure of nature. Nature itself is a *birth from God*, the *first manifestation of the hidden, inconceivable God*; and it is so far from being "out of nothing" that it is the manifestation of *all that in God* which was previously unmanifested. As nature is the first birth or manifestation of God, or the discovery of the Divine powers, so all creatures are the manifestation of the powers of nature, brought into a variety of births by the will of God *out of nature*. The first creatures, which are nearest to the Deity, are *out of the highest powers of nature* by the will of God—He willing that nature should be manifested in the rise and birth of creatures *out of it*. Nature, directed and governed by the wisdom of God, continues in the birth of one thing *out of another*. The spiritual materiality of heaven brings forth the bodies, or heavenly flesh and blood, of angels, just as the materiality of this world brings forth the birth of gross flesh and blood. The spiritual materiality of heaven, as far as the extent of the kingdom of the fallen angels reached, has, through various changes caused by their fall, gone through a variety of *births* or creations, until some of it came down to the *thickness of air and water* and the *hardness of earth and stones*. But when things have stood in this state for their appointed time, the last purifying fire, kindled by God, will take away all thickness, hardness, and darkness. It will bring all the divided things and elements of this world back again to be that *first glassy sea*, or heavenly *materiality*, in which the throne of God is set, as was seen by *St. John* in the revelation made to him.
> 
> But the fiction of the *creation out of nothing* is not only contrary to the letter and spirit of the Scriptural account of the rise and birth of things, but is in itself full of the grossest absurdities and horrid consequences. *It separates everything from God; it leaves no relation between God and the creature, nor any possibility for any power, virtue, quality, or perfection of God to be in the creature. For if it is created out of nothing, it cannot have something of God in it.* BUT I STOP HERE FOR, AS YOU KNOW, WE HAVE AGREED, IF GOD PERMITS, TO HAVE AN ENTIRE DAY'S CONVERSATION HEREAFTER ON THE NATURE AND PURPOSE OF THE WRITINGS OF JACOB BEHMEN, AND THE RIGHT USE AND MANNER OF READING THEM; AND ALL THAT AS PREPARATORY TO A MORE CORRECT ENGLISH EDITION OF HIS WORKS FROM THE ORIGINAL GERMAN LANGUAGE. THEREFORE, THIS AND SOME OTHER POINTS SHALL BE POSTPONED UNTIL THAT TIME. In the afternoon, we will proceed only on such matters as may further set Christian redemption in its true and proper light before your friend *Humanus*.

> In *The Appeal*, we have a system of uniform truths concerning the fall of angels, their spoiled and darkened kingdom, and the creation of this world as raised out of it. We have the creation and fall of man, his regeneration, and the manner of it, all opened and explained according to the letter and tenor of Scripture from their deepest ground, in such a manner as to give light and clarity to all the articles of the Christian faith; to expel all difficulties and absurdities that had crept into it; and the whole scheme of our redemption proved to be absolutely necessary, both from Scripture and from all that is seen and known in nature and the creature.
> 
> On the other hand, the opinion which is and must be received if the account in *The Appeal* is rejected appears to be a *fiction* that has no sense, no reason, no fact, no appearance in nature, nor one single letter of Scripture to support it. Instead, it stands in the utmost opposition to everything the Scripture says about the creation of all things, and is in itself full of the grossest absurdities, raising darkness and difficulties in all parts of religion that can never be removed from it. For a creation that has nothing of God in it can explain nothing that relates to God; for a creation out of nothing has no better sense in it than a creation into nothing."

Here we observe that Mr. Law was casually drawn aside from his main purpose to comment on the source of all the arbitrary theology which had characterized the church, and to support the fundamental refutation of that system of doctrine in *The Appeal*. But in order not to encumber this particular and practical work with irrelevant matter, he suggests his intention of devoting an entire day to conversation on the subject—that is, of publishing another work which should serve at the same time as an introduction to the *Works of Jacob Behmen* and to the right, evangelical use of them, as designed in their gift to these last ages, for which they have been termed the gospel. This purpose he had conceived long before, as expressed in his letter to a Mr. Stephen Penny, an extract of which was inserted in the note on page 45.

The work thus promised is the *Way to Divine Knowledge*, more especially that portion of it commencing with the "Second Dialogue"—the First Dialogue being an elision and sequence of the *Spirit of Prayer* as a means of knitting the two works together and giving continuity to the conversations, and appropriately summing up with the observations on "Gospel Christianity," cited on page 120, showing its true nature as the end of all the salvation dispensations of *God* to man.

[We have designated the *Spirit of Prayer* as the practical application of the *divine philosophy* opened in *The Appeal*; but it <unclear>may</unclear> <gloss>likewise</gloss> be considered an *Appendix* to the *Demonstration of the Fundamental Errors of the Plain Account of the Sacrament* where, in the latter portion of it, a brief and popular elucidation of the fallen state of man was set forth, by which to preach the gospel to Christian skeptics. And he would be no ill-instructed scribe or ill-qualified preacher of the gospel who (in addition to his own experience of Christianity) should have made himself thoroughly master of the contents of this last-mentioned treatise.]

Thus this Christian sage, in his retirement, was laying the foundation for carrying out the designs of the gospel revelation—that is, as the Divine Author of it wished "truth," or the pure, universal philosophy He taught, to be understood—by which to renew the face of moral nature even to the ends of the earth, and so to usher in the *great day*.

As we are elucidating it, he will doubtless raise his mind in astonishment that, from the apostolic ages down to this very day, so few individuals, or churches, have apprehended the exact views of Christ regarding the Gospel’s scope and efficacy, before the square-minded Christian philosopher, Law. For had Christianity—as taught by its author and summed up in Saint Paul’s Epistles—continued to be rightly understood and transmitted purely by the apostolic successors, the host of conflicting religious schemes which the last seventeen hundred years have brought forth could never have been conceived, or at all events would have been strangled at birth. But, blessed be God, the world is approaching daylight and will soon have the means of understanding the mind and spirit of Christ in his recorded declarations and those of his apostles.

We have remarked that the “First Dialogue” of the work under review is the natural conclusion of the “Spirit of Prayer.” In like manner, the last two Dialogues may be considered as supplementary to the “Appeal,” which the reader will understand as follows. Seeing that the world was distracted by the errors, absurdities of doctrine, and interminable sectarian divisions which had arisen in the once simple and united church of God, and convinced by everyday experience of the incapacity of Christianity in this state to pursue its natural mission, Mr. Law was led to consider the real source of all this Babel-like confusion and uncertainty. From the elevation at which he now stood, he was enabled clearly to detect the major mistake from which almost every other illusion had proceeded: which was, in short, the absurd notion that “all things were originally created out of nothing.” Strange to say, this fiction had prevailed as a matter of ordinary belief in every age since the loss of the tradition of St. Paul concerning “the great mystery of Christ,” about the second or third generation after the apostles. It had caused the Gospel revelation to be represented as the offspring of an arbitrary Deity; the scholars in each age outlined its features according to their blind concepts and attempted to reconcile them to the opposing natural sense of mankind by imaginary superstructures, opinions, and conjectures of their own based upon the abstract letter of Scripture. In this way, it appeared, every error of doctrine had originated, by which the wellsprings of *religion* and *philosophy* had been poisoned in Christian schools and centers of learning; these had at length arrived at such a pitch of extravagance and irrationality as to be not unworthy of Bedlam itself. Thousands of learned and often devout persons in the Protestant church held with implicit faith the Calvin-invented doctrines of unconditional election and reprobation, the imputation of Christ’s righteousness, justification by—that is, as the reward of—faith, and the non-freedom of the will. They also held reason to be the judge of revelation and of divine requirements, along with other enormities embraced by Arianism, Deism, Socinianism, and the ever-varying schools of free-thinkers. Still greater numbers in the Latin church might be found imbued with equal faith in papal infallibility, indulgences, purgatory according to the literal sense, and the deliverance of souls out of it for money by virtue of the priest’s office, the intercession of the Virgin Mary, etc.; not to mention the corresponding absurdities of the Greek church, which were doubtless quite as numerous. [We say nothing here with respect to the ancient Oriental or Jewish religions, etc., except that the mystery of iniquity has ever worked in one uniform way; and “there is no difference,” says the Apostle Paul.]

Thus, the various doctrines of Christianity had been driven from their true center and basis, and the most devoted persons were subject to illusion in points of understanding; although the essential knowledge of religious truth was always within reach of every honest soul that desired God and had been realized by a mystical “seven thousand” among every sect and denomination in all ages. At the time Mr. Law wrote the “Appeal,” therefore, it was obvious to him that the purification of Gospel truth, and indeed of philosophy generally, was the work especially demanded by the needs of the times; and that the first step toward effecting it would be the refutation, once for all, of the fundamental error to which we have alluded. This being done by the “Appeal,” and the “Spirit of Prayer” included as a practical episode to point the application of the whole <note>The printed words "as suggested by his crowning discovery in theology" are crossed out in ink in the original.</note> it remained simply to show that the philosophy of the “Appeal” was fully capable of explaining the basis and reason of redemption, as well as of creation. The explanation of this point, therefore (which in effect involved a mention of the writings of Boehme), is the particular characteristic of the “Way to Divine Knowledge,” though it is also hinted at in the “Appeal.” In that work, the fall of angels and afterward of man—with all the natural effects and consequences of each in connection with the true reason and origin of this temporal system, and the exact parallel between the operation of the laws of eternal nature in the world at large and the operations of the same laws in man—are all explained and described as in a working plan. It was designed by a wise master-builder for the guidance of workers in building a new and eternal Temple for all nations to worship in together. Thus, the great object of the whole is not to open but to close the field of controversy between *unbelievers* and *Christians* by establishing the great fact: *(1.) that there is only one life and only one death throughout all nature; and (2.) that the proposal of that life, and the call from that certain death, is the sum and purpose of the entire Gospel.* To quote Mr. Law’s own words:

> “To embrace the gospel is to enter with all our hearts into its terms of dying to all that is earthly, both within us and without us; and on the other hand, to find our faith, trust, and satisfaction in the things of this world is to reject the Gospel with our whole heart, spirit, and strength, as much as any infidel can do, even if we made any number of verbal assents and consents to everything that is recorded in the New Testament.

This, therefore, is the one true, essential distinction between the *Christian* and the *unbeliever*. The unbeliever is a man of this world, wholly devoted to it; his hope and faith are set upon it; for where our heart is, there, and there only, is our hope and faith. He has only such virtue, such goodness, and such a religion as entirely suits the interests of flesh and blood, and keeps the soul happy in the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life: this, and this alone, is infidelity—a total separation from God and a removal of all faith and hope from him into the life of this world. It does not matter whether this unbeliever is one who professes the Gospel, a disciple of Zoroaster, a follower of Plato, a Jew, a Turk, or an opponent of the Gospel history.

This difference of opinions or professions does not alter the matter; it is the love of the world instead of God that constitutes the whole nature of the unbeliever.

On the other hand, the Christian renounces the world as his horrible prison; he dies to the *will* of flesh and blood because it is darkness, corruption, and separation from God. He turns from all that is earthly, animal, and temporal, and remains in a continual inclination of faith, hope, and prayer to God to have a better nature, a better life and spirit, born again in him from above.

Wherever this faith exists, there is the Christian—the new creature in Christ, born of the Word and Spirit of God <note>whether called Pagan, Heathen, Papist, Turk, or Jew</note>; neither time nor place, nor any outward condition of birth and life, can hinder his entrance into the kingdom of God.

But where this faith <note>and practice</note> is not, *there is the true, complete unbeliever* <note>however he may talk, or even preach about Christianity and salvation</note>: *the man of the earth, the unredeemed, the rejecter of the Gospel—the son of perdition, who is dead in trespasses and sins, without Christ, an alien from the commonwealth of Israel, a stranger to the covenants of promise, having no hope and being without God in the world.*

Here, therefore (adds Mr. Law emphatically), I fix my true ground for converting men to Christianity <note>that is, Christian-born skeptics; for to convert an intellectual outsider to the Christian faith, it is necessary first of all to let him understand the basis of nature and grace—the expressed word of God in love and anger—with its re-expression both in the creation and the human life.</note> And how miserably they err (he continues) who place Christianity and infidelity in anything else but in the heart being devoted either to this world or to God.”

In accordance with our plan so far, we shall here give the general contents of the “Way to Divine Knowledge.” Like the Second Part of the “Spirit of Prayer,” it consists of Three *Dialogues* which are carried on by the same characters, except that Humanus is now no longer a *silent* listener. This change is in accordance with an intimation given at the end of the “Spirit of Prayer,” and it reveals a brilliant trait of the author’s genius in the skillful adoption of the method of the ancient philosophers. Before them, to encourage reflection, to elicit the birth of philosophic truth in the mind, and to impart the understanding of their deep discourses of wisdom, the initiates were compelled to observe perfect silence for a specific period and were afterwards allowed to ask such questions as they were then unable to resolve themselves. Owing to the wisdom of this method and the self-evident nature of the truths proposed by our theosopher, Humanus, at the end of the “Spirit of Prayer,” evidently had no other alternative as an honest seeker of truth than to become a thorough convert to Christianity. Mr. Law conveys this interesting fact, and the precise state of his mind as a result, to his reader in the opening passage of the “Way to Divine Knowledge”:

> “Oh, Theophilus, I must yield; and it is with great pleasure that I now enter into conversation with you. You have taken from me all power of caviling and disputing. I have no opinions that I choose to maintain, but have the utmost desire to enter further into this field of light, which you have so clearly opened to my view. I shall not trouble you with the account of what has passed in my soul, nor what struggles I have had with that variety of heathenish notions which have had their turn in my mind. It is better to tell you that they are dead and buried, or rather consumed to nothing by that new light which you have opened in so many great points that I was quite a stranger to before. To reject all that you have said concerning the fall of angels, the origin of this world, the creation and fall of man, and the necessity of a redemption as great as that of the gospel, is impossible; nothing can do it or stand against it but the most willful and blind obstinacy. <note>Note Well.</note>

> But these great points cannot be received in any true degree without seeing the vain contention of all those who either defend or oppose the gospel without any true and real knowledge of them. One group contends for and the other opposes not the Gospel, but a *system of empty words and historical facts branched into forms and modes of dividing one church from another; whereas the Gospel is no history of any absent, distant, or foreign thing, but is a manifestation of an essential, inherent, real life and death in every son of Adam. It is grounded on the certainty of his real fall from that state into an animal, earthly life of impure, bestial flesh and blood, and on the certainty of an inward redemption from it by the divine nature given to him again.* These three great points, with all the doctrines, duties, and consequences that are essentially contained in or flow from them, are the *Gospel of Jesus Christ*, to which, through your means, I have become a convert. I am now, dear Theophilus, strongly drawn in two different directions. *First*, I am all hunger and thirst after this new light, a glimpse of which has already raised me, as it were, from the dead; and I am in the utmost impatience to hear more and more of this divine philosophy, which, I so plainly see, opens all the mysteries both of Nature and Grace from the beginning to the end of time. What I have heard from you when I was obliged to be silent, and what I have since found and felt by much reading of the *Appeal* and that *Dialogue*, obliges me to speak in this ardent manner. They have awakened something in me which I never felt before—something much deeper than my reason and over which I have no power. It glows in my soul like a fire or hunger which nothing can satisfy but a further view of those great truths which I this day expect from your opening to us the mysteries of heaven revealed to that wonderful man, *Jacob Behmen*.

> On the other hand, I find in myself a vehement impulse to become a preacher among my former infidel brethren, which impulse I do not know how to resist. For having just been converted myself, I seem to know and feel the *true place* from which conversion must arise in others; and by the reluctance I felt in my passage from one side to the other, I also seem to know the *true ground* on which infidelity supports itself. And only he who preaches nothing but what he has first seen, felt, and found to be true *by a living sensibility and true experience of its reality and power in his own soul* is able to declare any truths with spirit and power, or bear a faithful testimony of their reality. All other preaching—whether from art, hearsay, books, or education—is, at best, only playing with words and mere trifling with sacred things. Being thus divided within myself, I hope to have your direction.”
