At this point Mr. Law proceeds with the plan of his work, and the topics under which his instructions may be categorized are as follows:

**FIRST DIALOGUE.**—The entire foundation of the Gospel, based on the certainty of man's original perfection and of his fall and redemption. The primeval fire and light still remain within the human soul. Salvation consists in the awareness or reopening of this hidden divine life. How it differs from any natural goodness, and yet must become a habit of life. This doctrine of the fall is the best and only safe means of converting unbelievers. Its proofs are not historical but are found within human nature itself. The possibility, occasion, and manner of the fall are briefly sketched. The difference between the fall of mankind and that of the fallen angels. The certain redemption of the former. Gospel Christianity is only its actual beginning, as involved in the glorification of Christ's humanity. 

**SECOND DIALOGUE,** (which, according to what we have said above, may be considered as a resumption of the *Appeal*.)—Learned interpretations of Scripture, like religious opinions, are utterly useless. The only purpose to be considered in Scripture is its use in advancing the new birth of the divine life. Behmen is the only original guide to the philosophy of this new life. The nature of Behmen's disclosures. For whom his works are intended, and by whom alone they can safely be consulted. The impossibility of searching into these things by mere human reason. True understanding is derived from the Spirit of God working in man, just as He works in nature. Hence, the only way to Divine knowledge is the way of the gospel, which proposes the new birth as the means of attaining light and love. How the path to this birth lies entirely in the will. How the will of man rules his own nature, just as the will of God rules eternal nature. The nature of this will, as proceeding from the latent divine life or power of redemption. Faith is nothing else than the *working* of this new will. 

**THIRD DIALOGUE.**—Both nature and God are known by their manifestation in the mind. The entire basis of religion is explained. Nature and God are both defined. The birth and generation of the properties of nature, as set forth by Behmen. The first *form* or principle of nature and its three properties. Their beatification by the light and love of God. How they constitute the substance in which the all-present, all-working, *supernatural* deity moves and shines, or becomes perceptible. The stages by which they become materialized. In what state the original substance (*or nature*) was brought forth. Its fundamental constitution was never intended to be known. The reason for its discovery and the creation of temporal nature as a consequence of the fall. Into which elements the wrathful properties finally passed. The birth of fire. The understanding of nature in seven properties. The place of the sun in their midst, or the Copernican philosophy explained from transcendental grounds. The end of temporal nature, and a general review of the providential design connected with its origin, existence, and termination. The philosophy of regeneration. The birth of fire, or the fourth form of nature in regeneration. Admonition concerning the right use of the Mystery revealed in Behmen. The practical religious value of this philosophy. <note>The reader should keep in mind, amid all these openings of the ground and origin of things and seemingly non-essential knowledge, that the design of the whole, as we have repeated to excess, is all directed toward the author's goal: namely, the everlasting establishment of Christianity on its true basis of philosophy and theology, and showing how it may be experimentally tested by every true, seeking, rational spirit without a possibility of delusion; also providentially embracing its ultimate conclusion, as implied in the extract in the note on page 496.</note>

The "Way to Divine Knowledge" was published during the first half of the year 1752, and before June of that same year, it was followed by a tract (which is now the "First Part" of "The Spirit of Love") titled the "Spirit of Love; being an Appendix to The Spirit of Prayer. In a Letter to a Friend." The very short time that passed between the publication of the "Way to Divine Knowledge" and this small treatise leaves nothing to be added to the narrative part of our remarks until after its appearance. Accordingly, we shall at once proceed to a notice of its contents as in the case of the other books.

The doctrine that God is *love*, that Christianity is the religion of *love*, and that all its gifts and graces are the gifts and graces of *love*—along with the delightful explanations of this in the preceding works—was exposed to two objections from those who had even seriously begun the practice of a Christian life, though without any acquaintance with the science of mystical divinity. These people had been so captivated by Mr. Law's discourses that they imagined that from then on it was impossible they could be or do anything but *love*. In the first place, they would find, when the occasion for exercising this divine principle arose (as it necessarily would in the course of things, under the various trials of life; amid the contention, opposition, and injuries of the world; and worse than all, under the stinging passions, tempers, and sinfulness of their own evil hearts); they would find, we say, that they had only acquired a new system of religious notions, which offered them no practical relief in the hour of trial. Because of these feelings of disappointment, they would also recall to mind the numerous expressions in the Bible concerning the righteousness, justice, and wrath of God; and, judging according to their own standard of theology, they would find it impossible to reconcile such representations of the Deity with those of Mr. Law. Thus, no matter what they did, they would find themselves unable, on one hand, to practice that perfection of Divine goodness which the doctrine of love seemed to require of them in order to be consistent with their convictions (<note>in other words, they would feel through experience what Mr. Law had been demonstrating all along: namely, that it was impossible for nature to overcome itself</note>). On the other hand, the Gospel, in this new light, appeared mysterious and contradictory. From this, they would rashly conclude that there was no reality in this evangelical doctrine and that Mr. Law's interpretations of it, though they could not explain how, were only ingenious melodic fictions. And, if they were of a hasty temperament and too much under the control of self-will, they might perhaps angrily denounce mystical divinity altogether as an infatuating and dangerous delusion; and so they would proceed in their own unscientific, haphazard way of studying the analogy of faith, without any knowledge of its ground or aid from experienced tutors and guides.

It therefore remained for Mr. Law's farsighted prescience to meet these last objections and thereby complete his series of explanations of Christianity with a formal and complete demon-

stration, (1) that the Spirit of Love is not a dead notion, but a spirit of life, which can only arise in its own time and place, and from its own natural cause. And (2) that those expressions of Scripture which attribute the manifestation of wrath to God are absolutely true, though there is no wrath in the Deity himself.

This, then, was what he accomplished by the “Spirit of Love,” which is very properly called an “Appendix to the Spirit of Prayer,” and as such is certainly the very capstone of the author’s scientific Christian writings; it leaves nothing to be desired, nor a single question to be asked by the attentive reader regarding the way to God and salvation, and the means of overcoming all obstacles that may block his path. That which the “Spirit of Prayer” had shown to be an essential part of the Christian process—namely, the absolute and voluntary death to self—is supported here, indeed, strictly demonstrated, from the universal ground or reason of things. Thus, seeing the intrinsic nature of self and of the powers of this world, and seeing with the same open eye the nature, the relations, the transactions, and the efficacy of Christ as a Redeemer, everything speaks as with a trumpet voice and calls to prayer; in other words, there is nothing, whether it be good or evil, that does not conspire to turn the soul wholly to God. Such is unquestionably the essential instruction which every Christian believer requires (though, perhaps, not so philosophically demonstrated as is done by Mr. Law) in order to work out his salvation without becoming the subject of various delusions from time to time. And such an opening of nature, it is equally manifest, is the one thing necessary for the conversion of unbelievers to the Christian faith.

Mr. Law’s own statement of the case regarding the occasion for writing the “Spirit of Love” is as follows; and the reader may consider the words of the author as addressed especially to him:

> “You say: there is nothing in all my writings that has more affected you than that spirit of love that breathes in them; and that you wish for nothing so much as to have a living sensibility of the power, life, and religion of love. But you have these two objections often rising in your mind: *First*, that this doctrine of pure and *universal love* may be too refined and imaginary; because you find that, however you like it, you still cannot attain to it or overcome all that in your nature which is contrary to it, do what you can; and so, you are only able to be an admirer of that love which you cannot lay hold of. *Secondly*, because you find so much said in Scripture of a *righteousness and justice*, a *wrath and vengeance of God*, that must be atoned and satisfied, etc., that though you are in love with that description of the Deity which I have given as a being that is *all love*, yet you have some doubt whether the Scripture will allow of it.” It is the first of these objections only which is answered in the portion of the work now under consideration; and though we have inserted it at full length in the first section of this treatise (see p. 64–77), we here present a brief specification of its contents, which may be summed up under the following heads of discourse:

(“Spirit of Love”—“First Part.”)—The nature and perfection of the spirit of love. No man can participate in this spirit until he lives freely, willingly, and universally according to it. Its indispensable necessity as the means of union between God and man. The state of nature and of man as deprived of the spirit of love by reason of the fall. The process of its recovery by purification. The fundamental reason of this process revealed in a description of nature and its seven properties. The similarity of these properties in the nature and being of man. All evil is the consequence of nature working in self, or in a state of separation from God. All good is the power and presence of the supernatural Deity, dwelling and working in the properties of nature. How His presence and the birth of the spirit of love are the same thing. Being a spirit of *life*, it can rise in only one way and from only one cause. Its birth, by the kindling of eternal fire and the consequent transformation of the life. Hence the truth and necessity of the Christian redemption and the doctrine of the Cross.

A letter which belongs to this place, according to the chronology of our biographical sketch, was inserted as a note in pages 69–72. It is of great merit in many respects—among others as involving the philosophy of <term>Homœopathy</term>, and likewise the process of the refinement of the soul for the <term>sibylline</term> and the <term>philosophic work</term>, such as the <term>forty days proba</term>. But reference is made to it here as providing a further illustration of the circumstances which we have previously alluded to as usually active in calling forth the various works of Mr. Law, and the “Spirit of Love” in particular; we mean the continual necessity of correcting the illogical conclusions of persons (even those of education and piety) upon the presentation of pure original truth to their minds, and of preventing that relapse into their ancient, fond conceptions and fantastic ground, which was found to be an almost inevitable consequence of their confused understanding and disappointment. This latter was no doubt the case in the instances referred to at the foot of the note on page 94, and occasioned the correspondence alluded to there.

The following letter, which was addressed by the author to his friend Mr. Langcake about this time, demonstrates the patient assurance with which Mr. Law left the progress of his writings to the over-ruling Divine wisdom, and his caution in admitting any controversy upon the truths which he might consider himself the special instrument of reducing into a settled, classic form for all future generations:

> “My dear friend,—Upon reading the papers you sent me, I could not help giving you the trouble of this note to caution you against a danger which your pious zeal may bring you into. To desire to communicate good to every creature to the degree we can, and that it is capable of receiving from us, is a Divine temper; for this is how God stands unchangeably disposed toward the whole creation. And therefore it was an instinct of true goodness that prompted you to put *The Appeal*, etc., into the hands of your friend. But when this is done, you are to stop there. *Your ministry*, and mine also, is then at an end.
>
> The next thing that belongs to us, and which is also God-like, is a true, unfeigned patience and meekness, showing every kind of goodwill and tender affection toward those who turn a deaf ear to us. Consider it to be just as contrary to God’s method and the good state of our own hearts to *dispute* with anyone in contentious words as it is to fight with him for the truths of salvation.
>
> As to your friend, the *Remarker*, I fully believe him to be of a humane, candid, and generous nature.”

...and frank nature, of lively character, and much candor; but entirely ignorant of the depth of the heart of man, and the necessities of human nature.

As yet, though he knows it not, he is only at play and passing time; pleasing himself with supposed "deep inquiries after strict truth," while he is only amusing himself with lively, wandering images of this or that, just as it happens to start up in his mind. All his remarks, from the beginning to the end, are proofs of this.

Could he see himself in the state of the poor distressed prodigal son, and find that he is the very person recorded there, he would then, but not till then, see the fitness of that redemption which you have laid before him. But alas! he is rich, he is sound, light is in his own power, and goodness is in his own possession. He feels no distress or darkness, but has a "crucible of reason and judgment," as he calls it, that on every occasion separates gold from dross. And therefore, he must be left to himself, in his own elysium, until something awakens him from these golden dreams.

He expressed himself rightly when he said, "Truth was his game"; but the truth in question will not be caught while so pursued. He frequently ascribes the highest virtue to himself; and ventures to aver that he has every goodness that any Christian can have, faith excepted. I mention this not to charge him with arrogance and presumption—that is not the matter. He only speaks what he thinks. But the reason for his thinking and speaking of himself this way is to be found in these words of his: "Excuse," says he, "the hurry I have written this in, while I chose to spread my ideas before you, just as my head was warmed with them." And yet this heated brain, spreading out its ideas in a hurry, is earlier called a hunting after truth as his "game"; and, what is still worse, is considered as a "crucible of reason" that separates gold from earth!

Judge now, my friend, whether I mistook the matter when I said that he was only at play and passing time, or whether a man of the lowest understanding, talking about the search after truth and the crucible of reason, could more mistake the nature of them and himself than this gentleman with his lively character has done.

I thought it necessary to say this much of this matter. I shall now only add my request that, as you value the peace which God has brought forth by His Holy Spirit in you, and as you desire to be continually taught by an unction from above, you would on no account enter into any dispute with anyone. "He that has ears to hear, let him hear," may be enough for you, just as it was for our blessed Lord.

You need not check your inclination to help others in every way you can. Only do what you do as a work for God, and then you will have reason to be content with the success God gives to it.

As to what you mention concerning Dr. Middleton, I leave all to your own discretion. Dear soul, be humble; dwell in love, in meekness, and the spirit of prayer, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is yours. Adieu.
->W. LAW.<-

It has been supposed by some clever and much-to-be-respected modern inquirers into the truth of ancient natural and Divine <term>magic</term> (whose research, by the way, appears to have been directed by the obscure traditions and assumptions of the foolish medieval speculators about the mystery, and the supposed vestiges of its existence in the allusions of the Greek and Roman poets, rather than by the supreme light of the gospel, with its classic developments of theosophical science and orthodox mystical experience and discoveries; for in Christ are all the treasures and prerogatives of Divine wisdom and power deposited for the faithful, regenerate children of God, who are qualified to use them aright)—it has been supposed by them that Mr. Law was unacquainted with high <term>magian</term> philosophy. But we have his assurance that he never wrote upon any subject until he had made it his own; and he certainly treats this topic as a familiar one in a letter of the published "Collection" dated October 16th, 1752. These observations, coupled with the published letter and other remarks interspersed in his "Way to Divine Knowledge" and elsewhere, would lead an unprejudiced reader to infer that he well understood the subject of the *philosophical work* in its foundation, and the boundaries of all that was practical and true in alchemy. Hence, he could afford to smile, as he now and then does, at the blindness and vain efforts of pretended artists and philosophers, knowing from a perusal of their writings their relative ability or position in the regeneration. And when we reflect further upon his clear, theosophical apprehension of the powers of nature and the manner of creation—as sparkling through his observations and arguments in his "Letter on Warburton's Legation"—the matter seems to acquire the utmost certainty. For nature and her laws, eternal and temporal, must of course be mutually regarded in every operation of the Divine <term>magus</term>. Regarding the subject of popular clairvoyance, its *nature and limits*, we may, perhaps, recur to it again. Suffice it to remark for the present that the sacred mystery of the Divine philosophy and powers is not to be pierced by the spasmodic efforts of the ignorant mountebank or the expert ecstatic; for except a man be born again, and that according to the gospel comprehension, he cannot see the kingdom of God, nor enjoy the true light of the spirit of wisdom.

of philosophy. Reference is also made to the same fact in the note on page 46, where an extract is presented from a letter by Mr. Law to the celebrated Dr. Cheyne. And in the last work, also "*The Way to Divine Knowledge*," the philosophy of temporal nature was particularly described. The candidate may now perhaps remember how, in a Prospectus attached to the Essay entitled "*The Present, Past, and Future, with Regard to the Creation*," it was proposed to describe the process by which Sir Isaac Newton was enabled to declare the system of the universe. Now, all that would be sufficient for that purpose would be merely to enlarge upon what Mr. Law has said in the above references; as is in effect done in the following quotation from a modern treatise entitled a "*Suggestive Inquiry into the Hermetic Mystery*," the author of which does not appear to make any pretensions to a knowledge of the ground or reason of what he writes, nor has he any true acquaintance with Mr. Law's writings, but simply states the facts as they are familiar to science.

> "Attraction (says he), is the first principle of motion in nature: this is generally admitted, but the origin of this universal attraction is occult and incomprehensible to the ordinary human understanding. Repulsion is the second principle, and a necessary consequence of the first by reaction. Circulation is the third principle, proceeding from the conflict of the first two.
> All motion is derived from this threefold source in its reciprocal relations, which are diversified according to its qualifications with the matter. The attraction, repulsion, and circulation in the sun and stars move the planets in their orbits; the same principle in each globe performs the rotation on its axis, and the satellites take part in the same motion from their primary bodies. Every quantity of matter—solid, fluid, or gaseous—when separated from the rest by its quality or discontinuity, is possessed individually by the same principles; however infinite the variety of substances, natural or artificial, great or small: vegetable and animal forms and motions are no less evidence of these three principles than the heavenly and earthly bodies. Hence chemical affinities unite: one is attractive and the other repulsive; when either attraction or repulsion predominates in a matter, the circulation is an ellipse; but when they are in equilibrium, a circle is produced. Repulsion, being produced in its origin by attraction, equals it, as reaction equals action: but in nature one principle *is everywhere more latent or inert, or weaker, than another; and there are degrees accordingly, in which either predominates in external manifestation; hence the different degrees of natural affinity for union. There are also degrees of strength, from harshness to mildness, and (in the operation of these three principles) from the compaction of a hard rock to the close adherence of the particles of a globule of mercury or dew; from explosion to expansion, and from a violent whirling motion to a gentle evolution. But the medium is always, in the circulation, produced from the action and reaction of centrifugal and centripetal forces; and the equality of this forms a circle, as was before observed, which labors to harmonize the conflict of these two, and will succeed if the matter be duly qualified for it.*" And so the author proceeds, applying these truths to his own transcendental subject.

These are the principles which, along with their philosophy, are opened up in Mr. Law's work now under consideration, and were first revealed by Behmen. Now, herein we say, the whole matter in question may be perceived; for, apply these principles by the aid of Geometry and Algebra to the problem of physical nature—working with data, facts, and experiments bequeathed by previous philosophers, as referred to in Maclaurin; exerting therein a noble power of imagination and range of thought—and we arrive at the Newtonian discoveries. Methodize these principles, elaborate and experiment with true ingenuity and the necessary materials, and we produce the Newtonian *Principia* and *Optics*, leaving such points as are not discoverable as queries. (We need not follow Sir Isaac into his alchemic torture-house, where he endeavored to make earth generate heaven.)

This much may suffice in reference to the subject for the present work; it will be duly enlarged upon in the proposed standard biography of Mr. Law.

This letter naturally brings the Second Part of the "*Spirit of Love*" under our notice, which was published in January 1754 as a full and satisfactory answer to the second objection alluded to on p. 548, which the author had reserved for another letter. In the interim, however, he had allowed the circumstances of the case, as in the instance of the "*Spirit of Prayer*," to influence his choice of the manner and style of the work, and again resorted to the form of Dialogues, on this occasion between three characters, namely, *Theogenes*, *Eusebius*, and *Theophilus*; of which the first two were new conceptions, expressly adapted to bring out the design and instruction of the present work and to point the application of its arguments. (*Theogenes* and *Eusebius* might well represent Wesley and his brother Charles, supposing them to have continued a little longer under their tutor, *Theophilus*, instead of breaking with him and setting up on their own account in 1738.)

This answer is contained in the first two dialogues, while the third consists of a practical evangelical application of the whole philosophy of God and nature opened in the preceding treatises.

<note>Apropos of the Hermetic philosophy, we observed in our remarks above that "in Christ are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge," and that they are all the prerogatives of those who have the requisite "faith on the earth"—"all are yours." "Greater works than these shall you do," said Christ (after my glorification). All Divine magical arts and power must, therefore, be comprehended in these assurances and promises. — Again, Christ, the manifestation in the flesh of the universal Deity, the wisdom and power of God, is One; "the same yesterday, today, and forever." Therefore, all that ever was true in the ancient natural magical, oracular, and sibylline powers and revelations must have been only so because they were faint coruscations of the glorious powers that belong to our day and <term>seculum</term>, and which only await the summons of the true children of the mystery, according to the graduation and faith-directing instructions of the "*Grammar of Wisdom*." — Again, Christ says, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No man comes to the Father but by me." "The pure in heart shall see God." Now the way or process of Christ, according to its true and comprehensive scope, is taking up the Cross, total denial and death to self, and prayer without ceasing, or close adherence to God. Therefore, all that was efficient in all the arts and ceremonies of the ancient Theurgic and Eleusian mysteries, etc., etc., for the purification of the spirit from the contagion, cloudiness, and darkness of matter, and its gradual restoration, through the phantasmic centers of reason, to its primary, intellectual ground, could only be so because they were imitations of that purifying process of Christ and the regeneration of the virgin humanity implied in the above declaration of our Lord; but which the latter could only have taken place since the glorification of human nature.

Thus, in these and all other instances of efficient arts and practices for the divinization of the human spirit, so much regarded in the ancient mysteries, it might be shown how all derived their virtue and effect from Christ, and were more or less powerful as they more or less approached that</note>

Why then look for the arts and practices of attaining to the true supersensual ground of life among the rudimentary ancients, when all is so completely set forth in the most perfect form in the standard principles of the Gospel, in the genuine working out of the same by the mystics, and in the full noon daylight of the theosophy of Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme</note>? The subjects of the "Second Part" of the *Spirit of Love* are as follows:—The Deity is an infinite ocean of pure, overflowing love and joy. All nature and creatures were brought forth to manifest and rejoice in this love and happiness. Nothing can be in God which is not infinite and eternal. What wrath is in itself. It can be nowhere but in nature, and that only in a state of disorder. The origin of wrath and evil is the same. In man, it exists at the separation of his twofold life—of God and nature. All man's salvation and good come from the manifestation of the life of God in the soul. Perpetual inspiration is essential to a life of goodness. The ground of salvation is the inspoken word or seed of the divine nature. This is the subject of all revealed dispensations. The earthly self is to be resisted and renounced. Wrath is attributed to God because the creature has changed its state in nature and therefore must experience God as He is manifested in nature. How wrath originates in nature, even though nature is a manifestation of the Deity. God and nature are distinguished. Wrath is kindled by the will of the creature when it breaks or loses the union of the seven heavenly properties. The Deity is a governing love and wisdom, always seeking the restoration of lapsed nature and creatures. The texts of Scripture confine the working of wrath to the powers of nature. Vengeance is not allowed to man because that is a working with fallen nature. It belongs only to God, who is supernatural; that is, to the love of God (to overcome it). 

SECOND DIALOGUE.—The atonement of the Divine wrath or justice, and the extinguishing of sin in the creature, are only different expressions for one and the same thing. The analogy of Scripture teaches this. The atonement is the one work of regeneration, rightly understood. The sufferings and death of Christ are the gracious effects of Divine love and goodness. In what sense the justice or righteousness of God is satisfied by them. Man's original righteousness is his law. There is no peace until this is perfectly restored. God's being all love does not abate the force of the Scripture denunciations of eternal torments and punishments for those who live and die in sin. The popular doctrine of the vicarious suffering of Christ is erroneous and opens a door either to superstition or to infidelity. "Christ's suffering and dying are nothing else but Christ conquering and overcoming all the false good and hellish evil of the fallen state of man. His resurrection and ascension into heaven, though great in themselves and necessary parts of our deliverance, are but the consequences and effects of his suffering and death—his entering into possession of what he had obtained by them." "There is no wrath in God, no fictitious atonement, no folly of debtor and creditor, no suffering for suffering’s sake; but a Christ suffering and dying is the same victory over death and hell as when he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven." The necessity and efficacy of the sufferings and death of Christ are what gave him power to become a common father of life to all who died in Adam. They are only acceptable to the love of God on that account. How we, by virtue of Christ's complete process, have victory over all the evils of our fallen state and shall rise to the glory of Christ—the heirs of God. The Bible is to be studied in this simple, adorable light. 

The "THIRD PART."—The *practical ground* of the spirit of Love. The goodness and amiability of this natural life are easily mistaken (by mere reasoners and transcendentalists) for the spirit of divine love in the soul. The danger of this delusion. The doctrine and the spirit of Love itself are two very different things. How we are to acquire the spirit of love. The Scripture doctrine of election and reprobation in its true ground. The figures under which it is represented. Nothing is elected but the seed of the New Man, or the heavenly birth within us; all else is rejected unto death. There are two ways of induction into virtue and goodness. One is by rules and precepts, the other is by the spirit itself born in the soul; the former must precede the latter. What Divine love is, and its effects within us. All that we are and have from Adam as fallen must be given up if the birth of divine love is to be brought forth in us. All our natural contrariety to divine love must be lost and swallowed up in it, as darkness is in the light. This was the state of the first man, previous to the fall. Concerning darkness and light. The priority and glory of light. In itself it is invisible and only known by possessing darkness or substantiality. Light is immaterial, though materiality is always with visible light. All light, whether in heaven or earth, is only so much darkness illuminated. All nature and creatures, as such, are darkness, and therefore can only work according to the powers of darkness. Nothing is evil or tormenting except that which nature or self does. Self or nature consists of the three properties of desire thrown into a fourth property of wrath through the loss of their only (supernatural) good. There is no possible deliverance from self except by the new birth of God in the soul. Desire is the ground of life and all sensibility of life. How this is manifest in outward productions to the invisible and hellish world. The way of abolishing all evil, or the art of dying to self. God must be and do all; the state of heart that the perfect conviction of this truth induces. The results of a true practical conformity to this conviction, or the *spirit of prayer*. The "marriage of the Lamb," or the birth of the *spirit of love*. The one simple way to attain it, as shown here, is the one infallible way, because the will is the leader of the creaturely life. Christ, having obtained an infinite power over human nature, must sooner or later see all enemies under his feet—all subdued to LOVE.—

In the completion of this work, behold at length the comprehensive design of this illustrious sage; which began after it had been discovered to his understanding how the doctrine of love is the fundamental tenet and ground of the whole process of Christ, and ended only by the complete demonstration of it and the removal of every objection which could be made against it. has been made known in its philosophical ground, so as to show that the eternal manifestation of God through nature, as a consuming fire (which is the ‘infinite wrath’ or ‘divine justice’ of the theologians), is not contradictory to it. This, however, was accomplished through the work of Mr. Law, who has the honor of having first reduced into a popular form the explanations of Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme</note> in Freher—as regards this particular subject. These consist in showing (1) how the ‘eternal opposition,’ or the rising of the inferior properties which form the body or ground of the eternal (septenary) manifestation of God through nature, is ‘eternally overcome’ by the influx and mixture of the light and love of the Deity. (Without this opposition, there could be no manifestation at all, as there would be nothing in which a reflection of the supernatural abyss could take place.) This process converts that which might otherwise well be called a dark and fiery chaos into a resplendent crystal ocean or “glassy sea” of divine powers—the fruitful mother of wonders and the perpetual source of ever-springing new forms and figures of life, to the praise of the riches of divine wisdom and glory. And (2) how these (three) lower fundamental properties, when severed (N.B.) *in the creature* from their original union with the fountain of all peace and gladness—and therefore necessarily experienced as mere wrath and anguish—are again subdued by the omnipotence of the love of God. This occurs when resistance ceases in the creaturely *self-will*, according to the free agency of man; that is, by the full, hearty practice of the Gospel requirements. We say this had never been done until now; much less had it been seen how that love was the overruling principle of the whole material and intellectual universe, and therefore the one bond of union between all philosophy and religion, which it clearly is in the above outline. So much so that we venture to say, taking the works of Behmen and Freher in conjunction with the popular application of them by Law, we now have a perfect system and framework of theology and philosophy. In this, every person may learn how to find their true place and move freely in the will of God, and thus work, according to their particular signature, towards the full manifestation of the wisdom and wonders of the Deity. His spirit would then freely act through man as his peculiar instrument and organism; and so the practical fulfillment of our Lord’s prayer would be attained: ‘Thy kingdom come; thy will be done, on earth as in heaven.’ [All of which, it should be observed, is expressed in and would proceed according to the divine declaration of Christ, given as a sure rule for all ages: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness (in its truth and fullness), and all other things shall be added to you.’ And it was specifically to set nature right, and in a right order of working, that Behmen composed his practical treatise, *The Way to Christ; of Repentance and Resignation*. In his tract *Of Divine Vision or Contemplation*—which we intend to present to the reader shortly when we consider the philosophical regeneration of the medical art—we have a brief illustration of this divine, classic order of procedure regarding the study of philosophy.]

The effects of this opening of the *center of nature*—which was the specific design of Mr. Law’s *Way to Divine Knowledge* and of Behmen’s entire writings (*Resig.* ii. 1–22; *Four Compl.* v. 136, 137) to make a matter of universal experience—would be seen, for example, if it were general and duly appreciated, in a pure philosophy of medicine, by which sickness would be gradually eliminated. As a beginning of the system, to put it into working order, we have proposed the establishment of a Theosophic College. In theology, the errors and delusions of the field would appear in their native deformity, and “the truth” would become equally understandable to *all nations*. In the magical or alchemical science of the occult forces, universal magnetism, etc. (a conversing even face to face with the spirit of nature, she being ever accessible and responsive to the graceful approach and summons of the true vestal); and thus throughout the whole range of natural philosophy, nothing might remain a secret, further than to exercise the human *ingenium* <note>natural talent or genius</note> in its respective tastes and characteristics.

It is admitted that Behmen’s philosophy, as it stands in his own writings, is apparently opposed to certain ‘facts’ which are generally assumed to have been established by “science.” In geology, for example, it takes no notice of the submarine stratification of the earth and the formation of gravel and sand from the wearing down of rocks, but accounts for the existence of those vast deposits by the operation of other laws which form a part of his system. Thus, it has no need for the vast cycles of time which are alleged to have elapsed since the first creation of this globe. Accordingly, it is again at odds on this point with alleged discoveries in ancient chronology by certain modern savants of Germany. In astronomy also, it admits of only one inhabitable earth, and apparently disallows the motion of the sun with its attendant planets through the starry heavens (round a central sun, and that system again round another central sun, and so on, *ad infin.* et *ad absurd.* <note>to infinity and to absurdity</note>); leaving it incumbent on ‘scientific men’ either to *disprove* its first principles or to regulate their own conjectures and discoveries by its pure, *a priori* light. Some other particulars might be mentioned in which the philosophy of Behmen will be found to differ from the current opinions of individuals whose “science” is solely confined to the motions of body or matter and the theories that have been founded upon such observations.

<margin>position that /</margin>The answer as printed contains an interpolation of three or four pages, which were certainly never in the original as sent to Mr. Law’s correspondent. The <gloss>fact is</gloss> that Mr. Ward and Mr. Langcake, both resident in London, manufactured (so to speak) a few of these letters from originals or copies which they had by them, cutting off certain portions from one letter and appending them to another according to their own taste and judgment. Finally, perhaps, they persuaded Mr. Law himself to touch up the parts which did not fit well together; he was also willing to please them and saw a little *providential use* in it regarding himself, to which we shall later allude. The passages thus inserted in *The Scruple letter* extend from the paragraph beginning "Do not my Friend," to the one ending "supernatural God of love." This interpolation, as we shall later notice, was a refutation of objections made concerning his books—as well as the writings of Boehme—in the empty, silly letter of "Mr. Horne of Oxford" (afterwards the bishop), a manuscript copy of which had been sent to him for reading from Ireland shortly after its appearance. In it, the writer affirms that "God is justice and truth as well as love; and his offended justice cannot pardon sinners until it has received an atonement, etc.," to which the interpolated remarks are especially directed; and likewise regarding Warburton.

To perceive the consistency of the letter as it originally stood, and the spirit of Mr. Law's mind at this period, as well as the explanation of the point just described in this work, we would recommend the candidate here to read the entire epistle as if restored to its original state. Indeed, it ought to form a note to the "Spirit of Love" in case of a republication of that treatise, instead of being placed among his letters.

We have more than once alluded to the extensive correspondence of Mr. Law, chiefly with those who sought his advice on account of his reputation as a casuistical divine <note>A theologian specializing in resolving moral problems or "cases of conscience."</note>, possessed of extraordinary light and solidity of judgment. Though, we may here remark, he was far from encouraging the recourse which his admirers thus had to him as a sort of confessor; rather, he enjoined them to be done with him as soon as they were convinced of the truths set forth in his writings, and to resign themselves wholly to God in the spirit of prayer. Letters of this kind from individuals, both learned and unlearned and of various ranks of life, had accumulated while he was engaged in writing the preceding work, so that at last, when his hands were free, as he informs Mr. Langcake, "he hardly knew what to begin first." Among others which had lain unanswered during this period was one from the *Countess of Huntingdon*, a devoutly-disposed woman who had given herself up to the zealous propagation of certain peculiar—or what she considered "evangelical"—views of the Gospel. Being a person of wealth and rank, she had necessarily become a kind of general or tutelar patroness of that class whose doctrines had captivated her taste and awakened her zeal for their promotion. We allude to the so-called doctrines of "Calvinism," which—by using the words "free grace," "predestination," "divine sovereignty," "the elect," "Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated," and other corresponding terms and ideas made up from isolated passages of St. Paul's Epistles (according to our English translation), and so chiming in with the sound of scripture truth—had a very attractive effect, particularly as they appeared to be highly honoring of "sovereign grace" and correspondingly demeaning of "vile, wretched, sinful man." And such is the mystery of the divine kindness and overruling wisdom regarding the ignorance and perverseness of human nature, that many souls have been turned seriously and lastingly to religion by hearing such doctrines preached and receiving a lively impression from them.

This little circle was only one among the numerous bands of enthusiastic, pious souls, at the head of whom were several devout clergymen who spread themselves over the country with all the earnestness and zeal of recruiting parties in God's service. Among these, the mystical writings of Mr. Law made a great commotion (not indeed unlike that of a blue pill <note>A common 18th/19th-century mercurial medicinal pill used as a purgative.</note> in the bowels of a very disordered constipated person). Of course, they were unable to understand Mr. Law's philosophy but obtained a glimpse here and there of what seemed contrary to popular views or their interpretations of Scripture, and which—thereupon, according to the common practice, assuming the office and capacity of judges—they solemnly condemned. It was not so easy, however, to overthrow Mr. Law's theology by argument. Accordingly, when Lady Huntingdon inquired of some of them their opinions about his writings, especially his exhibition of the real scripture doctrine of the atonement, their only refutation of it was a dogmatic affirmation of their own crude conceptions of it, with scripture quotations to support them; and when pressed by her more

We have not denied that sincere piety and true devotion to God might exist under the pitiable views (called the "first reformer's refreshing views of Christ" by the author of the "Christian Student," and "blessed soul-saving doctrines" by others) of those who, like Lady Huntingdon herself, were taken with Christianity and had entered zealously into it from the captivating and plausible representations alluded to, such as "unconditional election," "free grace," and the "imputation of Christ's righteousness to the sinner." It is quite natural for piously disposed but unlearned, untutored persons to fall suddenly under the delusion of such doctrines when they are earnestly preached to them, since enthusiasm, by its very nature, is contagious. But such people would do well to consider the remarks, commencing with "You tell me, my friend," to "these doctors" in the letter of Mr. Law's published "Collection" addressed "To a Clergyman of Bucks," as well as various other portions of these letters relating to the same subject.

We may be permitted to express our hope that the preceding letters and observations, and the researches to which they are intended to lead the reader, will at length abolish the fallacy concerning an outward atonement or sacrifice as commonly understood, and lead to a view of the divine procedure and atonement of Christ in that infinitely more ravishing light which springs from the central and cardinal doctrine of all: that God is *Love*. This view preserves all that is really touching and affecting in the former view and adds to it the overwhelming evidence and truth of a self-evident proposition. For, if God is love, then he can have no purpose toward man—his original son and heir—but what is essentially *full of love*; and all that he has done can be with no other object in view than that of enabling man to avoid the wrath of nature and enabling him to receive that indwelling of himself for which he created him, and from which alone can be derived any degree of happiness, wisdom, and perfection.

A special subject which occupied Mr. Law's attention this year (1754), after completing the "Spirit of Love," was the final settlement of the foundation of the schools and almshouses at King's-Cliffe, previously mentioned. At this time, it appears, the Master of the Boys' School became ill with no hope of recovery, as a result of which some inquiry had been started for a proper successor, and an application was received from a candidate in London. These circumstances were the occasion of the following two letters to Mr. Langcake:

> Feb. 9th, 1754. — My dear Langcake — I thank you heartily for your two letters. Had there been even more, they would have been very welcome to me. For I love to hear you talk.
> The reason for the enclosed letter is this. We have two Charity Schools in this town, one for the full clothing and education of girls, and the other for boys. A Master for the Boys' school will likely be needed in a short time.
> I know no more of the writer of the enclosed letter than his letter tells me, nor have I answered it. If you would be so good as to go to the school in Westminster where he says he was and engage in some sort of conversation with him—asking if he did not write to me, or receive an answer to it, or whatever you please, only to see his manner, etc.—I should be much obliged to you. He may, for all I yet know of him, be very proper or improper to be the master of the school. I want to have a young man who is an *awakened Christian*. I need describe him no further to you.
> There is a library of books of piety given to the school, which are to be lent out by the master to all the neighboring parishes. There is a very handsome house for the master, free from all charges of every kind. There is a salary of twenty pounds for the master and thirty shillings yearly to buy firewood. It is a pleasant situation for anyone who is the awakened Christian that I want.
> If this person should have left that place, please inquire after him, and if he is in London, find him. If he should not appear to be the man we want, I desire you to see among your acquaintance if you can find one. * * * I kiss you with the lips of my heart. W. Law.

> "King's-Cliffe. March 2nd, 1754. — My dear friend — I am sorry to put you to the expense of this letter, which is only to inform you that I have received your last, giving a further account of Mr. Holyday over a dish of tea.
> The master of the school is dead and buried. And upon consideration of your true, just, and well-meaning character of Mr. Holyday, I have made choice of a young man in the neighborhood for the school. I heartily thank you for the trouble you have taken in this matter, which I gave you on the supposition that you or your friends might know of some young sprout of piety who would have rejoiced at the offer of it.
> May the God of love and mercy and goodness in Christ Jesus bring forth the everlasting birth of heaven in your soul. W. Law."

To this year of Mr. Law's life properly belongs a notice of the improvement of medicine in the present day through the discoveries of Hahnemann, originally suggested and worked out—like the Newtonian philosophy—from the principles of Jacob Behmen. That Mr. Law foresaw this refinement of the healing art at no distant period—in fact, its elevation to the standard of the universal philosophy and its future practice with all the certainty of the exact sciences—is only a fair inference from certain expressions in the letters we are about to quote, as likewise from what he states concerning the nature of wrath (and body) in the Second Part of the "Spirit of Love"; and especially when we consider the basis he had for making such observations in the actual philosophy of medicine formally opened by Behmen (in his "Signatura Rerum," "Divine Vision or Contemplation," "Mysterium Magnum," and other of his writings, with the clarifications by Freher (see p. 322, §. xxiv., and elsewhere in his works). The second letter, to the first paragraph of which we call the reader's particular attention in connection with the subject under notice, is dated October 10th, 1756, and is consequently presented out of chronological order; but for this, its connection with the subject must be a sufficient excuse:
> "My dear friend,—I was much concerned at the account you sent me of the state of your health, and think it very advisable to seek help. But there is the difficulty: where to find it. Everything is so very superficial in the *art of medicine*, and based on such a poor foundation, that one has little reason to prefer one physician over another, except for his personal temperament and behavior. Air and gentle exercise, if pursued consistently, must be greatly beneficial to you. If your physician is right for your purpose, he will not load you with apothecary medicines, nor should you submit to anyone who does. Nothing can assist you but some simple regimen that gradually lessens the feverishness in your blood.
> My dear brother-pilgrim, be of good comfort; our road of life is such that weakness can help us along as fast as strength. Use outward medicines as if you used them not. The *universal* is within you, and whether you find it in a sickly or a healthy body is but a small matter.
> Daily, hourly [earnest prayer and] thankful resignation to God in everything is the best regimen you can enter into, both for soul and body. Every good wish attends my dear fellow-traveler out of time into eternity."

<margin>Aurora, chapter 2, sections 11, 113-19, 37.</margin>
Doubtless, if Mr. Law had had the time and opportunity, he would have followed the example of Boehme and suggested to the practicing physicians of his day a mode of searching into the philosophy of disease and its remedies, so that an art of such immediate and unremitting importance might no longer stand on "so poor a foundation"—depending exclusively on *a posteriori* data, which can only be ascertained at the expense of much suffering and danger to the subjects, and is otherwise so blind and uncertain. Indeed, we would not undervalue experimental science in any department, but it must always have a tendency to lower the understanding and close the eye within its own narrow limits in proportion to how much it is separated from *a priori* philosophy. Hence, Liebig's "Animal Chemistry," Oken's "Magnetism," etc., are only so many advertisements and aids to materialism, and some of the most confirmed skeptics are men eminent in "science." As a general illustration, however, of what we mean by a *pure philosophy of medicine*, we give the following outline:
Premises: (1.) There is a double virtue or twofold power of good and evil in all earthly things (as indicated in *Genesis 2:17*). (2.) All disease or sickness is the hunger, irritation, or fierce, undue action of some one of the <term>seven properties of nature</term>.—Hence we conclude:
*Regarding a person in health*: The powers of nature are in due proportion or equilibrium in the human body. There is no excess, no morbid excitement; no organ is too stimulated, too active, or too inactive; instead, heat and cold, or centripetal and centrifugal action, balance each other, and the circulation is equable.
*Regarding a person in sickness*: There is excessive action in one of the seven properties, the ailment being an overly eager stimulus, hunger, or desire. This abnormal action may be centripetal or centrifugal.
*Regarding medicine (whether vegetable or metallic)*: It contains both the two actions and the seven powers, but unequally.
*Regarding the cure*: It arises from the hunger (or the life in the blood) taking the power (or powers) from the administered medicine that will soothe or strengthen and satisfy it, so that it finds in that property what it requires. [Hence, the greatest science and experience are required not only in the <term>medicus</term> <note>physician</note>, but also in the artist preparing the medicine, to purify it from its wrathful properties and "body of death" so as to leave a pure, quintessential <term>tincture</term> and vitality, and then to incorporate this into a pure vessel so as to cause the respective properties to predominate, each in the exact degree and order that is necessary.]
*Regarding the influence of medicine on health*: The very property that cures or harmonizes would disturb the equilibrium of a healthy person, and so, inversely, create a disease of that kind.
Thus, the good and the evil combined in nature constitute medicines; and where there is disease, which is evil, the good will be taken to satisfy it. But if nature is in equilibrium, or good,

For the *seventh property or body of nature*, concerning the circulation of *life*, is in a peaceful state as long as the six properties work harmoniously together within it; but it becomes disordered in proportion to how much that harmony is disturbed, and thus it perishes. We see this on a small scale in many diseases that form scabs, and in the nature of illnesses and sores.

And this, by the way, is the basis of vaccination—the seven-fold body reacting to the virulent affection of certain properties from another body. Since this was such an *original* and *on-its-face* irrational theory and discovery, we would very much like to see the library list of Dr. Jenner, the reputed discoverer of this wonderful means of protection from that predominant deadly condition. We would like to see whether there were any little square volumes in it published between 1640 and 1665. We would also just suggest, *in passing*, concerning any radical and universal morbid action, that there is a corresponding inoculation which acts as a medicine to it; though it may produce another disease that would require a cure through the proper, effective transmutation. <note>The current practice of medicine is necessarily based on these principles, but there is so much irrelevant and coarse impurity alongside the living, tincturous properties in it, and so little enlightened understanding of the basis and workings of the degrees of nature among practitioners—not excepting the *homeopathists*—that the practice of it is little better than guesswork. It is not carried out with a sublime understanding of the nature of the disease and the remedies it requires, nor does it immediately adjust them in number, weight, and measure to the needs of the case; rather, as we say, it proceeds by blind, partial experience.</note> The hints above regarding Jenner's discovery also apply to the circulation of the *blood* (or the *life in the blood*), alleged to have been discovered by Harvey. They also apply to the pretensions of physiognomy, phrenology, etc. <note>Annotation: *Hydropathy*, when scientifically practiced, is perhaps the most effective popular art of physical purification yet discovered. It is founded on the basis of the heat and cold of life, or centripetal and centrifugal action. Its operation consists in promoting a free outflow of the vital fire through all the tissues of the human body, from the center to the circumference, or the *exits* of the pores of the skin. However, long-continued, regular physical exercise, such as walking, has a refining effect. The vital fire (provided it is duly supplied with pure fuel) is thereby made so brisk and free that it consumes all the impurity and coarseness in the blood, generating pure fleshly matter. Indeed, it renders the body an almost transparent organism, as was evident in the individual who was reported to have walked a thousand miles in a thousand consecutive hours last year (1850).</note>

If we were to dwell on particulars of this nature, we might show through numerous instances the philosophy of the generation of *living matter* by the various workings of the seven properties, both within the subject and in outward nature, and thus describe the boundaries of *a posteriori* as well as *a priori* philosophy. In this case, we might draw an illustration from a theosophical correction and orderly expansion of Swedenborg's theory regarding the way he says the “soul generates the body.”

For Swedenborg is entitled to high and complete respect as a philosophical genius and a scholar up to the year 1744, or the period alluded to in the following extract from a publication “on the writings of Swedenborg” dated Wakefield, 1782, by Wesley. (See also Pike's “Swedenborgianism Depicted,” Derby, 1820, and “Inquiry Respecting Swedenborg,” Manchester, 1794):

> “Many years ago the Baron came over to England and stayed at the house of a Mr. Brockmer. He informed me—and the same information was given to me by Mr. Mathesius, a very serious *clergyman* (both of whom were alive when I left London and, I suppose, still are)—that while he was at his house, he had a violent fever. In the height of it, being delirious, he broke away from Mr. Brockmer, ran into the street naked, proclaimed himself the Messiah, and rolled himself in the mire * * * From this time, we are undoubtedly to date that peculiar species of insanity which stayed with him, with scarcely any intermission, until the day of his death.”

The writer of this text quite concurs with this latter opinion. This conclusion comes after reading and hearing all that his most recent, complete, and ingenious biographer could argue in daily private conferences over several months. This biographer admitted that, since he had become acquainted with the basis and philosophy of Behmen, Freher, and Law (through the writer), Behmen was the great original light he had been seeking for years—and whom he had [in his invented scheme, or “Biographical Sketch, Rich, London, 1849”] made Swedenborg the personification of. But we propose to expand on this point when we come to consider Mr. Law's allusion to the “Arcana Celestia.” The reader who has read the “Biographical Sketch” will, by this time, undoubtedly be prepared to smile at the relative position Mr. Law is made to occupy in that work by the then-uninformed conception of the author, as well as at the gross absurdity of the assertion that Law was supposed to be the author of the *Arcana Celestia*!!—along with numerous other equally romantic statements. To come to the point: Swedenborg, in his researches up to the period named, as an ingenious and learned philosopher, had explored, as it were, backward to the very borders of physical nature. Wanting to understand what was beyond on the *a priori* side, and thus the dwelling place of God, but having no acquaintance with the ground and truth of gospel regeneration—which is the only gate of entrance to it—he was brought to a dead standstill. What did he do then in this dilemma (assuming his recovery from his illness)? Why, by a leap of *pure imagination*, he jumped over the wall. (His biographer described his procedure to the writer “like a man in a balloon descending in the middle of China and immediately beginning to write a description of the country and its inhabitants; therefore, he had no need to *explain* his basis or produce his divine credentials”!!) And so he solemnly resumed his ‘researches,’ writing about the spiritual world according to his knowledge of the material world, with which he makes it perfectly analogous, as he could do no other way. But, knowing nothing of the true origin and history of the latter and its present degraded state, his accounts of the spiritual world are more revolting to sober natural sense and Christian understanding—and overall more depressing—than even Mahomet's descriptions of it.

His writings, therefore, from the aforementioned period (partially including his work “On the Worship and Love of God”), are to be considered the outpourings of pure imagination and a disturbed brain,

Therefore, when devout and enlightened people read his writings expecting some *divine chord* in their souls to be struck by a similar harmony in the speaker, they are forced to set his books down in disappointment. They experience not the slightest spark or sound of spiritual vitality and response, but find everything to be cold, *moon-like death*; just as one might naturally expect from the reasonings of a kind and talented Hanwell lunatic—everywhere, indeed, are indications of “a fine genius, majestic, though in ruins,” but no holy spirit or divine life. The writer has not only told his admiring, imaginative biographer this but *proved* it to him in every instance he cited to the contrary: that regarding theology, the Baron’s writings were no more needed or useful to the world than “a fifth wheel to a wagon,” being entirely superfluous, even in those parts where he hits upon a vein of truth. He argued that after the publication of this current work, the Baron's writings, along with the delusions they caused, would only become one of the century's passing wonders. And while laughing honestly and heartily with those present at the absurdities of some of the Baron’s theological works (for example, *the most evangelical treatise mentioned above, while suggesting as an excuse that it might be like a poem*), his biographer candidly admitted that, understanding the *mystery of nature* as he now did through the light of Behmen and Law, if he were to write the “*Sketch*” again, he would do it very differently. Furthermore, if Behmen’s foundation and account of the origin of things were true, then the Baron’s entire theological <term>system</term> was a mass of delusion. Therefore, let those disciples of the Baron who *love and desire truth* consider this for themselves: if Behmen’s foundation, principles, and manifestation of the birth and order of things in eternity and time are true (and is not every lit, *burning piece of coal* in this world a demonstration of the *fall* of angels and eternal nature?), then the Baron’s theological writings are a *mass of delusion and falsehood*. There is no doubt that his writings have been helpful to some inexperienced and well-meaning minds, but they would have benefited much more from studying established orthodox writers on mystical and practical Christianity and supersensual truth. But to return to the main subject.

It is enough to repeat that the fundamental renewal of medicine follows the same laws of nature as every other science and results as naturally from the universal philosophy of Behmen as do the discoveries in planetary motion and electricity that we mentioned earlier. Therefore, it was always on Mr. Law's mind as one of those great developments—or rather, established laws of science and art—which would certainly happen as surely as tomorrow's sunrise, only waiting for a practical person to achieve it. This event *partially* occurred about half a century later, as we have already suggested, the agent being *Hahnemann*, whose famous formula <term>*Similia Similibus Curantur*</term> is the exact reflection and translation of the expressions Behmen used when speaking of medicine in his <term>“Signatura Rerum,”</term> and which Mr. Law so well understood in their foundation and philosophical application.

We take this opportunity to comment again on the ignoble spirit of certain men regarding their discoveries; who, having derived the actual basis, elements, and principles of their so-called discoveries from Behmen, Law, and others, have always carefully hidden the source. We charitably assume some did so out of “fear of man,” but we are nearly forced to believe it was mostly due to a desire for personal gain in money and honors. We have previously mentioned how Behmen is the sole origin and basis of Sir Isaac Newton’s reputation as an original philosopher, for his mechanical or mathematical talents are not the true source of his worldwide fame. We may add that the very ambiguous way he treated the <term>*vortical theory*</term>—allowing both sides to claim him as an authority—is fully explained by his debt to Behmen, since he could hardly have provided a definite doctrine on the subject without the source of the whole matter becoming obvious. As for Hahnemann and others mentioned above, we have said enough without returning to the honors and wealth that poor Behmen provided for them. Nor will we mention at this time others we are considering, hoping they will realize that it suits the noble philosophy they study to do everything possible to make the original and universal *panacea* known.

We have Euclid’s and Newton’s ‘Principia’ of mathematics and mechanical philosophy. Hahnemann’s work, regulated by high practical experience in the several various prevailing modes of cure, should have formed a *Principia* of medicine, or of the qualities of nature, whether in harmony or disorder in the body. And this work may serve (for the present) as a ‘Principia’ of the spiritual nature, of theology experimental and theoretic, embracing a *Principia* of electricity, natural as well as *divine*—awaiting the grand *Principia* of the Universal Scale of Wisdom and Life, illustrated with the needful diagrams and symbols, descending from the central throne of nature down to the lowest feces of her forms. The editor of this book merely proposes by it to give a general design or working drawing thereof, which must exist before the work can be completed; though in the present instance, the design is not to be considered a mere artificial invention of the imagination, but as a glance at, or index of, natural wisdom and forthcoming events, even introductory to the second coming of the Lord, who, when the work is complete, “will descend and crown his bride,” just, indeed, as Adam the first crowned the previous six days’ creation.

We have indicated herein the sources of a far more perfect Philosophy than was ever enjoyed by the Ancients or *Schoolmen*.]

<margin>were/</margin>
We may remark here that Mr. Law was now well advanced in years, and that his activities during the intervals that occurred between our notices of his active and more public life must have settled into the more meditative routine so fitting for old age, though the earnestness and vivacity of his spirit were never quenched. It was with him, indeed, as with the autumnal season of the year, when the noblest fruits of our temperate climate become fully ripe. Or as with the oak, when it towers in majestic strength after growing for ages, only becoming more firmly rooted by the lapse of time. The masculine vigor of his classical understanding and high wisdom, as we have already remarked, not only remained unimpaired even to the last hour of his life but increased in strength and brightness; and we can hardly conceive a more suitable illustration of this, or a more fitting conclusion to such a life, than his “Address to the Clergy,” of which we shall shortly speak.

The second letter is as follows:—
> “Sept 10th, 1755.—My dear Langcake—You receive this only because it will cost you nothing. But I find pleasure in writing it because it is to you; and you can have no pleasure in reading it, unless because it comes from me.
>
> Mr. Ward has persuaded me to reprint *The Case of Reason*. I have revised and corrected it, and have sent it by my nephew to Mr. Ward to be printed, provided he will take the trouble of proofreading; as it is being published at his request.
>
> Mrs. Hutcheson thanks you for the little book by Boehme. She joins with Mrs. Gibbon in their hearty regards to you. I am, with much truth, your most affectionate friend and servant, W. Law.”

Accordingly, we find that the “Case of Reason” was published in a “second edition, revised and corrected,” in 1755. In this edition, a few of the references to the leading publications and authorities that were prominent twenty years earlier were omitted. The work was now presented as a complete and independent treatise, whereas the former edition had *Part the First* on the title page, the author having clearly intended to address the subject more universally. But either the changing times or the circumstances of his own life delayed the completion of that intention, and it was never publicly resumed; though the writer of these lines, while looking over Mr. Law’s manuscripts, found several hundred pages of what appears to be a continuation of the work. This pamphlet, it should be remembered, was only an argument written in the most perfect manner, according to the purest scholastic science of all ages; but—as Mr. Law himself observes (in the letter of Sept. 8th, 1754)—“nothing of this kind touches [convinces] the Deist.” Whatever it was, therefore, that at first delayed the appearance of the Second Part, it was ultimately set aside due to the author’s acquaintance with Boehme (as we may indeed infer from the second paragraph of the letter we have just provided dated Nov. 25th, 1754), which enabled him to do effectively, and on the philosophical principles of revealed nature, what he had formerly proposed in the “Case of Reason.” This work, however, as we have said before, has its own intrinsic and peculiar merits. The class of unbelievers to whom it more particularly applies may be seen by a reference to Tindal’s book, which it aimed to answer; and it is equally applicable to the weakened and feeble modern forms of the ancient classic infidelity. At the beginning of the year 1756, "*A Letter to the Reverend Mr. Law*, occasioned by some of his late Writings," was published (as alluded to in the note on p. 91) by the celebrated John Wesley. <note>About this time Mr. Law was preparing for the press the Tract shortly afterward published under the title of "Christian Piety freed from the Delusions of Modern Enthusiasts of all denominations, by *Philelathes*."</note> The reception of a copy of Mr. Wesley's rash and childish outpouring is acknowledged by Mr. Law in these words, which we extract from a letter addressed to his friend, Mr. Langcake, on the 24th of January:—"I have much to thank you for in the zeal and diligence you have shown in sending me Mr. Wesley's letter. But I am sorry you and Mr. Richardson <note>the publisher</note> should have wasted so many franks, for I was in no eagerness to see it soon, nor under any expectation of being obliged to take any notice of it." In fact, no one knew the philosophical and mental caliber of Wesley better than Mr. Law, or could be less disposed to take advantage of his own superiority. The truth of this and the nobleness of his spirit are proved by his allusion to the subject in a letter to Lady Huntingdon, which he might well commence as he did, remembering what he himself knew and had experienced of Mr. Wesley’s disposition, as well as what he had seen and read of its effects as displayed by the author of the "*Enthusiasm of the Methodists and Papists compared*" some five years previously. We ought to observe in referring to this Letter that the lady to whom it was addressed had written to Mr. Law upon the subject and very justly remarked on the great good accomplished by the Methodists amid all their apparent disorder. <note>See the letter in the "Collection," dated Feb. 16th, 1756. Also one under date of Sept. 1756 to Mr. Langcake, and an unpublished one to Dr. Byrom of April 30th, 1757.</note>

We have noticed how Lady Huntingdon sought the acquaintance of Mr. Law and corresponded with him (though, by the way, we very much doubt the authenticity or seeming authorship of the letter attributed to Miss Gibbon in the compilation of "the Life and Times of Lady Huntingdon"). The origin of that acquaintance may perhaps be traced back to Lady Elizabeth Hastings, of pious memory, who had sought Mr. Law's spiritual directions but without giving her name. Her opinion of Mr. Law, apart from a knowledge of his books, might have been strengthened by what the devout Bishop Wilson had said to her, as we have presented on p. 356.

The following letters, written on the occasion of her sickness and death to either Lady Anne or Lady Frances Hastings, the half-sisters of the deceased lady, though out of the order of time, may not be unacceptable in this place. We may also just remind the reader how Mr. Law cleverly took occasion to pay a tribute of respect to the memory of that blessed lady in his "Animadversions upon Trap," published in the same year as the date of the last of these Letters:—

> "[1739.] Madam,—I pray God to direct me to say that which is proper for your state and condition. I agree with your ladyship that your situation has been very advantageous to your piety: for that good lady your sister, with whom I suppose you have spent most of your time, must have been very beneficial to you. And I have some fear upon me that she is your suffering friend, for whom you are so concerned.—Pious persons may depend upon this as an infallible truth: that when their trials and sufferings increase, or attack them in a new manner or with unusual violence, it is because God has fitted them for them and intends them some new degree of perfection thereby. When the time came that our blessed Savior sweat drops of blood, it seems as if he then had no merciful Father in heaven; and yet this greatness of distress came upon him immediately after he had made this prayer to God, namely, 'Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,' etc.—A plain proof to us that when we fall into the greatest distress, then is the time that we are most of all under the tender mercies of God, and only drinking our share of that bitter cup which God mixes for those whose prayers for their sanctification have been most accepted by him.
> 
> Your apprehension of your lack of true faith, resignation, and pure love to God is what I much like. It is good for you to know and believe this of yourself. And these virtues are then in their most beneficial state to you when you can discover the least of them and are, in your own thinking, the farthest driven from them. This is one benefit that we receive from our present disordered and corrupt state: that the confusion of our passions and the evil workings of flesh and blood conceal our virtues from us until we are in such a state as to be able to possess them without vanity. These storms and tempests help to make us sail with safety, and our greatest danger is in a calm, where all seems to be well.
> 
> There is nothing we so much wish for as to see the progress, growth, and stability of what we call our own virtues; and we are apt to think that we are then best advancing when we feel no opposition to such virtues stirring in our natures. But this is a delusion of self-love. For though
