Even if piety is a work of light, in a true and good sense, it grows best in darkness and must receive its purity from the fire of opposition, which seems to blacken and destroy it. This is most certain: we never deeply feel the smallness and imperfections of our own virtues until we have advanced far enough to hunger and thirst for righteousness. While we have only a natural, superficial love for any virtue, a small amount of it satisfies us, and we are seldom disappointed by it. But as soon as any virtue begins to be divinely active within us, it is sure to stir up everything in our nature that is contrary to it. For just as every virtue aims only to destroy the contrary vice born in us—which has grown in our nature for some time—every vice in our nature will fight for its own life. It exerts its strength most intensely through strange impulses when it is in the greatest danger of being destroyed. This is why people far advanced in humility will sometimes feel such struggles and impulses of pride that they never knew when they were less humble. It is the same with every virtue: as it grows, it provokes and stirs up its enemy; the stronger the virtue, the more violent its enemy becomes. For the greater a virtue is, the more it contradicts our corrupt nature, and consequently, the more it is opposed by it. And this is the *darkness* and *fire* through which every virtue must, by the grace of God, achieve its true purity.

We all have a twofold nature, which the Scripture calls the "outward" and the "inward" man. One is from above; the other is the mass of corruption derived from our fallen ancestors. All the mystery and perplexity of a pious life arises from the struggle and conflict between these two natures, and because we do not sufficiently distinguish our sins from our miseries.

Because some people have an easy natural temperament and delight in the outward aspects of religion—being as content with their own piety as they are with everything else they possess—they view this mental serenity as a sign of progress in piety and believe they possess all the blessings of a religious life. But most of these people are very little of what they believe themselves to be; the best among them are like gold that has never been refined in the fire. On the other hand, there are others whose piety is deep and constantly arising in the inward man, yet they find they cannot control the impulses of their outward nature.

->* * *<-

The second letter is as follows:—“Jan. 19th, 1740.—Madam,—Since I rarely see the newspapers, I did not hear of the death of Lady Elizabeth Hastings, of blessed memory, until sometime after the public had been informed. For two or three mail days after this, I felt a strong urge to write to your Ladyship, which I continually resisted; then, in the next mail, I had the honor of receiving your kind and obliging letter. This led me to view it as something truly providential.

My intention in writing to your Ladyship was to ask you to write an historical account of that blessed Lady’s spirit, life, and virtues, from your first knowledge of them, so that a memorial of her virtues might be shared with the world.

I recently discovered by accident that this good Lady had written several anonymous letters to me; it troubles me to think that I did not know I had such a correspondent at the time.

The way your Ladyship should respond to this great event in your life is to practice the highest acts of love and gratitude toward God for blessing you with such a close relative, whose virtues have been so eminent and edifying to this part of Christendom. This special circumstance of your happiness should fill you with the greatest comfort and ignite your heart with the sincerest fire of love for God. Observing the high character of a piety so dear to you—arising from your own flesh and blood—you are called to make an absolute gift of yourself to the glory and praise of God. You should desire nothing but for His will to be done in you, so that everything you are, have, and can do may be a sacrifice and service of love and devotion to Him who has called you. God has called you to take the place of your blessed sister, to maintain her spirit, life, and virtues in the world.

The way to be everything and do everything that God expects from you is the *way of love*. Let love be your religion, and then all the Law and the Gospel are fulfilled. *God is love, and whoever dwells most in love dwells most in God.*

Therefore, consecrate your heart to this Divine love <note>[as shown in the *Life of the Good Armelle*]</note>. Let it begin, sustain, and finish everything you do; then everything will equally benefit you and unite you to God.

To see all things as coming from the love of God, to do all things from a motive of love for God, and to be absolutely and gratefully resigned to Him in all things—this is a state of heart that consecrates everything around us and makes every internal and external change an equal blessing to us. An unlimited faith and resignation to God—which, with closed eyes, always says "God be praised"—and a pure, selfless love that seeks only to do or suffer everything in and for the love of God, is the only piety that is infallible. It is subject to no delusion and must lead the soul to its highest perfection. Every state of piety, though good and sincere, is subject to harmful scruples to the extent that it lacks this unlimited faith and pure love. It becomes perplexed with itself, always needing new light and new methods, constantly researching its own inward progress, and filled with anxious doubts about the number and greatness of its virtues. <note>[These remarks clarify the basis of Mr. Law’s criticisms of the Methodists in his treatise on *Regeneration*.]</note> The way to obtain this faith and love is to expect it and seek it solely from Jesus Christ—from His nature, spirit, and life brought into us by a faith that is always hungering and thirsting for His flesh and blood.

I hope your Ladyship is directed by God to choose the retirement you mentioned. I cannot advise you to completely stop the visits you speak of; since you make them not for self-gratification, but as prudent concessions to the order of human life, they will not harm your piety and may have better effects than usually occur. At the very least, it will be time enough to stop them when they appear to have ill effects. Good and edifying conversation is not always available, and yet your Ladyship may be edified even when you are obliged to say nothing.

Dr. Balthazar Walter. The responses are announced as not being according to external reason, but according to the spirit of knowledge, based on the principles of which the author has given the—

I have recently published a short work on “Christian Regeneration;” which, if your Ladyship has not seen it, I would be happy to send along with another small one currently in press, <note>the *Answer to Trapp’s Sermon?*</note> I shall always be exceedingly glad to hear from your Ladyship as often as it is not troublesome for you; and when your Ladyship honors me again, please send the letter by the Post. I remain, with hearty prayers to God to make you a true successor to the piety of your blessed sister, your Ladyship’s most dutiful, obliged, and obedient servant, W. Law.” To resume our notice of the published “Letter.”

Mr. Wesley seems to have been well aware (as the observations attributed to him at the end of the fourth volume of his Journals, in treating the ability of controversial writers, sufficiently testify) that no one had the power to inflict a more effective and lasting injury upon his claim to learning and philosophy—while still giving him full credit for his ingenuity, sincerity, devotion, and zeal—than Mr. Law. And if we did not well understand his mental constitution (shown indeed in his “inability to keep a secret”), it would have surprised us that he should have been so lacking in prudence and judgment as to presume that his right *intentions* were sufficient to shield him from the punishment usually inflicted with military precision by capable and severe casuists and enlightened theologians upon such offenders as himself. Still more surprising was the rashness of this attack upon Mr. Law after having recently suffered so much at the hands of Bishop Lavington, as we shall presently notice; assured, as he must have been, that if the former should condescend to take up the lash, the strokes would fall upon him with tenfold severity. Though possibly, his knowledge of Mr. Law’s principles might have led him to presume that he would be spared, remembering his observation in the “Answer to Trapp,” that “by the grace of God he would never engage in personal contention with any man.” Besides, there can be no doubt that his publication was the result of a sincere regard for what he conceived to be the interests of truth and Christianity. As we hinted in the second paragraph of the note on p. 361—common with other so-called evangelical writers since, who have not been trained in the strictly mathematical and classic discipline of thought and judgment, and who entertain eccentricities and strong views on particular theological points—he thought that Mr. Law was really unacquainted with the true and simple nature of the Gospel and therefore that he was in duty bound to try to set him right. This was despite what the latter had recently written at the conclusion of the first dialogue of the “Way to Divine Knowledge.” Indeed, it is evident from this publication that he felt a ‘great concern’ and even ‘pity’ for Mr. Law’s “ignorance of the way of simple faith” and of “justification,” and for his “fall into the mysticism of Jacob Behmen. . . . . .”

But to return to the Letter to Lady Huntingdon, in answer to her remarks on Wesley, we observe by it that Mr. Law was evidently now obtaining a glimpse of the peculiar character of his own Gospel call and mission. This was not only to make the whole world see, as if with open eyes, the philosophy and nature of Gospel Christianity (see pp. 524—530) as their birthright and atmospheric element, but also to endeavor to unite all the struggling, contending divisions and sections of Babylonian Christianity (as he expressed himself most justly on another occasion, “*Babel is not a city, it is the whole Christian world*”) into the unity of the spirit of the one simple, original Gospel church. “As to myself,” (he writes; see the entire letter in the “Collection” dated Feb. 16th, 1756), “I seem to myself to have no other part to act, nor any call to anything else in this hurry and struggle of zeal against zeal in such a variety of forms, but only and fully to assert the true ground, and broadly open all the reasons, of that one inward regeneration, which is equally the one thing necessary to every sect, and the only thing that can make any sect, or method, or outward form, not hurtful to those that adhere to it.”

We find from the same letter, as Mr. Wesley has himself admitted, that Mr. Law was once a “kind of oracle” to him. Indeed (as we have already stated, and are prepared to show by a series of extracts from the sermons and other publications of Mr. Wesley), Methodism itself is nothing more than a superstructure, of which the primary foundation is Mr. Law’s “Serious Call” and “Christian Perfection” as the true spirit and interpretation of the fundamental obligations and duties of the Gospel; these are to precede, give birth to, and then be the fruits of and strengthen the regenerate life. What Mr. Law adds concerning Mr. Wesley’s “subordination to his own spirit” is verified by all the acts of his life. These acts, notwithstanding his sincerity, devotion, and zealous practical application of the Gospel, testify that he did not experimentally understand, much less love, that great mystical, evangelical truth of the <term>all-workingness</term> of the Divine nature and the consequent necessity of *death to self*. In further proof of this lack of philosophic understanding, and at the same time of the good reason he thought he had to sit in judgment on the subject of our memoir, we might quote the remarks on Law inserted purposely in his “Journals.” For example, there is the passage where he designates Mr. Law’s treatise on *Regeneration* as “philosophical, speculative, uncertain, Behmenish, void, and vain,” and adds, “O what a fall is there!” In explanation of this, we ought to state that the objectionable points among the peculiarities of Mr. Whitefield’s Calvinism and Mr. Wesley’s doctrine of “faith and its tests” (which he had imported from the “Germans”) had been fundamentally examined in Mr. Law’s book, and their trivialities exposed in our author’s usual incontrovertible and lucid manner. Mr. Wesley, finding by this that a few of his favorite, novel constructions and theories of doctrine were grounded on mere temperament, and supposing these peculiar notions to stand at the heart of his evangelical system, felt very angry. We presume that as a matter of conscience, but with the weakness peculiar to him, he endeavored to cast shame on that book in his published selections and compilations from his Journals. His judgment of the matter has necessarily been the rule for his unquestioning followers up to the present time. Now, however, the tendency of the age and the liberal education which the respectable members of the community receive enable them to see things in their true natural and historical light; it even permits them in some instances to venture to look at Mr. Wesley’s proceedings in religion in the same light as they would view a schism and rebellion, under the pretense of greater spirituality, within their own body.

One of the ministers of that community, and one who occupies a very respectable position in the esteem of his brethren, made the following candid admission to the writer of these lines, af—

after having had Behmen's philosophy presented and explained to him, though only in a general way:—"I have (he said) previously read through all systems of philosophy, and am now convinced that Behmen's is the only true philosophy. They are, as it were, but parts of the circumference, while this comprises the center and the whole of truth." Such an admission in Wesley's day might, if known, have subjected the speaker to a *Galilean* condemnation.

An equally characteristic example of Mr. Wesley's understanding in the passage is his "Journals," where he alludes to Mr. Law's *Spirit of Prayer*: "There are many masterly strokes in it" (see vol. ii. p. 14,) up to the word "Christianity." Also, regarding his ability as a controversialist and strength of mind (notwithstanding his recently mentioned adventurous flippancy toward Mr. Law), see his Letter to the London newspaper, inserted in his Journals, vol. iii. p. 18, 8vo. ed., dated September 17, 1760. This letter claims to be an answer, and of course a refutation, of the charges against him in Mr. Law's published "Collection of Letters"; but it will be seen, by reference to them, that Wesley, as usual, has not given the original words, but his own version of them, which he has put in quotation marks to mislead the reader, as if they were genuine extracts from Mr. Law; and he has taken care to omit altogether those passages which constitute the gravest reflections on his character!! Yet this letter, placed intentionally in his "Journals" for posterity, constitutes his sole defense against the accusations in Mr. Law's "Letters."

On all of which we remark, that those who are inclined to maintain that Mr. Wesley was a logician must mean a logician of the flabby, weakened modern system of mental training, and not of the ancient, classic, rigorous intellectual discipline. Undoubtedly the views we have attributed to him regarding Mr. Law were the settled conviction of his mind, though a most egregious mistake. We have previously alluded (p. 94, 5) to the letters which he sent on breaking with his former tutor and spiritual parent in 1738 (which correspondence and procedure on Mr. Wesley's part, by the way, the judicious and pious editor of the Periodical of 1797 candidly laments): when, after leaving Mr. Law for a time and becoming acquainted with the "United Brethren," whose lifestyle, communal and devotional practices, etc., were necessarily highly appealing to a young, optimistic spirit full of an earnest desire and intention to be active in religion—he gave himself up to the propagation of these views and idiosyncrasies as the true understanding of evangelical Christianity. This is not an uncommon case, for you will find a young man who has served only half an apprenticeship to a business enter into a venture on his own account and, obtaining some sort of success in his own way, give himself up with impetuous passion to a new course of life, at the same time ridiculing the regular and respectable business habits of the old merchant or trader; and he may go on prosperously, chiefly by reason of his extraordinary energy and perseverance. Thus Mr. Wesley, when he found the effects of his newly adopted doctrines and preaching, attributed such results to these new opinions, or rather specific ways of thinking and expression concerning the atonement, faith, imputed righteousness, justification, etc.; forgetting all the while the sober, self-denying, humbling *gospel preparations* for the new birth in which he had been so formally initiated by Mr. Law's early writings and conversation. Whereupon, full of the passion peculiar to his character—*a quality, by the way, most invaluable and essential in itself for great purposes, especially when coupled with the discipline of self-government and strict, orderly business habits*—and of those new and enthusiastic interpretations of St. Paul's words about "faith" and "justification," he turned against Mr. Law in the manner related in the correspondence previously mentioned. And so far from profiting from what he then suffered, he, like a man willfully determined to receive punishment and martyrdom, rashly returns to the attack in the manner shown in the publication now in question.

The following is the beginning of this published "Letter," which, as it has been omitted from Wesley's collected Works, we provide here; it also justifies certain statements by ourselves as to the respect and veneration in which Mr. Law's abilities were held by the writer of the letter. It is further to be observed that the printer did not attach his name to this publication:—

> “REVEREND SIR,—It will be easily allowed by impartial judges that there are few writers in the present age who can compete with MR. LAW in beauty and strength of language; readiness, liveliness, and richness of thought; and (in many points) accuracy of sentiment. And these uncommon abilities you have long employed, not to gain either honor or promotion, but with a steady view to promote the glory of GOD and *peace and goodwill among men.* To this end, you have published several treatises which must remain as long as England stands as almost unequalled standards of the strength and purity of our language, as well as of sound practical divinity. How great a service these have been in reviving and establishing true, rational, scriptural religion cannot fully be known until the Author of that religion shall descend in the clouds of heaven.
> I cannot but earnestly desire that the fruit of these, your labors, may increase a thousandfold! I would gladly contribute my small part to make your writings still more useful; particularly the “Treatise on Christian Perfection” and the “Serious Call to a Holy Life.” Will you pardon me, Sir, if for this purpose I take it upon myself to mention something in your recent writings which seems not altogether consistent with them, nor equally conducive to the great end you pursue? Can you bear, Sir, that I should do this (I hope with modesty and respect, but yet with great plainness of speech), especially where I believe the revealed truths of GOD, and even the very essence of the gospel, are at stake.
> It may indeed seem strange, not only to you but to many, that someone like me should presume to speak this way to YOU, a person superior to me in so many respects beyond all degrees of comparison. But in some respects it is not impossible that the advantage may lie on my side. For (1) a dwarf standing on the shoulders of a giant may see farther than the giant himself. (2) Being conscious of my own weakness and liability to err, I am open to instruction from others, whereas it is doubtful whether you think any man in Great Britain is capable of instructing you. (3) *I am a man of one book.* In matters of religion, I regard no writings but the inspired ones. *Tauler, Behmen,* and a whole army of mystic authors are nothing to me compared to *St. Paul.* In every point I appeal to

Thus says the preface. But while Mr. Wesley thus flattered himself that he, “though but a dwarf in intellectual stature, was capable of seeing much farther than his former director, by standing upon a giant’s shoulders” (if he could but find such a personage), what was his astonishment when Mr. Law’s “Letter to the Bishop of London, regarding Warburton,” appeared as it did in the following year? Warburton, as we have suggested, had fiercely attacked Wesley and the Methodists, and Mr. Wesley might have been on the lookout for someone with adequate evangelical knowledge and scholastic ability to give his antagonist a taste of his own medicine (*quid pro quo*) when he finally heard of this publication. He undoubtedly obtained it immediately and read it with the delightful expectation of seeing the great opponent of Gospel evangelism severely scourged by someone he knew had the power to do it perfectly—indeed, to everyone's admiration. 

We say his astonishment was great, not merely to find his expectations in this respect fully realized, but to discover on almost every page of that pamphlet that what he had previously regarded as the advanced experimental Christian science unique to himself and the Methodists was treated throughout as mere basic Gospel knowledge. From time to time in his discourse, the author seemed to seize the reader, carrying him up as if on the wings of an eagle and exhibiting to his astonished vision glimpses of the entire field of Gospel truth—of the relative extent of which he previously had not had the least conception. As Mr. Wesley subsequently extracted almost the whole of this work in his published two volumes of “Selections from Mr. Law’s Writings,” we may conclude (for he did not afterward venture any more public judgments on Mr. Law’s later writings) that he not only looked upon Mr. Law with that trusting reverence which characterized his mind until he met with the “United Brethren,” but that this feeling toward him grew into a kind of awe, not only because of his abilities, but for his vast and sublime Gospel learning. 

In line with this, indeed, in his more mature years—though he did not actually make a confession of his early rash judgments and actions, except to confidential friends (see the bottom of page 91)—he acted like someone who was really sorry for them. He settled into a firm regard for many whom he had violently opposed in the first passion and inexperience of his itinerant ministry. 

<note>Not feeling, however, quite satisfied with the judgment an impartial future generation would pass upon him after reading Mr. Law’s remarks and observations in the “*Collection of Letters*,” we find the following appeal to mercy (*ad misericordiam*) introduced into the preface of his “Sermons.” These were specially revised by him for publication toward the close of his life:—“Are you persuaded (he writes) that you see more clearly than I? It is not unlikely that you may. <note>He no longer mentions “standing upon a giant’s shoulders”!</note> Then treat me as you would desire to be treated yourself if circumstances were reversed. Point me out a better way than I have yet known: show me it is so by plain proof of Scripture. And if I linger in the path I have been accustomed to tread, and am therefore unwilling to leave it, work with me a little: <note>this, after what transpired, as related on pages 94 and 95!!</note> take me by the hand and lead me as I am able to bear: I can go but feebly and slowly at best; then I should not be able to go at all!! May I not request of you further, not to give me hard names <note>referring to Law’s description of Wesley’s “Address to the Clergy, etc.”</note> in order to bring me into the right way. Suppose I were ever so much in the wrong, *I doubt* this would not set me right. Rather, it would make me run so much the farther from you, and so get more and more out of the way.” <note>!!</note> And this was the manly and elegant style of thought and composition by the man who had been the bold critic of Mr. Law! The actual instability of his judgment regarding the nature of certain favorite terms or topics of Gospel doctrine (through not understanding the philosophy of Christianity) will be readily discoverable by a reading of the doctrinal discussions related in Garrett’s *Digest*, 1827, pages 240–258. These certainly are more worthy of a council of schoolboys than of persons professing to instruct the world in the true theory of revelation. It was doubtless the reflection upon this intellectual blindness, and the exposure of his continual contradictions (*saying and unsaying*) then existing in print against him, that rendered Mr. Wesley <note>once so full of confidence</note> so very submissive at this period of his life.</note>

Continuing our observations on the published “Letter,” we cannot help but conclude that its author would have shown much greater wisdom had he simply pursued his own specific business: preaching the Gospel, converting souls, and forming them into little societies and bands all over the country. In doing this, we say, he was laying the groundwork for the civil and political improvement and growth of this nation (and the progressing renewal of the world) which has since followed as the result of the moral cultivation and regeneration of the root of society. He should have left philosophy and learning to those who are capable and skilled in hidden truth; for he was entirely unfit for handling such subjects, as is proved by his own journals, which are full of evidence of his ignorance and misunderstanding of such authors. 

His “Letter” to Mr. Law is described by that gentleman in the following words, in a presumed letter to Mr. Langcake:—“Mr. John Wesley is a clever man, and the reason why his letter to me is such a juvenile composition of emptiness and *rudeness*, falling below the character of any man who had been serious in religion for even half a month, is because it was not ability but necessity that put his pen into his hand.” 

We were desirous of testing this judgment by placing the letter in question in the hands of a lady for her to read. She is a member of the Wesleyan body and a great admirer of the benefits and superior advantages of such a community regarding the popular spread and cultivation of the blessings of practical piety and holiness, but who is also well-informed regarding the grounds and reasons of the Christian faith. The remark of this lady, then, after reading the pamphlet and being asked her opinion upon it, was in these words:—“It is not worth reading; there is no argument in it. It is like an ignorant person quoting an author’s words he does not understand and saying, ‘Isn’t that absurd? Who ever thought of that? Where do we find that or that in the Bible?’ Poor man! He meant well; he was a good man, but he couldn’t reason. Mr. Wesley was not made for philosophy: his talent was only practical.”

The “Letter” indeed is nothing but an inconsistent selection of sentences or *fragments of ideas* taken out of Mr. Law’s works, without the slightest understanding or grasp of the author's basis or principles. Indeed, we are sorry to say that Mr. Wesley stooped in this letter—whether intentionally or not is for the reader to consider—to actual misrepresentation of Mr. Law’s words. The

> "March 20th, 1756.—My dear Langcake,—I have sent you by the carrier of this week, in a parcel that comes to my nephew in Cornhill, a packet, in which is a letter to Mr. Freelove, and the *Letter* you desired, that was written to a Clergyman upon the point of going into the Roman Communion. I should be glad if you would see him, and from what you see of him, give him any of my books which you think will be most useful to him. Buy them, and take money from my nephew for them. * * *"

We have already observed that of the same empty, perverse, and stupid character as this published "*Letter*" are the "*Strictures upon Law and Behmen*" by (the then) Mr. Horne, in *Jones's account of his life*. This latter (a clergyman), it may be mentioned, edited a work called "*The Scholar Armed*," in which he awarded high praise to Mr. Law's defense of High Church principles in the Bangorian controversy: distinguishing our author's "*Three Letters*" as "incomparable for truth of argument, brightness of wit, and purity of English" (as did the "*British Critic*" only still more laudatorially in reviewing the "*Scholar Armed*"), but adding in a note: "We know and lament that the excellent Mr. Law afterwards adulterated his Christian doctrines with many novel and unsound speculations; but when he composed these Letters his mind was in its purest state; and they have no tincture of the errors he afterwards fell into during a life of too much abstraction and solitude." (The reader will here refer perhaps to our note on this subject at p. 92.) The truth of the matter is, Mr. Law, when his mind was more mature and independent, could not fail to observe how little the cause he had championed in his early days had to do with the real interests of Gospel Christianity; and it is possible that, in an impartial mood, he might even have given in to the representations of the nature of ecclesiastical authority (namely, distinguishing mere papistical, artificial, "apostolic succession" assumptions of authority from the true spiritual inherent authority of holiness in pastors, and order in the assemblies and worship of Christians all over the world) by his opponent and reviewer, Gilbert Burnet, M.A. 1718, whose work we would again recommend to be perused along with Law's "*Three Letters*" as stated in the note of p. 52.

The "*Letter*" (under review) Mr. Law then treated with that disregard which it merited; "for there was not anything properly argumentative in it." Indeed, for him to have attempted a reply would have been merely to write his series of books over again. There might also have been other reasons for his silence: he knew, for example, that when he came to deal with Warburton, as he probably felt he should soon be called to do—after his usual manner of not only knocking down the unsound supports of his antagonist's superstructure, but of rebuilding the edifice with all the materials in their right order of construction—he knew, we say, that such a procedure would include in its embrace all that could be necessary to subdue Wesley. He was also well aware, from private letters which came to him, and some of which are now extant, that much good was done by Wesley among the lower orders, and on this account might forbear to reply, being unwilling to throw the least obstacle in the way of any good he might be able to promote by diminishing his title to respect. Besides all this, Mr. Law, as we have before remarked, deemed it improper to take notice of any aspersions cast upon himself or his writings until a providential opportunity of so doing fairly presented itself; which he was aware would assuredly be the case through the harmonious working of nature, if he were not too hasty in anticipating the divine regulation of events. Accordingly, in the case before us, about four years after this period (Mr. Law being then about seventy-four years of age), his friends were solicitous for his permission to publish such letters of his as they could collect together that might prove of public edification. Here then was the opportunity presented to him to do justice to himself and bestow correction on his inconsiderate adversaries, which he skillfully availed himself of by inserting merely a few additional paragraphs, refutatory and ironical remarks, and reflections in certain of his letters, which, as the results evinced, were quite sufficient for the purpose; though his correspondence was by no means improved by similar alterations attempted by his friends.

We have observed that Mr. W. [Wesley] was completely in Law's power had the latter been capable of making "a mock of him"; and we may add that a weapon had been ready formed to his hand, had he required such auxiliary assistance, by the witty and learned Bishop Lavington, whose work, "*The Enthusiasm of Methodists and Papists compared*," had reached a third edition in 1752. In this book (and it is distinguished by a surprising amount of wit, genius, and labor), the proceedings of the Methodists, as disclosed in their own publications, are handled with the strict severity and unsparing criticism of one who is equally a master of strong sense as of sound learning, and fully capable of administering the judicial chastisement which his knowledge of human nature and the evidence before him dictated. The work consists of Three Parts, the first two of which were printed previously to the third, and were aimed chiefly at Whitefield, though Wesley is also no—

noticed therein. While the author is quite mistaken regarding the true intentions of those individuals—which he attributes to some Jesuitical or adventurous motives—the impartial reader should remember that this was a work written in *self-defense*. It should only be condemned to the extent that it actually misrepresents their intentions, and because it is itself imperfect due to a lack of greater seriousness and spirituality in the "Right Reverend Father in God," the author. For in the first place, Messrs. Whitefield and Wesley were in open rebellion against the author and his assistants, their lawful superiors, and this was contrary to their ordination *oath of obedience*. Secondly, they had preached, and were still preaching vehemently, against their fellow clergy (both deceased and living). In short, they were actual *revolutionists* against the established order of their profession and society. Lavington, therefore, was only maintaining a legal right, which he believed could be done most effectively by exposing to the test of reason and sound judgment the ignorance and delusions that were so heavily mixed with the ranting proceedings of the "Methodists." He sought to show that certain transactions or events, which they attributed to the Spirit of God as a divine confirmation of their preaching, were in fact mere fanaticism. Thus, we say, he was acting like a true bishop by attacking those he considered the enemies of ecclesiastical order and the plunderers of his flock. He used weapons of ridicule and defiance because they were best suited to the nature of the assailants; otherwise, such tactics would have been unjustifiable for a Christian watchman and overseer, regardless of the work's value as a labor of criticism and history.

The Two Parts first printed drew an answer from both of the people it attacked (Whitefield being the most conspicuous figure in it, as he was the originator of Methodist itinerancy); but our business is solely with Mr. Wesley. <insert>[A reading of "God's Dealings with George Whitefield, by Himself," and of the "List of Books sent out to him in Georgia by Mr. Charles Wesley," will provide a glimpse of the influence of Mr. Law's writings on his life, as well as on the evangelicalism of the American Continent, no less than that of England, etc.]</insert> The personal charges implied and expressed in Lavington's work were, as we have suggested, harsh and far from merited; for as weak as Mr. Wesley may be considered regarding his judgment on obscure topics, his religious motives were indisputably fervent and sincere, and his intention to do good was pure and simple. His reply to Lavington only brought a Third Part of the work before the public, in which it was now his turn to be the most prominent figure and pass completely through the *fiery ordeal*. In referring the reader to the preface of this part of the work, which takes the form of an Epistle to Mr. Wesley, it may be well to observe that the author's successful illustration of the peculiarities that distinguish every wide and ardent attempt to evangelize the ignorant, common, and brutal populace would have appeared in a somewhat different light had he reflected on them as accidental circumstances that must always accompany such a promotion and cultivation of good. Indeed, the very justice of his comparisons between the Montanists, the Papists, Pietists, Jesuits, etc., and the Methodists, ought to have suggested this to his mind. The truth of the matter is that he has written an admirable *textbook and index*, without intending to do so, regarding the instructive parallels found in different ages. These illustrate the *inseparable working of the Spirit of God and the spirit of fallen nature* within humanity; or the intermingling of good and evil so intimately that the one is seldom stirred to great activity without exciting the other.

The argument in the latter part of the letter (forming, as we say, the Preface to the Third Part of "The Enthusiasm of the Methodists and Papists Compared") is all very just and good, but it falls far short of the subject, which is finely presented in Mr. Law's "Answer to Trapp's Sermon." How, we would ask, are the masses of the lower classes (or indeed their superiors), who are swallowed up in sensuality and worldliness and are totally unacquainted with this "sedate, composed piety" and "steady course of sincere, habitual, unaffected religion" reflected upon here, to be roused out of their insensibility to divine things and spiritual death? This can only be done by men of faith, anointed by the Holy Spirit with true Christian zeal and love for their souls, rushing in among them and—at the risk of their own lives amid beatings, scourgings, etc.—snatching such "wild heifers of the devil" from destruction. It was this spirit that truly distinguished the first three generations of devoted, self-denying Christian men and women among the Methodists. Having themselves been the slaves of sin and vice and rescued by the proclamation of the gospel, they could not resist the holy impulse to go and preach the same divine love and humility to their poor, deluded brethren, who were steeped in brutality and sin and hastening toward everlasting misery. As for the objections regarding the irregularity of such proceedings, and the ignorance and even abstract sinfulness mixed with their movements and preaching, it is, as we have said before, no argument at all against the divine inspiration of their efforts. It is solely attributable to undiscerning ignorance and to the fact that the people were subjects of what may be called a new and magical action—the measure of the good they receive being greater than the attendant evil, provided that the manifested excitement is only the accompaniment of honest and sincere efforts to draw near to God. It would be easy to explain further the reason for this twofold working of good and evil when the sincere zeal of religion begins to operate, but it must suffice to point out that the Spirit of God has in all ages moved souls with such holy zeal against sin and evangelical love for the souls of sinners. In the present case, whatever extravagances might have occurred amidst such a mass of mixed materials, the good that was brought to life was like a small seed sown. Springing up under the favorable aspect of Protestant principles of civil and religious liberty, it became, as we have observed, a chief source of the current extraordinary exaltation of this nation and the progressing improvement of the world.

The distinguishing characteristic of the Methodists, compared to all previous revivals in the church of Christ, is that they have always kept to the simple words of Scripture and its *prima-facie* sense (leaving the implications of its scope and spirit to the "poor, dark, bewildered mystics"). Although their doctrine is distinguished by no more science and knowledge of the foundation of truth and nature than appears on the simple surface of Scripture—as understandable by a peasant—yet their plan of action, mode of evangelization, and discoveries of improved means of reaching and regenerating the root of society in the lower classes (as witnessed by the City Mission and Ragged School principles and American evangelical activities) in the introduction of the

Gospel into new locations, disregarding all presumed opposition, and pursuing the goals of their society—actually establishing themselves and forming a core group that grows into a large church body, which constantly offers the advantages and blessings of enlightened spiritual Christian fellowship and effective evangelical methods—all this, into which Methodism may be said to have resolved itself (though setting out with more general and vague views), is not only strictly in line with apostolic practice but also reflects the most experienced judgment of the people's condition and the adaptation of the Gospel to their moral needs and their social and political improvement and perfection. And Methodism, when correctly implemented (especially if considered as a pioneer and addition to the Established Church), is perhaps the best-designed system of Gospel work for the "poor" and the simple common people (whether they are the ignorant and reprobate or the educated and devoutly inclined) that has ever been discovered. For although it does not produce as thorough a total conversion and enlightenment of the soul as the spiritual training of the *Society of Jesus* or *La Trappe*, it has this great advantage over the former system: it is not as liable to such satanic abuse and corruption when its members lose the spirit of their order and fall back under the control of self-interest and a spirit of deception.

As for what constitutes the unique identity of Methodism, there are many points, but nothing is truly original except for the talent that directed and applied them. All the solid foundation of disciplined and devotional piety is that of the Church of England, as illustrated by Law, Jeremy Taylor, and other of her theologians. All its outward spirit and operation, and everything domestic regarding pastoral methods and inventions—which affect the religious life and <margin>the "United Brethren"</margin> capacity of man—were taken from the "United Brethren" (the Moravians). They probably had their real origin in the gathering of a few pious souls of a mystical inclination about a century earlier to practice Behmen's <note>Jacob Boehme</note> "Way to Christ." In their practical pursuit of this, they discovered and invented new tools for the cultivation of piety: spiritual, devotional hymns and tunes, prayer and band meetings, love-feasts, local and foreign missionary efforts, and so on.

But although these latter evangelical methods could be adopted by Wesley, they would not have been enough to promote the spirituality and unity of a large society without a corresponding and equally practical *Psalmody*. For the psalms and hymns that existed at the beginning of the last century were, with few exceptions, not divinely inspired poetry; they were not the outpouring of souls experiencing all the various states leading to or participating in the divine nature reborn in the soul. Because the true doctrines of regeneration had not been preached and *personally experienced* by the great body of Christians, how could hymns have been composed (and their matching musical expressions, natural tones of sound, or tunes discovered) that expressed the diverse experiences of the new reborn life of Jesus in humanity? But Gospel salvation, which had previously been restricted mostly to a few mystics, was now to be made popular through Methodism. What then did Wesley do when he began to understand the nature of the spiritual life? He converted his brother Charles, who almost breathed and thought in poetic rhythm; and together they selected the best spiritual hymns, expressions, and sentiments from the practical and mystical theology of France, Holland, Germany, Italy, Spain, the ancients, and our own country—the finest blossoms and flowers from every Christian land and tradition they knew. With admirable skill and genius, they transformed them into a volume of hymns and sacred poems with such natural expression and simple language that it surprises any reader who reflects on the circumstances. They also added many of their own original works. We currently have before us the fourth edition of these "Hymns and Sacred Poems" from 1743, which, through successive additions and refinements, has grown into the hymn book now used by the Methodists.

It is the preface to this book that Mr. Law refers to in the Letter to Lady Huntingdon (inserted at p. 91). Upon reading it, the enlightened reader of the present work will doubtless at once agree with the justice of the accusation that Wesley showed an indifference to strict truth—an attitude he was driven to by his own impulsive will and the promotion of his favorite ideas. However, any competent defender of the mystics might view this preface and everything Wesley ever wrote in his journals or elsewhere against mystical theology (though he was surprisingly blinded by his own temperament) as the most worthy, well-intentioned, and truly Christian statement of objections ever written. Although many authors have joined this same crusade, we do not find that they were as devoted, practical Christian men, or that they had as much experience with the evangelical world and its *practices* as Mr. Wesley. Despite all this, we believe that if the apologist we mention possesses the right spirit of understanding and discernment, he will easily address and overturn these objections by placing each one in its proper relation to the center of truth.

It is time, however, to conclude these remarks; and we cannot do so more appropriately than by paying a proper tribute to Mr. Wesley's character. In writing a work like this, we have felt obligated to describe things as they happened, rather than through the usual lens of a fifty-year-old idealization or the views of biased sectarians. Thus, while we hold Mr. Wesley's character of sincerity, devotion to God, and usefulness to the church in as high esteem *as anyone*, it has been our task to point out the unique characteristics of Mr. Law as a mystical prophet of God, a theologian, and a man of learning and genius. Indeed, we see him as one of the leading spirits of the age—not necessarily for his extensive study of specific branches of knowledge, but for his balanced and universal learning, along with high achievements in intellectual development. This was especially necessary since our narrative required us to comment on the irrational attacks made against the general tone of his later writings. Having spoken so uncomplimentarily in defense of our subject and our goal of edification, it will now give us equal pleasure to act with justice and truth by glancing at the inner spirit of Mr. Wesley as he surely stood before God.

We have already noted the genius and piety he displayed in obtaining the translations of spiritual hymns by foreign and domestic authors into simple and popular English poetry—the true, natural, unforced expressions of the soul’s abundance; and arranging them (over years and experience) under many various headings, adapted to the diverse experience of souls in the process of the Gospel. <note>By the way, justice requires us to add that he took for himself both poetry and prose whenever he found them to his liking, without the smallest acknowledgment or reference to the authors! So it is that in his modern published, collected "Works," as in his "Hymns," pieces are attributed to him to which he has not the slightest claim of authorship.</note> A second remarkable trait in his character was the tenacity with which he stuck to his determination of taking the Bible and its unique style of language as the only and universal standard, from then on, for the conception and expression of spiritual things. For, if religion was ever to be universalized, a universal form or signature of ideas was plainly necessary, however varied the ideas themselves might be, according to the diverse conceptions of the human mind and the denominational instruction which believers—both learned and uneducated—might be expected to receive. This was embodied again in what may be called a third distinguished character of his spirit, or rather his procedure and habit in the great work to which he was called; we mean the tenor of all his preaching and exhortation, which made no distinction or exception for either the rich or poor, learned or uneducated, but the same doctrine was addressed to all alike,
> "He who believes shall be saved; he who does not believe shall be damned. Unless you repent, you shall all likewise perish. We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. Unless a man is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. He who is born of God does not sin. To those who believed, he gave power to become sons of God. The Spirit of God bears witness with our spirit that <note>if</note> we are the children of God. Without holiness, no man shall see the Lord. Seek first the kingdom of God and its righteousness, and all things needed <note>for this life</note> shall be added to you."

The effect of this, especially among "the poor," was to free religion from all uncertainty, opinion, and guesswork, and place its highest benefits within the immediate reach of every person by promoting that disposition of soul to which alone prayer, or true seeking after God, is possible. With what simplicity of imagery and expression, yet vividness of imagination and fervor of spirit, he was accustomed to plead with the ungodly and endeavor to awaken in them a concern for their souls, may be understood to some extent from a reading of his publications, especially his "Sermons" and his "Collection of Hymns" under the headings of "Death" and "Judgment."

Driving the truth home as he usually did, personally to "the sinner," and then placing before his mind’s eye "Christ dying on the cross a sacrifice in his place," "to appease the wrath of God," and "now waiting to pardon all who believe," and that "we are saved by faith, not by works," etc., etc.—we leave to the reflecting reader to consider what effect all this, supported by abundant quotations from Scripture, must have had upon the uneducated and uncivilized, who had never before heard such earnest, plain preaching; and how, consequently, thousands turned from their ungodly ways to pursue righteousness. Thus he proceeded through the length and breadth of the land, and, according to his systematic habits, forming those who were awakened under his discourses into little circles or classes to build up each other in the good way, until he or his preachers should come around again to impart some further spiritual gift. And it must be kept in mind that Wesley himself was the first to practice all the duties he so zealously enjoined upon others—writing to Mr. Law, "after the model of your two practical treatises." He was the first in mortification and self-denial (for instance, in his early rising, he rose at four o'clock for devotion, had preaching at five, a prayer meeting at six, etc., thus indeed testing the faithfulness of his converts in "forsaking all" and "taking up the cross"). He was the first in self-restraint and fasting, in charity and almsgiving, in labor and living strictly by rule, and the universal practice of "whatever things were pure, Christian, lovely, and of good report." Such was his undisputed, acknowledged reputation before his societies, a course which he maintained until the end of his life.

We do not mean to say that this spirit was completely obvious to the outside world, for in the conflicts into which he was brought, and into which he brought himself by the intensity of his spirit and dominant self-will, he showed that he was "only a man." But we say that this was the sincere aim and intent of his soul. To confirm this, we may refer the reader to the authenticated histories of his life, his journals, and other publications—especially his "Sermons"—where he will find only a spirit of experiential holiness and the cultivation of the life of God, of hunger and thirst after righteousness, and the struggle to realize all the salvation that Christianity claims to give to its faithful disciples. In short, as we have said, his one desire was to be himself fully devoted to God, to be acquainted with true, holy Gospel people, to fan the divine fire into a flame of heavenly love in others, and to spread the experiential knowledge of Christ and redemption through every neglected corner of this nation and to the ends of the earth. What this kingdom and the world itself owes to his efforts under the providence of God (for example, the serious tone of mind present today, and the practices of Christian philanthropy now occurring, with their results, etc.) may someday be known and acknowledged. We might just remark, before we close, that the prominent points of Methodist religious action are the driving of people toward God—"compelling them to come in"—and the doctrine of "sanctification," or the full restoration of the life and image of God in the soul. Many eminent writers, ascetics, and mystics of the Roman Catholic Church have treated this latter state, and very sublimely at that; but in no body of Christians is the experience of it so clear, full, and scriptural as among the Methodists, and the pathway to it made so well-traveled and direct to achieve—for the general public. And should the reader wish to see a classic illustration of Mr. Law's grand doctrine of "regeneration" and "the spirit of love" (as of his "ideal of a Minister of the Gospel," pages 380-5), he may, for that purpose, refer to Sigston's *Memoir of Bramwell* and read the letters within it.

Bramwell's letters indeed should constitute an inseparable appendix to Mr. Law's evangelical doctrinal works. While in these works the pure philosophy of the Gospel would be found displayed, in those letters the pure, non-idiosyncratic practice, experience, and explanation of it would be presented. Oh, let him who desires to experience the blessing of full sanctification of soul, full regeneration, full spiritual...

Dec. 1851.

We would be permitted here for a moment to return to our remarks on page 177, and to observe, in reference to our venerable mother, the established Church of England, and to certain of her academic sons in particular who evidently see the necessity of a movement of some kind in religion, that the adoption of all the discovered, efficient, and judicious instruments of communal and individual piety is the only means by which she can be raised to her true power and influence, so as to swallow up all sectarianism in this country. The diverse research and experience of the last two centuries have laid open to popular view the simple nature, design, and practice of the Gospel. What we would say then is: superimpose these well-tested practices, arts, expedients, and aids upon your "sober principles of sedate, composed piety," if you would not be left behind in this age of experiment and march of improvement. What merchant, trader, or mechanic, for instance—and the procedure of men of business is only the right use of natural means—what enterprising person, we say, raises himself in the world from his old position, or above his competitors, by a "sedate, composed" manner of conducting his affairs? On the contrary, he adopts the best help, the latest discoveries, and improved methods, and applies himself with indomitable energy and perseverance to his goals. In the same way should the ministers and pastors of the national church proceed if they would develop the transcendent power it possesses in the large body of learned, devout, and accomplished members and writers of its communion; and in a few years, the sects and divisions of this nation would resemble the leafless, lifeless bushes of a barren heath compared with the rich and majestic oak towering aloft in a fertile and luxuriant country. And as for themselves personally, they would thereby soon rub off the corners, the stiffness, and awkwardness of their unexercised pastoral talents, and rise into—yes, greatly rejoice in—the *liberty* of the spirit of Christ, as workmen who feel themselves thorough experts at their business and who "need not be ashamed"—such as was the *vrai athlète* (**2 Timothy** 2:3) and accomplished minister of Jesus Christ just mentioned, Bramwell.

We return now to our remaining notices of Mr. Law’s life for the year 1756, which was the period we had arrived at when we were led into the preceding digression by the publication of Mr. Wesley’s "Letter." We observed that Mr. Law had an anonymous tract in the press at this time, and we find in a postscript to one of the manuscript letters already cited, dated January 24th, 1756, the following remark: "You have done the office of a very accurate proofreader, and the translation of the Latin is as well as it can be done." [The beginning of the letter ran thus: "I do not know how many letters I should thank you for here. The *Psychologia Vera* is the book that I wanted, but it falls much short of my expectation. It is a very neat translation of the *Forty Questions*; but the *Figure of the Philosophic Eye* is missing. But as it is, I am very glad to have it, which would never have happened to me except through your hands. . . ."] This was addressed to Mr. Langcake, we presume, upon the actual publication of the tract, as we find the following letter written about a month previously to the same gentleman:—

> "December 20th, 1755.—My dear friend—I like the translation of the Latin passages very much. I suppose you desire me to send the verses, though I believe there is no occasion for it:—
> In vain you hope for bliss on this poor earth, &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Mysterious passage, hidden from mortal eyes!
> Return, and seek your Father and your God.— &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Soaring you will sink, and sinking you will rise;
> Yet think not to regain your native sky, &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Let humble thoughts your wary footsteps guide;
> Borne on the wings of vain philosophy. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Regain by meekness what you lost by pride.

> The advertisement to the Behmenists is a very strange one. I would not have any of the books you have mentioned.—I can only add that you have as much of me as any creaturely being ought to have. W. Law."

<margin>Having recently read it (see page...), we perceive the promises of the paragraph are incorrect.</margin>
The verses recited in the above letter were written by a Dr. Arbuthnot; but being inscribed by Mr. Langcake on the blank leaf of a book sent by him to Mr. Law, Mr. Law supposed them to have been of his composition and directed them to be printed at the close of the anonymous tract mentioned above, then in the press, entitled "Christian Piety freed from the Delusions of Modern Enthusiasts of all Denominations."

Not having been able to procure a copy of this tract, we can only say we suppose it to be a practical, general application of the principles elucidated in the author’s treatise "on Christian Regeneration" or "Answers to Trapp"; and wherein might be found an exposure of the enthusiasm of religious ignorance and blind zeal, just as the enthusiasm of literary learning and learned ignorance in the things of God had been made the subject of rebuke on a former occasion, as inserted in the note on pages 62 and 63; at the same time, the true and proper nature of evangelical religion was duly stated.

The original correspondence of this year supplies us with a fine illustration of Mr. Law’s transcendent abilities as a spiritual physician and director of souls. While reading the following letters, the reader will remember the objections of a certain set of popular theologians—men, indeed, very sincere and devout in their way—to what they term the "vain philosophy" contained in Mr. Law’s later writings, regarded in a purely practical point of view. He will also remember what we have said, and the instances we have given of their natural effects upon unsophisticated minds, when not counteracted by the bias of some secret prejudice and imaginary theological knowledge. An instance of such effects in the case of a thoughtful and learned man is inserted in the note from pages 423 to 426, and the letter we are about to give will show the effects resulting from a right reading of his writings in the case of one who may be termed an intelligent clerk or warehouseman:—

> "London. November 18th, 1756.—Reverend Dear Sir—Having read most of your writings, I find the utmost opposition to all anger, ill-will, or resentment breathe through the whole: and as I have no reason to doubt their being a copy of your heart, so I am persuaded no liberty taken by one so altogether unworthy as I will meet with anything but your pity and your prayers, and your . . . . . . . . ."

...truly depicts the "man of desire," who offers prayers that his fellow men might seek true knowledge and the pure enjoyments of the spirit, drawing them from their own...

...good advice, which is all I ask. I do not doubt that you feel compassion for all of miserable mankind, and I have no doubt that your compassion is redoubled for those who are the most miserable of all men because they are so by their own fault—I mean poor, backsliding, self-destroyed sinners, among ten thousand of whom I am the chief. Before I was well past my childhood, the holy Immanuel, the blessed seed of life, began to be awakened in me; and I remember that by reading the works of Bishop Beveridge it was so called forth that, though I never had any gift for what is called prayer or conversation, yet in my private meditations, and especially at church, I have been in such a state that whether I was in the body or out of the body, God only knows. Being sent out into the world to earn my living in the prime of giddy youth, the heat of blood and spirits, evil examples, the lust of the flesh, and sinful opportunities soon choked to death and buried the good seed once more; and I think it almost utterly silenced the speaking Word of God in my heart. 

About my eighteenth year I came up to London, and there, through worldly disappointment and hearing Mr. Wesley preach once, such conviction was wrought in my heart that I lived in such bondage and misery that I only wished for no afterlife, and that it were lawful to end my own life. For six or seven years I continued in this poor, miserable way, praying from books until midnight and later, fasting until I hurt my health, and vowing and resolving to serve God; but the first strong temptation overthrew the entire fabric of my own works and leveled it to the ground. During this time, my reading consisted of volumes about original sin and the sin against the Holy Ghost, and Bishop Taylor's writings; I used to hear preaching on Sundays from morning to night, but to no purpose. All of it tended to stiffen me in that particular folly of laboring to establish my own righteousness. And as for the Scriptures, although I greatly venerated them and dared not say otherwise, they always seemed to me like a finely written poem about a lock of hair or a lady's lap-dog—like the laboring mountain that brought forth a mouse. They seemed, as you better express it, to have more height and mystery in the expression than in the thing itself. 

And I must and do lament that, despite all my misery from convictions—the stings and lashes of God's vicegerent, my conscience—I was not restrained from outward sin. Lust and anger were the mutual pests and plagues of my life, and made me bitterly wish I had never been born. Oh, what temptations did I undergo; it would be endless to tell. Blasphemous thoughts, thoughts of despair and reprobation, not only amazed my spirit but even depressed and bowed down my body, making me walk stooped, hardly able to do my work. Amidst all this, lust would beset me in the daytime, and uncleanness and perhaps fornication at night; and in the morning, anger at myself for my folly made me peevish and disagreeable to everyone around me, and so miserable in myself that, although the fear of the afterlife did restrain me from choosing hanging over such a life, I heartily wished it were lawful. And this is what I sadly lament: my being so accustomed to falling into sin that to this day it is the bane and destruction of the life of God in my soul. I have fallen into it again and again, so that it robs me of my peace, hardens my heart, and I suspect has nearly extinguished the good Spirit of God; for now I feel no such horror, remorse, and bitterness of heart for sinning as I used to feel then.

One night I committed two great evils: drunkenness and fornication. The next day, sick with intemperance and wounded by conviction, I was unable to do my work and was obliged to stay in my room. It so happened that your book *Regeneration* was at that moment put into my hands. With solemnity I looked at the preface; I prayed to God to give me understanding. I already had seriousness—my gripping conscience had produced that in me. I read, and surely the Spirit of God applied it; how clearly did I see my miserable, helpless, sinful self! But when I came to that "most glorious and edifying truth that ever possessed the heart of man," namely, that *God is all love, and in him is no anger at all*, I was amazed. I prayed to God and read it again, and the second time I read that blessed truth, it truly possessed and edified my heart. How my peevish, angry soul was melted into love! My misery fled away in a moment; the very memory of it perished. All the slavish fear of God, of hell, and of reprobation, as well as all that anger and lust that had harassed me to death, were instantly gone, and such a peace possessed my heart as surpasses human understanding; human words cannot express it, for it was indeed the peace of God. 

It was not more than a month before sin robbed me of that blessing again. Then I encountered the *Spirit of Prayer*, and every word brought conviction as I read; and a year after that I obtained the *Appeal*, and how joyful I was to find truth so plain and intelligible! Every word lifted my heart above itself, but when I came to that pathetic description of the *sufferings of our blessed Saviour's soul*, my heart was broken anew, and I did—like Peter—weep bitterly and repent. By the goodness of God, this introduced into my heart all those sweet and heavenly dispositions I had at the first. This same description in the *Appeal* has several times produced the same effect in me, but sooner or later sin has always robbed me of my peace. I have lately given way to folly and am at present in unspeakable misery—the greater because I do not feel it sufficiently; I feel neither enough happiness nor enough misery. A cold indifference and lukewarmness about the concerns of my soul seem to possess me at this time. 

And what shall I do? Yet I find great compassion in my heart for the miseries of other people, and more patience to bear affronts and injuries; I am afraid to give way to anger or resentment in any degree, and if it burns in my heart, my mouth is shut and it is smothered. But it is not so with lust; it gains dominion over me, and as it always was, it continues to be the very pest and perplexity of my life. Being only a servant, I cannot marry without bringing beggary and misery upon myself, and I see with open eyes the work of God destroyed in my soul, and I think I cannot help it. The Spirit strives only faintly, and my heart is so treacherous and desperately wicked, and I have been so accustomed to folly, that I am continually betrayed into sin, misery, and folly. I am at my wits' end, and yet all is calm and quiet within; my understanding and former experience show me my intolerable danger and misery, but my heart and affections seem to have no share in the matter, or are insensibly given up to something else. O dear Sir, consider my case, excuse this long and broken account, and if your wisdom can suggest to you the reason for my miserable situation, I hope your compassion will prompt you to favor me with good counsel in a letter directed to me.

Your most unworthy servant,  
THOMAS YATES.  
(at Mr. Hooke's in the Globe Court, Fish Street Hill, London.)

Here was a case of conscience indeed, set forth with all its symptoms in the clearest manner...

but one which, we may well suppose, if presented to some of our self-appointed evangelical doctors and critics, would have either totally stumped them, or have produced a volume of empty, confused instructions and advice, proceeding not from an actual understanding of the nature of grace and nature, but from mere theology learned by heart. And as nature would not be considered in that advice, so the root of the disorder would not be directly touched, nor would the cure be achieved in the true *homœopathic* <note>Law uses "homœopathic" here in a spiritual sense, meaning a cure that addresses the root nature of the ailment by using like to treat like, or addressing the internal spirit directly.</note> manner. Let us see how Mr. Law treats the case according to his principles, as explained in the closing Dialogue of the “Spirit of Love.” His reply we did not have, but it has been *accidentally discovered*, having been sent for publication to the “Monthly Ledger, or Literary Repository” for May, 1787, by the very person to whom it was addressed; and it is in the following terms:—

> “Poor honest man—Whom I much love and esteem, your letter has been lost among a massive pile of papers, and has only just been found by me. I am not without hope that God and time may have done that for you in a better way than I could have done it. To be left in distress is often the only way to be rescued from it; and when help seems to be the farthest off, then we are nearest to the place where it can only be found. Happy is that desolation, wherever it comes, that forces us to see no glimpse of relief except in giving ourselves blindly, implicitly, and wholly to the redeeming power and goodness of God, without the least thought or conceit of having any other or more goodness than what his holy Nature and Spirit bring forth in us. This is the one great point for you, and all your remedy lies in it. Your way is short; no variety of rules and practices, no methods of finding help from yourself or any worldly thing, no length or variety of beautifully written prayers, will do for you what you want to have done. All these things in your present case stand between you and God. They will only help you as that sick woman in the Gospel was helped—by spending all that she had on physicians and medicines. She was no better, but rather grew worse, until the time came that everything within her said, ‘If I may only touch the hem of his garment, I shall be healed.’ A blind, non-rational, absolute faith in God—offering up all your sins, without any overthinking of their nature, quality, or degree, to the mere mercy of God, to be consumed in that blessed furnace of love which made God become a suffering, dying Redeemer—is your only infallible and full relief. Any other way but this, however full of religious inventions, will only maintain both your weakness and your confusion under it. But to this faith, everything must yield. All things are possible to it: it draws Divine virtue from the hem of a garment; it can remove mountains, pluck up whole trees of sin by the roots, make lepers clean, and raise the dead to life.

If I end here, perhaps you will think my advice too short, but if I add nothing else to it, it is because I would have you only attentive to the one thing that is necessary, and the one thing only that is available for your salvation. Only, watch your outward life closely, be temperate in everything, and, as much as you can, avoid temptations. But in this and everything else, place no trust in your own care and resolutions; rather, do all that you do not as inventions to help yourself, but as acts of faith and dependence upon the power of God, living and working in your soul all that is or can be holy or good in it. Prayer of the heart is the most principal work or fruit of faith. And as our faith is, such will our prayers always be. But neither faith nor prayer is ours, except as they both come out of our own hearts.

The soul, therefore, that lives by faith will have no need of being outwardly taught the following *spirit of prayer*; it will be as constant as the beating of the pulse of the heart, always living in it and being inseparable from it: it will, with and without words, be continually crying to God—

> ‘O infinite, fathomless depth of never-ceasing love! save me from myself, from the disorderly workings of my own evil nature. Kindle, with the fire of your Divine love, the dead [latent] powers of that first holy life, which you breathed into the first created man.
>
> ‘O quicken and revive the heavenly seed, which your redeeming mercy in Christ Jesus has planted in my soul, so that it may come to full birth; that your holy Jesus may be truly formed and fully revealed in my soul; that I may be born again of him, be a new creature in him, led and governed by his holy Spirit, ever living, dwelling, and working all that is within me and proceeds from me.
>
> ‘O holy and adorable God of light and love, of mercy and goodness, of glory and majesty, everywhere present! manifest the power of your holy nature within me. Help me to such a true and living faith in you, such earnest hunger and thirst, and longing desire for your holy nature, that all that is within me may seek and find, worship and adore, the life-giving power of your holy presence in my soul. Let all that is within me be humbly, earnestly, and obediently resigned, devoted, and attentive to your holy Will, ever-speaking Word, and ever-sanctifying Spirit within me—turned away from every thing or thought that is not of you, your holy will, and your heavenly working in my soul.’

That every blessing of God may be continually with you is the hearty prayer of—Your most affectionate friend and servant—W. LAW.

P.S.—Never think of God as anything but an infinity of overflowing love, who intends nothing by the creation except to be the comfort, the blessing, and the joy of every life according to its capacity. And let this idea, which is the truth of truths, animate and govern all that you think, say, or do, either toward God or man.”

This was Mr. Law’s reply. The state of spiritual or legal bondage in which this honest and sincere Thomas Yeates was held when he wrote to Mr. Law has reminded the writer of the case of Dr. Johnson, who was certainly better acquainted with Law than may be generally supposed. As we wish to make no assertion which is not supported by facts, we must remind the reader that John Payne, as we have already mentioned, was so filled with the spirit of Law that he merely reproduced and published Law's thoughts and expressions almost exactly. We need not add that a man so influenced by extreme admiration of a writer is sure to make him a common subject of his intimate private conversations. Now we find from published historical notices that Payne supplied Johnson with money and aided him in producing *The Rambler*; in fact,
