<meta>This page continues the discussion of William Law’s influence on his contemporaries, specifically focusing on his impact on Samuel Johnson and his correspondence with seekers and fellow mystics.</meta>

“His system (writes Tourlet, the author of another *Historical Notice of Saint Martin*) aims to explain everything through man; man, according to him, is the key to every enigma, and the image of—”

---

was a great support to him in a variety of ways. It is certain that with such opportunities as this connection must have afforded him, he would not fail to make some impression on Johnson; and if we could only get at the facts, we should doubtless find that Johnson knew Law’s work thoroughly. This may indeed be inferred not only from his imitations of Law’s style of drawing characters in the previously mentioned periodical, but from other circumstances. We learn, for example, from Croker’s edition of Boswell, that a lady and Johnson were discussing Law’s writings when she expressed her opinion to him that the *Appeal* was the clearest of all his later works; and we are directly informed how familiar Johnson was with his early writings. 

For our own part, we conceive there to have been some misapprehension in Boswell—who, himself, most probably had not read Law’s works, nor was his taste inclined that way, even if he were at all conversant with the ideas and language of theology—when, in the “Life,” it is related that a conversation occurred between Johnson and others as to who were the most perfect logicians of the day. When Law’s name was submitted as the second or third in the series, Johnson replied, “Oh, Law does not know how to argue.” Now, Johnson’s whole life was a proof to the contrary—that he could not have thought so; for Law’s writings were, so to speak, a constant mirror before his mind of the true decency, rule, and perfection of human nature—of, in short, the law. In these writings, he saw himself, when he dared to reflect upon himself, as a swinish, self-condemned, sinful spirit. His was not an intellect to be affected by the crude declamations of popular theology, nor by anything less than strict demonstration. Because he did not apprehend the precise nature of Gospel Christianity, by which he might become renewed in moral purity according to his innate consciousness, and because he felt himself enslaved to his rational, hoggish tavern and table delights and sensualities, we see at once the secret of his constant mental depression and bondage. The spirit of his life was like that of a guilty criminal, always expecting the moment of his trial and execution.

In this connection, we shall provide a letter—though a little out of date—written by Mr. Law to a Mr. John Lewsley, a merchant of Bristol, in answer to one from him. it illustrates the edifying purpose and invariable tone of his spiritual advice. His whole remedy for those who applied to him in every case (from the date of his “Three Letters to a Lady inclined to enter into the Church of Rome” in 1732) consisted in an implicit faith and total abandonment to the sole operation of the all-working, redeeming spirit of Christ in the soul. This letter is invaluable in regard to its instruction:—

> “Kings Cliffe. July 9th, 1755. — My dear Friend — For so I must call you, though you are unknown to me—yours of the 27th of May arrived safely.
> 
> Your true conduct under your present light is to *turn inwards*, and endeavor to find and feel the truth and reality of those doctrines *there*, which you are beginning to see.
> 
> For all that I have written is only to help mankind, in this age of darkness, controversy, and delusion, to find the full truth and fundamental ground of all the doctrines of salvation. These are as plainly written and demonstrated in the essence, state, and condition of their own souls as they are in scripture. <note>This sentence might serve, among others, as a motto for Mr. Law’s later writings.</note>
> 
> Under such a conviction as this, you come to this knowledge: *that everything is to be transacted between God and yourself;* and that as you are, so is God toward you. Therefore, you are to look for no good except from such a state of heart, or *kind of prayer*, as keeps you continually uniting yourself to God, steadily believing and fully expecting to be delivered from all your evil through the merits, mediation, and heavenly birth of the holy Jesus in your own soul.
> 
> Form no idea of the progress you make, nor stand on watch for how it advances in you. Give God your heart; desire only to die to yourself and to everything that hinders your living for Him, and then your road is safe and good, whatever you meet upon it.
> 
> All my books will be of use to you at present, provided you read them as your instruction on how to find and know the misery and corruption of your fallen nature, and the absolute impossibility of ever being delivered from it except by turning to God through Jesus Christ. For they mean nothing else but to lead you away from me, and from yourself, and from all trust in created things, to expect and find all that you want in God alone, in the immediate operation of his *living* Word and Spirit in your soul.
> 
> In all your readings, read more with your heart than with your head; and never exercise your mind in trying to understand any difficult matters, nor dwell upon them whenever you encounter them.
> 
> Your heart, when given up to God, will have its sufficient daily illumination and, in its proper time, its true fitness for understanding every matter that can be a blessing to you. And be assured of this: that no knowledge except that which is born within you, from a heart in union with the eternal Word and Spirit of God, is worth a moment’s thought. — My dear friend, Adieu. — W. LAW.”

In the early part of this year, it would appear that Mr. Langcake had introduced a Mr. Richard Clarke—a numerical mystic <note>Richard Clarke was a writer known for interpreting biblical prophecy through symbolic numbers.</note> and prophetic writer—to the notice of Mr. Law to solicit a subscription on his behalf toward the publication of a spiritual work, as he was in impoverished circumstances. The following letter will show with what genuine kindness of heart the desired financial aid was afforded:—

> “Jan. 24th, 1756. — My dear friend — I had just sent mine to you by this day's post before yours arrived, and so you have the trouble of a second letter. I am much pleased that you acquainted me with Clarke’s affair; and it is a pleasure to me to do anything through your hands, as you are quite dear to me. You may go directly to my Nephew in Cornhill for the five pounds. Your demand for it in my name will be sufficient, and with my service, you may tell him that he will hear from me in a post or two. I have no time to say any more. — Dear soul, Adieu. — W. LAW.”

The following letter, written some months afterward, evidently relates to the same subject. The book, which Mr. Law proposed to *kindle his bedroom fire* with, was the very work to whose publication he had himself subscribed, according to the previous letter:—

> “Aug. 29th, 1756. — My dear Langcake — As it is usual for you to receive letters from me

—that may be said to have nothing in them but the good will of the writer, so I shall make no apology for this, which has no more to say for itself.

<margin>1</margin> I could not let my nephew come empty-handed to you from me, and if you will call this *something*, you will do it a great honor.

<margin>2</margin> Your friend Clarke’s piece will have its place among those books that, at certain times, help to kindle my fire. This is not through contempt or disregard for him or his pen, but because I know of no better use for such materials. It is all the good that I can get from them. <margin>4</margin> In the proper order of our narrative, we shall find occasion to notice this writer again, where Mr. Law refers to his prophetic calculations and the doctrine of final restoration. We may observe here that he claimed to have discovered the key to the secret numbers and symbols of scripture, and ventured to definitively foretell and publish the year (if not the exact day and hour) of the second coming of Christ, which was to be in the latter part of the last century. And his writings are composed, in large measure, of such unprofitable speculations concerning the counsels of divine wisdom. He followed in the wake of the old fanatics, though Swedenborg outdoes them all, as he said the last judgment actually happened in the year 1756, and that the disciples were then sent through the regions of spiritual nature to preach the Gospel!! (The gospel of the redemption of man from the fall by Jesus Christ, so that true believers at the hour of death follow Christ into paradise, and the unregenerate remain in the root of nature, having no light of him in them.) Such were the Baron’s conceptions of the scheme and constitution of Christianity.

We have mentioned the friendship which existed between the celebrated John Byrom of Manchester, M.D., poet and shorthand writer, and Mr. Law. Byrom, it would seem, had turned some part of Law’s writings into poetry, and on proposing to continue the transformation, had at first been encouraged by the latter to do so. This intimacy in all probability began in a similar way to other instances of friendship with an author who was sought, as we have said, by all classes of persons, learned and unlearned, not only as a spiritual adviser and sage, but as one of the foremost spirits of the age, whose friendship was highly honorable and beneficial to those who could secure it. This surmise is confirmed by Byrom’s application to Law in 1736, on account of a lady who was about to join the Quakers; on which occasion Law wrote the five letters mentioned in the note on pages 363-4. The attachment of Dr. Byrom was of such a chivalrous character that his whole arsenal of wit and learning was always ready in the defense of Mr. Law, in whose service he volunteered as a sort of champion. In illustration of this, we purpose to insert from the documents in our possession three letters of his correspondence with Warburton. They belong, indeed, to an earlier date than that at which we have arrived, but as it was in the year 1757 that Law himself took up the whip to scourge his rampant, flippant antagonist, we could not give them in a more appropriate place than the present.

Warburton, we have observed, following in the wake of Trapp, but in his own brutal style, had attacked Law (through Wesley and others), more particularly in a volume of sermons, which, after Mr. Law’s death, were expanded into the “Doctrine of Grace,” and made the occasion for a reply to Mr. Law’s criticisms in his “Address to the Clergy,” and “Letters.” It was against attacks of this nature, which Law himself could not stoop to notice, that Dr. Byrom had opposed himself in the correspondence we are about to cite; which, as we possess it, commences with the reply of Byrom to Warburton’s first letter. It should be stated that the copy of this correspondence we hold is in Byrom’s handwriting, being made out and sent to Mr. Law, accompanied by the following note:—

> “Tuesday Morning, April 21st, 1752.—There has been no opportunity of obeying your direction in sending the Answer to Mr. W.’s first [letter], of which you have a copy, and the short notice of one at present only affords leisure for a hasty transcription of it, together with his Second and its Answer, for your perusal and opinion of this new and unexpected correspondence; and how to manage in returning civilities, and preserving freedom properly, in case of a continuance. With which you will favor—his Excellency—Your Poet.”

The copy of the letter from Warburton alluded to above, we have not been able to discover; and the answer to it dated February 2nd, 1752, by Byrom, as well as Warburton’s mild and well-written reply, dated Prior Park, near Bath, April 3rd, 1752, and Byrom’s rejoinder of April 10th of the same year, on account of their great length, we (now) perceive we must defer to the proposed larger biography, as well as other interesting letters and correspondence with Law from the years 1736-7, and from Law with Byrom up to the year 1760.

This correspondence will clarify how Law was kept *au fait* of the treatment of him by Warburton and others, whose judgment did not sleep, as we are about to notice especially.

Byrom, as we have seen, subscribes himself “Your Poet” in writing to Law, and the second volume of his “Poems,” by the extensive versifications it contains of Law’s writings, almost in the original words, testifies how he, like Payne, must have been captivated with Law’s style of thought and expression. Wesley in his Journals of 1773 notices these Poems in the following words:—

> “Read Dr. Byrom’s Poems. He has all the wit and humor of Dr. Swift, together with much more learning, a deep and strong understanding, and above all, a serious vein of piety. A few things in the second volume are taken from Jacob Behmen; to whom I object, etc., etc.”; see the quotation and remarks upon it in the Note on p. 93.—He continues, “But setting these things aside, we have some of the finest sentiments that ever appeared in the English tongue; some of the noblest truths expressed with the utmost energy of language, and the strongest colors of poetry. So that, upon the whole, I trust this publication will much advance the cause of God, and of true religion.”

Now these very fine sentiments and noble truths were chiefly Mr. Law’s, put into verse by his admiring friend and poet. But what must be said of Wesley’s persistent judging of Behmen,

The late Dr. Newton, Bishop of Bristol, in his prophecies, volume 3, page 194, speaking of Savonarola, who in the fifteenth century preached against the luxury, vices, and debauchery of the Roman clergy, and was burned by them for doing so, says, "all persons of any note and eminence bear a double character in the world, and so does Savonarola—his admirers extolling him as the best of men and the prophet of God, his enemies reviling him as the worst of impostors and hypocrites; but if his works may speak for him, they are in the opinion of Dupin, full of grace and maxims of piety." Dr. Newton lived to see the above observation exactly verified. He himself thought well of Savonarola; but Dr. Warburton, the late Bishop of Gloucester, and Dr. Newton's contemporary, in his *Doctrine of Grace* falls most outrageously on Savonarola, giving him the worst and blackest character, and then (*Horresco referens* <note>Latin: "I shudder to relate it"</note>) compares Mr. Law to the deformed picture he had drawn, because Mr. Law had written an Answer to him which he could not refute.

And is there no enmity in the heart of Mr. Wesley against Mr. Law, for correcting him in his "*Letters*," on account of his illiberal and unchristian treatment of Mr. Law, in his *Preservative*?

We must not omit one detail regarding Byrom which, however minor, is worthy of observation because of the individual involved. We refer to the marriage of one of his relatives of the same name to the holy Bramwell, whom we have so often referred to as a classic model of a Gospel Christian or regenerate believer, and of a pastor and priest of Jesus Christ. He is especially notable for exhibiting, in his spiritual journey, *the pursuit of the proper goal of a religious life, namely the attainment of "the full birth of the spirit of love," "entire sanctification," and "the marriage of the Lamb," through the proper means of growth in grace and arrival at that state—namely, the due order and proportions of physical with psychical devotion.* Thus, in his practice, one may trace a direct, well-trodden path of ascent, without deviating either to the right or to the left, from the natural fallen state of man to the highest degree of spiritual, Christian renewal. Many have been the eminent examples of renewed, regenerate souls among those truly devoted to God in this country (some of whom the writer is acquainted with), and also among the foreign spiritualists, both Roman Catholic and Protestant; (and it would perhaps be difficult to conceive of purer sanctity and greater devotion than what distinguished Gregory Lopez and others who might be named from Spain and France). But we remark that probably the church has never produced a more accomplished example of a practical, solid, Gospel Christian and clergyman. His spiritual state was the pure growth and fruit not of religious theories or book knowledge, but of a simple acceptance of Gospel doctrine according to its *prima-facie* <note>at first sight; obvious</note> sense, and a diligent conformity in practice; especially in the case of persistent and unceasing prayer, and that total self-denial which is essential to the true and actual exercise of it. The precepts, counsels, example, and spirit of humility and meekness of Jesus Christ, along with the explanations of Apostolic thought and action, were his constant study. Thus he became what may be termed a *standard* regenerate man; the gravity and seriousness of his character were undoubtedly much aided by his natural temperament, which was of that inclination. No fiction of the popular, lazy "justification by faith" doctrine could confuse or delude him; there was no jumping into all the privileges and enjoyments of religion "simply by believing." Instead, the sensible old method of diligent, hard-working death to self—of striving, watching, praying, and agonizing—was the path he pursued. This was the preparation of the heart for God to raise up within it the perfect image of His well-beloved Son; this, we say, was Bramwell's orthodox doctrine and process of salvation, just as it was that of his master and redeemer, Jesus Christ. It is labor, exercise, and practice that make one perfect in salvation, as in other arts.

And had Bramwell been *called* to it, and favored accordingly with the "Word of Wisdom" through the theosophic explanations of Behmen <note>Jacob Böhme</note>, the world might have seen in him the true Christian worker of miracles described in *Mark* 16:17–18, and a divine magus or alchemist. This latter point (Note Well) can only arise from Bramwell's foundation of experience and regenerate manhood: his process and attainments being *the way* and the subordinate qualifications of the *philosophical artist. A word to the wise is sufficient.*

Saying goodbye to the pleasant, quaint old English poet, Byrom, we now resume our narrative, which left off at the beginning of the year 1757. We have already noticed the Babylonian confusion into which Protestant scholastic theology had sunk. We have also mentioned one or two strange doctrines which the enthusiastic sectarians and so-called "first Reformers" had adopted; though alas, ignorance of theological truth and its essential relations was not confined to these, or to the field preachers who overran this country and, to a lesser extent, Holland and Germany. The learned themselves, though many of them were very devout, were groping about in equal mental and spiritual darkness, just like *Newman* and other examples of the hybrid theological science and pretended spiritualism of our own times. The subjects of their intellectual arguments and quarrels with one another were not, however, the flagrantly blasphemous and absurd doctrines of election, reprobation, etc.; rather, they were of a more sober cast, as befitted scholarly minds. For instance, one of the subjects of learned discussion in the early part of the last century concerned the immortality of the soul, with the celebrated Mr. Henry Dodwell maintaining that immortality was not natural to it, but conferred by Christian baptism! It would be pointless to recount the varieties of monstrous errors brought forth by university learning when severed from a knowledge of the natural grounds of Christianity, or the plain letter, analogy, and sure guide of scripture. But we relate another instance which will bring us back to the course of our present narrative: namely, that Warburton—who was famous as a giant of scholastic learning and for his close familiarity with the insults (and filth) of classic poets of all ages down to the "Dunciad"—being in holy orders as a true son of the church, felt he must (thus equipped) write a learned book in defense of Christianity. One of the new hypotheses he proposed and most learnedly maintained, "*dragging (as it is said) the Scripture by the hair of the head*" to support his position, was that *the ancient Jews were not taught the knowledge of a future state by the writings of their great lawgiver Moses*. At the same time, he dared to treat Dr. Sherlock, the then Bishop of London, rather dismissively; Sherlock had incidentally affirmed the direct contrary in some of his published discourses. The work we refer to here, the "*Divine Legation of Moses*," the reader will undoubtedly be acquainted with as a mass of great learning; it was quite possibly intended by its author to form an eternal monument to his presumed unparalleled genius and erudition, if not a stepping stone (in the absence of a political pamphlet) to a high position in the school of Christ—if by that one understands the Anglican church establishment.

Now, it seemed to Mr. Law that the time had arrived to take his disrespectful opponent in hand; t

Now also, the opportunity was providentially presented (as in the case of Trap) for him to exhibit, for the edification and encouragement of the theological world, a new and further display of the lofty and enlightened science of mystical divinity and theosophy—such as we would propose to cultivate systematically, among other evangelical rights and divine attainments, in our projected theosophic college. There, indeed, the highest popular scholastic learning and intellectual ability might form mere basic qualifications for the student, who would then ascend through all the degrees of divine science, up to the refined light and wisdom of *pure theology* and all *philosophy*.

To attempt any specific description of how Mr. Law performs his proposed task in the work we are now noting, beyond what has already been stated, would only tend to diminish rather than clarify its merits. We shall therefore content ourselves with referring the reader to the work itself, not doubting that he will later fully agree with the sobriety and fairness of our representations of its character. However, it may be said that few men of his status have ever had to suffer such an exposure of incompetence as Warburton is made to undergo in this work. The title page reads as follows:—“A short but sufficient Confutation of the Rev. Dr. Warburton's Projected Defense (as he called it) of Christianity, in his ‘Divine Legation of Moses.’ In a Letter to The Right Rev. The Lord Bishop of London. A.D. 1757.”

We have noted how Wesley, in the “Selections” he published from Mr. Law’s writings—of what he considered evangelical and edifying—reprinted almost the entire work. Yet, though accessible to common understanding, every page of it teems with such mystical implications, science, and developments that he, on other occasions, would have rejected as “Behmenish, empty, and vain.” But here, the truth and its application to Warburton were so sharp and admirable that they were irresistible even to Mr. Wesley.

We cannot, however, conclude our notice of this work without specifying one of its unique practical features: it may be regarded as a model theological review, written according to the highest science. While refuting the unfounded claims of the author under examination and replacing them with the proper understanding, it throws out—wherever an opening in the argument allows, and as fast as the reader's mind can receive the knowledge without being dazzled and confounded—flashes of sublime instruction in the deepest and most significant mysteries of nature and the Gospel. These are truths demonstrated by such a mystical “eagle-eye” and powerful logical intellect as distinguished Mr. Law. In short, we have in this letter the conclusion of the philosophy of “The Appeal,” “The Way to Divine Knowledge,” and “The Spirit of Love,” along with an example of its applicability in solving theological problems. In this respect (coupling it with “The Case of Reason” for reasons that will be well understood upon reflecting on the capacity of that work), it may not be unfairly regarded as the capstone of the great bulwark of Christianity contained in the author's writings.

For while mere unguided reason in the speculating minds of Hume, Bolingbroke, Gibbon, Voltaire, and other free-thinkers—gazing up at nature, at the stars of heaven, those innumerable worlds of the universe among which the globe we inhabit is scarcely comparable in size to a grain of sand on the seashore, and considering the Great Spirit of life, power, and wisdom which must be present everywhere to sustain and move all—can feel no secret, intrinsic affinity between these things and the professed revelation of the Jewish and Christian scriptures, as might reasonably be expected if revelation were true. Especially, they question how this vast universe of worlds was made chiefly for this little grain of sand, our globe, and solely with reference to that little atom of intellectual life upon it: man. Furthermore, they consider that if man were what he is represented to be by revelation—the formal son of this Great Spirit—he would not be left by Him in such darkness regarding His nature and will. Instead, He would make Himself known, sensible, and evident to man; He would interpose for oppressed virtue and goodness, and openly threaten and punish the wickedness, injustice, and diabolical cruelty prevalent everywhere on the earth. 

Then again, they argue: how can any man enjoying his rational powers believe that this Great Spirit—who is always present beyond the remotest fixed star as He is here and everywhere—opened Himself at a central point and became a man? In this man, according to the Christian gospel, dwelt all the *fullness* of the Godhead bodily; yet not a hundred-thousandth part of the inhabitants of the earth, the workmanship of His hands, have the least accurate conception, if any belief at all, of this alleged truth. And they question how this mysterious incarnation in so-called fallen humanity died to atone for the sins of the world, as if the Great Universal Spirit, if necessary, could not have forgiven and restored man of His own accord. And then again, shrewdly remarking: how artfully Moses put together the Old Testament scriptures, and what a tale he tells to his own people—over whom he was more than an emperor, and who dared not disbelieve or oppose him on pain of instant death—of the creation of this universe only about six thousand years ago, and all within six days or one hundred and forty-four hours; of the making of man, and then some time afterward of woman; then how a serpent talked with her (as a donkey did afterward to a man) and deceived her, thus bringing death into the world. 

How the Great Universal Spirit of impartial goodness chose the Israelite nation to be His special favorites, despite the fraud, lies, and deceit that formed the basis of their particular establishment through Rebecca and Jacob, and the subsequent wickedness of their children. Indeed, they ask why He chose this little branch of the great human tree above all the trunk and other chief branches, with their learning, science, and religion, though they were undeniably descended from the great Shem, inheriting his knowledge and imitating him in the devout worship of this Great Spirit—from whom, indeed, Moses himself and they had derived all the knowledge they possessed. How, further (as Moses relates), the Great Spirit appeared to him and talked with him, and enabled him to lead the people out; how the Great Spirit, at his bidding, destroyed thousands upon thousands of (His other children) the poor, unoffending inhabitants of

Egypt with their innocent little ones, pitiful livestock, and their pastures, with such horrible plagues as would strain the imagination to conceive, and then drowned King Pharaoh and all his hosts in the Red Sea. And afterwards, he sanctioned (in these his alleged favorites) such butchering murders and horrible villainies as completely overshadow the murders of a Muhammad, an Alexander, or a Napoleon in their significance—all these horrors being inflicted by the Great Spirit of life and love upon such myriads of his children, purely for the sake of his favorite small number of Israelites. This is how Moses seems to represent it, though no documents or monuments have ever been found in Egypt bearing even the most remote allusion to such incredible, apocryphal, and great events. 

Furthermore, how he, Moses, brought the people into the sandy desert and kept them there for forty years, and fed them not with ordinary food but with bread actually sent down daily from the sky (though what is the sky?), indeed with the food of angels! (Representations of the Israelites stationed in the desert with their tents, and in the middle the strange Mormon-like or animal-pen looking <term>tabernacle of worship</term>, with the sand hills all around in the distance, are exhibited in the shop windows around town)—and this handful of illiterate, ignorant people, worse than Mormons, indeed! They are presented as the only favorites of that Being who, at that very moment, was blessing and fertilizing ten thousand lands, and imparting his spirit, light, and life to millions of rational and devout souls in all nations!! 

Then, again, consider how cleverly Moses provides against opponents and counter-evidence; for he distinctly kills every soul but two in less than forty years—everyone he had brought out of Egypt who knew how things were going on in the world. As for the <term>Chartists</term> and <term>Radicals</term>, he swallowed them up at the first signs of rebellion. And these two survivors, though he allowed them a little interaction with the outside for a special purpose, were not permitted to come within “the wholesome influence of the external world”; yet when they had served his purpose, they died also—and so forth, through all the other seemingly irrational events. (For objections against Jewish and Christian history, see the Deist writings of the early part of the last century, and others.)

Now we say, while unenlightened “reason” thus gazes at the alleged facts and the surface of biblical revelation—which, as has been observed, is “like a heifer looking at a new stall door,” wondering and unable to reconcile them with nature, sense, and experience—it simultaneously feels itself in a worse dilemma than the simple believer. It is totally submerged in an abyss of darkness and uncertainty regarding its origin, destination, and relationship to the Great Spirit of the Deity, which it fully acknowledges. 

This treatise, or “*Confutation of Warburton’s Projected Defense*” (with the “*Case of Reason*” added, as we have observed), summarily clears up (to the satisfaction of the qualified reader) the seeming paradoxes and inherently unaccountable events that characterize the Christian scheme. It shows the mystery and the golden thread that runs through all its parts, and exhibits the parallels (which would be impossible to invent by art) between the first and second Adam. It highlights the circumstances related to the creation and the fall of the former, and the birth and process of redemption of the latter. 

By demonstrating the truth of the divine economy of the Jews and the basis of the extraordinary facts regarding the history of Christianity narrated by Moses—doing so in a way that places all beyond dispute, as Mr. Law does succinctly therein—we believe we may fairly regard such a work as the capstone of the impregnable bulwark of Christianity found in his own (and his adopted) writings, and the conclusion of his philosophical explanations. For although he wrote afterwards (besides one or two minor pieces) the “*Address to the Clergy*,” this was not so much a book of divine philosophy as it was a trumpet-blast, or a powerful resonance and application of the harmony, sum, and object of his later—or rather his entire twofold *Elias* ministry.

The following letter, written by Mr. Law at this time to Mr. Langcake, shows that the Bishop of London, Dr. Sherlock, fully appreciated the merits of Mr. Law’s work and the honor Law had done him in its publication:

> “June 9, 1757.—My dear friend—I believe I have nearly half a dozen letters to thank you for, and I am just as far behind in the same acknowledgments to our good friend Mr. Ward. You must help one another to be patient with me.
>
> Mr. Gurney is here with us, but his hearing is so bad at this time that the speaking is all on his side and the hearing only on ours. What makes us listen to him with more pleasure is that he speaks so much about you.
>
> Nearly a fortnight ago, I received a very good and friendly letter from the Bishop of London. Fancying you might be interested in knowing what he says regarding my book, I send you his own words as follows:
>
> ‘Permit me to express my thanks to you for the honor you have done me in the letter you inscribed to me. In it, I find many things that give me great satisfaction, and which must carry great weight with all those who seek only for the truth.’
>
> I would like half a dozen of them covered with marble or blue paper sent to me by the first package that comes here. I would also like you to send forty copies of the ‘*Christian Piety*.’ Buy and pay for both of these yourself, and then collect all expenses from my nephew. Ask Mr. Richardson if he knows whether any of them have been sent to the Universities. I would not like the advertising of it to be dropped yet.—Adieu.—W. Law.”

We have already stated that this “Letter” or “Confutation” was never publicly acknowledged by Warburton. After Mr. Law’s death, when his “*Address to the Clergy*” was published, it was found to contain some further criticisms of Warburton’s writings and a note in which Law humorously remarks that, although Warburton had recently been made a prelate, Law would continue to refer to him as a plain “Mr. or Dr.” He was unwilling to attribute such glaring errors and inconsistencies as he had pointed out to a “Right Reverend Bishop” as he would to an ordinary man. 

A short time later, Warburton published his “*Doctrine of Grace*,” in which he pretended to answer these later criticisms. But we perhaps have no better proof of the sharp mental anguish he suffered from Mr. Law’s authoritative corrections in the earlier publication and in his “*Collection of Letters*” than the following raging and brutal remark. He uttered this after the man—perhaps the only man of whom he stood in terror—was no longer alive:

> “When I reflect (he writes, alluding to Mr. Law) on his wonderful infatuation, who has spent

<meta>This page continues the discussion of William Law's works and his intellectual interactions, specifically focusing on criticisms from Bishop Warburton, the writings of Dr. Nicholas Robinson, and Law's correspondence regarding John Gambold and the Moravians.</meta>

"...a long life spent hunting after, and devouring with an incredible appetite, the trash dropped from every species of mysticism; it reminds me of what travelers tell us of a horrid fanaticism in the East, where the devotee makes a solemn vow never to taste any food other than what has passed through the entrails of some impure or savage animal. Hence their whole lives are passed (like Mr. Law's among his ascetics) in woods and forests, far removed from the conversation of mankind."

But as Payne in the "Letter" attached to his "Evangelical Discourses, 1763," and Hartley in his "Defence of the Mystic Writers" added to his "Paradise Restored," have both sufficiently commented upon the relationship between Law and Warburton, we shall say no more, but refer the reader to those publications. Accidentally taking up a volume of Warburton's works one day, we observed that, in writing to a friend upon his state of health and spirits, he calls to mind that Law once said (in his "Animadversions on Trap's Reply"), that his brain was "painted all over with hieroglyphics," but adding, "Law was wrong."

Among the number of authors to which the "Appeal" immediately gave rise, we are here reminded of having omitted to name (in addition to Freke) one Dr. Nicholas Robinson of the Royal College of Physicians, London, who we conceive had been originally attracted to the leisurely study of theological philosophy by Mr. Law's writings. In the year 1741, after the appearance of the "Appeal," he published a book with the following title:—"The Christian Philosopher, or a Divine Essay on the Doctrines of Man's Universal Redemption. Proving from the Principles of Nature, the Maxims of Philosophy, and the Sacred Records of the Old and New Testaments, that the various revolutions of human nature, as they relate to the creation, fall, and redemption of man, are grounded upon eternal reason and the moral fitness of things." With an appendix (published in the following year), being "A Physico-Theological Discourse on the Nature, Attributes, and Properties of the Serpent that tempted Eve in Paradise. Demonstrating, from the common reasons of nature, that Moses, left to himself and unassisted by the Spirit of God, never could have sketched out such a plan of things as he has left us concerning the creation and fall of man." Prefaced by "A Supplemental Discourse on the Image of God, as it distinguished Adam from all other creatures in nature and set him at the head of the creation."

This work appears to be the production of a mind that had been deeply impressed with the sentiments and style of Mr. Law's writings, more particularly the "Case of Reason" and "Remarks on the Fable of the Bees," but which had been suddenly captivated by the novel manner of treating theological subjects in the "Appeal." Then, conceiving that superior advantages would arise from uniting the scholastic metaphysical style of argumentation from "the nature and fitness of things" with the modes of reasoning suggested by a knowledge of the deep truths of nature revealed by <term>Behmen</term> <note>Jacob Behmen, also known as Jakob Böhme, a German mystic</note>, he had accordingly composed this book, which is directed against deism and atheism, the objects of the two works mentioned above. But a student and imitator of Mr. Law is always found to confuse rather than clarify the subjects he has handled. This author proceeded no further with his avowed scheme, but remained passive until some twelve months after the publication of Mr. Law's "Confutation of Warburton," the perusal of which had evidently excited him afresh and set him to patching and enlarging his work. In this interval, he would appear to have read Pike's "Philosophia Sacra" and other writers of the Hutchinsonian school. He, however, in the year 1758, published a new edition of the "Christian Philosopher" in two volumes, which, though interesting in its subjects, large in its scope of comprehension, and written in a style somewhat partaking of the ease, spirit, and simplicity of Mr. Law's diction, is a most imperfect work. The author has evidently ransacked Law and Behmen for truths relating to his scheme, but not understanding the actual grounds of their philosophy, nor the mind of Newton and other illustrators of philosophical truth, nor yet stepping cautiously in all his movements from certainty to certainty, but seeking chiefly, we say, to support his own conjectures, his work—as much of it as is *his own*—is a tissue of facts and unsound speculations. And, while affecting to be surprised at certain positions of his original authors (as if indeed he had had no intimacy with them) and of other orthodox writers concerning nature, he immediately afterward repeats their meaning in his own form of expression. Still, his work may suggest a popular mode of representing the truths of Behmen, with their illustrations, regarding modern discoveries of science and experimental philosophy.

The next letter we notice in the unpublished correspondence of Mr. Law in our possession is the following:

> "September 27th, 1757.—My dear friend—I thank you for yours of yesterday, but have not time to speak to the particulars of it as I would,—only take care of doctors. Griffith has no title to be regarded in anything he says.
>
> I have returned Menoza and have had more than enough of the little I have read of him. I am very willing to make an acknowledgment to the bookseller, and would have you give as you think proper, and to his own satisfaction.
>
> The friendly salutation of this house waits upon my best beloved friend.—*Je vous porte dans mon cœur* <note>I carry you in my heart</note>.—W. LAW.
>
> P.S.—Mr. Gambold was with me both before and after he was a Moravian. At first he came with six or seven of his fellow Methodists from Oxford; he only then hung down his head, spoke now or then a word or two, with much show of humility, meekness, etc. I said to one of them, whom I had been more acquainted with, that I could not tell what to make of Mr. Gambold, or why he should come to me. He said it was his great modesty that made him act in that manner.
>
> When I afterward saw him by himself, and he was more open, I could see nothing in him but that same kind of soft, humble, and meek language that had nothing else in it. He afterward consulted me by a letter from Oxford, in which he desired me to consider him as one who had been deeply experienced in all that the mystics had written in every age. And yet his letter was a full demonstration of quite the contrary.
>
> Two or three of the chief Moravians made attempts upon me in the same show of meek, humble, and mighty deliberate language. This may perhaps have much helped forward Mr. Gambold's uniting with them, for what they say has nothing to recommend it but their manner of saying it.
>
> What a folly for a man to say he has read Behmen and the mystics, who can talk no better..."

<margin>From the *Life of Wesley*, 2nd edition, pages 38–41, regarding the Moravians</margin>
Regarding the systematic devotional practices of the "United Brethren"—a Society, by the way, which for the implicit obedience of its chief members to its head, Count Zinzendorf, is not unlike the Jesuits with their General—and their peculiar, exciting doctrines, which captivated Wesley so much during his visit to Herrnhut in the year 1738, as mentioned in his journals; and then his addition of parts of these to his own solid Church of England principles of piety, which he had absorbed from the works of Law;—upon all these points we have provided sufficient direction to the candidate in the previous pages of this work. What Wesley afterward thought and wrote of them may be gathered from his publications and from allusions in his "Enthusiasm of the Methodists and Papists Compared." There is evidently implied in these denunciations something of a scandalous and grossly immoral nature regarding their more secret and *sanctum sanctorum* (holy of holies) practices; and this is, no doubt, what *Rimius* published at length in his "Candid Narrative of the Herrnhuters," 8vo. 1751. All of this, indeed, is easily believable by those readers who have had any acquaintance with the uncontrolled popular workings of ignorant religious enthusiasm and antinomian principles in this country and America;—though with the Herrnhuters, the simple outer-court members were not initiated into, nor had any suspicion of, the infamous mysteries and discourses of the *inner love circle*. But Lavington's tract, "The Moravians Detected," will leave nothing more to be desired concerning these matters; in which also Mr. Wesley's celebrated "man of God," Peter Böhler (page 95, above), will be found to figure quite respectably. Such activities, however, can only last in a Society where the head who promotes them possesses almost unlimited power, and only during his life; the succeeding members and the former novices shall find it impossible to believe they ever took place. The active efforts of the Count's disciples in propagating their doctrines throughout this country (many of whom, though weak-headed, were sincerely pious and amiable men) were known to Mr. Law, as may be inferred from his letter of February 12th, 1753 (previously inserted), to Mr. Langcake. It appears Langcake was personally acquainted with some of these leaders, who had been telling him that he was only in a *legal state*, which induced him to seek Mr. Law's counsel, and so gave occasion to parts of Letter XIV (third edition) of his printed "Collection of Letters." Though, by the way, we have not been able to satisfy ourselves exactly as to the individuals alluded to there as a Mr. G. and a Mr. S., unless they are Stonhouse the Universalist and Gambold, of the self-styled Moravians.

Respecting their peculiar Gospel doctrines (see Letter, p. 551), we may remark here—though we shall have to return to the subject again in the course of our narrative—that it was this incessant *talk* and preaching about the "heart-truth," the "blood," and "the Lamb," and of themselves as "*little lambs lying in the Saviour's bosom, in whom he saw no sin*," that "his lambs might do as they would, for they were not under the law but under grace," and that it was "all glory and alleluia, whatever they did" (—at the *Agapemone*, "the day of judgment is past, and we, the elect, may lead a jolly life!!"). It was this incessant rant, we say, about the "blood," the "five wounds," the "lamb," "justification," "faith," "final perseverance," "election," and "salvation," that these "Germans," as they were familiarly termed, went preaching about the country, and by which they were so successful in making converts of the simple and ignorant.

One of their eminent proselytes and preachers was a young Mr. Ingram, who, by his "lamb" and "liberty" and "blessed soul-saving" preaching, had drawn into the number of his privileged flock Lady Huntingdon's two unmarried, older sisters, who, it would appear, followed the shepherd up and down wherever he went. The end of this was—as in the modern parallel case of the Prince of the Agapemone (N.B. probably an offshoot, through <unclear>Prince</unclear>, from the same original root or stem)—that one of these elderly matrons actually became Ingram's own bosom lamb! The simple editor of the "Life of Lady Huntingdon" speaks of these parties with great gravity and respect, but if the reader desires to obtain a true insight into their character, doctrine, and proceedings, along with the judgment of a man of sense and piety upon them, he may consult for that purpose the artless autobiography or "Memorial of John Nelson," 18mo., Mason, London.

Mr. Law, in his writings (alluding to the abuse that is made of spiritual science by *effortless, prayerless, ideal transcendentalists*), speaks on the folly of attempting to understand *divine mysteries* (which only mean the manifestations of the divine nature in the soul) before the proper time. This he does in the "Spirit of Prayer," but more emphatically in the "Way to Divine Knowledge," and lastly in the third dialogue of the "Spirit of Love." In reference to this practical point, and by way of relief to our narrative, we here insert the following 'Confession' made by the theosophical scholar, Freher, who occasionally (1715) frequented a society (a revival of the early Philadelphian Society; see Roach) which met together for the plausible purpose of spiritual edification and <margin>Statement corrected on page 583</margin> conversation upon the mysteries of Behmen, in whose theory and language they were well versed, where he commonly held his peace. Being reproached for his general silence as "hiding his talents under a bushel," and told that it was his duty to edify the church by his high wisdom and understanding and to make converts to the truth, he, in reply, promised to give his reasons for the conduct he had pursued, which are contained in this confession. The opportunity which he most judiciously uses for doing so is at that stage of his theosophical discourse upon the First of his "THREE TABLES," where, treating "of man in his primeval state," he is showing his original relations to the abyssal Deity, and consequently the steps that he must take in regeneration to regain his native place. He has brought the demonstration to that point which is denominated *fire*, in strict and proper spiritual language, and so termed by Mr. Law, page 75, above; which means that particular state in the spiral, inward-circlings of the life of nature through which the soul has to travel in its journey of regeneration or purification; in other words, the gate of the full birth of the spirit of love;—the further and more refined degrees or interior stages of which, described by one who intellectually had experience of the same in himself, namely Behmen, are justly and philosophically designated *Tincture*, *Majesty*, *Ternary*, and lastly, "in the deepest depth, the ineffable Holy Name," JEHOVAH; (though not all living souls are philosophers, or have their senses exercised to understand the terms of philosophy.)—The following quo-

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the Moravians and John Wesley to the theosophical writings of Dionysius Andreas Freher, specifically focusing on his "Confession" regarding the limits of theoretical study versus practical devotion.</meta>

...our intelligence; it is thus that we create the plan of an edifice and of any work whatsoever.

[Presen]tation, then, is Freher's "Confession," which we urgently recommend for reading in this place, for its practical value and for the suggestions it offers to the wise in heart. Though writing all his voluminous and indeed invaluable (in their way) interpretations, justifications, and demonstrations of Behmen as the original truths of God—at the earnest request and urging of others—he nevertheless finds that the application of his thoughts and mind to the subject and to the labor of writing is detrimental to that robust and *lively* growth in grace, purity, and perfection. This growth is and should be the sole end of all knowledge, yet writing withdraws the efforts of his body, spirit, and soul from devotion—a powerful stimulant and nourishment, or means to bring forth the divine life in the soul. In the proper exercise of prayer—*Bramwell-like* prayer is the most direct and proper means for the meditation of the reader and for the notice of the candidate—the substance of it must be made to preface and to close *all* that shall ever be set forth in *any* book or books recommending the study of theosophical truths. We would only add one remark, if necessary after what we provided on page 527 concerning the two ways of learning goodness and virtue, which is this: that we are justified in recommending the theoretical study of Behmen, Law, etc., to those who are called to education in divine knowledge until they grasp their foundation; for it is by such understanding and knowledge that they can become true, divine workmen themselves, regarding their own souls and with regard to the world at large. Without further observation, then, we present the extract:

> Having now finished with the *Fire* in the first rotation of our spiral line, on the front side of the figure of man looking into eternity; I should, according to my first intent and promise, go further to the second, third, and fourth—where *Tincture*, *Majesty*, and *Ternary* appear, along with their different characters, and lastly in the deepest depth, the ineffable name J E H O V A H. But I must declare that I cannot go further; for, being weary within and without, I must stop here and apply my mind entirely from now on to another more necessary business, which will be of much greater importance to my own soul. Accordingly, I here part with the pursuit of my first intention and ask pardon for having thoughtlessly promised something which, because of some deeper emerging occasion, I cannot perform; observing daily more and more that an inward progress in the only necessary work is hindered and delayed in my own soul by applying all my faculties so continually to writing with pen and ink. Yet I will not leave it so abruptly as to not first lay down, more explicitly, a solid and substantial ground and reason for doing so—even one that cannot but be acknowledged as good and firm, standing upon a solid foundation, both with respect to all of us in general and also with respect to myself in particular.
>
> With respect to all of us in general, it is undeniably true that we know already much more than we need to know of things requisite and necessary to that end which all our knowledge is meant to lead us to; and that we are also convinced in ourselves of the truth of it. For we all know and admit that the *Fire* (and the fundamental doctrine of conformity to Jesus Christ, so eminently implied in it) is the only gate through which we can be let in deeper; and before or without this, no one can see, much less possess and enjoy, what is behind or within that veil. And that it is that great point where all our duties from this side, and all our happiness from the other side, meet and concentrate themselves; and which, as long as it is not attained and passed through, must hinder and delay the attainment of all really great and solid matters in every soul—seeing that on this side of this great point, there is nothing really great, solid, and weighty. If we then strive in sincerity, earnestness, and constancy [taking as our model and guide, *Bramwell*] to enter through this gate and to reach this great central point, we shall find—every one in himself, according to his measure and degree—what *Tincture* is, what *Majesty* is, etc.; whereas without so finding it in ourselves, no angel from heaven can make us understand it from the outside. Why then should words be multiplied any further about such things that do not relate at all to what we shall do, but only to what we may expect in mercy when we have finished—or rather, in doing that which we know we are to do. And
>
> With respect to myself in particular, I must declare openly that all that I could say or write further concerning *Tincture*, *Majesty*, etc., would be said and written only as if on *this side* of that great gate and point. But pray, what can be said of it on this side? To what end, intent, and purpose can anything be said of it; and what benefit could be expected either to myself or to any other from such sayings and writings? Would I not wander about in empty notions and fill my own brain, as well as the brains of others, with shadows having no life, reality, and substance? How can I declare to any other what I have not seen myself, but only heard and read about? If I did say I have seen these things and know them in the foundation of my own soul, I would be a shameless liar before God and men. If I did say that I have read in J. B. <note>Jakob Böhme</note> and have heard of these things (of the *Light of Majesty* especially) both here and overseas, and never without perplexity and amazement, I would be telling the truth. And if I did say I can repeat the words, or at least the substance of them, written or spoken by others, I would also be telling the truth. But if I did undertake to bring forth words of my own concerning the *Tincture*, *Majesty*, etc.—even if they were ever so true, pertinent, and consistent with the foundation of my friend J. B.—I might justly be called presumptuous. And though I might not be called so by others, yet my own conscience would tell me that I am, and that I intend to set up a fine show and to make a name and reputation for myself, etc. No benefit could arise from it, neither to myself nor to any other; but harm rather, and detriment might be expected both on my side and on the side of those who might think my words are what they are not. But from this my plain declaration, and from the example of my breaking off—by which I declare both to myself and others that there is the highest necessity for us to do what we know we ought to do [that is, to pursue the *Bramwell*-process of devotion in order to attain "perfection"], but no necessity at all to speculate and search curiously after things not to be found in any reality but only as a shadow before we have done what our own heart tells us we are obliged to do—from this declaration and example, I say, more benefit may reasonably be expected.

<meta>This page continues the personal reflection or "Confession" of Dionysius Andreas Freher regarding his spiritual development and the nature of his writings on Jacob Boehme.</meta>

Notre faculté créatrice est vaste, active, inépuisable, mais en l'examinant de près, nous voyons

It is true that I have previously written something about these matters as well, though very briefly, because I knew then as well as I know now that I could do it only *historically*, not *through personal experience*. But at this time, the case is quite altered by many other circumstances. Therefore, I cannot do the same thing now that I could do then, but must break off before I come to the end of this "First Table." Regarding the other two Tables, I must say that not only are there many things in them which are already touched upon and at least implicitly stated in this "First Table," but also *that there is nothing in them which will not reveal and declare itself in reality and substance once this gate is opened and this point is reached.* If this is not a fully convincing argument, I am willing to be better informed; and if it is, the consequence is plain and evident: that it is much better for both myself and others to move forward within [in the true *Methodist* <note>In this context, "Methodist" refers to a disciplined, systematic way of seeking spiritual perfection, common in the 18th century.</note> way of seeking God and "entire sanctification"] than to run any further outside, although I may perhaps be blamed by one person or another for doing so. I may expect this all the more because such a thing has already happened several times lately. For,

One friend criticized me for living so privately or in secret and advised me to make myself known, to seek more conversation, to go out into the world, and to do some good with my talent in the present generation by instructing others and making converts to the truth. For, he said, I would find myself obligated to do so if I had the knowledge that you have, etc. I answered this friend only very briefly then, and now I think it not worth my while to take any further notice of it, for reasons best known to myself. But,

Another good friend of mine, soon after this, criticized me for keeping so much to myself, even among friends, that they could hardly get anything from me. He told me that others with whom we previously spoke more often had found the same fault, and the conclusion of all was this: that I was not fit for conversation. To this friend, I then made a serious promise that I would answer him and reveal to him my inner foundation and whole heart, without ambiguity or mental reservations. I will now perform this promise according to my best ability, without regard for what might arise in my own mind to dissuade me from such freedom, and without fear of his taking anything the wrong way or putting a wrong construction upon my words. I will do it (1.) with a more general respect to those other friends whose testimony he brought in, and then also (2.) with a more particular respect to the conversation between himself and me.

IN THE FIRST PLACE, it is undeniably true that this fault you find with me in outward conversation has its deep roots in an internal secret constitution, or the essential <term>signature</term> <note>A Behmenist term referring to the outward expression of an inner spiritual essence.</note> of my own mind. Furthermore, it is also true that if this signature were entirely of my own making, a much worse name than that of a "fault" might be justly given to it. But again, it is no less true that no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of man which is in him. Since you, my friend, according to this general rule, can as little know my affairs as I can know yours, you can judge no further than what outwardly appears to you and what you can understand. Therefore, to base your judgment upon a deeper foundation, I will reveal my affairs to you as much as the words of this world are able to open secret spiritual depths. If you find a self-justifying spirit in them, you may justly reject and condemn it, just as I have previously condemned and rejected such a spirit in another friend. But if you meet with a spirit of sincerity that speaks the naked truth, and speaks it for good ends, and speaks it as if in the presence of God without self-justification, *then be careful how you judge*, and do not trust your own deep-piercing and penetrating spirit, but say instead, *I do not understand it*.

This internal signature of my own mind, and consequently this fault you find with me, is indeed, in a large sense, of *my own making*. It was made by myself before I could well distinguish my right hand from my left, or when I was most terribly blind and ignorant. To that extent, therefore, it is evil and falls under the judgment of the Almighty. But He who brings good out of evil has made use of this evil of mine for my own good and for the preservation of my own soul. For by this disposition and signature of my mind, changed and improved by Him, I avoided many nets and snares, was kept from self-exaltation, restrained from rashly judging others, and was led through many strange things and dangerous passages without receiving hurt. Even by you yourself, my friend, I would have been led away and involved in one labyrinth after another *if it had not been for this internal disposition of my mind*. To that extent, therefore, it is *not of my own making*, but God, in His infinite *love, free grace, and mercy*, shall be praised and glorified by it forever and ever.

Now to give you a short verbal description of that inward invisible figure of my mind, considered as changed and improved by free grace, I tell you that after my dreadful, sudden [*spiritual*] *shock* (though indeed long before it I also had something much like it, but it never reached that level), I could never be satisfied with or much pleased by anything inferior to what I then perceived was attainable only by reaching that *great point* and entering through *that gate*. Besides this, I had from that time a deeper sense in my mind than the <term>astral spirit</term> <note>In theosophy, the mind or spirit tied to the physical and cosmic world rather than the divine.</note> can give to anyone living in this world, and a stronger impression of that sense in my soul than any words in this world can declare, concerning a vast or rather an immense difference or distance between knowledge and understanding. Therefore, when I was afterwards quite unexpectedly called, entreated, and mightily desired to write about <term>J. B.</term> <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), the German Christian mystic.</note>, I was often strangely amazed how it could happen that I could be so pressed to write of things which my own heart told me I did *not yet understand*. This was the true ground and reason why I never could nor did put any real value upon my own writings, forced out of me as they were; and why (I dare say) I could have seen them all burned without any inward concern. When I perceived afterwards that they were read, valued, and sought after, I was put into such a state of mind that I knew not what to think or say of it. I freely admit that I thought to myself, more than once and not superficially, *Surely all those who value so highly what I value so little must be completely blind and deplorably ignorant?* Yet at the same time, as I always had that commandment against me, *Judge not*; so I always also had this plain reason for me: *If they could see with their own eyes, and if they had a spirit able to discern between know-*

qu'elle n'est que secondaire, temporelle, dépendante, c'est-à-dire, qu'elle doit son origine à une

*knowledge and understanding, and between things really valuable and things of no great value, they would immediately perceive that all these books of mine were written before that* gate *was opened in me and that* great point *attained; and would therefore not value them any more than I can and do value them myself.*

Everyone who could speak of great things consistently with J.B., I thought must necessarily know something of this gate and point, <note>the birth of Love, see page 76</note> and must have such a discerning spirit; and I did not dare to freely entertain thoughts to the contrary about anyone, being restrained by a superior power for which I cannot account. And yet, I could never reconcile their actions and proceedings with what I bore in my own mind. If I had followed this too far with my imagination, it might have driven me to distraction. I know my words are very confused, yet I cannot help it; the invisible state of my mind was much more so. I cannot convey to you the internal sensation I had of it, nor the deep impression these things made upon my soul. But,

To come closer to the matter, let me tell you that on this basis—at that time when you were eager and busy to bring me over to that assembly which I joined later by other means (not knowing then yourself what you were about to do, nor that next year you would do quite the opposite)—at that time, I say, I had a higher opinion of those friends than of myself. I thought myself *not fit for their conversation* long before you heard them say so. Yet when I had come among them, this high opinion of them was soon mixed with great confusion within myself. For something in me would secretly suggest to my mind that this gate was still shut in them, and this *great point* not yet attained. And something else in me would reprimand me for thinking so, and would not let such thoughts settle in my mind as a certain truth.

The reasons for the former were these: (1) because I never heard any mention made of it; (2) because they valued so much what I could value so little; and (3) because I could never see any actual good effects, which I was sure could not have failed to follow the *opening of that gate* and the *attainment of that point*. A reason for the latter was that I heard so many excellent words, fluent discourses, and confident declarations of great, high, and glorious things. <note>It was undoubtedly to these matters that Mr. Law refers in his letter of April 8, 1747, to Mr. Stephen Penny of Bristol (a quotation from which was given at the head of the note on page 46) and not, as was there supposed, to the original Philadelphian Society, which was broken up upon Mrs. Lead's death in the year 1703 or 1704.</note>

Between these two positions, I sat in great doubt and hesitation; for I did not dare to say positively that they were under delusions, and I did not dare to utter such glorious things about myself. And so I fell so far and so deep into confusion that I did not know at all what to think or say, either of them or of myself. Regarding the effects this had on me, I say now only this: it made me, on one hand, increasingly sensible that I was not fit for their conversation, and on the other hand, increasingly weary of everything and almost everyone too, because I never knew what to say to them, nor what to accept from them. But a while later, the private disputes, frequent fallings out, continual discords, and the anger and animosity always present in that assembly gave me some relief and extricated me more and more from my confusion. They showed me and convinced me of the truth of what I was previously so slow, backward, and cautious to let settle in my mind. You know what was done on my part to compose all those differences and to maintain peace and union; and you know the effects and consequences of my doing so as well as I do. Could you see at that time that I kept so much to myself among those known friends—whose testimonies you now claim show they could hardly get anything out of me? If you did find me so then, tell me now, even though you did not tell me then. And if you did not find me so then, but must rather admit that they got from me ten times more than they ever would or could digest, then give me leave to tell you that in all those matters *I was not understood*, neither by yourself nor by others. For if you had understood, you would have taken other measures according to your own free and voluntary promise; indeed, you would have taken such measures as I should show you, which you never did, for want of understanding me.

You must necessarily allow that there is a vast difference between understanding the words of another *grammatically* and understanding him *essentially*. Grammatically, even though my words were not ordered according to the rules of English grammar, I was always understood well enough; for what I said or wrote was approved, its truth was acknowledged, and whenever I said, "I am not understood," I was always answered, "We understand you very well."

Who shall be the judge here of whether I was understood or not? I say my own internal essences (and likewise the essences of everyone who proposes any spiritual matter) can be the best and ought to be the *only* judges. For they alone can feel within themselves whether or not they have really reached and stirred the internal essences of the hearer, and whether or not they have raised in his essences a full harmony with themselves and an equal disposition of mind toward that which the speaker verbally acknowledges to be the truth. If they have, the intended good effects must necessarily follow. And if they have not, those internal essences in the speaker need no other testimony from outside but are clearly convinced within themselves of this plain truth: that they are not understood *essentially*, but only outwardly, grammatically, and superficially. Neither can they be blinded nor made senseless by any of those confident replies saying, "We understand you very well," for their feelings cannot be overcome by words.

If then, (1) in the state of that confusion I spoke of in the previous paragraph, the internal visible state of my mind was such as I declared, it is no wonder that I could, with more pleasure and readiness, "take a pipe" with those friends and talk of the Sultan and the Great Mogul rather than of things in which I had no great interest. I could not perceive those things to flow out of a solid ground, and I saw no prospect of any actual good effects being produced from them—having experienced how I had fared with my first declaration made to them concerning matters of practice. If this was a fault in me, let it be one without my contradicting it, and let it be as great or as little as they please to make it; for my part, I shall be neither better nor worse for it. (2) In that following state, when I had come out of the inward confusion and had the opportunity to utter many things, all for good ends and allowed to be good and true; if this was my condition,

...creative, superior, independent, and universal faculty, of which ours is only a faint copy,

that I could not be understood essentially, that we remained strangers in our inner foundation, and that discord and division increased among them as much as I tried to promote peace and union—and that I did not dare say, *I am not understood*, without being immediately contradicted—what should I have done then? You be the judge. Of my great secret, which I may call my *philosopher’s stone*—upon which the preservation of my earthly life depends, without being a burden to anyone—I did not dare utter one word, for twenty good, substantial reasons. To you, my friend, I gave several hints of it, but found that in your foundation, depth, practice, and *serious effort* toward practice, you were as much a stranger to it as I am a stranger to your stone.

I did not dare speak of mysteries and high speculations, because I did not value those things half as much as I valued things on the other side of the "great gate and point." I did not dare mention this gate and point, unless I wanted to willfully provoke a new dispute. Regarding matters relating to the *practice of Godliness*, the *doctrine of conformity with Jesus Christ*—to the reading of our own book, to judging no one but ourselves first, to looking first into our own dark root and foundation before we look into someone else's, to our being all one in both respects, etc.—you know that I have spoken much more than they could take in; for it was neglected (though not contradicted) for lack of practice and understanding.

Therefore, nothing was left for me to use my tongue or rather my pen for, except such things as most of them delighted to be entertained with: namely, *enjoyments*, *triumphant joys and exultations*, *openings of the second principle*, etc. If I had only praised, exalted, and admired these things, and had shown a desire to attain them in their way and manner, I would have been an excellent fellow in their opinion. But I had nothing to say about these things at all because, as they themselves rightly and truly said (and I thank them for speaking this truth), *I was not acquainted with such things*. If, then, I was not only unacquainted with those things but also declared openly that I did not desire them—and could nevertheless present many good and necessary things to them which they truly lacked and were not acquainted with—it is plain that my essence had embraced something with which theirs had no acquaintance. Their essence valued something which mine made little of; therefore, we were strangers to each other in our internal essences, and consequently, they were *as little suited for my conversation as I was for theirs*.

But now, MY FRIEND, with more specific respect to you and me, let me ask you this legitimate question: *What was our conversation?* You know that some of our acquaintances, whose testimonies you cited, knew nothing of this "gate" and "great point"; and that others did not deny or contradict what they heard of it but acknowledged the truth—some more and others less coldly, indifferently, and superficially. But my question shall not be extended to any of them; rather, just between you and me, I ask: *What was our conversation during the whole time of our acquaintance?* I will not answer it with a definition or description of my own making, because my own might be subject to various different objections; but Moses, the mediator of the old covenant, shall answer it for both of us. He says, *We spend our years as a tale that is told*. I admit, on my part, that these words are a plain, full, and true description of our conversation, which you should take notice of as much as I should. For I blame you no more with these words than I blame myself; yet not one bit less. Please remember, in serious reflection and inner examination of your mind and in the fear of God, how many fine tales were told between us concerning this gate and this great point; and do not misunderstand me, as if I were now condemning and rejecting everything that was spoken about this matter. No, no, God forbid! But I say only these three things, and you may know that I speak the truth. (1.) All these tales in which we spent these years never yet reached any solid stability, much less any true internal reality; and that spark of an almighty will which lies in our souls was never yet so essentially touched by those tales as to produce any good, great, or significant effect outwardly. What good you may have gained from them internally, I can judge as little as you can judge me. (2.) I say that, just as it is much better and more profitable to *proceed slowly and moderately, but steadily and constantly*, in the way we are in—maintaining the ground we stand upon, even if little or nothing is known or said of this gate and point—provided our way is right and straight, not wrong and crooked; so it is much worse and more harmful to *tell tales* about it and to show, in those tales, great earnestness and passion one day, only to be cool and negligent the next. (3.) I say to you, my friend, judge and decide for yourself: whose mind of the two is more harmless, and whose years are more innocently spent? His, *who tells more tales* and is on that account *more suited for conversation*? Or his who tells *fewer tales* and is less or not at all suited for it? For my part, I hereby freely and openly declare that I am, in my mind and spirit, as weary of *telling* and of *hearing tales* concerning this point and gate as I am weary of anything in this world.

On your part, my good friend, you have shown and proven more than sufficiently that you *are suited for conversation even with the greatest princes and courtiers in the world*. But allow me to tell you that you are better suited for conversation with such people than with simple, humble, and lowly people—although I admit that you can condescend and, in a way, force yourself to do it sometimes. To prove this, besides my own observation, I could cite against you such testimonies from my close friends as you have cited against me. But it would be great folly for me to do so, and it would give you a just reason to think that I was angry with you, that I took your words as an affront and wanted to be revenged on you. No such thing. How could I take them in anger when you said no more than what I myself have said many times—not out of an affectation of false humility, but from a deep sense and feeling of my own nature? And if I never took notice outwardly, and was not moved inwardly, when you once before called me a *fool*—distinguishing that "fool" on the outside from my foundation within—how should I now take this so poorly, which is not as harsh and rough as that? Besides, I know and acknowledge before God that your words, declaring me *not suited for conversation*, do not have such an extensive, harmful, and malicious meaning that they should be resented as much as I may seem—but only seem—to do. For I take them with a better distinction than you realize, and my intent in writing these things is directed elsewhere.
