I thank you sincerely for this expression of yours, because it has lifted a great burden from me and has made me feel more light and easy than I ever was before. Moreover, it has provided an opportunity to discover something that otherwise might have remained hidden until the end of my life. No evil will come of it, at least not on my part; but *good* may be produced on both sides if we—assisted by the grace of God—make ourselves capable of his blessing. Therefore, my friend, do not take anything I say the wrong way, but remember that I told you before I would be plain and open; and consider that sincerity, just as much as justice, is no respecter of persons.

On my part, and regarding my own person, I acknowledge again and again that I am *not fit for conversation*, and that I was made unfit for it, partly by the spirit of this world and partly by *that dreadful sudden shock* I hinted at before. For this gave me such a strong sense, and made such a deep, lively impression in my soul of my own *being nothing* and *having nothing*, that I shall never be able in this world to make any other soul—by any words of mine—as sensible of it as I *was* made, or to make myself understood as essentially as I *was* made to understand myself essentially within. Neither can I always represent it to myself as deeply as to have the same sensation and impression I had then; but I must be satisfied with this: that the same good effects and the same wholesome disposition of mind continue and remain with me; and through the grace of God, they shall remain as long as I live in this world. I do not doubt that you yourself also have a deep sense and impression in your soul of *your being nothing and having nothing*; I only say that your sensation and impression of it is not mine, and mine is not yours. For if it were, you would have been as little fit for conversation as I am; and it would have been an eternal impossibility for you (I know what I am saying) to have done the things you did.

Therefore, my kind request of you is this: that you would be pleased hereafter to find no more fault with my unfitness; for though you would do no harm to me, you might perhaps harm yourself, which I would not want you to do. What we call *conversation* in this world is rightly called *communion of saints* with respect to another world. Conversation includes a two-legged beast <note>the physical body or animal nature of man</note> which will be devoured by worms and turned into dust and ashes; but this *communion* excludes that beast, although during this mortal life, it cannot be entirely excluded in every sense. This *communion* must be the inward ground and foundation of conversation, if conversation is not to perish along with the beast and with this world. If conversation stands upon this ground and foundation and is animated by this communion, it is then blessed and sanctified and able to produce good fruits. But if not, it is a certain truth that the more one is fit for conversation in this world, and the more he cultivates and maintains it—even in the best way, sense, and manner—the greater damage and loss he must expect to meet in the world to come. This is because this *conversation* and all his fitness for it, having no eternal root and not being animated by this *communion*, cannot go with him through death, but must sink into the grave together with his beast. I, for my part, have reason to thank my God and Father in heaven that *I am not fit for it*. Neither can I pray to him to be made fit for it in this world and in this sense. But my prayer is rather for this: that I may be made *unfit* for it more and more, and that all the world and all its conversation (not standing upon this foundation and not being influenced and animated by this communion) may be crucified to me, and I to it. May God our Father, in his infinite love and mercy, make us altogether fit (as he is willing and ready to do, if we do not hinder him and do not think *we are fit already*) for a *conversation* not made up of *telling and hearing tales*, but of *finding, feeling, touching, embracing, and keeping each other in our inward renewed or renewing ground*. For by that, and only by that, our *conversation* may be in heaven within, even during this time already, while it is and must still be in the flesh without.

**HAVING THUS BY THIS ANSWER** discharged myself of the obligation I was under due to a promise to a friend, and having said before that I cannot go any further in the explanation of these TABLES, but that I would henceforth employ my mind wholly in another necessary business, I shall here, as a conclusion to all, explicitly declare what business I mean. This is not only so that the truth of my words may appear clearer to my friends (though it is of much greater importance to my soul), but also and even chiefly so that this declaration of mine, written by my own hand, may stand as a testimony against myself if I should not perform, or not continue in the performance of, what I intend and promise to do in secret before my *Father in heaven, who sees in secret*, through his grace.

My whole intent and purpose is to seek, through earnest and unceasing application to God my Savior, for his perfect manifestation in my soul; and, regarding my studies, to read and meditate only upon the Scripture and my worthy friend J. B. <note>Jakob Böhme</note>. By these two, I intend to be always excited and stirred up to recollect and turn my mind inward, whether I am at home or abroad—not letting it wander into unnecessary things; to remember always the saying of my Lord to Martha: "One thing is needful"; to keep my heart with all diligence, because the issues of life flow from it; to seek no conversation with the children of this world; to refrain my tongue from telling tales; to keep my ears open so that I may be ready to hear what God will speak in my own conscience; and to have my eye always intent and fixed upon Him, and him alone, as if no creature were in the world besides myself. Yet I will do so without ever excluding from my mind that inward foundation in any of my fellow members in whom even the smallest grain of grace is sown by his Spirit; but whatever I may desire for my own soul, I will desire for them also, and nothing for myself alone. For although these two things may seem, in some of my outward expressions, to be more or less inconsistent with each other, I know sufficiently that they are so coherent in substance and internal reality, and so firmly linked together, that they are inseparable; and the one relating to my own soul in particular cannot be pursued with any success without the other, which relates to all my fellow members in general. And this, through the grace of God and by his assistance, I intend to do without any outward hypocritical show, peculiar affectation, or ostentation, as if I were not like other men; in short, without any alteration from how I have appeared outwardly until now. Because I do not intend to make my outward *two-legged beast* holy and fit for heaven, but only to have a bridle put into its mouth and a hook into its nostrils, so that it may not kick and trample me under its feet, and turn again and tear me to pieces. <meta>This page continues the author's exploration of spiritual identity and the soul's relationship with God. It follows from the previous page's discussion of man as an "effigy" or "coin" that implies a "matrix" or mold of the Creator.</meta>

My ultimate goal in doing so will not be the salvation and happiness of my own soul: no. For if I were to make this my ultimate goal and reach no deeper into the spirit of my mind, I know that I would be acting from a very subtle, secret, and almost imperceptible root of *selfishness*. My ultimate goal, therefore, will be this (beyond which I know nothing further or deeper, and which is not invented by the subtlety of reason): that my whole created being in body, soul, and spirit, with all its essences and faculties without exception, may be possessed by Him who is its rightful and sole proprietor and purchaser; and that He may receive the reward due to His bloody labors, according to the promise made to Him by the Father, saying, *Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, etc.*: which, as it is said in general with respect to all the nations upon earth, is also applicable in particular to every individual person, and therefore to myself as well. And this alone I will constantly desire to be fulfilled and performed in me. "*For the laborer is worthy of his reward;*" and *for my soul he has labored and struggled*, and therefore ought not to be served by me in such a way as to have occasion to complain and say, *I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing*.

But seeing as I know the Father cannot give, and He cannot receive, any soul except one that is made conformable to Him by His Spirit, therefore His fundamental doctrine of *conformity to Him*, according to the sense He has given me of it, will be my principal rule. If I follow this, taking His yoke upon me—which is easy—and His burden—which is light—and learning from Him, I will have no need of <term>casuists</term> and commentators. Because He has promised that he who follows Him "*shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life;*" and have as a guide His Spirit, which leads into all truth necessary for salvation. I will only need simplicity, sincerity, humility, and love. I take special notice of these four and list them particularly for my own sake and for reasons best known to myself. Although I know very well that in each of them all the other three are implied; so that if I have one of them, I have them all in that one, because they are all inseparable companions, and none of them can really be had without having all the rest. And these four, I am certain, will be the best and most fit <term>casuists</term> and commentators—sufficient also for my necessary instruction in all cases and matters whatever.

And to this fundamental doctrine of *conformity with Him* I will apply my mind and spirit, neither out of fear of hell nor out of hope for heaven, but only because it is imprinted on my soul and spirit. I can read it there as plainly as I can read what I am writing now: that it ought to be so, without asking or answering any *Why*; without a prior examination of any arguments pro or con; without deliberation and consultation with flesh and blood; and without sour looks, murmuring, or complaining, but with gladness of heart, willingness of spirit, and cheerfulness of mind. Knowing and always remembering not only that my Lord and Master says of Himself, "*Behold, I come; in the volume of the book it is written of me, I delight to do your will, O my God;*" but also that in the same volume of the book it is written of me likewise, if I am to be numbered among those people of whom it is said, "*Your people shall be willing in the day of your power,*" or, according to the German translation, "After your conquest, your people shall serve you willingly"—not with uneasiness and reluctance, as if compelled by force, nor in a mercenary manner, like someone hired for wages, but freely, willingly, and with delight, having received this spirit of willingness from His own free grace.

This spirit of willingness in the soul not only implies and strongly confirms what I said before—that my ultimate goal in the spirit of my mind ought not to be the salvation of my own soul—and not only resolves the question of whether a person can love God and willingly do His will without fixing their eye on the reward promised to those who love Him, but it also sufficiently answers an objection made from the words of the Apostle, saying of our Lord and Savior that "*for the joy that was set before him, he endured the cross.*" This silly question cannot be asked, and this senseless objection—senseless in its internal <term>ground</term>, though specious enough in superficiality or to the sight of reason—cannot be made by anyone except those who know nothing in their own <term>ground</term> of the life and motions of this spirit of willingness, and very little of what our future salvation and happiness will be.

For my part, and to my own full satisfaction, I know that my Lord and Savior, having said, "*Behold, I come; I delight to do your will, O my God,*" immediately declares the deepest ground and only foundation of this delight in the following words: "*Yes, your law is within my heart.*" I know that here no other *why* is to be asked, and no deeper ground or reason to be searched for. Nevertheless, I know that in an inferior and exterior sense and respect, better suited to my own weak capacity and to excite in me the spirit of willingness (or to raise it when clouded or suppressed), it is rightly said of Him that "*for the joy that was set before him, he endured the cross.*" But I also know that it is a false conclusion to say He made this joy His ultimate goal in the spirit of His mind, or that He would not have delighted to do the will of His God if it had not been for this joy or for this necessary consequence of His delight. This, I say, is injurious to Him and to that spirit of willingness which He had in the highest perfection, because He also had the law of His God in the highest perfection within His heart.

And regarding my own future happiness, I know that it will be a necessary consequence, or an inseparable appendix, to that *ultimate goal* which I named above. This goal, relating to my Savior, is greater and more dignified than anything relating to myself can be; therefore, it would be perverse behavior if I were to make that which is lesser and inferior my ultimate goal. Furthermore, I also know that this salvation and happiness will consist of two things united into one: namely, on one side, the greatest riches, fullness, life, and glory of which I can be capable; and on the other side, the utmost poverty, emptiness, death, and nothingness of *myself* and of all that is my own. Or rather, it will consist in an everlasting, harmonious union of these two things which, in this world, are contraries. It is such a union as will bind and cement them together so that they shall be inseparable from each other forever and ever. Such a union that they shall make up *one perfect circle* wherein the beginning shall not be discerned from the end, nor the end from the beginning; indeed, such a union that I may freely and truly say of each of these two things: *This is that, and that is this*. For dying to myself perpetually is living to my Savior eternally in happiness and glory—and this living is that dying. Emptying myself continually of all my own

If then my merciful God and Father in heaven gives me a simple, sincere, humble, and loving heart; not according to the notions I might have of these words, but according to the sense in which his Spirit takes these words in the Scripture—a sense of which I cannot yet have a right, true, and adequate idea. If he gives me, I say—(though indeed this is a very silly expression, fit only for this world and for earthly senses, but altogether nonsensical in the internal ground; and a very striking instance showing what all our words are in this world when we try to express spiritual matters belonging to another world. For it implies something of an uncertainty, hesitation, or doubtfulness as to whether our merciful God and Father in heaven is willing to give it; whereas I know, not only that he on his side is *always ready and willing to give it*, even *giving it continually*, but also, that in those *earnest desires and longings for it*, which were his gifts, he *has given us* also the thing desired and longed for. Notwithstanding, at the same time I must own to my own shame, that I have it not; so that “he may be justified when he speaks and be clear when he judges.” But let me go on with my nonsensical expression, because it is so common in this world, and I can have no better; and let it suffice me that his Spirit understands the internal sense of my mind)—if, I say, he gives me such a heart, I shall be (according to my friend <term>Jacob's</term> words) <note>Referring to the mystic Jacob Boehme</note> *one of the richest and noblest men on earth*; because they are such riches and such a nobility as will continue and be perpetuated, and go along with me through death into life. Yet, just as I know I shall do in another world for all eternity, (N.B.) so I must begin to do in this world; I must lay them down entirely and continually at the feet of that merciful Giver, denying them to be *my own*, and owning myself to be *one of the basest, vilest, and poorest creatures among mankind*.—And this, (N.B.) I must not do in affectation or in imitation of such words as I may have heard from another and may admit to be good and true; for this would be very superficial, if not quite hypocritical. Neither must I do it only in a sincere assent and consent of my refined reason; for although this is good and necessary, yet I must not rest there, nor think to have attained the highest pitch by it. But I am to know that there is still something much deeper or higher and more solid: namely, a profound, substantial, unutterable sense or sensation of the truth of it. This sensation my refined reason can provide as little as it can give me a spirit of willingness, although it can apprehend and convince me both of the truth and of the necessity of it. But this sensation can be given only by that Spirit from above, which can also give a spirit of willingness; and without His giving it, no living soul can ever have it, let her reason be ever so much refined. Yet this refined reason may safely go on in this practice; for her sincere persistence in it will not be in vain, but will have a good and blessed success.—And this, my laying them down and denying them perpetually, I know will be my constant keeping, preserving, and securing them. *Poverty, therefore, and riches, baseness and nobility, are in this harmonious union not two, but only one thing—one everlasting life, happiness, and glory.*”

After the above quotation—for the length and redundancy of expression of which (the writer being a foreigner) no apology need be offered, much less for the insertion of it, speaking as it does a language of inestimable instruction and wisdom to the devout reader and aspiring theosopher, if he is not already experimentally conversant with the truths taught in it—after this quotation, we say, and as being in strict accordance with the design of the present treatise, we now offer for perusal (which we could not have ventured to do before) the following extracts from some unpublished letters in our possession. These illustrate the state of experience of a soul which had actually reached the end (which we have so often mentioned by way of suggestion) of a spiritual life. That the writer had attained to that *great point* and passed through *that gate* so much spoken of in the above quotation, even to a *high degree of divine union* (and this also by the classic *<term>Bramwell-process</term>*), <note>A method of intense, persistent prayer for entire sanctification, associated with the evangelist William Bramwell.</note> there is undoubted evidence in these letters, if in them “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth does (truly) speak.” The singular conformity of the writer's judgment with the views and sentiments contained in the above quotations from Freher's manuscript works, and also pervading Mr. Law's later publications, will doubtless strike the conversant reader with surprise. For what those illuminated authors declare as the result of their perfected science, this writer evidently utters from a natural ground of experience, from an original sensibility of life. And though some readers might expect a more solemn tone to pervade the expressions of a sanctified soul than appears here on a first perusal (for instance, such as is found in the “Biography and Diary of H. A. Rogers, Mason, London”), yet the Apostle's declaration must be ever kept in mind: namely, that there are “diversities of operations but the same Spirit.” There are diversities of complexions and <term>signatures</term> of humanity, as varied as the flowers of the field, but it is “one spirit” governing the soul where pure truth, light, and wisdom are the actual births and natural flashes of it. The writer of these letters was a woman, one immersed in the common occupations of life and the mother of a family; and this gives occasion to remark that the simplicity of purpose, sincerity of affection, and directness of action which is found to distinguish the <term>feminine tincture</term> <note>In Behmenist philosophy, the "tincture" refers to the essential quality or spiritual orientation of a being.</note> appears better to qualify that sex to receive divine impressions and energies, and to rise up into high spirituality and purity, than the naturally questioning, encumbered, and divided mind and will of the male character. She, it appears, did not fail to receive the standard credentials of those who “will live godly in Christ Jesus,” namely, persecution *by reason*. We, however, commit the extracts to the reader's own judgment and, if they are of the nature of paradise blossoms, to his instinct, to draw from them what spiritual honey and refreshment he may. Perhaps they may prove, as the authoress herself proposed, a staff for the Christian pilgrim to lean upon and an incitement to renewed diligence in climbing the steep and high hill of perfection. They are these:—

> “Christmas Eve, 1791.—Dear Sir—I found you had a desire for the hidden manna which has been, through the rich mercy of God, given to me—less than the least of all his dear people; yes, grace has taken to itself a body and has counted me worthy of that superlative, distinguished honor. This is the real cause of my giving you the trouble of a line—to encourage you to pursue

*Malgré le rapport ou la tendance que nous conservons vers ce centre commun, nous avons pu*

the "narrow way that leads unto eternal life," which few, very few find; and why? Because the way to the crown is the way of the cross. Deep sorrows and heavy afflictions are the portion of the Lord's favorites here below; this is the reason why so few attain this inestimable prize, in my humble opinion. I long to find souls who are thirsting for the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, and so hungry that they cannot be satisfied with the *husks* of outward preaching. No, they are starving for celestial food, and cannot be at rest without it. To those choice souls the Lord gives out of his hidden storehouse; for "there is a path which the vulture's eye has not seen"—a holy state, when the soul communes with the Lord without words. Drops of water assimilate, but acid and alkali cause an effervescence. Oh, how pleasant it is when the soul feels itself "filled with God," when the will, like sugar in hot water, melts and dissolves itself into union with Jehovah, and tastes paradisical pleasures! Go on, dear Sir, and press into the deep abyss of sovereign love. Paradise is to be entered into in this life, the tree of life is *here* on earth, and those who have passed through the first resurrection eat the fruit of it every day. Pardon me for obtruding my experimental joys on you; I only mean it as a staff for you to lean on while pursuing your pilgrimage to the heavenly city. I delight in the experience of real Christians, and I wish you, Sir, the dew of the heavenly grace to comfort you, and more of the Divine unction to instruct you, until you taste celestial enjoyments. I am, with cordial love, in gospel bonds, your friend and servant, MARY PRATT.

"January 16th, 1792. —— I was cautious when I wrote lest any misconstruction might be put on my letter, but the spirit of your writing breathes a different language.

My husband is a strenuous follower of the visionary Swedenborg, and as the writings of the Baron work against the pure doctrine and experience of God manifested in the flesh, I have no fellowship with my partner in religion; indeed, I have been most cruelly treated by him because of my progress in the super-celestial life.

I love and esteem Mr. ***; indeed, he is the only person I have any fellowship with; and although our experience differs, yet he is pressing after the prize in earnest, through many difficulties both inward and outward. "The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force."

You say, dear Sir, that you have read many mystic authors and have been a sojourner for thirty years. Blessed probation! Do not faint but hold out to the end, for I have eaten—yes, I daily feast on—"the grape brought from the land of Eshcol," one taste of which will overbalance all your tedious waiting. But perhaps you are among the number of those who look for perfection in the flesh! Alas, alas, the body is bestial, sensual, and devilish; it is "the son of the bondwoman who must be cast out, so that the son of the free woman may reign." I am confident from experience that one of Satan's deepest schemes is to show the soul its deformity, as if to say: Look here, how filthy you are! See how ugly sin has made you! Worse than a dog, or a pig, etc. These things have often bowed down my poor soul and made my chariot wheels drag heavily; but this was while I was in the earthly state. I am delivered from it, and experience the joys of the "new heaven and the new earth, and the former things have passed away," nor do they come into my mind at all. I truly live in paradise, having passed by the angel that stands at the gate to guard the tree of life. His flaming sword has cut off all that is *not God*, and I entered naked, without any garment. The undefiled righteousness of Jesus the anointed, Jah-Jehovah, has clothed me, and I see and rejoice in my own beauty—*not* by my own achievements, *not* by my sufferings though they were grievous and most terrible, *not* by vigils for twenty years, nor by fasting, abstraction, or prayer. No, it was the Lord's free gift. He made me see my own darkness, impotence, insufficiency, and extreme poverty and nakedness; and then (glory forever to his adorable love) he took me into his bosom, and I became his bride—the object in which his soul delights. He espoused vile me! I am his beloved and he is mine, and death or hell cannot part us; for those who are made "partakers of the first resurrection, over them the second death has no power." Come then, my very dear brother, beloved in the Lord, come, lift up your dejected head, "for he who shall come will come and will not tarry." "The Spirit and the bride say, come, and let him who hears say, come; all things are ready." Perhaps you may be looking for some outward testimony, as I was for a very long time; that is, I fear, a delusion, for the Lord is in the still small voice. Do you relish my writing? Do you have a taste for it? Can you find sweetness in the heavenly manna? Have you been enlightened by the Holy Ghost? Do you know the precious tincture of the water of life? Are you hungry—starving—ready to tear your flesh in pieces (speaking figuratively)? These are delightful signs. "Blessed are they who hunger and thirst after Truth"; they may—no, "they shall be filled." Dear Sir, do look more inward, *abandon yourself to the Lord*; say, "Lord, if I perish, I perish." Take all your shortcomings, your very deformities, and lay them at his blessed feet. Say, "Lord, my pollution needs your purity, my vileness your loveliness, my uncleanness your holiness"; and believe me, the Lord will smile and "wash you whiter than snow." I was one of the ugliest, dirtiest, raggedest objects I ever knew, and yet love took me in, and set me upon a throne, ordered my goings, "put a new song in my mouth," and I live only to praise him!

"July 17th, 1792. —— There is a very choice author whom I delight in, if only I could purchase any of his works. I have a sermon of his which is as clear as the sun to a spiritual eye. P. Sterry is entirely centered on the love principle; he also wrote with all the love and sweetness of Mr. Law. But books are dry and insipid unless illuminated by the Spirit of God while we read them. When the *seventh seal is opened in the soul*, every line of the Word of God appears in a new light, and that Scripture is verified which says, "Eye has not seen, nor has ear heard, the things that God has prepared for them that love him." This great mystery it has been the good will of Jehovah to bestow upon me—mere dust and ashes! And my tongue longs to exalt him, and my pen to show forth his praise. Then let me exhort my beloved brother not to faint, nor be weary in his passage to the new Jerusalem—the city of the living God, where Jehovah condescends not only to visit but to dwell; and the inhabitants of that glorious city "shall hunger no more, nor thirst any more. The sun shall not strike them, nor any heat. For the Lord God shall lead them to fountains of living waters, and all tears shall be eternally wiped away from their eyes." Oh, my dear friend, this is my state—unutterable bliss, where there is no satiety. May my pen stimulate you to "count all things but dross and dung" compared with the "pearl of great price"; and may

*en vertu de notre libre arbitre, nous en approcher ou nous en éloigner. La loi intellectuelle nous*

...grace make you willing to be stripped naked and bare, and to “suffer the loss of all things” so that you may be counted worthy to enter into the *holy of holies* in this life. No man can see the face of God and live, but the dead see him; those who have died the spiritual death—*of self*—they see him. This is the first resurrection; but not after the manner of the deluded Swedenborgians—they grasp at shadows. My partner in life is an adherent to these wild doctrines, who call themselves the New Jerusalem Church and are building chapels to preach the Baron’s doctrine in. Poor hoodwinked mortals! Led blindfolded by the seducer down the broad and easy way to their own destruction.

> August 25th, 1792. — I wish to know if you find any relish for the great mystery—“God manifest in the flesh?” If you do, you must be willing to die to *sense* and *reason*, which cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. All that sense and reason can apprehend will not defend us from the fear of eternal torment, but “perfect love casts out fear.” Love! Omnipotent love! is the *alpha* and *omega*. My own experience, before I was in this glorified resurrection state <note>a most just phrase</note>, was to believe contradictions and impossibilities; and by that means the Lord instructed me in revelation. There is no book I have yet found that describes my experience. Could the seventh seal be opened, surely the time had not come until it came to *me*? Do not be staggered, dear Sir, at my saying so, nor look at the humbleness of the instrument; for a soul that is parched with thirst drinks out of a humble vessel and forgets “through extreme pain” the outward vehicle. — You ask for my prayers. Perhaps the completion of six days’ labor is at hand; for the curse lasts for six days. You must therefore compose your spirits to a tranquil state, and like Esther the *type*, say, “though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.” In my humble opinion, to abandon oneself to the Lord is the only way to find true peace. Books are idols—our graces are idols—our holy walking is idolatry—even the Bible is an idol; it is not God. From all idols, God will cleanse you. Then throw yourself into the sea of his love and abandon everything but God. Suppose He allows you to feel yourself ugly and polluted, like a toad, or an ape, a viper, or anything else that is horrid; your business is to be content with it. Eh, you say, to be content to be, and appear to others, so very loathsome? Yes, this is the way, for all flesh stinks before him; and the great controversy is this: ministers, people, books, and teachers want to make the flesh—*the beast*—holy. Alas, “can the Ethiopian change his skin?” Therefore be content to wear the figure of a beast, as our Lord did; he had the bestial nature; he ate, drank, and slept like one of us. Had he not, he could not have “felt for us in every temptation.” My words may perhaps displease you when I say I have rejoiced at being counted worthy to be made “the filth and offscouring of all things.” I have been in *prison* for the cause and have been stripped of all things for the Lord’s sake. My relatives put me in a madhouse privately, where I stayed six weeks. From there my beloved, the Lord Jehovah, set me free, and I adore him for it. He is the same yesterday and forever; infinite in love and mercy. I praise Him for my liberty, my health, my food, and all that I enjoy; and as the “new heaven and the new earth” have begun, I do not fear the second death.

> September 11th, 1792. — Your state is a very safe state, being made very sensible of your wants. It is a great mercy to be emptied, and not only so, but to be filled—with an ardent, burning desire for God, the spouse of the bride, the church. All natural love is descriptive of spiritual love. How vehemently does the church described by Solomon pant after the Lord! Language is too poor to paint what souls feel under the agonies of divine love. May your vessel be thoroughly emptied, and every desire be brought into subjection to the Divine will. The greatest cross I ever found was to hear myself called unholy, impure, impatient, disobedient, and discontented—to feel all this unholiness and to be content with it is a miracle; yet so I found it. I know that the flesh is the son of perdition and my intolerable enemy; it cannot be made clean; it is filthy and will always remain so. People think they can bring a clean thing out of an unclean one; alas! they are washing the Ethiopian white. Our pollution follows us until mortal death. The dark spirits take much delight in worrying the soul that is seeking the Lord; “look,” they say, “at your deformity; can you imagine Jehovah will dwell with you?” I answer, Yes; it is by the light of grace that we feel our shortcomings and imperfection. Isaiah says, “Our holiness is a bed too short, and the curtains too narrow for a covering.” Is it not so? Then be content to be whatever it shall please the Lord to make you. In dryness or aridity still be quiet, for it is our tempers that move. The Lord is unchangeable; he is always the same. Suppose it is very painful, dreadful, or horrible—so it must be; it comes from a Physician who is infallible and a Sovereign whom none can control! Pure gold is refined seven times, and then it becomes ductile and will easily take any form or any impression; then and only then is it “fit for the master’s use.” Oh, that a divine and irresistible hunger may be awakened in your soul—an insatiable, tormenting thirst—a burning, implacable fire, never to be quenched but in the sublime enjoyment of Jehovah; for eye has not seen, nor has ear heard, nor can sense conceive the ecstatic rapture of a union with him—Jehovah, the Lord. You feel dissolved, annihilated, melted, liquefied, swallowed up in Him; and you have that ease, that familiarity, that oneness, so that all fear is banished forever. You will have no more respectful awe, filial awe, or sovereign awe. No, no, all will be love. You will be in ecstasies that feel no satiety; you will be transported with unutterable delight; your tears will be tears of tumultuous joy—rapturous yet tranquil. <note>This refers to Jacob Boehme's “Marriage of the Virgin Sophia with the Soul.”</note> I write not from books but from my own heartfelt experience; and I sincerely wish you may die daily to rise into celestial pleasure. Every place and every state is heaven to me, because Jesus-Jehovah is my beloved, and he is always with me as an omnipotent God: full, very full of all that can satisfy me. The dark spirits feel God as an omniscient God, as an omnipresent God; but as an omnipotent God or a God of love, they do not know him. Did they know his omnipotence, light would immediately, from its own brilliance, dissipate their darkness, and they also would be compelled to love. Oh my dear friend, I cannot pray for your case, but I pray for your extreme fires to begin; from those burning furnaces, the resplendent gold may be brought forth—more precious than the gold of Ophir. Do not be deceived, but expect the ordeal—the *proba*—so that you may be enabled to glorify God in the fire. Oh, how divinely brilliant, how divinely lustrous and transcendent will you then be! Everlasting joy will be on your head, and then you will enter into an everlasting rest. This alone is felicity and is given to those “who are worthy.” Who are they? Those who loved not their lives unto death.

...that celestial number Jehovah in great love has made me, and I am uniformly thankful, for his love dwells in me and has become my very essence. Farewell.”

“October 14th, 1792.—I had the pleasure of seeing * * *, and among other spiritual conversations, I asked him if he knew any precious souls who were *hungering and thirsting for the hidden manna*? He said he knew but very few and sent a minister to me who professed mysterious things; but weighing him in the balance of the sanctuary, I found him very deficient indeed. He showed me your letters, in which I perceived the true flavor of the hidden life, though in an imperfect state.

I greatly rejoiced in the prospect of communicating and receiving mutual benefits, if it were agreeable to Jehovah, who alone forms friendships upon celestial principles, and who is in my voice, my actions, my life, my all. Therefore, as a mariner casts the lead to find soundings, so am I directed to act. I throw out the line, and if what Jehovah gives me to say finds acceptance, it yields me unspeakable pleasure, for by that the Lord is glorified and my soul is refreshed.

But if any doubts arise, or *reason* dares to dictate, my correspondence ends, and why? All that flesh can say is but like “*sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal.*” I then conclude first, that the time has not come for my friend to receive mysteries; or secondly, that perhaps cursed pride might creep in and poison the water that I wish to communicate; or thirdly, perhaps Jehovah does not choose any instrument but will teach my dear friend more immediately by himself. And as I am not my own, but belong to Him, my adorable spouse, I am content to be considered simple, foolish, and void of understanding—yes, and to be laughed at, mocked, and reviled. For “the natural man (the *man of reason*) does not understand the things of God; they are folly to him”; besides, all that reason can teach or suggest is impure—*the root of reason is in death.* Our blessed Lord said to reason, “If I tell you of earthly things and you do not believe, how shall you believe if I tell you of heavenly things?” But truly, the truly hungry and the truly thirsty will drink and eat to satisfy the raging passion of nature even out of a very filthy vessel. Yes, the torment of spiritual hunger which I felt was so intolerable that I could have been taught by a dog, if it had pleased Jehovah to let him speak like Balaam’s donkey. My dear Sir, I am not afraid that the cause of an omnipotent God can suffer by the pen of one who is but dust and ashes; for the waters of eternal life are too clear; nothing that is created can soil them or cloud their incomparable beauty, let reason say what it may. <note>Her correspondent had replied that the religious world would hardly receive her testimony.</note> And although your delicate tenderness for me feels very deeply, and my soul loves and esteems you for it, yet I must write with Pilate, “What I have written, I have written,” being under the influence of the Holy Spirit who writes with my pen. I am a zero; all the numbers are from Jehovah, for the “kingdom is given up, in me, to the Father, that God may be *all in all*.”

Madame Guyon, Roach, Bourignon, Poiret, Boehme and Marsay, Francis de Sales, and every mystic author, Philadelphian and others, I have read; not one of them ever went into the garden to eat of the tree of life, which grows in the midst of the paradise of God. Pardon me, I do not deny that there may have been such souls, but no mystic book I have met with—whether French, English, German, or Italian, even Latin—ever mentions such an experience. Now the treasure is so immense that I am very confident the possessor would have published it. I have read manuscripts and many (almost all) Hermetic books; I have searched earth, sea, and air (speaking figuratively), yet never found a companion who had walked that path. <note>It must be kept in mind here that the “Memorials of Hester Ann Rogers,” “Bramwell,” and other Methodists were not then published.</note> Paul himself considered *himself* not to have captured that for which he was captured by Christ Jesus; but he followed on, leaving those things which were behind to press on toward perfection.

Indeed, I should publish this transcendent mystery, but I am grieved to say I have a persecuting husband and a dissolute son who is allowed plenty of money, while I am treated like *Hagar* the *Ishmaelite*, kept without a shilling; but I lack neither food nor clothing, and my high privileges bring me peace and contentment. My husband is a strict follower of Swedenborg; *that deluded society* is spreading contagion in London. But why do I say contagion? For it is no matter what persuasion people are of until they feel the pangs of the new birth. Then a child is born whose parent is God, and the child is immortal and will not be satisfied without proper nourishment from God its Father. Bromley’s “Sabbath of Rest” speaks highly of the hidden life. All the mystic writers used to give me pleasure, but now they are to me like a *horn-book.* I once had great need of them; that day was under the sixth seal—under the *seventh* there is no need for a teacher, for the “new heaven and the new earth” speak a superior, a celestial language. Those who live there are undefiled; nor can the truths they speak become contaminated, for they carry a dignity with them—a sovereignty which cannot be copied, and though obscure—deep, profound, incomprehensible—yet true. If *reason* could comprehend them, where then is the “mystery hidden from the foundation of the world”—the “seventh seal opened”—the “resurrection state”—the “new Jerusalem”—the “day of the Holy Spirit”? A blind man may as well attempt to paint the sun and stars as a person endeavor or presume to say what is right or what is wrong to souls under the peculiar influence of the Holy Spirit. <note>Most excellent truth.</note> The works of God are in the dark abyss and are to be viewed with astonishment and awful fear; but when revelation comes, every mystery is open. Though before we saw through a glass darkly, now all is clear as the sun at noon-day, and so exceedingly glorious that the possessor sinks into dust and ashes, considering the disparity between flesh and spirit—yet at the same time feels his own dignity and is delighted in contemplating his own beauty; for in equality, as between man and wife, the connubial endearments are in union, and they taste reciprocal delights: for “my beloved is mine and I am his, he feeds among the lilies”—or he feeds with me in spotless purity. Lilies are emblems of innocence. “Come walk in the gardens of love” and taste pure delight and inexpressible pleasure. “Eye has not seen nor ear heard, neither has it entered into the heart of man to conceive,” what Jehovah has given me and what he has been pleased to reveal to me. It is ecstatic—it is glorious—it is divine! Follow on, my dear brother; sink down, deep as death in self-abasement, and you also shall dwell in paradise.

Looking over your letter I perceive you say, “Some will doubt my testimony.” Be it so; it is only

the blind; besides, what harm can come to me? Suppose they say that I am in pain. If I do not *feel* it, it cannot hurt me. Not only so, but all *mysteries* are inconsistencies, let the "Nicodemuses" say what they will. What sense and reason can understand is not worth having—it is polluted. [Excellent, sublime truth.]

My soul exults in the prospect of a separation from the polluted hell I live in, namely the body. There is no other hell for those who have passed the first death; over them the second death has no power. This foul body is like a *beast*—its appetites, its passions, and its gratifications are vile, unbecoming the loveliness of a celestial inhabitant who is always attended by a host of blessed angels, “lest you dash your foot against a stone.” Oh, that every soul who is seeking this priceless *pearl* may soon find it! [As they will, if they “seek” as a *Bramwell* or a *Rogers* did, or as taught by Behmen’s “Way to Christ,” and the Gospel.] Oh, how they will dance for joy! My dearest Sir, I have danced for joy, yes, and sung too, until my body was quite exhausted, and I could say, “Sustain me with flagons, comfort me with apples, for I am sick with love.” Dear Sir, pursue the direct road to *death*—give up your time, your powers of soul and body to annihilation, to putrefaction; then shall you arise “fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners.” You will find my pen the “tongue of a ready writer,” for in this new state there is such an abundance of matter that it would be a pleasure to fill a volume if time would permit.” Thus much from Mrs. Pratt’s letters. To resume the narrative:

We find, on looking over Mr. Law’s published “Collection of Letters,” one addressed to Mr. Ward, dated April 10, 1757. This letter (in accordance with what we have before stated) was not an original, but was altered for publication, and, we think, partially by Mr. Law himself at the suggestion of his friend and editor, Mr. Ward. Ward might have deemed this a favorable opportunity for finally disposing of the senseless slander propagated by Warburton respecting the “Appeal.” This slander had formed one of the subjects of the expostulatory correspondence of Byrom, noticed on page 574; and was possibly forged by Warburton out of revenge, after being stung by the ironic allusions at the close of the “Animadversions on Trapp,” appended to the “Appeal.” On referring to the original, given on page 559, and then to this published letter, and further to that dated September 1756, it will appear that Mr. Law never honored Wesley by coupling him with the Pope as “having the same reasons for condemning, and not espousing the mystery revealed by God in Jacob Behmen (J.B.);” but that the remark originally applied to Warburton. And then it might only have been an adoption of Warburton’s own term in his remarks and correspondence with Byrom.

In this published Letter, with which must be associated the ‘second interpolation’ in the Scruple Letter (referred to on page 554), commencing “Let me here, sir, observe” etc., to “both of us like-minded,”—doubtless composed, though ingeniously inserted as an incidental remark for the same purpose—we cannot help but notice the grace with which Mr. Law turns the arrows of Warburton’s slanders against himself. Taking that in connection with the “Confutation” piece, we see how he makes good his own comparison in the above reference regarding Warburton “knocking his head against a post.” It will further be remarked that Mr. Law tacks on a postscript to this imaginary letter in order to pay a final compliment to Mr. Wesley’s qualifications and the spirit exhibited in the publication Wesley had addressed to him the previous year.

<margin>a/</margin>
The scope of this letter, we need hardly observe, has proved too difficult for the ordinary class of readers; (it being, moreover, of a prophetic character, and so embraced within the purpose of the next succeeding letter in the “Collection.”) But the secret of the second paragraph is the existence of an eternal nature or ground of being, sometimes called by Mr. Law the ‘glassy sea’ or ‘heavenly materiality,’ in which every form of life is raised up originally as a magic birth by the wisdom, will, and outflowing virtue of the abyssal Deity. It concerns the fact that the visible universe and every object in it on the face of the earth is so much of this unseen world (its separated ground) materialized and brought to view in a lower degree of manifestation. The whole creation constitutes one stupendous theater or platform on which divine things and characters are represented, not by the arbitrary will of an omnipotent *fiat*, but according to the necessary economy, so to speak, of the divine nature, which is triune in its essence and operation, and must therefore kindle and distinguish all natural life in a threefold manner. This philosophy, in which only the distinctions of God and nature are scientifically and virtually made, Mr. Law very justly holds up as that which Dr. Warburton—with his usual ill-luck when handling theological topics—represents as *Pantheism* or *Spinozism*. However, it not only makes a distinction between God and nature but shows how the Deity, opening and manifesting his own abyssal glory and perfection in the latter, is the fountain of its life and joy. The fire which penetrates and vivifies all material things, the light which makes them visible, and the spirit which preserves them in one bond and chain of being, are nothing else than the fire, the light, and the spirit of eternal nature, brought down through a variety of births into this temporal system, as described in the *first four verses of the book of Genesis*. How important and essential the acquisition of this science is for all who would be true *savants* in the understanding or manipulation of nature—according to the several main branches of her physical powers and developments, as well as with reference to the universal induction of “all nations” into Christianity and to the revelation of every secret that can concern man—is left for the intelligent reader to conceive. On this point Mr. Law speaks thus to those who have ears to hear (for our Lord submitted his parables “of heavenly things” only to such): “Not a book,” says he, “ancient or modern in all our libraries” (this does not include the ancient Egyptian and Chaldean learning and its repositories), “has so much as attempted to open the *ground of nature*, to show its *birth and state*, and its essential and unalterable distinction from the one abyssal *supernatural God*; and how all the glories, powers, and perfections of the hidden, unapproachable God have their wonderful manifestation in nature and creature. This is a blessing reserved by God for *these last times*, to be opened in his chosen instrument, the poor illiterate Behmen.”

The postscript of this letter, which we have already referred to, touches on a subject of great concern to the Christian world. “We seem,” remarks Mr. Law therein, “to be farther from the Gospel in point of spirit than in distance of time”;—a truth assuredly as applicable to our own day (with all its supposed Gospel light) as it was to the time when it was written; (though, considering the contents of this publication, must it not be said that “our salvation is nearer than...

...when we believed?”) For where are the happy souls who, comprehending the scope and mystery of the gospel as now revealed from heaven, realize every moment the prerogatives of their redeemed and restored birthright? Who, turning from all inferior, human, and earthly helps for any and every necessity, trial, weakness, or distress of soul, spirit, or body, live purely and totally by faith, seeking *every good* in and from God alone, manifested in Christ Jesus?

This subject, by the way, brings to mind the remarks of a respected friend who claims expertise in the high alchemical science. He was informed of the following circumstance: in the recent biography of the holy William Bramwell, published by some of his own family, the editor presented evidence—intended to show Bramwell's occasional weakness of judgment—that when he was attacked by severe bodily illness, instead of using the advice and usual remedies of doctors (which were kindly and freely offered to him), “he considered them a positive intrusion.” Instead, he would show (through the exercise of faith and prayer) a profound reliance upon God alone for relief. In short, he applied himself (like Gregory Lopez and other sublime contemplatives) immediately to the hyperphysical physician of human nature in its current relations under the gospel. By the touch of faith, he sought to draw from God’s all-pervading divine body whatever “virtue” or healing power he required for his physical as well as spiritual needs. When this was told to our friend, he expressed much surprise and gratification to find such an example of divine science existing among that group of active religious people, the Methodists. He most heartily commended the sound judgment of Bramwell’s procedure. At the same time, he remarked that the editor of the book—though he might be fit to write a sentimental religious novel—was clearly incapable of the task he had undertaken: depicting the mind and spirit of an enlightened Christian philosopher.

The short of the matter is this, which Mr. Law knew well—that men do not have that *faith* (or degree of faith) which our Lord meant when he said, “When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?” or as already quoted in *Mark 16:15–18* and elsewhere. This faith—without a spark of fanaticism in it—would do everything for the person who can exercise it by placing their total being in immediate *rapport* with the glorified Head and Heart of human nature, providing an all-sufficient satisfaction and remedy for all its wants and distresses whatsoever <note>see page 9</note>. It is just as attaching wires to a galvanic battery forms a medium through which the elemental fluid may be spread at the will or faith of the operator. The reason for this lack of faith—this all-powerful gospel faith—is that the science of it has been lost to the church. However, through the means of this treatise, it may be restored, and a new era may dawn upon the philosophy of natural and divine magic. It should also be observed that this faith includes all the levels of the reborn life, down to that of the uneducated, beginning believer. <note>See “Revelation of Revelations,” pages 60–68.</note>

Leaving the reader to refer at their pleasure to Mr. Law’s published letters according to their dates, we shall now confine ourselves chiefly to the manuscript correspondence we hold that passed between him and his friends. From these, we select the following two letters for insertion here:

> “December 12th, 1757. — My dear Langcake — I received both your letters and thank you for the little book by Mr. Norris. Who is he? He writes in the style of an ingenious quack. I am willing to have some small amount of his medicine with his directions, to make some trial of it.
>
> I must ask you to pick up the following books by Mr. Richardson on my account, namely: the “Appeal,” “Spirit of Prayer,” “Way to Divine Knowledge,” and the “Spirit of Love.” Let them be made up into a well-covered parcel with this direction: ‘*To Mr. John Burnett, at Rotterdam. — To be sent by the first Holland Packet Boat.*’
>
> I would like a slip of paper enclosed, showing the order in which these books were published, which is as they stand in this letter.
>
> Perhaps my nephew’s servant may be the safest way of carrying them to the boat, but I leave that to you. We are all well and full of all good wishes to my dear friend. Adieu.—W. LAW.”

> “April 9th, 1758.—My dear friend—I thank you for all the various trouble you have taken on my account.
>
> I liked the spirit of Penington in that book you sent me, which made me write for his Works as fit to be added to my Spiritual Library. If you send them, I would have them bound, but I leave it to you either to send them now or wait for a perfect copy.
>
> Please tell Mr. Ward that I want him to buy me the eighth volume of the “<term>Arcana Cœlestia</term>.” He bought the first seven volumes for me and so knows the volume that I do not have. I shall never go through them, but as I have gone so far in the expense, I shall take this last volume. My last volume ends with the 24th chapter of Exodus. Also, from the Quaker’s shop, get the “Godly Life of Luterman,” if it is in High Dutch (that is, German). I need not repeat to you and Mr. Ward to pay yourselves all charges in Sun Court.
>
> As soon as the little pieces are out of the press, I would like the whole of what is printed for me sent directly away; a hundred of each stitched in blue paper, and the rest in sheets. You and Mr. Ward may take what you please of both of them.—Yours affectionately—W. LAW.”

The particulars of this last letter offer us a subject for remark. We have already, from time to time, expressed Mr. Law’s opinion regarding the character and value of mystical writers—specifically those who he considered had a right evangelical understanding and experience, as distinguished from those who did not grasp the “single purpose and design of all the <term>dispensations</term> of God to man.” That purpose is to teach man to know and feel his great natural misery as a fallen being, and his great glory as a redeemed one, so that he shall willingly die to every motion and working of his natural spirit and, with all the energies of his being, reach for the full birth of the divine nature within him. That is, those mystical writers whose philosophy and instructions were centered on this latter *practical business*, and flowing from a pure ground of experience, he deemed *orthodox mystics*. Meanwhile, he set aside the writings of the former group as *beside the point*, as books not of the nature of the Gospel and therefore not worthy of a place in his library. But here we encounter a letter written by Mr. Law’s intimate friend Langcake to Henry Brooke of Dublin (Mr. Wesley’s friend, to whom Mrs. Pratt’s recent correspondence was addressed), immediately relating to this subject. Because of the interesting nature of its contents, we present it here in full:

> “Bristol. Dec. 29th, 1776.—My dear Sir—I received your most friendly and obliging favor, and I wish I were capable of fully satisfying you in every specific inquiry contained in your letter. Though I had the honor and happiness of being intimate with that divine and blessed man, Mr. Law, for several years, it was more through correspondence than personal interaction; and during the times I visited him, nothing occurred in conversation except what might have happened with any of his other disciples. It mainly turned upon his own writings during my first visit, and I well remember that, while walking together in his garden and talking about those who objected to them, he said, ‘the more capable the adversary, the better he should be pleased; but that *his principles could not be overthrown without tearing up the entire Christian religion by the roots.*’—Mr. Law had a high regard for the early Quakers and their writings, but as for *Isaac Pennington*, I do not recall having any conversation about him; though after Mr. Law’s death, I was personally satisfied that he had read him with great approval.—I never heard him mention a word about *Engelbrecht*; but a friend <note>Probably Mr. G. Ward or Stephen Penny</note> told me that he said *Swedenborg* was ‘very voluminous, and that was not his worst fault.’—As Mr. Law had read the mystic writers from every age of the church, Madame Bourignon could not have escaped his notice. He considered her—indeed, he said she was—an *enlightened woman, but petulant*. <note>Mr. Law’s very impartial opinion of Madame Bourignon is expressed *at length* in a letter to Dr. Byrom from 1736, given in answer to the latter’s specific inquiry.</note> He spoke with approval of Mr. Marsay’s pious pieces that are translated into English (in the Scottish volume); but regarding the foundation of *Nature*, he said it was never revealed to any man but *Jacob Behmen*, and so he did not approve of Marsay and other spiritual writers drifting into *philosophical conjectures and fancies of their own*.”

It is appropriate to mention that the letters exchanged between Mr. Langcake and Mr. Brooke, along with many others of a relatively interesting and spiritual nature, are in the possession of the author of these lines. From the correspondence of Henry Brooke, we make the following extracts, the second of which relates to our subject:—

> “Dublin. Jan. 2nd, 1781.—Your letter arrived at the right time as a sweet tonic to revive my weary spirit. I feel grateful for your kindness and am inspired to emulation by the glow of love that animates your writing.
>
> I had hoped that my last letter would have been delivered to you in person by Mr. R. T., a follower of J. B. and Mr. Law, but it seems he sent it by mail. He has given up friends, fortune, and fame for God, abandoned a seat in Parliament, and distributed his inheritance. At first, he enjoyed the love of God, but by neglecting private devotions and watchfulness, he lost his first love and is now in the anguish of a backslider’s return. May God, in His infinite mercy and love in Jesus Christ, quickly restore him—like Job—to all that he has lost, and ten times more besides. I can hardly tell you how deeply I have been interested in his welfare, but he kept his distance and would have none of my kindness. He saw that I lived in the world, a plain and common outward life, and that despite my professed respect for J. B. and the mystics, I had been connected with the Methodists for many years. These things caused him a certain spiritual repulsion toward me, especially as he thought (perhaps too rightly) that I lived in conformity with the world, while his inclinations were all toward austerity and retirement.
>
> My dear friend, I am sorry to say that here, as well as among you, we are all swallowed up in the vortex of self; indeed, there are, thank God, a few exceptions. But there is not one single exception to the observation that we all live on the surface of things—the externals of religion. My soul longs and sighs for a brother—a fellow traveler whose conversation might cheer me, whose instructions might strengthen me, and whose example might inspire me. I have a few people to talk with who are truly pilgrims. <margin>Z.</margin>The conversation of people of the world is a most wearying bondage to a spirit aspiring after heaven; but I cannot express the tediousness and the various emotions we feel in the company of those who think themselves whole and healthy, and yet do not know that they are poor, miserable, blind, and naked . . . .
>
> “Oct. 1782.—Our friend gave me reason to hope that you would not consider it troublesome to send me a copy of Mr. Law’s letter concerning the mystical writers, especially the Philadelphian Society and its members, among whom I value *Bromley, Lead, Pordage, etc.*
>
> I confess I have never ranked their writings higher than the third class. The Holy Scriptures stand first. *Jacob Behmen* is first in the second class, which includes *Dionysius, Macarius, Bertot, Molinos, John of the Cross, Canfield, Tauler, the two Catherines, etc.* And in the third class are the many who, in all the divided churches and even in Pagan and Muslim nations, taught their disciples to penetrate from the *outward* into the *inward* and seek after the divine life—of a God <margin>/</margin>in them, the *hope of glory.*” <note>It must be kept in mind that when this was written, the biographies of those eminent and *pure Methodist figures* such as *Bramwell, Longden, Rogers, etc.*, had not yet been published.</note>
>
> “Jan. 1783.—My heart is filled with gratitude for the kindness of your letter, which I should have answered sooner; however, the many internal exercises and conflicts I have been passing through, and am still somewhat burdened with, have taken away all desire for writing, even to those whose correspondence I value above all human connections.
>
> I believe Mr. T.’s pursuit, as well as mine, has so far been fruitless. *No completely renewed, entirely regenerate, and apostolic character* has yet appeared to reward the research of either. <note>The same remark as above applies here.</note> But let God be true, though every man is a liar. That such souls existed, that such may yet exist—indeed, that such are now actually living, breathing men with passions like our own—I firmly believe, just as I believe the word of God and my own existence. Yes, I truly believe it is the hope and high prize of our holy calling, and that he and I and you have fallen short of it, not through any failure on God's part, nor through any lack of instruction, opportunity, grace, or power from the sweet love and willingness of JESUS, but through our own hard and rebellious hearts, which have failed to cooperate with His grace and are inclined to backslide.
>
> Our dear friend is eagerly hungering and thirsting after the full salvation of God; and I believe he wages constant war with all the lusts, passions, and appetites of the fleshly heart. Blessed hunger—blessed warfare. Oh, may he go on from victory to victory until the shout of the King of Glory is heard in his heart. Yet I am protective of him; I trust not with an eye of envy—

or uplifting, for I feel myself in deed and in truth, not only less than the least of all saints, but the very chief of sinners and unfaithful, backsliding rebels. He has a spirit of rejection and condemnation that seems to narrow and embitter his mind both against himself and others; rejecting all who oppose, or even are doubtful about, the doctrine of perfect salvation and sinless obedience; and renouncing all the visitations and operations of God that are not immediately followed by perfect victory over corrupt nature, and entire renovation into the divine life. I cannot so understand the Scripture. Surely if he is right I have all along mistaken Jacob Behmen in many places, as well as in his *Book of Regeneration*, from verse 100 to the end. He evidently does not consider the gradations of the divine life, though in all things the commandment still stands against us, “*Strive to enter into that rest;*” “*watch and pray.*” I shall be thankful for a transcript of any of Mr. Law's unpublished letters; indeed, I think it is a real loss that they are not all made public. How many hungry and thirsty souls, who gasp after the water of life, might be directed by them to the *true fountain*, instead of being continually directed and led to the cracked and broken cisterns of some patched-up sect, or pulpit orator.”

> “June, 1783.—I hope this letter will be delivered to you by Mrs. B., the sister of our worthy friend Mr. R. T. She is taking her two children with her to England, principally motivated by the desire and expectation of meeting some of those *living characters*, whose principles and practice have been so exquisitely drawn by the pen of him who used to address you as “Dear son of my love.” About seventeen or eighteen years ago, she felt the kindlings of the divine fire while reading the writings of Mr. Law; since then, his most excellent female character, *Eusebia*, has been the object of her constant aspirations. She is now a widow with two children and an independent income like her, which she wishes and endeavors to devote in the same manner. I have had the favor of knowing her these five or six years—a privilege like many others, which I have neither improved nor cultivated as I ought. Oh, may my manifold infidelities and sins be blotted out forever by that cleansing blood that not only effaces the stains of the old Adam, but invigorates the new man; giving strength to the weak, and power to those who have no might.
>
> And now my dear friend, may the sweet Spirit of our long-suffering and infinitely patient Lord JESUS, draw us more and more from multiplicity into UNITY; teaching and giving us power and wisdom to cut off, renounce, and crucify to the very last gasp, the man of sin within us, so that our lives may at length be hidden with Christ in God.”
>
> “Jan. 1785.—I am exceedingly grateful for the copies of Mr. Law's letters, and cannot but lament that while the press swarms with childish, crude, and undigested trash, such excellent gems should be locked up in a desk or drawer, and by and by be cast out among the rubbish of waste papers, and devoured in the common flame that consumes the refuse. Surely the excellence of those already published is a very strong call upon you to let those you have, and all you can help to collect, be multiplied abroad; and though they may be scattered like the Sibyls' leaves, yet the breath of the adorable providence of God shall blow one here and another there to hearts disposed by his own Spirit, and prepared to receive them; and so good not only *may*, but *must* be done by them.
> 
> Remember the labors of honest Poiret, who was the industrious editor of an incredible number of the sacred mystics, [and of the “*Bibliotheca Mysticorum,*” given on pages 129—178.] And surely if a cup of cold water given in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward, how much more (if we cannot speak or write as Apostles ourselves) shall our extending and communicating the knowledge of spiritual wisdom and grace—through a spiritual and gracious motive—receive a spiritual and most gracious acceptance and reward. I must own I have blessed Poiret in my private room many a time for his labors of love. As also Elliston and Sparrow, etc., for their labors in the word and doctrine.
>
> As for myself, I do feel a share in the general revival and outpouring of grace, which seems to descend and visibly influence all spiritual worshippers of every denomination; and even to reach many in the National church, who remain shut up in the *frozen form of an invariable repetition.*”

> “August, 1785.—I cannot tell you how peculiarly timely your last precious transcript was. Indeed, Mr. Law’s Christian writings have from my earliest infancy had the easiest and most convincing entrance to my heart, until they had performed their Baptist-like ministry and led me on to the inestimable mines of Jacob Behmen, and opened the inexhaustible fountains of the sacred Scriptures; whereby we come finally to live in the Spirit, and draw water direct out of the *wells of salvation*, opened in our own souls.

>
> Mr. T. is married and has a son. His wife has all the sweetness of an elementary goodness, but is yet unawakened to the struggle of the two principles. May the divine call (“Adam, where are you?”) soon be heard, and the promise (of the seed of the woman or the working Word of Life) soon be felt within her, bruising the serpent's head.”

The extract we now give is from one Ralph Mather, about whom we accidentally found the following notice in Wesley’s journals:—“Jan. 29th, 1774.—This day, and several times in the following week, I had much conversation with Ralph Mather, a devoted young man, but almost driven out of his senses by mystic divinity. If he escapes out of this specious snare of the Devil, he will be an instrument of much good.” Thus Wesley wrote in his usual style of self-confidence and righteous phrasing when upon this topic (notwithstanding what we say regarding Matthew 7:1 and what he had written in his diary on November 30th, 1767). The extract we now propose to provide is from one of Mather's letters, dated November 1775, containing “A List of some Names and the Places of Residence of Persons in whose Minds the Light of God has arisen, or is graciously rising.” He was, it appears, simply a working artisan. The account, headed “Sing Praises,” proceeds as follows:

> “*Carrickfergus.* E. Pendril, a shoemaker and a married man, who under great persecution lives in continence and abstinence from animal food; he was visited about five years ago. He has a tender mind; he was formerly with the Quakers, but now fully believes in restitution and the universality of God's power and love. *Belfast.* William Forde, of Hercules Lane, is a poor man; he is not as solid as E. P. but is teachable and lives on roots and water. There is another in that debauched town, but I am waiting to see if they will prove to be like the seed sown in good ground. *England. Liverpool.* Richard Haughton, of Wolstenholme Square; this is a mind that is the very soul of your soul and spirit of your spirit. My relative R. Seddon Jr., an anchor-smith at the Old Dock, belongs to the Methodists. Give him R. M.'s love, and he will show you any civility, though he has no house of his own and merely rents a room. My sister also married his relative, but she, poor thing, and her husband—a captain of a ship—are in the dark world. *Warrington.* It is not impossible to find some simple minds here. James Worrall and William China, both well-meaning Methodists and my loving friends, can soon direct you to them. *Leigh.* Near this town lives William Crompton, a farmer; and in the town are R. Darwell, young George Darwell, and J. Marsh. These poor people love *Jacob Behmen* and *William Law*. My father and mother, T. and M. Westrey, live here; likewise two uncles, one named Joseph and the other H. Mather. *Bolton.* E. Hughes has passed into God; M. Owen is greatly advanced; M. Winkbridge has been fifteen years in purifications; several more are coming along. These, I think, are generally of low status in the world, but it is a school of female philosophers. Oh, how gladly would they see a mind desirous of getting out of the dark world! But these angelic souls are treated as the filth of the world and the scouring of all things. *Chester.* (I forgot). Enquire for Elizabeth Letsham at H. Rider's; she has a most tender mind. She was with the Methodists, and though she has a fairly handsome annuity, she sits alone and keeps silence. \*\*\*, a poor woman, has a large experience. A servant maid, an acquaintance of E. L., is very simple. J. Leadbetter, a painter, and many others have been visited; these are also held in derision as mystics, but though some do not come forward as one would wish, they have not departed from simplicity. *Manchester.* Sarah Lee in St. Ann's Square is one highly esteemed in the world, but of large experience. Thomas Clowes, a rector of one of the churches, is a pious, solid young man. \*\*\*, a curate of another church and an acquaintance of T. C., is more 'in the fire' yet seems promising. Samuel Mann of Radcliffe Street has been about eighteen years in the way; this dear man and his wife will show you the rest. A young woman in *Salford*, S. M., will conduct you to some others in this place who would claim the name of mystics, but I fear they are deceiving themselves. However, E. Watson and M. Brierly among the Methodists, though simple and of low status in the world, are worthy to be seen. So are some others who are simple; and if one could put books into their hands, such as I have done with Lady Guyon's “*Short Method of Prayer*,” it would be merciful, for they do not know the way, though the way is at hand. There were nearly four hundred Methodists here, and there are a large number in Bolton. Near Manchester, there are three simple, tender minds who have been seeking the true life for many years; Samuel Mann will therefore point them out. But there is another also, Mary Robinson, who has the most exquisite talents, genius, intrepidity, and docility; I am jealous for her, lest the Quakers get her into their society. If she escapes, she promises to be a star of the first magnitude; she has been a sprightly, quick, and gay frequenter of all scenes of pleasure. Near *Wellington*, in *Shropshire*, lives one Hatton, a preacher of the Episcopal church. This man's companion writes to E. Letsham in a sweet, broken strain. Not far from here, at *Madeley*, lives J. Fletcher. But should Leeds not be too far from Manchester, there is C. Cayley; the widow Crosby and a young maiden named Horrold are preachers there. And six miles from them lives M. Bosanquet, who also appears in public; I have been to her house. Among the many Methodists, of whom there are two or three thousand in that neighborhood, some must be deeply touched. In *Macclesfield*, there were some tender Methodists. In *Birmingham* (see *Wolverhampton*), there is one, if not more, of whom I hear a thirst for spirit and life has been kindled. *Jacob Behmen* and *William Law* are favorite authors with one of them. *Banbury.* Richard Cooper, the son of a timid, wealthy man, has given himself up to much solitude. Providence may make a way for conversation; I do not know him in person. A young man here, a grocer who lived in Bristol, professes a great veneration for the mystics, but I have found more brokenness in fewer words; yet he is not in the spirit of the world, but another turn of the wheel would lay his mind more deeply in the dust. *Worcester.* In this city there cannot help but be some seekers, but *Gloucester* is a dead place. I met a man at *Gloucester* who calls himself a prophet, but when I questioned him closely, he treated me with the greatest insolence and perversity, so I felt no freedom to see him anymore. *Cheltenham.* Enquire for \*\*\*, a schoolmistress; she has been brought down from her Calvinistic notions through the simplicity of a forlorn rector's wife who lives apart from her husband. But though the sister of this schoolmistress, with whom I had much conversation, is called the *Phoenix* of the Methodists in those parts, she cannot believe that her sister yet knows anything of religion. *Stroud* (and enquire for those at *Dursley*, etc.). John King at Bowbridge, his wife, and Sarah Niblet are tender minds, as are some three or four others, and two among the Methodists, especially a schoolmistress there; but J. King, his wife, and the rest now live separately from the Methodists. You must find satisfaction in them. J. K. was a schoolmaster but now lives on his own estate; the rest are poor. I have great hopes that, despite all the reluctance he (*J. K.*) feels, he will yet become an excellent man. *Bristol.* J. Castleman, a surgeon. His wife Letty has a sweet mind; she will lead you to my (and her) spiritual mother. I am persuaded God will give you admittance to her (if she is still alive), though she can by no means admit anyone except those whom her God and your God shall direct her to converse with.
