The youngest of these women, a most devoted soul, shows great promise of becoming a Teresa <note>referring to St. Teresa of Avila</note>. The others are not yet prepared for such communications.

Among the Methodists—of which sect there were eight hundred in the city of Bristol according to J. W.'s <note>John Wesley's</note> books—there is a handful laboring with a different spirit (L. Cas is one of them). Among these, J. Southest, S. Johnston (an elderly virgin), the widow Purnel, etc., might be included. But the Bristol society is mixed, consisting of five or six sorts: *first*, here and there an inward-looking mind. *Secondly*, a few who are very accustomed to the prayer of meditation. *Thirdly*, a division of these who are less certain in their active state. *Fourthly*, those who have passed into some consolations and the ecstatic state. *Fifthly*, some under their first convictions. *Sixthly*, a large body of chattering, vain, worldly minds who can talk about God and the world simultaneously, like someone trying to dictate to two writers at once, each writing on opposite subjects. But the hardest to convince, or to bring into any true union or nearness to God and His purity, are the second and the last groups; for one has gained spiritual riches, and the other temporal riches and sensuality. The fourth state is the gate to death; the fifth is the season of plowing and pruning in order to bring forth fruit. But as for the second and sixth—alas! how hard it is for those who have riches (whether in spiritual sweetness, in mental images, or in the world) to enter God's kingdom. With men it is impossible, but glory to God, all things are possible with Him. Upon inquiry, some hidden minds may be found. Dr. Stonhouse, a learned man, is strong in the doctrine of restitution, I hear; and in the large congregations of this professing city—for few churches are without a smattering of Christ's *salvation doctrine* in their speech—one might find the hungry, the weary, and the heavy-laden. In Bath, ask T. Mills for such people. In Bradford, near Bath, Joseph Yerbury: my dear brother and sister are both being drawn into the pure nature of God. Oh Jesus, touch many such souls!

London: Mary Roberts, a Methodist in Union Street, Oxford Market; you will see her husband’s name over the door. She has a select old matron with whom she converses. There are a few at the West End of the town to whom I would hope mercy has been offered. *Barnstaple* and *Bideford*: These towns may be too far away, otherwise it was there, or at Bishop's Tawton, where some were compelled to meet together, such as Prudence Scott, Edward Sage, William Harnet, John Nichols, etc. *Northampton*: At this town a Moravian preacher named Okely professes great love for the mystics; but at *Loughborough*, not far from there, nearly twenty people have turned from Methodism to Quakerism. Because of this, prejudice may have closed their hearts, except toward those who can speak "thee" and "thou," wear a broad-brimmed hat, and have learned their specific phrases. I am afraid this is also the case with those at Barnstaple, as many Quakers have visited them; but all things are possible with God. Should providence lead you through *Salop* <note>Shropshire</note>, there are doubtless some serious minds in that large town. But regarding Manchester and Bristol—the *Spring of Truth* seems to open most clearly there of any place I know. In Bolton, etc., they are universally accosted, derided, and treated with evil reproaches; and in Bristol, they are called whimsical, dreaming, enthusiastic visionaries. If, therefore, we are persecuted and suffer for righteousness' sake, we are happy; it is then that the *Spirit of God and of glory* rests upon us. Seeing, therefore, that on the one hand providence is laying before you hearts as well as books with which you may freely converse, and on the other, that it is in your power to give them—if not spoken, then at least such written consolation as the order of God may require—consider how the ties of divine love may be strengthened in that which does not perish, but lives and abides forever. Amen.”

This singular communication-doubtless led the ingenious Mr. Brooke to seek out some of the devoted individuals mentioned in it. writings; though it must be admitted they possess many deep and awakening truths. There is much written and much talked about concerning the divine life, but to *live it* is the thing much needed. —— The whole Christian world seems to be swallowed up in the vortex of *self*, whereas I want to see immortal spirits so refined as to go out of themselves, and truly embrace the whole human race in the arms of abundant love. Madame Guyon, whom you mention in your letter, seems to be a standard in this particular elevation of spirit. To be filled with that fullness of divine love she possessed is devoutly to be wished; it carried her everywhere in holy zeal to win souls for God. In this, by a faith that could remove mountains, she seems to have risen superior to all the most terrible events that could befall her during her mortal pilgrimage. Oh, how many internal experiences and deaths must the soul pass through before it is thus purified! And yet I was told by a friend who had a relative that corresponded with her, that toward the end she passed through some severe conflicts with the powers of darkness, but emerged from them into a luminous state before she died. In this, she realized what Mr. Law says in his book *Regeneration*: "What the soul shall feel and undergo in its last purifications, when the deepest roots of all selfishness—both spiritual and natural—are to be plucked up and consumed out of it, or how we shall be able to stand in that final trial, are both equally impossible for us to know beforehand. It is enough for us to know that we hunger and thirst, hourly and constantly, for the salvation which is in Christ Jesus; and that the deepest humility and most absolute resignation of our whole selves—soul, spirit, and body—to God, from moment to moment, by the most unbounded acts of faith, is our greatest and highest qualification to receive our greatest and highest purification at his hands."

The next subject we have to notice is the mention of the *Arcana Coelestia* in Mr. Law’s letter of April 9th, 1758. Among the correspondents of Mr. Law was one Mr. Stephen Penny, previously mentioned, whose address in the year 1747 was "at the Distillery by Castle Green, Bristol." It was to him that the letter we have inserted in the note on pages 45 and 46 was written, which was found among his papers on December 4th, 1780, after his death. This individual moved to Dartmouth, from where he once more addressed Mr. Law in the following manner. It appears that Mr. Langcake became acquainted with him toward the latter part of his life:—

> "Dartmouth, 30th Sept. 1755.—Rev. Sir—I had some years ago (then residing at Bristol) the pleasure of writing you a few lines about a new translation of the valuable works of Jacob Behmen; and of receiving your kind answer to it. And I have with great satisfaction, and I hope profit, read all the pieces you have published since that time. From some of them I conceived hopes of seeing the translation I so much long for, and though the Second Part of the *Spirit of Love* seemed in the conclusion to somewhat forbid that hope, yet I cannot entirely give it up without an order from your own hand; which I confess indeed would give me no small concern, as I do not know anything in the world I long for with so much ardor as to see a work so inestimable in itself introduced into the world by a hand, perhaps the only one in it, capable of the undertaking.
>
> Among my small circle of acquaintances in this obscure corner of England, I have a few who relish these writings, who had never so much as heard of them before my coming here; but what is remarkable (and yet may be well enough accounted for too), they are of the simple and uneducated sort. Others with school-learning despise us and ridicule the writings. It was of the first sort that the followers of the Savior of the world consisted when He was clothed with humanity. Happy ignorance that leads to so great wisdom!
>
> Give me leave before I conclude to express my hope that you will not stop the translation you seem to be so far advanced in, until you have finished the whole according to the design you apparently had (and I think promised) to do in some of your late pieces. It is not for me to describe to such an expanded mind the immensity of the benefit many people may receive from an acquaintance with those valuable writings, not only in your own lifetime, but for years and years after you are no longer on earth; and how great a happiness must flow into a good mind from the consciousness of being so instrumental in it, as you are enabled to become by divine grace. Pardon my freedom, since it is the love of mankind only that prompts me thus boldly to invade your blessed solitude, and if you could prevail upon yourself to indulge me with a line in answer, it would confer a very significant obligation on——Rev. Sir, your affectionate though unknown friend and humble servant—STEPHEN PENNY.
>
> P. S. What is your opinion of *Arcana Coelestia*, a book being published in Latin in London, the author being a Swedish nobleman called Emanuel Swedenborg?"

We notice this letter chiefly for the postscript, as it has been stated on the supposed authority of this Mr. Stephen Penny, in the recent *Biographical Sketch of Swedenborg* (1849), that the authorship of the *Arcana Coelestia*, on its first appearance, was ascribed to Mr. Law. But apart from the above letter, such a preposterous idea could not have entered the mind of the writer if he had had the least proper acquaintance with Mr. Law’s sentiments or writings. Nor do we understand how such a supposition could have been ventured in print (for it was from a printed document that the compiler of the "Sketch" took it), unless to add dignity and respectability to the inventor’s favorite author’s deep studies. We cannot discover if Mr. Law wrote an answer to Mr. Penny, though there is every probability of it. <note>Note: It was probably this mention of the work which led Mr. Law to direct Mr. Ward to procure it for him, only seven volumes of it being then published. What his feelings were on looking into it and reading the Baron’s explanations of the first chapters of Genesis may be more easily imagined than described! His criticisms in his two letters, in addition to the gospel-like, Christ-like tone of all his judgments, indicate them sufficiently. Being informed of the publication of the remaining eighth volume, he, as we have seen, directed it to be purchased in order to complete the set.</note>

We should very much like to have possessed a clear statement of Mr. Law’s opinions of the *Arcana Coelestia* in answer to Mr. Penny’s inquiry, to add to those illustrations of the character of his theology which we have already presented on pages 158–60, and which were drawn from Mr. Law, we have supposed, by his neighbor and friend the Rev. ->affections dépravées, et corriger en nous ces altérations faites à l'image vivante de la divinité ; nous<-

would have been, and that Mr. Law would, in his characteristically powerful and natural way of demonstrating—resulting from a perfect understanding of his subject and its relationship to truth—have completely extinguished Swedenborg’s claims to any respect from serious and enlightened Christians. For aside from his blatant, fundamental heresy, all the truths that are handled in his reasoning and presented as discoveries are merely weak explanations of what may be found expressed with vigor, conciseness, and fullness (to those initiated) in the Gospel and our excellent English church theologians.

And this is what the writer declared and proved on all occasions to his clever and admiring biographer, when specifically tested by portions of his writings selected and read to him by the latter for that purpose during several months of intimate conversation, as mentioned before. Nor could he ever present one seemingly original truth of the Baron’s [Swedenborg's] that the writer did not immediately produce or repeat in the superior form of the Gospel and established theological expression. And when turning to Mr. Law’s two letters and discussing the statement of the Baron’s doctrines there, this was allowed by him to be substantially accurate—with the exception of an alleged but only apparent inaccuracy in one minor point and the use of the term "illiterate" (which, however, only meant an "ignorance of the doctrines and documents of theological truth"). However, it must be said that Mr. Law’s conclusions and judgment appeared sadly unpleasant to him.

On another occasion, our candid friend informed us that among the strange views held by some of the Baron’s devoted followers and publicly promoted in their more exclusive gatherings and church meetings (held at coffee shops around town), one was that *St. Paul*, as an inspired apostle, *was not to be compared to their Seer; indeed, that St. Paul must be completely discarded if Swedenborg is to be understood,* for their principles were diametrically opposite! *This*, it may be noted, was an allusion to the Gospel doctrine of the *cross*. Furthermore, he stated that at one of these meetings, when the question was asked about the best or most likely means to convert people to the *New Church* doctrine (it being his turn to speak), he had suggested sincere and devout prayer, at which the company looked at him with astonishment and burst into laughter! Indeed, the writer himself once heard a very prominent member of that community state that he regarded the Bible only as any other book, that the New Testament Scriptures were in fact "but a kind of spiritual police," and in proof appealed to their favorite illustration: the passion of *carnal lust!* And further, that the doctrine of the Trinity was a gross delusion, for God was simply a man. 

On another occasion, we might remark that our clever literary friend, who had unbounded faith in the Baron’s spiritual vision (as his "Biographical Sketch" amply testifies), offered us what he considered absolute proof of it. He read certain passages from the Baron's recently discovered "*Diary*" regarding the state of a famous deceased religious figure in the spiritual world, as a result of certain secret, gross misconduct in this world. He added that nobody could have known this but the Baron himself at the time, though it had since been discovered that the individual was actually guilty of it. To our friend's astonishment, we produced a book published about six years before the date of the Baron’s "*Diary*" in which these very alleged misdeeds were openly charged against the individual while he was still living. Swedenborg had undoubtedly read this and, in his later reflective moments, had entered it into his "*Diary*" as a *vision!* 

From the Baron’s "*Diary*," we made the following extract, the substance of which our conversational partner admitted was the foundation *upon which all Swedenborg’s theology stands*. He admitted that if it were untrue—"absolutely false, even the very opposite of truth" (as the writer described it)—then everything the Baron had written of a theological nature was indeed only the outpourings of a disordered mind. The passage is this: "All the angels in heaven and all the wicked spirits in hell were once human beings on earth; and the common notion regarding the devil having been an angel in heaven, from which he fell through rebellion, is a mere fable that has neither scripture nor reason to support it."

Thus, the much-disputed question of the Baron’s mental sanity may be brought to a focus, separate from the absurdity—unavoidable in error—of his peculiar doctrines, as shown in part in the two letters from Mr. Law presented earlier.

Now our literary friend has obtained, through our books and conversation, what he admits is a true understanding of the "ground of nature," or the primary outward manifestations of the infinite Deity. To him, then, and to all others who understand *that fundamental point* and basis of all true knowledge, we offer Behmen’s "*Aurora*" and "*Signatura Rerum*," with the explanations of Freher and Law, and we will let the outcome of the case rest on the result. The matter, we say, may soon be decided without exposing the absurdities of the Baron’s doctrines through the common conventional method of theological argument. It simply rests here: in a clear, sensible *understanding of the true ground and principles of all things, and then in an examination of Behmen’s "Aurora"*—to see whether the *very opposite* of the statement in the quote above is not satisfactorily demonstrated there. 

But we suspect, from certain past observations, that the current generation of the Baron’s admirers *dare not* examine his claims in the way we have suggested, nor discuss them with a true <term>theosopher</term> <note>A practitioner of theosophy, specifically in the sense of Jacob Boehme's mystical philosophy.</note>. The possibility of finding themselves to have been the dupes of perhaps the most clever lunatic and audacious visionary that the powers of earthly reason ever produced would, we think, be considered too great a risk for such intellectuals to take. Leaving then, finally, the amiable and tireless reasoner and his admirers to their imaginary rambles in their elysian fields (having offered our remarks from time to time chiefly to guide the candidate’s judgment and views), and urging the general reader to stick to—and bless God for—the good old road of earnest devotion to God through mortification and self-denial, watchfulness and prayer, and all holiness and good works. This is the one "narrow way" through which alone every person from the first to the last must enter into life and be eternally happy. If they are members of the "*first resurrection*," we proceed with our notes and observations.

>
> My love to the philosophic doctor; but you need not tell him that a good brown loaf and cheese

> "Dec. 3rd, 1759. — My dear friend — I must begin this as you began your last to me, by acknowledging its lateness. I am always glad when you have no need for such an excuse, for your letters are both a pleasure and a benefit to me.
> The name of the author of 'Faith and Reason' is Mittenach, a German count. All his later works are in a book called 'Fides et Ratio'; they are chiefly translations from Madame Guyon.
> I thank friend Hinde for his offer of 'George Fox,' but I have no leisure for reading folios; though the man who wrote it has plenty of my esteem.
> Perhaps the operation of Dr. James's medicines may have done you no harm, but of this your own experience can only judge. However, I think you ought to be very cautious in your dealings with doctors.
> I wrote a letter to Mr. Clarke in answer to one of his. It was sent open to Mr. Ward, so that he might see the contents and show them to you, as well as two other letters for the judgment of you both. I do not know how far he has proceeded in preparing some of my letters for the press, or whether he and you are still of the opinion that they should be published.
> Next week I intend to send you a small parcel by the carrier, addressed to you in Sun Court, in which you will find another letter on a particular subject to be added to the other letters, if you and Mr. Ward judge it worthy. For you and he are to do for me what I cannot do for myself. I have no need for spectacles, but find great benefit in looking at things through your eyes.
> Give my love to the philosophic doctor. I have done what I never thought I would do: I have tasted his cordial, as the ladies have. We believe it is as good as anything of that kind can be. You do not need to tell him this unless you cannot help it.
> I am commanded by two of us to tell you that we all three love to think and talk of you. And so farewell. — W. LAW. — P.S. Mrs. Campbell died here on the 23rd of last month." <insert>[Note: She was the widow of the celebrated Rev. Archibald Campbell. Her two daughters inherited Mrs. Hutcheson's property upon her death in 1781; one of them was married to a Mr. Griffiths, whose descendant or son-in-law was a Mr. Bailey, an upholsterer on Mount Street, Grosvenor Square.]</insert>

In this letter, we find a reference to Mr. Clarke, the individual whom Mr. Law had previously assisted in the publication of a work at the request of Mr. Langcake, but whose book Mr. Law had placed among the list of authors whose publications, when sent to him, he used to light his bedroom fire. <insert>[It was this individual who wrote the Eulogy that appeared in print a short time after Mr. Law's death, which we propose to add to our other notices of Mr. Law in its proper place.]</insert> Mr. Clarke, as his writings show, was an author of a peculiar idiosyncrasy; the subjects of his thoughts and conversation were the transcendental mystical topics and prophecies of the old Jewish scriptures. One of his favorite topics was an artificial, sudden *millennium* (like the sun rising at midnight, or autumn happening in spring), and searching out, by calculations based on the figures of Daniel and Revelation, the exact year of its commencement, as well as the *conversion of the Jews*, which "at the furthest," he declared, "would be in 1811." The long and plausible, rambling dissertations on all these topics, which he occasionally introduced to the world in certain publications, found—and still find—their admirers among individuals of a similar turn of mind who look for extraordinary events, according to the old system of things before Christ. Thus, in all ages, there have been these positive prophetic determiners of the future of Christianity and the day and hour of the blossoming of the tree of good and evil of time, according to their childish conceptions of the mystery of the gospel and calculations made from data of ancient, obsolete, shadowy, and temporary Jewish matters. Such have been the occupations of individuals claiming the character of gospel Christians and the office of guides and leaders of the people in religion; in short, aiming at anything but the *one business* of high personal purification and sanctity, and leading souls to God—the source of all wisdom and truth.

But Mr. Law was too wise a man to be dazzled by false glare or to admit anyone into his select category of spiritual authors who could so mistake the design of the gospel as to indulge their fancy and lead the attention of their audience into such a wilderness of barren speculations as those we have described, however captivating they may be for those curious in such matters. The business of religion, and therefore of all orthodox spiritual writers, was, he knew, simple and unchanging, under whatever form a new "kaleidoscope" writer might represent the truths relating to it. He himself, in a word, describes the sort of books that alone are deserving of his attention:

> "Books of divinity," he says in his 'Way to Divine Knowledge,' "I am not finished with, but I will esteem none to be such except those that make known to my heart the inward power and redemption of Jesus Christ. Nor will I seek anything even from such books but that which I ask of God in prayer: namely, how to better know, more abhor, and resist the evil that is in my own nature, and how to obtain a supernatural birth of the divine life brought forth within me. All besides this is *pushpin*." <note>Pushpin: A trivial children's game; here used to mean something of no consequence or value.</note>

After these remarks, the reader will be prepared for the letter which Mr. Law, in the above communication to Mr. Langcake, states he had written to Mr. Clarke. It was as follows, and though inserted in the published "Collection," we provide it here in full:

> "Nov. 3rd, 1759. — Dear Sir — Mr. Ward will convey 'Rusbrochius' to you. — Everyone has his own proper way from God, if he is so happy as to find and follow it without seeking out one of his own. For many years, my mind has turned from, or rather passed by, every religious matter that requires critical abilities or that carries me to any help other than that which is to be found within me.
> I never could go through even the divine 'Rusbrochius' in his spiritualizing of the Mosaic tabernacle and all that belonged to it. His enlightened eye saw Christ figured and typified in every part, and what he saw he told the world.
> But as for myself, I cannot go back to search for the *shadow* of the mystery under its types and figures, because the substance itself has come. And I find more enjoyment of it by simply giving myself up to that which is to be had from a Christ, not as known under Jewish prophecies, but as having come in the flesh and being made man in everyone who receives him.
> Next to the Scriptures, my only book is the enlightened Behmen. And him I only follow so

Such were the principles of Mr. Law and his approach to the writings of spiritual authors, whose direct tendency was not to engage the heart in a simple conversion to God and, consequently, in earnest devotion and hardworking conformity to the practical model of the life of Jesus Christ. Some people may think differently and consider it quite consistent with the profession of the Gospel and the character of an evangelist to search for satisfaction and light in the workings of the imagination and in the objects and wonders of inferior nature; but they will not be among those who feel and know what our blessed Lord felt and knew when he said, "but one thing is necessary."

We may notice here another topic that later occupied the mind of this Mr. Clarke, as it had done for others who were not governed by the pure principles of this last-mentioned, oracular truth. We mean the doctrine of *universal restitution*, which, as we previously suggested, Mr. Clarke came to believe was not only implied but directly enforced in certain Jewish types and prophecies! Having caught the idea of restitution in his meditative speculations and followed the train of thought it induced within him, he ended, we say, by accepting it as a positive dogma taught by the word of God. According to his letters in the writer's possession, it was so binding upon him that his very salvation depended upon his preaching and publishing it openly to the world! He designated it the "everlasting Gospel," as Mrs. Jane Lead had done before him. In this way, good men are liable to be led astray (by not properly grasping this simple counsel of our Lord). Instead of regarding such topics with indifference, suitable only for conversation during occasional relaxation, they turn them into mental idols and obstacles to the work of personal salvation, if not occasions for sin. — "A multiplicity of wills," says Mr. Law, "is the great disease and misery of man. To have but one will and one love is the great remedy for all his evil."

These subjects were sometimes brought to Mr. Law's attention by Mr. Langcake, who was acquainted with people who advocated them. This led to the expression of his views in the letter we inserted in the note on page 216, which Mr. Law likely considered at the time to be fit only for private reading. Therefore, in preparing his letters for publication, he would only allow as much of that communication to be published as is attached to the end of the letter to Mr. T. L., numbered XIV in the latest edition of the "Collection." <note>We have reason to say that the Mr. S. mentioned in this published letter may mean one Mr. Shirley, if it does not refer to Stonhouse.</note>

The subject of "restitution" is one that surely occupied Mr. Law's private thoughts (as shown by extracts we possess in his handwriting from treatises relating to it and the "Last Judgment," etc.). However, he always kept it within its proper bounds, as might be expected from one so fully imbued with the classic mind and perception of Christ. The whole tone of his writings, apart from his individual expressions, shows how reluctant he was to give any particular attention to such mysterious points, or to make them subjects of conversation beyond a passing remark at a suitable time; just as we might suppose our Lord himself would have done, according to what St. Clement relates of some of Christ's private conversations. Guarded as the subject must necessarily be by our present observations, we have great pleasure in presenting here Mr. Law’s definite conjectures on the matter. These were uttered, it may seem to some, by a peculiar providence (like the remarkable last words he wrote) at the very close of his unique evangelical, *Elias ministration*: they are contained in a letter written by Mr. Langcake to Henry Brooke on August 1, 1790. Since Mr. Langcake's accuracy is not to be doubted, what he relates must be considered alongside what Mr. Law wrote on the subject in the letters referred to on page 216, in his "Way to Divine Knowledge," and with what we will soon present in a letter from Miss Gibbon to Edward Fisher. Mr. Langcake writes as follows:

> "Regarding this doctrine of universal redemption, I remember very well Mr. Law speaking of it during my last visit at Easter 1761, a few days before his death; for he died on April 9th, and Easter Sunday was on March 22nd that year. He said that <note>it would seem as if</note> not only the whole human race but even the fallen angels would all be delivered out of misery, but not until the Day of Judgment. He said there would be a gap in creation if they were not taken into happiness. But he added that this could not happen until they saw the entire creation made happy before them. When they saw this and felt the eternal fire fully operating upon them, it would produce the blessed effect of <note>quickening or</note> awakening that <note>original root of</note> goodness which lay dormant within them. For though that goodness might be locked away in a compaction seven times deeper or stronger than fire is in a flint, yet because it was locked up—<note>possibly not extinct or its essence destroyed, for what can die in eternity?</note>—and preserved in them, it would come forth. Thus, they also would be made happy, to the full display of God’s <note>wonderful wisdom and enchanting</note> love and goodness toward all His creatures. <note>Such a sight and experience would certainly melt every creature into humility, love, and adoration, and make the entire creation ring with *HALLELUJAHS*.</note>
> 
> This was essentially what Mr. Law said on that occasion, and nearly in his own words, as best as I can remember. I have never before written of these sentiments of Mr. Law to anyone but you; nor do I wish to circulate them. However, it may not be improper to place them safely in the hands of a dear friend, and so I entrust them to you, or rather repose them in your heart and in the hearts of your dear friends. Mr. Law spoke on the subject of his own accord after we had heard the Easter Sunday afternoon sermon and took a walk through the town of Kings-Cliffe. He then opened a gate into a field—it was on rising ground—and then he began"

From another part of Mr. Fisher's memorandum book, we extract the following note, without vouching for its accuracy. He might have heard Mr. Langcake mention something to the effect, if not the exact substance of it:—

If the light of this world were to be withdrawn, their power would be very great, and they would be even visible to us. When our Lord cast them out of those who were possessed, their request was that they might not be cast out into their own deep. They reside where the sun does not reach, and the reason they are not here in this upper visible world is that the sun and water abate their power.”

Let it then be distinctly understood that, in the above reported observations, Mr. Law merely indulged in a speculative conjecture, nor could he go beyond that. For, as he well knew and had repeatedly stated, no revealed wisdom or philosophy offers any ground upon which to form a definite judgment respecting the point; but rather, all that we do know of the constitution and working powers of eternal nature, and its relations to the Deity, forbids the hope of the restoration of the fallen Luciferian hierarchy.

<margin>
Formed in person first; reference to the Death of Christ, expressed in his Microcosmos.
</margin>

And **Boehme's** grand justifier (and Mr. Law's private tutor), **Freher**, even wrote a specific treatise (A.D. 1718) against this doctrine, which was adventurously and plausibly put forward in his day by some enthusiastic remnants of the **Philadelphian Society**, consisting of **Roach** and others. In this treatise, he examines the matter fundamentally and in all its comprehensiveness; showing, *first*, the great difference between Lucifer's and Adam's fall; then, the notion of the *everlasting gospellers*, with their eight chief arguments; further, he gives his own idea on the subject, accompanied with demonstrative explanations and symbols; and finishes by a methodical, thorough refutation of the aforementioned eight arguments.

The “mystery of Christ,” we may remark, is always represented to us in Scripture antithetically to that of Adam; and therefore does not comprehend the nature of the fallen angels, as indeed is especially declared in Hebrews 2:16. The question of their restoration may belong to the millennial kingdom of Christ and form the subject of a specific revelation to that *golden age* of love and wisdom, but certainly it has nothing in common with our present dispensation. Nor, perhaps, do we have capacities of a sufficiently extensive mathematical power and precision to apprehend distinctly the how and the why of the possibility or impossibility of their restoration. It is the deepest and most comprehensive geometrical problem of the intellectual universe to our present conceptions. Nay, it is embraced in that dazzling, overwhelming contemplation of St. Paul, where he exclaims in Romans 11:33, “Oh the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable his judgments, and his ways how past finding out!”—Let therefore upstart religionists beware of dogmatizing on this matter and keep to the essentials of sound Christian knowledge, for they have no ground to stand upon but imagination: let them, we say, beware of temptation even in this matter, which they will find to be the high road to sin if they do not flee from it.

The chief passages of revelation which (it has appeared to us) may be supposed to refer to the subject are those of St. Paul in *Ephesians* 1:10, *Colossians* 1:19, 20, and especially in his sublime fifteenth chapter of the *First of Corinthians*, from the twenty-second to the twenty-eighth verse, where he touches upon the order and intervals of redemption, thus:—**Christ**, risen and glorified, as the first-fruits; *secondly*, they who are **Christ's**, by gospel regeneration, at his coming; *thirdly* and *lastly*, the **END**, when, having reduced all opposing wills into subjection and become Lord of all, of an entire willing people, he shall deliver up his redeeming government <note>it being finished</note> to God and the Father: thereby leaving to Satan and his angels actually nothing, and so nothing to do. But <note>we say</note> the very commencement of the Apostle's declaration, as well as the whole tenor of his gospel, shows that his consideration regarded <note>if even it may be so liberally interpreted</note> only the restoration of the Adamic humanity.

It will not here be necessary for us to dwell upon the fact of Mr. Law's belief in the purification of all human nature as the ultimate effect of the mediation of Christ, inasmuch as he avowed it unhesitatingly whenever called to do so, and in no place with greater authority than in the “Address to the Clergy,” the close of which he wrote, as we have stated, a few days only before his death.

He undoubtedly knew well the basis from which he wrote and spoke, and was the last man in the world to put forth a conclusion that was not perfectly logical or drawn from indisputable premises. However, we do not think this same doctrine should be publicly promoted by others who do not themselves *certainly* understand its basis and philosophy. Since it is not an explicit revelation of the Gospel, it is not a suitable subject for the entertainment of the masses, whether in the world or the church. And woe to him who shall add anything to, or take anything from, the doctrine implied in the warning: "What shall it profit a man if he gain the whole world and *lose his soul*? Or what shall a man give in exchange *for his soul*?" For his own part, the writer of these lines will not entertain the question of *human or universal restoration* at all; but, according to the sound teaching of the church in all ages and the advice of her faithful, earnest, devoted, and regenerate children without exception, would stick to the plain doctrine and example of Jesus Christ,

<margin>
What is that to you? Follow me.
</margin>

Still, if any serious reader should think that this doctrine tends to weaken the force of the Bible's denunciations against the impenitent, or to soften the "terrors of the Lord" which will inevitably overtake a sinful life—let such a person consider the actual state of a soul deprived of the only light and refreshment of its spiritual, dark, and fiery ground. Its habitation is therefore in that root of nature which, because of its enclosed restriction, anguish, and despair, may be compared to an element of cold and darkness, ten thousand degrees below zero and ten thousand times denser than any iron; and yet also to a furnace such as could only be produced by three omnipotent, opposing, whirling, consuming, yet self-generating properties of *fire*. There, in a condition of gasping, perpetual dying, thirst, and aching sorrow, with ten thousand attendant horrors, it must remain (being unable to relieve itself in the least degree, but rather increasing its dreadful misery by its very motion), until such revolutions take place in the whole order and system of nature that it becomes possible for the divine light to reach and act upon this shut-up spirit. This is so that its imprisoned seed or principle of the divine life may have an atmosphere and the necessary external aids for growth; this process will occupy ages upon ages of duration to achieve, just as three hundred and sixty-five days are needed for the earth to revolve around the sun and for the production of mature autumnal fruit.

Let all this, we say, be duly considered—(though what heart can conceive the horrors of a soul that has lost its God? When even a brief awareness of it, permitted for a necessary purpose, caused the immaculate Jesus-Jehovah to break out into a bloody sweat)—and furthermore, that all this unspeakable misery will have been reached through contempt for the blood of the covenant and the patience, mercy, and help of God in Christ Jesus (which will be the reflection of such a soul): let all this be duly considered, and then let such a reader say whether this doctrine in any way detracts from the authority of Scripture, or tends to weaken the force of its denunciations against sin or its exhortations to "strive to enter through the narrow gate," to be a partaker of the "first resurrection," and to avoid the portion of the wicked "in the lake that burns with fire and brimstone, where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched."

It would indeed be horrible enough to experience such sensations in a dream or nightmare; and who has not felt them to some degree and rejoiced at the morning light, which has, through the medium of the physical organs of flesh and blood, dissipated the gloom of the mind? But oh! what must the *actual suffering* itself be, and that not to be relieved for ages? We may form some faint conception of the power of its external causes by considering how in the arctic regions—where (the wrathful, predominant action of the first property of nature being unmitigated by the fourth) the cold is so intense that, according to the accounts of Polish adventurers, it burns off the tongues of the little foxes (even in their native element) when they try to bite the iron traps by which they were caught and held. But this intense harshness of action is only a limited, temporal manifestation of the omnipotent, separated powers of attraction, or the basis of nature, in the spiritual world. For, as the reader is undoubtedly aware, cold and heat, want and satisfaction, are the two extreme points of the same line of nature; one end of which may be termed hell and absolute despair, and the other the glory and enjoyment of heavenly joy, while the middle may be compared to this world, with its fears, hopes, and gospel warnings.

Regarding the truth of these representations of the dreadful horrors and misery that will be the lot of the impure and unregenerate in the spiritual world—[—*that is, of those who have failed in this state of probation to use all diligence, pain, and labor to enter through the narrow gate and make their calling and election sure: first by faith, or the heart's desire turned in earnestness and urgency toward the universal Spirit of mercy and goodness; and secondly, by the practice of faith, or renunciation of the world, mortification and self-denial, slaying and sacrificing the self, mentally and physically, even to the very last gasp,*—] such, we say, have been the traditions of all nations. These traditions, therefore, originated in a Divine revelation, perhaps one as specific as our own New Testament Gospel, as suggested in the Annotation on pages 450–496. And these are the reasons for the self-immolations, the "penances, sacrifices, and other [so-called] peculiar superstitious practices of the Hindus," and other intellectual as well as unlettered nations of antiquity. These poor souls (see the engraving of their penances and the dissertation on them in Maurice's "Indian Antiquities," Vol. 5), though laughed at and pitied by our modern, easy, burly, well-to-do, broad-way Christians and "evangelical" converters of Jews and heathens, will assuredly never drop into that lake of perdition which they have so earnestly and continuously striven to avoid. Meanwhile, many a complacent, "fat and flourishing" talker about "salvation by faith alone" and many a rational Christian (both being practically and equally despisers of the doctrine of the cross) may find to their sorrow the terrible meaning of that truth: "many who are last shall be first, and the first, last."

And this brings to mind an observation which Mr. Law is reported to have once made to a friend: namely, that "thousands of simple, honest souls, who say humbly and sincerely, 'Lord have mercy upon me,' 'The Lord's will be done,' and know nothing further of their own spiritual state, may be at a great level of advancement in the kingdom of heaven; while those who are elevated by their learning, talents, and abilities, their theological knowledge, and acquaintance with gospel doctrines—being full of sophistry and self—will have their whole spiritual process to go through in another life."

The following letter was written by Mr. Edward Fisher to Miss Gibbon on the occasion mentioned therein—a letter he had received from her and a visit he had made, some months previously, to King’s Cliffe. It may have been to inquire concerning any literary remains of Mr. Law and the writings of Freher, which he had recently learned of and also discovered that Mr. Law had kept copies of some of them:

> “Compton-Greenfield, March 26th, 1789.—I have not been in a hurry to acknowledge the favor of good Mrs. Gibbon’s kind answer to my letter from Bristol, which reached my hands some months ago, though I was no less appreciative of my obligation to her for the effort, I believe, she must have taken to write it under the pressure of so much physical illness and weakness. * * *
> I recently asked my brother to visit Mr. Law at Sun Court, Cornhill, to inquire about your health, and I had the satisfaction of being informed that it was not worse on the whole (allowing only, perhaps, for the further advance of age and weakness) than when I had the pleasure of seeing you last summer. I congratulate you on having passed through the late severe winter so well; and I heartily wish you may enjoy the use of your mental faculties and as much freedom from physical pain as your weak condition will allow, while it shall please the Almighty to grant you a continued stay in this mortal state.
> Mr. Langcake, who continues to live in Bristol, was as well as he has usually been lately when I last saw him; his physical constitution is weak at best, and his health is subject to much interruption. He does not know I am writing to you at this time, or he would undoubtedly desire to be remembered to you. Nor did I know of his writing to you some months ago until he told me of it after he had sent his letter; I knew nothing of the contents until yours informed me that he had given you some account of Mr. Clarke’s visit with him. It is true that the Reverend Mr. Clarke (who is a regularly ordained clergyman and has been so for many years) came to Bristol, as he has been to other places, to preach; and also, I believe, to see what he could obtain in charitable donations for the relief of his temporary needs, which I understand were then very urgent, as he had a family of children to maintain along with himself, with very meager and insufficient means to do so. As he previously knew Mr. Langcake well, who had at one time lodged with Mr. Clarke at his house in Hoxton Square, London, he spent much time in his company at Bristol, but did not stay in the same house. Mr. Clarke afterwards went to Winchester upon notice that an older brother of his, who lived there in good circumstances, was in a very poor state of health and not likely to live much longer. That brother has since died and has left Mr. Clarke such a provision that, with economy and prudent management, may serve to place him above the financial difficulties and distresses he previously had to struggle with. His friends rejoice with him over this favorable turn in his circumstances.
> It is true that Mr. Clarke held the opinion of the final restoration of *all human souls*, in which he had the agreement of your truly valuable friend* Mr. Law; I view this as a significant confirmation of the truth of it. I am glad to see a doctrine that reflects so much glory on a God of love, and is so comforting to the poor, frightened souls of sinful men, so well-founded and supported. But what *calling* he had to preach that doctrine so generally, or to carry it further (if he did so) in his preaching, is a matter I will say nothing about here, but leave to him to answer for. <note>*From whose books he probably first drew it.</note>

These letters are three in number, the first dated in 1731 and the last in 1732. These letters by Mr. Law are excellently written for the purpose that prompted them and contain many things of *general use and edification*; as do the others that were published during the lifetime of the blessed author.</note> In a subsequent letter, Mr. Fisher writes:

> “Many excellent truths and directions are to be found in these letters, and a vein of piety runs through the whole that is very exalted and edifying. We have now only to add that as Mr. Clarke was acquainted with Mr. Ward (known as Mr. Langcake), upon whom he was perhaps accustomed to urge his calculations and opinions regarding the *millennium*, etc.—and who, through the agitation regarding these topics then prevailing in the religious world, might have felt some interest in knowing Mr. Law's views on the matter—it appears he addressed Mr. Law on the subject. This gave a most fortunate occasion for the expression of Mr. Law's opinion in the following letter, which, as the reader will perceive, is distinguished by that same piercing, divine common sense and simplicity which so pre-eminently illustrate everything that passed through his mind and to which expression was given. This letter was written about a year before his death. And just as he, in the course of his previous life and writings, not only indicated the path of a prophetic messenger suited to the times in which he lived—in which his own mystical portrait, unconsciously to himself but very clearly to us, is distinctly traced—so we find him, with the same unconsciousness yet extraordinary acuteness, fairness, and exactness, like an evangelical *Malachi* summing up the whole with a finished general description of himself and of the *nature and effects of his scriptural ministrations*. <note>And does not the present treatise follow in the train of these mystical messengers who are specially indicated in this letter, to precede or be instrumental to the introduction of that day? For here is the *key to the gospel*, which all nations will receive when it is rightly presented to them.</note> The letter in question is the following:

"April 2, 1760. My dear friend—Regarding the approach of THE GREAT DAY, it is certainly near, though it may not be strictly according to the scriptural arithmetic and calculations that have been presented to the public. That the seven-thousandth year is but a little way off is undeniable; and it may be affirmed on sufficient ground that the *six-day creation* lasts no longer than until it arrives. <note>N.B.</note>

And though the scriptural prophecies, figures, and numbers are certainly intended to point out the time, yet I am inclined to believe that the messenger of God (whether one or more) who is to proclaim this time as a forerunner will not be left to take his proof from them, but will be as much an original in his way as any of the prophets of old were. And though he may perform no more outward miracles than John the Baptist did, yet he will come burning and shining in such a light of divine distinction from all others that it may correspond in the Spirit to that which was formerly done in the flesh, when the blind saw, the deaf heard, the lame walked, the dead were raised, and the gospel was preached to the poor.

End all your letters to me as I end this, by only adding my name. Your name is compliment enough to me. —W. Law."

(Mr. Law is said to have remarked that Mede was the best who had written upon the calculations, meaning those of a prophetic nature in the Scriptures.) We may add that the sentiments in this letter were totally at variance with the enthusiastic views of Clarke, as well as those of the millenarians of our own day. And being published, they would necessarily be known abroad; therefore we find Clarke writing in a letter to Mr. H. Brooke:

"Chelsea. April 24, 1772. Dear Sir—I received yours dated April 4, and find by it that I was mistaken in thinking you another Mr. Brooke <note>that is, your uncle, the author of the "Fool of Quality."</note>. I am glad to find that he is on the path of true piety. I wished for the sake of others that some men of letters (for the world loves its own things) would appear in favor of the spiritual sense of Scripture. Such men have always been given by providence in the worst times, as the salt of the earth. But now the religious people, who began in the spirit, have ended in the flesh—in the dead letter, which is only a record, a memory of a divine and newborn man, whose seed lies in the soul of all men, beginning with the first covenant, though manifesting gradually in the ages of the gospel.

Although you may lack human learning, you have the best learning: that of the Scriptures and the Holy Spirit, the teacher of all truth. I put no value on my own learning, such as it is, nor did I ever understand the gospel by means of it, nor indeed by any means whatever! <note>!</note> For though I have seen traces of the same truths in the mystical writers, they have been only in general, but their foundation is true. I have read very few lately; for some years past I have read none. The law and gospel, Moses and Christ—the two witnesses prophesying in sackcloth for nearly 1260 years—are my only study; and my light is to and from them alone! <note>!</note> The world was to be in the state it is under now, just before the era of the *millennium* or the seventh trumpet of Moses in the seventh month, corresponding to the seventh of St. John; and from the types and language (which mostly correspond to each other, if not always), it will be sudden, without any notice or any notice that shall be regarded. Remember Egypt, the flood, the taking of old Babylon; compare our Lord's words, "*as it was in the days of Noah and Lot, so shall it be in the days of the Son of Man.*" The expectation, therefore, of such messengers as Mr. Law and the Roman Catholic Church expect will prove groundless: no Elijah, no John the Baptist will be sent, either in spirit or name! <note>!</note> *He comes as a thief in the night without a precursor or herald.*

How could the world be surprised if it were otherwise? *The spirit of prophecy is the only testimony of his advent, to take the nations who have not yet heard of him, and the kingdoms of this world, into his theocrasy, and into the vision and food of the cloud of glory.* <note>!</note>

The spirit of prophecy will be despised, as it always was before; yet Daniel says, "The wise and enlightened of God shall understand the times and seasons, and the signs of the times, both in nature and in revelation." The world is now in its fullest triumph over the spirit of the gospel, and as Dr. Oswald says over and over in his "Appeal in Favor of Religion," the world has, in a way, renounced the gospel. He is a man who has seen much of high life and knows the conversation and sentiments of the great. Expect no other signs, my friend, than those Christ has given; my own misconception in some respects was due to yielding too much to common opinion, built on passages of scripture poorly understood. Mr. Law himself was not in the mystery

I am, dear friend, your affectionate and obliged servant,

The following is an extract from a letter of Clarke to Mr. Brooke, written a short time previously:

“My ‘Daily Service of the Temple,’ I find, has been thought to open the regeneration more than any other tract. <note>!</note> The *first-born*, etc., is intended to explain one particular truth of great consequence to the true knowledge of the extent of the gospel: *but of this you will best judge for yourself.* We are certainly near the seventh trumpet, when the *mystery* ends, as St. John tells us. Seven trumpets blew from the month *Abib*, of first ripe fruits, to the *seventh* month; then comes the millennial kingdom, of which I can say little at present. The signs of the times in Moses, by days, weeks, months, and years, are clear enough in general; the exact measure God only knows and will reveal in His own manner. The second coming of *Christ in clouds* is a blessing; all the language of the gospel must be understood as good news. But this manifestation will be sudden and unexpected by the world in general, which it could not be if signs in earthquakes, wars, famines, and pestilences were to abound in all kingdoms. These things could not make men be as in the days of Noah, for even luxury itself could not subsist under such a combination of calamities. The external signs are sufficient for the serious; the internal is the spirit of prophecy, opening the *everlasting gospel*, which the angel flies through heaven and preaches to every creature. The wicked must be punished and purged. If we extend wrath beyond the work of love, love is a servant and wrath the master, but this cannot be. *** ”

Such is a sample of the conceptual rigmarole put forth by this individual as the spiritual sense of Scripture: all vapid talk and groundless assumption, proceeding neither from the spirit of holiness nor from the spirit of wisdom, nor yet from sound Christian knowledge.

Should the reader desire to see a truly common-sense as well as theosophic view concerning the millennium, and a judgment respecting the opinions that have prevailed in recent ages upon it—as well as the right way to attain to a true understanding of gospel mysteries—he is advised to consult the Fourth and Fifth of Behmen’s published “Epistles.” Behmen, it may be remarked, never uttered anything from conjecture, but only what he fundamentally and certainly knew. These two epistles were written in answer to the inquiries of a certain millenarian author in his own day and at his desire, who, it may be just stated, resolved the question according to the simple, scripture-number calculations of Clarke and the popular modern writers upon it (instead of according to nature, or the autumnal maturity of the tree of good and evil). Alluding to such a view of the matter, Behmen writes:

“When we look upon the words of Christ and his apostles, they will not in the least manner agree with it; and though there is mention made of a thousand years in the Revelation, yet the same is hidden from us; and we know not when they may begin, or whether they have begun. If the ‘first resurrection’ is paradisiacal, then it may be done without our knowledge.” And again, “It may please God to open the understanding of others <note>as to this matter</note>, and I should be ready and willing to learn, if I could see the ground of it in the light of nature. But it belongs not to man to make conclusions about secret mysteries without the command and light of God, lest he be found a liar before God.” Again, he observes, “Man hardly reaches that which is before his eyes, much less that which is hidden and mystical, unless God is his light.” And thus again, “For this world is confined and determined in the beginning of the creation, and then to the end,

Concerning the seventh day of rest, whether or not the world shall yet be at rest for a thousand years? Behmen concludes his long and admirable dissertations on the subject (in the two Epistles in question) in the following terms—which quotation, for its excellence despite its length, we deem worthy of special notice, as providing an important lesson of instruction and caution to future professed interpreters of Scripture times and seasons, which "God has reserved in his own power." > "And therefore I entreat you entirely as a brother and a Christian, that you would be pleased to take care that you apprehend the sabbath in the rest of Christ; and do not be so moved by the fervent prompting of your mind about a millennium according to the common notion of it, but search whether you are able to ground it in the light of nature. >

>

>

And accordingly his understanding must judge, and give it permission or reject and tame it, as necessity requires.

Law had before his mind’s eye, when he wrote the letter we last provided, thoughts regarding the approach of the GREAT DAY.

To return to the order of our narrative, it was in the early part of the year 1760 that the volume of Mr. Law’s “Letters,” which we have repeatedly alluded to, was published. This was done at the request, as we have stated, of his attached and admiring friends, Mr. Ward and Mr. Langcake, both of whom were then resident in London. This latter fact is apparent from a remark in one of the unpublished letters we have presented, as well as from other documents. To this residency may be mainly attributed the *alterations* we have from time to time pointed out as having been made in the originals of the letters inserted in the published collection; though in some cases, these were perhaps entirely effected by the master hand of Mr. Law himself. As we have suggested, he deemed it proper to inflict a corrective lashing on his perverse detractors and antagonists without compromising his dignity by a direct recognition of their childish folly or malignity.

<margin>
This letter is the original of the tract in Ruby type to page 570.
</margin>

The remarks we have made on particular letters (the *third or last edition* of the “Collection” being the one we have consulted) leave little to be said on this volume. We heartily recommend its entire contents to the attentive reading of any student of Mr. Law’s previous writings. Letter IV is particularly instructive to one who desires to worthily fulfill the office of the ministry. Letter VIII is an admirable answer to a well-educated man whose mind, having been completely mystified by the overbearing influence and seeming seriousness and piety of popular ‘evangelical’ talk, preaching, and phraseology, had lost its original balance of judgment and become altogether unsettled. In it, the author demonstrates the folly of flying to religious methods, opinions, forms, and ordinances as the means of attaining to goodness; thus restoring his correspondent’s mind to its original classic poise, while at the same time pointing out the true and natural way of Christian progress. These, with many others which we might point out, are fine examples of the doctrines of the “Spirit of Love” and “Spirit of Prayer” applied in actual life and enforced with the eloquence and zeal peculiar to the author. The last letter in particular, addressed to a Clergyman of Westmoreland, is an excellent commentary on the universal principles of theology, contrasting them as they are in themselves with the way in which they are generally understood. In short, we regard this book of “Letters” as a familiar introduction to the same life and practice as the “Spirit of Prayer,” adapted to various characters and circumstances, and recommended by the personal interest which always attaches to correspondence. It would be impossible to pick a single letter out of the “Collection” which would not stand being submitted to a judge of logic and rhetoric. We do not mean a modern evangelical preacher or writer, nor his Oratorian ultra-antagonist, but one who has been accustomed to strict argumentation in the pursuit of truth—such a mind, for example, as that of Lord Lyndhurst, after his well-disciplined intellect had applied itself to the examination of the theory and practice of Christianity, even to its very foundation. Such a person would commence with self-evidence and take no step except according to strict self-evidence. Such a person would be able to pull Christianity up by the very roots if it were untrue—that is, if its alleged true ground and whole philosophy were not established or demonstrated.

In the autumn of this year, the devout and amiable Francis Okely—an educated university man well known for his translation of German mystical writings and other works, and who was now a preacher among the “United Brethren”—addressed a letter to Mr. Law. He requested permission for himself and a friend to pay him a visit, as he stated, “for his instructive conversation on the spiritual life.” From a copy of Mr. Law’s reply to this letter (or the reply itself, which was later found among the papers of the celebrated John Ryland of Northampton), his friends presumed and announced that this letter was originally addressed to Mr. Ryland. However, the evidence we are about to furnish will doubtless convince others, as it has convinced us, that the reply was addressed to Mr. Okely, who might have given the original or a copy to Mr. Ryland, the friend alluded to in the request. Mr. Law, having had experience with the common critical disorder of the popular, erratic spiritualists of his day (as we have seen in the case of Wesley and some of the Moravians), was unwilling to refuse the request made to him. But at the same time, to protect himself and remain consistent with his uniform evangelical sentiment, he took care to provide such instruction in his reply that his correspondent—if he were really beyond the initial stages of divinity—should feel the visit was altogether unnecessary for its professed purposes. The reply he sent is the first letter in the published “Collection.”

The visit was paid in due course nonetheless, Mr. Okely being accompanied by Mr. Ryland; and we may judge of its agreeable nature from the following letter by Mr. Okely, addressed to the editor of “Lloyd’s Evening Post” on the occasion stated therein:

> “Northampton. July 19th, 1772. — Sir — Having observed in your paper a couple of letters from two clergymen, under the signatures of Ouranius and Theophilus, wherein, with a pious and disinterested view, they recommend to the public the writings of the late truly Reverend WILLIAM LAW, I am encouraged to hope you will not be averse to the addition of a third to the two former testimonies. They are ministers of the establishment, and I belong to another Protestant denomination. I would consider myself happy if, from the mouths or pens of two or three witnesses, the good opinion of the general utility of Mr. Law’s writings could be so far established that ministers and people of every denomination might be inclined to seriously read and truly practice the sound lessons of his works. Although we are to call no man ‘Master’ on earth, because there is only one who is perfect and infallible, yet I can state with truth that I have reason to believe the Lord has spoken, and still speaks to this age, through him. I also have, in this respect, a happiness beyond that of Ouranius and Theophilus. They lament having had no acquaintance with this worthy and faithful servant of Jesus. But though I did not know him long, I was, a few months before his death, indulged with an ample and intimate conversation with him upon the present state of religion in our time and nation, and on many other most interesting subjects. This I regard as a favor from God bestowed upon me, which I would not have been without for any consideration. I only wish to make the very best use of it in all respects.

We will notice, without going any further, that the unknown philosopher connects all the scien—

Mr. Law lived as he wrote, and died as he lived. I am informed on good authority that amidst the most excruciating pains of the stone <note>A common historical term for kidney or bladder stones.</note>, and at the age of seventy-five, immediately before his death, rising up in his bed, he said: "Take away these filthy garments; I feel a fire of love within, which has burned up everything contrary to itself and transformed everything into its own nature." Oh, that every minister and each of his flocks (both of the established church and every other denomination) might live the life and die the death of this truly righteous man!

To give a small specimen of the conversation that passed between us: "Sir," he said, "I am not fond of religious gossip; my best thoughts are in my works, and I recommend them to you. If I should seem to you to be a stubborn old man, I cannot help it, knowing well the basis from which I write. But, dear sir, above all things, be present with and attend carefully to your own heart. There you will be sure to meet with all evil, and there only can you meet with GOD and all real goodness." <note>A saying worthy of a divine ORACLE.</note>

Having already (through God's mercy) gained some benefit from this advice, I communicate it simply to the public for the same purpose. It is necessary; and may it prove, together with all his writings, a standard raised against the flood of unbelieving immorality and purely intellectual faith, and against the countless numbers of blatant sinners and hypocritical false saints who everywhere divide a fallen Christendom.

I do not have the least intention here to cast unkind reflections on the Clergy, or the ministers and people of any other denomination; my heart feels nothing of that sort. But I most earnestly beg leave to recommend, first to myself and then to them all, a passage in his *Answer to Dr. Trapp’s Discourse on the Folly, Sin, and Danger of being righteous over-much*, from page 58 to 69, fourth edition. If it were only read with godly sincerity, I am very certain that every reader would see reason to be thankful for having had it pointed out to him. This is one among ten thousand other pearls to be found in this brilliant and enlightened author's writings. — CHRISTOPHILUS.

This letter was subsequently published in an octavo pamphlet in the year 1774, entitled, *A Metrical Version of certain Select Passages taken from the Works of the late Rev. William Law A.M.*, which was written by Okely. In the preface to it, the author mentions a poetical friend who had committed his pen to the same purpose, meaning Dr. Byrom of Manchester.

Among Mr. Law's manuscripts, we find a letter from Okely, written after he had made the desired visit to King's Cliffe; at which time, it appears, Mr. Law was working on the project of the *Address to the Clergy*. The letter is as follows:

"Bedford. Nov. 13th, 1760. — Reverend and dear Sir — I hope it will not be considered a sign of over-boldness in me if I write a few lines to inform you that the visit I recently made to you proved so satisfactory to me that it has been fresh in my memory every day since. As you told me your books contained some of your choicest thoughts, I have made such use of them as to continue my conversation with you, and I am sure with more blessing for the heart than for the satisfaction of curiosity.

Should your heart and pen be led to consider the true nature of Justification according to truth and solid experience, as you have in effect already done in the latter part of the *Grounds and Reasons of Christian Regeneration*, I flatter myself that some good advantages might result from that for the present state of *awakened Christianity* among us. As God has made you and your writings a primary instrument in its beginning, you are the most likely person I know to help carry it on and perfect it. On that account, you carry a certain reputation which cannot help but give your words some weight and influence upon the hearts of all truly religious people. Certainly, I wish and pray that your pen may have all the advantages God can give it for the removal of all practical error and the propagation and establishment of *living truth* in the hearts of all the children of God.

And because I know that one of the most pointed and effective objections against you and your writings, among some persons claiming a *real heart-knowledge* of the redemption of Jesus Christ, has been and is: that there is far more abstract and difficult reasoning, notion, and speculation in your works (however much they sometimes seem to avoid it) than individual, *simple, heartfelt truth and enjoyment*; it would be a singular satisfaction to me to see you once, in the spirit and power of a *living witness and confessor of Jesus*, after the pattern of St. Paul, forced, as it were, to show the source of truth and infallibility out of which you think and write, and to boast a little—not of what you are, but of *what the grace of God is and does in you*." <note>This was a rather direct thrust at Mr. Law, but a very proper challenge to be made in its season to all who assume the office of directors in spiritual matters. What is the present state of your Christian experience? Do you consciously enjoy the light and love of God? Does the Spirit of God bear witness with your spirit and conscience now that you are his reborn, beloved child; that your guilt and iniquities are all "washed away," and the power of sin is entirely conquered within you; that in short, all within you and proceeding from you is the *holy Jesus*, with his divine wisdom and love, his heavenly meekness and humility, courage and zeal—all old things having passed away within you and all become new—the world, the flesh, and the devil under your feet? If so, and you have your rational understanding well-exercised in mystical theology and learning, then you are deserving of attention as a Christian doctor. "Show the source of truth and infallibility (says Mr. Okely to Mr. Law) out of which you write," in such a convincing, irresistible manner. But Mr. Law was gathered to his rest above before an opportunity was afforded him to respond to this summons; by which we may infer that he was not called to it, nor had occasion to do it.</note>

"Something of this nature might, I think, by God's blessing, silence, if not win over, this class of your opponents, as it would certainly crown all the other productions of your most excellent pen.

I must admit that whenever I hear or read the *true interior life* of any solid saint, of whatever time, place, or persuasion, I feel something thereby inexpressibly captivating to my heart. And as much as I cannot help preferring the work of God to that of man, so much is one grain of such *living truth* more esteemed by me than a hundred pounds of *dead general truth*, however well it is composed and delivered.

In this point of view, I have transcribed and enclosed for your perusal something I take to be—"

About three weeks *prior* to this time, as we find from the following letter, Mr. Law had sent his tract on *Justification by Faith and Works*:

> "Oct. 20th, 1760.—My dear Langcake—If this begins by saying, 'I am glad to see you,' you may understand it without considering it a strong figure of speech; for before I wrote your name at the top of this page, you were more than just present in my mind’s eye. If you think this sounds a little frantic, you must grant me the benefit of the old saying, *Amare et insanire idem est* <note>Latin: "To love and to be insane are the same thing."</note>.
> On Wednesday the 29th of this month, the carrier will bring a small box to Sun Court for Mr. Ward. In it will be found your *Three-fold Life* and a manuscript *Dialogue* to be reviewed by you and Mr. Ward.
> If you grant it an *imprimatur* <note>Official license to print.</note> (which I would not want unless you would grant it even to an enemy), please let it be published with typeface and paper as good as is consistent with a price of *six pence*, for it must not exceed that. Whether the name *Theophilus* or my own name shall appear on the title page is left to you and company, as you judge which one will get it into more hands.
> Adieu——W. LAW."

It may be necessary to remind the reader that the Methodists at this period were divided into two classes: the "Calvinistic" and the "Arminian." The latter represented the beliefs of Wesley and his societies (as well as those of the sober, *solid theologians of all ages*), while the former were the fondly cherished views of Lady Huntingdon and her party, of Whitefield and others (as well as many amiable religious people in our own day). The term "Methodist" was applied not only to the followers of these two main promoters of the religious excitement then occurring throughout the country, but also to certain clergymen who adopted their peculiar notions of justification by faith, the imputation of righteousness, atonement, election and reprobation, sovereign grace, final perseverance, etc., and who also practiced their style of preaching (especially Whitefield’s) in their own parish churches as well as in public. Among this latter group were, as we have mentioned, Berridge, Hervey <note>Spelled "Harvey" in the original.</note>, Venn, and others solemnly displayed in that modern newspaper-style work, the "Life of Lady Huntingdon." Such was the extent of their excitement and their elation *at their imaginary discoveries of Gospel truth* that, among other publications, Berridge ventured to publish two letters he had privately written to a fellow clergyman. These contained a view of these peculiar *converting* doctrines, along with an account of the author's own experience before and after adopting them, under the title of "A Fragment of the True Religion, being the Substance of Two Letters from a Methodist Preacher in Cambridgeshire to a Clergyman in Nottinghamshire, 1760." This work was full of absurd, jumbled "gospel" terms and Calvinistic, Zinzendorfian <note>Referring to Count Zinzendorf and the Moravians.</note> ranting, which he presented as the soul-saving, evangelical truth, in contrast to the old "dead, bedridden, legal" divinity and preaching of the Church of England. <note>To understand this subject fairly, the reader should consult Dr. Green's very calm and rational expostulation with Berridge and others regarding this publication, in a tract titled "The Principles and Practices of the Methodists Considered," 8vo, 1760, in addition to this "Dialogue" by Mr. Law and Berridge's own publication.</note>

Mr. Law had previously taken no public notice of the doctrinal extravagances that the zealous but injudicious Whitefield preached, published, and later confessed to, nor of the "cant and babble" of the Moravians. He had also ignored the famous excitement surrounding the ministries of the clergymen we have just mentioned, who (like experimenters in mesmerism after witnessing its effects) tried Whitefield’s peculiar style of preaching and doctrine and found similar results. However, upon the appearance of the pamphlet by the Reverend Mr. Berridge (regarding which the Reverend R. Whittingham, editor of the 1838 edition of "The Works of Berridge," justly remarked: "In this letter there are some expressions which he himself, when his knowledge and experience were more matured, would not have used"), Mr. Law now had the opportunity to formally expose all these *fantastic notions and doctrines*. He did this not with open ridicule, as Lavington <note>George Lavington, Bishop of Exeter, author of "The Enthusiasm of Methodists and Papists Compared."</note> did, but with sobriety and elevated evangelical instruction. These were essentially false, enthusiastic interpretations of true scriptural doctrine. He did not omit an allusion to a "late most elegant Gospel writer" (the author of *Theron and Aspasio* <note>James Hervey.</note>), as Berridge called him. At the same time, to the surprise of those who had been deceived—and who had not been convinced by the admissions and confessions of Whitefield and Wesley—he revealed the true secret behind all these supposed supernatural excitements and divine attestations, such as shrieks and groans. He argued that these things are not the work of the Spirit of God (for Muhammad had the same testimonies) but are due to natural causes. With his usual wisdom and complete demonstration, he summed up the matter by pointing out the true doctrines of salvation that should be preached by those desiring to convict sinners in the open highways, streets, and fields, as well as the proper conduct for their zeal
