in delivering the same. Finally remarking, that he should only be too glad to hear that not only this kingdom but the whole world was overrun with such preachers and missionaries.

This is what Mr. Law did in the little publication now before us, entitled "A Dialogue between a Churchman and a (Calvinistic) Methodist, upon Justification by Faith and Works." And when it is remembered who were the individuals encouraging and abetting these delusions, Mr. Law had occasion enough, it will be admitted, to step forward and endeavor to rescue Gospel truth from such audacious, run-riot distorters of it.

<margin>Christian Perfection and</margin>
It will be borne in mind that this tract did not so much embrace Wesley (except in one or two incidental points), nor was it leveled at him so much as at the strange infatuation and high-flown, ignorant declarations and theories we have just described, of the Whitefield and Huntingdon, Calvinistic and Moravian, party of the Methodists: though we cannot admit that Wesley was free from serious censure even in this latter particular. He had manufactured a system of arbitrary theoretic theology out of certain expressions of St. Paul, without understanding his ground: (as if an individual, unacquainted with the principles of Arithmetic, had met with a separate treatise on one of its branches, such as barter, profit and loss, etc., and being initiated into it practically, should thereupon frame a system of figures and calculations, all converging round this particular subject as a center and rule of all arithmetical science!) His chief doctrines, however (we do not allude to the practical divinity of the "Serious Call" etc.<gloss>The author refers to William Law's earlier practical works.</gloss>, which he maintained), were as to their substance, sound; the fault being in the invented, artificial mode of their representation. As for instance, his doctrine of the imputation of Christ's righteousness, set forth in his sermons, which (like some others) is only an idiosyncratic peculiarity of conception and expression, borrowed from the Zinzendorfians; which he would not have used (but would have adopted the classic, unsectarian terms of Mr. Law) had he been duly, scholastically tutored in the true science of the mystical doctrines of Christianity, of the exact parallel and ground of St. Paul's expression, of the 'first and second Adam,' and of the 'man Christ Jesus.' The actual physico-spiritual birth and growth of whom (with the due antecedent process) is everything with which we have to do, and the center round which all the Scriptures and revelations of God are built up. It is the bottom, the middle, and the peak of the *pyramid* of truth and life, human and divine.

What Mr. Law has presented upon the subject of "election and reprobation" in his published "Collection of Letters," and elsewhere, to say nothing of Behmen, is surely sufficient to forever settle the doctrine for all ministers of these kingdoms, and to show the relations of the idiosyncratic understanding of Lady Huntingdon and her party, and of our present "Christian Student" evangelicals (who talk about the "blessed first Reformer's doctrines," and maintain that "a moderate Calvinism is the doctrine of the articles of the Church of England!!")—to show, we say, the relations of Calvin's ignorant, detestable notions to the 'truth as it is in Jesus.'

This little treatise of doctrinal "Justification" by Mr. Law might very appropriately be appended to his "Regeneration" tract and "Answers to Trapp," and so recommended to every sectarian and established preacher and minister in these kingdoms, as a sequel study to the "Serious Call" and "Christian Perfection."

<margin>to be pur</margin>
We may also observe, that it is from the ground laid down in the last six pages of this tract, coupled with the scope and frame of Mr. Law's "Letter on Warburton's Legation," and the apprehension of the nature of the true Gospel kingdom under whose influences we dwell, and the mode of its realization,<gloss>The practical application of these spiritual principles.</gloss> that we always speak when expressing our views as to the proper course of evangelical philanthropy of action with respect to mankind, or our opinions of approval or disapproval of either religion or philosophy in any of their forms thrust upon the world.

The next letter of the unpublished correspondence of Mr. Law, which offers us a topic of remark, is the following:—

> "Nov. 22nd, 1760.—My dear Langcake—I thank you much for your two last letters. I am afraid you overrate the *Dialogue*, written by a man grown very old, in much haste, and through various interruptions.
> 
> But if you are not so clear-sighted with respect to anything of mine as in other matters, it is owing to that which is both my honor and pleasure, your friendly regard for me.
> 
> I would have you take what copies you please for yourself and friends, and to present one in my name to your friend Mr. Payne, and another to your street neighbor, the Brazier. [Mr. Langcake's address was, "at the New House in Hosier Lane, West Smithfield, London."]
> 
> If you can find out how to send one to Mr. Hartley, I should be glad.—I do not make my usual presents to the Gentry, but have proposed a consultation to be held by you and Mr. Ward at Richardson's shop, whether it might not be proper to make presents to some of the Bishops, and especially such as have these *new preachers* in their dioceses.
> 
> Is our philosophic doctor alive and flourishing?—I have the rheumatism in both my arms. There was an oil of mustard seed much in request for this complaint about forty years ago; if you can find it out, I should be glad to have it as soon as you can.
> 
> I intend to put a bit of gold into your hands in a little time, for Mr. Griffiths, the philosopher.
> W. LAW.—P.S. There must be one given to Mr. Clarke."

<margin>or rather</margin>
The Mr. Payne mentioned here has been already alluded to on several occasions; among others as having been instrumental in the posthumous publication of Mr. Law's "Three Letters to a Lady &c.," 1779: which it appears he also edited, and took upon himself to alter the form of the sentences as originally composed, comprising in one paragraph or volume of thought,<gloss>A dense or lengthy block of text.</gloss> what Mr. Law with his masterly taste and judgment had put in distinct sentences or arguments, which is the true style of argumentative writing, as for instance in the symbolic Euclid. The editor of an edition of the "Serious Call," published about the same period as these "Three Letters," and who may well be presumed to be Payne also, has therein taken the same liberty with that work. So far from placing a long or connected volume of thought into one paragraph in argumentative writing, it would be well if individuals would think and write so logically and justly that they would not be afraid to make every argument in their train of reasoning into a brief, single paragraph, whereby its strength or weakness, and its dependence, might be at once seen and tested by the reader. But this process would be the condemnation by the authors themselves of five-sixths of the books com-

The following is the letter Mr. Payne addressed to Mr. Law upon receiving the work, which Mr. Law, in the letter above, requested Mr. Langcake to present to his friend:—

> “London. Herald’s College, near St. Paul’s. December 25th, 1760.—Reverend and dear Sir—Though in these roles you have for some time lived in my heart, yet the freedom of such an address from one who is an entire stranger to you may need some apology. It would be hard if the favors you bestow should cause you any trouble; but I cannot any longer refrain from thanking you for the very acceptable present of your two latest pieces, which I received as a result of your direction to Mr. Langcake. I have, indeed, a much higher obligation to speak of: having learned from you all the good and evil that belongs to me as a fallen and redeemed spirit that is to live forever. And though this is the basis of that sincere esteem and affection I bear towards you, yet unless a particular and personal occasion had given me an opportunity of mentioning it, it would have been acknowledged only in silent thankfulness to the God of all grace and mercy, who has blessed you with the truth and made you the instrument of communicating it to me in common with the Christian world.
>
> To enter into a detail of my religious opinions would be a task almost as trifling and vain as the subject itself. It is sufficient to say that I received them as opinions are commonly received, from my outward situation, subject to the same mutability and change as all that is outward in human life; and having no deeper ground, they could produce no better effect than the formalities of an outward behavior, while the heart continued unchanged, a prisoner of darkness and a slave to all the evil of its fallen state.
>
> I entered into the world upon a narrow foundation; which, though afterwards enlarged by the unexpected favor of some who suddenly became my friends, was yet made more limited by their sudden and unexpected dislike. Along with the loss of them, I lost all hope of future success, and I resolved to disengage myself from business as well and as speedily as I could. In the meantime, it pleased the Almighty in one week to take from me three children, who were all I had left: one nine years old, another seven, and the third an infant. Under this visitation, by far the most awful as well as the most affecting I had known, the same merciful hand that had thus wounded me for my own good led me to your writings; and, through them, to the only remedy for all the disorders of the human heart, the only consolation for all its sorrows.
>
> I think I may justly consider this coincidence of two such circumstances as the most remarkable period of my life; indeed, may I not humbly look upon it as simultaneously the call of God to participate in His redeeming mercy and His direction on how to obtain it? For what benefit could be derived from an outward profession of Judaism? What more salutary ends could be answered by reading the history of the life and precepts of Jesus Christ than by reading the history of what was said and done by Pythagoras, Socrates, or Epictetus?
> 
> Indeed, my heart constantly recoiled from the doctrines of the <term>imputation of sin</term>, partial revelation, <term>vicarious righteousness</term>, and <term>absolute election</term> and <term>reprobation</term>, and it became the master of my sentiments with respect to those debated points. Not knowing the ground of the blessed Trinity—known only to the humble and repenting sinner—the pride of reason could easily reject that doctrine as an inexplicable mystery, the invention of <term>schoolmen</term>, and wholly repugnant to its eternal and immutable ideas. And what was left after this noble separation of truth from falsehood? Nothing but an idea of Christ as an outward teacher and example of virtue, raised in authority above the masters of the ancient schools only by a power of working miracles; while a Tully, a Hutcheson, and a Shaftesbury were secretly more regarded, as they explained morality in a more connected series and upon the deeper and more known principles of nature and life. Meanwhile, the language of the Blessed Redeemer, when discussing His Father, Himself, and the Holy Spirit, His work and His disciples, and the eternal and inseparable union that exists between Him and them, was coldly passed over and impiously excused as a strong metaphorical manner of speaking peculiar to Eastern nations.
>
> I thank my God, and esteem you as His instrument, for bringing me out of this tremendous darkness, superimposed upon the Gospel, into a marvelous light that reveals His holy being, with His kingdoms of nature and grace and all their operations, as harmoniously united in one blessed work, so that the will for all goodness may be the one universal will throughout the whole extent of being and the endless ages of eternity. However, as I can say but little about the influence of this new knowledge on my heart and life, let me not speak too freely as if it were my own. True as I believe your doctrine to be, I do not wish to receive it merely as changing one set of opinions for another; I would rather, in silence, humbly hope and patiently wait for its birth in the depth of my own soul, *looking only unto Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, in whom alone is life, and whose life is the only light of men.*
>
> I know your affectionate heart will not be displeased at my forcing this account of myself upon you; and your candor, I dare say, will excuse the general and imperfect manner in which I have given it. If I should be asked what my motive was for giving it at all, I must answer: so that I might share in your benevolent regard enough to receive that testimony which St. Paul has thrice spoken of as an evidence of his affection for repenting souls—being mentioned in your prayers at the Throne of Grace.
>
> But as it may happen that I shall never, through fair occasion and merit, justly obtain that privilege of communicating my thoughts to you which I have now in a manner usurped, permit me, before I lay down my pen, to say a few words, with all due deference, about the printing of your inestimable pieces.
>
> I have often lamented that, on account of your distance from town, so many inaccuracies should have escaped the press: not because I think the thing in itself deserves much anxiety; but because I fear there are people in the world who, lacking every other pretense, would endeavor to raise a hatred against your writings upon so wretched a foundation; and because I

<meta>This page continues the correspondence from Mr. Payne to William Law, dated December 25th, 1760. Payne is expressing his gratitude for Law's writings and offering his services as a proofreader, drawing on his professional background in the publishing business.</meta>

humain; et nous dirons franchement que la science peut beaucoup gagner à l'examen approfondi

...know there are others weak enough to become the dupes of such mean artifice: a significant shrug, a forced smile, or a single word expressing contempt is enough to discourage the majority of people from examining the basis of doctrines in which they have not been trained, and without which they find themselves perfectly at ease. While I was in business, I undertook the correction of the press for almost every book I published; and by that means, I acquired a skill in detecting typographical errors which are commonly overlooked by the eye that has not been accustomed to seek them out. That I have, therefore, always been ready to undertake the task of correcting the press for your service will, I hope, no longer be attributed to vanity, any more than the eagerness of a painter who, when a portrait is to be painted, should offer to undertake it in preference to someone who had never learned to draw. For all that a man can teach himself, or one man can teach another, is learned only through the combination of time, attention, and repeated practice; and it would have been no criticism of the skill of Sir Christopher Wren to have said that he could not build a ship. I would not, however, have it thought that I am insinuating that you should take this business out of the hands of any person to whom you have thought proper to entrust it, or assign him an assistant if an assistant would be disagreeable. It is a matter, even in my own opinion, of no greater importance than I have stated above; and if it were of much greater importance, it would surely be no excuse for giving a good person a moment's real pain about it. What was not done in a first edition may be done in a second; and upon that principle, I will, with your permission, send you a copy of the recent dialogue, with a few proposed corrections in the punctuation and other small matters marked in the margin. All these will be humbly submitted—as they ought always to be, whether in the revision of a printed book or a manuscript—to your better judgment; for I would no more alter another man's writing without his permission and approval than I would alter his dress.

But to come to a subject that may be more worthy of your attention. There are two groups of people who are, very deservedly, the objects of your earnest and affectionate concern: the Clergy and the Deists. It may be said that I have here joined together two very opposite characters; but I fear there is more real union between them—in spirit, life, and work—than the world is likely to suppose. In the "Answer to Dr. Trapp's Discourse" and the "Animadversions on his Reply," there is such a stirring address to the Clergy that no one in that important position can possibly read it without being the better for it; but how few see it there! Dr. Trapp and his *Discourse* are now almost forgotten; and most clergymen, I believe, are so set in their opinion regarding the passage in Solomon that they will not read anything that is published about it. Even Dr. Trapp, with all his zeal, would not, I think, have ventured a discourse upon it as the vehicle for his abuse of "enthusiasm" if he had not overlooked the circumstances of the case. And yet, to rectify a mistaken understanding of this text is the only subject that the world is encouraged to expect from the title page of your excellent "Answer." I have, therefore, earnestly wished that the address <insert>therein</insert> to the Clergy was stripped of that covering which hides it from those for whose benefit it was written; and if I could have afforded it, I would, with your permission, have printed it some time ago as a separate pamphlet and sent it to everyone who calls himself a preacher of the Gospel in the three kingdoms.

The case is nearly the same regarding Deists. What strength of argument and what tenderness of plea have you used in almost all your works for the everlasting good of those self-deluded souls! How accurately you have stated and explained—particularly in the "Answer to the Plain Account," etc.—the function and limits of human reason; how candidly you have allowed it all its own power, and how completely you have stripped it of that which it has so long usurped! And yet, none of this is specifically and separately addressed to the Deist; instead, it is generally a secondary part in connection with subjects that one Christian debates with another. And will the Deist think himself at all interested in the different opinions of Christians regarding Prayer, Regeneration, and the Lord's Supper? He knows there is such a difference of opinions, and that is enough for his purpose. But to awaken his own sensitivity to his own wretched and deplorable state—for Regeneration is the only possible way of his becoming good and happy, even if he had never seen the Bible or heard the name of Jesus Christ—he must, I think, be called upon in his own name and his own character. If heaven had granted me the ability, I would have done the same for him that I wished to do for the Clergy.

One thing more. In the book on "Regeneration," you have given only the simple proposition regarding man's divine origin as an image of the holy triune God; but the excellent and powerful proof and illustration of this blessed truth, contained in the "Appeal," is only referred to. Now, there are many who do or may buy the book on "Regeneration" who cannot afford to buy the "Appeal"; and many more receive the former from the hands of the benevolent who could never read it unless it were given to them. I wish, therefore, that when the book on "Regeneration" is printed again, all that is in the fourteen cited pages of the "Appeal" might be either incorporated into the text or inserted in a note. I am sure every reader of that invaluable work, whether rich or poor, would be the better for such an addition; and I think, even as a bookseller, that the sale of the "Appeal" would be rather increased than lessened by it.

After all: what can a poor, ignorant man do for others—I speak only of what has been proposed here—when he can do nothing for himself? We allow our blind passions and our blinder reason to be alive, active, and busy from morning until night; and, in our best moods, they lead us into a thousand trifling projects and contrivances for the good of ourselves and others. We do not consider that nothing can do good in, to, or for us and others but the Spirit of God; that His Spirit is continually doing good to every soul in its own blessed way; and that all the events and circumstances of outward life—whether great or small, national or personal—are overruled by the same Holy Spirit and made to serve the final accomplishment of the immutable, gracious purposes of infinite love. If this were the living sentiment of every heart, all might soon be well; and the sudden redemption of fallen nature would convince every man that he contributed as little to its recovery as to his first creation in his original glory.

If it was appropriate for me to begin with an apology, it is surely much more appropriate to conclude with one; as I fear I have said many presumptuous things, and with a freedom that could only be justified by long and familiar correspondence. But whatever I have written has proceeded from a sincere esteem and reverence for that Spirit which lives in you, and from a concern for the honor...

...of some of these works: in general his reasoning is full of strength; his logic

and success of the truth as it is in Jesus, and from a brotherly sympathy for the good and evil of those souls which Jesus came to redeem; and in this light, hoping you will receive it all, I remain, Reverend and dear Sir, your grateful and affectionate servant—J. PAYNE.”

Such is Mr. Payne’s letter, which is not distinguished by the cleverness, focus, and brevity that we might have expected on the occasion. Three years later (1763), he edited an edition of ‘Kempis’ (a work that will be found highly recommended by Mr. Law in the “Three Letters to a Lady”). His appreciation of our author’s writings is detectable in every page of it, but most especially in the preface, where he distinctly alludes to him, though without mentioning his name. Indeed, he was so thoroughly filled with the spirit and style of Mr. Law (as we have observed before) that his “Evangelical Discourses” and his “Letter to Warburton,” published about the same time, are for the most part nothing more than reappearances of Mr. Law’s very language.

We may add here that the Editor of the large edition of Kempis published by *Pickering* in 1828 notices the reproduction of the “Christian Pattern” by Payne in highly praising terms. However, the book itself (as beautifully as it is produced, with the subscription price being a guinea <note>A gold coin worth 21 shillings.</note>) is a mere literary ornament, totally lacking any real connection to the true spirit and power of the original. Indeed, it is rare to find such obvious lack of awareness of the mystery of the cross (and of the nature and spirit of divine love, the life of God ignited in the soul) as is shown by the editor of this new work—an educated theologian attempting to write *classical notes* on and republishing a *spiritual book*. As evidence of this, we may just refer to a reprint he has included in the preface of one of *Haften’s* plates from a celebrated ancient treatise, “Regia Via Crucis” (illustrating the various kinds of crosses that *Christians* have endured), with his own comments on it. He does this to expose (as he considers it) the “mysticism and vague rapture” of “perverted imaginations” regarding the doctrine of the *cross*, which he seems to think refers simply to the wooden cross on which our Lord was crucified. Had he been a master of his subject (like a *classical disciple of the cross*), he might have known, along with the author of “Regia Via Crucis” and of “Le Mystère de la Croix,” that the *cross* is the first, deepest, oldest, most central, and most universal of all the doctrines and truths of nature and grace. Indeed, it is the very basis of the outward glory and majesty of God, and of the blessedness of all the angels of heaven; and that the ‘cross of Christ’ is not that wooden cross on which he died, but that cross on which he was crucified, “a living sacrifice” all the days of his atoning, redeeming ministry on earth. It is that cross by which all the children of God are marked—internally and essentially as well as externally in holy baptism—who indeed are born on the cross, live on the cross, and die on the cross, and shall, as flames of love, forever rejoice upon and above the cross in the kingdom of glory. To return.

The ‘Justification’ tract was not only written in great haste, as Mr. Law expresses in the previous letter, but from the hint in the letter we are about to provide, it was evidently produced as a side project while the *Address to the Clergy* was being written. We should therefore consider Mr. Law to be engaged in his last labor, that work, during his periods of contemplation at the end of this year:

> “Nov. 29th, 1760.—My dear friend—This comes by the first post after receiving yours. I entirely agree with you regarding the gifts being made to the whole bench <note>The Bench of Bishops in the Church of England.</note>, not one excepted, if they are in or near town. If they can be friendly with this, they may be better prepared for what is to follow. Mr. Richardson has a letter from me today in which I mentioned that I am following your advice.
> Your waking thoughts are such as deserve everyone's attention, and especially mine; but as to your night dreams, they may perhaps be little better than my own.
> You have been very good to me in your care about mustard oil. There was an oil chemically extracted from mustard seed by a Dr. Rogers of Stamford; it was praised by prominent figures in the medical profession. It is not to be found here, and I suspect that Linden has changed it into his ‘Ethereal’ version.
> I am glad my philosophic doctor is well and cheerful, and in a little time I will send you a small contribution to be put into his treasury. Mr. Richardson may publish as soon as he likes, without any regard to those copies that are to be sent to me.—Do not forget Mr. Hartley. Farewell.—W. LAW.—P.S. I had no objection to presenting it to all the bishops, except that it seemed to suggest too much its own importance.”

The Mr. Hartley who is mentioned both in this and the previous letter as receiving a presentation copy of the ‘Justification’ tract was the rector of Winwick in Northamptonshire, whom we have referred to before as the author of “Paradise Restored” and other writings of a mystical character. He is perhaps better known today as an admirer and personal friend of Swedenborg; as we noted, he was one of the earliest translators of Swedenborg's works.

We have now arrived in the course of our narrative at the last year of Mr. Law's time on earth, and we find two letters which we propose to insert together:

> “Jan. 10th, 1761.—My dear Langcake—After Mr. Ward has seen the letter to Mr. Brotherson, I want you to seal it and put it into the penny post, or any other way that you like. I have no copy of it, nor do I think any needs to be taken. It took too much time to write it once.
> I have some rheumatic pain daily but use no medicines. The medicine you use may be helpful, and I should think it has no bad effects, which is something much to be considered when using medicines.
> Mr. Gurney has been here, but he is so deaf as to be hardly able to converse.—God be with you.”

The second letter is dated ten days later: 

> “Jan. 20th, 1761.—My dear friend—I think you have taken on unnecessary work in transcribing the letter <note>The one mentioned above to Mr. Brotherson.</note>. I hope to hear in your next that your enemy has had no power to hurt you.
> I want you to see that a copy of the ‘Dialogue’ is sent in a handsome cover to Lord Westmoreland in Hanover Square. <note>We find among Mr. Law’s papers a letter from Lady W., dated Bath, Feb. 8, 1759.</note>—Yours most affectionately—W. LAW.”

The Mr. Brotherson mentioned here as one of Mr. Law’s correspondents was a member of the ‘United Brethren’ <note>The Moravian Church.</note> who had written to Mr. Law because of his references in the tract on ‘Justification’ (and perhaps in previous writings) to Count Zinzendorf and the alleged doctrines

of the Moravians. It is a source of regret to us (for the sake of truth and justice) that we cannot present this reply from Mr. Law. It is evident that a copy of it was taken by Mr. Langcake, but we have been unable so far to discover it among the papers that have come into our possession. We hold, however, the original letter from Brotherson, which we now insert, only observing that Mr. Law undoubtedly believed in the purity and piety of this good man, as he did of many, if not most, of his simple, sincere, earnest, and devout brethren (see p. 550, 1). Nevertheless, Law deemed it necessary that the leaders and advocates of that society should answer the charges made by *Rimius* <note>Henry Rimius, a German critic who published attacks on the Moravians in the 1750s.</note> regarding their actions and principles abroad, as well as what had been publicly stated concerning certain of their proceedings in this country.

We feel it is a duty to express our conviction that, despite the evils alleged to be mixed up with their early conduct, the Moravians were the first and most natural *experimental gospel philosophers* of their day and of Protestantism. With them began that system of progress and proselytism in gospel enlightenment which became the *spirit* of Methodism, and whose developments are so wonderful and universally beneficial to mankind—morally, socially, and politically—at the present day. The following is the letter from Mr. Brotherson mentioned above, addressed by him to Mr. Law:

> "Rolls Buildings, London, Dec. 23rd, 1760.—Dear and honored Sir—I have read your book, 'Justification by Faith and Works.' Permit me to tell you a few thoughts that occurred to my mind. I am one of the United Brethren. I know there are many of our people who until now had a sincere veneration for Mr. Law; nor should we lose it if he showed us anything in our doctrines and practice by which we might discover our faults and improve. For that is the use we make of what our most bitter enemies write against us; we always examine ourselves by the best and most solid meaning of their criticisms.
>
> But when Mr. Law, who must now be near the end of his life, joins the list of our adversaries and blames us for the very opposite of what is taught publicly and privately among us—and suggests, in his way, a reputation for us which, if true, would be enough to make us hateful in the eyes of all sober men—then love makes me weep at the poor use he makes of his reputation.
>
> Instead of an answer, which modern controversialists might twist into a heresy, I will make a confession regarding those points which your book, Sir, chiefly treats of. This confession can at any time be confirmed by every true member of our church, whatever may be said to the contrary or blamed upon us by any runaway who—from motives of a carnal or proud mind, or an unwillingness to see his own spirit broken and subdued by the spirit of Christ—has left us and now seeks to ease the guilt of his own conscience. Almost to a man, our antagonists are of this class. Namely,
>
> ' We preach the love of our Savior to poor distressed sinners, which he has proved by be-
> ' coming man, suffering, and dying for us; this love of his we can never magnify enough. We
> ' have no notion that a human heart can by faith receive his grace and be saved by his merits
> ' without being at the same time sincerely desirous to be cleansed in soul and body from sin, which
> ' caused him so much pain; indeed, we dare not call ourselves children of God until we are truly made
> ' one spirit with him. And as for *works*, I will appeal to the conscience of everyone who has
> ' made a trial of living among us, whether the true reason for his leaving us was not this: that we
> ' went further in them than he found himself able to follow, for want of the true Spirit. And yet I
> ' admit that works are very little *spoken* of among us; for we think they must be done even cheer-
> ' fully and immediately forgotten by the one who does them, because there is more to be done.'
>
> We are so entirely of your opinion, dear Mr. Law, regarding the absurdity of separating works from faith, that though a man could speak ever so well of the experience of grace, his words and actions must prove that the Spirit of Jesus has taken possession of his heart. Otherwise, we know no greater faithfulness to show to such a man than to believe of him that he has neither seen nor known our Savior.
>
> This is the foundation of our *daily practice*, and upon that basis the Holy Spirit carries on the work of sanctification among us from within.
>
> Dear Mr. Law, I never before wrote to any man who thought it proper to slander the character of the Brethren; but the pleasure I have taken in reading several of your writings, and what I heard of you from several of my Brethren, made me believe that you had never taken the trouble to be rightly informed concerning what you claim about us. If you will please coolly weigh what I have said above, you may perhaps repent of your insinuations. I am grieved for your sake to have lived to see Mr. Law joining that set of spirits with whom it seems to be a rule, as soon as the question is about the Moravians, to use no restraint; in that case, we may see men who until now bore the character of patriarchs sin, and make thousands sin against the ten commandments without blushing.
>
> I write to you so plainly because I am unwilling to think of you as anything other than a lover of our Savior, who would not knowingly do the work of Satan. Our dear Savior will sooner let the entire existence of our community cease than suffer us to decay so far as to attack any servant of his outside our fold (among ourselves we are indeed sharp with one another); yes, there are many among us who are sorry for every line that was ever written in answer to those who attacked us.
>
> May I beg to be heard with patience when I tell you, dear Mr. Law, that I have lived for several years in the family of that nobleman <note>Presumably Count Zinzendorf, the leader of the Moravian Brethren.</note> whom you call a *successful deceiver*, and I can witness before God that he was taught, and did, the very opposite of what every reader of your book will conclude from what you say of him. He is now in his Lord's joy; but you cannot take it amiss that a friend of his, who is still left behind, reads your book with pain. Please, for once, set all theological controversies aside and consider what you have caused to be printed.
>
> I should be glad of an answer, and if I am favored with one, I shall rejoice to find that Mr. Law looks upon this as well-intended; for I have neither myself nor my brethren, but only him in view. My heart has dictated what I write; it is no apology. I humbly hope that no ill use will be made of it, for I call it an ill use to publish letters without the writer's intention or permission. I love dear Mr. Law, and am with much respect, his most obedient and humble servant, — ->**C. BROTHERSON**<-."

Around this period, or a little later, a portion of the “Address to the Clergy” was sent to the press. The correction of this work is the subject of our next letter, which also contains a promise for the remainder of the manuscript. This, consisting of only a few pages, was properly transcribed by Mr. Law but not sent by him to the press; for immediately upon finishing it, he was called to the court of his heavenly Lord and Master. As all his writings demonstrate, he had now fulfilled his mission as an *Elias* messenger of the completion of the gospel age to the world (see note p. 2). We shall remark on this “Address” in due course, after the notice of Mr. Law's death, to which we are immediately brought by the letter in question:—

<margin>r/</margin>
“March 27th, 1761.—My dear friend—We are all glad of your safe arrival.—I greatly approve of Mr. Ward's judgment in placing the note about *swearing* into the main text.
You have sent me two paragraphs. I would have them come immediately after the first, not with an (N.B.), but like this: *But here let it be well observed*, that nothing that has been, etc. Afterwards, where I say, *I am so far from blaming this*, add these words: *or looking upon it as the effect*, etc.—In the first line of your first paragraph, namely, instead of 'all this freedom from the evil of an imposed,' etc., let it be, 'all this *supposed* freedom,' etc.
Owen's book is a collection of rants and slander.—I intend to send you a parcel by the carrier next week, which will include the remainder of the manuscript for Mr. Ward.—We all say, God be with you.—W. LAW.” <note>Mr. Langcake has added these words to this letter: ‘The last letter I had from my most beloved friend.’</note>

The allusion to Mr. Langcake's *safe arrival* at the beginning of this letter is explained by a memorandum in Mr. Langcake’s handwriting on the fly-leaf of his copy of the “Address to the Clergy,” which is now before us. It reads as follows: “<note>The Gift of</note> The Rev. Mr. Law, my dear friend <note>who</note> died <note>Thursday</note> the 9th of April, 1761, while this last book of his was being printed. T. Langcake.—I was with him for a visit on Easter Sunday, March 22, 1761, only eighteen days before his death.” Some readers might here recall the postscript of the letter inserted at p. 601, addressed to Henry Brooke, in which this visit is mentioned. They may picture in their reverent minds how appropriate to the contemplation and spirit of such a divine Sage was that last private conversation. For he had not—as is evident from the letter quoted at the foot of p. 604—stated what Mr. Langcake recounts even to his most intimate friend and sole heir, Miss Gibbon. One may also deem it a remarkable providence that arranged for him to express his conjecture on that occasion, so that it will now descend (with the considerations by which the subject must always be guarded) to all generations. This is certainly no more singular a providence than that which preserved Behmen's works and also Freher's invaluable manuscripts.

Regarding the manner of Mr. Law's death, it is reported that during the annual Easter audit of the Schools, he caught a cold which produced inflammation and ended in the fatal disorder that was to conclude his days and his labors on earth. “The disease from which he suffered was sharp and painful, being of the nephritic <note>A condition relating to the kidneys.</note> kind; the torment of it wrung from his suffering and *feeling flesh* the cries and groans of nature.” This remark we find on a fragment of paper, and it probably applies to the beginning of the disorder. It likely gave rise to the doctor's report—upon hearing Mr. Law's earnest cries and prayers in his agony—that he was afraid of death and the future. How different the case actually was is shown not only by the evidence of his life and works, but by the repeated testimony of an eyewitness and ear-witness, Miss Gibbon. Among her papers, we have found various memoranda made by her concerning Mr. Law's death, as follows:

“Wednesday, April 8th, 1761. He said he had such an opening of the divine life within him that the fire of divine love completely consumed him <note>the last remains of self</note>.”

And again (as if uttered by Mr. Law, though we think it was not correctly noted down): “Oh, what have you done? You have awakened such a spark of divine love that it quite devours me. Who would have thought that all my learning should end in my dying a martyr to love!” To which is added, “The fire of divine love was so awakened in him that he knew not what to do.”

Elsewhere she wrote, “This death-bed, instead of being a state of affliction, was providentially a state of divine transport. As for the truth, all his behavior bore full testimony to it, and the gracious words that proceeded out of his mouth were all love, all joy, and all divine transport.” Again, “After taking leave of everyone in the most affecting manner, and declaring the opening of the spirit of Love in the soul to be all in all, he expired in divine raptures.”

On another fragment, we find: “Our departed friend ended his journey <note>process—alluding to the closing words of the ‘Address to the Clergy.’</note> with the words in which our divine Master and Saviour, Jesus Christ, ended his. And they may well be called his farewell speech to the world, calling all men to repent and believe the *gospel*, as he truly proclaimed it in his writings. For these words were written only a few days before his death, and the last time his blessed hand *was capable of holding a pen*.” <note>The singular fitness, justice, and propriety of these concluding words of Mr. Law's public ministry will be especially clear to the attentive reader of this work. It indicates the true and only means for the induction of all unbelievers into the Christian faith. For when the approaching event takes place—the great mystery revealed by God through Behmen finding its children and reducing all complexity of divine and natural knowledge back into the source unity from which it sprang—then Mr. Law's writings will be the universal primer, introductory to the spread and acquisition of that knowledge. And thus they will be with us to the end of the world.</note>

To the foregoing, Miss Gibbon added: “His eye was piercing, for it was the organ of his immortal soul, filled with divine light. His heart was filled with God, and therefore his voice was the sweet trumpeter of divine love.” And again, we find written by her on another fragment: “Mr. Law lived to the age of seventy-five without the infirmities of age; for though the age of man is said to be seventy years, and after that only labor and sorrow, yet it could not be said of Mr. Law, who retained the strength and vivacity, both in body and mind, of a man in the prime of life.”

He died Thursday, April 9th, 1761, between seven and eight o'clock in the morning. When near death, it is reported that he sang a hymn with a strong and very clear voice. This solemn act

...was in perfect accordance with all the previous measured performances of his consecrated life; and the sentiments he expressed there were worthy of that heavenly simplicity which, like a fountain, was opened in his soul and constituted his ordinary declarations as so many divine oracles of light and truth. The hymn he sang was a poetic rendering of the song of the heavenly choirs at the announcement to the shepherds in Bethlehem of the birth of the redeemer of mankind: "Glory to God in the highest, peace and love to mankind." We may consider this not only as a natural devotion of his refined spirit but also as a significant salutation to the world. It was as if he were suggesting that the mystical dispensation of the "knowledge of Christ after the flesh"—conducted in the limited, distorted, and imperfect manner of even the self-proclaimed evangelical church, which was opened by the above heavenly proclamation (though there always remained a true piety in the established Jerusalem church)—was about to be closed. He suggested that a new or further dispensation of the Spirit in its broad and universal development of life-giving power and holiness, reaching even the most sublime theosophic wisdom and magical <gloss>faith</gloss> powers, was about to be revealed through the influence of his own writings (though a true and deep evangelical piety would remain in the established churches of Christendom). This new dispensation would finally, like a torrent, sweep away all obstacles to the universal spread of the Gospel by revealing the foundation of all nature—of mind and matter, eternal and temporal, universal and *particular*—and of the "mystery of Christ," perceptibly to all mankind.

A short notice of Mr. Law’s death was inserted in the newspapers of the day. As appears from the following letter, this was composed by Miss Gibbon and only corrected by Mr. Ward and Mr. Langcake to preserve her wording; thus, it is not particularly remarkable for literary excellence. This announcement, with slight changes regarding his death, was the same one later inscribed on Mr. Law’s tomb. The letter in question, from Mr. Ward, reads as follows:

<margin>is/</margin>
> “London. April 22nd, 1761.—Madam—Several newspapers are sent with this, which include the character [obituary] of our dear and most invaluable friend. For my part, I feel as if I have lost the best, noblest, and most valuable part of myself, yet I still find God’s gracious goodness and presence with me. And I pray God that you may have His continual support and consolation.—I have again transcribed the inscription that is to be on the stone. Since it will remain for future generations, Mr. Langcake and I have consulted to make it as perfect as possible. By comparing it with the copy you have, you will find some variations, which are submitted to your judgment and final decision. You may wonder, Madam, why the first letter I take the liberty of writing to you should be such a hasty scrawl. But I have only just enough time to write it, having waited for the copy I had made of the part of the manuscript that is being sent. When you return it by the carrier, please direct it to be left at Mr. Crew’s and inform me of it by a line in the post. Mr. Fitzgerald said, when I was with him, that it was necessary for you to prove Mr. Law’s will; with his compliments and respects to you, he desires you to send the will and codicil to him for that purpose. With the most sincere desire for your health and happiness, and with respects to everyone with you,—I am, Madam, your most obliged servant—GEORGE WARD.”

The following is the inscription mentioned before, engraved on the front of Mr. Law’s tomb, erected in the churchyard of Kings-Cliffe, not far from where he lived: “HERE LIES THE BODY OF THE REV. WILLIAM LAW, M.A., WHO DIED APRIL 9TH, 1761, AGED 75 YEARS. He was well known to the world for several truly Christian, pious writings, exemplified by a life spent in a manner suitable for a worthy and true disciple of his heavenly, divine, crucified Master and Savior, Jesus Christ, who *lived and spoke in him and through him.*—In his younger days, he sufficiently distinguished himself by his talents and progress in human literature. Afterward, taking the advice of our Savior to the rich young man, he totally renounced the world and followed Christ in meekness, humility, and self-denial. And in his last years, he was wholly absorbed in his love for God and mankind, so that virtue in him was nothing but heavenly love and heavenly flame.

|---|---|
| In talents and sense, inferior to none— | His time was all employed in things divine, |
| With wit most amiable, with learning stored, | By serving God in goodness to mankind. |
| His talents great and high, were quite refined | The poor, the maimed, the blind, have lost in him, |
| In loving God with all his mind and heart. | The kind protector and the ready friend.” |

[This may be sufficient for the present, but we hope the time will soon come when Mr. Law’s remains will be transferred to Westminster Abbey, or some similar distinguished but more central location, with a suitable epitaph over them.]

The following is a copy of Mr. Law’s will and codicil; the latter, it appears, was made only three days before the testator’s death:

> “In the name of God, Amen. I, William Law of Kings-Cliffe in the County of Northampton, Clerk, being—I thank God—in good bodily health and sound mind, do make this my LAST WILL and Testament, in the following manner and form: *First*, I humbly recommend my soul to the mercies of God in Christ Jesus, and I commit my body to the earth, to be buried in the churchyard of Kings-Cliffe as my executrix, named below, sees fit. *Also*, I give to my nephew John Law five shillings. And as for the rest of my estate, of whatever nature, quality, or condition it may be—whether real estate, personal property, or mixed—of which I shall die owning or possessing, or to which I am now, or at the time of my death shall be entitled, whether in law or equity, in possession, reversion, or remainder, or otherwise however and wherever, I give and devise the same and every part and parcel of it, along with all my right, title, interest, property, claim, and demand whatsoever, to Hester Gibbon of Kings-Cliffe, gentlewoman: to hold the same, both freehold and copyhold, to the said Hester Gibbon, her heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns forever. And I hereby constitute, nominate, and appoint the said Hester Gibbon as the sole executrix of this my last Will and Testament, written with my own hand. In witness of this, I, the said William Law, have set my hand and seal here, this thirteenth day of September, in the year of our Lord one thousand seven hundred and fifty-three.—WILLIAM LAW. Signed, sealed, published, and declared as the last will and testament of the above-named William Law, in the presence of us the undersigned

The CODICIL reads as follows:
> “I, William Law, of Kings-Cliffe, in the County of Northampton, Clerk, do make and ordain this my Codicil (in the following manner) to my last will and testament, which is dated the thirteenth day of September, 1753. And since I have in my said Will given and bequeathed all my estate, whether real, personal, or mixed, to Hester Gibbon of Kings-Cliffe mentioned above, Gentlewoman, to hold for her, her heirs and assigns forever, and nominated her sole executrix: Now I do hereby order and direct, and give and bequeath all my said estates to the said Hester Gibbon, her heirs and assigns, to be disposed of and given by her or them to and among the descendants of my late brother George Law, of Kings-Cliffe mentioned above, deceased, in such shares and proportions, and at such time and times, as the said Hester Gibbon shall direct, limit and appoint: And I do make this my Codicil to be a part of my said Will and be attached to it. In witness of which I have set my hand and seal to this my first Codicil this sixth day of April in the year of our Lord one thousand seven hundred and sixty-one.—WILLIAM LAW. Signed, sealed and delivered in the presence of us who have subscribed our names as witnesses hereunto, in the presence of the said William Law.—Eliza Hutcheson. Tho. Jackson. Sarah Law.”

The “Address to the Clergy” was published after Mr. Law’s death. Having already descriptively referred to this work, we need only remark that, whether intentionally by the author, or so ordained by the providence of God, or in both instances, it was a judicious and accomplished finishing stroke to his Elias-baptist office under the Gospel. We submit this view of it to the judgment of the reader who has mastered Mr. Law’s writings.

Among Miss Gibbon’s correspondence we find the following letter from Richardson, Mr. Law’s publisher, which gives an interesting statement of the arrangements between them and the generous character of Mr. Law’s dealings:—

> “London. August 7th, 1761.—Madam—Mr. Ward mentioned to me your desire to have the accounts between the late Mr. Law, Mr. Innys, and myself; you will find that the papers accompanying this contain them. One part of these papers concerns Mr. Law and Mr. Innys, the other Mr. Law and myself: from Mr. Innys there is £26. 1s. 2¾d. due; to me a balance of £6. 15s. 6¼d. is due; the difference between these is £19. 5s. 8½d. to be paid. Now Mr. Law told me in one or two letters that whatever sums should appear due to him at any time, he would not think of taking money but rather the amount in books. I consider this declaration to have applied to himself; I place no stress upon it to you, but only mention it: for what might be within the circle of his designs is no obligation upon you, nor shall I expect it, but leave you to take the balance in the way most convenient and agreeable to yourself. As all accounts will be closed at this time, I wish you could think of a method that you would most like, so that they may no longer remain open. This may be done by paying money, or giving books with every impression, or should you choose for me to provide an account as the books are printed: I shall be agreeable to any of the three ways. I shall hope for your answer to the above; in the meantime—I am, Madam, your most sincere obedient servant—JO: RICHARDSON.
>
> P.S.—On the other side, to make everything as clear as possible, I have given a list of Mr. Law’s works, against which I have written how I stand in regard to their copyright.” [It reads as follows:]
>
> “Serious Call—Christian Perfection—Three Letters to Bishop Hoadley—Remarks on the Fable of the Bees 8vo.—On the Stage 8vo.—Case of Reason 8vo.—Answer to the Plain Account 8vo. These seven copies were sold to the late Mr. W. Innys; J. Richardson purchased them from his executors.
>
> Answer to Dr. Trapp 8vo.—Christian Regeneration 8vo. J. Richardson purchased these two, half from Mr. Innys and half from Mr. Manby, supposing them to be their property; but Mr. Law, in one of his letters to me, said they had only the right to the first impression; but since I had bought and paid the money, he would waive his claim.
>
> Spirit of Love, Two Parts. Presented to W. Innys and J. Richardson.—Appeal—Spirit of Prayer, 2 parts—Way to Divine Knowledge 8vo.—Confutation of Dr. Warburton—Justification—Letters—Address 8vo. These are half accounted for by the enclosed papers.”

The following is a subsequent letter relating to the same subject: “London. March 31st, 1762.—Madam.—Having printed a new edition of Mr. Law’s ‘Justification by Faith,’ you will receive fifty copies with this, being the proportion of one hundred in a thousand which I was to send to Mr. Law when that number was printed. I have only printed five hundred now, as I have many of the small edition still with me. You will also receive four hundred copies of the little ‘Extract.’ I have a new edition of the ‘Divine Knowledge’ in the press now, and am also printing the ‘Second and Third Letters to the Bishop of Bangor.’ I do this to have all Mr. Law’s works complete, and when they are ready, I hope you will give me leave to present you with a set of the worthy author’s complete works. Though I am a stranger to Mrs. Hutcheson, I beg my respects may be made acceptable to her, and with the same to yourself, I am, Madam, your most sincere obedient servant.—JO: RICHARDSON.”

The next letter we propose to insert as an interesting memorial of Mr. Law is also addressed to Miss Gibbon, and reads as follows:—

> “Lancaster. July 6th, 1761.—Good Madam—It is my duty to return you my thanks for the pleasant gift you were so kind as to give me through Mr. Richardson, of our late worthy friend Mr. Law’s last work, an ‘Address to the Clergy,’ which arrived safely, along with another copy for the Rev. Mr. Hunter. I have forwarded this to him, but as he lives at a distance from me, I have not yet heard of his having received it.
>
> I was greatly affected when I read in the newspaper an account of the death of my much esteemed and valuable friend, the pious Mr. Law, for whose character I had the highest regard and veneration. To comfort myself upon this melancholy occasion, I recollect what he said to me in his letter on the death of good Dr. Stratford, which I shall always remember. His words were, ‘Everyone must see your loss is very great, and yet I would like you to think that your happiness deserves all your attention, and that you ought, every time you think of your great friend, to sing *Te Deum*, both on his account and your own. On his, that he lived to grow so old in piety

I wrote to Mr. Richardson to inquire into the manner of my late friend's death, but he was able to give me little information. I suppose it must have been sudden, as the advertisement prefixed to his last '*Address*' mentions that some part of that work was written by Mr. Law not many days before his death. But to a person under such a continual state of preparation as he was, death could be no surprise.

Being so much a stranger, I cannot presume to trouble you by making any inquiries on this subject, though I am greatly desirous of knowing every particular relating to it. Accept, however, Madam, my grateful thanks for your kind remembrance of me through this gift of my great friend's last work from the press, a favor for which I am truly grateful. And most sincerely wishing you and Mrs. Hutcheson (to whom I beg my compliments) a long enjoyment of health and every blessing, I remain, Madam, your much obliged and most obedient servant—J. COLLINSON."

The following (previous) correspondence may prove of interest, as it also shows the occasion upon which the writer had made Mr. Law's acquaintance. It was addressed to Mr. Law:

> “Lancaster. Sep. 23rd, 1753.—Honored Sir—Your kind and obliging letter by Mr. Graves to the late Dr. Stratford came to my hands soon after the death of that most worthy man, of which I thought it my duty to take this notice. I was at that time (as I still am) deeply concerned on account of his death, which is an irreparable loss to me; for he was like a father to me and my most generous friend and benefactor. The sight of your letter added to my affliction, as I well knew it would have been the highest pleasure and satisfaction to him to have received such a letter; but we must submit to the will of heaven. For a long series of years, he has been employed in exercising the greatest acts of charity and beneficence, and I do not doubt that he is happy. He was seized with a paralytic disorder which deprived him of speech and, in a few days, of life, though without much seeming pain or agony. We called in the best physicians in this country; but alas! it was not in the power of their art to restore him, though I sometimes flattered myself there were hopes of his recovery, and that providence would be pleased to continue such a useful and valuable life for a while longer: but the ways of heaven are inscrutable to us. His loss is a public one. The poor in these and several other parts have lost their best patron and friend, and the world an eminent and shining example of Christian piety.
> 
> I came to live with this good man when I was very young, and have continued as his amanuensis and reader for more than eighteen years; and as long as I live, I shall ever esteem it my greatest happiness to have been early acquainted with such an amiable example. He was for many years a constant reader and great admirer of your pious and ingenious writings, and always spoke of them in the highest terms, especially '*Christian Perfection*' and the '*Serious Call*,' from which he has made large extracts.
> 
> By his Will (of which I am one of the executors), he has left to the **REV. MR. LAW**, *author of ‘Christian Perfection’ etc.*, one hundred pounds; and the bulk of his fortune, which is very considerable, he has directed to be applied toward feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, and other charitable purposes. I propose (God willing) to do myself the honor of waiting upon you at Kings-Cliffe sometime next spring, in order to pay this legacy and several others around Northampton, which by his Will he has expressly directed me to do.
> 
> If you are so obliging as to favor me with a line, a letter by the post directed to me as a Proctor at Lancaster will arrive safely. I most heartily and sincerely wish you the continuance of health and every other blessing, and am, with the greatest respect and esteem, honored Sir, your most obedient but much afflicted, humble servant—JAS. COLLINSON.”

In another letter, dated Jan. 15th, 1757, the same party writes, “I am greatly obliged to you for your last kind favor *** You would no doubt be informed of the death of your old friend Mr. Innys, who died lately at Bristol. The business will now be carried on by his partner, Mr. Jos. Richardson, a person that I have long known and for whom (upon account of his fair dealing and honesty) I have a great respect. *** I sincerely wish you (for my own sake and the good of mankind) many happy new years and the perfect enjoyment of your health and every comfort, and am, with a heart truly sensible of the many advantages received from you and your writings, your most obliged and most faithful humble servant.” And again, under the date of May 10th, 1760,

> “I lately saw in the papers an advertisement of ‘Letters on the most Important and Interesting Subjects’ shortly to be published, which gave me much satisfaction, as I judged from that that my worthy friend was still in health and good spirits. I have ordered one of these to be immediately sent to me upon publication; but it would add to my satisfaction if you would be kind enough yourself, by a single line, to acquaint me that you are well.
> 
> A friend of mine, a worthy clergyman and formerly a Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, mentioned that he had a curious manuscript of some part of the works of Jacob Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme</note>, and upon my expressing some desire (on your account) to see it, he promised to send it. He has done so, and I find it to be a large quarto, above 600 pages, very clearly written in eighteen chapters, ruled with red lines and handsomely bound. The title is *De Triplici Vitâ*, *by Jacob Boehme*. It is marked on the outside “Behmen’s State of Man.” The language is quite unintelligible to me, but I take it to be High Dutch <note>German</note>. It seems quite complete, and at the conclusion it is dated thus, Anno Christi, 1620. Great pains and care have been taken in the writing, which is very good, quite plain and legible, and the manuscript has been remarkably well preserved. Though you may have seen this manuscript, or perhaps it may have been translated and printed, yet as it came thus accidentally into my hands, I thought I would acquaint you with it, so that in case it should happen to be worth your acceptance, I might send it to you.
> 
> I shall esteem it a great favor to hear how you are, which was my chief view in troubling you with this; and sincerely wishing you a long continuance of health and every comfort, I am, with the greatest respect, honored Sir, your much obliged and most obedient servant—J. COLLINSON.” To return.

Upon this event, we find the following two letters addressed to Mrs. Gibbon:—

> "Clerkenwell. No. 7, Spa-fields. Dec. 6, 1774.——Madam—Last Sunday evening I buried that eminent Christian, the great and good Mr. Ward, after waiting eleven days for his brother and sister to come to town, but to no effect. The Rev. Mr. Clarke, Mr. Langcake, and myself, along with his old servant, attended him to the grave in Bunhill Fields burial ground, the spot he selected some little time before his death; his desire was strictly followed, except for a brick-lined grave. I wrote to the brother on the third day, informing him that as the Will could not be found, I had a claim of twenty pounds on Mr. Ward's effects, which if he pleased, I would most cheerfully give up for the construction of this grave; but I received no answer to that—not even an order for his burial in any manner, but only a request that I would take care of his most valuable effects. I have, however, purchased the ground and ordered a headstone and footstone to be put up so that he might not be disturbed. I have no doubt that this covetous man will insist on my paying for it, but that I shall do with pleasure.
>
> Permit me to inform you that I have taken into my keeping the whole of the manuscript of **Jacob Boehme** <note>J. Behmen in the original</note> together with the rest of the plates, as your property. Mr. Taylor the engraver demands eighty pounds; there is about thirty pounds due to Mr. Baldwin on this fourth volume. Now Madam, I have some doubt whether these hundred guineas which I found were not your property, intended to have been used for the payment of those debts. I shall be much obliged to you for information on this matter, because it will enable me better to settle the affairs with the brother.
>
> This, Madam, has been the most severe trial I have ever experienced, but through the rich mercy of God to me, a poor unworthy creature, I am enabled to say 'O Lord, thy will be done!'—Please present my most dutiful respects to Mrs. Hutcheson, and let her know that in searching for the Will, I found a letter from Mr. Law and *several others*, which I have taken proper care of. <note>We have discovered that the copies of the two letters on Swedenborg, inserted on pages 158—160, are in the handwriting of this Mr. Selfe.</note>—I am most respectfully yours—S. SELFE."

The other letter reads as follows:—

> "Dec. 15, 1774.——Madam—I have received your letter, and think myself greatly obliged both to Mrs. Hutcheson <note>The text likely meant Mrs. Hutcheson here despite saying Mr.</note> and yourself for the concern you express for my late worthy friend, whom I had for some years respected as my father and obeyed in all things as such.
>
> Mr. Ward's Will has not been found. The morning he fell ill, he told me he had not seen it since he moved, but that he had brought it to the house and would find it when he put his things in order. There was a Will, because I have read it more than once, and a copy of it is now in the possession of Mr. Taylor, an attorney in Clifford's Inn.
>
> How wonderful is the goodness of God to those who faithfully serve and love Him! For in almost everything, Mr. Ward's desire will be as truly executed as if the Will had been found; for I have received an order from the brother empowering me to act as his agent. In consequence of this, I have sold the goods and cleared the house, in hopes of finding the Will, but to no purpose. I found in the breast pocket of his coat some shares of lottery tickets: do you know anything of them? I had no doubt when I first found the hundred guineas but that they were Mrs. Hutcheson's or your property. I knew the money was not likely to be Mr. Ward's, but do you have any acknowledgments in his handwriting? Because if not, I think it most advisable to let Mr. Taylor make out his bill for the coloring of the plates of Jacob Boehme, which Mr. Ward made his own responsibility. The engraving of the plates is paid for. I have put an entire stop to the work on Jacob Boehme; there is about thirty pounds due to Mr. Baldwin for printing. The books, <note>N.B.</note> together with his papers, his philosophical and chemical equipment, are safely stored at my house and will remain there until I have your orders concerning them. I can witness to his bringing a very considerable sum with him from the country, because I disposed of the underweight gold and weighed the whole, and understood it was for finishing Jacob Boehme with all possible speed.
>
> Please, Madam, accept and likewise present my most dutiful respects to Mrs. Hutcheson.—I am your most faithful, humble servant—S. SELFE."

This letter mentions that a complete halt was put to the publication of Jacob Boehme. However, it was resumed some time later, and the fourth volume was printed before Mrs. Hutcheson's death in that year, though it was not immediately published due to a dispute with the publisher, Robinson. We should state that after part of the print run of this fourth volume had been issued, the party responsible for supervising its completion—following Mr. Ward's death—found among Mr. Ward's papers a manuscript in Mr. Law's handwriting. This was a paraphrase or expansion of the main part of Jacob Boehme's treatise *The Supersensual Life*. It appears that this had been marked for insertion in Boehme's works by Mr. Ward, who had likely received it among a number of papers and drawings formerly belonging to Mr. Law from his friends at Kings-Cliffe, to enable him to further the publication of Boehme. Mr. Ward thus concluded it was Mr. Law's own composition; whereas it was merely a copy Law had made of part of the manuscripts of Lee, which had been lent to him by Mrs. De La Fontaine (Lee's daughter), as mentioned before. Both the copy and the original are now in our possession.

It is, nevertheless, very sweet to my spirit—as affecting as this account was to me—to contemplate her being called away from us, conducted by the holy angels to heaven, full of years, full of good works, and ripe for glory. This is a matter of strong consolation, and I sincerely rejoice with you on this blessed occasion. Dear departed saint, in

> "October 3, 1782.—I am particularly led to write as I do because I have lately transcribed with great pleasure some glorious manuscripts of our dearly beloved Mr. Law, which have providentially fallen in my way. This happened initially through Mr. Selfe, who came into possession of the books and papers of Mr. Ward; he purchased them from Mr. Ward's brother-in-law, who succeeded to the rights and possession of his effects after Mr. Ward died without any will that could be found. Among them were found these manuscripts of dear Mr. Law. On reading them, I found they contained a great treasure of natural and divine truths, which tend to give the mind a sublime and noble turn of thought; and I hope that, with your support, the public will in due time be enriched with such a great blessing. We are now approaching the close of the general sketch and suggestions which we have deemed necessary to provide in respect to a complete and classic biography of Mr. Law. We might have presented a considerable number of letters written to him in his spiritual capacity, as well as intimate communications of his own with his immediate friends (such as Miss Gibbon in the earlier part of his retirement from town and previously), and of his family and friends with himself, as well as his manuscript remains, papers, a sermon, etc. These, however, can be made use of if necessary (and a perfect analysis of all Mr. Law’s writings in the order of their appearance can be given) in the proposed memorial. What we have attempted has been merely a general outline of his life, and to show the *spirit and views* in which his future biography should be written. We think that by a proper reading of this entire work, the candidate may not be at a loss in this respect, nor will it be difficult to fill in the gaps of Mr. Law’s life we have left open and to connect the whole into one unbroken and truly edifying narrative. For a general example of the spirit of seriousness and earnestness, of holy Christian experience, judgment, and heavenly wisdom which ought to be infused into the composition of such a work, we might again refer to the seventh, eighth, ninth, nineteenth, and twentieth chapters of the “Serious Call,” as well as the general tone of the “Christian Perfection” and other writings by Mr. Law. In reviewing these, it may be said most truly of all of them without exception (as was said of the works of his Great Master, whom he so closely studied and whom he so much resembled in his mental perspective), “He has done all things well.” The biography in question should ideally be that of a <term>CLASSIC MAN</term> who had attained the highest level of solid learning, moral, and intellectual perfection. We think we have furnished in the preceding pages (and what may follow) a just conception of, and a direct clue to, the peculiar proportions of literary, erudite, scientific, Christian, and theosophic knowledge and ability required in the candidate to execute such a design—or rather to enable him to present a true portrait of nature in her respective developments, degrees, and harmonies, as seen in such a man—a <term>BOEHME-FREHER-LAW</term> or a <term>LAW-FREHER-BOEHME</term>. Let it be remembered that what we propose is with a view to the improvement of the world and the blessing of future ages; so that in the contemplated work, everyone who looks into it—whether regarding learning, politeness, religion, or divine philosophy—may find there not only a *beau-ideal* of the highest perfections and accomplishments of human nature, but a practical exemplification of them, with *every step, as it were*, leading to such attainments laid down in an orderly manner. We do not doubt the reader’s agreement with the sobriety of our hopes in this respect after a proper understanding of and meditation upon the present work when it is completed.

The document in question (which, as exhibiting the sum and end of all mystical science and conducting the soul to the very threshold of wisdom's <note>theosophic</note> temple, will require close and oft-repeated perusal) proceeds as follows:

### ABSTRACT OF THE SECOND PART, OR APPENDIX OF FATHER JOHN EVANGELIST'S 'KINGDOM OF GOD IN THE SOUL,' ENTITLED, THE DIVISION BETWEEN THE SOUL AND SPIRIT, OR, THE ASCENT OF THE BRIDE, THROUGH THE DEGREES OF PURE LOVE.

Chap. I.—Of the inward state of a [regenerate] soul, striving forward to perfection [or purity of] heart. *Matthew 5:8* is generally, briefly, and simply described. Here it is shown that such a soul can no longer be satisfied, as it was formerly, with her usual exercises of contemplation, meditation upon the passion of Christ, and prayers, etc., but finds effectively that by all these things she loses her time and is scattered; instead of drawing near to God, she comes to be at a greater distance from him. This occurs when she also perceives, on the other hand, that in her most inward ground a certain rest, tranquility, and serenity of mind and uniformity of spirit is presented and offered to her, etc.

Chap. II.—Of the soul's gathering herself to herself. The author declares that the soul, in this beginning state, not knowing how to attain to that rest, learns by good advice and is confirmed by her own experience that she can attain to it only by the operations of the Will. In this, therefore, she exercises herself gradually (the manner and means of which are described here) until she comes to taste something of that internal rest and sweetness. But successively these operations are also found by the soul to be too gross, outward, and imperfect, hindering more than furthering her; so that at length she can hardly use them in her practice any more.

Chap. III.—Of the soul's introversion. Here the soul's progress is described at length, made chiefly by a simple apprehension of, or laying hold on God, by faith. After a comparison of the soul's current operations with her former exercises (where the different effects of both are excellently declared), the author says that in such a manner the soul begins to build or raise in herself a place of rest and peace, and an inward city of refuge from the tumors and noises of this world. There, she is frequently visited by God's ineffable goodness, instructed by Divine wisdom, and formed and taught how to worship God henceforth in spirit and in truth.

Chap. IV.—Of the soul's penetrating herself. Here the author declares that when the soul has attained to some degree of constancy and perfection in the aforementioned state, she still finds all these things too human, too natural, and superficial, and can no longer acquiesce in them. For she perceives herself to stand too much in herself, and wishes that she might be able to unload and throw herself out from herself. And yet she does not know what it is that causes her such hindrances, much less how she may be freed from them. This causes in her a great perplexity and anxiety, yet without disturbance of the mind, seeing it makes her full of longings and desires to know thoroughly and to subject herself wholly to God. Here the author excellently declares (1.) the soul's fruitless and ineffectual endeavors; (2.) the great mercy of God, kindling as it were a beacon upon a high tower, whereby the present state of the soul—and also that which she is to advance toward—is shown to her, and that she is still a great way distant from her desired haven; (3.) the soul's progress; and (4.) her several delusions, which she brings upon herself by taking up wings and intending to fly before the wings are given her from above. Till at length she comes to see that God has dealt with her most graciously, leading her through various winding paths <note>ambages</note> so that she might overcome that great difficulty of ascending straight away to the top of a steep mountain. But still, says the author, there is a deceit remaining, cleaving to the innermost marrow, and this is *self-love*: before this has breathed its last breath, the soul cannot enter into the *sanctum sanctorum*.

Chap. V.—Of the soul's raising herself above herself. Here the author declares how the soul further comes to the inward operations of a perfect abnegation and poverty of spirit, renouncing not only all her rest in and delightful cleaving to her own exercises, but also all her taste and comfort in the gifts of God, intending to attend only to the divine drawings within her; to be obedient to them, and to continue all her lifetime in such an abnegation—nay, to all eternity also, if God would have it so, etc. In these most highly abstracted operations, the soul, he says, continues for a time, but finds afterward that she cannot attain to their perfection by herself, because this surpasses the powers of nature. Therefore, she then comes into a total [abnegation] (of which he had treated above) and is still deeper swallowed up into that internal *obscurity*, mistrusting and despairing of herself; she continues therein longer than she could hitherto. In this (namely, in this *obscurity*) she begins now to observe that she has within her a very secret power, which she did not know until now; and that the extreme perfection consists in the *knowledge* and use of it. Here she begins also to know and discern that this same power is what she had formerly looked upon as the image of God. But she sees all this as yet only obscurely, and without true distinction. The author represents these things most pleasantly and plainly by the similitude...
