Chap. VI.—*How difficult it is for the soul to raise herself above herself.* The soul (says the author on this point), having now discovered herself to her deepest depths, is full of wonder and rejoicing; but her joy and wonder are soon mixed with pain, fear, and care or sorrow. With pain, because she indeed sees a treasure but does not have it in her possession—indeed, she finds herself at a greater distance from it than she had previously believed herself to be, seeing that the very thing she had conceived to be the end was really but the middle, etc. With fear, because she sees this is so high a state that, by reason of her weakness and especially her instability, she is apt to think that she will never attain it, etc.; everything that until now she had thought to be clear and pure now seems but obscure, dark, and impure—which the author explained regarding several particulars. With care or sorrow, because she sees no way to raise that noble power within her, considering her present state, which is now thoroughly detected. And after a distinct description of this, represented by the author under the simile of two pieces of different wax melted together into one lump, and so mingled and incorporated with each other that they make up only one substance—when a division and separation are nevertheless absolutely required if each of them is to have its own existence by itself—he says that when the soul perceives *this*, it makes her truly believe that nothing under heaven can be more confused, perplexed, and irregular than this her inward state, etc. She indeed wills that this division and separation be done in her and prepares herself for it, but perceives also that this very self-willing and preparing is but a hindrance and an occasion for new darkness, etc. But all these truly inexpressible difficulties can really achieve nothing else but a total lack of confidence in herself and confidence in GOD, whom she perceives is ready to assist her, when all the difficulties arise only on her own side. At length the soul is convinced of the indispensable necessity for this separation; so that, even if she did not expect any future reward or punishment, she still could not rest in this disordered state without striving against it as much as she can. A great compassion also arises now in the soul for all people, and a great wonder that they all carry such a noble treasure within them and yet know nothing of it, etc. Upon all this, the soul's new resolution for a deeper and more universal resignation is declared, etc.

Chap. VII.—*Of the manner in which the soul is raised above herself.* Here, the author says, <term>Human instructions, precepts, or rules</term> can help very little and are only profitable so far as they may encourage the soul to perseverance. For a soul thus abstracted, stripped bare, and simplified cannot listen to, nor be directed by, what is prescribed to her from the outside, etc. He grants that the soul is still active, and here also continues to be so, and says that the gathering of all the powers within is a "sitting," which is indeed quiet but not idle; for it is incomparably busier, more active, and more laborious than what the soul was doing before. She clearly sees that here she cannot be idle for even one moment without being actually driven back, and that she is like a bird in the air which can never cease to move its wings. And this he further explains and confirms from the nature of love.—*Of these operations he says, they are so secret and spiritual that the soul, used to coarse activity, can hardly distinguish them from idleness, but recognizes them best by their effects.* Concerning especially the manner and the operations by which the division and separation is achieved in the soul, he describes it indeed largely and plainly enough to the end of the chapter; but the contents of this description cannot be given in brief; a translation of the whole context would be required.

Chap. VIII.—*Concerning the way and manner of the operations of the soul, now raised up above herself.* Although this, he says, is inexplicable, yet so that the efficacy, nature, and property of this power which has no name may be made known in some measure, he will declare as much of it as God will give him, in the following points (represented here only in short positions): [N.B. What now follows also refers to pages 9, 43, 44, 505, etc.; whereby the uniformity of truth will be seen, from whatever side, or by whatever eye, she may be approached and viewed.]

(1.) <term>This secret inward power</term> shows itself like a spark, or rather like a *flame*, which arises suddenly in the innermost depths of the soul and is very quick and nimble in motion, as well as capable of being expanded or dilated and contracted. It arises only in the highest abstraction, rest, and inward silence, and ascends immediately into God its center; but it is swallowed up by the senses in the very first moment if the soul does not respond by immediately turning herself inward to God.

(2.) This <term>introversion</term> of the soul must be done with great simplicity and purity, so that nothing of her usual operations may participate; but all the senses and powers must be silenced, and this power is to be exercised. Therefore, when it is said the soul must "answer," this is to be understood negatively—which is to say, the soul must not move herself. The introversion is done through the operation of this power only, and in the twinkling of an eye, and everything the soul tries to contribute only nullifies and spoils it.

(3.) This <term>introversion</term> is answered most internally by the <term>Divine presence</term>; God manifests himself here, not indeed clearly and distinctly, but as the condition of this life can bear—that is, obscurely and mixedly—yet so that the soul finds herself to be with GOD immediately (without any [intermediary]), she <note>The OCR reads "templates," likely meaning "contemplates."</note> contemplates GOD in a manner unknown to herself and always in the same way, except only that sometimes she can do it more clearly. [N.B.]

Here the soul stands open, without hindrance, to receive the Divine influences, and is in the most direct way fit and capable of being raised up higher, to a clearer and more distinct contemplation of God. <note>N.B.</note>

Here the soul dare not and cannot strive for, or desire, any particular revelation, but commits all this to Him, whom she finds to be satisfied and well-pleased with her, if she is only diligent in such a manner as to exclude and keep out, according to her power, all impediments between Him and her.

Here the soul is made wholly God-like (*dei-formis*), so that she can desire nothing else but that the Will of God—both in herself and in all people—may be most perfectly performed, according to that end and aim which He had in the creation and redemption, etc.

(4.) This introversion of the soul is done either by ascending above all things and surpassing herself also, or by descending and sinking down under all things and under herself also. The inward power is suited for both. And by the one as well as by the other (but not without them both), this union and communion with God can be achieved.

In the first case, the aforementioned most inward power of the soul leaves the lowest place (the lowest parts of the chest) and rises up to the highest (to the crown of the head); and in the second, conversely. Above this, this power cannot rise, and beyond that it cannot go deeper down. <note>To understand the author's meaning here, a translation of the whole context would be required, containing several things.</note>

(5.) When the soul stands thus exalted in God above herself, or when she is swallowed up in Him downwards, the use of the outward senses is utterly stopped and hindered; yet not so much that she could not hear or feel, etc., but only that she cannot turn toward or take any notice of what is done in and about her without immediately interrupting her introversion.

She cannot smell or taste at all; but she can hear, see, and even speak. As for feeling, this is unique: namely, that by feeling something pleasant and taking notice of it, her introversion is immediately dissolved; but if the sensory object is painful, that power of the soul can fully and immediately apply itself to the pain, receiving and embracing—even beholding and contemplating—it. This is *wonderful* but certain, from innumerable experiences, etc.

(6.) All the parts of the body are deprived of their natural operations, so that all stretching and contracting must cease, and no motion can be performed—not even so much as the opening or shutting of an eye—without a total breaking of the soul’s introversion. Nevertheless, a person may bow, stand, or even walk, if it is done without any notice being taken of it. <note>The soul must become again a will-less, imagination-less, desire-less, pure mirror-Eye, whose only selfhood is the *seeing* of Divine wisdom.</note>

Breathing also ceases, and the lack of it is inwardly compensated for in a secret manner; so that the warmth of the heart is, all this time, at a better temperature than when breathing performs its office. <note>N.B.</note>

It is the soul’s last and most difficult struggle, which she must undergo with or concerning this breathing, etc. And it is the most certain outward sign by which she can know whether she has been properly introverted.

(7.) This stopping of the breath can continue for the space of two hours, more or less, etc.

No weariness arises from this long duration of introversion, but rather the soul and body are wonderfully strengthened and refreshed by it. Though indeed, the *inward* power loses something through the long duration, and is also sometimes quite exhausted and passes away. <note>The author also declares what the effects and dangers of this are, and how they are to be remedied.</note>

(8.) Concerning the use of this power during outward affairs, it is much more difficult to explain this than what has been treated of so far. For this manner of working is so spiritual and so high that the soul can hardly reach it with her sight, and so come to the knowledge of it. <note>What the author gives us regarding this from No. 8 to 12 cannot be represented by fragments, but a translation of the whole would be required if his meaning is to be understood. In the conclusion, he says what follows.</note>

To this power belongs, and is to be referred, everything that the mystic writers have delivered, though sometimes obscurely and confusedly, because of the most secret and very little known manner of operation which they felt in themselves, and which can hardly be expressed in words. Now, to the manifestation or *knowledge*, use, and practice of this power, the soul comes ordinarily and usually in the manner that is described (in this treatise). But nevertheless, God is not confined to this method; for to some, He sometimes reveals this most internal and most noble power at the very beginning of their conversion; but they cannot come to the constant use of it otherwise than after many years, and by faithful and diligent exercise. Amen.

Despite what we have previously stated as to our intention to conclude the extracts from Freher with those already presented, we cannot resist the impulse we feel—considering, moreover, that Freher was probably Mr. Law's constant private tutor for Behmen from about the year 1736—to add one or two more before closing the present SECTION. Therefore (without further apology), we offer the following edifying and practical fragment, in elucidation of the nature, depth, and universality of what is termed theologically *original sin*; this may serve as an appendix to the mystical "Abstract" inserted in the annotation on pages 623–28, wherein the "last remains of original sin" is especially referred to. This is the secret root of selfishness in the soul, which, as a last grand obstacle, must be removed from it before it can attain perfect union with God. (See "H. A. Rogers's Life and Experience" for a practical gospel illustration of this subject.) This particular point was also necessarily embraced in Mr. Law's philosophical treatise on "Regeneration," though perhaps without a systematic consideration of the subject such as we now offer, his scope and remarks may not be duly understood; as indeed they have not been for the most part until now, but, in some instances (e.g., § 46), have given great offense to many well-meaning religious people not versed in the science of deep gospel truth. By this, then, we say, a reader may attain a full and distinct contemplation of the entire tree of selfishness and sin, both original and actual, in human nature, and of the necessity of its destruction down to its deepest spiritual roots—and how God only is "sufficient for these things," to whom therefore "earnest cries and tears" must be offered up (Luke xviii. 7) for that end. This critical knowledge or understanding, it will be admitted, is of the utmost importance to the advanced regenerate Christian, no less than to beginning believers of all ages and all times. The fragment in question reads as follows:—

"XCV.—That the corruption of human nature, reaching to its very bottom, did indeed show itself mightily by the answer Adam and Eve gave to their Creator here; specifically, that neither he nor she would find and own the cause of their fall in their own bosom—Adam laying the same upon the woman whom God (as he said) had given him, and the woman upon the serpent. The serpent, by not shifting the fault from himself onto the devil, but silently owning and bearing it, as it were, behaved better than both of them. But notwithstanding this, into this hu—

a mist or vapor, as it occurs in drunkenness), but that in the superior part are the spirits, the forms or images of things, and all in a greater tranquility.

That the more subtle spirits are either drawn up into that superior part, or are therein made so thin and subtle, or as *St. Thomas* says, simplified. And that the most subtle images, which are nearest to intellectual thoughts, are in that superior part, namely, in the superior corners or turnings of the brain, etc.

That this spark of the fantastic or imaginative light, which forms the images, can be so kindled and ruled by God's natural providence and direction, that it must be subservient to the supernatural glimpse of the intellect, etc.

That this fantastic light is given to assist the superior part of the soul in the warfare of the spirit against the soul, so that the spirit more easily may extricate and separate itself from the soul. And that, therefore, this fantastic light is, as it were, a helping medium and instrument of the superior light, by which the spiritual part weakens the soulish part.

That herein lies the ground why, to a soul used to introversion, it may be as easy to remain in Contemplation as it is to live a natural life. As *Rusbroch, in his Book of the Perfection of the Children of God, witnesses. Chap. xiii.* [N.B.]

That *J. Evangelist* has often confessed to him that always early in the morning, as soon as he was awakened, this flame of light used to arise into the region of his brain and did shine therein with its usual clarity, until the least imperfection or <term>veniale peccatum</term> (venial sin), committed perhaps by him, obscured the glimpse of it like a mist.

That the confession and declaration about this matter ought to be believed, and is not to be accounted as a dream or fancy, under the pretense that only a few* have come so far as to have experience of it. *St. Bernard, Rusbroch, Tauler, Harphius*, and other eminent men say many things to the same purpose. <note>Few indeed, in this country, even have any conception of this advanced Christian progress or purity of heart.</note>

That the sincerity and holy life of *P. J. Evangelist*, known to many who are still alive, makes him free from all suspicion of hypocrisy, of his own invention, or of any devilish delusion.

That he has already spent about twenty years in such abstractions and Divine contemplations, and has nevertheless esteemed this grace so little that many times he said to him (*Fromundus*) in familiar discourse: "I wish I could give and deliver up to you all that I have received from God concerning this; for I know [N.B.] that true holiness does not consist in, nor depend upon, this or similar gifts of grace."

That though these illuminations appear suddenly like lightning, and suddenly also vanish away (according to *St. Bernard* and *Francis Suarez*), yet all depends principally on Divine grace, to which nothing is impossible, etc.

That such persons who continue whole days, months, and years in this exalting and cleaving to heaven seem to be of that sort of which *St. Gregory Nazianzen* speaks in *Orat. xxix*.

That it appears from *St. Augustine* and *St. Bernard* that the formation of those likenesses, by which we see divine things as in a glass, or in an obscure word (in <term>ænigmate</term>), is sometimes performed by the ministry of holy angels.

That the best counsel and surest direction for those who are not yet so far advanced, and yet still

XCVI.—And regarding this, we believe that it was not merely a simple promise of something that would happen after several thousands of years, but also a grace already beginning and actually manifesting itself even then. Into which Adam and Eve, along with all their posterity, were not only received again as children of grace, but also had so much power given to them that they could rule over the sin dwelling within them, by the assistance of that grace, grasped by faith and taken into their spirit; as this ruling over sin was soon after required of Cain.

XCVII.—Also, that not only the eternal Word, the Father’s only begotten Son, had already placed himself as a mediator in the middle, between fallen humanity and the anger of God ignited within it, to prevent that anger from devouring these two poor creatures; but also that the heavenly Virgin [or Divine handmaid], who had departed from Adam during his sleep, now again in union and communion with the eternal Word, approached fallen humanity. However, she did not give herself into the soul in a way that could be grasped, much less into the soul's own will, but only stood in her own principle of light, opposite the soul, or in the innermost depths of the human mind, manifesting herself there and opening, as it were, a door of possibility for all people, through which they can return to their lost heavenly image. Because in this spoken grace of the serpent treader, and in the promise of the blessed woman’s seed, she has espoused herself anew to the human soul and promised to walk with the soul through the dangerous valley of this world, to warn, conduct, and guide it safely, and at length, in perfect regeneration, to take it into her arms as her espoused bridegroom.

XCVIII.—But especially we believe that this holy woman’s seed, which alone is the true serpent treader, was spoken chiefly and directly into the woman, not into the man—that is, not into the masculine fire-ground, or Adam’s fiery tincture separated from the light, but into that light and water tincture which had disappeared in Eve. And thus it was set in opposition to the fiery will of the soul in Adam, and against that sinful source which first began in him. Indeed, it could not have been spoken into the man in such a manner; because this same fiery will and tincture of the soul in Adam, separated from the holy light and soft water, was and is still that serpent in humanity, whose head was to be bruised by the soft tincture of holy light and water—that is, whose power was to be broken by it, and whose dominance was to be taken away. XCIX.—This inspoken grace or covenant of grace, we believe, was propagated from generation to generation, yet only in its own inward ground and not in flesh and blood, until the time was fulfilled and had run to its end (scope, limit, period) in the blessed Virgin Mary. Although we cannot properly call it a propagation, because it was not done by the efficiency of men, nor by their concurrence (assistance), but by the efficiency of this covenant of grace which was made here, and by virtue of the promise made within it: according to (in performance of) which, this inspoken grace moved itself freely and opened itself from its center, more or less and in different degrees, from generation to generation.

C.—We hold that herein lies one of the strongest arguments against a particular and partial election of only some to life, and the reprobation of others to damnation. Because this grace was inspoken, and this promise made to the whole life of humanity, which as yet was still only one, like the single trunk of a tree, before it could have spread itself out into boughs and branches; indeed, before these two first parents (who, with respect to propagation, are to be looked upon as only one) were cast out from the garden of Eden. This grace and promise, therefore, can press forward upon all their children, no less than death has done from one to all.

CI.—After the sentence was passed upon Adam and Eve, and this promise was made to them, they were, we believe, as Moses says, cast out (driven out) from the garden of Eden (for they had already lost paradise before then) by a cherub with a flaming sword, turning every way. And though we believe the account of Moses to be fully true even in its literal sense, yet we also believe and know by experience that this cherub with his sword has something in it much greater and deeper than what was outwardly done at that time; and we are also well assured that every person born of man and woman without exception, on their way returning home to paradise, shall find this cherub and his sword in their own souls, yet each one according to his peculiar state and condition.

CII.—With St. Paul we believe God willed it so, that all the generations (families) and nations upon earth should come forth from one blood; and that therefore, this single trunk of the human tree has propagated and spread itself successively into innumerable boughs and branches. But especially, that not only from the beginning of the first world, with the children of Adam, but also and even more conspicuously in the beginning of the second world, with the three sons of Noah, it has divided itself into three great, principal branches; continuing to drive forth its growth even to this day in three lines or parties and sorts of people. And these three lines or generations of men have divided themselves, and still do so, according to the manner and property of the three principles, divided in humanity.

<margin>Jn</margin>CIII.—The first we rightly call the line of the serpent's seed, which showed itself in Cain, the firstborn of Adam, and afterwards in Ham, who was cursed by his father. The second is the line of the woman's seed, the line of grace or of the covenant of grace, which opened itself in Abel, further in Seth, and among the sons of Noah, in Shem. And the third we call the line of nature, or of the natural wonders, which in the first world—as far as the account given to us by Moses—had not yet so distinctly separated and manifested itself in various persons and families, but kept mostly to Cain's posterity; but in the second world, it distinctly opened itself in Japheth, and displayed itself in the heathen (gentiles) who were of his posterity.

->LINES TO THE MEMORY OF THE REV. WILLIAM LAW, A.M.,<-

FAREWELL, GOOD MAN!—whose great and heavenly mind,
In love embraced the whole of human kind;
From earth's dark scene, to realms of joy and light,
Your soul, congenial, took her happy flight;
With kindred spirits mixed, and bright as they,
You drink with them the streams of endless day!
While we below lament your absence most,
Like all true worth, then dearest when it is lost.—
Bound to no *sect*, to no one party tied,
To sons of God in every clime allied;
Like *light's* great orb, to no one realm confined,
Your heaven-taught soul, capacious, grasped mankind!—
Of pains severe you felt the torturing smart,
While grace poured comfort on your better part,
Your will resigned, with breath unmurmuring, bore
The last sharp passage to the heavenly shore.—
Your heart's best image, still, your *Writings* shine,
One spirit breathe—the dove and lamb *divine!*
Though soft your tongue, your soul's *strong breathings* charm;
Though cold your clay, your *ardent thoughts* still warm:
Awakened by you, we feel the heavenly fire,
And, with seraphic flames, to God aspire.

<column-break/>

Your pious zeal, transfused to other hearts,
New springs of bliss and nobler life, imparts.—
No time, no numbers can exhaust your mine,
Your gifts are full—*posterity is yours!*
Through future ages shall your labors go,
Like streams enriching nations, as they flow;
*Who, while perusing, catch the sacred fire,
Fetch the deep sigh, and pant with strong desire
For glory lost!* HEAVEN lent your pencil rays
To paint that glory and diffuse its blaze!
Though for these days, your colors are *too bright,*
And hurt weak eyes, by their too radiant light,
Yet Wisdom's sons, though few, to good awake,
Drink your sweet spring, and bread celestial break!
'Midst Babel's various tongues, though thousands stray,
In you, the wanderer finds his Master's way.—
In heaps let critics, commentators, lie,
Your Works will make a Christian's LIBRARY!
In vain shall *malice* seek to wound your name,
Or *ignorance* your *solid worth* defame.—
To pride of science, wisdom's fount is sealed;
To humble hearts, her treasures are revealed.
Yet *this her child* wants no man's pen to praise,
Nor slander dreads, in these degenerate days;—
Far nobler monuments will guard his fame,
Deep in their breasts, the good engrave his name.

CIV.——By the third line of nature, or of natural wonders, we mean the honest, wise, and prudent among the heathen, who, according to the letter, knew nothing of grace and were not outwardly included (like the Jews) in the covenant of grace, but lived as rational men according to the testimony of their consciences or the light of nature. Many of them made great progress in the knowledge of God, of outward nature, and of themselves. And these, we say, have the promise that "they shall dwell with Japhet in the tabernacle of Shem."

CV.——The second line, which is that of the woman’s seed or of the covenant of grace, we take either in a narrower sense—referring only to the seventy-two generations that follow in orderly succession in the genealogy of Christ, from the first Adam down to the Virgin Mary—or in a larger and more extensive sense, for all those related generations, tribes, or even individuals who were included in the covenant of grace and conducted themselves accordingly in their lives and behavior.

CVI.——But by the first line of the serpent’s seed, we mean the thoroughly wicked crew of those who despise, and even mock, both the light of grace and the light of nature, and who live according to their own lusts like animals, if not worse. These, we say, are excluded from the tabernacle of Shem and are accursed with Ham. However, we do not mean that Noah cursed his son Ham completely in soul and body, but only the serpent’s seed and spirit dwelling in him and operating through him.

CVII.——We do not distinguish or separate these three lines so far as to say, on one hand, that all the children of grace are entirely holy from the inside out and have nothing of the serpent’s seed or the outward corrupt nature in them. Nor do we say, on the other hand, that all the children of nature and of the serpent’s seed are totally excluded in body, soul, and spirit from the covenant of grace, with no possibility of obtaining grace. No; we distinguish them only so far as to say that the children of nature, and especially the children of the serpent’s seed, do not have the covenant of grace as a moving (working) life within them. This is because the corrupt nature and the serpent’s life in them suppresses and, as much as possible, kills the movement of the covenant of grace, which lives in itself or in its own internal principle within them. Yet they still have the possibility within them to pull back their will and sink it down into the grace that lies within them—though in many it is deeply shut up—which calls to them in their consciences and wishes to manifest itself in them. This is because no man was ever born solely from a serpent’s seed; all are born from the one human seed into which the serpent’s seed had indeed crept, but into which grace was also spoken, even before any man was generated from it. On the other hand, we say that all the children of grace and of the covenant also bear the serpent’s seed and the corrupt nature outwardly. There is no one to be found, not even the most sanctified, who dares to boast of being wholly free from it; but they do not allow these things to rule in them, because grace is active within them, existing as a working life that continually suppresses and casts out everything that is not from itself.

CVIII.——For we believe and confess that regarding the outward life—if it is considered only by itself, separate from the grace living and operating within—there is no other difference between men than this: one man perhaps sticks more deeply than another in this or that particular kind of dirt and mire, while the other may stick more deeply in another sort. In this way, both are so polluted that neither is able to enter that city where no pollution is admitted. Therefore, <insert>[ ☞ WE REQUEST THE MOST SERIOUS AND CONSIDERATE ATTENTION OF EVERY READER TO EVERY LINE AND WORD FOLLOWING, UNTIL THE END OF THESE POSITIONS.]</insert> no one has any reason to reproach another for his defilement and to boast of his own purity, even if, in the sight of others and his own eyes, he might be truly pure of this or that particular filth with which he sees his neighbor is abominably defiled. This is because both come from the serpent's seed, and both together belong to the corrupt nature; also, both must confess of themselves, "Behold, I was brought forth in a sinful seed, and in iniquity my mother conceived me."

<margin>*Of this generating and conceiving in sin...*</margin> CIX.——*Of this generating and conceiving in sin we believe that it concludes everyone under sin; that is, not only those who generate, conceive, and bear, but also those who are generated and born.* Since sin is already acting and working in those who generate, conceive, and bear, and since it cannot produce or bring forth anything other than what is like itself, there must necessarily be sin in those who are generated and born as well, even if it cannot immediately act and work in them in the same way from their birth. From this arises the well-known distinction between so-called original sin and actual sin.

<margin>w/</margin> CX.——Concerning original sin, we believe that although it is not in itself a doing, acting, or working as actual sin is, it nevertheless bears the name of sin justly and properly. This is because it is the inward root, ground, and foundation, and the universal origin of all those outward evil works that are called sins.

CXI.——In short, it consists of nothing other than that disorder and corruption which the first Adam, quite contrary to his creation and the will of his creator, introduced into all the properties of human nature and manifested in all his essences. By this, he displaced the three principles within himself from their proper place and order, giving so much room and permission to the spirit of this world that it could exalt itself above the paradisiacal life in him. This turned the heavenly image of God into an earthly beast regarding the outward life. From this, nothing else could arise but darkness in the intellect, perversity in the will, a false love turned toward the self in the heart, and a great weakness in all powers and faculties.

CXII.——This disorder and corruption is indeed inactive by itself in children during their conception and birth, so it cannot immediately break out into actual sins. Nevertheless, it is the true and only root from which actual sins must necessarily and unavoidably spring up and break out when the child reaches a certain age, though it may be more in one person and less in another. Absolutely nothing else but sin and what follows sin—and never anything good and pleasing to God—can be generated out of it. Indeed, this is even less possible than for a thistle to produce figs, or for a thorn-bush to bear grapes.

CXIII.——Adam must necessarily and unavoidably have brought upon and communicated to his children, in their conception and natural birth, all this disorder and corruption, along with everything belonging to this fruitful root of sin, because he could not have generated out of

himself any other image but what he was himself, and could not raise up another and better life in them than he had in himself. And that again, his children must necessarily have propagated to their children and children’s children from generation to generation this root of sin; because none of them all could, in this case, have given to his children a better portion than what he himself before had received from his father.

CXIV.—We hold that, if a proper name should be given to this original sin, a more fitting and convenient one could hardly be found than selfhood or *selfishness*, provided only that it is understood more deeply than is commonly done. It is commonly understood that selfhood or selfishness is the same as own-will and self-love, and all these three together are to be accounted as actual sins: which in a certain sense we grant, and do not criticize, but willingly leave to everyone the understanding they have of it. But we understand here by *selfishness*, <note>N.B.</note> human nature as it is broken off from its right and true inward center, as it has entered into its own government of the divided and contrary (fighting) properties of life, as it stands upon a ground and foundation of its own making, and as it has settled itself, as it were, to rest only in and upon itself. This nature is such in every person, even from their conception and birth; and is in its own inward spiritual signature in the sight of God so qualified and conditioned even before any will or love can move or stir within it perceptibly, or can act and operate in the least.

CXV.—For we must rationally conclude this: everything that corrupt human nature, by means of its sinful activity in every person born of man and woman, operates and effects, that very same it has already received in the mother’s womb as a natural inclination, disposition, and ability to operate and effect; otherwise, it could not work those sins which it works. Just as no tree in this world could bear such or such fruits if its peculiar kind and property, together with a natural disposition or tendency for bearing such fruits, had not been in the seed before. Or just as no person in this outward macrocosm could either inwardly contrive anything with his thoughts and senses, or outwardly create any works with his hands, if he had not received within his own microcosm, when the same was prepared in his mother’s womb, such senses and hands, together with a natural genius, inclination, and disposition for this or that, even before he was able to employ them—indeed, before he knew anything of the one or the other.

CXVI.—This sinful inclination and disposition to actual sins, we know not how to express or represent by words better than by saying: when the sinful seed is sown by the male and conceived by the female, then already all the disordered and corrupted properties—indeed, the whole fallen human nature—lie within it. Just as a whole tree with all its boughs, leaves, fruits, and qualities lies in a kernel, though these things are not yet unfolded into distinct parts. And this human nature, both in this sown sinful seed and in the parents from whom it comes, is even then already formed in itself, as it were in a circle like a serpent in a coil; for instead of stretching forth and tending directly to the Creator of the true paradisiacal life, it bends and turns itself crookedly or in a circle, enters into itself, joins its own end firmly with its beginning, makes in this circle both its own circumference and its own center, and settles itself there exactly in the nature of a serpent, which, from the middle of its coil, lifts up its head and prepares himself to strike like an arrow from a bow. Such a signature, we say, human nature has even in the seed sown in the mother’s womb, and before the rising of its natural life. And <note>N.B.</note> this we call *selfishness* with respect to its own spiritual figure; and with respect to parents and children together, we call it *original sin*.

CXVII.—This selfishness, propagated to us all from the first Adam—or this seed or character imprinted in us all by our parents when we were still but a seed, which seal has not only engraved upon it, as it were from without, an image of the serpent, but is also in its own selfish being a true image of the old serpent; the impression of which makes us all the first corrupt Adam’s natural children, indeed children of wrath and guilty of death—this selfishness, I say, we acknowledge to be the *deepest ground* of our corruption. We compare it justly to the root of a tree firmly fixed wide and broad, stretching itself forth, or rather comprising all in itself and bringing forth all out of itself, but continuing always deeply hidden underground: and this tree we call the *tree of death*.

CXVIII.—But own-will and self-love, which denote and carry with them a more outward and more perceptible activity of sin sprung up out of that root, we compare to a gross, thick, and twofold trunk of the same tree; yet so that these two are strongly grown together, firmly united (interwoven), and inseparable from each other. This trunk is indeed the next immediate ground of all the branches and fruits that stand above it; but it nevertheless also still has a deeper ground beneath it, standing in the middle between the root and the branches, just like the trunk of every natural tree.

CXIX.—But all the other activities, together with the external works or actual sins—not only of the gross earthly flesh but also of the subtle senses and reason, indeed of the whole natural life and of all its powers and faculties—we compare, according to their differences and degrees, partly to the greater or lesser branches, and partly also to the blossoms, leaves, and fruits of this tree; saying that death is the end of them all, just as death was also their beginning.

CXX.—But here we also expressly include all those good works that were performed before regeneration, and thus did not proceed from a renewed ground; where they might have had a form of goodness—indeed, even more than a mere form of it—and might have been called good in the sense of this outward world and in comparison to those that were notoriously evil. For, because they did not come out of faith (which faith belongs to regeneration and to the spoken-in (incorporated) grace) and because without faith no person can please God, they must necessarily be sins, as the Apostle testifies.

CXXI.—Yet we hold that, between these so-called good works before regeneration, there is still a considerable difference to be observed, because the persons who performed them must be distinguished. For first, some remain in their unregenerate state, and so depart this life and fall into death. Secondly, others return, enter into repentance, attain at least to the beginning of regeneration, and sink down through death into life. And thirdly, others again may backslide from their good beginning of regeneration, in which they had performed good works, turn with the dog to its own vomit again and with the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire, and continue to lie there until their end, and then fall into a deeper damnation. And the works of all these three follow after them, but with a great difference.—Of the *first*, we believe that all

their so-called good works—which were not good before God but originated from the evil root of selfhood and were coated, as it were, only from the outside with a shining form of goodness from the astral light—such works, we say, as well as those other works of theirs that were notoriously evil, shall go with them into perdition. Concerning the *second* group, we believe that all their works, washed in the Lamb's blood, separated from all evil, and made as white as snow—though they might have been as red as blood before—shall stand before them forever as an eternal hymn of praise and thanksgiving for their redemption. And of the *third* group, we believe that all their truly good works shall be remembered no more, but shall be taken from them and placed into 그 good principle from which they were born, while they themselves shall go without them into their own place; because every principle is to gather its own fruits into its barn, and neither of them can receive anything except what has grown out of and according to its own properties.

CXXII.—Of this tree of death, whose root is *selfishness*, whose trunk is *self-will* and *self-love*, and whose entire upper part consists of *all other actual sins*—we further believe and know by sure experience that many of these evil fruits may be plucked off and cast away. Indeed, a man, through the assistance of the Spirit of God, may powerfully resist and prevent others like them from coming forth in their place; and yet, the trunk that bears them all may still remain in itself unaltered and also unknown to such a man. Furthermore, even this trunk, which is much thicker and stronger than can be shaken by human strength, may be truly shaken by an Almighty arm and hand stretched out from on high, so that everything standing upon it in that man must tremble; and yet, the root of this tree may still stand fast and immovable in the ground, and its specific serpentine form and properties may still remain unknown to such a man. And lastly, this *root* in its own form (signature) cannot be seen and known by anyone living, unless a strong spiritual earthquake from the first principle violently shakes his entire ground; and only then are the very foundation pillars of all his natural being moved and weakened, everything within him to the very depths is laid bare, and all must tremble, both what is above and what is beneath, by whatever name it might be called.

CXXIII.—And we believe this same root was primarily what created the most difficult battle in the *spirit* of the *second Adam*, our only Savior and Redeemer. It caused the greatest and most intense anxiety in his soul and forced a bloody sweat from his holy body when he was to lay hold of the human nature he had assumed, to powerfully pull it up by this root from its own selfish ground, and to transplant it again into its right field, or into its first Divine origin. For he was sent by his heavenly Father for this very purpose: that he might destroy the works of the devil (which altogether, as far as they concerned corrupt humanity, centered in *this root*), and that he might procure a perfect redemption for the whole of human nature. Indeed, for this same purpose, God made him who knew no sin to be not only a sacrifice for sin, as St. Paul says in one place, but also, as he says in another place, he was made sin for us, that we might become in him not only righteous but also righteousness.

CXXIV. [We possess this position in German, but the English translation of it, along with the remainder of this invaluable piece in manuscript, as we have stated, is no longer to be found.]

Pursuing our goal regarding practical edification, we would next have inserted FOUR LETTERS addressed by Freher, between the years 1712 and 1715, to a religious assembly he attended (at the special request of one of its members), which held its meetings in Bow Lane, having begun its existence around the year 1706. We find that Freher's remarks in the quotation inserted on pages 582–5 applied to the conduct of certain members of this meeting, and not, as we have supposed and stated until now, to the "Philadelphian Society," with which this group had no connection, though it appears their goals were not dissimilar. And we have reason to conclude that Mr. Law was likewise mistaken in the statements of his letter to Mr. Penny, given previously; the objects of his censures were undoubtedly the individuals referred to by Freher in these letters and the recent quotation. Mr. Law, when transcribing these writings, might have supposed them to be Philadelphians, but this was not the case, as is clearly evident from one of the original letters we hold, dated November 24, 1712, from a correspondent of that assembly residing in Scotland, one James Inglis, and from Freher's reply to the said Mr. Inglis, dated September 20, 1715. Nor is this meeting among those mentioned or referred to in Roach's treatises. What we would call attention to in these LETTERS is their pure and illuminated evangelical character regarding personal holiness, the nature and blessedness of the communion of saints, and the duties of members of a Gospel Society, as well as exposing the delusions and sinful proceedings of a certain individual referred to in the above-mentioned extract. But we find we must postpone the publication of these most edifying letters until another opportunity; merely observing that, if convenience had allowed, we should have inserted them here. In this place and context, the candidate should turn to and carefully read them: this will lead his spirit out of the coldness and insensibility of abstract mystical study into the warm sunshine and refreshment of heavenly light and life.

We now end the present POSTSCRIPT, which has extended to a length we did not imagine<note>*</note> at its commencement (on page 188), but which seemed to grow naturally as we proceeded, the contents appearing necessary to accomplish our design for this work. And with it, we also end the SECTION.

## SECTION III.

We now resume the immediate subject of this work (from which we diverged on page three into a long digression that has continued until the end of the last Section) regarding the literary and other qualifications needed for the editorship of the proposed biography.

Treatises I, II, III, IV, V, and VI are to be regarded as general models for the writing style and the earnest, serious spirit mentioned in the Advertisement. We would also add that the particular subject-word or words of each sentence or proposition, as well as those upon which the argument depends, should be placed in *italic letters*. Specific words or nouns, according to their importance, should be set in large or small capital letters. In the former case, this follows the style of Mr. Law’s early writings and "Case of Reason"; in the latter, it follows the method (though improved and more consistent) used in that ingenious and *admirable* little work, Dr. Fordyce’s "Elements of Moral Philosophy." In this way, the reader (like a talented musician with a properly marked piece of music before him) may perceive at a glance the relationships between all the various divisions, sentences, words, thoughts, propositions, and arguments of the discourse, both to each other and to the conclusion. This may then serve as an exact spoken "word," a platform, mirror, and embodiment of the writer's entire just conception, reasoning, and judgment.

To those who are not already familiar with the writings offered here as general models of style, it may simply be noted that their great ease, purity, abundance, and correctness place them among the purest and—

---

printing of it, having formed only a general plan for our projected work, we intended to comprise what we had to offer in about five or six sheets; but as we proceeded, we found it necessary—to do justice to the subject and for the reader's sake—to enter into explanations, which also required further notes; thus, the Section grew to its current size. But despite the imperfections of the entire work, as we believe it will help achieve its intended purpose, we are content to let it remain and so proceed with our task. Had we waited until we were able to produce a faultless work with the same goal, we feel certain we would never have done anything. We would have left the world just as ignorant of the rich treasures of divine wisdom and knowledge given by God's counsel and grace as we found it. Or rather, had we been able to write with that perfection of logic and rhetoric which we recognize as necessary, this preliminary treatise would have been unneeded; for we ourselves would have performed the very task we are seeking to achieve through it.

But our talent is limited to the architectural science for such a work—one deemed necessary for this age, encompassing a systematic, universal revelation of the mystery of Nature and its development, as well as of "God the Father, and Christ"—and to searching out and collecting the necessary materials for its construction from the finest sources, workshops, and schools. The mechanical or handicraft portion of the labor is beyond our ability. We have endeavored to perform this calling faithfully, having been uniquely aided by Divine providence. Our faith and hope is that our labor will not be in vain in the Lord, but that through it, ultimately, Divine wisdom and Christian truth, revealed through Behmen <note>Jacob Boehme</note>, shall flourish to the ends of the earth, and all nations will come to know the Lord, even *Jesus Christ*. 

We may just remind the reader that the last Section, in its contents, was originally intended to be an annotation to the following Section III, as a further explanation and development of the holy spiritual life. That life is specifically referred to there as something the candidate must experience and understand to do justice to his subject; in fact, everything we have stated from page three onward is of the same character: intended to initiate him into the qualifications for that same end. Having therefore cleared the way by what has been presented, the remainder of our task will necessarily be very brief and simple, though we may find it appropriate to expand again as we proceed, wherever the best interests of humanity may be served by what could be offered and suggested.

the most classic models of English composition; while for richness of wit, sharp irony, power of ridicule without ever compromising the dignity of the subject, skill in argument, and correctness of conclusion, they stand unrivaled. A Whately, or some other modern professor of logic or literature, may have a smoother style of diction, or even a more refined individual characteristic than the sum of those which distinguish Mr. Law's compositions. However, for the accomplished qualifications we have named above and previously—as combined in his talent—not to mention his robust sense, and the musical rhythm and natural aspiration of his sentences, we do not remember meeting any writer who may be compared with him, or whose style may be so justly held up as a standard of pure English and general literary excellence. Nor can anyone be expected to write like him on moral and religious topics, whether philosophically or casuistically, unless they have been well-grounded in youth and early manhood in the same solid and enlightened, ancient ascetic principles and Spartan discipline of wisdom and piety.

We incidentally mentioned on page 4 a number of treatises that the Candidate should study—if not well-versed in evangelical science—before entering upon the consideration of the Works of Behmen, a view of the contents of which was then about to be presented. In our Second Section, we inserted a large Catalogue of writers upon spiritual truth—each, it is true, according to his own peculiar mode of understanding. We must now say, regarding the theological qualifications for the editorship of the work contemplated by the present treatise, that it will be absolutely necessary for the Candidate to master the scope of understanding of these writings. In this way, the diverse spiritual erudition and the profound and accomplished Christian science and experience contained in them may be blended with the exalted views and purified principles of holiness of the aforementioned models of style (like so many additional beauties and fragrances in a refreshing bouquet), and the concentrated spirit of the whole may be skillfully infused through every page of the work in question. But as the number of such authors and treatises is so great, and as what is sufficient for the Candidate to acquire in this respect may be derived from the study of a well-chosen few from among them, we shall here list such a selection for his guidance, referring him to the Catalogue itself for a more extensive variety. He may also consult, for the same purpose, more recent treatises of spiritual piety in the French, German, and English languages.

The particular objects of these selections will be found described and attached to each, as with their predecessors in the series (pages 1 and 2). By the due perusal and study of them, in the order in which they are set forth, the Candidate, we say, may have his mind thoroughly imbued with the perfect principles of evangelical sanctity, free from partial, abusive, sectarian dogmas and opinions. For he is recommended to pass over all merely Roman Catholic, or indeed Protestant, peculiarities of doctrine, crudities, and idiosyncrasies that he may meet with in his researches, and simply extract from each work the pure Christian honey and edifying instruction contained therein. Such a foundation of qualification, we may remark, is necessary not only to do justice to the personal subject or subjects of the biography, but also with regard to the world at large. This is because the work is proposed to be rendered a kind of standard textbook of divine science—elementary and profound—in all its solid theoretical and practical diversities, with rules and directions for its attainment, all being set forth in the purest classic simplicity.

evangelism that this country has ever witnessed. By this, however, we mean both the spirit of religious philanthropy now so universally active (which was instrumentally started by it) and the religious principles more directly designated by that name. This simple system of practical Gospel doctrine, and of preaching and applying it—being *combined*, so to speak, with the vast and varied learning and experiences of the great masters of spiritual science from previous ages, from the ascetic and mystic schools, and further refined with the maturing light of Theosophy—may no longer remain a mere elementary and dogmatic theology. Such basic theology is adapted to the masses of our own country or foreign lands, who can receive and believe without logical proof, and who, indeed, for the most part, are incapable of logical and metaphysical research (of tracing all the results of a conclusion back to the premises, or the perfect development of the premises in the conclusion, so as to know for certain that the beginning and the end are one; or again, of discerning whether the offered and received doctrines of faith, in all their parts and complexities, are in harmony or identical with natural and infallible abstract truth). 

But, we say, it shall be exalted into a perfect philosophy or complete logical science, proving and justifying itself by the highest demonstration. This is achieved not only through rational explanation from the basis of nature and a clear interpretation of the signatures and forms of its science and qualities in its plant life, but also by the display and evidence of a complete mastery over all the manifested powers of the dark principle, transforming by a touch (or by a mere act of the will upon a proper subject) all their dominant evil qualities into nothing but more sublime vitality. All of this was continually referred to by our Lord as being the natural rights of his faithful, enlightened, perfect disciples after the redemption and glorification of humanity; and it was confirmed by him after his resurrection from the dead, as summarized at the close of St. Mark’s Gospel. 

Then, we say, the Gospel shall be rightly and fully preached, and no rational mind (whether of the East or the West), upon hearing it (*Romans 10:8–17*), shall be able to contradict or resist believing it. Then, as we have observed, missionaries may go forth who shall be capable of meeting the honest objections and just demands of the most refined rationalist or stubborn skeptic by demonstrating (as well to his *senses* as to his understanding, soul, and spirit) the truths of the Christian faith and their identity with the universal voice of nature (which is perhaps included in the scope of the prophetic declaration inserted in the note on page 496).

The following, then, is the selection of works in question, whose distinguishing, edifying sentiments and spirit the candidate will make his own, so as to incorporate them (so far as they may be original) with those of the treatises already presented as models of style.

To form a right foundation for the high superstructure of a perfect Christian, regenerate, divine life: In the first place, inducing in the mind a profound and piercing conviction of the vanity and emptiness of all worldly things, and of the degraded sinful state of humanity by nature; and therewith an earnest conversion of the soul to God. Secondly, to arm the mind with a steadfast, immovable purpose to follow Christ fully in his process of *regeneration*; in the way of his precepts, counsels, and example—the narrow way, the way of the cross, the way of faith; as being the only true and direct way from defilement to purity, from sin to holiness, from darkness to light, from death to life. And thirdly, to furnish the soul with principles to walk manfully and surely in that way;—that is, in the perfect spirit and power of prayer, of self-denial, of contempt of the world, of divine love and universal charity; of humility, of patience, of meekness, long-suffering, obedience, silence, and resignation; in heavenly foretastes of the world to come, in absolute trust and dependence upon God, with all that is earthly and temporal—all the goods and evils of the present life—under the feet.

* The antiquity of Mystical Theology (writes the Editor of the *Theosophical Transactions*, in commenting upon the above treatise, regarding *ASCETICS*,) is here traced down from Noah; and the examples of Melchizedek, Abimelech, the two Pharaohs, Jethro the Midianite, Rebekah, Balaam, and Job, with his friends, are cited to prove that it was anciently believed in all nations that there were *means* by which men and women might come to have some acquaintance and communication with God. The tradition and succession of this through the Colleges of the Prophets among the *Jews*; through the Priestly colleges of the eastern Magi among the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Arabians; and through the Pythagorean and Platonic schools—if it were accurately and judiciously done, it would be a significant work; but this is not to be expected within a few pages. And as for the media which the Gentiles used to attain the intimacies and communications of their peculiar Deities, or of the Soul of the world, or of the supreme Demiurge and Creator, a particular and distinct explanation of them would necessarily lead us into an investigation concerning the ancient *Theurgic* mysteries.
What the spirit of *Plotinus* and *Iamblichus* was, and what also the spirit of *Porphyry* was, cannot be thoroughly understood without a more than ordinary insight into these. The *Porphyrian spirit* is a very great mystery. But as it is in witchcraft, or in demoniacal obsessions, so also is it here. The evil demons are unable to do anything of themselves: it is Nature that performs everything and produces those strange and wonderful operations. They also know how to apply active forces to passive ones, and leave her to bring about what they intend; to which the present corrupt state of nature is subservient, and to which they do not fail to add some of their own malice. Such, then, are the series of works which are considered calculated to afford to the Candidate a correct general understanding of the profound and universal theological science of the chief subject of our proposed standard Biography. Likewise, it provides a conception of his far-seeing ideal realizations of the effects that should flow from his own Elias-restoring, Baptist-purifying ministry: not only in the general diffusion of a simple practical gospel Christianity among the unsophisticated of the earth, as we see in progress in our day; but also regarding the induction of the intellectual aliens and unbelievers of all nations into the Christian faith—which is yet to be accomplished as the final result of the revelation of the mystery in <term>Behmen</term> <note>Jakob Böhme</note>, and of the refinement of all natural knowledge, philosophy and theology, arts and sciences, which has followed as a consequence or development of it.

As a suitable close to these remarks and to the present Section, the following Fragment is offered for the Candidate’s consideration:
> “It is for lack of considering religion as a new nature, an inward life, a seed of God, a plant of paradise, and therefore as something that is to be nursed and cherished, to be cultivated and raised up to perfection; as something that is to be made part of our business, that is to be improved with care and contrivance, by art and method, and a diligent use of the best helps and most expedient means or instruments; it is for lack of considering it in this light that so many people are so little benefited by it, and live and die strangers to that interior renovation or new birth prescribed to them in their baptism—that spirit of holiness, purity, and heavenly love which, by a prudent use of proper means, they might have enjoyed in a super-eminent degree.
> 
> For though the spirit of holiness is the gift of God and not attainable by any mere power of our own, yet it is mostly given and never withheld from those who, by a wise and diligent use of proper means, prepare themselves for the reception of it.
> 
> And it is amazing to see how eagerly men of science and business employ their abilities, their sagacity, time, study, application, and exercise—how all helps are called to their assistance when anything is intended and desired in worldly matters; and how dull, negligent, and unimproved they are—how little they use their abilities, sagacity, and talents to quicken and cultivate the incorruptible seed of grace, of the Word and Spirit of God (which is the source or root of all holiness, truth, heavenly life, and divine knowledge), sown in the soul.”

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of cultivating a devout life, using the characters Mundanus and Classicus to illustrate how even intelligent and learned people often neglect spiritual growth despite their excellence in secular pursuits.</meta>

*Mundanus* is a man of excellent talents and clear understanding. He is well advanced in years and has been a prominent figure in business. Every aspect of trade and business he has encountered has been improved by him; he is always devising ways to bring every method of doing something well to its highest potential. *Mundanus* aims for the greatest perfection in everything. The soundness and strength of his mind, along with his accurate way of thinking, make him focused on removing all imperfections.

He can tell you all the defects and errors in all the common methods, whether in trade, building, the improvement of land, or manufacturing. The clarity and strength of his understanding—which he constantly improves through continual practice in these matters, by often organizing his thoughts in writing and testing everything in every possible way—has made him a great master of most concerns in human life.

Thus, *Mundanus* has continued to increase his knowledge and judgment as he has grown older.

The only thing that has not been improved or benefited from his discerning mind is his devotion. This remains in the same poor state it was in when he was only six years old.

Thus *Mundanus*—who hardly ever saw the simplest utensil or held the smallest trifle without considering how it might be improved or used to better advantage—has lived his whole life without ever considering how much the spirit of devotion can be improved, how many resources a person can use for help, and how necessary it is that our prayers be expanded, varied, and suited to the particular state and condition of our souls.

Now, how poor and pitiable is the conduct of this man of sense, who possesses so much judgment and understanding in everything except that which constitutes the entire wisdom of man!

And how miserably do many people, who are considered geniuses, more or less imitate this behavior!

All of this seems to be due to a strange, infatuated state of negligence that prevents people from considering what religion actually is. For if they would only go so far as to *reflect* on it, or ask themselves any questions about it, they would soon see that the spirit of religion (that is, the spirit of love, with its fruits of perfect humility, meekness, patience, and resignation to God) is like any other faculty or understanding. It can only be improved through study, care, application, and the use of the means and aids necessary to make a person proficient in any art or science.——

Similarly, *Classicus* is a man of learning, well-versed in all the best authors of antiquity. He has read them so much that he has entered into their spirit and can very skillfully imitate the style of any of them. All their thoughts have become his thoughts, and he can express himself in their language. He is such a great supporter of this mental improvement that if he happens upon a young scholar, he never fails to advise him regarding his studies.

*Classicus* tells the young man that he must not think he has done enough by simply learning languages; rather, he must converse daily with the best authors, reading them repeatedly to catch their spirit by "living" with them. He insists there is no other way to become like them or to make himself a man of *taste* and *judgment*.

How wise *Classicus* might have been, and how much good he might have done in the world, if he had only thought as accurately about devotion as he does about learning!

Indeed, he never says anything shocking or offensive about devotion because he never *thinks* or *talks* about it. It suffers nothing from him except neglect and disregard.

The two Testaments would not even have a place among his books if it weren't for the fact that they are both available in *Greek*.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the character of Mundanus to that of Classicus, illustrating how intellectual pursuits in the classics are often prioritized over the systematic cultivation of spiritual devotion.</meta>

*Classicus* thinks that he sufficiently shows his regard for the Holy Scriptures when he tells you that he has no other book of piety besides them.

It is very well, *Classicus*, that you prefer the Bible to all other books of piety; anyone who is not of your opinion lacks judgment.

But if you will have no other book of piety besides the *Bible* because it is the best, how is it, *Classicus*, that you do not content yourself with *one* of the best books among the *Greeks and Romans*? How is it that you are so greedy for all of them? How is it that you think the knowledge of one is a necessary help to the knowledge of the other? How is it that you are so earnest, so hardworking, and so expensive with your time and money to restore *broken periods and scraps of the ancients*?

How is it that you read so many commentators on *Cicero*, *Horace*, and *Homer*, and yet read nothing regarding the high, heavenly, Divine spirit of the gospel? How is it that your love of *Cicero* and *Ovid* makes you love to read an author who writes like them, and yet your esteem for the gospel gives you no desire—indeed, prevents your reading—such *spiritual books as breathe the very spirit of the gospel*?

How is it that you tell your young scholar he must not content himself with barely understanding his authors, but must be continually reading them *all* as the only means of entering into their spirit and forming his own judgment according to them?

Why, then, must the Bible lie alone in your study? Is not the spirit of the saints, and are not the holy contemplative exercises and practical piety of the devoted followers of Jesus Christ, as good and necessary a means of entering into the *spirit and taste* of the gospel as the reading of the ancients is of entering into the spirit of antiquity?

Is the spirit of poetry to be enkindled by much reading of poets and orators? And is not the spirit of devotion to be also assisted in the same way, by a frequent reading and meditation upon the holy thoughts and pious strains of devout and heavenly-minded men?

Is your young poet to search after *every line that may give new wings to his fancy or direct his imagination*?

And is it not as reasonable for him who desires to advance in the divine life to study all the certain means of sanctification and purity; to imitate Jesus Christ in his spirit of entire self-denial, renunciation of the world, and devotion to God; to live by strict rule, to rise early, to watch, to fast, and to pray without ceasing, to walk in fellowship with the people of God, and heartily join in every pious and charitable exercise that may strengthen and perfect the Spirit of heaven in the soul?

Do you advise your Orator to translate the best orations, to commit much of them to memory, and to be frequently exercising his talent in this manner so that habits of thinking and speaking justly may be formed in his mind? And is there not a similar benefit and advantage to be derived from books of spiritual piety, hymns, and devotions? Should not a man use them in the same way, so that the spirit of perfect charity may be well formed and well supported in his soul, and so that he may be enabled powerfully to awaken, to edify, and to inflame the hearts of others with the love of God and all holiness and purity of life—by the deep experience and piercing vigor of his discourses and the seraphic ardors of his devotions?

Now the reason why *Classicus* does not think and judge thus reasonably of devotion is owing to his never thinking of it in any other manner than as repeating a *form of words*. It never in his life entered into his head to think of devotion or religion as a *state of the heart*, as an *improvable talent* of the mind, or as a seed of the *Divine life* that is to grow and increase (like our reason and judgment) and to be formed and raised up to perfection, to the *stature of a man in Christ Jesus*, by such a regular, diligent use of proper—

<summary>Through the character of Classicus, the author argues that true devotion is an improable talent of the heart that requires the study of spiritual writings and disciplined practice, just as secular mastery requires wide reading and exercise.</summary>
