## APPENDIX.

->“It is clear to me that all our education must be Christian, and not sectarian.”—DR. ARNOLD. *See Life, Vol. ii. p. 23.*<-

As the present treatise may perhaps fall into the hands of some who have the direction of education in this country—those who would gladly assist in the establishment of a system of tuition based entirely upon the purest and most enlightened principles of Christianity—somewhat analogous, indeed, regarding the cultivation of pure wisdom and perfecting self-discipline, to that of the ancient Egyptian, Pythagorean, and Platonic schools; or, to that magnificent institution which arose under the rule of the Roman episcopacy in the sixteenth century of Christianity, and which, during the brilliant period of its early and healthy existence, may be said to have left no degrees of lofty sanctity unattained, or of practical piety unfamiliar to the world; “no treasures of knowledge unexplored, and no field of literature uncultivated,” and all from a pure, angelic regard for the greater glory of God; (or again, to that still later refined institute of *Port Royal des Champs*, near Paris), the following general hints and suggestions on how to begin the experiment, without encroaching upon existing educational studies, are subjoined here for consideration as an appendix to the present section, and having reference to the leading subject of this work:—

But the thing I now mean—the education that I intend here—is such as would be expected from virtuous and wise parents and learned and devout tutors and governors in a Christian country.

If we had remained perfect, as God created the first man, perhaps the perfection of our nature would have been sufficient self-instruction for everyone. But as sickness and diseases have created the necessity for medicines and physicians, so the change and disorder of our *rational nature* have introduced the necessity of education and tutors.

And as the only end of the physician is to restore nature to its own state, so the only end of education is to restore our rational nature to its proper state. Education, therefore, is to be considered as *reason borrowed at second-hand*, which is, as far as it can, to supply the loss of original perfection. And as medicine may justly be called *the art of restoring health*, so education should be considered in no other light than as *the art of recovering for man the use of his reason*.

Now, as the instruction of *every art or science* is founded upon the *discoveries, wisdom, experience, and maxims* of the several great men who have labored in it; so *human wisdom or the right use of our reason*, to which young people should be called by their education, is nothing else but the *best experience and finest reasonings* of men who have devoted themselves to the study of wisdom and the *improvement of human nature*.

Therefore, all that *great saints and dying men*—when they are most full of light and conviction, and after the highest improvement of their reason—all that they have said of the necessity of *piety*, of the excellence of *virtue*, of their *duty to God*, of the emptiness of riches, and of the vanity of the *world*; all the *sentences, judgments, reasonings, and maxims* of the wisest philosophers, when in their highest state of wisdom, should constitute the common lessons of instruction for youthful minds.

This is the only way to make the *young and ignorant* part of the world the better for the *wisdom and knowledge* of the wise and ancient.

An education which is not *wholly intent* upon this is as much beside the point as an art of *medicine* that had little or no regard for the restoration of health.

The youths who attended Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, and Epictetus were educated in this way. Their everyday lessons and instructions were so many lectures upon the *nature of man*, his *true end*, and the *right use of his faculties*; upon the immortality of the soul, its relation to God, the beauty of virtue, and its agreement with the divine nature; upon the dignity of reason, the necessity of temperance, fortitude, and generosity, and the shame and folly of indulging our passions.

Now, as Christianity has, as it were, newly created the *moral and religious world* and set everything that is reasonable, wise, holy, and desirable in its true light; one would expect that the education of youth should be as much bettered and amended by Christianity as the *faith and doctrines of religion* are amended by it.

As it has introduced such a new state of things and so fully informed us of the *nature of man*, the *ends of his creation*, and the *state of his condition*; as it has fixed all our *goods* and *evils*, taught us the means of purifying our souls, pleasing God, and becoming eternally happy; one might naturally suppose that the government of every Christian country would take care and see that it abounded with *schools for teaching*—not only a few questions and answers of a catechism, but for the *actual forming, training, and practicing* of all our rising youth in such an outward course of life as the *highest precepts, the strictest rules, and the sublimest doctrines* of Christianity require.

An education under Pythagoras or Socrates had no other end but to teach youth to *think, judge, act*, and follow such *rules of life* as Pythagoras and Socrates used.

And is it not just as reasonable to suppose that a Christian education should have no other end but to teach youth how to think, and judge, and act, and live according to the *strictest laws of Christianity*?

At least one would suppose that in all Christian schools, the teaching of youth to begin their lives in the spirit of Christianity—in such severity of behavior, such abstinence, sobriety, humility, and—

<summary>This appendix argues that education should be the "art of recovering reason" and restoring man's fallen nature through the study of the wisdom of saints and philosophers. It calls for a Christian educational system as rigorous as those of the ancient Greeks or the historic religious institutions of Europe.</summary>
<keywords>Christian education, rational nature, Pythagoras, Socrates, human wisdom, piety, self-discipline, Dr. Arnold, Port Royal des Champs</keywords>

--- Page 683 ---
<meta>This page continues the Appendix concerning a truly Christian education, moving from general principles to a specific critique of how modern education fosters pride and envy under the guise of "emulation."</meta>

*Devotion, as Christianity requires, should not only be more, but a hundred times more regarded than any or all things else.*

For our education should imitate our *guardian angels*, suggesting nothing to our minds but what is *wise and holy*; helping us to discover and subdue every vain passion of our hearts, and every false *judgment of our minds*.

And it is as sensible and reasonable to expect and require all this benefit from a Christian education, as to require that medicine should strengthen all that is right in our nature, and remove that which is sickly and diseased.

But alas! our *modern* education is not of this kind.

The *first disposition* that we try to awaken in children, is *pride*; a passion as dangerous as that of *lust*. We stir them up to vain thoughts of themselves, and do everything we can to puff up their minds with a sense of their own abilities.

(1.) To give an example, in the first place, regarding our *sons*; whatever way of life we intend for them, we apply to the *fire and vanity* of their minds, and exhort them to everything from corrupt motives. We stir them up to action from principles of *strife* and *ambition* from *glory*, *envy*, and a desire for distinction, so that they may excel others, and shine in the eyes of the world.

We repeat and instill these motives into them, until they think it a part of their duty to be proud, envious, and vainglorious of their own accomplishments.

And when we have taught them to refuse to be outdone by anyone, to tolerate no *rival*, to thirst after every instance of applause; to be content with nothing but the highest distinctions; then we begin to take comfort in them, and promise the world some mighty things from youths of such a *glorious spirit*.

If children are intended for *holy orders*, we set before them some eminent orator, whose *fine preaching* has made him the *admiration* of the age, and carried him through all the *dignities and preferments* of the Church.

We encourage them to have these *honors* in their eye, and to expect the reward of their studies from them.

If the youth is intended for a *trade*, we bid him look at all the rich men of the *same trade*, and consider how many now are carried about in their stately carriages who began in the same low status as he now does. We awaken his ambition and endeavor to give his mind a *right turn*, by often telling him how very rich such and such a tradesman *died*.

If he is to be a *lawyer*, then we set great counselors, *Lords*, *Judges*, and *Chancellors*, before his eyes. We tell him what *great fees*, and great *applause* attend fine pleading. We exhort him to take fire at these things, to raise a spirit of emulation in himself, and to be content with nothing less than the highest honors of the *long robe* <note>The "long robe" refers to the legal profession or the judiciary.</note>.

That this is the nature of our *best education*, is too plain to need any proof; and I believe there are few parents, but would be *glad* to see these instructions *daily* given to their children.

And after all this, we complain of the effects of pride; we wonder to see *grown men* actuated and governed by ambition, envy, scorn, and a desire of glory; not considering that they were all the time of their youth *called upon*, to base all their action and industry upon the same principles.

You teach a child to refuse to be outdone, to thirst for distinction and applause; and is it any wonder that he continues to act all his life in the same manner?

Now if a youth is ever to be so far a Christian as to govern his heart by the *doctrines* of humility, I would like to know at what time he is to begin it; or if he is ever to begin it at all, why do we train him up in views and temperaments quite contrary to it?

How dry and poor must the doctrine of humility sound to a youth who has been spurred up to all his industry by ambition, envy, emulation, and a desire of *glory and distinction*? And if he is not to act by *these principles* when he is a *man*, why do we call him to act by them in his *youth*?——

*Envy* is acknowledged by all people to be the most ungenerous, base and wicked passion that can enter into the heart of man.

And is this a temperament to be instilled, nourished and established in the minds of young people?

I know it is said that it is not *envy*, but *emulation*, that is intended to be awakened in the minds of young men.

But this is said in vain. For when children are taught to tolerate no *rival*, and to refuse to be outdone by any of their age, they are plainly and directly taught to be *envious*. For it is impossible for anyone to have this refusal of being outdone, and this contention with *rivals*, without burning with *envy* against all those that seem to excel him, or get any distinction from him. So that what children are taught is *rank envy*, and only covered with a *name* of a less odious sound.

Secondly, If *envy* is thus confessedly bad, and it be only emulation that is endeavored to be awakened in children, surely there ought to be great care taken that children may know the one from the other. That they may loathe the one as a great crime, while they give the other admission into their minds.

But if this were to be attempted, the *subtlety* of the distinction between envy and emulation would show that it was easier to divide them into words than to separate them in action.

For *emulation*, when it is defined in its best manner, is nothing else but a *refinement upon envy*, or rather the *most plausible part* of that black and venomous passion.

And though it is easy to separate them in *theory*, yet the most acute philosopher or scholar who understands the art of distinguishing ever so well, if he gives himself up to *emulation*, will certainly find himself deep in *envy*.

For *envy* is not an *original* disposition, but the natural, necessary, and unavoidable effect of emulation, or a *desire of glory*.

So that he who establishes the one in the minds of people, necessarily fixes the other there. And there is no other possible way of destroying envy but by destroying emulation, or a desire of glory. For the one always rises and falls in proportion to the other.——

I know it is said in defense of this method of education, that ambition and a desire of glory are necessary to excite young people to industry; and that if we were to press upon them the doctrines of humility, we should discourage their minds and sink them into *dullness and idleness*.

But these people who say this do not consider that this reason, if it has any strength, is just as strong against pressing the doctrines of humility upon *grown men*, for fear we should discourage their minds and sink them into dullness and idleness.

For who does not see that middle-aged men need the assistance of pride, ambition, and vainglory to spur them to action and industry just as *children do?* And it is very certain that the precepts of humility are more contrary to the designs of such men, and more grievous to their minds when they are pressed upon them, than they are to the minds of young persons.

This reason, therefore, which is given for why children should not be trained in the principles of true humility, is as good a reason why the same humility should never be required of grown men; it at once goes to uproot Christianity.

*Thirdly*, let those people who think that children would be spoiled if they were not educated this way consider this:

Could they think that if any children had been educated by *our blessed Lord* or his holy *Apostles*, their minds would have sunk into dullness and idleness?

Or could they think that such children would not have been trained in the profoundest principles of a strict and true humility? Can they say that our blessed Lord, who was the meekest and humblest man that ever was on earth, was hindered by his humility from being the *greatest example* of worthy and glorious actions that were ever done by man?

Can they say that his Apostles, who lived in the humble spirit of their master, therefore ceased to be *laborious and active instruments* of doing good to all the world?

A few such reflections as these are sufficient to expose all the poor pretences for an education such as the *Christian* world at present bestows upon its *sons*.

(2.) And then with respect to the *education of daughters*: That turn of mind which is taught and encouraged in the education of *daughters* makes it exceedingly difficult for them to enter into such a sense and practice of humility as the spirit of Christianity requires.

The right education of the *sex* is of the utmost importance to human life. There is nothing that is more desirable for the common good of all the world. For though *women* do not carry on the *trade and business* of the world, yet as they are *mothers* and mistresses of families—who for some time have the care of the education of their children of both sorts—they are entrusted with that which is of the greatest consequence to human life. For this reason, *good or bad*, women are likely to do as much good or harm in the world as good or bad men in the greatest business of life.

For just as the *health and strength*, or weakness, of *our bodies* is very much owing to *their methods* of treating us when we were young, so the soundness or folly of our minds is no less owing to those *first tempers* and ways of thinking which we eagerly received from the *love, tenderness, authority*, and constant *conversation* of our mothers.

Just as we call our first language our *mother-tongue*, so we may justly call our first tempers our *mother-tempers*; and perhaps it may be found easier to forget the *language* than to part entirely with those *tempers which we learned in the nursery*.

It is therefore much to be lamented that this *sex*, on whom so much depends, who have the first forming of both our *bodies* and our *minds*, are not only educated in pride, but in the silliest and most contemptible part of it.

They are not, indeed, allowed to dispute with us the proud prizes of *arts and sciences*, of *learning* and *eloquence*—in which I strongly suspect they would *often* prove our superiors—but we turn them over to the study of *beauty and dress*, and the whole world conspires to make them think of nothing else. *Fathers and mothers, friends and relations* seem to have no other wish for the *little girl* but that she may *have a fair skin, a fine shape, dress well, and dance to admiration*.

Now, if a fondness for *our persons*, a desire for *beauty*, and a love of *dress* are parts of pride (as they surely are a most contemptible part of it), the first step toward a *woman's conversion* to God seems to require a repentance of her education.

For it must be owned that, generally speaking, good parents are never more fond of their daughters than when they see them too fond of themselves and dressed in such a manner as is a great reproach to the gravity and sobriety of the Christian life.

And what makes this matter still more to be lamented is this: that women are not only spoiled by this education, but we spoil *that part of the world* which would otherwise furnish *most instances* of an eminent and exalted piety.

For I believe it may be affirmed that, for the most part, there is a *finer sense*, a *clearer mind*, a *readier apprehension*, and *gentler dispositions* in *that sex* than in the other.

All these tempers, if they were truly improved by proper studies and sober methods of education, would in all probability carry them to greater heights of piety than are to be found among the generality of men.

For this reason, I speak on this matter with so much openness and plainness, because it is much to be lamented that persons so naturally qualified to be great examples of piety should, by an erroneous education, be made poor and *gaudy spectacles of the greatest vanity*.

The Church has formerly had eminent saints in that sex; and it may reasonably be thought that it is purely owing to their poor and *vain* education that this honor of their sex is for the most part confined to *former ages*.

The corruption of the world indulges them in great vanity, and mankind seem to consider them in no other view than as so many *painted idols* that are to allure and gratify their passions; so that if many women are *vain, light, gewgaw creatures*, they have this to excuse themselves: that they are not only what their *education* has made them, but what the *generality of the world* allows them to be.

But then they should consider that the *friends to their vanity* are no friends of theirs. They should consider that they are to live for *themselves*; that they have as great a share in the *rational nature* as men have; that they have as much *reason to pretend* and as much *necessity to aspire* after the highest accomplishments of a Christian and solid virtue as the *gravest and wisest among Christian philosophers*.

They should consider that they are abused, *injured*, and betrayed from their only perfection whenever they are taught that anything is an ornament in them that is not an ornament in the wisest among mankind.

It is generally said that women are naturally of *little and vain minds*; but this I look upon to be as false and unreasonable as to say that *butchers are naturally cruel*; for just as their cruelty is not owing to their *nature* but to their *way of life*, which has changed their nature, so whatever littleness

...and vanity is observed in the minds of women; it is like the cruelty of *butchers*, a temperament that is worked into them by the life they are *taught and accustomed to lead*.

At least this much must be said: we cannot blame their nature until we ensure it is not perverted by their education.

On the other hand, if it were true that they were naturally vain and frivolous, then how much more blameworthy is an education that seems designed to *strengthen and increase* this folly and weakness of their minds? For if it were a virtue for a woman to be proud and vain, we could hardly find better ways to encourage this passion in her than those currently used in her education.

Some people who judge hastily will perhaps say here that I am being too severe against women.

But more reasonable people will easily see that I entirely spare the *sex* and only indict *their education*; that I not only spare them, but plead *their interest*, assert *their honor*, set forth *their perfections*, commend *their natural temperaments*, and only condemn *that education* which is so *injurious to their interests, so debases their honor, and deprives them of the benefit of their excellent natures and temperaments*.

I admit I cannot spare their education; but the only reason is that it is *their greatest enemy*. It deprives the world of so many blessings and the Church of so many saints that might reasonably be expected from people so formed by their natural temperaments for all goodness and tenderness, and so fitted by the clarity and brightness of their minds to contemplate, love, and admire everything that is holy, virtuous, and divine.

If it should be said here that I place too *much blame* on *their education*, and that they are not *as harmed* by it as I imagine:

It may be answered that, although I do not claim to state the *exact degree* of harm caused by it, its plain and natural tendency to do harm is sufficient to justify its *most absolute condemnation*.

Now, taking for granted that the reader will be able to infer from the preceding remarks what is implied by a wise and enlightened Christian education, and the necessity of attempting its establishment in this country—it is asked: what simpler or more efficient method can be suggested for introducing the principles (as well as the practice) of exalted wisdom and piety into currently established systems of education (and, at the same time, the almost lost, invaluable *habit* of strictly logical thinking, writing, and speaking), than by immediately making the tracts arranged and composed as the **Grammar of Wisdom** (see p. 8, 9, *above*) a common, everyday schoolbook? This would be a grammar of experimental Christianity, containing the principles of sound, practical piety and, at the same time, the elements of the most sublime *Theosophy*, which every pupil of a certain age should learn by heart—just as the classical student learns his Eton grammar—until he can repeat at least the **First Part** correctly and perfectly.

After the pupil (or a class of pupils) can repeat from memory the first three chapters, then nine, and then thirteen, along with the conclusion (for that is how the sections of the **First Part** are divided), let him begin to be examined by the tutor in every sentiment, reason, argument, inference, dependency, and connection of the discourse. (However, for this purpose, assuming the book becomes a regular class book, a series of questions would need to be skillfully prepared.)

This should be accompanied by critical observations on the logical construction, the ease, simplicity, and rhetorical beauty of the composition; the pure and correct, though high, standard of duty and sentiment; the fundamental exactness of the reasons and the mathematical strictness, so to speak, of the argumentation; the order and method of the author’s procedure, the fairness of his conclusions (and, as the case may be, the application of the truths demonstrated); the inference leading to the next step in the order of thought toward the intended final conclusion; then the method of proceeding again, the objections—including all that can be offered, whether they are substantial, or untenable though plausible, or only those of hasty, irrational thinkers—with the answers to them in logical order. And so on, not failing to strongly impress on the students' attention the duties and moral obligations as they become clear in the course of the argument.

We say, let the pupils be exercised in this way every day until they really KNOW the various named sections and the entire discourse; until its principles, duties, and sentiments become the very approved *natural feelings and reflections* of their own minds\*; and the logical construction, the objects, the foundation, reasons, arguments,

**SECTION FIRST.** Devotion consists not in prayers, whether public or private, but in giving and devoting the entire life to God.
*Chapter I.*—On the nature and extent of Christian devotion.
*——— II.*—An inquiry into the reason why the generality of *Christians* fall so far short of the holiness and devotion of Christianity.
*——— III.*—On the great danger and folly of not intending to be as eminent and exemplary as we can in the practice of all Christian virtues.)
**SECTION SECOND.** It is in the several *instances and details* of our common life that we must exercise devotion.
*Chapter I.*—We can please God in no state or employment of life except by *intending and devoting it all* to his honor and glory.
*——— II.*—Persons who are free from the necessity of labor and employment are to consider themselves as devoted to God in a *higher degree*.
*——— III.*—The great obligations and the great advantages of making a wise and religious use of our estates and fortunes.
*——— IV.*—How the imprudent use of an estate corrupts all the temperaments of the mind and fills the heart with poor and ridiculous passions through the whole course of life: this represented by a character.
*——— V.*—How the wise and pious use of a fortune naturally carries us to great perfection in all the virtues of the Christian life: this represented by a character.
*——— VI.*—Some reflections upon the character last described; and showing how it may, and ought to be, imitated.
**SECTION THIRD.** Devotion is the *duty of all persons* of every rank and condition, and the only source of peace and happiness.
*Chapter I.*—How all orders and ranks of men and women of all ages are obliged to devote themselves to God.
*——— II.*—How great devotion fills our lives with the greatest peace and happiness that can be enjoyed in this world.
*——— III.*—The happiness of a life wholly devoted to God, further proved from the vanity, the sensuality, and the ridiculous, poor enjoyments which they are forced to put up with who live according to their own humors. This represented in various characters.
*——— IV.*—That not only a life of vanity or sensuality, but even the most regular kind of life that is not governed by great devotion, sufficiently shows its miseries, its wants, and emptiness to the eyes of all the world. This represented in various characters.
**CONCLUSION.** On the excellence and greatness of a devout spirit.

# SECTION FIRST.

->Proving that Devotion consists not in prayers, or any particular instances of piety, but in giving and devoting the *whole life* to GOD.<-

## CHAPTER FIRST.

->Concerning the nature and extent of Christian devotion.<-

<margin>[Q.E.R.]</margin>
I. 1. **DEVOTION is neither private nor public prayer,**
. but prayers, whether private or public, are particular parts or instances of devotion.
2. **DEVOTION signifies a life given or devoted to GOD.**
3. ... **HE therefore is the devout man,**
. who lives no longer according to his own *will*, or the *way* and *spirit* of the world, but according to the sole *will* of GOD;
.. who considers GOD in everything;
.. who serves GOD in everything;
<margin>[1. 1. 32.]</margin>
.. who makes all the parts of his *common life* parts of piety,
.. by doing everything in the name of GOD and under such rules as conform to his glory.

4. ... **WE readily acknowledge**
. that GOD ALONE is to be the rule and measure of our *prayers*;
.. that in them we are to look wholly to him and act *wholly* for him;
.. that we are only to pray in such a *manner*, for such *things*, and for such *ends* as are suitable to his glory.

<margin>[Q.E.D.]</margin>
5. ... **NOW let anyone but find out the reason** why he is to be strictly pious in prayers,
. and he will find that same reason is as *strong* a reason to be as strictly pious in all the other parts of his life.

# SECTION SECOND.

->Proving that it is in the several instances and particulars of our *common life* that we are to exercise devotion.<-

## CHAPTER FIRST.

->We can please GOD in no state or employment of life except by *intending* and *devoting* it all to his honor and glory.<-

I. 1. HAVING in the first chapter stated the *general nature* of devotion,
<margin>[I. i. 9.]</margin> . and shown that it does not imply any *form of prayer*,
. but a certain form of life that is offered to GOD, *not* at any particular *times* or *places*, but everywhere and in everything;
. I shall now move to specific details and show
. how we are to devote our *labor* and *employment*, our *time* and *fortunes* unto GOD.

2. AS a good Christian should consider every place holy,
. because GOD is there,
. so he should look upon every part of his life as a matter of holiness,
<margin>[Q. E. D.]</margin> . because it is to be offered unto GOD.

3. ... THE profession of a *clergyman* is a *holy profession*
. . because it is a ministry in *holy things*,
. . an attendance at the *altar*,
. but worldly business is to be made holy unto the Lord
. by being done as a service to him,
<margin>[Q. E. D.]</margin> . and in conformity to his divine will.

4. ... ... ... FOR as all men and all things in the world truly belong to GOD,
. just as much as any *places, things,* or *persons* that are devoted to Divine service;
. so all things are to be *used*
. and all persons are to *act* in their several states and employments
. for the glory of GOD.

5. ... Men of worldly business, therefore, must not consider themselves free to live for themselves,
. . to indulge their own *moods* and *tempers*,
. because their employment is of a worldly nature;
. but they must consider
. that as the world and all worldly professions truly belong to GOD as much as *persons* and things that are devoted to the *altar*,
. so it is as much the duty of men in worldly business to live wholly for GOD
. as it is the duty of those who are devoted to divine service.

6. ... ... ... AS the whole world is GOD's,
(a) . so the whole world is to act for GOD.
(b) As all men have the same *relation* to GOD,
. as all men have all their powers and faculties from GOD,
. so all men are obliged to act for GOD with all their powers and all their faculties.
(c) As all things are GOD's,
. so all things are to be used and regarded as the things of GOD.
. For men to abuse things on *earth* and live for themselves is the same rebellion against GOD as for angels to abuse things in *heaven*,
. because GOD is exactly the same Lord of all on earth as he is the Lord of all in heaven.
(d) Things *may* and must *differ* in their *use*,
. but yet they are all to be used according to the will of GOD.
(e) Men may and must differ in their *employments*,
. but yet they must all act for the same ends as dutiful servants of GOD, in the right and pious performance of their several callings.

## SECTION THIRD.

->Proving that *devotion* is the duty of *all* men, of every rank and condition, and the *only* source of peace and happiness.<-

### CHAPTER FIRST.

->Showing how all orders and ranks of men and women of all ages are *obliged* to devote themselves to GOD.<-

<margin>[II. throughout.]</margin>
I. 1. I HAVE in the previous chapters gone through the several great examples of Christian devotion,
. and shown that all the parts of our common life—our employments, our talents, and gifts of fortune—are all to be made holy and acceptable to GOD by a wise and religious use of everything, and by directing our actions and designs to such ends as are suitable to the honor and glory of GOD.
2. I SHALL now show that this regularity of devotion,
. this holiness of common life,
. this religious use of everything we have,
<margin>[Q.E.D.]</margin>
. is a devotion that is the duty of all orders of Christian people.

3. ... ... *FULVIUS* has had a learned education and taken his degrees at the university;
. he came from there so that he might be free from any rules of life.
4. ... ... HE takes no employment upon himself, nor enters into any business, because he thinks that every employment or business calls people to the careful performance and just discharge of its several duties.
5. ... ... ... WHEN he is serious he will tell you
(a) . that he did not enter into holy orders, because he looks upon it as a state which requires great holiness of life,
. and that it does not suit his disposition to be so good.
(b) . He will tell you
. that he never intends to marry, because he cannot commit himself to that disciplined life and good behavior which he takes to be the duty of those who are at the head of a family.
(c) . He refused to be godfather to his nephew
. because he will have *no trust* of any kind to answer for.
6. ... ... *FULVIUS* thinks he is conscientious in his conduct,
. and is therefore content with the most *idle, trivial, and careless life*.
. He has no religion, no devotion, no claims to piety.
. He lives by no rules,
. and thinks all is very well because he is neither a *priest*, nor a *father*, nor a *guardian*, nor has any employment or family to look after.
<margin>[II. iv. 13, 27—32.]</margin>
7. ... ... BUT *Fulvius*, you are a rational creature,
. and as such are as much obliged to live according to *reason and order*
. as a *priest* is obliged to attend at the *altar*,
. or a guardian to be faithful to his trust.
. If you live contrary to reason,
<margin>[II. iv. 33.]</margin>
. you do not commit a small crime,
. you do not break a small trust;
. but you break the *law of your nature*,
. you rebel against GOD who gave you that nature,
. and put yourself among those whom the GOD of reason and order will punish as *apostates and deserters*.
<margin>[II. i. 9.]</margin>
8. (a)... ... THOUGH you have no employment, yet as you are baptized into the profession of Christ's religion, you are as much obliged to live *etc.*

another subject of common instruction in the course of the studies mentioned above. For instance (assuming a pure, devout regard for the glory of God and for the public good, without which motive every occupation—especially that of a public writer—loses its innocence and piety and only makes salvation more difficult), the pupil would first of all feel that he is a perfect master of the foundation and philosophy of the subject upon which he has to express a discriminating judgment. He would then read over and analyze the treatise to be reviewed until he sufficiently understood its scope and details. Should those foundations, or the structure in any of its parts, feel inconsistent with the principles and developments of truth, sound reason, and real knowledge—which will have been well formed in his mind by the educational process we propose—he would, after a little reflection and examination, easily discover where, why, and how the discrepancy exists, whether in the premises, the reasoning, or the conclusion. And so, having clearly understood the source and nature of the errors, whether fundamental or partial, and the briefest way to effectively refute them, he would proceed in the usual classical order: first, to state the case of the question simply and clearly for the understanding of the most common, dullest reader; then give a fair summary in a series of propositions of the various grounds on which the question rests, verifying his statements; then, by pure argumentation from self-evident or concisely demonstrated principles (in whatever purity, elegance, or oratory his taste and judgment deem suitable), he would proceed in logical order to expose from various perspectives the fallacy of the propositions, the author's misunderstanding, or the incorrectness of his reasoning, until the unsound edifice—however plausible and imposing its general appearance or famous its architect—appears in its true character as an unsound and dangerous structure.

<margin>Blackwall's *Introduction to the Classics*, 12mo, 1737, should be well considered in reference to the art of perfecting the English language.</margin>
Moreover, as an accomplished and scholarly finish to the review, and as previously observed, always having regard for the public good (like a strict yet benevolent sage and guardian of truth), he would, at every suitable opening in the argument, make a digression to provide some masterful theosophical and edifying information incidentally related to the subject under discussion. He would sum up the whole with a well-executed finishing stroke of some clear and stirring truths, designed to impress, captivate, and win over the reader's understanding, judgment, and affections.

Again, for further exercises, the pupils might be directed to look through Law's *Christian Perfection* or similar rigorous casuistical dissertations on the essential duties and obligations of wisdom and Christianity; or perhaps of patriotism and moral virtue. (The work on *British Education and Eloquence* by Thomas Sheridan, M.A., 8vo, London, 1769, is strongly recommended here for reading and consideration.)

And now the inquiry may be made: would it not be perfectly consistent with the true spirit and genius of Protestantism, as well as the nature and design of pure Christianity, to establish a kind of religious Colleges of Retreat? Here, young people, after reaching a certain age or when their education is said to be finished, might, if they were so inclined, enter and remain for a period of five or seven years for the simple and stated purpose of being taught and practiced in the most *extensive application* of the divine virtues of Christianity. Thus, after being daily trained by a holy and enlightened Superior and his assistants in everything that could strengthen and perfect them in evangelical virtue, they might be properly prepared to enter public life and serve as living examples of the purity and glory of the Gospel. If only such establishments had long been common in our land, and if our senators, our priests, our public journalists, and leading public men had undergone such a wise and devout course of practical discipline as an essential qualification for their respective roles in life—then the public manners and condition of this nation, and of the world itself, would currently be enjoying the most blessed effects of it.

In such a place, all that is evil, unamiable, or biased in the human mind would, through ingeniously devised private and public trials and exercises, be made to show itself in its glaring opposition to the nature of the Divine will and the happiness of creation; where all that was wise,

Goodness, generosity, nobility, dignity, meekness, humility, patience, silence, resignation, loveliness, impartiality, and heavenliness would be made to vigorously grow as natural births of the new life of Jesus, following the gradual destruction and death of their opposing traits. Now, although the qualifications for the heads of such an establishment must be as high as can be imagined—where each leader, from the *Xavier-like* superior down, would be elected solely for his surpassing excellence of understanding, profound wisdom, great experience, high sanctity, and hardworking, *Bramwell-like* devotional spirit—yet we think no fears need be entertained regarding a lack of qualified individuals to fill such offices, if the system were once in operation and a single college established on these principles. Indeed, we believe the world would be more astonished by the wonders of human nature flowing from such a *newly opened source* of life than it has ever been by the greatest marvels of natural or inspired effort. Meanwhile, ample precautions *would* be provided through the watchfulness of the public, the growing universal sentiment of piety, the reckless liberty of the anonymous press, the strict action of pure principles, and a holy jealousy and mutual vigilance among the members themselves. By these and other providential means, we think the Institute might be *kept for fifty years* from being abused or degraded by a Jesuitical spirit and selfish interests. Such Christianity as is contemplated here does not allow for secrecy and scheming but requires the most open simplicity, the most tender purity of mind, and the constant pursuit of perfect goodness. It may not be entirely unnecessary to observe once more that the simple and sole intent of what we propose here is the—so to speak—*Spartan* cultivation of a perfect and enlightened morality, or Christian perfection, with which to enter into the common every-day duties of life. But to return.

For another exercise, the pupils might take the two volumes of Kempis, or the *Spiritual Combat*, or similar works, selecting from them all the purest and most evangelical counsels and precepts concerning self-government, holiness, and perfection that might not have been specifically covered in their former studies. They should preserve their original passion and spiritual richness while turning them into logical, spirited tracts on Christian virtues or finely expressed holy devotions. (And the same remarks also apply to the sentiments of *moral prudence* found in several wise treatises published in the early eighteenth century.)

Again, another most profitable exercise for pupils who have become moderately proficient in these studies could be letter writing, addressed to individuals supposed to be suffering from various kinds of spiritual distress (whether "children," "young men," or "fathers" in Christ). They could also write to others oppressed by the various troubles and trials to which human life is subject every day. These letters would be critically examined and corrected by the superior, and thus the pupils would acquire the qualifications for the essential office of a wise director and comforter of souls.

A further and very important exercise would be that of *devotional biography*, the channel through which so much valuable instruction can be effectively conveyed to the world. For instance, having practiced describing and portraying characters with classic talent, spirit, force, accuracy, a charming depiction of perfect virtue, and an ironical exposure of the deformity and folly of vice—as in the *Serious Call*—the pupil might select a few of the most edifying biographies from Butler’s *Lives of the Saints* (or other modern pious works). From their current tame, monotonous, and inelegant style, the pupil could reproduce them in Law’s simple, spiritually rich, and masculine style of thought and expression. They would add original sentiments of virtue while keeping edification, truth, and pure history steadily in view as the sole aim of everything written. At the same time, they should omit all Roman Catholic or Protestant peculiarities and praises. In short, they should merely extract the pure Christian honey and necessary historical facts. Thus (with natural, clever introductory remarks and concluding reflections into which the characters and incidents would be integrated), they would create a standard and fascinating example for the reader to win their attention and to provoke as well as guide their imitation.

The same remarks generally apply to the writing of *fables*, another invaluable source of instruction. When fables are concise, elegant, weighty, and pointed—that is, when the previously mentioned rhetorical skills are displayed in their construction—they form another charming literary ornament and relief, as well as

Other suggestions of equally manifest utility might be offered, but without entering further into the subject, it may be remarked in conclusion that through a simple practical course such as has been sketched and proposed here (indeed, in the spirit of *Sheridan* in his work on *British Education* previously recommended, or of the *school in Germany* described in the "Theosophical Transactions"), the minds of youth might be easily imbued with the sublimest spirit of heavenly wisdom and piety. At all events, these exercises might serve as a beginning, leaving it to the natural course of time and experience to mature and perfect a simple, comprehensive system of instruction in the theory and practice of pure, natural religion and evangelical virtue—in other words, a religion that is perfectly Christian yet non-sectarian. This, we say, can be achieved without harmfully infringing upon the existing methods and routines of education.

### SECTION IV.

We have now completed what we intended by this work, which was to fully clarify the scope of the *Advertisement* inserted at its beginning, regarding the specific understanding and talent deemed necessary for the adequate and just representation of the character of Mr. Law, and of the extraordinary individuals, agencies, and events which, under God, were instrumental in its formation or development.

This undertaking is, in effect, contained in the first three and the last fourteen pages, which, with an additional sheet or two, constituted the extent of the publication we had in mind when we began; but which, as explained in the Note on page 631 above, is now found to have expanded to its present large dimensions.

The entire work may then be considered as a general plan and specification for the construction of a noble building, or temple, dedicated to the Deity of Christianity—that is, to the true, rational understanding and worship of the universal Spirit of wisdom, goodness, and truth, according to his now complete revelation of himself. Furthermore, it furnishes the necessary materials for its construction or provides directions on where to obtain them.

It only remains for us to add a few words by way of conclusion. The candidate is supposed to have qualified himself as indicated for the great and noble work that is presented to his genius by this entire treatise—a work that, if properly executed, cannot fail to have a most important and happy influence on the future destinies of the world. Should it now seem desirable to him to test his abilities, the subject we would suggest to him for that purpose, first, regarding theology and literary power, is contained in the following writings, where they are summarized yet completely handled: (1.) the tract on *Regeneration*, described on page 40 above; (2.) the tract on *Repentance*, page 41; (3.) the book of *Prayers*, page 44; (4.) the tract on *Temptation*, page 42; (5.) the tract on *Resignation*, page 43; and (6.) the treatise on the *Supersensual Life*. The sum and tenor of the whole is a comprehensive and practical explanation of this grand truth and text of Scripture: "*unless a man is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God*." For the purpose in question, this might be rendered into the following proposition: namely, that it is the indispensable obligation of all men to be born again and to grow up in such new spiritual humanity toward perfection; otherwise they cannot have any divine knowledge, nor become true magical artists in nature or the creation.

By this or some similar proposition, we believe, the candidate may test his powers to do justice to the biography of so eminent a son of wisdom and mystic evangelical prophet as Mr. Law was. That is, regarding theoretical theology and mystical, spiritual, experimental divinity, he would clarify the *scope* and *implications* of the text or proposition, according to the orthodox science and experience set forth in the tracts specified above and the other works listed in series on pages 634–41 above; meanwhile, the style of language and argumentation would necessarily follow the prescribed models and their defined characteristics. In this way, among its general illustrations, sketches of modern character could be introduced as sacred ingenuity might dictate, showing its common phases of injustice, baseness, depravity, and folly. These would be placed in strong contrast or subjection to the inflexible requirements and sure reactionary, retaliatory laws of universal justice, righteousness, truth, and wisdom. This would especially involve scrutinizing conventional pretensions to honor, justice, respectability, and sanctity—probing them to the quick and, as groundless claims, exhibiting their moral degradation and loathsomeness in its true light. Yet all this should be touched with the charming delicacy of a La Fontaine, the happy brevity and irony of a La Bruyère, and the devout wisdom, robust sense, and pungent wit displayed in the fine moral sketches of the* *“Serious Call.”* In short, the essay might present a spirited exhibition of the talent and genius of the writer in the instances named above, embracing all necessary general and particular instructions concerning the states and degrees, the experiences, and the doctrines of Christian regeneration. I.—What is GOD, considered *outside of nature and the creature*, in himself?
II.—What is the ABYSS of *ALL* things, where there is no creature, namely, the unsearchable NOTHING?
III.—What is the love and the wrath of God? How is he an angry God, whereas he himself is unchangeable love?
IV.—What existed before the angels and the creation? *Col. 1:17.*

VII.—What moved Lucifer so that he lusted against God and turned himself away from the good?

X.—What did the devil desire, causing him to depart from God’s love?
XI.—What was the conflict between Michael and the Dragon? *Rev. 12:7.* What are Michael and the *Dragon*; or how is the defeat and expulsion carried out?

How may a man truly understand this basis of the deep UNITY?
XIII.—How is the expulsion of the *Dragon* and the legions of *Lucifer* carried out? To where is he cast, *Rev. 12:9*, so that he can be without God, whereas *God fills all things, Jer. 23:24?* Or what is the foundation of *hell* where he dwells?
XIV.—What is the office of *Lucifer* in hell, with his legions?
XV.—Did the foundation of hell have a *temporary* beginning, or has it existed from eternity? Or how may it exist eternally, or not?
XVI.—Why has God poured out such fierce wrath, in which there shall be eternal perdition? *Rev. 17:8, 11.*
XVII.—Since God is and remains eternally undivided, what then is his work in the place of *hell*? Is there indeed a specific place called hell, or not?
XVIII.—Where is the place of heaven, in which the angels dwell? How is it severed and *distinguished* from hell? Also, is it a specific place, and how is that to be understood?
XIX.—What are the dominions, or thrones, and principalities of angels, *evil* and *good*, in the invisible world? *Col. 1:16, Eph. 6:12.* How may the spiritual nature of eternity be understood in the visible world? Also, are they divided from each other by space and location, or what is the inward foundation?
XX.—Out of what is the *visible* world created, seeing the Scripture says, *God has made all things by his Word?* *John 1:3.* How is that to be understood? (*Three Principles, 22:11.*)
XXI.—Since God and his Word are only *good, Gen. 1:25*, from what, then, has the *evil* in the substance of this world flowed forth, such as venomous, poisonous worms, beasts, herbs, and trees, as also in the earth and other things? (*Mysterium Magnum, 61:63, 68.*)
XXII.—Why must there be strife and contrariety, or opposing wills in nature?
XXIII.—What is the basis of the *four elements*? How is the division carried out, so that out of one element, *four* have come to be?

XXV.—What is the basis of the temporal nature *light* and of the *darkness? Gen. 1:2–6.* From what did they originate?
XXVI.—What is the heaven created *out of the midst of the waters*? And what is the separation of the waters *above the firmament from the waters beneath the firmament? Gen. 1:6, 7.*

XXVIII.—What are the principles in the *spirit of this world* of the superior and inferior substance?
XXIX.—What is the *sperm* <note>meaning the seed or originating principle</note> of the generation of all things?

These, then, are the propositions or questions into which the subject, contained in the passages of Scripture referred to, has been resolved. They are offered to the candidate as a further exercise of his abilities, specifically with respect to <term>theosophical science</term>.
As a suggestion, however, regarding his mode of treating them—in terms of both brevity and detail—we venture in conclusion to submit for his consideration the following answers to a few of the earlier questions:

### Question I.—*What is GOD, considered without nature and creature, in himself only?*

Answer. (1.) God is the eternal Unity (comparable more to the zero than to the first of natural numbers), namely the universal or unmeasurable Good; which has nothing after it or before it that can give or provide anything to it. Without any inclinations or properties, and without the origin of time, it is in itself only ONE—a mere clarity, purity, or stillness. It has no space or place anywhere, nor does it need any for its home, but it is outside and inside the world equally; and it is deeper than a thought or an imagination can reach. Indeed, if for a hundred thousand years together, someone were to speak myriads of numbers concerning its greatness and depth, he would not have even begun to express its profundity, for it is endlessness or infinity.
Everything that can be numbered or measured is natural and imaginable, but the <term>Divine Unity</term> cannot be expressed; for it is equally the same through and through everything all at once. It is therefore called and understood to be the Good, because it is the eternal meekness and the highest beneficence in the <term>inventibility</term> (the capability of being discovered) of Nature and creature—namely, the perceptible or discoverable sweet Love.
(2.) For the Unity—the Good—flows forth from itself, and with such outflowing, introduces itself into willing and motion. There the Unity loves or thoroughly inhabits the desiring or motion, and the desiring or motion grasps the meekness of the Unity—the ground of the love in the Unity: *concerning which it is that Moses says, "The Lord our God is one only God and no other." 1 Cor. 8:6.*
(3.) And the matter is not as unenlightened reason supposes—that God dwells only above or outside the location of this world. There is no place prepared for him where he dwells separately; rather, only his revelation or manifestation is distinguishable.
He is through, with, and in all. And wherever he, in a *life*, becomes active with his Love, there God is manifested or revealed in his working; that is, his Love (the Unity) is there flowing forth, desirous, and perceptible or discoverable. There God has made himself a place—namely, in the ground of the soul, in the eternal <term>IDEA</term> or object or representation of the eternal desiring in the Love, wherein the Love wills and perceives or finds itself; as it is to be understood in the angels and in blessed souls.

### Question II.—*What is the Abyss of All things where there is no creature, namely, the abyssal Nothing?*

Answer. (1.) It is a dwelling place of God’s Unity, for the opening—or the "something" of the nothing—is God himself. The opening is the Unity, an eternal life and desiring, a <term>mere velleity</term> or will, which yet has nothing it can desire but itself. Therefore, the will is a mere desirous love-longing delight—an exit of itself toward its own perceptibility or discoverability.
(2.) This *will* is first the eternal *Father* of the <term>byss</term> (the ground); secondly, the *perceptibility* of the love is the eternal *Son,* whom the will generates in itself into a perceptible love-power; and thirdly, the exit of the desirous, perceptible Love is the *Spirit* of the Divine life.
(3.) And this is the eternal Unity, or threefold, unmeasurable, unbeginning Life, which stands—

...exists in mere desiring; in conceiving, comprehending, and finding itself, and in an eternal departure from itself.

(4.) And that which has gone forth from the Will, from the Love, and from the Life, that same thing is the *Wisdom* of God, namely the Divine vision, contemplability, and joy of the Unity of God, where Love eternally introduces itself into powers, colors, wonders, and virtues.

(5.) In this opening life of the Divine Unity, five clear and loud-sounding senses become understood in the perceptibility of the Love of life, namely AEIOU, in which the Divine desiring and working stand. This brings itself into an out-breathing or out-speaking, for the understanding of the one only Trinity, by which the eternal life finds and understands itself.

(6.) The Trinity manifests itself out of the Unity with a threefold breathing, so that this threefold breathing enters into itself in a threefold manner, toward a *self-possession*. And this threefold *sense* is called by its sensory name IEHOVA.

(7.) For the Unity, namely the I, goes into itself into a threefold substance, which is called IE. And that IE is the Father, who brings himself with his breathing will into HO, that is, into a formation of Love; and in the HO the word of all powers is understood, for it makes a circumference or surrounding of itself, namely the eternal "somewhat" or "something." From this goes forth the Love-longing or delight, whose departure is the Spirit, which comprehends and forms itself into VA. For the V is the Spirit, namely the outgoing, and A is the Wisdom, in which the Spirit forms itself* into a working life. <note>Note the distinction between the Deity or triune life and its seat or body of manifestation—its looking-glass of self-contemplation, or its magic Wonder-eye. One, it will be perceived, is all-active, the other all passive; one is the abyssal, formless will, the other is the revelation of that will, the discovery of itself in an essential form, and that form is a virgin. This supernatural, eternal virgin is yet further a mother, indeed the bride of God, and you, O reader, are one of her conceptions as to your inmost signature. In this respect you are God’s own veritable child—his own little image; yes, and in you, in this wisdom signature, God is ever waiting to reveal to you your portion of the glories of the Deity! Retire then into this your inward, pure, peaceful, happy, intellectual ground, away from the exterior bestial, hellish, reasoning life: as you are called anew to it by this philosophy, which is all practical, all about yourself, your inward being, and your way back to God (see p. 43, above), to teach you only to KNOW YOURSELF, and be happy.</note>

(8.) And then this threefold breathing or speaking life is in itself O, A. For the uncomprehended longing delight is the O, namely the eye of the one only seeing, a pure or clear vision; and the A is the threefold entrance into itself—that is, to the perceptibility of the desiring, which opens itself through the eternal breathing or speaking.

(9.) The opening, namely the *property* in the *sense* of the perceptible opening, is called ADONAI, and consists of six powers: out of which the *Mysterium Magnum*, namely the high name TETRAGRAMMATON, flows; from this, all substances visible and invisible have proceeded forth and come into form and images.

(10.) In the word ADONAI, namely in these six powers, lie the six properties of eternal nature, that is, of the natural life, out of which the angels and souls have flown forth according to the inwardness of their IDEA; and also the six days of the creation of this world, which, with the seeing life (that images itself in the midst of the substance, namely the O), became shut into the rest; wherein the six powers stand and rest in the still love, namely in the eternal Unity, and yet with their own self-working, they do will and go forth without ceasing.

(11.) And that is the O, the seventh day, in which God rested from all his works and eternally rests; that is, the six powers (namely, *first*, desirousness or astringency; *secondly*, mobility; *thirdly*, sense or perceptibility; *fourthly*, fire or life; *fifthly*, light or love; *sixthly*, sound, distinction, or understanding) rest in that from which they arose, namely in the O, in the place of God. In this, the eternal Love is signified, namely the Unity, or the I-hood of the Unity, which is the eternal Sabbath of all things, the good substance.

(12.) Thus we understand first that the eternal Nothing, which is without any beginning, is a clear, pure shining—namely, the Eye of eternal seeing. For in that, namely in the nothing, all things see; and just as "something" has arisen out of this seeing, so the nothing, namely the eternal Unity, sees through all things unhindered.

(13.) And secondly, we understand further that God himself is the seeing and finding of the nothing. It is called a "No-thing" (though it is clearly God himself) because it is incomprehensible and inexpressible.

### Question III.
*—What is God’s love and wrath, how is he an angry jealous God, though he in himself is the unchangeable Love? How may love and wrath be one only thing; or what is the Divine nature as distinguished from the supernatural abyssal Unity? (Or, what is the qualification of that nature or element, in which we, spiritually, live and have our being?)*

### Answer.

(1.) Although we may be difficult for the reader to understand, yet he may understand all in the divine power and by calling upon God, if this is done in right earnest sincerity. For all lies in man: he is a living book of God and of all things.

(2.) The reader must know that in *Yea* (the *A* shown above)† and *Nay*, all things consist, whether they are divine, devilish, earthly, or whatever can be named. <note>† Symbolized by two equilateral triangles crossing each other, the lower, inverted one (the Nay) being black, and the upper one, with the circle in which they stand, being white.</note> The *One*, namely the *Yea*, is mere power and life, and is the truth of God, or God himself. This would be in itself unapprehensible, and therefore would be neither joy nor exultation without the *Nay*. The *Nay* is an object of the *Yea* or

of the truth, so that the Truth may be manifest, and there be something in which there is a *contrarium,* and that may be loved, wherein the eternal Love is working, perceptible and desirous.

(3.) And yet we cannot say that the *Yea* is separated from the *Nay*, and that they are two things, one besides the other; but they are only one thing, yet sever themselves into two principles (*principia*), and make two centers (*centra*), wherein each works and wills in itself. Like as the day in the night, and the night in the day, are two centers, and yet unsevered, that is, they are severed only with their own will and desire. For they have a twofold fire in them, *namely first,* the day or the heat opening, and *secondly,* the night, or the cold enclosing; and yet both together are but one fire, and neither of them without the other would be manifest or working. For the cold is the root of the heat, and the heat is the cause that the cold is perceptible: without these two, which yet stand in continual strife, all things would be a nothing, and stand still without moving.

(4.) This is also to be understood concerning the eternal Unity of the Divine power. If the eternal Will did not flow forth from itself, and introduce itself into a receptivity, then there would be no form nor distinctness, but all powers would be only One power; also there would be no understanding, for the understanding arises in the distinctness of the multiplicity, where one property sees, proves, and wills the other properties. In like manner, also, there would be no joy.

(5.) Now if there must exist a receptivity, then there must be a desire for self-perception, that is, a self-will for the receptivity, which is not, nor wills like the only Will. For the one only Will wills only the one Good which it is itself; it wills no other than itself in the equilibrium (*æquilibrio*) or balance (*temperature*); but the out-flowed will wills inequality, that it may be distinguished from the balance, and be its own "something" in order that there might be something which the eternal Seeing may see and feel. And out of the own-will or self-will has proceeded the *Nay,* for it brings itself into a selfhood, that is, into a receptiveness of itself; it wills to be something, and does not liken itself to the Unity, for the Unity is an outflowing *Yea* or A, which eternally stands in a breathing-forth of itself, and is an imperceptibility, for it has nothing in which it might find itself, save in the receptiveness of the outgoing will, *namely* in the *Nay,* which is an opposite of the *Yea*, wherein the *Yea* becomes manifest, and wherein it has something that it can desire.

(6.) For the One has nothing in itself that it can desire, unless it doubles itself, so that it becomes two; also it cannot find itself in the Unity, but in the duality it finds itself. Understand the ground aright, thus:

(7.) The self-separated will has gone forth out of the equilibrium of the eternal desiring, and also has nothing that it can desire itself. Now seeing it is a "something" in respect of the Unity, (which is Nothing and yet All,) therefore it brings itself into a desire for itself, and desires itself, and also the Unity, out of which it has flown forth.

(8.) The Unity it desires, as the perceptible love-longing, that the Unity may be perceptible in it; and itself it desires, as the moving, apprehending and understanding, that there may be a separability in the Unity, so that powers might exist. And though the power has no ground nor beginning, yet so do distinctions arise in the receptiveness, out of which distinctions NATURE does exist.

(9.) This out-flowed will brings itself into a desire, and the desire is magnetic, that is, in-drawing, and the Unity is out-flowing. So that now it is a *contrarium,* like as *Yea* and *Nay,* for the Out-flowing has no ground, but the in-drawing makes a ground. The Nothing does will out from itself, that it may be manifested, and the "something" does will into itself, that it may be perceptible in it. Nothing, in order that the Unity may become perceptible in it. Thus is the *Out* and *In* an inequality.

(10.) And the *Nay* is therefore called a *Nay,* because it is an in-turned desire, that is, negatively enclosing; and the *Yea* is therefore called *Yea,* because it is an eternal outgoing and the ground of all being, that is the clear-sounding Truth. For it has no *Nay* before itself, but the *Nay* first exists in the out-flowed will of the receptiveness.

(11.) This out-flowed desirous will is in-drawing or attracting, and conceives itself in itself, whence come forms and properties. The *first* property is acid sharpness, whence arise hardness, coldness, dryness, and darkness, for the attractiveness overshadows itself; and this is the true ground of the eternal and also temporal darkness, and the hardness and sharpness is the ground of the perceptibility. The *second* property is the motion in the attracting, which is the separating. The *third* property is the true perception between the hardness and the moving, wherein the will perceives or is sensible of itself, for it finds itself in a great sharpness, like a great anguish, in respect to the placid, soft Unity, so to speak. The *fourth* property is the fire, that is the flash of the glance, which exists from the conjunction of the great anguishing sharpness, and the Unity. For the Unity is gentle and still, and the movable hard sharpness is terrible, and is a ground of the painfulness.

(12.) Now in this conjunction there is a great terror, and in this terror the Unity is grasped or seized, and becomes a flash or glance, like an exulting joy. And thus arises the light in the midst of the darkness, for the Unity becomes a light, and the receptiveness of the desirous will, in the properties, becomes a spirit-fire, which takes its source and original out of the astringent cold sharpness, in the moving and perceptibility in the darkness; and it is even its very being, *namely,* a terrible consuming quality.

(13.) And according to this, is God called an *angry, jealous God,* and a *consuming fire*; not according to what he is within himself, without or beyond all receptiveness, but according to this eternal fire-ground. And in the darkness is understood the foundation of hell, as a forgetfulness of the Good; which darkness is totally hidden in the light, as night in the day: as *John* i. 5 is to be understood. (See Note below.)

This process describes how light emerges from darkness and how God’s nature can be perceived as both gentle love and consuming fire.</summary>

(14.) Thus we see in the above-mentioned properties, God's <term>wrath</term>, namely, the first property of the contracting of the <term>Nay</term>; for that does not assimilate itself with the <term>Yea</term>, namely, the <term>Unity</term>, because it makes a <term>darkness</term> within itself, which is an extinguishing of the Good.

(15.) *Secondly*, it makes a sharpness within itself, which is the ground of the eternal dying of the gentleness of the amiable Unity. *Thirdly*, it makes a <term>hardness</term> within itself, which is the eternal death, like a state of helplessness. *Fourthly*, it makes in itself such hardness of death, a perpetual painful awareness. *Fifthly*, it makes within itself an anguishing <term>fire</term> source. Now, in these properties, God's wrath and the <term>hell</term>ish fire are to be understood; and it is called hell, or the pit, because it is a hiding place or a confinement. It is also called an enmity against God because it is painful, and the Unity of God is pure gentleness. Therefore, one is against the other, like fire and water; from which fire and water in the substance of this world also took their origin.

(16.) In this kindling of the out-flowed will, the *fifth* property is now born: the perceptibility of the Unity of God—namely, the <term>Love</term>—which in the fire becomes movable and desiring. It makes another <term>principium</term> within the fire (that is, in the painfulness)—namely, a great Love-fire. For it is the cause and the ground of the <term>Light</term>, so that the light springs up in the fire's essence. It is the Love-power in the light, for in this way the Unity brings itself into movement and perceptibility, so that the eternal power may be felt, and so that a desire and distinctness may be within it; otherwise, the Unity would be an eternal stillness and without feeling.

(17.) This Love and Light dwell in the fire and penetrate the fire, so that the fire's essence becomes changed or transmuted into the highest joy, and no wrath can any longer be perceived, but only a pure taste of love from the Divine perceptibility.

(18.) For in this way the eternal Unity inflames itself everywhere, so that it is a Love, and so that there is something that may be loved. For if the love of the Unity did not exist in the fire-burning nature, then it would not be *essential*, and there would be no joy or movement in the Unity.

(19.) Thus, God's wrath may now be understood in the fire's essence; and in the love-perceptibility—that is, the perceptible Unity—the divine Love-fire is understood. These make two centers in only one ground, which is a twofold fire.

(20.) Namely, first, the wrath-fire in the out-flowed will of receptivity is a ground of the eternal Nature, from which the angels and the soul of man have received their foundation. This is called <term>Mysterium Magnum</term>, and out of this eternal Nature this visible world was also produced and created as an *objectum* or *mirror* of the inwardness.

(21.) *Secondly*, the center of the love is the *Yea*—namely, the fire-flaming breathing, which is called the <term>Word of God</term>. This is the breathing of God's Unity, the *foundation* of the power, in which the true Holy Spirit is understood in the outflow of the Love-breathing—namely, the movement or life of Love. Thus, the angelic spirit, as well as the soul's spirit, is understood within it, where God is manifest and dwells.

(22.) But the foundation of the soul and the angels, according to their nature, is understood in the eternal Nature-fire. For the clear Deity does not become creaturely (for it is an eternal Unity), but it dwells through Nature, just as fire glows through iron.

(23.) And at this place, we understand the possibility of the perdition or damnation of angels and souls; if they lose the Love-fire—that is, turn away from the divine Unity and enter into self-desire—then the wrath-fire burns in them, and it becomes their own life.

(24.) But if the divine Love-fire burns in their central fire, then their fire-life is a perfect joy and a lovely well-being; and God's fire and the fire of Nature stand in them as one single ground.

(25.) In this *fifth* property, the glory and majesty of God become manifest as a light of Love. Of this the Scripture says, *God dwells in a light that no man can approach unto*, 1 Tim. 6:16; thereby signifying that no creature has ever been born out of the central fire of the Love, for that is the Most Holy fire, even *God* himself in his <term>Ternary</term>.

(26.) And out of this Holy fire has flowed the *Yea*, A, as a beam of the perceptible Unity. The same is the highly precious name <term>JESUS</term>, which has redeemed the poor soul from the wrath-fire again. By assuming humanity, he gave himself into the separated central fire of God's wrath in the soul, kindled it again with the love-fire, and united it with God. Oh, reader, observe this well!

(27.) Thus, now understand the right foundation. In God there is no wrath, but only pure Love; but in the foundation by or through which the Love becomes movable, there is the wrath-fire. In God it is only a cause of the joy and the powers, but in the center of the wrath-fire, it is the greatest and most terrible darkness, pain, and anguish.

(28.) And these two are within one another as day and night, where neither one may comprehend the other, but one dwells in the other, and they make two *principia*, that is, two eternal beginnings.

(29.) One beginning is the kingdom of God in the Love; and the other beginning is called the kingdom of God's wrath—namely, the foundation of hell, where the outcast spirits dwell.

(30.) The foundation of the kingdom of God is pure *Yea*—namely, the powers of the differentiated *Word*. And the foundation of the wrath of God is pure *Nay*, from which the *lie* exists; which is why Christ said *that the devil was a father of lies*, John 8:44, for his foundation is pure *Nay* and a contradiction of the Truth—namely, of the *Yea*.

(31.) The *sixth* property in the out-flowed will is the sound, voice, understanding, discourse, or distinctions—namely, the true understanding—and it stands in both central fires alike at once. In the center of the self-receptivity of the Nature-fire, without the co-working of the Holy fire (where these two fires are separated, as in the devils and damned human souls), it is not understanding, but only cunning and craft. That is, a testing of the foundation of Nature, a mere misuse of the powers of Nature, from which deceit, suspicion, folly, trickery, and wantonness originate.

(32.) In this sixth power stand the *Holy Names*—namely, the divine powers in the opening of the Unity, in the working and desiring; and they stand in both the fires alike at once—namely, in the fire of the Natural mobility and in the fire of the Love-flame.

(33.) And here stands the *wonder-working Word* in its workings; for the great name of God, <term>TETRAGRAMMATON</term> (<term>IeHovah</term>), is here the center of the wonders of God, which works in both the central fires; which the evil spirits, in their transformation according to the center of the fire's nature, do misuse.

(34.) And the ground of the whole <term>CABALA</term> and <term>Magia</term> is comprehended in this foundation; for

From this, the visible world existed, and by the moving of the *wonder-working Name*, it flowed forth, or grew, and transitioned into divisibility and forms.
