**VOL. VIII.—THE FIFTEENTH CONFERENCE.** Concerning a MS. of Bishop Sanderson, as far as his Ninth Position, upon the modern doctrine of Predestination, the Series of the Decrees of God, and the Causes and Means of Men's Salvation: as also many questions which are now most in agitation, not only in the Church of England, but in many foreign churches also, popish and reformed. Written by him, partly in Latin and partly in English, but now (upon a certain emergent occasion) translated and transcribed entirely in English by one who heartily wishes that Babel might be pulled down, and that the Spirit of God might be built up in Jerusalem.—**THE SIXTEENTH CONFERENCE.** Concerning the same MS. from the Bishop's Ninth Position to the End. Also further considering several distinctions between Grace and Grace, which are used by Predestinarians.

**NOTE.**—These sixteen conferences are considered to have been written by the author, chiefly in the year 1715; who, it is presumed, adopted the dialogue mode of representation as being best calculated to elucidate his very profound subjects without too much wearying the attention and patience of the reader. Still, it were to be wished that the substance of the Third to the Ninth Conferences had been presented in a more condensed form, as indeed the worthy author would appear to have proposed to do in and by the "*Immanuel*" Fragment, referred to in the notices of the contents of VOL. G, above, but which, whether completed or not, does not now appear. The theosophical student may very profitably go through these intermediate six conferences and extract out of them that which is purely of solid instruction. This work is duly illustrated with symbols.

**(4.) FIVE CONFERENCES,** concerning THE ABSOLUTE NECESSITY of all the HOLY SUFFERINGS and DEATH of JESUS CHRIST upon the CROSS. With a large HIEROGLYPHICAL FIGURE, representing the PROCESS of CHRIST in effecting the REDEMPTION.—**THE FIRST CONFERENCE.** Being Preliminary to the Arguments against the position—'That the Mediation of Christ implies no Necessity of his Death;' and giving an Account of the Origin of the said Opinion.—**THE SECOND, THIRD and FOURTH CONFERENCES.** Proving the Necessity of the Death of Christ from the Ground of Scripture. **THE FIFTH CONFERENCE.** Wherein is demonstrated the Necessity thereof under some Emblematical Figures.

**NOTE.**—This work is supposed not to have been completed by the author, though the special mention of *two more conferences*, made at the end of the Fifth Conference, and also of the *large hieroglyphic figure* which was to be the subject of these remaining portions of it, would seem to imply the contrary. If the two deficient conferences were really written, they were not with the author's other MSS at the time of his decease, nor have they been in the possession of his intimate friends and admirers of his writings since, up to the present moment. The original copy of this work, which is supposed to have been written A.D. 1716, is likewise no longer known to be in existence.—The portion of it which will be of most esteem with the theosophical student is the Fifth Conference. And we are not sure that, in case of a republication of the 'Third to the Ninth Conferences' of the 'Predestination' work in a separate form, this last or fifth conference of this work might not very judiciously be placed before them, though an "unfinished" piece.

**(5.) MICROCOSMOS,** or the **Formal IMAGE of DEITY and all NATURE, MAN.** Considered in his PRIMEVAL STATE, his FALLEN STATE, and his STATE of REGENERATION. In **THREE TABLES** or **SYMBOLS**, with their EXPLANATIONS.

**NOTE.**—As may have been perceived by the annotation made on VOL. E. of the *Elucidations*, etc., these Tables with their explanations were originally composed immediately <insert>before</insert> that said treatise; but the author's improved knowledge in subsequent years of his reflections led him to make a great enlargement of the explanation of the First Table; though for want of convenience, he left the other two in their original state. ### (6.) EPISTLES. WRITTEN in London, during the YEARS 1713—1717.

(1.) THE FIRST LETTER. To the Church or Religious Meeting in Bow Lane. Written in the early part of the year 1713. (2.) THE SECOND LETTER. To the same. Also including PART OF A LETTER read by the author at the conference held according to the proposal in this second letter. (3.) THE THIRD LETTER. Read and delivered by the author to the church in Bow Lane, November 1st, 1713. (4.) THE FOURTH LETTER. Written probably in 1714, or early in 1715. This meeting was not, as has been incorrectly stated in a letter from Mr. Law on April 8th, 1747, the celebrated Philadelphian Society (which arose about A.D. 1697 and continued until A.D. 1703 or 1704, and the spirit of which, as appears from Roach’s writings, was maintained to some extent up to the date of his two publications). Instead, it was a society formed around A.D. 1706 by a number of persons who were also well-versed in the terms and phraseology of the writings of <term>Bohemius</term>, though it appears some of them made a lamentable abuse or perversion of them. These letters, as the observations at the end of the ‘Explanation’ of the first table of <term>Microcosmos</term> show, explain how their author was induced to visit and assemble with that society around 1712, and what he thought of its proceedings; they contain his views on how to render the company a truly spiritual church.

(5.) THE FIFTH LETTER, addressed to a Mr. Inglis in Scotland, dated September 20th, 1715. In this work is found the symbol of the Eye of Eternity, seeing at one view, within itself, all that is past, present, and future.</note>

### (7.) A TREATISE AGAINST THE DOCTRINE of the RESTORATION of ALL THE DEVILS and LOST SPIRITS.
In this is shown, FIRST, THE GREAT DIFFERENCE between the FALL of LUCIFER and THAT of ADAM. NEXT, the notion of the <term>Everlasting Gospellors</term>, together with their EIGHT CHIEF ARGUMENTS. FURTHER, THE AUTHOR’S IDEA ON THE SUBJECT, accompanied by EXPLANATIONS AND ILLUSTRATIVE SYMBOLS. And LASTLY, the METHODICAL ANSWER to the said eight arguments of the <term>Everlasting Gospellors</term>. Written in the German language, in London, A.D. 1718.

<note>This treatise is one of the most elaborately illustrated of all the author’s writings, and perhaps the deepest metaphysical or logical treatise that was ever presented to the world upon such subjects of hidden truth as those it addresses.</note>

### (8.) A TREATISE of GOOD and EVIL.
In which good and evil are considered, FIRST, as in this OUTWARD THIRD PRINCIPLE. SECONDLY, as in the TWO INTERIOR WORLDS, yet as BEFORE THE DAY OF SEPARATION. And LASTLY, as AFTER THE DAY OF SEPARATION. In a conference between A and B. Written in the German language, in London, A.D. 1720.

<note>In the author’s original of this work, now before us, the fourth or last conference is no longer to be found; nevertheless, it is contained in the copy of it which we also hold, made by Leuchter. This treatise commences at “page 561,” facing which is an ‘antiscript’ by the author, calling attention to this circumstance; this is to intimate that this treatise implies an antecedent one, and the due understanding of it, in order to apprehend the present work. From a note at the head of it, it appears to have been drawn up to clear a scruple. On looking over the author’s own writings, we can find no work to which this remark may be supposed to refer, except perhaps the ‘Sixteen Conferences on Predestination,’ the pages of which are double pages. Page 560 therein we find to be in the eleventh conference, the subject of it (see the title given above) being <term>Voluntas signi et bene placiti</term>. This page begins with the words, ‘ever any other man’—and the bottom of the said double page ends with these words, ‘which the triune God.’—Were the original of the work “against the restoration of devils” numbered within this extent of pages, then we should conclude this treatise to have been an appendix to that work.</note>

# *ANNOTATIONS regarding the ORIGINALS and COPIES of this AUTHOR'S WRITINGS, where they are deposited, and which Copy ought to be FOLLOWED in CASE of PUBLICATION, with other incidental Notices.*

### (I.)—*On the Serial Elucidations of J. B.'s Philosophy and Theology, Vols. A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H and I.* A.D. 1699—1703—1710.

(1.) The Author's own original of this entire series, with the mentioned Index, is in our possession. No other copies have the Index to them, which refers to the pages of this original copy. These treatises, as we have suggested, were written at different times, as is evident by the paper and style of writing. They have clearly been read many times; marks and references here and there upon their pages show them to have been examined, among others, by Francis Lee, and also by Mr. Law, as well as by the aforementioned Rev. Mr. Waple, etc. They are all bound in calfskin and labeled. Volumes A and B are in octavo, the remainder in quarto. Volume I, forming the Index to their contents, is backed only with strong paper. In case of publication, *this original* should be followed, as it was first written and punctuated, but removing the "continentalisms" such as *for to see*, *for to understand*, etc., and making only such simple alterations. The references to J. B. in all the Author's own compositions are to the German edition of 1682; but in some of the *copies* of them, the references are altered to the *English* translation.

<margin>A B ^</margin>
(2.) There is good reason to suppose Mr. Law made an entire copy of this Series, as we hold his copy of Volumes F and G, but not of the other Volumes. In copying them out, he gave a better English phrasing to some of the sentences of the German Author's original, besides shortening sections in places where it might be done judiciously.

(3.) The next best written copy (of A to H only) of this series is that in the British Museum, *Additional MSS.*, No. 5767—5774, which is by Leuchter, in quarto vellum. The Author's writings deposited there are entitled, **FUNDAMENTA MYSTICA JACOBI BOHEMII TEUTONICI, EXPLICATA. BY ANDREAS DIONYSIUS FREHER.** (*Add. MSS. 5767—5792.*) They were presented to the Museum by Mr. Edward Fisher of Bath and Bristol, through or from whom the greater part of the same Author's manuscripts we hold have come into our hands. Volume No. 5767 has a portrait of the Author, like the one prefacing our copy of the 'Letter to Gildersleeve.'

(4.) We also have in our possession another uniform copy (A to H) in quarto vellum made by Allan Leppington, except Volume B, which is in another handwriting, at the end of which is written October 27, 1728; and further excepting Volume G, which is bound in calf like the Author's original, though the writing in it is in a very distorted hand.

(5.) We also hold a copy of Volume A in the same handwriting as Volume B above; at the end of which is written July 22, 1727. Also a copy by Mr. Law (with his mentioned alterations) of Volumes F and G. Also, a copy in large quarto calf of volumes A to H in a more recent hand. This forms a part of the last three of the Six Volumes in quarto containing copies of the main part of the Author's writings, which were originally purchased at the sale of the books of Richard Cosway, Esq., R.A., and F.R.S., Portrait Painter to the Prince Regent (about 1818—20); who was also the intimate friend of Lady de Clifford and Mrs. Udney: which two ladies jointly had the forming of the mind of the lamented Princess Charlotte. Several copies of one or two of the A and B Volumes of this series, by Leppington and others, originally belonging to a Mr. Holdcroft, which were rejected by the writer when purchasing his library, were afterwards sold in London, A.D. 1849.

(6.) Regarding the *Fragments of Treatises* specified in the description of Volume G, *above*—the original of the 'Substance of Three Conferences between an English Divine and a German Theosophist,' in the Author's handwriting, is in the British Museum, *Add. MSS.* 5784, half-bound. It expressly indicates the parties in question to be Mr. Waple and this Author. We hold a copy of this treatise in the handwriting of Edward Fisher.

Secondly—the original of the Fragment headed 'Immanuel,' on the 'Seven Properties of Nature,' we ourselves have in our possession in the Author's own handwriting; which exactly corresponds in the style of its writing and other particulars with the above-mentioned 'Conference' Fragment in the British Museum. We also have a copy of it by Fisher.

Thirdly—the Fragment of the 'Theosophic Confession of Faith' we hold the original of itself, as referred to in the note on Volume G *above*. Also a copy by Leppington.—We repeat that it is much to be lamented that the additional portions of this valuable piece (as with the 'Immanuel' Fragment) are no longer in existence, to our knowledge, after many inquiries.

### (II.)—*On the Hieroglyphica Sacra, or Thirteen Theosophic Emblems.* A.D. 1703, 10.

(1.) As we have said before, the author's own original is in our possession; the first four Tables having been composed as an explanation of the Emblem at the end of Volume A, or

rather of the truths symbolized within them. We have also suggested that the following Nine Tables were added some time later, and have set that period around A.D. 1710. However, the designs for the treatise ‘against the Restoration of Devils’ have led us to suppose that these remaining Tables might have been added after that work was finished; yet the handwriting and paper lead us back to the original conclusion, and further suggest that the designs from that German treatise (against Universal Restoration), insofar as they resemble those in this work, might have been adapted for that treatise from the present work. It should be noted that these Symbols begin at the end. The reason for this is that the first four are considered as only one, or a fourfold Figure; the fourth represents pure Eternal Nature, or God, or God in Trinity, or the outward immediate manifestation or birth of the abyss of Deity, “wherein all the powers, glories, and perfections of the hidden, unapproachable, supernatural Deity, have their wonderful manifestation,” and subsequently in the creatures born out of it. The first three plates, therefore, represent the *motion* or *speaking* of that eternal, enduring, and eternally generated essence, <term>ternarius sanctus</term> <note>Latin for "holy triad," referring to the kingdom of heaven or the manifestation of the Trinity in nature.</note>, or the kingdom of heaven shown in the fourth plate; in other words, the working ground or root of all nature and natural being. Within these, the theosophic student will observe the birth of the two co-eternal principles and the seven properties of nature, along with its three constituent parts: these are the ground or working powers of all things, whether of mind or matter, eternal or temporal, including all qualities and sensibilities of all life. They were previously published in volume 2 of Jacob Boehme’s Works, quarto, 1764.

(2.) We also possess two copies of this series of Emblems, both by Leuchter: one follows the author’s original exactly, with the descriptions facing the images; the other is a later copy with the tables proceeding in the regular order and the descriptions placed together at the beginning. There is also a similar copy by the same artist in the British Museum, *Additional Manuscripts* 5790.

### (III.)—*On the Sixteen Conferences concerning Predestination.* A.D. 1715.

(1.) We have in our possession the author’s originals of this work, with the exception of Conferences 4, 5, 6, 9, 12, 15, and 16; these are most probably lost, as they have certainly not been heard of by collectors of these writings for the past sixty years. They were originally contained in about thirteen volumes, bound in brown paper and labeled. Using this clue and other notices in this sketch, it is possible that the author’s missing manuscripts and fragments may be traced and recovered at a future time.

(2.) There is, however, a very beautiful and complete copy of this work in the British Museum, made by Leuchter, *Additional Manuscripts* 5775–83. These were arranged by Leuchter into eight volumes, as this was the most equal and appropriate division for them. All of Leuchter’s copies of this author’s writings—though he was a German like the author—are written with great care and in a very clear, round hand, being probably those he made for his own use. However, they were sold (as we shall state later in our collected memoranda respecting this author) at an auction in Islington in the year 1772, and were bought by old Mr. Denis, a bookseller of New Bridge Street, Blackfriars. At the death of Mr. John Denis's son at the close of the last century, these were obtained by Mr. Edward Fisher, and the greater part of them were presented to the *British Museum*. If published, the ‘Conferences’ in quarto which are stated above as missing from the author’s original should be supplied from this source. Or rather, the *copies* which we hold (besides the originals) of all these missing Conferences—with the exception of Conferences 12, 15, and 16—might be compared with this British Museum copy to see if they are correct and the *italicized words properly distinguished*. It would then only be necessary to copy out the aforementioned 12th, 15th, and 16th Conferences.

(3.) In the six quarto volumes, bound in calfskin, containing extracts from this author’s works (formerly in the possession of the late R. Cosway, Esq., which we hold, as previously mentioned), there is a copy of all the first nine of these Conferences. Among our collection of manuscript books will also be found a recent quarto copy of the first three Conferences, bound in calf by a modern hand, and again, of the fourth in quarto, bound in calf with a copy of Canfield’s *Third Part of ‘Rule of Perfection,’* etc.; but these latter are not to be depended upon.

(4.) We have no doubt these Conferences were written in the year 1715—perhaps the concluding ones in 1716, and the earlier ones possibly in 1714. At that time, and for several years prior to 1715 or 1716, the author resided in Eagle Court, St. John’s Lane, near Smithfield.

### (IV.) *On the Five Conferences concerning the Necessity of the Holy Sufferings and Death of Christ upon the Cross. With a large Hieroglyphical Figure.* A.D. 1716.

(1.) As we have noted, we have not been able to trace the original of this treatise, but we possess the original draft of the large Symbolical Figure. In the large portrait drawing of the author, prefixed to the fair copy we hold (bound together in one large quarto volume in green vellum, containing all the illustrative diagrams and tables of the author’s writings made by Leuchter), this large Symbol is represented as lying open on his table. His other writings (with the exception of the ‘First Table’) are shown standing in order beside him, bound, with their titles labeled on each. We may just mention that this last work (the collection of the symbols and other illustrative designs of the author’s writings) came into our hands by a remarkable providence, as did indeed all his writings, both originals and copies, as well as those of Mr. Law, Francis Lee, and others. By this work, or rather by the notification of his writings contained within it, we were enabled to determine whether all of them had been preserved for us, which we happily find to be the case. Without this clue, we would have been unable to trace this fact or to present the details contained in these pages regarding them. We rejoice at being the instrument of preserving and making known such inestimable, unique, and—as will be found regarding the promotion of theosophy or divine wisdom—essential writings and instructions to the world.

(2.) We hold a good copy of these Five Conferences, made by Leppington, in two quarto volumes bound in vellum. There is also a fine copy of the same by Leuchter, in one quarto volume bound in vellum, deposited in the *British Museum*. This copy also has inserted at its beginning a clever reduced copy of the large hieroglyphic Symbol, which was to have been particularly and entirely explained in the now-missing sixth and seventh conferences. At the end of this volume (of the fifth conference),

There is a remark in Leuchter's handwriting that this work was not finished. Possibly, as we have stated our guess to that effect, the author abandoned the completion of this undertaking to begin the refutation of the doctrine of Universal Restoration. He especially mentions this in the First of these Conferences as one of the great Babylonian errors of his age, which would necessarily involve the resolution of the chief points that would have come under special review in these two concluding conferences of the present work. As he expresses himself on that occasion:
> “Now this opinion of the restoration of devils is based by these Babylonians on almost the same foundation as the non-necessity of the death of Christ.” See also some similar observations by him relating to this matter in the concluding part of the Sixth Conference on Predestination.

In this copy in the British Museum, *Add. MSS.*, 5785, there is also found a very striking bust portrait of our author, which certainly should not be omitted if his writings are published. This portrait would require comparison with the others of him in his regular costume—for instance, with the large portrait we mentioned before at the beginning of the *Collection of the illustrations of his works*, also with the one at the beginning of our copy (in a formal modern handwriting) of the ‘*Epistle to Gildersleve*,’ and with the two corresponding portraits in Nos. 5767 and 5789 *Add. MSS.* in the British Museum. All these, however, must further be compared with the portrait in the ‘*Paradoxa, Emblemata*’ work of the author in our possession; this portrait is undoubtedly the most accurate and authentic, being probably done at the very time that copy of the emblems was drawn up, which was, we judge, almost contemporary with the author’s own original. In contrast, the former, larger-featured portraits, which make the author’s face appear younger, were necessarily done at a later date. We are almost decided to regard this latter ‘*Paradoxa*’ portrait as providing a good idea of the general effect of the author’s person; still, we are much pleased to see this *bust design*, which has indeed a natural, unsophisticated air and sentiment that we well understand and feel to be consistent with the spirit which the worthy original acknowledges in himself in his ‘*Epistle to Gildersleve*.’ This spirit is also manifest in his pious, deeply felt ‘*Letters to the Church in Bow Lane*,’ in his confessions appended to the ‘*Explanation of the First Table*,’ and indeed throughout all his writings.

(3.) The large Hieroglyphical Figure of these Conferences was formerly engraved and inserted in the first volume of the incomplete edition of J. B.’s <note>Jacob Boehme</note> works, published A.D. 1764—82. This was done at the sole expense of Mrs. Hutcheson (Miss Hester Gibbon not having, as formerly guessed, joined in that expense) out of respect to the memory of her esteemed friend, companion, and spiritual advisor, Mr. Law, who died A.D. 1761. We may here repeat that Mr. Law had nothing whatever to do with that publication, which was seen through the press by a Mr. George Ward—an old friend and correspondent of Mr. Law and a great admirer of his talents—who showed honest zeal but great incompetence for such an important business. Assistance in this work may have also been rendered, especially in the completion of the Fourth volume after Mr. Ward’s death, by a Mr. Langcake, another friend of Mr. Law, who was perhaps just as incompetent an editor for such a task as Mr. Ward was.

(5.) We know of no other copies of this work than those mentioned above, except for one more that we hold, contained in the previously mentioned Selections of the author’s writings in six quarto volumes, formerly in the possession of Mr. Cosway. We have stated our belief that this work was written in 1716, immediately after the *Conferences on Predestination* were completed, and that after finishing the Fifth conference, the author laid aside the undertaking for a time, if not altogether. He then (1717) added the final touches, revisions, and appendix to the ‘*Explanation of the First Table*.’ In that work, it will be found how tired he says he is of writing so continuously (indeed, he must have labored almost night and day with his pen as well as his mind), but he adds that he will nevertheless not abandon it all at once.

From observations scattered throughout these writings, it appears the author was intimately acquainted with P. Poiret between A.D. 1670 and 1680. See also the Philadelphian writings, Lee’s *Letter to Dodwell* (pp. 194—221 above), Roach’s two publications, and other books in German and English from about A.D. 1690—1725—not to mention others from earlier or later times—regarding the topic of the “everlasting gospel” and “universal restitution,” which gave rise to the author’s next original treatise, as mentioned before. Freher, like Law and their great master in divine science, Bohemius <note>Jacob Boehme</note>, by the constitution of their uniformly developed and *well-balanced* intellect and judgment, had as great and instinctive an antipathy to all unsound and Babylonian confusion of Christian theology and empty, profitless religious idiosyncrasies of doctrine (however plausibly presented) as St. Paul himself had to the ideas of Simon Magus and alchemical pretenses for the purification of the soul in the first ages of Christianity.

->*(V.) On the Microcosmos, or Three symbolic Tables, with their respective Explanations. A.D. 1703—1717—1727.*<-

(1.) We have not seen or heard of the first original manuscript of the *Explanation of the First Table*, though we hold a fragment copy of its beginning, which clearly shows how much the present work improves upon the first draft. Neither have we heard of the author's original manuscript of this current revised work; yet we think it must have been in Mr. Law's hands when he made his copy of it, for he would hardly have wanted to copy from a copy of such an important and valuable treatise. The author's original manuscripts of the ‘*Explanations of the Second and Third Tables*’ are in the British Museum, *Add. MSS.* 5787; the style of the handwriting sufficiently proves to us when it was composed by him. At the end of it is a Latin note by a friendly hand, dated November 1712. These two Explanations, as noted by the author at the end of the ‘*Explanation of the First Table*,’ were left as they were originally written. Although he might have considerably enlarged and improved them, as he had indeed intended, he was (as he states) so tired of writing, and furthermore, what remained to be declared regarding them would be fully evident to every reader and student who had become personally acquainted with and mastered the contents of that ‘*Explanation of the First Table*,’ which was indeed its sole object. In fact, a further explanation was not necessary, and therefore he would give up his original purpose and leave the Explanations of those latter Tables as they were first composed. We cannot help but regret this with respect to future schools of theosophy, as we consider it desirable that the entire practical scope of man's nature and relations had been fully explained by this divinely enlightened and intellectually learned sage. We would recommend the

The reader should look over, if it is in his power, the German work mentioned before by Graber and Gichtel from 1696, titled ‘*Theosophia Practica*, or a Brief Explanation of the Three Worlds and Principles in Man, illustrated with Plates;’ in order to form a just conception of the origin of the present work. This work was intended as a brief, practical, yet deep exposition and application of Jacob Boehme's declaration on that subject in his THREEFOLD LIFE. Who Graber was, we do not know; but if he originated the drawings while Gichtel attended to the literature, he possessed great ingenuity of talent as well as high theosophical science—more especially so if he also originated the designs or symbols for the early German editions of Jacob Boehme's Works.

(2.) The beautiful copy of this work (of the literal portion of it) by Leuchter, in quarto, with the first volume in vellum and the two later Discourses in a paper back, is in our possession. Likewise, we possess the copy made by Mr. Law for himself of the ‘*Explanations of the First Table*,’ in quarto green vellum, and of the Second and Third Tables, bound up with, but preceding the discourse of Volume F *above*, of ‘*Nothing and Something*.’

The copy of the First Table Explanation in the British Museum, *Add. MSS 5786*, is in a very deformed hand, and we question whether it is a perfect copy. We hold a copy of the self-same treatise in the same kind of writing. We also hold a copy of the same treatise in folio vellum written by Leppington.

We also hold a copy of the Second and Third Table Explanations, along with a fragment of the very original of the First Table Explanation (as stated before) in a fair hand. We should perhaps observe here that the title ‘*Microcosmos*’ is only given to this work by ourselves; or rather, it was written in Mr. Law’s copy of the ‘*Explanation of the First Table*’ by Mr. Langcake during the time he had the manuscript in his charge. And probably it was the finding of such treatises among Mr. Ward’s papers by Mr. Selfe, his friend and executor, that led to the knowledge of Freher’s writings by Langcake, and then by Fisher, by whom they were subsequently hunted up.

(3.) Respecting the ‘*Tables*’ themselves, the finest and best copy, from which the plates were made that were inserted in Volume III of the quarto edition of Jacob Boehme of 1772, is, as stated before, in our possession. These are for the original English ‘*Explanations*.’ We also, as we observed, hold the original draft of these ‘*Tables*,’ though with the descriptive names on the figures and veils in German; also the amended rough draft, with the substitution of the *Peacock* for the *Hunting Dog*, to accompany the German translation of their ‘*Explanation*,’ is also in the British Museum, *Add. MSS 5788*, which is colored. The above-mentioned ‘*rough drafts*’ in our possession were probably originals to this completed, but not highly finished (yet very striking, because it is colored) copy of all the ‘*Three Tables*,’ which may serve as a guide for coloring future drawings of these Tables. Also, the colored drawing of the ‘*Tree of the Soul*,’ with its relations to all the worlds in which man stands, along with other unmentioned colored symbols in our possession, may serve for a similar purpose.

## (VI.) *On the Author’s Epistles*. A.D. 1713—1717.

(1.) The copy of the Four Letters to the Church in Bow Lane, and of the Fifth addressed to Mr. Inglis (which latter is signed “D. A. F., a zealot for the blessed memory and the sacred writings of Jacob B.”), made by Leuchter in quarto vellum, is in our possession. Likewise, we have the copy of the same made by Leppington, quarto, half-bound. Also, we have the copy (if they are not the originals) of the two letters from James Inglis in Scotland, dated 1712 and, we suppose, 1713, together with a manuscript in the same handwriting (which is also the same writing as the fragment copy of the first original First Table ‘*Explanation*,’ as named before) to the Bow Lane Society. Of these letters, there does not appear to be any copy in the British Museum. The author’s originals of them we have never seen or heard of.

(2.) We are not aware that the original of the long ‘*Epistle to Gildersleve*’ is in existence, nor the remainder of the letters which are generally found together with this Epistle—for instance, the letter titled “To my friends,” and the one “to the Bishop of Bangor, 1717.” The best-written copy of these three letters (in one volume half-bound, by Leuchter, to which is added a copy of the author’s letter in German addressed to Mr. Lúctbecher) is in the British Museum, *Add. MSS 5791*. We ourselves hold a very clearly written copy in a modern hand, quarto vellum bound, illustrated with a bold portrait of the Author, including also a copy of the letter to Lúctbecher. Also, we have a copy in folio vellum in the handwriting of Leppington, at the end of which are the initials ‘J. D. Oct. 4th, 1782’ (the year in which old Mr. Denis bought Leuchter’s and other copies of our author’s writings at Islington, as observed before).

## (VII.) *On the Treatise against the Restoration of the Devil and all Lost Spirits*. (Written in the German language and character.) A.D. 1718.

(1.) The Author’s original of this work—if he ever made anything but rough drafts of the very elaborate and perfected theosophic symbols contained in it—we have never heard of. There is no copy of this treatise in the British Museum. We hold a perfect copy of it in folio, green vellum, by Leuchter, the German words being in English letters. Also, we hold a copy by Leuchter of the Drawings and Symbols only, the literary portion of it being lost. This was evidently once a perfect copy, and matches in size, paper, and German lettering the ‘*Explanation of the First Table*’ in the British Museum, *Add. MSS 5792*, in the German character; but it has been taken to pieces to copy. The owner, however, did not part with the Drawings at the time, which were therefore preserved and have come into our hands. We have had them bound up again with blank leaves, on which the literary portions of the work may be transcribed, so the whole may again be a perfect book. We do not know of any other copy in existence besides the one mentioned above of this splendid treatise. Having already stated its special nature in our incidental remarks in previous notices of these works, we need say no more upon the subject here. Very probably it was intended by the author to be a kind of finishing stroke to his profound theosophical labors for the benefit of mankind, not knowing, however, how this might take place, yet doing all with a single eye and in the fullness of faith to the divine glory. And yet, notwithstanding that his writings have been only in manuscript and tossed about in the world, have been put up to public auction, and subject to all kinds of chances and dangers arising from the death of friends and admirers, and falling into the hands of persons who might have no esteem for them, but have regarded them as enthusiastic mysticism and

folly, and so have destroyed them; together with a thousand other possible misadventures—yet, we say, despite all these possibilities, the providence of God has still preserved them, safe up to the present moment; and it may be that they may yet perform their well-adapted and, we think, *predestined* function of being, instrumentally, a universal blessing to all nations of the world! We consider the preservation of these writings to manifest a similar kind of special providential care and intervention to that which was so signally evidenced in the preservation of the diverse manuscript writings of this author's great master, Bohemius, as related in the A.D. 1730 edition of his writings. We cannot help but greatly rejoice in being the depository of these inestimable, forever useful productions, and the instrument of thus making them known to the world. Bohemius is the divinely appointed original Christian fountain of the true philosophy of the universe of intellectual and physical nature, of God, Nature, and all things. All that can be revealed touching the true ground and mystery of things, it has pleased God to open in his writings, with such an amazing power of light and conviction as must almost strike the mind of the properly discerning reader with awe and astonishment, yet gratitude and love. All that is mysterious and incomprehensible to superficial or even philosophical readers—unless they possess a very piercing, devout, illuminated, and composed intellect (and even these may sometimes have difficulty with clear perception)—all their possible and ordinarily occurring doubts and misapprehensions of the deep truths contained in J. B.'s writings are all met or anticipated, cleared, and resolved in the clear and academic writings of the extraordinary genius of our Author. May we be enabled by divine favor to present to the world a serial publication, in the right order of study, of the writings of Law, Bohemius, and this Author, with all necessary notes and instructions, elucidated by all the discoveries of the established applied sciences; last but not least, those in the sphere of intellectual and animal magnetism. Then the philosophy of nature and religion will be complete, and the world will only have to experiment upon it and realize all that refinement of the divine nature in man of which it is capable, along with the blessings, wonders, and discoveries to which such moral or rather divine elevation of the spirit and mind of man must necessarily lead, and which belong to it. We presume the symbols and drawings in this work may be supposed to be carried to their highest perfection of clarity and accuracy of representation regarding deep theological truth.

### (VIII.) *On the Treatise of Good and Evil.*—(In the German language.) **A.D. 1720.**

The nature and construction of this work, not being, so to speak, an original new development of theosophic truth, but rather intended to clear up a certain scruple, has already been explained. The Author's original, as we have stated, is in our possession, with the exception of the last Conference; however, that is contained in the copy we hold of this work made by Leuchter, both being in the German script and beautifully written. The dedication, however (to young Jeremiah Leuchter), with several large and elaborate drawings inserted by the author in the middle of the First Conference, is not contained in the copy by Leuchter. The author's lettering upon the paper backs of these 'Conferences' (now, however, bound by us in one vellum quarto volume with blank leaves for the insertion of the last missing Conference) was as follows, in German: 'The First Conference and First Continuation of the Same, [after the said Dedication] of Good and Evil—The Second Continuation of the First Conference of Good and Evil—The Third Continuation of the First Conference of Good and Evil.' There is not any copy of this treatise in the British Museum, nor do we believe any other exists besides those mentioned here as being in our possession.

### (IX.) *On the Paradoxa, Emblemata, etc., Volume.* **A.D. 1717, 1718, 1720.**

(1.) We have never heard of the author's original manuscript of this work. The copy we hold in a small vellum folio with clasps is by Leuchter and appears to have been made immediately after the original was completed. In this copy, there are two emblems on each page with their Latin inscriptions, while the English translations are in a separate loose pamphlet accompanying it. This, as we stated, contains a portrait of the author, along with his coat of arms, which are attached to all the regular portraits of him.

There is also a copy of this work in the British Museum, *Add. MSS. 5789*, by Leuchter, but it is manifestly of a later date than the one in our possession. It is likewise embellished with a bold portrait of the author. The emblems in this copy are each made to occupy single pages, while the English translations, instead of being in a separate book, are inserted under each emblem with its Latin inscription; this arrangement enables the work to be presented in octavo. This is altogether a very beautiful copy, and its arrangements should be strictly followed in case of publication. We know of no other copy than those mentioned here.

### (X.) *On the large millboard Symbol or Hieroglyphic of Deity and Nature.*

This original, as we have observed, which was engraved and inserted in Volume IV of J. B.'s works, published in 1782, and which is there headed "The True Principles of All Things," is in our possession. In the engraving in question, the various depths or indentations of the figure, expressive of the various degrees and relations of the principles to each other, are not attempted to be indicated in any way whatsoever, which is a great failure in this plate. The original itself is rightly colored, though now much faded, and in case Theosophy—or the true science of the mutual relations and magical laws of Deity and Nature, and of the essential constitution of the latter, both external to and internal within man and all beings—ever becomes a common elementary school study, as it ought to become (being the science of ourselves, of our Father, of our lost patrimony and promised re-inheritance, etc.), then copies might be made of this large millboard Symbol (as indeed of all the other chief symbols) to erect in such establishments for the exercise and questioning of the classes of students in the principles and truths of Theosophic Science.

**POSTSCRIPT.**—Our beautiful copy of all the symbols, diagrams, and illustrations of this Author's writings (in one quarto volume by Leuchter) may serve, in case of their publication, as a guide to the engraver and draftsman employed upon them.

## FOR WHICH AN EDITOR IS REQUIRED.

The fundamental qualifications of mind presumed to be in the candidate, upon which the knowledge described above is to be added, are these following—

1. The possession of sound classical learning, clear common sense, sharp ironical wit, and vigorous strength of reason and judgment.
2. —of high rhetorical art, and pure Saxon simplicity of language.
3. —of precise exactness of logical power and demonstration.
4. —of easy, natural aspiration of thought, regarding the length and rhythm of sentences, with great practice in argumentative composition.
5. —of a devout and serious spirit, or mental temperament. And,
6. —regarding religion, of the ancient Methodist views on the necessity and blessedness of earnest devotion to God, and the attainment of perfect sanctity or holiness of spirit, and outward practical life.

NOTICE.—This pamphlet is a reprint of part of the preface of a 688-page book of the same page size, but printed in <term>nonpareil</term> type—which is titled as follows:

> “*To the Christianity, Philosophy, Learning, Science, and Noble Intelligence of the Age.*—*Notes and Materials for a Precise and Proper Biography of the Celebrated Clergyman and <term>Theosopher</term>, William Law. Including an explanation of the purpose and contents of the writings of Jacob Böhme and his great illustrator, Dionysius Andreas Freher; with a notice of Mystical Theology and the most curious and solid science of all ages. Also, an indication of the true means for bringing intellectual ‘Heathen,’ Jewish, and Muslim nations into the Evangelical faith. Printed for Private Circulation. London. A.D. 1848-56.*”

The original goal of this work was to find or create an Editor to write the BIOGRAPHY of Mr. LAW in a worthy manner. His unpublished manuscripts and papers (along with those of other DISTINGUISHED PHILOSOPHERS) had come into the Advertiser’s possession. The goal was to provide a candidate, who might already have the necessary academic foundation, with the means to perfect themselves in the unique and specialized knowledge—and spirit—required for the task. At the same time, it was thought appropriate to outline the main features of the information intended for the planned biography for their further education. This outline was included in this treatise, which is why it grew to its current size. With the original goal still in mind, and to provide what is considered a timely benefit to the world (while awaiting the publication of Volumes II and III of the *Introduction to <term>Theosophy</term>*), the Advertiser has reprinted this extract for general distribution. He does not doubt that the results of all this will eventually appear, to the great glory of God and the fulfillment of his own earnest hopes and desires. *Christmas*, 1856.

### THE "EXTRACT"—BEING A RECAPITULATION OR SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE WORK.

The following advertisement appeared some time ago in a public newspaper. However, because the specific talent required might not be clearly understood from the terms of that announcement, it was decided to provide a more detailed and comprehensive statement regarding the subject; hence this treatise.

> WANTED: A person of high literary talent and deep devotional spirit, at least forty years old. During their academic studies, they should have become well-versed in the <term>casuistry</term> and <term>metaphysics</term> of classical theology. Their writing style should be one of strict logical reasoning, even if its rigor is softened by the simplicity and beauty of rhetoric, to assist in writing an elevated religious and philosophical biography.

The following series of books and tracts have been selected as general models. By studying them according to the notes attached to each, one may understand the exact nature of the required talent.

1.—*Serious Call to a Holy Life*, by *W. Law, M.A.*—*The Case of Reason, or Natural Religion, Fairly and Fully Stated, 2nd edition.* By *W. Law, M.A.*

These treatises (along with the author's “Christian Perfection” and his “Three Letters to a Lady inclined toward the Church of Rome”) may be taken as examples of the desired argumentative writing style, showing the necessary amount of metaphysical knowledge. They also demonstrate a masterful use of wit, a vivid imagination, a sharp observation of life, a classic and skillful portrayal of character, and an easy, flowing, and complete treatment of the subjects being discussed.

**II.—***Earnest and Serious Answer to Trapp.—Remarks on Trapp's Reply.* Both contained in Vol. i. of “*Introduction to Theosophy.*”

As models for a clever and dignified style of address, for elevated sentiments of Christian purity and holiness, and for the earnest and serious spirit which must breathe through the work. The qualities of the previously mentioned treatises should be incorporated with the characteristics of the current tracts.

**III.—***Short Confutation of Warburton's ‘Defence of Christianity’ in his “Divine Legation.”* This also in Vol. I. of “*Introduction to Theosophy.*”—*An Address to the Clergy.* By *W. Law, M.A.*

The first of these treatises (in which the literary and other perfections of the previously named works may be said to be embodied) may be taken as a model of the authoritative style and power of philosophical writing desired. The second should be taken for the *Elias-Baptist* spirit of divinely animated zeal, irresistible truth, and elevated wisdom, in which the biography should be composed from first to last—written, indeed, in such a holy, reverent glow of spirit, as if composed by a seraph; so as to inflame the hearts of all its readers with the love of God and all holiness and perfection of life.

The preceding notices relate mainly to the literary qualifications of the author: the following series of works express the foundation of understanding, or the mental outlook, from which the work should be dictated.

**IV.—***Treatise of Christian Perfection.* By *W. Dublin, 1830—considering therein what is of the essence of Christianity, or of useful practice for regeneration; and absorbing its earnest and serious spirit.

To form a right foundation for the high structure of a perfect Christian, reborn, and divine life. In the first place, inducing in the mind a profound and piercing conviction of the vanity and emptiness of all worldly things, and of the degraded sinful state of humanity by nature; and with it an earnest conversion of the soul to God. Secondly, to arm the mind with a steadfast, immovable purpose to follow Christ fully, in his process of *regeneration*—in the way of his precepts, counsels, and example—the *narrow way*, the way of the cross, the way of faith; as being the only true and direct way from defilement to purity, from sin to holiness, from darkness to light, from death to life. And thirdly, to provide the soul with principles to walk courageously and surely in that way; that is, in the *perfect spirit and power* of prayer, of self-denial, of contempt for the world, of divine love, and universal charity; of humility, patience, meekness, long-suffering, obedience, purity, silence, and resignation; in heavenly foretastes of the world to come, in absolute trust and dependence upon God, with everything earthly and temporal—all the goods and evils of this present life—under one's feet.

**V.—***W. Law, M.A. Serious Call to a Holy Life.* With his *Case of Reason*; and his *Three Letters to a Lady inclined to the Church of Rome*, 8vo., London.—*Life of Baroness de Chantal* (translated by Mrs. Blachford), 12mo., 1787.

The tradition and succession of this through the Colleges of the Prophets among the *Jews*; through the Priestly Colleges of the Eastern Magi among the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Arabians; and through the Pythagorean and Platonic schools, if it were accurately and judiciously documented, would be a significant work; but this is not to be expected within a few sheets. The evil demons are able to do nothing on their own: it is Nature that works all, and produces those strange and wonderful operations. They also know how to apply active forces to passive subjects, and leave her to bring about what they design; the present corrupt state of nature is subservient to this, and they do not fail to add something of their own malice to it.

**NOTE.**—After having gone through the present division of study (referring also to the Notes on pages 522–24, 549, 550, 553, 556, 559, and of 467–9, 464, 449, 495, and to the text of page 320, etc.), the student will perceive its scope and object. It opens to him a glimpse of the whole field of *natural* and *divine magic*, and of the accidental entrances made there by the astral spirit and by faith up to the present time. Furthermore, it enables him to advocate with superlative force of reason and earnestness of zeal for the necessity of establishing *Theosophic Colleges* for the perfect triumphs of the Gospel. These should be, not mere elementary schools of the prophets, nor even like the ancient *philosophical academies*; but brilliant evangelical seminaries, worthy of the age, for the rearing or training of children of God up to the *highest perfection of sanctity and wisdom*, according to the insights of this work—even to the matured understanding and exercise of those *angelic arts and powers* which are the prerogatives of regenerate humanity.

The considerations that will follow a review of this particular study will also elucidate the original doctrines and mysteries of Christianity, such as the *laying on of hands* (by a regenerate and official medium), *baptism*, the *Lord's Supper*, etc.—yes, even the *supplementary sacraments* of the Roman Church. Here may be read—*Law on the Sacrament*. Query: Who or what was the stranger who so impressively approached BÖHME when he was a youth (as related in his Life), and what followed from it? Also, regarding the polished platter, by the luster of which reflected upon him, he became entranced with "double consciousness" into the central *ground* of all Nature; he, however, being manifestly qualified for such a baptism and revelation! Is this not the secret clue to BÖHME’S character (which we here offer to the judicious future editor of his life), namely, that he was a pure, simple child of nature, of a highly delicate tincture and complexion of spirit (as is indeed evident from the existing painting of him in this country), and accordingly susceptible to magic or "magnetic" action? Hence his early vision on the *Land’s Crown* mountain; and also, after being "baptized" by the supposed *Rosicrucian*, his center-life became still more opened, and he became *more lucid*? And now, seeking God and salvation in the true, orthodox, gospel mode (*in the style of Bramwell*), namely, by total penitence and earnest, wrestling, unflinching faith and prayer; and obtaining what he thus sought, even the *full liberty and witness of the Spirit*—in this state of clear and now greatly augmented salvation, being again "magnetized" by the inward solar power and tincture in the reflection from the polished platter, he became a *perfect clairvoyant*! That is, he realized the full prerogatives of his state at that time as a highly regenerate man, in respect to both the *temporal* and *eternal vision*, and other senses. Consequently, he wrote down his understandings of Nature as he was able to conceive and express them through the astral reason and our defective *Babel language*. This original view or discovery of BÖHME’S character, which has presented itself to us, is, we consider, the true key to his peculiar genius as displayed in his writings; in this respect, it may also serve as a qualifying note to our other descriptions of him in these pages. But the true subjects of a right Theosophic College and its training— — —*If only some noble-minded philanthropist would dedicate a hundred thousand pounds to the foundation of such a scheme in the name of the holy, holy, holy, eternal SOPH-IAH, and to his own high honor!*— — —might, we consider, be made to far excel BÖHME, as they would enjoy equal clearness of spiritual sense, but, being thoroughly grounded in modern science, would therefore be enabled to elucidate technically the "mystery" and *virtues* of things, and thus be of greater practical utility to the Church and the world.
->End of MAGICAL INTERSECTION.<-

VIII.—The *Old and New Testaments* of the Lord, JESUS CHRIST—the pillar and standard of practical evangelical truth. This is the popular and devotional light in which the Holy Scriptures are to be regarded. The other, or theosophical consideration of them (which affords a proof of their Divine Inspiration, though loose and partial in detail and composed separately), is as brief chronicles of the divine origin or creation, and of the degeneration or bestial-diabolic transformation of human nature in Adam, its natural head; and then of the entire process of its redemption, re-transformation, and deification, by the “mystery of Christ” in the person of JESUS, as the second and divine head of the same nature.

Hence it is that the working of these two principles of life—the rational-animal spirit of fallen man, and the holy, Sophian Spirit of Christ—forms the mystical ground of every narrative of the Scriptures, however historically true; and the line and virtue of the Covenant is the *golden thread that runs through and illumines the whole*. And hence they conclude with presenting to view the person of the Second Adam and Conquering Prince, fully perfected, glorified, and divine: and thereupon inviting and admonishing all men to “follow him in the regeneration.” That is, to cultivate the *seed* or spirit of grace, of *moral holiness* or love, of heaven or the heavenly humanity, or the virgin wisdom of God, of the “divine nature,” or—*himself* within them, into a powerful and all-predominant life; even to its full maturity or manhood-development, as thus visible in himself, the “perfect,” “justified,” “glorified” Son of Man, and heavenly Virgin form of substantial light and Love, in whom the earthly nature or spirit is swallowed up, “hidden in God.” This transformation is therefore possible to be accomplished in us—as he is the spi-

Those laws and requirements are revealed to us in the gospel, in the precepts and counsels of Christ, and in the subsequent explanations and exhortations of his apostles, having been all fulfilled in his own example on earth. These consist in the continual crucifixion of our fallen natural or diabolical spirit, and the renunciation of our animal, earthly will and wisdom: in other words, in a *daily dying to all self*, spiritual and natural, and in a turning of the faith, hope, and earnest prayer—or *hungering desires* of the soul—constantly and absolutely to God; into the *love of God, the humility, meekness, and patience of the divine light*, for deliverance from "self" and growth in grace, or salvation. This spiritual diligence, labor, and watchfulness, or passive submissiveness on our part, must be persevered in until the "new birth" is fully brought forth in us by our heavenly regenerator and *magnetist*; until the last remains of "self" in the will are finally absorbed in the power of God, and our *life* is thereupon transformed into a *spirit of love*: which, and which only, is the gospel salvation! —— The sum and end of the whole labor is this: "that man (the spirit of his soul being clothed with the regenerate, heavenly humanity, corporeity, or ‘flesh and blood of Christ’) may be able even in this world to magically re-enter paradise and ‘eat of the tree of life’ in the midst of it (as witnessed in the experience of Mrs. Pratt, related on pages 588–90 *following*), and so walk and act on the earth *in divine power and understanding*;* and that, upon his mortal death, he may be found a *qualified subject and participant* of those nameless, ravishing manifestations of wisdom, power, and love, which shall spring up and break forth in fresh and constant wonders as displays of the unfathomable riches and glories of the Godhead in the kingdom of heaven—but especially in the souls of its redeemed inhabitants, even for all eternity: —— in a word, that he may be a partaker of that same glory with which JESUS, the King of Glory and Lord of All—the Alpha and Omega—here exhibits himself crowned! —— Thus are brought to a close the *words of the prophecy of this book*; or the "counsel of God" concerning man in his creation, his fall, and his redemption in Christ! And such is the theosophic scope, spiritual unity, and divine certainty of the INSPIRED VOLUME; the contents of which may well be termed the *blessed gospel—or good tidings of great joy to all people*! And how the whole forms a glorious demonstration of the love of God! Or, that GOD, as our God—as in CHRIST JESUS—is MERE LOVE, the POWER OF LOVE! —— Which *power* is in very deed the universal basis of all things; and that quickening element wherein, as observed before, our *self-constrained, iron-hardened, insensible, ungrateful, and unbelieving* hearts and souls have their momentary life and being! *Ephesians* 3:8-19. *2 Corinthians* 2:6, 7, etc.

# CONCLUSION.

Such, then, are the series of works which are considered suitable to provide the reader with a correct general understanding of the profound and universal theological science of the primary subject of our proposed Biography. This includes a conception of his far-seeing *faith-based* realizations of the effects that should flow from his own *Elias-restoring, Baptist-purifying* ministry:—not only in the general diffusion of a simple, practical gospel Christianity among the *unsophisticated* of the earth, as we see progressing in our day; but also regarding the induction of *intellectual* unbelievers of all nations into the Christian faith. This is yet to be achieved as the final result of the revelation of the "*mystery of Christ*"—of Deity, Nature, and all things—in BOHEMIUS, and of the refinement of all natural knowledge, philosophy and theology, the arts and sciences, both mechanical and magical, which has followed, and shall hereafter follow, as a consequence or development of it.

As a close, the following EXTRACT is offered for the reader's consideration:—

> It is because people do not consider the *spirit of holiness* as a new nature, as a *seed of God, a plant of paradise* in the soul—and therefore as something that is to be nursed and cherished, to be cultivated and raised to *perfection* by care and planning, by skill and method, and a diligent use of the best means and most expedient instruments—it is because they do not consider it in this light that so many people benefit so little from it, and live and die strangers to that interior renovation, that holy, spiritual "*oneness*" with the glorified nature of the Lord Jesus (*John xvii. 21—24*), which they might have attained had they only intended it.
> 
> For though the *spirit of devotion* is the gift of God, and not attainable by any mere power of our own—yet it is mostly given, and *never withheld* from those who rightly seek and prepare themselves to receive it.
> 
> And it is amazing to see how eagerly men of science and business employ their talents, their sagacity, time, study, application, and exercise—how all helps are called to their assistance when anything is intended and desired in *worldly matters*; and how *dull, infatuated, and unimproved* they are—how little they use their talents, sagacity, and abilities to *quicken and cultivate* the *incorruptible seed of grace*, or the *Light and Spirit of God*—which is the source of every divine blessing of holiness, power and wisdom, and with it every necessary earthly good—implanted and hidden in the ground of the soul.

---

This much is said by way of specifying the talent deemed indispensable for the proper representation of the genius and character of MR. LAW (as contemplated by this work); or rather, of the means and instruments whereby the artist who is qualified by nature and education for such a task (being of pure Methodist origin and understanding in religion) may attain the special ability, science, and experience necessary for its adequate performance. In a word, it is to present the portrait of a man which, whether regarding its subject or the manner of its execution, may serve as a classic standard or practical model of divine wisdom, solid learning, and rhetorical art for all future generations of the British people and of mankind.—*Communications on the subject (or for permission to make extracts from this work) should be addressed to the* "**Editor of Law's Memorial,**" *and left at 24, Ludgate-street, London. Christmas, 1856.*

<header>APPENDIX.—LAW’S PHILOSOPHICAL WRITINGS.</header>

The following is an **ABSTRACT** of the treatises of **MR. LAW**, which are intended to constitute **VOLS. II.** and **III.** of the “**INTRODUCTION TO THEOSOPHY**.” These, together with the previous volume, present a perfect, logical demonstration of Christianity, universal and evangelical, based on the grounds of Nature.

### BOOK V.—THE APPEAL: OR, THE FUNDAMENTAL DOCTRINES OF CHRISTIANITY DEMONSTRATED. (Forming a Practical Guide to the Science of True Metaphysics.)

*Chapter I.*—Concerning creation in general. The origin of the soul. From where will and thought originate in the creature. Why the will is free. The origin of evil comes solely from the creature. This world was not a first, immediate creation of God. How the world came to be in its present state. The first perfection of man. All things prove a trinity in God. Man has the triune nature of God within him. Arianism and deism refuted by nature. That life is uniform through all creatures. That there is only one kind of death to be found in all nature. The fallen soul has the nature of hell within it. Regeneration is a real birth of a divine life in the soul. That there is only one salvation possible in nature. This salvation is only to be had through Jesus Christ. All the deist’s faith and hope are proved to be false.

*Chapter II.*—Concerning eternal and temporal nature. How nature comes from God and is the scene of His action. How creatures exist outside of it. Temporal nature was created out of that which is eternal. The fallen angels brought the first disorders into nature. This world was created to repair those disorders. The source of good and evil in everything in this world. How heaven and hell are the foundation of, or make up the entirety of, this world. How the fire of this world differs from eternal fire, and how the matter of this world differs from the materiality of heaven. Eternal nature is the kingdom of heaven, the blessed manifestation of the triune Deity. The Deity is pure love and goodness. How wrath and anger came to be attributed to God. Concerning fire in general. Concerning the beginningless fire. Concerning the spirituality of fire. How fire comes to exist in material things. From where the possibility of kindling fire in the things of this world arises. Every man is, and must be, the kindler of his own eternal fire.

*Chapter III.*—The true ground of all the doctrines of the gospel discovered. Why Adam could make no atonement for his sins. Why and how Jesus Christ alone can make this atonement. The reason for the shedding of blood for the forgiveness of sins. What wrath or anger it is that is quenched and atoned for by the blood of Christ. Concerning the final sufferings of Christ. Why and how we must eat the flesh and drink the blood of Jesus Christ.

### BOOK VI.—THE SPIRIT OF PRAYER, OR WAY TO REGENERATION. IN THREE PARTS.—(A Popular Treatise on the Art of Restoring the Displaced Principles of Man’s Threefold Life, or Nature, to their Original Created Order, Relations, and Subservience. According to the Grounds established in the preceding BOOK V.)

**PART FIRST.** *Chapter I.*—The indifference and insensibility of people in general toward their eternal interests. The original state of man as the son of God, or child of the total divine nature. His trial and fall. The commencement of his redemption. His real nature and state because of sin. How it differs from that of fallen angels. The means of his salvation, or recovery of the Light and holy Spirit of God. *The new birth* is not a figurative expression, but a real, living process, or moral growth. The whole chapter is a familiar discussion of matters preparatory to the spirit of prayer.

*Chapter II.*—In what salvation, or the regenerate life, consists; namely, in the manifestation of *the nature, life, and spirit of Jesus Christ in the new inward man.* The means of attaining such a state lie in faith, or the right direction and earnest working of the will. How the ground or *principle* of faith—which is a seed of “Christ,” called in scripture the “seed of the woman,” or the “*engrafted word*”—lies implanted in every soul. Its opening or development is the only way of salvation. The signs by which the regenerate life reveals itself. Everything depends on adhering to it and removing all impediments of earthly lusts from around it. The infallible truths by which we may be assured that our dependence is well-grounded. The abandonment of *self*, and the true nature and worth of self-denial and mortification. No activity of our own is of any direct use for salvation. The only way is the *desire of the soul turned toward God.* <insert>[The further clarification of these points will be found in the last dialogue of the following treatise, “The Spirit of Love.”]</insert>

**PART SECOND**, <insert>[the argument being set forth in the form of Dialogues between (1.) *Theophilus*, a learned sage and master of the science contained in the writings of **JACOB BÖHME**, surnamed the *central philosopher*, (2.) an academic, or university theologian and metaphysician, (3.) a plain, unlettered, honest, common-sense Christian, and (4.) a rationalist or natural moralist, whether Deist, Unitarian, or modern *Swedenborgian*.]</insert>

*Dialogue I.*—Introduction, on the vanity of spiritual knowledge where there is no religion or true conversion of the heart to God. Spiritual books are only useful as calls to the absolute renunciation of self and the cultivation of the new life. The nature of *self* is described, and the necessity of its complete sacrifice or death is demonstrated. The actual grounds of this necessity are shown here to be in the nature of things, and not in the arbitrary provisions of God’s providence. How the will of the creature stands between God and nature as the only opener of all good and evil. Its turning to God in true faith and earnestness of desire is the means of bringing heaven into the soul; that is, of attaining the heavenly birth of the soul’s life. The agreement of these doctrines with Scripture. There is only one death and only one life throughout all nature. Vindication of the ‘Appeal.’ <insert>[This discourse, which involves an explanation of the writings of **BÖHME**, is deferred to another occasion, when *Theophilus* proposes to describe the true nature and end of those writings, and the right use and manner of reading them. The concluding Fifth and Sixth Dialogues of this **BOOK** will accordingly be found to be devoted to that object.]</insert>

*Dialogue II.*—The philosophy of the gospel doctrine of redemption and salvation continued.

How Adam stood in his state of perfection, or creation. The gradual fall or decline of his will through earthly imagination. The division of Adam (the embodied idea, or Virgin image of God, nature, and all things) into male and female (like the earthly animals, *Gen.* 1:25–27). The fall completed, by which the inward nature of man became diabolic, and the outward nature became wild, coarse, and beast-like. The means of human recovery by the promised redeemer, or covenant of the "seed of the woman." The argument for the *renunciation of self and the world* resumed (from the first dialogue) on the rational grounds of this philosophy. What constitutes the great apostasy—"the sin of all sins, and heresy of all heresies." Hours and forms of prayer considered.

**Dialogue III.**—The difficulty attending the total conversion of the heart to God. The whole life of the fallen nature must be given up, and yet there is no possibility for man to do it by himself. The omnipotence of the love of God, and how it overcomes all evil and opposition when the heart turns to God with a right understanding and faith. How this love has followed and inspired man from the beginning, as the "Immanuel" or *seed of Christ*, treasured in the ground of every soul. The beginning of salvation by the awakening or germination of this holy virgin seed. The new creature formed, or the spirit of divine love opened and working in man. How this spirit is obtained and recognized so as to avoid delusion. The prayer or breathing of this spirit is the only genuine devotion. No other spirit in man (and therefore no mere speculation or reasoning, however transcendental) works toward salvation. The consistency of this doctrine with free will. Prayer as the continual and habitual state of the will, depending on whether it works with the Spirit of God or the spirit of its own selfish nature, fallen from God. All the soul's goodness, or growth in holiness, depends on the continuity and earnestness of the state of the will, or desire (as surrendered to God). The outward expression of prayer justly distinguished. How far manuals of devotion, or set forms of prayer, are profitable. The degrees of prayer, or steps of the spiritual life toward its perfection (the state of *Jesus glorified*, Phil. 3:12–15). Why the motion, "drawing," or magnetism of the Holy Spirit (*John* 12:32) is the source of every aspiration to unite with the goodness and holiness of God. How this Spirit (or life of the element of *Jesus-God*) is known by the pure, free, universal goodness, patience, meekness, and love which it inspires. These dispositions in man, as the aim of his life, are the certain effects of the Holy Spirit's presence and influence, and evidence to him that he is in the process of regeneration. 1 *John* 3:24.

**Dialogue IV.**—The whole foundation of the gospel, based on the certainty of man's original perfection, his beast-like and diabolic fall, and his redemption. The primeval fire and light still lodged in the human soul. Salvation consists in the awareness or reopening (or growth and blossoming) of this hidden, divine life. How it differs from any natural goodness, yet must become a habit of life, even the "life of our life, and the spirit of our spirit." The doctrine of the fall is the best and only safe means for converting unbelievers. Its proofs are not historical but are lodged in human nature itself and are self-evident to every sober, rational mind. (See also, "*Introduction to Theosophy*," Vol. 1, Book 1, pp. 39–62.) The possibility, occasion, and manner of the fall briefly sketched. The difference between the fall of mankind and that of the *Luciferian* angelic hierarchy. The certain redemption of the former. Gospel Christianity is only its actual commencement, as involved in the glorification of Christ's humanity. How gospel Christianity is distinguished from the original, universal Christianity which began with Adam; was the religion of the patriarchs and their descendants in the direct main lines of the East; of the divergent branch of Abraham, of Moses, and the prophets; and in short, of every penitent man in every part of the earth who had *faith and hope* toward God to be delivered from the evil of this world. For whom his works are intended, and by whom alone they can safely be consulted. The impossibility of searching into these things—*belonging to the supernatural sphere* of divine wisdom—by mere human reason. How the will of man rules his own nature, just as the will of God rules eternal nature. The nature of this will, as proceeding from the hidden divine life or power of redemption in the soul. Faith, in the true Scripture sense as it relates to salvation, is nothing else than the *working* of this new, engrafted divine power in the will of the soul.

How they constitute the substance, or working powers of darkness, in which the supernatural Deity moves and shines, or becomes perceptible. VIRGIN SOPHIA.] In what state the original, eternal nature, or substance of heaven, was brought forth.
